Gastroesophageal reflux disease with peptic stricture
Esophageal or gastric cardia malignancy causing pseudoachalasia
Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi infection)
Eosinophilic esophagitis
Scleroderma-related esophageal dysmotility
Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) causing destruction of myenteric plexus with achalasia-like esophageal dysfunction
Barium esophagram — shows esophageal dilation with distal 'bird's beak' tapering and poor emptying
High-resolution esophageal manometry — confirms diagnosis via absent peristalsis and impaired LES relaxation, and subtypes achalasia (I–III)
Upper endoscopy — mandatory to exclude a mechanical or malignant cause (pseudoachalasia) at or near the gastroesophageal junction
Endoscopic ultrasound or CT chest/abdomen — used selectively when pseudoachalasia from tumor infiltration is suspected
Serology for Trypanosoma cruzi — considered in patients from endemic regions to exclude Chagas disease
Timed barium swallow — assesses esophageal emptying and is useful for monitoring treatment response
Chest imaging — may incidentally reveal a dilated, air/fluid-filled esophagus or absent gastric air bubble
Peptic or malignant esophageal stricture
Esophageal or gastroesophageal junction carcinoma (pseudoachalasia)
Diffuse esophageal spasm
Scleroderma esophagus
Eosinophilic esophagitis

Achalasia results from degeneration of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus of the esophagus, leading to loss of coordinated peristalsis in the esophageal body and failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax appropriately with swallowing. The cause is usually idiopathic, though an autoimmune or postviral inflammatory process targeting these neurons is suspected in many cases. Similar clinical pictures can arise secondarily from infiltrative or destructive processes affecting the myenteric plexus, such as Chagas disease or tumor invasion at the gastroesophageal junction (pseudoachalasia).

Progressive dysphagia to both solids AND liquids from the outset is the classic clue distinguishing achalasia from a mechanical stricture or malignancy, where solid-food dysphagia usually predominates and progresses later to liquids.
Regurgitation of undigested food (especially at night, with risk of aspiration) and slow, gradual weight loss are common accompanying features.
Retrosternal chest pain/discomfort with meals occurs in a subset of patients, more often early in the disease course.
Patients often learn compensatory maneuvers — eating slowly, holding arms overhead, or performing repeated swallows/Valsalva — to help push food through the non-relaxing lower esophageal sphincter.
Barium esophagram classically shows a dilated esophagus tapering to a smooth 'bird's beak' narrowing at the gastroesophageal junction.
Manometry is the gold standard: it shows absent/incomplete lower esophageal sphincter relaxation together with loss of normal peristalsis in the esophageal body.
New-onset 'achalasia-like' symptoms in an older adult, especially with rapid weight loss, should prompt evaluation for pseudoachalasia from a malignancy at the gastroesophageal junction.
Chagas disease should be considered in patients from or with travel history to endemic areas of Latin America presenting with an achalasia-like picture.
Attributing dysphagia to reflux disease and delaying manometry, since achalasia can be misdiagnosed as GERD for years
Failing to perform endoscopy to exclude a malignant or infiltrative cause before treating for idiopathic achalasia
Overlooking Chagas disease in patients with relevant epidemiologic exposure
Assuming a normal-caliber esophagus on barium study excludes achalasia; early disease may show minimal dilation despite abnormal manometry

With appropriate treatment (pneumatic dilation, surgical myotomy, or peroral endoscopic myotomy), most patients achieve durable symptomatic improvement, though the underlying esophageal aperistalsis is not reversed and long-term surveillance is often needed. Untreated or longstanding disease carries risk of progressive esophageal dilation, aspiration, malnutrition, and a modestly increased long-term risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
Rapid symptom onset or significant weight loss in an older patient, raising concern for pseudoachalasia due to malignancy
Recurrent aspiration pneumonia from nocturnal regurgitation
Severe odynophagia or evidence of esophageal perforation
Marked, progressive esophageal dilation (megaesophagus) with risk of retained food and aspiration
New or worsening symptoms despite treatment, warranting re-evaluation for an underlying malignant cause
Achalasia (non-infective) — Gastroenterology Also: achalasia cardia, esophageal achalasia, cardiospasm, failure of LES relaxation, esophageal aperistalsis, megaesophagus
Community-acquired pneumonia (distinguished by a new infiltrate on chest radiography and focal exam findings) (p.1024).
Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis / COPD (p.1024).
Heart failure (p.1024).
Pulmonary embolism (p.1024).
Influenza and nonspecific upper respiratory infection, which overlap clinically with lower-tract infection (p.252).
Pneumonia (cough plus sputum, dyspnea, chest pain, fever, and a new infiltrate point to pneumonia rather than bronchitis) (p.1537, p.1024).
Influenza (overlapping cough and systemic features; can be complicated by secondary bacterial infection) (p.1537).
Pertussis / subacute postinfectious tracheobronchitis (a frequent cause of cough persisting 3-8 weeks) (p.272).
Chest radiography should be obtained whenever pneumonia is suspected, to confirm the absence of an infiltrate that defines acute bronchitis (p.1537).

Specific viral diagnosis is generally unnecessary but, when needed, RT-PCR/multiplex respiratory panels are the most sensitive tests; results must be interpreted cautiously because viral genome can persist for weeks after a resolved infection (p.1537).

Acute coronary syndrome / myocardial infarction presenting as cough and dyspnea, illustrated by a fatal case in which exertional dyspnea and chest heaviness were prematurely labeled acute bronchitis (p.21).
Cough-variant asthma (p.272).
Gastroesophageal reflux (p.272).
Rhinosinusitis with postnasal drainage (p.272).
ACE-inhibitor-induced cough (p.272).
Inhalation of noxious chemicals or smoke, and aspiration, as causes of acute cough (p.272).

Acute bronchitis is predominantly a viral infection of the lower airways below the vocal cords, caused by common respiratory viruses; the inflammatory airway response produces cough that may be dry or productive, without parenchymal consolidation. Bacterial involvement is uncommon, in contrast to chronic bronchitis where bacteria contribute more prominently (p.1537).
Defined as a dry or productive cough lasting <3 weeks, occurring without clinical or radiographic signs of pneumonia; it is most common during winter (p.1537).
Sputum purulence does not distinguish viral from bacterial cause; in acute bronchitis the cough is predominantly viral, whereas bacteria play a larger role in chronic bronchitis (p.1537).
Among acute respiratory infections, only acute otitis media, sinusitis, streptococcal pharyngitis, and pneumonia warrant antibiotics; acute bronchitis is not on that list (p.252).
Acute bronchitis and sinusitis are common at all stages of HIV infection, with more severe disease at lower CD4+ counts (p.1595).
An individual episode of acute bronchitis does not typically cause lasting reductions in pulmonary function (p.1537 context; long-term lung-function data p. respiratory infections section).

Prescribing antibiotics for acute bronchitis is inappropriate stewardship; roughly half of ambulatory antibiotic prescriptions for acute respiratory infections are unnecessary, and antibiotics cause adverse effects, C. difficile infection, microbiome disruption, and resistance (p.252).
Treating purulent sputum as evidence of bacterial infection is a mistake, since purulence does not reliably indicate bacterial etiology in acute bronchitis (p.1537).

Premature closure: relying on a rapid 'URI/bronchitis' protocol can cause clinicians to miss life-threatening conditions such as myocardial infarction; a patient who does not look 'sick' may be wrongly assumed to have a benign illness (p.21).
Not eliciting a full dyspnea history (exertional onset, chest heaviness, relief with rest) can lead to a dangerous misdiagnosis of acute bronchitis (p.21).

Acute bronchitis is a self-limited illness; the cough usually resolves within about 3 weeks, and antibiotics neither speed resolution nor prevent complications in most acute respiratory infections. A dry, irritative postbronchitic cough may linger for more than 2 months, particularly in winter, and a residual subacute cough of 3-8 weeks is common after tracheobronchitis (p.252, p.272-273).
Dyspnea, especially exertional dyspnea or chest heaviness/pain, which should trigger consideration of cardiac or thromboembolic disease rather than acute bronchitis (p.21).
Cough accompanied by sputum, fever, chest pain, or focal chest signs suggesting pneumonia, prompting chest radiography (p.1537).
Hemoptysis or weight loss (raising concern for malignancy or other serious pulmonary disease) (p.272).
Cough persisting beyond a few weeks, warranting reassessment and chest radiography for serious causes (sarcoidosis, lymphoma, lung cancer, tuberculosis) (p.272-273).
None routinely required — Diagnosis is clinical; investigations are reserved for atypical course, prolonged symptoms, or red-flag features suggesting pneumonia.
Chest X-ray (only if pneumonia cannot be excluded clinically) — To rule out consolidation if exam findings are equivocal or symptoms persist beyond expected course.
Acute Bronchitis (infective) — Respiratory
veryLikely: Respiratory viruses (rhinovirus, influenza, RSV, coronavirus); likely: Bordetella pertussis (if prolonged cough >2 weeks, paroxysmal, or known exposure)
Decompensated chronic liver disease (cirrhosis with acute-on-chronic liver failure)
Severe acute hepatitis without encephalopathy (acute liver injury short of failure)
Ischemic hepatitis (shock liver)
Acute Budd-Chiari syndrome and other vascular liver outflow obstruction
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy / HELLP syndrome
Malignant infiltration of the liver causing acute hepatic dysfunction
Viral hepatitis A, B, D (with B), and E
Herpes simplex virus hepatitis
Cytomegalovirus hepatitis

Prothrombin time/INR — core diagnostic criterion and key prognostic marker
Arterial ammonia level — correlates with risk of cerebral edema and severe encephalopathy
Acetaminophen level and detailed drug/toxin/supplement history — identifies the most common treatable etiology
Viral hepatitis serologies (A, B, C, D, E) and, where relevant, HSV/CMV testing — identifies infectious causes
Autoimmune markers (ANA, smooth muscle antibody, immunoglobulins) and ceruloplasmin/copper studies — screens for autoimmune hepatitis and Wilson disease
Doppler ultrasound of hepatic and portal vasculature — evaluates for vascular outflow obstruction
Arterial blood gas, lactate, and renal function — assess systemic perfusion and evolving multiorgan dysfunction
Blood and other cultures with a low threshold for infection screening — ALF patients are prone to occult sepsis
Acetaminophen (paracetamol) toxicity
Idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury (including certain antituberculous and antiepileptic agents, and herbal/dietary supplements)
Autoimmune hepatitis presenting acutely
Wilson disease presenting with acute decompensation
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy and HELLP syndrome
Mushroom (Amanita) poisoning and other hepatotoxins
Acute Budd-Chiari syndrome / ischemic hepatopathy
Malignant hepatic infiltration (lymphoma, metastatic disease)

Massive hepatocyte necrosis or dysfunction outstrips the liver's regenerative capacity, causing simultaneous failure of synthetic function (coagulation factors, albumin), detoxification (ammonia, other neurotoxins), and metabolic homeostasis. Accumulating ammonia and inflammatory mediators drive astrocyte swelling and cerebral edema, producing hepatic encephalopathy and raised intracranial pressure. The systemic inflammatory response and impaired hepatic clearance of pathogens also predispose to circulatory dysfunction, renal impairment, and secondary infection, contributing to a multiorgan failure picture.

Defined by acute severe liver injury with coagulopathy (INR generally above 1.5) and any degree of encephalopathy in a patient without pre-existing chronic liver disease, developing within about 26 weeks of illness onset

Speed of onset matters clinically: hyperacute presentations (encephalopathy within roughly a week or two of jaundice) are typically from acetaminophen toxicity or viral hepatitis and, despite dramatic cerebral edema risk, often carry better spontaneous recovery odds than slower subacute forms
Acetaminophen overdose and drug-induced liver injury are the leading causes in resource-rich settings, while viral hepatitis (especially hepatitis B and E) dominates in many other regions
Cerebral edema and raised intracranial pressure are the most feared early complications and a major cause of death, particularly in hyperacute presentations
Coagulopathy in ALF reflects a rebalanced but fragile hemostatic state rather than pure bleeding tendency; INR is used mainly for prognosis and monitoring, not as a routine transfusion trigger
Early transfer to a liver transplant center should be considered as soon as ALF is recognized, since deterioration can be rapid and unpredictable
Look actively for a treatable cause (acetaminophen, autoimmune hepatitis, Wilson disease, HELLP/acute fatty liver of pregnancy, vascular causes) since specific therapy can be life-saving
Infection and sepsis are common complications during the course of ALF and should be surveilled for proactively rather than only when clinically obvious
Assuming a normal or mildly elevated bilirubin excludes liver failure — hyperacute acetaminophen-related ALF can present with striking coagulopathy and encephalopathy before marked jaundice develops

Using INR alone to guide prophylactic correction with plasma products — this does not reflect true bleeding risk in the rebalanced coagulopathy of ALF and can complicate assessment of hepatic synthetic recovery
Delaying transfer to a transplant-capable center while pursuing additional outpatient-type workup — deterioration can be abrupt
Overlooking a treatable etiology (Wilson disease, autoimmune hepatitis, pregnancy-related liver disease) because acetaminophen or viral hepatitis seems statistically likely

Outcome depends heavily on etiology and speed of onset: hyperacute presentations from acetaminophen or hepatitis A/E often have a better chance of spontaneous recovery than subacute presentations, which have lower native-liver survival. Emergency liver transplantation substantially improves survival in appropriately selected patients who do not recover spontaneously.
Any new alteration in mental status or asterixis in a patient with acute severe liver injury — signals encephalopathy and true liver failure
Rapidly rising INR with jaundice — suggests impending or established failure requiring urgent transplant center contact
Signs of raised intracranial pressure (hypertension with bradycardia, pupillary changes, posturing) — medical emergency
Hemodynamic instability, oliguria, or lactic acidosis — herald multiorgan involvement
Grade III–IV encephalopathy — generally warrants intensive care and consideration of airway protection
Any suspicion of acetaminophen ingestion, even with a vague or denied history — treatable and time-sensitive

Acute liver failure (non-infective) — Hepatology Also: acute liver failure, fulminant hepatic, fulminant hepatic failure, ALF, acute hepatic failure, acute liver injury with encephalopathy, hyperacute liver failure, subacute liver failure

Serum ferritin and glycosylated ferritin fraction — marked elevation with low glycosylated fraction supports diagnosis
Complete blood count with differential — neutrophilic leukocytosis typical; cytopenias raise concern for macrophage activation syndrome
Liver function tests — transaminitis is common
Blood cultures and viral serologies — to exclude infectious mimics before immunosuppression
ANA and rheumatoid factor — expected negative, helps exclude other connective tissue disease
Imaging or lymph node biopsy — to exclude lymphoma when lymphadenopathy is prominent
Joint imaging — assess for erosive arthritis, notably of the wrist, in chronic disease

Systemic lupus erythematosus

AOSD is an autoinflammatory disorder driven by innate immune activation rather than autoantibody-mediated disease, with overproduction of proinflammatory cytokines including interleukin-1, interleukin-6, interleukin-18, and tumor necrosis factor. This cytokine storm produces the systemic febrile illness, marked acute-phase response, and hyperferritinemia seen clinically. The absence of a clear autoantibody or defined trigger, along with strong similarity to systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, supports its classification as an autoinflammatory rather than autoimmune condition.
Classic triad is quotidian (once- or twice-daily) high spiking fever, evanescent salmon-pink rash that appears with fever spikes, and arthritis/arthralgia
Rash is typically truncal and on proximal limbs, non-pruritic, and often elicited or worsened by scratching (Koebner-like phenomenon)
Sore throat and cervical lymphadenopathy are common early features and can mimic infection
Markedly elevated ferritin, often more than five times normal, is a strong clue but not specific
Rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibody are typically negative, helping distinguish AOSD from other connective tissue diseases
Neutrophilic leukocytosis with left shift and elevated inflammatory markers accompany the fever spikes
Diagnosis is one of exclusion after infections, malignancy, and other rheumatologic diseases are ruled out
Watch for macrophage activation syndrome, a life-threatening complication marked by falling counts and rapidly rising ferritin
Treating as fever of unknown origin with prolonged empiric antibiotics before considering an autoinflammatory cause
Missing the diagnosis because the evanescent rash is absent at the time of examination
Anchoring on markedly elevated ferritin as diagnostic without excluding lymphoma and macrophage activation syndrome
Delaying immunosuppressive therapy while pursuing an exhaustive infectious workup in a clinically deteriorating patient

Course is variable: some patients have a self-limited monophasic illness, others a chronic intermittent pattern, and a subset develop chronic destructive polyarthritis. Most patients respond well to anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive therapy, though macrophage activation syndrome significantly increases morbidity and mortality.
Cytopenias, coagulopathy, or precipitous rise in ferritin suggesting macrophage activation syndrome
Hepatic failure or disseminated intravascular coagulation
Cardiac tamponade from serositis
Adult respiratory distress syndrome from pulmonary involvement
Persistent fever despite broad antimicrobial coverage without an identified infectious source
Adult-onset Still disease (non-infective) — Rheumatology Also: adult onset still, AOSD, still disease, adult still's disease, systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis adult equivalent
Pyogenic liver abscess (the most important imaging-based distinction once a hepatic abscess is identified) (p.1801)
Malaria (p.1801)
Typhoid/enteric fever (p.1801)
Pulmonary disease (p.1801)
Gallbladder disease (p.1801)
Any febrile illness with few localizing signs / fever of unknown origin, since 10-15% present with fever alone (p.1799, p.1801)
Pyogenic liver abscess (p.1801)
Malaria (p.1801)
Typhoid (enteric) fever (p.1801)
Serum alkaline phosphatase and aminotransferases (enzymes often normal/minimally elevated; raised aminotransferases suggest acute disease or complication) (p.1800)
Full blood count for leukocytosis >10,000/uL, present in about three-quarters of patients, especially with acute or complicated disease (p.1800)
Enzyme immunoassay for the Gal/GalNAc lectin antigen, usable on stool and on liver-abscess aspirates (p.1800)
Multiplex PCR for E. histolytica DNA (near 100% sensitivity/specificity) (p.1800)
Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) on abscess pus as a low-cost molecular option (p.1800)
Diagnostic aspirate sent for Gram stain and bacterial culture when distinguishing amebic from pyogenic abscess (p.1801)
Gallbladder disease (p.1801)
Pulmonary disease presenting with right-sided pleural/pleuritic findings (p.1801)

Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites invade colonic mucosal venules and travel via the portal venous system to the liver; the organism is resistant to complement-mediated lysis, which is critical to its survival in the bloodstream. An early acute infiltrate (predominantly neutrophils) is followed by lysis of those neutrophils on contact with amebae, and the released neutrophil toxins are thought to contribute to hepatocyte necrosis. The liver parenchyma is progressively replaced by necrotic material surrounded by a thin rim of congested liver tissue, producing the classically described (but variably colored) 'anchovy paste' that is sterile and largely acellular, with amebae found mainly at the capsule. Genetically, a leptin-receptor substitution (Q223R) increases the risk of amebic liver abscess in adults (p.1798-1799).

Most patients are febrile with right-upper-quadrant pain that may be dull or pleuritic and may radiate to the shoulder; point tenderness over the liver and a right-sided pleural effusion are common, whereas jaundice is rare (p.1799).
Invasive amebiasis does not elicit eosinophilia (p.1800).
Although the colon is the initial site of infection, fewer than one-third of patients with an amebic abscess have active diarrhea at presentation (p.1799).

Strongly age- and sex-dependent: men aged 30-60 are infected at a rate roughly 10-12 times that of women in the same age group; testosterone-modulated NK-T-cell interferon-gamma signaling is implicated experimentally (p.1798).

Young patients tend to present acutely with prominent symptoms of under 10 days' duration, while older patients from endemic areas more often follow a subacute course over months with weight loss and hepatomegaly; only about one-third of those with chronic presentations are febrile (p.1799).
Of travelers who develop an amebic liver abscess after leaving an endemic area, 95% do so within 5 months (p.1799).
Amebic liver abscesses are always preceded by intestinal colonization, which may be entirely asymptomatic (p.1799).
On imaging, more than 80% of patients symptomatic for over 10 days have a single right-lobe abscess, but about 50% of those symptomatic for under 10 days have multiple abscesses (p.1800).

The classic necrotic 'anchovy paste' contents are variable in color and bacteriologically sterile, composed of granular debris with few or no cells; amebae, when present, sit near the abscess capsule rather than in the aspirable necrotic center (p.1799).

Liver enzymes are usually normal or only minimally elevated even with large abscesses; alkaline phosphatase is the most commonly elevated value, while aminotransferase elevation suggests acute disease or a complication (p.1800).
Expecting concurrent dysentery: fewer than one-third of patients have active diarrhea, so a negative stool examination or absent diarrhea does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1799).
Trophozoites are rarely recovered from liver aspirates because they reside in the abscess capsule, not in the necrotic center that is actually aspirated (p.1799).
Up to 10% of patients with acute amebic liver abscess have negative serology early; titers usually become positive within a week (p.1799).

Microscopy cannot distinguish E. histolytica cysts from non-pathogenic E. dispar, E. moshkovskii, or E. bangladeshi; species-specific diagnosis on microscopy requires seeing trophozoites that have ingested erythrocytes (p.1799).
In endemic areas serology may stay positive for years (indirect hemagglutination up to ~10 years), complicating interpretation (p.1799).
Follow-up imaging may be confusing because abscesses resolve slowly and can transiently enlarge despite a good clinical response (p.1800).

With early diagnosis and treatment, mortality from uncomplicated amebic liver abscess is under 1%, and over 90% of patients respond dramatically with reduced pain and fever within 72 hours; recurrence is rare. Abscesses resolve slowly and may even enlarge despite clinical improvement, so follow-up ultrasonography can be misleading; complete resolution within 6 months is expected in about two-thirds of patients, while roughly 10% have persistent imaging abnormalities for up to a year. A hepatobronchial fistula carries a good prognosis, whereas pericardial rupture (usually from left-lobe abscesses) carries the gravest prognosis (p.1799-1801).
Pleuropulmonary involvement (reported in 20-30%, the most frequent complication): contiguous spread or frank rupture into the pleural space, the latter requiring drainage (p.1799).
Large abscess (>10 cm) in the superior right lobe, which may rupture into the pleural space (p.1800).
Left-lobe abscess, which may rupture into the pericardium, the complication carrying the gravest prognosis and able to occur even during medical therapy (p.1799-1800).
Rupture into the peritoneum, presenting as an indolent leak or as an acute abdomen (p.1799).
Hepatobronchial fistula causing cough productive of large amounts of necrotic material (p.1799).
Lack of clinical response within 3-5 days or threat of imminent rupture (p.1801).
Abdominal ultrasound or CT — Characterizes the abscess (typically single, right lobe, in amoebic disease) and guides the decision on aspiration.
Amoebic serology (IgG) — Highly sensitive for invasive amoebiasis and useful when aspiration is not performed or is inconclusive.
Stool microscopy for E. histolytica (trophozoites/cysts) — Supportive if positive, but a substantial proportion of liver abscess patients have negative stool studies at the time of presentation.

Diagnostic aspiration (if no improvement in 5-7 days, large/left-lobe abscess, or diagnostic uncertainty) — Classic 'anchovy paste' aspirate supports amoebic etiology; also allows bacterial culture to exclude/identify a pyogenic or mixed process.
Amoebic Liver Abscess (infective) — Hepatobiliary / Tropical Fever
veryLikely: Entamoeba histolytica; possible: Concurrent or preceding intestinal amoebiasis (only a minority have concurrent diarrhea at presentation)

[guideline] empiric → Metronidazole / Followed by a luminal agent (Paromomycin or Diloxanide furoate) Highly effective tissue amoebicide for invasive disease including liver abscess, with response typically seen within days; first-line for amoebic liver abscess based on strong clinical/imaging suspicion.
[guideline] alternative → Tinidazole (alternative tissue amoebicide)
Foreign-body/food aspiration causing major-airway obstruction with atelectasis and nonspecific inflammation, managed by removal rather than antibiotics (p.1418)
Chemical (acid) pneumonitis, e.g., Mendelson syndrome from regurgitated gastric contents (p.1418)
Pneumococcal pneumonia, distinguished by its more acute presentation (p.1418)
Lung abscess (subacute anaerobic infection) as a related/overlapping entity (p.1072, p.1418)
Pneumococcal pneumonia presenting more acutely than indolent anaerobic aspiration infection (p.1418)

Chest radiography looking for consolidation in dependent lung segments (basilar lower-lobe segments if aspiration occurred upright; posterior segment of the upper lobe or superior segment of the lower lobe if supine) (p.1418)
Gram stain of sputum, which characteristically shows a mixed bacterial population with many polymorphonuclear leukocytes (p.1418)
Bronchoscopic protected-brush specimens or bronchoalveolar lavage, which may recover anaerobes from the lower tract with less oropharyngeal contamination (role still being defined) (p.1418)
Assessment of dentition/oral hygiene, given the association of severe dental disease with aspiration pneumonia (p.1418)
Chemical pneumonitis (Mendelson syndrome) from aspiration of acidic gastric juices, with rapid alveolar injury and pulmonary edema, often without fever and frequently needing no antibiotics (p.1418)
Foreign-body/food aspiration with airway obstruction and atelectasis (p.1418)

Macroaspiration of oropharyngeal or gastric contents delivers a high microbial burden directly into the lower airways; lung involvement reflects this rather than invasion of a sterile space, since the lungs normally harbor a microbiota. Mechanical defenses (nasal hairs/turbinates, branching airways, mucociliary clearance, gag and cough reflexes) reduce but do not fully block bacterial access to the lower respiratory tract. Bacterial aspiration pneumonia develops over several days to weeks (not hours) through a combination of increased bacterial burden, increased virulence of aspirated organisms, and potential airway damage from aspirated gastric fluid. This contrasts with chemical pneumonitis (Mendelson syndrome), where aspirated acidic gastric juice causes rapid, direct destruction of the alveolar lining with fluid transudation into the alveolar space within hours (p.1066, p.1418).

Aspiration pneumonia is best viewed as a point on a continuum that also includes community-acquired and hospital-acquired pneumonia, defined by a phenotype with macroaspiration risk factors and involvement of characteristic gravity-dependent lung locations (p.1066).
Aspiration pneumonia is estimated to account for roughly 5-15% of community-acquired pneumonia cases; reliable figures for the hospital-acquired setting are not available (p.1066).

The historical view that aspiration pneumonia is caused mainly by anaerobes has shifted: when acquired in the community or hospital, the likely pathogens mirror those of CAP or HAP, with anaerobes still relevant mainly in poor dentition, lung abscess, necrotizing pneumonia, or empyema (p.1067).

Anaerobic aspiration infections tend to follow an indolent course, a clinical clue that helps separate them from more acutely presenting conditions such as chemical pneumonitis or pneumococcal pneumonia (p.1418).
Sputum in bacterial aspiration pneumonia is characteristically NOT malodorous unless the process has been ongoing for at least about a week (p.1418).

Expectorated sputum is unreliable for anaerobic culture because of inevitable contamination by normal oral microbiota; reliable anaerobic specimens historically required transtracheal or transthoracic aspiration, techniques rarely used now (p.1418).
In CAP overall, no specific etiology is identified in more than half of cases despite careful history, examination, and imaging (p.1067).

Failing to distinguish chemical pneumonitis (Mendelson syndrome) from bacterial aspiration pneumonia: chemical pneumonitis is a non-infectious acid injury that usually resolves with supportive care and does NOT warrant antibiotics unless bacterial superinfection develops (p.1418).
Routinely covering anaerobes for all aspiration pneumonia: anaerobic coverage is unnecessary unless dentition is poor or there is lung abscess or necrotizing pneumonia (p.1070).
Expecting an acute, foul-smelling presentation: bacterial aspiration pneumonia evolves over days to weeks and sputum is usually not malodorous until the process has lasted about a week (p.1418).
Relying on expectorated sputum for anaerobic culture, which is invalid because of oral-flora contamination (p.1418).
Gross hemoptysis suggesting necrotizing pneumonia (p.1067)
Progression to respiratory failure; in chemical pneumonitis a chest x-ray can evolve from normal to a complete bilateral whiteout within 8-24 hours (p.1067, p.1418)
Septic shock and organ failure in severe pneumonia (p.1067)
Weight loss and anemia indicating a more chronic process (p.1418)
Development of lung abscess or complicated/empyematous pleural effusion (pleural fluid pH <7.2, glucose <2.2 mmol/L, or LDH >1000 U/L, or organisms seen/cultured indicates need for drainage) (p.1072)
Chest X-ray — Aspiration classically affects dependent lung segments (posterior upper lobes if aspirated supine, basal segments of lower lobes if upright) — helpful in confirming the diagnosis.
Swallowing assessment (if recurrent or ongoing risk) — Identifies the underlying mechanism (dysphagia, reduced consciousness) to prevent recurrence.
CBC, CRP — Supports severity assessment and baseline for response monitoring.
Aspiration Pneumonia (infective) — Respiratory

veryLikely: Oral anaerobes (Peptostreptococcus, Prevotella, Fusobacterium), Streptococcus pneumoniae; likely: Staphylococcus aureus, Enterobacteriaceae (if hospital-associated aspiration); possible: Klebsiella pneumoniae (classically associated with aspiration in alcoholics)

[guideline] alternative → Clindamycin (penicillin allergy)
[guideline] alternative → Piperacillin-tazobactam (hospital-associated or severe)

Serum and CSF autoimmune/paraneoplastic antibody panel (NMDAR, LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA, and onconeural antibodies) — confirms specific antibody-mediated syndrome
MRI brain with contrast — assesses for mesial temporal/limbic T2-FLAIR signal change and excludes structural or infectious mimics
CSF analysis (cell count, protein, oligoclonal bands, HSV PCR) — distinguishes autoimmune from infectious causes and supports diagnosis
EEG — detects epileptiform activity, extreme delta brush pattern (suggestive of anti-NMDAR encephalitis), or non-convulsive status epilepticus
Whole-body imaging (CT/MRI chest-abdomen-pelvis, pelvic ultrasound/MRI in women, testicular ultrasound in men) — screens for occult tumor, especially ovarian teratoma or thymoma
FDG-PET brain — may show characteristic regional hyper- or hypometabolism when MRI is unrevealing

Autoimmune encephalitis results from antibody-mediated or T-cell-mediated attack on neuronal surface or intracellular antigens, producing limbic or diffuse cortical dysfunction. Surface-antigen antibodies (e.g., against the NMDA receptor, LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B receptor) directly disrupt synaptic receptor function and are often reversible with immunotherapy, whereas antibodies against intracellular (onconeural) antigens reflect cytotoxic T-cell-mediated neuronal injury and are less responsive to treatment. A subset is paraneoplastic, triggered by tumor expression of neuronal antigens (e.g., ovarian teratoma expressing NMDA receptors), while others arise post-infection (e.g., following herpes simplex encephalitis) or without any identifiable trigger.

Subacute (days to a few weeks) behavioral change, memory decline, psychiatric symptoms, seizures, or movement disorder should prompt consideration of autoimmune encephalitis, especially in young adults or children.

Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis classically evolves through a viral-like prodrome, then psychiatric/behavioral disturbance, followed by seizures, movement disorder (orofacial dyskinesias), autonomic instability, and decreased consciousness.
Faciobrachial dystonic seizures are a highly characteristic, near-pathognomonic sign of anti-LGI1 encephalitis and often precede overt cognitive decline.
Always search for an underlying tumor (ovarian teratoma in anti-NMDAR disease, thymoma, small-cell lung cancer) since paraneoplastic triggers are common and tumor removal aids recovery.
MRI can be normal or show only subtle mesial temporal T2/FLAIR signal change; a normal scan does not exclude the diagnosis.
CSF often shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and oligoclonal bands; antibody testing should be sent on both serum and CSF since CSF sensitivity is higher for some antibodies (e.g., NMDAR).
Response to immunotherapy can be slow (weeks to months), and early aggressive treatment plus tumor removal improves long-term outcome.
Relapses occur in a meaningful proportion of patients, particularly with anti-NMDAR encephalitis, warranting longitudinal follow-up.

Excluding the diagnosis because MRI or initial antibody testing is negative — antibody testing can be falsely negative early, and CSF testing may be more sensitive than serum
Failing to empirically treat for herpes simplex encephalitis while autoimmune work-up is pending
Overlooking the need for repeated or interval tumor screening, since a causative tumor may not be apparent at initial presentation

Many patients, particularly those with anti-NMDAR or anti-LGI1 encephalitis, achieve substantial or full recovery with prompt immunotherapy and tumor removal when applicable, though recovery may take many months and some residual cognitive or behavioral deficits can persist. Relapses occur in a meaningful minority, and outcomes are generally worse with delayed treatment, intracellular (onconeural) antibody syndromes, or need for prolonged intensive care.

AIH results from a breakdown in immune self-tolerance leading to T-cell-mediated attack on hepatocytes in a genetically susceptible host, often triggered by an environmental factor such as a viral infection or drug exposure. Autoantibody production (ANA, anti-smooth-muscle antibody, or anti-LKM1) accompanies the T-cell-driven injury but is thought to be a marker rather than the primary mediator of hepatocyte damage. Chronic interface hepatitis with ongoing necroinflammation can progress to fibrosis and cirrhosis if untreated.
Consider AIH in any patient with unexplained acute or chronic hepatocellular injury, especially young to middle-aged women, but it can occur at any age and in either sex.
Presentation is highly variable, from asymptomatic transaminase elevation to fulminant acute liver failure or established cirrhosis at diagnosis.
Marked hypergammaglobulinemia (especially elevated IgG) out of proportion to the degree of liver injury is a classic clue.
Two broad serologic patterns exist: type 1 (ANA and/or anti-smooth-muscle antibody positive) and type 2 (anti-LKM1 positive, more common in children).
Concurrent autoimmune conditions (autoimmune thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes, celiac disease, ulcerative colitis) support the diagnosis.
Liver biopsy showing interface hepatitis with a dense plasma cell infiltrate is characteristic and helps confirm diagnosis and grade severity.
A dramatic biochemical response to immunosuppressive therapy is itself supportive of the diagnosis and is used as a diagnostic criterion when the picture is ambiguous.
Overlap syndromes with primary biliary cholangitis or primary sclerosing cholangitis occur and should be considered when cholestatic features coexist.

With timely immunosuppressive treatment, most patients achieve biochemical remission and have a favorable long-term prognosis, though relapse after treatment withdrawal is common and many require long-term maintenance therapy. Untreated or refractory disease can progress to cirrhosis, liver failure, and the need for liver transplantation.

Intact brain parenchyma is relatively resistant to infection; bacterial invasion generally requires preexisting or concomitant ischemia, necrosis, or hypoxemia in brain tissue. Abscesses arise by direct contiguous spread (sinusitis, otitis media, mastoiditis, dental infection), by inoculation after penetrating trauma or neurosurgery, or by hematogenous seeding from a distant focus; about a quarter are cryptogenic with no identified source. Hematogenous abscesses are often multiple, frequently lie at the gray-white junction in the middle cerebral artery territory, and tend to be poorly encapsulated. Once established, the lesion evolves through stages: early cerebritis (days 1-3, perivascular inflammation around a core of coagulative necrosis with marked edema), late cerebritis (days 4-9, expanding necrotic center with macrophage/fibroblast infiltrate and a developing thin capsule), early capsule formation (days 10-13, capsule better formed on the cortical than ventricular side, correlating with the ring-enhancing appearance on imaging), and late capsule formation (day 14 onward, dense collagenous capsule, regressing edema, and surrounding gliosis with reactive astrocytes that may underlie later seizures). In right-to-left cardiac or pulmonary shunts, bacteria bypass the pulmonary capillary filter while shunt-related hypoxemia and polycythemia create ischemic nidi favoring abscess formation (p.1178-1179).
The classic triad of headache, fever, and a focal neurologic deficit is present in fewer than half of cases, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1178).
Headache is the single most common symptom (more than 75% of patients), typically a constant, dull ache that becomes progressively more severe and refractory to treatment (p.1178).
Fever is present in only about half of patients at diagnosis; its absence should not be used to rule out a brain abscess (p.1178).

Most patients present a relatively long time after symptom onset (commonly around 11-12 days), and a brain abscess usually behaves like an expanding mass lesion rather than an obvious infection (p.1178).
Meningismus is generally absent unless the abscess has ruptured into the ventricle or infection has reached the subarachnoid space (p.1178).
Diffusion-weighted MRI helps distinguish abscess from tumor: an abscess shows restricted diffusion (high DWI signal, low ADC) within the cavity, whereas necrotic tumors typically do not (p.1178).
Lesion location predicts the source and the deficit: otogenic abscesses favor the temporal lobe and cerebellum, while sinus and dental abscesses favor the frontal lobes (p.1179).
New-onset partial seizures are the most common manifestation of neurocysticercosis, an important focal CNS lesion in patients from Latin America (p.1181).
Relying on the classic triad: headache, fever, and focal deficit coexist in fewer than half of patients (p.1178).
Excluding the diagnosis because the patient is afebrile - fever is absent in roughly half of cases (p.1178).
Performing a lumbar puncture in a patient with a suspected focal intracranial infection, risking herniation without diagnostic benefit (p.1179).
Misreading a ring-enhancing lesion as tumor when diffusion-weighted imaging would point to abscess (p.1178).
Forgetting that glucocorticoid therapy can alter the imaging appearance of the abscess capsule (p.1178).
Overlooking cerebral toxoplasmosis, which characteristically reactivates and causes ring-enhancing lesions in HIV-infected and other immunocompromised patients (p.1181).
Dismissing a cryptogenic abscess as having no source - many are in fact attributable to occult dental infection (p.1179).

With modern neuroimaging, stereotactic aspiration, and improved antibiotics, mortality has fallen to typically less than 15% in recent series. However, significant sequelae - including seizures, persisting weakness, aphasia, or mental impairment - occur in at least 20% of survivors (p.1180).

Lumbar puncture should NOT be performed when a focal intracranial infection such as abscess or empyema is known or suspected, because CSF analysis adds nothing and LP increases the risk of herniation (p.1179).
Signs of raised intracranial pressure (papilledema, nausea/vomiting, drowsiness or confusion) can dominate the presentation, particularly with cerebellar abscesses (p.1178).
Rupture of an abscess into the ventricle (heralded by new meningismus) is an ominous development (p.1178).
High risk (about 35%) of focal or generalized seizures (p.1180).
Glucocorticoids and prior treatment can alter the CT/MRI appearance of the capsule, potentially masking or modifying the imaging picture (p.1178).

Harrison describes a staged histopathologic/radiologic evolution rather than a clinical severity score: early cerebritis (days 1-3), late cerebritis (days 4-9), early capsule formation (days 10-13, when ring enhancement appears), and late capsule formation (day 14 and beyond) (p.1178).

High-resolution chest CT - imaging modality of choice; more specific than chest radiograph; look for airway dilation as 'tram tracks' or the 'signet-ring sign' (airway diameter at least 1.5x the adjacent vessel), lack of bronchial tapering, bronchial wall thickening, and inspissated secretions in a 'tree-in-bud' pattern (Harrison 22e p.2243)

Bronchoscopy - almost always required in focal bronchiectasis to exclude airway obstruction by mass or foreign body; consider with BAL in diffuse disease if no pathogen is identified (Harrison 22e p.2243)
Pulmonary function testing - functional assessment, typically showing mild-to-moderate airflow obstruction (Harrison 22e p.2243)

Etiologic workup for diffuse disease: sputum stains/cultures for bacteria, acid-fast bacilli, and fungi; immunoglobulin levels and CBC with differential; HIV testing; sweat chloride and genetic testing for CF; alpha-1 antitrypsin level; nasal/respiratory brush or biopsy for ciliary dyskinesia; autoimmune serologies; ABPA workup (Aspergillus skin test/precipitins, serum IgE, eosinophils); swallowing/neuromuscular assessment (Harrison 22e p.2242)

Traction bronchiectasis from underlying lung fibrosis (e.g., idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, post-radiation fibrosis) - dilated airways from parenchymal distortion rather than active infection (Harrison 22e p.2242-2243)
Autoimmune/rheumatologic airway disease (rheumatoid arthritis, Sjogren's syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease) (Harrison 22e p.2242)
Recurrent aspiration (e.g., from esophageal motility disorders such as scleroderma) (Harrison 22e p.2242)

The dominant mechanism of infectious bronchiectasis is the 'vicious cycle hypothesis': susceptibility to infection plus impaired mucociliary clearance permits microbial colonisation of the bronchial tree; the persistent microbial presence incites chronic inflammation that damages the airway wall, which further impairs secretion and microbial clearance, perpetuating the infectious-inflammatory cycle. Some organisms, notably Pseudomonas aeruginosa, are especially adept at colonising damaged airways and evading host defences. Impaired mucociliary clearance may be inherited (e.g., cystic fibrosis, dyskinetic cilia syndrome), and a single severe infection such as Bordetella pertussis or Mycoplasma pneumoniae can cause enough airway damage to seed the cycle. Pathologically there is small-airway wall inflammation with larger-airway wall destruction and dilation, and loss of elastin, smooth muscle, and cartilage; inflammatory cells release proteases, reactive oxygen species, and proinflammatory cytokines that damage larger airways while ongoing small-airway inflammation produces airflow obstruction. Antiproteases such as alpha-1 antitrypsin help neutralise neutrophil elastase, and bronchiectasis/emphysema occur in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Molecular endotypes with distinct inflammatory and microbiome signatures may correlate with exacerbation risk. Noninfectious mechanisms include immune-mediated bronchial wall damage (e.g., Sjogren's syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis) and traction from parenchymal fibrosis. (Harrison 22e p.2242-2243)
Bronchiectasis is irreversible airway dilation, classically categorised as cylindrical/tubular (most common), varicose, or cystic; it may be focal or diffuse (Harrison 22e p.2242).

An acute exacerbation is defined primarily by a change in sputum character - increased volume and increased purulence - rather than by classic infection signs; fever and new infiltrates may be absent (Harrison 22e p.2243).
The usual clinical picture between exacerbations is a persistent productive cough with thick, tenacious sputum, often with crackles, wheeze, and sometimes digital clubbing (Harrison 22e p.2243).
Pseudomonas aeruginosa preferentially colonises damaged airways and evades host defences; its colonisation marks more severe disease and worse outcomes (Harrison 22e p.2242-2243, p.2244).

The pattern of lung-field involvement on imaging hints at the underlying cause: upper-zone in CF and post-radiation fibrosis, lower-zone in chronic aspiration/end-stage fibrosis/immunodeficiency, midlung in NTM (MAC) and dyskinetic cilia syndrome, and central-airway in ABPA (Harrison 22e p.2242-2243).
MAC-related bronchiectasis classically affects nonsmoking women over 50 years of age (Harrison 22e p.2242).
Up to 25-50% of patients referred for bronchiectasis have idiopathic disease after workup (Harrison 22e p.2242).
Expecting classic infection signs: an exacerbation may lack fever or new infiltrates, so reliance on these can miss it - the defining change is sputum volume and purulence (Harrison 22e p.2243).
Chest radiographs lack sensitivity for bronchiectasis; a normal or unremarkable film does not exclude it, and CT is needed for confirmation (Harrison 22e p.2243).

Positive NTM cultures may reflect colonisation rather than true infection; consensus diagnostic criteria (e.g., two positive sputum cultures, or one positive BAL, plus symptoms and radiographic findings) should be applied before attributing disease (Harrison 22e p.2243).
Focal bronchiectasis should prompt bronchoscopy to exclude an obstructing mass or foreign body rather than being attributed to infection alone (Harrison 22e p.2243).

Outcomes vary widely with the underlying etiology and comorbidities, and are influenced by exacerbation frequency and, in infectious disease, the specific pathogens involved - Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonisation is associated with worse outcomes. Lung-function decline in non-CF bronchiectasis can resemble that of COPD, with FEV1 falling roughly 50-55 mL/year versus 20-30 mL/year in healthy controls. (Harrison 22e p.2244)

Hemoptysis - bronchiectatic airways are dilated, inflamed, and highly vascular (supplied by the high-pressure bronchial circulation), so exacerbations can produce massive, life-threatening hemoptysis (Harrison 22e p.2243-2244, p.1408 hemoptysis chapter)
Massive hemoptysis - may require intubation to stabilise the patient, protection of the nonbleeding lung, and bronchial artery embolisation or surgery (Harrison 22e p.2244)
Emergence of antibiotic-resistant organisms after recurrent infections and repeated antibiotic courses (Harrison 22e p.2244)
Sputum culture (every exacerbation) — Tracks colonization status over time and directly informs both current and future empiric choices.
Chest X-ray (if new symptoms or to exclude complications) — Excludes pneumonia or other acute complications superimposed on chronic bronchiectatic changes.
Pulse oximetry — Assesses for hypoxia, particularly relevant in patients with significant structural lung disease.

Pneumonia results from proliferation of microbial pathogens in the alveoli together with the host inflammatory response. Organisms reach the lower respiratory tract chiefly by microaspiration of oropharyngeal flora, but also by inhalation and direct mucosal spread; mechanical defenses (nasal hairs/turbinates, branching airways, mucociliary clearance, gag and cough reflexes) are imperfect barriers. Rather than simple invasion of a sterile space, current models view pneumonia as an emergent disturbance of the lung microbiota driven by self-reinforcing positive-feedback loops: an inciting epithelial/endothelial injury (often a viral infection plus microaspiration) releases cytokines, chemokines, and catecholamines that can selectively favor growth of organisms such as S. pneumoniae and P. aeruginosa, amplifying inflammation. When innate and adaptive immunity fail to contain this, mediators (IL-6 and TNF cause fever; IL-8 and G-CSF recruit neutrophils) drive an alveolar-capillary leak producing hypoxemia and radiographic infiltrates. Bacterial toxins amplify inflammation, and some pathogens blunt hypoxic vasoconstriction, worsening hypoxemia; reduced compliance, increased secretions, raised respiratory drive, and intrapulmonary shunting cause dyspnea and, when severe, respiratory failure (Harrison 22e p.1066). Pathologically, classic (lobar pneumococcal) pneumonia passes through edema, red hepatization, gray hepatization, and resolution; a bronchopneumonia pattern predominates in nosocomial disease while a lobar pattern is more typical of bacterial CAP, and viral pneumonias are alveolar rather than interstitial processes (Harrison 22e p.1066).

Typical and atypical pathogens cannot be reliably separated on clinical or radiographic grounds because both can produce overlapping syndromes; atypicals (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella) are not seen on Gram stain or grown on standard media and are intrinsically resistant to beta-lactams (Harrison 22e p.1067).

In more than half of CAP cases no specific pathogen is identified despite history, examination, and imaging; in one large emergency-department series an etiology was established in under 8% (Harrison 22e p.1068).

Physical examination has limited diagnostic accuracy in pneumonia (sensitivity ~58%, specificity ~67%), so a compatible clinical picture plus a new infiltrate on chest film remains the diagnostic standard (Harrison 22e p.1068).
In the elderly the presentation may be subtle, manifesting as new or worsening confusion or decompensation of a chronic illness with few classic respiratory findings (Harrison 22e p.1068).
Gross hemoptysis raises concern for necrotizing pneumonia, such as that caused by community-associated MRSA (Harrison 22e p.1067).
Up to about 20% of patients have gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea) in addition to constitutional and pulmonary findings (Harrison 22e p.1067-1068).

Aspiration pneumonia sits on a continuum with CAP/HAP and accounts for roughly 5-15% of CAP cases; modern organisms mirror the usual CAP/HAP flora, with anaerobes mainly relevant in poor dentition, lung abscess, necrotizing pneumonia, or empyema (Harrison 22e p.1066-1067).

Epidemiologic exposures can flag specific organisms (e.g. birds for Chlamydia psittaci/Histoplasma, recent hotel or cruise stay for Legionella, local influenza activity for influenza/pneumococcus/S. aureus) (Harrison 22e p.1067).

CAP can be complicated by cardiovascular events (heart failure, arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, stroke), especially in the elderly with pneumococcal or influenza pneumonia, attributed to increased myocardial load and inflammation-driven plaque destabilization, and these events may occur acutely or up to a year later (Harrison 22e p.1072).
Treating a macrolide as adequate empirical monotherapy where high-level pneumococcal macrolide resistance is prevalent risks treatment failure (Harrison 22e p.1069).

Relying on chest radiography or clinical features to determine etiology is unreliable; imaging often cannot distinguish CAP from other conditions and seldom yields a specific organism (Harrison 22e p.1068).
Using procalcitonin or CRP in isolation to decide on or withhold antibiotics is inappropriate, as neither is sufficiently accurate for diagnosing bacterial CAP (Harrison 22e p.1068-1069).
Neither PSI nor CURB-65 is designed to determine the need for ICU admission, so they should not be used for that purpose (Harrison 22e p.1069).
Delayed ICU transfer of a deteriorating ward patient is associated with higher mortality than initial ICU monitoring of equally ill patients (Harrison 22e p.1069).
Inability to expectorate sputum may reflect dehydration rather than absence of disease; rehydration can yield a productive sample and a more apparent infiltrate (Harrison 22e p.1068).
Pneumonia that relapses or recurs in the same lung segment should prompt evaluation for an underlying neoplasm or focal abnormality such as bronchiectasis (Harrison 22e p.1072).

Outcome depends on age, comorbidities, and site of care. Young patients without comorbidity generally recover fully in about 2 weeks, whereas older patients or those with comorbid illness may take several weeks longer. Overall mortality is under 5% for outpatients but ranges from roughly 12% to 40% for hospitalized patients depending on the patient category and the timeliness of appropriate antibiotics; in older patients the 1-year mortality after CAP exceeds the 30-day mortality. Fever and leukocytosis typically resolve in 2-4 days in otherwise healthy patients, while chest radiographic clearance is slowest (4-12 weeks). About 18% of hospitalized CAP patients are readmitted within a month (Harrison 22e p.1067, p.1072).

Room-air oxygen saturation <92% (Harrison 22e p.1069)
Confusion or disorientation, including new or worsening confusion in the elderly (Harrison 22e p.1068-1069)
Respiratory rate >=30 breaths/min (Harrison 22e p.1069)
Multilobar infiltrates (Harrison 22e p.1069)
Hypotension requiring aggressive fluid resuscitation (Harrison 22e p.1069)
Gross hemoptysis suggesting necrotizing pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.1067)

Two validated tools guide the site-of-care decision. The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) is a prognostic model using 20 variables (age, comorbidities, abnormal exam and laboratory findings) that stratifies patients into five classes with rising mortality (class 1 ~0.1%, class 2 ~0.6%, class 3 ~2.8%, class 4 ~8.2%, class 5 ~29.2%); classes 1-2 are generally suitable for outpatient care and class 3 for an observation unit. CURB-65 scores one point each for Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate >=30/min, low Blood pressure (systolic <=90 or diastolic <=60 mmHg), and age >=65: a score of 0 (30-day mortality ~1.5%) suggests outpatient treatment, 1-2 generally warrants admission (unless driven only by age >=65), and >=3 (mortality ~22%) may need ICU care. PSI is better validated and more discriminating but harder to compute. Severe CAP (Harrison/IDSA-ATS criteria) is defined by either major criterion (invasive mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure, or septic shock requiring vasopressors), mandating ICU admission; presence of at least 3 of 9 minor criteria (RR >=30/min; PaO2/FiO2 <=250; multilobar infiltrates; confusion/disorientation; uremia with BUN >=20 mg/dL; leukopenia <4000/uL; thrombocytopenia <100,000/uL; hypothermia <36 degrees C; hypotension needing aggressive fluids) warrants ICU or high-level monitoring. Independent of these scores, inability to maintain oral intake, concerns about compliance (e.g. cognitive impairment, homelessness), or room-air O2 saturation <92% are indications for hospitalization (Harrison 22e p.1069).

Carcinoid syndrome arises from a neuroendocrine tumor (most often midgut origin) that secretes serotonin and other vasoactive substances (histamine, tachykinins, prostaglandins, kallikrein) directly into the systemic circulation, bypassing hepatic inactivation once liver metastases develop or when the primary tumor drains outside the portal system. These circulating mediators produce the characteristic flushing, diarrhea, and bronchoconstriction, while chronic exposure to serotonin and related factors promotes fibrous plaque deposition on cardiac valves, producing carcinoid heart disease.
Classic triad is episodic flushing, secretory diarrhea, and bronchospasm/wheezing, but full triad is present in only a minority of patients
Syndrome typically only manifests once hepatic metastases are present, since liver normally clears vasoactive mediators from portal circulation before they reach systemic circulation
Midgut (small bowel/appendiceal) tumors are the classic cause; bronchial and other extra-intestinal primaries can bypass hepatic first-pass metabolism and cause symptoms without liver metastases
Right-sided (and occasionally left-sided) valvular heart disease from fibrotic plaque deposition is a hallmark late complication and a major driver of morbidity/mortality
Flushing is usually dry, reddish-violet, and involves face/neck/upper trunk, lasting minutes; triggers include alcohol, certain foods, emotional stress, and palpation of the tumor
Niacin deficiency (pellagra-like features) can occur because tryptophan is diverted toward serotonin synthesis rather than niacin production
Carcinoid crisis — profound flushing, bronchospasm, and hemodynamic instability — can be precipitated by anesthesia, tumor manipulation, or invasive procedures and requires pre-procedural prophylaxis
Attributing episodic flushing/diarrhea to anxiety, menopause, or irritable bowel syndrome, delaying diagnosis for years
Obtaining urinary 5-HIAA without dietary restriction (serotonin-rich foods) or accounting for interfering medications, leading to false results
Overlooking carcinoid heart disease until advanced right heart failure develops
Failing to anticipate and prevent carcinoid crisis before surgery, biopsy, or anesthesia in a patient with known tumor

Prognosis depends primarily on tumor grade, extent of metastatic disease, and presence of carcinoid heart disease; with modern somatostatin analog therapy and multidisciplinary management, many patients experience prolonged survival and symptom control, though cardiac involvement significantly worsens outcomes if untreated.
Signs of carcinoid heart disease (new murmur, right heart failure symptoms) warrant urgent echocardiography and cardiology referral

Refractory diarrhea causing dehydration or electrolyte derangement needs prompt correction

Castleman disease is a heterogeneous group of lymphoproliferative disorders characterized by distinctive lymph node architectural changes, most driven by dysregulated interleukin-6 (IL-6) signaling. In unicentric disease the process is localized and follicular/vascular changes predominate, while multicentric disease reflects a systemic cytokine-driven process, frequently linked to lytic HHV-8 infection in immunocompromised hosts, producing viral IL-6 and human IL-6 that fuel plasmablast proliferation and systemic inflammation. Idiopathic multicentric disease lacks HHV-8 but shares a similar IL-6-driven inflammatory phenotype, sometimes with an associated clonal or autoimmune-like process.
Consider Castleman disease when lymphadenopathy (localized or generalized) is accompanied by unexplained constitutional symptoms, cytopenias, or hypergammaglobulinemia.
Unicentric disease is usually indolent, presenting as a single enlarged lymph node mass, and is often curable with excision.
Multicentric disease is a systemic illness with fevers, weight loss, organomegaly, and multi-organ dysfunction driven by excess IL-6 signaling.
HHV-8 infection drives most multicentric cases in HIV-positive patients; idiopathic multicentric disease occurs without HHV-8 or HIV.
POEMS syndrome and TAFRO syndrome are important clinical variants/associations that change management and prognosis.
Excisional lymph node biopsy with expert hematopathology review is essential — needle biopsies are often non-diagnostic.
Multicentric disease carries an increased risk of progression to lymphoma and of concurrent Kaposi sarcoma in HHV-8-positive/HIV-positive patients.
Attributing lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms solely to infection or malignancy without considering Castleman disease, delaying diagnosis
Relying on core needle biopsy alone, which frequently yields non-diagnostic or misleading architecture compared to excisional biopsy
Failing to test for HIV and HHV-8 in patients with multicentric disease, missing a treatable driver
Overlooking associated syndromes (POEMS, TAFRO) that substantially alter prognosis and treatment approach

Unicentric Castleman disease has an excellent prognosis after complete surgical excision, with cure in most cases. Multicentric disease, particularly HHV-8-associated or TAFRO-variant forms, follows a more relapsing and potentially life-threatening course, with outcomes improved by IL-6-pathway-targeted therapy but still carrying elevated risk of lymphoma and organ dysfunction.

Catastrophic APS represents an accelerated, disseminated form of antiphospholipid antibody-mediated thrombosis affecting predominantly small vessels and multiple organs simultaneously, rather than the single medium/large-vessel thrombi seen in classic APS. Antiphospholipid antibodies (anticardiolipin, anti-beta2-glycoprotein I, lupus anticoagulant) activate endothelium, platelets, and complement, driving a systemic thrombo-inflammatory cascade that resembles disseminated intravascular coagulation but with predominant thrombosis rather than bleeding. A triggering event (infection, surgery, trauma, or abrupt anticoagulant discontinuation) is thought to initiate a self-amplifying cytokine storm and complement activation, leading to a vicious cycle of endothelial injury and microthrombosis across organs. This results in a systemic inflammatory response with multi-organ failure occurring within days to weeks.
A fulminant, multi-organ variant of antiphospholipid syndrome causing widespread small-vessel thrombosis over days, in contrast to the single large-vessel events typical of classic APS
Suspect in any patient with known or suspected antiphospholipid antibodies who develops rapidly progressive multi-organ dysfunction
Roughly half of cases are precipitated by an identifiable trigger such as infection, surgery, trauma, anticoagulation withdrawal, or malignancy
Renal, pulmonary, cerebral, cardiac, cutaneous, and adrenal involvement are the most commonly affected sites
Thrombocytopenia and schistocytes may be present, creating overlap with thrombotic microangiopathy syndromes and complicating diagnosis
Mortality remains high despite treatment, so early recognition and aggressive combination therapy are critical
A definite diagnosis requires histopathologic confirmation of small-vessel occlusion in at least one organ, though treatment should not be delayed pending biopsy in critically ill patients
Mistaking catastrophic APS for straightforward sepsis-related multi-organ failure or DIC and delaying antibody testing
Withholding anticoagulation and immunosuppression while awaiting confirmatory biopsy in a rapidly deteriorating patient
Failing to identify and treat the precipitating trigger (e.g., untreated infection) alongside the antibody-driven process
Overlooking coexisting thrombotic microangiopathy, which may require additional therapies beyond standard APS management

Catastrophic APS carries a high mortality rate even with aggressive combination treatment, though survival has improved with earlier recognition and multimodal therapy. Survivors remain at risk for recurrent thrombotic events and organ damage, requiring long-term anticoagulation and monitoring.

Urinary catheters and other foreign bodies (stones, stents, nephrostomy tubes) provide an inert surface for bacterial colonization and formation of a persistent biofilm, and catheterization dramatically increases bacterial entry into the urinary tract. The catheter serves as a conduit allowing organisms to ascend into the bladder, making bacteriuria nearly universal during catheterization. Biofilm on the catheter shelters organisms and acts as a nidus for reinfection, which is why catheter exchange or removal is central to clearing infection. The microbiology is more diverse than in uncomplicated cystitis; while E. coli remains predominant, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, enterococci, Staphylococcus aureus, and Candida are important additional pathogens (Harrison 22e pp.1087-1088, 1094).

CAUTI is diagnosed only when localizing urinary and/or systemic symptoms (e.g., fever) are present together with pyuria and bacteriuria; bacteriuria and pyuria alone do not establish the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1090).

Because the catheter is a conduit for bacterial entry, bacteriuria is essentially inevitable with catheterization, so an abnormal urinalysis alone should not be the endpoint of evaluating a febrile catheterized patient (Harrison 22e p.1090).
The accepted bacteriuria threshold for CAUTI is at least 10^3 colony-forming units per mL of urine (Harrison 22e p.1090).
Typical UTI features (pain, urgency, dysuria, fever, peripheral leukocytosis) have lower predictive value in catheterized patients than in non-catheterized patients (Harrison 22e p.1090).

The catheter should be exchanged or, if feasible, removed during treatment to clear biofilm-associated organisms; ideally the exchange precedes urine culture collection so results reflect bladder rather than catheter-wall microbiology (Harrison 22e p.1094).

Very high pyuria levels are common with urinary stasis (e.g., end-stage renal disease, obstructed catheters) and the degree of pyuria should not influence the distinction between asymptomatic bacteriuria and true UTI in an asymptomatic patient (Harrison 22e p.1089).

Candiduria is common in catheterized patients, especially after antimicrobial therapy for CAUTI or inappropriate treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria; removal of the catheter alone resolves candiduria in over a third of asymptomatic cases (Harrison 22e pp.1088, 1095).

Urine nitrite is detectable only with Enterobacterales and adequate accumulation, so it can be falsely negative with non-Enterobacterales pathogens (e.g., enterococci, Pseudomonas, Candida) that are prominent in CAUTI (Harrison 22e pp.1090-1091).

Treating catheter-associated asymptomatic bacteriuria: apart from pregnancy (and pre-urologic-procedure screening), urine culture and treatment are not indicated for asymptomatic catheterized patients, and treating it does not reduce subsequent infection (Harrison 22e pp.1147, 1095).

Attributing nonspecific symptoms such as confusion in an elderly catheterized patient to bacteriuria without excluding other time-sensitive causes of delirium, leading to premature diagnostic closure (Harrison 22e pp.1089, 1147).
Improper treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria followed by repeat 'test-of-cure' cultures, driving a vicious cycle of escalating antimicrobial use and resistance (Harrison 22e p.1147).
Sending urine cultures in catheterized patients lacking signs/symptoms of UTI (poor diagnostic stewardship), which promotes overdiagnosis and overtreatment (Harrison 22e pp.1089, 1147).

Sampling urine through the existing biofilm-laden catheter rather than from a newly placed catheter, yielding culture results that reflect the catheter wall rather than the bladder (Harrison 22e p.1094).
Routinely using antimicrobial (silver- or nitrofurazone-impregnated) catheters to prevent CAUTI, which has not shown significant clinical benefit (Harrison 22e p.1094).

Asymptomatic bacteriuria is common in catheterized and elderly patients but does not itself increase risk of infection or death, which argues against treating it. In the absence of anatomic abnormalities (e.g., reflux, obstruction), recurrent urinary infection does not lead to chronic pyelonephritis or renal failure; however, with underlying renal abnormalities such as obstructing stones, infection can accelerate renal parenchymal damage. A randomized trial found more relapses with 3 versus 14 days of therapy, supporting longer treatment than for uncomplicated cystitis (Harrison 22e pp.1094-1095).
Fever, rigors, nausea/vomiting, or flank/costovertebral angle pain suggesting infection has extended beyond the bladder (pyelonephritis or bloodstream)
Signs of sepsis in a catheterized patient with systemic symptoms
Isolation of S. aureus from urine, which should prompt consideration of concomitant bacteremia
Persistent fever and/or bacteremia despite appropriate therapy, suggesting renal/perinephric abscess or obstruction requiring drainage

CAUTI falls within the complicated UTI category, defined by infection in the setting of intermittent or indwelling urinary catheterization. Severity ranges from localized symptomatic infection to infection extending beyond the bladder (pyelonephritis, bacteremia) signaled by fever, rigors, flank pain, and systemic toxicity (Harrison 22e pp.1086-1087, 1089).

Coeliac disease is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by dietary gluten (from wheat, barley, and rye) in genetically susceptible individuals, most of whom carry HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8. Deamidation of gluten peptides by tissue transglutaminase enhances their binding to these HLA molecules, driving an aberrant T-cell response that damages small intestinal enterocytes. The resulting villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytosis impair mucosal absorptive surface area, leading to malabsorption of macronutrients and micronutrients.
Consider in any patient with chronic diarrhoea, bloating, weight loss, or unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia, even without overt GI symptoms
Can present atypically with isolated osteoporosis, infertility, elevated transaminases, peripheral neuropathy, or dental enamel defects
Dermatitis herpetiformis is a specific cutaneous marker and is essentially pathognomonic when biopsy-confirmed
Serologic testing must be performed while the patient is still on a gluten-containing diet, otherwise antibody titres normalise and results are falsely negative
First-degree relatives and patients with type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease, or Down/Turner syndrome have markedly increased prevalence and warrant screening
Selective IgA deficiency can cause false-negative IgA-based serology, so total IgA should be checked concurrently
Symptomatic response to a gluten-free diet supports but does not confirm the diagnosis; histology and serology should ideally precede dietary change
Testing serology after the patient has already started a gluten-free diet, producing false-negative results
Relying on serology alone without confirmatory duodenal biopsy, or biopsying too few sites reducing diagnostic yield
Missing the diagnosis in atypical presentations (isolated anaemia, infertility, elevated liver enzymes) because classic diarrhoea is absent
Failing to screen at-risk relatives or patients with associated autoimmune conditions

Most patients respond well to strict, lifelong adherence to a gluten-free diet, with resolution of symptoms and mucosal healing over months to years. A small subset develops refractory disease or, rarely, enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma, particularly with prolonged undiagnosed or poorly controlled disease.
Persistent or worsening symptoms despite strict gluten-free diet — consider refractory coeliac disease or alternative diagnosis
New abdominal pain, obstruction, or GI bleeding in a known coeliac patient — raises concern for enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma or ulcerative jejunoileitis
Severe malnutrition, hypoalbuminemia, or electrolyte derangement requiring urgent nutritional support

Signs of adrenal or severe metabolic crisis from long-standing malabsorption

Bacteria reach the dermis and subcutaneous soft tissue after disruption of the epidermal barrier by cracks, abrasions, cuts, burns, insect bites, surgical incisions, IV catheters, trauma, tinea/fungal infection, or pressure and venous-stasis ulcers. Organisms already colonizing the skin (notably S. aureus and group A streptococci) most readily exploit such breaks, though many exogenous bacteria can be introduced. Streptococcal disease characteristically spreads diffusely via lymphatics, producing lymphangitis, whereas staphylococcal disease spreads from a central focus such as an abscess or infected foreign body. Much of the expanding erythema reflects the action of bacterial extracellular toxins and host-derived inflammatory mediators rather than high bacterial burden. Progression to deeper structures with loss of vascular integrity (purple bullae, ecchymosis, cutaneous anesthesia) signals possible necrotizing infection (Harrison 22e p.1095, p.1007).

Non-purulent cellulitis (no associated abscess, focal purulence, or drainage) is a rapidly spreading, diffuse process typically due to S. pyogenes, often accompanied by lymphangitis and fever; purulent cellulitis arising from a focal lesion (furuncle, carbuncle, abscess, surgical wound) is more likely staphylococcal (Harrison 22e p.1095).

Even with needle aspiration of the advancing edge or punch biopsy of involved tissue, cultures are positive in only about 20% of cases, suggesting low bacterial numbers and that much of the spreading erythema is driven by extracellular toxins and host inflammatory mediators (Harrison 22e p.1095).

When a draining wound or visible portal of entry is present, Gram stain and culture of that material can give a definitive microbiologic diagnosis, unlike cultures of intact cellulitic skin (Harrison 22e p.1095).

A careful exposure/epidemiologic history is diagnostically valuable because many less common causative organisms occupy characteristic ecological niches (e.g., cat/dog bite, freshwater laceration, fish/swine handling, aquarium water) (Harrison 22e p.1095).
Bilateral, symmetric lower-leg involvement favors a mimic such as stasis dermatitis, whereas true cellulitis is usually unilateral (Harrison 22e p.428).
Routine cultures of intact cellulitic skin are frequently negative (positive in only ~20% even with aspiration or biopsy), so negative cultures do NOT exclude cellulitis (Harrison 22e p.1095).

When patients labeled 'cellulitis' are reviewed by dermatology, roughly one-third have an alternative diagnosis (e.g., eczema, lymphedema), so an overcall risks unnecessary hospitalization and antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.93).
Bilateral symmetric lower-extremity erythema is more likely stasis dermatitis than cellulitis (Harrison 22e p.428).
Early necrotizing fasciitis may present with pain or unexplained fever as the only manifestation; do NOT rely on overt cutaneous inflammation to exclude it (Harrison 22e p.1095).
Purple/hemorrhagic bullae, ecchymosis, or cutaneous anesthesia suggesting loss of vascular integrity and possible necrotizing fasciitis or myonecrosis (Harrison 22e p.1095)
Pain or tenderness disproportionate to visible skin findings, or unexplained fever with deep soft-tissue pain even without overt skin inflammation (Harrison 22e p.1095)
Brawny edema, dark-red induration, skin friability with bluish/maroon/black discoloration, or systemic toxicity/shock indicating deep necrotizing infection (Harrison 22e p.1095)

Harrison distinguishes non-purulent cellulitis (diffuse, spreading, typically streptococcal, often with lymphangitis and fever) from purulent cellulitis (associated with a focal lesion such as furuncle, carbuncle, abscess, or surgical wound, typically staphylococcal, the FDA-preferred term for these). Loss of vascular integrity (purple bullae, ecchymosis, cutaneous anesthesia, systemic toxicity) marks progression toward necrotizing infection (Harrison 22e p.1095).
