Thrombosis of a dural venous sinus or cortical vein obstructs cerebral venous drainage, raising venous and capillary pressure. This leads to impaired CSF resorption with intracranial hypertension, and can progress to vasogenic edema, venous congestion, and eventually venous infarction with secondary hemorrhage. Because venous drainage territories overlap and are variable between individuals, resulting deficits are often atypical for a single vascular distribution.
Suspect in a young patient (especially female on estrogen-containing contraception or postpartum) with new headache plus seizure, focal deficit, or altered consciousness
Headache is the most common presenting symptom and can be subacute, progressive, or thunderclap-like, sometimes mimicking idiopathic intracranial hypertension
Papilledema from raised intracranial pressure may occur even without a clear focal deficit
Deficits often do not respect a single arterial territory and may be bilateral or migrate, reflecting venous rather than arterial infarction
Hemorrhagic venous infarcts are common and should not by themselves prompt withholding anticoagulation
Seizures, especially with focal onset, occur more frequently than in typical arterial ischemic stroke
A normal non-contrast CT does not exclude the diagnosis; dedicated venous imaging is required
Consider an underlying prothrombotic, infectious, or inflammatory trigger in every confirmed case
Dismissing headache as migraine or tension-type without considering CVST in at-risk patients (pregnancy, postpartum, hormonal contraception, thrombophilia)
Withholding anticoagulation because of hemorrhagic venous infarction, which is generally still an indication for treatment rather than a contraindication
Relying on a normal non-contrast CT to exclude the diagnosis instead of obtaining dedicated venous imaging
Attributing bilateral or non-arterial-territory deficits to a psychiatric or functional cause rather than pursuing venous imaging

Most patients who receive timely anticoagulation have a favorable outcome with good functional recovery, though a minority develop persistent neurological deficits, chronic intracranial hypertension, or, rarely, death from extensive venous infarction or herniation. Recurrence risk depends on the presence and persistence of underlying prothrombotic risk factors.

Extensive bilateral hemorrhagic venous infarction on imaging

CHIKV is an arthropod-borne alphavirus (family Togaviridae) spread by Aedes mosquitoes. It produces an acute febrile illness with prominent joint involvement; rheumatic manifestations span arthralgia with or without inflammatory signs (periarticular redness, swelling, immobility). Adults experience more severe and articular-predominant disease than children. Chronic musculoskeletal sequelae are thought to relate to host factors, with increased risk in patients who have preexisting osteoarthritis, severe acute disease, or the HLA-B27 subtype, and may be associated with cryoglobulins (Harrison 22e p.1712).

Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) is an arthritogenic alphavirus transmitted by Aedes (yellow-fever and Asian tiger) mosquitoes; after a 2-10 day incubation it causes abrupt high fever, sometimes with a saddleback pattern, plus severe arthralgia (Harrison 22e p.1712).

Migratory polyarthritis predominantly involves the small joints of the hands, wrists, ankles, and feet, though larger joints may also be affected; periarticular swelling and immobility are common, while frank effusions are less frequent (Harrison 22e p.1712).

A rash appears at onset or several days in, often coinciding with defervescence around day 2-3, is most intense over trunk and limbs, and may desquamate; children more often develop a bullous rather than maculopapular/petechial rash (Harrison 22e p.1712).

Although petechiae and epistaxis are occasionally seen, CHIKV should not be classified as a cause of viral hemorrhagic fever; older reports of 'chikungunya hemorrhagic fever' largely reflected concurrent dengue coinfection (Harrison 22e p.1712, p.1706).

A recovery period of weeks is common, and a substantial proportion of middle-aged to older patients go on to develop chronic, sometimes disabling arthritis or arthralgia syndromes typically involving the same joints (Harrison 22e p.1712).

Pregnant women are not at increased risk of severe disease, but there is a high risk of maternal-fetal transmission, especially intrapartum, which has occasionally led to fetal death (Harrison 22e p.1712).

A live-attenuated chikungunya vaccine was approved in the United States in 2023 for adults at increased exposure risk and is contraindicated in immunocompromised persons; about 12% of recipients developed chikungunya-like symptoms in trials (Harrison 22e p.1060).
Do not label CHIKV as a viral hemorrhagic fever despite occasional petechiae/epistaxis; apparent 'hemorrhagic' cases historically reflected concurrent dengue infection (Harrison 22e p.1712, p.1706).
Do not assume severe disease in pregnancy; the principal pregnancy concern is intrapartum vertical transmission rather than maternal severity (Harrison 22e p.1712).
Do not consider the live-attenuated vaccine safe in immunocompromised persons, in whom it is contraindicated (Harrison 22e p.1060).

Life-threatening illness is rare; most patients recover, though recovery may take weeks. A significant fraction of middle-aged to older patients develop chronic, potentially disabling arthritis/arthralgia. Deaths have been reported, typically in the setting of large outbreaks. Children generally have milder disease and are less frequently hospitalized (Harrison 22e p.1712, p.1060).
Cardiorespiratory, neurologic, renal, or ocular complications in severe acute disease (uncommon but reported, typically in hospitalized patients) (Harrison 22e p.1712)
Pregnancy near delivery, given high risk of intrapartum maternal-fetal transmission and reported fetal death (Harrison 22e p.1712)

Acute cholangitis arises from infection within an obstructed biliary tree, most often due to choledocholithiasis (common duct stones complicate about 10-15% of cholelithiasis). At least partial obstruction to bile flow combined with bacterial colonization of bile produces inflammation; rising intrabiliary pressure in an obstructed system promotes translocation of organisms into the bloodstream, causing bacteremia and biliary sepsis. In suppurative cholangitis, pus accumulates under pressure within a completely obstructed duct, driving severe toxicity (Harrison 22e p.2489, p.2735).
The classic presentation is Charcot's triad: biliary pain, jaundice, and spiking fevers with rigors; it is present in roughly 70% of patients with ascending cholangitis (Harrison 22e p.2489, p.2735).
Addition of shock and confusion to Charcot's triad constitutes Reynolds's pentad, which signals high mortality and should trigger urgent biliary drainage (Harrison 22e p.2489).
Bile cultures are positive in approximately 75% of patients with acute cholangitis early in the symptomatic course, and blood cultures are frequently positive (Harrison 22e p.2735).
Most acute cholangitis is the nonsuppurative form, which often responds relatively quickly to supportive care and antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.2735).

Initial medical management (fluids and IV antibiotics) usually stabilizes the patient and buys a window of about 24 hours within which biliary drainage should be established, typically by ERCP (Harrison 22e p.2489).
The bile duct may not yet be dilated on early ultrasound during acute biliary obstruction, so a normal-caliber duct does not exclude cholangitis (Harrison 22e p.2489).
Relying on antibiotics alone in suppurative cholangitis; biliary decompression is required because antibiotic response is poor and mortality is very high without it.
Excluding cholangitis because the bile duct appears non-dilated on early ultrasound, which can occur in acute obstruction.
Awaiting the full Charcot's triad before acting, since not all patients display all three components.
Mistaking the relentless toxicity of suppurative disease for simple sepsis without recognizing the need for urgent source control.

Nonsuppurative acute cholangitis generally responds well to antibiotics and supportive care. Suppurative acute cholangitis carries a far worse prognosis: response to antibiotics alone is poor and mortality approaches 100% unless prompt endoscopic or surgical relief of the obstruction with drainage of infected bile is achieved. Reynolds's pentad and undue delay in drainage both predict increased morbidity and mortality (Harrison 22e p.2489, p.2735).
Reynolds's pentad (Charcot's triad plus shock and confusion) indicating suppurative cholangitis and high mortality
Mental confusion, bacteremia, and septic shock signaling suppurative cholangitis with pus under pressure
Failure to respond to antibiotics, which in suppurative disease is associated with multiple hepatic abscesses
Delay in establishing biliary drainage beyond the ~24 h stabilization window, risking recrudescent sepsis

Harrison distinguishes nonsuppurative acute cholangitis (the more common, milder form responsive to antibiotics) from suppurative acute cholangitis (pus under pressure in a completely obstructed duct, with severe toxicity, bacteremia, septic shock, and very high mortality without drainage). Clinically, Charcot's triad (pain, jaundice, fever/rigors) defines the typical syndrome, and progression to Reynolds's pentad (adding shock and confusion) marks the severe/suppurative end of the spectrum requiring urgent biliary decompression (Harrison 22e p.2489, p.2735).
Blood cultures — Frequently positive in cholangitis and identifies organism/susceptibility for de-escalation.
Liver function tests — Cholestatic pattern (elevated bilirubin, ALP, GGT) supports the diagnosis and tracks resolution after drainage.
Abdominal ultrasound — First-line imaging to identify biliary dilation and the level of obstruction.
MRCP or CT abdomen (if ultrasound inconclusive) — Better characterizes the cause and location of obstruction (stone, stricture, malignancy) to guide definitive drainage strategy.
Bile culture (at time of ERCP/drainage) — Identifies the causative organism directly from the infected source for the most targeted de-escalation.

chunks.text: Acute cholecystitis is acute inflammation of the gallbladder wall that usually follows obstruction of the cystic duct by a stone. Three mechanisms drive the inflammatory response: mechanical inflammation from increased intraluminal pressure and distention producing mucosal/wall ischemia; chemical inflammation from release of lysolecithin (via phospholipase action on biliary lecithin) and other local tissue factors; and bacterial inflammation, which contributes in roughly 50-85% of cases. Chronic cholecystitis is almost always associated with gallstones and results from repeated bouts of subacute/acute inflammation or persistent mechanical irritation of the wall by stones (Harrison 22e pp.2732-2733).

CIDP results from a T-cell and antibody-mediated autoimmune attack on peripheral nerve myelin and, in some cases, the nodal/paranodal region, producing segmental demyelination and secondary remyelination with onion-bulb formation. Some patients harbor antibodies against paranodal proteins (e.g., neurofascin, contactin-1), which behave more like a nodopathy than classic demyelination and may predict differential treatment response. Chronic or repeated inflammatory injury can eventually cause secondary axonal degeneration, which correlates with residual disability.
Presents as a progressive or relapsing symmetric polyneuropathy evolving over at least 8 weeks, distinguishing it from Guillain-Barre syndrome which peaks by 4 weeks
Weakness typically affects both proximal and distal muscles, unlike the length-dependent pattern of most axonal neuropathies
Large-fiber sensory loss (vibration, proprioception) predominates over pain, and reflexes are diffusely diminished or absent
Cranial nerve and autonomic involvement can occur but are less prominent and severe than in Guillain-Barre syndrome
CSF classically shows albuminocytologic dissociation (elevated protein with normal cell count), similar to acute demyelinating polyneuropathy
Electrodiagnostic studies showing multifocal demyelination (conduction block, temporal dispersion, prolonged distal latencies, slowed conduction velocities) are central to diagnosis
A meaningful subset responds to immunotherapy, so early recognition matters because untreated disease can lead to irreversible axonal loss and disability
Some patients have an underlying paraprotein, diabetes, HIV, or other systemic association that should be screened for
Mistaking CIDP for a slowly evolving Guillain-Barre syndrome, or vice versa, based solely on time course without full electrodiagnostic correlation
Over-reliance on CSF protein elevation alone, which is nonspecific and can be seen in diabetes and other conditions
Missing an underlying paraproteinemia or nodopathy antibody profile that changes expected treatment response
Attributing residual deficits solely to inadequate treatment when secondary axonal degeneration has already occurred

Most patients improve substantially with timely immunotherapy, though relapses are common and some require long-term maintenance treatment. Delayed diagnosis or predominant axonal involvement is associated with greater residual disability.
Rapidly progressive weakness with respiratory compromise mimicking Guillain-Barre syndrome requires urgent evaluation and monitoring
Significant axonal loss on electrodiagnostic testing suggests a worse prognosis and need for prompt treatment escalation
Asymmetric or purely motor presentations should prompt consideration of multifocal motor neuropathy rather than CIDP
Coexisting monoclonal gammopathy warrants hematologic workup to exclude POEMS syndrome or malignancy
Lack of any response to appropriate first-line immunotherapy should trigger diagnostic reconsideration

chunks.text: Tuberculous meningitis in adults does not arise acutely from direct hematogenous seeding of the meninges. Rather, during hematogenous dissemination of primary infection, miliary (millet seed-sized) tubercles form in the brain parenchyma; these enlarge and usually caseate. Whether a caseous focus produces meningitis depends on its proximity to the subarachnoid space (SAS) and how quickly it becomes fibrous-encapsulated. Subependymal caseous foci discharge bacilli and mycobacterial antigens into the SAS; rupture of a subependymal tubercle into the subarachnoid space is a recognized route. The mycobacterial antigens trigger an intense inflammatory reaction producing a thick exudate that fills the basilar cisterns and encases the cranial nerves and the major blood vessels at the base of the brain - explaining the basal enhancement, cranial nerve palsies, arteritic infarcts and obstructive hydrocephalus seen clinically. Meningitis can also result from hematogenous spread of primary or postprimary pulmonary TB, and is a particular concern in very young children and immunocompromised persons (e.g., people living with HIV) (p.1127, 1389).

chunks.text: If unrecognized, tuberculous meningitis is uniformly fatal. The disease responds to chemotherapy, but neurologic sequelae are documented in about 25% of treated cases - most often when the diagnosis was delayed. Adjunctive glucocorticoids may speed resolution of CSF abnormalities and raised CSF pressure and lower rates of death or severe disability and relapse; in one trial adjunctive dexamethasone improved survival in patients >14 years but did not reduce the frequency of neurologic sequelae. Among people living with HIV, a placebo-controlled study showed no survival or secondary-endpoint benefit from a 6-8 week tapering course of adjunctive dexamethasone (p.1389). Pharmacogenomic data suggest only a subset of patients benefit from steroids: those homozygous for the proinflammatory LTA4H allele were most helped, whereas those homozygous for the anti-inflammatory allele may be harmed (p.1026).

Most UTIs arise by ascent of bacteria from the urethra to the bladder, with further ascent up the ureter producing renal parenchymal infection; the hematogenous route accounts for under 2% of cases and typically involves virulent organisms such as S. aureus and Salmonella (isolation of either from urine should prompt consideration of concomitant bacteremia). Whether bladder entry leads to symptomatic infection depends on the interplay of host, pathogen, and environmental factors. Conditions causing urinary stasis or obstruction (vesicoureteral reflux, ureteral obstruction from prostatic hypertrophy, neurogenic bladder, urinary-diversion surgery) and foreign bodies that support biofilm all predispose to infection. Uropathogenic E. coli virulence factors include P fimbriae (mediating binding to renal epithelial receptors and important in pyelonephritis and bloodstream invasion) and type 1 pili (mediating mannose binding and initiating bladder infection), plus toxins, iron-acquisition systems, biofilm formation, and capsules. Candiduria is pathogenetically distinct in that the hematogenous route is more common, and in non-instrumented immunocompetent patients its presence implies either genital contamination or possible widespread visceral dissemination (p.1131).

Harrison defines complicated UTI as infection extending beyond the bladder (e.g., prostatitis, pyelonephritis, bacteremia) or UTI occurring in the setting of intermittent or indwelling catheterization; this is a shift from the older approach that automatically labeled any UTI in men, diabetics, the immunocompromised, or those with anatomic abnormalities as complicated (p.1129-1130).
Recurrent UTI is not inherently complicated; individual episodes may be uncomplicated and managed as such (p.1130).

Fever, rigors, and unilateral back or flank pain are incompatible with infection confined to the bladder and should trigger evaluation for infection beyond the bladder (kidney, prostate, or bloodstream) (p.1132).

In men, UTI is uncommon outside the context of catheterization/instrumentation or obstructive uropathy from prostatic hypertrophy; a urine culture should be obtained in every case of male UTI (p.1132).
Men with febrile UTI, even at first episode, should undergo imaging (CT or ultrasound) if not done previously, specifically to assess for urinary tract abnormalities or obstruction (p.1132).

Predictors of a surgically correctable disorder in men with febrile UTI include urinary retention symptoms, early UTI recurrence, hematuria at follow-up, and voiding difficulties; men with none of these had normal urinary tracts on workup (p.1132).
Early recurrence within 2 weeks is regarded as relapse rather than reinfection and may signal a sequestered focus of ongoing infection that needs evaluation (p.1130).
Foreign bodies such as stones, stents, and catheters provide an inert surface for bacterial colonization and persistent biofilm formation, serving as a nidus for recurrent infection (p.1130-1131).
Initial evaluation of recurrent cystitis should include imaging to identify renal calculi or another nidus of infection and assessment for urinary retention (p.1138).

Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria outside pregnancy or pre-urologic-procedure settings: it does not reduce future UTI and may even increase risk, possibly by promoting colonization with more virulent/resistant pathogens (p.1129, p.1136).

Ending the workup of a febrile catheterized patient at an abnormal urinalysis: bacteriuria and pyuria are essentially inevitable with catheterization, so other infectious and noninfectious causes must be systematically excluded before diagnosing CAUTI (p.1133-1134).
Premature diagnostic closure in elderly patients with isolated delirium; collateral history is needed and a reported history of recurrent UTIs may actually reflect persistent ASB (p.1132).
Relying on a negative urine dipstick to rule out bacteriuria in pregnancy; it is not sensitive enough and culture-based ASB screening is required (p.1135).

Using nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin as if they treat tissue-invasive disease; they do not achieve adequate renal tissue levels and should not be used for pyelonephritis, and nitrofurantoin is inactive against many Proteus, Providencia, Morganella, Pseudomonas, Serratia, and some Klebsiella/Enterobacter (knowledge of intrinsic resistance) (p.1136-1137).
Interpreting a mixed-flora urine culture as infection; it usually represents contamination except in long-term catheterization, chronic retention, or urinary-enteric/genital fistula (p.1135).

Most simple cystitis carries a low risk of serious complication, but tissue-invasive complicated disease (pyelonephritis and beyond) carries greater risk and patients are often systemically ill. Pyelonephritis may be complicated by acute papillary necrosis with obstruction (requiring relief of obstruction to preserve renal function), perinephric or renal cortical abscess (often requiring percutaneous drainage), emphysematous pyelonephritis (a severe form, almost exclusive to poorly controlled diabetes), and xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (suppurative renal destruction associated with chronic obstruction, often by staghorn calculi, that can mimic renal malignancy and frequently requires nephrectomy). Bilateral papillary necrosis is rare but may present with a rapid rise in creatinine (p.1133, p.1137).
Fever, rigors, nausea/vomiting, and flank pain suggesting severe pyelonephritis or infection beyond the bladder (p.1133)
Continued fever and/or bacteremia despite antibacterial therapy, suggesting intraparenchymal renal abscess (p.1133)
Failure to respond clinically within 72 h, prompting evaluation for an uncontrolled source of infection (p.1137)
Gas in renal/perinephric tissues (emphysematous pyelonephritis), almost exclusive to poorly controlled diabetes (p.1133)
Acute papillary necrosis with sloughed papillae obstructing the ureter complicating pyelonephritis (p.1133)
Isolation of S. aureus or Salmonella from urine, raising concern for concomitant bacteremia / hematogenous seeding (p.1131)
Symptoms of urinary retention, early UTI recurrence, hematuria at follow-up, or voiding difficulty in men with febrile UTI (predict surgically correctable disease) (p.1132)

Harrison frames the practical categorization around whether infection is confined to the bladder (uncomplicated cystitis) versus extends beyond it (complicated UTI: prostatitis, pyelonephritis, bacteremia) and whether catheter-associated (CAUTI). The key bedside questions are whether the patient is stable for outpatient management, whether a recalcitrant/recurrent source (e.g., obstructing calculi) must be identified, and whether the chosen agent must reach adequate blood and renal-tissue levels in addition to urine. Pyelonephritis itself ranges from mild (low-grade fever +/- back or costovertebral angle pain) to severe (high fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting, flank pain) (p.1130, p.1133).
Urine culture and sensitivity — Essential in complicated UTI given higher rates of resistant organisms — guides definitive therapy.
Renal function tests — Assesses baseline renal function, particularly relevant if structural abnormality or obstruction is suspected.
Renal ultrasound (if recurrent or treatment failure) — Evaluates for obstruction, stones, or structural abnormality contributing to complicated infection.

Pneumonia - the most frequent abnormal finding on chest imaging in this setting; about 25% of x-rays obtained for moderate-to-severe exacerbations in severe COPD are abnormal (p.2301).

Arterial blood gas in patients with advanced COPD, a history of hypercarbia, altered mental status (confusion, sleepiness), or significant distress; hypercarbia is defined as PCO2 >45 mmHg and carries treatment implications (p.2301).
Chest x-ray or chest CT in patients with severe underlying COPD, moderate-to-severe distress, or focal examination findings (p.2301).

C-reactive protein, as part of emerging expert-consensus objective criteria (combining dyspnea, vital signs, CRP, and arterial blood gases) to diagnose and stage exacerbation severity, mainly of use in the emergency department (p.2301-2302).
Pulmonary embolism - should be actively considered because the incidence of PE is increased during COPD exacerbations (p.2301).
Congestive heart failure - a common alternative or contributing finding on imaging in patients presenting as an exacerbation (p.2301).
Pneumothorax - asymmetry on chest examination may indicate pneumothorax (or large-airway obstruction) mimicking an exacerbation (p.2301).

A variety of stimuli converge on a final common pathway of airway inflammation with increased respiratory symptoms. Viral respiratory infection, once thought less common than bacterial infection, is detected by PCR-based studies in over half of exacerbations; acquisition of a new bacterial strain is associated with increased near-term exacerbation risk. Non-infective contributors include air pollution, allergens, and environmental/Aspergillus sensitization, and in a significant minority no specific precipitant is identified (p.1756, p.2301).

An exacerbation is defined clinically as an episodic acute worsening of respiratory symptoms (increased dyspnea, cough, and/or a change in sputum volume and character), usually evolving over fewer than 14 days; it may or may not be accompanied by fever, myalgias, or sore throat (p.2301).

COPD exacerbation is a clinical diagnosis; no single test confirms it, and measurement of pulmonary function (unlike in asthma) has not been shown to aid diagnosis or management of a COPD exacerbation (p.2301).

The strongest single predictor of future exacerbations is a history of a previous exacerbation, and the single greatest risk factor for hospitalization is a history of a previous hospitalization (p.2301).

The cardinal symptoms of a bacterial exacerbation are increased cough with increased sputum production, sputum purulence, and increased dyspnea relative to baseline; nontypeable H. influenzae exacerbations typically show only low-grade fever and no infiltrate on chest x-ray (p.1305-1307).

Exacerbation frequency rises as airflow obstruction worsens: patients with severe obstruction (FEV1 <50% predicted) average 1-3 episodes per year, though some severely obstructed patients are not frequent exacerbators (p.2301).

A target oxygen saturation of 88-92% is used; in patients with acute or chronic hypercarbia, supplemental O2 does not reduce minute ventilation but may modestly raise arterial PCO2 by altering ventilation-perfusion relationships - this should not deter giving the oxygen needed to correct hypoxemia (p.2302).
Withholding needed supplemental oxygen for fear of CO2 retention is an error; oxygen should be titrated to 88-92% saturation to correct hypoxemia despite a possible modest PCO2 rise (p.2302).

Contraindications to noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation that must be screened for include cardiovascular instability, impaired mental status, inability to cooperate, copious or unclearable secretions, and craniofacial abnormality or trauma preventing mask fit (p.2302).
M. catarrhalis is easily mistaken for commensal Neisseria species on respiratory culture and was historically overlooked as a pathogen, so culture interpretation requires care (p.1308).

Mortality for patients requiring mechanical ventilatory support during a COPD exacerbation is 17-49% for that hospitalization. After any hospitalization for COPD, about 20% are rehospitalized within 30 days and 45% within a year, and mortality is approximately 20% in the year after discharge. Because of the high mortality of invasive ventilation, advance directives (e.g., resuscitation preferences) should be discussed in the outpatient setting (p.2302).

Respiratory acidosis with hypercarbia (PCO2 >45 mmHg, pH <=7.35) - an indication for noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation, which reduces mortality, need for intubation, complications, and length of stay (p.2302).

Severe respiratory distress, severe hypercarbia and/or acidosis despite noninvasive ventilation, markedly impaired mental status, respiratory arrest, or hemodynamic instability - indications for invasive mechanical ventilation via endotracheal tube (p.2302).
New or worsening hypoxemia, severe underlying COPD, or significant comorbidity such as heart failure - features suggesting the need for inpatient treatment (p.2301).

Inability to speak in complete sentences, accessory muscle use, perioral or peripheral cyanosis, tachypnea, tachycardia, altered mental status, or paradoxical abdominal wall motion on examination (p.2301).

Assessment should grade both the severity of the acute exacerbation and the severity of preexisting COPD; the more severe either component, the greater the likelihood of needing hospital admission. An expert consensus has proposed more objective criteria to diagnose and stage exacerbation severity using dyspnea, vital signs, C-reactive protein, and arterial blood gases, although this schema is more useful in the emergency department than the outpatient setting (p.2301-2302).
Pulse oximetry / ABG — Assesses for hypoxia or hypercapnic respiratory failure, which determines need for ventilatory support and site of care.
Chest X-ray — Excludes pneumonia, pneumothorax, or other alternative/complicating diagnoses presenting similarly.
Sputum culture (if frequent exacerbator or treatment failure) — Identifies resistant or atypical organisms (e.g., Pseudomonas) in patients with recurrent exacerbations.

chunks.text: Most cystitis arises by ascending infection: gut flora (typically E. coli) colonize the vaginal introitus and periurethral area, then ascend the urethra into the bladder. Introduction of bacteria into the bladder does not inevitably cause sustained symptomatic infection; normal voiding and innate bladder defenses often clear organisms (e.g., after intercourse). Outcome reflects the interplay of host, organism, and environmental factors. Anything that increases bacterial entry or retention raises risk. The shorter female urethra is considered the primary anatomic reason cystitis predominates in young women over young men. Uropathogenic E. coli express virulence factors including type 1 pili (fimbriae) that bind mannose on bladder uroepithelium and initiate bladder infection (P fimbriae are more relevant to pyelonephritis/bloodstream invasion); toxins, iron-acquisition systems, biofilm formation, and capsules also contribute. Disruption of the normal vaginal lactobacilli (e.g., by spermicide/nonoxynol-9, or estrogen loss after menopause) permits Gram-negative colonization and bacteriuria. Hematogenous spread accounts for under 2% of UTIs. Intracellular bacterial communities within bladder epithelium are demonstrated in models but their clinical significance in humans is unclear (p.1088).

chunks.text: Ingested spores of toxigenic C. difficile survive gastric acid, germinate in the small bowel, and colonise the lower gut once antibiotic exposure has disrupted the protective microbiota. There they elaborate two large clostridial toxins: toxin A (an enterotoxin and potent neutrophil chemoattractant) and toxin B (a cytotoxin). Both glucosylate Rho-family GTP-binding proteins that regulate the actin cytoskeleton, causing loss of cell shape, adherence and tight junctions, with epithelial barrier breakdown, fluid leakage, diarrhoea and pseudomembrane formation. Toxin B appears to be the dominant virulence factor: disease occurs with toxin A-negative but not toxin B-negative strains. A third (binary) toxin, CDT, is present in all NAP1/BI/027 epidemic isolates but its pathogenic role is undefined. Disease typically requires at least three events: antibiotic exposure establishing susceptibility, acquisition of a toxigenic strain, and an inadequate host (anamnestic antibody) immune response. Notably, patients colonised by (often nontoxigenic) strains who have not previously had CDI actually have a DECREASED, not increased, risk of subsequent CDI (Harrison 22e p.1082-1084).

Dengue is caused by the four flavivirus (orthoflavivirus) serotypes DENV-1 to DENV-4, transmitted mainly by Aedes aegypti (and the secondary vector Aedes albopictus), which bite during the day. After infection of one serotype, the cross-protection against a different (heterotypic) serotype is only transient and wanes within weeks to a few weeks of convalescence; subsequent heterotypic infection can produce classic dengue or, less often, severe dengue. The progression to severe disease centers on immune-mediated enhancement, in which enhancing, non-neutralizing antibodies are implicated, whereas neutralizing antibodies are associated with lower viremia on reinfection. The hallmark of severe dengue is a vascular-leak syndrome producing increased capillary permeability, intravascular volume depletion, hypoalbuminemia, and serosal (pleural, ascitic) effusions; recent evidence assigns the DENV NS1 protein a key role in this vascular leak. Host/viral risk modifiers include age (susceptibility to severe dengue drops markedly after 12 years), the specific sequence and timing of serotype infections (e.g., DENV-1 then DENV-2 tends to be more severe), and viral-variant heterogeneity (p.1711, 1721).

Symptomatic dengue evolves through three phases: febrile, critical (plasma leakage), and recovery; most patients never enter the critical phase, but the possibility must be actively considered in every case (p.1714).

The critical/plasma-leakage phase characteristically begins around the time fever subsides (defervescence, roughly days 3-5), so worsening at this transition - not at peak fever - signals deterioration (p.1721).
A 'saddle-back' fever pattern (recurrence of fever after defervescence and a brief remission) can occur in a subset of patients (p.1714).
Most primary DENV infections are subclinical, and only about 25% of the ~400 million annual infections cause clinical illness (p.1711).
Incubation is approximately 4-7 days (p.1714).
A positive tourniquet test (>=10 new petechiae per square inch on the upper arm after BP-cuff inflation for 5 min) reflects microvascular damage and is more often linked to severe dengue (p.1714).
Near defervescence a maculopapular rash typically starts on the trunk and spreads to the extremities and face; a separate transient macular rash may appear at illness onset (p.1714).
During recovery a patchy erythematous pruritic rash that desquamates may develop as extravascular fluid and effusions are reabsorbed (p.1722).
Early IgG appearing about 4 days after onset and rising rapidly suggests a secondary (rather than primary) infection, where IgG otherwise appears later and at much lower titers (p.1721).
Anchoring on the febrile phase and missing the critical phase, which paradoxically begins as fever declines rather than at its peak (p.1721).
Serologic cross-reactivity with antigenically similar orthoflaviviruses (yellow fever, Zika, Japanese encephalitis virus) - including after vaccination - can confound serologic diagnosis (p.1721).
Relying on antigen/nucleic-acid tests outside their acute-phase window: after about day 5 diagnosis must shift to serology (p.1721).
Failing to distinguish secondary from primary infection: early, rapidly rising IgG points to secondary infection and higher severe-disease risk (p.1721).

Most patients with uncomplicated dengue recover from the acute illness within 7-10 days, though convalescence may be prolonged and post-acute fatigue and depression are recognized sequelae. Among the millions of annual DENV infections, about 500,000 progress to severe dengue, with an overall case-fatality rate near 2.5%; with early recognition and good supportive care most patients with severe dengue respond well, and CFR at experienced tropical centers can be as low as ~1% (p.1714, 1721-1722).
Onset of restlessness or lethargy together with thrombocytopenia (<100,000/uL) and hemoconcentration 2-5 days into illness, typically at defervescence (p.1721)
Signs of plasma leakage: rising hematocrit/hemoconcentration, hypoalbuminemia, and serosal effusions (pleural effusion, ascites) (p.1721)
Circulatory compromise with narrowed pulse pressure, hepatomegaly, and cyanosis progressing to shock (p.1721)
Severe or spontaneous bleeding in the absence of a predisposing lesion (p.1721)
Severe organ dysfunction: altered mental status or seizures (CNS), arrhythmias (cardiac), acute kidney injury (renal), hepatic injury (p.1721)
Respiratory distress from plasma leakage (p.1721)

Harrison endorses the WHO pragmatic categories that replaced the older 'dengue fever / dengue hemorrhagic fever / dengue shock syndrome' terminology: dengue without warning signs, dengue with warning signs (which directs inpatient management), and severe dengue. Severe dengue is defined as confirmed or presumptive dengue plus at least one of: (1) plasma leakage severe enough to cause shock or respiratory distress, (2) severe bleeding, or (3) severe organ dysfunction. Every patient with presumptive dengue of any severity should be assessed up front for warning signs and for the criteria of severe dengue, with the provisional diagnosis of severe dengue made clinically (p.1704, 1721).
NS1 antigen (early, days 1-5 of fever) — Detects dengue viral antigen early in illness before antibody response develops.
Dengue IgM/IgG serology (later in illness) — Confirms diagnosis when NS1 is negative or testing occurs later in the course; IgG pattern can also suggest primary vs. secondary infection.
CBC with platelet count (serial) — Tracks thrombocytopenia and hematocrit trends, central to monitoring for plasma leakage and bleeding risk.
Hematocrit (serial) — A rising hematocrit with falling platelets signals plasma leakage and impending severe dengue — the single most important trend to follow.
Liver function tests — Transaminitis is common in dengue and severe elevation can indicate more severe disease.
Dengue Fever (infective) — Tropical Fever
veryLikely: Dengue virus (DENV-1 to DENV-4)
Left-sided native-valve or prosthetic-valve endocarditis (may coexist with or be mistaken for CIED-IE) (Harrison 22e p.1078, p.1084)
Bloodstream infection from an extracardiac focus (e.g., gram-negative, streptococcal, or enterococcal bacteremia) not arising from the device (Harrison 22e p.1084)
Remote-site metastatic infection complicating bacteremic CIED infection, such as vertebral osteomyelitis (Harrison 22e p.1084)
Non-device bloodstream infection from a separate source presenting with fever and sepsis in a CIED patient (Harrison 22e p.1084)

Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE): detects vegetations in >90% of patients with definite IE; an initial study may be falsely negative in a minority, so a negative TEE when IE is likely should be repeated in 7-10 days rather than used to exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1083).

Three or more separate blood culture sets (two-bottle, ~10 mL per bottle) from different venipuncture sites; if negative at 48-72 h, obtain additional sets and consult the lab for optimal techniques (Harrison 22e p.1082-1083).
FDG-PET/CT: less sensitive than TEE for intracardiac pathology in CIED-IE but useful for assessing CIED pocket and lead infection and extracardiac/remote complications (Harrison 22e p.1083).
Aspiration of any pyogenic collection at the device/pocket site, combined with blood cultures, to establish the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1201).
Echocardiographic assessment is specifically indicated in monomicrobial S. aureus bacteremia when an intracardiac device is present (Harrison 22e p.1084).

Cardiac implantable electronic devices (pacemakers, implantable defibrillators, cardiac resynchronization devices) and other prosthetic intravascular hardware provide an avascular foreign surface that organisms colonize and on which they persist. Infection localizes to the generator pocket and/or the intravascular leads, and may extend to the endothelium at points of lead contact, producing endocarditis (CIED-IE). Staphylococci dominate because skin flora is the principal portal; S. aureus and coagulase-negative staphylococci cause the majority of CIED-IE cases. Once organisms establish on the foreign material, antimicrobial therapy alone usually fails to eradicate them, because the retained device continues to act as a nidus for persistent or recurrent infection (Harrison 22e p.1078, p.1201).

CIED-related endocarditis (CIED-IE) involves either the device hardware itself or the endothelium at points of device contact, and occasionally coexists with concurrent valvular infection (Harrison 22e p.1078).

The timing of CIED-IE is split roughly into thirds: about one-third present within 3 months of implantation or manipulation, one-third between 3 and 12 months, and one-third more than a year afterward (Harrison 22e p.1078).

CIED infection can be obvious from a generator pocket infection (especially within 6 months of device manipulation) or cryptic, arising through bacteremic seeding without any visible pocket involvement (Harrison 22e p.1082).
Risk of device-associated endocarditis is reported as higher on implanted defibrillators and resynchronization devices than on permanent pacemakers (Harrison 22e p.1078).

In a patient with a CIED, an unexplained Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia (and persistent coagulase-negative staphylococcal bacteremia) without another source is likely to indicate CIED-IE or valvular IE and should be investigated and managed as such (Harrison 22e p.1084).

Relapse of bloodstream infection after a course of antimicrobial therapy in a CIED patient increases the likelihood that the device is the source and warrants treatment as CIED-IE (Harrison 22e p.1084).

S. aureus device-related infections tend to be acute with both local and systemic manifestations and to progress more rapidly than the indolent course seen in non-S. aureus staphylococcal infections; a pyogenic collection at the device site is relatively common (Harrison 22e p.1200-1201).
Treating an infected CIED with antibiotics alone (salvage/suppression) usually fails and should not be the default approach (Harrison 22e p.1084).
Using a negative TEE to rule out CIED-IE when clinical suspicion is high, rather than repeating the study in 7-10 days (Harrison 22e p.1083).
In critically ill patients already on antibiotics for other indications, blood cultures may be negative and device-related endocarditis missed (Harrison 22e p.1200-1201).

Assuming every bloodstream infection in a CIED patient indicates the device: gram-negative, streptococcal, or enterococcal bacteremia from an extracardiac focus may not be device-related, though relapse afterward raises suspicion for CIED-IE (Harrison 22e p.1084).

Removal of the infected CIED during the initial hospitalization is associated with increased 30-day and 1-year survival compared with antibiotic therapy and device retention. Attempted salvage of an infected device with antibiotics alone plus long-term suppressive therapy is usually unsuccessful and is reserved only for patients whose devices cannot be removed or who decline removal; left in place, the device remains a nidus for persistent or recurrent infection (Harrison 22e p.1084, p.1085, p.1201).
S. aureus bacteremia in a patient with a CIED with no alternative source (Harrison 22e p.1084)
Persistent or relapsing bacteremia after antimicrobial therapy in a device patient (Harrison 22e p.1084)
Generator pocket inflammation/pyogenic collection at the device site (Harrison 22e p.1082, p.1201)
Lead vegetation >2 cm, which carries a risk of pulmonary embolism (Harrison 22e p.1085)

Harrison distinguishes generator pocket infection without bacteremia (more localized) from bacteremic CIED infection and CIED-IE (more severe, with risk of coincident left-sided valve infection or remote metastatic foci); complete hardware removal is required across the spectrum of established CIED-IE and pocket or intracardiac lead infection (Harrison 22e p.1084, p.1085).

Blood cultures (peripheral and through each catheter lumen if not removed) — Differential time-to-positivity (catheter culture positive significantly earlier than peripheral) supports a catheter-related source.
Catheter tip culture (if removed) — Confirms the device as the source when growth matches blood culture results.
Echocardiography (if S. aureus bacteremia, prosthetic valve, or persistent bacteremia) — Screens for endocarditis, a serious complication of device-related bacteremia, particularly with S. aureus.
Repeat blood cultures after line removal/initiation of therapy — Confirms clearance of bacteremia, especially important for S. aureus where persistent positivity changes management significantly.

veryLikely: Coagulase-negative staphylococci, Staphylococcus aureus; likely: Enterococcus species, Candida species (especially with prolonged central line dwell time, TPN); possible: Gram-negative bacilli (less common but seen, especially with femoral lines or GI source)
[guideline] empiric → Vancomycin Empiric coverage for staphylococci including MRSA, the dominant pathogens in device-related infection, pending blood culture and device culture results.
[guideline] alternative → Daptomycin (if vancomycin intolerance or treatment failure)
Charcot neuroarthropathy (neuropathic joint disease) — can mimic or coexist with foot osteomyelitis (p.1111, 3272)
Purely neuropathic ulcer without infection (p.3272)
Cellulitis without underlying ulceration (p.3272)
Probe-to-bone test with a blunt sterile instrument as a bedside clinical assessment (p.92, 1112, 3272)
Bone biopsy with culture (preferred basis for diagnosing/treating osteomyelitis given poor swab-to-bone correlation) (p.1112)
Cultures taken from the debrided ulcer base, purulent drainage, or wound aspiration rather than superficial swabs (p.3272)
MRI when pretest probability is lower or imaging needed (sensitivity 80-100%, specificity 80-90%) (p.1112)
Nuclear medicine studies (PET, CT/SPECT) or labeled white-cell scans as alternatives to MRI (p.3272)
Ankle-brachial index screening for peripheral arterial disease in diabetics >50 years with risk factors (p.3272)
Charcot (neuropathic) arthropathy with bony deformity, which can radiographically and clinically resemble osteomyelitis (p.1111, 3272)
Callus or pressure changes from abnormal foot biomechanics (p.3271)

Diabetic foot infection arises from the interaction of peripheral sensory, motor, and autonomic neuropathy with abnormal foot biomechanics, peripheral arterial disease, and impaired wound healing. Sensory neuropathy removes protective pain sensation, allowing unrecognized repetitive or major trauma; impaired proprioception causes abnormal weight-bearing and callus/ulcer formation. Motor and sensory neuropathy produce structural deformities (hammer/claw toe, prominent metatarsal heads, Charcot joint). Autonomic neuropathy causes anhidrosis with dry, fissured skin. Peripheral arterial disease and poor healing then allow minor skin breaks to enlarge and become infected. Foot osteomyelitis is almost always acquired by the exogenous (contiguous) route, progressing from skin/soft-tissue infection into bone, and can also follow deep wound infection after foot surgery (p.1111, 3271).

A wound that probes to bone (rock-hard, gritty base without intervening soft tissue) strongly predicts underlying osteomyelitis; the probe-to-bone test has a positive predictive value of ~90% in high-pretest-probability populations (p.1112).

In a hospitalized diabetic patient with a chronic deep foot ulcer, the pretest probability of osteomyelitis is high (~65%), so a positive probe-to-bone test can often establish the diagnosis clinically without imaging (p.91, 1112).
A negative probe-to-bone test lowers the likelihood of osteomyelitis (likelihood ratio ~0.2) (p.92).

An infected ulcer is a clinical diagnosis; superficial swab cultures recover multiple organisms of uncertain significance and correlate poorly with bone biopsy (only ~24% concordance in one study) (p.1111-1112, 3271-3272).
Culture-pathogen concordance between deep samples and bone is best for S. aureus (40-50%) and poorest for coagulase-negative staphylococci, anaerobes, and gram-negative bacilli (p.1112).
About 34% of people with diabetes develop a foot ulcer in their lifetime; among those with an ulcer, ~5% per year progress to foot osteomyelitis (p.1111).
Gas gangrene-like findings may occur in a diabetic foot wound even in the absence of clostridial infection (p.3272).
Do NOT rely on superficial swab cultures to guide therapy — they grow contaminants/colonizers and correlate poorly with bone culture (p.1112, 3272).
Plain x-rays have limited sensitivity (30-90%) for diabetic foot osteomyelitis and are mainly useful for follow-up of confirmed cases, not for early diagnosis (p.1112).
A negative probe-to-bone test does not fully exclude osteomyelitis, especially when pretest probability is low — pursue MRI (p.1112).
Antiseptic agents should be avoided and topical antibiotics are of limited value in wound care (p.3272).

Diabetes is the leading cause of nontraumatic lower-extremity amputation. Diabetic foot osteomyelitis increases amputation risk; a foot ulcer (or subsequent ulceration) carries a 14-24% risk of eventual amputation. Adequate management of early-stage infection lowers the amputation rate, and wound debridement combined with antibiotics makes amputation unnecessary in roughly two-thirds of patients (p.1111-1112, 3271).
Wound that probes to bone (high likelihood of osteomyelitis) (p.1112, 3272)
Chronic ulcer failing to respond to therapy (prompt plain radiographs to assess for osteomyelitis) (p.3272)
Underlying peripheral arterial insufficiency / ischemic limb (contributes to non-healing and amputation risk) (p.3272)
Charcot foot deformity complicated by chronic osteomyelitis (p.1111)

Harrison references the IWGDF/IDSA 2023 guidelines for diagnosis and treatment of diabetes-related foot infections but does not reproduce the detailed IDSA/IWGDF grading scale in this text. Infections are described broadly as mild/non-limb-threatening versus more severe (p.1112, 3272).
Deep tissue/bone culture (avoid superficial swab alone) — Superficial swabs poorly correlate with the true infecting organism; deep culture better guides targeted therapy.
Plain X-ray of the foot — Screens for osteomyelitis and gas in soft tissue.
MRI (if osteomyelitis suspected and X-ray inconclusive) — More sensitive for early osteomyelitis than plain films.
HbA1c and glycemic control assessment — Poor glycemic control impairs healing and infection clearance; relevant to overall management.
Vascular assessment (ABI/Doppler) — Peripheral arterial disease impairs healing and antibiotic delivery to tissue — relevant to overall treatment plan and need for revascularization.

veryLikely: Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus species; likely: Enterobacteriaceae (E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus) — especially in chronic or previously treated wounds; possible: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (if wound exposed to water/soaking), Anaerobes (if deep, necrotic, or malodorous wound)

[guideline] empiric → Mild infection: Cephalexin or Amoxicillin-clavulanate / Moderate-severe: Piperacillin-tazobactam Mild infections without deep tissue involvement can be treated with narrow-spectrum oral agents targeting staphylococci and streptococci.
[guideline] alternative → Clindamycin + Ciprofloxacin (penicillin allergy)
[guideline] alternative → Vancomycin (if MRSA risk) added to above regimens
Disseminated fungal infection (a differential when miliary or interstitial pulmonary infiltrates and multi-organ involvement are present) (Harrison 22e p.1390)
Dilated fundoscopic eye examination for choroidal tubercles (pathognomonic, up to ~30% of cases) (Harrison 22e p.1390)
Bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial biopsy for improved bacteriologic confirmation (Harrison 22e p.1390)

Full blood count for hematologic clues (anemia with leukopenia, lymphopenia, neutrophilic leukocytosis/leukemoid reactions, polycythemia; pancytopenia in nonreactive form; DIC reported) (Harrison 22e p.1390)
Liver function tests including alkaline phosphatase (elevated with hepatic involvement) (Harrison 22e p.1390)
Tuberculin skin test (may be falsely negative in up to half of cases) (Harrison 22e p.1390)
Xpert MTB/RIF as the initial test when TB meningitis is suspected; positive results prompt immediate treatment (Harrison 22e p.1393)

Miliary/disseminated TB results from hematogenous spread of M. tuberculosis when an acquired immune response fails to contain infection. Bacilli carried to regional lymph nodes reach the central venous return and the systemic circulation, seeding multiple organs with innumerable small (1-2 mm) yellowish granulomas resembling millet seeds. Occult hematogenous dissemination commonly follows primary infection; in the very young and the immunocompromised (including people living with HIV), insufficient immunity allows progression to fatal miliary disease or tuberculous meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1386, 1390).

Presentation is notoriously nonspecific and protean, varying with the organs predominantly seeded; constitutional features (fever, night sweats, anorexia, weakness, weight loss) dominate in most patients (Harrison 22e p.1390).

Choroidal tubercles on fundoscopic eye examination are pathognomonic of miliary TB and are present in up to roughly 30% of cases, so dilated fundoscopy is a high-yield bedside step (Harrison 22e p.1390).
A high index of suspicion is essential; the diagnosis is easily missed and untreated miliary TB is lethal, whereas early treatment is curative (Harrison 22e p.1390).
Sputum-smear microscopy is negative in most cases, so a negative smear does not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1390).
The tuberculin skin test may be negative in up to half of patients, with reactivity sometimes returning during chemotherapy; a negative TST therefore cannot rule out disease (Harrison 22e p.1390).
In adults miliary TB may arise from either recent infection or reactivation of old disseminated foci, whereas in children it more often follows primary infection (Harrison 22e p.1390).
Granulomas are often found on liver or bone-marrow biopsy, and bronchoalveolar lavage with transbronchial biopsy improves bacteriologic confirmation (Harrison 22e p.1390).
Relying on sputum-smear microscopy or the tuberculin skin test to exclude the diagnosis, since both are frequently negative in miliary TB (Harrison 22e p.1390).

Expecting a typical chest radiograph: early in the course, and especially among people living with HIV, the CXR may show no abnormality; findings may instead be large or interstitial infiltrates or pleural effusion rather than the classic miliary reticulonodular pattern (Harrison 22e p.1390).
Overlooking cryptic miliary TB in elderly patients with only mild intermittent fever and anemia (Harrison 22e p.1390).

Unrecognized miliary TB is lethal, but with proper early treatment it is amenable to cure. Cryptic miliary TB (seen in the elderly) runs a chronic course with mild intermittent fever and anemia, ultimately progressing to meningeal involvement before death. The nonreactive (acute septicemic) form is rapidly fatal with multiple necrotic, nongranulomatous lesions at postmortem. Glucocorticoid therapy has not proved beneficial in miliary TB (Harrison 22e p.1390).
Meningismus, present in fewer than 10% of cases, signals possible concurrent tuberculous meningitis and warrants urgent CNS evaluation (Harrison 22e p.1390).
Pancytopenia with an acute septicemic course suggests nonreactive miliary TB, a rare and rapidly fatal form from massive dissemination (Harrison 22e p.1390).
Disseminated intravascular coagulation has been reported and indicates severe disease (Harrison 22e p.1390).
Chest X-ray / CT chest — Classic miliary pattern (diffuse small nodules) supports the diagnosis, though it may be subtle or absent early.

Blood culture for mycobacteria (if available) and AFB smear of any accessible fluid/tissue — May provide microbiological confirmation; mycobacterial blood culture has reasonable yield in disseminated disease, particularly in HIV co-infection.

Liver or bone marrow biopsy (if hepatosplenomegaly/cytopenias and other tests inconclusive) — Can provide histological confirmation (caseating granulomas, AFB on staining) when other less invasive tests are unrevealing.
HIV testing — Essential given the strong association between disseminated TB and immunosuppression, with direct treatment implications.
Lumbar puncture (if any neurological signs) — Screens for concurrent CNS involvement, which would extend treatment duration.
Disseminated (Miliary) Tuberculosis (infective) — Systemic / Tuberculosis
veryLikely: Mycobacterium tuberculosis

[guideline] empiric → Isoniazid + Rifampicin + Pyrazinamide + Ethambutol (HRZE) Standard four-drug regimen; duration should be extended if disseminated disease is found to involve the CNS or skeletal system on further workup, which would change the continuation phase length.

[guideline] alternative → Drug-resistant TB regimens — see the Tuberculosis treatment pathway workspace For rifampicin-resistant / MDR / pre-XDR / XDR TB, the specific regimen is selected by drug-susceptibility testing and eligibility — see the structured, NTEP-sourced regimen cards (with eligibility, dosing, monitoring and safety gates) rather than a generic 'modified regimen'.

DRESS is a severe, delayed T-cell-mediated drug hypersensitivity reaction, thought to arise from impaired drug detoxification pathways or specific HLA associations that lead to a robust immune response against drug-modified proteins. The resulting systemic activation of eosinophils and lymphocytes drives multi-organ inflammation. Reactivation of latent herpesviruses, particularly HHV-6, is commonly observed and may amplify and prolong the immune response, contributing to the characteristic waxing-waning course.
Onset is classically delayed, typically 2-8 weeks after starting the culprit drug, distinguishing it from more immediate hypersensitivity reactions.
Look for the triad of fever, widespread morbilliform (often confluent and edematous) rash, and facial edema, especially periorbital swelling.
Systemic involvement is the hallmark: lymphadenopathy plus at least one internal organ (liver most common, also kidney, lung, heart) helps separate DRESS from simple drug rash.
Peripheral eosinophilia and/or atypical lymphocytosis on blood smear strongly support the diagnosis but may lag behind skin findings.
Common culprits include aromatic anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides, and certain antibiotics — always take a careful medication history covering the prior 2 months.
Symptoms can worsen for days to weeks even after the offending drug is stopped, and relapses/flares are common during the recovery phase.
Human herpesvirus-6 reactivation is frequently detected during the illness and may contribute to prolonged or relapsing disease course.
Cross-reactivity exists among structurally related anticonvulsants, so the entire drug class should generally be avoided going forward.
Attributing the rash only to the most recently started drug while missing a culprit introduced weeks earlier due to the characteristic delayed onset.
Discontinuing suspected culprit and expecting immediate improvement — worsening despite drug withdrawal is common and should not prompt reinstatement.
Underestimating disease severity because eosinophilia or organ involvement may be absent or delayed at initial presentation.
Failing to screen for and monitor internal organ involvement once the skin findings are recognized, since mortality is driven by visceral disease, not the rash itself.

DRESS carries a mortality risk of roughly 5-10%, primarily related to fulminant hepatic, cardiac, or pulmonary involvement. Even after recovery, patients can develop delayed autoimmune sequelae such as thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes, or other autoimmune conditions over the following months to years, warranting longitudinal follow-up.
Evidence of fulminant hepatitis or rising transaminases suggesting hepatic failure
Signs of myocarditis (chest pain, arrhythmia, heart failure) or interstitial pneumonitis
Acute kidney injury with rising creatinine
Rapidly progressive skin involvement raising concern for overlap with SJS/TEN
Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis-like features (cytopenias, hyperferritinemia, hepatosplenomegaly)

chunks.text: Inflammatory bowel disease - a first flare of ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease can be clinically indistinguishable from invasive bacterial dysentery, particularly in industrialised settings; travel history and stool studies help discriminate, and IBD should not be diagnosed until invasive infection (e.g. Campylobacter, amoebiasis) is excluded (p.1366, p.1306)

chunks.text: Dysentery results from injury to the colonic (and distal small-bowel) mucosa by two overlapping mechanisms. (1) Bacterial invasion: Shigella and enteroinvasive E. coli invade mucosal epithelial cells, multiply intracellularly and spread cell-to-cell, producing acute colitis mainly of the distal colon and rectum with edematous, hemorrhagic, ulcerated mucosa. (2) Cytotoxin production: organisms such as Shigella dysenteriae type 1, Shiga toxin-producing/enterohaemorrhagic E. coli and Vibrio parahaemolyticus elaborate cytotoxins that destroy mucosal cells; Shiga toxins inhibit the 60S ribosomal subunit, shut off protein synthesis, and after systemic translocation injure renal and cerebral microvascular endothelium. The resulting mucosal destruction yields small-volume bloody, mucopurulent stools containing inflammatory cells. Salmonella invades the bowel mucosa and causes inflammatory diarrhoea but generally does not destroy enterocytes or produce the full dysentery syndrome. Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites adhere via the Gal/GalNAc lectin, degrade mucus and extracellular matrix with proteases, and kill epithelial and inflammatory cells by contact-dependent (apoptosis, trogocytosis, pore-forming peptides) and contact-independent cytotoxicity, producing characteristic flask-shaped colonic ulcers and bloody diarrhoea, and can invade the portal venous system to seed the liver (p.306, p.1076-1077, p.1366, p.1754-1755).

chunks.text: Dysentery is bloody diarrhoea arising from mucosal invasion or cytotoxin injury to the colon, not from secretory/enterotoxin mechanisms; the triad of high fever, abdominal pain and grossly bloody stool points to invasive disease rather than toxin-mediated watery diarrhoea (p.306, p.1077).

chunks.text: An appendicitis-like presentation (right-sided pain, tenderness) should raise Yersinia enterocolitica, which invades the terminal ileum and proximal colon; Campylobacter and amoebic caecal involvement can similarly mimic appendicitis (p.306, p.1078).

chunks.text: The single most useful initial distinction is inflammatory vs noninflammatory diarrhoea: grossly bloody or mucoid stool, plus fecal leukocytes or a positive fecal lactoferrin/calprotectin, defines the inflammatory (dysenteric) category and a colonic/distal small-bowel locus (p.1079, p.1077).

chunks.text: Tenesmus (painful rectal spasm with a strong urge but little stool passage) signals proctitis and is characteristic of the distal-colonic involvement of shigellosis and amoebiasis (p.1078).

chunks.text: Bloody diarrhoea with a low-grade fever or no fever is a clinical clue to Shiga toxin-producing/enterohaemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC, e.g. O157:H7), which can be mistaken for noninfectious disease such as ischaemic or inflammatory bowel disease (p.1081, p.1288).

chunks.text: Unlike most watery diarrhoeal syndromes, dysenteric illness rarely presents with major dehydration; in shigellosis the stools are small-volume and dehydration is uncommon (p.1366).

source.page: Harrison 22e: Ch 49 (Diarrhea and Constipation) pp.348-350; Ch 138 (Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning) pp.1119-1124; Ch 166 (Diseases Caused by Gram-Negative Enteric Bacilli, E. coli pathotypes) pp.1331-1332; Ch 167/168 (Campylobacter) pp.1306,1348-1349; Ch 172 (Shigellosis) pp.1366-1368; Ch 230 (Amebiasis) pp.1753-1757

chunks.text: Shigellosis classically evolves through four phases: incubation (usually 1-4 days), initial watery diarrhoea, then dysentery with frequent small bloody mucopurulent stools, tenesmus and cramps, followed by a postinfectious phase (p.1366).

chunks.text: On stool microscopy, abundant PMNs in every field favour bacterial enteroinvasive disease (especially Shigella), whereas erythrophagocytic trophozoites with few PMNs favour Entamoeba histolytica (p.1366).

chunks.text: Fewer than ~40% of patients with amoebic dysentery are febrile, in contrast to bacterial dysentery; nearly all have heme-positive stools, and amoebic colitis typically has a more gradual onset over 2-6 weeks (p.1754).

chunks.text: EHEC/STEC stools are commonly grossly bloody with abdominal pain and fecal leukocytes in ~70% of cases, yet fever is characteristically absent (p.1288).

source.page: Harrison 22e: Ch 49 (Diarrhea and Constipation) pp.348-350; Ch 138 (Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning) pp.1119-1124; Ch 166 (Diseases Caused by Gram-Negative Enteric Bacilli, E. coli pathotypes) pp.1331-1332; Ch 167/168 (Campylobacter) pp.1306,1348-1349; Ch 172 (Shigellosis) pp.1366-1368; Ch 230 (Amebiasis) pp.1753-1757

chunks.text: Do NOT give antibiotics for suspected enterohaemorrhagic/Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (grossly bloody diarrhoea, often afebrile) - antibiotics induce Shiga toxin-producing phage replication, can increase toxin production roughly 20-fold, and raise the risk of HUS; this caution applies especially to children (p.1081, p.1289).

source.page: Harrison 22e: Ch 49 (Diarrhea and Constipation) pp.348-350; Ch 138 (Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning) pp.1119-1124; Ch 166 (Diseases Caused by Gram-Negative Enteric Bacilli, E. coli pathotypes) pp.1331-1332; Ch 167/168 (Campylobacter) pp.1306,1348-1349; Ch 172 (Shigellosis) pp.1366-1368; Ch 230 (Amebiasis) pp.1753-1757

chunks.text: Avoid antimotility/antiperistaltic agents (e.g. loperamide, diphenoxylate-atropine) in febrile or bloody dysentery - they may prolong fever and shedding in Shigella, increase the risk of toxic megacolon, and have been implicated in HUS in EHEC-infected children (p.349, p.1077, p.1367).

source.page: Harrison 22e: Ch 49 (Diarrhea and Constipation) pp.348-350; Ch 138 (Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning) pp.1119-1124; Ch 166 (Diseases Caused by Gram-Negative Enteric Bacilli, E. coli pathotypes) pp.1331-1332; Ch 167/168 (Campylobacter) pp.1306,1348-1349; Ch 172 (Shigellosis) pp.1366-1368; Ch 230 (Amebiasis) pp.1753-1757

chunks.text: Do not diagnose inflammatory bowel disease before excluding invasive infection - Campylobacter and amoebic colitis can closely mimic and even be histologically confused with ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease (p.1306, p.1755).

source.page: Harrison 22e: Ch 49 (Diarrhea and Constipation) pp.348-350; Ch 138 (Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning) pp.1119-1124; Ch 166 (Diseases Caused by Gram-Negative Enteric Bacilli, E. coli pathotypes) pp.1331-1332; Ch 167/168 (Campylobacter) pp.1306,1348-1349; Ch 172 (Shigellosis) pp.1366-1368; Ch 230 (Amebiasis) pp.1753-1757

chunks.text: Exclude amoebiasis (stool studies plus serology) before giving glucocorticoids for presumed IBD - unsuspected amoebic colitis can become fulminant or develop toxic megacolon on steroids (p.1755-1756, p.1757).

chunks.text: A negative fecal leukocyte/lactoferrin test or absence of fever does NOT rule out invasive disease - STEC/EHEC frequently lacks reliable fecal leukocytes and fever, which is why both Shiga toxin testing and culture are recommended in all community-acquired diarrhoea (p.1080, p.1289).

chunks.text: Shigella is fragile and is easily lost in transport (temperature/pH changes); inoculate promptly or use a holding medium (Cary-Blair) and sample the bloody/mucopurulent stool portion or use a rectal swab to maximise yield (p.1367).

chunks.text: Microscopy cannot distinguish E. histolytica cysts from non-pathogenic E. dispar (and E. moshkovskii/E. bangladeshi); a microscopic species diagnosis of E. histolytica requires demonstrating trophozoites that have ingested erythrocytes (use antigen/molecular testing) (p.1080, p.1756).

chunks.text: Empirical antimotility therapy should be avoided more broadly with febrile dysentery; bismuth subsalicylate should be avoided in immunocompromised or renally impaired patients (bismuth encephalopathy risk) (p.349).

chunks.text: Most invasive bacterial dysentery is self-limited: shigellosis usually resolves within about a week (faster with appropriate therapy), and STEC/EHEC illness typically lasts 5-10 days. Severe outcomes and death cluster in children under 5 (especially the malnourished) and the elderly. Adverse prognostic features in clinically severe shigellosis include nonbloody diarrhoea, moderate-to-severe dehydration, bacteraemia, absence of fever, abdominal tenderness, rectal prolapse, and altered consciousness. Haemolytic-uraemic syndrome occurs in roughly 15% of infected children under 10 with STEC/EHEC; with dialysis support its mortality is under 10%, but survivors often have persisting renal and neurological dysfunction; acute renal failure complicates 55-70% of HUS cases yet renal function recovers in most. Postinfectious sequelae include reactive arthritis (after Shigella flexneri, Salmonella, Campylobacter, Yersinia) and, after Campylobacter, Guillain-Barre syndrome; postinfectious irritable bowel syndrome may follow, particularly after Campylobacter (p.306, p.1288, p.1306, p.1366).

chunks.text: Grossly bloody diarrhoea with low-grade or absent fever - suspect STEC/EHEC and the risk of haemolytic-uraemic syndrome (p.1081, p.1288)

chunks.text: Harrison frames severity primarily by the inflammatory vs noninflammatory distinction and by host/feature risk rather than a single formal dysentery score. Inflammatory (dysenteric) disease is defined by grossly bloody/mucoid stool with fecal leukocytes/lactoferrin and a colonic locus. Indications that mark an episode as severe and warranting evaluation/empirical therapy include profuse diarrhoea with dehydration, overtly bloody stools, fever >=38.5C (>=101F), duration >48 h without improvement, severe abdominal pain in patients over 50, and elderly (>=70) or immunocompromised hosts. Dehydration is graded clinically as mild (thirst, dry mouth, decreased urine output), moderate (orthostatic hypotension, skin tenting, sunken eyes/fontanelle), and severe (lethargy, obtundation, feeble pulse, hypotension, shock). For shigellosis, severe disease is signalled by features such as bacteraemia, altered consciousness/seizures, toxic megacolon, perforation, severe dehydration, and occurrence in malnourished young children or the elderly (p.306, p.1077-1078, p.1366).

chunks.text: Encephalitis is inflammation of the brain parenchyma, usually viral (or from a primary autoimmune process). Neurotropic viruses tend to injure characteristic CNS regions, producing the clinical pattern. Associated meningeal inflammation (meningoencephalitis) is common, and spinal cord or nerve-root involvement may co-occur (encephalomyelitis, encephalomyeloradiculitis). HSV has a predilection for the inferomedial frontotemporal/limbic regions, producing the characteristic temporal-lobe imaging and EEG changes and a hemorrhagic/necrotizing process; punctate microhemorrhages explain CSF red cells in some cases. Flaviviruses such as West Nile and Japanese encephalitis virus preferentially involve deep grey structures (thalamus, basal ganglia, brainstem). VZV tends to produce a CNS vasculopathy with hemorrhagic and ischemic infarction rather than a true parenchymal encephalitis. Some viral encephalitides (notably HSV, and Japanese encephalitis) can trigger a subsequent antibody-mediated autoimmune encephalitis, e.g. anti-NMDA-receptor antibodies after HSV (p.1111-1114, p.746).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.1111-1117 (Ch.142 Encephalitis); arboviral/Japanese encephalitis p.1670-1671; autoimmune/anti-NMDAR encephalitis p.746-747

chunks.text: Encephalitis differs from meningitis by the presence of altered brain function itself - altered consciousness (confusion, behavioural change, lethargy to coma) and focal or diffuse neurologic signs - whereas uncomplicated meningitis spares brain parenchymal function (p.1111).

chunks.text: Outcome varies widely by etiology and host factors. For HSV encephalitis treated with aciclovir, roughly 81% survive but only about half of survivors have no or minor sequelae; outcome is directly related to patient age and to the level of consciousness at the start of therapy - younger patients with good neurologic function do markedly better, while those comatose (GCS ~6) at treatment initiation die or survive with severe deficits. Eastern equine encephalitis carries very high sequelae rates (~80% of survivors severely impaired), whereas EBV, California (La Crosse) and Venezuelan equine encephalitis rarely cause severe sequelae. West Nile survivors frequently have prolonged cognitive impairment, weakness, tremor, myoclonus and parkinsonism, with recovery taking many months. Japanese encephalitis case-fatality in hospitalized patients is high (~20-30%) with common long-term neurologic disability; rabies is almost invariably fatal. (p.1115-1117, p.1671)

chunks.text: CSF PCR for HSV (and other relevant viruses) — Definitive test to confirm or exclude HSV encephalitis and guide duration of acyclovir.
MRI brain — Temporal lobe involvement is characteristic of HSV encephalitis and supports the diagnosis pending PCR results.
EEG — May show characteristic findings (e.g., periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges) supporting HSV encephalitis and helps detect non-convulsive seizures.
CSF routine analysis, Gram stain, culture — Evaluates for bacterial meningoencephalitis as an overlapping or alternative diagnosis.
