Buffy-coat (centrifuged blood) culture — speeds isolation because most S. Typhi reside in the mononuclear-cell/platelet fraction, though it does not raise overall sensitivity (p.1360).
Bone marrow culture — about 80% sensitive and, unlike blood culture, its yield is not reduced by up to 5 days of prior antibiotics (p.1360).

Culture of intestinal/duodenal secretions (noninvasive duodenal string test) — can be positive even when bone marrow culture is negative; combining blood, marrow and intestinal-secretion cultures gives a yield over 90% (p.1360).
Stool culture — often negative in the first week (negative in 60-70%) but may turn positive by the third week in untreated patients (p.1360).
Culture of rose-spot punch biopsies (p.1360).

Rapid immunodiagnostic serologic tests (e.g., Tubex, Typhidot detecting IgM/IgG to O and H antigens) — point-of-care, low cost, but only ~70-80% sensitive and ~80-90% specific, so insufficient to replace blood culture (p.1360).
Blood PCR for S. Typhi/S. Paratyphi — reported sensitivity ~40-100% depending on gene target (p.1360).

After ingestion (infectious dose ~200 to 10^6 CFU; lower gastric acidity or impaired intestinal integrity raises susceptibility), S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi traverse the small-bowel mucosa via M cells overlying Peyer's patches, using a type III secretion system to induce membrane ruffling and bacterium-mediated endocytosis. Crossing the epithelium, they are phagocytosed by macrophages but survive the intracellular environment by remodeling their surface (e.g., via the PhoP/PhoQ regulatory system) and by delivering effector proteins across the phagosome to remodel the Salmonella-containing vacuole for survival and replication. Carried within macrophages, the organisms disseminate via lymphatics and colonize reticuloendothelial tissue (liver, spleen, lymph nodes, bone marrow); the patient is largely asymptomatic during this incubation. Fever and abdominal pain emerge once a critical bacterial load triggers macrophage/epithelial cytokine release recognized by innate immune receptors; hepatosplenomegaly reflects mononuclear-cell recruitment and acquired cell-mediated immunity. Recruitment of mononuclear cells and lymphocytes to Peyer's patches over subsequent weeks causes marked enlargement and necrosis, the basis for later intestinal complications. Many S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi A strains also produce a toxin within host cells that is exported extracellularly and probably contributes to systemic and neuropsychiatric features. This contrasts with the mononuclear (rather than neutrophilic) bowel infiltrate that distinguishes enteric fever from nontyphoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis (p.1358-1359).
Both 'enteric fever' and 'typhoid fever' refer to the same systemic illness caused by dissemination of S. Typhi or S. Paratyphi; the names are used interchangeably (p.1358).

Chronic asymptomatic carriage (S. Typhi shed in stool or urine for over a year) develops in 2-5% and is more common in women, infants, and those with biliary disease; organisms persist by forming biofilms on gallstones (p.1360).

The classic 'hallmarks' of fever plus abdominal pain are actually variable: fever is present at presentation in over three-quarters of cases, but abdominal pain is reported in only about 30-40% (p.1358).
Prolonged fever (roughly 38.8-40.5 C) is the most prominent symptom and can persist up to about 4 weeks if untreated (p.1359).
Mean incubation for S. Typhi is about 10-14 days (range 5-21), shortened by larger ingested inoculum (p.1359).
Relative bradycardia at the peak of high fever is described in under half of patients (p.1359).

Rose spots are faint, salmon-colored, blanching maculopapular lesions on the trunk/chest, appearing in about 30% near the end of the first week and fading in 2-5 days; they are hard to see in highly pigmented skin and Salmonella can be cultured from punch biopsies of them (p.1359-1360).

Headache (~80%) and coated/furred tongue are among the most common symptoms/signs; in a Nepal series S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi A infections were clinically indistinguishable even though Paratyphi A is generally thought milder and more GI-predominant (p.1359).
Diarrhea is somewhat more common than constipation in enteric fever, contrary to older teaching (p.1359).
Up to ~10% of treated patients have a mild relapse, typically 2-3 weeks after fever resolves, with the same strain and susceptibility profile (p.1360).

No single laboratory test other than a positive culture is diagnostic; the presentation is nonspecific, so a high index of suspicion is needed in any febrile returning traveler from an endemic region (notably the Indian subcontinent, Southeast Asia, or Africa) (p.1358, p.1360).

Blood culture sensitivity is only ~40-60% and falls further with low sample volume, prior antibiotics, or sampling in the first week, because very few organisms (<15/mL) circulate — a negative blood culture does not exclude enteric fever (p.1360).
Rapid serologic/immunodiagnostic tests are not accurate enough to replace blood culture for diagnosis (p.1360).

Leukopenia/neutropenia occur in only ~15-25%; counts can instead be normal or, especially in children or with perforation/secondary infection, show leukocytosis — so the WBC count is unreliable for ruling the diagnosis in or out (p.1360).

The textbook triad is fluid: abdominal pain is present in only ~30-40% and splenomegaly/hepatosplenomegaly are documented in a minority on exam, so their absence does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1358-1359).

Fluoroquinolones should no longer be used empirically in regions with high decreased-ciprofloxacin-susceptibility prevalence (Indian subcontinent, parts of Africa); travel from Pakistan raises concern for XDR/ceftriaxone-resistant strains (p.1361).

Overall case-fatality is about 2.5%, rising to ~4.5% in hospitalized patients and to 10-30% in untreated disease; prompt appropriate antibiotics prevent severe complications and cut mortality to under 1%. Complications occur in roughly 27% of hospitalized patients and correlate with longer symptom duration before admission, host factors, strain virulence/inoculum, and antibiotic choice. Chronic S. Typhi carriage carries an increased long-term risk of gallbladder cancer, especially in endemic regions like the Indian subcontinent (p.1360-1361).
Gastrointestinal hemorrhage (~6%) — most often in the third and fourth weeks; life-threatening, needs fluid resuscitation and possible surgery (p.1360).
Intestinal (ileal) perforation (~1%) — from necrosis/ulceration of ileocecal Peyer's patches, typically weeks 3-4; requires urgent surgery and broadened cover for polymicrobial peritonitis (p.1360).
Neuropsychiatric deterioration ('muttering delirium' or 'coma vigil', picking at bedclothes/imaginary objects) (p.1360).
Neurologic complications — meningitis, Guillain-Barre syndrome, neuritis (p.1360).
Shock and obtundation, marking critically ill / severe typhoid (p.1361).
Disseminated intravascular coagulation, hemophagocytic syndrome, myocarditis/pericarditis/endocarditis, severe pneumonia, or hemolytic-uremic syndrome as uncommon severe complications (p.1360).

Harrison does not give a formal grading scale; it distinguishes uncomplicated enteric fever (manageable at home with oral therapy) from disease warranting hospitalization (persistent vomiting, diarrhea, or abdominal distension) and from critically ill / severe typhoid characterized by shock and obtundation, plus complicated disease with GI hemorrhage, intestinal perforation, or other end-organ involvement (p.1360-1361).

Eosinophilic oesophagitis is a chronic, immune/antigen-mediated condition in which food and aeroallergens drive a Th2-skewed inflammatory response leading to dense eosinophilic infiltration of the esophageal mucosa. Persistent inflammation promotes epithelial barrier dysfunction and, over time, subepithelial fibrosis and smooth muscle remodeling, producing the strictures, rings, and narrow-caliber esophagus seen in longstanding disease. It is closely linked to atopic disease and shares overlapping pathways with asthma, allergic rhinitis, and atopic dermatitis.
Consider EoE in young adults (often male) presenting with recurrent solid-food dysphagia or food bolus impaction, especially with a personal or family history of atopy, asthma, or allergic rhinitis.
In children, presentation is often less specific — feeding difficulty, vomiting, abdominal pain, or failure to thrive rather than classic dysphagia.

Endoscopy may show characteristic esophageal rings ('trachealization'), linear furrows, whitish exudates/plaques, and mucosal fragility ('crepe-paper' esophagus), but can appear normal in a subset of patients.
Diagnosis requires both compatible clinical symptoms and esophageal biopsies showing eosinophil-predominant inflammation, after excluding other causes of esophageal eosinophilia.

Proton pump inhibitor-responsive esophageal eosinophilia exists on the same clinical spectrum and no longer excludes an EoE diagnosis; PPIs are considered a treatment option rather than purely a diagnostic exclusion test.
Take multiple biopsies (typically several from proximal and distal esophagus) since eosinophilic infiltration can be patchy.
Dietary elimination approaches (empiric or allergy-testing-directed) and topical swallowed corticosteroids are mainstay therapies alongside consideration of PPIs.
Esophageal dilation may be needed for fibrostenotic disease but carries a higher perforation risk than in other esophageal strictures due to mucosal fragility.
Assuming a normal-appearing esophagus on endoscopy excludes EoE — mucosal appearance can be unremarkable despite significant histologic eosinophilia.
Relying on a single biopsy site, missing patchy involvement and underestimating eosinophil counts.
Treating all esophageal eosinophilia as pure GERD without considering the overlapping PPI-responsive EoE spectrum.
Performing aggressive dilation without recognizing the higher perforation risk from mucosal fragility and lack of prior gentle approach.

EoE is a chronic, relapsing condition requiring long-term management; without maintenance therapy, symptoms and inflammation typically recur. Untreated or undertreated disease can progress to fibrostenotic remodeling with strictures and recurrent food impactions, but sustained dietary or pharmacologic control can maintain remission and reduce complications.
Acute food bolus impaction causing complete dysphagia — requires urgent endoscopic evaluation and possible removal
Suspected esophageal perforation, especially after dilation given increased mucosal fragility
Progressive weight loss or failure to thrive in pediatric patients
Signs of a tight fibrostenotic stricture on imaging/endoscopy before attempting dilation
Unexplained esophageal eosinophilia not responding to standard measures — reconsider alternative diagnoses (hypereosinophilic syndrome, Crohn disease)

Cellulitis (deeper dermal/subcutaneous involvement, with less sharply demarcated borders) (Harrison 22e p.1210)

Staphylococcus aureus cellulitis, which can produce a similar appearance, especially when the lesion is atypical, less intensely red, fades into surrounding skin, or arises around a wound or ulcer (Harrison 22e p.1210-1211)

Streptococcus pyogenes infecting the epidermis is translocated laterally to deeper structures via lymphatics, producing the characteristic rapid superficial spread of erysipelas. Subsequent engorgement or obstruction of lymphatics causes flaccid edema of the epidermis. The infection is confined to the superficial dermis and superficial lymphatics (in contrast to cellulitis, which involves deeper subcutaneous tissue), and extension to deeper soft tissues is rare (Harrison 22e p.1051-1052, p.1210).
Abrupt onset of fiery-red swelling of the face or extremities, with well-defined indurated margins (notably along the nasolabial fold), rapid progression, and intense pain (Harrison 22e p.1052).

The sharply demarcated, raised border distinguishes erysipelas from cellulitis and reflects involvement limited to the superficial (upper) dermis and superficial lymphatics rather than the deeper subcutaneous tissue (Harrison 22e p.1051, p.1210).
A peau d'orange (orange-peel) texture of the skin is characteristic and is thought to reflect involvement of superficial lymphatics (Harrison 22e p.1210).
Lesion typically develops over a few hours and is accompanied by fever and chills; flaccid superficial blebs/bullae may appear on the second or third day (Harrison 22e p.1052, p.1210).
Classic distribution is the malar area of the face (often extending over the bridge of the nose to the contralateral malar region) or the lower extremities (Harrison 22e p.1210).
Infants and elderly adults are most commonly affected, and the severity of systemic toxicity varies (Harrison 22e p.1052).
Desquamation of the involved skin occurs roughly 5-10 days into the illness (Harrison 22e p.1052).
Classic cases with typical features are almost always due to beta-hemolytic streptococci, usually group A and occasionally group C or G (Harrison 22e p.1210).

Atypical erysipelas may involve an unusual anatomic site, appear less intensely red, fade into surrounding skin, or cause only mild systemic illness, in which case a specific clinical diagnosis cannot reliably be made and broader empirical coverage (including S. aureus) is prudent (Harrison 22e p.1210-1211).
Extension to deeper soft tissues is rare in true erysipelas; if present, reconsider the diagnosis and exclude a deeper or necrotizing infection (Harrison 22e p.1052).

In most parts of the world, acute rheumatic fever is NOT a sequela of streptococcal skin infection (unlike pharyngitis), though post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis may follow either skin or throat infection (Harrison 22e p.1210).

Generally responds well to therapy; with appropriate treatment, fever, pain, and the intense red color diminish, although swelling may continue to progress initially. Recurrence at the same site (sometimes years later) is not uncommon, particularly where normal lymphatic drainage has been disrupted (Harrison 22e p.1052, p.1210-1211).

Edema with purple bullae, ecchymosis, and cutaneous anesthesia suggests loss of vascular integrity and necessitates exploration of deeper structures for necrotizing fasciitis or myonecrosis (Harrison 22e p.1051).
Unexplained fever with disproportionate pain and tenderness in soft tissue, even without acute cutaneous inflammation, should raise suspicion for a deeper necrotizing process (Harrison 22e p.1051).
None routinely required — Diagnosis is clinical based on the characteristic appearance; cultures of intact skin have low yield.

Erythema nodosum is a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction resulting in inflammation centered on the subcutaneous fat septae (septal panniculitis), triggered by circulating immune complexes or antigen-driven T-cell responses to a variety of infectious, inflammatory, or drug antigens. The septal inflammatory infiltrate initially contains neutrophils and later becomes predominantly lymphohistiocytic with multinucleated giant cells, without primary vasculitis. The overlying epidermis and dermis are typically spared, which explains the absence of ulceration or scarring despite the deep tenderness.
Presents as tender, erythematous, non-ulcerating nodules typically over the bilateral pretibial surfaces, sometimes extending to knees, ankles, or extensor forearms
Lesions evolve in color like a bruise (bright red to violaceous to yellow-green) over 1-2 weeks without ulcerating or scarring
Often accompanied by fever, malaise, arthralgia, and sometimes frank arthritis of ankles/knees
Far more common in women, with peak incidence in the second to fourth decades of life
Most cases are idiopathic or post-streptococcal, but a broad secondary workup is warranted, especially with atypical features
Lesions are typically bilateral and symmetric; unilateral or ulcerating nodules should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis
Represents a hypersensitivity reaction pattern rather than a single disease, so the search for an underlying trigger is central to management
Usually self-limited, resolving over 3-6 weeks even without treatment of an identifiable cause
Assuming erythema nodosum is always idiopathic without pursuing a directed search for streptococcal infection, sarcoidosis, IBD, tuberculosis, or drug causes
Confusing erythema nodosum with nodular vasculitis/erythema induratum, which favors the posterior calf and can ulcerate, changing management implications
Overlooking Löfgren syndrome (EN plus bilateral hilar adenopathy and arthritis) as a distinct, generally self-limited sarcoid presentation with a favorable prognosis
Performing a superficial punch biopsy instead of a deep incisional biopsy, which may miss the septal panniculitis needed for histologic confirmation

Erythema nodosum is typically self-limited, with lesions resolving spontaneously over 3-6 weeks without scarring, though it may recur if the underlying trigger persists or recurs. Prognosis is generally excellent and closely tied to management of any identified underlying condition.

Recurrent or refractory episodes despite removal of an identified trigger, warranting rheumatologic referral

chunks.text: Most cytotoxic chemotherapeutic agents suppress bone marrow function, and polymorphonuclear neutrophils, with their very short circulating half-life of roughly 6-8 hours, are the cell line most rapidly and severely depleted. As the neutrophil count falls, the host loses the first-line cellular defense that normally contains commensal flora at mucosal surfaces; below an ANC of 500/uL control of endogenous mouth and gut organisms is impaired, and below 200/uL the local inflammatory response is essentially absent, so signs of infection are blunted. The combination of profound neutropenia and chemotherapy-induced mucosal barrier injury allows translocation and rapid dissemination of bacteria from the patient's own gut and oral flora. Neutropenia is most commonly iatrogenic, arising from cytotoxic or immunosuppressive therapy. (Harrison 22e p.499-500, p.617)

chunks.text: Febrile neutropenia is defined by fever together with neutropenia (granulocytes below ~1500/uL, with clinically significant risk concentrated at ANC <500/uL and severe impairment of host defense at ANC <200/uL) (Harrison 22e p.499, p.617). Risk stratification for management intensity is performed with validated tools such as the MASCC risk index, which separates low-risk from high-risk febrile neutropenia (referenced in existing curated investigations; specific scoring not detailed in this Harrison excerpt).

FSGS results from podocyte injury and loss that a glomerulus cannot adequately repair, leading to segmental capillary collapse and scarring in a portion of glomeruli. In primary disease a circulating permeability factor is suspected to injure podocytes directly, whereas secondary forms arise from maladaptive hyperfiltration in remnant or overworked nephrons, viral cytopathic effects on podocytes, direct podocyte toxicity from certain drugs, or inherited defects in podocyte structural proteins. Ongoing podocyte depletion below a critical threshold triggers a self-perpetuating cycle of glomerulosclerosis and eventual global glomerular loss.
FSGS is a histologic lesion with multiple causes (primary/idiopathic, genetic, virus-associated, drug-induced, and adaptive/secondary to nephron loss or hyperfiltration), not a single disease
Primary FSGS typically presents with abrupt-onset nephrotic-range proteinuria, low serum albumin, and edema, resembling minimal change disease clinically
Secondary (adaptive) FSGS from obesity, reduced nephron mass, or reflux tends to present with subnephrotic proteinuria, preserved albumin, and a more indolent course
Collapsing variant is the most aggressive subtype, historically linked to HIV infection and other viral triggers, and carries the worst renal prognosis
APOL1 high-risk genotype markedly increases risk of FSGS and more rapid progression in patients of recent African ancestry
Diagnosis requires kidney biopsy with light microscopy showing segmental sclerosis in a subset of glomeruli, since sampling can miss focal lesions

Response to immunosuppression is more likely in primary FSGS with diffuse podocyte foot-process effacement than in secondary/adaptive forms, which generally do not respond to immunosuppressive therapy
Recurrence in the transplanted kidney is common in primary FSGS, particularly in patients whose native disease progressed rapidly to kidney failure
Treating all FSGS as a single steroid-responsive disease rather than recognizing that secondary/adaptive forms generally do not benefit from immunosuppression
Missing the diagnosis on a biopsy specimen that under-samples glomeruli, since the sclerotic lesions are segmental and focal rather than global
Failing to search for an underlying secondary cause (obesity, reduced nephron mass, viral infection, drug exposure) before committing a patient to prolonged immunosuppressive therapy
Overlooking genetic/familial forms in young patients or those with a family history, which alters both prognosis and treatment approach

Outcomes vary widely by FSGS subtype: primary FSGS achieving remission (spontaneous or treatment-induced) has a favorable long-term renal outlook, whereas resistant primary disease and most secondary/collapsing forms carry a substantial risk of progression to kidney failure over years. The collapsing variant has the most aggressive course among the subtypes.
Rapidly rising creatinine or oliguria suggesting an aggressive or collapsing variant
Nephrotic syndrome with severe hypoalbuminemia and high thrombotic/infectious risk requiring closer monitoring
Resistance to standard immunosuppressive therapy, suggesting secondary/genetic FSGS that will not benefit from continued immunosuppression
New heavy proteinuria in a transplant recipient with a history of primary FSGS, raising concern for disease recurrence
Uncontrolled hypertension or severe edema/anasarca needing urgent management

chunks.text: Acute infectious diarrhea results when an ingested pathogen overwhelms or bypasses host defenses (gastric acid, intestinal motility/peristalsis, mucus layer, secretory IgA, and the protective resident microbiota). Mechanistically there are two broad patterns. Noninflammatory disease arises in the proximal small bowel and is mediated by enterotoxins (e.g., cholera toxin, E. coli heat-labile [LT] and heat-stable [ST] toxins) or by viral injury; cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates a GTP-binding protein to persistently activate adenylate cyclase, raising cyclic AMP, increasing chloride secretion and decreasing sodium absorption, producing watery secretory diarrhea without mucosal destruction. Inflammatory disease affects the colon or distal small bowel through mucosal invasion (Shigella, enteroinvasive E. coli, Salmonella) or cytotoxins (S. dysenteriae type 1, Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, C. difficile), destroying epithelium and producing dysentery with fecal leukocytes. Viral pathogens (norovirus, rotavirus) injure the small-intestinal villous epithelium: rotavirus destroys mature absorptive enterocytes and the loss of brush-border enzymes leaves unmetabolized disaccharides, generating combined secretory and osmotic diarrhea, with the nonstructural protein NSP4 acting as an enterotoxin. Crucially, glucose-coupled sodium absorption in the small intestine remains intact even during toxin-driven secretion, which is the physiologic basis for oral rehydration therapy (p.1076-1077, p.1081, p.1629).

chunks.text: Most acute infectious gastroenteritis is self-limited and resolves within days; viral norovirus/sapovirus illness typically lasts 1-3 days and rotavirus 3-7 days. Death is uncommon in healthy adults but occurs chiefly from dehydration in infants and debilitated elderly; globally acute diarrhea remains a leading cause of childhood death. Oral rehydration has dramatically reduced mortality (e.g., cholera case fatality from >50% untreated to <1%). Recognized post-infectious sequelae include reactive arthritis (after invasive Shigella/Salmonella/Campylobacter/Yersinia), Guillain-Barre syndrome (after Campylobacter), hemolytic-uremic syndrome (after Shiga toxin-producing bacteria), post-infectious IBS (notably after Campylobacter), and transient post-infectious lactase deficiency; recurrent childhood diarrhea in resource-poor settings causes environmental enteropathy with growth and developmental stunting (p.302, p.305, p.1077-1078, p.1081, p.1628-1629).

chunks.text: Severity is graded clinically by functional impact and dehydration rather than by a single score. Mild: activity unrestricted. Moderate: activities altered. Severe: incapacitated. Dehydration assessment is the key severity measure on examination - mild = thirst, dry mouth, reduced axillary sweat, decreased urine output, slight weight loss; moderate = orthostatic blood-pressure fall, skin tenting, sunken eyes (or sunken fontanelle in infants); severe = lethargy/obtundation, feeble pulse, hypotension, and shock. Frequency of stools forewarns impending dehydration. By duration, diarrhea is acute (<2 weeks), persistent (2-4 weeks), or chronic (>4 weeks) (p.302/304, p.307, p.1078).

Anti-GBM disease results from autoantibody binding to a conformational epitope on the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen, an antigen shared by the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes. Antibody deposition activates complement and recruits neutrophils and macrophages, producing crescentic glomerulonephritis and, when pulmonary capillaries are involved, diffuse alveolar hemorrhage. Loss of pulmonary capillary integrity (from smoking, infection, or inhalational injury) is thought to expose the alveolar antigen and precipitate lung bleeding in genetically susceptible individuals (HLA-DR15 association).

Three factors are central to VAP pathogenesis: colonisation of the oropharynx with pathogenic organisms, aspiration of those organisms into the lower respiratory tract, and compromise of host defences (p.1073). The endotracheal tube is the single most important risk factor: it bypasses normal anti-aspiration mechanisms, and although it blocks large-volume aspiration, microaspiration is worsened by secretions pooling above the cuff. The tube and suctioning damage tracheal mucosa and facilitate colonisation, and pathogenic bacteria form a protective glycocalyx biofilm on the tube surface that shields them from antibiotics and host defences; biofilm fragments can embolise to distal airways or be dislodged during suctioning to reinoculate the trachea (p.1073). Normal oropharyngeal flora is frequently replaced by pathogenic organisms under antibiotic selection pressure, cross-infection, severe systemic illness, and malnutrition (p.1073). Almost all intubated patients have transient colonisation, but progression to pneumonia reflects a large bacterial inoculum overwhelming host defences amid post-admission immunoparalysis (p.1073). More broadly, pneumonia is now viewed as an emergent disturbance of the lung microbiota driven by self-accelerating inflammatory feedback rather than simple invasion of a sterile space (p.1066).

VAP is defined as pneumonia with onset 48 hours or more after the start of mechanical ventilation; research on HAP has centred on VAP, but the same principles extend to ventilated HAP and to non-ICU HAP (p.1072).

Absence of bacteria on a Gram stain of an endotracheal aspirate makes pneumonia an unlikely cause of the fever or infiltrate; presence of an MDR pathogen can be excluded as a target if tracheal aspirate cultures (or sensitive molecular tests) are negative, enabling de-escalation (p.1074).

Anaerobes may be somewhat more common in nonintubated HAP than in VAP because of greater macroaspiration risk and lower lower-airway oxygen tension, but they usually contribute only to polymicrobial pneumonia and rarely need specific targeted therapy (p.1076).

A bronchopneumonia pattern is most common in nosocomial pneumonias, in contrast to the lobar pattern more typical of bacterial CAP; in VAP, respiratory bronchiolitis may precede a radiologically apparent infiltrate (p.1066).

The 'healthcare-associated pneumonia' category has been abandoned because it did not reliably predict resistant-organism infection and drove excessive broad-spectrum antibiotic use; resistance risk should instead be judged individually from comorbidities, recent hospitalisation, and recent antibiotic therapy (p.1066).

About 70% of HAP cases are acquired outside the ICU and 30% within it; roughly 35% of all HAP patients require mechanical ventilation, which makes ventilated HAP a distinct entity whose bacteriology and outcome resemble those of VAP (p.1072).

In nonintubated HAP an expectorated sputum sample is used for microbiologic diagnosis but is confounded by frequent colonisation with oral pathogens; deep lower respiratory tract samples in VAP/ventilated HAP are more reliable yet may still contain colonising organisms (p.1072).

The non-MDR 'core pathogens' of VAP closely mirror those of severe CAP and predominate when pneumonia develops in the first 5-7 days of admission; with risk factors (especially prior antibiotics) MDR pathogens become a concern even early (p.1072).
Most hospitals contend with P. aeruginosa and MRSA, but the specific MDR organisms are institution-specific and can differ even between critical-care units in the same hospital (p.1072).
Prior antibiotic exposure is by far the dominant risk factor for colonisation with pathogenic organisms; P. aeruginosa almost never infects patients with no prior antibiotic exposure (pp.1073, 1076).

Only about one-third of colonised intubated patients go on to develop VAP, indicating that the final step is overwhelming of host defences by a large bacterial inoculum rather than colonisation alone (p.1073).

Severely ill septic or trauma patients appear to enter a state of immunoparalysis several days after ICU admission, coinciding with the period of greatest VAP risk; hyperglycaemia and frequent transfusions adversely affect immune response (p.1073).
Serial changes in oxygenation may detect HAP/VAP earlier than other findings and can also serve to monitor response to therapy (p.1073).

Applying CAP-type clinical criteria to ventilated patients consistently overdiagnoses VAP, owing to frequent tracheal colonisation, multiple alternative causes of radiographic infiltrates, and many other sources of fever in the critically ill (pp.1073-1074).

No single set of criteria reliably diagnoses pneumonia in a ventilated patient; over-reliance on portable chest radiographs is limited by frequent pre-existing infiltrates and poor portable film quality (p.1073).

Effective antibiotic given in the 24-48 h before sampling can drive quantitative cultures below the diagnostic threshold and yield false-negative results; conversely, counts above threshold during therapy suggest the current antibiotics are ineffective (p.1074).

Sampling too early in the course, or after an effective host response has already reduced bacterial counts, can also give sub-threshold results; ideally sample as soon as pneumonia is suspected and before starting or changing antibiotics (p.1074).
Chest radiographs often worsen initially during treatment, making them less reliable than clinical criteria as indicators of response (p.1076).

Recurrent VAP with the same organism can occur because the endotracheal tube biofilm allows persistence and reintroduction; about half of recurrent Pseudomonas cases are actually due to a new strain (p.1075).

Crude VAP mortality is reported as high as 50-70%, but the key measure is attributable mortality, since many VAP patients have underlying disease that would itself be fatal. Attributable mortality exceeded 25% in one matched-cohort study, whereas more recent estimates are much lower (5-10%); VAP complicating COVID-19 carries higher attributable mortality than other VAP. VAP in trauma patients shows no attributable mortality, likely because many were previously healthy. MDR pathogens carry significantly greater attributable mortality than non-MDR organisms, and some pathogens (e.g., S. maltophilia) chiefly mark a severely immunocompromised, high-risk host. Nonintubated non-ICU HAP has lower mortality and lower risk of antibiotic failure than VAP and ventilated HAP because of better host defences (pp.1076).

Harrison frames empirical management around two risk axes rather than a discrete severity score: (1) presence or absence of risk factors for MDR pathogens (prior antibiotic therapy, prior hospitalisation, local antibiogram; for MRSA additionally known MRSA colonisation, chronic haemodialysis, or local MRSA pneumonia rate >10% or unknown), and (2) predicted risk of death, with a mortality risk of 15% or less considered low risk. The frequency of VAP also varies with duration of ventilation, with the highest hazard in the first 5 days, a plateau (~1%/day) after about 2 weeks, and a cumulative rate up to ~70% by 30 days of ventilation (pp.1073, 1075).

Advanced liver disease with portal hypertension causes marked splanchnic arterial vasodilation, which reduces effective circulating arterial volume despite total-body volume overload. This triggers compensatory activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, sympathetic nervous system, and vasopressin release, producing intense renal vasoconstriction and a progressive fall in glomerular filtration despite normal renal histology. Systemic inflammation and bacterial translocation from the gut further worsen splanchnic vasodilation and renal hypoperfusion, and superimposed infection frequently precipitates the acute form.
A diagnosis of exclusion: renal failure in advanced cirrhosis/portal hypertension (with or without ascites) that fails to improve after volume expansion and stopping diuretics

Defective or overwhelmed cytotoxic lymphocyte function fails to clear antigen-presenting and infected cells, so antigen persists and continuously stimulates CD8+ T cells and macrophages. The result is unrestrained secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines (notably interferon-gamma, IL-6, IL-10, TNF and IL-18) — a cytokine storm — that activates macrophages to phagocytose erythrocytes, leukocytes and platelets (hemophagocytosis) in the marrow and reticuloendothelial system. This drives the cardinal features: fever from systemic inflammation, cytopenias from marrow consumption and hemophagocytosis, hepatosplenomegaly and transaminitis from organ infiltration, hyperferritinemia and hypertriglyceridemia from macrophage activation, and hypofibrinogenemia with coagulopathy that can progress to disseminated intravascular coagulation and multi-organ failure.

HLH is a hyperinflammatory syndrome of uncontrolled immune activation: over-activated CD8 T cells and macrophages drive a cytokine storm and widespread hemophagocytosis (immune cells engulfing blood cells), producing fever, cytopenias and organ injury rather than effective clearance of the trigger.

Two broad forms exist — primary/familial HLH from inherited defects of lymphocyte cytotoxicity (e.g. perforin/PRF1, UNC13D), usually presenting in infants and children; and secondary/acquired HLH triggered by infection (classically EBV), malignancy (especially lymphoma), or autoimmune/autoinflammatory disease, where it is termed macrophage activation syndrome (MAS).

The clinical hallmark is persistent high fever that does NOT respond to antibiotics, with hepatosplenomegaly and progressive cytopenias affecting two or more lineages — a picture that closely mimics severe sepsis but fails to resolve with antimicrobials alone.

A markedly elevated serum ferritin is the most useful bedside clue: values in the tens of thousands are strongly suggestive in adults, and a rising ferritin with falling cell counts and falling fibrinogen should prompt urgent evaluation.

Diagnosis commonly uses the HLH-2004 framework (five or more of eight features): fever; splenomegaly; cytopenias in two or more lineages; hypertriglyceridemia and/or hypofibrinogenemia; hemophagocytosis on marrow, spleen or lymph node; low or absent NK-cell activity; ferritin at or above 500 micrograms/L; and elevated soluble CD25 (soluble IL-2 receptor). The H-score is an alternative probability tool for secondary HLH in adults.
Anchoring on 'sepsis' and continuing antibiotics while HLH progresses — suspect HLH when a septic picture does not improve and the ferritin is very high.
Assuming a normal early bone marrow excludes HLH; hemophagocytosis can appear later, and the diagnosis is clinical plus biochemical, not marrow-dependent.
Treating the syndrome without an aggressive search for the trigger (infection, malignancy, autoimmune) — outcome depends on identifying and treating it.
Over-relying on a ferritin of 500 micrograms/L alone, which is not specific; it is the very high values and the overall pattern that matter.

Untreated HLH is frequently fatal. Outcome depends on prompt recognition, the underlying trigger (malignancy- and EBV-associated disease carry the worst prognosis), and timely trigger-directed and immunosuppressive therapy. Macrophage activation syndrome arising in rheumatic disease generally has a better prognosis when recognised and treated early.

The prototypic lesion is the vegetation - a mass of platelets, fibrin, microorganisms and scant inflammatory cells - usually on heart valves but also on the low-pressure side of a ventricular septal defect, on mural endocardium injured by aberrant blood jets or foreign bodies, or on intracardiac devices. Intact endothelium resists most bacteria; endothelial injury (e.g., at sites of high-velocity jet impact or on the low-pressure side of a structural lesion) permits direct infection by virulent organisms or formation of a sterile platelet-fibrin thrombus (nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis, NBTE) that becomes a nidus for bacterial seeding during transient bacteremia. NBTE is most often associated with mitral regurgitation, aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, ventricular septal defects and complex congenital heart disease, and also arises from hypercoagulable states (marantic endocarditis of malignancy/chronic disease and the bland vegetations of SLE and antiphospholipid syndrome). Circulating organisms adhere via surface adhesins (MSCRAMMs) - fibronectin-binding proteins, S. aureus clumping factor, enterococcal Fss2/Ace/Ebp pili, streptococcal glucans/FimA; S. aureus can even invade intact endothelium via fibronectin-binding proteins and von Willebrand factor, allowing infection of previously normal valves. Adherent organisms proliferate into microcolonies, induce platelet deposition and a local procoagulant (tissue-factor) state, and become buried in fibrin; deep organisms are metabolically inactive and relatively antibiotic-resistant while surface organisms are continuously shed into the blood. Clinical manifestations arise from intracardiac structural damage, embolization of vegetation fragments causing remote infarction/infection, hematogenous seeding during bacteremia, and immune-complex deposition; constitutional symptoms reflect cytokine release.

IE spans a clinical continuum from acute to subacute, and the causative organism largely dictates the tempo: beta-hemolytic streptococci, S. aureus and pneumococci tend to produce an acute, rapidly destructive course, whereas viridans streptococci, enterococci, CoNS and HACEK organisms usually cause subacute disease (Bartonella, T. whipplei, C. burnetii and M. chimaera are exceptionally indolent).

Up to half of arterial emboli precede the diagnosis of IE; embolic risk falls rapidly once effective antibiotics begin, so emboli occurring late during or after therapy do not by themselves indicate treatment failure.

In hemodynamically stable patients with suspected subacute IE, empirical antibiotics can reasonably be withheld initially to allow uncontaminated blood cultures, but patients with sepsis or deteriorating hemodynamics should be treated immediately after the first three culture sets are drawn.

Surgery is indicated (as a knowledge concept, distinct from antibiotic regimens) for optimal outcome when there is moderate-severe CHF/shock from valve dysfunction, paravalvular extension with abscess/fistula/heart block, persistent bacteremia without an extracardiac source despite 7-10 days of therapy, lack of effective antimicrobial therapy (fungal, Brucella, multidrug-resistant gram-negative), or an unstable partially dehisced prosthetic valve; it is strongly considered for large (>10 mm) hypermobile vegetations with prior embolus and valve dysfunction, very large (>30 mm) vegetations, S. aureus PVE with intracardiac complications, and relapse after optimal therapy. Removal of all hardware is recommended for established CIED-IE.

Fever is present in 80-90% of cases and a heart murmur in 80-85%, but in subacute IE fever is typically low-grade (rarely above 39.4 C) and may be blunted altogether in elderly, severely debilitated, or renal-failure patients.
A new or worsening regurgitant murmur is heard in only 20-50% of cases; in acute IE on a previously normal valve a murmur may be absent at first but is ultimately detected in about 85%.

Classic peripheral stigmata (Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, Roth spots, subungual/splinter hemorrhages) appear in only about 2-15% of cases and have become infrequent with earlier diagnosis; their absence does not exclude IE.

Janeway lesions are nonsuppurative painless hemorrhagic macules of the palms/soles classically linked to prolonged subacute infection, whereas septic emboli (subungual hemorrhages, Osler nodes) mimicking these lesions are common in acute S. aureus IE.
Three independent predictors of embolization are S. aureus etiology, mobile vegetations larger than 10 mm, and involvement of the anterior mitral leaflet.

In people who inject drugs, 35-60% of IE is confined to the tricuspid valve and presents with fever but faint or absent murmur and no peripheral stigmata, often with septic pulmonary emboli (cough, pleuritic pain, nodular infiltrates).

S. aureus bacteremia carries an 8-14% prevalence of IE and high mortality, so echocardiography (high-quality TTE, preferably TEE) is recommended routinely; intracardiac device, emboli, 2 or more positive cultures, community acquisition, vertebral osteomyelitis or persistent bacteremia each raise IE risk and argue for early TEE.

About 12-17% of patients with E. faecalis bacteremia and about 7% with non-beta-hemolytic streptococcal bacteremia have IE, justifying echocardiographic screening when predictive features are present.
Relying on a new/worsening murmur alone - it is a physical-exam minor criterion only; a major imaging criterion requires echocardiographic evidence of new valvular regurgitation, not auscultation.

Treating a negative TTE (or even a negative initial TEE) as ruling out IE; TTE misses vegetations under 2 mm and is poor for prosthetic valves, and initial TEE is falsely negative in 6-18% (especially TAVR-PVE) - repeat in 7-10 days when suspicion persists.
Forgetting that 5-15% of IE is blood-culture negative, often because of prior antibiotics; withholding empirical therapy when stable preserves diagnostic yield.
Interpreting persistent organism DNA detected in excised valves (in ~45% of patients who completed therapy) as antibiotic failure - relapse after surgery for active IE is actually uncommon.
Misattributing emboli that occur late during or after effective therapy to treatment failure.
Overlooking that prior antibiotics within 2 weeks blunt culture yield and that nontypical organisms require 3 or more positive sets (plus no extracardiac focus) to count as a major criterion.
Assuming antithrombotic therapy prevents systemic emboli in NVE - it does not.

Overall survival in developed countries is about 80-85%, but varies markedly by subgroup. About 85-90% survive NVE caused by viridans streptococci, HACEK organisms, or synergy-susceptible enterococci. Non-injecting patients with S. aureus NVE have 55-70% survival; injecting patients have 85-90%, but 1-year mortality rises to 20-30% if substance-use disorder is not addressed. Prosthetic-valve IE arising within 2 months of surgery carries 40-50% mortality versus only 10-20% for late-onset PVE; elderly TAVR-PVE in-hospital mortality is 35-50%, rising to 60-75% at 1 year. Crude survival after successful treatment is roughly 80-90% at 1 year and 70-80% at 2 years. Death often reflects comorbidities and end-organ complications rather than antibiotic failure. Adverse outcomes are linked to older age, severe comorbidity/diabetes, delayed diagnosis, prosthetic or aortic valve involvement, virulent or resistant pathogens (S. aureus, P. aeruginosa, yeast), intracardiac and major neurologic complications, and health care-associated infection.

Persistent fever or persistently positive blood cultures despite appropriate antibiotics, indicating uncontrolled infection
New or worsening regurgitant murmur or prosthetic valve dehiscence
Large (over 10 mm) mobile vegetation, particularly on the anterior mitral leaflet, with high embolic risk
Acute S. aureus or fungal IE, and any prosthetic-valve involvement

Diagnosis uses the 2023 Duke-International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases (Duke-ISCVID) update of the modified Duke criteria (sensitivity 80-93%). MAJOR criteria: (1) Microbiologic - a typical IE organism in 2 or more separate blood culture sets (S. aureus, S. lugdunensis, E. faecalis, all streptococci except S. pneumoniae and S. pyogenes, Granulicatella/Abiotrophia/Gemella, HACEK group; and, when intracardiac prosthetic material is present, CoNS, C. striatum, C. jeikeium, S. marcescens, P. aeruginosa, C. acnes, nontuberculous mycobacteria and Candida), OR a nontypical organism in 3 or more sets; positive PCR/single culture/serology for C. burnetii, Bartonella spp. or T. whipplei. (2) Imaging - echocardiography or cardiac CT showing vegetation, perforation/leaflet aneurysm, abscess, pseudoaneurysm or fistula, OR new valvular regurgitation, OR new prosthetic dehiscence; OR abnormal FDG-PET/CT activity on a valve/graft/lead/prosthetic material. (3) Surgical - IE seen at direct surgical inspection. MINOR criteria: predisposing condition (prior IE, injection drug use, prosthetic valve, prior valve repair, congenital heart disease such as bicuspid aortic valve, CIED, more-than-mild regurgitation/stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy); fever over 38.0 C; vascular phenomena (arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial/conjunctival hemorrhage, Janeway lesions); immunologic phenomena (glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots, positive rheumatoid factor); microbiologic evidence not meeting a major criterion; and PET/CT activity within 3 months of prosthetic implantation. CLASSIFICATION: DEFINITE IE = pathologic confirmation OR 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria. POSSIBLE IE = 1 major + 1 minor, or 3 minor. REJECTED = firm alternative diagnosis, or resolution with under 4 days of antibiotics, or no histologic evidence at surgery/autopsy after under 4 days of therapy. IE is also classified by tempo (acute vs subacute), site (native vs prosthetic valve, right-sided/tricuspid), cause, and predisposition (injection drug use, health care-associated).

Blood cultures (≥3 sets from separate sites, before antibiotics) — The single most important diagnostic step — identifies the organism and is a major Duke criterion; false-negative cultures from premature antibiotics significantly complicate diagnosis and management.

Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), followed by transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) if TTE inconclusive or high suspicion persists — Identifies vegetations, abscess, or valve destruction — a major Duke criterion and essential for surgical planning.
ECG — Screens for new conduction abnormalities (e.g., new heart block), which can indicate perivalvular abscess extension.
CBC, ESR/CRP, renal function — Supports overall assessment of inflammatory burden and any renal involvement (e.g., immune complex glomerulonephritis).

Disease arises from circulating poorly galactosylated IgA1 molecules that form immune complexes, which deposit in the glomerular mesangium and trigger mesangial cell proliferation and matrix expansion. This deposition activates complement and local inflammatory pathways, leading to variable degrees of mesangial hypercellularity, segmental sclerosis, endocapillary proliferation, and interstitial fibrosis depending on disease severity. Mucosal immune stimulation (e.g., respiratory infection) is thought to transiently boost production of these abnormal IgA1 complexes, explaining the synpharyngitic timing of gross hematuria flares.
Most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide, typically presenting in the second or third decade of life.

Classic presentation is episodic gross (macroscopic) hematuria occurring within 1-2 days of an upper respiratory or mucosal infection, distinguishing it from post-streptococcal GN which lags 1-3 weeks.
Can also present as asymptomatic microscopic hematuria with mild proteinuria found incidentally on urinalysis.
Diagnosis requires kidney biopsy showing dominant or codominant mesangial IgA deposition on immunofluorescence.
Course is highly variable: some patients have a benign lifelong course while roughly 20-40% progress to end-stage kidney disease over 20 years.
Recurrent gross hematuria episodes typically resolve completely between attacks, but persistent proteinuria or hypertension signals higher risk.
IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura) is considered a systemic variant of the same underlying disease process affecting skin, gut, and joints.
Renal biopsy findings are graded using the Oxford (MEST-C) classification to help predict prognosis and guide therapy intensity.
Attributing recurrent gross hematuria solely to urologic causes and delaying nephrology referral or biopsy.
Assuming normal complement levels rule out all forms of glomerulonephritis rather than supporting IgA nephropathy specifically.
Underestimating long-term risk in patients with isolated microscopic hematuria who lack proteinuria monitoring over time.
Confusing timing of hematuria onset relative to infection with post-streptococcal GN, missing the synpharyngitic pattern typical of IgA nephropathy.

Course ranges from indolent with preserved kidney function over decades to progressive decline, with an estimated 20-40% of patients reaching end-stage kidney disease within 20 years of diagnosis. Higher risk features include persistent proteinuria, hypertension, reduced GFR at presentation, and unfavorable histology on Oxford classification.
Rapidly rising creatinine suggesting crescentic (rapidly progressive) IgA nephropathy requiring urgent nephrology evaluation
Nephrotic-range proteinuria or nephrotic syndrome at presentation
New or worsening hypertension poorly responsive to therapy
Systemic features (purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain) suggesting IgA vasculitis with renal involvement
Persistent proteinuria greater than 1 gram per day despite optimized supportive therapy

Factitious or surreptitious insulin/sulfonylurea administration
Non-islet cell tumor hypoglycemia (IGF-2-secreting mesenchymal or epithelial tumors)
Post-bariatric surgery hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia / nesidioblastosis

Severe hepatic failure or sepsis-related hypoglycemia
72-hour supervised fasting test — reference standard to document Whipple triad with paired glucose, insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin
Plasma insulin and C-peptide during hypoglycemia — inappropriately elevated levels confirm endogenous hyperinsulinemia
Sulfonylurea/meglitinide screen — excludes factitious hypoglycemia from oral secretagogues
Insulin antibody testing — helps exclude autoimmune insulin syndrome or exogenous insulin use
Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of pancreas — initial anatomic localization of tumor
Endoscopic ultrasound — high sensitivity for small intrapancreatic lesions not seen on cross-sectional imaging
Somatostatin-receptor or GLP-1 receptor based functional imaging — localizes lesion when anatomic imaging is negative
Genetic/family screening for MEN1 — indicated when tumors are multiple, recurrent, or early-onset

Insulinoma is a neuroendocrine tumor arising from pancreatic beta cells that autonomously secretes insulin independent of glucose feedback regulation. This unregulated insulin release drives glucose into tissues and suppresses hepatic glucose output, producing hypoglycemia. The resulting fall in plasma glucose triggers counter-regulatory adrenergic activation and, when severe or prolonged, neuroglycopenia due to inadequate glucose delivery to the brain. Most tumors are sporadic and benign, but a subset occurs in the context of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1.
Presents with Whipple triad: symptoms of neuroglycopenia/adrenergic surge, documented hypoglycemia, and relief with glucose intake.
Neuroglycopenic symptoms (confusion, behavioral change, visual disturbance, seizure, coma) often dominate and can mimic a primary neuropsychiatric or seizure disorder.
Fasting-induced hypoglycemia is classic, but symptoms can also occur postprandially or with exertion in some patients.
Most insulinomas are small (<2 cm), solitary, benign, and confined to the pancreas; only a minority are malignant or multiple.
Multiple or recurrent insulinomas should raise suspicion for MEN1 syndrome, especially in younger patients or with a family history.
Weight gain is common because patients learn to eat frequently to avoid symptomatic hypoglycemia.
Diagnosis rests on a supervised fasting study demonstrating inappropriately elevated insulin and C-peptide during hypoglycemia, not just cross-sectional imaging.
Localization can be difficult since many tumors are very small; a negative scan does not exclude the diagnosis.
Relying on a single random glucose or insulin level instead of a supervised fasting protocol, leading to missed or false diagnosis.
Failing to exclude factitious hypoglycemia (exogenous insulin/sulfonylurea) before pursuing extensive tumor imaging.
Assuming a negative CT/MRI excludes insulinoma, when small tumors frequently require endoscopic ultrasound or functional imaging for localization.
Overlooking the possibility of MEN1 in patients with multiple or recurrent insulinomas, delaying appropriate family and genetic evaluation.

Most insulinomas are benign and solitary, and surgical resection is curative in the large majority of cases. Malignant or MEN1-associated multifocal disease carries a less favorable outlook and requires longer-term surveillance.
Severe neuroglycopenia with seizure, coma, or altered mental status requiring urgent glucose correction
Recurrent or multifocal tumors suggesting MEN1 and need for broader endocrine screening
Imaging or biochemical features suggesting malignant insulinoma with metastatic potential
Hypoglycemia unresponsive to standard glucose repletion, suggesting an alternative or coexisting cause
Signs of another MEN1-associated tumor (parathyroid, pituitary) in a patient with insulinoma

Pulmonary function tests with DLCO — documents restrictive pattern and gas-transfer impairment, tracks progression
Serologic autoimmune panel (ANA, rheumatoid factor, myositis antibodies) — screens for occult connective tissue disease
Six-minute walk test with oximetry — assesses functional capacity and exertional desaturation
Surgical or transbronchial cryobiopsy — considered when HRCT is indeterminate and histopathology would change management

Detailed exposure and medication history — identifies occupational, environmental, or drug-related causes of fibrosis

IPF is thought to result from repeated micro-injury to alveolar epithelium in a genetically susceptible, typically older individual, triggering an aberrant wound-healing response rather than a primarily inflammatory process. This dysregulated repair leads to fibroblast/myofibroblast proliferation and excessive extracellular matrix deposition, producing the patchy, temporally heterogeneous fibrosis and architectural distortion characteristic of the usual interstitial pneumonia pattern. Progressive scarring impairs gas exchange and lung compliance, culminating in restrictive physiology and hypoxemia.
Consider IPF in an older adult (usually over age 60) with progressive exertional dyspnea and dry cough lasting months, especially with a smoking history.
Bibasilar, fine 'Velcro-like' end-inspiratory crackles are the classic auscultatory finding.
Digital clubbing is present in roughly half of patients and supports the diagnosis.

High-resolution CT showing a definite UIP pattern (subpleural, basal-predominant reticulation with honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis, absence of features suggesting an alternative diagnosis) can obviate the need for lung biopsy.
IPF is a diagnosis of exclusion — connective tissue disease, chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, drug toxicity, and occupational/environmental exposures must be ruled out first.
Course is highly variable: most patients decline gradually, but acute exacerbations with rapid, often fatal deterioration can occur unpredictably.
Antifibrotic therapy slows the rate of decline in lung function but does not reverse existing fibrosis, so early diagnosis and referral matter.
Early referral for lung transplant evaluation should be considered at diagnosis given the poor natural history.
Attributing crackles and dyspnea to heart failure or COPD without pursuing HRCT, delaying diagnosis
Missing an underlying connective tissue disease or exposure history that would reclassify the disease and change management
Relying on chest x-ray alone, which is insensitive for early fibrotic change
Assuming a stable course; failing to monitor for acute exacerbations or gradual functional decline

IPF carries a poor prognosis with median survival historically around 3-5 years from diagnosis, though the trajectory is heterogeneous and antifibrotic therapy has modestly slowed functional decline. Acute exacerbations and progression to respiratory failure are the major causes of death, and lung transplantation remains the only intervention altering long-term survival.
Acute worsening of dyspnea over days to weeks (acute exacerbation), which carries high short-term mortality
Resting hypoxemia or significant desaturation on exertion
Rapidly declining forced vital capacity or DLCO on serial testing
Signs of cor pulmonale or pulmonary hypertension
Superimposed respiratory infection, which can precipitate acute decompensation

ESR and CRP — markedly elevated, supports diagnosis and tracks inflammatory activity

Kawasaki disease is thought to arise from an exaggerated innate and adaptive immune response, possibly triggered by an unidentified infectious agent, in a genetically susceptible host. The resulting medium-vessel vasculitis targets the coronary arteries, causing panvasculitis with destruction of the internal elastic lamina and media, which weakens the vessel wall and predisposes to aneurysm formation and later stenosis or thrombosis. Systemic inflammation also produces the mucocutaneous and lymph node findings that define the clinical syndrome.
Acute self-limited vasculitis of childhood, mainly under age 5, that preferentially targets medium-sized arteries, especially the coronary arteries.

Classic diagnosis needs fever for five or more days plus four of five criteria: bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, oral mucosal changes (cracked lips, strawberry tongue), polymorphous rash, extremity changes (edema, erythema, later periungual desquamation), and cervical lymphadenopathy usually unilateral and over 1.5 cm.
Incomplete (atypical) presentations are common in infants under 6 months and older children, and this group carries a higher, not lower, risk of coronary aneurysm.
Irritability out of proportion to exam findings and marked perineal desquamation in the diaper area are supportive clues.
Untreated disease leads to coronary artery aneurysms in roughly a quarter of children; timely therapy sharply reduces this risk.
Think of Kawasaki disease in any young febrile child with unexplained sterile pyuria, gallbladder hydrops, or aseptic meningitis.
Highest risk of coronary aneurysm formation is in the subacute phase, roughly one to four weeks after fever onset, coinciding with marked thrombocytosis.
Dismissing the diagnosis because not all classic criteria are present, especially in infants who often have incomplete disease with greater cardiac risk
Delaying treatment while awaiting full criteria, since early therapy within the first ten days of fever meaningfully lowers aneurysm risk
Overlooking overlap with MIS-C in the appropriate epidemiologic context, which requires additional testing and different considerations
Failing to arrange long-term cardiology follow-up in children with documented coronary changes

With prompt recognition and treatment most children recover fully with resolution of fever and inflammation within days. Coronary artery aneurysms, when they occur, may regress over time but can also persist, predisposing to late stenosis, thrombosis, or ischemic events, so children with cardiac involvement need long-term surveillance.
Evidence of coronary artery dilation or aneurysm on echocardiogram warrants urgent cardiology involvement
Signs of myocarditis, pericardial effusion, or hemodynamic instability (Kawasaki disease shock syndrome)
Persistent or recrudescent fever after initial therapy suggesting treatment resistance
Very young infants or children with incomplete presentations, who are at higher risk of coronary complications
Marked thrombocytosis in the subacute phase increasing thrombotic risk in dilated vessels

Bilirubin, aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase (bilirubin may be high; transaminase rises typically only moderate) (p.1443)
Chest radiograph / CT (patchy bilateral lower-lobe alveolar pattern from alveolar hemorrhage; pleura-based densities; ground-glass ARDS pattern) (p.1443)
ECG (nonspecific ST/T changes; repolarization abnormalities and arrhythmias are poor prognostic signs) (p.1443)
CSF examination when meningitis suspected (pleocytosis from a few to >1000 cells/uL, lymphocytic but may be PMN-predominant early; protein normal or slightly raised, glucose normal) (p.1443)
Co-testing for rickettsiae, dengue, and hantavirus given overlap and reported dual infections (p.1443)

Microscopic agglutination test (MAT) using live leptospiral strains — paired acute/convalescent sera seeking a fourfold rise; single high titer (1:200-1:800 depending on endemicity) supportive (p.1443)
IgM ELISA and commercial rapid lateral-flow / latex agglutination tests (useful where MAT/culture unavailable) (p.1443)
Blood/urine/CSF culture (special media; may take weeks to months) (p.1441, 1443)
C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, ESR (raised inflammatory markers) (p.1443)
Coagulation profile / DIC markers (D-dimer, antithrombin, protein C) in severe disease (p.1443)
Serum amylase (often elevated even without overt pancreatitis) (p.1443)
Serum electrolytes including magnesium (urinary magnesium loss is characteristic; hypokalemia, hyponatremia) (p.1443)
Urinalysis (leukocytes, erythrocytes, hyaline/granular casts, mild proteinuria) (p.1443)

Leptospires enter through cuts, abraded skin, or mucous membranes (especially conjunctival and oral). The highly motile organisms proliferate, cross tissue barriers, and disseminate hematogenously to all organs (leptospiremic phase), evading innate immune mechanisms such as complement-mediated killing and phagocytosis; an exaggerated proinflammatory response correlates with mortality. With the immune phase, antibodies appear and leptospires clear from blood but persist in liver, lung, kidney, heart, and brain. Renal pathology shows acute tubular damage and interstitial nephritis, progressing to interstitial edema and acute tubular necrosis, with dysregulated nephron transporters causing impaired sodium absorption, potassium wasting, and polyuria. Liver histology shows focal (not widespread) hepatocellular necrosis, inflammation, bile canaliculus plugging, and hepatocyte apoptosis, with disruption of intercellular junctions and bile leakage. Petechiae and hemorrhages occur across many organs. Hemorrhage is associated with thrombocytopenia (likely platelet consumption); a consumptive coagulopathy with elevated coagulation-activation markers, reduced anticoagulant markers, and dysregulated fibrinolysis may progress to overt DIC. Endothelial cell activation (raised soluble E-selectin and von Willebrand factor) correlates with severity, and leptospires/leptospiral proteins disrupt endothelial barrier function, increasing permeability. The LPS has unusually low endotoxic potency, yet serovar-specific anti-LPS antibodies are central to protective humoral immunity (p.1441-1442).

Classically biphasic: an acute leptospiremic phase (fever lasting ~3-10 days, organism culturable/PCR-detectable in blood) followed by an immune phase in which symptoms may resolve as antibodies appear and leptospires can be recovered from urine; the two phases are not always distinct, mild cases may lack the second phase, and severe disease can be monophasic and fulminant (p.1442).
Idea that specific serogroups cause distinct clinical syndromes has been refuted, although some serovars tend to cause more severe disease (p.1442).
Serology lacks sensitivity in the early acute phase (up to day 5) and cannot guide a timely treatment decision; PCR (notably real-time PCR) can confirm diagnosis during the first 5 days (p.1443).
MAT antibodies generally do not reach detectable levels until the second week of illness, and the antibody response may be blunted by early antibiotics (p.1443).
Incubation is usually 1-2 weeks but ranges from 2 to 30 days (p.1442).
Conjunctival suffusion (redness without exudate) is a characteristic but non-pathognomonic sign; muscle pain is intense, especially in the calves, back, and abdomen (p.1442).
Headache is intense and frontal or retro-orbital, sometimes with photophobia, resembling dengue (p.1442).
Weil's syndrome denotes the severe triad of jaundice, acute kidney injury, and hemorrhage (p.1442-1443).

Severe pulmonary hemorrhage (with or without jaundice) is increasingly recognized as an important and widespread presentation; hemoptysis may not become apparent until the patient is intubated (p.1439, 1442).
Jaundice occurs in only ~5-10% of patients, can be deep with an orange skin cast, and is usually NOT associated with fulminant hepatic necrosis (p.1442).

Aseptic meningitis is more common in children than adults; altered mental status in severe disease may reflect leptospiral meningitis, which can occur in anicteric patients lacking other hallmarks (p.1442-1443).
Autoimmune-associated uveitis is a recognized, potentially chronic late sequela (p.1443).
Absence of a travel or freshwater-exposure history does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1443).
Absence of renal involvement does not rule out leptospirosis (p.1443).
Relying on serology in the first ~5 days risks a false-negative; antibodies are often undetectable until the second week and early antibiotics blunt the response (p.1443).
Cross-reactions are frequent in MAT, so the infecting serovar/serogroup cannot be definitively identified without isolating the organism (p.1443).
Leptospiral meningitis may present without jaundice or other classic severe-disease hallmarks, making it easy to miss (p.1443).
Jaundice can be profound yet usually does not signify fulminant hepatic necrosis, so hepatic transaminase rises are only moderate (p.1442-1443).
The transient rash may be misdiagnosed as scrub typhus or a viral exanthem (p.1442).
Dual infection (e.g., with dengue, rickettsiae, or hantavirus) can occur, so a positive alternative test does not exclude leptospirosis (p.1443).

Most patients recover, with renal and hepatic function typically returning to normal in survivors (hemodialysis can be lifesaving). Overall mean case-fatality is near 10% for severe cases; severe leptospirosis carries a case-fatality of 1-50%. Mortality is highest in the elderly and those with pulmonary hemorrhage or Weil's syndrome. Untreated leptospiral meningitis has reported mortality of ~13% versus ~2% with antibiotics. Pregnancy is associated with high fetal mortality. Post-leptospirosis sequelae include prolonged fatigue, myalgia, malaise, headache, depression-like symptoms persisting for years, and chronic autoimmune uveitis (p.1443-1444).
Age >40 years
Pregnancy (high fetal mortality)
Altered mental status
Acute kidney injury / oliguria or anuria
Respiratory insufficiency, hemoptysis, or pulmonary hemorrhage
Hypotension / septic shock
Cardiac arrhythmias and repolarization abnormalities on ECG
Jaundice with bleeding (Weil's syndrome triad)
Thrombocytopenia (platelet count <=100 x10^9/L) — linked to bleeding and renal failure

Harrison distinguishes mild leptospirosis (sudden-onset flu-like febrile illness with headache, myalgia, conjunctival suffusion; usually self-limiting over 7-10 days, low mortality) from severe leptospirosis, which is often rapidly progressive with multiorgan involvement. Severe disease classically presents as Weil's syndrome (triad of jaundice, acute kidney injury, and hemorrhage) and/or severe pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome, with a case-fatality of 1-50% (p.1442-1443).

Leptospira IgM ELISA / MAT (microscopic agglutination test) — Confirms diagnosis serologically; MAT is the reference standard but often only available at referral labs, so treatment should not be delayed pending results.
Renal function tests — Assesses for acute kidney injury, a hallmark of severe leptospirosis (Weil's disease) with major prognostic significance.
Liver function tests — Jaundice with relatively modest transaminase elevation (compared to viral hepatitis) is a classic pattern in leptospirosis.
CBC, coagulation profile — Screens for thrombocytopenia and bleeding risk, relevant to hemorrhagic complications.
CPK (creatine phosphokinase) — Often elevated due to myositis, supporting the diagnosis and explaining myalgia.

chunks.text: Supportive labs: leukocytosis (~77%), normochromic normocytic anaemia (~50%), hypoalbuminaemia (~33%); concomitant bacteraemia in one-third to one-half of patients (p.1117).

chunks.text: For suspected hypervirulent K. pneumoniae, the string test for hypermucoviscosity is suggestive but not optimally sensitive or specific; the most accurate identification uses the biomarkers iucA, iroB, peg-344, rmpA, and rmpA2 (p.1290).

chunks.text: Pyogenic liver abscesses arise either from haematogenous spread of bacteria or from local spread from contiguous intraperitoneal infection. The organism reaches the liver by several routes: ascending biliary infection (currently the most common associated source), portal venous seeding via suppurative thrombosis of the portal vein (pylephlebitis, classically from pelvic or other intra-abdominal infection), direct contiguous spread, or systemic bacteraemic (haematogenous) seeding. Historically, ruptured appendicitis was the leading source. Hypervirulent (hypermucoviscous) K. pneumoniae causes a distinct community-acquired monomicrobial syndrome in which the organism establishes a primary liver abscess and then disseminates metastatically; this contrasts with the polymicrobial, source-driven pattern of biliary or enteric abscesses. (p.1117, p.1289-1290)

source.page: Harrison 22e p.1117-1118 (pyogenic/intraabdominal abscesses); p.1289-1290 (hypervirulent K. pneumoniae); p.1755-1757 (amebic liver abscess)

chunks.text: The liver is the visceral organ most prone to abscess formation; in one series of intraabdominal abscesses, hepatic abscesses accounted for roughly half of all visceral abscesses (p.1117).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.1117-1118 (pyogenic/intraabdominal abscesses); p.1289-1290 (hypervirulent K. pneumoniae); p.1755-1757 (amebic liver abscess)

chunks.text: Fever is the most common presenting feature; about half of patients with a liver abscess have no localizing signs (no hepatomegaly, right-upper-quadrant tenderness, or jaundice), so the liver may not be obviously implicated on examination (p.1117).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.1117-1118 (pyogenic/intraabdominal abscesses); p.1289-1290 (hypervirulent K. pneumoniae); p.1755-1757 (amebic liver abscess)

chunks.text: In the elderly, liver abscess may present solely as fever of unknown origin, so abdominal imaging (especially of the right upper quadrant) should form part of any FUO workup (p.1117).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.1117-1118 (pyogenic/intraabdominal abscesses); p.1289-1290 (hypervirulent K. pneumoniae); p.1755-1757 (amebic liver abscess)

chunks.text: An elevated serum alkaline phosphatase is the single most reliable laboratory abnormality, present in about 70% of patients; bilirubin and aminotransferases are often normal or only modestly raised (p.1117).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.1117-1118 (pyogenic/intraabdominal abscesses); p.1289-1290 (hypervirulent K. pneumoniae); p.1755-1757 (amebic liver abscess)

chunks.text: The microbiology of pyogenic liver abscess tracks with the source: biliary-tract origin yields enteric gram-negative aerobic bacilli and enterococci, pelvic/intraperitoneal origin yields a mixed aerobic-anaerobic flora (B. fragilis most common), and haematogenous seeding usually yields a single organism such as S. aureus or a Streptococcus milleri (anginosus)-group streptococcus (p.1117).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.1117-1118 (pyogenic/intraabdominal abscesses); p.1289-1290 (hypervirulent K. pneumoniae); p.1755-1757 (amebic liver abscess)

chunks.text: Anaerobes are not typically involved in liver abscesses arising from biliary infection unless prior surgery has occurred (p.1117).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.1117-1118 (pyogenic/intraabdominal abscesses); p.1289-1290 (hypervirulent K. pneumoniae); p.1755-1757 (amebic liver abscess)

chunks.text: Candida liver abscess characteristically follows fungaemia in patients receiving chemotherapy and often becomes clinically apparent as neutrophil counts recover after a period of neutropenia (p.1117).

chunks.text: Failing to distinguish pyogenic from amebic liver abscess: amebic serology is positive in >95% of amebic cases, amebic abscesses are classically a single right-lobe lesion, and most travellers with amebic abscess present within ~5 months of leaving an endemic area — so travel history, lesion location, and serology should be sought before committing to a purely bacterial diagnosis (p.1117, p.1755-1756).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.1117-1118 (pyogenic/intraabdominal abscesses); p.1289-1290 (hypervirulent K. pneumoniae); p.1755-1757 (amebic liver abscess)

chunks.text: Aspirating an amebic abscess for trophozoites is low-yield: trophozoites reside in the abscess capsule, not in the readily aspirated necrotic ('anchovy-paste') centre, so their absence on aspirate does not exclude amebiasis (p.1756).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.1117-1118 (pyogenic/intraabdominal abscesses); p.1289-1290 (hypervirulent K. pneumoniae); p.1755-1757 (amebic liver abscess)

chunks.text: Up to 10% of patients with acute amebic liver abscess have negative serology early on, usually seroconverting within a week — a single early negative test does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1757).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.1117-1118 (pyogenic/intraabdominal abscesses); p.1289-1290 (hypervirulent K. pneumoniae); p.1755-1757 (amebic liver abscess)

chunks.text: Assuming anaerobic coverage is always required: anaerobes are generally not involved in abscesses of biliary origin (unless prior surgery), whereas pelvic/intraperitoneal-source abscesses are typically polymicrobial with B. fragilis (p.1117).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.1117-1118 (pyogenic/intraabdominal abscesses); p.1289-1290 (hypervirulent K. pneumoniae); p.1755-1757 (amebic liver abscess)

chunks.text: Attributing a cryptogenic pyogenic liver abscess solely to the liver: because biliary, portal (pelvic/appendiceal), and other intra-abdominal infections are leading sources, the underlying source must be sought and addressed (p.1117).

chunks.text: Overlooking that ampicillin/amoxicillin exposure within the prior 30 days has been associated with increased risk of the hypervirulent K. pneumoniae liver abscess syndrome, presumably via selection for the causative strain (p.1117).

chunks.text: Mortality from pyogenic liver abscess averaged about 15% despite treatment in the data cited; outcome is poorer with delayed source control or factors predicting failed percutaneous drainage. For hypervirulent K. pneumoniae infection, survivors may suffer catastrophic sequelae from metastatic spread, including vision loss (endophthalmitis) and major neurologic deficits. (p.1118, p.1289)

chunks.text: Features suggesting hypervirulent K. pneumoniae with metastatic spread — concurrent endophthalmitis (threatening vision loss), meningitis/brain abscess, or septic pulmonary nodules — mandate urgent evaluation of distant sites (p.1289-1290).

chunks.text: Abdominal ultrasound or CT — Confirms presence, size, number, and location of abscess(es), and guides drainage planning.
Image-guided aspiration with Gram stain, culture, and microscopy — Definitively distinguishes pyogenic from amebic abscess and identifies the specific organism for targeted therapy.
Amebic serology (IgG) — Supports diagnosis of amebic liver abscess, especially useful when aspiration is not performed or is inconclusive.
Blood cultures — May identify the causative organism in pyogenic abscess, particularly Klebsiella, without requiring aspiration.
HbA1c/blood glucose — Diabetes is a major risk factor for Klebsiella liver abscess and affects overall management.
Liver Abscess (infective) — Hepatobiliary

veryLikely: Klebsiella pneumoniae (especially in diabetics, particularly in Asia), Escherichia coli; likely: Streptococcus species, Anaerobes (Bacteroides, if biliary or colonic source); possible: Entamoeba histolytica (amebic liver abscess — common in endemic regions including India, typically single right lobe lesion)

[guideline] empiric → Ceftriaxone + Metronidazole This combination covers the most likely pyogenic pathogens (Klebsiella, E. coli, anaerobes) while metronidazole simultaneously provides empiric amebic coverage, addressing both major causes pending specific identification.
[guideline] alternative → Piperacillin-tazobactam (monotherapy for pyogenic coverage)
