A lung abscess is necrosis and cavitation of lung parenchyma after microbial infection, typically a single dominant cavity >2 cm. In primary disease, anaerobes and microaerophilic streptococci colonizing the gingival crevices are aspirated into a susceptible host who carries an overwhelming aspirated burden or cannot clear it. An initial pneumonitis (worsened by gastric-acid tissue damage) progresses over about 7-14 days to parenchymal necrosis and cavitation, with anaerobes driving more extensive synergistic tissue destruction in polymicrobial infection. Secondary abscesses follow the predisposing mechanism: post-obstructive (tumor/foreign body) impairment of secretion clearance, or impaired host defense in immunocompromise allowing a broad pathogen range. Abscesses may also arise hematogenously from septic emboli (e.g., tricuspid endocarditis, Lemierre's syndrome).

Roughly 80% of lung abscesses are primary, arising from aspiration in the absence of an underlying pulmonary or systemic disease; the remaining ~20% are secondary to a predisposing process such as bronchial obstruction or immunocompromise (p.1034).

A foul-smelling (putrid) breath, sputum, or empyema is considered essentially diagnostic of an anaerobic lung abscess; abscesses with no isolated pathogen (about 40%) are termed nonspecific and anaerobes are presumed (p.1035).

Primary abscesses favor the dependent segments (posterior segments of upper lobes, superior segments of lower lobes), and the right lung is involved more often than the left because the right mainstem bronchus is less angulated (p.1035).

Anaerobic abscesses often present indolently with night sweats, fatigue, and anemia, whereas non-anaerobic causes such as S. aureus can produce a fulminant course with high fevers and rapid progression (p.1035-1036).

Edentulous patients are thought very unlikely to develop a lung abscess, since teeth (especially with gingivitis/periodontal disease) provide the nidus for the anaerobic/microaerophilic colonization that seeds the lung (p.1034).

Lemierre's syndrome (oropharyngeal infection, classically Fusobacterium necrophorum, with septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein) is a recognized embolic source of lung abscess (p.1034-1035).
Metronidazole alone is inadequate because it covers anaerobes but not the microaerophilic streptococci that are commonly part of the mixed flora of primary abscesses (p.1036).

Failure to exclude an obstructing malignancy: in older patients, those with malignancy risk factors, or those lacking clear aspiration risk, early bronchoscopy/biopsy and CT are indicated rather than assuming a primary anaerobic abscess (p.1035-1036).
Treating a presumed primary abscess that does not improve without re-evaluating for a secondary cause (obstruction, unusual pathogen) (p.1036).
Sputum culture may miss the diagnosis: infection is usually polymicrobial and routine cultures often fail to reflect anaerobes (p.1035).
Using metronidazole as monotherapy, which misses microaerophilic streptococci (p.1036).
Misclassifying a peripheral abscess as a pleural infection (empyema) or vice versa, since empyema may need urgent drainage (p.1035).
Underestimating risk in immunocompromised hosts, who are fragile, infected by a wide pathogen range, and warrant early culture-directed diagnostics (p.1035).

Mortality for primary lung abscess can be as low as ~2%, but secondary abscesses carry a much higher mortality, reported as high as 75% in some series. Adverse prognostic factors include age >60, malignancy-associated abscess, presence of aerobic bacteria, sepsis at presentation, symptom duration >8 weeks, and abscess size >6 cm. Defervescence on appropriate therapy can take up to 7 days, and 10-20% of patients fail to respond. Larger cavities at presentation predispose to persistent pneumatoceles or bronchiectasis. Prevention centers on airway protection, oral hygiene, minimizing sedation, head-of-bed elevation in aspiration-prone patients, and pathogen prophylaxis in selected immunocompromised hosts (p.1036).
Life-threatening hemoptysis (p.1036)
Massive aspiration of abscess contents into the airway (p.1036)
Extension to the pleural space with empyema, which may require urgent drainage (p.1035-1036)
Failure to defervesce or radiographic progression despite appropriate therapy (10-20% of patients do not respond) (p.1036)
Abscess >6-8 cm in diameter, which is less likely to respond to antibiotics alone (p.1036)
Sepsis at presentation (poor prognostic factor) (p.1036)

Lung abscesses are classified as primary (~80%, aspiration-related, anaerobe-predominant, no underlying lung/systemic disease) versus secondary (underlying obstruction, systemic illness, or immunocompromise); and by chronicity as acute (<4-6 weeks) versus chronic (~40% of cases). Size >6-8 cm marks lesions less responsive to antibiotics alone (p.1034, p.1036).

Chest X-ray and CT chest — CT better characterizes cavity size, wall thickness, and surrounding parenchymal involvement, and helps distinguish abscess from other cavitary lesions (e.g., malignancy, TB).
Sputum culture (including anaerobic culture if obtainable) — May identify causative organisms, though anaerobic cultures are technically difficult to obtain without invasive sampling.
Blood cultures — May identify the organism if bacteremic spread has occurred.
Lung Abscess (infective) — Respiratory

veryLikely: Oral anaerobes (Peptostreptococcus, Prevotella, Fusobacterium, Bacteroides); likely: Streptococcus species (including microaerophilic strains), Staphylococcus aureus; possible: Klebsiella pneumoniae (necrotizing pneumonia, especially in diabetics/alcoholics)

[guideline] empiric → Ampicillin-sulbactam Reliable anaerobic and streptococcal coverage appropriate for the prolonged course required in lung abscess; IV therapy initially with oral step-down once clinically stable.
[guideline] alternative → Clindamycin
Acute viral illness / minor febrile viral syndrome (early nonspecific malaria mimics this) (Harrison 22e p.1763)
Bacterial meningitis (severe headache in malaria, but neck stiffness and photophobia are absent in malaria) (Harrison 22e p.1763)
Sepsis / bacteremia with incidental parasitemia, especially in high-transmission areas (Harrison 22e pp.1765, 1767)
Dengue fever (myalgia is prominent but usually more severe in dengue) (Harrison 22e p.1763)
Leptospirosis (muscle tenderness, which malaria lacks; petechial hemorrhages a feature) (Harrison 22e p.1763)
Typhus/rickettsial illness (tender muscles, unlike malaria) (Harrison 22e p.1763)
Viral hemorrhagic fevers (petechial hemorrhages, which are very rare in malaria) (Harrison 22e p.1763)
Nontyphoidal Salmonella and other bacteremia complicating or coinciding with malaria (Harrison 22e p.1765)
Thick blood film (concentrates parasites ~40-100x over thin film, increasing sensitivity; examine 100-200 fields before calling negative) (Harrison 22e pp.1766-1767)
Thin blood film for species identification and parasite quantification (parasitized cells per 1000 RBCs) (Harrison 22e pp.1766-1767)
Giemsa (pH 7.2) or other Romanowsky stain; acridine orange for rapid detection of low-level parasitemia (Harrison 22e p.1766)
Rapid diagnostic tests detecting PfHRP2, parasite LDH, or aldolase (note PfHRP2/3 gene-deletion false negatives and that RDTs do not quantify parasitemia) (Harrison 22e p.1767)

PCR / ultrasensitive PCR for species confirmation and detection of low-density/asymptomatic infection (reference setting; too sensitive for primary diagnosis in endemic areas) (Harrison 22e pp.1767-1768)
Plasma lactate and bicarbonate (best biochemical prognosticators in severe malaria) (Harrison 22e p.1764)
Coagulation studies (PT, aPTT, fibrinogen) and platelet count in severe disease (Harrison 22e pp.1764-1765, 1768)
Assessment of malaria pigment in neutrophils (>5% pigment-containing) and proportion of mature pigmented trophozoites/schizonts as severity/prognostic markers (Harrison 22e pp.1764, 1767)
Diabetic ketoacidosis / ketoacidosis (acidotic 'respiratory distress' breathing overlaps with severe malaria acidosis; ketoacidosis can contribute in children) (Harrison 22e pp.1764-1766)
Hematologic malignancy / lymphoproliferative disorder (hyperreactive malarial splenomegaly with massive splenomegaly and pancytopenia can be mistaken for it) (Harrison 22e p.1766)

Infection begins when a female Anopheles inoculates sporozoites, which reach the liver and undergo preerythrocytic schizogony, each sporozoite yielding 10,000 to >30,000 merozoites. Released merozoites invade red cells, becoming trophozoites that multiply roughly 6- to 20-fold each asexual cycle (every 48 h for P. falciparum/P. vivax/P. ovale, 72 h for P. malariae, 24 h for P. knowlesi); symptoms begin around densities of ~50 parasites/uL. In P. vivax and P. ovale a fraction of liver forms persist as dormant hypnozoites for weeks to a year or more, causing the relapses characteristic of these species (P. falciparum, P. malariae, and P. knowlesi do not relapse). Disease results from red-cell invasion and destruction plus the host inflammatory response: schizont rupture releases material that activates monocytes/macrophages and proinflammatory cytokines, producing fever. The central pathology of severe falciparum malaria is cytoadherence: ~12-15 h after invasion 'knobs' on the infected red cell extrude the variant adhesin PfEMP1, which binds endothelial receptors (ICAM-1 and endothelial protein C receptor in brain, VAR2CSA/chondroitin sulfate A in placenta, CD36 elsewhere). Cytoadherence, rosetting (adherence to uninfected red cells), and agglutination sequester mature parasites in vital organs, especially the brain, obstructing microcirculatory flow and metabolism while escaping splenic clearance. Uninfected red cells also become less deformable in severe disease. P. falciparum invades cells of all ages and can reach very high densities (P. knowlesi can also, owing to its 24-h cycle), whereas other species spare most red cells and rarely exceed ~2% parasitemia. The spleen augments clearance and 'pits' damaged ring forms; severe lactic acidosis arises from anaerobic glycolysis in sequestered beds, parasite lactate production, gut-derived acids, and failed hepatic/renal clearance, and hypoglycemia from impaired gluconeogenesis with increased glucose consumption. (Harrison 22e pp.1760-1765)

Malaria is not a clinical diagnosis: any patient in or from an endemic area with fever needs thick and thin blood smears (or a rapid test if reliable microscopy is unavailable) to confirm infection and identify the species (Harrison 22e p.1766).
Specific retinal changes (patchy retinal opacification/whitening, vessel decolorization, pale-centered hemorrhages) on funduscopy support a diagnosis of cerebral malaria (Harrison 22e pp.1764-1765).

In severe malaria the usual adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycemia (sweating, tachycardia, gooseflesh) are absent and its neurologic effects cannot be distinguished from the disease itself, so glucose must be checked actively (Harrison 22e p.1764).
Quinine can provoke hypoglycemia by stimulating pancreatic insulin secretion, compounding the hypoglycemia of severe malaria (Harrison 22e p.1764).

Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema may appear even after several days of effective antimalarial therapy and is readily precipitated by over-vigorous IV fluids; mortality exceeds 80% (Harrison 22e p.1764).
Acidotic ('respiratory distress') breathing in a child with severe anemia is usually due to metabolic acidosis, not 'anemic heart failure' as previously mislabeled (Harrison 22e pp.1765-1766).

Approximately 6% of children and <1% of adults with severe malaria have concomitant bacteremia (higher with >20% parasitemia in adults), and nontyphoidal Salmonella bacteremia is specifically associated with P. falciparum (Harrison 22e p.1765).

In high-transmission areas low-density parasitemia is a common incidental finding, so severe malaria is easily overdiagnosed and must be distinguished from sepsis with coincidental parasitemia (Harrison 22e pp.1765, 1767).
Sudden delayed hemolysis can follow artesunate treatment of hyperparasitemia in nonimmune patients, from synchronous loss of once-parasitized 'pitted' red cells (Harrison 22e p.1765).

Early symptoms are nonspecific (malaise, headache, fatigue, abdominal discomfort, myalgia, then fever) and resemble a minor viral illness, so a high index of suspicion is essential (Harrison 22e p.1763).

The classic regular febrile paroxysms (chills, rigors, fever spikes at fixed intervals) are now unusual and, when present at presentation, suggest P. vivax or P. ovale (often a relapse); prompt effective treatment prevents the synchronized fever pattern from developing (Harrison 22e p.1763).
Mild thrombocytopenia is usual in malaria; a normal platelet count should call the diagnosis into question (Harrison 22e pp.1765, 1768).
In falciparum malaria, peripheral parasitemia underestimates true parasite burden because mature parasites sequester in deep vascular beds and only younger ring forms circulate (Harrison 22e p.1762).

A PfHRP2-based rapid test can stay positive for weeks after treatment, which helps diagnose severe malaria in a patient who has already taken antimalarials and cleared peripheral parasites but is a drawback in high-transmission settings (Harrison 22e p.1767).

Persistent gametocytemia after a full treatment course does not indicate drug resistance or a need to re-treat, because mature P. falciparum gametocytes are unaffected by most antimalarials (Harrison 22e p.1767).
Any obtundation, delirium, abnormal behavior, or generalized seizure in falciparum malaria must be taken seriously as a possible herald of cerebral malaria (Harrison 22e pp.1763-1764).
Cerebral malaria is a diffuse symmetric encephalopathy without true meningism; focal neurologic signs are unusual and signs of meningeal irritation are absent (Harrison 22e p.1764).
Treating malaria as a clinical diagnosis; confirmation by smear or rapid test is required (Harrison 22e p.1766).
Mistaking acidotic breathing in a severely anemic child for 'anemic congestive cardiac failure' (Harrison 22e pp.1765-1766).
Accepting a normal platelet count without question, as mild thrombocytopenia is the rule in malaria (Harrison 22e pp.1765, 1768).
Relying on peripheral parasitemia to gauge true burden in falciparum malaria, since mature parasites are sequestered (Harrison 22e p.1762).
Overdiagnosing severe malaria in high-transmission areas where low-density parasitemia is a common incidental finding, missing concurrent sepsis (Harrison 22e pp.1765, 1767).
Over-vigorous IV fluid administration, which can precipitate noncardiogenic pulmonary edema (Harrison 22e p.1764).
Missing hypoglycemia because its usual autonomic signs are absent in severe disease and its neurologic effects mimic malaria itself (Harrison 22e p.1764).
Re-treating on the basis of persistent gametocytemia, which does not signify drug resistance after a full course (Harrison 22e p.1767).
False-negative RDTs from PfHRP2/3 gene-deleted parasites (notably in the Horn of Africa); RDTs also cannot quantify parasitemia (Harrison 22e p.1767).
Using serology to diagnose acute illness; serology has no role in acute diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1768).

Promptly and appropriately treated uncomplicated falciparum malaria has a mortality of <0.1%, but risk rises steeply once vital-organ dysfunction occurs or parasitemia exceeds 2%. Cerebral malaria carries roughly 20% mortality in adults and 15% in children even with treatment; about 10% of surviving children (especially with hypoglycemia, severe anemia, repeated seizures, or deep coma) have residual neurologic deficits, most of which improve or resolve within 6 months, though persistent language and cognitive deficits, increased epilepsy risk, and reduced life expectancy occur in some. Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema in adults has >80% mortality. Plasma bicarbonate and lactate are the best biochemical prognosticators. Among complications, poor prognosis is indicated by >20% mature pigment-containing parasites or >5% of neutrophils containing pigment, and by hyperparasitemia. In severe acute renal failure that survives, urine flow returns in a median of 4 days and creatinine normalizes in a mean of 17 days; early dialysis improves survival. (Harrison 22e pp.1763-1765, 1767)
Impaired consciousness, delirium, abnormal behavior, or unarousable coma (cerebral malaria) (Harrison 22e pp.1763-1764)
Spontaneous bleeding / DIC (Harrison 22e p.1764)
Hyperparasitemia (>5% in nonimmune, >10% in any patient) or >100,000/uL (Harrison 22e pp.1763-1764)
Prostration / inability to sit or stand unaided (Harrison 22e p.1764)
Low core temperature <36.5C, marked agitation, jaundice (bilirubin >50 umol/L) with vital-organ dysfunction (Harrison 22e p.1764)
Generalized or repeated convulsions (>2 in 24 h), or subtle seizure activity such as tonic-clonic eye movements (Harrison 22e p.1764)
Acidotic deep ('respiratory distress') breathing, hyperlactatemia >=5 mmol/L, or acidemia (arterial pH <7.25) (Harrison 22e p.1764)
Hypoglycemia (plasma glucose <2.2 mmol/L, <40 mg/dL) (Harrison 22e p.1764)
Hypotension/shock with impaired perfusion (Harrison 22e p.1764)
Severe anemia (hematocrit <15% or Hb <50 g/L with high parasitemia; Hb <=3 g/dL on presentation carries increased mortality) (Harrison 22e pp.1764-1765)
Macroscopic hemoglobinuria / blackwater fever (black, brown, or red urine) (Harrison 22e pp.1764-1765)

Severe falciparum malaria (WHO-based criteria, Harrison 22e Table 231-2, p.1764) is defined by one or more of: unarousable coma/cerebral malaria (no localizing response, coma >30 min after a generalized convulsion, Glasgow Coma Score <11 or Blantyre <3 in young children); acidemia/acidosis (arterial pH <7.25, base deficit >8 meq/L, or plasma bicarbonate <15 mmol/L; venous lactate >=5 mmol/L; deep labored 'respiratory distress' breathing); severe normochromic normocytic anemia (hematocrit <15% or Hb <50 g/L with parasite density >10,000/uL); renal failure (creatinine >265 umol/L / >3 mg/dL); noncardiogenic pulmonary edema/ARDS (or O2 sat <92% on room air with respiratory rate >30/min); hypoglycemia (glucose <2.2 mmol/L / <40 mg/dL); hypotension/shock (systolic BP <70 mmHg in children 1-5 y or <80 mmHg in adults with impaired perfusion); significant bleeding/DIC; convulsions (>2 generalized seizures in 24 h); hemoglobinuria (macroscopic black/brown/red urine, not due to oxidant drugs or G6PD deficiency); extreme weakness/prostration; hyperparasitemia (>5% in nonimmune, >10% in any patient); and jaundice (bilirubin >50 umol/L / >3 mg/dL) with parasitemia >100,000/uL or other vital-organ dysfunction. Note: criteria thresholds for renal failure are for adults; lower values define severe disease in children. (Harrison 22e p.1764)

MCTD is an overlap autoimmune connective tissue disorder characterized by immune-mediated vasculopathy and fibrosis affecting skin, synovium, muscle, esophagus, lungs, and vasculature. It is strongly associated with high titers of antibody against the U1-RNP component of the spliceosome, which is thought to contribute to immune complex formation and endothelial injury. The vascular pathology, particularly intimal proliferation in pulmonary and other vessels, resembles that seen in systemic sclerosis and underlies the propensity for pulmonary arterial hypertension.
Consider MCTD in a patient with overlapping features of SLE, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis who does not neatly fit any single diagnosis.
Puffy, swollen ('sausage') fingers and severe Raynaud phenomenon are classic early findings, often preceding other manifestations by years.
High-titer anti-U1-ribonucleoprotein (anti-U1-RNP) antibody is the serologic hallmark and is required for diagnosis.
Pulmonary arterial hypertension is the leading cause of death and can develop insidiously, so periodic screening is warranted even when patients feel well.
Esophageal dysmotility and other sclerodermoid features are common, similar to limited systemic sclerosis.
Renal disease and severe CNS involvement are less frequent than in classic SLE, but can occur and should not be dismissed.
Clinical phenotype can evolve over time, and some patients eventually reclassify into a more defined connective tissue disease such as scleroderma or SLE.
Myositis in MCTD tends to respond well to glucocorticoids compared with some other overlap myopathies.
Attributing puffy hands and Raynaud phenomenon solely to early scleroderma without checking anti-U1-RNP and considering MCTD.
Failing to screen asymptomatic patients periodically for pulmonary arterial hypertension, the dominant cause of mortality.
Assuming a single high anti-U1-RNP titer alone confirms diagnosis without correlating with the required overlapping clinical features.
Overlooking that clinical features can evolve over years, sometimes prompting reclassification into a more defined connective tissue disease.

Overall prognosis is generally better than diffuse systemic sclerosis but variable, with outcomes largely determined by the degree of pulmonary vascular and interstitial lung involvement. Pulmonary arterial hypertension is the most significant predictor of mortality, making regular cardiopulmonary surveillance essential.

Burkholderia pseudomallei is a motile, aerobic, gram-negative bacillus that survives in soil and surface water in endemic tropical regions and enters the host through skin breaks, inhalation of aerosols, or ingestion. It is a facultative intracellular organism capable of escaping the phagosome, moving between cells via actin-based motility, and inducing multinucleated giant cell formation, which contributes to its capacity for chronic latency and later reactivation. Hematogenous dissemination from a primary site produces multifocal abscesses, and impaired cell-mediated and neutrophil function, as occurs in diabetes, markedly increases susceptibility to severe and disseminated disease.
Caused by the gram-negative soil and water saprophyte Burkholderia pseudomallei, endemic to Southeast Asia and northern Australia, with expanding recognition in South Asia, including India
Acquisition is via percutaneous inoculation, inhalation, or ingestion of contaminated soil/water, especially during monsoon/rainy season and after flooding
Diabetes mellitus is the dominant risk factor; other predispositions include chronic kidney disease, alcohol excess, chronic lung disease, thalassemia, and immunosuppression
Clinical spectrum ranges from localized cutaneous/subcutaneous infection to pneumonia (most common presentation) to overwhelming septicemia with multiple abscesses

Classically described as 'the great mimicker' because it can resemble tuberculosis radiographically (cavitary upper-lobe disease) and can produce abscesses in almost any organ, including spleen, liver, and prostate
Can present as an acute fulminant illness or as a chronic, indolent infection persisting for months to years, and may reactivate after decades of latency ('Vietnamese time bomb')
Requires laboratory alert to the microbiology lab, since B. pseudomallei can be mistaken for a contaminant or misidentified as another Burkholderia/Pseudomonas species on automated systems
Treatment is biphasic: an initial intensive intravenous phase followed by a prolonged oral eradication phase, reflecting the organism's propensity to relapse if therapy is inadequate
Dismissing B. pseudomallei growth in culture as an environmental contaminant, leading to missed or delayed diagnosis
Attributing cavitary lung disease to tuberculosis without considering melioidosis in endemic-exposure patients, delaying appropriate therapy
Underestimating the need for prolonged eradication-phase oral therapy, which risks relapse if truncated

Untreated septicemic melioidosis has historically carried very high mortality, and even with modern intensive-phase antimicrobial therapy, severe disseminated or septic shock presentations remain associated with substantial mortality, particularly in patients with diabetes or other comorbidities. With appropriate biphasic treatment and adequate follow-up, localized and non-septicemic disease generally carries a favorable outcome, though relapse can occur if eradication therapy is incomplete.

Membranous nephropathy results from in-situ formation of immune complexes along the subepithelial aspect of the glomerular basement membrane, most often triggered by autoantibodies against a native podocyte antigen (chiefly PLA2R, less commonly THSD7A or other targets) or against a planted exogenous/tumor antigen in secondary forms. Complement activation at the site of deposits leads to podocyte injury, cytoskeletal disruption, and a marked increase in glomerular capillary wall permeability to protein without significant inflammatory cell infiltration. Ongoing antigen-antibody deposition drives basement membrane thickening and the characteristic 'spike and dome' appearance seen on silver-stained biopsy over time. This process explains the disease's predominantly nephrotic (rather than nephritic) presentation.
Most common cause of primary nephrotic syndrome in non-diabetic White adults, typically presenting with heavy proteinuria and edema but preserved renal function early on.
About 70-80% of primary (idiopathic) cases are associated with circulating anti-PLA2R antibodies; a minority have anti-THSD7A antibodies instead.
Always screen for an underlying secondary cause (malignancy, autoimmune disease, infection, or drug exposure) before labeling disease as primary/idiopathic, especially in patients over 50-60 years.

Follows a 'rule of thirds' natural history in untreated primary disease: roughly one-third spontaneously remit, one-third have persistent proteinuria with stable function, and one-third progress to kidney failure over years.

Renal vein thrombosis and other thromboembolic events are disproportionately common because of the profound hypercoagulable state associated with heavy proteinuria and urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins.
Microscopic hematuria may be present, but heavy nephritic-range findings (red cell casts, marked hematuria) suggest an alternative or superimposed diagnosis.

Immunofluorescence classically shows granular capillary loop deposits of IgG (often IgG4-dominant in primary disease) and C3, with electron microscopy showing subepithelial deposits and spike formation on the basement membrane.
Response to therapy is slow (months), so treatment decisions and reassessment of remission should be based on sustained trends in proteinuria rather than short-term fluctuations.

Making treatment decisions based on a single proteinuria measurement rather than sustained trends, given the naturally fluctuating course and slow treatment response
Overlooking the markedly elevated thromboembolic risk and failing to consider prophylactic anticoagulation in severe nephrotic syndrome
Misinterpreting a negative anti-PLA2R antibody test as excluding membranous nephropathy, since a meaningful subset of primary cases are antibody-negative or have other target antigens

Renal outcomes are highly variable, with roughly equal proportions of patients undergoing spontaneous remission, persistent stable proteinuria, or progression to kidney failure over years if untreated; lower proteinuria, preserved renal function at diagnosis, and declining PLA2R antibody titers portend a better outcome, while persistent heavy proteinuria and reduced eGFR predict progression.

chunks.text: Bacterial meningitis is an acute purulent infection of the subarachnoid space accompanied by a CNS inflammatory reaction that can cause decreased consciousness, seizures, raised intracranial pressure and stroke; meninges, subarachnoid space and brain parenchyma are often jointly involved (meningoencephalitis). The leading organisms (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis) first colonize the nasopharynx, cross or breach the epithelium into the bloodstream, evade neutrophil phagocytosis and complement killing via their polysaccharide capsule, and reach the CSF through the choroid plexus or cerebral capillary endothelium. They multiply readily in CSF because normal CSF has few leukocytes and little complement/immunoglobulin, so opsonization and phagocytosis are poor. Much of the neurologic injury comes from the host inflammatory response rather than direct bacterial damage, so injury can progress even after antibiotics sterilize the CSF. Lysis of bacteria releases cell-wall components (gram-negative LPS; pneumococcal teichoic acid and peptidoglycan) that drive production of TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, chemokines and other mediators by microglia, astrocytes, monocytes, endothelium and CSF leukocytes. These cytokines increase blood-brain barrier permeability (vasogenic edema and protein leakage), the proteinaceous/leukocytic exudate obstructs CSF flow and resorption (obstructive and communicating hydrocephalus, interstitial edema), and neutrophil degranulation plus reactive oxygen/nitrogen species and excitatory amino acids produce cytotoxic edema and cell death (notably in the hippocampal dentate gyrus). Cerebral blood flow rises early then falls with loss of autoregulation; vasculitis and thrombosis of arteries, cortical veins and dural sinuses cause ischemia/infarction. The combined interstitial, vasogenic and cytotoxic edema raises ICP and can lead to coma and herniation (p.1118-1120).

chunks.text: Case-fatality varies by organism: roughly 3-7% for H. influenzae, N. meningitidis or group B streptococcal meningitis, about 15% for Listeria, and around 20% for pneumococcal meningitis. Risk of death rises with decreased consciousness on admission, seizures within 24 h, signs of raised ICP, age (infancy or >50 years), comorbidities such as shock or need for mechanical ventilation, and delay in starting treatment. A markedly low CSF glucose (<40 mg/dL) and very high CSF protein (>300 mg/dL) predict worse outcomes in some series. About 25% of survivors have moderate-to-severe sequelae, commonly decreased intellectual function, memory impairment, seizures, sensorineural hearing loss with dizziness, and gait disturbance (p.1123).

chunks.text: Harrison 22e does not provide a formal graded severity score for acute bacterial meningitis; it frames the disease as a medical emergency (goal: antibiotics within 60 min of arrival) and lists adverse prognostic markers (decreased consciousness on admission, seizures within 24 h, signs of raised ICP, age extremes, comorbidities such as shock/ventilation, treatment delay, very low CSF glucose, very high CSF protein). For distinguishing bacterial from aseptic meningitis in children, the prospectively validated Bacterial Meningitis Score is cited: very low probability (NPV ~99.7%) when all of negative CSF Gram stain, CSF neutrophils <1000/uL, CSF protein <80 mg/dL, peripheral ANC <10,000/uL, and no seizures are met (p.1123-1124).

chunks.text: Lumbar puncture with CSF analysis (cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, culture) — Confirms the diagnosis, identifies the organism, and guides definitive duration and choice of therapy — but should follow, not precede, empiric antibiotics if there is any delay.
Blood cultures (before antibiotics if no delay incurred) — Frequently positive in bacterial meningitis and may identify the organism if LP is delayed or contraindicated.

CT head (before LP only if specific indications: papilledema, focal neurological deficit, severely altered consciousness, seizures) — Screens for mass effect/herniation risk before LP in specific high-risk presentations — not required routinely and should not delay antibiotics.
Acute Bacterial Meningitis (infective) — Central Nervous System

veryLikely: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis; likely: Listeria monocytogenes (neonates, elderly, immunocompromised, pregnant); possible: Haemophilus influenzae (unvaccinated populations), Gram-negative bacilli (post-neurosurgery, immunocompromised)
Red flags: Immediate empiric antibiotics required

Microscopic colitis is thought to result from a dysregulated mucosal immune response to luminal antigens (including bile acids, bacterial products, and certain drugs) in a genetically or immunologically susceptible host, producing intraepithelial lymphocytic infiltration with or without subepithelial collagen deposition. This impairs colonic epithelial barrier function and fluid/electrolyte absorption, producing a secretory-type watery diarrhea without gross mucosal ulceration. The strong drug and autoimmune associations support an immune-mediated rather than structural mechanism.
Classic presentation is chronic, non-bloody, watery diarrhea in an older adult (often 60s-70s) with a grossly and endoscopically normal-appearing colon
Female predominance is marked, especially for the collagenous subtype
Strongly associated with NSAID use, proton pump inhibitors, SSRIs, and statins — a careful drug history is essential
Frequently coexists with autoimmune conditions such as celiac disease, autoimmune thyroiditis, and other connective tissue or rheumatologic disorders
Diagnosis requires random biopsies from multiple colonic segments even when mucosa looks endoscopically normal, since gross findings are typically absent
Two histologic subtypes — collagenous (thickened subepithelial collagen band) and lymphocytic (increased intraepithelial lymphocytes) — share similar clinical behavior and management
Nocturnal diarrhea and fecal urgency/incontinence are common and can significantly impair quality of life despite the benign histology
Weight loss and abdominal pain can occur but are typically milder than in classic inflammatory bowel disease
Assuming a normal-appearing colonoscopy excludes colitis — biopsies are mandatory since gross findings are usually absent
Failing to obtain biopsies from multiple segments, as histologic changes can be patchy or segment-specific
Overlooking a causative medication and treating chronically without attempting drug discontinuation
Missing coexisting celiac disease or bile acid diarrhea, which can perpetuate symptoms despite colitis-directed therapy

Microscopic colitis is a benign, non-progressive condition that does not increase colorectal cancer risk and often responds well to drug withdrawal or medical therapy, though relapses are common after treatment discontinuation and a subset of patients follow a chronic intermittent course.
Rectal bleeding, anemia, or weight loss suggesting an alternative or coexisting diagnosis rather than uncomplicated microscopic colitis
Severe dehydration or electrolyte disturbance from high-volume diarrhea
Failure to respond to standard therapy — warrants reassessment for IBD, celiac disease, or bile acid diarrhea
New abdominal pain, fever, or peritoneal signs, which are atypical and require evaluation for another process
Persistent symptoms despite discontinuation of an implicated drug
Microscopic colitis (non-infective) — Gastroenterology Also: microscopic colitis, collagenous colitis, lymphocytic colitis, MC, chronic watery diarrhea syndrome, minimal change colitis
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)
Membranous nephropathy
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis

Post-infectious glomerulonephritis

HIV-associated nephropathy
Urinalysis with microscopy — assess for selective proteinuria and absence of significant hematuria or cellular casts
24-hour urine protein or spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio — quantify nephrotic-range proteinuria
Serum albumin and lipid panel — confirm hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia typical of nephrotic syndrome
Renal function panel (creatinine, eGFR) — establish baseline and monitor for atypical renal impairment
Renal biopsy with electron microscopy — required in adults or steroid-resistant cases to confirm diagnosis and exclude FSGS/other glomerulopathies
Serum complement levels — typically normal in minimal change disease, helps exclude complement-mediated glomerulonephritides
Age-appropriate malignancy screening in adults — evaluate for underlying lymphoproliferative disease, especially if steroid-resistant
Coagulation studies/consideration of thromboembolic risk — nephrotic syndrome predisposes to venous thromboembolism
NSAID-induced acute interstitial nephritis with nephrotic-range proteinuria
Paraneoplastic nephrotic syndrome (Hodgkin lymphoma, other lymphoproliferative disorders)
Diabetic nephropathy
Amyloidosis

Minimal change disease is thought to result from a circulating permeability factor or T-cell/immune dysregulation that injures podocytes, causing effacement of their foot processes and loss of the glomerular filtration barrier's charge/size selectivity without structural glomerular damage visible by light microscopy. This leads to massive selective loss of albumin into the urine, producing hypoalbuminemia, decreased plasma oncotic pressure, and edema, along with compensatory hepatic lipoprotein synthesis causing hyperlipidemia. The glomerular basement membrane and capillary architecture otherwise remain intact, distinguishing it from other primary glomerulopathies.
Most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children (peak age 2-6 years) but also occurs in adults, sometimes elderly patients.
Presents with abrupt-onset heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and edema; renal function and blood pressure are typically preserved at onset.
Light microscopy is essentially normal ('minimal change'); diagnosis relies on electron microscopy showing diffuse podocyte foot-process effacement.
Excellent response to corticosteroids is characteristic and considered almost diagnostic in children; failure to respond should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis.
Frequent relapses and steroid dependence are common, often requiring steroid-sparing agents over time.
Can be triggered or associated with recent upper respiratory infection, atopy/allergy, immunizations, NSAID use, or (in adults) underlying lymphoproliferative disease (especially Hodgkin lymphoma).
Selective proteinuria (predominantly albumin, low IgG) on urine protein electrophoresis supports the diagnosis.
Thromboembolic risk and increased infection susceptibility parallel the severity of nephrotic syndrome regardless of underlying cause.
Assuming a normal light microscopy biopsy excludes glomerular disease without electron microscopy to assess podocyte foot processes
Delaying biopsy in adults presenting with nephrotic syndrome, where minimal change disease is less common and other etiologies must be excluded
Misclassifying steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome as minimal change disease when it more likely represents FSGS or another glomerulopathy
Overlooking secondary causes (drugs, malignancy) in adult-onset minimal change disease

Minimal change disease has an excellent overall prognosis, with the large majority of children and most adults achieving remission with corticosteroid therapy and rarely progressing to chronic kidney disease. However, relapses are common and some patients become steroid-dependent or frequently relapsing, necessitating steroid-sparing immunosuppressive strategies.
Steroid resistance or failure to achieve remission — reconsider diagnosis (likely FSGS) and pursue biopsy
Significant hematuria, hypertension, or renal impairment at presentation — atypical for minimal change disease, suggests alternative diagnosis
Signs of thromboembolism (limb swelling, chest pain, dyspnea) given hypercoagulable state of nephrotic syndrome
Severe hypovolemia or acute kidney injury from aggressive diuresis in the setting of low oncotic pressure
Signs of serious infection (peritonitis, cellulitis, sepsis) due to functional hypogammaglobulinemia and immunosuppressive therapy
New systemic symptoms (weight loss, lymphadenopathy, night sweats) in adults raising concern for occult malignancy
Minimal change disease (non-infective) — Nephrology Also: minimal change, MCD, minimal change nephropathy, nil disease, lipoid nephrosis, MCNS
Single-species P. falciparum malaria with an undetected coexisting vivax/ovale component (the central diagnostic trap of mixed infection)
P. knowlesi infection, which on RDT/microscopy may be misidentified as P. falciparum and can reach dangerously high densities (24-h cycle)
Recrudescent falciparum vs. true vivax/ovale relapse vs. reinfection as the cause of recurrent fever after treatment
Dengue (myalgia typically more severe than in malaria)
Leptospirosis (tender muscles, unlike malaria)
Typhus
Viral hemorrhagic fevers (petechiae/rash, which are very rare in malaria)
Bacterial sepsis with incidental parasitemia (concomitant bacteremia coexists with severe malaria and is hard to distinguish, especially in children)
Thick and thin Giemsa-stained blood films examined immediately for parasite demonstration AND species identification; examine 100-200 fields before calling a thick film negative
PCR amplification for definitive speciation and genotyping when mixed infection is suspected (more sensitive than microscopy/RDT for detecting and distinguishing species)
Combination RDT carrying a P. falciparum-specific antigen plus a pan-malaria or P. vivax band
Quantification of parasitemia (RDTs do not quantify) and assessment of parasite maturity/pigment for prognostic stratification
G6PD status (knowledge basis for safe hypnozoite-directed therapy of the vivax component) — testing rationale only

Sporozoites inoculated by anopheline mosquitoes reach the liver and undergo pre-erythrocytic schizogony; a single sporozoite yields thousands of merozoites that invade RBCs and multiply (every 48 h for P. falciparum and P. vivax). In P. vivax (and P. ovale) infection, a fraction of intrahepatic forms do not divide but persist as dormant hypnozoites for weeks to a year or more, later reactivating to cause relapses — a feature absent in P. falciparum. In a mixed P. falciparum + P. vivax infection, the falciparum component drives the risk of severe disease through cytoadherence (PfEMP1 binding endothelial receptors), rosetting, and agglutination, causing sequestration of mature parasites in vital organs; only ring forms circulate, so peripheral parasitemia underestimates true burden. P. vivax preferentially invades young reticulocytes and produces lower parasitemia (seldom >2%), while P. falciparum invades RBCs of all ages and can reach very high densities. The simultaneous presence of a vivax hypnozoite reservoir means blood-stage cure of both species does not prevent later vivax relapse (p.1760-1763).

Mixed infections (most commonly P. falciparum together with P. vivax) are frequently under-detected by light microscopy and rapid antigen tests; PCR is the most sensitive method and is increasingly used specifically for speciation and genotyping in mixed infections (p.1767).

Because microscopy and RDTs may detect only the dominant species, a smear or RDT reported as single-species (especially P. falciparum) does not exclude a coexisting vivax/ovale component carrying dormant liver-stage hypnozoites.
P. vivax + P. falciparum is recognized as a distinct co-circulating pattern in endemic mapping, with roughly equal prevalence of the two species in Oceania (p.1761-1762).

Standard combination RDTs typically carry one P. falciparum-specific band plus a pan-malaria or P. vivax band; this design distinguishes falciparum from the 'less dangerous' malarias but is not optimized to flag concurrent dual infection (p.1766).

RDTs may miss low-level P. vivax (and P. ovale/P. malariae) parasitemia and PfHRP2-based tests can be falsely negative where parasites carry HRP2/3 gene deletions — both failure modes can mask one component of a mixed infection (p.1766).

The classic regularly-spaced febrile paroxysm at presentation suggests P. vivax or P. ovale (often relapse); its presence in a patient with confirmed falciparum should raise suspicion of a coexisting vivax/ovale component.
Apparent vivax/ovale relapses arising after treatment of a mixed infection reflect persistence of liver-stage hypnozoites, which are not cleared by standard blood-stage schizonticides.

Treating an apparently single-species falciparum infection as if vivax were absent: the coexisting vivax hypnozoite reservoir is not cleared by blood-stage drugs and later causes relapse — manage mixed infection as falciparum AND provide hypnozoite-directed coverage for vivax.
Relying on microscopy or RDT alone to exclude a second species — both under-detect the minor component; PCR is needed to confirm/exclude mixed infection.
Misreading PfHRP2 RDT positivity that persists for weeks after a prior infection as evidence of the current species mix.
Mistaking persistent P. falciparum gametocytemia after treatment for treatment failure or active infection.
Attributing all post-treatment fever to falciparum recrudescence when it may be a true vivax/ovale relapse from the mixed-infection liver reservoir.
Misidentifying P. knowlesi as P. falciparum on microscopy/RDT, distorting the apparent species picture.

Promptly treated uncomplicated falciparum malaria has a mortality of <0.1%, but risk rises steeply once vital-organ dysfunction occurs or parasitemia exceeds ~2%. In a mixed infection the falciparum component dictates the severe-disease prognosis; cerebral malaria carries ~20% mortality in adults and ~15% in children even with treatment, and ~10% of child survivors have residual neurologic deficits (most improving within 6 months). Poor-prognosis features include hyperparasitemia (>100,000/uL), predominance of mature pigment-containing parasites (>20%), pigment in >5% of neutrophils, hypoglycemia, hyperlactatemia, acidemia, and coagulopathy. The vivax component does not usually drive mortality but, if its hypnozoite reservoir is not addressed, predisposes to later relapse and recurrent anemia (p.1763-1767).
Coma, obtundation, delirium, or abnormal behavior (cerebral malaria) — attributable to the falciparum component
Prostration / inability to sit or stand unaided
Repeated or generalized convulsions (>2 in 24 h)
Respiratory distress / acidotic deep breathing (acidosis, lactate >=5 mmol/L)
Hypoglycemia (<2.2 mmol/L)
Shock / hypotension with impaired perfusion
Severe normocytic anemia (Hct <15%) and/or spontaneous bleeding / DIC
Hemoglobinuria (black/brown/red urine)
Acute kidney injury (creatinine >265 umol/L)
Hyperparasitemia (>2% indicates increased risk; >5-10% defines severe disease) — a falciparum-driven marker

Severity is governed by the P. falciparum component per Harrison Table 231-2 (Manifestations of Severe Falciparum Malaria): major criteria include unarousable coma/cerebral malaria, acidosis (arterial pH <7.25 / lactate >=5 mmol/L), severe normocytic anemia (Hct <15%), renal failure (creatinine >265 umol/L), noncardiogenic pulmonary edema/ARDS, hypoglycemia (<2.2 mmol/L), hypotension/shock, bleeding/DIC, and repeated convulsions; other criteria include hemoglobinuria, prostration, and hyperparasitemia (>5% nonimmune, >10% any patient). Uncomplicated disease = patient can sit/stand unaided and swallow, with no vital-organ dysfunction and parasitemia <2% (p.1763-1764).

Peripheral blood smear (thick and thin film) confirming both species — Definitive method to confirm mixed infection and quantify parasitemia of each species, directly determining treatment approach and monitoring intensity.
Rapid diagnostic test (combination P.f/P.v if available) — Can support or suggest mixed infection rapidly, though smear remains the definitive confirmatory test.
G6PD testing — Mandatory before primaquine administration to avoid precipitating hemolysis in deficient patients.
CBC, renal function, blood glucose, LFTs — Screens for organ dysfunction that would classify this as severe/complicated malaria requiring IV therapy and escalated care.
Mixed Malaria (P. falciparum + P. vivax) (infective) — Tropical Fever
veryLikely: Plasmodium falciparum, Plasmodium vivax
Red flags: Urgent antimalarial therapy required (NOT an antibiotic)
Clostridial myonecrosis / gas gangrene (distinguished from clostridial NF by muscle biopsy)
Streptococcal necrotizing myositis (GAS infection extending into muscle)
Pyomyositis (usually S. aureus; localized, shock uncommon unless toxin-producing)
Synergistic nonclostridial anaerobic myonecrosis (necrotizing cutaneous myositis / synergistic necrotizing cellulitis) — a mixed aerobic-anaerobic variant
Cellulitis / erysipelas (superficial; skin more abnormal but pain mild-moderate)
Halophilic Vibrio vulnificus infection (can be as fulminant as NF; Gulf/Atlantic water exposure or raw seafood in cirrhosis)
Aeromonas soft-tissue infection (freshwater laceration exposure)
Aggressive cellulitis from Vibrio vulnificus or Aeromonas hydrophila
Ecthyma gangrenosum (Pseudomonas, neutropenic hosts)
Clostridial myonecrosis

Soft-tissue plain radiography, CT, and MRI to assess depth of infection and detect tissue gas or a localized abscess — most useful when lesions progress rapidly or SIRS is present; note imaging may show only soft-tissue swelling and is NOT specific for fulminant GAS NF/myonecrosis, where gas is typically absent
Gram stain and aerobic/anaerobic culture of surgically excised tissue to identify GAS vs mixed flora vs MRSA vs Clostridium
Frozen-section histology of aspirate or punch biopsy (valuable in NF), though aspiration/biopsy is negative in ~80% of cases
Serum CPK (markedly elevated when myonecrosis coexists)
Lactate, d-dimer, coagulation, liver and renal function as markers of systemic toxicity/organ failure
Thrombophlebitis (a common early misdiagnosis)
Muscle strain or contusion (the minor trauma at the deep nidus)

NF is infection of the superficial and/or deep fascia investing the muscles of an extremity or trunk, with extensive necrosis of subcutaneous tissue and fascia. Infection spreads rapidly along fascial planes and via venous channels and lymphatics, typically sparing the muscle itself in pure fasciitis. Two main microbiologic patterns: a mixed aerobic-anaerobic (type I) process beginning with a breach of a mucosal barrier (GI/GU tract), and a monomicrobial group A streptococcal (type II) process. In GAS disease, organisms reach deep fascia either by transient bacteremic seeding at a site of minor non-penetrating trauma (no portal) or by spread from cutaneous infection/penetrating trauma. Thrombosis of dermal vessels produces progressive skin necrosis; infarction of cutaneous nerves causes the characteristic late anesthesia. NF caused by Clostridium perfringens or extending into muscle (clostridial/streptococcal myonecrosis) carries very high systemic toxicity with hemolysis. PVL-producing MRSA strains have been reported as a cause.

Pain out of proportion to physical findings is the classic early clue: physical signs may be minimal (only soft-tissue edema and mild erythema) while pain and fever are severe; this disparity helps distinguish NF from superficial cellulitis, where skin appearance is more abnormal but pain is only mild-to-moderate.

Early disease is frequently misdiagnosed (e.g., as thrombophlebitis) and patients may be sent home with analgesics, especially in the strep type that begins deep at a site of non-penetrating minor trauma (bruise, muscle strain) with no visible portal of entry.

Classic late signs evolve sequentially: swelling and brawny edema/tenderness, then dark-red (violaceous) induration, then bullae filled with blue/purple fluid, then friable bluish-maroon-to-black skin; thrombosis of dermal-papillae vessels is extensive by this stage.
Paradoxical decrease in pain or progression to anesthesia over the involved area is an ominous sign reflecting thrombosis of small vessels and infarction of cutaneous nerves.
GAS NF can be preceded by varicella, childbirth, or muscle strain, and most patients deny an antecedent streptococcal infection.
The inoculation site may be inapparent and remote from clinical involvement (e.g., minor hand trauma manifesting as infection over the shoulder or chest).
Myositis/myonecrosis coexists with NF in roughly 20-50% of cases and serum creatine phosphokinase (CPK) may be markedly elevated, signaling deeper muscle involvement.
Early physical findings are minimal relative to pain/fever, leading to underestimation of severity and misdiagnosis as thrombophlebitis or simple cellulitis.
Absence of gas does NOT exclude NF: gas is usually absent when the cause is GAS or MRSA and is seen mainly with mixed/clostridial infection.
Normal or nonspecific imaging does NOT rule out NF — CT/MRI may show only soft-tissue swelling and are not specific for fulminant GAS NF/myonecrosis.
A negative aspirate or frozen-section biopsy does NOT exclude NF (negative in ~80% of cases).
Decreasing pain should not be reassuring — it can signal nerve infarction and disease progression rather than improvement.
Do not wait for imaging or cultures when NF is suspected with systemic toxicity; surgical exploration is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

Mortality for NF is roughly 11-34% overall and rises substantially when associated with toxic shock syndrome. GAS/clostridial fascial-muscle infection historically carried 20-50% mortality with penicillin alone. Survivors of GAS NF often require repeated surgeries including amputation. Clostridial NF/myonecrosis is far more lethal: spontaneous (nontraumatic) myonecrosis mortality exceeds 65% (often C. septicum with underlying malignancy); trunk infection ~63% vs limb ~12% mortality. Any delay in surgery increases the risk of death; early aggressive surgery markedly improves outcomes.
Pain out of proportion to examination findings
Rapidly progressing lesion with signs of systemic inflammatory response / toxicity
Violaceous (blue/purple) bullae, skin sloughing, dusky/mottled erythema
Progression of tenderness to anesthesia over the lesion (cutaneous nerve infarction)
Crepitus or gas in deep tissue (suggests mixed/clostridial infection)
Renal impairment that may precede shock, plus hypotension/multiorgan failure
Urgent surgical exploration supersedes other diagnostic or therapeutic maneuvers — debridement is life-saving and must not be delayed

Microbiologic/clinical typing: Type I = mixed aerobic-anaerobic, begins at a mucosal-barrier breach (GI/GU), common in diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, malignancy, surgery, or abdominal penetrating injury; Fournier gangrene is the perineal/scrotal form. Type II = monomicrobial group A streptococcal (GAS implicated in ~60% of NF cases), can occur in otherwise healthy hosts, two presentations (with vs without a defined portal of entry). PVL-producing MRSA is a recognized monomicrobial cause. NF qualifies as soft-tissue necrosis under the CDC streptococcal toxic shock syndrome case definition (hypotension plus >=2 of: renal impairment, coagulopathy, hepatic impairment, ARDS, generalized erythematous desquamating rash, soft-tissue necrosis/NF/myositis/gangrene). (LRINEC score not described in this source.)

Urgent surgical exploration (diagnostic AND therapeutic) — The definitive diagnostic test — direct visualization of necrotic fascia confirms the diagnosis and simultaneously allows debridement; imaging should not delay surgery when clinical suspicion is high.
Blood cultures and intraoperative tissue/fluid cultures — Identifies the causative organism(s) to guide de-escalation.
CT or MRI (only if diagnosis uncertain and patient stable enough to tolerate delay) — May show fascial thickening/gas, but should never delay surgery in a patient with high clinical suspicion.
CPK — Markedly elevated levels suggest muscle involvement (myonecrosis), affecting the extent of surgical debridement needed.

LRINEC score (Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis) — Can support clinical suspicion using CRP, WBC, hemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, and glucose, though it should not override strong clinical suspicion if score is low.
Necrotizing Fasciitis (infective) — Skin & Soft Tissue

veryLikely: Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus) — monomicrobial type II, Polymicrobial flora including anaerobes and Enterobacteriaceae — type I (more common, often in diabetics/immunocompromised); likely: Staphylococcus aureus (including community-associated MRSA), Clostridium species (if gas gangrene/myonecrosis); possible: Vibrio vulnificus (if marine/brackish water exposure), Aeromonas species (if freshwater exposure)
Red flags: Immediate empiric antibiotics required

[guideline] empiric → Piperacillin-tazobactam + Clindamycin + Vancomycin This combination covers polymicrobial type I infection (pip-tazo), provides antitoxin effect against streptococcal/staphylococcal toxin production (clindamycin, via protein synthesis inhibition), and covers MRSA (vancomycin) — maximal reasonable empiric coverage is justified given the extreme mortality risk.
[guideline] alternative → Meropenem + Clindamycin + Vancomycin (broader gram-negative coverage if indicated)
[guideline] alternative → IVIG (adjunctive, for confirmed streptococcal toxic shock features)

Acute pharyngitis (symptoms generally present for days) is most often caused by respiratory viruses; group A beta-hemolytic streptococci (GAS, Streptococcus pyogenes) are a frequent bacterial cause, with other contributors including Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Epstein-Barr virus, HIV, non-group-A streptococci (groups C and G), Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae. Complications of GAS pharyngitis arise from both suppurative spread (e.g., peritonsillar abscess, sinusitis, other invasive GAS infection) and nonsuppurative immune-mediated sequelae (acute rheumatic fever, poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, scarlet fever) (Harrison 22e p.300-301).

Sore throat is not synonymous with pharyngitis: it may also arise from submandibular/retropharyngeal/peritonsillar space infections, thyroiditis, gastroesophageal reflux, tumors, or postnasal drainage (Harrison 22e p.300).

In children the Centor criteria are less specific, so GAS pharyngitis should be confirmed by testing; children with pharyngitis but no viral signs (conjunctivitis, runny nose, cough, hoarseness, nonexudative oral lesions) warrant testing (Harrison 22e p.301).
In developed countries the prevalence of rheumatic fever is extremely low, and antibiotic treatment does not prevent poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (Harrison 22e p.300).

Full-blown infectious mononucleosis (EBV) appears in only about one-fourth of cases and is a triad of clinical, hematologic, and serologic findings; new EBV causes 1-6% of pharyngitis in young adults and is rare over age 40 (Harrison 22e p.301).
Heterophil antibody is detectable in only ~40% of mononucleosis patients in the first week but in 80-90% by the third week, so an early negative test does not exclude EBV (Harrison 22e p.302).

Gonococcal pharyngitis is more often asymptomatic than symptomatic; suspect it with persistent sore throat unresponsive to presumptive strep treatment and relevant sexual exposure (Harrison 22e p.302).
Diphtheria produces only mild pharyngitis beneath its characteristic grayish pseudomembrane (Harrison 22e p.302).
Acute HIV infection causes sore throat in roughly half of cases; consider it when sore throat accompanies headache, fever, myalgias, lymphadenopathy, anorexia, and rash (Harrison 22e p.302).
Pharyngeal erythema is most commonly seen with viral infection (common cold, influenza), not bacterial disease (Harrison 22e p.300).

Pharyngeal exudate can be mimicked by Candida (cottage-cheese appearance, scrapes off leaving a bleeding surface) or leukoplakia (cannot be scraped off) — do not equate exudate with bacterial pharyngitis (Harrison 22e p.300).
GAS is the only common cause of sore throat that warrants antibiotics; most non-GAS pharyngitis is viral and self-limited (Harrison 22e p.300).
About 10% of adults with sore throat have GAS; in children the prevalence may reach ~35%, peaking at ages 5-15 years, and is higher in winter and early spring (Harrison 22e p.300).

Risk of GAS pharyngitis is elevated in health care and child care workers, teachers, parents of young children, and contacts of known strep cases; clinicians should watch for local outbreaks in military and institutional settings (Harrison 22e p.300).
GAS carriage is common (up to ~20% of schoolchildren, ~5% of adolescents/young adults); rapid antigen tests and culture cannot distinguish true infection from carriage (Harrison 22e p.301).

In adults meeting zero or one Centor criterion, a positive GAS test is very likely a false positive and/or represents carriage; indiscriminate testing of adults with sore throat is discouraged (Harrison 22e p.301).

Lower the threshold to test/treat GAS in patients with a history of acute rheumatic fever, documented strep exposure in the past week, those in a community strep epidemic, and diabetic or immunocompromised patients (Harrison 22e p.301).
Prescribing antibiotics to the majority of adults with sore throat despite only ~10% having GAS — most cases are viral (Harrison 22e p.300).
Testing adults who meet zero or one Centor criterion: 40-60% of adults with pharyngitis fall here, and a positive test is highly likely to be false-positive or carriage (Harrison 22e p.301).
Relying on throat culture or rapid test to distinguish active infection from GAS carriage — neither can (Harrison 22e p.301).
Applying adult Centor criteria to children, in whom they are less specific (Harrison 22e p.301).
Mistaking Candida or leukoplakia for bacterial pharyngeal exudate (Harrison 22e p.300).
Attempting to examine or swab the posterior pharynx in suspected epiglottitis — this can provoke laryngospasm and should only be done in a controlled setting (Harrison 22e p.302).
Assuming antibiotic treatment of GAS prevents poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis — it does not (Harrison 22e p.300).
A negative early heterophil antibody test does not rule out EBV mononucleosis (Harrison 22e p.302).

Both streptococcal and nonstreptococcal pharyngitis should resolve within 3-5 days. Nonsuppurative complications are rare, and even streptococcal pharyngitis is self-limited in the vast majority of cases; outside the U.S., because complications are rare, some guidelines do not recommend routine GAS testing or antibiotic treatment of sore throat (Harrison 22e p.301).
Shaking chills/rigors, neck swelling beyond lymphadenopathy, trouble swallowing, drooling, or symptoms persisting >5 days without improvement should prompt urgent re-evaluation (Harrison 22e p.301)
Stridor, dyspnea, hoarseness, or tripod/forward-leaning posture with drooling — suggests epiglottitis and impending airway obstruction (Harrison 22e p.302)
Non-GAS pharyngitis that is not resolving in a teenager/young adult with rigors, neck pain or swelling, or extrapharyngeal symptoms — suspect Lemierre syndrome (Harrison 22e p.302)

Centor criteria (4 findings, 1 point each): history of fever, absence of cough, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and tonsillar exudate or swelling. For an adult pretest probability of ~10%, post-evaluation probability of GAS is ~2% at 0 points, ~3% at 1, ~8% at 2, ~19% at 3, and ~41% at 4 points (area under the curve 0.79). Conceptually: 0-1 criteria -> neither test nor treat; 2-3 -> rapid antigen test to guide management; 4 -> rapid test or empirical treatment. (Harrison 22e p.300-301).

PNH arises from an acquired somatic mutation in the X-linked PIGA gene within a hematopoietic stem cell, impairing synthesis of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor required to display several surface proteins. Loss of the complement regulators CD55 (decay-accelerating factor) and CD59 (membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis) leaves the abnormal red cell clone vulnerable to unchecked complement-mediated intravascular lysis. The clonal population expands, often in the setting of an immune-mediated marrow injury that gives PIGA-mutant cells a relative survival advantage, producing the combination of hemolysis, cytopenias, and a pro-thrombotic state linked to platelet and microparticle complement activation.

Acquired clonal stem-cell disorder from a somatic PIGA gene mutation, leading to loss of GPI-anchored surface proteins (including CD55 and CD59) that normally protect red cells from complement attack.
Classic triad is intravascular hemolysis, marrow failure/cytopenias, and a marked thrombotic tendency, though most patients present with only one or two of these features.
Morning hemoglobinuria is a well-known feature but is actually seen in only a minority of patients; hemolysis is often chronic and low-grade rather than dramatically episodic.
Thrombosis is the leading cause of death and characteristically occurs at unusual sites — hepatic (Budd-Chiari), portal, mesenteric, cerebral (dural sinus), and dermal veins.
Consider PNH in any patient with unexplained hemolysis plus cytopenia, or with venous thrombosis at an atypical site, especially with a normal or low platelet count.
PNH clones frequently coexist with, precede, or follow aplastic anemia and myelodysplastic syndrome, reflecting a shared marrow-failure background.
Smooth muscle dystonia (esophageal spasm, erectile dysfunction, abdominal pain) results from free-hemoglobin-mediated nitric oxide scavenging rather than mechanical obstruction.
Flow cytometry for GPI-anchored proteins (e.g., FLAER, CD55/CD59) on granulocytes and red cells is the diagnostic test of choice, replacing older Ham's and sucrose lysis tests.
Assuming hemoglobinuria must be present and grossly visible; many patients have only subclinical or intermittent hemolysis
Missing the diagnosis in a patient with unexplained thrombosis at an atypical site because cytopenias are mild or absent
Relying on outdated Ham's/sucrose lysis tests instead of flow cytometry, which is far more sensitive and specific
Overlooking a coexisting or antecedent marrow failure syndrome (aplastic anemia, MDS) when a PNH clone is found

Historically PNH carried significant mortality, largely from thrombosis and marrow failure, but complement-inhibitor therapy has markedly improved survival and quality of life. Long-term outcome also depends on clone size and any associated bone marrow failure syndrome, with a small risk of progression to MDS or acute leukemia over time.

Severe abdominal or chest pain with hemolysis flare, which may signal smooth-muscle dystonia or thrombotic event
Pregnancy in a known PNH patient, which carries substantially increased maternal thrombotic and fetal risk
Acute kidney injury from massive hemoglobinuria or renal vein thrombosis

POEMS syndrome arises from an underlying monoclonal, lambda-restricted plasma cell disorder that drives systemic overproduction of proinflammatory and proangiogenic cytokines, most notably vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). This cytokine excess is thought to underlie the vascular, neurologic, and organ-based manifestations rather than direct tumor infiltration, distinguishing the disease from classic multiple myeloma. The resulting syndrome combines a chronic demyelinating polyneuropathy with multisystem involvement including bone, endocrine, dermatologic, and extravascular fluid abnormalities.
Rare paraneoplastic disorder driven by an underlying clonal plasma cell process, almost always with lambda light-chain restriction.
Peripheral polyneuropathy is typically the presenting and most disabling feature — usually a symmetric, ascending, demyelinating sensorimotor pattern resembling CIDP.
Suspect POEMS when 'CIDP' fails to respond to standard immunotherapy, especially if accompanied by systemic features.
Sclerotic bone lesions (solitary or multiple) are common and often visible on skeletal survey or CT even without lytic disease typical of myeloma.
Papilledema, extravascular volume overload (ascites, edema, effusions), and thrombocytosis/erythrocytosis are distinctive clues that separate POEMS from typical myeloma or CIDP.
Markedly elevated serum VEGF is a hallmark biomarker reflecting disease activity.
Endocrinopathies (commonly hypogonadism, hypothyroidism, or glucose intolerance) are frequent but nonspecific, and should not be over-interpreted alone.
Skin changes (hyperpigmentation, thickening, hypertrichosis, glomeruloid hemangiomas) support the diagnosis when present alongside neuropathy.
Misdiagnosing as idiopathic CIDP and treating with standard immunotherapy (e.g., IVIG/plasma exchange) alone, which is typically ineffective since the underlying plasma cell clone is not addressed
Overlooking sclerotic bone lesions on imaging because they lack the classic lytic appearance of multiple myeloma
Failing to check serum VEGF or overinterpreting an isolated endocrinopathy without considering the full multisystem picture
Anchoring on a single feature (e.g., organomegaly) rather than recognizing the required combination of core diagnostic criteria

With clone-directed therapy, many patients achieve meaningful and durable improvement in neuropathy and systemic features, and overall survival is generally more favorable than multiple myeloma. However, residual neurologic deficits are common, and relapse or progression can occur, warranting long-term surveillance of the monoclonal marker and VEGF level.
Rapidly progressive neuropathy with respiratory or bulbar involvement
New papilledema suggesting raised intracranial pressure
Signs of extravascular volume overload (ascites, pleural effusion, peripheral edema) indicating advancing systemic disease
Evidence of pulmonary hypertension or thrombotic events, which portend higher morbidity
Rapid rise in serum VEGF or new osteolytic transformation suggesting progression or evolution toward myeloma

Autonomous, renin-independent overproduction of aldosterone from one or both adrenal glands leads to sodium retention, potassium and hydrogen ion wasting, and volume-mediated hypertension. The excess mineralocorticoid activity suppresses plasma renin and can produce hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, though many patients remain normokalemic. Beyond hemodynamic effects, chronic aldosterone excess produces direct pro-fibrotic and pro-inflammatory effects on the heart, vasculature, and kidney that account for disproportionate target-organ damage relative to blood pressure alone.
Consider in any hypertensive patient with spontaneous or diuretic-induced hypokalemia, treatment-resistant hypertension, or an incidentally found adrenal mass
Most patients are normokalemic at presentation; hypokalemia is present in only a minority, so a normal potassium does not exclude the diagnosis
Plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio is the preferred screening test and should be checked before starting mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists

Screening should target patients with sustained BP above standard thresholds, resistant hypertension, hypertension with an adrenal incidentaloma, or hypertension with sleep apnea or a family history of early-onset hypertension/stroke
Unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma and bilateral adrenal hyperplasia are the two dominant subtypes and require different management (surgery versus mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist)
Adrenal vein sampling is generally required to distinguish unilateral from bilateral disease before considering surgery, since imaging alone is unreliable in this regard

Correcting the underlying aldosterone excess improves blood pressure control and reduces the excess cardiovascular and renal risk associated with this condition beyond what is expected from hypertension alone
Failing to correct hypokalemia and withdraw interfering drugs (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, high-dose diuretics) before aldosterone-to-renin ratio testing, leading to false results
Relying on adrenal CT alone to decide unilateral versus bilateral disease instead of adrenal vein sampling, risking inappropriate or missed surgery

With correct subtype classification, unilateral disease treated surgically often achieves cure or major improvement of hypertension and hypokalemia, while bilateral disease managed medically with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists generally achieves good blood pressure control. Untreated or unrecognized disease carries excess risk of cardiovascular events, stroke, and chronic kidney disease compared with blood-pressure-matched essential hypertension.

PBC is an autoimmune, T-cell-mediated process that progressively destroys small and medium intrahepatic bile ducts, producing chronic cholestasis. Ongoing bile duct injury leads to periportal inflammation, fibrosis, and eventually biliary-type cirrhosis if untreated. Genetic susceptibility combined with environmental triggers is thought to break tolerance to mitochondrial autoantigens, driving the characteristic antimitochondrial antibody response.
Consider in middle-aged women with fatigue, pruritus, and an isolated cholestatic (alkaline phosphatase-predominant) liver panel
Pruritus often precedes jaundice by months to years and may be the presenting complaint

Hyperlipidemia is common but does not appear to confer the usual cardiovascular risk seen in the general population
Fat-soluble vitamin deficiency and metabolic bone disease (osteoporosis) develop as cholestasis progresses

PSC is thought to result from an immune-mediated process in genetically susceptible individuals, possibly triggered by altered gut permeability and microbial translocation related to colonic inflammation, leading to periductal inflammation and concentric fibrosis of bile ducts. Progressive fibro-obliteration produces multifocal strictures with intervening dilations, eventually causing biliary obstruction, secondary bacterial cholangitis, and biliary cirrhosis. The disease can involve both intra- and extrahepatic ducts, and a small-duct variant exists without visible cholangiographic changes.
Chronic cholestatic disease marked by progressive fibrosing inflammation and stricturing of intra- and/or extrahepatic bile ducts
Strongly linked to inflammatory bowel disease, particularly ulcerative colitis; colitis may be quiescent or diagnosed after PSC
Predominantly affects young to middle-aged men; often discovered incidentally via persistently elevated alkaline phosphatase
Fluctuating cholestatic pattern (elevated alkaline phosphatase and GGT) is typical, with variable bilirubin depending on stricture burden
Cholangiography (MRCP preferred over ERCP for initial diagnosis) shows characteristic multifocal strictures alternating with normal or dilated segments (beaded appearance)

Carries increased lifetime risk of cholangiocarcinoma, gallbladder cancer, and colorectal cancer (in those with concurrent colitis)

PSC follows a variable but generally progressive course over years to decades, often culminating in biliary cirrhosis and end-stage liver disease; median transplant-free survival historically has been reported around a decade or more from diagnosis, though course varies widely between patients. Cholangiocarcinoma and colorectal cancer (in those with IBD) are major contributors to morbidity and mortality.
