Chronic bacterial prostatitis (CBP) — presents insidiously as recurrent episodes of cystitis, sometimes with pelvic and perineal pain, usually without systemic signs of infection; should be suspected with recurrent UTI not in the context of catheterization (Harrison 22e p.1089, p.1136).
Pyelonephritis — another febrile genitourinary infection that must be excluded as the anatomic source before attributing systemic symptoms to ABP (Harrison 22e p.1136).
Acute cystitis in men — uncommon and warrants caution; urine culture should be obtained in all male UTI to help identify a prostatic focus (Harrison 22e p.1089).
Pyelonephritis — overlapping febrile UTI presentation; distinguished by flank/costovertebral angle pain and an upper-tract source (Harrison 22e p.1089).

Urethritis — urethral pain, pruritus, or discharge should prompt evaluation for sexually transmitted infections (Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium) rather than assuming prostatitis (Harrison 22e p.1087).

Urine culture in all male UTI — documenting bacteriuria differentiates bacterial prostatitis from chronic pelvic pain syndrome; dipstick and/or microscopy alone are not sufficient (Harrison 22e p.1089).

Cross-sectional imaging (CT or ultrasound) for men with febrile UTI, including the first episode, if not previously done, to evaluate for urinary tract abnormalities or obstruction (Harrison 22e p.1089).
Evaluation for urinary retention / prostatic focus in men with recurrent cystitis (Harrison 22e p.1089).
Urologic consultation referral if the diagnosis of UTI is unclear or UTI is recurrent (Harrison 22e p.1089).

Chronic pelvic pain syndrome (formerly chronic prostatitis) — a noninfectious disorder that is the far more common cause of prostatic-type symptoms, with NO bacteriuria and NO response to antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.1089).
Benign prostatic hypertrophy with obstructive uropathy / urinary retention — can produce lower urinary tract symptoms and predispose to UTI (Harrison 22e p.1089, p.1131).

Prostatitis can complicate ascending cystitis or arise hematogenously, for example as a metastatic focus of Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia. Infectious prostatitis is almost always bacterial and is far less common than the noninfectious chronic pelvic pain syndrome. In general, most genitourinary infections in men ascend from the urethra to the bladder, with the prostate becoming involved as part of febrile UTI; less than 2% of UTIs are hematogenous, usually from virulent organisms such as S. aureus and Salmonella. Obstruction from prostatic hypertrophy after age 50 promotes urinary stasis and is a major reason UTI incidence in older men approaches that in women (Harrison 22e p.1087, p.1089, p.1131).

Acute bacterial prostatitis (ABP) typically presents as a severe illness with dysuria, urinary frequency, and pain in the prostatic, pelvic, or perineal region, and may be accompanied by fever, rigors, and/or bladder outlet obstruction (Harrison 22e p.1089).

The prostate is involved in the majority of febrile UTI cases in men; ABP should be specifically suspected when a man presents with UTI plus systemic symptoms but no other clear anatomic source such as pyelonephritis (Harrison 22e p.1089, p.1136).

Bacteriuria documented on urine culture is what distinguishes the less common bacterial prostatitis syndromes (acute and chronic) from the far more common chronic pelvic pain syndrome, which is NOT associated with bacteriuria and is NOT improved by antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.1089).

Men with febrile UTI may show an elevated serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) and an enlarged prostate and seminal vesicles on ultrasound, supporting prostatic involvement; PSA is therefore not interpretable as a cancer marker during acute infection (Harrison 22e p.1089).

Prostatitis is largely unrepresented in UTI clinical trial data, so complicated-UTI practice guidelines cannot be assumed to apply to prostatitis; older literature suggests prolonged therapy with prostate-penetrating agents may be needed (Harrison 22e p.1087).

Do not attribute prostatic-type symptoms to bacterial prostatitis without bacteriuria; absence of bacteriuria points to chronic pelvic pain syndrome, which will not respond to antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.1089).
Do not interpret an elevated PSA during febrile male UTI as a cancer marker — acute prostatic infection itself raises PSA and prostate/seminal vesicle size on imaging (Harrison 22e p.1089).

Do not assume complicated-UTI guideline regimens and durations apply to prostatitis, since prostatitis is largely absent from UTI trial data and may require prolonged prostate-penetrating therapy (Harrison 22e p.1087).
Do not overlook a prostatic focus or urinary retention in men presenting with recurrent cystitis (Harrison 22e p.1089).

ABP is typically a severe acute illness but is amenable to therapy with prostate-penetrating antimicrobials. A prostatic abscess is a recognized complication requiring urologic intervention. Chronic bacterial prostatitis recurrences are not uncommon. Men with febrile UTI and none of the warning features (retention, early recurrence, hematuria, voiding difficulty) generally have normal upper and lower urinary tracts on urologic workup, implying a favorable structural prognosis (Harrison 22e p.1089, p.1136).
Bladder outlet obstruction or urinary retention accompanying ABP (Harrison 22e p.1089).
Fever and rigors indicating a severe, systemic illness (Harrison 22e p.1089).
Identification of a prostatic abscess — should prompt urologic specialist consultation (Harrison 22e p.1136).
Symptoms predictive of surgically correctable disease in men with febrile UTI: urinary retention, early UTI recurrence, hematuria at follow-up, and voiding difficulties (Harrison 22e p.1089).

Prostatitis is categorized as acute bacterial prostatitis (ABP) versus chronic bacterial prostatitis (CBP). ABP is a typically severe illness with systemic features (fever, rigors, possible bladder outlet obstruction); CBP presents insidiously as recurrent cystitis with pelvic/perineal pain and typically without systemic signs, often managed in the ambulatory setting. Both are distinct from noninfectious chronic pelvic pain syndrome (Harrison 22e p.1089, p.1136).
Urinalysis and urine culture — Identifies the causative organism; this is preferred over prostatic secretion sampling in the acute setting given bacteremia risk with prostatic massage.
Blood cultures (if febrile/systemically unwell) — Bacteremia is not uncommon in acute prostatitis and positive cultures help confirm the organism.

Post-void residual / bladder scan (if retention suspected) — Urinary retention is a recognized complication requiring catheterization (suprapubic preferred over urethral if prostatitis is causing obstruction).
STI testing (NAAT for gonorrhea/chlamydia) if risk factors present — Identifies sexually transmitted causes requiring different management and partner notification.
Acute Bacterial Prostatitis (infective) — Genitourinary

veryLikely: Escherichia coli; likely: Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis, Enterococcus species; possible: Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis (younger sexually active men — different management)

[guideline] empiric → Ciprofloxacin Fluoroquinolones achieve excellent prostatic tissue penetration, which is essential since many antibiotics with good urinary concentration do not adequately penetrate prostatic tissue; prolonged duration (longer than typical UTI) reduces the risk of chronic prostatitis.
[guideline] alternative → Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (if susceptible)
[guideline] alternative → Ceftriaxone + Azithromycin/Doxycycline (if STI risk in younger sexually active men)
Bronchogenic carcinoma (lung cancer) - upper-lobe mass/cavity, hemoptysis, weight loss; patients with such radiographic findings often undergo bronchoscopy/biopsy to distinguish from TB (p.1393)

Nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease (e.g., M. avium complex, M. kansasii) - AFB-positive smear with limited CXR abnormality, favoured by absence of TB risk factors and presence of underlying chronic lung disease (p.1393)

Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis / aspergilloma colonising an old TB cavity - hemoptysis, weight loss, fatigue, often misdiagnosed as TB recurrence; Aspergillus IgG precipitins and a fungal ball within a cavity suggest the diagnosis (p.1390-1391)
Bacterial lung abscess / necrotising pneumonia (cavitary lesion with air-fluid level) (p.1386)
Nontuberculous mycobacteria (M. avium complex, M. kansasii) causing AFB-positive cavitary or nodular lung disease (p.1393)
Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis / aspergilloma in residual cavities mimicking TB relapse (p.1390-1391)
Bacterial lung abscess or necrotising pneumonia producing upper-lobe cavitation (p.1386)
Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra (next-generation NAAT with higher sensitivity in smear-negative and HIV-positive cases) (p.1392)
Urine lateral-flow lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) assay in advanced HIV (p.1393)
Chest CT to clarify equivocal plain-film findings (p.1393)

Tuberculin skin test (TST/PPD) and IFN-gamma release assays (IGRA: QuantiFERON-TB Gold/Plus, T-SPOT.TB) to identify TB infection - note both have low predictive value for who will progress and cannot distinguish infection from active disease (p.1393-1394)
M. tuberculosis antigen-based skin tests (TBSTs using ESAT-6/CFP-10) with accuracy similar to IGRA (p.1394)
Truenat MTB / MTB Plus and Truenat MTB-Rif Dx - portable, battery-operated molecular tests for peripheral settings (p.1392)
Line probe assays (LPAs) for rapid detection of rifampin (rpoB) and isoniazid (katG, inhA) resistance, and second-line LPAs for fluoroquinolone/injectable resistance (p.1393)
Liquid culture (MGIT) as WHO reference standard; solid media (Lowenstein-Jensen, Middlebrook 7H10/7H11) require 4-8 weeks (p.1392)
Universal drug-susceptibility testing - at minimum rifampin DST on all initial isolates (p.1392-1393)
Targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) and whole-genome sequencing for comprehensive resistance profiling (p.1393)
Sputum induction with hypertonic saline when spontaneous sputum cannot be produced (p.1393)
Fiberoptic bronchoscopy with bronchial brushings, endobronchial/transbronchial biopsy, and bronchoalveolar lavage (submit for Xpert, culture, AFB smear) (p.1393)
Early-morning gastric lavage / induced sputum for children unable to expectorate (p.1393)
Bronchogenic carcinoma presenting as a cavitary upper-lobe mass with hemoptysis and weight loss (p.1393)
Solitary pulmonary nodule - TB can present as one, overlapping with neoplastic causes (p.1393)
Sarcoidosis and other granulomatous diseases (caseating vs non-caseating granuloma distinction) (granuloma differential, p.1384)

M. tuberculosis is an aerobic acid-fast bacillus whose mycolic-acid-rich cell wall confers acid fastness and low permeability (reducing antibiotic efficacy). Transmission is by airborne droplet nuclei (<5-10 um) from a person with infectious pulmonary or laryngeal TB; cavitary cases are most infectious (10^5-10^7 AFB/mL of sputum). Inhaled bacilli reaching the alveoli are phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages; the bacillus arrests phagosome maturation and phagosome-lysosome fusion, replicates, and (via the ESX-1/RD1 secretion system) ruptures the macrophage to infect newly recruited phagocytes. Around 2-4 weeks, cell-mediated (TH1/IFN-gamma-driven, CD4+ T-cell-dependent) macrophage activation and a delayed-type hypersensitivity tissue-damaging response develop; their balance determines disease form. Granulomas (tubercles) of activated macrophages, epithelioid and giant cells form, with central caseous (cheese-like) necrosis in which low oxygen and pH inhibit but do not kill bacilli. When the macrophage-activating response is weak, delayed hypersensitivity causes progressive caseous liquefaction, bronchial and vascular erosion, and cavity formation; bacilli multiply within cavities and are discharged into airways, driving transmission and bronchogenic spread of satellite lesions. Lymphohematogenous dissemination can seed distant organs (miliary disease, meningitis). The continuum from infection to disease is governed largely by host immune competence; only ~10% of immunocompetent infected persons progress to active disease over a lifetime, about half within ~18 months. (pp.1380-1385)

Pulmonary TB is traditionally split into primary (soon after initial infection, often middle/lower lung zones, common in children) and postprimary/adult-type (reactivation or recent reinfection, apical-posterior upper lobes); molecular data show many adult cases in endemic areas reflect recent infection rather than old reactivation (p.1385).
Because HIV-associated TB cavitates less, such patients are often less infectious; PLWH with culture- and smear-positive disease may even have a normal chest radiograph (p.1382, p.1391-1393).
Urine lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) is a point-of-care adjunct for TB diagnosis specifically in PLWH with advanced disease or low CD4 counts, not a general test (p.1393).

MDR-TB is defined as resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampin; rifampin resistance (RR-TB) is used as a practical proxy for MDR; pre-XDR adds fluoroquinolone resistance, and XDR-TB adds resistance to a fluoroquinolone plus at least one additional group A drug (e.g., bedaquiline or linezolid) (p.1380-1382).
Postprimary disease favours the apical and posterior segments of the upper lobes and the superior segments of the lower lobes, where higher local oxygen tension favours mycobacterial growth (p.1386).

Cough develops in up to ~90% of cases and is often nonproductive initially before becoming purulent; hemoptysis occurs in 20-30%, and constitutional symptoms (diurnal fever, night sweats, weight loss, anorexia, malaise) are typical but nonspecific (p.1386).
Absence of fever does not exclude TB; physical examination is frequently normal even with significant parenchymal disease, so reliance on exam findings can mislead (p.1386).

Xpert MTB/RIF is the WHO first-line diagnostic, simultaneously detecting M. tuberculosis and rifampin resistance in under 2 hours; overall pulmonary sensitivity ~85% (up to 98% in smear-positive, ~70% in smear-negative), specificity 98% (p.1391-1392).
A negative NAAT (Xpert/Ultra) does NOT exclude TB and requires further workup; conversely culture remains the gold standard for definitive diagnosis (p.1390-1393).

Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra adds sensitivity (notably in smear-negative/culture-positive cases and PLWH) but its 'trace calls' can detect nonviable bacilli; trace calls in recently treated patients may represent dead-bacillus DNA (p.1392).
At least one to two early-morning sputum specimens should be submitted for both AFB smear and mycobacterial culture; tissue for culture must NOT be placed in formaldehyde/preservative (p.1392).

In HIV with partially preserved immunity, pulmonary TB looks classic (upper-lobe infiltrates and cavitation); with CD4 <200/uL it shifts to a primary-like pattern with diffuse/subtle interstitial infiltrates, little or no cavitation, pleural effusion and intrathoracic adenopathy (p.1391).

Treating on clinical/radiographic grounds alone: CXR has high sensitivity but poor specificity and no pattern (including a normal film) is pathognomonic in the HIV era - bacteriologic confirmation must always be pursued (p.1393).

Interpreting a negative Xpert/NAAT or negative smear as ruling out TB - smear microscopy sensitivity is only 40-60% and a negative molecular test still requires culture and further workup (p.1392-1393).

AFB microscopy cannot distinguish M. tuberculosis from nontuberculous mycobacteria, and urine/gastric specimens are prone to false negatives (low organism load) and false positives (commensal mycobacteria) (p.1392).
Relying on the chest exam: physical findings are of limited use and may be entirely normal in significant pulmonary TB (p.1386).
Missing diagnosis in atypical hosts (elderly nursing-home residents, teenagers, immunosuppressed/PLWH with lower-zone or noncavitary disease) (p.1391).

TST/IGRA pitfalls: false-negative TST in immunosuppression and overwhelming TB; false-positive from NTM or BCG; the TST 'boosting phenomenon' can mimic conversion; neither test distinguishes latent infection from active disease (p.1393-1394).
Putting tissue intended for culture into formaldehyde, which kills the organism and precludes culture (p.1392).

Untreated, TB is often fatal: about one-third of patients die within 1 year of diagnosis, and historically ~70% (weighted mean) of smear-positive cases died within 10 years; paucibacillary smear-negative disease had a lower ~20% case-fatality at 5 years, and ~60% of 5-year survivors underwent spontaneous remission. With timely, proper drug-susceptible treatment the vast majority are cured. Improper therapy lowers mortality but generates chronic infectious, often drug-resistant cases. A substantial proportion of cured survivors suffer post-TB lung disease - chronic airflow impairment, dyspnea, residual cough, bronchiectasis, pulmonary hypertension, and predisposition to aspergilloma/chronic pulmonary aspergillosis in residual cavities. (pp.1383, 1386, 1390-1391)
Massive hemoptysis from erosion of a vessel in a cavity wall or rupture of a Rasmussen's aneurysm - potentially life-threatening (p.1386)
Extensive disease causing dyspnea progressing to acute respiratory distress syndrome (p.1386)
Features of hematogenous/miliary dissemination (miliary reticulonodular CXR, hepatosplenomegaly, choroidal tubercles) - high mortality if unrecognised (p.1389)
Meningismus, headache, altered sensorium or cranial nerve palsy suggesting tuberculous meningitis - uniformly fatal if untreated (p.1388-1389)
Advanced HIV with possible TB: NAAT-positive results warrant immediate treatment because diagnostic delay can be fatal (p.1391, p.1393)

Harrison frames severity primarily by disease form and host rather than a numeric score: primary vs postprimary (cavitary) pulmonary disease; pulmonary vs extrapulmonary vs disseminated (miliary) TB; and by drug-resistance category - drug-susceptible TB, rifampin-resistant (RR-TB), multidrug-resistant (MDR-TB: resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampin), pre-XDR-TB (MDR/RR plus fluoroquinolone resistance), and extensively drug-resistant (XDR-TB: MDR plus fluoroquinolone resistance and resistance to at least one additional group A drug such as bedaquiline or linezolid). Infectiousness grades with cavitation and sputum bacillary load (smear-positive cavitary > smear-negative/culture-positive > culture-negative/extrapulmonary, the last essentially noninfectious). (pp.1380-1386)
Sputum smear for AFB (at least 2 samples) — Rapid, widely available test; positive smear supports diagnosis and indicates infectiousness for public health purposes.

CBNAAT / Xpert MTB-RIF (or equivalent rapid molecular test) — Provides faster diagnosis than culture and simultaneously detects rifampicin resistance, directly informing regimen choice — should be prioritized where available.
Sputum culture (liquid or solid media) — Gold standard for diagnosis and allows full drug-susceptibility testing if initial molecular testing suggests resistance or treatment failure occurs.
Chest X-ray — Supports diagnosis (upper lobe infiltrates, cavitation) and provides a baseline for treatment response monitoring.
HIV testing — TB-HIV co-infection changes management (ART timing, drug interactions) and is a standard part of TB workup per national guidelines.
Pulmonary Tuberculosis (infective) — Respiratory / Tuberculosis
veryLikely: Mycobacterium tuberculosis; possible: Non-tuberculous mycobacteria (if AFB smear positive but culture/PCR does not confirm M. tuberculosis)

[guideline] empiric → Isoniazid + Rifampicin + Pyrazinamide + Ethambutol (HRZE) Standard first-line four-drug regimen for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB, started ONLY after microbiological confirmation (or strong programmatic criteria per national guidelines) — not empirically on clinical suspicion alone.

[guideline] alternative → Drug-resistant TB regimens — see the Tuberculosis treatment pathway workspace For rifampicin-resistant / MDR / pre-XDR / XDR TB, the specific regimen is selected by drug-susceptibility testing and eligibility — see the structured, NTEP-sourced regimen cards (with eligibility, dosing, monitoring and safety gates) rather than a generic 'modified regimen'.
drugRefs: DST-driven DR-TB regimens (BPaLM · 9–11-mo shorter oral · 18–20-mo longer oral M/XDR · isoniazid mono/poly-resistant)

chunks.text: Infective endocarditis (including culture-negative endocarditis from fastidious organisms - nutritionally variant streptococci, HACEK group, Coxiella burnetii, Tropheryma whipplei, Bartonella) - one of the more common infectious causes (pp.150-151)
Adult-onset Still's disease (NIID, relatively common in FUO) (p.150)
Large-vessel vasculitis and giant cell arteritis / polymyalgia rheumatica (pp.150, 153)
Systemic lupus erythematosus (p.150)
Sarcoidosis (p.150)
Familial Mediterranean fever and other autoinflammatory syndromes (rare except in specific regions) (p.150)
Schnitzler's syndrome - urticaria, bone pain, monoclonal gammopathy (p.150)

VEXAS syndrome - adult-onset, middle-aged/elderly males, recurrent inflammation, chondritis, skin lesions, lung disease, venous thrombosis, arthritis, MDS; bone-marrow vacuoles in myeloid precursors; somatic UBA1 variants (p.150)
Malignant lymphoma - by far the most common neoplastic cause; fever may precede detectable lymphadenopathy (p.150)
Common solid tumors causing fever: breast, colon, hepatocellular, lung, pancreatic, renal cell carcinoma (p.151)
Extrapulmonary and miliary tuberculosis - up to half of infections in non-Western FUO are M. tuberculosis; miliary TB is especially hard to diagnose (pp.150, 153)
Diverticulitis (p.150)
Vertebral osteomyelitis / spondylodiscitis (pp.150-151)
Q fever (Coxiella burnetii) - consider with rural exposure, animal contact, valve disease, aortic aneurysm, or vascular prosthesis; test by immunofluorescence assay (pp.150-151)
Whipple disease (Tropheryma whipplei) - consider with unexplained CNS, GI, or joint symptoms; PCR on stool and blood early (p.150)
Intraabdominal / hepatic / renal / pelvic abscesses (p.151)
Endemic infections after relevant travel/residence: malaria, visceral leishmaniasis, histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis (p.150)
Acute HIV infection (p.150)
Culture-negative endocarditis - sterile cultures may simply reflect ongoing antibiotic therapy rather than a noninfectious cause (pp.151-152)
Marantic (nonbacterial thrombotic) endocarditis - sterile, paraneoplastic, especially with adenocarcinomas, mimics infective endocarditis (p.151)
Sterile endocarditis of SLE and antiphospholipid syndrome (p.151)

Obligatory baseline panel: ESR and CRP, platelet count, leukocyte count with differential, hemoglobin, electrolytes, creatinine, total protein, alkaline phosphatase, ALT, AST, LDH, creatine kinase, ferritin, antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, protein electrophoresis, urinalysis, three blood cultures, urine culture, chest x-ray, abdominal ultrasonography, and TST or IGRA (p.149)

Specialized blood cultures held long enough for fastidious organisms (e.g., HACEK); inform the lab and use special media for Histoplasma or Legionella; >3 blood cultures or >1 urine culture is useless without PDCs (p.153)
Q fever serology by immunofluorescence assay; T. whipplei PCR on stool/blood (pp.150-151)
Temporal artery biopsy in patients >=55 years for suspected giant cell arteritis (p.153)
CSF examination (HSV especially type 2, Cryptococcus, M. tuberculosis) when FUO is accompanied by headache (p.153)
Later-stage PDC-driven biopsies for pathology and/or microbiology (p.154)
Cryoglobulins - useful low-cost screening test (p.153)
Fundoscopy by an ophthalmologist - early, to exclude retinal vasculitis when PDCs are absent or misleading (p.153)

18F-FDG-PET/CT - established next step when PDC-guided tests are unrevealing; ~50% total diagnostic yield; best performed during active inflammation (elevated CRP/ESR or fever) and before glucocorticoids; outperforms gallium and labeled-leukocyte scintigraphy (pp.152-154)
Gallium-67 citrate or 111In/99mTc-labeled leukocyte scintigraphy - alternatives when PET/CT unavailable (lower yield; gallium localizes ~1/3, leukocyte ~1/5 of cases) (p.154)
Whole-body MRI - one study reported yield comparable to PET/CT (needs confirmation) (p.154)
Echocardiography - low yield without PDCs; reserve for high suspicion of endocarditis (p.153)
Liver biopsy (acid-fast smear, culture, PCR) - highest yield if miliary TB suspected; bone marrow / lymph node biopsies are alternatives (p.153)
Mycobacterial PCR alongside cultures - may shorten time to TB diagnosis (p.153)

Drug-induced fever - virtually any drug, even after long-term use; common culprits include allopurinol, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin, sulfasalazine, furosemide, and antimicrobials (sulfonamides, minocycline, vancomycin, beta-lactams, isoniazid); fever persisting >72h after stopping the drug makes it an unlikely cause (pp.150, 153)
DRESS / drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome - often with eosinophilia and extensive lymphadenopathy (p.150)

Benign or exercise-induced hyperthermia - elevated temperature WITHOUT raised CRP/ESR or other inflammation; may be postinfectious (triggers similar to chronic fatigue syndrome: EBV, Q fever, COVID-19) (p.150)
Factitious fever - artificially induced (e.g., IV injection of contaminated water); suspect with access to medical equipment (p.150)
Fraudulent fever - patient is normothermic but manipulates the thermometer; simultaneous multi-site measurement (rectum/ear/mouth) and pulse-temperature dissociation are clues (p.150)
Central thermoregulatory disorders - brain tumor, stroke, encephalitis, hypothalamic dysfunction (p.151)
Peripheral thermoregulatory causes - hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma, heat stroke (p.151)

FUO is a syndrome, not a single disease - a final prolonged febrile illness in which intensive standard evaluation has failed to localize a cause. Etiologies cluster into four groups: infections, noninfectious inflammatory diseases (NIIDs: autoimmune, autoinflammatory, granulomatous, and vasculitides), malignancy, and miscellaneous, with a substantial undiagnosed fraction. The spectrum has shifted over time: intraabdominal abscesses, tumors, and infective endocarditis have declined as CT, ultrasound, blood culture, and echocardiography improved, while entities such as acute HIV and autoinflammatory syndromes are now recognized. NIIDs may precede their typical clinical or laboratory features by months, requiring prolonged observation. The 'FUO paradox' describes how, despite better imaging (CT/MRI/PET-CT), the undiagnosed proportion is now higher (>50% in some Western cohorts) because most febrile illnesses are diagnosed before 3 weeks elapse, leaving only the most difficult cases to meet FUO criteria (pp.149-150).

Current (post-Petersdorf) FUO definition requires all of: fever >=38.3C (101F) on at least two occasions, illness lasting at least 3 weeks, no known immunocompromised state, and a diagnosis still uncertain after thorough history, examination, and a defined set of obligatory investigations (p.149).

Geography shapes the differential: infections (especially TB) dominate non-Western cohorts, while noninfectious inflammatory diseases (NIIDs) are the most common cause in Western cohorts, accounting for up to one-third of cases (p.150).
Investigation of cryoglobulins is a useful low-cost screening test in FUO given the frequent absence of specific symptoms (p.153).
Inflammation of unknown origin (IUO) shares the FUO definition but lacks the temperature criterion (elevated CRP/ESR with normal temperature); its causes and workup are identical to FUO (p.149).
FUO usually reflects an ATYPICAL presentation of a COMMON disease rather than a rare disease; pattern recognition explains the higher diagnostic yield at expert centers (pp.150, 153).

The cornerstone of the workup is the search for potentially diagnostic clues (PDCs) - all localizing signs, symptoms, and abnormalities pointing toward a diagnosis - via repeated history, examination, and obligatory tests; further testing should be PDC-driven (pp.152-153).
Examination should pay special attention to the eyes, lymph nodes, temporal arteries, liver, spleen, prior surgical sites, the entire skin surface, and mucous membranes (p.152).

History should capture fever pattern (continuous vs recurrent) and duration, prior medical history, current/recent drugs, family and sexual history, country of origin, recent and remote travel, environmental/hobby exposures, and animal contacts (p.152).
Giant cell arteritis is notably prevalent among FUO patients, with rates up to 17% in the elderly; temporal artery biopsy is still recommended for patients >=55 years (p.153).
FUO with headache should prompt CSF microbiologic examination for herpes simplex virus (especially type 2), Cryptococcus neoformans/gattii, and M. tuberculosis (p.153).

In patients with recurrent/episodic FUO, ask the patient to return DURING a febrile episode; further tests should be done during an inflammatory episode since abnormalities may be absent between episodes (pp.152-153).
Starting empirical therapeutic trials before a diagnosis - should be AVOIDED except when the patient is rapidly deteriorating, because most undiagnosed patients resolve spontaneously (p.154).

Continuing antibiotics/glucocorticoids during workup - they mask disease: cultures become unreliable and glucocorticoids shrink lymph nodes regardless of cause; stop them before further testing (p.152).

Early empirical glucocorticoids - can mask fever while infection or lymphoma spreads and reduce the chance of diagnosing a treatable malignancy; avoid until infection and lymphoma are sufficiently excluded (p.155).

Ordering more screening tests without PDCs - low yield; immunologic and microbiologic serologies without PDCs more often give false-positives; better to wait for new PDCs unless the patient deteriorates (pp.153-154).
Over-culturing - performing >3 blood cultures or >1 urine culture is useless absent PDCs (p.153).
Failing to recognize PDCs already present in available information is a frequent cause of diagnostic delay (p.154).
Interpreting a negative TST/IGRA as excluding TB - it does not; results may be indeterminate in miliary TB, malnutrition, immunosuppression, or with anti-IFN-gamma autoantibodies (p.153).

Misreading PET/CT - physiologic FDG uptake in brain, heart, bowel, kidneys, and bladder can obscure pathology (e.g., cardiac uptake masking endocarditis - mitigate with a pre-scan low-carbohydrate diet) (p.153).
Not excluding factitious/fraudulent fever and drug fever early, especially when inflammatory markers are normal (pp.150, 153).

Prognosis depends chiefly on the underlying diagnosis. When FUO remains unexplained after extensive evaluation, outlook is favorable: large cohorts report high rates of spontaneous fever resolution and mortality of 8% or less over several years of follow-up. The greatest mortality risk is during the early diagnostic phase. A normal 18F-FDG-PET/CT is associated with higher rates of spontaneous resolution and may help predict who will resolve. A symptom duration >12 months and a normal PET/CT both lower the chance of ever reaching a final diagnosis (pp.150, 154).
Clinical deterioration without new PDCs - the trigger to escalate workup (rather than wait) and the situation where empirical therapy may be justified (pp.152-153)
Hemodynamic instability or neutropenia - good indications for empirical antibiotic therapy (p.155)
Granulomatous disease on liver or bone marrow biopsy - should prompt (re)consideration of miliary tuberculosis (p.153)
Early phase of evaluation carries the highest FUO-related mortality risk (deaths occurred during index admission in cohort data; intravascular lymphoma and pneumonia found at autopsy) (p.154)

FUO categories (by host/setting), each requiring a distinct approach: (1) classic FUO - the immunocompetent adult per the formal definition; (2) nosocomial FUO; (3) neutropenic FUO; and (4) HIV-associated FUO. The contemporary Harrison definition explicitly EXCLUDES immunocompromised states, which need a different, more aggressive approach. Etiologies are grouped into four diagnostic categories - infections, noninfectious inflammatory diseases (NIIDs), malignancy, and miscellaneous - with a large 'no diagnosis' fraction (pp.149-150).
Repeat detailed history and serial examinations — New localizing signs often emerge over time and are the single most valuable step in PUO workup.
CBC, ESR, CRP, LFTs, RFTs, urinalysis — First-tier screening tests that can reveal a localizing clue (e.g., abnormal LFTs pointing to liver abscess or biliary source).
Blood cultures (multiple sets, including for fastidious organisms if endocarditis suspected) — Identifies bacteremic causes including culture-negative endocarditis pathogens with extended incubation.
Chest X-ray and abdominal ultrasound — First-line imaging to screen for occult infection (TB, abscess) or malignancy.
CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (second-tier) — More sensitive for occult abscess, lymphadenopathy, or malignancy if first-tier workup is unrevealing.
Echocardiography (if any murmur, risk factors, or persistent bacteremia) — Screens for infective endocarditis as a cause of prolonged fever.
Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (infective) — Systemic
veryLikely: Diagnosis-dependent — broad differential includes infective (TB, enteric fever, infective endocarditis, abscess), neoplastic (lymphoma), and autoimmune/rheumatologic causes
Acute prostatitis in men presenting with febrile UTI (Harrison 22e p.1137)
Complicated UTI (fever in a patient with structural/functional urinary abnormality, immunocompromise, or instrumentation) (Harrison 22e p.1133-1134)
Sexually transmitted infection mimicking UTI, particularly Chlamydia trachomatis cervicitis/urethritis (Harrison 22e p.1133-1134)
Renal/ureteral calculus with obstruction (renal colic) presenting with flank pain and pyuria (Harrison 22e p.2493)
Acute prostatitis (Harrison 22e p.1137)
Cervicitis or urethritis due to Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Harrison 22e p.1133-1134)
Vaginitis (Candida albicans, Trichomonas vaginalis) or herpetic urethritis causing dysuria (Harrison 22e p.1133-1134)

Upper-tract imaging (CT or renal ultrasound) to evaluate for obstruction, abscess, or anatomic abnormality, especially in men, in patients not responding within 72 hours, or when complicated infection is suspected (Harrison 22e p.1132, 1137)

Urine dipstick (nitrite, leukocyte esterase) and microscopic urinalysis as point-of-care tests; note nitrites detect only Enterobacterales and may be falsely negative with non-Enterobacterales organisms (Harrison 22e p.1134-1135)
Imaging for gas in renal/perinephric tissues when emphysematous pyelonephritis is suspected in a diabetic patient (Harrison 22e p.1090)
Renal/ureteral stone with proximal obstruction, which may present exactly as acute pyelonephritis (Harrison 22e p.2493)
Interstitial cystitis or noninfectious vulvovaginal irritation causing dysuria (Harrison 22e p.1133-1134)
Sloughed renal papilla or blood clot causing ureteral obstruction without infection (Harrison 22e p.2493)
Musculoskeletal flank/back pain, herpes zoster, abdominal aortic aneurysm, duodenal ulcer (differential for flank pain) (Harrison 22e p.2493)

Pyelonephritis usually develops as an ascending infection: uropathogens move from the urethra to the bladder and then continue up the ureter to the renal parenchyma, which is the route for most renal parenchymal infection. Its microbiology therefore mirrors that of acute cystitis. A minority arises hematogenously (<2% of UTIs overall), typically with relatively virulent organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus and Salmonella; isolation of either from urine should prompt consideration of concomitant bacteremia, and hematogenous seeding can produce focal renal abscesses. Anatomic factors causing urinary obstruction or retention (congenital anomalies, cystocele, pelvic-organ prolapse, neurogenic bladder, benign prostatic hypertrophy) impede the protective flushing action of micturition and predispose to renal involvement. A foreign body such as a stone or catheter provides an inert surface for colonization (Harrison 22e p.1088, 1130-1131).

Fever is the principal feature distinguishing pyelonephritis from simple cystitis; presence of fever, back/flank pain, rigors, nausea or vomiting signals infection that has extended beyond the bladder (Harrison 22e p.1086-1090, 1133).

Severity spans a wide spectrum: mild disease may present only with low-grade fever with or without costovertebral angle pain, whereas severe disease manifests with high fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting, and flank pain; onset is generally acute and may or may not be preceded by cystitis symptoms (Harrison 22e p.1090).
Pyelonephritis represents tissue-invasive disease and patients are often systemically ill, so the threat of progression to bacteremia and urosepsis is real (Harrison 22e p.1090, 1137, 1329).

In a woman presenting with at least one localizing urinary symptom (dysuria, frequency, hematuria, or back pain) and no complicating factors, the combined probability of acute cystitis or pyelonephritis is about 50% (Harrison 22e p.1133).

Men with febrile UTI should undergo upper-tract imaging (CT or ultrasound) if not done previously, to evaluate for urinary tract abnormality or obstruction, and elevated PSA with enlarged prostate/seminal vesicles suggests prostatic involvement (Harrison 22e p.1132).

Pregnant patients are at unusually high risk of developing pyelonephritis, which can adversely affect pregnancy outcome (preterm delivery, low birth weight); this underlies routine prenatal screening for asymptomatic bacteriuria (Harrison 22e p.1086, 1329).

Treating presumed UTI when the true cause is an STI (e.g., C. trachomatis); vaginal discharge should prompt STI consideration since symptoms alone do not reliably distinguish them (Harrison 22e p.1133-1134).

Stopping the workup at an abnormal urinalysis in a catheterized or febrile patient: pyuria and bacteriuria are expected with catheterization and do not by themselves establish UTI as the cause of fever (Harrison 22e p.1133-1135).
Mistaking an obstructing stone with proximal infection for uncomplicated pyelonephritis and missing the need for emergent drainage (Harrison 22e p.2493).
Misattributing xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis to renal malignancy because its mass effect can mimic tumor (Harrison 22e p.1090).
Delayed/withheld antimicrobial therapy in true UTI carries a small increased risk of progression to pyelonephritis (Harrison 22e p.1136).

Most pyelonephritis treated effectively resolves, though fever may take 5-7 days to clear completely even with appropriate therapy. Renal parenchymal damage and loss of renal function are uncommon and occur primarily in association with urinary obstruction (preexisting, or, rarely, de novo in diabetic patients with papillary necrosis). Chronic bacterial pyelonephritis is rarely a cause of chronic renal failure because it seldom affects both kidneys. Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis arises from chronic obstruction (often staghorn calculus) plus chronic infection causing suppurative destruction of renal tissue and frequently requires nephrectomy (Harrison 22e p.1090, 1137, 1329, 2493).

Acute papillary necrosis with sloughed papillae obstructing the ureter, producing obstructive uropathy that requires intervention to relieve obstruction and preserve renal function (Harrison 22e p.1090, 1137)
UTI in the setting of ureteral obstruction is a medical emergency requiring immediate restoration of drainage by ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy (Harrison 22e p.2493)

Emphysematous pyelonephritis: gas production in renal and perinephric tissues, occurring almost exclusively in patients with poorly controlled diabetes; a particularly severe form (Harrison 22e p.1090)
Continued fever and/or bacteremia despite antibacterial therapy should raise suspicion for intraparenchymal, perinephric, or renal cortical abscess (Harrison 22e p.1090, 1137)
Failure of clinical response within 72 hours warrants evaluation for an uncontrolled source of infection (Harrison 22e p.1137)
Persistently elevated/increasing fever, flank pain, and rising neutrophil counts should prompt evaluation for intrarenal/perinephric abscess and/or obstruction (Harrison 22e p.1329)
Bilateral papillary necrosis may present first as a rapid rise in serum creatinine (Harrison 22e p.1090)

Harrison describes a clinical spectrum rather than a formal score: mild pyelonephritis (low-grade fever, with or without lower back or costovertebral angle pain) versus severe pyelonephritis (high fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting, flank pain). Distinct severe/complicated entities include emphysematous pyelonephritis (gas-forming, almost exclusively in poorly controlled diabetes), xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (chronic obstruction plus infection causing suppurative renal destruction), and pyelonephritis complicated by papillary necrosis with obstruction or by intrarenal/perinephric abscess. Acute pyelonephritis is one of the systemic UTI presentations that may be grouped as urosepsis or febrile UTI, with or without bacteremia (Harrison 22e p.1090, 1329).

Pyoderma gangrenosum is a neutrophilic dermatosis thought to arise from dysregulated innate immune activation and neutrophil chemotaxis/function, often in a genetically predisposed host. Cytokine-driven neutrophilic infiltration in the skin, without a demonstrable infectious trigger, produces sterile abscess-like tissue destruction. The tendency for lesions to develop at sites of trauma (pathergy) reflects this exaggerated local inflammatory response. Its frequent association with inflammatory bowel disease, inflammatory arthritides, and myeloid dyscrasias suggests a shared systemic inflammatory or clonal process in many patients.
Starts as a tender pustule or nodule that rapidly breaks down into an ulcer with a violaceous, undermined, overhanging border
Classic feature is pathergy — new or worsening ulceration at sites of minor trauma, injection, or surgical incision
About half of cases are associated with an underlying systemic disease, most commonly inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, or a hematologic malignancy/paraproteinemia
Diagnosis is one of exclusion; there is no single confirmatory laboratory or histologic test
Ulcer base often shows purulent, necrotic tissue with a boggy, undermined edge rather than a clean granulating base
Lower extremities (especially pretibial region) are the most common site, but PG can occur anywhere including peristomal skin
Debridement and skin grafting can worsen lesions via pathergy and should generally be avoided until disease activity is controlled
Response to immunosuppressive therapy, when it occurs, supports the diagnosis retrospectively
Treating PG as an infected wound and pursuing aggressive debridement, which can worsen the ulcer through pathergy
Assuming a positive wound culture confirms infection rather than colonization of a chronic ulcer
Delaying diagnosis by relying on a single confirmatory test rather than the clinical picture and exclusion of mimics
Missing an underlying systemic disease (IBD, arthritis, hematologic disorder) that drives disease activity and recurrence risk

Course is variable and often relapsing, particularly when an underlying systemic disease remains active; lesions can heal with characteristic cribriform (atrophic, often hyperpigmented) scarring. Prompt recognition, avoidance of unnecessary surgical intervention, and treatment of any associated systemic condition improve outcomes.
Rapidly expanding ulcer with systemic toxicity — reconsider necrotizing infection and seek urgent surgical/infectious disease input
Worsening of the ulcer after debridement or grafting, consistent with pathergy, warrants stopping surgical intervention and escalating immunosuppression
New PG lesions in a patient with known IBD may signal a disease flare requiring gastroenterology involvement
Unexplained cytopenias or monoclonal gammopathy alongside PG should prompt hematologic evaluation for underlying malignancy
Peristomal PG in patients with ostomies can be mistaken for a wound infection and mismanaged

Reactive arthritis is thought to result from an aberrant immune response to bacterial antigens (or bacterial components/DNA persisting in synovium) following a distant mucosal infection, rather than from direct joint infection. HLA-B27 appears to shape the immune response to these triggering pathogens, promoting a sterile inflammatory synovitis, enthesitis, and mucocutaneous inflammation. It is classified with the spondyloarthritis family, sharing pathogenic overlap with ankylosing spondylitis and psoriatic arthritis.
Asymmetric oligoarthritis, predominantly of the lower limbs, arising 1-4 weeks after a genitourinary or gastrointestinal infection
Classic triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis/uveitis, and urethritis/cervicitis occurs in only a minority of patients — most present with incomplete forms
Enthesitis (especially Achilles tendon and plantar fascia) and dactylitis ('sausage digit') are characteristic clues pointing away from a purely infectious arthritis
Strongly associated with HLA-B27, particularly in cases following genitourinary infection or with axial/sacroiliac involvement
Triggering organisms include Chlamydia trachomatis, and enteric pathogens such as Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, and Campylobacter
Mucocutaneous findings — keratoderma blennorrhagicum and circinate balanitis — can mimic psoriasis or STI-related dermatoses
Synovial fluid is inflammatory and sterile; cultures and PCR are negative for the triggering organism, distinguishing it from septic arthritis
Most cases are self-limited over months, but a subset develops chronic or relapsing joint disease, especially those who are HLA-B27 positive
Assuming a sterile inflammatory joint effusion excludes infection without adequate synovial fluid culture and clinical correlation
Missing the diagnosis in incomplete presentations lacking the full urethritis-arthritis-conjunctivitis triad
Overlooking a preceding GI or GU infection because the interval before joint symptoms can be several weeks
Confusing mucocutaneous lesions (keratoderma blennorrhagicum, circinate balanitis) with psoriasis or sexually transmitted skin disease

Most episodes resolve within 3-12 months with appropriate anti-inflammatory management, but relapses and progression to chronic spondyloarthritis occur in a meaningful minority, particularly HLA-B27-positive individuals. Chronic disease may involve persistent enthesitis, axial disease, or recurrent ocular inflammation requiring long-term rheumatologic follow-up.
Fever with a hot, markedly swollen single joint — must exclude septic arthritis before attributing to reactive arthritis
Acute visual symptoms or eye pain suggesting uveitis — requires urgent ophthalmology referral
Signs of aortitis or cardiac conduction disease in longstanding HLA-B27-associated disease
Rapidly progressive axial disease or neurologic symptoms suggesting cauda equina involvement
Systemic sepsis features that suggest disseminated gonococcal or other bacteremic process rather than reactive arthritis

chunks.text: Rickettsiae and Orientia are obligately intracellular gram-negative coccobacilli that primarily infect vascular endothelial cells. After tick saliva inoculates organisms into the dermis (in RMSF after roughly 6 h of feeding), they spread lymphohematogenously and infect contiguous foci of endothelium throughout the body, producing a widespread infectious vasculitis with increased vascular permeability. The resulting edema, hypovolemia, and tissue ischemia (rather than occlusive thrombosis) drive the organ injury: prerenal azotemia, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, and CNS dysfunction. Platelet consumption causes thrombocytopenia in about a third to half of RMSF cases, but frank DIC with hypofibrinogenemia is rare; the coagulation changes appear to be homeostatic responses to endothelial injury forming nonocclusive hemostatic plugs (p.1454, p.1456).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.137-141 (Ch.21 Fever and Rash); p.1454-1459 (Ch.192 Rickettsial Diseases); p.1488 (Ch.189 Leptospirosis differential)

chunks.text: All acute rickettsial illnesses look alike for roughly the first 5 days: fever, headache, and myalgias, often with nausea, vomiting, or cough; the distinguishing features (rash, eschar, pneumonitis, meningoencephalitis) emerge only as the illness progresses (p.1454).

chunks.text: Outcome is strongly time-dependent: untreated RMSF carries mortality of roughly 20-25% (historic) with confirmed-case fatality around 9-10% where R. rickettsii is the sole agent, versus ~3-5% when treated early; delayed recognition and treatment markedly increase death. For unclear reasons RMSF case-fatality approaches 50% in Mexico and Brazil. Severe Mediterranean spotted fever has mortality near 50% without treatment but improves dramatically with even a single day of appropriate therapy. Untreated epidemic typhus historically killed up to 60% and still exceeds 10-15% in outbreaks. Many survivors of severe RMSF recover fully, but permanent neurologic deficits and gangrene requiring amputation can follow severe illness (p.1456-1457; p.1488 / Ch.21).

chunks.text: Harrison does not give a formal grading scale, but stratifies along a spectrum: (1) self-limited febrile illness that resolves without evolution; (2) classic disease with rash and/or eschar; and (3) severe/complicated disease with organ involvement - pneumonitis/ARDS, meningoencephalitis, acute kidney injury, hemorrhage/skin necrosis/gangrene, sepsis/septic shock, and (rarely) fulminant RMSF fatal within 5 days. Higher-risk groups include children <10 years, adults >70 years, the immunosuppressed, and (for fulminant RMSF) males with G6PD deficiency (p.1454-1457).

Neurosarcoidosis results from non-caseating granulomatous inflammation infiltrating the meninges, cranial nerves, hypothalamic-pituitary axis, brain parenchyma, or spinal cord. The granulomas provoke a perivascular and leptomeningeal inflammatory response that can cause direct compressive or infiltrative neurologic deficits, hydrocephalus from impaired CSF flow, or vasculopathy. Because it is part of a systemic multisystem granulomatous disease, isolated CNS presentations without other organ involvement are diagnostically challenging.
Symptomatic nervous-system involvement occurs in roughly 5-10% of sarcoidosis patients, though subclinical granulomas are more common at autopsy
Facial nerve palsy (often bilateral or recurrent) is the single most characteristic cranial neuropathy seen
Basilar leptomeningeal enhancement on MRI is a classic pattern, reflecting the predilection for meninges at the base of the brain
Hypothalamic-pituitary involvement can cause diabetes insipidus, hyperprolactinemia, or other endocrinopathies and should prompt pituitary axis testing
CSF findings are nonspecific — lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and sometimes low glucose — mimicking tuberculous or fungal meningitis
Neurologic disease can be the presenting manifestation of sarcoidosis before systemic disease is recognized, so tissue confirmation elsewhere (e.g., mediastinal nodes, skin) is valuable
Spinal cord involvement can mimic a longitudinally extensive myelitis or an intramedullary tumor on imaging
Response to immunosuppression supports but does not confirm the diagnosis, since some infections also transiently respond to steroids
Starting empiric immunosuppression before adequately excluding infectious mimics (especially TB and fungal disease) can worsen unrecognized infection
Relying solely on elevated CSF or serum ACE for diagnosis, as this is neither sensitive nor specific
Assuming a favorable steroid response confirms sarcoidosis, since infections and other inflammatory conditions may also improve transiently
Overlooking neurosarcoidosis in a patient without known systemic sarcoidosis, since isolated CNS presentation occurs in a meaningful subset of cases

Course is variable — many patients respond to immunosuppressive therapy with partial or complete resolution, but a subset experience chronic, relapsing, or progressive disease, particularly with parenchymal brain or spinal cord involvement, which carries a worse functional outcome.

Optic neuropathy, which can threaten vision and warrants prompt treatment

SBP is spontaneous infection of ascitic fluid in the absence of an intraabdominal surgical source. The presumed mechanism is bacterial translocation: gut flora cross an edematous, leaky intestinal wall into mesenteric lymph nodes, producing bacteremia that seeds the ascites, which is a good growth medium. Susceptibility in cirrhosis reflects impaired hepatic filtration from a diseased liver and altered portal circulation, low ascitic complement levels (lower than in non-cirrhotic ascites), and diminished opsonic and phagocytic function of PMNs in advanced liver disease. Cirrhosis is also associated with gut dysbiosis (increased Enterobacteriaceae), small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth, reduced Paneth-cell defensins, decreased intestinal motility, reduced pancreatobiliary secretions, and portal-hypertensive enteropathy, all of which promote pathologic translocation. SBP occurs in up to ~30% of hospitalized cirrhotics with ascites but is an uncommon event overall, affecting 10% or fewer of cirrhotic patients. (Harrison 22e p.1070, 2715)
An ascitic-fluid PMN (neutrophil) count of at least 250/microL is diagnostic of SBP, irrespective of whether cultures grow an organism (Harrison 22e p.329, 372, 1070).
SBP virtually always arises on a background of preexisting ascites, which predates the infection (Harrison 22e p.1070).

A repeat paracentesis after 48 hours of therapy should confirm at least a 25% fall in the ascitic PMN count from baseline; failure to fall, or persistent ascitic leukocytosis after treatment, should prompt a search for an alternative or secondary diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.329, 1071).

Fever is the single most common manifestation, present in roughly 80% of cases; abdominal pain, acute onset, and peritoneal signs aid diagnosis but their absence does not rule SBP out (Harrison 22e p.1070).
Abdominal tenderness is found in only about 40% of patients and rebound tenderness is uncommon, so a benign abdomen does not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.329).

SBP can present with no abdominal symptoms at all, instead manifesting as new or worsening hepatic encephalopathy, altered mental status, jaundice, or acute kidney injury without another explanation (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070, 2715).

In any cirrhotic patient hospitalized with ascites who deteriorates or shows signs of infection, a diagnostic paracentesis is mandatory; tapping within 12 hours of admission lowers mortality through early SBP detection (Harrison 22e p.329, 2715).

Ascitic fluid should be injected directly into blood-culture bottles at the bedside to improve yield, and blood cultures drawn simultaneously, since the organism burden in the fluid is low and bacteremia frequently coexists (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070).
Culture samples should be obtained before antibiotics are started to maximize recovery of the organism (Harrison 22e p.1070).
SBP is almost always monomicrobial; a single isolate is the rule (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070).
Gram stain of ascitic fluid is frequently negative in SBP and a negative result should not deter treatment (Harrison 22e p.1070).
Diagnosis rests on the ascitic PMN count >=250/microL, not on a positive culture; ascitic cultures are often negative because the organism burden is low (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070).

Recovery of more than one organism (a mixed flora, especially with anaerobes) alongside an elevated PMN count points to SECONDARY peritonitis from a ruptured viscus or abscess, not SBP, and demands a search for a surgical source (Harrison 22e p.329, 1071).
Multiple organisms WITHOUT an elevated PMN count suggest bowel perforation by the paracentesis needle rather than true infection (Harrison 22e p.329).

Failing to perform a diagnostic paracentesis in a decompensated cirrhotic who deteriorates (encephalopathy, AKI, sepsis) misses SBP, since the abdomen may be benign and tenderness is present in only ~40% (Harrison 22e p.329, 2715).
A low ascitic total protein (<1.0-1.5 g/dL) reflects low opsonic activity and identifies patients at higher risk for SBP; this group warrants heightened suspicion (Harrison 22e p.330, 1071).

The 250/microL PMN threshold is specific to SBP and should not be applied to secondary peritonitis or to peritoneal-dialysis peritonitis, where lower leukocyte cutoffs are used (Harrison 22e p.1070, p.2486 context).
Gastric acid suppression (e.g., proton-pump inhibitors) has been associated with increased SBP risk in observational data (Harrison 22e p.1071).

SBP is a common and potentially lethal complication of cirrhotic ascites and carries significant morbidity and mortality, largely because it tends to occur in patients with the most advanced liver disease. In-hospital mortality is roughly 17-25%; one tertiary-center series reported ~23% mortality at 30 days and ~37% at 90 days. Recurrence is high, with up to ~70% of patients having another episode within a year. Patients with PBP usually respond to appropriate antibiotics within about 72 hours. The underlying prognosis of cirrhosis with ascites is itself poor, with under 50% surviving 2 years after ascites onset in some series, so SBP should prompt consideration of liver transplantation. (Harrison 22e p.1071, 2715-2716, 373)
New or worsening hepatic encephalopathy or altered mental status in a cirrhotic with ascites (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070, 2715)
Unexplained acute kidney injury, jaundice, or nonlocalizing malaise/fatigue in a susceptible patient (Harrison 22e p.1070)
Multiple organisms recovered from ascitic fluid, especially with anaerobes, suggesting secondary peritonitis requiring source control (Harrison 22e p.329, 1071)
Free air under the diaphragm on imaging, signaling perforation (Harrison 22e p.1070)
Concurrent GI/variceal bleeding, which markedly increases SBP frequency (Harrison 22e p.330, 2716)

Harrison does not provide a formal severity grading system specific to SBP. Risk stratification is framed around predictors of poor outcome and renal injury: higher SBP risk in patients with low ascitic-fluid total protein (<1.0-1.5 g/dL), impaired renal function (creatinine >=1.2 mg/dL, BUN >=25 mg/dL, or serum sodium <=130 mEq/L), and advanced liver failure (Child-Turcotte-Pugh score >=9, bilirubin >=3 mg/dL); these are used to identify candidates for prophylaxis. The greatest benefit of adjunctive albumin is seen in those presenting with serum creatinine >=1 mg/dL, BUN >=30 mg/dL, or total bilirubin >=5 mg/dL. (Harrison 22e p.1071)

Diagnostic paracentesis with ascitic fluid cell count and culture — Defines the diagnosis (neutrophil count ≥250/mm³) and identifies the organism for targeted therapy — essential before committing to a full antibiotic course where feasible.
Blood cultures — Frequently positive and may identify the organism even when ascitic fluid culture is negative (culture-negative neutrocytic ascites).
Renal function tests — Guides decision on adjunctive albumin and assesses for hepatorenal syndrome, a major complication of SBP.
Liver function tests and coagulation profile — Establishes baseline severity of underlying liver disease, relevant to prognosis and overall management.

Serology is the mainstay of laboratory diagnosis: indirect fluorescent antibody, indirect immunoperoxidase, enzyme immunoassays, and rapid lateral-flow chromatographic tests (Harrison 22e p.1460).
PCR amplification of Orientia genes is effective when performed on eschar material, but is less sensitive on blood (Harrison 22e p.1460).

Serum sodium: hyponatremia is a recognized associated finding across the rickettsioses (Harrison 22e p.1455).
Hepatic aminotransferases: mild to moderate elevation is commonly seen (Harrison 22e p.1455).

Scrub typhus is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi, an obligate intracellular organism placed in a separate genus within the family Rickettsiaceae. It differs substantially from Rickettsia species both genetically and in cell-wall composition, notably lacking lipopolysaccharide. Disease results from infection of vascular endothelial cells with increased vascular permeability (a mechanism shared across the rickettsioses). The organism is maintained in nature by transovarial transmission within trombiculid mites; infected larval mites (chiggers, the only mite stage that feeds on a vertebrate host) inoculate the organism into the skin during feeding. Severe disease reflects widespread vascular injury, producing the encephalitis and interstitial pneumonia that characterize advanced cases. Closely related Orientia species (O. chuto, Candidatus O. chiloensis) cause scrub typhus-like illness in newly recognized foci (Harrison 22e p.1455-1456, p.1460, p.3773).

The classic triad of an inoculation eschar at the chigger feeding site, regional lymphadenopathy, and a maculopapular rash is the textbook description, but these signs are seldom seen in indigenous (local endemic) patients (Harrison 22e p.1460).
Among returning travelers, fewer than 50% develop an eschar and fewer than 40% develop a rash; when a rash does appear it typically emerges on day 4-6 of illness (Harrison 22e p.1460).

Eschar formation occurs at the site of mite/chigger feeding and may develop during the incubation period; an eschar is a useful diagnostic clue that should prompt consideration of scrub typhus (Harrison 22e p.1455).

Onset after a 6-21 day incubation is characterized by fever, headache, myalgia, cough, and gastrointestinal symptoms; some patients recover spontaneously after a few days while others progress to severe disease (Harrison 22e p.1460).
Chigger bites may be asymptomatic, so the absence of a recalled bite does not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.3773).

Immunity to scrub typhus is short-lived: protection against the homologous strain wanes over 1-3 years, and the organism's marked antigenic diversity means cross-protective immunity can be lost in as little as 1 month, so reinfection is possible (Harrison 22e p.1460).

Relying on the classic triad: eschar, rash, and lymphadenopathy are frequently absent (eschar <50% and rash <40% of travelers; signs seldom seen in indigenous patients), so a negative skin exam does not exclude scrub typhus (Harrison 22e p.1460).
Expecting a recalled bite: chigger bites may be asymptomatic and the mites are tiny and rarely noticed (Harrison 22e p.3773).

Assuming geographic exclusion: although classically eastern/southern Asia, northern Australia, and Pacific/Indian Ocean islands, emerging and reemerging foci (e.g., Chile, parts of South/Central America, Africa, Arabian peninsula via related Orientia species) challenge the traditional epidemiology (Harrison 22e p.1460, p.3773).
Note that PCR on blood is less sensitive than PCR on eschar material (Harrison 22e p.1460).
Some Thai isolates are poorly responsive to doxycycline or chloramphenicol (Harrison 22e p.1460).

Illness ranges from mild and self-limiting to fatal. The case-fatality rate for untreated classic cases is about 6% and would likely be lower if all mild cases were captured; overall reported mortality varies widely by location (cited as 1% to 70%). Risk of death rises with increasing age and with the presence of myocarditis, delirium, pneumonitis, or signs of hemorrhage. Recognized in time, the disease responds well to appropriate antibiotic therapy (Harrison 22e p.1035, p.1460).
Altered mental status / encephalitis (meningoencephalitis is a feature of severe disease) (Harrison 22e p.1035, p.1455).
Interstitial pneumonia / pneumonitis with dyspnea or progression toward respiratory failure (Harrison 22e p.1035, p.1460).
Myocarditis (Harrison 22e p.1035).
Signs of disseminated intravascular coagulation or hemorrhage (Harrison 22e p.1035).
Renal failure (Harrison 22e p.1035).
Progressive hypotension and multiorgan failure (a severe-disease pattern shared by the rickettsioses) (Harrison 22e p.1455).

Harrison does not give a formal severity score; it contrasts mild/self-limiting illness with severe disease. Severe scrub typhus is marked by encephalitis/meningoencephalitis and interstitial pneumonia due to vascular injury, and may progress to myocarditis, DIC, renal failure, hypotension, and multiorgan failure (Harrison 22e p.1035, p.1455, p.1460).

Careful skin examination for eschar — Eschar (a painless, often overlooked necrotic lesion at the chigger bite site) is highly specific for scrub typhus when found — actively look in skin folds, axillae, groin.
Scrub typhus IgM ELISA / Weil-Felix (less specific) — Confirms diagnosis serologically, though treatment should not wait for results when clinical suspicion is high.
CBC, LFTs, renal function — Assesses organ involvement; transaminitis and thrombocytopenia are common supportive findings.
Chest X-ray (if respiratory symptoms) — Screens for ARDS, a recognized complication of severe/delayed scrub typhus.

chunks.text: Sepsis arises when an infection provokes a dysregulated, self-amplifying host response rather than a contained local one. Pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs, e.g., LPS, bacterial cell-wall components, microbial nucleic acids) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs, e.g., histones, HMGB1, S100 proteins, mitochondrial/double-stranded DNA, ATP released from injured cells) are sensed by pattern-recognition receptors (TLRs, CLRs, RAGE, RIG-I, NOD-like receptors) on innate immune and parenchymal cells. This triggers exuberant release of cytokines and chemokines and upregulation of vascular adhesion molecules. Myeloid cells (neutrophils, monocytes, M1 macrophages, dendritic cells) drive injury through phagocytosis, degranulation, reactive oxygen/nitrogen species, and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), while emergency granulopoiesis releases immature neutrophils (a poor-prognosis marker). Lymphoid responses are dysregulated, with lymphocyte apoptosis, exhaustion, and myeloid-derived suppressor cells producing a state of immunosuppression that predisposes survivors to secondary infection. The endothelium is activated and injured: glycocalyx breakdown, loss of VE-cadherin/tight junctions, and apoptosis cause capillary leak, interstitial edema, and a widened oxygen-diffusion distance. A prothrombotic shift (increased tissue factor, vWF, PAI-1; depleted antithrombin, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, and protein C; complement activation with C3a/C5a and the C5b-9 membrane attack complex) generates microvascular thrombi and, once clotting factors and platelets are consumed, bleeding. Excess nitric oxide drives systemic vasodilation. The net result is impaired oxygen delivery, uptake, and utilization; even when oxygen delivery is adequate, mitochondrial and metabolic dysfunction impairs ATP generation and ion homeostasis, producing multiorgan cellular injury and dysfunction (p.2317-2319).

source.page: 2310-2324 (Harrison 22e; principal sepsis chapter 315, p.2316-2324; shock chapter 314, p.2310-2316; ICU scoring chapter 311, p.2291-2292)

chunks.text: Sepsis-3 (2016) reframes sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, not merely a systemic inflammatory state; the older SIRS-based criteria and the term 'severe sepsis' were discarded for poor specificity (p.2316).

chunks.text: Lactate is central to risk-stratifying sepsis: elevation reflects tissue hypoperfusion/anaerobic metabolism, correlates with worse outcome, and serial measurements help track response to resuscitation (p.2313).

chunks.text: Overall in-hospital mortality is roughly 15% among hospitalized adults with sepsis, rising to up to ~40% with septic shock; globally an estimated ~11 million sepsis-related deaths occur yearly (about one in five deaths worldwide). Mortality climbs with age and is higher in men. Elevated SOFA scores and machine-learning-defined phenotypes track population-level outcome (e.g., alpha/beta/gamma/delta phenotypes with ~2%/5%/15%/32% mortality) but cannot reliably predict an individual patient's outcome. Survivorship carries a heavy long-term burden: physical (prolonged fatigue, muscle loss, weakness, reduced functional capacity), cognitive (cognitive decline, dementia), and psychological (depression, reduced quality of life) sequelae, plus increased risk of cardiovascular events, recurrent infection, and readmission. About half of survivors are rehospitalized within a year and roughly one in six die within the first year, with most post-sepsis deaths in the first 6 months and elevated death risk persisting up to ~2 years (p.2316-2317, 2324). No FDA-approved host-targeted/immunomodulatory therapy exists for sepsis (p.2324).

chunks.text: Sepsis-3 (Singer et al., JAMA 2016) is the current framework: (1) Infection (suspected or confirmed) without organ dysfunction is not sepsis. (2) Sepsis = suspected/confirmed infection with an acute increase of >=2 points in the SOFA score from baseline (life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response). The SOFA score grades six systems 0-4: respiratory (PaO2/FiO2), coagulation (platelets), liver (bilirubin), cardiovascular (MAP / vasopressor requirement), CNS (Glasgow Coma Scale), and renal (creatinine / urine output). (3) Septic shock = sepsis with vasopressor requirement to maintain MAP >65 mmHg AND serum lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation. qSOFA (>=2 of RR >=22/min, altered mentation, SBP <=100 mmHg) is a rapid bedside risk-stratification prompt for poor outcome in suspected infection, not a diagnostic criterion. The prior 1991/1992 SIRS-based definitions and the term 'severe sepsis' are obsolete under Sepsis-3 (p.2292, 2316, 2320).

source.page: 2310-2324 (Harrison 22e; principal sepsis chapter 315, p.2316-2324; shock chapter 314, p.2310-2316; ICU scoring chapter 311, p.2291-2292)

chunks.text: Blood cultures (x2, before antibiotics if feasible) — Identifies the causative organism and susceptibility for de-escalation.
Lactate — Core Sepsis-3/Surviving Sepsis Campaign marker of tissue hypoperfusion; guides resuscitation and risk-stratification toward septic shock.
Source-specific cultures (urine, sputum, wound, CSF as guided by clinical exam) — Identifies and confirms the infectious source to allow targeted therapy.
CBC, renal function, liver function, coagulation profile — Assesses organ dysfunction (SOFA components) and supports staging severity.
Imaging directed by suspected source (CXR, abdominal ultrasound/CT) — Localizes the source and identifies any need for source control (drainage, debridement).
Sepsis (infective) — Systemic

veryLikely: Organism depends entirely on the suspected source (e.g., E. coli for urosepsis, S. pneumoniae for pulmonary sepsis); likely: Polymicrobial flora if source is intra-abdominal; possible: Resistant organisms if healthcare-associated or recent antibiotic exposure
Red flags: Immediate empiric antibiotics required

[guideline] empiric → Piperacillin-tazobactam (broad empiric, source unclear) / Add Vancomycin if MRSA risk, line-associated, or skin/soft tissue source Broad empiric gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic coverage is reasonable when the source is not yet localized, pending rapid source identification to allow narrowing.
[guideline] alternative → Source-directed narrow-spectrum therapy (preferred once source identified)
Other causes of distributive shock: pancreatitis, severe burns, liver failure, anaphylaxis, neurogenic shock from brain/spinal cord injury, and adrenal insufficiency/adrenal crisis (p.2353-2354)

chunks.text: Septic shock is the most common form of distributive shock, in which the primary hemodynamic derangement is a fall in systemic vascular resistance (vasoplegia) rather than a primary loss of preload or pump function. The vasodilatory profile is distinctive: SVR is reduced, cardiac output is typically increased as a compensatory response, and both central venous pressure (CVP) and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) tend to be low (p.2353-2354). Arterial and venous vasodilation is mediated in part by excess nitric oxide; vasopressin deficiency may also contribute to refractory hypotension. The dysregulated host response begins when pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs, e.g. LPS, microbial nucleic acids) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs, e.g. histones, HMGB1, mitochondrial DNA, ATP) are sensed by pattern-recognition receptors (TLRs, CLRs, RAGE, RIG-I, NOD receptors) on neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages, and parenchymal cells, triggering proinflammatory cytokine/chemokine release and upregulation of endothelial adhesion molecules. Activated neutrophils release reactive oxygen species and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs); endothelial activation/injury, glycocalyx degradation, and loss of VE-cadherin tight junctions cause capillary leak, interstitial edema, and increased oxygen-diffusion distance. A prothrombotic state arises from tissue-factor-driven coagulation, platelet/vWF microthrombi, complement activation (C3a, C5a, C5b-9 membrane attack complex), reduced anticoagulants (antithrombin, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, activated protein C), and impaired fibrinolysis (elevated PAI-1); consumption of clotting factors and platelets can then produce hemorrhage. The net effect is hypotension (from vasodilation, myocardial depression, and hypovolemia), microcirculatory dysfunction, and mitochondrial/metabolic failure, so that oxygen delivery, uptake, and utilization are all impaired and cellular injury occurs even when bulk oxygen delivery appears adequate (p.2317-2320). Sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy can add a cardiogenic component, producing mixed shock (p.2355).

chunks.text: Septic shock carries up to ~40% mortality, far higher than the ~15% overall mortality among US hospitalized adults with sepsis (p.2316). In emergency-department shock cohorts, septic and cardiogenic shock have the highest 90-day mortality (reported ~56% and ~52% respectively), and septic shock predominates among ICU shock (~62% of ICU shock patients in one multicenter series), whereas hypovolemic shock has lower mortality (p.2355). Mortality rises with age and is higher in men; comorbidities such as diabetes, obesity, neurologic/respiratory/cardiac disease, renal or hepatic insufficiency, cancer, and immunosuppression worsen outcomes (p.2317). SOFA scores predict mortality at the population level but not for individual patients; proposed clinical 'phenotypes' (alpha/beta/gamma/delta) carried roughly 2%, 5%, 15%, and 32% mortality (p.2317). Survivors face substantial long-term sequelae: physical (fatigue, muscle loss, weakness), cognitive and psychological (cognitive decline, dementia, depression), and increased risk of cardiovascular events, recurrent infection, and readmission. Roughly half of survivors are rehospitalized within 1 year and about one in six die within the first year, with most post-sepsis deaths in the first 6 months and elevated risk persisting up to 2 years (p.2321).

chunks.text: Sepsis-3 spectrum: (1) Sepsis = life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response to infection, operationalized as an acute increase of >=2 points in the SOFA score in a patient with suspected/confirmed infection. (2) Septic shock = a subset of sepsis with profound circulatory, cellular, and metabolic abnormalities and higher mortality, operationally defined as a septic patient who, despite adequate fluid resuscitation, requires vasopressors to maintain MAP >65 mmHg AND has serum lactate >2 mmol/L. qSOFA (RR>=22, GCS<15, SBP<=100; score >=2) is a rapid risk-stratification screen, not a diagnosis. The historical Sepsis-1/2 terms 'severe sepsis' and SIRS-based septic shock (SBP<90 or drop >=40 mmHg) have been superseded (p.2316, p.2320).
