Pneumonia results from proliferation of microbial pathogens in the alveoli combined with the host inflammatory response. Organisms reach the lower respiratory tract by inhalation, microaspiration of oropharyngeal flora, or direct mucosal spread; mechanical defenses (nasal hairs/turbinates, the branching airway, mucociliary clearance, gag and cough reflexes) are insufficient to fully exclude bacteria, and the lung is now understood to harbor a microbiota rather than being sterile. An inflammatory/epithelial-endothelial injury event releases cytokines, chemokines, and catecholamines that can selectively promote growth of organisms such as S. pneumoniae and P. aeruginosa, generating a positive-feedback loop; in CAP the trigger is often a viral infection compounded by microaspiration. Inflammatory mediators (IL-6, TNF) cause fever, while IL-8 and G-CSF recruit neutrophils; mediators from macrophages and neutrophils produce alveolar-capillary leak with impaired oxygenation, hypoxemia, and radiographic infiltrates. Some pathogens interfere with hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, worsening hypoxemia. Reduced compliance from capillary leak, increased respiratory drive and secretions, and intrapulmonary shunting drive worsening dyspnea, and when severe, reductions in lung volume/compliance and shunting can precipitate respiratory failure. Pathologically, classic (lobar pneumococcal) pneumonia evolves through edema, red hepatization, gray hepatization, and resolution phases.
Neither the Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) nor CURB-65 accurately determines the need for ICU admission; they predict mortality/site of care but not ICU need (p.1026).
Gross hemoptysis suggests necrotizing pneumonia, e.g., due to CA-MRSA (p.1024).
In the elderly, severe CAP may present atypically as new-onset or worsening confusion or decompensation of a chronic illness with few classic respiratory findings (p.1025).
Recent data show a mortality benefit for corticosteroids in severe CAP, particularly when there is a high level of systemic inflammation (CRP >15 mg/dL) (p.1029).

Patients with septic shock requiring vasopressors or acute respiratory failure requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation meet a major criterion and should be admitted directly to an ICU (p.1026).
Presence of three or more of the nine minor severe-CAP criteria warrants admission to an ICU or high-level monitoring unit (p.1026).

Late or delayed ICU admission is associated with increased mortality; less-ill patients placed on a general ward who then deteriorate fare worse than equally ill patients monitored in the ICU from the outset (p.1026).
In ICU-admitted CAP specifically, treatment directed at an identified pathogen may be superior to empirical therapy, so etiologic workup carries more weight in severe disease (p.1025).
The microbial spectrum of severe (ICU) CAP differs from milder CAP: Legionella tends to cause more serious disease, and S. aureus and gram-negative bacilli become more prominent (p.1024).

Prior respiratory-tract isolation of MRSA or P. aeruginosa within the past year is a stronger (more robust) risk factor for these pathogens than recent hospitalization plus parenteral antibiotic exposure (p.1028).
Procalcitonin (PCT) is insufficiently accurate to diagnose bacterial CAP and must NOT be used as a basis for withholding initial antibiotics; CRP is even less sensitive than PCT (p.1026).

If only a viral pathogen (e.g., influenza or SARS-CoV-2) is found and no bacterial pathogen is evident, antibacterial therapy can be stopped — BUT in severe illness, bacterial-viral co-infection must still be considered (p.1028).
Using PSI or CURB-65 to decide ICU admission - neither is accurate for that purpose (p.1026).
Withholding initial antibiotics based on a low procalcitonin - PCT is too inaccurate to exclude bacterial CAP (p.1026).
Assuming hospitalization alone is a significant risk factor for MRSA or P. aeruginosa - it is no longer considered so; severity plus specific risk factors drive coverage decisions (p.1028).
Requiring all three drug-resistance risk factors (recent hospitalization, recent oral/IV antibiotics, local validation) before considering resistant pathogens - any can apply (p.1028).
Stopping antibacterials when a virus is identified in a severely ill patient without considering bacterial-viral co-infection (p.1028).

Attributing failure to improve to the wrong cause: consider resistant or unexpected pathogen (CA-MRSA, M. tuberculosis, fungus), a sequestered focus (lung abscess, empyema), wrong drug/dose, or nosocomial superinfection (p.1029).
Routinely covering anaerobes in aspiration-related severe CAP - unnecessary unless poor dentition, lung abscess, or necrotizing pneumonia (p.1027).

Prognosis depends on age, comorbidities, and site of treatment. For hospitalized CAP, overall mortality ranges from 12% to 40%, the higher end reflecting ICU-level disease and care-process factors such as timely administration of appropriate antibiotics (vs <5% for outpatients). CURB-65 scores >=3 carry an overall ~22% mortality and may indicate ICU admission; PSI class 5 has a ~29.2% mortality. CAP is a leading infectious cause of death in patients >65 years; about 18% of hospitalized CAP patients are readmitted within a month, and recent data show 1-year mortality after CAP (especially in older patients) exceeds 30-day mortality. Severe-CAP complications (respiratory failure, shock, multiorgan failure) and pneumonia-associated cardiovascular events worsen outcomes.

IDSA/ATS severe-CAP criteria (Harrison 22e Table 131-3, p.1026). MAJOR criteria (either qualifies for ICU): (1) respiratory failure requiring invasive mechanical ventilation; (2) septic shock requiring vasopressors. MINOR criteria (>=3 warrant ICU/high-level monitoring): respiratory rate >=30 breaths/min; PaO2/FiO2 ratio <=250; multilobar infiltrates; confusion/disorientation; uremia (BUN >=20 mg/dL); leukopenia (WBC <4000/uL); thrombocytopenia (platelets <100,000/uL); hypothermia (core temperature <36 C); and hypotension requiring aggressive fluid resuscitation. Prognostic tools PSI (5 mortality classes, class 5 ~29.2%) and CURB-65 (confusion, urea >7 mmol/L, RR >=30, SBP <=90 or DBP <=60 mmHg, age >=65; score >=3 ~22% mortality) assess severity/site of care but are NOT accurate for determining ICU need.
Blood cultures (x2) — Bacteremia rate is higher in severe CAP; identifies organism and susceptibility for de-escalation.
Sputum culture and Gram stain — Helps target and de-escalate empiric therapy.
Urinary antigen (pneumococcal and Legionella) — Rapid, useful for severe presentations to guide targeted therapy.
ABG — Quantifies hypoxia/hypercapnia and guides ventilatory support decisions.
Chest X-ray / CT chest — Defines extent (multilobar disease, effusion, cavitation) which affects prognosis and management.
Lactate — Screens for tissue hypoperfusion and helps gauge severity/sepsis overlap.

chunks.text: Sinusitis is inflammation of the paranasal sinuses; when the nasal passages are also involved the term rhinosinusitis is used. Most acute disease begins as a viral process. Bacterial sinusitis, when it occurs, is usually a secondary superinfection of the obstructed/inflamed sinus and is most often caused by S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, or M. catarrhalis. Invasive fungal disease arises when host defenses are impaired (uncontrolled diabetes, transplant/immunocompromise), allowing Mucorales or Aspergillus to invade tissue and spread beyond the sinus (pp. 298-299).

Status epilepticus arises from a failure of the mechanisms that normally terminate seizure activity, leading to sustained abnormal neuronal hypersynchronization. This results from a relative excess of excitatory (glutamatergic) neurotransmission and depletion or dysfunction of inhibitory (GABAergic) signaling, with progressive receptor trafficking changes that make prolonged seizures increasingly resistant to GABA-acting drugs over time. Prolonged seizure activity can itself cause excitotoxic neuronal injury independent of the underlying cause, and is accompanied by systemic derangements including hyperthermia, acidosis, hypoxia, and autonomic instability that compound neuronal damage.

Defined operationally as a single seizure lasting beyond the time most seizures of that type would normally stop (roughly 5 minutes for convulsive seizures) or recurrent seizures without recovery of consciousness in between.
Treat convulsive status epilepticus as a time-critical emergency — earlier treatment initiation strongly predicts easier termination and better outcome.
Airway, breathing, circulation, glucose, and thiamine should be addressed simultaneously with, not after, anticonvulsant therapy.
Always check a bedside glucose early; hypoglycemia is a rapidly reversible cause that mimics or precipitates status epilepticus.

Non-convulsive status epilepticus should be suspected in any patient with unexplained persistent altered consciousness, especially after a convulsive seizure has been treated but the patient fails to wake up.
Continuous EEG monitoring is essential once convulsions have stopped to confirm electrographic seizure resolution, particularly in patients who remain unresponsive.
Refractory status epilepticus (persisting despite adequate first- and second-line therapy) generally requires escalation to continuous anesthetic infusions with EEG guidance in an ICU setting.

Identifying and treating the underlying etiology is as important as stopping the seizure itself, since ongoing precipitants (e.g., infection, toxin, structural lesion) will otherwise perpetuate the episode.
Assuming convulsions have stopped means the seizure is over — non-convulsive status epilepticus can persist electrographically with only subtle clinical signs.
Delaying anticonvulsant administration while awaiting imaging or laboratory results, which worsens the chance of terminating the seizure.
Underdosing initial therapy out of caution about respiratory depression, which increases the risk of treatment failure and need for escalation.
Failing to search for and treat the underlying precipitant, allowing the episode to recur despite initial seizure control.

Outcome depends heavily on etiology, age, and duration of status before treatment, with prolonged or refractory episodes carrying substantially higher morbidity and mortality. Even with successful seizure termination, patients face risk of cognitive sequelae and recurrent epilepsy, particularly when status is due to an acute severe brain insult.

TSS results from exotoxins produced by Staphylococcus aureus (notably TSST-1) or by Streptococcus pyogenes acting as superantigens that bind directly to MHC class II molecules and T-cell receptors outside the conventional antigen groove. This bypasses normal antigen processing and triggers massive, non-specific polyclonal T-cell activation with a resulting cytokine storm (IL-1, IL-2, TNF, interferon-gamma). The surge in inflammatory mediators produces capillary leak, vasodilation, hypotension, and secondary multi-organ dysfunction, explaining why the clinical picture can be severe even with a small, localized focus of infection or colonization.
Consider TSS in any acute febrile illness with diffuse macular erythroderma, hypotension, and multi-organ involvement, even without an obvious focal infection source.
A retained tampon, nasal packing, surgical wound packing, or postpartum/post-surgical site should always be actively sought and removed as part of initial assessment.
Streptococcal TSS typically presents with a clear, severe, deep soft-tissue focus (necrotizing fasciitis or bacteremia) and is far more often bacteremic than the staphylococcal form.
Desquamation of the palms and soles is a late finding, occurring one to two weeks after illness onset, and should never be relied upon to make the initial diagnosis.
Hypotension plus involvement of three or more organ systems (renal, hepatic, hematologic, mucosal, CNS, muscular/GI) in a febrile diffuse-rash illness supports the syndromic diagnosis.
Early aggressive fluid resuscitation is often required because of profound capillary leak, and volume needs can be extreme in the first 24-48 hours.
Source control (removing foreign material, draining/debriding infected tissue) is as critical as antimicrobial therapy and delays worsen outcomes.
Blood cultures are frequently negative in staphylococcal TSS since the syndrome is toxin-mediated rather than driven by bloodstream invasion.
Dismissing the diagnosis because blood cultures are negative — staphylococcal TSS is toxin-mediated and frequently culture-negative.
Waiting for classic desquamation before considering the diagnosis, which delays treatment since desquamation occurs late in the course.
Failing to perform a thorough examination for retained foreign bodies (vaginal, nasal, surgical) as the driving source.
Underestimating streptococcal TSS severity because the cutaneous findings can be subtler than staphylococcal disease despite higher mortality.

Staphylococcal TSS has a lower mortality (roughly a few percent) when recognized early and the source is controlled, whereas streptococcal TSS carries a substantially higher mortality, often cited around 30-70%, particularly when associated with necrotizing soft-tissue infection or bacteremia. Prompt source control, resuscitation, and antimicrobial therapy are the main determinants of outcome.

Rapid destruction of malignant cells releases large quantities of intracellular potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids into the circulation. Nucleic acid catabolism generates a surge of uric acid that can precipitate in the relatively acidic, low-flow environment of the renal tubules, producing obstructive nephropathy. Hyperphosphatemia from cell lysis exceeds the solubility product for calcium phosphate, causing tissue and renal deposition and consequent hypocalcemia. The resulting acute kidney injury further impairs excretion of potassium, phosphate, and uric acid, creating a self-amplifying metabolic crisis.

Emerges when bulky, rapidly proliferating tumours (especially high-grade lymphomas and acute leukemias) undergo massive cell death, either spontaneously or within hours to days of starting cytotoxic therapy
Classic biochemical tetrad is hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, and secondary hypocalcemia
Risk correlates with tumour bulk, proliferation rate, and baseline chemosensitivity — Burkitt lymphoma and acute lymphoblastic leukemia carry the highest risk
Pre-existing renal impairment, volume depletion, and acidic urine markedly increase risk of uric acid nephropathy
Onset is typically 12–72 hours after initiating effective therapy but can occur before any treatment is given in highly proliferative tumours
Acute kidney injury is usually the dominant clinical threat, driven by uric acid and/or calcium phosphate precipitation in renal tubules
Cardiac arrhythmia from hyperkalemia and hypocalcemia is the most immediately life-threatening complication
Aggressive risk stratification and prophylaxis before chemotherapy is far more effective than treating established syndrome
Assuming TLS only occurs after chemotherapy — spontaneous lysis can precede any treatment in highly proliferative tumours
Correcting hypocalcemia aggressively without addressing hyperphosphatemia first, which can worsen calcium-phosphate precipitation
Underestimating risk in patients with bulky, chemosensitive tumours and pre-existing renal impairment or dehydration
Delaying prophylactic measures until after laboratory abnormalities appear rather than initiating them proactively

With prompt recognition, risk stratification, and preventive management, most cases resolve without permanent renal impairment; outcomes worsen substantially once oliguric acute kidney injury or refractory hyperkalemia develops, occasionally requiring dialysis.

Nonspecific URI is an acute infection of the respiratory tract above the vocal cords, most commonly caused by respiratory viruses acquired through direct contact with infected people, contaminated surfaces, and large and small respiratory droplets. Susceptibility depends on prior exposure and immunity, general health, genetics, microbiome factors, and psychosocial factors including stress. Because immunity is serotype-specific (rhinovirus, adenovirus) or weak/short-lived (coronaviruses, parainfluenza, RSV, metapneumovirus), reinfection is frequent (Harrison 22e pp.295-296).

The nonspecific URI ('common cold') is defined as a respiratory tract infection in which no single symptom predominates, distinguishing it clinically from more localized syndromes such as pharyngitis, sinusitis, or otitis media (Harrison 22e p.296).

The overwhelming majority of acute respiratory infections are caused by common respiratory viruses and are self-limited; antibiotics neither speed resolution nor prevent complications, which is why at least half of ambulatory antibiotic prescriptions for these infections are inappropriate (Harrison 22e p.295).

Nasal mucus in a viral URI can range anywhere from watery to frankly purulent, so purulent or discolored nasal discharge by itself does not indicate bacterial infection or warrant antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.296).

Symptoms typically begin gradually after a 2-8 day incubation, peak early, and usually last 5-10 days but may persist up to 14 days; patients remain infectious as long as symptoms are present (Harrison 22e pp.296-297).

Adults average 2-4 URIs per year and children 6-10 per year; reinfection is common because immunity to the many rhinovirus and adenovirus serotypes is serotype-specific and immunity to coronaviruses, parainfluenza, RSV, and metapneumovirus is weak or short-lived (Harrison 22e pp.295-296).
Myalgias may occur but are usually less prominent than in influenza, a useful bedside discriminator from influenza (Harrison 22e p.296).

Making a specific viral diagnosis is not practical, cost-effective, or necessary; multiplex RT-PCR panels may be overly sensitive and yield false positives from recent prior infection (Harrison 22e p.296).
URI can be reduced by hand hygiene, physical distancing, masking, isolation of ill persons, and environmental cleaning (Harrison 22e p.295).

Prescribing antibiotics for a viral URI: they do not shorten illness or prevent complications and risk adverse drug effects, microbiome disruption, C. difficile infection, increased cost, and antibiotic resistance (Harrison 22e p.295).
Interpreting purulent nasal discharge as evidence of bacterial infection; viral URI mucus normally ranges from watery to purulent (Harrison 22e p.296).

Drivers of inappropriate prescribing include time pressure, fear of missing a rare bacterial diagnosis, concern about a rare complication, low salience of antibiotic harms, and the mistaken belief that patients demand antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.295).

Delayed antibiotic prescriptions are conceptually flawed for self-limited respiratory infections, shift decision-making to patients, and send a mixed message; they should be avoided (Harrison 22e p.296).
Procalcitonin testing has been ineffective and CRP testing not durable for reducing inappropriate ambulatory antibiotic use (Harrison 22e p.296).

Many popular cold remedies are ineffective, of questionable benefit, or harmful, including echinacea, zinc, inhaled steam, vitamin C, vitamin D, garlic, antihistamines, intranasal corticosteroids, saline nasal irrigation, and antiviral drugs (Harrison 22e p.296).
Cough and cold medicines should not be used in children under 6 years because of the risk of adverse effects (Harrison 22e p.296).

Nonspecific URI is self-limited. Symptoms peak early and generally resolve within 5-10 days, though some last up to 14 days. Although the cold can occasionally be complicated by otitis media or bacterial sinusitis, for any individual patient an antibiotic is more likely to cause an adverse reaction than to prevent a complication (Harrison 22e pp.296-297).

chunks.text: The endotracheal tube is the single most important risk factor for VAP. While it blocks large-volume aspiration, it worsens microaspiration of secretions that pool above the cuff, and the tube plus suctioning damages tracheal mucosa and promotes tracheal colonization. Pathogenic bacteria form a glycocalyx biofilm on the tube surface that shields them from antibiotics and host defenses; suctioning can dislodge organisms that reinoculate the trachea, and biofilm fragments can embolize to distal airways carrying bacteria. Ventilator circuit tubing can harbor organisms that wash back if manipulated, so circuits are changed only when soiled or with a new patient. In critically ill patients, normal oropharyngeal flora is replaced by pathogens, driven mainly by antibiotic selection pressure, cross-infection, severe systemic illness, and malnutrition. Severely ill patients with sepsis or trauma appear to enter a state of immunoparalysis several days after ICU admission, coinciding with peak VAP risk; the mechanism is unclear but hyperglycemia and frequent transfusions adversely affect immunity (p.1029-1030).

chunks.text: Crude mortality rates for VAP are reported as high as 50-70%, but the clinically meaningful figure is attributable mortality, since many patients have underlying diseases that would be fatal regardless. Attributable mortality exceeded 25% in one matched-cohort study, while more recent estimates are lower (5-10%); VAP complicating COVID-19 has higher attributable mortality. Mortality varies with patient type and ICU; VAP in trauma patients is generally not associated with attributable mortality (these patients were often previously healthy). The causative pathogen matters: MDR pathogens carry significantly greater attributable mortality than non-MDR pathogens, and infection with organisms such as S. maltophilia mainly marks a severely immunocompromised host at high risk. Beyond death, the major complication is prolonged mechanical ventilation with longer ICU and hospital stays; long-term sequelae of necrotizing infection include bronchiectasis and parenchymal scarring with recurrent pneumonia, prolonged oxygen need, a catabolic state, and (in the elderly) loss of independent function (p.1032-1033).

None of the hepatitis viruses is ordinarily directly cytopathic to hepatocytes; the clinical manifestations and outcome of acute liver injury are largely determined by the host immune (chiefly cell-mediated/cytolytic T-cell) response to infected hepatocytes. In hepatitis B the existence of inactive carriers with normal histology and the more severe disease seen with defective cellular immunity support an immune-mediated mechanism; in immunocompetent adults the degree of liver injury correlates with the level of HBV replication (HBV DNA). HBV enters hepatocytes via the sodium taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide (NTCP) receptor and replicates through reverse transcription of a pregenomic RNA, forming covalently closed circular DNA in the nucleus. HDV likewise enters via NTCP but depends on HBV helper function for complete virions and liver injury (p.2643-2645, p.2651).

Five hepatotropic viruses cause almost all acute viral hepatitis: HAV, HBV, HCV, HDV (delta), and HEV. All are RNA viruses except HBV, which is a DNA virus that replicates via reverse transcription like a retrovirus (p.2643).
Isolated anti-HBc usually represents remote past HBV infection (IgG class); rarely it reflects low-level viremia with HBsAg below detection, or a false-positive (p.2646).

IgM anti-HBc can reappear with high titer during acute flares of chronic hepatitis B, so IgM vs IgG anti-HBc does not always reliably separate de novo acute hepatitis B from an exacerbation of chronic HBV; history and serial follow-up help (p.2646-2647, p.2657).

HBeAg is a qualitative marker of active HBV replication and high infectivity; HBV DNA is the quantitative marker. HBeAg-positive HBsAg-positive mothers transmit to >90% of offspring versus only 10-15% if anti-HBe positive (p.2645-2646).

Precore/core-promoter mutant HBV cannot make HBeAg, producing HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis with detectable HBV DNA and anti-HBe; it can run a more aggressive course and is the predominant form in the Mediterranean and Europe (p.2646-2647).

Anti-HCV (IgG) is the available antibody marker (no clinically useful IgM anti-HCV exists); with contemporary assays it is detectable early in acute hepatitis C and persists after recovery and during chronic infection (p.2657).

HCV RNA is the most sensitive test and the diagnostic gold standard; it appears before aminotransferase rise and before anti-HCV. Detectable anti-HCV with negative HCV RNA signifies cleared/cured infection (p.2657-2658).

Recovery from hepatitis C leaves persistent anti-HCV but does NOT protect against reinfection; in people who inject drugs, anti-HCV plus HCV RNA may indicate reinfection rather than chronic infection (p.2657-2658).
Serum aminotransferase levels do not correlate well with the degree of liver cell damage; peak ALT/AST does not predict severity (p.2655-2656).
A low-grade fever (38-39 C) is more typical of hepatitis A and E than of B or C, except when hepatitis B presents with a serum sickness-like syndrome (p.2655).

HDV is a defective virus that requires HBV (HBsAg envelope) for replication; negative HBV serology excludes hepatitis D, and the duration of HDV infection cannot outlast HBV infection (p.2646-2647, p.2658).

All five types produce a clinically similar acute illness, so the type cannot be reliably distinguished by clinical or epidemiologic features alone; specific serologic testing is the accurate way to tell them apart (p.2643, p.2651).

In acute hepatitis with HBsAg and anti-HDV, the anti-HBc class clarifies the relationship: IgM anti-HBc indicates simultaneous acute HBV-HDV co-infection, whereas IgG anti-HBc indicates HDV superinfection on chronic HBV (p.2658).
Among healthy adults, acute hepatitis B is self-limited in ~95-99%, whereas acute hepatitis C is self-limited in only ~15-20% (chronicity is the rule for HCV) (p.2655-2656).

Only the bloodborne agents (HBV, HCV, HDV) can become chronic and progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma; HAV and HEV do not cause chronic liver disease in immunocompetent hosts (p.2643, p.2659-2660).

Hepatitis A is diagnosed during acute illness by detecting IgM anti-HAV; IgM persists ~3 months (rarely 6-12). IgG anti-HAV appears in convalescence, remains detectable indefinitely, and confers lifelong immunity to reinfection (p.2643-2644, p.2656).

The serologic/virologic course of acute hepatitis E mirrors hepatitis A: brief fecal shedding and viremia, an early IgM anti-HEV response dominating ~the first 3 months, then long-lasting IgG anti-HEV (p.2658).
Acute hepatitis can be evaluated with five serologic tests: HBsAg, IgM anti-HAV, IgM anti-HBc, anti-HCV, and HCV RNA (p.2657-2658).
HBsAg positive plus IgM anti-HBc indicates acute (or acute reactivation) hepatitis B; HBsAg positive with IgG anti-HBc (IgM negative) indicates chronic HBV (p.2657-2658).
In about 1-5% of acute HBV infections HBsAg is below the detection threshold; in that window the presence of IgM anti-HBc establishes the diagnosis of acute hepatitis B (p.2646, p.2656).
The anti-HBc 'window' period (HBsAg already cleared, anti-HBs not yet detectable) is now rarely encountered because of higher-sensitivity HBsAg/anti-HBs assays (p.2646).
Relying on HBsAg alone can miss acute hepatitis B: in ~1-5% of cases HBsAg is below detection and only IgM anti-HBc reveals the diagnosis (p.2656, p.2657-2658).
Retrospective diagnosis of self-limited simultaneous acute HBV-HDV co-infection is difficult because anti-HDV is often transient and disappears once HBsAg clears (p.2658).
Patients with acute viral hepatitis tolerate surgery poorly; biliary disease should be excluded clinically and with imaging before any operation (p.2660).
IgM anti-HBc can re-emerge during an acute exacerbation of chronic HBV, so it does not always distinguish true acute hepatitis B from a chronic flare (p.2646-2647, p.2657).
False-positive IgM anti-HAV occurs in rheumatologic disease (rheumatoid factor) and rarely in EBV infection; false-positive IgM anti-HBc occurs with high-titer rheumatoid factor (p.2656).
Anti-HCV immunoassays can be falsely positive (low pretest probability, rheumatoid factor); confirm with HCV RNA (p.2657).
In immunosuppressed patients anti-HCV may be undetectable, so HCV RNA testing is required to diagnose hepatitis C (p.2655, p.2657).
HBsAg titer does not reflect disease severity - an inverse correlation exists, with very low HBsAg in fulminant hepatitis (p.2656-2657).
Coexisting HBsAg and anti-HBs in chronic HBV does not signal imminent HBsAg clearance; these patients still have chronic HBV infection (p.2646, p.2657).
A normal or only mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase and normal albumin are expected in uncomplicated acute hepatitis; abnormal values suggest an alternative or complicated course (p.2656).
The serum sickness-like prodrome of acute hepatitis B (arthralgia, rash, angioedema) is often misdiagnosed as a rheumatologic disease before jaundice appears (p.2659).

Hepatitis A and acute hepatitis B in previously healthy persons usually resolve completely (HBV self-limited in ~95-99% of healthy adults; HAV essentially always), with an overall case-fatality of ~0.1% (1% among hospitalized acute hepatitis B). Hepatitis A and E cause no chronic liver disease in immunocompetent hosts. Acute hepatitis C becomes chronic in ~85-90%; among chronic HCV, cirrhosis develops in up to ~20% over 10-20 years, with an annual decompensation risk ~4% and annual HCC risk ~1-4% (about 3.36%) once cirrhotic - rates declining with effective direct-acting antiviral therapy. Chronic hepatitis B carries an enhanced HCC risk, especially with infection in infancy/childhood and high HBV DNA/HBeAg; risk of cirrhosis and HCC rises with the level of HBV replication. Waterborne hepatitis E (genotypes 1 and 2) in India/Asia has a case-fatality of 1-2%, rising to 10-20% in pregnant women. Acute HBV-HDV co-infection mortality is usually similar to HBV alone (~5% in some injection-drug-user outbreaks), but HDV superinfection of chronic HBV markedly worsens outcome (annual cirrhosis rate ~4% in chronic hepatitis D; annual HCC ~3% once cirrhotic) (p.2658-2660).
Hepatic encephalopathy (confusion, disorientation, somnolence, progression to coma) - hallmark of fulminant hepatitis with very high mortality (>80% in deep coma without transplant) (p.2659)
Acute hepatitis E or other insult superimposed on chronic liver disease (acute-on-chronic liver failure) (p.2659-2660)
Markedly prolonged prothrombin time / INR (reflects severe synthetic failure and extensive hepatocellular necrosis) (p.2656, p.2658-2659)
Rapidly shrinking liver size with rapidly rising bilirubin even as aminotransferases fall - indicates massive hepatic necrosis (p.2659)

No formal grading system for acute viral hepatitis is given; severity is judged clinically. Features indicating severe hepatocellular disease warranting prompt hospital admission include prolonged prothrombin time, low serum albumin, hypoglycemia, and very high serum bilirubin; presenting ascites, edema, or encephalopathy indicate a poorer prognosis. Progression to fulminant hepatitis (massive hepatic necrosis) is marked by encephalopathy with rapidly shrinking liver size, rapidly rising bilirubin, and markedly prolonged PT even as aminotransferases fall (p.2658-2659).

Liver function tests — Marked transaminase elevation (often >10x upper limit of normal) with hyperbilirubinemia is characteristic of acute viral hepatitis and helps distinguish it from other causes of jaundice.
Hepatitis A IgM, Hepatitis E IgM — Confirms the most likely causes in this setting; both are the standard first-line serologic tests for acute fecal-oral hepatitis.
Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), IgM anti-HBc — Identifies acute Hepatitis B, which has different counseling, monitoring, and contact-tracing/vaccination implications than A or E.
Coagulation profile (PT/INR) — A rising INR is the key early warning sign of evolving acute liver failure and should be tracked closely.
Mental status assessment (serial) — Screens for hepatic encephalopathy, the clinical hallmark of progression to acute liver failure requiring urgent escalation of care.

Viral meningitis is inflammation of the meninges, most often caused by enteroviruses, with a self-limited course in immunocompetent hosts. Inflammation is largely confined to the meninges, producing meningeal irritation without the parenchymal brain involvement that characterizes encephalitis; preservation of higher cerebral function distinguishes meningitis from encephalitis. CSF oligoclonal IgG bands directed against viral proteins can occur, though they are nonspecific (Harrison 22e p.1166-1167).

Profound alterations in consciousness (stupor, coma, marked confusion), seizures, focal neurologic signs, or neuroimaging evidence of parenchymal involvement do NOT occur in viral meningitis; their presence points instead to encephalitis or another CNS process (p.1166).

Consider LCMV when aseptic meningitis occurs in late fall/winter with exposure to house mice or pet/laboratory rodents or their excreta, particularly when accompanied by leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, or abnormal liver function tests (p.1169).

Headache is almost invariably present, often frontal or retroorbital, with photophobia and pain on eye movement; nuchal rigidity is usually present but may be mild, appearing only near the limit of neck anteflexion (p.1166).

A specific viral cause is identified in 60-90% of cases using combined CSF PCR, culture, and serology; roughly two-thirds of culture-negative 'aseptic' meningitis cases have a viral etiology found by CSF PCR (p.1166).
Enteroviruses account for >85% of cases with an identified etiology and predominate in summer and fall, especially in children <15 years (p.1167-1168).

HSV-2 causes most adult uncomplicated HSV meningitis (HSV-1 causes ~90% of HSV encephalitis); ~20% of HSV meningitis patients develop recurrent attacks, and most recurrent/'aseptic' meningitis, including cases formerly called Mollaret's meningitis, is due to HSV (p.1168).
Many HSV meningitis patients give no history and show no active genital herpes lesions at presentation, so absence of genital lesions does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1168).
VZV is increasingly recognized as a cause of meningitis even WITHOUT rash, so absence of chickenpox or shingles does not exclude it (p.1168).

Cranial nerve palsies (most often V, VII, or VIII) are more common in HIV meningitis than in other viral meningitides; HIV seroconversion may be delayed, so seronegative suspected cases warrant repeat testing (p.1168).

Mumps meningitis is suggested by parotitis, orchitis, oophoritis, pancreatitis, or raised serum amylase/lipase, but their absence does not exclude it; a documented prior mumps infection (lifelong immunity) does exclude it (p.1168-1169).
Failing to recognize partially or incompletely treated bacterial meningitis, which can produce a lymphocytic-predominant CSF that mimics viral meningitis (p.1167)
Up to 15% of enteroviral meningitis patients (most often young infants) have a NORMAL CSF leukocyte count, so a normal cell count does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1168)

PMNs may predominate during the first 48 h of viral meningitis (e.g., echovirus 9, WNV, EEE, mumps); WNV PMN pleocytosis occurs in ~45% and can persist a week or more before shifting to lymphocytes — do not assume early neutrophilia means bacterial infection (p.1167-1168)
Treating a normal CSF glucose as ruling out viral meningitis is wrong, but conversely low CSF glucose can occur in 10-30% of mumps or LCMV and rarely with enteroviruses, HSV-2, or VZV (p.1167)
CSF viral culture has generally poor sensitivity for viral meningitis (unlike its utility in bacterial infection), so reliance on culture alone underdiagnoses (p.1167)
Enterovirus detected in stool is NOT diagnostic of acute CNS infection — it may reflect residual shedding from a prior infection or asymptomatic carriage during epidemics (p.1167)
Enteroviral RT-PCR has low sensitivity for EV71; specific testing may be required (p.1168)
EBV CSF PCR false-positives may reflect viral reactivation or latent viral DNA in recruited lymphocytes rather than true EBV meningitis (p.1168)
Routine serology is unhelpful for high-seroprevalence viruses (HSV, VZV, CMV, EBV) (p.1167)

In adults the prognosis for full recovery from viral meningitis is excellent; treatment of almost all cases is primarily symptomatic. Rare adult patients have persisting headache, mild mental impairment, incoordination, or generalized asthenia for weeks to months. Outcome is less certain in infants and neonates (<1 year), in whom intellectual impairment, learning disabilities, hearing loss, and other lasting sequelae have been reported. Enteroviral meningitis outside the neonatal period is usually benign with recovery without sequelae, but chronic/severe infection can occur in neonates and in people with hypo- or agammaglobulinemia (Harrison 22e p.1168-1169).
Depressed or markedly altered consciousness (stupor, coma, marked confusion) — suggests encephalitis or alternative diagnosis, not simple viral meningitis (p.1166)
Seizures (p.1166)
Focal neurologic signs/symptoms or neuroimaging abnormalities indicating parenchymal brain involvement (p.1166)
CSF PMN pleocytosis without an established diagnosis — should prompt consideration of bacterial or parameningeal infection (p.1166-1167)

Lymphocytic pleocytosis WITH low CSF glucose (hypoglycorrhachia) — should raise suspicion of fungal, tuberculous, or Listeria meningoencephalitis, or noninfectious causes such as sarcoid or neoplastic meningitis (p.1167)
Atypical CSF profile or immunocompromising condition/treatment — warrants hospitalization and neuroimaging (p.1167)

Harrison does not give a formal severity grading for viral meningitis; it instead frames disposition by risk. Immunocompetent patients with a classic CSF profile (lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, negative Gram stain), no focal signs, and no significant alteration in consciousness may not require hospitalization if home monitoring and follow-up are assured. Hospitalization is indicated for immunocompromised patients, those with significant alteration in consciousness, seizures, or focal signs suggesting encephalitis/parenchymal involvement, and those with an atypical CSF profile (Harrison 22e p.1169).

Lumbar puncture with CSF cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, culture — The decisive test distinguishing viral from bacterial meningitis and guiding the decision to continue or stop empiric antibacterial therapy.
CSF viral PCR (enterovirus, HSV) — Identifies the specific viral cause; HSV PCR specifically changes management since HSV meningitis/encephalitis is treated with acyclovir.
Blood cultures — Performed alongside LP workup to support the broader diagnostic picture, particularly if bacterial meningitis cannot yet be excluded.

Waldenström macroglobulinaemia is a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma in which clonal B-lymphoplasmacytic cells infiltrate the bone marrow (and sometimes lymph nodes and spleen) and secrete large quantities of monoclonal IgM. The pentameric structure of IgM raises serum viscosity disproportionately to its molar concentration, producing the hyperviscosity syndrome, and the paraprotein may also deposit in nerves, precipitate in the cold (cryoglobulinemia), or bind red cells (cold agglutinin disease). Somatic activating mutations in MYD88 (and often CXCR4) drive NF-κB signaling and are central to disease pathogenesis.
Consider WM in an older adult with fatigue, weight loss, and an incidental monoclonal IgM spike on protein electrophoresis.
Hyperviscosity symptoms (visual blurring, headache, mucosal bleeding, dizziness) reflect the very large size of the pentameric IgM molecule rather than tumor burden alone.
Bone lesions are characteristically absent, unlike multiple myeloma, which helps distinguish the two at the bedside.
Peripheral neuropathy (often demyelinating, anti-MAG antibody mediated) can be a presenting or dominant feature.
Cold agglutinin disease and cryoglobulinemia are important IgM-related complications that can cause hemolysis or vasculitis-like skin findings.
Bone marrow involvement by small lymphoplasmacytic cells with a mast-cell-rich infiltrate is a classic morphologic clue.
MYD88 L265P mutation is present in the great majority of cases and is a useful diagnostic and prognostic marker.
Asymptomatic patients with low IgM levels can often be observed without treatment (watch-and-wait).
Attributing an incidental IgM paraprotein to benign MGUS without adequate marrow and clinical evaluation when other features are present
Delaying plasmapheresis in symptomatic hyperviscosity while awaiting definitive chemoimmunotherapy
Missing WM as a cause of unexplained demyelinating peripheral neuropathy in older adults
Confusing WM with IgM myeloma or misinterpreting lytic bone lesions as consistent with WM (they are not typical)

The disease course is typically indolent with survival often measured in many years, and asymptomatic low-burden disease can be observed safely. Prognosis is influenced by age, cytopenias, beta-2-microglobulin level, and genetic features such as CXCR4 mutation status, with most patients eventually requiring treatment for symptomatic progression.

Zollinger-Ellison syndrome results from a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor (gastrinoma), most often located in the duodenum or pancreas, that drives unregulated gastric acid hypersecretion. The resulting profound acid load overwhelms mucosal defenses and inactivates pancreatic enzymes, producing severe/recurrent peptic ulceration and secretory diarrhea with malabsorption. A substantial minority of cases occur in association with MEN1, reflecting a hereditary predisposition to multiple endocrine tumors.

Suspect ZES in patients with severe, recurrent, or refractory peptic ulcers, ulcers in unusual locations (distal duodenum, jejunum), or ulcers with prominent diarrhea that improves with acid suppression.
Chronic secretory diarrhea plus peptic ulcer disease is a classic combination that should prompt gastrin testing.
About 20-30% of gastrinomas occur as part of MEN1 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1) — screen for hyperparathyroidism and pituitary tumors.
Most gastrinomas arise within the 'gastrinoma triangle' bounded by the cystic duct, junction of the pancreatic head/neck, and duodenal junction.
Fasting serum gastrin should be measured off proton pump inhibitors when clinically feasible, since acid suppression can falsely elevate gastrin.
A markedly elevated fasting gastrin with an inappropriately low gastric pH strongly supports the diagnosis.
Roughly half of gastrinomas are malignant with a tendency for lymph node and hepatic metastases at diagnosis.
Somatostatin-receptor imaging (e.g., DOTATATE PET) is the preferred modality for tumor localization given high sensitivity.

Prognosis depends primarily on tumor biology and extent of disease at diagnosis; localized, resectable gastrinomas carry a favorable long-term outlook, while metastatic disease (especially hepatic spread) is associated with reduced survival. Effective acid suppression has greatly reduced ulcer-related morbidity, shifting long-term outcome toward tumor-related factors.

Aneurysm is a pathologic dilation of the aortic wall; a true aneurysm involves all three wall layers, versus a pseudoaneurysm in which intima and media are disrupted and the dilated segment is contained only by adventitia (and sometimes perivascular clot). Most abdominal aortic aneurysms are degenerative and atherosclerotic. Wall failure results from degradation or abnormal production of the structural matrix proteins elastin and collagen, driven by inflammation, oxidative stress, proteolysis, and biomechanical wall stress. B- and T-lymphocytes, macrophages, inflammatory cytokines, and matrix metalloproteinases degrade elastin and collagen, reducing tensile strength and the aorta's ability to tolerate pulsatile stretch; histology shows elastin/collagen destruction, loss of vascular smooth muscle, neovascularization, and inflammation (p.2208).
Most abdominal aortic aneurysms are asymptomatic and are found as an incidental imaging finding or as a palpable, pulsatile, expansile, nontender mass on routine abdominal exam (p.2211).
New aneurysmal pain is usually a harbinger of rupture and constitutes a medical emergency; however, acute rupture more often occurs without any prior warning (p.2211).
Acute pain plus hypotension is the presentation of frank rupture and mandates emergency open or endovascular repair (p.2211).
At least 90% of abdominal aortic aneurysms >4.0 cm are atherosclerotic, and most lie below the level of the renal arteries (infrarenal) (p.2211).
Cigarette smoking is the most potent modifiable risk factor; incidence rises with age and the condition is more common in men (p.2211).
Mural thrombus within the aneurysm sac can be a source of peripheral (distal) embolization (p.2211).
A rupturing AAA can be misattributed to renal/ureteric colic when pain radiates to the flank or genitalia (p.154).
Plain x-ray cannot exclude an aneurysm because roughly a quarter are non-calcified (p.2211).
Aortography may underestimate aneurysm diameter when mural thrombus narrows the lumen (p.2211).
Premonitory pain may persist for several days before rupture and collapse, so an evolving symptomatic aneurysm should not be dismissed (p.154).

Prognosis depends on aneurysm size and on the severity of coexisting coronary and cerebrovascular disease. Rupture risk rises sharply with diameter: the 5-year rupture risk is roughly 1-2% for aneurysms <5 cm versus 20-40% for aneurysms >5 cm. At smaller diameters the rupture risk is higher in women than in men (p.2211-2212).
New or worsening aneurysmal pain (abdomen, lower back, chest, or scrotum) signals impending rupture (p.2211).
Abdominal pain radiating to sacrum, flank, or genitalia should always raise suspicion of a rupturing AAA (p.154).
Acute pain with hypotension indicates rupture — emergency repair required (p.2211).

Rupture-risk stratification is driven by maximal aortic diameter. Per Harrison: a true abdominal aortic aneurysm is dilation 50% greater than the adjacent normal segment; aneurysms >=4.0 cm affect 1-2% of men >50. 5-year rupture risk is ~1-2% for <5 cm and ~20-40% for >5 cm. Repair thresholds: any size if rapidly expanding or symptomatic; for asymptomatic aneurysms repair is indicated at >=5.5 cm in men and >=5.0 cm in women, with smaller aneurysms followed by ultrasound surveillance (p.2210-2212).

Normal menstruation depends on cyclical ovulation producing coordinated oestrogen and progesterone effects, followed by orderly progesterone withdrawal and controlled endometrial shedding with effective local haemostasis. Abnormal bleeding arises when this is disrupted: structural lesions (polyps, adenomyosis, fibroids, hyperplasia or cancer) distort the endometrium and its vasculature; anovulation leads to unopposed oestrogen with an unstable proliferative endometrium that sheds erratically; systemic coagulopathy impairs haemostasis; and local disturbances of endometrial prostaglandins and fibrinolysis increase menstrual loss.
Abnormal uterine bleeding describes any bleeding that is abnormal in frequency, regularity, duration, or volume in a non-pregnant woman of reproductive age

A. baumannii has greater virulence potential than other Acinetobacter species, partly through its ability to grow at 37 degrees C and resist macrophage uptake. Colonization is facilitated by adherence to surfaces and human cells and by biofilm formation, which is linked to exopolysaccharide production and pilus formation; a quorum-sensing molecule encoded by the abaI autoinducer synthase gene contributes to biofilm on abiotic surfaces. The organism modifies its lipid A structure to survive harsh environments, decreasing susceptibility to antibiotics and antimicrobial peptides and enhancing desiccation survival. An extracellular capsule protects against complement-mediated killing and can be upregulated in the presence of subinhibitory antibiotic levels, producing a hypervirulent phenotype. Phospholipase C and D act as cytotoxic virulence factors aiding epithelial invasion, and siderophore-based iron-acquisition systems permit growth despite host iron limitation. Multiple protein-secretion systems (type II with the LipA lipase substrate, type V trimeric autotransporter mediating biofilm and matrix adherence, and a type VI system secreting antibacterial toxins) plus outer-membrane vesicles carrying OmpA, proteases, and phospholipases contribute to pathogenesis and innate immune activation. Antimicrobial resistance arises from reduced porin expression, overexpressed efflux pumps (removing quinolones, tetracyclines, chloramphenicol, disinfectants, and tigecycline), and beta-lactamases including intrinsic AmpC cephalosporinases (upregulated when the ISAba1 insertion sequence is placed next to the AmpC gene) and acquired serine and metallo-beta-lactamases. Carbapenem resistance is mostly tied to Ambler class D oxacillinases (group 2d), some intrinsic/chromosomal (e.g., OXA-51-like) and others acquired (e.g., OXA-23-, 24-, 58-, 143-, 235-like). The small A. baumannii core genome with a large accessory genome confers high genomic plasticity and ready uptake of resistance genes by horizontal gene transfer.

Acinetobacter are gram-negative, oxidase-negative, nonmotile, nonfermenting coccobacilli readily grown on standard media; A. baumannii is the most clinically relevant species. Phenotypic differentiation between species is difficult, so molecular methods such as MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry or quantitative real-time PCR are often needed for accurate identification.

Risk factors for health care-associated colonization/infection include nursing home residence, prolonged ICU stay, central venous catheterization, tracheostomy, mechanical ventilation, enteral feeding, and prior third-generation cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, or carbapenems; carbapenem-resistant strains are most common after carbapenem exposure.

Urinary tract infection is infrequent and usually catheter-associated, reflecting biofilm formation on devices; rare community-acquired cases occur with nephrolithiasis or after renal transplantation.
Less common manifestations include contact lens-associated keratitis and native- or prosthetic-valve endocarditis.
A. baumannii can survive environmental desiccation for weeks, allowing it to persist on hospital surfaces and equipment - a key reason it drives health care-associated outbreaks.

A. baumannii is a notorious cause of nosocomial pneumonia, especially with prolonged mechanical ventilation; onset tends to be later than with other gram-negative bacilli, and the usual clues are fever and increased sputum production.

Airway colonization with A. baumannii does not by itself confirm pneumonia, but it is a recognized risk factor for subsequent infection - distinguishing colonization from true infection is a recurring clinical challenge.
On a CSF Gram stain, Acinetobacter can mimic Neisseria meningitidis since both appear as gram-negative paired cocci; a petechial rash was described in up to 30% of one meningitis case series.

Bloodstream infection most often arises in ICU patients with a central venous catheter or as a secondary complication of ventilator-associated/hospital-acquired pneumonia; fever occurs in over 95% of cases and polymicrobial growth is reported in roughly 20-36% of bacteremia episodes.

In combat-trauma soft tissue infection, the described clinical evolution progresses from an edematous peau d'orange appearance to a sandpaper appearance with overlying vesicles, then to a necrotizing process with hemorrhagic bullae; necrotizing fasciitis has been reported.

Community-acquired Acinetobacter pneumonia is relatively rare but severe, with fever, prominent respiratory symptoms, multi-organ dysfunction, lobar consolidation on imaging, and mortality exceeding 50%.

A. baumannii is an important burn-unit pathogen; large burns provide ideal growth conditions, facilitate patient-to-patient transmission, and wound colonization is a risk factor for bloodstream infection.

Infections carry high mortality, driven largely by the severity of the patient's underlying illness and by drug resistance of the infecting strain. Crude mortality with nosocomial pneumonia has been reported as high as 65%, though attributable mortality is hard to establish because affected patients are typically debilitated. Community-acquired pneumonia mortality exceeds 50%. Crude bloodstream infection mortality reaches about 40% overall and as high as 70% with carbapenem-resistant isolates. Wound colonization/infection contributes to healing delays and graft loss in burn patients.

chunks.text: The anterior cruciate ligament runs from the posterior femoral intercondylar notch to the anterior tibial plateau and is the principal restraint to anterior translation of the tibia and a key stabiliser against rotational and pivoting forces. Sudden deceleration, landing, or a valgus-external rotation force with the foot planted overloads the ligament, causing partial or complete rupture, frequently near its femoral origin. Because the ligament is intra-articular and vascular, rupture produces a rapid haemarthrosis. The ACL has poor intrinsic healing capacity, so complete tears generally do not reunite. Persistent instability increases shear on the menisci and articular cartilage, accelerating degenerative change.

chunks.text: Acne results from four interacting processes within the pilosebaceous unit: increased sebum production driven by androgens, abnormal keratinisation of the follicular lining producing microcomedones, proliferation of Cutibacterium acnes, and inflammation. Trapped sebum and keratin form comedones; bacterial activity and the host immune response generate inflammatory mediators that produce papules, pustules, and deeper nodules. Rupture of the follicular wall extends inflammation into the dermis, and disordered wound healing can result in atrophic or hypertrophic scarring. Hormonal influences, genetic predisposition, and certain drugs modulate severity.

chunks.text: Acoustic neuroma is a benign neoplasm of Schwann cells, most often originating at the transition zone of the vestibular nerve within or near the internal auditory canal. As it grows it first fills the canal, compressing the cochlear and vestibular fibres and their blood supply to produce sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and imbalance. Continued expansion into the cerebellopontine angle displaces and stretches adjacent structures: the trigeminal nerve above, the facial nerve alongside, and eventually the brainstem and cerebellum. Large tumours can obstruct cerebrospinal fluid flow and raise intracranial pressure. Most cases are sporadic and unilateral, while bilateral tumours are the hallmark of neurofibromatosis type 2.

Myocardial ischemia (angina pectoris) arises from an imbalance between myocardial oxygen demand (raised by heart rate, ventricular wall stress, and contractility) and oxygen supply (set by coronary blood flow and arterial oxygen content). ACS is typically precipitated by acute coronary atherothrombosis. When ischemia is sufficiently severe and prolonged (as little as ~20 min), irreversible cellular injury and MI occur. Symptoms can also be driven predominantly by increased demand (e.g., intense psychological stress) or reduced delivery (anemia, hypoxia, hypotension), underlying the type 2 MI concept (Harrison 22e p.145).
ACS encompasses unstable angina, NSTEMI, and STEMI, and the term is generally reserved for ischemia precipitated by acute coronary atherothrombosis (Harrison 22e p.145).

Unstable ischemic heart disease is sub-classified by whether acute myocardial injury is detectable and whether ST-segment elevation is present: unstable angina = no detectable acute injury; NSTEMI/STEMI = acute injury without/with ST elevation (Harrison 22e p.145).

Type 1 MI (acute coronary thrombosis) is distinguished from type 2 MI, which results from another imbalance of myocardial oxygen supply and demand; type 2 may be driven by anemia, hypoxia, hypotension, or intense psychological stress (Harrison 22e p.145, p.150).
An ECG is recommended within 10 minutes of presentation, primarily to identify ST-segment elevation candidates for immediate reperfusion (Harrison 22e p.150).
Resting ECG sensitivity for ischemia is poor (as low as ~20%), so a normal ECG does not exclude ACS; serial ECGs every 30-60 min are recommended early in suspected ACS (Harrison 22e p.150).
Physical examination findings may be entirely normal in unstable ischemic heart disease, so an unremarkable exam is not reassuring (Harrison 22e p.149).

Relief of pain by nitroglycerin is neither sensitive nor specific for ischemia (esophageal spasm also responds); relief delayed beyond ~10 min suggests either a non-ischemic cause or severe ischemia such as acute MI (Harrison 22e p.149).
Chest wall tenderness on palpation does not exclude myocardial ischemia (Harrison 22e p.150).
Relying on a normal resting ECG or unremarkable physical exam to exclude ACS - both can be normal in unstable ischemic heart disease (Harrison 22e p.149-150).
Treating nitroglycerin response as diagnostic - esophageal spasm also responds and ischemic relief is non-specific (Harrison 22e p.149).
Attributing pain to the chest wall because palpation reproduces it - tenderness does not exclude ischemia (Harrison 22e p.150).

Some patients with ischemia deny 'pain' and report only dyspnea or vague anxiety; women and the elderly may present with anginal equivalents (dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, fatigue, faintness) (Harrison 22e p.149).
Inferior MI may present with nausea/vomiting (vagal / Bezold-Jarisch reflex), simulating a GI disorder (Harrison 22e p.149).

High-sensitivity troponin detects injury in many non-ACS cardiopulmonary conditions; without a dynamic rise/fall and clinical correlation, a single elevated value can be misinterpreted as MI - chronic elevation occurs with structural heart disease, end-stage renal disease, or interfering antibodies (Harrison 22e p.150).
Non-ischemic injury (e.g., myocarditis) can raise troponin but should not be labeled MI (Harrison 22e p.150).
Confusing diagnostic decision-aids (HEART, EDACS) with prognostic risk scores (TIMI, GRACE), which are intended for patients with already-established ACS, not for diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.151).

Among unselected ED chest-pain populations, only ~10-20% (as low as 5%) are ultimately diagnosed with ACS, while gastrointestinal causes predominate; historically 2-6% of patients discharged with presumed non-ischemic pain were later found to have had a missed MI. In patients stratified as low risk (excluding ST elevation or definite noncardiac pain), the estimated 30-day major cardiovascular event rate was ~2.5%. Validated clinical decision pathways combining ECG and serial high-sensitivity troponin can achieve ACS miss rates <0.5%, and a single very low hs-troponin >2-3 h after symptom onset carries a negative predictive value >99% for MI (Harrison 22e p.145, p.150-151).

ACS is categorized along two clinical decision-making lines. (1) Diagnostic/disposition risk in undifferentiated chest pain uses clinical decision pathways such as the HEART score (history, ECG, age, risk factors; low risk 0-3) and EDACS, combined with serial high-sensitivity troponin, to classify patients as low/intermediate/high risk. (2) Prognostic risk in established ACS uses the TIMI and GRACE risk scores to estimate event risk - these are explicitly not intended for diagnostic use. Common high-risk elements across tools: typical ACS symptoms, older age, known/atherosclerotic risk factors, ischemic ECG changes, and elevated troponin (Harrison 22e p.151).

chunks.text: Actinic keratosis is an intraepidermal proliferation of atypical, dysplastic keratinocytes driven by cumulative ultraviolet radiation. UV exposure induces characteristic DNA mutations, including in the TP53 tumour-suppressor gene, that impair repair and apoptosis and allow clonal expansion of abnormal keratinocytes confined to the epidermis. The result is disordered maturation and hyperkeratosis producing the palpable scale. Because the whole photo-damaged area shares this mutational burden (field cancerisation), multiple lesions and recurrences are common, and continued genetic damage can lead to full-thickness dysplasia and invasion characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma.

The etiologic agents are members of the normal oral, gastrointestinal, and female genital flora. The critical initiating step is disruption of the mucosal barrier, allowing local infection. Once established, the infection spreads contiguously in a slow, progressive fashion that disregards normal tissue planes. Although acute inflammation may occur initially, the hallmark is a chronic indolent phase with indurated lesions, central necrosis (neutrophils plus sulfur granules), and dense fibrotic walls. Sinus tracts to skin, adjacent organs, or bone may develop over time. Foreign bodies, particularly IUDs, facilitate infection, and ulcerative mucosal infections (e.g., HSV, CMV) may promote disease (Harrison 22e p.1364).

An uncommon, indolent, slowly progressive infection caused by anaerobic or microaerophilic bacteria—primarily Actinomyces species—that normally colonize the mouth, colon, and vagina; it has been called one of the most frequently misdiagnosed diseases (Harrison 22e p.1363).

Foreign bodies (especially IUDs) and immunocompromising states—HIV, transplantation, common variable immunodeficiency, chronic granulomatous disease, and certain immunosuppressive therapies—are recognized predisposing factors (Harrison 22e p.1364).
FDG-PET may show hypermetabolism in actinomycotic lesions, potentially compounding confusion with malignancy (Harrison 22e p.1365).

Three classic presentations should trigger suspicion: a chronic mass-like lesion that crosses tissue planes and mimics malignancy, a sinus tract that spontaneously resolves and recurs, and a refractory or relapsing infection after a short course of therapy (Harrison 22e p.1363).

Most infections are polymicrobial; companion organisms such as Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, Eikenella corrodens, Enterobacteriaceae, Fusobacterium, and Bacteroides are commonly co-isolated, though their pathogenic contribution is uncertain (Harrison 22e p.1363).

Disease spreads contiguously, ignoring tissue planes; the characteristic chronic phase produces single or multiple indurated lesions with fibrotic walls classically described as wooden (Harrison 22e p.1364).
Central necrosis containing neutrophils and sulfur granules is virtually diagnostic; over time, sinus tracts to skin, adjacent organs, or bone develop (Harrison 22e p.1364).
Lymphatic spread with lymphadenopathy and distant hematogenous seeding are uncommon—an important contrast with malignancy and tuberculosis (Harrison 22e p.1364).
Oral–cervicofacial disease is the most frequent presentation, typically at the angle of the jaw, often precipitated by dental disease or procedures (Harrison 22e p.1364).

Pelvic actinomycosis is strongly associated with intrauterine contraceptive devices (IUDs) and other foreign bodies such as surgical mesh; risk increases the longer the device remains in place and is low when in place under one year (Harrison 22e p.1364-1365).

Sulfur granules represent an in vivo matrix of bacteria, calcium phosphate, and host material; on hematoxylin-eosin staining they may be surrounded by a radiating fringe of eosinophilic clubs (Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon) (Harrison 22e p.1365).
Diagnosis is rarely considered prospectively—actinomycosis is often first identified by the pathologist after extensive (and avoidable) surgery (Harrison 22e p.1365).

Prior antibiotic exposure or failure to obtain appropriate anaerobic cultures frequently precludes microbiologic identification; even a single antibiotic dose can prevent isolation (Harrison 22e p.1365).

Because actinomycetes are normal oral and genital-tract flora, their detection in sputum, bronchial washings, or cervicovaginal secretions without sulfur granules may reflect colonization rather than infection (Harrison 22e p.1365).

Detection of Actinomyces-like organisms on Papanicolaou smear in IUD users has low positive predictive value; in an asymptomatic patient this warrants education and follow-up, not routine IUD removal (Harrison 22e p.1365).
Isolation of Actinomyces from blood cultures without a defined focus may represent contamination or transient bacteremia from a mucosal site (Harrison 22e p.1366).
Elevated CA-125 in pelvic disease and FDG-PET hypermetabolism can reinforce a mistaken cancer diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1365).

Actinomycosis is usually curable with medical therapy alone, even in extensive disease, and an awareness of its clinical spectrum can expedite diagnosis and minimize unnecessary surgery, morbidity, and mortality. Cure of established disease requires prolonged treatment, and relapse is a clinical hallmark if therapy is stopped too early; refractory disease has been described in HIV-infected individuals (Harrison 22e p.1363, p.1366).

chunks.text: Acute abdomen results from inflammation, obstruction, perforation, ischaemia, or haemorrhage of intra-abdominal organs. Visceral pain is initially poorly localised because of autonomic innervation, but once inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum the pain becomes sharp and localised. Perforation releases luminal contents causing chemical then bacterial peritonitis; obstruction causes distension, third-space fluid loss, and potential strangulation; and vascular occlusion causes bowel ischaemia and infarction. These processes can precipitate hypovolaemia, sepsis, and shock, making the acute abdomen a potentially life-threatening presentation.

chunks.text: Acute agitation is a final common pathway of many disturbances of brain function. Global cerebral dysfunction (delirium) arises from hypoxia, hypoperfusion, hypoglycaemia, metabolic derangement, sepsis, drug intoxication or withdrawal, and structural brain injury, all of which impair the neural networks governing attention and behaviour. In the trauma setting, agitation may be the earliest external sign of inadequate cerebral oxygen delivery from hypoxia or haemorrhagic shock. Primary psychiatric illness and severe pain also contribute, but organic causes must be excluded because they are frequently reversible and can be fatal if missed.

Immune checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis and vaccine-associated myocarditis

Infectious agents injure the myocardium both by direct cellular invasion (disrupting normal cellular processes) and by activating immune responses, with or without persistent infection. Viral myocarditis has classically been described in three phases from murine enterovirus (coxsackie B) models: (1) direct myocardial invasion, with viral entry sometimes enhanced by coxsackie/adenovirus receptor variants and enteroviral protease degrading dystrophin to trigger apoptosis and impair autophagy; (2) host immune response to conserved antigenic patterns, activating macrophages and expanding T- and B-cell populations, which can produce 'virally triggered' myocarditis even without direct viral injury, possibly via molecular mimicry between viral and cardiac antigens; and (3) progression to chronic cardiomyopathy, demonstrated in animal models. Direct genome entry occurs with enteroviruses, HIV, and dengue, but most common viruses do not appear to damage the heart directly, and early injury is often driven by cytokine storm and nonspecific immune activation. Notably, this initial immune response appears crucial to recovery, since early immunosuppression worsened viral replication and cardiac injury in animals. Viral 'hijacking' of cellular machinery to produce extracellular vesicles carrying viral RNA may allow protected spread to other cells. In Chagas disease, acute infection produces dense parasitic pseudocysts that rupture and cause diffuse myocyte necrosis, while chronic disease reflects persistent parasitemia plus depopulation of cardiac and gastrointestinal parasympathetic neurons. Noninfective inflammatory myocarditis (sarcoid granulomas, giant cell, eosinophilic, autoimmune, checkpoint inhibitor) reflects antigen-driven, dysregulated immune attack on myocardium; the paradigm is cardiac transplant rejection, which showed that antibodies and cytokines, not only lymphocytes, mediate reversible myocardial depression and that antigens are exposed by prior injury or infection (p.2011-2014).

Myocarditis is inflammation of heart muscle that can present acutely, subacutely, or insidiously, with outcomes ranging from full resolution to a relapsing course or progression to chronic cardiomyopathy; it is termed acute when symptoms have lasted under a month, often only days (p.2011).

Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) is the most common infective cause of cardiomyopathy worldwide; after a usually silent initial infection patients enter an 'indeterminate phase' lasting decades, during which persistent low-level parasitemia is now recognized as the major driver of progression to chronic heart failure (p.2013).

Diphtheria toxin (Corynebacterium diphtheriae) interferes with cardiac protein synthesis and especially affects the conduction system; cardiac involvement is the most common cause of death in this infection, and clinical suspicion alone justifies giving antitoxin with higher priority than antibiotics (p.2013).

Combined immune checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis is the most dramatic noninfectious form: troponin is often elevated, biopsy shows extensive lymphocytic infiltration, and it should be suspected immediately with any acute cardiac presentation in a treated patient; CCU admission is recommended for elevated troponin with ECG changes (p.2014).

Chest pain is the most common symptom of acute myocarditis, occurring in more than 80% of patients, who frequently also have dyspnea or arrhythmias; fever is present in over half of cases and a viral prodrome may precede onset by days to weeks (p.2011).
Acute myocarditis in adults typically occurs between roughly 30 and 45 years and is more common in men, whereas women tend to present after age 45 (p.2011).

At presentation about one-fourth of acute myocarditis cases have an LVEF below 0.50, ventricular arrhythmias, or shock; fulminant myocarditis (circulatory shock) is reported in about 3-9% of cases (p.2011).

Diagnosis can now be made noninvasively when a typical symptomatic presentation is accompanied by elevated troponin plus cardiac MRI showing both myocardial edema and nonischemic injury without another cause; biopsy is no longer strictly required for a 'definite' diagnosis (p.2011-2012).

Because chest pain, ECG changes, and elevated troponin overlap between acute myocarditis and myocardial infarction, coronary imaging is often the first differential step; myocarditis is later diagnosed in up to one-third of patients with MINOCA (myocardial infarction with nonobstructed coronary arteries) (p.2011).

Eosinophil counts should be checked routinely because hypereosinophilia is present in most cases of eosinophilic myocarditis; right bundle branch block should raise suspicion for sarcoidosis or Chagas rather than typical cardiomyopathies, in which left bundle branch block predominates (p.2011, p.2013, p.2014).

Around one in five patients with inflammatory myocarditis carry genetic variants considered pathogenic for cardiomyopathy, and 20-40% of dilated cardiomyopathy patients have variants sufficient to explain their disease; CMR fibrosis patterns once attributed to prior viral myocarditis are now recognized as common in genetic cardiomyopathy too (p.2011, p.2012).

Giant cell myocarditis accounts for 10-20% of biopsy-proven myocarditis, occurs equally in men and women (typically older than viral cases), is more often linked to systemic autoimmune disease, and usually presents acutely with rapidly progressive heart failure and tachyarrhythmias (p.2014).
Assuming any chest pain/ECG change/troponin elevation is infarction can miss myocarditis, which underlies up to one-third of MINOCA cases (p.2011).
Sarcoid granulomas are scattered and commonly missed on endomyocardial biopsy, so a negative biopsy does not exclude cardiac sarcoidosis (p.2014).
Eosinophilic myocarditis may be overlooked in milder presentations if hypereosinophilia is not assessed (p.2014).

Viral titers and detection of viral genome fragments or anticardiac antibodies in chronic cardiomyopathy are of uncertain significance, as the same viruses (e.g., parvovirus B19, HHV6) are also found in normal control hearts and these assays are not in routine clinical use (p.2011, p.2012).

There are no data supporting routine immunosuppression for presumed viral acute myocarditis, and immunosuppression for nonspecific lymphocytic chronic myocarditis has not shown convincing benefit (p.2012).
Initial care of suspected checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis should generally not be delayed to obtain endomyocardial biopsy (p.2014).

Prognosis is good for 'uncomplicated' acute myocarditis (LVEF >=0.50 without ventricular arrhythmias or shock), which represents about three-fourths of patients; spontaneous recovery is common, almost all retain LVEF >=0.50 on follow-up, and they survive without transplantation at 5 years. Among the one-fourth with complicated presentations, roughly 18% die or undergo transplantation over the next 5 years. In fulminant myocarditis, more than half of affected patients recover to near-normal LVEF despite presenting with refractory cardiogenic shock. Reduced LVEF at presentation predicts chronic cardiomyopathy. Chagas cardiomyopathy has lower survival than other cardiomyopathies once overt heart failure develops, and LVEF improvement is uncommon. Most patients with giant cell myocarditis in cardiogenic shock require urgent mechanical support or transplant. Checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis fatality was initially very high but is improving with earlier recognition and treatment (p.2011-2014).

Ventricular arrhythmias or syncope, which may precede sudden cardiac death (inflammatory myocarditis found in 3-10% of sudden deaths in previously healthy young adults)

Harrison distinguishes uncomplicated acute myocarditis (LVEF >=0.50, no ventricular arrhythmias, no shock; ~75% of cases, good prognosis) from complicated acute myocarditis (LVEF <0.50, ventricular arrhythmias, or shock; ~25%, higher 5-year death/transplant rate). Fulminant myocarditis (~3-9%) denotes circulatory shock requiring high-dose inotropes or mechanical circulatory support. Diagnostically, 'probable myocarditis' requires at least one symptom plus one supporting finding (elevated troponin, consistent ECG, or reduced LVEF/wall-motion abnormality on imaging), while 'definite myocarditis' historically required a positive endomyocardial biopsy with lymphocytic infiltrate (p.2011).

chunks.text: In predisposed eyes with a shallow anterior chamber and short axial length, the peripheral iris crowds the drainage angle. When the pupil becomes mid-dilated, relative pupillary block impedes aqueous flow from the posterior to the anterior chamber, so pressure builds behind the iris and bows it forward against the trabecular meshwork. This apposition abruptly obstructs aqueous outflow, causing a rapid and severe rise in intraocular pressure that compromises the optic nerve head and corneal endothelium if not relieved promptly.

For peritonitis: in stable patients with ascites, diagnostic paracentesis is indicated with testing of fluid for protein and LDH and a cell count; radiographs may show bowel dilatation and wall edema, and free air or other leakage may represent a surgical emergency (Harrison 22e p.2597).
A left shift toward immature polymorphonuclear leukocytes is present in >95% of cases (Harrison 22e p.2596).
Serum amylase and lipase should be measured; sickle cell preparation may be prudent in patients of African, Spanish, Mediterranean, or Indian ancestry (Harrison 22e p.2596).

Urinalysis to help exclude genitourinary mimics; a few red or white cells may be a nonspecific finding, and an inflamed appendix abutting the ureter or bladder may cause sterile pyuria or hematuria (Harrison 22e p.2596).

Ultrasonography: highly operator dependent; overall sensitivity ~0.86 and specificity ~0.81; appendix may not be visualized even in skilled hands; especially useful (including intravaginal techniques) for pelvic pathology in women. Suggestive findings: wall thickening, increased appendiceal diameter, free fluid (Harrison 22e p.2596).

CT: sensitivity at least 0.94 and specificity at least 0.95; high negative predictive value; suggestive findings include dilatation >6 mm with wall thickening, a lumen that does not fill with enteric contrast, and periappendiceal fatty stranding or air. Presence of luminal air or contrast is NOT consistent with appendicitis; nonvisualization of the appendix is nonspecific and should NOT be used to rule out appendiceal/periappendiceal inflammation (Harrison 22e p.2596).
