Etiology is not completely understood. Obstruction of the appendiceal lumen (by fecaliths/appendicoliths, incompletely digested food residue, lymphoid hyperplasia, intraluminal scarring, tumors, bacteria, viruses, or inflammatory bowel disease) is believed, though not proven, to be an important early step at least in some cases. Obstruction leads to bacterial overgrowth and luminal distension with increased intraluminal pressure that can inhibit lymph and blood flow; vascular thrombosis and ischemic necrosis with perforation of the distal appendix may then follow. Perforation near the base of the appendix should raise concern for another disease process. Appendicoliths are found in ~50% of patients with gangrenous appendicitis who perforate but are rarely seen in simpler disease, suggesting differing underlying pathophysiology. Uncomplicated appendicitis does not always progress to perforation; some cases of simple acute appendicitis may temporarily resolve or be managed with antibiotics, though at least one-third will subsequently require appendectomy. When perforation occurs, the leak may be contained by omentum or surrounding tissues to form an abscess, whereas free perforation normally causes severe peritonitis (p.2594-2595).

Classic history is migration of vague, intermittent, crampy epigastric or periumbilical pain to the right lower quadrant over 12-24 h, where it becomes sharper and localizes as transmural inflammation irritates the parietal peritoneum (p.2595).

Examine the entire abdomen systematically, starting in a non-tender area; all patients should have a rectal examination, and a pelvic examination in women is mandatory to exclude PID, ectopic pregnancy, and ovarian torsion (p.2596).
Appendicitis should be included in the differential diagnosis of abdominal pain for every patient of any age unless it is certain the appendix has been previously removed (p.2595).
Maximal tenderness is classically at or near McBurney's point in the right lower quadrant, about one-third of the way along a line from the anterior iliac spine to the umbilicus (p.2596).

Nausea, if present, characteristically follows the onset of abdominal pain (helping distinguish appendicitis from gastroenteritis, in which nausea precedes pain); emesis is typically mild and scant and also occurs after pain onset (p.2595).
Anorexia is so common that the diagnosis of appendicitis should be questioned in its absence (p.2595).
Rovsing's sign: palpation/gentle pressure in the left lower quadrant elicits pain in the right lower quadrant (p.2596).
Iliopsoas sign: extending the right hip causes pain along the posterolateral back and hip, suggesting a retrocecal appendix (p.2596).
Obturator sign: internal rotation of the hip causes pain, suggesting an inflamed appendix located in the pelvis (p.2596).

Patients with appendicitis tend to lie quite still to avoid peritoneal irritation; some report discomfort with a bumpy car ride, coughing, sneezing, or Valsalva-type maneuvers. Parietal peritoneal irritation is often best elicited by gentle percussion, jiggling the bed/gurney, or mildly bumping the feet (p.2596).

Simple appendicitis patients usually appear only mildly ill with pulse and temperature only slightly above normal; temperature >38.3 C (~101 F) or rigors should raise concern for another process or for complications such as perforation, phlegmon, or abscess (p.2596).

Atypical presentations and pain patterns are common, especially in the very old and very young; signs and symptoms can be subtle in the elderly, who may not react vigorously, with nausea/anorexia/emesis predominating (Harrison 22e p.2596).

Retrocecal or pelvic (below the pelvic brim) appendix may prompt very little anterior abdominal wall tenderness; pelvic appendicitis may present with dysuria, urinary frequency, diarrhea, or tenesmus and only suprapubic or rectal/pelvic-exam tenderness (Harrison 22e p.2596).

Appendiceal location varies widely (right lower quadrant, pelvis, right flank, right upper quadrant, or even the left side with malrotation/redundant colon), influencing presentation; delay in diagnosis is more likely when the appendix is unusually positioned (Harrison 22e p.2595).

Diagnosing appendicitis in children is challenging (dramatic response to stimulation, difficult history); the smaller pediatric omentum may be less able to wall off a perforation (Harrison 22e p.2596).

Pregnancy: appendicitis is the most common extrauterine general surgical emergency in pregnancy; early symptoms (nausea, anorexia) may be overlooked and the enlarging/gravid uterus may displace the appendix higher and obscure typical findings (Harrison 22e p.2596).
Immunocompromised patients may present with only mild tenderness; do not be overly cautious and delay operation in those believed to have appendicitis (Harrison 22e p.2596).
Laboratory testing alone does not identify appendicitis, and no currently available decision tool obviates the need for expert clinical opinion (Harrison 22e p.2596).
A fecalith is not diagnostic of appendicitis, though its presence in an appropriate location with pain is suggestive and associated with greater likelihood of complications (Harrison 22e p.2596).

Mortality from simple appendicitis is currently <1%, and for uncomplicated nonperforated appendicitis the operative mortality rate is 0.1-0.5% (approximating the risk of general anesthesia). Mortality for perforated or otherwise complicated disease is much higher, ranging from ~3% overall to as high as 15% in the elderly. For acute peritonitis, mortality can be <10% in reasonably healthy patients with relatively uncomplicated, localized disease but >40% in the elderly or immunocompromised (Harrison 22e p.2597).
Free perforation normally causes severe (generalized) peritonitis; perforation risk is ~10-20% and is significantly higher in patients <5 or >65 years of age (Harrison 22e p.2594).
Temperature >38.3 C (~101 F) or rigors suggest a complication (perforation, phlegmon, abscess) or another diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2596).
Persistent symptoms not improved over 48 h are more likely to perforate or develop other complications (Harrison 22e p.2595).
Rare but dreaded complication: infective suppurative thrombosis of the portal vein and its tributaries with intrahepatic abscesses, with very poor prognosis (Harrison 22e p.2595).

Diffuse abdominal tenderness with guarding and rigidity indicates generalized peritonitis; tachycardia, hypotension/volume depletion, significant leukocytosis, and severe acidosis are signs of serious disease (Harrison 22e p.2597).
In pregnancy, perforation raises fetal mortality fourfold (from ~5% to ~20%) (Harrison 22e p.2596).
Postoperative fever and leukocytosis persisting beyond 5 days should raise concern for an intraabdominal abscess (Harrison 22e p.2597).

No formal grading scale is presented; disease is broadly distinguished as simple/uncomplicated appendicitis (without gangrenous necrosis, appendicoliths, perforation, or tumors) versus complicated disease (gangrene, perforation, phlegmon, abscess). Peritonitis is classified as secondary (most commonly from perforation of a hollow viscus, e.g., appendix, colonic diverticula, stomach/duodenum) versus primary or spontaneous (no identifiable intraabdominal source; >90% occur in patients with ascites or hypoproteinemia <1 g/L), and either type may be localized or diffuse; aseptic/chemical peritonitis (e.g., from gastric juice, bile, pancreatic enzymes, blood, or urine) is also distinguished (Harrison 22e p.2595-2597).

Bacterial invasion of the supraglottic tissues produces intense inflammation and oedema of the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, and surrounding structures. Because these tissues sit at the laryngeal inlet, swelling rapidly narrows the airway, and the loose submucosa allows oedema to accumulate quickly. Progressive obstruction, worsened by agitation and secretions, can culminate in acute total airway occlusion.
A rapidly progressive, life-threatening bacterial infection of the epiglottis and supraglottic structures that can cause sudden complete airway obstruction.
Historically caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b; its incidence has fallen dramatically since Hib immunisation, so other organisms and unimmunised children now feature prominently.
Classic presentation is abrupt onset of high fever, severe sore throat, drooling, muffled 'hot potato' voice, and difficulty swallowing, usually without the barking cough of croup.
The child characteristically sits upright in a tripod position, leaning forward with the neck extended to maximise the airway.
This is an airway emergency: keep the child calm, avoid distressing procedures such as throat examination or venepuncture, and do not lay the child flat.
Definitive airway management is secured in a controlled setting, ideally the operating theatre with experienced anaesthetic and ENT support, before other interventions.
Once the airway is secure, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics targeting likely pathogens are given.
A lateral neck radiograph may show the classic 'thumbprint' sign, but imaging must never delay airway management and is unnecessary in an unstable child.
Direct visualisation of a cherry-red swollen epiglottis confirms the diagnosis but should only be performed where the airway can be immediately secured.
Examining the throat or performing painful procedures that can precipitate obstruction
Laying the child supine or forcing separation from a caregiver
Delaying airway management to obtain imaging or bloods
Assuming the diagnosis is excluded in an immunised child, since non-Hib causes still occur
With prompt airway control and antibiotics, recovery is usually rapid and complete; outcomes are poor if the airway obstructs before it is secured, making early recognition critical.
Stridor, drooling, and respiratory distress indicating imminent obstruction
Tripod positioning and refusal to lie flat
Cyanosis, exhaustion, or decreasing level of consciousness
Muffled voice with inability to swallow secretions
Rapid clinical deterioration
Acute Epiglottitis (infective) — Respiratory Also: epiglottitis, supraglottitis, acute supraglottitis
IgA nephropathy
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
Lupus nephritis
Henoch-Schonlein (IgA) vasculitis nephritis
Haemolytic uraemic syndrome
Alport syndrome or thin basement membrane disease
Urinalysis and microscopy for red cell casts and dysmorphic red cells
Serum complement (C3 and C4)
Evidence of streptococcal infection (ASO, anti-DNase B, throat or skin swab)
Renal function and electrolytes
Urine protein quantification
Renal biopsy if the course is atypical, complement stays low, or renal function deteriorates

Immune complexes involving streptococcal antigens deposit in or form within the glomerular basement membrane, activating the complement cascade (predominantly the alternative pathway). This drives glomerular inflammation with endothelial and mesangial proliferation and neutrophil influx, reducing the glomerular filtration surface. The result is a fall in filtration rate, sodium and water retention, haematuria, and proteinuria producing the nephritic syndrome.
The classic nephritic picture is gross haematuria (often described as tea- or cola-coloured urine), oedema, and hypertension.
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is the most common cause in children and typically follows a group A streptococcal throat infection by about 1-2 weeks or a skin infection by 3-6 weeks.
Although labelled non-infective as a glomerular process, it is an immune-mediated sequela of a preceding streptococcal infection rather than active kidney infection.
Look for evidence of recent streptococcal infection with elevated antibody titres (such as ASO) and a low serum C3 that typically normalises within 6-8 weeks.
Fluid overload from sodium and water retention can precipitate hypertension, pulmonary oedema, and hypertensive encephalopathy.
Urinalysis characteristically shows red blood cells, red cell casts, and mild to moderate proteinuria.
Management is largely supportive with salt and fluid restriction and control of hypertension; the condition is generally self-limiting in children.
Persistently low complement beyond 8 weeks should prompt consideration of an alternative diagnosis such as membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis or lupus nephritis.
Assuming all paediatric nephritis is post-streptococcal and missing lupus or membranoproliferative disease when complement stays persistently low
Overlooking hypertension, which may be asymptomatic yet dangerous, by not measuring blood pressure
Fluid overloading a child with impaired filtration
Attributing dark urine to dehydration rather than examining the urine sediment

The great majority of children with post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis recover completely, with resolution of gross haematuria within weeks and normalisation of complement within about two months; microscopic haematuria may persist for a year or more. A small minority develop chronic kidney impairment.
Severe hypertension or hypertensive encephalopathy (headache, seizures, altered consciousness)
Pulmonary oedema or respiratory distress from volume overload
Rapidly rising creatinine suggesting rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis
Oligoanuria or features of acute kidney injury requiring dialysis
Hyperkalaemia with associated arrhythmia risk
Acute Glomerulonephritis (Child) (non-infective) — Renal Also: acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, APSGN, acute nephritic syndrome, paediatric acute glomerulonephritis

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Stool culture for Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter in febrile inflammatory diarrhea (MacConkey/Salmonella-Shigella agar/selenite broth; Campylobacter requires 42 degrees C microaerophilic culture)

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Selective culture for V. cholerae on TCBS or TTG agar, plus rapid diagnostic tests when cholera is suspected

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Sorbitol-MacConkey culture and/or Shiga toxin/PCR testing of visibly bloody stools for E. coli O157:H7

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: C. difficile toxin A/B testing (enzyme immunoassay, latex agglutination, or PCR) for nosocomial or antibiotic-associated diarrhea

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Rapid antigen, immunofluorescence, or PCR (and less sensitive microscopy) for Giardia, Cryptosporidium, and Entamoeba histolytica

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Multiplex nucleic acid amplification panels for viral/bacterial/parasitic pathogens - faster and more sensitive than culture, but may detect multiple organisms and complicate interpretation; CDC advises follow-up culture to allow susceptibility testing and outbreak typing

chunks.text: Inflammatory bowel disease (acute diarrheal illness may be its initial presentation or an exacerbation, sometimes precipitated by traveler's diarrhea)

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Acute infectious diarrhea results from a contest between ingested enteric pathogens and host defenses. Pathogens overcome defenses through small infective inoculum, adherence/colonization factors (e.g., V. cholerae toxin-coregulated pilus; enterotoxigenic E. coli colonization factor antigen; attaching-effacing lesions of enteropathogenic and enterohemorrhagic E. coli), and the elaboration of toxins or direct invasion. Three broad mechanisms produce three clinical patterns: (1) Noninflammatory enterotoxin-mediated disease in the proximal small bowel causes watery diarrhea without fecal leukocytes - the cholera-toxin/LT pathway elevates cyclic AMP (increased Cl- secretion, decreased Na+ absorption) and ST elevates cyclic GMP. (2) Inflammatory disease in the colon/distal small bowel results from cytotoxins (e.g., Shiga toxin of S. dysenteriae type 1 and Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, V. parahaemolyticus, C. difficile) or from mucosal invasion (Shigella, enteroinvasive E. coli, Salmonella), producing dysentery with fecal leukocytes and blood. (3) Penetrating organisms (Salmonella Typhi, Y. enterocolitica) traverse intact mucosa, multiply in lymphoid tissue, and disseminate to cause enteric fever. Neurotoxins (staphylococcal, B. cereus emetic) are typically preformed outside the host and act on the nervous system to cause rapid-onset vomiting. Host protection depends on the intestinal microbiota's colonization resistance, gastric acidity, intestinal motility/peristalsis, the mucin barrier, mucosal and systemic immunity, and genetic factors; impairment of any of these (achlorhydria/acid suppression, antimotility drugs, antibiotic-altered flora, immunocompromise) raises infection risk and severity.

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Diarrhea is defined as the passage of three or more loose or watery stools (conforming to the shape of the container) within a 24-hour period; illness lasting more than 2 weeks is generally classified as chronic and shifts the likely differential away from typical acute infectious causes (Harrison 22e p.1078, 1079).

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Blood group O confers increased susceptibility to disease from V. cholerae, Shigella, E. coli O157, and norovirus (Harrison 22e p.1077).

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Salmonella Typhi and Yersinia enterocolitica can penetrate intact mucosa, multiply in Peyer patches/lymph nodes, and disseminate to cause enteric fever - fever, headache, relative bradycardia, abdominal pain, splenomegaly, and leukopenia (Harrison 22e p.1077).

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Cholera toxin is the prototype enterotoxin: its A subunit ADP-ribosylates a GTP-binding protein, persistently activating adenylate cyclase, raising cyclic AMP, increasing Cl- secretion and decreasing Na+ absorption to drive secretory diarrhea; E. coli LT acts identically, while ST acts via guanylate cyclase and cyclic GMP (Harrison 22e p.1076-1077).

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: The first practical step is to separate noninflammatory from inflammatory disease: watery diarrhea with no fecal leukocytes and minimal/no fecal lactoferrin points to proximal small-bowel enterotoxin-mediated disease, whereas fecal polymorphonuclear leukocytes and high fecal lactoferrin point to colonic invasion or cytotoxin (dysentery/inflammatory diarrhea) (Harrison 22e p.1077-1079).

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Infective dose varies enormously and shapes transmission: as few as 10-100 organisms/cysts of Shigella, enterohemorrhagic E. coli, Giardia, or Entamoeba cause infection and allow person-to-person spread, while 10^5-10^8 Vibrio cholerae must be ingested, often requiring growth in food first (Harrison 22e p.1076).

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Neurotoxin-mediated food poisoning (Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus emetic form) is caused by toxin preformed outside the host, giving the shortest incubation (1-6 h), prominent vomiting, and usually no fever (Harrison 22e p.1076-1077, 1080).

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Stool appearance is diagnostically informative: bloody/mucoid stool suggests large-bowel ulceration/inflammation; profuse rice-water stools suggest cholera or a similar toxigenic process; bulky white/gray stools suggest a malabsorptive small-bowel process (Harrison 22e p.1078).

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Bloody stools WITHOUT fecal leukocytes should specifically raise suspicion for Shiga toxin-producing enterohemorrhagic E. coli (e.g., O157:H7) (Harrison 22e p.1078).

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Severity is judged largely by dehydration: thirst and dry mouth indicate mild dehydration; orthostatic blood-pressure fall, skin tenting, and sunken eyes/fontanelle indicate moderate dehydration; lethargy, obtundation, feeble pulse, hypotension, and shock indicate severe dehydration (Harrison 22e p.1078).

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Recent or current antibiotic use shifts suspicion toward Clostridioides difficile; C. difficile is the predominant cause of nosocomial diarrhea in U.S. adults, and stool culture for other pathogens in the hospital setting is low-yield (Harrison 22e p.1078-1080).

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Host defenses against enteric pathogens include the intestinal microbiota (colonization resistance, >99% anaerobic colonic flora with acidic pH/volatile fatty acids), gastric acid, peristalsis, the mucus barrier, mucosal/secretory IgA immunity, and host genetics (Harrison 22e p.1077).

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Relying on the fecal leukocyte smear alone - its predictive value is debated, and fecal lactoferrin is more sensitive (Harrison 22e p.1079).

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Routine stool culture cannot distinguish pathogenic E. coli from normal flora, and enterotoxin assays are unavailable in most clinical labs, so a negative routine culture does not exclude E. coli disease (Harrison 22e p.1080).

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Sending broad stool cultures for nosocomial diarrhea is low-yield and not cost-effective; initial workup should focus on C. difficile (Harrison 22e p.1080).

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Antimotility agents (e.g., diphenoxylate-atropine) and opioids can prolong fever and organism shedding in Shigella infection and increase bacteremia risk in Salmonella - impaired motility favors bacterial overgrowth (Harrison 22e p.1077).

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Multiplex NAAT panels may detect multiple pathogens, complicating interpretation, and the absence of an isolate prevents susceptibility testing and outbreak typing - CDC advises follow-up culture (Harrison 22e p.1080).

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Reheating/frying contaminated fried rice may not destroy preformed heat-stable B. cereus toxin or its heat-resistant spores (Harrison 22e p.1080).

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Missing infection outside the GI tract (e.g., malaria) as a cause of fever and diarrhea/vomiting (Harrison 22e p.1078).

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Most acute diarrheal episodes are mild and self-limited. Traveler's diarrhea is typically self-limited, lasting 1-5 days, and Clostridium perfringens food poisoning rarely lasts more than 24 h; toxin-mediated staphylococcal/B. cereus emetic illness generally lasts under 12 h. Globally, however, acute diarrheal disease remains a leading cause of illness, associated with an estimated 1.57 million deaths per year, and in low- and middle-income countries it accounts for about one in ten deaths in children under 5; recurrent intestinal infection contributes to stunting, wasting, micronutrient deficiency, and malnutrition. Outcome is worse in immunocompromised hosts, where dehydration can also compromise renal function and increase immunosuppressive drug toxicity. Postdiarrhea complications include chronic diarrhea (~1% of travelers; protozoa account for about one-third), postinfectious irritable bowel syndrome (~10% of those with traveler's diarrhea), reactive arthritis (especially after Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter, Yersinia), hemolytic-uremic syndrome (Shiga toxin-producing bacteria), and Guillain-Barre syndrome (especially after Campylobacter).

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Signs of severe dehydration: lethargy, obtundation, feeble pulse, hypotension, and shock

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Fever, which often signals invasive disease

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Bloody or mucoid stools (dysentery) indicating large-bowel ulceration

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Bloody stools without fecal leukocytes - alert for Shiga toxin-producing enterohemorrhagic E. coli and risk of hemolytic-uremic syndrome

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Diarrhea in an immunocompromised host (cell-mediated immunity defects/AIDS, hypogammaglobulinemia, cancer), where infection can be life-threatening with persistent infection, bacteremia, and metastatic seeding

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Profuse rice-water stools suggesting cholera, with risk of rapid life-threatening volume loss

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Diarrhea in infants <2 years with moderate dehydration, fever >24 h, bloody stools, or prolonged duration

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Severity is graded clinically by degree of dehydration (Harrison 22e p.1078). Mild dehydration: thirst, dry mouth, decreased axillary sweat, decreased urine output, slight weight loss. Moderate dehydration: orthostatic fall in blood pressure, skin tenting, sunken eyes (or sunken fontanelle in infants). Severe dehydration: lethargy, obtundation, feeble pulse, hypotension, and shock. The complementary classification is mechanistic/syndromic per Table 138-1: noninflammatory (enterotoxin, proximal small bowel, watery diarrhea, no fecal leukocytes), inflammatory (invasion or cytotoxin, colon/distal small bowel, dysentery, fecal PMNs and high lactoferrin), and penetrating (distal small bowel, enteric fever, fecal mononuclear cells).

chunks.diseaseName: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
chunks.text: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning (infective) — Gastrointestinal Also: acute infectious diarrhea, acute gastroenteritis, bacterial food poisoning, infectious diarrhea
Postoperative ileus (functional obstruction following intraabdominal surgery)
Colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's syndrome)
Obstructive colon cancer (may mimic small-bowel obstruction when the ileocecal valve is incompetent)
Crohn's disease and other inflammatory strictures
Acute mesenteric ischemia (pain out of proportion to findings)
Complete blood count and serum electrolytes/creatinine with serial assessment (mild hemoconcentration and slight leukocytosis are common in simple obstruction)
Upright/cross-table lateral abdominal radiographs ('staircasing' of dilated small-bowel loops >2.5 cm, air-fluid levels, 'coffee bean' shadow in volvulus)
CT with enteral and IV contrast (location, closed-loop, and ischemia features such as altered wall enhancement, mesenteric venous gas, pneumatosis, pneumoperitoneum)
Markers possibly suggestive of strangulation: serum D-lactate, creatine kinase BB isoenzyme, intestinal fatty acid binding protein
Contrast enema or colonoscopy for suspected colonic obstruction; ultrasound when radiation is contraindicated (e.g., pregnancy)
Adynamic ileus from metabolic/electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hyponatremia, uremia, severe hyperglycemia)
Drug-induced dysmotility (opiates, antihistamines, anticholinergics, some psychotropics)
Colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's syndrome)
Intestinal ischemia presenting with functional dysmotility
Collagen vascular disease (e.g., lupus, scleroderma) causing visceral dysmotility

Acute obstruction is either mechanical (extrinsic, intrinsic bowel-wall, or intraluminal lesions) or functional (dysmotility without blockage). Increased contractility proximal and distal to the block is characteristic; peristalsis then slows as proximal bowel dilates and fills with secretions and swallowed air, with additional luminal gas from fermentation and CO2 production. Rising intraluminal pressure exceeding venous pressure impairs venous and lymphatic drainage, producing wall edema and proximal hypoxemia, with epithelial necrosis identifiable within 12 h. Progressive arterial compromise can cause full-thickness ischemia, necrosis, and perforation. Inflammatory edema generates reactive oxygen species and recruits neutrophils and macrophages, disrupting secretory and neuromotor function. Loss of absorptive capacity plus fluid sequestration in the bowel wall and peritoneum causes dehydration; anorexia and emesis worsen volume depletion, and high-grade distal obstruction with vomiting causes loss of gastric potassium, hydrogen, and chloride while dehydration drives proximal tubular bicarbonate reabsorption (metabolic alkalosis). Closed-loop obstruction, in which both ends of a segment are occluded (e.g., volvulus, hernia), is the most common precursor to strangulation and carries high risk of vascular insufficiency and irreversible ischemia (Harrison 22e p.2590-2591).

The cardinal features are colicky abdominal pain, abdominal distention, emesis, and obstipation; distal obstruction tends to produce more distention and later, sometimes feculent, vomiting, whereas proximal obstruction produces more pronounced vomiting with less distention (Harrison 22e p.2591).

Stasis raises bacterial counts in the jejunum and ileum; organisms such as Escherichia coli, Streptococcus faecalis, and Klebsiella may be recovered from intestinal cultures, mesenteric nodes, and blood (Harrison 22e p.2590).

CT is the most frequently used modality, with sensitivity ~95% (78-100%) and specificity ~96% for high-grade obstruction, but accuracy for closed-loop obstruction is much lower (~60%) (Harrison 22e p.2592).
Contrast appearing within the cecum 4-24 h after oral water-soluble contrast predicts improvement with high (~95%) sensitivity and specificity (Harrison 22e p.2592).

Obstruction is characterized as partial, high grade, or complete, which generally tracks with the risk of complications and the urgency of intervention; it is termed simple versus strangulated when vascular insufficiency and ischemia are present (Harrison 22e p.2589).

Roughly 80% of cases involve the small bowel, and about one-third of small-bowel cases show significant ischemia; obstruction accounts for about 1-3% of hospitalizations and a quarter of urgent/emergent general surgery admissions (Harrison 22e p.2589).

Postoperative adhesions are the single most common cause (>50% overall), followed by neoplasms (~20%) and hernias (~10%); lower abdominal operations (appendectomy, colorectal, gynecologic) are especially adhesiogenic (Harrison 22e p.2589-2590).

Classic early small-bowel obstruction produces high-pitched 'musical' tinkling bowel sounds and peristaltic rushes (borborygmi), which later become absent or hypoactive; in ileus/pseudo-obstruction sounds are typically absent or hypoactive from the start (Harrison 22e p.2591).
A tender abdominal or groin mass strongly suggests an incarcerated hernia; pain out of proportion to physical findings can mimic acute mesenteric ischemia (Harrison 22e p.2591).

Carcinomatosis causing obstruction most often originates from the ovary, but can arise from the pancreas, stomach, or colon, and rarely from distant sites such as breast or skin (Harrison 22e p.2589).

In adult intussusception the lead point is typically a polyp or tumor; in gallstone 'ileus' the most common obstruction site is the ileum (~60%), with the stone usually entering via a cholecystoduodenal fistula (Harrison 22e p.2590, 2593).

Sigmoid colon volvulus comprises about two-thirds of all volvulus cases and ~4% of large-bowel obstruction; risk factors include institutionalization, neuropsychiatric conditions on psychotropics, chronic constipation, and advanced age (seventies-eighties) (Harrison 22e p.2589-2590).

Barium should never be given orally until obstruction is excluded; in significant obstruction it may form concretions and renders later cross-sectional imaging or angiography uninterpretable (Harrison 22e p.2592-2593).
No laboratory test reliably distinguishes simple from strangulated obstruction; reliance on labs may delay needed intervention (Harrison 22e p.2592).
Bowel sounds are notoriously unreliable for diagnosis, and pain may be out of proportion to physical findings, masking strangulation or mimicking mesenteric ischemia (Harrison 22e p.2591).
Distal colonic obstruction with an incompetent ileocecal valve can present late and mimic distal small-bowel obstruction (Harrison 22e p.2591).
Imaging intervention should not be delayed when signs strongly suggest high-grade/complete obstruction or bowel compromise (Harrison 22e p.2592).

Overall morbidity and mortality appear to be decreasing. The mortality rate for patients with strangulation operated on within 24-30 h of symptom onset is about 8% but roughly triples thereafter. Most postoperative adhesive obstructions are partial and resolve spontaneously, and about 60-80% of selected mechanical obstructions can be managed conservatively; recurrence requiring readmission within 10 years occurs in ~20% of conservatively treated and 5-30% of operatively managed patients. Major complications after operation occur in roughly 12-47%, with higher risk for resection therapies and for patients with ASA class III or higher (Harrison 22e p.2589, 2593).
Fever, which raises concern for strangulation or systemic inflammation
Severe localized pain or peritoneal signs, suspicious for strangulated or closed-loop obstruction
Leukocytosis with immature forms plus metabolic acidosis, worrisome for ischemic necrosis and sepsis
Cecal diameter exceeding 10-12 cm in distal colonic obstruction with a competent ileocecal valve (impending ischemic perforation)
Free intraperitoneal air in a patient who has not recently had surgery (perforation)
Oliguria, hypotension, and tachycardia indicating severe intravascular volume depletion

Mechanical obstruction is graded as partial, high grade, or complete, correlating with complication risk and urgency. It is further classified as simple versus strangulated when vascular insufficiency and ischemia supervene, and closed-loop when both ends of a segment are occluded (highest risk of strangulation) (Harrison 22e p.2589-2590).

chunks.text: Acute leukaemia is a clonal proliferation of immature, poorly differentiated haematopoietic precursors (blasts) that infiltrate marrow, blood and other tissues; AML arises from myeloid progenitors and ALL from lymphoid (B- or T-lineage) progenitors. Genome sequencing indicates most AML arises from a small number of mutations that accumulate with age - up to 5-6% of normal people over 70 carry premalignant clones (clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential, CHIP, commonly DNMT3A/TET2/ASXL1), which carries a ~10-fold increased risk of haematologic malignancy though additional 'hits' are required to progress to overt leukaemia. Genetic lesions drive both phenotype and behaviour: for example t(15;17)/PML-RARA defines APL and predisposes to DIC, while NPM1 and FLT3 mutations associate with high leukocyte counts. Marrow replacement by blasts produces anaemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, accounting for the dominant clinical features (Harrison 22e p.825-828, p.844).

In AML, cytogenetic/molecular findings at diagnosis are the strongest predictors: t(15;17)/APL has a very good prognosis (~85% cured), core-binding-factor AML (t(8;21), inv(16)) is favourable (~55% cured), normal-karyotype AML is intermediate (~40% cured), and TP53 mutation, complex karyotype, t(6;9), inv(3) or monosomy 7 are adverse with little chance of cure without transplant. NPM1 mutation without FLT3-ITD is favourable, whereas FLT3-ITD is adverse. Advancing age, poor performance status, antecedent haematologic disorder/preceding cytopenias, therapy-related disease and high presenting WBC all worsen outcome; only ~32% of AML patients survive 5 years overall. In ALL, outcome is strongly age-dependent - cure rates ~90% in children falling to <10% in elderly/frail adults; achievement of molecular complete remission (MRD negativity) is the most important on-treatment prognostic factor (Harrison 22e p.825-828, p.846-847).

Malignant transformation of lymphoid progenitor cells in the bone marrow or lymphatic system produces a clone of immature, nonfunctioning lymphoblasts. Progressive marrow infiltration crowds out normal hematopoiesis, yielding anemia, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia. Blasts may also infiltrate lymph nodes, liver, spleen, mediastinum, and the central nervous system (a pharmacologic sanctuary site). Subtypes correspond to arrest at defined stages of B-cell or T-cell differentiation and carry characteristic cytogenetic/molecular lesions such as t(9;22)/BCR-ABL1, t(4;11)/MLL-AF4, t(1;19)/PBX-E2A, and t(8;14) in mature B-ALL, as well as newer entities including early T-precursor (ETP) ALL and Ph-like (BCR-ABL1-like) ALL driven by IKZF1 deletion, CRLF2 overexpression, and tyrosine kinase-activating rearrangements (ABL1, JAK2, PDGFRB).

In ALL the malignant clone arises from hematopoietic progenitors in marrow or lymphatic tissue, producing immature nonfunctioning blasts; marrow infiltration causes anemia, granulocytopenia, and thrombocytopenia, so fatigue, infection, and hemorrhage (rather than tumor bulk) are usually the presenting complaints.

Achieving a molecular complete remission after induction predicts disease-free survival around 70% versus under 40% for MRD-positive patients, the single most relevant independent prognostic factor in both pediatric and adult ALL.
Mature B-ALL (Burkitt leukemia, ~3-4% of adults) expresses surface IgM, shows L3 morphology, and has short relapse kinetics (up to ~1-1.5 years) with frequent organ and CNS involvement.

Down syndrome carries a roughly 20-fold increased leukemia risk (ALL predominating in childhood, AML at older age), and other congenital disorders raising risk include Klinefelter, Fanconi anemia, Bloom syndrome, ataxia-telangiectasia, and neurofibromatosis.

Tumor-bulk features such as lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly from leukemic infiltration, and CNS involvement (meningeosis leukemica) may occur but are less often the reason a patient first seeks care.

ALL is the most frequent neoplasm of childhood with an early peak at age 3-4 years; in adults the incidence ranges from about 0.7 to 1.8 per 100,000 per year, higher in adolescents/young adults and rising again in the elderly.

The WBC count is normal or reduced in roughly 40% of patients, and in about 8% no circulating blasts are seen, so automated counters may fail to flag the diagnosis; only about 16% present with WBC above 100 x 10^9/L.

Bone marrow is typically heavily packed, with more than 90% blasts in about 70% of patients and near-absent normal hematopoiesis; a biopsy is essential to confirm acute leukemia and distinguish ALL from AML.

Immunophenotyping is the principal tool for subclassification: more than 70% of adult ALL is B-lineage (common ALL being most frequent, CD10+), while about 25% is T-lineage (all express CD7 and cytoplasmic/surface CD3).
An immunologic marker is considered positive when more than 20% of cells stain with the monoclonal antibody.
Philadelphia chromosome-positive ALL (t(9;22), BCR-ABL1) is seen in roughly half of elderly B-lineage patients; subtype frequencies shift substantially with age.

Minimal residual disease detected by flow cytometry, RT-qPCR for clonal Ig/TCR rearrangements or fusion transcripts (limit ~0.1-0.001%, lower with NGS/ddPCR) is the most important prognostic factor during therapy; patient-specific markers should be banked from diagnostic marrow.
Because the WBC is normal or low in about 40% of patients and roughly 8% have no circulating blasts, automated blood counts may miss the diagnosis; a manual smear and marrow biopsy are required.
Failing to bank diagnostic marrow for patient-specific markers compromises later MRD follow-up.
Assuming an MRD-negative result guarantees cure: 20-30% of MRD-negative adults still relapse, attributable to loss of assay sensitivity, evolving subclones, or extramedullary disease.

Performing lumbar puncture without an adequate platelet count (>20 x 10^9/L) or in the presence of clinical hemorrhage; potentially seeded blasts should be addressed with intrathecal therapy at the first tap.
Overlooking that L1/L2 FAB morphology has no clinical bearing while only L3 morphology indicates mature B-ALL.
Misclassifying Ph-like ALL as Ph-positive: Ph-like ALL is BCR-ABL1 negative despite similar genetic lesions and requires molecular testing to identify.

Outcome is strongly age-dependent, with cure rates around 90% in children falling to under 10% in elderly or frail patients. Prognostic stratification rests on age, WBC count at diagnosis, immunophenotype, cytogenetic/genetic lesions, and especially MRD response: molecular complete remission after induction predicts disease-free survival near 70% versus under 40% if MRD-positive. The greatest relapse risk is within the first 2 years and is much lower after 5 years. Relapse kinetics vary by subtype, being short (up to ~1-1.5 years) in mature B-ALL, intermediate (~3-4 years) in T-ALL, and prolonged (up to 5-7 years) in common ALL. CNS relapse, usually accompanied by marrow involvement, carries a dismal outcome.
Platelet count below 20 x 10^9/L, signaling high bleeding risk
Neutropenia with neutrophils below 0.5 x 10^9/L, signaling high infection risk
Hemoglobin below 7-8 g/dL (present in nearly one-third of patients)

Lineage/immunophenotypic subtyping (EGIL-type) divides ALL into B-lineage (pro-B, common, pre-B, mature B/Burkitt) and T-lineage (early/ETP, cortical-thymic, mature) categories. MRD-based response categories (Harrison Table 111-3) include complete hematologic remission (<5% marrow blasts), complete molecular remission/MRD negativity (<=0.01%, i.e. <=1 leukemic cell in 10,000 marrow cells), molecular failure/MRD positivity (>0.01% with hematologic remission), molecular relapse, and hematologic relapse (>5% blasts in marrow or blood). Risk stratification assigns standard-risk patients (no risk factors) versus high-risk patients (one or more of advanced age, high WBC, adverse immunophenotype, or adverse cytogenetic/genetic lesions).

CSF examination is the diagnostic cornerstone; classic bacterial findings are PMN pleocytosis >100/uL (90%), low glucose <2.2 mmol/L (<40 mg/dL) and/or CSF/serum glucose ratio <0.4 (~60%), elevated protein >0.45 g/L (90%), and raised opening pressure >180 mmH2O (90%) (Harrison 22e p.1120-1121)
CSF Gram stain positive in >60% and bacterial culture positive in >70-80%; culture remains required for susceptibility testing (Harrison 22e p.1120-1121)
Blood cultures should be obtained immediately when bacterial meningitis is suspected (Harrison 22e p.1120)

CSF multiplex PCR (e.g., FilmArray Meningitis/Encephalitis panel) detects S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, E. coli, L. monocytogenes, H. influenzae, S. agalactiae, plus HSV-1/2, enteroviruses, VZV, HHV-6, and parechovirus, but does not replace culture (Harrison 22e p.1121, p.1124)

Neuroimaging before LP (CT or MRI) when immunocompromised, recent head trauma, depressed consciousness, papilledema, or focal deficits; MRI preferred for edema/ischemia and shows diffuse meningeal enhancement after gadolinium (Harrison 22e p.1120-1121)

For suspected viral meningitis: CBC with differential, liver and renal function, ESR, C-reactive protein, electrolytes, glucose, creatine kinase, aldolase, amylase, and lipase; CSF PCR is the diagnostic procedure of choice for enteroviral and HSV CNS infection (Harrison 22e p.1124)

Bacterial meningitis is an acute purulent infection of the subarachnoid space accompanied by a CNS inflammatory reaction that may cause decreased consciousness, seizures, raised ICP, and stroke, with meninges, subarachnoid space, and parenchyma often jointly involved (meningoencephalitis). The leading organisms (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis) colonize the nasopharynx, cross or bypass epithelial tight junctions to enter the bloodstream, evade neutrophil phagocytosis and complement via a polysaccharide capsule, then reach the CSF through the choroid plexus or cerebral capillary endothelium. Bacteria multiply readily in CSF given its scarce leukocytes, complement, and immunoglobulin, which impair opsonization. Lysis of bacteria releases cell-wall components (LPS of gram-negatives, teichoic acid and peptidoglycan of pneumococci) that drive microglia, astrocytes, monocytes, and endothelium to produce TNF-alpha and IL-1 beta; these cytokines synergistically increase blood-brain barrier permeability (vasogenic edema, protein leakage), and the proteinaceous leukocytic exudate obstructs CSF flow and arachnoid resorption causing hydrocephalus and interstitial edema. Leukocyte adhesion and degranulation, excitatory amino acids, and reactive oxygen/nitrogen species produce cytotoxic edema and cell death (notably in the hippocampal dentate gyrus). Loss of cerebrovascular autoregulation, basal arterial narrowing/vasculitis with thrombosis, and venous/sinus thrombosis cause ischemia and infarction; combined interstitial, vasogenic, and cytotoxic edema raise ICP and may produce herniation (Harrison 22e p.1118-1120). Viral (aseptic) meningitis produces meningeal irritation with a CSF inflammatory profile but, by definition, does not produce the parenchymal dysfunction of encephalitis (Harrison 22e p.1123).

The classic triad of fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity each occurs in more than 80% of adults with acute bacterial meningitis, but the complete triad is frequently absent; a depressed level of consciousness is seen in over 75% (Harrison 22e p.1119).
Profound CNS depression, seizures, or focal deficits should never be attributed to uncomplicated viral meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1123).

A lymphocytic pleocytosis combined with a low CSF glucose should raise suspicion for fungal, tuberculous, or Listeria meningitis or noninfectious causes such as sarcoid or neoplastic meningitis rather than typical viral meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1124).

Neurologic injury in bacterial meningitis can progress even after CSF sterilization because much of the damage stems from the host inflammatory response rather than direct bacterial injury (Harrison 22e p.1119).
Acute presentation can be either fulminant over hours or subacute over several days; nausea, vomiting, and photophobia are common (Harrison 22e p.1119).

Nuchal rigidity is the pathognomonic sign of meningeal irritation; Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs are classic but of uncertain sensitivity/specificity and may be absent in the very young, elderly, immunocompromised, or obtunded (Harrison 22e p.1119-1120).

S. pneumoniae (~50%) and N. meningitidis (~25%) are the leading causes of community-acquired bacterial meningitis; group B streptococci (~15%) and L. monocytogenes (~10%) follow, with H. influenzae type b now <10% (Harrison 22e p.1118).

Petechial or purpuric skin lesions are an important clue to meningococcal infection; the rash starts as a maculopapular eruption resembling a viral exanthem then becomes petechial on trunk, extremities, mucosae, conjunctivae, and sometimes palms/soles (Harrison 22e p.1118, p.1120).

Listeria meningitis should be considered in neonates, pregnant women, those over 60, and immunocompromised hosts; infection is acquired from contaminated foods such as soft cheeses, unpasteurized milk, deli meats, and uncooked hotdogs (Harrison 22e p.1119).

Seizures occur in 15-40% of bacterial meningitis cases; focal seizures suggest focal ischemia/infarction, cortical venous thrombosis with hemorrhage, or focal edema, while generalized seizures may reflect hyponatremia or cerebral anoxia (Harrison 22e p.1120).
More than 90% of bacterial meningitis patients have a CSF opening pressure above 180 mmH2O, and 20% exceed 400 mmH2O; raised ICP is the major cause of obtundation/coma (Harrison 22e p.1120).

Viral meningitis is distinguished from encephalitis by the absence of stupor, coma, marked confusion, seizures, or focal neurologic signs; their presence points toward encephalitis or another process (Harrison 22e p.1123).
Awaiting LP or neuroimaging to start therapy: blood cultures and empirical treatment must not be delayed in suspected bacterial meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1120)
Assuming antibiotics given a few hours before LP invalidate the CSF; they do not significantly alter WBC count or glucose, nor reliably prevent Gram stain or PCR detection (Harrison 22e p.1120)
Relying on multiplex PCR alone: it omits S. aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci, and many gram-negatives, and cannot provide susceptibility data (Harrison 22e p.1121)
Interpreting meningeal enhancement on MRI as diagnostic of meningitis; it occurs in any condition with increased blood-brain barrier permeability (Harrison 22e p.1121)

Overreliance on Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs, which have uncertain sensitivity/specificity and may be absent in vulnerable groups; cervical spine disease in the elderly can cause false-positive nuchal rigidity (Harrison 22e p.1119-1120)

Misreading an early PMN pleocytosis in viral meningitis (e.g., echovirus 9, WNV, EEE, mumps) as bacterial; a PMN-predominant CSF without a diagnosis should prompt consideration of bacterial or parameningeal infection (Harrison 22e p.1123-1124)
Forgetting that giving IV 50% glucose before LP can take hours to alter CSF glucose, so it rarely confounds early sampling (Harrison 22e p.1120-1121)

Mortality from bacterial meningitis varies by organism: about 3-7% for H. influenzae, N. meningitidis, or group B streptococci; ~15% for L. monocytogenes; and ~20% for S. pneumoniae. Risk of death rises with decreased consciousness on admission, seizures within 24 h, signs of raised ICP, age in infancy or over 50, comorbidities such as shock or need for mechanical ventilation, and delayed treatment; very low CSF glucose (<2.2 mmol/L) and very high CSF protein (>3 g/L) also predict worse outcomes. Moderate-to-severe sequelae occur in roughly 25% of survivors, including impaired intellect, memory loss, seizures, hearing loss, dizziness, and gait disturbance. In adults, recovery from viral meningitis is excellent, with only rare lingering headache, mild cognitive complaints, or asthenia; outcomes in infants/neonates under 1 year are less certain, with reported intellectual impairment, learning disability, and hearing loss (Harrison 22e p.1123, p.1125).
Petechial or purpuric rash suggesting meningococcemia, which can be fulminant and fatal within hours of symptom onset (Harrison 22e p.1118)

Deteriorating consciousness, papilledema, dilated poorly reactive pupils, sixth nerve palsy, decerebrate posturing, or the Cushing reflex (bradycardia, hypertension, irregular respirations) indicating raised ICP (Harrison 22e p.1120)
Cerebral herniation, the most disastrous complication of raised ICP, reported in 1-8% of bacterial meningitis cases (Harrison 22e p.1120)
Focal neurologic findings, which mandate prompt MRI to detect focal suppurative infection (Harrison 22e p.1121)
Seizures or status epilepticus at presentation (Harrison 22e p.1120)
Stupor, coma, or marked confusion in a presumed viral meningitis, which instead suggest encephalitis or an alternative diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1123)

No single formal grading scale is given for acute meningitis; instead Harrison enumerates prognostic risk factors for death in bacterial meningitis (decreased consciousness on admission, seizures within 24 h, raised ICP, age <1 or >50, shock or need for ventilation, treatment delay, CSF glucose <2.2 mmol/L, CSF protein >3 g/L). For distinguishing bacterial from aseptic meningitis, a prospectively validated bacterial meningitis score yields a negative predictive value of about 99.7% in children, and CSF protein >0.5 g/L and serum procalcitonin >0.5 ng/mL favor bacterial over aseptic meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1123-1125).

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) - distinguished by flow cytometry/immunophenotype; presence of Auer rods confirms AML and excludes ALL
Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) - may precede/evolve into AML; AML-MR is defined by antecedent MDS or MDS/MPN and/or specific cytogenetic/molecular features
Myeloproliferative neoplasm (including chronic myeloid leukemia) - antecedent hematologic disorder that can transform to AML
Therapy-related (post-chemotherapy) AML - after alkylating agents (4-6 yr latency) or topoisomerase II inhibitors (1-3 yr latency)

Myeloproliferative neoplasms (e.g., CML in blast crisis)

AML results from clonal proliferation of poorly differentiated myeloid progenitor (blast) cells that infiltrate the marrow, blood, and tissues, crowding out normal hematopoiesis and producing pancytopenia (anemia, neutropenia/leukocyte dysfunction, thrombocytopenia). Leukemogenesis is driven by accumulating somatic mutations; clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP), most often involving epigenetic regulators DNMT3A, TET2, and ASXL1, carries a ~10-fold increased risk of hematologic malignancy, though additional 'hits' are required to progress to leukemia. Recurrent genetic lesions define disease biology and presentation: fusion genes (e.g., PML-RARA from t[15;17]; RUNX1-RUNX1T1 from t[8;21]; CBFB-MYH11 from inv[16]/t[16;16] core-binding-factor AML; MLLT3-KMT2A; DEK-NUP214) and gene mutations (NPM1, present in ~30% of AML and ~60% of cytogenetically normal AML; FLT3, activating ITD or TKD mutations in ~30%; CEBPA; TP53; IDH1/IDH2 producing the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate that disrupts epigenetic processes). KMT2A rearrangements and monocytic differentiation favor extramedullary/tissue infiltration; t(15;17) APL drives DIC.

AML is a clonal neoplasm characterized by infiltration of blood, bone marrow, and other tissues by proliferative, poorly differentiated myeloid cells (myeloblasts); historically the diagnosis required a marrow or blood myeloid blast count of >=20%, though the 2022 WHO classification eliminated the blast-percent requirement for cases with specific defining genetic aberrations (Harrison 22e p.825, p.826).

Infectious complications during neutropenia are the major cause of morbidity and death during induction and postremission chemotherapy; fever develops in most patients but infection is documented in only about half of febrile patients, and empiric broad-spectrum antibacterial/antifungal therapy at onset of neutropenic fever has substantially reduced infectious deaths (Harrison 22e p.832).

Most cases are idiopathic; genome sequencing suggests the majority arise from a limited number of mutations that accumulate with age. AML is the most common acute leukemia in older patients (median age at diagnosis 69 years) and causes 62% of leukemic deaths; only ~32% of patients survive 5 years (Harrison 22e p.825).

Auer rods are abnormal rod-shaped cytoplasmic granules; they are NOT uniformly present, but when seen they establish AML (and exclude acute lymphocytic leukemia) with certainty. AML blasts show fine lacy chromatin with one or more nucleoli and primary (nonspecific) cytoplasmic granules (Harrison 22e p.829).

Presentation is usually nonspecific and gradual (sometimes abrupt), reflecting marrow failure: fatigue (frequent first symptom) and anemia, abnormal hemostasis/bleeding and easy bruising from thrombocytopenia, and fever +/- infection from neutropenia/leukocyte dysfunction. Fever is the initial symptom in ~10% of patients (Harrison 22e p.828).

Multiparameter flow cytometry helps distinguish AML from acute lymphoblastic leukemia and identify subtypes (e.g., myeloid antigens CD13/CD117 in minimally differentiated AML; platelet antigens CD41/CD61 in acute megakaryoblastic leukemia); it has only a supportive role for WHO subtyping given the paramount importance of genetics, and is increasingly used to measure measurable residual disease (MRD) (Harrison 22e p.827).

Cytogenetic/molecular testing at diagnosis provides the most important prognostic information and drives risk stratification (European LeukemiaNet 2022 categories: favorable, intermediate, adverse). All AML cells contain genetic mutations, most recurring; the majority of patients now have a genetic lesion that can be specifically targeted (Harrison 22e p.826, p.827).

Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), defined by t(15;17)(q22;q12) / PML-RARA fusion, is a distinct, highly curable subtype (~85% long-term survival) treated uniquely with tretinoin (ATRA) and arsenic trioxide; it is excluded from the ELN risk table and is a coagulopathy emergency (Harrison 22e p.826, p.833).

Myeloid sarcoma is a tumor mass of myeloid blasts at sites other than marrow (commonly skin, lymph node, GI tract, soft tissue, testis); it may precede or coincide with blood/marrow involvement, is associated with t(8;21), and patients with isolated myeloid sarcoma typically develop blood/marrow disease quickly and cannot be cured by local therapy alone (Harrison 22e p.828).

Infiltration of gingiva, skin, soft tissues, or meninges with leukemic blasts at diagnosis is characteristic of the monocytic subtypes and those with KMT2A chromosomal abnormalities; gum hypertrophy is a classic monocytic finding (Harrison 22e p.828, p.830).
Auer rods are not uniformly present in AML, so their absence does NOT exclude AML; their presence, however, confirms AML over ALL

Diagnosis based on blast percent alone is outdated - cases with defining genetic abnormalities (e.g., t[15;17], t[8;21], inv[16], KMT2A rearrangement, NPM1 mutation) qualify as AML even with <20% blasts; genetic/cytogenetic testing is mandatory for precise diagnosis

APL must be recognized urgently - delay or treating it like ordinary AML risks fatal DIC; high-risk APL (WBC >10,000/uL) requires immediate cytoreduction because ATRA can precipitate life-threatening differentiation syndrome and rapidly rising leukocyte count
Even infirm older patients generally benefit from treatment over supportive care alone - age and comorbidity should not automatically exclude therapy

Even patients with undetectable MRD remain at risk for relapse; without postremission therapy virtually all CR patients eventually relapse, and there is no consensus on the optimal MRD technique or its use to direct therapy
NPM1 prognostic favorability is negated by co-existing FLT3-ITD; prognostic mutations are not mutually exclusive (>80% of patients carry two or more)
Anemia at diagnosis is usually present but not typically severe and is normocytic normochromic - a 'mild' blood count abnormality can still herald AML

Untreated AML is uniformly fatal; overall only ~32% of US patients survive 5 years. Cytogenetic/molecular risk is the dominant prognostic determinant: t(15;17)/APL has a very good prognosis (~85% cured), t(8;21) and inv(16) (core-binding-factor AML) a good prognosis (~55% cured), cytogenetically normal AML an intermediate outcome (~40% cured), and TP53 mutation, complex karyotype, t(6;9), inv(3), or monosomy 7 confer adverse risk with very poor outcomes and virtually no cure without transplantation. NPM1 mutation without FLT3-ITD is favorable; in-frame bZIP CEBPA mutation is favorable; FLT3-ITD carries negative prognostic impact. Clinical adverse factors include advancing age (the most important clinical factor), poor performance status, high presenting leukocyte count, antecedent hematologic disorder (MDS/MPN) or prolonged preceding cytopenias, and therapy-related (post-chemotherapy) AML. Achievement of complete remission (CR) and MRD-negative status predict longer survival.

Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL, t[15;17]/PML-RARA): coagulopathy/DIC emergency - presents with DIC-associated hemorrhage (may include significant GI, intrapulmonary, or intracranial bleeding); requires immediate recognition and ATRA-based therapy
Disseminated intravascular coagulation - classically in APL but also in monocytic AML and with extreme leukocytosis or thrombocytopenia; note thrombosis is also a recognized feature of DIC in APL
Hyperleukocytosis (WBC >100,000/uL, seen in ~20% at presentation) with pulmonary leukostasis and early CNS bleeding - associated with poor outcomes
Intracranial hemorrhage / CNS bleed - headache, vision changes, nonfocal neurologic abnormalities
Febrile neutropenia - fever in a neutropenic patient mandates immediate evaluation and empiric broad-spectrum antibacterials covering gram-negative organisms

Tumor lysis syndrome / uric acid nephropathy - hyperuricemia (aggravated by initiating chemotherapy); allopurinol/hydration started at diagnosis, rasburicase for severe cases (avoid in G6PD deficiency)

APL differentiation syndrome - within first 3 weeks of ATRA (or less commonly ATO): fever, fluid retention, dyspnea, chest pain, pulmonary infiltrates, pleural/pericardial effusions, hypoxemia; ~10% mortality if unrecognized

Risk stratification per 2022 European LeukemiaNet (ELN) by genetics at diagnosis (APL excluded): Favorable - t(8;21)/RUNX1-RUNX1T1, inv(16) or t(16;16)/CBFB-MYH11, mutated NPM1 without FLT3-ITD, in-frame bZIP-mutated CEBPA. Intermediate - mutated NPM1 with FLT3-ITD, wild-type NPM1 with FLT3-ITD (without adverse lesions), t(9;11)/MLLT3-KMT2A, and abnormalities not classified as favorable or adverse. Adverse - t(6;9)/DEK-NUP214, KMT2A rearrangements, t(9;22)/BCR-ABL1, inv(3)/t(3;3) MECOM(EVI1), -5/del(5q), -7, -17/abn(17p), complex or monosomal karyotype, mutated ASXL1/BCOR/EZH2/RUNX1/SF3B1/SRSF2/STAG2/U2AF1/ZRSR2, and mutated TP53 (>=10% VAF). Classification (2022 WHO): AML with defining genetic abnormalities versus AML defined by differentiation; the >=20% blast requirement is removed for cases with specific defining genetic aberrations.

chunks.text: Acute otitis media is an acute suppurative inflammation of the middle ear cleft, usually arising when Eustachian tube dysfunction (commonly from a viral upper respiratory infection or adenoid obstruction) impairs middle ear ventilation and drainage. Negative middle ear pressure and mucosal oedema allow pathogens to ascend from the nasopharynx and proliferate, producing an inflammatory exudate that becomes purulent. Rising pressure causes the tympanic membrane to bulge and may lead to necrosis and perforation with discharge, after which the process typically resolves. Untreated or aggressive infection can extend to adjacent structures.

chunks.text: Respiratory failure occurs when gas exchange fails to maintain adequate oxygenation or carbon dioxide elimination. Hypoxaemic (type 1) failure arises mainly from ventilation-perfusion mismatch and shunt, as in pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, and acute respiratory distress syndrome, where alveoli are filled or collapsed. Hypercapnic (type 2) failure results from reduced alveolar ventilation due to depressed respiratory drive, neuromuscular weakness, increased airway resistance, or chest wall problems, so carbon dioxide accumulates. Both cause tissue hypoxia; hypercapnia additionally produces respiratory acidosis. Fatigue of the respiratory muscles can convert a compensated state into rapid decompensation and arrest.

chunks.text: Always request: electrocardiogram (ECG), echocardiogram, complete blood count (CBC), C-reactive protein (CRP), and streptococcal serology (antistreptolysin O [ASO] and anti-DNase B [ADB]) (Harrison 22e p.2857).

Echocardiography should be performed on all possible cases to aid diagnosis (including detection of subclinical carditis/valvulitis) and to establish baseline carditis severity; auscultation is poorly sensitive and specific for RHD in asymptomatic patients (Harrison 22e p.2855, p.2857).

Because most cases lack a positive throat swab culture or rapid antigen test, serologic evidence of preceding group A strep infection is usually needed (ASO and anti-DNase B titers), ideally with locally derived age-specific reference ranges (Harrison 22e p.2856).

In relevant situations: throat swab, skin sore swab, blood cultures, synovial fluid aspirate (cell count, microscopy, culture, gonococcal PCR), pregnancy test, and creatinine/UEC (since NSAIDs can affect renal function) (Harrison 22e p.2857).

Tests to exclude alternative diagnoses (per clinical presentation/local endemic infections): autoantibodies, double-stranded DNA, anti-CCP antibodies; urine molecular testing for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis; serology for viral hepatitis, Yersinia, CMV, parvovirus B19, respiratory viruses, Ross River virus, Barmah Forest virus (Harrison 22e p.2857).

Inflammatory markers should be monitored every 1-2 weeks until normalized (usually within 4-6 weeks), and a repeat echocardiogram performed after 1 month to assess for progression of carditis (Harrison 22e p.2858).

ARF results from an autoimmune reaction to group A streptococcal infection, classically of the upper respiratory tract, with increasing evidence for a role of streptococcal skin infection. The most widely accepted theory is molecular mimicry: an immune response to streptococcal antigens (mainly the M protein) cross-reacts with human tissues. Antigen-presenting cells of the innate immune system present streptococcal antigens to T cells, activating humoral and cellular immunity; cross-reactive antibodies bind heart-valve endothelial cells, activating VCAM-1 with recruitment of activated lymphocytes and complement-mediated lysis, releasing peptides (laminin, keratin, tropomyosin) that activate cross-reactive T cells invading the heart, amplifying damage and causing epitope spreading. An alternative hypothesis proposes initial damage from streptococcal invasion of epithelial surfaces with M-protein binding to type IV collagen, rendering it immunogenic but not through molecular mimicry. Susceptibility is inherited (~3-6% of a population susceptible; 44% concordance in monozygotic vs 12% in dizygotic twins; heritability ~60%), with associations to HLA class II alleles, TNF and mannose-binding-lectin polymorphisms, the IGH locus (IGHV4-61*02), and complement factor H (Harrison 22e p.2854-2855).

ARF is a multisystem autoimmune sequela of group A streptococcal infection; almost all manifestations resolve completely, the major exception being cardiac valvular damage (rheumatic heart disease, RHD), which may persist after other features disappear (Harrison 22e p.2854).

Revised Jones criteria (2015 AHA): for all populations with evidence of preceding group A strep infection, initial ARF requires 2 major OR 1 major plus 2 minor manifestations; recurrent ARF requires 2 major OR 1 major plus 2 minor OR 3 minor manifestations. Separate, more sensitive criteria apply to moderate/high-risk populations versus low-risk populations (Harrison 22e p.2856-2857).

Major manifestations: carditis (clinical and/or subclinical), arthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, and subcutaneous nodules; in moderate/high-risk populations arthritis includes monoarthritis and polyarthralgia (Harrison 22e p.2857).

Secondary prevention with long-term penicillin prophylaxis is the mainstay of controlling ARF and RHD, best delivered through a register-based RHD control program; patients should be entered on an ARF registry, educated, and linked to follow-up before discharge (Harrison 22e p.2857-2858).

Mainly a disease of children aged 5-14 years; initial episodes are rare in persons aged >30 years, whereas recurrent episodes remain relatively common in adolescents and young adults. RHD prevalence peaks between 25 and 40 years (Harrison 22e p.2854).
There is no clear gender association for ARF, but RHD more commonly affects females, sometimes up to twice as often as males (Harrison 22e p.2854).

Latent period of ~3 weeks (range 1-5 weeks) between the precipitating group A streptococcal infection and onset of ARF; the exceptions are chorea and indolent (low-grade) carditis, which may follow prolonged latent periods of up to 6 months (Harrison 22e p.2855).

Most common clinical features are polyarthritis (60-75% of cases) and carditis (50-75%); chorea prevalence varies from <2% to 30% between populations; erythema marginatum and subcutaneous nodules are now rare, found in <5% of cases (Harrison 22e p.2855).

Up to 75% of patients with ARF progress to RHD; the mitral valve is almost always affected, sometimes with the aortic valve. Isolated aortic valve involvement is rare. The characteristic manifestation of carditis in previously unaffected individuals is mitral regurgitation, sometimes with aortic regurgitation (Harrison 22e p.2855).

ARF arthritis is typically a migratory polyarthritis of large joints (knees, ankles, hips, elbows), asymmetric, severe and disabling, and highly responsive to salicylates/NSAIDs (Harrison 22e p.2855-2856).

Sydenham's chorea often occurs in the absence of other manifestations, follows a prolonged latent period, and is found mainly in females; more than 50% of patients presenting with chorea will have carditis, so echocardiography should be part of the workup (Harrison 22e p.2856).

Erythema marginatum is an evanescent serpiginous rash (pink macules clearing centrally) usually on the trunk, sometimes the limbs, but almost never on the face. Subcutaneous nodules are painless, mobile, occur over bony prominences, appear 2-3 weeks after onset, and are commonly associated with carditis (Harrison 22e p.2856).

The preceding group A streptococcal infection is commonly subclinical, so the absence of a reported sore throat or a negative throat swab/rapid antigen test does not exclude ARF; serologic confirmation is usually required (Harrison 22e p.2855-2856).

Diagnosis of ARF is often missed, particularly in resource-poor settings, so children, adolescents, and young adults may have undiagnosed RHD; echocardiographic screening can detect these cases (Harrison 22e p.2855).
Early commencement of anti-inflammatory medication before the typical migratory pattern is established may produce an atypical presenting picture such as aseptic monoarthritis (Harrison 22e p.2856).

Recurrence of fever, joint manifestations, and elevated acute-phase reactants up to 3 weeks after stopping anti-inflammatory medication does NOT indicate a true ARF recurrence and is managed by briefly recommencing anti-inflammatory agents (Harrison 22e p.2857).

Glucocorticoid use in ARF carditis remains controversial; two meta-analyses failed to demonstrate benefit over placebo or salicylates, though included studies were >40 years old and used outdated medications (Harrison 22e p.2857-2858).
Salicylates/NSAIDs are of no proven value in the treatment of carditis or chorea (they treat arthritis, arthralgia, and fever) (Harrison 22e p.2857).

Medications to control choreiform movements do NOT alter the duration or outcome of chorea; IVIg shows no benefit on short- or long-term carditis outcome and is not recommended except in severe chorea refractory to other treatments (Harrison 22e p.2858).

Untreated, ARF lasts on average 12 weeks; with treatment, patients are usually discharged within 1-2 weeks. Almost all non-cardiac manifestations resolve completely. Inflammatory markers usually normalize within 4-6 weeks. Up to 75% of patients with ARF progress to RHD, the long-term consequence being valvular damage; people with RHD are often asymptomatic for many years before progression to cardiac failure. There is no treatment proven to alter the likelihood or severity of RHD; apart from heart-failure management, treatment of ARF is symptomatic. RHD is the most common cause of acquired heart disease in children in low- and middle-income countries and a major cause of adult mortality and morbidity, with >40 million people affected worldwide and >300,000 deaths annually (Harrison 22e p.2854, p.2857-2858).
Severe carditis causing congestive heart failure; treatment of heart failure may be lifesaving (Harrison 22e p.2857).
Myocardial inflammation affecting conduction, causing P-R interval prolongation (first-degree AV block, rarely higher-level block) (Harrison 22e p.2855).
More than 50% of patients presenting with chorea have underlying carditis, mandating echocardiographic workup (Harrison 22e p.2856).
Advanced RHD complications: heart failure, arrhythmia, stroke, and infective endocarditis (Harrison 22e p.2856).

RHD detected by echocardiography is staged (2023 World Heart Federation guidelines) into: Stage A (minimal echocardiographic criteria for RHD, individuals aged <=20 years, mild MR or AR without morphologic features); Stage B (mild RHD, mild valvular regurgitation plus morphologic feature(s)); Stage C (advanced RHD at risk of clinical complications - moderate/severe MR or AR, any MS or AS, pulmonary hypertension, decreased LV systolic function); Stage D (advanced RHD with established clinical complications such as cardiac surgery, heart failure, arrhythmia, stroke, infective endocarditis). The 2015 revised Jones criteria additionally separate low-risk populations (ARF incidence <=2 per 100,000 school-age children, or all-age RHD prevalence <=1 per 1000) from moderate/high-risk populations, applying more sensitive criteria to the latter (Harrison 22e p.2856-2857).

chunks.text: Acute tonsillitis is acute inflammation of the palatine tonsils, usually from viral or bacterial infection of the tonsillar crypts and parenchyma. Pathogens invade the crypt epithelium, provoking an inflammatory response with hyperaemia, oedema and crypt exudate. Streptococcal infection can trigger immune-mediated sequelae elsewhere in the body. Local spread of infection beyond the tonsillar capsule can produce peritonsillar or deep neck space abscesses, and marked tonsillar and adenoid enlargement may compromise the airway.

chunks.text: Acute urinary retention is the abrupt failure to empty the bladder, arising from mechanical obstruction (most often prostatic enlargement, but also urethral stricture, clot, or stone), increased outlet tone, impaired detrusor contractility, or neurogenic causes. chunks.text: The adenoid (nasopharyngeal tonsil) is part of Waldeyer's ring and undergoes physiological enlargement with repeated exposure to inhaled and ingested antigens in childhood. Recurrent infection and allergy drive lymphoid hyperplasia so the pad enlarges enough to obstruct the posterior nasal choanae and the nasopharyngeal openings of the Eustachian tubes. Choanal obstruction forces mouth breathing and impairs sinus drainage, while Eustachian tube dysfunction interferes with middle ear ventilation, favouring effusion and recurrent otitis media. Chronic mouth breathing during the years of facial growth alters craniofacial and dental development, and narrowing of the upper airway during sleep produces snoring and obstructive sleep apnoea. The adenoid tissue can also act as a reservoir of infection and biofilm.

Acute adrenal insufficiency reflects an absolute or relative deficiency of cortisol, in primary disease compounded by loss of aldosterone (mineralocorticoid). Glucocorticoid deficiency impairs vascular tone, gluconeogenesis and loss of feedback inhibition of AVP release (contributing to hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia), while mineralocorticoid deficiency causes renal salt wasting with volume depletion, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and rising creatinine. The result is hypotension that may decompensate into hypovolaemic shock. Crisis is usually unmasked by a stressor that exceeds the inadequate cortisol reserve — intercurrent illness, surgery or other stress, or increased glucocorticoid inactivation as in hyperthyroidism (p.3111).
Adrenal crisis typically emerges after a prolonged prodrome of nonspecific complaints rather than appearing out of the blue (p.3111).
Crisis is more frequent in PRIMARY adrenal insufficiency because both glucocorticoid AND mineralocorticoid secretion are lost (p.3111).
Postural hypotension can progress to frank hypovolaemic shock (p.3111).
Prospective data: about 8.3 adrenal crises per 100 patient-years and roughly 0.5 crisis-related deaths per 100 patient-years (p.3111).
Adrenal crisis is classified as a form of endocrine/distributive shock (p.2353).
In suspected crisis, it is reasonable to draw a baseline cortisol (and ACTH), start replacement, and defer formal stimulation testing — diagnostic testing must never delay treatment (p.3111).

Starting thyroid hormone replacement in an undiagnosed patient can precipitate adrenal crisis, because thyroid hormone shortens cortisol half-life; screen for adrenal insufficiency before treating hypothyroidism in possible polyendocrine syndrome (p.3133).
Do NOT let diagnostic testing delay treatment in suspected crisis (p.3111).

Random/baseline serum cortisol has limited diagnostic value because levels may be coincidentally low from normal diurnal rhythm, and many secondary cases have near-normal baseline cortisol that only fails on stimulation testing (p.3111).
Do NOT start thyroid hormone before excluding/treating adrenal insufficiency — it can precipitate crisis (p.3133).
Hyperthyroidism increases glucocorticoid inactivation and can trigger crisis (p.3111).
Adrenal insufficiency can be masked by concurrent primary hypothyroidism, which prolongs cortisol half-life (p.3133).
Acute adrenal insufficiency is potentially lethal (p.636). Even with established care, crises and crisis-related deaths continue to occur (~8.3 crises and ~0.5 deaths per 100 patient-years) (p.3111).

[guideline] adjunct → IV/IM hydrocortisone maintenance Continues cover after the initial bolus while the precipitant (often infection) is treated; a continuous infusion (~200 mg/24 h) is an alternative. Taper as the patient recovers.

ACTH-independent adrenal Cushing's: cortisol-producing adenoma, adrenocortical carcinoma, primary bilateral macronodular adrenal hyperplasia, primary pigmented nodular adrenal disease (Carney complex), McCune-Albright syndrome

Mineralocorticoid excess differential: bilateral micronodular hyperplasia vs unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn's); glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism (GRA/FH-I) and other familial primary aldosteronism; apparent mineralocorticoid excess (HSD11B2 deficiency); Liddle's syndrome (ENaC mutations); deoxycorticosterone excess from CAH (CYP11B1 or CYP17A1 deficiency)
