Cushing's screening: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test, late-night (midnight) salivary cortisol, 24-h urinary free cortisol (three collections); low-dose dexamethasone test if confirmation needed

Cushing's differential: plasma ACTH; pituitary MRI; high-dose dexamethasone test; CRH or desmopressin stimulation; bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling; unenhanced adrenal CT for ACTH-independent disease

Aldosteronism: aldosterone-renin ratio with serum potassium normalized; confirmatory saline infusion / oral sodium loading / fludrocortisone suppression test; unenhanced adrenal CT; adrenal vein sampling; 24-h urinary steroid profile (GC/MS) for familial/mimicking forms

Adrenal insufficiency: short cosyntropin (Synacthen/ACTH) stimulation test; plasma ACTH; plasma renin; adrenal steroid (21-hydroxylase) autoantibodies; insulin tolerance test as alternative; adrenal CT if autoantibody-negative; very-long-chain fatty acids in autoantibody-negative males (exclude X-ALD); pituitary MRI for secondary disease

Incidentaloma: 1 mg-DST in all; plasma/urine metanephrines if HU >10; paired renin and aldosterone plus potassium if hypertensive; 17-OHP, DHEAS, androstenedione (and sex steroids) if ACC suspected; unenhanced CT for size and attenuation (HU); chemical-shift MRI for indeterminate lesions

CAH: measurement of precursor steroids accumulating before the enzymatic block (notably 17-hydroxyprogesterone for 21-hydroxylase deficiency), preferably by mass spectrometry; androstenedione and testosterone for monitoring
Common population conditions overlapping Cushing's: obesity, type 2 diabetes, diastolic hypertension, hirsutism, depression, osteoporotic vertebral fractures
Pseudo-Cushing states (alcohol, major depression, morbid obesity)
Chronic adrenal insufficiency mistaken for depression or anorexia (nonspecific fatigue, weight loss)
Adrenal crisis mimicking acute abdomen or neurologic disease (stupor/coma)
Polycystic ovary syndrome phenotype mimicked by nonclassic CAH (hirsutism, oligomenorrhea)
Other causes of hypokalemic hypertension: licorice ingestion inhibiting 11beta-HSD2; renovascular/malignant hypertension (secondary hyperaldosteronism)

The adrenal cortex produces glucocorticoids (cortisol, zona fasciculata under HPA/ACTH control), mineralocorticoids (aldosterone, zona glomerulosa under renin-angiotensin-aldosterone control), and adrenal androgens. Cushing's syndrome reflects chronic glucocorticoid excess: ~90% of endogenous cases are ACTH-dependent (mostly a pituitary corticotrope adenoma = Cushing's disease, or ectopic ACTH from carcinoid/small-cell lung cancer), ~10% are ACTH-independent adrenal causes (adenoma, carcinoma, or bilateral macronodular/pigmented nodular hyperplasia). Cortisol excess upregulates gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, and protein catabolism, and when 11beta-HSD2 is overwhelmed cortisol activates the mineralocorticoid receptor, producing hypertension, hypokalemia, and edema. Primary mineralocorticoid excess (primary aldosteronism) is autonomous aldosterone production by the zona glomerulosa (bilateral hyperplasia or unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma/Conn's); MR over-activation causes sodium retention with volume expansion, potassium and hydrogen loss (hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis), and direct cardiac/renal damage. Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's) is destruction or dysfunction of the adrenal cortex (most often autoimmune adrenalitis, also TB, adrenoleukodystrophy, hemorrhage, infiltration, CAH), causing combined glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency; secondary insufficiency is HPA/pituitary-hypothalamic failure (tumor, surgery, irradiation, apoplexy/Sheehan's, or iatrogenic glucocorticoid suppression) with isolated glucocorticoid deficiency. CAH results from inherited steroidogenic enzyme defects (commonly CYP21A2) causing glucocorticoid deficiency, loss of feedback, raised ACTH, and adrenal androgen excess, with mineralocorticoid deficiency or excess depending on the enzymatic block.

Cushing's: most clinical features (obesity, diabetes, diastolic hypertension, hirsutism, depression) are nonspecific; the more discriminatory signs are thinning/fragile skin with easy bruising, broad (>1 cm) purplish striae, and proximal myopathy (difficulty rising from a chair or climbing stairs). Suspect when several features cluster, or when a feature appears at an unusual age (e.g., osteoporosis in a young patient). (p.3056-3057)

Primary adrenal insufficiency loses both glucocorticoid AND mineralocorticoid secretion; secondary (central) disease loses glucocorticoid only because the adrenal stays responsive to the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Adrenal androgen secretion is lost in both. (p.3067)

Hyperpigmentation (palmar creases, friction/shear areas, sun-exposed skin) from excess POMC/ACTH is the hallmark distinguishing primary adrenal insufficiency; secondary insufficiency instead causes an alabaster-pale skin from ACTH lack. (p.3067)

Hyponatremia is present in ~80% of primary adrenal insufficiency at presentation and hyperkalemia in ~40%. Hyponatremia can also occur in secondary insufficiency via reduced cortisol inhibition of ADH (mild SIADH-like picture). (p.3067)

All patients with an incidentally discovered adrenal mass need a 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test to exclude cortisol excess; add plasma/urine metanephrines if HU >10 (exclude pheochromocytoma), and paired renin/aldosterone plus potassium if hypertensive. Confirm any Cushing's as ACTH-independent by measuring plasma ACTH. (p.3063-3064)

On unenhanced CT, adrenal lesion attenuation is the key discriminator: lipid-rich adenomas are typically <10-20 HU, whereas adrenocortical carcinoma and pheochromocytoma have high attenuation (>20 HU). Hounsfield assessment only applies to unenhanced CT, not post-contrast. (p.3064)

Mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS) = abnormal 1 mg dexamethasone test with no overt clinical Cushing's; it still carries excess risk of hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, osteoporosis, cardiovascular events, and mortality. A subset of primary aldosteronism patients have co-existing MACS ('Connshing' syndrome). (p.3061, p.3064)

CYP21A2 (21-hydroxylase) deficiency causes 90-95% of congenital adrenal hyperplasia; it impairs glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid synthesis and drives ACTH-mediated adrenal androgen excess. 17-hydroxyprogesterone is the diagnostic marker steroid. Severity spans classic salt-wasting (neonatal), simple virilizing, to nonclassic (presents in adolescence/adulthood). (p.3071)

Screen for endogenous Cushing's only after excluding exogenous (iatrogenic) glucocorticoids in any form. First-line screening tests: increased 24-h urinary free cortisol (three collections), failure to suppress morning cortisol after a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone test, and loss of diurnal rhythm shown by raised late-night (midnight) serum/salivary cortisol. Diagnosis is considered established when several tests are consistently abnormal. (p.3057)

Establish the diagnosis of Cushing's beyond doubt BEFORE doing any differential-diagnosis or imaging tests; most management errors (unnecessary imaging or surgery) come from not following this sequence, because pituitary and adrenal nodules are common incidental findings in the general population. (p.3057)

Cushing's differential diagnosis order: measure plasma ACTH first. Suppressed ACTH = ACTH-independent (adrenal) excess -> unenhanced adrenal CT. Normal/high ACTH = ACTH-dependent -> pituitary MRI plus dynamic tests (high-dose dexamethasone, CRH or desmopressin); pituitary MRI can be normal in up to 40% because microadenomas are small. (p.3057-3058)

Inferior petrosal sinus sampling (central:peripheral ACTH ratio >2 at baseline, >3 after CRH) distinguishes Cushing's disease from ectopic ACTH when dynamic tests are discordant; it cannot be used to lateralize the tumor within the pituitary, and no cortisol-lowering drugs should be used before it. (p.3058)

Primary aldosteronism is far more common than historically appreciated: prevalence 5-12% of hypertensives, higher in hypokalemic or drug-resistant hypertension. Screen only selected hypertensives (drug-resistant/severe hypertension, hypokalemia, adrenal mass, onset <40 years, or family history of primary aldosteronism), not all comers. (p.3060-3061)

Primary aldosteronism screen = aldosterone-renin ratio (ARR); correct hypokalemia first. Stop MR antagonists at least 4-6 weeks before testing; beta-blockers cause false positives and ACE inhibitors/ARBs cause false negatives. A positive ARR is followed by confirmatory testing (e.g., saline infusion test) by an endocrinologist. (p.3061)

After biochemical confirmation of aldosteronism, unenhanced adrenal CT plus adrenal vein sampling distinguish unilateral adenoma (Conn's, surgically curable by unilateral adrenalectomy) from bilateral hyperplasia (treated medically with an MR antagonist). AVS is only needed when surgery is feasible and desired. (p.3061)

Adrenal insufficiency: short cosyntropin (Synacthen) test is the safe, reliable first-line diagnostic test; failure is cortisol <450-500 nmol/L (16-18 microg/dL) at 30-60 min. Then measure plasma ACTH: high ACTH = primary (Addison's), inappropriately low ACTH = secondary/central. Increased plasma renin confirms mineralocorticoid deficiency in primary disease. (p.3068)
Performing imaging or surgery before biochemically confirming Cushing's beyond doubt - pituitary/adrenal nodules are common incidental findings and lead to misdiagnosis
Forgetting to exclude exogenous (iatrogenic) glucocorticoid use as the cause before working up endogenous Cushing's

Dexamethasone test pitfalls: false non-suppression from oral estrogens/contraceptives (raise CBG/total cortisol; retest after 4-6 weeks off estrogen) and rapid dexamethasone inactivation by CYP3A4 inducers (antiepileptics, rifampicin); antibody-based urinary free cortisol assays have specificity problems improved by tandem mass spectrometry
Not normalizing potassium before, or failing to stop MR antagonists (4-6 weeks) before, ARR testing; beta-blockers give false-positive and ACE inhibitors/ARBs false-negative ARR results
Relying on the ARR alone when renin is very low increases false positives; only 10-40% of primary aldosteronism patients are hypokalemic, so normokalemia does not exclude it

Using random serum cortisol to diagnose adrenal insufficiency - baseline levels may be coincidentally low (diurnal rhythm), and secondary insufficiency often shows near-normal baseline cortisol that fails only on stimulation
Stopping exogenous glucocorticoids abruptly can precipitate iatrogenic adrenal insufficiency even though the patient still looks cushingoid

Judging adrenal mass attenuation on post-contrast CT - Hounsfield-unit discrimination of benign vs malignant only applies to unenhanced CT; lipid-poor adenomas (high HU) overlap with ACC and pheochromocytoma
Mistaking testicular adrenal rest tumors (TART) in CAH for testicular neoplasms

After successful removal of an ACTH- or cortisol-producing tumor the HPA axis remains suppressed and may take months to years (or never) to recover; recovery rates differ by cause - ectopic ACTH best (~80%, median ~7 months), Cushing's disease intermediate (~60%, ~17 months), adrenal Cushing's lowest (~40%, ~30 months). Even after cure, long-term quality of life can remain impaired with increased cardiovascular and osteoporotic-fracture risk depending on duration and degree of cortisol excess. Primary aldosteronism carries increased osteoporosis, type 2 diabetes, and cognitive dysfunction. Adrenal crisis is potentially lethal, with prospective data of 8.3 crises and 0.5 crisis-related deaths per 100 patient-years. MACS is associated with increased mortality. In CAH, fertility may be compromised (anovulation in women, testicular adrenal rest tumors and fibrosis in men).

Adrenal crisis (acute adrenal insufficiency): postural hypotension progressing to hypovolemic shock, often after a prolonged period of nonspecific complaints; may mimic acute abdomen or neurologic decline (stupor/coma); can be triggered by intercurrent illness, surgery/stress, or increased glucocorticoid inactivation (e.g., hyperthyroidism) - treat immediately, do not let testing delay therapy
In suspected adrenal crisis, draw a baseline cortisol, start replacement, and defer formal stimulation testing - tests must never delay treatment
Cushing's hypercoagulable state with risk of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism
Acute paranoid or depressive psychosis in severe cortisol excess
Severe hypokalemia in aldosteronism causing arrhythmias, rhabdomyolysis, or hypokalemic paralysis; severe alkalosis causing tetany
Classic salt-wasting CAH in male neonates presenting as life-threatening adrenal crisis in the first weeks of life

Adrenal insufficiency is classified as primary (Addison's, combined glucocorticoid + mineralocorticoid deficiency, high ACTH) vs secondary/central (isolated glucocorticoid deficiency, low/inappropriate ACTH), with acute adrenal crisis as the life-threatening acute form. Endogenous Cushing's is classified as ACTH-dependent (~90%; Cushing's disease vs ectopic ACTH) vs ACTH-independent (~10%; adenoma, carcinoma, hyperplasia). Cortisol excess severity ranges from overt Cushing's to mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS). Primary aldosteronism is divided into unilateral (adenoma/Conn's, surgically curable) vs bilateral (hyperplasia, medical therapy). CAH (21-hydroxylase deficiency) is graded by severity into classic salt-wasting, simple virilizing, and nonclassic forms. Adrenocortical carcinoma is staged by the ENSAT/TNM system (Stage I T1 <=5 cm to advanced/metastatic).

chunks.text: Age-related macular degeneration results from cumulative damage to the retinal pigment epithelium, Bruch's membrane, and choriocapillaris at the macula. Impaired clearance of metabolic debris leads to drusen deposition, and oxidative stress, complement-mediated inflammation, and lipofuscin accumulation injure the photoreceptor-RPE complex. In the atrophic form this causes progressive loss of central photoreceptors, whereas in the neovascular form ischaemia and VEGF release drive abnormal choroidal new vessels that leak and bleed beneath and within the retina, rapidly destroying central vision.

chunks.text: In prerenal states, a fall in true or effective arterial volume lowers mean arterial pressure and triggers sympathetic activation, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and vasopressin release; GFR is sustained by prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar dilatation and angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction. Once mean arterial pressure falls below about 80 mmHg, GFR declines steeply. This autoregulation explains why NSAIDs (which block prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilatation) and ACE inhibitors/ARBs (which reduce efferent constriction) can precipitate hemodynamically mediated AKI when volume or perfusion pressure is already reduced, and why patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis (or stenosis of a solitary kidney) are especially susceptible to a precipitous GFR fall on ACEi/ARBs. Sustained hypoperfusion progresses to ischaemic ATN. Nephrotoxic ATN results from a combination of intrarenal vasoconstriction, direct tubular toxicity, and intratubular obstruction (p.340).

Ethanol is a CNS depressant that acutely enhances GABA activity (notably at GABA-A receptors) and inhibits postsynaptic NMDA excitatory glutamate receptors; chronic exposure produces compensatory downregulation of GABA-related activity and upregulation of NMDA receptor subunits. Falling blood levels after chronic use therefore unmask a hyperexcitable state, explaining withdrawal phenomena. Acute alcohol raises dopamine in the ventral tegmentum and nucleus accumbens, releases beta-endorphins, and increases serotonin and stress hormones (cortisol, ACTH), driving reward, craving and relapse. Cellular (pharmacodynamic), metabolic (up to ~30% faster hepatic metabolism after 1-2 weeks) and learned/behavioral mechanisms contribute to acquired tolerance. Cellular adaptations may take weeks to resolve, so rapid drops in blood level produce withdrawal that is most intense in the first 5 days but with protracted symptoms (disturbed sleep, anxiety) lasting up to 4-6 months (Harrison 22e p.3675-3676).
A standard drink contains roughly 10-12 g of ethanol; one typical drink raises the blood ethanol level by about 0.02 g/dL (Harrison 22e p.3675).

Useful blood markers of regular heavy intake are GGT (>35 U) and carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (CDT >20 U/L or >2.6%), with the combination more accurate than either alone; high-normal MCV (>=91) and elevated uric acid also support the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.3678-3679).
Continued heavy drinking shortens life span by about 10 years, with leading causes of early death being heart disease, cancer, accidents and suicide (Harrison 22e p.3678).

'Holiday heart' refers to atrial or ventricular arrhythmias, especially paroxysmal tachycardia, occurring temporarily after heavy drinking in people with no other evidence of heart disease (Harrison 22e p.3677).

Behavioral, psychomotor and cognitive impairment appears at only 0.02-0.04 g/dL (one to two drinks); 'legal intoxication' in most U.S. states is 0.08 g/dL, with 0.04 g/dL applied to pilots and to drivers in some countries (Harrison 22e p.3676).

In a person without tolerance, light coma with depressed vital signs occurs around 0.30 g/dL and death between 0.30 and 0.40 g/dL; alcohol probably causes more overdose deaths than any other drug (Harrison 22e p.3676).

Heavy drinking while fasting can cause transient hypoglycemia within 6-36 h by suppressing gluconeogenesis, producing temporarily abnormal glucose tolerance that can be misread as diabetes until 2-4 weeks of abstinence (Harrison 22e p.3675).

Most ethanol is metabolized in the liver: the cytosolic alcohol dehydrogenase pathway generates acetaldehyde (then cleared by aldehyde dehydrogenase), while the microsomal ethanol-oxidizing system (MEOS) handles >=10% at high blood levels (Harrison 22e p.3675).
Blackouts (temporary anterograde amnesia while awake) occur in about 35% of drinkers, with en bloc blackouts at levels >0.20 and fragmentary blackouts at >0.12 (Harrison 22e p.3676).

Alcohol disrupts sleep architecture, reducing early-night REM and deep sleep and relaxing pharyngeal muscles to worsen snoring and apnea; sleep apnea symptoms occur in about 75% of men with AUD aged >=60 (Harrison 22e p.3676).
DSM-5 diagnoses AUD when >=2 of 11 criteria cluster in the same 12-month period; severity is mild (2-3), moderate (4-5) or severe (>=6 items) (Harrison 22e p.3677-3678).

Roughly 60% of the risk for AUD is genetic; a flushing response (ALDH variant seen in Japanese, Chinese and Korean individuals) lowers risk, while a low level of response to alcohol predicts future heavy drinking and problems (Harrison 22e p.3678).
Misreading alcohol-induced transient hypoglycemia/abnormal glucose tolerance as diabetes before 2-4 weeks of abstinence (Harrison 22e p.3675)
Misdiagnosing alcohol ketoacidosis as diabetic ketosis (Harrison 22e p.3675)

Treating substance-induced psychiatric symptoms with long-term medication when they typically resolve within days to ~4 weeks of abstinence (only short-term antipsychotics for substance-induced psychosis are usually needed) (Harrison 22e p.3676-3677)

Giving routine IV fluids in withdrawal - most patients are normally hydrated or mildly overhydrated, so fluids should be avoided unless there is a specific medical indication, bleeding, vomiting or diarrhea (Harrison 22e p.3680)
Relying on questionnaires (e.g., AUDIT) alone - they are screening tools and a face-to-face interview is required for diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.3679)
A false-negative tuberculin skin test from impaired delayed-hypersensitivity in chronic heavy drinkers (Harrison 22e p.3677)
Assuming AUD spares affluent or professional patients - lifetime risk among physicians is similar to the general population (Harrison 22e p.3678)

With at least a year of follow-up after treatment, more than half of people with AUD achieve a marked reduction in drinking and related problems or full abstinence, and even without formal treatment or self-help groups there is at least a 20% chance of spontaneous long-term remission. Many alcohol-related organ changes are reversible with abstinence: blood pressure normalizes within weeks, GGT/CDT return toward normal within weeks, thrombocytopenia usually resolves within a week (unless cirrhosis or congestive splenomegaly), MRI/CT brain changes generally reverse, and acute myopathy improves though may not fully remit. Continued heavy drinking shortens life span by roughly 10 years, mainly through heart disease, cancer, accidents and suicide (Harrison 22e p.3677-3678).
Withdrawal seizure (about 2% of patients), with higher risk in older age, concomitant medical problems, polydrug misuse and larger alcohol quantities (Harrison 22e p.3680)
Withdrawal delirium / delirium tremens (about 1%): agitated delirium with confusion, fluctuating consciousness, tremor and marked autonomic overactivity (Harrison 22e p.3680)
Autonomic overactivity during withdrawal: rising pulse, respiratory rate, sweating and body temperature (Harrison 22e p.3680)
Severe intoxication with respiratory depression, cardiac arrhythmias or blood pressure instability; light coma near 0.30 g/dL and death 0.30-0.40 g/dL (Harrison 22e p.3676, 3679)
Gastrointestinal bleeding from hemorrhagic gastritis or a Mallory-Weiss tear after violent vomiting (Harrison 22e p.3677)
Pregnancy: any drinking risks fetal alcohol spectrum disorder; complete abstinence advised (Harrison 22e p.3677)

Effects of blood alcohol levels without tolerance: 0.02 decreased inhibitions; 0.08 reduced complex cognition and motor performance; 0.20 slurred speech, incoordination, poor judgment; 0.30 light coma with depressed vital signs; 0.40 death (Harrison 22e p.3676).

Ethanol is rapidly absorbed in the upper GI tract and metabolized predominantly in the liver, reaching it via the portal vein. Most ethanol is oxidized by alcohol dehydrogenase 1 (ADH1) to acetaldehyde in hepatocytes; chronic consumption also induces CYP2E1, which similarly generates acetaldehyde. Beyond direct acetaldehyde toxicity, ethanol metabolism generates reactive oxygen species causing hepatocyte injury through lipid peroxidation and DNA damage. Acetaldehyde is then oxidized to acetate by acetaldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH); inherited ALDH2 deficiency (common in Asian populations) causes acetaldehyde accumulation with nausea and cutaneous flushing. Steatosis arises because acetate becomes acetyl-CoA feeding fatty acid/triglyceride synthesis, alcohol upregulates lipogenic genes (partly epigenetically) while suppressing fatty acid transport/oxidation, and the increased NADH/NAD+ ratio reduces mitochondrial beta-oxidation; alcohol also mobilizes fatty acids from adipose and intestine into the liver. A subset develop gut dysbiosis and increased intestinal permeability, allowing microbial components (e.g., bacterial LPS) to reach the liver via the portal vein, driving inflammation, hepatocyte death, and fibrotic pathway activation; sustained alcohol use progresses to cirrhosis with portal hypertension. Impaired liver regeneration may contribute to acute alcohol-associated hepatitis arising in underlying cirrhosis (p.2698).

ALD is a spectrum: alcohol-associated fatty liver (steatosis) and steatohepatitis progress to fibrosis and cirrhosis; acute alcohol-associated hepatitis is an acute-on-chronic form associated with liver failure and high mortality (p.2697).
In confirmed cirrhosis, HCC surveillance with liver ultrasonography and serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) every 6 months and upper GI endoscopy to screen for varices are recommended (p.2699).
Only 10-20% of individuals with alcohol-induced hepatic steatosis develop progressive liver disease and cirrhosis; women develop ALD at a lower daily alcohol intake (p.2698).

Characteristic biochemical signature: AST/ALT ratio >1 (commonly cited as >2:1 for alcoholic liver disease), with serum AST rarely exceeding 300 IU/L; in alcohol-associated hepatitis AST and ALT do not exceed 400 IU/L and the AST/ALT ratio is >1.5 with serum bilirubin >3 mg/dL (p.2699).
Steatosis and steatohepatitis are clinically silent; symptoms typically appear only when alcohol-associated cirrhosis decompensates or alcohol-associated hepatitis develops (p.2699).

Alcohol-associated hepatitis is defined clinically by heavy drinking (>40 g/d women, >50-60 g/d men) for >6 months with <60 days abstinence before symptom onset, presenting with rapid-onset jaundice (bilirubin >3 mg/dL), often with fever, malaise, and tender hepatomegaly (p.2698).
Prolonged alcohol abstinence is the most effective therapy to reduce progression and reverse ALD; steatosis and steatohepatitis are reversible with cessation of alcohol consumption (p.2699).
There are currently NO approved drugs for treatment of alcohol-associated steatosis or steatohepatitis with or without fibrosis (p.2699).

Severity of alcohol-associated hepatitis is stratified by Maddrey discriminant function (MDF) and MELD: severe disease (MDF >=32 or MELD >20) carries high short-term mortality (~30% at 3 months) and may benefit from glucocorticoids; moderate disease (MDF <32 or MELD <=20) still carries ~20% 1-year mortality (p.2700).

Lille score >=0.45 after 7 days of glucocorticoid treatment identifies non-responders unlikely to benefit from continued therapy; glucocorticoids should be stopped and early liver transplantation considered (p.2700).
Liver transplantation for alcohol-associated decompensated cirrhosis or HCC is the leading indication for liver transplantation in the United States (p.2699-2700).

Diagnosis of ALD requires exclusion of other liver diseases in heavy drinkers; do not attribute liver disease to alcohol without ruling out viral hepatitis, Wilson's disease, autoimmune liver disease, and DILI.

Atypical laboratory values (AST <50 IU/L or >400 IU/L, or AST/ALT ratio <1.5) argue against alcohol-associated hepatitis and warrant transjugular liver biopsy - 10-20% of clinically diagnosed cases have a different disease on biopsy.

Do not give glucocorticoids when contraindications are present: uncontrolled infection/sepsis, AKI/hepatorenal syndrome, uncontrolled upper GI bleeding, concomitant viral hepatitis/HCC/pancreatitis/DILI/active TB/HIV, multiorgan failure, or shock; glucocorticoids may be used only once infection, sepsis, and GI bleeding are adequately controlled.
Liver biopsy is rarely needed to diagnose simple steatosis or steatohepatitis - reserve invasive biopsy for confounding/atypical cases.
Distinguish ALD from NAFLD/MASLD by the AST/ALT pattern (ALD favors AST/ALT >2:1).

Steatosis and steatohepatitis are reversible with abstinence, but only 10-20% of those with steatosis progress to cirrhosis. In alcohol-associated hepatitis, short-term mortality is predicted by MDF, MELD, or ABIC scores: moderate disease (MDF <32 or MELD <=20) carries ~20% 1-year mortality, whereas severe disease (MDF >=32 or MELD >20) carries ~30% 3-month mortality. Glucocorticoids reduce risk of death in severe disease within 28 days but not over the following 6 months. While short-term prognosis depends on disease severity at presentation, long-term prognosis (>1 year) largely depends on alcohol abstinence and underlying cirrhosis. Non-responders to medical therapy have high 30-day mortality (p.2700).

Alcohol-associated hepatitis severity: Moderate AH = MDF <32 or MELD <=20 (~20% 1-year mortality); Severe AH = Maddrey discriminant function (MDF) >=32 or MELD >20 (~30% 3-month mortality), candidates for glucocorticoids if no contraindication. MDF = 4.6 x (prothrombin time prolongation above control in seconds) + serum bilirubin (mg/dL). Day-7 Lille score >=0.45 defines glucocorticoid non-response. Cirrhosis prognosis assessed by Child-Pugh-Turcotte (CPT) and MELD (or sodium-MELD). Fibrosis staging by liver stiffness: <6 kPa normal, >8 kPa indicates >=F3 advanced fibrosis, >12.5 kPa indicates F4 cirrhosis.

chunks.text: Chronic alcohol exposure enhances inhibitory gamma-aminobutyric acid signalling and suppresses excitatory glutamatergic (NMDA receptor) activity; the brain adapts by downregulating GABA and upregulating glutamate systems. chunks.text: Allergic rhinitis is an IgE-mediated inflammatory response of the nasal mucosa to inhaled allergens. On re-exposure, allergen cross-links IgE bound to mast cells, triggering an early-phase release of histamine and other mediators that produce sneezing, itching, rhinorrhoea and congestion within minutes. A late-phase reaction, driven by recruited eosinophils, basophils and T cells, sustains mucosal inflammation and congestion hours later and heightens nasal reactivity. Chronic inflammation causes mucosal oedema and hyperresponsiveness, and shared airway inflammation links the condition to asthma.

chunks.text: Alopecia areata is an organ-specific autoimmune disorder in which the immune privilege of the hair follicle breaks down, allowing a T-cell-mediated attack focused on the anagen-phase follicular bulb. Interferon-gamma and other cytokines signalling through the JAK-STAT pathway drive a peribulbar lymphocytic infiltrate classically likened to a swarm of bees. Affected follicles prematurely enter catagen and telogen and produce dystrophic hairs, but the follicular stem-cell compartment is preserved, which is why regrowth remains possible even after long-standing loss. A polygenic predisposition interacts with environmental triggers, and there is overlap with other autoimmune diseases.

Ascent lowers barometric pressure and thus the partial pressure of inspired oxygen, reducing the pressure gradient driving oxygen diffusion along the oxygen cascade. Hypobaric hypoxia is the central trigger for all forms of altitude illness. The normal struggle response is increased ventilation (the cornerstone of acclimatization) mediated by the carotid bodies; this can produce marked respiratory alkalosis (arterial pH may exceed 7.7 at extreme altitude) and dehydration, with alkalosis blunting ventilatory drive in sleep and causing periodic breathing and hypoxemia. Early acclimatization includes renal carbonic-anhydrase suppression with dilute alkaline urine to correct pH, plus increased sympathetic tone, rising erythropoietin/hemoglobin and red cell mass, greater tissue capillary density and mitochondrial numbers, and elevated 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate. Hypoxia-inducible factor governs transcriptional hypoxia responses; the EPAS1 gene (HIF-2alpha) and EGLN1/PPARA influence adaptation in Tibetan highlanders (lower hemoglobin than Han Chinese or Andeans). In AMS/HACE, raised intracranial pressure, increased sympathetic activity, relative hypoventilation, fluid retention/redistribution, and impaired gas exchange contribute; MRI evidence points to vasogenic (interstitial) cerebral edema, especially in the splenium of the corpus callosum, that may become cytotoxic in severe HACE, with hemosiderin deposits as long-lasting footprints. Impaired cerebral autoregulation with hypoxic vasodilation, altered blood-brain-barrier permeability via histamine, arachidonic acid, and VEGF, and venous outflow obstruction raising capillary pressure all promote edema. HAPE results from patchy hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction with regional overperfusion and capillary stress failure at normal wedge pressure; endothelial dysfunction with reduced nitric oxide availability and elevated endothelin-1, exaggerated sympathetic drive (pulmonary venoconstriction), and impaired transepithelial alveolar fluid clearance are implicated. Inflammation in HAPE is regarded as an epiphenomenon rather than the primary cause, although inflammatory/viral respiratory processes can predispose to it.

Altitude illness encompasses a spectrum: acute mountain sickness (AMS, the benign form) and the two life-threatening forms, high-altitude cerebral edema (HACE) and high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE) (Harrison 22e p.3754).

Sickle cell disease is one of the rare exposures in which altitude can provoke vaso-occlusive crisis, reported even at passes as low as 2500 m; thalassemia has not been linked to high-altitude problems (Harrison 22e p.3759).

Hypertensive patients are not more prone to altitude illness, and most with well-controlled hypertension can be reassured that blood pressure stays relatively stable; antihypertensives should be continued at altitude (Harrison 22e p.3759).

High-altitude cough can be severe enough to cause rib fracture above 5000 m; it is multifactorial (cold dry air plus hypoxia and respiratory water loss), and infection is generally not a common cause (Harrison 22e p.3758).

AMS is a clinical diagnosis presenting 6-12 h after ascent with nonspecific symptoms (headache, nausea, fatigue, dizziness) and few physical findings; the Lake Louise Scoring System is used for research uniformity (Harrison 22e p.3755).

AMS and HACE are viewed as opposite ends of one neurologic continuum; HACE (not AMS) is an encephalopathy whose hallmarks are ataxia and altered consciousness with diffuse cerebral involvement, typically without focal deficits, and progression can be rapid (Harrison 22e p.3755).

The two most important risk factors for altitude illness are a rapid rate of ascent and a prior history of high-altitude illness; exertion is a risk factor, but lack of physical fitness is not (Harrison 22e p.3755).

Illness is likely above 2500 m but has been documented at 1500-2500 m; in the Everest region about 50% of trekkers ascending above 4000 m over 5+ days develop AMS, rising to 84% with direct flight to 3860 m, whereas HACE and HAPE incidence is far lower (roughly 0.1-4%) (Harrison 22e p.3754).

HAPE is primarily a pulmonary disorder and need not be preceded by AMS; it develops within 2-4 days of arrival and rarely after 4-5 days at the same altitude owing to vascular remodeling and adaptation (Harrison 22e p.3757).

HAPE is a noncardiogenic pulmonary edema with normal pulmonary artery wedge pressure, driven by patchy hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction causing regional overperfusion, capillary pressures above 18 mmHg, and capillary stress failure (Harrison 22e p.3757).

Retinal hemorrhages are common at altitudes of 5000 m or more even without AMS/HACE symptoms; most resolve on descent, but macular hemorrhage can cause devastating, occasionally permanent visual loss (Harrison 22e p.3755, 3759).

Gradual ascent with time for acclimatization is the best preventive measure; a conservative target above 3000 m is graded gain of no more than ~300 m per sleeping-altitude night with an extra acclimatization day every third day of gain (Harrison 22e p.3756).
Treating AMS as trivial - symptoms overlap with exhaustion, dehydration, hypothermia, hangover, and hyponatremia, and it can progress to life-threatening HACE.
Relying on pulse oximetry alone to predict AMS during a trek - readings should not be used predictively unless guided by clinical signs.
Assuming HAPE is always preceded by AMS - it is primarily pulmonary and may present without headache or nausea, sometimes only as fatigue and rest dyspnea.
Misreading HAPE chest opacities as pneumonia (cold) or as heart failure - Kerley B lines and bat-wing pattern are absent in HAPE.
Confusing sudden neurologic events (TIA, stroke, subarachnoid hemorrhage, cranial nerve palsy) at altitude with altitude illness - AMS evolves gradually whereas these typically occur suddenly.
Mistaking reentry HAPE in returning highlanders for a viral illness.
Injudicious prophylactic glucocorticoid use by climbers to boost performance - can be tragic owing to severe side effects, especially with prolonged use.
Overhydration - adequate (not excessive) hydration is intended; potent diuretics such as furosemide should be avoided in HAPE.
Comet-tail/B-line lung ultrasound is sensitive but not specific, since B-lines also appear in individuals who never develop clinical HAPE - clinical correlation is essential.

AMS is benign and usually self-limited; once symptoms abate (with or without acetazolamide) the patient may reascend gradually. HACE and HAPE are life-threatening but generally reversible with prompt recognition and descent. In HAPE the lung architecture is typically well preserved with rapid reversibility (radiographic opacities can clear in about 2 days), allowing some patients to reascend slowly after a few days of descent and rest; after HACE, reascent within the same trip may be inadvisable. Severe AMS-related debilitating fatigue on descent is an important predictor of death in mountaineers, and macular hemorrhage can rarely cause permanent visual loss. HACE complicated by globus pallidus lesions has been reported to lead to parkinsonism.

Any hint of HAPE or HACE mandates descent

Debilitating fatigue consistent with severe AMS on descent from a summit (important risk factor for death in mountaineers)
Papilledema or retinal hemorrhages, especially macular hemorrhage with visual loss
Worsening symptoms despite halting ascent

AMS is graded clinically as mild versus moderate, a subjective judgment based on headache severity and the presence/severity of nausea, fatigue, and dizziness (the Lake Louise Scoring System, without the sleep score, is used for research). The overall spectrum runs from benign AMS to the life-threatening forms HACE (neurologic, the severe end of the AMS-HACE continuum) and HAPE (pulmonary), which can coexist.

chunks.text: On contact with water or gastric acid, aluminium phosphide releases phosphine gas, which inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase and generates reactive oxygen species, arresting oxidative phosphorylation across tissues. The heart is especially vulnerable, developing myocardial depression, myocarditis, and arrhythmias, while widespread vasodilatation and cellular energy failure produce profound refractory shock. Lipid peroxidation and oxidative injury drive a severe metabolic (lactic) acidosis and multi-organ dysfunction affecting the liver, kidneys, and adrenal glands.

Dementia with Lewy bodies (early parkinsonism with fluctuating alertness, visual hallucinations, delusional misidentification) (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Parkinson's disease / Parkinson's disease dementia (resting tremor, stooped posture, bradykinesia, masked facies) (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Frontotemporal dementia (prominent behavioral changes with intact navigation and focal anterior-predominant atrophy) (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease / prion disease (rapid progression over weeks-months with rigidity and myoclonus) (Harrison 22e p.3476, p.3482)

Limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy (LATE) and primary age-related tauopathy (PART) - can mimic AD clinically, especially in biomarker-negative older patients with progressive amnestic dementia (Harrison 22e p.3476, p.3477)
Huntington's disease and rare hereditary ataxias when family history of dementia is present (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Primary or metastatic brain neoplasm (early focal seizure) (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Viral or bacterial encephalitides (listed as causes of rapidly progressive dementia in the CJD differential) (Harrison 22e p.3483)
MRI/CT structural imaging - mainly to exclude other disorders; AD shows posterior-predominant cortical and medial temporal (hippocampal) atrophy and may be normal early (Harrison 22e p.3476)
FDG-PET - shows hypometabolism in posterior temporal-parietal cortex (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Amyloid PET ([11C]PIB, [18F]florbetapir, [18F]florbetaben, [18F]flutemetamol) - confirms neuritic/diffuse Abeta plaques (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Tau PET ([18F]flortaucipir and research tracers) - estimates density/distribution of neurofibrillary tangles (Harrison 22e p.3476-3477)
CSF biomarkers - decreased Abeta42 and Abeta42/Abeta40 ratio, increased p-Tau181/p-Tau217 (Harrison 22e p.3477)
Plasma biomarkers - decreased Abeta42/Abeta40 ratio, increased p-Tau181/p-Tau217/p-Tau231 (Harrison 22e p.3477)
EEG - usually normal or nonspecific slowing; prolonged EEG to seek intermittent nonconvulsive seizures (Harrison 22e p.3476)
ApoE genotyping - recommended before initiating anti-Abeta antibody therapy to inform ARIA risk (Harrison 22e p.3480-3481)
Systemic laboratory tests to exclude reversible dementia mimics (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Vitamin B12 deficiency (loss of joint position and vibration sensibility with Babinski signs; especially with autoimmune disease, small bowel resection/irradiation, or veganism) (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Normal-pressure hydrocephalus (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Depression-related cognitive impairment (depressive pseudodementia) (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Chronic drug intoxication (history of treatment for insomnia, anxiety, psychiatric disturbance, or epilepsy) (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Thyroid and other reversible/metabolic causes of dementia to be excluded per Tables 31-1, 31-3, 31-4 (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Hashimoto's encephalopathy, CNS vasculitis, CNS lymphoma, paraneoplastic/autoimmune syndromes (rapidly progressive dementia differential) (Harrison 22e p.3483)

AD is characterized by extracellular neuritic plaques containing amyloid beta (Abeta) and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs) of hyperphosphorylated tau, with Abeta also accumulating in cortical and leptomeningeal blood vessel walls (amyloid angiopathy). Abeta is a 39-42 amino acid peptide cleaved from amyloid precursor protein (APP) by beta and gamma secretases; excess production of Abeta42 is a key initiator of cellular damage, and soluble oligomers are thought to be the early toxic species before fibril/plaque formation. Hyperphosphorylated tau can no longer stabilize microtubules and redistributes from axon to cytoplasm and dendrites, with prion-like templating proposed to drive tau spread. Earliest and most severe degeneration is in the medial temporal lobe (entorhinal/perirhinal cortex, hippocampus), inferolateral temporal cortex, and nucleus basalis of Meynert; atrophy spreads to temporoparietal and frontal cortices. Biochemically there is depletion of acetylcholine (degeneration of cholinergic nucleus basalis of Meynert neurons) plus noradrenergic and serotonergic loss from locus coeruleus and dorsal raphe. Genetic contributors include autosomal dominant mutations in APP (chromosome 21), PSEN-1 (chromosome 14, most common cause of early-onset familial AD), and PSEN-2 (chromosome 1), plus the ApoE epsilon4 risk allele (chromosome 19) and >40 minor GWAS risk variants in innate immunity, lipid metabolism, and synaptic pathways (e.g., CLU, PICALM, CR1, TREM2). (Harrison 22e p.3475, p.3478-3480)
Most common cause of dementia, contributing an estimated 60-70% of all cases; in the U.S. ~10% of people over 65 have AD (3% at age 65-74, 17% at 75-84, 32% at 85+) (Harrison 22e p.3475, p.3478).

ApoE epsilon4 is the most important genetic risk factor for sporadic AD: one allele raises risk ~2-3 fold (higher in women), two alleles raise it ~10-15 fold; each allele shifts onset ~10 years earlier (Harrison 22e p.3475, p.3479-3480).

Lecanemab (anti-Abeta protofibril) and donanemab (anti-pyroglutamate Abeta) are FDA-approved disease-modifying antiamyloid antibodies for early-stage AD, showing ~22-27% slowing of clinical decline; restricted to MCI/mild dementia with biomarker-confirmed Abeta pathology (Harrison 22e p.3480-3481).

Antiamyloid antibodies carry risk of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA-E edema, ARIA-H microhemorrhage/siderosis); risk rises with each ApoE epsilon4 allele and is highest in epsilon4 homozygotes, prompting an FDA box warning (Harrison 22e p.3481).

Treatment with lecanemab or donanemab should be considered a contraindication to peripheral thrombolysis, as catastrophic multifocal hemorrhages and death have been reported when antiamyloid-treated patients received thrombolytics for stroke (Harrison 22e p.3482).
Medications with strong anticholinergic effects (e.g., diphenhydramine sleep aids, oxybutynin) should be vigilantly avoided in AD (Harrison 22e p.3482).

Typical symptomatic duration is 8-10 years (range 1-25 years); death often results from malnutrition, secondary infections, pulmonary emboli, heart disease, or, most commonly, aspiration (Harrison 22e p.3476).

Typical presentation is insidious loss of episodic memory followed by slowly progressive multidomain dementia, with cognitive change progressing from memory to executive, language, and visuospatial deficits (Harrison 22e p.3475-3476).

About 20% of patients present with nonmemory complaints; atypical variants include posterior cortical atrophy (visual processing), logopenic progressive aphasia, corticobasal (akinetic-rigid-dystonic) syndrome, and a dysexecutive/behavioral (frontal) variant (Harrison 22e p.3475-3476).
Depression, social withdrawal, and anxiety may occur early and represent a prodrome before cognitive symptoms are apparent (Harrison 22e p.3476).

~50% of patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), roughly 12% per year, progress to dementia over 4 years; the MCI construct is increasingly replaced by 'early symptomatic AD' (Harrison 22e p.3476).
Preclinical biomarker changes may precede clinical symptoms by 20 years or more, creating a window for early treatment and prevention (Harrison 22e p.3476).

Core 1 biomarkers (amyloid PET, CSF/plasma Abeta and p-Tau) are considered necessary and sufficient for biological diagnosis of AD under the revised Alzheimer's Association criteria; tau PET is a core 2 biomarker used for staging (Harrison 22e p.3477).
A negative amyloid PET scan in a patient with dementia makes an AD diagnosis unlikely; a positive scan can establish eligibility for amyloid-lowering therapy (Harrison 22e p.3477).

Decreases in the CSF Abeta42/Abeta40 ratio and increases in p-Tau181 or p-Tau217 correlate with AD pathology; plasma biomarkers show high concordance with amyloid PET and are entering clinical use (Harrison 22e p.3477).

Failing to exclude reversible/treatable mimics early in the course - vitamin B12 deficiency, thyroid disease, normal-pressure hydrocephalus, and depression-related cognitive impairment should be excluded before attributing dementia to AD (Harrison 22e p.3476).

A clinical diagnosis of AD is confirmed at autopsy only ~70-80% of the time; misdiagnoses are usually LATE (with or without hippocampal sclerosis), PART, Lewy body disease, vascular pathology, or FTLD (Harrison 22e p.3476).

Amyloid PET positivity is not specific: ~25% of cognitively unimpaired older adults have positive scans, and a positive scan can reflect comorbid (incidental) AD pathology rather than the primary cause of impairment (Harrison 22e p.3476).
A completely negative tau PET does not rule out early neurofibrillary pathology (Braak stages I-III) (Harrison 22e p.3477).
Increased total tau in CSF is nonspecific - seen in AD but also other neurodegeneration (Harrison 22e p.3477).

Plasma Abeta and p-Tau concentrations can be altered by comorbidities (reduced creatinine clearance, elevated BMI), causing false-positive or false-negative results near the threshold (Harrison 22e p.3477).
ApoE epsilon4 is neither necessary nor sufficient to cause AD - many AD patients lack epsilon4 and many epsilon4 carriers never develop dementia (Harrison 22e p.3479-3480).

Estrogen, statins, vitamin E, ginkgo biloba, and NSAIDs appeared protective in observational studies but did NOT show efficacy in randomized controlled trials; consumer 'memory-enhancing' supplements lack evidence (Harrison 22e p.3478, p.3482).
Antipsychotics carry an FDA black box warning in elderly dementia patients (increased risk of death) and should be used with caution for neuropsychiatric symptoms (Harrison 22e p.3482).

Typical duration of symptomatic AD is 8-10 years, with a course ranging from 1 to 25 years. Some patients decline steadily while others have prolonged plateaus. Late stages bring rigidity, mutism, incontinence, and a bedridden state with dependence for eating, dressing, and toileting; hyperactive tendon reflexes and myoclonic jerks may occur. Death most commonly results from aspiration, and also from malnutrition, secondary infections, pulmonary emboli, or heart disease. Approved disease-modifying antiamyloid antibodies slow but do not halt clinical decline (~22-27% slowing over the trial periods). (Harrison 22e p.3476, p.3480-3481)
Rapid progression over weeks to months with rigidity and myoclonus suggests CJD rather than AD (Harrison 22e p.3476, p.3482)
Early prominent gait disturbance with mild memory loss suggests vascular dementia or normal-pressure hydrocephalus (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Early focal seizure suggests a metastatic or primary brain neoplasm (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Loss of joint position/vibration sense with Babinski signs suggests vitamin B12 deficiency (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Stroke-like symptoms in a patient on anti-Abeta monoclonal antibody require immediate MRI to differentiate acute stroke from ARIA before any thrombolysis (Harrison 22e p.3482)
Seizures (focal or generalized) can herald AD and occur even before dementia onset, especially in younger patients and autosomal dominant mutation carriers (Harrison 22e p.3476)

Clinical staging is performed independent of biomarkers, based on functional impairment along a continuum: preclinical AD (biomarker evidence of amyloid pathology without symptoms) -> subjective cognitive decline -> mild cognitive impairment / early symptomatic AD (functionally compensated) -> dementia stages (early/middle/late/end-stage). Biological staging under the revised Alzheimer's Association criteria uses core 1 biomarkers (amyloid PET, CSF/plasma Abeta and p-Tau) for diagnosis and tau PET (core 2) for biomarker-based disease staging. (Harrison 22e p.3476-3478)

chunks.text: Amblyopia results from abnormal visual experience during the critical period of cortical visual development. When the two eyes receive unequal or degraded input (from misalignment, unequal refractive error, or media opacity), competitive cortical mechanisms favour the better eye and suppress the input from the affected eye. This leads to persistent cortical under-development of that eye's pathway and reduced acuity that is not correctable by optical means alone once the sensitive period has passed, though it remains treatable if addressed early.

E. histolytica is acquired by ingesting viable cysts from fecally contaminated water, food, or hands (food-borne exposure being most common). Motile trophozoites excyst in the small intestine; in most patients they remain as harmless commensals in the large bowel and re-encyst, shedding infectious cysts in stool. In some patients trophozoites invade the colonic mucosa (causing colitis) or enter the portal bloodstream (causing distant abscesses, most often hepatic). Trophozoites attach to colonic mucus and epithelium via the Gal/GalNAc adherence lectin and release glycosidases, proteases, and cysteine proteinases that degrade mucus, collagen, elastin, immunoglobulins, and complement anaphylatoxins; mucosal damage follows via contact-dependent cytotoxicity (apoptosis, trogocytosis, lysis of inflammatory and epithelial cells) and contact-independent mechanisms (inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandin E2). Resistance to reactive oxygen/nitrogen species and to complement-mediated lysis are virulence factors. The earliest lesions are mucosal microulcerations of the cecum, sigmoid, or rectum; submucosal extension beneath viable surface mucosa produces the classic 'flask-shaped' ulcer with trophozoites at the margins. Human infection is notable for a paucity of inflammatory cells (in part because trophozoites kill neutrophils) (p.1753-1755).
Amebiasis is infection with Entamoeba histolytica, an intestinal protozoan; ~90% of infections are asymptomatic cyst passage and only ~10% are invasive (p.1753).

E. histolytica infection is widespread in the Indian subcontinent, Africa, parts of East Asia, and Central/South America, often affecting children under 5 in areas of poor sanitation; in developed countries returning travelers, immigrants, MSM, military personnel, and institutional inmates are the main at-risk groups (p.1753).
Invasive amebiasis does not elicit eosinophilia (p.1757).

Symptomatic amebic colitis develops 2-6 weeks after ingestion of infectious cysts, with gradual-onset lower abdominal pain and mild diarrhea progressing to malaise, weight loss, and dysentery (p.1755).
In full-blown dysentery patients may pass 10-12 stools per day consisting mainly of blood and mucus with little fecal material; virtually all have heme-positive stools (p.1755).
In contrast to bacterial diarrhea, fewer than 40% of patients with amebic dysentery are febrile and stools show a paucity of neutrophils (p.1755).
Cecal involvement may mimic acute appendicitis (p.1755).

Definitive diagnosis of amebic colitis requires demonstration of hematophagous (erythrocyte-ingesting) trophozoites of E. histolytica; this is the only way microscopy can identify the species (p.1756).

Because trophozoites are rapidly killed by water, drying, or barium, at least three fresh stool specimens should be examined; wet mounts, iodine-stained concentrates, and trichrome-stained preparations confirm diagnosis in 75-95% of cases (p.1756).

Stool antigen detection (Gal/GalNAc lectin EIA, sensitivity 87%, specificity >90%) and multiplex PCR (sensitivity/specificity approaching 100%) are more sensitive, specific, and rapid than microscopy (p.1757).

Serology (ELISA) is positive in >90% of cases of colitis, ameboma, or liver abscess; results usually revert to negative within 6-12 months, so positivity with a compatible syndrome suggests active disease (p.1756).

E. histolytica cannot be distinguished microscopically from the non-pathogenic commensal E. dispar (nor from E. moshkovskii or E. bangladeshi); most asymptomatic carriers actually harbor E. dispar, which is incapable of invasive disease and does not warrant treatment, so species-specific antigen detection or PCR is needed (p.1754, p.1756).
Cysts must also be differentiated from non-pathogenic Entamoeba hartmanni, Entamoeba coli, and Endolimax nana, which do not cause disease (p.1756).

Amebiasis must be excluded before starting glucocorticoid therapy for suspected inflammatory bowel disease; unsuspected amebiasis treated with steroids can precipitate severe colitis or toxic megacolon (p.1755-1757).
An ameboma can be mistaken for cancer on barium studies; positive serology or biopsy can prevent unnecessary surgery (p.1755).
Sigmoidoscopy/biopsy and barium studies are dangerous during fulminant or acute colitis because of the risk of perforation (p.1756-1757).
Trophozoites are rapidly killed by water, drying, and barium and may be confused with neutrophils, so examination must use multiple fresh specimens with experienced microscopy (p.1756).

Outcome relates to the clinical syndrome: about 90% of infections are asymptomatic and self-limited, and uncomplicated amebic colitis responds well to therapy with ulcers characteristically healing with little or no scarring. Fulminant colitis, toxic megacolon, and perforation are rare but carry a poor prognosis. Treated colitis generally resolves, but severe disease (notably in those given glucocorticoids or in children with fulminant infection) markedly worsens outcome (p.1755-1756).

Harrison describes a clinical spectrum rather than a formal grading scheme: (1) asymptomatic cyst passage (~90% of infections); (2) symptomatic amebic colitis/dysentery with bloody mucoid stools; and (3) rare fulminant intestinal infection (severe pain, high fever, profuse diarrhea, predominantly in children) that may progress to toxic megacolon, full-thickness necrosis, or perforation (p.1753, p.1755).

Genetic mutation, abnormal processing, or aging-related decline in protein quality control causes precursor proteins to undergo reversible unfolding/misfolding. Misfolded subunits adopt a common antiparallel beta-pleated-sheet conformation and assemble into oligomers, higher-order polymers, and ultimately 10-nm fibrils that deposit extracellularly in tissues/organs. Soluble oligomeric intermediates are thought to be the most toxic species (generating reactive oxygen species and stress signaling), while fibrillar deposits mechanically interfere with organ function. Fibrils co-deposit accessory molecules including serum amyloid P component, apolipoproteins E and A-IV, glycosaminoglycans, and metal ions. Precursors include monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (AL; lambda subtypes predominate), transthyretin (ATTR; wild-type or >130 described mutations), and the hepatic acute-phase protein serum amyloid A (AA) (p.895, p.897, p.899).

Amyloidosis is a group of protein-misfolding disorders defined by extracellular deposition of insoluble polymeric protein fibrils with a common antiparallel beta-pleated-sheet structure; nomenclature is AX, where A = amyloidosis and X = the fibril precursor protein (p.895).

AA amyloidosis arises from the acute-phase reactant serum amyloid A (SAA) in chronic inflammatory or infectious disease and typically begins in the kidneys; cardiomyopathy is a late manifestation in about 10-25% (p.895, p.899).
Abdominal subcutaneous fat aspiration is the most accessible diagnostic tissue, positive in >80% of systemic amyloidosis, avoiding surgical biopsy (p.895).
Amyloid deposits show characteristic apple-green birefringence under polarized light when stained with Congo red, whereas other regular protein structures such as collagen appear white (p.895).

AL amyloidosis (formerly primary systemic amyloidosis) is composed of monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains from a clonal B-cell/plasma-cell disorder and is the most common systemic type in North America; it can occur with myeloma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, or Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia (p.895, p.897).
In AL amyloidosis the kidneys are involved in 60-70% (proteinuria, often nephrotic range, with hypoalbuminemia) and the heart in 70-80%; cardiac involvement is the leading cause of death (p.897).
Macroglossia and periorbital ('raccoon-eye') ecchymoses are pathognomonic signs of AL amyloidosis but each is seen in only about 10% of patients (p.897).
Easy bruising in AL amyloidosis is due to amyloid deposits in capillaries or to acquired factor X deficiency from binding of factor X to amyloid fibrils (p.897).
ATTR amyloidosis is the most prevalent hereditary amyloidosis and derives from wild-type or mutated transthyretin (TTR); it targets the peripheral and autonomic nerves and the heart (p.895, p.899).

The TTR variant V122I occurs in nearly 4% of African-American and Afro-Caribbean populations and causes late-onset cardiac amyloidosis; suspect it in African-American patients with concentric cardiac hypertrophy and diastolic heart failure, especially without hypertension or valvular disease (p.899).

Wild-type ATTR (ATTRwt, formerly senile systemic amyloidosis) is a disease of aging, not inheritance; it predominates in men from the seventh decade and is found at autopsy in 25% of hearts of men >=80 years, and is now the most prevalent and fastest-growing form of amyloidosis worldwide (p.899).

Carpal tunnel syndrome, tendinopathy, and spinal stenosis (soft-tissue disease) can precede ATTR nerve or heart disease by one to two decades, and ATTRwt patients frequently report bicipital, patellar, or Achilles tendon rupture (p.899).

Amyloid typing pitfall: commercial immunohistochemistry antibodies may be inaccurate and some AL deposits bind light-chain antibodies nonspecifically; accurate typing (mass spectrometry / immunoelectron microscopy / genetic testing) is essential because therapy differs by type (p.895, p.899).

Serum and urine protein electrophoresis are NOT useful screening tests for AL because the clonal light chain is often insufficient to produce a detectable M-spike; immunofixation and free light chain assays are required (p.897).

A monoclonal protein alone is not diagnostic of amyloidosis since MGUS is common in older patients; conversely, AF carriers may have a coincidental monoclonal gammopathy, so screen for BOTH plasma-cell disorder and protein mutations (p.897, p.899).

Renal insufficiency can falsely elevate cardiac biomarkers (NT-proBNP, troponin) and nonspecifically raise both free light chain isotypes, so the free light chain ratio (not just absolute level) must be examined (p.896, p.897).

In amyloid cardiomyopathy digitalis, calcium channel blockers, and beta blockers are relatively contraindicated because they interact with amyloid fibrils and can cause heart block and worsening heart failure (p.899).
Interstitial (rather than glomerular) renal amyloid can cause azotemia WITHOUT proteinuria (p.897).
Apparent sporadic ATTRv (no family history) often reflects incomplete penetrance rather than a true spontaneous case (p.899).
Mass spectrometry detects amino-acid sequence variation but does not definitively identify specific protein variants; DNA sequencing is the standard for hereditary (AF) mutations (p.899).

AL amyloidosis is often rapidly progressive; historically untreated median survival was only ~1-2 years, but outcomes have improved markedly over four decades with newer plasma-cell-directed therapy. Cardiac stage (Mayo system based on NT-proBNP and troponin) is the strongest determinant of management and survival; very low dFLC (<50 mg/L) predicts better outcome regardless of cardiac stage. High-risk patients (~15-20%) with advanced cardiac stage IIIb or NYHA III-IV heart failure are largely excluded from trials. ATTR cardiac disease is better tolerated than AL: untreated median survival from heart failure presentation is ~42-48 months for ATTR versus ~6 months for AL. Untreated ATTR survival after onset ranges 4-15 years depending on predominant cardiac versus neurologic involvement (p.897, p.899).
Macroglossia or periorbital ('raccoon-eye') ecchymoses (pathognomonic of AL)
Concentric ventricular hypertrophy with diastolic dysfunction plus low-voltage ECG (voltage-mass mismatch)
Easy bruising or bleeding diathesis from acquired factor X deficiency
Multisystem involvement (unexplained nephropathy, cardiomyopathy, neuropathy, enteropathy) in a patient with fatigue/weight loss

AL amyloidosis is staged primarily by the Mayo 2004 cardiac staging system (NT-proBNP and cardiac troponins), modified by European investigators to identify very-high-risk patients; the Mayo 2012 revision adds clonal burden via dFLC (difference between involved and uninvolved free light chains). A Boston University system uses BNP and troponin I. A separate renal staging system based on 24-h urine protein and eGFR predicts progression to dialysis at 2 years. ATTR cardiac involvement is graded by stage (e.g., advanced stage IIIb) and NYHA functional class (p.897).
Amyloidosis (non-infective) — Hematology / Multisystem Also: AL amyloidosis, ATTR amyloidosis, AA amyloidosis

Constrictive pericardial disease (the classic and most important differential, sharing dominant right-sided failure, edema, ascites, elevated JVP and Kussmaul sign; echocardiography readily distinguishes the two today) (Harrison 22e p.2020-2022)
Hypertensive heart disease (usually shows LVH on ECG and requires years of severe uncontrolled hypertension to reach amyloid-degree wall thickening) (Harrison 22e p.2021)
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (rarely presents with peripheral edema and usually has LVH on ECG; distinction from amyloidosis is usually fairly clear) (Harrison 22e p.2021)
Fabry disease and other infiltrative cardiomyopathies (may have typical skin manifestations and usually LVH on ECG) (Harrison 22e p.2021-2022)

Mitochondrial cardiomyopathy (echocardiographic appearance can mimic amyloidosis but with distinct noncardiac features such as maternally inherited diabetes, deafness, and recurrent strokes) (Harrison 22e p.2022)
Advanced diabetic heart disease with heavy proteinuria (obvious diabetes history and echocardiogram lacking amyloid features) (Harrison 22e p.2022)

Echocardiography showing increased LV wall thickness without dilation, frequent biatrial enlargement, increased RV free-wall thickness, restrictive diastolic filling pattern, and a small transmitral A wave (the latter associated with increased thromboembolic risk) (Harrison 22e p.2022-2023)
Longitudinal strain imaging demonstrating apical-sparing 'bull's-eye' pattern (Harrison 22e p.2022-2023)
Cardiac magnetic resonance with extracellular volume measurement, abnormal myocardial nulling, and extensive late gadolinium enhancement (Harrison 22e p.2023-2024)
Bone-avid radionuclide imaging (technetium PYP, DPD, or HMDP) with SPECT and ideally cardiac CT to confirm myocardial rather than blood-pool uptake (Harrison 22e p.2023-2026)

Serum free light chains plus serum and urine protein electrophoresis and immunofixation to detect or exclude a plasma cell dyscrasia (immunofixation is more sensitive than electrophoresis for the low paraprotein levels of AL amyloidosis) (Harrison 22e p.2023-2026)

Tissue biopsy (subcutaneous fat pad aspirate or deep-skin biopsy first; endomyocardial biopsy if needed, positive in well over 90% of cardiac amyloid cases) with amyloid typing ideally by mass spectrometry (Harrison 22e p.2024-2026)
TTR gene sequencing to distinguish familial (variant) from wild-type TTR when AL is not clearly established (Harrison 22e p.2026)

NT-proBNP (often disproportionately high for the degree of heart failure, frequently 1000-2000 pg/mL even with mild symptoms) and high-sensitivity troponin (frequently mildly elevated, risking misdiagnosis as ischemic disease) (Harrison 22e p.2023-2024)
ECG, which may show abnormally low voltage (particularly in AL) though not invariably (Harrison 22e p.2022)
Constrictive pericarditis
Hypertensive heart disease with left ventricular hypertrophy
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (including sarcomere-variant forme fruste presenting as RCM)
Fabry disease and other infiltrative or storage cardiomyopathies
Mitochondrial cardiomyopathy
Hemochromatosis (iron storage)

Restrictive cardiomyopathy results from a noncompliant ventricle with markedly impaired diastolic filling; most cases are 'infiltrative,' due to deposition of abnormal substances between myocytes (amyloid being the most common), with additional causes from intramyocyte storage of metabolic products (e.g., iron in hemochromatosis, Fabry disease, glycogen storage disease) or acquired fibrosis (radiation, scleroderma, endomyocardial/hypereosinophilic injury, carcinoid). In amyloidosis, fibrillar proteinaceous material is deposited extracellularly; amyloid stains with Congo red and shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light, and electron microscopy reveals nonbranching fibrils about 10 nm in diameter. Extracellular amyloid deposition expands the extracellular space, increasing heart mass and ventricular wall thickness while reducing compliance; the left ventricular cavity may be relatively small (restrictive physiology) and both atria dilate from chronically elevated biventricular filling pressures. AL amyloidosis is a plasma cell disorder closely related to multiple myeloma in which excess abnormal free light chains (more often lambda than kappa) deposit in multiple organs, with heart and kidney most commonly affected. TTR amyloidosis arises from liver-produced transthyretin, either wild-type (ATTRwt) or from a destabilizing genetic variant (ATTRv); variant TTR is generally considered less stable than wild-type. Both wild-type and variant TTR cardiomyopathy have a subclinical phase of probably several years, and by the time heart failure occurs 30-50% of the involved heart weight may be amyloid (Harrison 22e p.2020-2022).

Restrictive cardiomyopathy is dominated by abnormal diastolic function in a noncompliant ventricle with usually only mildly reduced contractility; ejection fraction is often 30-50% and both atria are typically enlarged, sometimes massively (Harrison 22e p.2020).

In the United States the most common variant causing TTR amyloid cardiomyopathy is Val122Ile, present in about 3.5% of people of African descent, presenting as a late-onset restrictive cardiomyopathy usually from the seventh decade with incomplete penetrance (Harrison 22e p.2022).

Wild-type TTR amyloidosis (ATTRwt) is now considered the most common form of amyloidosis, affecting predominantly older men (men roughly 20 times more likely than women); the heart is usually the sole clinically involved organ, though lung and gut deposits are often found histologically (Harrison 22e p.2022).

Atrial arrhythmia, especially atrial fibrillation or flutter, is a common presenting feature (particularly in TTR amyloidosis) and its onset often precipitates or worsens heart failure; refractory atrial arrhythmia in a patient in the mid-60s or older without other cause should raise suspicion for TTR cardiac amyloidosis (Harrison 22e p.2021-2027).

Despite biventricular elevation of filling pressures, restrictive disease and cardiac amyloidosis tend to present with predominantly right-sided symptoms such as peripheral edema, abdominal discomfort, and ascites (Harrison 22e p.2020-2021).

In sinus rhythm a fourth heart sound is more typical than a third in RCM generally, but in cardiac amyloidosis both an S3 and an S4 are unusual because restrictive physiology impairs relaxation and the infiltrated atrium generates little contractile pressure; jugular venous pressure is elevated and may rise paradoxically on inspiration (positive Kussmaul sign) (Harrison 22e p.2020-2021).

The two precursor proteins causing most cardiac amyloidosis are transthyretin (TTR, produced in the liver) and light chains (produced by abnormal plasma cells); precise typing of the precursor is essential because therapy is type-specific and incorrect typing leads to inappropriate treatment (Harrison 22e p.2020).

Periorbital purpura is virtually pathognomonic of AL amyloidosis (occurring in about 20-30% of cases) and macroglossia occurs in roughly 10%; an unusually hard liver may reflect amyloid hepatic infiltration, which occurs in AL but not TTR amyloidosis (Harrison 22e p.2021).

A history of bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, spinal stenosis, or a ruptured biceps tendon — often 5-8 years before heart failure — points toward TTR amyloidosis, reflecting TTR's predilection for ligaments and tendons (Harrison 22e p.2021-2022).

Longitudinal strain imaging classically shows relatively preserved apical strain with severely impaired basal strain, producing a 'bull's-eye' color pattern highly suggestive of cardiac amyloidosis (Harrison 22e p.2022-2023).

On cardiac MRI, abnormal nulling of the myocardium with poor myocardium-to-cavity distinction plus extensive transmural late gadolinium enhancement and markedly increased extracellular volume are near-pathognomonic of amyloid infiltration (Harrison 22e p.2022-2024).

Bone-avid tracers (technetium pyrophosphate/PYP, DPD, HMDP) are normally not taken up by the heart but show avid myocardial uptake in TTR amyloidosis; a positive scan with a negative plasma cell dyscrasia workup confirms TTR amyloidosis without biopsy (Harrison 22e p.2023-2026).
Mildly elevated high-sensitivity troponin may lead to misdiagnosis as ischemic heart disease (Harrison 22e p.2023-2024).

AL amyloidosis can occasionally show myocardial uptake on bone-avid tracer scans, so a positive nuclear scan must never be interpreted as diagnostic of TTR without first excluding a plasma cell dyscrasia (Harrison 22e p.2023-2026).

Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) is common in older patients and not uncommonly coexists with TTR amyloidosis, so abnormal plasma cell dyscrasia testing does not automatically equal AL amyloidosis and may require hematology input (Harrison 22e p.2023-2026).
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis may miss the low-level paraprotein of AL amyloidosis; immunofixation is more sensitive and should be performed (Harrison 22e p.2024).

The sedimentation rate is usually normal or only minimally elevated in AL amyloidosis, unlike the marked elevation in multiple myeloma, so a normal ESR does not exclude AL amyloidosis (Harrison 22e p.2024).
Immunohistochemical typing of amyloid is fraught with diagnostic uncertainty and can be misleading; typing is ideally done by mass spectrometry (Harrison 22e p.2024-2026).
There is no definitive noninvasive test for AL cardiac amyloidosis, so a tissue biopsy is always required to confirm it (Harrison 22e p.2024).
Rare variant TTR forms can have negative bone-tracer imaging, so a negative scan does not entirely exclude amyloidosis when clinical suspicion remains high (Harrison 22e p.2026).

Prognosis depends heavily on amyloid type. AL cardiac amyloidosis is aggressive and, with cardiac involvement, carries the worst survival, with median survival from onset of heart failure to death of about 6 months in untreated patients, underscoring the urgency of diagnosis. Among TTR forms, untreated Val122Ile variant disease tends to progress relatively rapidly with median survival of 2-3 years from onset of heart failure, whereas wild-type TTR amyloidosis has an untreated median survival of about 4-5 years, with death usually from progressive congestive heart failure rather than sudden death; wild-type disease occurring in women tends to present later and follow a more indolent course. There is a high risk of thromboembolism in cardiac amyloidosis, and sudden cardiac death may occur (more common in advanced AL disease). Overall, cardiac amyloidosis is now recognized as far more common than previously appreciated, and earlier diagnosis with the advent of disease-modifying therapy has improved outlook (Harrison 22e p.2021-2028).
Heart failure with a thick left ventricle but without a history of severe hypertension and without LVH on ECG
Disproportionately elevated NT-proBNP relative to clinical heart failure severity
Periorbital purpura or macroglossia (suggesting AL amyloidosis)
Refractory atrial fibrillation/flutter in a patient in the mid-60s or older without other cause (suggesting TTR amyloidosis)
Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, spinal stenosis, or ruptured biceps tendon preceding heart failure (suggesting TTR amyloidosis)
Abnormal postural blood-pressure drop indicating autonomic neuropathy (AL or some variant TTR forms)
Unexplained nonpostural dizziness or syncope with bifascicular or left bundle branch block in TTR amyloidosis, indicating risk of high-degree atrioventricular block
Significant proteinuria with hypoalbuminemia (renal AL involvement)

Harrison does not provide a single formal staging scale within this chapter; severity is gauged clinically and prognostically by amyloid type and stage of cardiac involvement. Adverse markers include disproportionately elevated NT-proBNP (often 1000-2000 pg/mL even with mild heart failure) and elevated high-sensitivity troponin, with the proportion of heart weight composed of amyloid reaching 30-50% by the time heart failure occurs in TTR disease. AL cardiac involvement confers the worst prognosis among the types (Harrison 22e p.2022-2024).
