Motor neuron degenerative disorder marked by death of lower motor neurons (anterior horn cells and their brainstem bulbar homologues) and upper/corticospinal motor neurons (layer-five motor cortex neurons descending via the pyramidal tract). Affected neurons shrink and accumulate lipofuscin; the motor neuron cytoskeleton is affected early, with proximal axonal 'spheroids' composed of neurofilament accumulations. Both sporadic and familial ALS show ubiquitin-positive aggregates frequently associated with the protein TDP43, plus astroglial/microglial proliferation (neuroinflammation). Loss of cortical motor neurons thins the corticospinal tracts; lateral-column fiber loss and fibrillary gliosis impart firmness (lateral sclerosis), while muscle denervation and atrophy give rise to the term amyotrophy. Neuronal cell death is strikingly selective: the sensory apparatus, cerebellar coordination structures, ocular-motility neurons, and the sacral parasympathetic sphincter neurons (nucleus of Onuf) are characteristically spared. Familial ALS most commonly involves mutations in C9orf72, SOD1, TDP43, and FUS/TLS (p.3519-3521).

ALS is the most common progressive motor neuron disease and ultimately causes progressive loss of BOTH upper (corticospinal) and lower motor neurons; in the absence of clear involvement of both motor neuron types, the diagnosis of ALS is questionable (p.3519-3520).

Lower motor neuron features: insidious asymmetric weakness usually first distal in one limb, progressive wasting/atrophy, and fasciculations (spontaneous twitching of motor units); in the hands a preponderance of extensor over flexor weakness is common (p.3521).

Upper (corticospinal) motor neuron features: hyperactive muscle-stretch reflexes (tendon jerks), spastic resistance to passive movement, and muscle stiffness often out of proportion to weakness (p.3521).

Bulbar onset presents with difficulty chewing, swallowing, and moving the face and tongue; corticobulbar degeneration causes dysarthria and pseudobulbar affect (involuntary excess weeping or laughing) (p.3521).

World Federation of Neurology criteria: simultaneous upper AND lower motor neuron involvement with progressive weakness and exclusion of all alternative diagnoses; 'definite' when 3-4 regions involved (bulbar, cervical, thoracic, lumbosacral), 'probable' when 2, 'possible' when 1 (p.3521).

Elevated CSF/serum neurofilament light chains (Nfl) or phosphorylated neurofilament heavy chains are markers of neurodegeneration in most cases; higher levels correlate with more aggressive disease and more rapid progression (p.3521).

About 10% of cases are inherited as an autosomal dominant trait (familial ALS); FALS is clinically indistinguishable from sporadic ALS apart from its inheritance. C9orf72 is the most common genetic cause (~45-50% of FALS), followed by SOD1 (~20%) (p.3521).
ALS may arise concurrently with frontotemporal dementia (particularly in familial cases), with early behavioral abnormalities reflecting frontal lobe dysfunction (p.3520-3521).

Because ALS is currently untreatable, it is imperative to exclude potentially remediable mimics - especially cervical cord compression/cervical spondylotic myelopathy, which can produce weakness, wasting, fasciculations in the arms and leg spasticity that closely resembles ALS.

Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block (MMCB) must be excluded: unlike ALS it lacks corticospinal signs, often has elevated anti-GM1 antibodies, and may respond dramatically to IVIG or chemotherapy.
Diagnosing ALS without clear involvement of BOTH upper and lower motor neurons is questionable - reconsider the diagnosis.

Features favoring ALS over a compressive mimic: absence of pain or sensory changes, normal bowel and bladder function, and normal spinal radiology and CSF. Sensory, sphincter, ocular-motility, and cognitive functions are preserved even late (except when concurrent frontotemporal dementia is present).

Relentlessly progressive; median survival is 3 to 5 years, with death typically from respiratory paralysis. Stabilization or regression is very rare. Higher serum/CSF neurofilament light chain levels correlate with more aggressive disease and more rapid progression. No treatment arrests the underlying pathologic process (p.3521, 3524).

Respiratory involvement: weakness of the muscles of respiration may rarely cause death before the disease is advanced elsewhere; the illness is relentlessly progressive, leading to death from respiratory paralysis - respiratory failure determines prognosis.
Bulbar dysfunction (difficulty chewing/swallowing) risks aspiration pneumonia and compromised nutrition/hydration.

Atypical features warranting search for a remediable mimic: restriction to only upper OR only lower motor neurons, involvement of non-motor neurons, or evidence of motor conduction block on electrophysiology.

World Federation of Neurology diagnostic categories based on number of body regions with combined upper and lower motor neuron involvement (bulbar, cervical, thoracic, lumbosacral): 'definite' ALS = 3-4 regions; 'probable' = 2 regions; 'possible' = 1 region. Exception: progressive upper and lower motor neuron signs at one site plus a SOD1 mutation also qualifies (p.3521).
Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) (non-infective) — Neurology Also: ALS, motor neuron disease, Lou Gehrig disease
Thrombosed external haemorrhoid or perianal haematoma

chunks.text: An anal fissure is a longitudinal tear in the anoderm of the distal anal canal, usually initiated by the passage of a hard or bulky stool. Resulting pain triggers spasm and hypertonia of the internal anal sphincter, which raises resting anal pressure and reduces blood flow to the relatively poorly perfused posterior midline. This local ischaemia impairs mucosal healing, converting an acute tear into a chronic non-healing ulcer. Persistent inflammation produces the sentinel tag, papilla hypertrophy, and exposure of sphincter fibres seen in chronic fissures.

chunks.text: Anaphylaxis is driven by mediators released chiefly from mast cells, basophils, and eosinophils. The most common mechanism is allergen cross-linking of IgE bound to FcepsilonRI on mast cells and basophils, triggering degranulation. Preformed granule contents include histamine, proteases (tryptase, chymase), proteoglycans (heparin, chondroitin sulfate), and TNF-alpha; newly generated arachidonic-acid products include cysteinyl leukotrienes, prostaglandin D2, and platelet-activating factor (PAF). Histamine produces flushing, urticaria, pruritus and, at high levels, hypotension and tachycardia; cysteinyl leukotrienes and PGD2 cause bronchoconstriction and increased microvascular permeability, with PGD2 also recruiting eosinophils and basophils. Serum PAF correlates with severity and is inversely related to PAF acetylhydrolase. Tryptase and chymase activate complement (generating the anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a) and the kallikrein-kinin system, with mediator effects likely additive or synergistic. Reactions can also be non-IgE-mediated: direct mast-cell activation (e.g., via MRGPRX2 by neuromuscular blockers, quinolones, icatibant; or opiates, vancomycin, radiocontrast, NSAIDs), complement activation (e.g., Cremophor-solubilized paclitaxel), or contact-system/bradykinin generation (e.g., oversulfated chondroitin sulfate heparin contaminant). (p. 2812-2813)

chunks.text: Cutaneous features (urticaria, flushing, generalized warmth) are the most common manifestation, present in over 90% of cases (p. 2812).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch. 364 (Anaphylaxis), pp. 2812-2814; distributive-shock context p. 2358

chunks.text: Cross-linking of allergen with IgE bound to FcepsilonRI receptors on mast cells and basophils is the usual initiating mechanism; sensitization requires prior exposure, so repeated exposure to the antigen is a key risk factor (p. 2812-2813).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch. 364 (Anaphylaxis), pp. 2812-2814; distributive-shock context p. 2358

chunks.text: Some severe reactions are non-IgE-mediated and can occur on first known exposure, because direct mast-cell activation needs no prior sensitization (e.g., via the MRGPRX2 receptor with neuromuscular blockers, quinolones, and icatibant) (p. 2813).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch. 364 (Anaphylaxis), pp. 2812-2814; distributive-shock context p. 2358

chunks.text: Severe Hymenoptera sting anaphylaxis, especially with prominent hypotension, may be the first presentation of underlying systemic mastocytosis; checking a baseline tryptase screens for this (p. 2812-2813).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch. 364 (Anaphylaxis), pp. 2812-2814; distributive-shock context p. 2358

chunks.text: Failure to give epinephrine within the first 20 minutes of symptoms is a risk factor for poor outcomes (p. 2813).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch. 364 (Anaphylaxis), pp. 2812-2814; distributive-shock context p. 2358

chunks.text: About 6% of Western populations carry hereditary alpha-tryptasemia, an extra TPSAB1 allele giving a high baseline tryptase that can confound interpretation and may itself be a risk factor for severe reactions (p. 2813).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch. 364 (Anaphylaxis), pp. 2812-2814; distributive-shock context p. 2358

chunks.text: Treat with epinephrine first - antihistamines, glucocorticoids, and bronchodilators are ancillary agents for residual urticaria/angioedema and bronchospasm once the patient is hemodynamically stable, not initial therapy (p. 2813).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch. 364 (Anaphylaxis), pp. 2812-2814; distributive-shock context p. 2358

chunks.text: Biphasic reactions in 10-20% recur an hour or more after apparent recovery, so a period of observation is needed after initial resolution (p. 2812).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch. 364 (Anaphylaxis), pp. 2812-2814; distributive-shock context p. 2358

chunks.text: A normal tryptase does not exclude anaphylaxis - it is not elevated in scombroid poisoning (exogenous histamine), and an acutely 'normal' value may still be diagnostic relative to a low individual baseline (apply the 20% + 2 rule) (p. 2813).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch. 364 (Anaphylaxis), pp. 2812-2814; distributive-shock context p. 2358

chunks.text: Non-IgE-mediated reactions can occur on first exposure, so the absence of prior exposure does not rule out an anaphylactic reaction (p. 2813).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch. 364 (Anaphylaxis), pp. 2812-2814; distributive-shock context p. 2358

chunks.text: Beta blockers can blunt the response to epinephrine; consider an alternative antihypertensive in patients at high risk of needing emergency epinephrine (p. 2813).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch. 364 (Anaphylaxis), pp. 2812-2814; distributive-shock context p. 2358

chunks.text: Skin/serum specific-IgE testing to foods has relatively poor predictive value, so a positive test alone does not confirm clinical reactivity (p. 2814).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch. 364 (Anaphylaxis), pp. 2812-2814; distributive-shock context p. 2358

chunks.text: Severe and even fatal complications can develop within minutes of symptom onset, making early recognition critical; deaths occur via airway/bronchial obstruction, laryngeal angioedema, or vascular collapse. Delaying epinephrine beyond the first 20 minutes worsens outcomes. Risk is higher with underlying asthma or cardiovascular disease. Natural history varies by trigger: most childhood egg, milk, soy, and wheat allergy resolves, whereas about 80% of peanut allergy persists for life. (p. 2812-2813)

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch. 364 (Anaphylaxis), pp. 2812-2814; distributive-shock context p. 2358

chunks.text: Hypotension or hypoxia - the most dangerous features, risking cardiovascular collapse or respiratory failure (p. 2812)

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch. 364 (Anaphylaxis), pp. 2812-2814; distributive-shock context p. 2358

chunks.text: Laryngeal edema (sensation of a lump in the throat, hoarseness, stridor) or angioedema of the epiglottis/larynx threatening mechanical airway obstruction (p. 2812)

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch. 364 (Anaphylaxis), pp. 2812-2814; distributive-shock context p. 2358

chunks.text: Bronchial obstruction (chest tightness, wheezing), especially severe in patients with underlying asthma, who have increased mortality (p. 2812)

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch. 364 (Anaphylaxis), pp. 2812-2814; distributive-shock context p. 2358

chunks.text: Underlying asthma or cardiovascular disease - predisposes to more rapid decompensation (p. 2812)

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch. 364 (Anaphylaxis), pp. 2812-2814; distributive-shock context p. 2358

chunks.text: Severe GI involvement (vomiting, crampy abdominal pain); bowel-wall angioedema can deplete intravascular volume enough to cause cardiovascular collapse (p. 2812)

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch. 364 (Anaphylaxis), pp. 2812-2814; distributive-shock context p. 2358

Serum tryptase
Anaphylaxis (non-infective) — Allergy / Emergency
Acute hypotension with urticaria/angioedema and bronchospasm after exposure indicates anaphylaxis.
Red flags: IM adrenaline immediately

[guideline] management → IM Adrenaline 1:1000 First-line and most time-critical agent — reverses airway oedema, bronchospasm and vasodilatory shock. Paediatric dose is weight-based via the paediatric formulary.

[guideline] adjunct → IV crystalloid bolus / Nebulised salbutamol / IV adrenaline infusion (refractory) / Corticosteroid (second-line, not a substitute for adrenaline) / Antihistamine (symptomatic, second-line) Corrects distributive hypotension from capillary leak; large volumes may be required.

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: Serial hemoglobin/hematocrit measurements — recognizing that early values are misleadingly normal and fall over hours as volume is restored (p.807)

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: Reticulocyte count and erythropoietin level — rise during the marrow recovery phase (p.807)

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: Targeted physical examination for signs of concealed hemorrhage (Grey Turner sign, Cullen sign, chest dullness) (p.807)

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: Hemolysis — also presents as anemia with an elevated reticulocyte count and a brisk marrow response, mimicking the recovery phase of acute blood loss (p.807)

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: Hypovolemic shock from non-hemorrhagic causes (dehydration, fluid sequestration) can reproduce the early hypovolemic picture before any fall in hemoglobin (p.807)

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: Blood loss produces anemia by two mechanisms: direct loss of red cells, and — if the bleeding is protracted — gradual depletion of iron stores leading to iron-deficiency anemia (the latter covered separately). Acute posthemorrhagic anemia follows the former. Hemorrhage may be external (trauma, obstetric) or internal (gastrointestinal tract, splenic rupture, ruptured ectopic pregnancy, subarachnoid hemorrhage, leaking aneurysm). After a sudden large loss there are three sequential clinical/pathophysiologic stages: (1) hypovolemia dominates and threatens high-flow organs (brain, kidneys), so impaired consciousness and acute renal failure are early dangers, while the blood count still appears normal because hemoglobin concentration is unchanged; (2) baroreceptor and stretch-receptor activation triggers vasopressin and other peptide release and a shift of fluid from the extravascular into the intravascular space, producing hemodilution that converts hypovolemia into measurable anemia proportional to the volume lost; (3) provided bleeding ceases, increased marrow erythropoiesis (reflected by elevated reticulocytes and erythropoietin) gradually ameliorates the anemia. Tissue oxygen delivery is defended by rightward shifts of the oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve (acute Bohr effect from lower pH/higher CO2; chronic rise in 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate) and by shunting blood away from organs with relatively rich supply (kidney, gut, skin) (p.807).

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: In the first hours after a sudden large bleed the routine blood count typically does NOT reveal anemia, because hemoglobin concentration is initially unchanged; the dominant problem at this stage is hypovolemia, not a low hemoglobin (p.807).

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: Compensation is partly achieved by a rightward shift of the oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve: with mild loss via the Bohr effect (lower pH / higher CO2), and in more chronic anemia via rising intracellular 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, which aids oxygen unloading (p.807).

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: Surgery is an important iatrogenic cause of acute posthemorrhagic anemia; blood loss can be substantial (e.g., up to about 2 L with radical prostatectomy) and should be measured and monitored (p.807-808).

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: Hemoglobin falls only gradually over several hours to days as the intravascular volume is restored — either by intravenous fluids given acutely, or by the body's own fluid shift from the extravascular into the intravascular compartment (hemodilution) — so the measured hemoglobin lags behind the true blood loss (p.807).

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: The degree of anemia eventually reflects the amount lost: as a rough guide, a hemoglobin around 7 g/dL after about 3 days implies roughly half of the total blood has been lost (p.807).

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: If bleeding stops, the marrow response (rising reticulocyte count and erythropoietin) gradually corrects the anemia; this reticulocyte rise mirrors the marrow response seen in hemolysis (p.807).

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: Acute blood loss and hemolysis are the two principal causes of anemia accompanied by an elevated reticulocyte count (p.807).

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: Signs of vascular instability appear once roughly 25% or more of total blood volume is lost; donating a unit of blood (~20% of volume) is usually only minimally symptomatic (p.807).

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: Bedside signs of concealed bleeding include the Grey Turner sign (flank ecchymosis, suggesting retroperitoneal hemorrhage), the Cullen sign (periumbilical ecchymosis, suggesting intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal bleeding), and dullness to chest percussion (suggesting intrapleural blood) (p.807).

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: The amount of blood lost is frequently overestimated when a scene appears bloody; careful repeated examination and directed investigations (e.g., ultrasound, endoscopy) are needed to localize occult bleeding (p.807).

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: Whenever hemoglobin drops abruptly, acute posthemorrhagic anemia should be suspected regardless of the history initially offered by the patient (p.807).

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: Mistakenly excluding significant hemorrhage because an early blood count shows a normal hemoglobin — the fall is delayed until volume is restored (p.807).

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: Overestimating blood loss from the bloody appearance of a scene rather than from careful clinical assessment (p.807).

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: Failing to suspect occult internal bleeding after trauma, where even large losses may not be immediately obvious (p.807).

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: Focusing on the anemia number rather than on hypovolemia and organ perfusion, which are the true early threats in large acute losses (p.807).

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: Outcome depends on the rapidity and volume of loss and on whether the source can be controlled. If bleeding is stopped, the marrow's compensatory rise in red cell production gradually corrects the anemia. The acute danger is not the anemia itself but hypovolemia and impaired organ perfusion: losses above ~30% of blood volume overwhelm normal compensatory mechanisms, and losses >40% (>~2 L in an average adult) produce hypovolemic shock with significant vital-organ perfusion deficits (p.807).

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: Loss of consciousness or acute renal failure early on, reflecting hypovolemic threat to brain and kidneys before any anemia is detectable (p.807)

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: Postural hypotension and tachycardia with a preference to remain supine, indicating sudden loss exceeding ~30% of blood volume that overwhelms sympathetic compensation (p.807)

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: Hypovolemic shock — confusion, dyspnea, diaphoresis, hypotension, tachycardia — indicating loss >40% (>~2 L in an average adult) and significant vital-organ hypoperfusion (p.807)

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: Tachycardia, tachypnea, narrowed pulse pressure, cold, pale, mottled skin and reduced urine output signaling sympathetic compensation for ongoing loss (p.807)

chunks.diseaseName: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss
chunks.text: Severity tracks the fraction of total blood volume lost: ~20% (one unit) is usually minimally symptomatic; signs of vascular instability emerge at ~25% or more; sudden loss of >30% overwhelms sympathetic compensation and produces postural hypotension and tachycardia; loss of >40% (>~2 L in an average-sized adult) causes hypovolemic shock (confusion, dyspnea, diaphoresis, hypotension, tachycardia). Symptomatic chronic/progressive anemia from slower loss often becomes apparent only when hemoglobin falls below ~70-80 g/L (7-8 g/dL), and intrinsic compensation maintains normal tissue oxygen delivery only across about a 20-30 g/L (2-3 g/dL) hemoglobin deficit (p.807).

chunks.text: Anemia results from a defect in any of the three requirements for normal red-cell production: renal erythropoietin (EPO) output, a functioning erythroid marrow, and adequate substrate (especially iron). EPO rises logarithmically once haemoglobin falls below ~100-120 g/L, but in chronic kidney disease and chronic inflammation EPO is inappropriately low for the degree of anemia. With adequate EPO and substrate, marrow red-cell output can rise four- to fivefold over 1-2 weeks. Mechanistically anemia is either hyperproductive/regenerative (blood loss or haemolysis, with reticulocytosis) or hypoproliferative (nutritional deficiency, marrow replacement, absent precursors, stem-cell defects, or EPO deficiency). Inflammatory cytokines such as TNF lower EPO and raise hepcidin, which blocks iron absorption and release from stores, producing the anemia of inflammation (p.443-450).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.66 Anemia and Polycythemia (printed p.444-451); Ch.106 Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss (printed p.850-851)

chunks.text: Symptoms and signs of anemia correlate poorly with the actual haemoglobin/haematocrit; clinical severity reflects the rate of onset and the patient's cardiovascular reserve rather than the absolute level (p.444).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.66 Anemia and Polycythemia (printed p.444-451); Ch.106 Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss (printed p.850-851)

chunks.text: A high RDW favours iron deficiency (anisocytosis), whereas a low/normal RDW with microcytosis favours thalassaemia, where cells are more uniform in size (p.449).

chunks.text: Iron-deficiency pica and the neuropathy of B12 deficiency are deficiency-specific clues to seek on history and examination (p.444).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.66 Anemia and Polycythemia (printed p.444-451); Ch.106 Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss (printed p.850-851)

chunks.text: In acute blood loss the haemoglobin/haematocrit initially does NOT reflect the volume lost; the early picture is hypovolaemia, and the haemoglobin only falls over hours as fluid shifts and resuscitation dilute the blood (p.850).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.66 Anemia and Polycythemia (printed p.444-451); Ch.106 Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss (printed p.850-851)

chunks.text: Slowly developing anemia is remarkably well tolerated because three compensatory mechanisms develop over time: rapid rise in cardiac output (minutes), a rise in 2,3-DPG that lowers haemoglobin oxygen affinity and improves tissue oxygen offloading (hours to days), and an expansion of plasma volume (weeks) (p.444).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.66 Anemia and Polycythemia (printed p.444-451); Ch.106 Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss (printed p.850-851)

chunks.text: Plasma-volume expansion can occasionally overwhelm the heart and precipitate features of heart failure/oedema in chronic anemia (p.444).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.66 Anemia and Polycythemia (printed p.444-451); Ch.106 Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss (printed p.850-851)

chunks.text: Patients with limited cardiac reserve or atherosclerosis become symptomatic (angina, TIA/stroke) at a higher haematocrit than those with normal cardiovascular function (p.444).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.66 Anemia and Polycythemia (printed p.444-451); Ch.106 Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss (printed p.850-851)

chunks.text: The absolute reticulocyte count is the key first branch point for mechanism: an elevated count points to blood loss or haemolysis, while a low or inappropriately low count points to impaired production (p.448-449).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.66 Anemia and Polycythemia (printed p.444-451); Ch.106 Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss (printed p.850-851)

chunks.text: Manual percentage reticulocyte counts must be corrected for the haematocrit (a 1% count becomes an apparent 2% at a haematocrit of ~23%); the machine-derived absolute reticulocyte count needs no such correction (p.447).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.66 Anemia and Polycythemia (printed p.444-451); Ch.106 Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss (printed p.850-851)

chunks.text: Around 75% of all anemia is hypoproliferative, most often from mild-to-moderate iron deficiency or inflammation (p.449).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.66 Anemia and Polycythemia (printed p.444-451); Ch.106 Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss (printed p.850-851)

chunks.text: Anemia is frequently multifactorial (e.g., chronic inflammation plus occult GI blood loss in a patient on anti-inflammatory drugs), so iron status should be evaluated fully before and during treatment of any anemia (p.450).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.66 Anemia and Polycythemia (printed p.444-451); Ch.106 Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss (printed p.850-851)

chunks.text: Serum ferritin is an acute-phase reactant: it can be raised several-fold by inflammation and mask coexisting iron deficiency, whereas a ferritin <30 ug/L reliably indicates depleted body iron stores (p.449).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.66 Anemia and Polycythemia (printed p.444-451); Ch.106 Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss (printed p.850-851)

chunks.text: Anchoring on a normal haemoglobin in early acute haemorrhage and underestimating blood loss; an abrupt fall in haemoglobin should prompt suspicion of acute posthemorrhagic anemia regardless of the given history (p.850).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.66 Anemia and Polycythemia (printed p.444-451); Ch.106 Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss (printed p.850-851)

chunks.text: Estimates of blood volume lost at a bloody scene are often overestimated, while concealed internal bleeding may be missed entirely (p.850).

chunks.text: Relying on ferritin alone during inflammation, which can falsely normalise or elevate it despite true iron deficiency (p.449).

chunks.text: Two complementary classifications. (1) By red-cell size (Wintrobe): microcytic (iron deficiency, thalassaemia, sideroblastic, anemia of inflammation), normocytic (renal disease, marrow invasion, myeloma, aplastic anemia, pure red cell aplasia, endocrinopathies), and macrocytic - subdivided into oval macrocytes (B12/folate deficiency, myelodysplasia, drugs) and round macrocytes (alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, hypoxia, reticulocytosis, smoking, dysproteinemia). (2) By mechanism: hyperproductive (blood loss, haemolysis - reticulocytes high) versus underproductive/hypoproliferative (nutritional deficiency, absent precursors, lack of EPO, marrow replacement, stem-cell defects - reticulocytes low/inappropriate). The absolute reticulocyte count plus MCV drive the diagnostic algorithm (p.448-451). For acute blood loss: vascular instability appears with sudden loss of ~25% of total blood volume, and >30% loss exceeds compensatory mechanisms (p.851).

chunks.text: ACE inhibitors block angiotensin-converting enzyme, which normally also degrades the vasodilator peptide bradykinin; inhibition leads to delayed bradykinin breakdown and accumulation, increasing vascular permeability in the deep dermis and subcutaneous/submucosal tissues and producing angioedema (pp. 2807, 2024). This is mechanistically the same bradykinin pathway implicated in hereditary angioedema, where deficient or dysfunctional C1 inhibitor (C1INH) fails to restrain activated factor XII (Hageman factor) and kallikrein, generating excess bradykinin (p. 2808). Because the mechanism is bradykinin- rather than histamine-/IgE-mediated, there is no associated urticaria or pruritus, and the process is fundamentally distinct from allergic mast-cell-driven angioedema (p. 2808). The same bradykinin-accumulation mechanism explains the increased angioedema risk seen with combined ACE/neprilysin inhibition, since neprilysin also degrades bradykinin (Ch. 265, p. 1995).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 363 (Urticaria, Angioedema, and Allergic Rhinitis), pp. 2807-2809; with supporting context from Ch. 265 (Heart Failure: Management) p. 1995 and Ch. 271 (Hypertensive Vascular Disease) p. 2024.

chunks.text: ACE-inhibitor angioedema occurs in roughly 0.2-0.7% of exposed patients and is driven by impaired (delayed) degradation of bradykinin rather than by an IgE/mast-cell allergic mechanism (p. 2807).

chunks.text: Recognized risk factors for ACE inhibitor-related angioedema include Black race, prior organ transplant, female sex, smoking, and increasing age (p. 2807).

chunks.text: Bradykinin-mediated angioedema (whether from an ACE inhibitor or from C1-inhibitor deficiency) is characterized by the conspicuous ABSENCE of accompanying urticaria or pruritus (p. 2808).

chunks.text: Anorectal abscesses usually begin with obstruction and infection of an anal gland at the base of an anal crypt (cryptoglandular infection). Pus tracks along planes of least resistance from the intersphincteric space into the perianal, ischiorectal, or supralevator spaces, and can extend circumferentially in a horseshoe pattern. The causative organisms are typically gut flora, including coliforms and anaerobes. Underlying conditions such as Crohn's disease, diabetes, and immunosuppression predispose to formation and to more extensive spread. Persistence of the primary gland infection after drainage creates the epithelialised track of a fistula-in-ano.

chunks.text: Anterior uveitis is inflammation of the iris and ciliary body (anterior uveal tract). Breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier allows inflammatory cells and protein to leak into the anterior chamber, seen clinically as cells and flare. The process may be immune-mediated (often HLA-B27 associated or linked to systemic autoimmune disease), infective, or triggered by trauma. Inflammatory adhesions can form between the iris and lens (posterior synechiae) or the iris and trabecular meshwork (peripheral anterior synechiae), and secondary complications include raised intraocular pressure, cataract, and macular oedema.

chunks.text: Bacillus anthracis spores enter through skin abrasions, inhalation or ingestion, germinate, and multiply while producing a poly-D-glutamic acid capsule that resists phagocytosis and a tripartite toxin. Protective antigen mediates entry of lethal factor and oedema factor into cells; lethal factor is a protease that disrupts intracellular signalling and triggers massive inflammatory and cytotoxic effects, while oedema factor raises cyclic AMP causing the striking tissue oedema. Systemic dissemination produces toxaemia, vascular leak, haemorrhage and shock, which drive the high mortality of non-cutaneous disease.

APS is an autoantibody-mediated acquired thrombophilia. The major autoantibodies target phospholipid-binding plasma proteins, chiefly beta2-glycoprotein I (beta2GPI, a 43-kDa apolipoprotein of 326 amino acids in five domains) and prothrombin; anti-domain I IgG is associated with increased thrombotic risk, while the antithrombotic function of beta2GPI depends on its fifth domain. Lupus anticoagulant is a separate group of antibodies against phospholipid-binding proteins that prolongs in vitro clotting time which is not corrected by adding normal plasma. Antibody induction is thought to begin with endothelial injury (from infections, oxidative stress, or major physical stress such as surgery or trauma) in a permissive genetic background (HLA associations), driving increased endothelial apoptosis, autoantigen presentation, and an autoimmune response. Binding of aPL to disrupted endothelium produces a proinflammatory, prothrombotic state with monocyte and platelet activation, adhesion molecules and proinflammatory cytokines, complement and neutrophil activation, neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, and thrombus formation. Type I interferon pathway activation and an imbalance between type I and III interferons have recently been proposed as mechanisms of thrombosis and obstetric complications (Harrison 22e p.2837).

APS is an autoantibody-mediated acquired thrombophilia defined by recurrent arterial or venous thrombosis, microvascular manifestations, and/or pregnancy morbidity; it affects primarily young females (Harrison 22e p.2837).
Thrombocytopenia and autoimmune hemolytic anemia are the main hematologic manifestations of APS (Harrison 22e p.2837).

DOACs have recently been shown to increase the risk of arterial events, especially in patients with triple positivity or previous arterial thrombosis, and a meta-analysis found prior thrombosis type did not change this increased arterial risk versus VKAs (Harrison 22e p.2839).
APS may occur alone (primary) or in association with other autoimmune diseases, mainly SLE; about one-third of SLE patients carry aPL antibodies and 10-15% of those develop APS (Harrison 22e p.2837).

Diagnosis should be seriously considered with thrombosis, cerebrovascular accidents in individuals younger than 55 years, or pregnancy morbidity, particularly in the presence of livedo reticularis or thrombocytopenia (Harrison 22e p.2838).

The three classical laboratory antibodies are lupus anticoagulant (LA), anticardiolipin (aCL), and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I (anti-beta2GPI); higher-risk profiles include triple positivity, IgG isotype, moderate-to-high titers, and persistent positivity (Harrison 22e p.2838-2839).
Laboratory criteria require persistence: moderate (40-79 units) or high (>=80 units) aCL/anti-beta2GPI titers confirmed on two occasions 12 weeks apart (Harrison 22e p.2838-2839).

In patients receiving anticoagulation, LA test positivity should be interpreted with caution; when features are highly reminiscent of APS but classical aPL are absent, antiphosphatidylserine/prothrombin antibody testing may have a diagnostic role (Harrison 22e p.2837).

Deep venous thrombosis occurs primarily in the lower extremities and often causes pulmonary emboli; cerebral venous thrombosis may present with intracranial hypertension and focal deficits (Harrison 22e p.2837).
Arterial thrombosis most commonly affects cerebral arteries, manifesting as transient ischemic attack, stroke, migraine, or cognitive dysfunction (Harrison 22e p.2837).
Libman-Sacks endocarditis (small, usually <1 cm, organized platelet-fibrin valve vegetations) and valve thickening are characteristic cardiac manifestations (Harrison 22e p.2837).

Paradoxical pitfall: lupus anticoagulant prolongs in vitro clotting tests (e.g., aPTT) yet is associated with thrombosis in vivo, not bleeding; the prolongation is NOT corrected by mixing with normal plasma, distinguishing it from a factor deficiency.

aPTT has variable sensitivity to lupus anticoagulant depending on the reagent used; aPTT prolongation is not specific because factor deficiencies or other inhibitors also prolong it, so confirmation requires lack of correction on mixing and correction with added phospholipids (Harrison 22e p.~700).
In patients receiving anticoagulation, lupus anticoagulant positivity should be interpreted with caution.
Classification requires that clinical manifestations with other equally or more likely explanations than APS not be counted toward the criteria.
aPL antibodies are frequently transiently positive, so persistence must be confirmed (titers on two occasions 12 weeks apart) before attributing disease.

Thrombotic and obstetric event risk is closely tied to the underlying aPL profile, depending on antibody type (IgG high risk vs IgM low risk), number of antibodies (two or three classical autoantibodies confer higher risk than a single antibody), titer (moderate-high vs low), and persistence on repeated measurements. Catastrophic APS is life-threatening and rapidly progressive. APS antibodies increase with age, though it is questionable whether they induce thrombotic events in elderly individuals (Harrison 22e p.2837-2839).

Catastrophic APS (CAPS): a rare, life-threatening, rapidly progressive thromboembolic disease simultaneously involving three or more organs, typically with microvascular thrombosis developing in less than a week

2023 ACR/EULAR classification criteria require at least 3 points from clinical domains AND at least 3 points from laboratory domains. Clinical domains: (1) venous thromboembolism, (2) arterial thrombosis, (3) microvascular events, (4) obstetric complications, (5) cardiac valve disease, (6) hematologic manifestations. Laboratory domains: (1) lupus anticoagulant, (2) anticardiolipin, and/or (3) anti-beta2GPI antibodies at moderate (40-79 units) or high (>=80 units) titers on two occasions 12 weeks apart. Definite CAPS requires all four: thrombosis in >=3 organs/systems; development in less than a week; histologic small-vessel thrombosis in at least one organ; and aPL presence (probable CAPS when a combination is present) (Harrison 22e p.2838-2839).

Dissection begins with a tear of the intima, most often along the high-shear right lateral wall of the ascending aorta or in the descending thoracic aorta just below the ligamentum arteriosum. Pulsatile flow dissects along the elastic lamellar plates of the media to create a false lumen; the initiating event may be a primary intimal tear with secondary dissection into the media, or a medial hemorrhage that secondarily disrupts the intima. The dissection usually propagates distally (sometimes proximally), may be limited distally by atherosclerotic plaque, and can re-enter the true lumen through a secondary distal intimal disruption. Underlying medial degeneration and conditions that raise aortic wall stress predispose to dissection. Two related radiologic/pathologic variants are intramural hematoma (rupture of vasa vasorum bleeding into the wall, without an intimal flap) and penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer (plaque erosion into the media); both can progress to dissection and rupture (Harrison 22e p.2168-2169).
Pain characteristically migrates as the dissection propagates, often shifting to the interscapular region of the back (Harrison 22e p.2169).
Systemic hypertension coexists in about 70% of patients with aortic dissection (Harrison 22e p.2168).
Peak incidence is in the sixth and seventh decades, with men affected about twice as often as women (Harrison 22e p.2169).

A normal ECG showing no ischemia helps distinguish dissection from myocardial infarction in a patient with chest pain, though dissection can rarely involve a coronary ostium and cause an actual MI (Harrison 22e p.2169).

On chest x-ray, ascending dissection often produces a widened superior mediastinum; a pleural effusion (usually left-sided) may appear and is typically serosanguineous rather than a sign of rupture unless accompanied by hypotension and a falling hematocrit (Harrison 22e p.2169).
Although 'tearing' or 'ripping' pain is classic, acute aortic emergencies also commonly present with knifelike pain (Harrison 22e p.106).
Stanford type A or B classification is more practical for management than DeBakey, because DeBakey types I and II are managed similarly (Harrison 22e p.2168).

Aortic dissection is a classic disease that is misdiagnosed as acute myocardial infarction — a dangerous error because anticoagulant/thrombolytic therapy for presumed MI can be catastrophic (Harrison 22e p.102, p.2169).
A left pleural effusion in dissection is usually serosanguineous and does not by itself indicate rupture unless there is accompanying hypotension and a falling hematocrit (Harrison 22e p.2169).
Transthoracic echocardiography is insensitive for arch and descending dissections, so a negative TTE does not exclude dissection (Harrison 22e p.2169).

In-hospital mortality after surgical treatment of dissection is reported at about 15-25%; for medically treated uncomplicated type B dissection it is about 12%. Major perioperative causes of death and morbidity include myocardial infarction, paraplegia, renal failure, tamponade, hemorrhage, and sepsis. With careful follow-up the long-term outlook after discharge is generally good, with roughly 60% 10-year survival; patients with Marfan syndrome are at high risk for post-dissection complications (Harrison 22e p.2170).

Stanford classification: type A involves the ascending aorta (proximal dissection) regardless of tear site or distal extension; type B is limited to the arch and/or descending aorta (distal dissection). DeBakey classification: type I — intimal tear in ascending aorta with propagation to arch, descending and possibly abdominal aorta; type II — limited to the ascending aorta; type III — tear in the descending aorta with distal propagation. Stanford A/B is more practical for management since DeBakey I and II are managed similarly (Harrison 22e p.2168).

The total LV stroke volume (effective forward stroke volume plus regurgitant volume) is increased; in severe AR the regurgitant volume may equal the effective forward stroke volume. Unlike MR, the entire LV stroke volume is ejected into the high-pressure aorta. The major compensation is an increase in LV end-diastolic volume (increased preload); dilation and eccentric hypertrophy allow a larger stroke volume without increased myofibril shortening, so severe AR can occur with a normal effective forward stroke volume and normal LVEF together with elevated LV end-diastolic pressure and volume. By Laplace's law LV dilation increases systolic wall tension, so chronic AR is a state of both increased preload and afterload. Adaptive measures eventually fail; deterioration of LV function often precedes symptom onset. Considerable LV wall thickening occurs and hearts can weigh >1000 g. The reverse aorta-to-LV diastolic pressure gradient decreases through diastole, accounting for the decrescendo murmur. In acute severe AR the LV is unprepared for the volume load, compliance is normal or reduced, diastolic pressures rise rapidly (occasionally >40 mmHg), and the reversed pressure gradient closes the mitral valve prematurely. Myocardial ischemia may occur because of elevated oxygen demand (LV dilation, hypertrophy, increased systolic tension) combined with reduced coronary perfusion (most coronary flow is diastolic, when aortic pressure is low), affecting particularly the subendocardium even without epicardial CAD (p.2043-2044).

Chronic severe AR can have a long latent period, with patients remaining relatively asymptomatic for 10-15 years; exertional dyspnea is usually the first symptom of diminished cardiac reserve, followed by orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (p.2044).

A wide arterial pulse pressure (systolic hypertension plus low diastolic pressure) is characteristic of chronic severe AR, producing peripheral signs such as the water-hammer (Corrigan's) pulse, Quincke's capillary pulsations, Traube's pistol-shot femoral sounds, and Duroziez's sign (p.2043-2044).

The murmur of chronic AR is a high-pitched, blowing, decrescendo diastolic murmur heard best in the third intercostal space along the left sternal border; it is best appreciated with the patient sitting up, leaning forward, breath held in forced expiration (p.2044).
A diastolic murmur louder along the right sternal border suggests AR caused by aneurysmal dilation of the aortic root rather than primary valvular disease (p.2044).

The Austin Flint murmur is a soft, low-pitched rumbling mid-to-late diastolic murmur in severe AR, probably from diastolic displacement of the anterior mitral leaflet by the regurgitant stream; it is NOT associated with hemodynamically significant mitral obstruction (p.2044).
Anginal chest pain can occur in severe AR even without coronary artery disease and even in younger patients, may occur at rest, and often responds poorly to sublingual nitroglycerin (p.2044).
On echocardiography, a rapid high-frequency diastolic fluttering of the anterior mitral leaflet, produced by the impact of the regurgitant jet, is a characteristic finding (p.2044).
Auscultatory features of AR are intensified by sustained handgrip, which augments systemic vascular resistance and increases LV afterload (p.2044).
In acute severe AR, the elevated LV end-diastolic pressure leads to early (premature) closure of the mitral valve, a soft S1, and a soft, short early diastolic murmur (p.2044).

Sphygmomanometer diastolic pressure can be hard to read because systolic sounds may persist with the cuff fully deflated; the muffling point (Korotkoff phase IV) corresponds reasonably to true intra-arterial diastolic pressure (p.2044).

As chronic AR progresses and LV end-diastolic pressure rises, the arterial diastolic pressure may actually rise (aortic diastolic pressure cannot fall below LV end-diastolic pressure), so a less-wide pulse pressure does not exclude severe disease (p.2044).
A mid-systolic ejection murmur and systolic thrill in isolated AR can be loud without signifying aortic valve obstruction and do not necessarily indicate coexisting AS (p.2044).

Deterioration of LV function often precedes the development of symptoms, so waiting for symptoms risks irreversible dysfunction; serial noninvasive follow-up is essential to time surgery (p.2043-2044, p.2046).

Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) is NOT recommended for patients with severe AR who are surgical candidates (technical success limited by annular dilation and paucity of valvular/annular calcium) (p.2046).

Operative and late mortality risks depend largely on disease stage and myocardial function at operation. Overall operative mortality for isolated AVR for pure AR is ~1-2%; the risk doubles when aortic surgery is added. Patients with marked cardiac enlargement and established LV dysfunction have an operative mortality of ~5-10% and a late mortality of ~3-5% per year from LV failure despite technically satisfactory operation; nonetheless, because of the very poor prognosis with medical management, even patients with advanced LV systolic dysfunction should be considered for operation. If surgery is delayed too long (>1 year from onset of symptoms or LV dysfunction), it often does not restore normal LV size and function (p.2046-2047).

Acute severe AR (as in infective endocarditis, aortic dissection, or trauma): the LV cannot dilate enough to maintain stroke volume, LV diastolic pressure rises rapidly with marked LA and PA wedge pressure elevation, and pulmonary edema and/or cardiogenic shock may develop rapidly - a surgical emergency requiring operation usually within 24 h (prompt 24-48 h surgery may be lifesaving) (p.2044, p.2046-2047).

Acute severe AR may show only slight widening of pulse pressure and invariably presents with tachycardia (heart rate increases to preserve cardiac output), unlike the wide pulse pressure of chronic AR (p.2044).
In acute severe AR, intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation is contraindicated and beta blockers are best avoided (p.2045).
Onset of symptoms or LV systolic dysfunction in chronic severe AR is an indication for surgery (p.2045).

Severe AR is characterized by central jet width >65% of the LV outflow tract on color Doppler, vena contracta >0.6 cm, regurgitant volume >=60 mL/beat, regurgitant fraction >=50%, effective regurgitant orifice >=0.3 cm2, and holodiastolic flow reversal in the proximal descending thoracic aorta. AHA/ACC staging (per Fig. 273-2): asymptomatic (Stage C, with C2 denoting LV dysfunction EF <=55%) versus symptomatic (Stage D). Surgical thresholds for asymptomatic severe AR include LVEF <55%, LV end-systolic dimension >50 mm (>25 mm/m2), or LV end-diastolic dimension >65 mm on serial studies (p.2044, p.2046).

Hyperdynamic flow murmurs without structural disease (fever, thyrotoxicosis, pregnancy, anemia, normal childhood/adolescence) can produce midsystolic murmurs (Harrison 22e p.1908).

Aortic stenosis is most often caused by gradual progression of valvular calcification of either normal trileaflet or congenitally bicuspid valves, producing fixed left ventricular outflow obstruction. The pressure overload drives left ventricular hypertrophy, which manifests on the ECG as LVH that increases with severity. The combination of increased myocardial oxygen demand and impaired endocardial perfusion can cause ischemia/angina even with normal coronaries. Syncope in AS reflects a structural disorder compromising cardiac output, and inappropriate reflex vasodilation may be provoked by increased ventricular contractility against the fixed obstruction (Harrison 22e p.203-204, 285, 329, 1933).

The murmur of AS is a crescendo-decrescendo (midsystolic/ejection) murmur, usually loudest in the second right intercostal space and radiating into the carotids; it is the most common midsystolic murmur in adults (Harrison 22e p.328).

Apical transmission of the AS murmur, where it becomes higher-pitched, is common (Gallavardin effect) and may be mistaken for mitral regurgitation; the AS murmur intensifies in the beat following a premature beat and varies directly with cardiac output, whereas the MR murmur stays constant beat-to-beat (Harrison 22e p.328).

Auscultatory features pointing to severe AS include a soft or absent A2, paradoxical splitting of S2, a late-peaking systolic murmur, an apical S4, and (at normal output) a systolic thrill and a grade 4 or louder murmur (Harrison 22e p.328).

An early ejection sound (click) in children/young adults signifies a flexible, noncalcified bicuspid valve and localizes obstruction to the valvular level rather than sub- or supravalvular (Harrison 22e p.328).
Bicuspid aortic valve is one of the most common congenital anomalies and predisposes to both aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation (Harrison 22e p.1933).

AS can precipitate myocardial ischemia and anginal chest pain even without obstructive coronary atherosclerosis, by creating extreme myocardial oxygen demand with impaired endocardial blood flow (type 2 ischemia mechanism) (Harrison 22e p.285).

Heyde's syndrome is the association of aortic stenosis with bleeding gastrointestinal vascular ectasias (acquired von Willebrand disease); such patients appear to benefit from aortic valve replacement (Harrison 22e p.361).

Avoid aggressive preload/afterload reduction: aggressive treatment of cardiac failure with diuretics and/or vasodilators can precipitate orthostatic hypotension in patients with structural disease such as AS (Harrison 22e p.203).
Transvalvular pressure gradients underestimate severity in severe LV dysfunction; rely on valve area by continuity equation (Harrison 22e p.1933-1934).
In low-flow/low-gradient AS the valve may behave stenotic simply because of the low gradient; provocative dobutamine testing is needed to distinguish true severe stenosis (Harrison 22e p.1934).
The carotid parvus-et-tardus sign is less discriminatory in older patients with stiffened arteries (Harrison 22e p.329).
Aortic sclerosis can produce a murmur indistinguishable on auscultation from significant AS (Harrison 22e p.1908).

Patients with good left ventricular function can tolerate severe AS for a considerable period, so valve area or gradient alone should not dictate timing of surgery, which remains a clinical decision (Harrison 22e p.1934).
A weak and delayed carotid pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus) indicates severe AS (Harrison 22e p.329, 1905).
Soft or absent A2, paradoxical splitting of S2, late-peaking murmur, and an apical S4 indicate severe AS (Harrison 22e p.328).
A softening AS murmur in the setting of heart failure/low cardiac output is misleading and does not indicate mild disease (Harrison 22e p.328).
Syncope (including reflex/exertional) from AS reflects structural compromise of cardiac output (Harrison 22e p.203-204).

Echo: peak instantaneous velocities of 3.0 m/s or higher (often >4.0 m/s) correspond to gradients of ~36 and ~64 mmHg and indicate at least moderate AS; aortic valve area <1.0 cm2 is generally severe and <0.6 cm2 critical (Harrison 22e p.1933-1934). Catheterization: a valve area <1.0 cm2 with a mean gradient >40 mmHg indicates severe AS (Harrison 22e p.1950). Aortic sclerosis (non-obstructive) is defined by a Doppler jet velocity of 2.5 m/s or less (Harrison 22e p.1908).

ARDS results from diffuse lung injury, either direct (e.g., pneumonia, aspiration, toxic inhalation, pulmonary contusion) or indirect (e.g., sepsis, severe trauma, multiple transfusions, pancreatitis). It evolves through three phases. In the EXUDATIVE phase (first ~7 days), alveolar capillary endothelial cells and type I pneumocytes are injured, the tight alveolar barrier is lost, and protein-rich edema fluid accumulates in the interstitial and alveolar spaces. Proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha) and lipid mediators recruit neutrophils, and condensed plasma proteins plus cellular debris and dysfunctional surfactant form hyaline membranes (diffuse alveolar damage). Pulmonary vascular injury occurs early with microthrombi. Dependent alveolar collapse reduces lung compliance, producing intrapulmonary shunting, hypoxemia, and increased work of breathing; microvascular occlusion raises dead space and pulmonary vascular resistance, so hypercapnia and pulmonary hypertension can also occur. The PROLIFERATIVE phase (~day 7-21) brings lung repair, organization of exudates, a shift from neutrophil- to lymphocyte-predominant infiltrates, and proliferation of type II pneumocytes that regenerate surfactant and differentiate into type I cells; most patients recover. Some progress to the FIBROTIC phase, with alveolar-duct and interstitial fibrosis, emphysema-like bullae, vascular occlusion and pulmonary hypertension, increased pneumothorax risk, reduced compliance, and increased dead space (Harrison 22e p.2299, p.2300, p.2301, p.2302).

ARDS is a clinical syndrome of severe dyspnea of rapid onset, hypoxemia, and diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates leading to respiratory failure, caused by diffuse lung injury (Harrison 22e p.2299).

By 2012 expert consensus, ARDS is graded as mild, moderate, or severe by the degree of hypoxemia (PaO2/FiO2 ratio), and these stages correlate with mortality risk and duration of mechanical ventilation in survivors (Harrison 22e p.2299, p.2300).

Most cases (>80%) arise from a small number of disorders: pneumonia and sepsis (~40-60%), followed by aspiration of gastric contents, trauma, multiple transfusions, and drug overdose; risk rises with more than one predisposing condition (Harrison 22e p.2299).
The natural history has three phases - exudative (first ~7 days), proliferative (~day 7-21), and fibrotic - each with characteristic clinical and pathologic features (Harrison 22e p.2299, p.2301).

Cornerstone of management is recognizing and treating the underlying trigger (pneumonia, sepsis, aspiration, trauma) plus standardized bundled ICU care, rather than ARDS-specific drug therapy (Harrison 22e p.2302).

Lung-protective ventilation with low tidal volume (6 mL/kg predicted body weight) and limited plateau pressure (<=30 cmH2O) significantly lowers mortality versus conventional higher tidal volumes; this is the only therapy graded by the strongest evidence (Harrison 22e p.2302, p.2303).

Prone positioning early in severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <150 mmHg) reduced 28-day mortality in a randomized trial; it requires a team experienced in proning because repositioning critically ill patients can be hazardous (Harrison 22e p.2302).

A conservative fluid strategy - reducing left atrial filling pressure with fluid restriction and diuretics - shortens ICU stay and duration of ventilation, limited only by hypotension and organ hypoperfusion (Harrison 22e p.2302).
Mortality in ARDS is largely due to nonpulmonary causes, with sepsis and nonpulmonary organ failure accounting for >80% of deaths (Harrison 22e p.2303).

ARDS radiographic findings are characteristic but not specific and can be indistinguishable from cardiogenic pulmonary edema; unlike cardiogenic edema, ARDS often lacks cardiomegaly, pleural effusions, or pulmonary vascular redistribution. Hydrostatic edema must not be the primary cause - if no ARDS risk factor is present, objective evaluation (e.g., echocardiography) is required to exclude a cardiac etiology (Harrison 22e p.2300, p.2301).

Mechanical ventilation, though life-saving, can aggravate lung injury via volutrauma (alveolar overdistention from excess tidal volume), barotrauma (high alveolar pressure), and atelectrauma (recurrent alveolar collapse); because ARDS lung is heterogeneous, fully inflating consolidated regions can overdistend and injure more normal lung (Harrison 22e p.2302).

Routine glucocorticoids are NOT supported by current evidence for ARDS itself; recruitment maneuvers combined with higher baseline PEEP increased mortality in one study; routine early neuromuscular blockade is not beneficial in all moderate-to-severe ARDS (reserve for ventilatory dyssynchrony despite sedation); surfactant replacement and inhaled vasodilators (e.g., inhaled nitric oxide) do not improve survival (Harrison 22e p.2302, p.2303).
Pulse oximetry may overestimate oxygen saturation in patients with darker skin tones, so correlation with PaO2 should be considered when feasible (Harrison 22e p.2300).

Hospital mortality in the LUNG SAFE study was approximately 34.9% for mild, 40.3% for moderate, and 46.1% for severe ARDS, with a trend toward improved outcomes over time. Increasing Berlin-defined severity predicts higher mortality. Most deaths are nonpulmonary, with sepsis and nonpulmonary organ failure causing >80%. Major mortality risk factors are nonpulmonary: advanced age (~60% mortality in patients >75 vs ~20% in those <45), preexisting organ dysfunction (chronic liver disease, chronic alcohol abuse, chronic immunosuppression); direct lung injury carries nearly twice the death risk of indirect injury. Among survivors, the lung has notable resolving power: most regain nearly normal lung function, usually within 6 months, and more than a third have normal spirometry and diffusion capacity one year after extubation. However, exercise limitation and reduced physical quality of life are often documented at 5 years despite near-normal pulmonary function, and survivors and family caregivers carry a substantial burden of depression and posttraumatic stress disorder (Harrison 22e p.2303, p.2304).

Berlin definition (2012): severity is graded by oxygenation (PaO2/FiO2 assessed on at least 5 cmH2O PEEP) - Mild: 200 mmHg < PaO2/FiO2 <=300 mmHg; Moderate: 100 mmHg < PaO2/FiO2 <=200 mmHg; Severe: PaO2/FiO2 <=100 mmHg. Onset must be acute (within 1 week of a clinical insult or new/worsening respiratory symptoms), chest imaging must show bilateral opacities consistent with pulmonary edema not fully explained by effusions, lobar/lung collapse, or nodules, and respiratory failure must not be primarily due to hydrostatic (cardiogenic) edema (objective evaluation such as echocardiography required if no ARDS risk factor present). Proposed 2023 updates extend criteria to nonintubated patients on high-flow nasal oxygen or noninvasive ventilation, add SpO2/FiO2 (S/F) ratios, permit ultrasound imaging, and allow application in resource-limited settings. A more recent global definition has also been proposed that does not rely on arterial blood gases, chest radiography, or PEEP (Harrison 22e p.2299, p.2300).

Thrombus formation reflects dysregulated hemostasis involving the vessel wall, coagulation and fibrinolytic proteins, and platelets. In arterial thrombosis, vessel-wall damage exposes subendothelial collagen and von Willebrand factor; the platelet GPIb-IX-V complex mediates adhesion, platelets are activated through seven-transmembrane receptors (thrombin/PAR1, PAR4, ADP receptors P2Y1 and P2Y12, prostaglandin and lipid receptors), release thromboxane A2, serotonin, and ADP from granules, and undergo a calcium-dependent conformational change in GPIIb/IIIa that allows high-affinity fibrinogen binding and irreversible aggregation. Most arterial thrombi are superimposed on disrupted atherosclerotic plaque whose thrombogenic core triggers platelet-rich thrombus. In venous thrombosis, the coagulation cascade is initiated chiefly by exposure of tissue factor: factor VII/VIIa-tissue factor complex activates factor X (directly or via factor IX/VIIIa), FXa with cofactor FVa converts prothrombin to thrombin, thrombin converts fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin and activates FXIII to cross-link the clot. Amplification lets a small stimulus generate large amounts of fibrin. Venous thrombi typically originate in valve cusps of calf deep veins or muscular sinuses where sluggish flow lowers oxygen delivery, activating endothelial cells that express adhesion molecules; tissue-factor-bearing leukocytes and microvesicles adhere, neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) provide a scaffold that binds and activates platelets and activates factor XII, and impaired clearance of activated clotting factors worsens local thrombosis. Hypercoagulability (heritable or acquired), stasis, and vascular dysfunction (Virchow's elements) underlie venous events. Inflammation links the two: platelet P-selectin binds leukocyte PSGL-1, induces monocyte tissue factor and CD40 ligand expression, and Toll-like receptors (TLR2/3/4, TLR7/8) connect infection to platelet-dependent thrombosis.

Thrombosis is essentially hemostasis occurring in the wrong place at the wrong time; the same processes that protect against hemorrhage can, under certain conditions, produce pathologic arterial or venous occlusion.

Loss-of-function CYP2C19 polymorphisms are the strongest single determinant of reduced antiplatelet response to clopidogrel (a prodrug requiring hepatic activation) but account for only about 5-12% of the variability in ADP-induced platelet aggregation.

Antithrombin reactions governed by normal endothelium become pivotal in limiting clot extension into adjacent uninjured vessel once a protective clot has formed; antithrombin, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, heparin cofactor II, and protein C/protein S all restrain thrombin generation.
Hemostasis and thrombosis arise from interplay among three elements: the vessel wall, the coagulation/fibrinolytic proteins, and platelets.

Arterial thrombosis is dominated by platelet adhesion to an injured vessel wall and the state of the wall itself, whereas venous thrombosis is driven mainly by activation of the coagulation cascade in the setting of stasis or hypercoagulability.
Platelets are small anucleate cells (1-5 microns) circulating at roughly 200,000-400,000/microL with a 7-10 day lifespan, derived from marrow megakaryocytes under the control of thrombopoietin.

The platelet GPIb-IX-V complex binds exposed subendothelial von Willebrand factor to initiate adhesion, and signaling converts the GPIIb/IIIa integrin from a low-affinity to a high-affinity fibrinogen receptor that cross-links platelets into an aggregate.

Inflammation and infection transiently raise thrombotic risk: acute upper respiratory infection, bacterial and viral infections (including SARS-CoV-2, HIV, hepatitis C, dengue) are linked to increased myocardial infarction, stroke, and VTE.
Roughly 5-8% of the U.S. population carries a genetic risk factor predisposing to venous thrombosis, and multiple risk factors frequently coexist in a single patient.
Cancer confers an approximately fourfold increased risk of VTE compared with the general population, and VTE in cancer patients is associated with reduced survival.

Although factor V Leiden and the prothrombin G20210A mutation are established risk factors for DVT and PE, their contribution to arterial thrombotic events such as acute coronary syndromes is not well established.

Assuming hypercoagulable (thrombophilic) states that drive venous thrombosis are equally important for arterial events; their role in acute coronary syndromes is poorly defined and often not clinically significant.
Genotyping to optimize aspirin therapy is not currently clinically indicated, as ex vivo studies have not firmly established a pharmacogenetic interaction between aspirin and COX1.

Over-relying on CYP2C19 genotype for clopidogrel decisions, since loss-of-function alleles explain only a small fraction (about 5-12%) of antiplatelet response variability and genetics do not appreciably affect outcomes with prasugrel or ticagrelor.
Forgetting that up to 10% of venous thromboembolic events occur outside the lower extremities and lungs.
Treating many older single-gene thrombophilia associations as definitive when larger contemporary studies have called several into question.

Thrombosis is a major cause of morbidity and mortality. Coronary disease and stroke account for a large share of deaths; arterial thrombosis underlies most acute MI, ischemic stroke, and limb gangrene. For VTE, up to 30% of patients die within 30 days, about one-fifth experience sudden death from PE, and roughly 30% develop recurrent VTE within 10 years. The ARIC study reported a 9% 28-day fatality from DVT and 15% from PE; cancer-associated PE carries about 25% fatality. Incidence of first DVT rises sharply with age (from about 2-3 per 10,000 person-years at 30-49 years to about 20 per 10,000 at 70-79 years). Increasing age, obesity, malignancy, and acute extremity paresis independently predict recurrence.

In atherosclerotic PAD, segmental plaques with calcium deposition, medial thinning, patchy loss of muscle and elastic fibers, fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina, and platelet-fibrin thrombi narrow large and medium vessels, preferentially at branch points where turbulence, altered shear stress, and intimal injury occur. Principal sites are the abdominal aorta/iliac arteries (about 30% of symptomatic patients), femoral/popliteal arteries (80-90%), and tibial/peroneal vessels (40-50%); distal disease predominates in the elderly and in diabetics. Hemodynamically significant stenoses lower distal systolic pressure (reflected in a reduced ABI). During exercise, vasodilation distal to a stenosis drops perfusion pressure below interstitial tissue pressure generated by working muscle, producing claudication. Buerger disease shows early neutrophilic infiltration of vessel walls with a preserved internal elastic lamina and a cellular inflammatory luminal thrombus, evolving to mononuclear/giant-cell infiltration, then perivascular fibrosis, organized thrombus, and recanalization. Raynaud phenomenon reflects digital arterial vasospasm; inherited erythromelalgia involves gain-of-function SCN9A (Nav1.7 sodium channel) mutations in sensory/sympathetic nerves.

Peripheral artery disease (PAD) means stenosis or occlusion of the aorta or limb arteries; atherosclerosis is the dominant cause in patients over 40, while thrombosis, embolism, vasculitis, fibromuscular dysplasia, entrapment, cystic adventitial disease, and trauma account for the remainder.

Acute limb ischemia is sudden cessation of limb blood flow most often from cardiac embolism (atrial fibrillation, MI, ventricular aneurysm, endocarditis, prosthetic valves, atrial myxoma), in-situ thrombosis, dissection, or trauma; emboli lodge at bifurcations, most commonly the femoral artery in the leg.

Atheroembolism (cholesterol/fibrin/platelet debris from proximal plaque or aneurysm) classically spares large vessels, so distal pulses remain palpable; it causes the painful 'blue toe' syndrome, livedo reticularis, and may show cholesterol crystals on skin or muscle biopsy.

Raynaud phenomenon is episodic digital ischemia with sequential pallor (vasospasm), cyanosis (deoxygenated blood in dilated capillaries), and rubor (reactive hyperemia) after cold or emotional stress; over half of cases are primary/idiopathic, with women affected roughly five times more often and onset typically between ages 20 and 40.

Risk factors mirror those for coronary and cerebral atherosclerosis: cigarette smoking, diabetes mellitus, hypercholesterolemia, elevated lipoprotein(a), hypertension, and renal insufficiency; prevalence is similar between sexes but greater in Black than non-Hispanic white persons and in lower socioeconomic groups.

More than half of PAD patients are asymptomatic; the classic symptom is intermittent claudication (pain, ache, cramp, numbness, or fatigue in muscle that appears with exertion and resolves with rest), and the symptomatic muscle group lies distal to the obstructing lesion (e.g., buttock/hip/thigh with aortoiliac disease, calf with femoral-popliteal disease).

Chronic limb-threatening ischemia produces rest pain or a cold/numb foot that worsens at night when legs are horizontal and improves with dependency; signs include hair loss, thickened nails, shiny atrophic skin, coolness, pallor or cyanosis, and ultimately ulcers or gangrene.

Ankle-brachial index (ABI) is the key noninvasive test: normal 1.00-1.40, borderline 0.91-0.99, and abnormal/diagnostic of PAD at 0.90 or below; values above 1.40 indicate noncompressible, calcified vessels (as in diabetes or chronic kidney disease).
When the ABI is unreliable because of medial calcification, a toe-brachial index of 0.70 or below is considered abnormal and supports the diagnosis.

A drop in ABI immediately after treadmill exercise helps confirm PAD when resting findings are equivocal; MRA, CTA, and catheter angiography are reserved for revascularization planning, not routine diagnosis.

Fibromuscular dysplasia is a non-inflammatory hyperplastic arteriopathy of medium and small (sometimes large) arteries, predominant in women, classically renal and carotid/vertebral, with a multifocal 'string of beads' or focal pattern, and can cause stenosis, dissection, aneurysm, or thrombosis.

Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease) is an inflammatory occlusive disorder of distal small and medium arteries and veins, strongly linked to tobacco, typically in men under 40, presenting with a triad of distal claudication, Raynaud phenomenon, and migratory superficial thrombophlebitis; brachial and popliteal pulses are normal while distal pulses are reduced or absent.
Relying on the ABI in calcified, noncompressible vessels (ABI above 1.40) where it falsely appears normal or high; use the toe-brachial index instead.
Ordering routine MRA/CTA/angiography for diagnosis when history, examination, and ABI usually suffice and imaging is meant for revascularization planning.
Confusing atheroembolic digital ischemia (often one or two digits, palpable distal pulses) with Raynaud phenomenon.
Mistaking acrocyanosis for Raynaud phenomenon; acrocyanosis is persistent rather than episodic, extends proximally from the digits, and lacks a blanching phase.
Missing the strong tobacco link in Buerger disease and overlooking it in young male smokers presenting with distal ischemia and Raynaud features.
Overlooking secondary causes of Raynaud (scleroderma, SLE, blood dyscrasias, drugs, vibration injury) and labeling the disease primary prematurely.
Failing to perform provocative maneuvers in suspected thoracic outlet or popliteal entrapment syndromes, where the resting examination is often normal.
Applying massage, ice water, or extreme heat to frostbite, which are contraindicated; rewarming should use a 40-44 C water bath.

PAD natural history is driven largely by coexisting coronary and cerebrovascular disease: roughly one-third to one-half of symptomatic patients have clinical/ECG evidence of CAD and over half have significant disease on coronary angiography. PAD carries a 15-25% 5-year mortality and a two- to fourfold increased risk of cardiovascular death, with the highest mortality in those with most severe disease. Over 5 years the ABI worsens in nearly 40% and symptoms progress in about 20-25%; roughly 11% of symptomatic patients ultimately develop chronic limb-threatening ischemia, and without revascularization about 25% of those with chronic limb-threatening ischemia undergo amputation within a year. Prognosis is worse in continued smokers and diabetics. In thromboangiitis obliterans the outlook is worse in continued smokers and remains discouraging even after cessation. Primary Raynaud disease is generally mild, with fewer than 1% losing part of a digit, spontaneous improvement in about 15%, and progression in about 30%; primary acrocyanosis and benign livedo reticularis have favorable outcomes without ulceration or gangrene.
Rest pain, ulceration, or gangrene indicating chronic limb-threatening ischemia
Sudden severe pain, paresthesia, numbness, coldness, pallor, and pulselessness within an hour signaling acute limb ischemia
Paralysis, loss of sensation, and absent Doppler signal in both arteries and veins, marking a nonviable limb requiring amputation
Blue toe syndrome with progressive digital necrosis suggesting ongoing atheroembolism
Ischemic fingertip ulcers progressing to gangrene and autoamputation in scleroderma-associated Raynaud
Subclavian/axillary vein thrombosis (Paget-Schroetter) in venous thoracic outlet syndrome
High-output cardiac failure and cardiomegaly from a large arteriovenous fistula

PAD severity is graded hemodynamically by ABI: normal 1.00-1.40, borderline 0.91-0.99, abnormal/diagnostic at 0.90 or below, and noncompressible above 1.40 (toe-brachial index 0.70 or below abnormal). Clinically the spectrum runs from asymptomatic disease, to intermittent claudication, to chronic limb-threatening ischemia (rest pain, ulceration, gangrene). Acute limb ischemia is assessed for limb viability by presence of sensation, motor function, and Doppler-detectable arterial and venous flow; loss of all three defines a nonviable limb.
