chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: These arthritides share the theme of an underlying systemic disorder injuring joints rather than a primary autoimmune synovitis. In acromegaly, excess growth hormone and IGF-I stimulate cartilage, periarticular connective tissue, and bone, producing hypertrophic then degenerating cartilage that is prone to fissuring, with ligamentous laxity worsening joint discomfort. In hemochromatosis, parenchymal iron deposition damages cartilage: iron catalyzes superoxide-dependent lipid peroxidation, interferes with collagen formation, increases lysosomal enzyme release from synovium, and inhibits synovial pyrophosphatase, favoring chondrocalcinosis. Hemophilic arthropathy results from repeated intraarticular bleeding; blood persists because intrinsic clotting factors and tissue thromboplastin are absent in the synovium, and recurrent hemarthrosis leads to chronic noninflammatory fibrotic joints. Sickle cell musculoskeletal disease stems from vasoocclusion and marrow/cortical bone infarction, splenic dysfunction predisposing to osteomyelitis and septic arthritis, and avascular necrosis (notably femoral head); marrow hyperplasia widens medullary cavities and thins cortices. In neuropathic joints, loss of deep pain/proprioception plus dysregulated autonomic blood flow leads to bone resorption, repeated microtrauma, ligament tears, and fractures with progressive disorganization. HOA pathogenesis centers on circulating cells/platelet particles and growth factors (PDGF, VEGF) bypassing pulmonary clearance and stimulating peripheral connective tissue and periosteal proliferation, with endothelial activation reflected by elevated von Willebrand factor antigen.

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: Acromegaly drives an osteoarthritis-like picture from growth hormone/IGF-I overstimulation of cartilage and bone; prominent wrist involvement (unusual for primary OA), early radiographic joint-space WIDENING from cartilage hypertrophy, carpal tunnel syndrome in roughly half, and Raynaud phenomenon in about a third.

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: Achilles tendinitis and migratory large-joint arthritis can be the first clinical sign of familial hypercholesterolemia, preceding the appearance of tendinous xanthomas; synovial fluid is noninflammatory and crystal-negative.

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: Neuropathic (Charcot) joint disease arises from loss of pain sensation and/or proprioception with impaired protective reflexes; diabetes mellitus is the most frequent cause, classically affecting the tarsal and tarsometatarsal joints.

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy combines digital clubbing with periosteal new-bone formation; secondary HOA points to intrathoracic malignancy, suppurative/hypoxemic lung disease, congenital heart disease, or hepatopulmonary disease and may precede the underlying illness.

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: In hemochromatosis, arthropathy may be the FIRST clinical clue: degenerative-type involvement that characteristically starts at the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints (joints generally spared by routine OA), often with hooklike MCP osteophytes and frequent calcium pyrophosphate deposition.

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: An early hemochromatosis diagnosis is suggested by a high serum transferrin saturation, which is more sensitive than ferritin elevation; dominant 2nd/3rd MCP findings warrant ferritin and iron/total iron-binding capacity testing.

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: Hemophilic recurrent spontaneous hemarthrosis (factor VIII or IX deficiency) typically begins after age 1 when the child walks/runs and targets knees, ankles, elbows, shoulders, and hips, progressing to chronic fibrotic deforming arthropathy.

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: Hemarthrosis is characteristic of hemophilia but NOT of von Willebrand disease, factor V deficiency, oral anticoagulation, or thrombocytopenia.

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: Low-grade temperature can accompany acute hemarthrosis, but fever above 38.3 C (101 F) should raise concern for joint infection and prompt aspiration; clotting factor should be corrected before arthrocentesis.

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: Sickle cell dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome) in children under 5 produces diffuse swelling/tenderness of hands and feet from marrow and cortical bone infarction and is rarely seen after age 5; it generally resolves without residual damage.

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: Distinguishing osteomyelitis from bone infarction in sickle cell disease is clinically difficult; Salmonella is a notably associated cause of osteomyelitis, whereas S. aureus and Streptococcus are the more common organisms in sickle cell septic arthritis.

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: Up to ~40% of sickle cell patients are hyperuricemic (urate overproduction plus interstitial renal disease) and can develop acute, sometimes polyarticular, gouty arthritis; arthrocentesis distinguishes gout from infection or synovial infarction.

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: Attributing acromegalic or hemochromatotic arthropathy to ordinary osteoarthritis and missing the atypical joint distribution (wrist; 2nd/3rd MCP) that should prompt endocrine or iron-overload workup.

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: Relying on ferritin alone for early hemochromatosis when transferrin saturation is the more sensitive marker.

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: Mistaking acute hemarthrosis for septic arthritis (or vice versa) in hemophilia; failing to correct clotting factor before aspirating.

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: Aspirating a hemophilic intramuscular cyst, which can provoke further bleeding (relatively contraindicated unless secondarily infected, and then only after factor repletion).

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: Using a technetium bone scan to try to separate osteomyelitis from neuropathic arthritis, since uptake is increased in both.

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: Overlooking that nonselective NSAIDs impair platelet function and should be avoided where feasible in hemophilic bleeding.

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: Treating isolated clubbing as benign and missing an associated malignancy or lung/cardiac disease.

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: Outcomes are determined largely by the underlying disorder. Acromegalic joint pain may persist even after the acromegaly is treated. In hemochromatosis, established arthritis and chondrocalcinosis often progress despite phlebotomy. Hemophilic hemarthrosis usually resolves with joint function returning to baseline over about two weeks, but recurrent bleeding causes chronic fibrotic, flexion-deformed, function-limiting arthropathy. Sickle cell dactylitis resolves without residual damage, but avascular necrosis (about 5% femoral head involvement) and osteomyelitis carry greater morbidity. Neuropathic joints can disorganize rapidly and are largely unaffected by treating the underlying disease; early recognition and offloading of a diabetic Charcot foot can prevent severe disease. In primary HOA, symptoms typically disappear on reaching adulthood.

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: Fever above 38.3 C (101 F) with an acute hemarthrosis in hemophilia, suggesting joint infection

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: Femoral neuropathy from iliopsoas hematoma in hemophilia (hip held in flexion with preserved rotation)

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: Diabetic foot with callus/ulcer over metatarsal heads progressing to infected ulcer and osteomyelitis

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: Rapidly disorganizing (Charcot) joint developing over weeks with pain disproportionately mild for the degree of destruction

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: New digital clubbing or HOA, which may signal occult intrathoracic malignancy

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: Statin-associated rising muscle enzymes raising concern for necrotizing autoimmune myopathy

chunks.diseaseName: Arthritis Associated with Systemic Disease, and Other Arthritides
chunks.text: No single formal grading scheme; severity is judged by the staging of the underlying arthropathy. Hemophilic arthropathy progresses radiographically from capsular distention, to juxtaarticular osteopenia with marginal erosions and subchondral cysts, to late joint-space narrowing with osteoarthritis-like bony overgrowth. Neuropathic arthritis evolves from early osteoarthritis-like changes (joint-space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, osteophytes, effusions) to marked destructive/hypertrophic disorganization. HOA progresses from periostitis with a radiolucent zone between new periosteal bone and cortex to multilayered cortical thickening.

These taxonomically diverse zoonotic RNA viruses (Togaviridae/Alphavirus; Flaviviridae/Orthoflavivirus; the bunyaviricete families Arenaviridae, Hantaviridae, Nairoviridae, Peribunyaviridae, Phenuiviridae; Orthomyxoviridae; Bornaviridae and Rhabdoviridae; and the reovirus families) circulate in nature between arthropod vectors (mosquitoes, ticks, sandflies, midges) or chronically infected rodents and vertebrate reservoirs. Arboviruses establish chronic systemic infection of the vector after a blood meal and reach the salivary glands during extrinsic incubation (1-3 weeks in mosquitoes); vertical transovarial transmission also maintains some viruses. In arboviral encephalitis, an initial lymphoid-origin viremia seeds multifocal CNS entry, presumably via olfactory neuroepithelium/cribriform plate or brain capillary endothelium; CNS injury results partly from direct neuronal infection and partly from edema, inflammation, and host immune response, with focal neuronal necrosis, glial nodules, and perivascular lymphoid cuffing. LCM meningitis is T-cell-mediated immunopathology. VHF agents share a core pathophysiology of disrupted vascular function, stability, and integrity producing multisystem organ dysfunction and capillary leak; in HPS, widespread pulmonary capillary leak with depressed cardiac output produces noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and shock.

Most arthropod-borne (arbovirus) and rodent-borne zoonotic viral infections in humans are subclinical or unrecognized; humans are usually accidental, dead-end hosts and are not important amplifiers of these viruses (Harrison 22e p.1664-1665).

Lassa fever: most Lassa virus infections are subclinical or mild, onset is gradual (characteristic of mammarenavirus VHFs), and overt hemorrhage occurs in only about 15-30% of patients; about 30% of survivors develop sensorineural deafness (Harrison 22e p.1675-1676).

Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is the most significant VHF today, with over 100,000 severe cases annually in Asia; major agents are Hantaan (Eastern Asia), Dobrava (the Balkans), and Puumala (Europe) (Harrison 22e p.1676).

Arboviral CNS disease can leave residual deficits; spinal/motor-neuron (poliomyelitis-like) disease has been documented after West Nile virus and Japanese encephalitis virus infection, and difficulty concentrating, fatigability, tremor, and personality change are common during recovery (Harrison 22e p.1671).

Recognized illness usually falls into one of five overlapping syndromic categories: fever and myalgia (F&M), arthritis and rash (A&R), encephalitis, pulmonary disease, and viral hemorrhagic fever (VHF); a single virus may cause several of these (Harrison 22e p.1664-1665).

Fever and myalgia is by far the most common and most benign syndrome, with abrupt fever, chills, intense myalgia, malaise, anorexia, and headache with photophobia/retroorbital pain; true arthritis is absent and physical findings are minimal (Harrison 22e p.1665-1666).

A history of tick bite has more diagnostic significance than a history of mosquito exposure; clinical and epidemiologic clues may allow presumptive diagnosis in epidemics, but laboratory confirmation is required in all cases (Harrison 22e p.1664).

Arthropod vectors acquire arboviruses from viremic vertebrate blood meals; the virus must disseminate to the salivary glands (extrinsic incubation, typically 1-3 weeks in mosquitoes) before the vector can transmit; transovarial transmission to progeny is an alternative maintenance mechanism (Harrison 22e p.1664).

Rodent-borne viruses are maintained by chronically infected rodents; humans are typically infected by inhalation of or contact with aerosolized rodent excreta/secreta, and most show a high degree of rodent-virus specificity (Harrison 22e p.1664).

Lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) is acquired from the house mouse and classically causes a biphasic illness with a febrile phase followed by a CNS (meningeal) phase; patients with neuroinvasive LCM, including frank encephalitis, almost always recover fully, but the virus can cause fetal microcephaly and has been transmitted by organ transplantation (Harrison 22e p.1666-1667).

Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) begins after a 2-3 week incubation with a nonspecific 3-4 day prodrome, then rapidly progresses to noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and hypoxemic respiratory failure; coincident thrombocytopenia, circulating immunoblasts (atypical lymphocytes), and a left shift are considered almost diagnostic (Harrison 22e p.1673).

In suspected HPS, aggressive IV fluid resuscitation is hazardous because of widespread capillary leak and depressed cardiac output; management is hemodynamic/respiratory support, with ECMO for the most critically ill (Harrison 22e p.1673).

Anchoring on the most severe known phenotype of a virus; many agents most commonly cause mild F&M rather than their eponymous severe disease (e.g., West Nile, Venezuelan equine encephalitis, Rift Valley fever).
Treating the F&M syndrome as benign and self-limited without watching for evolution into A&R, neuroinvasive, pulmonary, or VHF syndromes for which it can be a prodrome.
Using acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) in these febrile illnesses, given the risk of exacerbated bleeding and Reye syndrome.
Giving aggressive IV fluids in HPS, which worsens noncardiogenic pulmonary edema because of capillary leak and depressed cardiac output.
Relying on a negative CSF RT-PCR to exclude arboviral encephalitis; viruses generally cannot be isolated from blood or CSF and RT-PCR cannot rule out the diagnosis.
Misreading the gradual onset of mammarenavirus VHF (Lassa, Argentinian/Bolivian) and expecting prominent early hemorrhage, which is often absent or late.
Treating a single positive heterotypic IgG cross-reaction as diagnostic in HPS serology given very low background seroprevalence.
Overlooking person-to-person/nosocomial transmission risk (Lassa virus, Andes virus, mammarenaviruses) and sexual transmission during early convalescence.

Outcome depends heavily on syndrome and specific virus. The F&M syndrome generally resolves completely within 2-5 days, though prolonged asthenia may follow LCMV or dengue infection. A&R illness resolves over days, but joint pain/arthritis may persist for months to years without deformity. Encephalitis ranges from full recovery (often slow, over weeks to months) to permanent deficits or death. HPS carries a case-fatality rate of approximately 30-40% even with appropriate care, though most patients surviving the first 48 hours of hospitalization recover without long-term sequelae. Argentinian and Bolivian hemorrhagic fevers can reach case-fatality rates over 50% in individual outbreaks. About 20% of Lassa virus infections become Lassa fever; survivors have roughly a 30% rate of (usually bilateral) sensorineural deafness, and pregnancy markedly worsens prognosis.
Altered mental status, seizures, focal neurologic signs, or coma indicating neuroinvasive disease
New dry cough, tachypnea, hypoxemia, and early pulmonary edema heralding the HPS cardiopulmonary phase
Hypotension, hemoconcentration, and marked thrombocytopenia with left shift
Mucosal/overt hemorrhage, marked thrombocytopenia, and CNS dysfunction in suspected VHF
CNS features, facial/neck edema, hypotension, hemorrhage, or jaundice in Lassa fever (markers of fatal outcome)
Pregnancy, especially the last trimester, in Lassa fever (very high case fatality and ~90% fetal death)
Oliguria and rising creatinine signaling acute kidney injury in HPS/VHF
Marked confusion, tremor, and cerebellar signs in South American mammarenavirus hemorrhagic fevers

No single unified severity scale; severity is framed by syndrome. The five-syndrome heuristic (F&M, arthritis and rash, encephalitis, pulmonary disease, viral hemorrhagic fever) stratifies expected severity, with F&M most benign and encephalitis/pulmonary/VHF most severe. Encephalitis severity grades clinically from asymptomatic through febrile headache and aseptic meningitis to full encephalitis with coma. HPS is staged by progression from nonspecific prodrome to the cardiopulmonary phase with respiratory failure and shock. Lassa fever severity/fatality is predicted by high viral load, high serum creatinine and AST, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, CNS features, face/neck swelling, hypotension, hemorrhage, jaundice, and pregnancy.

chunks.text: Ingested Ascaris eggs hatch in the small intestine; larvae penetrate the gut wall, travel via the portal circulation to the liver and then the lungs, break into the alveoli, ascend the tracheobronchial tree, are swallowed, and mature into large adult worms in the small intestine. The pulmonary phase provokes an eosinophilic hypersensitivity reaction. In the gut, large numbers of worms can form a bolus that obstructs the lumen, and individual worms may migrate into the biliary tree, pancreatic duct or appendix, producing obstructive and inflammatory complications. Chronic infection contributes to malabsorption and nutritional deficits.

Aspergillus is a ubiquitous hyaline septate branching mold whose conidia (spores) are inhaled from indoor/outdoor air; only species growing at 37C cause invasive disease. Disease form depends on host immunity. Invasive disease arises with profound neutropenia, glucocorticoid use, phagocyte dysfunction (CGD, advanced HIV, relapsed leukemia) and underlying respiratory disease, with angioinvasion and hemorrhagic infarction; from the lungs (>80% of cases) it may disseminate hematogenously (most often to brain). Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis occurs in apparently immunocompetent hosts with prior lung disease and a suboptimal TH1-like inflammatory response. Allergic forms (ABPA, SAFS) reflect a TH2-like hypersensitivity response to A. fumigatus, classically complicating asthma and cystic fibrosis. Multiple gene variants underlie susceptibility to each form (Harrison 22e p.1713-1714).
A. fumigatus causes most invasive aspergillosis, >95% of chronic aspergillosis, and most allergic syndromes; only species that grow at 37C cause invasive infection (Harrison 22e p.1713)

HEPA filtration is often protective and should be installed and monitored in operating rooms, burn units, and areas housing high-risk patients; hospital outbreaks usually relate to a contaminated air source or construction (Harrison 22e p.1713)

The disease spectrum spans three categories: invasive (acute/subacute in the immunocompromised), chronic/saprophytic (chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis, aspergilloma/fungal ball), and allergic (ABPA, severe asthma with fungal sensitization, allergic fungal rhinosinusitis) (Harrison 22e p.1713, 1714)

Invasive aspergillosis is one of the most common diagnostic errors revealed at autopsy; keys to early diagnosis are a high index of suspicion, circulating antigen screening (in leukemia), and urgent thoracic CT (Harrison 22e p.1714)

On thoracic CT the halo sign (ground-glass hemorrhagic infarction around a nodule/consolidation) appears for ~7 days early in neutropenic patients and is a good prognostic feature reflecting early diagnosis; the air-crescent/cavitation appears later (Harrison 22e p.1716)

Galactomannan antigen detection on respiratory samples (e.g., tracheobronchial/BAL fluid) is more sensitive than serum and is critical in ventilated/ICU patients where radiology is nonspecific; positive serum antigen usually precedes clinical or radiologic features by several days (Harrison 22e p.1714, 1716)

Antigen, beta-D-glucan, and real-time PCR are faster and far more sensitive than culture, as only 10-30% of invasive aspergillosis cases yield a positive culture; antifungal therapy reduces antigen sensitivity (Harrison 22e p.1716)

Aspergillus IgG antibody is detectable in ~90% of chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis and ~65% of Aspergillus nodules; ABPA is diagnosed by Aspergillus-specific IgE (or positive skin-prick test) plus elevated total IgE, usually >1000 IU/mL (Harrison 22e p.1714, 1715)

Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis follows pulmonary tuberculosis in ~6-13% of treated cases and is often initially mistaken for tuberculosis; >90% of chronic cavitary cases occur in patients with prior lung disease (Harrison 22e p.1713, 1715)

On tissue histology Aspergillus hyphae are hyaline, narrow, and septate with branching at 45 degrees; angioinvasion with vascular invasion by hyphae is characteristic in neutropenia (Harrison 22e p.1716)
Requesting only bacterial culture rather than fungal culture may miss the diagnosis (bacterial agar is less sensitive); only 10-30% of invasive cases have a positive culture
Fluconazole is commonly used for prophylaxis but has NO activity against Aspergillus species
No prophylactic regimen is completely successful
Antifungal therapy reduces the sensitivity of antigen detection
Aspergillus IgG may not be positive on initial testing in subacute/nonneutropenic invasive disease
A positive respiratory culture may represent only noninvasive disease or airway colonization, not invasion
Contrast CT of the brain is often contraindicated by poor renal function and unenhanced CT is usually nonspecific; MRI is the most useful immediate investigation for cerebral disease
Surgery is problematic in chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis and often causes serious complications; bronchial artery embolization is preferred for problematic hemoptysis

Invasive aspergillosis is curable if immune reconstitution occurs, whereas allergic and chronic forms are not curable. Mortality of invasive aspergillosis is 30-70% if treated but ~100% if the diagnosis is missed; cerebral aspergillosis, Aspergillus endocarditis, bilateral extensive invasive pulmonary disease, late-stage AIDS, relapsed uncontrolled leukemia, and liver failure carry very poor outcomes. Untreated chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis causes clinical deterioration in ~70%; with antifungal treatment mortality is 15-20% in the first year, ~40% over 5 years, and 50-60% over 10 years, with treatment failure in ~30% (more with azole resistance). ABPA/SAFS respond to glucocorticoids and antifungals (~60% to itraconazole, ~80% to voriconazole/posaconazole) but relapse after discontinuation is common (Harrison 22e p.1717).
Life-threatening / massive hemoptysis (the most significant complication of chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis and may be the presenting manifestation)
Neurologic deterioration: mood change, focal signs, seizures, declining mental status suggesting cerebral aspergillosis (hemorrhagic infarction/abscess)

By disease category: INVASIVE (acute course <=1 month, subacute 1-3 months) - angioinvasive/nonangioinvasive/granulomatous pulmonary, invasive sinusitis, tracheobronchitis, disseminated, cerebral, endocarditis, cutaneous, keratitis/endophthalmitis. CHRONIC - chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis, chronic fibrosing pulmonary aspergillosis (destroyed lung), Aspergillus bronchitis, Aspergillus nodule, chronic invasive and chronic granulomatous sinusitis. SAPROPHYTIC - aspergilloma (single fungal ball), airway colonization, maxillary sinus fungal ball. ALLERGIC - ABPA, severe asthma with fungal sensitization (SAFS), allergic fungal rhinosinusitis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis (Harrison 22e p.1714-1715).

Asthma is characterized by episodic, usually reversible airway obstruction with airway hyperresponsiveness, generally accompanied by airway inflammation (most often eosinophilic, sometimes neutrophilic, occasionally with no obvious inflammation). Exacerbations are episodes of acute bronchospasm driven by luminal narrowing from airway smooth-muscle constriction, airway edema and mucus secretion, superimposed on chronic airway inflammation. Triggers activate mast cells/basophils and inflammatory cells (releasing bronchoconstrictors and mediators) and stimulate sensory nerves acting on smooth muscle. Allergen exposure can cause an immediate (early) bronchospasm and a late response 2-24 h later with airway narrowing and inflammation. Structural airway-wall thickening (smooth-muscle hypertrophy/hyperplasia, subepithelial collagen deposition, edema, mucosal inflammation) increases the tendency to narrow disproportionately. In severe airflow obstruction there may be air trapping with dynamically elevated FRC and increased residual volume; mild hypoxemia from ventilation-perfusion mismatch (oxygen-responsive) is common (p.2216-2217, p.2221, p.2222-2223).
An exacerbation is an episode of acute bronchospasm that may be severe enough to require emergency care or hospitalization and can be fatal (p.2216).
During an acute attack patients typically show tachypnea, tachycardia and accessory-muscle use, with wheezing and a prolonged expiratory phase (p.2222).
As airway obstruction worsens the chest may become 'silent' with loss of breath sounds, indicating a more dangerous attack rather than improvement (p.2222).
Most patients in an attack are hypocapnic from a high respiratory rate; a normal or near-normal PaCO2 in a distressed asthmatic signals impending respiratory failure (p.2227).
PEFR, FEV1 and FEV1/FVC are reduced in obstruction, but these may appear normal during an attack or after recent bronchodilator use, so a normal value does not exclude severe disease (p.2222-2223).

In urgent care, PEFR/FEV1 should be measured; patients with PEFR >60% predicted often respond to beta2-agonists alone, whereas failure to reach >60% or persistent severe tachypnea over 4-6 h should prompt hospital admission (p.2227).
Severe exacerbations requiring systemic corticosteroids may themselves accelerate long-term lung-function decline (p.2221).
More than one-third of patients carrying a physician diagnosis of asthma do not actually meet diagnostic criteria, so consider mimics when an 'asthmatic' fails to respond (p.2222).
Some patients cannot distinguish an anxiety attack from an asthma attack, which can confound assessment of an apparent exacerbation (p.2222).
Interpreting a 'silent chest' or quieting wheeze as improvement when it actually signals worsening, life-threatening obstruction (p.2222).
Being reassured by a normal/normalizing PaCO2 - in a distressed asthmatic this is an ominous sign of impending respiratory failure, not stability (p.2227).
Relying on PFT/PEF values that may look normal during an attack or shortly after bronchodilator use (p.2222-2223).
Overlooking mimics such as vocal-cord dysfunction, heart failure or COPD in 'difficult' or treatment-refractory presentations - over one-third of diagnosed asthmatics do not meet criteria (p.2222).
Missing precipitants such as beta-blockers (including ophthalmic drops), aspirin/NSAIDs in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, or ACE-inhibitor cough (p.2221).
Giving antibiotics routinely in an exacerbation - they should be used only if there are signs of infection (p.2227).

Asthma causes significant morbidity and mortality; roughly 3000-4000 people die from asthma each year in the United States. Death can occur even in mild asthma (at lower rates than severe asthma). Mortality in patients over 65 is about five times that of younger cohorts. High-risk features for asthma death include prior ICU admission or intubation for asthma, illicit drug use, depression, a new diagnosis within the past year, two or more emergency visits in the past 6 months, severe psychosocial problems, lower socioeconomic status, and being on daily prednisone before admission. Severe exacerbations may accelerate long-term lung-function decline (p.2221, p.2227).
Silent chest with loss of breath sounds (life-threatening) (p.2222)
Normal or near-normal PaCO2 in a distressed asthmatic, or a rising PaCO2 - signals impending respiratory failure and possible need for mechanical ventilation (p.2227)
Respiratory exhaustion / failure to respond to repeated beta2-agonists (p.2227)
Failure to achieve PEFR >60% predicted or persistent severe tachypnea over 4-6 h (warrants admission) (p.2227)
Need for hourly beta2-agonists for several hours despite treatment (p.2227)
Status asthmaticus: severe attack in which mechanical ventilation is difficult due to high airway resistance/pressures (p.2227)

Harrison stratifies acute deteriorations practically rather than by a fixed table. Mild-to-moderate deteriorations can initially be managed with frequent beta2-agonists; failure to control with hourly beta2-agonists for several hours warrants urgent care. In urgent/ED care, PEFR or FEV1 guides severity: PEFR >60% predicted usually responds to beta2-agonists alone, whereas failure to reach PEFR >60% or persistent severe tachypnea over 4-6 h indicates a severe attack needing admission. Life-threatening / near-fatal features include silent chest, respiratory exhaustion, and a normal or rising PaCO2 signaling impending respiratory failure; status asthmaticus denotes a severe refractory attack with high airway resistance making ventilation difficult (p.2227).

Ataxia results from dysfunction of the cerebellum and the pathways connecting it to the rest of the nervous system, including the spinocerebellar tracts and the frontopontocerebellar pathway arising in the rostral frontal lobe. In the inherited polyglutamine spinocerebellar ataxias, expanded CAG triplet repeats produce mutant ataxin proteins with abnormally long polyglutamine tracts (generally toxic beyond ~40 glutamines); these proteins misfold into beta-pleated aggregates, are abnormally transported into the nucleus, bind and impair other polyglutamine proteins such as TATA-binding protein and CREB-binding protein, disrupt the ubiquitin-proteasome protein-turnover system, and trigger neuronal apoptosis, yielding a relatively disease-specific pattern of neuronal loss and gliosis. Longer repeats correlate with earlier onset and more aggressive disease across generations (anticipation). In Friedreich's ataxia, an expanded GAA repeat in the first intron of the frataxin gene silences frataxin expression; frataxin is a mitochondrial protein involved in iron homeostasis, so its loss causes mitochondrial iron accumulation, deficiency of iron-sulfur cluster enzymes, reduced ATP production, oxidative injury, and irreversible cell death, with predominant degeneration of the spinal cord (spinocerebellar tracts, lateral corticospinal tracts, posterior columns), dorsal root ganglia, and peripheral nerves.

The core ataxic syndrome is gait impairment, scanning (unclear) speech, blurred vision from nystagmus, limb incoordination, and tremor on movement, reflecting disease of the cerebellum and its afferent/efferent pathways including the spinocerebellar and frontopontocerebellar tracts (p.3533).

Retinal pigmentary degeneration (blue-yellow color blindness progressing to macular degeneration and visual loss) is the distinguishing feature of SCA7 among the spinocerebellar ataxias (p.3535-3536).

Episodic ataxia type 1 causes brief (minutes-long) attacks of ataxia with myokymia and nystagmus, while type 2 produces longer attacks lasting hours to days; type 2 stems from CACNA1A mutations (the same calcium-channel gene as SCA6 and familial hemiplegic migraine) (p.3536).
A treatable mimic to always exclude in chronic symmetric gait ataxia is hypothyroidism; infectious causes to consider include meningovascular syphilis/tabes dorsalis and Lyme disease (p.3534).

True cerebellar ataxia is an unsteady, imbalanced gait without vertigo, light-headedness, or sense of movement; vestibular/labyrinthine disorders by contrast produce gait disturbance accompanied by prominent dizziness (p.3533).

Sensory (proprioceptive) ataxia can mimic cerebellar imbalance but is distinguished because instability worsens markedly when visual input is removed (positive Romberg sign); rarely proximal leg weakness also mimics cerebellar disease (p.3533).

The tempo and pattern of onset guide etiology: gradual, bilateral, symmetric progression points to genetic, metabolic, immune, or toxic causes, whereas focal unilateral signs with headache and depressed consciousness, ipsilateral cranial nerve palsies, and contralateral weakness suggest a space-occupying cerebellar lesion (p.3533).

Acute, reversible symmetric ataxias commonly follow intoxication with alcohol, phenytoin, lithium, or barbiturates and exposures such as toluene, gasoline/glue sniffing, methyl mercury, or bismuth (p.3533-3534).

Subacute symmetric ataxia raises suspicion of alcoholic-nutritional vermal degeneration (thiamine/B12 deficiency), paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, immune-mediated ataxia, or a prion disorder (p.3533-3534).
Friedreich's ataxia is the most common inherited ataxia, accounting for about half of all hereditary ataxias, and is autosomal recessive (p.3536).

Friedreich's ataxia features onset before age 25 with progressive staggering gait, areflexia, extensor plantar responses, loss of vibratory/proprioceptive sensation, and frequently pes cavus and scoliosis (p.3536).

Among the dominant ataxias, the polyglutamine SCAs (SCA1, SCA2, SCA3/Machado-Joseph, SCA6, SCA7, SCA17) arise from expanded CAG triplet repeats; genotype, not phenotype, is the diagnostic gold standard because clinical pictures overlap (p.3534).
Mislabeling vestibular or sensory (proprioceptive) imbalance as cerebellar ataxia; absence of vertigo and a positive Romberg sign help distinguish them.
Overlooking readily treatable and reversible causes such as hypothyroidism, vitamin E/B1/B12 deficiency, and intoxications.
Relying on clinical phenotype alone to classify inherited ataxias, since SCA phenotypes overlap and genotype is the diagnostic gold standard.
In Machado-Joseph disease type I, the stiff broad-based lurching gait results from spasticity rather than true ataxia and lacks truncal titubation, which can be misread.
Failing to recognize an acute focal cerebellar lesion as a neurosurgical emergency because of herniation risk.
Forgetting that some SCAs have prominent non-cerebellar features (e.g., retinal degeneration in SCA7, parkinsonism/extrapyramidal signs in SCA1/SCA2, peripheral neuropathy in MJD type III).

Prognosis depends on cause: several acquired ataxias (intoxications, postinfectious ataxia, hypothyroidism, vitamin deficiencies) are reversible, whereas the inherited degenerative ataxias progress relentlessly. In Machado-Joseph disease (SCA3) deficits invariably progress to death from debilitation within about 15 years of onset (especially types I and II), with intellect usually preserved. Friedreich's ataxia has a median age of death around 35 years, and women have a significantly better prognosis than men. Larger triplet-repeat expansions correlate with earlier onset and more aggressive disease, and anticipation produces earlier, more severe disease in successive generations.
Acute focal ataxia with headache, depressed consciousness, and ipsilateral pontine/cranial nerve signs suggesting cerebellar infarction or hemorrhage with brainstem compression

Rapidly worsening focal cerebellar signs raising concern for posterior fossa hematoma, abscess, or tumor at risk of rostral (tentorial) or downward (foramen magnum/tonsillar) herniation, which can be devastating and may require emergent surgical decompression

Recurrent pulmonary infections and lymphoreticular malignancy risk in ataxia-telangiectasia

No single formal severity score is given; etiologic and temporal frameworks are used instead. Cerebellar ataxia is categorized as symmetric/progressive versus focal/ipsilateral, each subdivided by tempo into acute (hours to days), subacute (days to weeks), or chronic (months to years) per Table 450-1. Inherited ataxias are classified genomically by mode of inheritance: autosomal dominant (SCAs, DRPLA, episodic ataxias), autosomal recessive (Friedreich's ataxia, ataxia-telangiectasia, RFC1-related CANVAS), and mitochondrial. Machado-Joseph disease is further graded into clinical types I (ALS-parkinsonism-dystonia), II (ataxic, most common), and III (ataxic-amyotrophic).

chunks.text: Atopic dermatitis arises from the interplay of a defective epidermal barrier and a skewed type-2 immune response. Loss-of-function variants in the filaggrin gene and reduced barrier lipids increase transepidermal water loss and allow penetration of allergens and microbes. This drives activation of type-2 cytokines (including interleukins 4, 13, and 31) that promote inflammation, further barrier breakdown, and the sensation of itch. Scratching perpetuates an itch-scratch cycle, causing lichenification, and the barrier defect predisposes to colonisation and infection with Staphylococcus aureus and herpes simplex virus.

chunks.text: Multifocal atrial tachycardia (>=3 distinct P-wave morphologies with clear isoelectric intervals and a slower atrial rate than AF; typically in chronic pulmonary disease and acute illness) (p.1989).

Other supraventricular tachycardias including atrial flutter, focal atrial tachycardia, AV nodal reentry, and AV reciprocating tachycardia, distinguished by 12-lead ECG appearance and response to AV nodal blockade (p.1976-1977).
Preexcited (accessory-pathway) AF, presenting as an irregular wide-complex tachycardia with bizarre, beat-to-beat-variable QRS morphology (p.1985-1986).
Transesophageal echocardiography to exclude left atrial appendage thrombus before cardioversion when AF duration is >48 h or unknown (p.1992).
Cardiac CT angiography with delayed-acquisition imaging as an alternative to TEE for left atrial appendage thrombus detection, with high sensitivity and specificity (p.1992).
Ambulatory ECG monitoring, implantable loop recorders, or wearable/home ECG devices to capture intermittent or subclinical episodes (p.1991, 1993).

AF is characterized by disorganized, rapid, irregular atrial electrical activation with loss of organized atrial mechanical contraction; the AV node filters these impulses to produce an irregular ventricular rate. The pathophysiology is multifactorial and incompletely understood, with a proposed 'final common pathway' in which risk factors (age, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, diabetes, obesity, alcohol, sleep-disordered breathing) drive electrophysiologic changes in atrial tissue. Altered membrane channel regulation produces abnormal excitability; pulmonary vein musculature (and other foci such as the posterior left atrial wall, superior vena cava, coronary sinus, vein of Marshall) shows enhanced automaticity generating ectopic beats that initiate AF. Progressive cellular and tissue remodeling shortens atrial refractory periods and creates functional reentry, with eventual fibrosis and left atrial enlargement, explaining the typical progression from paroxysmal to persistent to long-standing persistent disease. Loss of atrial systole reduces cardiac output, and variable ventricular filling produces variable stroke volume (p.1990-1992).
AF is the most common sustained arrhythmia; prevalence rises steeply with age (~20% of those over 80), and the lifetime risk for a 40-year-old man is roughly one in four (p.1990).
On the ECG, AF shows absence of organized atrial activity (no P waves) with an irregularly irregular ventricular response; the chaotic atrial activity is often best seen in lead V1 (p.1990, 1991).

The conducted ventricular rate is variable and usually rapid (commonly 110-160/min), but may exceed 200/min, or be inappropriately slow when there is high vagal tone or AV nodal conduction disease (p.1990).
Many patients are unaware of the irregular heartbeat, so AF is frequently asymptomatic; absence of AF on intermittent monitoring does not establish low risk (p.1990, 1993).

AF is categorized by temporal pattern: paroxysmal (self-terminating, usually within 7 days), persistent (continuous >7 days but <1 year), and long-standing persistent (>1 year); these patterns correlate with progressive left atrial enlargement and scar burden (p.1990, 1991).

Stroke and bleeding risks are estimated as concepts using the CHA2DS2-VASc score (stroke risk: congestive heart failure, hypertension, age, diabetes, prior stroke/TIA, vascular disease, sex) and HAS-BLED score (bleeding risk), respectively (p.1993).

AF burden does not predict stroke risk; the approach to paroxysmal AF is the same as for persistent AF, and even apparently infrequent episodes carry risk because asymptomatic episodes are common (p.1993).
Subclinical AF detectable only on long-term continuous monitoring is associated with roughly 2.5-fold increased stroke risk (p.1993).
AF detected after cryptogenic stroke using insertable cardiac monitors in up to ~8.9% of patients within 6 months, supporting prolonged rhythm monitoring in this setting (p.1990).
Relying on AF burden or symptom frequency to gauge stroke risk is mistaken; anticoagulation decisions should rest on the risk-factor profile, not how often AF is documented (p.1993).
A normal intermittent monitor does not exclude clinically important AF, since asymptomatic episodes are common (p.1993).

Cardioverting AF of >48 h (or unknown) duration without anticoagulation or thrombus exclusion risks thromboembolism, which can occur even days later because of post-conversion atrial stunning (delayed recovery of mechanical function) (p.1992).
Nonvalvular AF (AF without mitral stenosis) differs in management from valvular AF; rheumatic mitral stenosis and mechanical valves carry especially high thromboembolic risk (p.1993).

AF is not benign: it carries a 1.5- to 1.9-fold increased mortality after adjusting for underlying cardiac disease, and causes approximately 25% of all strokes. It increases the risk of dementia, MRI-detected silent embolic infarcts, congestive heart failure, and cardiomyopathy. Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy is generally reversible once ventricular rate is controlled. AF tends to be progressive, with no definitive durable cure, and patients maintaining sinus rhythm generally have better survival than those who remain in AF (p.1990, 1992, 1994).
Acute AF with significant haemodynamic compromise, pulmonary oedema, or evidence of coronary ischaemia indicates need for emergent cardioversion (p.1992).

Preexcited AF over an accessory pathway with very rapid repetitive conduction (minimum R-R <250 ms occurs in ~25% of preexciting pathways) is potentially life-threatening, predisposing to ventricular fibrillation and sudden death (p.1985-1986).
Syncope or presyncope from bradycardia/pauses, including offset pauses on spontaneous conversion to sinus rhythm, suggesting coexisting sinus node dysfunction (tachy-brady syndrome) (p.1992).
Sustained uncontrolled rapid ventricular rates risk precipitating heart failure and tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy (p.1990, 1992).

By temporal pattern: paroxysmal AF (self-terminates or is cardioverted within 7 days; normal-to-mildly enlarged left atrium, low scar burden), persistent AF (continuous >7 days but <1 year; mild-to-severe LA enlargement, moderate scar), and long-standing persistent AF (>1 year; severely enlarged LA, high scar burden). A newer staged framework (at risk of AF, pre-AF, AF, permanent AF) reframes AF as a disease continuum. Mitral stenosis defines valvular versus nonvalvular AF for risk purposes (p.1991, 1993, 1996).

chunks.diseaseName: Atrial Myxoma and Other Cardiac Tumors
chunks.text: Cardiac tumors are classified as primary (benign, chiefly myxoma; or malignant, chiefly sarcoma) or secondary/metastatic. Myxomas are gelatinous masses of myxoma cells in a glycosaminoglycan-rich stroma, usually arising from the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis and most often projecting into the left atrium on a fibrovascular stalk. Clinical effects arise from three mechanisms: mechanical obstruction or valvular interference (mimicking mitral stenosis/regurgitation, or outflow obstruction for ventricular tumors), embolization of tumor fragments or associated thrombus, and constitutional effects from tumor-secreted cytokines such as interleukin-6. Familial myxomas relate to PRKAR1A inactivation within the Carney complex. Metastatic tumors reach the heart by hematogenous or lymphangitic spread or direct invasion, most often involving the pericardium, then myocardium of any chamber, and rarely the endocardium or valves.

chunks.diseaseName: Atrial Myxoma and Other Cardiac Tumors
chunks.text: Cardiac tumors are broadly divided into primary tumors (arising in the heart) and metastatic tumors from a distant source; metastatic involvement is far more common and is seen in up to roughly 20% of patients with end-stage metastatic cancer.

chunks.diseaseName: Atrial Myxoma and Other Cardiac Tumors
chunks.text: Rhabdomyomas and fibromas are the most common cardiac tumors of infants and children, usually ventricular; rhabdomyomas occur in about 50% of children with tuberous sclerosis (TSC1/TSC2 mutations) and tend to regress, whereas fibromas (PTCH1) tend to grow.

chunks.diseaseName: Atrial Myxoma and Other Cardiac Tumors
chunks.text: Malignant primaries are almost all sarcomas (angiosarcoma most common in adults, rhabdomyosarcoma in children), frequently right-sided, rapidly growing, and often invade the pericardium; about one-third are metastatic at diagnosis, usually to the lungs.

chunks.diseaseName: Atrial Myxoma and Other Cardiac Tumors
chunks.text: Tissue histology remains the gold standard for diagnosis; echocardiography is the usual initial test, with cardiac MRI (gadolinium) helping differentiate tumor from thrombus and benign from malignant lesions.

chunks.diseaseName: Atrial Myxoma and Other Cardiac Tumors
chunks.text: Primary cardiac tumors are rare (about 1 in 2000 in autopsy series); roughly three-quarters are histologically benign, and most of those benign tumors are myxomas, while malignant primaries (almost all sarcomas) make up about 25%.

chunks.diseaseName: Atrial Myxoma and Other Cardiac Tumors
chunks.text: Myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults, comprising one-third to one-half of cases at postmortem and about three-quarters of surgically treated tumors; it favors the third through sixth decades with a female predilection.

chunks.diseaseName: Atrial Myxoma and Other Cardiac Tumors
chunks.text: Roughly 90% of myxomas are sporadic; the remainder are familial (autosomal dominant), often as part of the Carney complex (cardiac/skin/breast myxomas, lentigines or pigmented nevi, and endocrine overactivity), associated in about 70% of cases with inactivating mutations in the PRKAR1A tumor-suppressor gene.

chunks.diseaseName: Atrial Myxoma and Other Cardiac Tumors
chunks.text: Sporadic myxomas are typically solitary, pedunculated on a fibrovascular stalk, and arise from the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis, most often in the left atrium; familial/syndromic myxomas occur in younger patients, are often multiple, may be ventricular, and recur more often.

chunks.diseaseName: Atrial Myxoma and Other Cardiac Tumors
chunks.text: Myxomas most commonly produce obstructive features mimicking mitral valve disease (stenosis from prolapse into the mitral orifice, or regurgitation from valvular trauma); symptoms may be sudden or positional because of gravitational effects on tumor position.

chunks.diseaseName: Atrial Myxoma and Other Cardiac Tumors
chunks.text: A characteristic low-pitched early or mid-diastolic 'tumor plop' may be heard, attributed to the tumor striking the mitral valve or ventricular wall.

chunks.diseaseName: Atrial Myxoma and Other Cardiac Tumors
chunks.text: Myxomas can cause peripheral or pulmonary embolic events (tumor fragments or associated thrombus) and constitutional/cytokine-mediated features (often interleukin-6), so they are frequently misdiagnosed as endocarditis, collagen vascular disease, or a paraneoplastic syndrome.

chunks.diseaseName: Atrial Myxoma and Other Cardiac Tumors
chunks.text: Papillary fibroelastomas are the most common tumors of the cardiac valves (friable, frond-like, usually solitary) and, although often silent, may embolize to cause TIA, stroke, or myocardial infarction.

chunks.diseaseName: Atrial Myxoma and Other Cardiac Tumors
chunks.text: Misdiagnosing myxoma as infective endocarditis, collagen vascular disease, or a paraneoplastic syndrome because of fever, embolism, and laboratory abnormalities (e.g., elevated ESR/CRP, anemia, hypergammaglobulinemia).

chunks.diseaseName: Atrial Myxoma and Other Cardiac Tumors
chunks.text: Catheterizing the chamber harboring a tumor, which risks tumor embolization; angiography/catheterization is no longer mandatory when noninvasive imaging is adequate and coronary disease is unlikely.

chunks.diseaseName: Atrial Myxoma and Other Cardiac Tumors
chunks.text: Failing to screen first-degree relatives of young patients with multiple myxomas or syndromic features.

chunks.diseaseName: Atrial Myxoma and Other Cardiac Tumors
chunks.text: Attributing cardiac symptoms in cancer patients solely to the tumor when radiotherapy/chemotherapy-induced myocarditis, pericarditis, or cardiomyopathy can produce identical findings.

chunks.diseaseName: Atrial Myxoma and Other Cardiac Tumors
chunks.text: Overlooking that a left-sided sarcoma may be mistaken for a myxoma.

chunks.diseaseName: Atrial Myxoma and Other Cardiac Tumors
chunks.text: Benign myxoma is generally cured by surgical excision; recurrence is about 1-2% in sporadic cases but 12-22% in familial cases (multifocal disease or incomplete resection). Malignant primary tumors carry a poor prognosis: sarcomas typically progress rapidly to death within weeks to months from hemodynamic compromise, local invasion, or metastasis, and respond poorly to radiotherapy/chemotherapy. The notable exception is primary cardiac lymphoma, the most chemotherapy-sensitive primary cardiac malignancy, with long-term survival in about 40% of treated patients. Metastatic cardiac involvement usually occurs with advanced disease, is clinically apparent only about 10% of the time, is rarely the cause of death, and carries an overall poor prognosis.

An opening in the atrial septum allows blood to shunt from the higher-compliance left atrium toward the right atrium, the direction favoured because the right ventricle is more compliant than the left. This left-to-right shunt volume-loads the right atrium, right ventricle, and pulmonary circulation while the left-sided output is maintained by the shunt returning through the lungs. Chronic volume overload dilates the right heart; over many years a minority develop elevated pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary hypertension, and the resulting right atrial stretch predisposes to atrial arrhythmias.
A communication in the atrial septum permitting left-to-right shunting; the secundum type in the region of the fossa ovalis is the most common form.
Most children are asymptomatic and are detected through an incidental murmur or, later, right heart enlargement; heart failure in infancy is uncommon.

The characteristic auscultatory finding is a widely and fixedly split second heart sound, accompanied by a soft systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border from increased pulmonary flow.
A larger shunt may produce a mid-diastolic rumble at the lower left sternal border from increased flow across the tricuspid valve.
The murmur reflects increased flow through the pulmonary valve rather than turbulent flow across the defect itself, which is low-velocity and inaudible.
Echocardiography defines the defect type and size, direction of shunt, and degree of right atrial and right ventricular volume overload.
Small secundum defects frequently close spontaneously in early childhood; a defect must be distinguished from a normal patent foramen ovale.
Significant defects are closed, often by transcatheter device for suitable secundum defects, to prevent later right heart enlargement, arrhythmias, and pulmonary vascular disease.
Untreated large defects may lead in adulthood to atrial arrhythmias, pulmonary hypertension, and, rarely, paradoxical embolism.
Mistaking a normal patent foramen ovale for a true atrial septal defect
Dismissing the subtle findings and missing a significant defect until right heart enlargement is advanced
Attributing fixed splitting of the second heart sound to a benign murmur
Assuming all defects require closure when many small secundum defects close spontaneously
Overlooking associated anomalous pulmonary venous drainage

Isolated secundum defects, whether closed spontaneously, by device, or surgically, have an excellent outlook when addressed before irreversible pulmonary vascular disease. Late, unrepaired large defects carry increasing risk of arrhythmia and pulmonary hypertension in adulthood.

Autism arises from atypical early brain development influenced by a strong and heterogeneous genetic basis, including many single-gene syndromes, copy number variants, and polygenic risk, interacting with prenatal and perinatal factors. These influences alter neuronal connectivity, synaptic function, and the balance of excitation and inhibition during critical periods, affecting circuits underlying social cognition, language, and behavioural flexibility. No single mechanism or biomarker accounts for all cases, reflecting the disorder's biological heterogeneity.
A neurodevelopmental disorder defined by persistent deficits in social communication and interaction together with restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests, or activities.
Symptoms are present from early development, though they may become fully apparent only when social demands exceed the child's capacities.
It is more frequently diagnosed in boys and shows a strong genetic contribution, with increased recurrence risk in siblings.
Early signs include reduced eye contact, limited joint attention and pointing, absent or delayed social smiling, and lack of response to name.
Repetitive behaviours may include hand-flapping, lining up objects, insistence on routines, and unusual sensory responses.
Diagnosis is clinical and based on developmental history and structured observation rather than a laboratory test.
Routine developmental surveillance and autism-specific screening in toddlerhood aid early identification.
Early intensive behavioural and educational intervention improves functional outcomes.
Common co-occurring conditions include intellectual disability, ADHD, anxiety, epilepsy, sleep problems, and gastrointestinal symptoms, and no evidence links vaccines to autism.

Outcomes vary widely; language ability and cognitive level are important predictors, and early intervention improves adaptive functioning, though most individuals have lifelong needs requiring ongoing support.

APS-1 is a monogenic, classically autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the AIRE (autoimmune regulator) gene on chromosome 21. AIRE is most highly expressed in thymic medullary epithelial cells, where it promotes expression of tissue-specific self-antigens; its loss reduces this expression and is thought to allow autoreactive T cells to escape central (thymic) deletion. Over 100 mutations are described, with higher frequency in certain ethnic groups (Iranian Jews, Sardinians, Finns, Norwegians, Irish). Newly recognized autosomal dominant mutations cluster in the PHD1 domain and tend to cause later-onset, less aggressive disease. Patients develop anticytokine autoantibodies (anti-IL-17A, IL-17F, IL-22, and type 1 interferons). In contrast, APS-2 is polygenic, with the dominant risk in the HLA complex on chromosome 6: Addison's disease in APS-2 is strongly linked to HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4, with additional contributions from HLA-B8, DQ2, DQ8, and DRB1 subtypes. Non-HLA immune genes including MIC-A (the 5.1 allele strongly associated with Addison's), PTPN22, CTLA4, and IL-2R-alpha variants further modulate susceptibility. Organ damage in both syndromes is mediated by organ-specific autoantibodies and autoreactive T cells against targets such as 21-hydroxylase, GAD65, thyroid peroxidase, transglutaminase, and intrinsic factor (Harrison 22e p.3089-3091).

Autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes (APS) are divided into two principal categories: APS type 1 (APS-1) and APS type 2 (APS-2); some authors further split APS-2 into APS-3 and APS-4, but this added subdivision adds little to understanding pathogenesis or guiding management (Harrison 22e p.3089).

Antibody screening can detect risk years before clinical disease: anti-21-hydroxylase antibodies are highly predictive of future adrenal insufficiency, and presence of two or more islet autoantibodies with normal glucose tolerance is defined as stage 1 type 1 diabetes with a near-100% lifetime risk of clinical disease (Harrison 22e p.3091).

About 50% of patients with Addison's disease develop another autoimmune disorder during their lifetime, so a new diagnosis of Addison's should prompt broader screening for linked conditions (Harrison 22e p.3091).

Although the underlying autoimmunity predominantly targets endocrine glands, many nonendocrine tissues can be affected, so a range of nonendocrine disorders is recognized as part of these syndromes (Harrison 22e p.3089).

APS-1 (APECED) is defined by a triad of chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and Addison's disease; the diagnosis is usually made clinically when two of these three major components are present (Harrison 22e p.3089).

APS-1 is rare (<500 reported cases) and classically is autosomal recessive, caused by mutations in the AIRE gene on chromosome 21; AIRE is most highly expressed in thymic medullary epithelial cells where it drives expression of tissue-specific self-antigens such as insulin (Harrison 22e p.3089).

Anticytokine autoantibodies are characteristic of APS-1: anti-IL-17A, anti-IL-17F, and anti-IL-22 underlie the mucocutaneous candidiasis, while detection of anti-interferon alpha and anti-interferon omega antibodies identifies nearly 100% of APS-1 cases and is not seen in other autoimmune disorders (Harrison 22e p.3089-3090).

APS-1 typically begins in infancy with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (mouth and nails more than skin/esophagus), followed by hypoparathyroidism (>85% of cases) and then Addison's disease (nearly 80%); the interval between components can be many years and the order is variable (Harrison 22e p.3089-3090).

APS-2 is more common (prevalence 1-2 per 100,000), shows a female predominance (at least 3:1), has multigenerational inheritance, and usually presents in adulthood with peak incidence between 20 and 60 years (Harrison 22e p.3090).

APS-2 is defined by two or more of: primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease, 50-70%), Graves' disease or autoimmune thyroiditis (15-69%), type 1 diabetes (40-50%), and primary hypogonadism; associated conditions include celiac disease, myasthenia gravis, vitiligo, alopecia, serositis, and pernicious anemia (Harrison 22e p.3090).

Adrenal insufficiency can be masked by coexisting primary hypothyroidism because low thyroid hormone prolongs the half-life of cortisol; patients with hypothyroidism and possible APS should be screened for adrenal insufficiency, since starting thyroid hormone first can precipitate an adrenal crisis (Harrison 22e p.3090).
Initiating thyroid hormone before excluding/treating adrenal insufficiency, precipitating adrenal crisis
Failing to recognize that one component disorder warrants screening for others, and that siblings of an APS-1 patient should be considered affected even with a single component
Attributing chronic candidiasis purely to local infection rather than recognizing it as a marker of APS-1
Missing functional asplenism (Howell-Jolly bodies) in APS-1, which raises infection risk
Overlooking subclinical/preclinical disease detectable only by autoantibodies and physiologic testing

These are chronic, progressive disorders in which individual component diseases continue to emerge over years to decades, so cumulative prevalence rises with age and lifelong surveillance is required. APS-1 typically presents earliest (often infancy) and its chronic candidiasis is nearly always present and poorly responsive to treatment. In APS-2, autoantibodies can precede clinical disease by many years, allowing early detection; about half of patients with Addison's disease develop an additional autoimmune disorder over their lifetime, and individuals with two or more islet autoantibodies have a near-100% lifetime risk of clinical type 1 diabetes. With timely hormone replacement and monitoring, prognosis for individual endocrinopathies is generally favorable, but unrecognized adrenal insufficiency or precipitated adrenal crisis is potentially fatal (Harrison 22e p.3089-3091).
New thyroid hormone replacement in an undiagnosed patient with adrenal insufficiency can precipitate an adrenal crisis
Treatment of mucocutaneous candidiasis with ketoconazole in a patient with subclinical adrenal insufficiency may also precipitate adrenal crisis
Hyperpigmentation, unexplained hyponatremia/hyperkalemia, or hypotension signaling evolving Addison's disease
Tetany or seizures from hypocalcemia indicating hypoparathyroidism
Howell-Jolly bodies on smear indicating functional asplenism and increased infection risk in APS-1
Refractory diarrhea or obstipation suggesting autoimmune destruction of enterochromaffin(-like) cells
Chronic oral candidiasis with leukoplakia-like atrophic change carrying a risk of future carcinoma

No formal severity grading is defined; classification is by type (APS-1 vs APS-2, with proposed APS-3/APS-4 subtypes) based on the constellation of component autoimmune disorders. For type 1 diabetes risk within APS-2, presence of two or more islet autoantibodies with normal glucose tolerance is staged as stage 1 disease (Harrison 22e p.3089-3091).
Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndromes (non-infective) — Endocrine Also: APS, APS-1, APS-2, APECED, autoimmune polyglandular syndrome, polyglandular deficiency syndrome

Organ-specific AD (e.g., Hashimoto thyroiditis, Graves disease, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia/autoimmune gastritis, myasthenia gravis, multiple sclerosis, vitiligo, autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis) (p.2822)
Systemic AD (SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, primary antiphospholipid syndrome, Sjogren syndrome, systemic sclerosis, idiopathic inflammatory myopathies, mixed connective tissue disease) (p.2822)

Systemic vasculitides (giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis, polyarteritis nodosa, ANCA-associated vasculitis, anti-GBM/Goodpasture disease, cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, IgA/Henoch-Schonlein vasculitis, Behcet disease) (p.2822)
Paraneoplastic autoimmune syndromes (Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, paraneoplastic pemphigus, dermatomyositis, anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis with ovarian cancer) (p.2826)
Drug-induced lupus (antihistone-antibody positive) and immune checkpoint inhibitor-related immune adverse events (p.2826)
Infections that trigger or mimic autoimmune flares: group A streptococcal infection underlying rheumatic fever via M-protein/myosin cross-reactivity (p.2825)
Coxsackievirus (myocarditis, Hashimoto thyroiditis, T1DM) and influenza A (T1DM, IgA vasculitis) as proposed autoimmune triggers (p.2825)
Epstein-Barr virus linked to SLE, MS, RA, celiac disease, and Sjogren syndrome (p.2825)
SARS-CoV-2-associated myocarditis, antiphospholipid syndrome, MIS-C, Kawasaki disease, and Guillain-Barre syndrome (p.2826)

Disease-specific autoantibody panels: anti-dsDNA and anti-RNP (SLE); anti-Ro/anti-La and rheumatoid factor (Sjogren); ACPA, anti-carbamylated antibodies, rheumatoid factor (RA); anti-MPO and anti-PR3 (ANCA-associated vasculitis); anti-type IV collagen (Goodpasture) (p.2825)
Anti-TSH-receptor antibodies (Graves); anti-thyroid peroxidase and anti-thyroglobulin (Hashimoto) (p.2825)

Islet-related antibodies in T1DM: anti-insulin, anti-GAD (glutamic acid decarboxylase), anti-protein-tyrosine-phosphatase/IA-2; antibodies to multiple targets confer higher risk of progression (p.2825)
Anti-parietal cell antibodies in pernicious anemia (present in 70-90% of patients) and antimitochondrial antibodies (anti-pyruvate dehydrogenase) in primary biliary cholangitis (p.2825)
Myositis-specific antibodies (anti-aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase, anti-Mi2, anti-MDA5, anti-TIF1-gamma, anti-HMGCR, anti-cN1A) for risk stratification in inflammatory myopathies (p.2825)
Antihistone antibodies for suspected drug-induced lupus (p.2826)
Serum tryptase, 24-h urinary 5-HIAA, and metanephrines to exclude mast-cell, carcinoid, and pheochromocytoma mimics when relevant (contextual) (p.2821)
Paraneoplastic syndromes presenting before a cancer diagnosis (e.g., dermatomyositis, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, immune thrombocytopenia, vitiligo, thyroiditis) (p.2826)
Drug-induced autoimmunity from antibiotics, antihypertensives, antiarrhythmics, TNF inhibitors, antiseizure agents (p.2826)
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia and mast-cell activation disorders presenting with multisystem symptoms (contextual, adjacent chapter) (p.2821)

Autoimmune disease reflects a failure of self-tolerance in a genetically predisposed host exposed to environmental and stochastic 'hits'. Central tolerance (deletion of autoreactive T cells in the thymus and high-affinity autoreactive B cells in the marrow) and peripheral tolerance (anergy from lack of costimulation, regulatory lymphocyte suppression, inhibitory costimulation, removal of autoreactive cells) normally restrain autoreactivity; impairment of these mechanisms allows pathogenic autoimmune responses. Susceptibility is largely polygenic (HLA-DR types, complement deficiencies, type I IFN-pathway and B-/T-cell genes such as STAT4 and PTPN22), with rare monogenic forms, and epigenetic programming (histone modifications, altered DNA methylation, trained immunity) further shapes risk. On the innate side, dysregulated or proinflammatory cell death (apoptosis, pyroptosis, necroptosis, NETosis) plus impaired clearance of dead-cell debris and defective nucleases prolong exposure of modified nucleic-acid autoantigens; endosomal TLR-7/8/9 and cytosolic sensors then drive type I interferon production and inflammasome activation. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells (major IFN-alpha producers), conventional dendritic cells, neutrophils/low-density granulocytes with aberrant NET formation, monocytes/macrophages with defective phagocytosis, and NK cells are all implicated. On the adaptive side, autoreactive CD4/CD8 T cells, Treg deficiency, and imbalance between costimulatory and inhibitory pathways (PD-1, CTLA-4) and cytokines (IL-2, IL-6, IL-17, IL-33) promote disease; pathogenic high-affinity IgG autoantibodies form immune complexes that deposit in tissue, fix complement, opsonize, engage activating Fc receptors, and drive type I IFN production. Inflammatory cytokines (TNF, IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-17, type I IFNs) sustain and amplify tissue injury. Female sex (sex hormones, X-chromosome dosage) and immune aging (inflammaging with senescent, proinflammatory cells) further potentiate autoimmunity.

Autoimmunity (development of autoantibodies or autoreactive T-cell responses against self-antigens) is present in essentially all individuals and tends to increase with age; it does not by itself imply disease. Autoimmune disease (AD) arises only when a loss of tolerance produces clinically relevant, pathogenic responses (p.2821-2822).

Infections can both trigger AD and provoke flares via molecular mimicry, epitope spreading, bystander/adjuvant effects, release of hidden self-antigens, and epigenetic changes; EBV is linked to SLE, MS, RA, celiac disease, and Sjogren, and SARS-CoV-2 has been associated with myocarditis, new APS, MIS-C, Kawasaki disease, and Guillain-Barre (p.2825-2826).

Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) cause immune-related adverse events in up to 85% of treated patients (dermatitis, arthritis, thyroiditis, colitis among the most common); most are mild and overall survival/time to progression is generally not influenced by their occurrence (p.2826).
Drug-induced lupus is a well-recognized iatrogenic AD characterized by antihistone antibodies; in many cases discontinuing the offending drug is sufficient to abate symptoms (p.2826).

Roughly 150 organ-specific and systemic ADs have been described; in 2009 the U.S. prevalence was estimated at 7.6-9.4% of the population (about 25-31 million people), likely an underestimate, with an apparent ongoing rise in incidence and prevalence (p.2822).

ADs predominantly affect women and, as a group, rank among the top 10 leading causes of death in women; an affected person carries a higher risk of developing a second autoimmune condition, of autoimmunity in relatives, and of certain cancers and premature cardiovascular disease (p.2822).

AD is a multistep process: genetic and environmental factors drive immune dysregulation and loss of tolerance, and autoantibodies can be detectable years before clinical symptoms appear (p.2822-2825).

HLA haplotype is considered the best single predictor of AD risk; specific HLA-DR types, complement-component deficiencies, and genes in the type I interferon and B-/T-cell pathways raise risk, and many susceptibility genes (e.g., STAT4, PTPN22) are shared across several ADs (p.2822-2823).

Autoantibodies serve as diagnostic tools and, in some diseases, as markers of activity or worse outcome; however, for several autoantibodies a specific pathogenic role has not been established, and the relevant autoantigens of many ADs remain unknown (p.2825).

Natural autoantibodies are mainly IgM, encoded by unmutated V(D)J genes with moderate self-affinity, and are not pathogenic; the harmful autoantibodies of AD are high-affinity, somatically mutated IgG generated by somatic hypermutation, class switching, and antigen-driven clonal selection (p.2824-2825).

Dysregulated type I interferon signaling is implicated across SLE, primary Sjogren syndrome, and idiopathic inflammatory myopathies; neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation externalizes modified autoantigens and is implicated in SLE, ANCA-associated vasculitis, myopathies, antiphospholipid syndrome, and RA (p.2823-2824).

Many ADs are female-predominant; two X chromosomes (women, and men with Klinefelter XXY) increase expression of X-linked immunity genes such as TLR-7/8 and IRAK-1, and breakdown of X-inactivation has been linked to autoimmunity (p.2823).

Equating autoimmunity with autoimmune disease: autoantibodies/autoreactivity occur in healthy individuals (and relatives) and increase with age without necessarily causing disease (p.2821-2822, p.2825).
Assuming any detected autoantibody is pathogenic — several are used only as diagnostic or activity/outcome markers without a proven causal role (p.2825).
Overlooking that classification criteria (e.g., for SLE) were designed for clinical-trial enrollment, not for individual diagnosis (contextual, p.2827).
Attributing AD to infection on circumstantial grounds — causality is often unproven and supported mainly by animal models (p.2825-2826).
Missing iatrogenic causes: failing to recognize drug-induced lupus (antihistone antibodies) or checkpoint-inhibitor irAEs, where stopping the agent may resolve symptoms (p.2826).

ADs are described as chronic, incurable conditions that significantly impair quality of life and, in many cases, carry accelerated mortality; as a group they are among the top 10 leading causes of death in women. An individual with one AD has elevated risk of additional autoimmune conditions, certain cancers, and premature cardiovascular disease. Autoantibodies (e.g., ACPA in RA, islet antibodies in T1DM, antimitochondrial antibodies in PBC) may precede clinical disease by years to a decade and can mark worse prognosis. Better understanding of pathophysiology is hoped to enable primary or secondary prevention (e.g., trials of oral insulin in T1DM-autoantibody-positive infants and at-risk RA studies), though more data are needed (p.2822, p.2825-2826).

New autoimmune-pattern symptoms in a patient on an immune checkpoint inhibitor (irAE such as colitis, thyroiditis, arthritis, dermatitis) — can be severe and may persist after stopping therapy (p.2826)
Sudden new autoimmunity or autoantibody synthesis following SARS-CoV-2 or other viral infection (APS, myocarditis, MIS-C, Guillain-Barre) (p.2826)
Autoimmune presentation that may herald an occult malignancy (paraneoplastic syndromes often precede cancer diagnosis) (p.2826)
Anti-Ro-positive pregnancy: IgG anti-Ro crosses the placenta and can cause neonatal lupus and congenital heart block in the fetus (p.2825)
Multiple positive autoantibody specificities (e.g., several islet antibodies in at-risk individuals) signaling high likelihood of progression to overt disease (p.2825)

No single unifying severity grading exists for autoimmunity as a whole; severity and classification are disease-specific and covered in the individual disease chapters. Autoantibody breadth/titer (e.g., number of islet antibodies in T1DM risk) and specific specificities (e.g., anti-TIF1-gamma marking cancer-associated myositis, anti-HMGCR statin-induced myositis, anti-cN1A inclusion body myositis) help stratify risk and outcome (p.2825).
Autoimmunity and Autoimmune Diseases (non-infective) — Immune-mediated / Rheumatologic Also: Autoimmune disease, AD, Loss of immune tolerance, Autoimmunity

Giemsa-stained thin blood smear (microscopy) — definitive diagnosis; trophozoites appear as ring/ameboid forms, and merozoites arranged in tetrads form the pathognomonic 'Maltese cross'
Real-time PCR amplifying the parasite 18S rRNA gene (detects 1–10 parasites/uL; allows speciation; used to monitor low-grade infection and relapse risk)
Complete blood count (anemia, often severe thrombocytopenia preceding severe anemia; WBC may be low, normal, or high) and reticulocyte count
Hemolysis markers: low haptoglobin, elevated LDH, elevated total bilirubin
Liver enzymes (alkaline phosphatase, AST, ALT) and renal function (BUN, creatinine)
Urinalysis (urobilinogen, hemoglobinuria, proteinuria)
