Babesia parasites invade and lyse red blood cells. RBC debris from hemolysis can accumulate in the renal vasculature and cause renal failure. Free hemoglobin is complexed by haptoglobin, then the oxidized heme group by hemopexin; excess free hemoglobin scavenges nitric oxide, promoting thrombus formation and vascular inflammation. RBC lysis in splenic capillaries can trigger localized necrosis and splenic infarction; oxidatively stressed, poorly deformable RBCs are filtered and phagocytosed by splenic macrophages, and erythrophagocytosis with the immune response contributes to splenomegaly and rupture. Fever, chills, and sweats reflect a systemic inflammatory response to RBC lysis, and excessive inflammation drives end-organ (renal and pulmonary) damage. The spleen is the immunodominant organ, explaining why asplenia is a major risk factor for severe disease; protective immunity involves CD4+ Th1 cells (severe disease in AIDS and transplant recipients), and B cells/antibodies appear critical for clearance in some patients (relapsing disease after rituximab). Persistent anemia after infection clears has been attributed to autoantibodies tagging RBCs for clearance (p.1778).

Emerging tick-borne infection caused by intraerythrocytic protozoa of the genus Babesia that invade and lyse red blood cells; most U.S. cases are due to Babesia microti, transmitted by the deer tick Ixodes scapularis, with ~90% presenting June through August (p.1775, 1777).

Presents as a flu-like illness: gradual-onset fatigue/malaise followed within days by fever (can reach 40.9 C) with chills, night sweats, headache, myalgia, and anorexia; dark urine and jaundice raise suspicion of severe hemolytic anemia (p.1777).

Because the same I. scapularis tick co-transmits Borrelia burgdorferi and Anaplasma phagocytophilum, co-infection is common: about one-half of patients diagnosed with babesiosis are also infected with B. burgdorferi, so a babesiosis diagnosis should prompt evaluation for Lyme disease, and vice versa (p.1778).
Most symptomatic patients (~80%) are 50 years or older; hospitalized patients are roughly a decade older (median 68 years) (p.1777).
Splenic complications (infarction, subcapsular hematoma, rupture) can occur even with low-grade parasitemia (median ~1%) and typically affect young, healthy patients (p.1777, 1780).

Misidentifying Babesia as malaria on the blood smear: distinguish by absence of central brownish hemozoin pigment, presence of extracellular merozoites, absence of gametocytes and schizonts, and the pathognomonic tetrad ('Maltese cross'); a negative BinaxNOW malaria test helps rule out falciparum malaria when microscopy is ambiguous (p.1779).
Relying on a single positive serology for diagnosis — antibodies persist for over a year after the parasite is cleared (p.1779).

Missing co-infection: failing to evaluate for Lyme disease (and other tick-borne pathogens) when babesiosis is diagnosed, or for babesiosis when Lyme symptoms worsen or fail to abate on appropriate antibiotics (p.1778).
Overlooking splenic complications, which can occur with low-grade parasitemia and in young, otherwise healthy patients (p.1777, 1780).

Routine follow-up PCR is not recommended in immunocompetent patients (parasite DNA detectable up to 3 months) since relapse is unlikely, and persistent fatigue alone does not warrant extending or resuming therapy (p.1779).

With first-line atovaquone plus azithromycin, a fatal outcome is rare; of 7612 CDC-reported cases in 2011–2015, 46 (0.6%) ended in death. Older regimens (clindamycin plus quinine) had fatality rates of 5–9%. Death is more frequent in those 65 years or older. Among Medicare recipients diagnosed 2006–2013, ~1% died within 30 days; fatality was ~3% among hospitalized patients. Fatality is high in immunocompromised patients (~20%) and in those with splenic rupture or infarction (~6%). Fatigue may persist for weeks to months after treatment. Highly immunocompromised patients are at risk of persistent, relapsing infection (p.1778).
Severe disease especially in asplenic (congenital, functional, or post-splenectomy), elderly, and immunocompromised (HIV/AIDS, transplant, malignancy, B-cell-depleting/rituximab therapy) patients
Dark urine and jaundice indicating severe hemolytic anemia, with scleral icterus on examination
Left-sided abdominal pain, unexplained hypotension with tachycardia, or hemodynamic instability suggesting splenic infarction or rupture
Acute renal failure (leading complication, ~20%) and acute respiratory failure (~7%); also DIC, shock, arrhythmia, heart failure
Parasitemia >4% (risk factor for severe, complicated disease; can reach 30–40% in immunocompromised patients)
Diagnosis delayed >7 days after symptom onset predisposes to severe complicated disease
Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis from massive phagocytosis of blood cells (fatal)

Severe babesiosis requires hospital admission (median stay 4 days). Severe, complicated babesiosis is defined as illness requiring ICU admission; complicated by ARDS, heart failure, or shock; or requiring dialysis, intubation, or RBC exchange. Diarrhea and nausea/vomiting are strong predictors of severe disease, and asplenia and autoimmune disorders predispose to it. Parasitemia is typically 0.1–10% in immunocompetent patients (up to 30–40% in immunocompromised); parasitemia >4% is a risk factor for severe complicated disease (p.1777-1778).

chunks.text: Bacterial keratitis develops when the corneal epithelial barrier is breached (by trauma, contact lens wear, dry eye, or surgery), allowing bacteria to invade the corneal stroma. Bacterial proliferation and the release of enzymes and toxins, together with the host inflammatory response and recruited neutrophils, cause stromal necrosis and an infiltrate. Collagen-degrading enzymes can rapidly thin the cornea, leading to ulceration, descemetocele formation, and perforation. Healing occurs with scarring that reduces corneal clarity, particularly when the visual axis is involved.

Trichomonas vaginalis infection
Physiological or cyclical vaginal discharge
Retained foreign body such as a tampon
Desquamative inflammatory vaginitis
Cervicitis from gonorrhoea or chlamydia
Measurement of vaginal pH, which is typically elevated above 4.5
Whiff (amine) test with potassium hydroxide to detect a fishy odour
Saline wet-mount microscopy for clue cells and reduced lactobacilli
Gram stain scoring of vaginal flora where laboratory diagnosis is used
Testing for co-existing sexually transmitted infections when risk factors are present

The healthy vagina is dominated by lactobacilli that produce lactic acid and hydrogen peroxide, maintaining an acidic environment that suppresses other organisms. In bacterial vaginosis this population is depleted and replaced by a polymicrobial overgrowth of anaerobes such as Gardnerella vaginalis, Prevotella, Mobiluncus, and Atopobium, often organised into a biofilm on the epithelium. The resulting rise in vaginal pH and production of amines generates the typical odour and discharge, while the biofilm contributes to treatment resistance and recurrence.
Bacterial vaginosis reflects a shift in the vaginal microbiome away from protective lactobacilli toward an overgrowth of anaerobes rather than a single infecting pathogen
The characteristic feature is a thin, homogeneous, greyish-white discharge with a fishy odour that is often most noticeable after intercourse
It is typically not associated with significant inflammation, so vulval itching and soreness are usually mild or absent, distinguishing it from candidiasis and trichomoniasis
Clinical diagnosis using the Amsel criteria combines discharge characteristics, raised vaginal pH, a positive whiff test with potassium hydroxide, and clue cells on microscopy
Clue cells are vaginal epithelial cells studded with adherent bacteria and are a hallmark microscopic finding
Treatment targets anaerobes with agents such as metronidazole or clindamycin, but recurrence is common and reflects failure to re-establish a lactobacillus-dominant flora
In pregnancy it is associated with an increased risk of preterm birth, late miscarriage, and postpartum endometritis, so symptomatic pregnant women are treated
It also increases susceptibility to sexually transmitted infections including HIV and to post-procedural pelvic infection
Mistaking it for candidiasis and treating with antifungals
Overtreating asymptomatic women outside pregnancy or pre-procedure settings
Failing to consider it in recurrent or malodorous discharge with minimal inflammation
Not screening for concurrent sexually transmitted infections when risk exists
Overlooking its role in preterm birth in symptomatic pregnant women

Symptoms usually respond well to appropriate antibiotic therapy, but recurrence within months is frequent because the protective lactobacillus flora and the biofilm are difficult to eradicate permanently. It is not itself a serious infection but its associations with adverse pregnancy outcomes, post-procedural infection, and enhanced susceptibility to sexually transmitted infections give it clinical importance.
Symptomatic bacterial vaginosis in pregnancy given the association with preterm birth and miscarriage
Signs of ascending infection such as pelvic pain, fever, or cervical motion tenderness suggesting pelvic inflammatory disease
Bacterial vaginosis before termination or intrauterine procedures, increasing post-procedure infection risk
Persistent atypical discharge not responding to treatment, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Coexisting features of a sexually transmitted infection

Obstruction of the Bartholin duct, often following inflammation or inspissated secretions, causes retention of mucus and cystic dilatation of the gland. Stasis within the obstructed duct favours bacterial proliferation, and secondary infection with mixed vaginal, enteric, and occasionally sexually transmitted organisms produces a walled-off collection of pus. The resulting abscess generates local inflammation, oedema, and pain, and if untreated may point and rupture spontaneously or recur once the duct re-obstructs.

The Bartholin glands lie at the posterior aspect of the vaginal introitus and secrete mucus for lubrication; obstruction of their duct leads to cyst formation and secondary infection produces an abscess
An abscess typically presents as a painful, tender, fluctuant swelling in the posterolateral labium majus that can make sitting and walking difficult
Infection is usually polymicrobial with vaginal and enteric flora, though sexually transmitted organisms such as gonorrhoea and chlamydia should be considered
Definitive treatment relies on drainage rather than antibiotics alone, and simple incision and drainage alone has a high recurrence rate
Placement of a Word catheter or marsupialisation creates an epithelialised tract that allows continued drainage and reduces recurrence
Antibiotics are reserved for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, immunocompromise, or high-risk sexually transmitted infection rather than routine drained abscesses
In women over the age of forty, and particularly postmenopausal women, a persistent or atypical Bartholin mass should raise concern for the rare Bartholin gland carcinoma and prompt biopsy
Sitz baths and analgesia support symptom relief and can encourage spontaneous drainage of small abscesses
Treating with antibiotics alone without adequate drainage
Relying on simple incision and drainage, which frequently recurs, instead of a definitive drainage procedure
Failing to test for sexually transmitted infections when relevant
Overlooking Bartholin carcinoma in an older woman with a persistent solid mass
Not investigating recurrent abscesses for underlying diabetes

Most Bartholin abscesses resolve well after adequate drainage, and techniques that create a lasting drainage tract, such as catheter placement or marsupialisation, substantially lower recurrence. Recurrent disease may require repeat procedures or gland excision, and the outlook is excellent overall provided malignancy is excluded in older or atypical cases.
Spreading vulval cellulitis, systemic sepsis, or features suggesting necrotising infection
Rapidly enlarging or irregular mass, or one in a postmenopausal woman, raising suspicion of carcinoma
Recurrent abscesses that may indicate underlying diabetes or immunosuppression
Severe pain with induration extending beyond the gland
Failure to resolve after adequate drainage

chunks.text: Basal cell carcinoma is a malignancy of the basal keratinocytes of the epidermis and follicular structures, driven predominantly by ultraviolet-induced DNA damage. Aberrant activation of the Hedgehog signalling pathway, commonly through inactivating mutations in the PTCH1 tumour-suppressor gene or activating changes in SMO, is central to tumour development, alongside UV signature mutations in TP53. The tumour grows as nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and a surrounding fibromyxoid stroma. Its behaviour is locally invasive rather than metastatic, and infiltrative or morphoeic patterns spread with subclinical extension that explains higher recurrence when margins are inadequate.

chunks.diseaseName: Basic Biology of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: The cardiovascular system develops from cardiac progenitors in lateral splanchnic mesoderm that fuse into a linear heart tube of endocardium and spontaneously beating cardiomyocytes, then undergo asymmetric looping and chamber specification with continued addition of second-heart-field cells (Islet-1 positive). Septation separates the cardiac chambers and divides the truncus arteriosus into aorta and pulmonary artery; endocardial cushions, rich in hyaluronic-acid 'cardiac jelly', undergo epithelial-mesenchymal transformation to form valves. Neural crest cells direct aortic arch remodeling and supply smooth muscle to the great vessels, while proepicardial cells form coronary vasculature. Blood vessels share a trilaminar architecture (intimal endothelium, smooth-muscle media, fibroblast-rich adventitia), with capillaries reduced to an endothelial tube and pericytes and large vessels nourished by vasa vasorum. The endothelium maintains vascular homeostasis through balanced production of vasodilators (NO, prostacyclin) and vasoconstrictors (endothelin), regulation of leukocyte adhesion, and modulation of coagulation; loss of these functions underlies atherosclerosis, hypertension, capillary-leak states, and immune-mediated vascular injury. Vascular smooth-muscle tone is set by intracellular calcium and myosin light chain phosphorylation, integrated through sympathetic, parasympathetic, and nonadrenergic/noncholinergic (nitrergic, peptidergic) autonomic signaling. In the myocardium, the sarcomere is the contractile unit; excitation-contraction coupling links the action potential and T-tubular calcium entry to RyR2-mediated SR calcium release, troponin C activation, and actin-myosin cross-bridge cycling, with relaxation driven by SERCA2A reuptake and Na+/Ca2+ exchange. Cardiac output reflects the interplay of preload, afterload, and contractility (Frank-Starling mechanism).

chunks.diseaseName: Basic Biology of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: The heart arises from crescent-shaped fields of lateral splanchnic mesoderm; a primary (first) heart field forms the linear heart tube while a second heart field, marked by Islet-1 expression, later adds myocardium to the inflow/outflow poles and contributes much of the right ventricle and outflow tract.

chunks.diseaseName: Basic Biology of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Cardiac contraction follows the sliding-filament model: an L-type calcium current during the action potential plateau triggers calcium-induced calcium release from the SR via the ryanodine receptor RyR2; calcium binds troponin C, relieving troponin-tropomyosin inhibition so actin and myosin cross-bridge cycling (ATP-dependent) can occur.

chunks.diseaseName: Basic Biology of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Relaxation depends on lowering cytosolic calcium by SR reuptake via SERCA2A (regulated by phospholamban) and sarcolemmal Na+/Ca2+ exchange; PKA phosphorylation of phospholamban speeds reuptake and produces the lusitropic (enhanced relaxation) effect.

chunks.diseaseName: Basic Biology of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Cytoplasmic calcium is the principal determinant of inotropic state: positive inotropes such as digitalis glycosides and beta-adrenergic agonists act by raising cytosolic calcium (beta agonists via Gs-adenylyl cyclase-cyclic AMP-PKA phosphorylation of sarcolemmal calcium channels).

chunks.diseaseName: Basic Biology of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Ventricular stroke volume is set by three factors: preload (muscle length at contraction onset), afterload (tension developed during contraction), and contractility; contractile force is optimal near a sarcomere length of about 2.2 micrometers, the structural basis of the Frank-Starling relationship.

chunks.diseaseName: Basic Biology of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Neural crest cells are required for aortic arch remodeling and truncus arteriosus septation; because these cells are sensitive to vitamin A and folic acid, maternal deficiency of these vitamins is associated with congenital defects of aortic arch remodeling.

chunks.diseaseName: Basic Biology of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Coronary arteries depend on epicardial cells derived from the proepicardial organ (a septum transversum derivative that also forms the fibrous diaphragm and contributes to the liver), which supply coronary smooth muscle and help pattern the vessels.

chunks.diseaseName: Basic Biology of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: The cardiac conduction system differentiates from cardiomyocyte precursors into slow-conducting proximal components (SA and AV nodes) and fast-conducting distal components (His bundle, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers); developmental defects can produce congenital heart block or pre-excitation (Wolff-Parkinson-White).

chunks.diseaseName: Basic Biology of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Decremental conduction across the AV node delays atrial-to-ventricular impulse transmission to allow sequential contraction and protects the ventricle by limiting transmission of rapid atrial rates.

chunks.diseaseName: Basic Biology of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: The endothelium is a selectively permeable barrier and a major homeostatic organ: under physiologic conditions it favors vasodilation, an antithrombotic/profibrinolytic state, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties; endothelial dysfunction reverses each of these (vasoconstriction, prothrombotic, proinflammatory, prooxidant, impaired barrier).

chunks.diseaseName: Basic Biology of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Endothelium-derived vasodilators include nitric oxide (NO), prostacyclin, endothelium-derived hyperpolarizing factor, and hydrogen peroxide; flow-mediated dilatation (brachial artery cuff occlusion/release with ultrasound) is used to assess endothelial vasodilator function in humans.

chunks.diseaseName: Basic Biology of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Excess reactive oxygen species (e.g., superoxide generated under high angiotensin II exposure) inactivate NO, and inflammatory stimuli/endotoxin/angiotensin II drive endothelial production of PAI-1 and tissue factor, shifting balance toward thrombosis (contributing to DIC in sepsis and to hyperglycemia-related prothrombotic states).

chunks.diseaseName: Basic Biology of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Vascular smooth-muscle contraction is governed by cytosolic calcium and the balance of myosin light chain kinase (calcium/calmodulin-activated) versus myosin light chain phosphatase; voltage-dependent L-type calcium channels and IP3-triggered sarcoplasmic reticulum release raise intracellular calcium.

chunks.diseaseName: Basic Biology of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Treating these molecular and developmental concepts as purely theoretical: shared embryonic origins of cardiovascular cell types explain syndromic associations between congenital heart disease and extracardiac anomalies.

chunks.diseaseName: Basic Biology of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Overlooking that true regeneration of a complete three-layered blood vessel does not normally occur in adult mammals, so adult arteriogenesis/angiogenesis reflects growth and collateral expansion rather than new full-thickness vessel formation.

chunks.diseaseName: Basic Biology of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Assuming adult vascular smooth-muscle cells are quiescent; they proliferate and migrate after injury or inflammatory activation, contributing to atherosclerotic stenosis, hypertensive arteriolar remodeling, and restenosis.

chunks.diseaseName: Basic Biology of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: As a foundational chapter, prognosis is framed at the level of mechanism: increased arterial stiffness with aging or disease raises left ventricular afterload and portends a poor outcome, and sustained high-flow states (e.g., left-to-right shunts) drive pulmonary smooth-muscle proliferation and pulmonary hypertension. Outcomes in specific cardiovascular diseases are detailed in their respective chapters.

chunks.diseaseName: Basic Biology of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Inherited or acquired disturbances of SR calcium handling (RyR2/regulatory protein abnormalities) can impair contraction and predispose to heart failure or ventricular arrhythmias.

chunks.diseaseName: Basic Biology of the Cardiovascular System

chunks.text: Developmental conduction-system defects may present as congenital heart block or pre-excitation (Wolff-Parkinson-White).

Diagnosis is clinical; no specific laboratory, imaging, or histologic test confirms it, so investigations mainly serve to exclude mimics.

International Study Group (ISG) criteria: recurrent oral ulceration (at least 3 times in 12 months) plus two of recurrent genital ulcers, skin lesions, eye lesions, or a positive pathergy test (sensitivity ~95%, specificity ~96%).
Pathergy test: dermal insertion of a 20-gauge (20-21 gauge) needle, read at 24-48 h.

The cause and pathogenesis are unknown. Family studies suggest a possible genetic predisposition, and heightened inflammation with involvement of both innate and adaptive immunity is implicated. Neutrophil hyperreactivity is present, though it is unclear whether this is primary or secondary to cytokine-driven activation. The disorder sits between classic autoimmune and autoinflammatory conditions: unlike typical autoimmune disease it is not generally associated with autoantibodies, Raynaud's phenomenon, Sjögren's syndrome, thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, photosensitivity, serosal involvement, or increased risk of other autoimmune diseases; unlike classic autoinflammatory disease it tends to abate over time, lacks the mutations seen in autoinflammatory syndromes, and is more prevalent than disorders such as familial Mediterranean fever. Retrospective cohort data suggest distinct disease clusters (e.g., acne lesions clustering with arthritis and enthesitis) that may have differing pathogeneses.

A systemic vasculitis presenting with various combinations of oral and genital ulcers, skin lesions, uveitis, arthritis, large vessel (arterial and venous) disease, and gastrointestinal and neurologic involvement, with manifestations appearing in differing sequences over time.
Ocular disease (most often bilateral panuveitis) usually appears within the first 2 years after diagnostic criteria are met, is most severe early, then tends to abate.
Most new manifestations appear within the first 5 years, and the natural history for most patients is one of diminishing symptoms that may culminate in remission.

Oral ulcers occur in essentially all patients (~98%) and are usually the first manifestation; they are typically multiple, resemble ordinary canker sores, last about 10 days, and recur unless treated, with only the uncommon major ulcers tending to scar.
Genital ulcers are the most specific lesion, most often on the scrotum or labia; they are larger, deeper, slower to heal than oral ulcers, and tend to scar.
The pathergy reaction (a papule or pustule forming 24-48 h after a needle prick) is a fairly unique nonspecific skin hyperreactivity and is part of the diagnostic criteria.
Hypopyon (intense anterior chamber inflammation), seen in about 10% of patients with eye disease, is quite specific for Behçet syndrome.
Superficial thrombophlebitis often occurs in men and is associated with deep-vein thrombosis; its presence should prompt a workup for other vascular involvement including pulmonary artery aneurysm.
HLA-B*51 is positive in up to 50-60% of patients depending on geographic origin, but it is not diagnostic because roughly 20% of the normal population also carries it.
Most prevalent in Turkey (about 1 in 250 adults); patients are most commonly from the Middle East, Mediterranean, and Far East. Onset before the late teens or after age 50 is uncommon.
Sexes are affected roughly equally, but males tend to have more severe disease and worse outcomes; eye involvement may reach ~70% in males.
Diagnosis may take months to years as the full constellation of features evolves; a tentative diagnosis often precedes a definitive one.
HLA-B*51 is not a diagnostic test because it is common in the general population.
Gastrointestinal Behçet is easily mistaken for Crohn's disease unless extraintestinal manifestations are evident.
Pathergy and eye lesions each occur in only about half of patients, so their absence does not exclude the diagnosis.
Regional variation matters: gastrointestinal involvement is common in Japan and seen in ~30% of US patients but rare in Turkey.

Most patients follow a course of diminishing symptoms over time with potential remission, often eventually requiring no ongoing medication, and most new manifestations emerge within the first 5 years. Young male patients tend to have worse outcomes. Poor ocular prognostic factors include male sex, posterior involvement, frequent attacks (>3 per year), strong vitreous opacity, and macular edema. Pulmonary artery aneurysms are associated with a 5-year mortality of about 20-25%.
Superficial thrombophlebitis in a male should trigger evaluation for deeper vascular involvement including pulmonary artery aneurysm.
Pulmonary artery aneurysms carry a 5-year mortality of about 20-25%.
Subacute severe headache with cranial nerve palsy, dysarthria, ataxia, or hemiparesis suggests parenchymal CNS involvement (telencephalic-diencephalic junction, brainstem, spinal cord).
Deep, round ileocecal ulcers are prone to perforation.
Clustering thrombotic events (deep-vein thrombosis, Budd-Chiari syndrome, IVC syndrome, intracardiac thrombosis, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis).

No formal severity grade; management and outlook are stratified by the type and severity of organ involvement (mucocutaneous, ocular, vascular, gastrointestinal, neurologic), with young male sex and posterior/severe eye disease marking higher-risk disease.

chunks.text: Bell's palsy is an acute mononeuropathy of the facial (seventh cranial) nerve, widely attributed to inflammation and oedema of the nerve, often linked to reactivation of herpes simplex virus. Swelling of the nerve within the narrow bony facial canal causes compression, ischaemia, and demyelination, producing unilateral weakness of all facial muscles on the affected side. Depending on the segment involved, taste, lacrimation, and stapedius function may also be impaired.

chunks.text: Benign prostatic hyperplasia is a proliferation of glandular epithelial and stromal cells in the transition zone of the prostate, driven by ageing and androgen (dihydrotestosterone) activity. The enlarging gland produces a static component of obstruction by mechanical narrowing of the prostatic urethra and a dynamic component from increased smooth muscle tone mediated by alpha-1 adrenergic receptors. Chronic outflow obstruction leads to detrusor muscle hypertrophy, trabeculation, and eventually detrusor decompensation, incomplete emptying, and rising post-void residual volumes, with risk of upper tract dilatation and renal impairment in advanced cases.

chunks.text: Benzodiazepines enhance the inhibitory action of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) at the GABA-A receptor by increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening, producing central nervous system depression. Because they modulate rather than directly open the channel, there is a ceiling to their respiratory depressant effect when taken alone, which explains their relatively wide margin of safety in isolated overdose. When combined with other central depressants such as opioids or alcohol, this ceiling is lost and dangerous synergistic respiratory depression can occur.

Mutations in the beta-globin gene reduce (beta+) or abolish (beta0) beta-chain synthesis, creating an imbalance with relatively excess alpha-globin chains. Unpaired alpha chains precipitate within red cell precursors, causing their destruction in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis) and shortened survival of circulating red cells (haemolysis). The resulting chronic anaemia drives erythropoietin-mediated marrow expansion and extramedullary haematopoiesis, while increased gastrointestinal iron absorption and transfusional iron together produce progressive tissue iron overload.
An inherited disorder of reduced or absent beta-globin chain production, most common in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, South Asian, and Southeast Asian populations.
Beta-thalassaemia major typically presents in the second half of the first year of life as protective fetal haemoglobin declines, with progressive pallor, poor growth, and hepatosplenomegaly.
The blood film shows a severe microcytic hypochromic anaemia with marked anisopoikilocytosis, target cells, and nucleated red cells.
Haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC demonstrates elevated HbF and often raised HbA2, with little or no HbA in the major form.
Chronic transfusion is required in transfusion-dependent disease to sustain growth and suppress ineffective erythropoiesis.
Repeated transfusion inevitably causes iron overload, so iron chelation is essential to prevent cardiac, hepatic, and endocrine damage.
Untreated or under-transfused children develop characteristic skeletal changes from marrow expansion, including frontal bossing and maxillary overgrowth.
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation offers a potential cure, and newer gene-based therapies are emerging.
Splenomegaly may lead to hypersplenism and rising transfusion requirements; genetic counselling and antenatal screening are important for at-risk families.
Misdiagnosing microcytic anaemia as simple iron deficiency and giving unnecessary iron
Under-transfusing and allowing marrow expansion and skeletal deformity to progress
Neglecting or delaying iron chelation, leading to preventable organ damage
Overlooking endocrine complications such as hypothyroidism, diabetes, and delayed puberty

With regular transfusion and effective iron chelation, survival into adulthood with good quality of life is achievable; outcomes are limited chiefly by iron-related cardiac and endocrine complications, and stem cell transplant can be curative in selected patients.

A fibro-obliterative process destroys the extrahepatic and often intrahepatic bile ducts, obstructing bile flow. Retained bile causes progressive hepatocellular injury, portal tract inflammation, and bile ductular proliferation, leading to fibrosis and, if untreated, biliary cirrhosis with portal hypertension and liver failure. The initiating cause is uncertain and probably heterogeneous, involving developmental, immune, and possibly viral mechanisms.
The most common cause of neonatal cholestasis leading to liver transplantation, resulting from progressive inflammatory obliteration of the extrahepatic bile ducts.
Classic presentation is a term infant with prolonged jaundice, pale (acholic) stools, and dark urine, usually with otherwise good early growth.
Any infant jaundiced beyond about two weeks of age should have a fractionated bilirubin measured; a raised conjugated (direct) fraction signals cholestasis and needs urgent evaluation.
Early diagnosis is critical because the success of surgery falls sharply with age, ideally before about 8 weeks (60 days) of life.
The Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy aims to restore bile drainage; the earlier it is performed, the better the chance of clearing jaundice.
Even after a successful Kasai procedure, many children progress to cirrhosis and ultimately require liver transplantation.
A subset have the biliary atresia splenic malformation syndrome with situs and other congenital anomalies.
Ultrasound may show an absent or small gallbladder and the 'triangular cord' sign; a hepatobiliary scan shows hepatic uptake without excretion into the bowel.
Dismissing prolonged neonatal jaundice as physiological or breast-milk jaundice without checking a split bilirubin
Failing to inspect stool colour
Delaying referral and surgery beyond the window where the Kasai procedure is most effective
Relying on a normal ultrasound to exclude the diagnosis
Overlooking associated congenital anomalies in the splenic malformation syndrome

Outcome depends heavily on the age at surgery; early Kasai portoenterostomy can restore bile flow and delay or avoid transplantation, but many children eventually progress to end-stage liver disease. Overall long-term survival is good when transplantation is available.

chunks.text: Biliary colic results from transient obstruction of the cystic duct (or common bile duct) by a gallstone migrating out of the gallbladder. The obstruction raises intraluminal pressure and distends the viscus; because repetitive biliary contractions cannot overcome or relieve the blockage, a steady visceral pain is generated. When the stone disimpacts or falls back, pressure normalizes and the pain resolves spontaneously, so an uncomplicated episode is self-limited and is NOT accompanied by inflammation, fever, or sustained cholestasis. Underlying stones are usually cholesterol stones (>90% in Western populations), which form when bile becomes supersaturated with cholesterol, cholesterol monohydrate crystals nucleate, and gallbladder hypomotility allows stasis and stone growth; gallbladder emptying is frequently impaired in stone formers. Distinct mechanisms (mechanical, chemical from lysolecithin, and bacterial) convert simple obstruction into acute cholecystitis when the cystic duct stays blocked (p.2727-2732).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.357 (Diseases of the Gallbladder and Bile Ducts) p.2728-2735; Ch.332 (Approach to GI Disease) p.2460-2461; Ch.52 (Jaundice) p.325

chunks.text: Uncomplicated biliary colic is self-limited; the individual attack resolves once the transient obstruction clears. The natural history of the underlying gallstones is generally favorable: 60-80% of asymptomatic stone carriers stay symptom-free for up to 25 years, the chance of developing symptoms is only ~2-4% per year in the first 5 years after diagnosis (falling to 1-2% thereafter), and the yearly incidence of complications is only ~0.1-0.3%. The cumulative risk of death from gallstone disease under expectant management is small. However, once biliary pain has occurred, the likelihood of recurrent attacks and of complications requiring intervention rises substantially; younger patients at diagnosis are more likely to become symptomatic than those over 60 (p.2731).

chunks.text: Hematuria from malignancy in females is frequently mistaken for a urinary tract infection (Harrison 22e p.691).
Urine cytology (detects cancer in only about 50% of high-grade bladder cancers) (Harrison 22e p.691).

Cystoscopy for direct bladder visualization; blue light or narrow-band imaging cystoscopy improves detection of small or flat noninvasive tumors and is used routinely in monitoring (Harrison 22e p.691).
CT urogram (or MR urogram if renal function is impaired) for the kidneys and upper tract (Harrison 22e p.691).

Adjunct urine molecular tests (FISH for chromosomal changes, nuclear mitotic proteins, bladder tumor-associated antigens) used mainly for detecting recurrence, as they can be falsely positive (Harrison 22e p.691).
Ureteroscopy or retrograde pyelography when upper-tract tumors are suspected with a normal bladder (Harrison 22e p.691).
Transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) or endoscopic resection of upper tract tumors for histologic diagnosis and staging (Harrison 22e p.691).
Genomic sequencing of tumor tissue and/or circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) recommended in all metastatic patients (Harrison 22e p.690).
In females, malignant hematuria may be misattributed to menstrual bleeding (Harrison 22e p.691).

Intravesical BCG side effects (dysuria, urinary frequency, bladder spasms, hematuria) overlap with infection/cystitis, and in <5% a systemic inflammatory response can mimic disseminated BCG infection (Harrison 22e p.692).

Urothelial carcinoma arises from the lining of the bladder, renal pelvis, ureter, and urethra and displays a biphasic clinical behavior. Loss of portions of chromosomes 9q and 9p (loss of heterozygosity) is an early molecular event in both phenotypes; candidate genes in these regions include CDKN2A and TSC1. Low-grade papillary tumors are characterized by RAS/RAF pathway alterations with activating FGFR3 mutations or fusions in 60-80% of patients, whereas the high-grade invasive phenotype features early deleterious TP53 and RB1 mutations, CDH1 (E-cadherin) alterations, and increased VEGFR2 expression. Chronic inflammatory states drive squamous-type bladder cancer, classically chronic schistosomiasis infection and chronic indwelling catheters in paraplegic patients. Carcinogenic exposures include aromatic amines (benzidine, beta-naphthylamine) in industrial dyes and arsenic-contaminated drinking water. The Cancer Genome Atlas defined five intrinsic molecular subtypes (luminal papillary, luminal infiltrated, luminal, basal squamous, neuronal) resembling breast cancer subclasses (Harrison 22e p.691-692).

Painless hematuria, either gross or microscopic, is the initial manifestation of urinary tract cancer in most patients; in males painless hematuria is almost always abnormal and must be worked up (Harrison 22e p.691).

In females, hematuria due to malignancy is often mistaken for a urinary tract infection or menstrual bleeding; antibiotics are warranted if a concurrent UTI is found, but persistent hematuria still requires further workup (Harrison 22e p.691).

Initial investigation in either sex includes urine cytology plus visual examination of the bladder by cystoscopy, together with radiographic evaluation of the kidneys and upper tract by CT urogram (MR urogram if renal function is poor) (Harrison 22e p.691).

Smoking of tobacco products is the overwhelming leading risk factor; 90% of new bladder cancer diagnoses occur in current or former smokers, and roughly one-third of cases could be prevented by smoking cessation (Harrison 22e p.692).

Urothelial carcinoma (formerly transitional cell carcinoma) is the most common histology, seen in about 90% of cases; nonurothelial variants (squamous cell, adenocarcinoma, small-cell, carcinosarcoma) collectively account for 10% or less (Harrison 22e p.690-691).

Disease is divided into non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC: carcinoma in situ, Ta, or T1 not reaching the muscularis propria; ~75% at presentation) and muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC: T2 invasion of muscularis propria and beyond) (Harrison 22e p.691-692).

Urothelial carcinoma shows a biphasic phenotype: low-grade papillary tumors that frequently recur but rarely invade or metastasize, and high-grade often flat tumors that invade early and lead to lethal metastatic disease (Harrison 22e p.691).
Urine cytology is insensitive, identifying cancer in only about 50% of high-grade bladder cancers, so a negative cytology does not exclude malignancy (Harrison 22e p.691).
Treating presumed UTI without follow-up risks missing malignancy; persistent hematuria after antibiotics still requires workup (Harrison 22e p.691).
Adjunct urine molecular tests may be abnormal in patients without cancer (false positives) and are best reserved for surveillance of known cancer (Harrison 22e p.691).
Systemic inflammatory reaction after intravesical BCG can mimic disseminated BCG infection (Harrison 22e p.692).

Outcomes correlate closely with stage at diagnosis. About 75% present with non-muscle-invasive disease, 18% with muscle-invasive disease, and only 3% with metastatic spread. 5-year overall survival is 70-90% for disease confined to the bladder (stage I-II), 39-50% for disease penetrating through the bladder or involving regional lymph nodes (stage III), and only 8% for metastatic disease (stage IV) (Harrison 22e p.692).
Painless gross or microscopic hematuria warrants investigation for urothelial cancer; in males it is almost always abnormal (Harrison 22e p.691).
Persistent hematuria despite treatment of a concurrent UTI requires further workup (Harrison 22e p.691).
Flank pain with an upper tract renal pelvis/ureter cancer, or hydronephrosis from a bladder tumor obstructing the ureteral orifice (Harrison 22e p.691).
Cachexia and widespread metastatic disease at presentation (rare) (Harrison 22e p.691).

Staging is driven primarily by depth of invasion (T stage). NMIBC: Tis (CIS) and Ta (epithelial layer only) or T1 (into connective tissue/lamina propria below urothelium but not muscularis propria). MIBC: T2 (into muscularis propria), T3 (through muscularis propria to serosa), T4 (adjacent pelvic organs - rectum, prostate, vagina, cervix). Nodal: N1 (single true pelvic node), N2 (two true pelvic nodes), N3 (common iliac nodes); disease beyond common iliac nodes or distant spread is M1. Stages 0a-II are defined by T stage alone without nodal/metastatic disease; regional pelvic or common iliac nodal involvement is stage III; any distant metastasis is stage IV (Harrison 22e p.691-692).

chunks.text: An explosion generates a high-pressure blast wave that transmits energy across tissue interfaces of differing density. Where gas meets fluid or solid, as in the alveoli, middle ear, and gut, shearing and implosion-reexpansion forces rupture delicate structures, producing pulmonary haemorrhage and oedema (blast lung), tympanic perforation, and bowel contusion or perforation. Secondary injury results from fragments propelled by the blast causing penetrating wounds, tertiary injury from the body being thrown, and quaternary effects from burns, crush, inhalation, and toxic exposure. Blast lung can allow air to enter pulmonary veins, producing systemic air embolism to the brain or coronary circulation.

Blastomyces is a thermally dimorphic species complex (including B. dermatitidis, B. gilchristii, B. helicus, B. percursus, B. emzantsi). In soil at 22-25 degrees C it grows as septate hyphae producing infectious conidia; inhalation into the lungs and conversion at the mammalian core temperature of 37 degrees C yields a pathogenic broad-based budding yeast that upregulates yeast-phase virulence factors and downregulates host immune defenses, eliciting pyogranulomatous inflammation. Shared virulence traits with other dimorphic fungi (Histoplasma, Coccidioides, Sporothrix, Paracoccidioides) include thermotolerance at 37 degrees C, intracellular survival, and the ability to infect immunocompetent hosts. Blastomyces can also replicate outside macrophages. Notably, immunosuppression has only minimal influence on dissemination, suggesting fungal virulence factors outweigh host defenses; the infecting species and duration of pulmonary symptoms (and concomitant AIDS) influence dissemination, with B. dermatitidis more likely to disseminate than B. gilchristii. (p.1700-1702)

A pyogranulomatous disease acquired by inhaling Blastomyces conidia or hyphal fragments from disturbed soil; typically a pulmonary infection, with a subset progressing to disseminated disease involving skin, bone, brain, or genitourinary system (p.1699).
Urine galactomannan antigen testing (sensitivity 85-93% urine, 57-82% serum) has supplanted older serology and can monitor treatment response as levels decline (p.1702-1703).
Treatment is recommended for ALL patients because there are no criteria to identify which untreated cases will self-resolve; antifungals are amphotericin B formulations and triazoles (p.1699, 1703).
A primary fungal pathogen: it infects persons with intact as well as impaired immune systems (p.1699).

Endemic mainly in North America (Mississippi/Ohio and St. Lawrence River basins, Great Lakes states, southeastern states) but of global importance with cases in Africa and Asia; outbreaks linked to construction, soil excavation, water sports, compost piles, and beaver dams (p.1699-1700).
Yeast form (37 degrees C) is a broad-based budding yeast, 4-29 micrometers, with a doubly refractile cell wall, allowing distinction from other fungi (p.1700, 1702).
After a 3-week to 3-month incubation, about 50% of those exposed develop symptomatic infection; the long incubation means cases present year-round (p.1701).

Pulmonary disease occurs in 69-93% of symptomatic patients (most common feature) and may present as asymptomatic infection, influenza-like illness, acute pneumonia, chronic pneumonia, or ARDS (p.1701).
Disseminated disease occurs in 15-48%; skin is the most common site (papules, ulcers, verrucous lesions, abscesses), followed by bone (osteomyelitis of spine, long bones, ribs) (p.1701).
CNS (meningitis/abscess/mass), laryngeal, and genitourinary (prostate, epididymis) dissemination each occur in fewer than 10%, usually with concurrent lung or skin involvement (p.1701).

Diagnosis combines microscopy of stained specimens, fungal culture, and antigen testing; serology (complement fixation 9%, immunodiffusion 28%) is diagnostically dispensable, though a newer anti-BAD1 antibody test has higher sensitivity/specificity (p.1702).

Called 'the great pretender' because it mimics infectious and noninfectious diseases; pulmonary blastomycosis is commonly misdiagnosed, and patients often receive two or three antibiotic courses before diagnosis (p.1701).

No distinctive radiographic features differentiate blastomycosis from other pulmonary diseases (consolidation, mass, nodules, miliary, cavitary patterns all possible); a mass lesion can mimic malignancy (p.1701).

Diagnosis requires a high index of suspicion and a detailed exposure history (about 50-60% of patients have environmental risk factors); failure to consider Blastomyces in the differential delays treatment (p.1701).
Serology by complement fixation/immunodiffusion has poor sensitivity and is diagnostically dispensable (p.1702).
Echinocandins are ineffective (minimal beta-(1,3)-glucan in the yeast cell wall) and should not be used (p.1703).
Antigen testing cross-reacts with other dimorphic fungi, notably H. capsulatum which shares the same endemic region (p.1703).

Overall mortality ranges from 5 to 13% (7.9% in 11,776 U.S. hospital admissions, 2010-2020), with most deaths from respiratory failure due to ARDS. Mortality is higher in older patients and those with COPD or concomitant solid/hematologic malignancy, and is increased when diagnosis is delayed. The vast majority who recover from pulmonary blastomycosis do not have long-term loss of pulmonary function; cutaneous blastomycosis typically heals with scarring. (p.1703)
Unexplained respiratory failure or ARDS in a person from or visiting an endemic area; 4-15% of pulmonary cases develop ARDS with a fulminant course and 40-89% mortality (p.1701)
Pneumonia that fails to improve despite antibiotics, or pneumonia with extrapulmonary features (skin lesions, osteomyelitis, CNS involvement) (p.1701)
Skin ulcers unresponsive to standard therapy (p.1701)
AIDS with CD4+ count <100/microliter: increased risk of CNS dissemination (p.1702)
B. helicus infection (commonly causes fungemia, usually in immunosuppressed hosts, high mortality ~71%) (p.1702)

Harrison does not give a formal numeric severity scale. Severe blastomycosis is operationally defined as disease requiring hospitalization (medical ward, intermediate care, or ICU). Risk factors for severe pulmonary disease include diabetes, solid organ transplantation, immunosuppression, and multilobar pneumonia; ARDS (in 4-15%) represents the most severe pulmonary form with high mortality. Special high-risk/severity categories warranting intensified management include CNS, severe pulmonary, and severe disseminated disease. (p.1701-1703)

chunks.text: Blepharitis is chronic inflammation of the eyelid margins with overlapping mechanisms. Anterior blepharitis involves bacterial (chiefly staphylococcal) colonisation of the lash bases and an inflammatory reaction to bacterial products, or seborrhoeic changes with excessive scaling. Posterior blepharitis reflects meibomian gland dysfunction, in which altered and inspissated meibomian secretions block the glands, destabilise the lipid layer of the tear film, and promote evaporative dry eye. Bacterial lipases and inflammatory mediators contribute to ocular surface irritation, and the condition is frequently linked to rosacea.

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease

chunks.text: Hypomagnesemia: malabsorption, proton pump inhibitor use, alcoholism, Gitelman and Bartter syndromes, claudin 16/19 mutations, TRPM6 mutation, drug-induced (cisplatin, aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, cyclosporine, cetuximab), diabetic glycosuria

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: Mineral homeostasis is maintained by integrated handling of calcium, phosphate, and magnesium across gut, kidney, and bone under hormonal control by PTH, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, and FGF23. Bone provides both mechanical support and the major reservoir of these ions; it is constantly remodeled, with osteoblasts (mesenchymal lineage, driven by Runx2, osterix, Ihh, Wnt and BMP signaling) forming and mineralizing type I collagen matrix and osteoclasts (hematopoietic lineage, driven by M-CSF and RANK ligand, opposed by osteoprotegerin) resorbing it via acidification and proteases such as cathepsin K. Osteocytes sense mechanical load, secrete the Wnt inhibitor sclerostin and the phosphaturic hormone FGF23, and orchestrate remodeling. Ionized calcium in the extracellular fluid is sensed by the calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid cells and renal tubule; low calcium raises PTH, which mobilizes bone calcium, enhances distal renal calcium reabsorption, lowers renal phosphate reabsorption, and stimulates renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase to make 1,25(OH)2D, which in turn increases intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption. Phosphate balance is governed largely by proximal tubular NaPi-2a/2c transporters, which are downregulated by PTH and FGF23; FGF23 from osteocytes additionally suppresses 1,25(OH)2D synthesis. Vitamin D is produced in skin or absorbed from diet, 25-hydroxylated in liver, and 1-alpha-hydroxylated in kidney, with 24-hydroxylase (CYP24A1) providing inactivation. Disturbances at any node (dietary extremes, renal failure, hormone deficiency/excess, intestinal disease, or genetic transporter/enzyme defects) disrupt the narrow regulation of ionized calcium and lead to skeletal and systemic disease.

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: Bone is continuously remodeled by a basic multicellular unit: osteoblasts (mesenchymal origin) lay down and mineralize osteoid, osteoclasts (hematopoietic/macrophage lineage) resorb matrix, and long-lived embedded osteocytes coordinate both and act as mechanosensors (Harrison 22e p.3259).

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: Optimal intestinal calcium absorption requires gastric acid; achlorhydria, proton pump inhibitors, or post-bariatric surgery impair absorption of poorly dissociable salts like calcium carbonate, so calcium citrate or dosing with meals is preferred (Harrison 22e p.3262).

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: Active vitamin D-dependent transcellular calcium and phosphate absorption uses specific apical channels/transporters (TRPV6 and Npt2b in the gut, TRPV5 in the distal tubule); thiazides lower urinary calcium (useful in hypercalciuria) while loop diuretics and saline promote calciuresis (Harrison 22e p.3262).

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: Serious neuromuscular sequelae of hypophosphatemia (seizures, paralysis, rhabdomyolysis) occur mainly when phosphate falls below about 0.25 mmol/L, reflecting ATP depletion; up to 30% of patients with acute hypophosphatemia have CPK elevations peaking 1-2 days after the phosphate nadir (Harrison 22e p.3264).

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: Roughly half of total serum calcium is ionized; the rest is bound to albumin/immunoglobulins or complexed to anions, so total calcium must be interpreted with the serum protein level. A useful correction adds about 0.8 mg/dL to total calcium for each 1 g/dL the albumin is below normal, but in acute illness measure ionized calcium directly with a calcium-selective electrode (Harrison 22e p.3261-3262).

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: Acidosis raises ionized calcium by reducing calcium binding to protein; alkalosis does the opposite, which helps explain tetany seen with respiratory alkalosis (Harrison 22e p.3262).

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: Serum phosphate varies by up to 50% over a day with a morning nadir, and IV dextrose, insulin, or alkalosis can drop it acutely, so phosphate should be measured fasting and in the basal state (Harrison 22e p.3262-3263).

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: Because only about 1% of body magnesium is in the extracellular fluid, a normal serum magnesium does not exclude significant total-body magnesium depletion (Harrison 22e p.3266-3267).

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: Hypomagnesemia frequently causes refractory hypocalcemia and hypokalemia; at very low serum magnesium (below roughly 0.4 mmol/L) PTH secretion is impaired and there is cellular PTH resistance, so calcium and potassium will not correct until magnesium is repleted (Harrison 22e p.3267).

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: FGF23, secreted by osteocytes, is a phosphaturic hormone that both lowers proximal-tubule phosphate reabsorption and suppresses 1-alpha-hydroxylase (lowering 1,25(OH)2D); excess FGF23 underlies XLH, ADHR, and tumor-induced osteomalacia, whereas deficient/inactive FGF23 causes tumoral calcinosis (Harrison 22e p.3263-3265).

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: Vitamin D is effectively a hormone, not a true vitamin: skin synthesizes it from 7-dehydrocholesterol under UV light, the liver performs unregulated 25-hydroxylation (25(OH)D is the storage/measured form), and the kidney performs the tightly regulated 1-alpha-hydroxylation to active 1,25(OH)2D (Harrison 22e p.3268).

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: Renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase is stimulated by PTH and hypophosphatemia and suppressed by calcium, FGF23, and 1,25(OH)2D itself; granuloma/lymphoma macrophages express an unregulated 1-alpha-hydroxylase, explaining hypercalcemia in sarcoidosis and lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.3268).

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: Relying on total serum calcium without correcting for albumin, or on corrected calcium during acute illness, can mislead; ionized calcium should be measured directly when accuracy matters

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: A normal serum magnesium does not exclude total-body magnesium depletion because the extracellular pool is tiny

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: The body phosphate deficit cannot be predicted from a single serum phosphate; repletion must be empirical and monitored, since the nadir often occurs hours into insulin/glucose therapy

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: Giving IV magnesium alone to a patient with combined hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, and hypophosphatemia can worsen hypophosphatemia by abruptly restoring PTH secretion; give calcium and magnesium together

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: Failing to recognize that hypocalcemia and hypokalemia are refractory until magnesium is repleted

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: Overlooking 1,25(OH)2D-mediated hypercalcemia from granulomatous disease or lymphoma, where calcium does not suppress the ectopic 1-alpha-hydroxylase

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: Phosphate measured non-fasting or after IV dextrose can be spuriously low; rapid phosphate correction risks heterotopic calcification if the calcium-phosphorus product is allowed to rise

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: Prognosis depends entirely on the underlying disorder rather than on bone and mineral metabolism per se. Acute redistributive electrolyte derangements (hypophosphatemia, hypomagnesemia) are typically reversible with appropriate repletion, and respiratory/cardiac dysfunction from severe hypophosphatemia improves with phosphate replacement. Tumor-induced osteomalacia resolves within hours to days after successful tumor resection. Chronic renal phosphate-wasting disorders (XLH, ADHR) generally cannot be fully normalized but can be controlled. Persistent dysregulation, as in chronic kidney disease with secondary hyperparathyroidism and hyperphosphatemia, leads to progressive skeletal and vascular consequences.

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: Severe hypophosphatemia below about 0.25 mmol/L (0.8 mg/dL): risk of seizures, ascending paralysis, rhabdomyolysis, respiratory and cardiac failure, coma

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: Acute severe hyperphosphatemia: widespread calcium-phosphate precipitation with tetany, seizures, acute renal failure, and pulmonary/cardiac calcification including heart block

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: Hypermagnesemia above ~2 mmol/L: refractory hypotension, neuromuscular blockade, hyporeflexia progressing to respiratory failure, heart block, and asystole near 10 mmol/L

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: Severe hypomagnesemia: tetany, seizures, cardiac arrhythmias, prolonged QT and enhanced digitalis toxicity

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: Very high calcium intake or milk-alkali syndrome: hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis, progressive renal failure

chunks.diseaseName: Bone and Mineral Metabolism in Health and Disease
chunks.text: Hypophosphatemia is graded by serum phosphate (mild-moderate ~0.5-0.8 mmol/L [1.5-2.5 mg/dL] with mainly musculoskeletal/reversible cardiorespiratory effects; severe <0.5 mmol/L [<1.5 mg/dL]; life-threatening <0.25 mmol/L [<0.8 mg/dL] with paralysis, seizures, rhabdomyolysis). Hyperphosphatemia in adults is defined as fasting phosphate >1.8 mmol/L (5.5 mg/dL). Hypomagnesemia is usually asymptomatic above ~0.5 mmol/L; defects in PTH secretion appear below ~0.4 mmol/L. Hypermagnesemia produces vasodilation/neuromuscular blockade above ~2 mmol/L, coma and hyporeflexia above ~4 mmol/L, and asystole near 10 mmol/L.

chunks.diseaseName: Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia
chunks.text: Bone marrow failure results from severe damage to the hematopoietic cell compartment. In aplastic anemia the marrow is replaced by fat, CD34+ early hematopoietic cells are greatly diminished, and the stem cell pool in severe disease may be reduced to about 1% or less of normal. Three principal mechanisms underlie an empty marrow: physical/chemical damage (high-dose radiation, benzene and its reactive hydroquinone/quinolone metabolites, cytotoxic chemotherapy), immune-mediated stem cell destruction, and constitutional genetic defects. Acquired aplastic anemia is most often immune: activated cytotoxic T cells suppress hematopoietic progenitors, type 1 cytokines including interferon-gamma upregulate Fas on CD34+ cells driving apoptosis, and immune selection can produce HLA-loss and PNH clones. Genetically determined immune-response features (HLA, cytokine and T-cell polarization gene polymorphisms) likely convert a normal response into sustained autoimmunity, explaining why aplasia is rare despite common exposures. Idiosyncratic drug-induced aplasia is attributed to abnormal generation of or failure to detoxify reactive electrophilic drug intermediates that bind cellular macromolecules. Constitutional syndromes are intrinsic stem cell defects: Fanconi anemia involves a DNA interstrand cross-link repair pathway (most often FANCA; the gene products monoubiquitinate FANCD2), telomere biology disorders involve telomerase complex (DKC1, TERC, TERT) or shelterin (TINF2) defects that limit replicative capacity, and GATA2/RUNX1 mutations disrupt hematopoietic transcriptional regulation; Diamond-Blackfan and Shwachman-Diamond syndromes are ribosomopathies. MDS is a clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder of aging marrow characterized by disordered proliferation, impaired differentiation and ineffective hematopoiesis producing cytopenias plus risk of leukemic progression; both chromosomal instability (non-random losses of 5, 7, 20, trisomy 8) and accumulating somatic mutations in ~100 recurrently mutated myeloid genes drive disease, with clonal succession of founder clones acquiring further mutations during evolution to AML.

chunks.diseaseName: Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia
chunks.text: Marrow failure cytopenias reflect deficient production, distinguishing them from peripheral destruction (hemolysis, ITP, immune leukopenia, hypersplenism); the syndromes are categorized by the dominant marrow morphology, with aplastic anemia (fatty/empty marrow), MDS (dysplastic marrow), and single-lineage aplasias forming a related spectrum.

chunks.diseaseName: Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia
chunks.text: Marrow blast percentage is the strongest morphologic prognostic determinant in MDS; the WHO threshold of 20% marrow blasts separates AML from MDS, and blasts should be enumerated manually on smear and by flow cytometry.

chunks.diseaseName: Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia
chunks.text: 5q deletion MDS arises from heterozygous loss of a ribosomal protein gene, effectively mimicking constitutional red cell aplasia; SF3B1 mutation is strongly associated with ring sideroblasts and a relatively favorable outcome.

chunks.diseaseName: Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia
chunks.text: Severity grading in aplastic anemia and recovery thresholds are defined by blood counts (see severity criteria); absolute reticulocyte and lymphocyte numbers are better predictors of treatment response than the classic severity definition in the immunosuppression era.

chunks.diseaseName: Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia
chunks.text: Immune (acquired) aplastic anemia is classically a young person's disease with abrupt pancytopenia in a previously well adolescent or young adult; the age distribution is biphasic with peaks in the teens-twenties and again in older adults.

chunks.diseaseName: Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia
chunks.text: In aplastic anemia bleeding (bruising, gum oozing, epistaxis, menorrhagia, petechiae) is typically the earliest symptom, whereas infection as a first symptom is unusual; lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly are highly atypical and should prompt search for another cause of pancytopenia.

chunks.diseaseName: Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia
chunks.text: Clues to an inherited bone marrow failure syndrome: short stature and cafe au lait spots with thumb/radial anomalies (Fanconi anemia); dystrophic nails, mucosal leukoplakia and reticular hyperpigmentation (dyskeratosis congenita); premature hair graying plus a family history of pulmonary or hepatic fibrosis (telomere biology disorders); recurrent warts and unusual infections (GATA2 deficiency).

chunks.diseaseName: Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia
chunks.text: A detectable PNH clone by flow cytometry is found in up to half of patients at presentation of aplastic anemia and strongly suggests immune-mediated pathophysiology and likely responsiveness to immunosuppression; patients can later cross over between aplastic and hemolytic PNH phenotypes.

chunks.diseaseName: Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia
chunks.text: MDS is predominantly a disease of older adults (mean onset over 70) with a slight male predominance; anemia (often macrocytic) dominates the early course and at least half of patients are asymptomatic, discovered incidentally on routine blood counts.

chunks.diseaseName: Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia
chunks.text: Persistent parvovirus B19 infection is a treatable cause of pure red cell aplasia; the marrow shows giant pronormoblasts (the cytopathic signature), and diagnosis requires detection of viral DNA because IgG/IgM antibodies are commonly absent in immunodeficient hosts.

chunks.diseaseName: Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia
chunks.text: B19 parvovirus uses the erythrocyte P antigen as its receptor; in patients with underlying hemolysis it can precipitate a transient aplastic crisis with abrupt worsening of anemia from arrested erythropoiesis.

chunks.diseaseName: Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia
chunks.text: Macrocytosis (elevated MCV) is a frequent finding across marrow failure states; in aplastic anemia the smear shows large red cells with a paucity of platelets and granulocytes, near-absent reticulocytes, and the elevated MCV often persists even after recovery.

chunks.diseaseName: Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia
chunks.text: Clinical drug/chemical and viral associations with aplastic anemia are not proof of causation; the implicated agent may merely have been used to treat the earliest symptoms (antibiotics for fever, NSAIDs causing petechiae in an already thrombocytopenic patient).

chunks.diseaseName: Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia
chunks.text: Marrow cellularity correlates imperfectly with disease severity: 'empty' biopsies can occur in moderate disease and focal 'hot spots' of hematopoiesis can be seen in severe aplasia, so a single small or dilute sample can mislead (a dry tap suggests fibrosis or myelophthisis rather than aplasia).

chunks.diseaseName: Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia
chunks.text: Distinguishing acquired from constitutional aplastic anemia is essential; constitutional marrow is usually morphologically indistinguishable and physical anomalies may be subtle or absent (adults with telomere disorders can present without anomalies, only premature graying).

chunks.diseaseName: Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia
chunks.text: Hypocellular MDS can be mistaken for aplastic anemia; the boundary with low-risk MDS is blurred (del 13q/20q may respond to immunosuppression, and DNMT3A/ASXL1 mutations occur in both).

chunks.diseaseName: Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia
chunks.text: Dysplastic marrow changes are not specific to MDS, occurring with vitamin deficiencies, copper deficiency, drug effects, alcohol and acute viral infection; interobserver agreement on dysplasia morphology is imperfect.

chunks.diseaseName: Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia
chunks.text: Germline genomic panel results may take weeks to return, a problem in the severely pancytopenic patient who needs prompt management.

chunks.diseaseName: Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia
chunks.text: In transplant-eligible aplastic anemia patients, transfusing blood from family members risks alloimmunization and should be avoided; HLA typing should be ordered as soon as the diagnosis is made.

chunks.diseaseName: Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia
chunks.text: Glucocorticoids are not effective primary therapy for aplastic anemia and increase fungal infection risk.

chunks.diseaseName: Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia
chunks.text: Untreated severe aplastic anemia deteriorates rapidly and is fatal; spontaneous recovery is rare. The dominant prognostic factor is the blood count: severe disease has historically required two of three of an absolute neutrophil count <500/uL, platelets <20,000/uL and corrected reticulocyte count <1% (or absolute reticulocytes <60,000/uL), while in the immunosuppression era higher absolute reticulocytes (>25,000/uL) and lymphocytes (>1000/uL) better predict response and survival. A PNH clone, very short telomeres and somatic myeloid mutations (e.g., ASXL1) further influence outcome and risk of clonal evolution. Clonal evolution to MDS or leukemia occurs in roughly 10-15% of immunosuppression-treated patients over a decade. In MDS, median survival ranges from years (5q- or sideroblastic anemia) to only months (high blast count disease); the IPSS-R and emerging molecularly informed IPSS-M stratify risk. Even lower-risk MDS carries meaningful morbidity and mortality; most patients die of complications of pancytopenia rather than leukemic transformation, and about a third die of unrelated comorbidities. Therapy-related MDS has an extremely poor prognosis with rapid progression to refractory AML. Pure red cell aplasia is generally compatible with long-term survival with supportive care, and persistent parvovirus B19 PRCA almost always responds to immunoglobulin.

chunks.diseaseName: Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia
chunks.text: Severe aplastic anemia has historically been defined by the presence of at least two of three criteria: absolute neutrophil count <500/uL, platelet count <20,000/uL, and corrected reticulocyte count <1% (or absolute reticulocyte count <60,000/uL). In the immunosuppressive-therapy era, absolute reticulocyte count >25,000/uL and absolute lymphocyte count >1000/uL are better predictors of response and long-term outcome. For MDS, prognostic severity is assessed by the Revised International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS-R), which integrates marrow blast percentage (categories at <=2%, >2-<5%, 5-10%, >10-30%), refined cytogenetic risk groups, depth of cytopenias (hemoglobin, platelets, neutrophils), and additional features (age, performance status, ferritin, LDH, beta-2-microglobulin) into five risk categories; the molecularly enhanced IPSS-M is emerging as the current standard.

chunks.text: Borderline personality disorder is understood through a biosocial model in which a heritable predisposition to emotional vulnerability and impulsivity interacts with an invalidating or traumatic developmental environment. Neurobiological findings include altered function of limbic structures such as the amygdala and of prefrontal regulatory regions, contributing to heightened emotional reactivity and impaired regulation, with disturbances in serotonergic and stress-response systems.

Disease is caused by botulinum neurotoxins (BoNTs) produced by Clostridium botulinum (rarely C. butyricum or C. baratii), gram-positive, spore-forming, anaerobic bacteria whose heat-resistant spores are ubiquitous in soil. Serotypes A, B, E, and F cause human disease. BoNT is a metalloprotease whose heavy chain mediates neurospecific binding and internalization and whose light chain enters the cytosol and cleaves SNARE-family proteins (e.g., SNAP-25, VAMP), disrupting synaptic vesicle fusion and blocking acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, producing flaccid paralysis of voluntary muscles. Toxin binding is effectively irreversible, so recovery requires regeneration of nerve endings over weeks to months. Routes differ by form: foodborne (ingestion of preformed toxin in improperly preserved foods, often home-canned low-acid vegetables), wound (spore germination in wounds/necrotic tissue, notably from black tar heroin injection), infant and adult intestinal colonization (in situ toxin production by colonizing Clostridium), iatrogenic (high-dose therapeutic BoNT injection), and inhalational (aerosolized toxin as a bioweapon). (Harrison 22e p.1233-1234)
Classic syndrome: bilateral cranial nerve palsies followed by symmetric, descending flaccid paralysis, in a patient who is afebrile and fully conscious with normal sensorium (Harrison 22e p.1235).

First neurologic manifestation is usually ptosis, which can be striking; ocular findings include blurred/fuzzy vision or diplopia from extraocular palsies of cranial nerves III, IV, and VI (Harrison 22e p.1235).

Bulbar onset: dysarthria, difficulty swallowing, and nasal/oral regurgitation reflect cranial nerve involvement; descending weakness then spreads to neck, shoulders, and limbs, with proximal groups affected before distal (Harrison 22e p.1235).
Paralysis descends symmetrically and distal tendon reflexes diminish symmetrically; constipation from intestinal paralysis develops in almost all patients (Harrison 22e p.1235-1236).

In a U.S. series of 332 cases, the most common reported symptoms were difficulty swallowing (86%), fatigue (85%), blurred vision (80%), and slurred speech (78%); signs included afebrile temperature (99%), descending paralysis (93%), alert/oriented status (93%), and ptosis (81%) (Harrison 22e p.1236).

BoNTs irreversibly block acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, so paralysis persists for weeks to months until nerve endings regenerate; the clinical approach is the same for all toxin types causing human illness (Harrison 22e p.1234, p.1236).

Four naturally occurring forms (foodborne, infant, wound, adult intestinal colonization) plus iatrogenic and inhalational forms; the neurologic syndrome is essentially identical across all forms and all ages (Harrison 22e p.1233-1235).

Every case of foodborne botulism is a public health emergency, as it may be the first in an outbreak; clinicians should contact the state health department emergency line to reach a CDC botulism consultant (Harrison 22e p.1235, p.1237).
More than 95% of noninfant botulism patients in the U.S. recover, and the infant botulism survival rate is near 100% (Harrison 22e p.1236).

Misclassifying the paralysis as ascending: botulism is a DESCENDING (cranial-first, then downward) symmetric flaccid paralysis, whereas GBS presents as an ASCENDING paralysis in about 95% of cases - this descending-versus-ascending distinction is central, though the Miller Fisher GBS variant (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia) may resemble early descending paralysis (Harrison 22e p.1236).

Mistaking intact sensorium for altered consciousness: cranial nerve palsies, ptosis, dysarthria, and gait instability can give a false impression of obtundation or be wrongly attributed to alcohol/substance intoxication, even though patients remain fully conscious (Harrison 22e p.1235-1236).

Sporadic (lone) cases are commonly misdiagnosed because of the rarity of botulism and clinician unfamiliarity; an incomplete neurologic examination is a frequent cause of delayed or missed diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1236).
Waiting for laboratory confirmation: confirmation may take >=24 h, so treatment must rely on rapid clinical diagnosis rather than awaiting lab results (Harrison 22e p.1236-1237).

Assuming normal CSF excludes GBS too early: in GBS, CSF protein elevation may lag symptom onset by days, so a normal early CSF must be interpreted with symptom duration and the lumbar puncture may need repeating (Harrison 22e p.1236).

Reported paresthesias are not explained by the known activity of botulinum toxin, and GI symptoms (nausea/vomiting) are seen in foodborne but have NOT been reported in wound botulism (Harrison 22e p.1235-1236).

More than 95% of noninfant botulism patients in the United States recover, often after protracted intensive care and rehabilitation, even without antitoxin; the survival rate for infant botulism is near 100%. Paralysis lasts weeks to months while affected nerve endings regenerate. Serotype A is associated with more rapid progression, more frequent respiratory compromise and mechanical ventilation, and longer-duration paralysis; type B is milder and shorter; type F progresses rapidly but recovers faster. Untreated, early death results from airway obstruction and inadequate tidal volume from respiratory muscle paralysis. (Harrison 22e p.1236)
Pharyngeal muscle flaccidity causing airway collapse and respiratory arrest early in the course
Falling vital capacity / diaphragmatic and accessory muscle weakness signaling impending respiratory failure
Rapidly progressive descending paralysis (especially BoNT type A or F)
A placid, expressionless appearance masking the agitation expected with respiratory distress
Autonomic dysfunction producing hemodynamic instability
Two or more patients with the same syndrome (near-pathognomonic and signals an outbreak / public health emergency)

Harrison does not provide a formal numeric severity score; severity is described as varying greatly between patients and is probably governed by toxin dose. At the mild end, some untreated patients progress no further than ptosis and mild palsy of one or two cranial nerves; at the severe end, others develop fulminant cranial nerve palsies and rapidly progressive descending flaccid paralysis affecting most or all voluntary muscles with respiratory failure requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation within hours. (Harrison 22e p.1236)

chunks.text: Mechanical obstruction of a hollow viscus classically elicits intermittent (colicky) pain that is less well localized than the parietal pain of peritoneal irritation; distension of the viscus may also produce steady pain with only occasional paroxysms. With superimposed strangulating obstruction, traction on the root of the mesentery can refer pain to the lower lumbar region. As the obstructed proximal bowel progressively dilates it loses muscular tone, so colicky pain may wane and peristaltic sounds may weaken. Obstruction must be distinguished from adynamic ileus (loss of peristalsis) and from colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's syndrome), in which the bowel is dilated without a mechanical lesion (Harrison 22e pp.110-113, p.327).
