chunks.text: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo is caused by displacement of otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals) from the utricular macula into a semicircular canal, most often the posterior canal. In the common canalithiasis form, these free-floating particles move under gravity when the head changes position, creating abnormal endolymph flow that deflects the cupula and generates a transient, mismatched sensation of rotation. The brief latency, short duration and fatigability of symptoms reflect the settling of the particles. A less common cupulolithiasis form, with particles adherent to the cupula, produces more persistent positional nystagmus.

Bradyarrhythmias arise from abnormalities of the specialized conduction tissues. The sinoatrial (SA) node is the natural pacemaker (resting rate 60-100/min); its pacemaker cells have no true resting potential and depolarize spontaneously in phase 4 driven by the funny current (If) plus T- and L-type calcium currents, with calcium (not sodium) carrying the slow phase-0 upstroke. SA node function is dominated by parasympathetic tone at baseline (intrinsic heart rate ~100-110/min after autonomic blockade); intrinsic rate declines ~5-6 beats/min per decade of age. SA node dysfunction reflects problems of impulse formation (sinus arrest) or impulse conduction (sinoatrial exit block), and is most often due to age-related fibrosis and loss of pacemaker myocytes. In the AV node, conduction is decremental and depends on L-type calcium current; the node and proximal His are richly innervated by autonomic input, whereas the His bundle and distal conduction system are NOT influenced by autonomic tone. Acquired AV conduction disease is most commonly due to fibrosis/sclerosis/calcification of the conduction system (~50% of cases: senile degeneration/Lev's disease, Lenegre's disease, aortic-annular calcification). Block is anatomically nodal (vagally modulated, stable narrow escape) or infranodal (His-Purkinje, unstable wide escape, higher risk).

Sinus node dysfunction (SND), also termed sick sinus syndrome, typically presents with fatigue, exercise intolerance, dyspnea, or syncope from a slow rate or pauses; the key diagnostic step is correlating symptoms with bradycardia/pauses on ECG or ambulatory monitoring (p.1917-1918).

Initial management of any bradyarrhythmia is to identify and eliminate reversible causes and assess the safety/reliability of the escape rhythm before deciding on temporary or permanent pacing (p.1922, p.1929).

Tachycardia-bradycardia (tachy-brady) syndrome is a subset of SND: high rates (most commonly atrial fibrillation) alternating with symptomatic bradycardia or offset pauses after the tachycardia terminates; the drugs needed for rate control often worsen the bradycardia, frequently prompting pacemaker implantation (p.1919).

AV block is classified on ECG: first-degree = fixed PR prolongation >200 ms with all impulses conducted; second-degree = intermittent failure of conduction (Mobitz I/Wenckebach with progressive PR prolongation before a dropped beat vs Mobitz II with fixed PR before a dropped beat); third-degree = complete AV dissociation with ventricular rate slower than atrial rate (p.1925-1926).

Mobitz I (Wenckebach) AV block typically involves the AV node, is hemodynamically stable, and in the absence of symptoms does NOT usually warrant pacing; Mobitz II is usually infranodal, associated with QRS widening and a less reliable escape rhythm, carries a risk of sudden death, and requires permanent pacing even when asymptomatic (p.1925).

Escape morphology localizes block: a narrow QRS escape implies AV-nodal/proximal-His block with a faster, more stable junctional rhythm, whereas a wide QRS escape implies distal His or bundle-branch block with a slower, less reliable rhythm (p.1926).

AV block from acute MI is more common with inferior MI but is usually proximal (AV node), with a stable narrow escape >40/min and often reversible; AV block in anterior MI is usually distal/infranodal, gives wide unstable escape rhythms, and carries a worse prognosis with high mortality (p.1926-1927).

Lyme carditis is a classic reversible infectious cause of AV block (usually nodal, narrow junctional escape >40/min) that typically resolves within about a week of antibiotic therapy; AV block with infective endocarditis should raise concern for a perivalvular abscess requiring urgent surgical consultation (p.1927).

AV block that develops at a younger age (≤60 years) warrants advanced imaging (cardiac MRI, CT, or FDG-PET) to evaluate for infiltrative disease such as sarcoidosis, since age-related progressive conduction-system fibrosis is otherwise the most common cause (p.1928).

Permanent pacing is the only reliable long-term therapy for symptomatic irreversible bradycardia; there is NO established heart-rate threshold below which pacing is automatically indicated, and the decision is driven by symptom-bradycardia correlation (p.1917, p.1922).
Treating asymptomatic sinus bradycardia or sleep/athletic vagal pauses with a pacemaker - these generally are NOT pacing indications; always check whether pauses occurred during sleep.
Missing reversible causes (drugs, hypothyroidism, hyperkalemia/electrolytes, ischemia, sleep apnea, increased vagal tone, hypothermia, raised ICP) before committing to permanent pacing.
Overlooking Lyme carditis as a reversible cause of AV block (typically resolves within ~1 week of antibiotics) - a treatable cause that should not lead to an unnecessary permanent pacemaker.
Failing to suspect a perivalvular abscess when AV block develops during infective endocarditis.
Treating Mobitz II or high-grade/complete infranodal block as benign - it requires pacing even without symptoms, unlike Mobitz I.
In 2:1 AV block, ECG cannot reliably distinguish Mobitz I from Mobitz II; clues (PR <160 ms with wide QRS suggesting infranodal) or EP study may be needed.
Missing chronotropic incompetence because a patient achieves a normal maximum heart rate on standard exercise testing despite inadequate rate during daily activity.
Misjudging a normal heart-transplant resting rate (~90-110/min due to denervation) as normal when it may represent chronotropic incompetence.

Asymptomatic sinus bradycardia has NOT been associated with adverse outcomes and generally does not warrant pacing; symptomatic SND is benign in terms of mortality and is treated to relieve symptoms. AV block prognosis depends critically on the level of block: AV-nodal (Mobitz I) block tends to be stable with a reliable junctional escape and good prognosis, whereas infranodal block (Mobitz II, distal third-degree) has unreliable escape rhythms and risk of sudden death. AV block complicating anterior MI carries high mortality, while inferior-MI nodal block is often transient and reversible. With appropriate permanent pacing, symptomatic bradyarrhythmias have an excellent prognosis. An HV interval >100 ms predicts ~10% annual progression to complete block.

ECG-based AV block grading: First-degree (PR >200 ms, all impulses conducted, usually AV-nodal delay) -> Second-degree (intermittent failure; Mobitz I/Wenckebach = progressive PR prolongation before dropped beat, usually nodal/stable; Mobitz II = fixed PR before dropped beat, usually infranodal/wide QRS/unstable) -> Third-degree/complete (complete AV dissociation, ventricular rate slower than atrial). SND subtypes: sinus arrest, sinoatrial exit block (type I, type II Mobitz I/II), tachy-brady syndrome, chronotropic incompetence. Pacing-indication classes (ACC/AHA/HRS): Class I (complete/high-grade or acquired Mobitz II block when irreversible - pace regardless of symptoms; symptomatic irreversible 2nd/3rd-degree block), Class IIa/IIb (symptom- or disease-dependent for milder block), Class III: Harm (asymptomatic physiologic bradycardia/pauses).

Metastatic brain tumour - three times more common than all primary brain tumours combined in adults; commonest sources lung and breast, with melanoma having the greatest propensity to metastasize to brain (p.716, p.723)
Diffuse glioma - the most common malignant PRIMARY brain tumour; subdivided into IDH-mutant astrocytoma, IDH-mutant 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendroglioma, and IDH wild-type glioblastoma (p.717-718)
Meningioma - now the most common primary brain tumour overall (~35%); extra-axial dural-based lesion, WHO grades I-III (p.720-721)
Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) - ~9% of primary brain tumours, presents with progressive unilateral hearing loss/tinnitus/dizziness (p.721)
Primary CNS lymphoma - densely enhancing, often periventricular/basal ganglia/corpus callosum; associated with immunosuppression and EBV in HIV (p.720)
Pituitary adenoma - amenorrhoea/galactorrhoea with headache suggests a prolactinoma (p.157, p.721)
Pineal-region tumour presenting with Parinaud's syndrome and hydrocephalus (p.720)
Colloid cyst of the third ventricle - intermittent hydrocephalus, rarely sudden death (p.722)
Brain abscess - shares a ring-enhancing radiographic appearance with metastasis and high-grade glioma (p.723)
Cerebral toxoplasmosis - in immunocompromised patients, multiple ring-enhancing lesions can be hard to distinguish from PCNSL or metastases (p.721)
MRI with gadolinium is the preferred test; CT only if MRI cannot be done (p.716)
Neuroimaging is often the only test needed to diagnose a brain tumour; laboratory tests are rarely useful (p.716)

General/raised-ICP symptoms arise as the enlarging tumour plus surrounding vasogenic edema raises intracranial pressure or obstructs CSF circulation, producing hydrocephalus; focal deficits reflect local invasion or compression (p.716). Primary tumours develop through stepwise acquisition of genetic changes - loss of tumour-suppressor genes (p53, CDKN2A/B, PTEN) and amplification/overexpression of oncogenes such as EGFR and PDGFR - and glioblastomas in particular show marked molecular heterogeneity (p.717). The 2021 WHO CNS classification integrates molecular markers (e.g. IDH mutation, 1p/19q co-deletion) with histology into the diagnosis (p.717-718). Brain metastases spread hematogenously, lodging in terminal arterioles at the grey-white junction in watershed territory, so distribution follows blood flow (~85% supratentorial, ~15% posterior fossa) (p.723).

Presenting features split into general (raised-ICP) symptoms - headache +/- nausea/vomiting, cognitive change, personality change, gait disorder - and focal/lateralizing signs such as hemiparesis, aphasia or visual field loss; many patients have both (p.716).

The classic morning-predominant headache that eases through the day occurs in only a minority of patients; brain-tumour headache is more often a nondescript dull ache, and migraine produces this pattern far more often than tumour (p.716, p.157).
Vomiting preceding headache by weeks is highly characteristic of posterior fossa tumours, and headache disturbs sleep in about 10% (p.157).
Seizures from a brain tumour always have a focal onset whether or not this is clinically apparent (p.716).
New de novo headache in a patient with known malignancy should raise suspicion of cerebral metastases or carcinomatous (leptomeningeal) meningitis (p.157).

On MRI, malignant tumours (primary or metastatic) typically enhance with gadolinium, have central necrosis and surrounding white-matter edema, whereas low-grade gliomas usually do NOT enhance and are best seen as increased signal on FLAIR (p.716).
Meningiomas and vestibular schwannomas are extra-axial, densely enhancing lesions; a meningioma characteristically shows a dural tail and compresses but does not invade brain (p.716, p.721).

Leptomeningeal disease produces multilevel neuraxis signs (radiculopathies, cranial neuropathies, seizures, confusion, raised-ICP encephalopathy); isolated focal deficits like hemiparesis are rarely from it unless brain is directly infiltrated (p.724).
Parinaud's syndrome (impaired upgaze and accommodation) points to a pineal-region mass (p.720).

A ring-enhancing lesion is non-specific - the differential includes brain abscess, toxoplasmosis, PCNSL, demyelination, sarcoidosis, radiation necrosis and primary brain tumour, so do not assume tumour without context (p.721, p.723).

Withholding the diagnosis of glioma can be hard for diffusely infiltrative non-enhancing tumours (formerly gliomatosis cerebri), which often present only with cognitive decline and confluent FLAIR signal without mass effect (p.718).
Do not give glucocorticoids before biopsy in suspected PCNSL - their cytolytic effect can yield non-diagnostic tissue (p.720).
Prophylactic antiepileptic drugs have no role in tumour patients who have not had a seizure (only perioperative use is sometimes appropriate) (p.716).
A normal or migrainous headache pattern is far more often migraine than tumour - tumour headache is frequently nondescript (p.157).
Imaging-negative leptomeningeal disease is common; a single negative CSF cytology does not exclude it (positive in only ~50% on first LP) (p.724).

Outcome is tumour-specific. Low-grade (grade 2) IDH-mutant astrocytoma usually transforms to higher grade with median survival around 10 years; high-grade IDH-mutant astrocytoma roughly 3-9 years (p.718). Oligodendrogliomas (IDH-mutant, 1p/19q co-deleted) are more therapy-responsive with median survival in excess of 10 years (p.718). Glioblastoma (IDH wild-type) is the most common malignant primary tumour and invariably recurs; with standard combined therapy median survival is ~15-18 months and 5-year survival ~10%; adverse factors include older age, unmethylated MGMT promoter, poor performance status and unresectable tumour (p.718-719). Diffuse midline glioma H3K27-altered carries a poor prognosis (~1 year) regardless of grade (p.719). Pilocytic astrocytoma (grade 1) and completely resected meningiomas/ependymomas can be cured (p.719-721). Brain metastases treated with WBRT have median survival of only ~4-6 months, though SRS achieves local control in 80-90% and occasional cure (p.724).

WHO CNS grading (2021 integrated histologic + molecular classification): diffuse gliomas graded 2-4 by histologic malignancy and molecular markers, with CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion conferring grade 4 to otherwise lower-grade IDH-mutant astrocytomas; pilocytic astrocytoma is grade 1. Meningiomas are graded I (benign), II (atypical) and III (malignant) by increasing aggressiveness (p.717-718, p.720-721).

chunks.text: A breast abscess is a localised collection of pus within breast tissue. In lactating women, milk stasis and nipple trauma allow skin organisms, chiefly Staphylococcus aureus, to enter and proliferate, progressing from mastitis to a walled-off abscess. In non-lactating women, periductal mastitis, strongly linked to smoking, causes duct damage, squamous metaplasia, and duct obstruction, with secondary infection by mixed aerobic and anaerobic organisms producing periareolar collections and sometimes a mammary duct fistula. Untreated collections enlarge, may point to the skin, and can cause tissue necrosis.

chunks.text: Inflammatory breast cancer is sometimes confused with mastitis or other breast infection (Harrison 22e p.638).
Benign breast pathology such as atypical ductal or lobular hyperplasia (raises risk about four- to fivefold) and lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS, raises risk 7- to 12-fold) (Harrison 22e p.633).

Mastitis or other breast infection can be mimicked by inflammatory breast cancer, which presents with rapid onset of erythema, swelling, and tenderness of the breast; breast or skin biopsy is critical when breast inflammation fails to resolve after antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.638).
Image-guided core biopsy for pathologic confirmation, tumor grade/morphology, and biomarker testing (ER, PR, HER2 protein, and potentially HER2 gene amplification) (Harrison 22e p.634).
Diagnostic breast imaging: mammography, ultrasonography, and MRI if indicated; bilateral breast imaging because up to 3% have unsuspected contralateral disease (Harrison 22e p.634).

Germline panel testing for breast cancer susceptibility mutations on DNA from peripheral blood or saliva after appropriate counseling (not recommended for the general population) (Harrison 22e p.633).

For symptoms or findings of advanced disease (large tumor, skin changes, extensive adenopathy): CT and radionuclide bone scanning to look for overt metastatic disease, with biopsy of suspicious lesions to confirm metastatic disease (Harrison 22e p.635).

Genomic transcriptional profiling assays for early-stage ER-positive disease (Oncotype Dx 21-gene, MammaPrint 70-gene, ProSigna 50-gene, EndoPredict 12-gene, Breast Cancer Index) to inform adjuvant chemotherapy decisions; ordering more than one per case is discouraged (Harrison 22e p.636).
Skin biopsy showing dermal lymphatic invasion with tumor cells supports diagnosis of inflammatory breast cancer (Harrison 22e p.638).

Evolving changes in the pregnant breast can make diagnosis of breast cancer during pregnancy difficult, so suspicious lumps or skin or nipple changes still require formal evaluation (Harrison 22e p.638).

Breast cancer is predominantly a disease resulting from prolonged exposure of the breast to estrogen. Most breast cancers begin in epithelial cells within the lobules or ducts and proceed through a conceptual continuum of atypia and hyperplasia to in situ malignancy, then invasion into surrounding tissue, intravasation into lymph and blood channels, spread to regional lymph nodes, and distant metastases (though not all cancers progress through every stage). Hereditary breast cancer susceptibility genes account for 5-10% of cases; these genes participate in DNA damage repair, and inherited autosomal dominant mutations generally cause protein truncation and loss of function of DNA repair proteins. The most common are BRCA1 (chromosome 17q21) and BRCA2 (chromosome 13q12), conferring a 50-80% lifetime risk of invasive breast cancer by age 80 and a 30% risk of ovarian cancer; other germline mutations include TP53 (Li-Fraumeni), PALB2, ATM, STK11 (Peutz-Jeghers), and PTEN (Cowden). Ashkenazi Jews have a higher BRCA mutation incidence (Harrison 22e p.632-633).

Most common nonskin cancer in women worldwide; predominantly a disease of prolonged estrogen exposure, with female gender and increasing age the most common risk factors (about 70% diagnosed at 55 years or older, median age 63) (Harrison 22e p.632).

Clinical signs and symptoms suggestive of breast cancer may include a breast lump, skin or nipple changes, or palpable regional nodes; with mammographic screening many patients are asymptomatic and present only with an imaging abnormality (mass, distortion, or suspicious microcalcifications) (Harrison 22e p.634).

Diagnosis rests on pathologic confirmation, generally by image-guided core biopsy, which also assesses tumor grade and morphology and performs biomarker evaluation for estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and HER2 protein expression and potentially HER2 gene amplification (the triple assessment of clinical/imaging/pathology with biomarkers) (Harrison 22e p.634).

Suspicious axillary nodes should be biopsied via image-guided techniques, and both breasts should be imaged because up to 3% of women with newly diagnosed breast cancer have unsuspected contralateral disease (Harrison 22e p.634).

Invasive breast cancer is divided into at least four molecular subtypes: luminal A and luminal B (both ER positive; luminal B has reduced PR or higher Ki67 proliferation and worse outcome), HER2 subtype (high HER2 expression, benefits from HER2-targeted therapy), and basal/triple-negative (TNBC, lacking ER, PR, and HER2) (Harrison 22e p.636).

Most invasive breast cancers are ductal; about 10-15% are lobular, which are usually ER positive and HER2 negative, distinguished by absence of E-cadherin, and have a propensity to spread to serosal surfaces (omentum, pleura, meninges) and parenchyma (ovaries, GI tract) (Harrison 22e p.636).
Family history is a critical risk factor, yet only 20% of women diagnosed with breast cancer have a family history; a first-degree relative with breast cancer doubles the risk (Harrison 22e p.633).

A common disease-specific diagnostic pitfall is ordering a mammogram for a woman with a palpable breast lump and, when it returns normal, reassuring her that cancer has been ruled out; any unexplained palpable mass needs further testing and biopsy where warranted (Harrison 22e p.45).

Lobular cancers can recur at unusual sites (serosal surfaces, ovaries, GI tract), producing atypical presentations that may delay diagnosis if metastatic disease is not considered (Harrison 22e p.636).
Up to 3% of newly diagnosed patients have unsuspected contralateral disease, so both breasts must be imaged (Harrison 22e p.634).
Inflammatory breast cancer may be mistaken for mastitis or infection; biopsy is critical when inflammation fails to resolve after antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.638).
Germline panel testing can yield variants of unknown significance (VUS) and includes genes with poorly defined clinical risk, causing patient confusion and discomfort (Harrison 22e p.633).

5-year relative survival in the United States is currently about 91%. Outcomes are directly related to stage at presentation (and vary by race/ethnicity): 5-year relative survival is over 99% for stage I, about 93% for stage II, about 75% for stage III, and about 29% for stage IV. Less than 10% present with de novo metastatic (M1) disease. Luminal B tumors carry a poorer outcome than luminal A; TNBC carries a poorer prognosis; mucinous and pure medullary cancers have very favorable prognoses with local therapy only; higher Nottingham grade is associated with poorer prognosis. About 20-25% of patients treated for early breast cancer subsequently develop metastatic disease (Harrison 22e p.635-638).

Inflammatory breast cancer: rapid onset of erythema, swelling, and tenderness of the breast (a subset of locally advanced disease); breast inflammation failing to resolve after antibiotics warrants breast or skin biopsy, and up to one-third have detectable metastasis at diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.638).

Any unexplained mass or lesion palpable on physical examination needs further assessment including biopsy where warranted; a normal mammogram does NOT rule out cancer in a woman with a palpable breast lump (Harrison 22e p.45).
Locally advanced features: large primary tumor, involvement of skin or chest wall, or fixed tumor or axillary nodes (Harrison 22e p.638).

Staging follows the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) eighth edition TNM (tumor-node-metastasis) system, which has evolved to incorporate molecular biomarkers (ER, PR, HER2) and certain genomic tests (e.g., Oncotype 21-gene assay). Conceptually, stages I and II are early-stage disease confined to breast and ipsilateral nodes; stage III is locally advanced disease; and stage IV (M1) is metastatic disease. Staging may be clinical (c), pathologic after surgery (p), or post-neoadjuvant (y prefix). Common metastatic sites are soft tissues, lung, bone, liver, and brain (Harrison 22e p.634-635).

Viral infection of the small airway epithelium causes inflammation, oedema, and necrosis of epithelial cells with increased mucus production. Sloughed cellular debris and mucus, together with airway wall swelling, partially or completely obstruct the small bronchioles. Because infant airways are narrow, this obstruction produces air trapping, hyperinflation, atelectasis, and ventilation-perfusion mismatch, leading to wheeze, hypoxaemia, and increased work of breathing.
A common lower respiratory tract infection of infants, typically under 2 years and peaking around 2-6 months, most often caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).
Begins with upper respiratory symptoms (coryza, cough, low-grade fever) that progress over a few days to tachypnoea, wheeze, crackles, and increased work of breathing.
Diagnosis is clinical; routine viral testing, chest radiographs, and blood tests are usually unnecessary and can be misleading.
Management is supportive: ensure adequate hydration and feeding, maintain oxygenation, and provide gentle nasal suction as needed.
Bronchodilators, corticosteroids, and antibiotics are generally not beneficial in typical bronchiolitis and are not routinely recommended.
Apnoea can be an early and sometimes presenting sign, particularly in young or premature infants.
Risk factors for severe disease include prematurity, age under 2-3 months, congenital heart disease, chronic lung disease, and immunodeficiency.
Most cases are self-limiting over 1-2 weeks, though cough can persist longer.

Most previously healthy infants recover fully within one to two weeks; a minority, especially high-risk infants, require hospitalisation, and some children have recurrent wheeze afterwards.

In the immature lung, the combination of oxidative stress from supplemental oxygen, mechanical injury from positive-pressure ventilation, inflammation, and antenatal or postnatal infection disrupts normal alveolar septation and pulmonary microvascular growth. The result is fewer, larger, simplified alveoli with an abnormal vascular bed, variable airway smooth-muscle and interstitial changes, and impaired gas exchange. Pulmonary vascular remodelling can lead to pulmonary hypertension.
A chronic lung disease of prematurity, usually defined by a persisting need for supplemental oxygen or respiratory support at around 36 weeks postmenstrual age.
Occurs mainly in very preterm, very-low-birth-weight infants, often those who required prolonged mechanical ventilation and oxygen for respiratory distress syndrome.
The modern ('new') form reflects arrested alveolar and pulmonary vascular development rather than the severe fibrotic airway injury seen historically.
Contributing factors include oxygen toxicity, ventilator-induced volutrauma and barotrauma, inflammation, infection, and a patent ductus arteriosus.
Lung-protective strategies, such as early CPAP, gentle ventilation targeting acceptable gas exchange, and judicious oxygen targeting, help prevent it.
Management emphasises adequate nutrition and calories for lung growth, careful fluid balance, and weaning of respiratory support as tolerated.
Systemic corticosteroids can facilitate extubation but carry neurodevelopmental risks, so their use is weighed carefully and generally limited.
Affected infants are prone to recurrent wheeze, respiratory infections, and pulmonary hypertension, and benefit from RSV prophylaxis and immunisation.
Caffeine therapy for apnoea of prematurity is associated with a lower rate of bronchopulmonary dysplasia.
Using liberal oxygen targets that worsen lung and retinal injury
Overlooking pulmonary hypertension as a cause of persistent oxygen need
Excess fluid administration precipitating pulmonary oedema
Prolonged or high-dose systemic steroid courses despite neurodevelopmental risk
Underestimating nutritional needs required for lung repair and growth

Most infants gradually improve as the lung grows during early childhood, but many have increased respiratory morbidity, exercise limitation, and abnormal lung function later; severe disease with pulmonary hypertension carries higher mortality and long-term risk.

Brucellae are small, gram-negative, unencapsulated, nonsporulating coccobacilli that behave as facultative intracellular parasites. Following entry by ingestion, inhalation, or mucosal/percutaneous exposure, initial replication is presumed to occur within cells of the lymph nodes draining the entry point, with subsequent hematogenous spread that can establish chronic localizing infection at almost any site, most often the reticuloendothelial system, musculoskeletal tissues, and genitourinary system. The macrophage is the key target cell; Brucella is a "stealth" pathogen that evades innate immunity and survives within monocytic cells by restricting fusion of type IV secretion system-dependent Brucella-containing vacuoles with lysosomes, inhibiting apoptosis of infected cells, and preventing dendritic cell maturation and T-cell activation. Smooth LPS has low endotoxin activity and contributes to pyrogenicity and resistance to phagocytosis and serum killing. Antibodies aid clearance of extracellular organisms but alone cannot eradicate infection; control depends on macrophage activation and IFN-gamma/TH1 responses. Tissue responses range from acute and chronic inflammation to granuloma formation, with or without necrosis and caseation, and abscesses may develop in chronic localized infection (p.1332).

A bacterial zoonosis caused by Brucella species, transmitted directly or indirectly from infected animals, predominantly domesticated ruminants and swine; B. melitensis (sheep, goats, camels) is the most common cause of symptomatic human disease, with B. abortus (cattle/buffalo), B. suis (swine), and B. canis (dogs) also implicated (p.1331).
Diagnosis rests on a history of potential exposure, a compatible presentation, and supporting laboratory findings, because the clinical picture is not distinctive (p.1333).

Isolation of brucellae from blood, CSF, bone marrow, joint fluid, or a tissue aspirate/biopsy is definitive and succeeds in about 50-70% of cases; modern automated blood culture systems (e.g., Bactec) usually turn positive within 7 days (p.1333).

Serology often provides the only positive laboratory finding; in endemic or occupationally exposed settings agglutinin titers of 1:320-1:640 or higher are considered diagnostic, while in nonendemic areas a titer of at least 1:160 is significant, with no single universal cutoff (p.1334).

Human infection is usually associated with occupational or domestic animal exposure (farmers, shepherds, goatherds, veterinarians, slaughterhouse and meat-processing workers, laboratory staff); travelers and urban residents typically acquire it through contaminated food (p.1332).

Dairy products, especially soft cheeses, unpasteurized milk, and ice cream, are the most frequently implicated sources; acquisition may occur by ingestion, inhalation, or mucosal/percutaneous exposure (p.1332).

Almost invariably causes fever, which may be accompanied by profuse sweats, especially at night; untreated, the fever classically shows an undulating pattern persisting for weeks before an afebrile period that may be followed by relapse (p.1332-1333).
Fever is associated with musculoskeletal symptoms and signs in about half of patients; nonspecific features include apathy, fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, myalgia, headache, and chills (p.1333).

Presentation often fits one of three patterns: a typhoid-like febrile illness but less severe; fever with acute monoarthritis (typically hip or knee) in a young child; and long-lasting fever with misery and low-back or hip pain in an older person, especially men (p.1333).

Focal musculoskeletal involvement is the most common complication (~40%): osteomyelitis favors lumbar and low thoracic vertebrae, and septic arthritis most often affects knee, hip, sacroiliac, shoulder, and sternoclavicular joints, as monoarthritis or polyarthritis (p.1333).
Roughly one-quarter of patients have hepatosplenomegaly and 10-20% have significant lymphadenopathy; up to 10% of men develop acute epididymo-orchitis (p.1333).
Endocarditis occurs in about 1% of cases, most often affecting the aortic valve (native or prosthetic), and is the usual cause of death when the outcome is fatal (p.1333, p.1335).
The clinical picture is not distinctive and definitive diagnostic signs may be lacking, so exposure history and laboratory support are essential (p.1331, p.1333).
Routine biochemistry is usually normal; peripheral leukocyte counts are typically normal or low with relative lymphocytosis, so normal blood counts do not exclude the disease (p.1333).

Brucella may be misidentified by gallery strips as Agrobacterium, Ochrobactrum, or Psychrobacter (Moraxella) phenylpyruvicus; after taxonomic changes Ochrobactrum isolates may now be reported as a Brucella subspecies despite completely different management, so culture reports should be confirmed with the laboratory before therapeutic decisions (p.1333-1334).
Rough strains such as B. canis and B. ovis do not react in conventional serologic tests and will give false-negative results; consult the laboratory if B. canis is suspected (p.1334).

Serologic cross-reactions occur with other gram-negative bacteria including Yersinia enterocolitica O:9, E. coli O157, Francisella tularensis, Salmonella enterica group N, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, and Vibrio cholerae (p.1334).
Live B. abortus vaccine strain RB51 does not elicit antibody in tests using smooth antigens, which must be considered when following accidental vaccine exposures (p.1334).
Elevated CSF adenosine deaminase cannot be used to distinguish tubercular meningitis, as it may also be raised in brucellosis (p.1333).

Existence of a prolonged chronic brucellosis state after successful treatment remains controversial; evaluation requires careful exclusion of malingering, chronic fatigue syndromes, and other causes of sweating such as alcohol abuse and obesity (p.1335).

Fewer than 1% of patients die of brucellosis; when fatal, death is usually due to cardiac involvement and, more rarely, severe neurologic disease. Despite low mortality, recovery is slow and the illness can cause prolonged inactivity. Relapse occurs in up to 30% of poorly compliant patients, so clinical follow-up for up to 2 years is recommended; relapse responds to a prolonged repeat course of the original therapy. General well-being and body weight are better guides to absence of relapse than serology, since IgG agglutination titers can stay in the diagnostic range for more than 2 years after cure. Immunity is not solid and reinfection can occur after repeated exposures (p.1335).
Endocarditis, most often of the aortic valve (native or prosthetic), the leading cause of death in fatal cases (p.1333, p.1335).
Neurobrucellosis: lymphocytic meningoencephalitis mimicking neurotuberculosis, and rarely intracerebral abscess, cranial nerve deficits, or ruptured mycotic aneurysms (p.1333).
Vertebral osteomyelitis (spondylitis) and sacroiliitis (p.1333).
Disseminated intravascular coagulation with raised fibrinogen degradation products and thrombocytopenia (p.1333).
Increased fetal loss in infected pregnant women (though teratogenicity has not been described and abortion is much less pronounced in humans than in animals) (p.1333).

Harrison distinguishes acute nonfocal brucellosis (duration under about 1-2 months) from complex or focal disease (e.g., spondylitis, neurobrucellosis, endocarditis), the latter requiring more prolonged and tailored therapy. Patterns by species are also noted: B. melitensis tends toward a more acute, aggressive presentation, B. suis toward focal abscess formation, and B. abortus toward a more insidious onset that is more likely to become chronic (p.1333-1334).

chunks.text: Bulimia nervosa involves interacting genetic, temperamental, and sociocultural factors, with dysregulation of serotonergic systems affecting satiety, mood, and impulse control. chunks.text: Bullous pemphigoid is caused by autoantibodies directed against hemidesmosomal proteins of the dermal-epidermal junction, principally BP180 (collagen XVII) and BP230. Antibody binding activates complement and recruits inflammatory cells, particularly eosinophils, which release proteases that degrade the anchoring structures holding the epidermis to the dermis. This produces a subepidermal split, giving tense blisters with an intact epidermal roof. The urticarial prodrome reflects the inflammatory phase before frank blistering. Disease predominates in the elderly and may be associated with neurological disease and, in some cases, drug exposure.

chunks.text: Candida species (most often C. albicans) are normal saprophytic commensals of the gastrointestinal tract and skin. They overgrow and become pathogenic when local or systemic host defenses are disrupted, e.g., by broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy, diabetes mellitus, or immunosuppression. Mucocutaneous disease results from overgrowth at moist, macerated surfaces; invasive disease arises when the organism gains bloodstream access, frequently via intravascular catheters or the gut in neutropenic hosts (endogenous flora), producing candidemia and hematogenous (disseminated) seeding to organs, skin, and the eye (Chap. 60, p.432-433; Chap. 79, p.578).

Delta-9-THC is mainly a partial agonist at G protein-coupled cannabinoid receptors CB1R and CB2R, with euphorigenic effects mediated through CB1Rs on excitatory glutamatergic and inhibitory GABAergic interneurons and glial cells in brain regions processing stress, mood, and reward. These receptors are effectors of the endocannabinoid system (ECS), physiologically driven by endogenous ligands 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG, a full agonist) and anandamide (a partial agonist) that are synthesized and degraded on demand to give temporally and regionally precise modulation. Exogenous cannabinoids, defined by dose and duration rather than this 'just-in-time' synaptic signaling, disrupt ECS neuroregulation. Reward is thought to be mediated by modulation of glutamatergic and GABAergic activity in the ventral tegmental area, from which dopaminergic neurons project to the nucleus accumbens where rewarding experiences are reinforced; anxiolytic effects are mediated via the amygdala. Regular use is associated with broad but reversible reduction in cannabinoid receptor density (recovering by ~28 days of abstinence). Perturbation of ECS signaling during early fetal development can affect neuronal development, migration, and connectivity.

Cannabis is among the most widely used psychoactive substances; surveys cited estimate tens of millions of monthly users in the U.S., including a substantial number of adolescents and young adults aged 12-25.

Chronic high-dose use can cause cannabis hyperemesis syndrome, presenting as recurrent cycles of severe nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain, and is a growing reason for ED visits and hospitalization.

High-potency cannabis (>10% THC) can trigger acute psychotic episodes even on first exposure; these are usually transient but may become chronic with continued use and can trigger or worsen schizophrenia in vulnerable individuals.

Synthetic Delta-9-THC (dronabinol) is approved for chemotherapy-induced nausea and appetite stimulation, and a Delta-9-THC:CBD formulation is approved in some countries for chronic pain and MS-related spasticity (efficacy in MS largely based on patient report); there are currently no FDA-approved medications specifically for CUD.

Marijuana is legally distinguished from hemp by Delta-9-THC content: material exceeding 0.3% Delta-9-THC by dry weight is marijuana, while 0.3% or less is hemp; the principal euphoric and medicinal effects are mediated by Delta-9-THC acting on type 1 cannabinoid receptors (CB1R).

Product potency has risen sharply: flower can contain 20-30% Delta-9-THC, vape concentrates are advertised up to ~75%, and solid extracts ('shatter') up to ~95%, though many high claims appear exaggerated; higher potency is linked to greater addiction and psychosis risk.

Inhalation (smoking, vaping, 'dabbing') gives rapid, highly bioavailable absorption with quick onset, conditions associated with increased addiction risk; edibles have slower, less predictable onset and carry a higher risk of accidental overdose, particularly in children and inexperienced users.

Following smoking, plasma Delta-9-THC peaks within 5-10 minutes, but a hysteresis exists because brain levels keep rising during the early distribution (alpha) phase (t1/2 ~6 min) even as plasma falls; subjective peak effects occur at 20-30 minutes and total effect lasts roughly 4-8 hours.

Urine drug testing detects the inactive metabolite 11-nor-carboxy-THC (11-COOH-THC), whose terminal half-life is ~20 to 35+ hours, so cannabis remains detectable for days in occasional users and weeks in frequent users with saturated fat stores.

Regular use produces tolerance, so a given plasma Delta-9-THC level does not reliably predict impairment, which has hampered regulation of cannabis-impaired driving; Delta-9-THC nonetheless impairs judgment, motor coordination, and reaction time, increasing crash risk.

Cannabis use disorder (CUD) is a DSM-5 diagnosis defined by a problematic pattern of use causing clinically significant impairment or distress; criteria include craving, tolerance, a withdrawal syndrome, and failure to meet role obligations from recurrent use and drug seeking.

The withdrawal syndrome peaks within 1-3 days of stopping and manifests as anxiety, restlessness, insomnia, depression, and reduced appetite; most symptoms resolve within about 2 weeks, but insomnia often persists longer and may drive relapse.
Assuming a plasma Delta-9-THC level reliably reflects impairment; tolerance breaks this correlation and complicates impaired-driving assessment.
Underestimating edible dosing: delayed and variable onset (amplified by fatty meals increasing bioavailability 200-400%) leads naive users to redose and overdose.
Overstating the clinical role of minor cannabinoids (e.g., CBD) or terpenes at the concentrations found in marijuana, where evidence of relevance is limited and largely unproven.
Trusting product potency labels, which testing has shown to be frequently inflated.
Perceiving intoxicating hemp-derived products (e.g., Delta-8-THC and others) as safe or 'legal'; some such products can be considerably more potent than Delta-9-THC.
Overlooking EVALI risk historically tied to vitamin E acetate diluent rather than cannabis itself.

Most acute psychotic episodes are transient, but regular use can render them chronic, and cannabis may trigger or worsen schizophrenia in vulnerable individuals; adolescent and higher-frequency, higher-potency use carries the strongest associations with later psychotic disorder. Receptor downregulation is largely reversible, recovering toward control levels within about 28 days of abstinence. Withdrawal generally resolves within roughly 2 weeks, although insomnia may persist and promote relapse. Earlier age of initiation, higher use frequency, and higher-THC products increase the risk of developing CUD and of progression to other substance use disorders. Adolescent use has been associated with lower grades, lower IQ, and higher school dropout, though causation is not established.

chunks.text: Carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless gas produced by incomplete combustion. It binds haemoglobin with roughly 200-250 times the affinity of oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin, which both reduces oxygen-carrying capacity and shifts the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve leftward, impairing oxygen release to tissues. CO also binds myoglobin and inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase, causing cellular hypoxia and oxidative stress. The brain and heart, with high oxygen demand, are most vulnerable, and a lipid peroxidation and inflammatory cascade underlies the delayed neurological injury.

Metastatic neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumours, typically of midgut origin with hepatic metastases, secrete serotonin and other vasoactive mediators into the systemic circulation. These substances stimulate fibroblast proliferation and deposition of fibrous tissue on the endocardium and valve leaflets, predominantly on the right side of the heart. The resulting plaque-like fibrosis retracts and immobilises the tricuspid and pulmonary valves, causing regurgitation and stenosis that lead to volume overload and right ventricular failure. Pulmonary inactivation of serotonin largely protects the left heart.
Carcinoid heart disease is a complication of the carcinoid syndrome caused by vasoactive substances, particularly serotonin, released by metastatic neuroendocrine tumours
It characteristically affects the right-sided heart valves, producing tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonary stenosis or regurgitation with fibrous plaque-like thickening of the endocardium
Left-sided valve involvement is uncommon because the lungs inactivate circulating serotonin, but it can occur with a patent foramen ovale or bronchial carcinoid
It usually develops in patients with liver metastases, since hepatic clearance of tumour products is then bypassed
Right heart failure with peripheral oedema, ascites, and elevated venous pressure is the typical late presentation
Urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid and echocardiography are central to diagnosis, and elevated NT-proBNP supports cardiac involvement
Somatostatin analogues control syndrome symptoms and tumour secretion, while significant valve disease may require surgical valve replacement
Attributing right heart failure to more common causes and missing an underlying neuroendocrine tumour
Not screening for cardiac involvement in patients with established carcinoid syndrome
Failing to prevent and treat carcinoid crisis around surgery and interventions
Delaying valve surgery until right ventricular function is irreversibly impaired

Cardiac involvement is a major determinant of survival in carcinoid syndrome and historically indicated advanced disease with a poor outlook, but somatostatin analogue therapy, tumour-directed treatment, and timely valve surgery have improved outcomes.
Progressive right heart failure with ascites and oedema
Carcinoid crisis with flushing, haemodynamic instability, and bronchospasm, especially around procedures
Severe symptomatic valve dysfunction requiring surgical evaluation
Rapidly rising cardiac biomarkers indicating advancing cardiac disease

Thorough history (risk factors, prior surgeries, family history) and physical exam including digital rectal exam in men and breast/pelvic exam in women (Harrison 22e p.731)
Mammography (and breast MRI if mammogram/ultrasound negative) in women with metastatic adenocarcinoma, especially isolated axillary adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.732)

Lymphoma, metastatic melanoma, and metastatic sarcoma (excluded from CUP because they have specific histology/staging) (Harrison 22e p.731)
Peritoneal mesothelioma mislabeled as peritoneal carcinomatosis (calretinin/D2-40 positive; BerEp4/MOC-31 negative) (Harrison 22e p.735)

The reasons cancers present without an identifiable primary remain unclear. One hypothesis is that the primary tumor regresses after seeding metastases or stays too small to detect, possibly contained or eliminated by host defenses including the immune system. Alternatively, CUP may reflect a distinct malignant event producing increased metastatic spread or survival relative to the primary; whether CUP metastases represent a genetically and phenotypically unique clone is unresolved. Searches for a unique CUP signature have been unrevealing: aneuploidy occurs in about 70% of metastatic adenocarcinoma/undifferentiated CUP, and overexpression of RAS, BCL2 (about 40%), HER2 (about 11%), and P53 (about 26-53%) is seen but is shared with many other malignancies. Adenocarcinoma CUP is more often driven by RTK/Ras/MAPK pathway alterations than non-adenocarcinoma CUP. No distinct molecular signature has been established (Harrison 22e pp.731-734).

CUP is a biopsy-proven malignancy whose anatomic site of origin stays unidentified despite a standardized, detailed diagnostic workup; it ranks among the 10 most frequently diagnosed cancers worldwide and accounts for roughly 3-5% of all malignancies (Harrison 22e p.731).

Liver is a common site of CUP presentation, so intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is frequently misdiagnosed as CUP; cholangiocarcinoma incidence is rising while CUP incidence is declining, partly due to improved molecular diagnostics and clinician awareness (Harrison 22e p.731).

DNA methylation profiling predicted a primary in about 87% of 216 CUP patients in one study, and tissue-of-origin classifier assays suggest a plausible primary in roughly 70-80% of patients, though accuracy cannot be fully verified because the true primary is by definition unconfirmed (Harrison 22e pp.733-734).

Latent primary cancers (a new primary emerging after months to years) are uncommon with modern imaging, occurring in 5% or fewer of CUP patients, typically in indolent presentations or highly treatment-responsive disease (Harrison 22e p.732).

Most authorities restrict the CUP label to epithelial or undifferentiated cancers and exclude lymphoma, metastatic melanoma, and metastatic sarcoma, since those have distinct histology and stage-based management even without an identified primary (Harrison 22e p.731).

On light microscopy about 60-65% of CUP is adenocarcinoma and roughly 5% is squamous cell carcinoma, with the remaining 30-35% being poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma/carcinoma or poorly differentiated neoplasm; neuroendocrine tumors make up about 2% (Harrison 22e p.732).

Most serum tumor markers (CEA, CA-125, CA 19-9, CA 15-3) are nonspecific and do not localize the primary; in contrast, PSA tissue/serum staining and thyroglobulin are among the most specific markers but have low yield because prostate and thyroid cancers rarely present as CUP (Harrison 22e pp.731-732).

CK7 and CK20 cytokeratin patterns help narrow the putative primary: CK7 marks lung, ovary, endometrium, breast, and upper GI/pancreaticobiliary tumors, while CK20 is expressed in GI epithelium, urothelium, and Merkel cells (Harrison 22e p.733).

TTF-1 nuclear staining is positive in about 68% of lung adenocarcinomas and roughly 25% of squamous lung cancers and helps distinguish a lung primary from metastatic adenocarcinoma in pleural, mediastinal, or parenchymal sites (Harrison 22e p.733).

Comprehensive genomic profiling shows about 85% of CUP samples carry at least one clinically relevant genomic alteration, averaging about 4.2 alterations per tumor; the most common are TP53 (about 55%), KRAS (about 20%), CDKN2A (about 19%), and ARID1A (about 11%) (Harrison 22e pp.733-734).

Tissue-agnostic biomarkers matter in a minority of CUP cases: MSI-high / mismatch-repair-deficient tumors and high tumor mutational burden tumors, as well as NTRK fusion-positive tumors, identify candidates for established histology-agnostic therapy (Harrison 22e p.734).

Adequate tissue acquisition (preferably excisional or core needle biopsy rather than fine-needle aspiration alone) is critical, both for histology/IHC and for molecular profiling that can suggest a primary and actionable biomarkers (Harrison 22e p.732).
No IHC stain is 100% sensitive or specific; under- or overinterpretation should be avoided, and poor differentiation reduces sensitivity even of hallmark markers (Harrison 22e p.732).
CDX-2 positivity, while used for GI adenocarcinomas, can also occur in tumors with enteric/mucinous differentiation from other sites such as mucinous ovarian cancer (Harrison 22e p.733).

Tissue antigenicity and IHC interpretation are affected by antigen retrieval, fixation/processing, observer variability, antibody performance, and tissue heterogeneity or inadequacy from small biopsies (Harrison 22e p.733).
Pathologic features should not always override clinical or radiologic findings when deciding to test for therapeutic biomarkers such as EGFR, ALK, or HER2 (Harrison 22e p.733).
More IHC stains are not necessarily better; staining must be interpreted alongside clinical presentation and imaging, with close clinician-pathologist communication (Harrison 22e p.732).
Not all peritoneal carcinomatosis in women is primary peritoneal serous carcinoma; careful pathology can reveal a colon or pancreaticobiliary profile or mislabeled mesothelioma (Harrison 22e p.735).

Two randomized trials of gene-expression-directed site-specific therapy versus empiric chemotherapy failed to show a significant survival benefit, so molecular classifier results must be interpreted cautiously (Harrison 22e pp.733-734).

Median survival for most patients with disseminated CUP is about 6-10 months, and the prognosis for advanced disease remains poor with early resistance to available cytotoxic therapy. Prognosis is heterogeneous: favorable subsets (e.g., women with isolated axillary adenopathy treated as breast cancer, women with primary peritoneal serous carcinoma treated as ovarian cancer, men with midline poorly differentiated carcinoma resembling germ cell tumor, squamous cervical adenopathy, solitary metastatic sites, low-grade neuroendocrine tumors, and men with blastic bone metastases and elevated PSA) can achieve prolonged survival and occasionally cure. Recognized prognostic factors include performance status, site and number of metastases, response to therapy, and serum LDH; prognostic models (Culine using performance status and LDH; Raghav nomogram using gender, ECOG performance status, histology, number of metastatic sites, and neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio) stratify outcomes (Harrison 22e pp.734-735).
Liver, brain, or adrenal metastatic involvement, which carries a poor prognosis (Harrison 22e p.735)
Disseminated disease with two or more involved sites (Harrison 22e pp.734-735)
Poor performance status and elevated serum LDH, which are adverse prognostic factors (Harrison 22e p.734)
Peritoneal carcinomatosis from metastatic adenocarcinoma, raising concern for gastric, appendiceal, colon, or pancreaticobiliary primaries (Harrison 22e p.735)

No single formal staging system; risk stratification distinguishes favorable prognostic subsets (treatable as a specific putative primary, with potential for prolonged survival/cure) from unfavorable disseminated disease. Prognostic models include the Culine model (performance status plus serum LDH, dividing patients into two outcome subgroups) and the Raghav nomogram (gender, ECOG performance status, histology, number of metastatic sites, and neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio) (Harrison 22e pp.734-735).

chunks.text: Cardiac arrest is the sudden cessation of effective cardiac output. Shockable rhythms arise from disorganised (ventricular fibrillation) or excessively rapid (pulseless ventricular tachycardia) electrical activity that prevents coordinated contraction, most often on a background of ischaemic heart disease. Non-shockable arrest reflects either absent electrical activity (asystole) or organised electrical activity without a pulse (pulseless electrical activity), commonly due to a profound reversible insult. Regardless of mechanism, cessation of circulation causes global ischaemia; the brain tolerates only minutes before injury begins, so restoration of perfusion by chest compressions and treatment of the cause is time-critical.

chunks.text: In advanced (stage D) heart failure the myocardium can no longer maintain adequate output despite maximal medical therapy, producing a low cardiac output state with elevated filling and pulmonary pressures, intolerance of neurohormonal antagonists, and progressive cardiorenal dysfunction. Cardiac transplantation replaces the failing heart with an allograft that is surgically denervated, so it depends initially on circulating catecholamines and cannot mount reflex heart-rate responses. Allograft rejection follows two mechanisms: ACR, a T cell-mediated lymphocytic assault on donor myocardium (perivenular in mild disease, diffuse interstitial with myocyte necrosis and hemorrhage in severe disease), and AMR, an antibody/complement-mediated injury with immunoglobulin deposition, endothelial swelling, interstitial edema, and arteriolar vasculitis. Over the long term, immunologic insults (brain death, ischemia-reperfusion, alloimmunity) combined with nonimmunologic metabolic factors (hypertension, hyperlipidemia, dysglycemia from chronic immunosuppression) drive cardiac allograft vasculopathy, a diffuse fibrotic intimal proliferation narrowing the coronary tree. For mechanical support, continuous-flow LVAS divert blood from the LV apex to the aorta via a pump whose output depends on the LV-to-aorta pressure gradient; the non-physiologic flow path imposes shear stress that degrades von Willebrand factor multimers and causes hemolysis. LV unloading lowers right-sided afterload, but increased device flow raises RV preload and the displaced septum reduces RV contractile efficiency, promoting RV dilatation and maladaptation.

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiac Transplantation and Prolonged Assisted Circulation
chunks.text: Advanced heart failure is a distinct syndrome marked by refractoriness to conventional therapy, intolerance of guideline-dose neurohormonal antagonists, worsening renal function, poor cardiopulmonary reserve, and a low-output state with elevated pulmonary pressures; therapeutic goals shift toward surgical support of the failing heart (Harrison 22e p.2028).

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiac Transplantation and Prolonged Assisted Circulation
chunks.text: LVAS-related shear stress can cause low-grade hemolysis and acquired von Willebrand disease (loss of high-molecular-weight vWF multimers), predisposing to gastrointestinal bleeding from intestinal arteriovenous malformations and to iron-deficiency anemia (Harrison 22e p.2032).

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiac Transplantation and Prolonged Assisted Circulation

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiac Transplantation and Prolonged Assisted Circulation
chunks.text: Posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorders are usually Epstein-Barr virus driven and are the most frequent malignancy; solid cancers most often manifest as basal- and squamous-cell skin malignancies, so routine sunscreen is advised (Harrison 22e p.2030).

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiac Transplantation and Prolonged Assisted Circulation
chunks.text: Transplant candidacy generally requires refractory heart failure with a peak VO2 below ~14 mL/kg per min (below 12 if on beta blockers) or percent-predicted VO2 under 50%, combined with intolerance of disease-modifying therapy, cardiorenal syndrome, inotrope dependence, or need for an LVAS (Harrison 22e p.2028).

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiac Transplantation and Prolonged Assisted Circulation
chunks.text: Age is not an absolute contraindication, but frailty is a relative one; BMI above 35 should prompt weight loss, eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 is a relative contraindication possibly requiring combined kidney transplant, and tobacco use in any form must cease for at least 6 months (Harrison 22e p.2028).

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiac Transplantation and Prolonged Assisted Circulation
chunks.text: The transplanted heart is surgically denervated and unresponsive to sympathetic or parasympathetic stimuli; early postoperatively high-dose catecholamines are needed, and allograft bradycardia does NOT respond to atropine, so isoproterenol or temporary pacing is used (Harrison 22e p.2029).

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiac Transplantation and Prolonged Assisted Circulation
chunks.text: Donor ischemia (out-of-body) time is typically limited to about 4 hours unless novel ex situ normothermic perfusion transport techniques are used; allocation considers urgency, waiting-list time, distance, and ABO blood group, while HLA matching is usually impractical given time constraints (Harrison 22e p.2029).

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiac Transplantation and Prolonged Assisted Circulation
chunks.text: Acute cellular rejection (ACR) is a T cell-mediated process with myocardial lymphocytic infiltrates that occurs early and declines after about 6 months, whereas antibody-mediated rejection (AMR) is a noncellular, donor-specific antibody-driven process with complement fixation, endothelial swelling, and arteriolar vasculitis that carries worse allograft survival and predisposes to vasculopathy (Harrison 22e p.2029-2030).

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiac Transplantation and Prolonged Assisted Circulation
chunks.text: Cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV) is an accelerated, diffuse coronary intimal proliferation that is commonly clinically silent; intravascular ultrasound or optical coherence tomography is more sensitive than routine angiography for detection (Harrison 22e p.2030).

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiac Transplantation and Prolonged Assisted Circulation
chunks.text: Angiographic CAV is present in roughly 30% of patients by 5 years and about 50% by 10 years after transplant; retransplantation is the only definitive therapy for advanced CAV (Harrison 22e p.2030).

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiac Transplantation and Prolonged Assisted Circulation
chunks.text: Continuous-flow LVAS generate forward flow dependent on the pressure gradient between the LV cavity and aorta, so flow is critically sensitive to systemic blood pressure; because pulse is often undetectable, blood pressure is measured by Doppler (mean/opening pressure) and the target mean arterial pressure is at or below 90 mmHg (Harrison 22e p.2032).

chunks.text: More than 150,000 patients have undergone cardiac transplantation worldwide, with 1-year survival above 80%, median survival of ~12.5 years, and conditional survival of ~14.8 years for those surviving the first year. With the fully magnetically levitated HeartMate 3 LVAS, median survival exceeds 5 years (about 60% survival at 5 years), and in younger patients (under 50) without comorbidity and an uncomplicated course the 5-year survival can rival transplantation (~75%). Without such support, patients with severe refractory systolic heart failure (peak VO2 <12 mL/kg per min or inotrope dependence) often have a median survival under 1 year. CAV grade correlates with prognosis and remains a leading limit on late allograft survival.

chunks.text: Cardiac allograft vasculopathy is graded by the ISHLT 2010 scheme as CAV0 (absent), CAV1 (mild), CAV2 (moderate), and CAV3 (severe), based on extent of angiographic disease and presence of allograft dysfunction by echocardiography or restrictive physiology. Transplant allocation urgency is tiered, with the highest status for critically ill patients on ECMO or temporary biventricular mechanical support, then those needing daily invasive hemodynamic monitoring plus IV inotropes or with durable LVAD complications, and lower status for ambulatory patients stable at home.

Blunt forces (rapid deceleration, direct chest impact, crush, or blast) and penetrating objects damage the myocardium, valves, coronary arteries, pericardium, and great vessels. Myocardial contusion produces injury pathologically similar to infarction, with necrosis arising either directly or from traumatic coronary laceration, dissection, or thrombosis, predisposing to arrhythmias and conduction block. More severe injury causes free wall rupture (hemopericardium and tamponade) or ventricular septal rupture (intracardiac shunting). Valvular apparatus rupture (most often tricuspid or aortic) causes acute incompetence. Aortic rupture or transection, typically just above the aortic valve or at the ligamentum arteriosum tethering point, is the most common vascular deceleration injury. Commotio cordis represents a purely electrical mechanism: a chest blow during the susceptible repolarization window induces ventricular fibrillation without structural damage.
Cardiac injury is broadly divided into penetrating trauma (most often gunshot or knife wounds, where the entry site is usually obvious) and nonpenetrating, or blunt cardiac injury (BCI).
Iatrogenic cardiac perforation can complicate central/intracardiac catheter placement, pacemaker or defibrillator lead insertion, RV endomyocardial biopsy, and intracoronary stent deployment.

Post-cardiac injury syndrome (an inflammatory process resembling the postpericardiotomy syndrome) can develop weeks to months after blunt chest trauma, presenting with pericarditis and/or pericardial effusion.

Survivors of penetrating cardiac injury may present days to weeks later with a new murmur or heart failure from an occult or evolving valvular regurgitation or intracardiac shunt, so trauma patients should be re-examined several weeks after injury.

BCI most commonly follows motor vehicle collisions (rapid deceleration or chest impact) but can also result from falls, crush and blast injuries, assault, or vigorous contact in sports; significant cardiac injury may occur even when there are no external signs of thoracic trauma.

There is no single sign, symptom, or test that confirms BCI, and clinical, laboratory, and radiographic findings are frequently nonspecific in the setting of major trauma, so a high index of suspicion is essential.

An ECG should be obtained in every patient presenting with chest trauma; abnormalities can resemble those of infarction or pericarditis and include sinus tachycardia, RBBB, heart block, ST-T changes, and atrial or ventricular arrhythmias.
Cardiac troponin is more specific than CK-MB for myocardial damage; a normal troponin combined with a normal ECG at 6-8 hours after chest trauma essentially excludes BCI.

Echocardiography is the most useful modality for detecting the structural and functional sequelae of BCI, including regional wall motion abnormalities, pericardial effusion, valvular dysfunction, and ventricular or septal rupture; the RV, interventricular septum, and LV apex are most commonly involved.

Commotio cordis is ventricular fibrillation triggered by a blunt, often innocent-appearing chest impact in the absence of structural injury, occurring most often in adolescents during sports when the blow lands during the vulnerable phase of repolarization (just before the T-wave peak); survival depends on prompt defibrillation.
Sudden emotional or physical stress, even without direct cardiac trauma, may precipitate a transient catecholamine-mediated cardiomyopathy (takotsubo / apical ballooning syndrome).
Because of its anterior position in the chest, the right ventricle is the most frequently injured chamber in penetrating trauma, followed by the left ventricle; isolated atrial injury is uncommon.
Overlooking cardiac injury because attention is focused on more obvious external injuries.
Relying on sternal or rib fractures to gauge cardiac risk; there is no proven association, and significant cardiac injury can occur with a normal-appearing chest wall.
Using CK-MB to confirm BCI; it is elevated in only ~20% of blunt chest trauma and is falsely raised by massive skeletal muscle injury.
Attributing post-traumatic chest pain solely to musculoskeletal causes when it may reflect myocardial ischemia or pericardial injury.
Assuming a hemodynamically stable penetrating chest injury excludes cardiac involvement; up to ~20% harbor occult cardiac trauma.
Missing delayed complications (post-cardiac injury syndrome, late valvular regurgitation, intracardiac shunt) by not re-examining the patient weeks after injury.

Outcome depends on injury mechanism, chambers involved, and clinical condition at presentation. Although myocardial rupture is generally fatal, up to ~40% of patients reach a specialized trauma center alive. In penetrating injury, gunshot wounds carry higher mortality than stab wounds (about 20% of shooting victims survive versus up to ~65% of stabbing victims), partly because ballistic injuries more often involve multiple chambers; multichamber involvement carries a worse prognosis than single-chamber injury, and RV injury may carry a better prognosis than LV injury. Patients in hemodynamic collapse on arrival have a mortality near 90%, whereas roughly 75% of those stable enough to reach the operating room survive. Iatrogenic penetrating injuries generally have a better prognosis owing to more limited injury and prompt corrective therapy.
Hemodynamic instability or collapse at presentation (penetrating injury mortality approaches 90% in those in hemodynamic collapse)
New loud murmur with rapidly progressive heart failure (traumatic valvular rupture)
Signs of pericardial tamponade (pericardial rub, distant heart sounds, hypotension)
ST-segment elevation suggesting coronary dissection/occlusion
Mediastinal widening on chest x-ray with upper-extremity hypertension and diminished lower-extremity pulses (aortic rupture)
Sudden collapse during chest impact in an athlete (commotio cordis requiring immediate defibrillation)
Even a small pericardial effusion on echo in a penetrating chest injury (suggests occult cardiac perforation)

Blunt cardiac abnormalities span a spectrum: ECG changes (sinus tachycardia, RBBB, heart block, ST-T changes, arrhythmias), elevated biomarkers (troponin most specific), focal wall motion abnormality or hematoma (RV free wall, LV apex, septum), valvular insufficiency (most often mitral/tricuspid, occasionally aortic), myocardial rupture (VSD or free wall), coronary artery injury (often LAD, presenting as STEMI), and pericardial effusion/tamponade. Risk stratification: stable patients with a normal ECG and normal serial troponins are low risk; an abnormal ECG and/or elevated troponin with a normal echo warrants telemetry monitoring; mechanical complications and hemodynamic instability constitute the highest-acuity group.

chunks.text: A profound fall in myocardial contractility initiates a self-perpetuating spiral: reduced cardiac output and stroke volume lower blood pressure and coronary perfusion, worsening ischaemia and further depressing contractility, which left untreated leads to death. Ineffective stroke volume is the inciting event, but inadequate circulatory compensation also contributes. Early peripheral vasoconstriction may transiently improve coronary and peripheral perfusion but raises afterload and can worsen ischaemia. Over time, systemic inflammation from acute cardiac injury induces pathologic vasodilatation; inflammatory cytokines and inducible/endothelial nitric oxide synthase increase NO and its by-product peroxynitrite, which are negatively inotropic and cardiotoxic. Lactic acidosis and hypoxaemia compound the cycle because severe acidosis blunts the efficacy of endogenous and exogenous catecholamines. Bleeding and transfusion during ICU care can further trigger inflammation. Left-ventricular failure accounts for roughly 80% of cardiogenic shock complicating acute MI, with acute severe mitral regurgitation, ventricular septal rupture, predominant RV failure, and free-wall rupture/tamponade making up the remainder (p.2325).

chunks.text: In-hospital mortality ranges from roughly 40-60% depending on shock severity and underlying cause; cardiogenic and septic shock carry the highest mortality among shock types (90-day mortality around 52% for cardiogenic shock in one ED cohort). Higher lactate, elevated admission glucose, hepatic hypoperfusion and progressive renal impairment are adverse markers. Untreated shock progresses through compensated (preshock), decompensated, and finally irreversible stages with permanent organ dysfunction and multi-organ failure. Reperfusion and modern care have reduced the incidence of shock complicating acute MI to about 5-10% (p.2311, p.2325).

chunks.text: SCAI shock classification (2019, updated): Stage A 'at risk' — no current signs/symptoms; Stage B 'beginning'/preshock — relative hypotension or tachycardia without hypoperfusion; Stage C 'classic' — manifest hypoperfusion requiring intervention (inotropes, vasopressors or MCS, excluding ECMO) beyond volume; Stage D 'deteriorating' — like C but worsening and failing initial therapy; Stage E 'extremis' — cardiac arrest with ongoing CPR and/or ECMO. The updated definition adds a three-axis model: (1) shock severity, (2) phenotype/aetiology, (3) risk modifiers such as cardiac arrest. Lactate >8 mmol/L marks stage E (p.2325-2326).

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiovascular Collapse, Cardiac Arrest, and Sudden Cardiac Death
chunks.text: Most sudden cardiac death stems from a lethal ventricular tachyarrhythmia (polymorphic VT degenerating to ventricular fibrillation) arising on a vulnerable myocardial substrate, though bradyarrhythmia, asystole, and pulseless electrical activity are increasingly common terminal rhythms. Coronary artery disease is the predominant substrate, acting through acute ischemia/infarction or through reentry around scar from a healed infarct. Nonischemic processes - dilated, hypertrophic, infiltrative, and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathies, valvular disease, congenital surgical scars, and myocarditis - produce replacement fibrosis, hypertrophy, ventricular stretch, electrical heterogeneity, altered ion-channel function, and abnormal calcium handling that lower the threshold for sustained arrhythmia. In structurally normal hearts, inherited channelopathies (long QT, Brugada, CPVT), pre-excited atrial fibrillation in Wolff-Parkinson-White, and QT-prolonging drug toxicity cause primary electrical arrest. Pulseless electrical activity reflects mechanical or metabolic catastrophe - massive MI, pulmonary embolism, exsanguination, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, profound hypoxia or acidosis. Heightened autonomic (sympathetic) tone is the common thread linking precipitants such as vigorous exertion, emotional and environmental stress to arrhythmogenesis. After return of circulation, global ischemia-reperfusion brain injury becomes the dominant determinant of outcome.

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiovascular Collapse, Cardiac Arrest, and Sudden Cardiac Death
chunks.text: Harrison distinguishes three overlapping terms: cardiovascular collapse is sudden loss of effective circulation that may revert spontaneously (e.g., neurocardiogenic syncope) or require intervention; cardiac arrest is abrupt cessation of cardiac function with loss of circulation potentially reversible by prompt intervention; and sudden cardiac death is unexpected death from cardiac arrest occurring within roughly 1 hour of symptom onset (p.2332-2333).

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiovascular Collapse, Cardiac Arrest, and Sudden Cardiac Death
chunks.text: Depressed left ventricular function is the best-validated risk marker in structural heart disease; after myocardial infarction, SCD risk rises gradually as LVEF falls toward 40% and then increases exponentially below that (p.2338-2339).

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiovascular Collapse, Cardiac Arrest, and Sudden Cardiac Death
chunks.text: Following an MI, the risk of sudden death rises up to roughly 10-fold, with the highest absolute rates in the first 30 days; early deaths are more often non-arrhythmic (myocardial rupture, reinfarction) while later deaths are predominantly scar-related ventricular arrhythmias (p.2334-2335).

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiovascular Collapse, Cardiac Arrest, and Sudden Cardiac Death
chunks.text: Commotio cordis - ventricular fibrillation triggered by blunt, non-penetrating precordial impact - is a rare cause of sudden death in otherwise healthy individuals, especially after a chest blow during the vulnerable repolarization window (p.2335).

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiovascular Collapse, Cardiac Arrest, and Sudden Cardiac Death
chunks.text: Sudden cardiac death accounts for about 15% of all deaths and roughly half of all cardiac deaths; in the United States the text cites an estimated 350,000 EMS-attended out-of-hospital arrests and 210,000 sudden cardiac deaths in adults yearly (p.2332).

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiovascular Collapse, Cardiac Arrest, and Sudden Cardiac Death
chunks.text: Up to two-thirds of sudden cardiac deaths occur as the first clinical manifestation of previously undiagnosed heart disease, limiting the ability to predict and prevent events at the population level (p.2332).

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiovascular Collapse, Cardiac Arrest, and Sudden Cardiac Death
chunks.text: Coronary heart disease underlies the majority of sudden cardiac deaths, but the proportion attributable to coronary disease varies markedly by demographics: roughly 70% in white men versus 40-50% in women and black individuals, and under 40% in Asian populations (p.2333-2334).

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiovascular Collapse, Cardiac Arrest, and Sudden Cardiac Death
chunks.text: The text emphasizes the chain of survival for out-of-hospital arrest, and that survival is strongly time-dependent: neurologic recovery falls rapidly and is under 30% by 5 minutes from collapse to return of spontaneous circulation when no bystander CPR is given (p.2335-2338).

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiovascular Collapse, Cardiac Arrest, and Sudden Cardiac Death
chunks.text: Gasping (agonal) respirations and brief seizure-like activity are common during arrest and may be misinterpreted as breathing or responsiveness, leading to delayed resuscitation; a pulse check by a trained provider should take no longer than 10 seconds (p.2335-2336).

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiovascular Collapse, Cardiac Arrest, and Sudden Cardiac Death
chunks.text: The initial recorded rhythm carries prognostic and etiologic weight: ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation (shockable rhythms) have the best outcomes, while pulseless electrical activity and asystole carry a poor prognosis (p.2335-2336).

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiovascular Collapse, Cardiac Arrest, and Sudden Cardiac Death
chunks.text: The proportion of arrests found in ventricular fibrillation has fallen from over half in the 1970s to only 20-25% in recent series, with pulseless electrical activity and asystole now most common; because arrhythmias are unstable after collapse, the rhythm at EMS arrival may not reflect the initiating rhythm (p.2334).

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiovascular Collapse, Cardiac Arrest, and Sudden Cardiac Death
chunks.text: Inherited arrhythmia syndromes without structural heart disease (long QT, Brugada, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT, early repolarization, idiopathic VF) are a more important cause of sudden death in the young and in Asian populations, accounting for around 10% of cases in Asia versus 1-2% in Western countries (p.2334).

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiovascular Collapse, Cardiac Arrest, and Sudden Cardiac Death
chunks.text: Mistaking agonal gasping or brief seizure activity for effective breathing or responsiveness, delaying CPR

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiovascular Collapse, Cardiac Arrest, and Sudden Cardiac Death
chunks.text: Outcomes are dominated by time to resuscitation and the presenting rhythm. Survival to hospital discharge for out-of-hospital arrest has improved but remains low - the chapter states about 90% of patients do not survive to discharge, and roughly 20% of survivors are left with severe neurologic or physical disability. Shockable rhythms (VT/VF) carry the best prognosis, with survival approaching 30% in some regions, whereas PEA and asystole carry poor outcomes. Success of resuscitation declines sharply after 5 minutes from collapse. Ischemia-reperfusion brain injury accounts for over two-thirds of post-arrest deaths; reliable neurologic prognostication is generally deferred at least 72 hours after return to normothermia (typically 4-5 days post-arrest). Features predicting poor neurologic outcome include absent pupillary light reflex, status myoclonus, absent EEG reactivity, and persistent burst suppression.

chunks.diseaseName: Cardiovascular Collapse, Cardiac Arrest, and Sudden Cardiac Death
chunks.text: Harrison frames the spectrum by terminology and reversibility: cardiovascular collapse (may revert spontaneously, includes syncope) -> cardiac arrest (rarely reverts spontaneously; reversibility depends on mechanism, setting, and speed of intervention) -> sudden cardiac death (death within ~1 hour of symptom onset). Acute risk and outcome stratify by presenting rhythm - shockable (VT/VF, better) versus non-shockable (PEA/asystole, worse). Chronic SCD risk in structural heart disease is graded chiefly by LVEF and presence of heart failure, with risk rising gradually as LVEF falls to 40% and exponentially below it.
