chunks.text: The carpal tunnel is a rigid osseofibrous canal bounded by the carpal bones and roofed by the flexor retinaculum, through which the median nerve passes alongside the flexor tendons. Any increase in the contents or reduction in the capacity of this fixed space raises pressure on the median nerve. Compression impairs the nerve's microcirculation and, if sustained, causes segmental demyelination and eventually axonal loss. Conditions that increase tissue volume (fluid retention in pregnancy, synovial thickening in rheumatoid arthritis, tenosynovitis from overuse) or reduce tunnel size (wrist fractures, deformity) precipitate symptoms. Sensory fibres are usually affected first, with motor weakness and thenar wasting appearing later.

Serology (immunofluorescence or enzyme immunoassay) is the most commonly used diagnostic, but has variable sensitivity/specificity; CSD serodiagnosis is often based on IgG alone (in the absence of IgM) and seroconversion may take a few weeks, complicating interpretation (p.1352).

PCR of pus aspirated from a lymph node or the primary inoculation lesion is highly sensitive and specific and is particularly useful for definitive, rapid diagnosis in seronegative patients; PCR of a lymph node biopsy specimen may be less sensitive (possibly due to sampling error) (p.1352).

Histopathology shows early lymphoid hyperplasia, later stellate granulomata with necrosis, coalescing microabscesses and occasional multinucleated giant cells (nonspecific but may narrow the differential) (p.1352).

For endocarditis: blood cultures (even with lysis-centrifugation or EDTA tubes) are positive in only ~25% of cases (mostly B. quintana, rarely B. henselae) and require prolonged incubation up to 6 weeks; high-titer (>=1:800) IgG serology supports the diagnosis but cross-reacts between B. quintana and B. henselae and with C. burnetii and Chlamydia; species-level identification usually requires PCR and DNA sequencing of valve tissue (p.1353).

For bacillary angiomatosis/peliosis: diagnosis is by histologic examination; Warthin-Starry silver staining of lesions reveals clusters of bacilli; cultures are usually negative though blood cultures may be positive (p.1355).
Lymphoma / malignancy (weight loss and night sweats of CSD, and CSD-associated FUO, can mimic malignancy)

Bartonella adapt to specific domestic/wild mammalian hosts where prolonged intraerythrocytic and endothelial-cell infection creates an immune-protected reservoir, producing chronic bacteremia that may persist even after prolonged antimicrobial therapy. Adhesion and entry to endothelial cells and erythrocytes is facilitated by Bartonella adhesin A or variably expressed outer-membrane proteins; the organism evades host immunity by modifying virulence factors (lipopolysaccharide, flagella) and attenuating the immune response. Humans are incidental hosts for most species except B. quintana and B. bacilliformis (which are not zoonotic). In CSD, the cat-to-human transmission mode is undetermined: B. henselae-infected cat saliva spreads to claws by self-licking and contaminated flea feces can be inoculated by a scratch or bite (mucous-membrane/conjunctival inoculation also possible). Lymphatic drainage to regional nodes in immunocompetent hosts triggers a TH1 response producing necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis, with dendritic cells and chemokines driving granuloma formation. In bacillary angiomatosis, Bartonella angiogenic factor A (a proangiogenic autotransporter in B. henselae) activates the host vascular endothelial growth factor pathway to drive angiogenesis (p.1350-1355).

Bartonella are fastidious, facultative intracellular, slow-growing gram-negative bacteria; clinical presentation depends on both the infecting species and the host's immune status. Of the >40 species/subspecies, B. bacilliformis, B. quintana and B. henselae are most commonly identified human pathogens (p.1350).

Bacillary angiomatosis (caused by B. henselae or B. quintana) is a neovascular proliferative disease of severely immunocompromised patients, presenting as non-painful tan/red/purple cutaneous lesions, tender subcutaneous nodules, ulcerated plaques or verrucous growths; nodular forms resemble fungal or mycobacterial infection (p.1354-1355).

Bacillary peliosis is a related angioproliferative disorder caused by B. henselae involving primarily the liver (peliosis hepatis) and also spleen and lymph nodes, with blood-filled cystic structures (microscopic to several mm). In advanced immunodeficiency, B. henselae and B. quintana are important causes of FUO (p.1355).

Trench fever (5-day/quintan fever) is caused by B. quintana, transmitted by the human body louse; it has reemerged as chronic bacteremia in homeless people (urban/contemporary trench fever), with alcoholism and louse infestation as risk factors (p.1354).

B. henselae is the principal etiologic agent of cat-scratch disease (CSD); rare cases are associated with Afipia felis and other Bartonella species. Apparently healthy bacteremic cats (especially kittens) are the major reservoir; person-to-person transmission does not occur and intrafamilial clustering is rare (p.1351).

Typical CSD (85-90% of cases) is a usually self-limited subacute regional lymphadenopathy; a small (0.3-1 cm) painless erythematous papule/pustule appears at the inoculation site within days to 2 weeks in about one-third to two-thirds of patients, with nodes enlarging 1-3 weeks (or longer) after cat contact (p.1351-1352).

Affected nodes are usually painful and suppurate in ~10% of cases; axillary/epitrochlear nodes are most commonly involved, then head/neck, then inguinal/femoral. About 50% have fever, malaise and anorexia; weight loss and night sweats can mimic lymphoma (p.1351-1352).

Atypical (extranodal) CSD occurs in 10-15% and includes Parinaud's oculoglandular syndrome, neuroretinitis (often unilateral visual deterioration), hepatosplenic disease, encephalitis/seizures/myelitis/cranial-nerve palsies, FUO, pneumonitis, debilitating myalgia, arthritis/arthralgia (mostly women >20 yr), osteomyelitis (incl. multifocal) and erythema nodosum (p.1353).

CSD-associated FUO is a unique, sometimes severe and debilitating syndrome that often mimics malignancy and may involve multiple organs (hepatosplenic space-occupying lesions, abdominal/mediastinal lymphadenopathy, ocular disease, multifocal osteomyelitis); fever may be continuous or relapsing (p.1353).
In elderly patients (>60 yr), lymphadenopathy is more often absent, whereas encephalitis and FUO are more common than in younger patients (p.1353).

Coxiella burnetii and Bartonella species are the most common causes of culture-negative endocarditis; in one French series Bartonella accounted for 28% of 348 culture-negative endocarditis cases. B. quintana and B. henselae are the species most often implicated (p.1353).

Bartonella endocarditis often presents as a prolonged, minimally febrile or even afebrile indolent illness lasting weeks to months; initial echocardiography may not show vegetations and acute aggressive disease is rare. Most cases are native-valve, ~60% aortic; B. henselae usually infects preexisting valvulopathy while B. quintana often infects normal valves (p.1353).

Bartonella is a key but easily missed cause of culture-negative endocarditis; routine blood cultures are positive in only ~25% of cases and serology cross-reacts with C. burnetii and Chlamydia, so a high titer to one organism may reflect cross-reactivity rather than the true pathogen (p.1353).
CSD is a frequently overlooked cause of FUO; CSD-associated FUO can mimic malignancy with multiorgan space-occupying lesions, leading to unnecessary investigation for cancer (p.1353).

Negative serology does not exclude CSD: 10-20% of patients have negative acute- and convalescent-phase sera, and seroconversion may take weeks; PCR of aspirated pus is preferred in seronegative patients (p.1352).
Suppurative nodes should be drained by large-bore needle aspiration, NOT by incision and drainage, to avoid chronic draining tracts (p.1353).
In elderly patients, lymphadenopathy is more often absent, so CSD may be missed when it presents instead as encephalitis or FUO (p.1353).

In immunocompetent individuals, CSD (whether typical or atypical) usually resolves without treatment and without sequelae; resolution is slow, requiring weeks for fever/pain and months for node shrinkage, and lifelong immunity is the rule. Some ophthalmologic manifestations may occasionally result in moderate to severe vision loss. Bartonella endocarditis is often diagnosed late, and the proportion of patients requiring valvular surgery (~60%) is high, probably as a consequence of delayed diagnosis (p.1352-1353).

Persistent constitutional symptoms with failure of spontaneous regression of node size, and negative acute- and convalescent-phase sera (10-20% of CSD patients) — malignancy must be ruled out (p.1352).
Seronegative CSD with lymphadenopathy and severe complications (encephalitis or neuroretinitis) — early biopsy is important to establish a specific diagnosis (p.1352).
Unilateral visual deterioration (neuroretinitis) in suspected CSD — ophthalmologic manifestations may occasionally cause moderate to severe vision loss (p.1353).
Culture-negative endocarditis, especially in a homeless/alcoholic patient with body louse infestation (B. quintana) or significant cat exposure (B. henselae) (p.1353).

Cat-scratch disease is described along clinical lines rather than a formal grading scale: (1) Typical CSD (85-90%) — subacute regional lymphadenopathy, usually self-limited; (2) Atypical/extranodal CSD (10-15%) — extranodal manifestations (Parinaud's oculoglandular syndrome, neuroretinitis, hepatosplenic disease, neurologic disease, FUO, osteomyelitis, etc.). Severe/disseminated Bartonella disease (bacillary angiomatosis and peliosis) occurs primarily in HIV-infected persons with CD4+ T-cell counts <100/uL and in other immunosuppressed patients; Bartonella endocarditis is a separate severe culture-negative-endocarditis presentation (p.1351-1355).

chunks.text: A cataract is any opacification of the normally transparent crystalline lens. With age, lens proteins (crystallins) undergo aggregation, oxidation, and cross-linking, while accumulation of pigment and changes in hydration reduce lens transparency and scatter incoming light. Depending on where these changes concentrate, opacity develops in the nucleus, cortex, or beneath the posterior capsule, each producing a distinct visual disturbance. Metabolic, traumatic, inflammatory, and toxic insults accelerate similar biochemical changes.

chunks.text: Cauda equina syndrome results from compression of the bundle of lumbar and sacral nerve roots within the spinal canal below the termination of the spinal cord. Because these are peripheral nerve roots, compression produces lower motor neuron deficits, radicular pain, and disruption of the sacral parasympathetic and somatic supply to the bladder, bowel, and perineum. Sustained compression causes ischaemia and mechanical injury to the roots, and delayed relief risks irreversible loss of sphincter and sexual function.

chunks.text: Central retinal artery occlusion results from acute interruption of blood flow in the central retinal artery, most often from an embolus (carotid or cardiac) or from thrombosis, arteritis, or vasospasm. The inner retina, supplied by this artery, is exquisitely sensitive to ischaemia; sudden occlusion causes rapid infarction and oedema of the inner retinal layers. The fovea, supplied by the underlying choroid, retains its colour and stands out as a cherry-red spot against the surrounding pale, opaque ischaemic retina. Irreversible neuronal damage occurs within a short ischaemic window.

chunks.text: Central retinal vein occlusion results from thrombosis of the central retinal vein at or posterior to the lamina cribrosa, where the central retinal artery and vein share a common adventitial sheath; arteriosclerotic thickening of the artery compresses the vein and promotes turbulent flow and thrombus formation. The resulting rise in venous and capillary pressure causes widespread retinal haemorrhage, oedema, and, when perfusion fails, capillary non-perfusion and retinal ischaemia. Ischaemic retina releases vascular endothelial growth factor, driving macular oedema and neovascularisation of the retina, optic disc, and iris, which can lead to neovascular glaucoma.

Cerebral palsy results from injury or maldevelopment of the immature brain from any of a range of prenatal, perinatal, or early postnatal insults. In preterm infants, periventricular white-matter injury (periventricular leukomalacia) commonly affects descending motor tracts, producing spastic diplegia; in term infants, hypoxic-ischaemic injury, malformations, stroke, or kernicterus may be responsible. The primary lesion is non-progressive, but secondary musculoskeletal changes such as contractures and bony deformity evolve over time.
A group of permanent disorders of movement and posture caused by a non-progressive injury or malformation of the developing brain, though the clinical picture can change as the child grows.
It is the most common cause of chronic motor disability beginning in childhood.
Classified by motor type (spastic, dyskinetic, ataxic, or mixed) and by topography (hemiplegia, diplegia, quadriplegia).
Spastic forms are most common; early signs include abnormal tone, persistent primitive reflexes, delayed motor milestones, and early hand preference before one year.
Preterm birth, low birth weight, intrauterine growth restriction, perinatal hypoxic-ischaemic injury, infection, kernicterus, and brain malformations are recognised risk factors.

Frequent comorbidities include intellectual disability, epilepsy, visual and hearing impairment, feeding and swallowing difficulties, communication problems, and orthopaedic complications such as hip subluxation and contractures.
Diagnosis is largely clinical; MRI often identifies the underlying lesion and helps establish aetiology.
Management is multidisciplinary and supportive, aiming to maximise function and participation with therapy, orthotics, spasticity treatment, and orthopaedic care rather than cure.
Because the disorder is static, clear progression or regression of neurological signs should prompt a search for an alternative, evolving diagnosis.

Oncogenic HPV integrates into the host genome of cervical epithelial cells, and its E6 and E7 oncoproteins inactivate the tumour suppressor proteins p53 and retinoblastoma protein, deregulating the cell cycle and permitting accumulation of genetic damage. Most infections clear spontaneously, but persistent infection produces cervical intraepithelial neoplasia that may progress over years to invasive carcinoma. Invasion typically begins at the transformation zone and extends locally into the cervical stroma, vagina, and parametrium, then to pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes and distant sites.
Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus, especially types 16 and 18, underlies the great majority of cases and drives progression from precursor lesions to invasive disease
Squamous cell carcinoma is the commonest histological subtype, followed by adenocarcinoma, which tends to arise higher in the endocervical canal and can be missed on cytology
Abnormal vaginal bleeding, particularly postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding, together with an offensive or blood-stained discharge, are classic early symptoms
Diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy of visible lesions or by colposcopically directed biopsy, not by cytology alone
Staging is clinical and increasingly incorporates imaging, with tumour size, parametrial spread, and nodal involvement determining management
Early-stage disease may be treated with surgery (radical hysterectomy or fertility-sparing trachelectomy in selected women) while locally advanced disease is managed with concurrent chemoradiation
Organised cytology and HPV-based screening programmes with prophylactic HPV vaccination markedly reduce incidence and mortality
Advanced disease may present with pelvic or leg pain, lymphoedema, ureteric obstruction, or fistula formation into the bladder or rectum

Prognosis depends strongly on stage at diagnosis: disease confined to the cervix carries high cure rates, whereas parametrial extension, nodal involvement, and distant spread substantially reduce survival. Tumour size, histological subtype, and depth of invasion further influence outcome, and screening plus vaccination continue to shift diagnosis toward earlier, more curable stages.

chunks.text: With ageing the cervical intervertebral discs lose height and hydration, transferring load to the facet and uncovertebral joints, which develop osteophytes. These bony spurs, together with disc bulging, ligamentum flavum thickening, and reduced canal diameter, encroach on the neural foramina and spinal canal. Foraminal narrowing compresses nerve roots to cause radiculopathy, while central canal stenosis compresses the spinal cord, producing myelopathy through direct pressure and impaired vascular supply. Dynamic factors during neck movement can aggravate cord compression. The degenerative process is gradual, and neurological compromise may accumulate slowly before becoming clinically apparent.

Cestodes are segmented flatworms (Platyhelminthes, subphylum Cestoda) whose adult worms live in the gut of the definitive host while larval cystic forms inhabit tissues of the intermediate host. The adult tapeworm attaches to intestinal mucosa by suckers or hooks on a scolex; proglottids bud from the neck to form the ribbon-like strobila and shed eggs. In intestinal taeniasis humans are definitive hosts (T. saginata, T. asiatica, T. solium, D. latus, D. caninum). In somatic disease, ingested eggs release oncospheres that penetrate the gut wall, disseminate via blood, and encyst as a cysticercus (single scolex), coenurus (multiple scolices) or hydatid (cyst with daughter cysts and protoscolices). Cysticercosis follows ingestion of T. solium eggs (fecal-oral, including autoinfection in tapeworm carriers); lodged cysticerci initially provoke little inflammation, but as the cyst degenerates an inflammatory response develops, producing seizures, and accompanying arachnoiditis or ventricular obstruction can cause hydrocephalus. In echinococcosis ingested eggs of canine tapeworms release oncospheres that seed liver, lung and other organs; E. granulosus forms slowly enlarging unilocular hydatid cysts containing brood capsules and protoscolices, while E. multilocularis grows by invasive peripheral budding of the germinal layer like a malignancy. (Harrison 22e p.1832-1837)

Cestodes (tapeworms) cause two clinically distinct patterns: intestinal infection by adult worms (taeniasis) and somatic/larval-tissue infection (e.g., cysticercosis, hydatid disease) (Harrison 22e p.1832).

High-dose glucocorticoids should always accompany antiparasitic therapy of neurocysticercosis, since dying parasites provoke an inflammatory response that can worsen seizures or hydrocephalus (Harrison 22e p.1834).
Bruns' syndrome is intermittent acute hydrocephalus triggered by positional change, caused by a ventricular cysticercus acting as a ball valve (Harrison 22e p.1833).
In Latin America and immigrants from Latin America, T. solium (neurocysticercosis) is the most common cause of brain abscess / focal CNS mass lesion (Harrison 22e p.1136).

Echinococcosis (hydatid disease) is larval Echinococcus infection: E. granulosus sensu lato causes unilocular cystic hydatid disease; E. multilocularis causes locally invasive, tumor-like alveolar disease (Harrison 22e p.1835-1836).
In cystic echinococcosis the liver is involved in about two-thirds and the lungs in about 20% of cases; alveolar echinococcosis involves the liver in nearly all cases (Harrison 22e p.1836).
Echinococcal cysts often remain asymptomatic for years and are frequently found incidentally on x-ray or ultrasound (Harrison 22e p.1836).

Identification of daughter cysts within a larger cyst, or eggshell/mural calcification on CT, is diagnostic of cystic echinococcosis; 'hydatid sand' is visible protoscolices/brood capsules within cyst fluid (Harrison 22e p.1837).
ELISA/immunoblot serology is positive in about 90% of hepatic hydatid disease but only about 50% of pulmonary cysts, and a negative test cannot exclude echinococcosis (Harrison 22e p.1837).

The fish tapeworm Dibothriocephalus latus (formerly Diphyllobothrium latum) is the longest human tapeworm (up to 25 m) and its avid vitamin B12 receptors can cause B12 deficiency with megaloblastic/pernicious-type anemia and neurologic sequelae (Harrison 22e p.1838-1839).

Rodentolepis nana (dwarf tapeworm, formerly Hymenolepis nana) is the most common human cestode infection and the only one not requiring an intermediate host, perpetuated by intestinal autoinfection (Harrison 22e p.1838).

Neurocysticercosis is the most common parasitic disease of the CNS worldwide; humans acquire it by ingesting food contaminated with Taenia solium eggs, not by eating cysticerci-containing pork (which instead causes intestinal taeniasis) (Harrison 22e p.1833, p.1138).

Seizures are the most frequent manifestation of neurocysticercosis and are associated with inflammation of brain parenchyma around the cysticercus; new-onset partial seizures with or without secondary generalization are the classic presentation (Harrison 22e p.1833, p.1138).

On neuroimaging a cystic lesion with a mural nodule representing the scolex ('dot-in-hole') is diagnostic of neurocysticercosis; lesions evolve through vesicular, colloidal, granulonodular and nodular-calcified stages (Harrison 22e p.1833-1834, p.1138).

CT is more sensitive for calcified lesions, whereas MRI is more sensitive for small cystic lesions, scolices and enhancement; FIESTA/3D-CISS sequences best detect ventricular and subarachnoid cysts (Harrison 22e p.1834).

The enzyme-linked immunoelectrotransfer blot (EITB) using lentil-lectin-purified glycoproteins is >99% specific/sensitive in patients with multiple cysts, but patients with a single intracranial lesion or only calcifications may be seronegative; serum is more sensitive than CSF (Harrison 22e p.1834).
Crude-antigen ELISA antibody tests have high false-positive and false-negative rates and should be avoided for neurocysticercosis (Harrison 22e p.1834).

In endemic-area patients with a single enhancing 5-20 mm round CT lesion, seizures, a normal exam and no systemic disease (no fever, adenopathy or chest abnormality), the lesion is almost always neurocysticercosis (validated in India) (Harrison 22e p.1834).

Antiparasitic treatment of neurocysticercosis is never an emergency; initial management focuses on controlling seizures and hydrocephalus and on excluding intraocular disease before any cysticidal therapy (Harrison 22e p.1834).

Do not aspirate or rupture a hydatid cyst carelessly: spillage of protoscolices can disseminate infection and provoke anaphylaxis; aspiration/PAIR should only be done by experienced operators with albendazole cover and through solid tissue.
Infusion of scolicidal agents during surgery is no longer recommended because of hypernatremia, intoxication and sclerosing cholangitis.

Never start antiparasitic drugs in neurocysticercosis with elevated intracranial pressure, and avoid them in diffuse cerebral edema from multiple inflamed lesions (glucocorticoids are the mainstay there).
Always give high-dose glucocorticoid cover when treating neurocysticercosis, because dying cysticerci can worsen seizures and hydrocephalus.
Treating T. solium intestinal taeniasis with praziquantel may occasionally trigger a CNS inflammatory response if occult (cryptic) cysticercosis is present.
Avoid antiparasitic drugs before neurosurgical removal of ventricular cysticerci: they make the cyst friable and harder to extract.
Crude-antigen ELISA antibody tests for cysticercosis are unreliable (high false-positive/false-negative rates) and should not be used.
A negative echinococcosis serology cannot exclude the diagnosis, and sensitivity is especially low (~50%) for pulmonary cysts.
Eggs/proglottids are shed intermittently, so single stool examination may miss intestinal taeniasis; Taenia species eggs are morphologically indistinguishable.
For ocular and spinal cysticercosis, drug-induced inflammation may cause irreversible damage; intraocular disease should be managed surgically.

Intestinal tapeworm infections (taeniasis, R. nana, diphyllobothriasis, dipylidiasis) are usually mild or asymptomatic and respond to a single course of treatment. In neurocysticercosis, single enhancing lesions often resolve and seizure medication can frequently be tapered after about 6 months; calcified lesions carry a higher risk of recurrent seizures, particularly with perilesional edema, and subarachnoid/ventricular (extraparenchymal) disease is more difficult to treat and requires prolonged therapy. Cystic echinococcosis is often curable with stage-appropriate medical therapy, PAIR or surgery, with relapse rates after skilled PAIR comparable to surgery; inactive CE4/CE5 cysts need only periodic surveillance. Alveolar echinococcosis behaves like a malignancy: most cases are diagnosed too late for complete resection and require indefinite antiparasitic therapy, since even after liver transplantation immunosuppression promotes parasite recurrence. (Harrison 22e p.1834-1838)
New-onset seizures or focal neurologic deficit in a patient from a cysticercosis-endemic area (e.g., Latin America, sub-Saharan Africa, China, India, Southeast Asia)
Signs of raised intracranial pressure or obstructive hydrocephalus (headache, vomiting, papilledema, altered mental status) from intraventricular/subarachnoid cysticerci
Bruns' syndrome: intermittent acute hydrocephalus precipitated by head position change
Subarachnoid/basal cysticerci causing chronic meningitis, arachnoiditis, vasculitis, infarction or hemorrhage
Sudden pruritus, urticaria, eosinophilia or anaphylaxis from rupture/leakage of a hydatid cyst
Pulmonary hydatid rupture into the bronchial tree (sudden expectoration of cyst fluid/membranes) or pleura (hydatid empyema)

Cystic echinococcosis of the liver is staged by the WHO Informal Working Group ultrasound classification, reflecting cyst viability: active cysts (CL = cystic lesion with no visible wall, CE1 = visible wall with internal echoes/snowflake sign, CE2 = visible wall with internal septation), transitional cysts (CE3a = detached laminar membranes, CE3b = partially collapsed), and inactive cysts (CE4 = nonhomogeneous mass, CE5 = thick calcified wall). Neurocysticercosis is categorized by parasite location and viability and by lesion stage on imaging (vesicular, colloidal, granulonodular, nodular-calcified); diagnosis uses the Del Brutto revised criteria (absolute, neuroimaging [major/confirmative/minor], and clinical/exposure criteria). (Harrison 22e p.1834-1837)

Chagas megacolon: Hirschsprung's disease and other causes of severe chronic constipation (p.1789)
T. b. gambiense HAT systemic features: hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency (but thyroid/adrenal function tests are normal) (p.1794)
HAT neuropsychiatric presentation: primary psychiatric illness (mental disorder is a key HAT feature easily misdiagnosed) (p.1794)
T. b. rhodesiense acute febrile illness: malaria (suspect HAT especially if malaria tests are negative) (p.1794)
Malaria (acute febrile illness overlapping T. b. rhodesiense HAT; HAT suspected when malaria tests are negative) (p.1794)
Other febrile/systemic infections in returned travelers from endemic areas (p.1794)
Chagas acute/reactivation: blood microscopy after concentration (Strout method, microhematocrit) or PCR of peripheral blood, CSF, or other body fluids (p.1790)
Supportive HAT labs (nonspecific): anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated C-reactive protein and IgM (p.1794)

Chagas chronic: serology for anti-T. cruzi IgG - conventional/recombinant ELISA and immunofluorescence; two positive tests with different techniques/antigens to confirm (third test if discordant); immunochromatographic rapid tests for first-line screening where labs are limited (p.1790)

Chagas congenital: cord/peripheral blood microscopy or PCR in first days/weeks (testing after 4 weeks most accurate; earlier PCR may be falsely positive); serology at 9 months once maternal antibodies cleared (p.1790)

Chagas cardiac staging: 12-lead ECG with 30-s strip; echocardiography and 24-h Holter for chamber dilation, apical aneurysm, ventricular dysfunction, arrhythmias; MRI or electrophysiologic studies as indicated (p.1791)
Chagas digestive staging: barium esophagography and barium enema (first-line); esophageal manometry (p.1791)
Chagas comorbidity workup: screen for other cardiovascular risk factors, immunosuppressive conditions, and other chronic infections (e.g., Strongyloides stercoralis, HIV) (p.1791)
HAT T. b. gambiense screening: card agglutination test for trypanosomiasis (CATT) or lateral flow tests; ELISA/immunofluorescence/indirect hemagglutination in reference labs (p.1795)

HAT confirmation: microscopy of trypanosomes in lymph (cervical lymph node puncture), blood (microhematocrit centrifugation; most sensitive is miniature anion-exchange centrifugation, ~90%), skin biopsy, or CSF; thin/thick Giemsa smears and concentration for T. b. rhodesiense (p.1795)
HAT staging: lumbar puncture with CSF examination (leukocyte count, trypanosomes after centrifugation) (p.1795)
Achalasia (Chagas megaesophagus) (p.1789)
Hirschsprung's disease (Chagas megacolon) (p.1789)
Dilated/ischemic cardiomyopathy (Chagas cardiomyopathy) (p.1790)
Hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency (HAT systemic features, but endocrine tests normal) (p.1794)
Primary psychiatric illness (HAT neuropsychiatric features) (p.1794)

Chagas (T. cruzi): trypomastigotes inoculated via triatomine feces enter the bloodstream, infect nucleated cells (notably cardiac, skeletal, and smooth muscle) and differentiate into amastigotes. An innate response to parasite mucins/DNA drives a predominantly Th1 response with proinflammatory cytokines and CD8+ T-cell activation that reduces parasitemia to subpatent levels in 4-8 weeks (end of acute phase). Immune evasion permits lifelong low-intensity amastigote proliferation. Chronic damage is thought to arise from parasite persistence plus a dysregulated host immune response (Th1/Th2 imbalance, excess proinflammatory cytokines), with secondary microcirculatory abnormalities and dysautonomia; the role of autoimmune mechanisms remains unresolved. In myocardium, chronic inflammation causes cellular destruction and fibrosis, segmental loss of contractility, chamber dilation, apical aneurysm, ventricular arrhythmias, and conduction-system scarring, plus autonomic (vagal/sympathetic) denervation. In the gut, a direct toxic effect on intramural autonomic ganglion cells causes loss of neural cells, motility disorders, and organ dilation (megaviscera). African trypanosomiasis (T. b. gambiense/rhodesiense): these subspecies infect humans because they resist human serum lytic factor apolipoprotein L-1 (T. b. rhodesiense via serum resistance-associated protein; T. b. gambiense via TgsGP glycoprotein and other mechanisms). After tsetse bite and local inflammation (chancre), parasites disseminate through the hematolymphatic system, multiply in blood (with cyclic density fluctuation due to variant surface glycoprotein antigenic switching - a repertoire of ~1000 VSGs) and extravascular tissues (skin, muscle, serous membranes, heart). CNS invasion (second stage) follows weeks-to-months (rhodesiense) or months-to-years (gambiense), with predominantly white-matter perivascular astrocyte/microglial proliferation and Mott (morular) cells containing IgM; the cortex and neurons are spared until terminal stages, and inflammatory lesions are largely reversible so neuropsychiatric features may resolve with treatment (p.1789-1790, 1793-1794).

Three trypanosome species cause human disease: T. cruzi causes Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis); T. brucei gambiense and T. b. rhodesiense cause human African trypanosomiasis (HAT, 'sleeping sickness'). Both are vector-borne neglected tropical diseases (p.1788).

T. b. gambiense HAT is a slowly evolving illness with a long incubation (months to years); T. b. rhodesiense HAT is an acute febrile illness with a short (<3-week) incubation and a shorter (weeks to months) course (p.1794).

A trypanosomal chancre may develop at the tsetse bite site (more common in travelers and in T. b. rhodesiense); it is nonpurulent, painful, itchy, and resolves spontaneously in 1-3 weeks (p.1794-1795).
Enlarged cervical lymph nodes are a classic HAT sign (38-85% of patients); posterior cervical involvement is the Winterbottom sign - cervical palpation is essential in suspected HAT (p.1794).

HAT is called 'sleeping sickness' because of CNS (second-stage) sleep disturbances - daytime somnolence, nocturnal insomnia, dysregulated sleep/wake cycle and fragmented sleep - plus neuropsychiatric features (mood/behavioral change, psychosis, motor/extrapyramidal/cerebellar syndromes) that may mimic primary psychiatric illness (p.1794).

HAT staging is by CSF examination: second-stage (CNS) disease is defined by CSF leukocytes >5/uL and/or trypanosomes; T. b. gambiense screening uses serology (card agglutination test, CATT, or lateral flow tests) and confirmation by microscopy of trypanosomes in lymph, blood, skin, or CSF (p.1795).

T. b. rhodesiense diagnosis is usually simpler because parasites are more numerous in blood; wet mounts, thin/thick Giemsa smears, and concentration techniques serve for both screening and confirmation, and parasites may be seen in chancre aspirate (p.1795).

T. cruzi evades immunity to persist as low-grade amastigote replication; immunosuppression (HIV, post-transplant, hematologic malignancy) can cause reactivation with increased parasitemia and CNS/cardiac/skin lesions - clinically manifest reactivation is an AIDS-defining opportunistic infection (~20% risk in untreated HIV when CD4 <100/uL) (p.1789).

Chagas is transmitted mainly by intradomiciliary triatomine ('reduviid') bugs whose feces, deposited during a nighttime blood meal, carry the infective metacyclic form that enters through skin breaks, mucosae, or conjunctivae; nonvectorial routes include congenital, blood transfusion, organ/tissue transplant, and oral (contaminated food/drink) transmission (p.1788).
Acute Chagas is asymptomatic or a mild febrile illness in >90% of cases; characteristic local swelling at the inoculation site is the Romaña sign (eyelid) or chagoma (skin) (p.1789-1790).

After acute infection T. cruzi persists for life in most patients; 60-70% remain in the indeterminate form (no apparent tissue damage), while 30-40% progress over decades to determinate disease - cardiac (20-30%), digestive (5-20%), or mixed (5-10%) (p.1789).

Chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy produces a dilated cardiomyopathy with fibrosis, segmental contractility loss, left ventricular apical aneurysm, ventricular arrhythmias, and conduction system disease; advanced cardiac damage carries a worse prognosis than other cardiomyopathies including ischemic disease (p.1789-1790).

Digestive Chagas (megaviscera) results from destruction of intramural autonomic ganglion cells: esophageal involvement mimics achalasia and colonic involvement mimics Hirschsprung's disease, with severe constipation, fecaloma, and risk of volvulus and toxic dilation; megacolon is diagnosed when sigmoid/descending colon diameter is >=6.5 cm (p.1789, 1791).

Chagas diagnosis is stage-dependent: detect circulating parasites by blood microscopy after concentration (Strout, microhematocrit) or PCR during acute phase/reactivation; rely on serology (anti-T. cruzi IgG) once parasitemia is subpatent in the chronic phase - two positive tests using different techniques and antigens confirm chronic infection (p.1790).

12-lead ECG (with 30-s strip) is a good screening test for Chagas cardiomyopathy; common abnormalities are right bundle branch block, left anterior fascicular block, ventricular premature beats, repolarization disorders, Q waves, and low QRS voltage (p.1791).

HAT is restricted to sub-Saharan Africa, matching the range of its tsetse fly (Glossina) vector; T. b. gambiense (western/central Africa, humans are main reservoir, slow chronic course) differs from T. b. rhodesiense (eastern/southeastern Africa, zoonotic animal reservoirs, acute course) (p.1792-1793).
More than 90% of Chagas infections go undiagnosed and are often identified late once chronic complications develop; the majority of infected individuals are asymptomatic (indeterminate form) (p.1790)
HAT systemic features may mimic hypothyroidism or adrenal insufficiency but thyroid/adrenal tests are normal; mental disorder may be misdiagnosed as primary psychiatric illness (p.1794)
Trypanids (HAT rashes) are almost impossible to detect on dark skin and have been reported only in Caucasians (p.1794)
HIV co-infection does not appear to increase HAT risk, and the virus's effect on HAT presentation is unknown (p.1794)
Eflornithine is ineffective against T. b. rhodesiense, so melarsoprol remains in use for second-stage rhodesiense disease (KNOWLEDGE only) (p.1796)
International tourists visiting endemic areas are at very low risk of Chagas and travel-related cases are rare - the at-risk group is migrants from endemic regions, not casual travelers (p.1789)
There is no evidence that bedbugs transmit T. cruzi to humans despite laboratory potential (p.1788)
There is no predictor of which chronic-phase Chagas patients will progress to clinical disease (p.1790)

Chronic-phase Chagas PCR has limited sensitivity (50-80%): a negative result cannot be interpreted, so patients with negative PCR but persistent positive serology should still be considered potentially infective (p.1790, 1792)
Early congenital Chagas PCR may be falsely positive (maternal T. cruzi DNA fragments); testing after 4 weeks of age is most accurate (p.1790)

In adults with chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy, benznidazole has no impact on disease progression or mortality, and neither benznidazole nor nifurtimox is effective against digestive complications (KNOWLEDGE only - no dosing) (p.1791-1792)
HAT clinical/biologic features (anemia, thrombocytopenia, raised CRP and IgM) are not specific enough to treat on suspicion - diagnostic confirmation is required in all patients (p.1794)
Absence of fever does not rule out T. b. gambiense HAT (fever is more frequent in travelers than natives) (p.1794)

Chagas: 5-10% of acute (early) infections resolve spontaneously without treatment; most become chronic, of whom 60-70% never develop tissue damage (indeterminate form) and 30-40% progress over decades to cardiac, digestive, or mixed disease. Acute-phase mortality is low (0.1-5% with oral transmission or myocarditis/encephalitis). Determinate chronic disease 5-year mortality is 2-63% depending on extent of cardiac damage, with cardiac failure, sudden death, and stroke the leading causes; advanced cardiac damage carries a worse prognosis than other cardiomyopathies. African trypanosomiasis: untreated HAT is usually fatal. With properly followed guidelines, >95% of first- and second-stage T. b. gambiense HAT patients are definitively cured (fexinidazole, pentamidine, nifurtimox-eflornithine), overall case-fatality <1% except in very advanced cases; relapses can occur long after treatment, so follow-up every 6 months for at least 2 years is advised. Second-stage T. b. rhodesiense HAT carries a 5-10% risk of death during/after melarsoprol treatment, though relapses are very rare (p.1790, 1796).

Chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy with high risk of sudden death - bundle branch block is often the first sign and may be asymptomatic for years before serious conduction disease, arrhythmias, and LV dysfunction; 5-year mortality 2-63% depending on cardiac damage, leading causes cardiac failure and sudden death, then stroke (p.1790)
Chagas digestive determinate disease: dysphagia, regurgitation, severe constipation, fecaloma, volvulus, and toxic colonic dilation (p.1790)
Intramural thrombus or LV apical aneurysm in Chagas cardiomyopathy - risk of cardioembolic stroke (p.1790-1791)

Chagas reactivation in immunosuppression (HIV with CD4 <100/uL, post-transplant, hematologic malignancy): myocarditis, Toxoplasma-like focal brain lesion, meningoencephalitis - AIDS-defining when clinically manifest (p.1789-1790)
Untreated HAT is usually lethal - early diagnosis is crucial; second-stage (CNS) disease with decreased consciousness, dementia, epilepsy progressing to coma and death (p.1794)
T. b. rhodesiense terminal sepsis-like illness with disseminated intravascular coagulation and multi-organ failure, plus more rapid evolution to coma and death than gambiense (p.1794)

Severe second-stage HAT signs warranting non-fexinidazole staging/treatment: mental confusion, abnormal behavior, logorrhea, anxiety, ataxia, tremor, motor weakness, speech impairment, abnormal gait/movements, or seizures (p.1795)

Chagas (T. cruzi infection stages, Table 234-1): Acute phase (including congenital, vector-borne, oral, transfusion, transplant) lasting 2-8 weeks, mostly asymptomatic; Chronic indeterminate form (normal exam and ECG, no attributable mortality, lifelong or until determinate phase); Chronic determinate form (cardiac, digestive, or mixed organ damage years to decades after infection); Acute reactivation in severe immunosuppression. chunks.text: A chalazion forms when a meibomian gland orifice becomes obstructed and retained sebaceous secretions leak into the surrounding tarsal tissue. chunks.text: Chemical injury damages the ocular surface through direct chemical action on cells and the extracellular matrix. Alkalis dissolve cell membrane lipids and penetrate deeply by liquefactive necrosis, reaching the anterior chamber and damaging the limbal stem cells, corneal stroma, trabecular meshwork, and intraocular structures. Acids denature and precipitate proteins, producing coagulative necrosis that can form a barrier limiting deeper spread, though strong acids still cause severe injury. Destruction of limbal stem cells impairs corneal epithelial regeneration, leading to persistent epithelial defects, conjunctivalisation, and scarring, while ischaemia and inflammation predispose to stromal melting and perforation.

Childhood obesity results from a chronic positive energy balance in which caloric intake exceeds expenditure, leading to excess adipose tissue. This arises from a complex interplay of genetic susceptibility, dietary patterns, physical inactivity, sleep, and environmental and socioeconomic influences. Expanded and dysfunctional adipose tissue drives insulin resistance, low-grade inflammation, and altered adipokine signalling, which underlie the associated metabolic, hepatic, cardiovascular, and endocrine complications. Rare monogenic and syndromic disorders disrupt central appetite regulation (notably the leptin-melanocortin pathway).

In children and adolescents obesity is defined using body mass index relative to age- and sex-specific percentiles rather than fixed adult cut-offs, with obesity typically at or above the 95th percentile.
The vast majority of cases are related to lifestyle and energy balance; a monogenic or endocrine cause is uncommon but should be considered in specific circumstances.
A tall child growing well who is obese is usually exogenously obese, whereas an obese child who is short or growing poorly raises suspicion of an endocrine or syndromic cause.
Ask about diet, physical activity, screen time, sleep, family history, and psychosocial factors, as these shape both cause and management.
Screen for comorbidities including type 2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia, hypertension, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and obstructive sleep apnoea.
Acanthosis nigricans is a clinical clue to insulin resistance and increased type 2 diabetes risk.
Management centres on sustainable family-based lifestyle change addressing nutrition, activity, sleep, and behaviour rather than short-term restrictive dieting.
Early-onset severe obesity, particularly with hyperphagia, may suggest a monogenic cause and warrants specialist evaluation.
Assuming all obesity is lifestyle-related and missing an endocrine, syndromic, or monogenic cause when growth is impaired
Failing to screen for comorbidities such as type 2 diabetes, fatty liver, and sleep apnoea
Focusing on the child alone rather than engaging the whole family in change
Overlooking psychosocial factors, stigma, and mental health in management

Chlamydiae are nonmotile, gram-negative, obligate intracellular bacteria that lack peptidoglycan (structural integrity depends on disulfide cross-linking of outer-membrane proteins) and are energy parasites using host-cell ATP. They have a unique biphasic growth cycle alternating between the infectious, extracellular-adapted elementary body (0.25-0.35 um) and the metabolically active, non-infectious intracellular reticulate body (0.5-1 um), which divides by binary fission within a membrane-bound cytoplasmic inclusion while preventing phagosome-lysosome fusion; the cycle lasts ~48-72 h, giving a long clinical incubation (generally 1-3 weeks). C. trachomatis has two biovars (trachoma and LGV) and 18 serovars (trachoma A/B/Ba/C; oculogenital D-K; LGV L1-L3); the trachoma biovar parasitizes squamocolumnar epithelium whereas the more invasive LGV biovar involves lymphoid cells. Disease is driven largely by immunopathology rather than direct cytotoxicity: the chlamydial heat-shock protein shares epitopes with human and other bacterial proteins and, with repeated/persistent infection, drives fibrosis and mucosal scarring leading to tubal-factor infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain (genital) or cicatricial trichiasis and blindness (ocular). Antigenic variation in the major outer-membrane protein (omp1) permits reinfection because immunity to one serovar is not protective against others (Harrison 22e p.1467-1469).

C. trachomatis genital infection is the most prevalent bacterial STI worldwide and is reported more than any other infectious disease in the United States; case counts are heavily dependent on screening coverage (Harrison 22e p.1469).

Neonatal exposure during vaginal delivery causes inclusion conjunctivitis (in ~20-30% of exposed infants) and, in 10-15%, pneumonia at 2 weeks to 4 months of age; standard gonococcal ocular prophylaxis does NOT prevent chlamydial conjunctivitis (Harrison 22e p.1471-1472).

Most genital infections are silent: up to 80-90% of women and >50% of men with C. trachomatis genital infection lack symptoms, and pharyngeal/rectal infection is typically asymptomatic and may persist for years, sustaining a large transmission reservoir (Harrison 22e p.1469).
C. trachomatis is the most common cause of nongonococcal urethritis (NGU) and postgonococcal urethritis (PGU), implicated in 30-50% of NGU cases (Harrison 22e p.1469-1470).

NAATs are the CDC-recommended diagnostic assay of choice; less-invasive specimens (urine for both sexes, vaginal swabs for women) are acceptable, and self-collected or clinician-collected vaginal swabs are slightly more sensitive than urine in women (Harrison 22e p.1472-1473).
Because of frequent co-infection, testing for or treating chlamydia should be considered in patients diagnosed with N. gonorrhoeae (Harrison 22e p.1474).

Trachoma (serovars A, B, Ba, C) remains a leading cause of preventable infectious blindness worldwide; the WHO SAFE-era programs target elimination as a public health problem by 2030 (Harrison 22e p.1474-1475).

LGV (serovars L1, L2, L3) is an invasive STI presenting classically as a transient painless genital ulcer followed by painful inguinal lymphadenopathy with bubo formation, or as hemorrhagic proctocolitis in MSM (Harrison 22e p.1469, 1472).

C. pneumoniae causes atypical (community-acquired) pneumonia, bronchitis, pharyngitis and sinusitis, accounting for as many as 10% of CAP cases though more typically 1-2%; PCR of respiratory secretions is the preferred diagnostic method (Harrison 22e p.1476).

Psittacosis (C. psittaci) is a zoonosis acquired from birds (psittacines, poultry) presenting as atypical pneumonia or systemic febrile illness; person-to-person transmission has never been demonstrated (Harrison 22e p.1475).

NAATs detect nucleic acid, not viable organisms - residual DNA may yield a positive result for up to 3 weeks after effective therapy, so NAATs should not be used as a test of cure before 3 weeks; routine test of cure is not recommended except in pregnancy.
C. psittaci is a biohazard category B biothreat agent associated with laboratory-acquired infections.
Single-dose penicillins or cephalosporins used for gonorrhea lack activity against chlamydiae - hence postgonococcal urethritis and the need to co-treat or exclude chlamydia.
Standard gonococcal ocular prophylaxis does NOT prevent neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis; the most effective prevention is antenatal screening and treatment.
Chlamydial and gonococcal conjunctivitis cannot be distinguished from other neonatal conjunctivitis on clinical grounds - laboratory diagnosis is required.
CF and LPS-based serologic tests identify chlamydiae only to the genus level (cross-reactive across all chlamydiae) and must be interpreted cautiously.
Serology (including a single high IgG titer) over-attributes C. pneumoniae to atypical pneumonia; cross-reactivity limits specificity, and PCR is preferred.
Serology is never recommended for diagnosis of uncomplicated genital cervical/urethral/lower-tract infection or for asymptomatic screening.
Fluoroquinolones are contraindicated in pregnancy; beta-lactams and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are not active against C. pneumoniae.
Most genital infections are asymptomatic, so clinical recognition of cervicitis requires a high index of suspicion - no genital symptom is specific for chlamydial cervical infection.

Uncomplicated genital chlamydial infection responds well to recommended antibiotics, and clinically significant drug resistance has not been observed in C. trachomatis; apparent treatment failure usually reflects non-adherence or reinfection. However, untreated or recurrent genital infection causes substantial long-term morbidity through mucosal scarring - PID with tubal-factor infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain - and women bear the greatest burden of sequelae. Reactive arthritis episodes typically last 2-6 months. Untreated ocular disease progresses to blinding trachoma; the WHO estimates ~6 million people have been blinded and ~1.3 million remain blind from trachoma. Untreated psittacosis pneumonia can be fatal in up to 10% of cases. Previous chlamydial infection raises the risk of reinfection, prompting rescreening at 3 months (Harrison 22e p.1469-1475).
Acute unilateral testicular pain - exclude testicular torsion promptly by imaging or surgical exploration before attributing to epididymitis
Failure of unilateral intrascrotal pain/swelling to respond to antimicrobials - exclude testicular tumor or chronic infection such as tuberculosis
Hemorrhagic proctocolitis with severe anorectal pain in MSM - consider invasive LGV serovars (often with HIV co-infection)

Untreated maternal infection - risk of neonatal inclusion conjunctivitis and infant pneumonia

No formal grading scale. Genital C. trachomatis infections are categorized as uncomplicated (lower genital tract) versus complicated (e.g., PID, epididymitis) requiring longer therapy; LGV is treated as invasive disease with extended therapy. Trachoma is described by phase - active trachoma (follicular conjunctivitis) versus cicatricial disease (conjunctival scarring, trichiasis, entropion) - underpinning the WHO clinical signs used for diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1474-1475).

Supportive labs in dehydrated patients: elevated haematocrit (haemoconcentration) in non-anaemic patients, mild neutrophilic leukocytosis, raised blood urea nitrogen and creatinine (prerenal azotaemia), normal sodium/potassium/chloride, markedly reduced bicarbonate (<15 mmol/L), elevated anion gap and low arterial pH (~7.2) (p.1328)
Severely dehydrating secretory diarrhoea of non-infectious aetiology, to which the term cholera has at times been loosely applied (p.1325)

Cholera is fundamentally a toxin-mediated disease. After ingestion (most often via faecally contaminated water, though contaminated food and human-to-human transmission also contribute), V. cholerae colonises the small intestine, a process dependent on the toxin-coregulated pilus (TCP), with cholera toxin, TCP and other virulence factors coordinately regulated by ToxR and by quorum sensing. The organism elaborates cholera toxin, a protein enterotoxin made of a monomeric enzymatic A subunit and a pentameric B-subunit binding moiety. The B pentamer binds GM1 ganglioside on the epithelial cell surface, delivering the A subunit, whose activated form (A1) irreversibly ADP-ribosylates the GTP-binding regulatory component of adenylate cyclase. This upregulates adenylate cyclase, raising intracellular cyclic AMP, which inhibits absorptive sodium transport in villus cells and activates secretory chloride transport in crypt cells, driving accumulation of sodium chloride in the lumen; water follows passively to maintain osmolality, producing isotonic fluid that exceeds the gut's reabsorptive capacity and results in watery diarrhoea. Cholera toxin also enhances secretion via prostaglandins and/or neural histamine receptors. Unless lost fluid and electrolytes are replaced, profound dehydration leads to hypovolaemic shock and bicarbonate loss leads to acidosis. The cholera toxin genes (ctxAB) are carried on the bacteriophage CTX-phi, which uses TCP as its receptor, allowing horizontal transfer to generate new toxigenic strains (p.1326-1327).

Cholera is an acute toxin-mediated diarrhoeal disease caused by Vibrio cholerae serogroup O1 or O139 (the serogroups with epidemic potential) that can progress to profound, rapidly progressive dehydration and death within hours (p.1325-1326).

After a 24-48 h incubation in a non-immune individual, illness begins with the sudden onset of painless watery diarrhoea that can rapidly become voluminous; vomiting is common and fever is usually absent (p.1327).

The characteristic stool is non-bilious, gray, slightly cloudy fluid flecked with mucus, containing no blood, with a fishy, inoffensive odour, described as rice-water stool because it resembles water in which rice has been washed (p.1327).
In severe cases (cholera gravis) volume loss can exceed 250 mL/kg in the first 24 h, and muscle cramps from electrolyte disturbance are common (p.1327).

Symptoms parallel the degree of volume contraction: thirst at <5% body-weight loss; postural hypotension, weakness, tachycardia and decreased skin turgor at 5-10%; and oliguria, weak or absent pulses, sunken eyes (sunken fontanelles in infants), wrinkled washerwoman skin, somnolence and coma at >10% (p.1327-1328).
If fluids and electrolytes are replaced adequately, complications are averted and the illness is self-limited, resolving in a few days (p.1328).
The organism is not recovered on routine media; V. cholerae must be specifically sought using selective medium, or the diagnosis will be missed (p.1328).
Diagnosis is often syndromic and many endemic countries under-report to the WHO, so the true burden and distribution are unknown and cases may be unrecognised (p.1326).
Cholera should still be suspected in severe acute watery diarrhoea or death even in areas not known to have cholera (p.1328).
Fever is usually absent, so its absence should not dissuade from the diagnosis (p.1327).
Immunity to V. cholerae O1 is not protective against O139 (and vice versa), so prior infection does not guarantee protection against the other serogroup (p.1327).

Death from cholera is due to hypovolaemic shock. Historically the disease carried high mortality, but prompt aggressive fluid repletion and supportive care can obviate this. With adequate fluid and electrolyte replacement, complications are averted and the illness is self-limited, resolving over a few days. Complications derive exclusively from volume and electrolyte depletion and include renal failure due to acute tubular necrosis. Untreated cholera carries very high case-fatality (historically >50% in untreated severe cases), which falls dramatically with rehydration (p.1326, p.1328).

Signs of severe dehydration: unconsciousness, lethargy or floppiness, weak or absent pulse, inability to drink, sunken eyes (sunken fontanelles in infants), >10% loss of body weight (p.1328)
Voluminous ongoing stool losses (volume loss exceeding 250 mL/kg in the first 24 h in severe cases) (p.1327)
Features of hypovolaemic shock, oliguria, somnolence and coma (p.1327-1328)

Harrison stratifies dehydration in cholera into: (1) None or mild (diarrhoea present) - thirst in some cases, <5% loss of total body weight; (2) Moderate - thirst, postural hypotension, weakness, tachycardia, decreased skin turgor, dry mouth/tongue, no tears, 5-10% loss of total body weight; and (3) Severe - unconsciousness, lethargy or floppiness, weak or absent pulse, inability to drink, sunken eyes (sunken fontanelles in infants), >10% loss of total body weight. This dehydration assessment guides the intensity of rehydration (p.1328).

chunks.text: Cholesteatoma consists of a sac of keratinising stratified squamous epithelium (matrix) that sheds keratin into the middle ear and mastoid, where it accumulates and cannot escape. Acquired disease most often follows persistent Eustachian tube dysfunction that produces a retraction pocket in the pars flaccida or posterosuperior pars tensa; trapped desquamated epithelium enlarges the pocket, or squamous epithelium migrates through a marginal perforation. The expanding mass and its associated chronic inflammation release enzymes and mediators that resorb surrounding bone, progressively destroying the ossicular chain and eroding toward the facial nerve, semicircular canals and intracranial cavity. Superimposed infection produces the characteristic foul discharge and accelerates the destructive process.

Chorioamnionitis most commonly results from ascent of bacteria from the vagina and cervix into the normally sterile amniotic cavity, particularly once the membranes are ruptured or the cervix is dilated. The organisms provoke a maternal and fetal inflammatory response with release of cytokines and prostaglandins that can precipitate or accelerate labour. Inflammation of the membranes, cord, and placenta may compromise the fetus directly through infection and indirectly through the fetal inflammatory response syndrome, which is implicated in preterm birth and neurological injury. Less commonly infection reaches the cavity haematogenously or via invasive procedures.
Chorioamnionitis is inflammation or infection of the fetal membranes and amniotic fluid, most often from ascending organisms from the lower genital tract
It is strongly associated with prolonged rupture of membranes, prolonged labour, repeated vaginal examinations, and preterm labour
Clinical diagnosis is suggested by maternal fever combined with features such as maternal or fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, and purulent or foul-smelling amniotic fluid
Infection is typically polymicrobial, involving genital tract flora including anaerobes, group B streptococcus, and enteric organisms
Management centres on prompt broad-spectrum antibiotics and expediting delivery, as the infection will not resolve while the pregnancy continues
It is an important cause of maternal sepsis and can lead to postpartum endometritis, wound infection, and, rarely, septic shock
For the neonate it raises the risk of early-onset sepsis, pneumonia, and, particularly in preterm infants, neurological injury and cerebral palsy
Delivery does not preclude ongoing infection, so mother and baby require continued observation and treatment after birth

With prompt antibiotics and timely delivery most mothers recover fully, though the condition carries risks of postpartum infection, haemorrhage from uterine atony, and rarely septic shock. Neonatal outcome depends on gestation and the severity of the fetal inflammatory response; term infants generally do well with treatment, whereas preterm infants exposed to intrauterine infection face higher risks of sepsis and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment.

Chronic inflammation of the meninges (pia, arachnoid, dura) generates neurologic deficits whose pattern is determined by the anatomic site of inflammation and its consequences. CSF, produced by the choroid plexus and circulating from the ventricles through the basal cisterns over the convexities to arachnoid villi, provides a conduit for rapid spread of infectious or infiltrative processes over the brain, cord, and nerve roots; organisms may also track along perivascular (Virchow-Robin) spaces into brain parenchyma. Intracranial inflammation stimulates meningeal nociceptive fibers (headache, neck/back pain) and may obstruct CSF flow at the cerebral aqueduct or arachnoid villi, causing hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure. Inflammatory exudate seeded around the brainstem and cranial nerves at the skull base produces basal meningitis with multiple cranial neuropathies, while spinal exudate injures nerve roots and may encircle the cord to cause myelopathy. Vasculitis of subarachnoid vessels can lead to infarction and cognitive/behavioral decline. A recently identified dural lymphatic system drains the dura, but its role in chronic meningitis is not yet established.

Chronic meningitis is defined by a characteristic neurologic syndrome persisting beyond 4 weeks together with a sustained CSF inflammatory response (white cell count >5/uL); appropriate treatment hinges entirely on identifying the underlying cause.

Meningeal enhancement patterns localize the process: leptomeningeal enhancement follows gyri and basal cisterns (typical of infection), whereas pachymeningeal enhancement is thick, linear or nodular along dura/falx/tentorium (e.g., lymphoma, IgG4-related disease).

In about one-third of cases the cause remains undiagnosed despite thorough evaluation; many causative organisms require weeks of culture, so diagnostic patience is balanced against the risk of progressive neurologic deterioration.

Repeated large-volume lumbar CSF samples (three or more), and if needed cervical cisternal sampling near the basal meninges, raise the yield for fungal and malignant causes; ventricular fluid may appear sterile despite active lower lumbar infection.

Five disease categories account for most cases: meningeal infections, malignancy, autoimmune inflammatory disorders, chemical meningitis, and parameningeal infections; some recurrent cases reflect monogenic autoinflammatory disorders.

Cardinal manifestations are persistent nonfocal headache, signs of hydrocephalus, cranial neuropathies, radiculopathies, and cognitive or personality change; classic meningeal signs (Kernig/Brudzinski) are actually uncommon in the chronic form.

Basal meningitis, where exudate collects at the skull base, presents as multiple cranial neuropathies; lower cranial nerves are involved more often because the inflammatory exudate gravitates to the base of the brain.

Spinal involvement produces multiple radiculopathies (radicular pain, sensory loss, weakness, sphincter dysfunction) and may progress to arachnoiditis with clumping of lower nerve roots, again because cells settle at the bottom of the intrathecal space.

Two clinical forms exist: a chronic persistent form and a recurrent form in which all clinical and CSF abnormalities resolve completely between discrete episodes (e.g., Mollaret's meningitis from HSV-2, chemical leak from epidermoid tumor, autoimmune conditions, drug hypersensitivity).

Worldwide, M. tuberculosis is the most common infectious cause, followed by Cryptococcus neoformans; in immunosuppressed patients these may present with little or no headache, fever, or meningeal signs and even a pauci-cellular CSF.

In most chronic (non-recurrent) meningitides mononuclear cells predominate; a neutrophilic CSF after 3 weeks points to Nocardia, Actinomyces, Brucella, certain fungi (Blastomyces, Candida, Histoplasma, Aspergillus, Pseudallescheria, Cladophialophora), or noninfectious causes (SLE, chemical meningitis).

An eosinophilic CSF response suggests parasitic disease (Angiostrongylus, Gnathostoma, Baylisascaris, Toxocara, cysticercosis, schistosomiasis, echinococcosis, toxoplasmosis), coccidioidal fungal meningitis (6-20% eosinophils with lymphocytic pleocytosis), neoplasia, or sarcoidosis.

Assuming a normal or pauci-cellular CSF excludes meningitis in immunosuppressed or HIV patients, in whom signs are attenuated

Failing to recognize that ventricular CSF can appear sterile while active infection persists in the lower lumbar space

Outcome depends on the underlying etiology and the speed of diagnosis and treatment; many causes are effectively treatable, but untreated disease produces progressive, potentially fatal damage to the CNS, cranial nerves, and roots. Even with treatment, tuberculous meningitis carries high rates of morbidity. Fatal levels of raised intracranial pressure can occur (notably in cryptococcal meningitis) even without ventricular enlargement, and repetitive or continuous CSF drainage may be needed to prevent abrupt deterioration and death. Some recurrent forms (e.g., chronic benign lymphocytic meningitis) resolve over 2-6 months.
Signs of raised intracranial pressure (vomiting, drowsiness, papilledema, visual loss, impaired upgaze, sixth-nerve palsy) warranting imaging before lumbar puncture
Rapidly progressive neurologic deterioration requiring urgent treatment rather than awaiting culture results

Immunosuppression or untreated HIV, where meningeal signs are attenuated and any persistent headache or mental status change mandates CSF examination

No formal grading scale is given; severity is gauged clinically by the rate of neurologic progression, the presence of raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus, and the degree of disability, which together determine whether to await culture results or proceed to meningeal biopsy and empiric therapy.

Chronic constipation reflects disordered colonic transit, defecatory mechanics, or both. In slow-transit constipation, reduced colonic propulsive activity, often linked to abnormalities of enteric neurons and interstitial cells of Cajal, delays stool passage. In defecatory disorders, impaired coordination of the pelvic floor and anal sphincter (dyssynergia) or structural pelvic floor abnormalities prevent effective evacuation. Normal-transit constipation, the most common type, involves normal stool movement with perceived difficulty, often overlapping with irritable bowel syndrome. Secondary causes act through metabolic, endocrine, neurological, or pharmacological effects on gut motility.
Constipation is defined by symptoms including infrequent stools, straining, hard stools, and a sense of incomplete evacuation rather than by stool frequency alone
Most chronic constipation is functional and can be categorised as normal-transit, slow-transit, or a defecatory (pelvic floor) disorder
A careful history and rectal examination are essential and can reveal a defecatory disorder such as dyssynergic defaecation
Secondary causes including hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, diabetes, neurological disease, and constipating medications should be identified and treated
Increasing dietary fibre and fluid with graded use of osmotic and stimulant laxatives is the mainstay for most patients
Defecatory disorders respond poorly to laxatives alone and are best treated with biofeedback-directed pelvic floor retraining
Anorectal manometry with a balloon expulsion test and, where needed, transit studies guide management of refractory cases
Escalating laxatives without recognising an underlying defecatory disorder that needs biofeedback
Failing to exclude secondary and structural causes before treating symptomatically
Overlooking constipating medications, particularly opioids
Omitting the rectal examination, which often reveals the mechanism of constipation

Chronic constipation is generally benign but frequently persistent and can significantly reduce quality of life; most patients improve with lifestyle measures and laxatives, and biofeedback is effective for defecatory disorders, though a minority remain refractory.

Chronic hepatitis comprises liver disorders of varying cause in which hepatic inflammation and necrosis persist for at least 6 months. Broad categories include chronic viral hepatitis (B, B plus D, C), drug- or toxin-induced chronic hepatitis, alcohol-associated liver disease, metabolic dysfunction-related (steatotic) liver disease, and autoimmune chronic hepatitis; idiopathic/cryptogenic cases are also believed largely autoimmune. In chronic hepatitis B, all forms can be progressive but progression occurs primarily in patients with active HBV replication, and HCC risk is highest with continued high-level replication. In autoimmune hepatitis, progressive injury results from a cell-mediated immunologic attack on hepatocytes in the setting of lost/failed tolerance for self-liver antigens; predisposition is inherited (HLA-B8, DR3, DR4, DRB1*0301/*0401) while liver specificity is triggered by environmental factors (chemicals, drugs such as minocycline, viruses, and reported triggers including COVID-19 and COVID-19 vaccination); molecular mimicry activates infiltrating CD4+ T cells and impaired regulatory CD4+CD25+ T-cell control contributes (p.2673, 2693-2694).

Chronic hepatitis is defined as hepatic inflammation and necrosis continuing for at least 6 months; milder forms are nonprogressive or slowly progressive, whereas more severe forms cause scarring and architectural reorganization that, when advanced, lead ultimately to cirrhosis (p.2673).

Cirrhosis from any cause of chronic hepatitis carries a risk of hepatocellular carcinoma; in cirrhotic hepatitis C the annual HCC rate is 1-4%, occurring primarily after 30 or more years of infection, warranting HCC surveillance (p.2685).

Liver biopsy is imperative to diagnose AIH; classic features include interface hepatitis extending beyond portal tracts, plasma cells in the infiltrate, central vein perivenulitis, hepatocellular rosette formation, and frequent septal/bridging fibrosis and cirrhosis (p.2695).

Classification rests on three axes: (1) cause, (2) histologic activity or grade (necroinflammatory activity), and (3) degree of progression based on fibrosis or stage; neither clinical features alone nor histology alone are sufficient to characterize disease (p.2673).

Grade reflects necroinflammatory activity (periportal/piecemeal necrosis or interface hepatitis, bridging necrosis, focal lobular necrosis, portal inflammation) and is scored by the histologic activity index (HAI, used in the U.S.) or METAVIR (used in Europe); chronic hepatitis is graded mild, moderate, or severe (p.2673-2674).

Stage reflects fibrosis on a numerical scale (0-6 HAI or 0-4 METAVIR); when fibrous septa surround parenchymal nodules and alter normal lobular architecture, the lesion is defined as cirrhosis (p.2674).
Hyperglobulinemia and circulating autoantibodies are distinctly ABSENT in chronic hepatitis B, in contrast to autoimmune hepatitis; this helps distinguish viral from autoimmune disease (p.2674).

Autoimmune hepatitis has a strong female predominance (~75% of cases) with a bimodal age distribution (one peak age <30, a second often >60); fatigue is the most common symptom (~85%) and ~25% are diagnosed when asymptomatic on abnormal liver tests (p.2694-2695).

Type I AIH (classic, North America/northern Europe, young women) is associated with ANA in a homogeneous pattern and anti-smooth-muscle antibody (ASMA); type II AIH (often children, Mediterranean) is associated with anti-LKM1 (directed against cytochrome P450 2D6) rather than ANA (p.2695).
Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (>2.5 g/dL) is common in AIH; smooth-muscle antibodies are detected in 63% of cases and, combined with a positive ANA, have high specificity (p.2695).

Anti-LKM1 (against cytochrome P450 2D6) seen in type II AIH is the same antibody found in some patients with chronic hepatitis C; rarely AIH patients with hyperglobulinemia give false-positive anti-HCV immunoassays (p.2685-2695).

Histopathologic-only classification (chronic persistent/lobular vs chronic active hepatitis) has been replaced because its presumed prognostic implications were not corroborated; classification now combines cause, grade, and stage (p.2673).
Laboratory features of chronic hepatitis B do not reliably distinguish histologically mild from severe disease (p.2674).

Low-titer ANA or ASMA occurs in other liver diseases including MASLD (~20% ANA-positive, ~14% ASMA-positive in one series) and viral hepatitis, so positive autoantibodies are not specific for AIH (p.2695).

Rarely AIH patients with hyperglobulinemia have false-positive anti-HCV; conversely some confirmed chronic hepatitis C patients have circulating anti-LKM1, blurring the distinction between viral and autoimmune disease (p.2685-2695).
ICI hepatitis resembles AIH but lacks female preponderance and is less likely to have ANA (low-titer if present) or plasma cell infiltrates (p.2695).
Overlapping types of hepatitis (e.g., viral plus steatotic, alcohol plus nonalcohol steatotic) are encountered not infrequently given the high prevalence of steatotic liver disease (p.2673).

Outcome depends on grade and stage. In untreated chronic hepatitis B, 5-year survival was 97% for mild, 86% for moderate-to-severe, and 55% for those with cirrhosis (15-year survival 77%, 66%, 40% respectively); all forms can progress, primarily with active HBV replication. In chronic hepatitis C, liver histology is the best prognostic indicator; mild disease has an excellent prognosis, while moderate-to-severe necroinflammation or bridging fibrosis makes cirrhosis highly likely over 10-20 years. In compensated HCV cirrhosis, 10-year survival is ~80%, with mortality 2-6%/year, decompensation 4-5%/year, and HCC 1-4%/year. In autoimmune hepatitis, 10-year survival is 80-98% for treated versus 67% for untreated patients; severe symptomatic disease carries up to ~40% 6-month mortality without therapy; in a Dutch cohort, mortality exceeded the general population only in patients with cirrhosis (p.2674, 2685-2686, 2694-2695).
Complications of cirrhosis: ascites, edema, bleeding gastroesophageal varices, hepatic encephalopathy, coagulopathy, hypersplenism

Staged by fibrosis: HAI 0-6 or METAVIR F0-F4, with cirrhosis defined when fibrous septa surround parenchymal nodules and alter lobular architecture (Table 352-2, p.2674).
