Mantle cell lymphoma (CD5+, but CD23-negative, cyclin D1+, moderate/bright CD20 and surface Ig) — distinguished by immunophenotype (p.852)
Marginal zone lymphoma (CD5 -/+, CD23 -/+, bright surface Ig) (p.852)
Follicular lymphoma (CD5-negative, CD10-positive, CD23-positive) (p.852)
Monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis (clonal B cells below the CLL threshold without organ involvement or cytopenias) (p.852)
Small lymphocytic lymphoma (tissue-based counterpart with identical molecular features) (p.852)
B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia arising from CLL (clinically and therapeutically distinct, though classified under Richter's transformation) (p.853-854)

Reactive lymphocytosis from viral infection — viral infections produce larger reactive lymphocytes with abundant cytoplasm, in contrast to the increased small lymphocytes and smudge cells of CLL (p.443)
Flow cytometry of peripheral blood for the characteristic immunophenotype (CD19, CD20, CD22, CD23, CD200, CD5, dim surface Ig) — diagnostic test of choice (p.852)
FISH for recurrent abnormalities del(13)(q14.3), trisomy 12, del(11)(q22.3), del(17)(p13.1); repeated before each line of therapy to detect acquired del(17p) (p.851)
Stimulated metaphase karyotype, including assessment for complex karyotype (≥3 abnormalities) (p.851)
Sequencing for TP53 and IGHV mutational status for prognostication (p.854)
β2-microglobulin and LDH (prognostic; component of CLL International Prognostic Index) (p.853-854)
Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test for warm IgG antibody when autoimmune hemolytic anemia is suspected (Coombs-negative cases can occur) (p.853)
Reticulocyte count, bilirubin, LDH, haptoglobin to evaluate suspected hemolysis (p.853)

18FDG-PET/CT to localize a biopsy site when Richter's transformation is suspected (SUV <5 consistent with CLL; SUV >5 suspicious; ≥10 very concerning); excisional biopsy preferred over fine-needle aspiration (p.853-854)
CLL International Prognostic Index integrating TP53 status, IGHV status, β2-microglobulin, clinical stage, and age (p.854)
Other CD5+ or low-grade B-cell lymphoproliferative disorders (mantle cell, marginal zone, follicular lymphoma) distinguishable by flow cytometry immunophenotype, morphology, or cytogenetics (p.852)

CLL is a monoclonal expansion of mature B lymphocytes; the definitive cell of origin is not established (mature/memory B cell, stepwise transformation, or hematopoietic stem cell are all proposed). Distinct BCR signaling — low-level IgM, tonic antiapoptotic pathway activation — drives tumor survival, with upregulation of BCR-pathway genes in lymph nodes and marrow versus blood. The CLL genome is relatively simple (~20 nonsynonymous and ~5 structural changes) with no unifying driver; recurrent mutations include SF3B1, NOTCH1, MYD88, ATM, and TP53 (mostly enriched in IGHV-unmutated disease, except MYD88 which favors IGHV-mutated/indolent disease). Key cytogenetic lesions: del(13)(q14.3) (sole, indolent; causes loss of the miR15/16 cluster that normally suppresses BCL2 and other antiapoptotic genes), trisomy 12 (intermediate), del(11)(q22.3)/ATM (bulky disease, aggressive), and del(17)(p13.1)/TP53 (poorest prognosis). Immune dysregulation pervades the disease: innate defects (reduced complement, neutrophil and NK cell defects), adaptive defects (CD4+ T-cell exhaustion, Th1-to-Th2 shift, expanded T regulatory cells), nurse-like tumor-associated macrophages, and humoral hypogammaglobulinemia (p.849-852).
CLL is a monoclonal proliferation of mature B lymphocytes defined by an absolute clonal B-cell count of ≥5 × 10⁹/L in the blood; it is a disease of older adults (median age at diagnosis 71) (p.849).
Bone marrow biopsy is not undertaken until therapy is initiated, except in cases of unexplained cytopenias; CT imaging is usually unnecessary at diagnosis (p.854).
A watchful-waiting strategy is used for most patients, with therapy reserved for symptomatic disease, as multiple trials show no survival advantage to earlier therapy (p.854).

Hypogammaglobulinemia affects all immunoglobulin subclasses and occurs in ~85% of patients at some point; low IgG and IgA correlate with infection risk, but isolated IgM reduction does not seem to confer excess infection risk (p.852).

Most commonly diagnosed incidentally on routine blood work showing an elevated lymphocyte count in an asymptomatic individual; the natural history is heterogeneous, with some patients never requiring therapy (p.849, p.853).

On the peripheral blood smear, the small lymphocytes are increased and many rupture during smear preparation, leaving nuclear material without surrounding cytoplasm — smudge cells, which are rare in the absence of chronic lymphoid leukemia (p.443).

Diagnosis is confirmed by flow cytometry on peripheral blood; the typical immunophenotype is CD19+, CD20+, CD22+, CD23+, CD200+, the T-cell marker CD5+, and dim surface immunoglobulin (kappa or lambda). A clonal B-cell count ≥5 × 10⁹/L needs no further workup to confirm CLL (p.852).

Small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) is the tissue-based counterpart of CLL (lymphadenopathy/splenomegaly with a small clonal blood population); genetic and molecular features are identical and SLL is managed identically to CLL (p.852).

Monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis (MBL) is a precursor: clonal B cells below the CLL threshold without nodal/organ involvement or cytopenias; high-count MBL progresses to overt CLL at ~1–2% per year, whereas low-count MBL has a negligible progression rate (p.849, p.852).

IGHV mutational status is a key prognostic factor: ~60% have IGHV ≥2% mutated from germline (more indolent course), while ~40% are IGHV-unmutated (more rapid progression, shorter survival before BCR-targeted therapy) (p.850).
B-cell receptor (BCR) signaling is central to CLL pathogenesis, characterized by low-level IgM expression and tonic activation of antiapoptotic pathways promoting tumor survival (p.850).
FISH (with or without karyotype) should be checked before every line of therapy because cytogenetics can evolve even without treatment, mainly to detect acquisition of del(17)(p13.1) (p.851).

When anemia or thrombocytopenia appear, distinguish autoimmune cytopenia from marrow replacement — the therapeutic approaches differ, and autoimmune cytopenias often respond without treating the underlying CLL (p.853)
AIHA can be Coombs-negative, so a negative direct antiglobulin test does not exclude it (p.853)

ITP can be hard to distinguish from disease progression because no lab test directly identifies the platelet-destruction mechanism; isolated thrombocytopenia and rapid platelet decline without alternative cause point to ITP (p.853)

del(13)(q14.3) seen on banded karyotype (rather than only on FISH) indicates a larger deletion involving the retinoblastoma gene, which negates the favorable prognosis usually associated with this marker (p.850)
Live vaccines should be avoided in CLL because of the small risk of viral reactivation in an immunocompromised host (p.853)
Fine-needle aspiration should be discouraged for diagnosing suspected Richter's transformation; excisional biopsy is preferred (p.854)
Cytogenetics can change without therapy, so prior FISH results may be outdated — recheck before each line of treatment (p.851)

Heterogeneous: many patients are asymptomatic and never require therapy while others need multiple lines and die of disease. Overall survival has improved markedly (5-year OS 70% in 1980, 92% in 2015, likely higher today), and only a small minority now die of CLL itself. Infections cause ~30–50% of CLL-related deaths. Favorable markers: IGHV-mutated disease, sole del(13)(q14.3), MYD88 mutation. Adverse markers: IGHV-unmutated disease, del(17p)/TP53, del(11q)/ATM, NOTCH1, complex karyotype, and high β2-microglobulin/LDH. The CLL International Prognostic Index stratifies 5-year survival from ~93% (low risk) to ~23% (very high risk) in training-set data, though it has not been validated in the era of novel targeted therapies. Richter's transformation carries a poor prognosis, with median survival of 6–16 months for clonally related DLBCL versus ~5 years for clonally unrelated lymphomas (p.849, p.851, p.853-854).

Richter's transformation — transformation to an aggressive lymphoma (most commonly DLBCL; Hodgkin lymphoma is a recognized variant). Suspect with rapid progression of adenopathy (often localized), constitutional symptoms (fatigue, night sweats, fever, weight loss), and usually high LDH (p.853-854)
del(17)(p13.1)/TP53 loss or mutation — poorest prognosis, rapid progression, poor response to DNA-damaging therapy (p.850-851)
Complex karyotype (≥3 abnormalities) — adverse impact on time to treatment and overall survival, worsening with increasing complexity (p.851)
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia — death from uncontrolled AIHA can occur without appropriate supportive care; immediate therapy is almost always necessary (p.853)

Symptoms indicating need for therapy: progressive marrow failure, massive/progressive/symptomatic splenomegaly or lymphadenopathy, lymphocyte doubling time <6 months, autoimmune cytopenia unresponsive to standard therapy, or constitutional symptoms (p.854)

Two staging systems, both based on physical exam and labs (no imaging or marrow required). Rai system (more common in the US): low risk (stage 0) = lymphocytosis only; intermediate risk (stage I/II) = lymphocytosis with lymphadenopathy, with or without splenomegaly/hepatomegaly; high risk (stage III/IV) = lymphocytosis with anemia or thrombocytopenia from marrow involvement. Binet system (more common in Europe): A = <3 areas of lymphadenopathy; B = ≥3 areas of lymphadenopathy; C = hemoglobin ≤10 g/dL and/or platelets <100,000/μL. The CLL International Prognostic Index refines outcome prediction using TP53 status, IGHV status, β2-microglobulin, clinical stage, and age (p.854).
Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) (non-infective) — Oncology / Hematology Also: CLL, small lymphocytic lymphoma, SLL
Leukemoid reaction (reactive leukocytosis) - distinguished from CML by a high/normal leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score (CML has a LOW LAP) and absence of BCR::ABL1 (Harrison 22e p.837)

Atypical CML (BCR::ABL1-negative) - lacks the Ph chromosome/BCR::ABL1, does not respond to TKI therapy, associated with SETBP1 (about 25%) and some CSF3R mutations, poor prognosis with median survival ~2-3 years (Harrison 22e p.835)
Chronic neutrophilic leukemia - frequently CSF3R-mutated (about 80%); may respond to ruxolitinib (Harrison 22e p.835)
Chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (Harrison 22e p.835)
Myelodysplastic syndrome/myeloproliferative neoplasms, including MDS/MPN-RS-T (SF3B1-mutated) (Harrison 22e p.835)
Essential thrombocythemia and other Ph-negative MPNs presenting with thrombocytosis - when JAK2 V617F is absent, cytogenetics/FISH for BCR::ABL1 are required to exclude CML (Harrison 22e p.832-833)

Bone marrow aspiration with routine G-banding cytogenetics - required to confirm the Ph chromosome, detect additional chromosomal abnormalities (which FISH will not detect), and quantify marrow blasts and basophils; a diagnosis of CML must always rely on marrow analysis with cytogenetics (Harrison 22e p.837)
FISH analysis for BCR::ABL1 on peripheral blood - quantifies percentage of Ph-positive cells; preferred when a Ph cytogenetic study is negative or for monitoring (Harrison 22e p.837)

Quantitative RT-PCR for BCR::ABL1 transcripts on the International Scale - baseline transcript typing at diagnosis (to avoid spurious 'undetectable' results on follow-up with atypical transcripts) and serial molecular monitoring of response (Harrison 22e p.837-838)
ABL1 kinase domain mutation analysis - assessed when resistance/loss of response is suspected (e.g., to detect T315I) (Harrison 22e p.836-837)
Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score - characteristically LOW in CML, helping distinguish it from a leukemoid reaction (Harrison 22e p.837)
Supportive biochemistry - high vitamin B12, uric acid, lactate dehydrogenase, and lysozyme are commonly seen (Harrison 22e p.837)

Leukemoid reaction (reactive leukocytosis from infection, inflammation, or other stress) - mimics the leukocytosis with left shift of CML but lacks BCR::ABL1 and shows a high/normal (not low) leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score (Harrison 22e p.837)
Other myeloproliferative neoplasms and MDS/MPN overlap syndromes that can produce leukocytosis, basophilia, or splenomegaly without the Philadelphia chromosome (Harrison 22e p.835)

CML is a clonal myeloproliferative stem cell neoplasm caused by the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene arising from the reciprocal balanced translocation t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2) (the Philadelphia chromosome). DNA from the ABL1 proto-oncogene on chromosome 9 is juxtaposed to the breakpoint cluster region (BCR) gene on chromosome 22, generating a hybrid oncogene whose product (most commonly the p210BCR::ABL1 oncoprotein from e13a2 or e14a2 transcripts) has constitutive tyrosine kinase activity. This drives increased proliferation and reduced apoptosis, giving CML cells a growth advantage and progressively suppressing normal hematopoiesis. Constitutive BCR::ABL1 activation triggers autophosphorylation and downstream signaling via RAS, MAP kinases, STAT, PI3K, MYC and others, mediated by adapter proteins (GRB-2, CRK, CRK-L, SHC). Most TKIs bind the ATP-binding domain to inhibit kinase activity; asciminib (a STAMP inhibitor) instead binds the ABL1 myristoyl pocket. BCR::ABL1 induces genetic instability favoring acquisition of additional defects (e.g., double Ph, trisomy 8, isochromosome 17/17p loss of TP53, 3q26 abnormalities, mutations in TP53, RB1, RUNX1, p16) that drive transformation from chronic to accelerated to blastic phase. Notably, the BCR::ABL1 rearrangement is detectable in the blood of up to 25% of normal adults and 5% of infants but is not sufficient to cause overt CML in the overwhelming majority. (Harrison 22e p.834-836)
CML is a clonal hematopoietic myeloproliferative stem cell neoplasm driven by the BCR::ABL1 chimeric gene, which encodes a constitutively active tyrosine kinase (Harrison 22e p.834).

Diagnosis depends on documenting t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2), identified by G-banding in 90% of cases; FISH and PCR aid diagnosis and estimate disease burden, and can be done on peripheral blood (Harrison 22e p.837).

TKIs have revolutionized CML: the estimated 10-year survival with imatinib now exceeds 85% and approaches that of a normal age-matched population; allogeneic HSCT (curative but riskier) is offered as later-line therapy after TKI failure (Harrison 22e p.834).

Molecular monitoring on the International Scale (IS) guides therapy: complete cytogenetic response (0% Ph) is roughly equivalent to BCR::ABL1 <=1% (MR2); major molecular response (MMR/MR3) is BCR::ABL1 <=0.1%; deep molecular response MR4 is <=0.01% and MR4.5 is <=0.0032% (Harrison 22e p.837-838).

The T315I 'gatekeeper' kinase-domain mutation prevents binding of, and causes resistance to, imatinib and the second-generation TKIs (dasatinib, nilotinib, bosutinib); third-generation agents (e.g., ponatinib, asciminib) retain activity against it (Harrison 22e p.836).

BCR::ABL1 results from a balanced reciprocal translocation between the long arms of chromosomes 9 and 22, t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2), known as the Philadelphia chromosome (Ph); the t(9;22) is present in >90% of classical CML cases (Harrison 22e p.834-835).

The most common transcript in CML encodes the p210BCR::ABL1 oncoprotein; p190BCR::ABL1 is present in two-thirds of Ph-positive ALL but rare in CML, and p230BCR::ABL1 is rare and associated with a more indolent course (Harrison 22e p.835).
Untreated, CML is typically biphasic or triphasic: an early indolent chronic phase, often followed by an accelerated phase, and a terminal blastic phase (Harrison 22e p.834).
Most patients (about 90%) present in chronic phase; in developed countries 50-60% are diagnosed on routine blood tests with minimal symptoms such as fatigue (Harrison 22e p.836).
Common symptoms, when present, are manifestations of anemia and splenomegaly: fatigue, malaise, weight loss, early satiety, and left upper quadrant pain or mass (Harrison 22e p.836).
Splenomegaly is the most common physical finding (20-70% depending on screening frequency); hepatomegaly (5-10%) and lymphadenopathy (5%) are less common (Harrison 22e p.836-837).

Untreated CML shows leukocytosis (10-500 x 10^9/L) with left-shifted myeloid hematopoiesis: neutrophils plus bands, myelocytes, metamyelocytes, promyelocytes, and blasts (usually <=5%); basophils and/or eosinophils are frequently increased (Harrison 22e p.837).

Thrombocytosis is common; thrombocytopenia is rare and, when present, suggests worse prognosis, disease acceleration, or an unrelated etiology. Anemia is present in one-third of patients (Harrison 22e p.837).

PITFALL: Mistaking a reactive leukemoid reaction for CML - the leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score is LOW in CML but high/normal in a leukemoid reaction, and CML requires demonstration of BCR::ABL1 (Harrison 22e p.837).

Atypical transcripts (e13a3, e14a3, e19a2, etc.) not detected at diagnosis can produce falsely 'negative/undetectable' BCR::ABL1 on follow-up PCR, giving a false impression of complete molecular response; transcript type must be documented at diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.835, 837).
FISH does NOT detect additional chromosomal abnormalities, so a marrow cytogenetic analysis is still required at diagnosis; relying on FISH/PCR alone can miss clonal evolution (Harrison 22e p.837).
Both FISH and PCR can be falsely positive at low levels or falsely negative for technical reasons, so diagnosis must always rely on marrow analysis with routine cytogenetics (Harrison 22e p.837).

In about 10% of patients marrow blasts and basophils are significantly higher than in peripheral blood, conferring poorer prognosis or representing transformation that peripheral counts alone would miss (Harrison 22e p.837).
Failure to achieve MMR or DMR should NOT automatically be considered 'failure' of a given TKI or an indication to switch TKI or proceed to allogeneic HSCT (Harrison 22e p.838).

TKIs have transformed CML prognosis. Before the TKI era median survival was 3-7 years with annual mortality of 10% in the first 2 years and 15-20% thereafter. With imatinib, annual mortality has fallen to about 1-2%, the 10-year survival rate is about 85% (CML-specific survival ~90%), and the 10-year incidence of blastic transformation is only 5-6%; more than half of deaths are now from non-CML causes. Treatment-related response milestones are the dominant modern prognostic factors: achievement of complete cytogenetic response (MR2) is the major endpoint associated with improved survival, while durable deep molecular response (MR4/MR4.5) may permit treatment-free remission (TFR rate about 50% after 2+ years of durable DMR and 80%+ after 5+ years). Historical pretreatment models (Sokal, Hasford, EUTOS) and adverse features (age, splenomegaly, anemia, high blasts/basophils, marrow fibrosis, additional chromosomal abnormalities) have lost much of their prognostic weight in the TKI era. Accelerated phase (historical median survival <2 years) and blastic phase carry the worst outcomes; de novo accelerated phase on TKI now has an estimated 8-year survival of 60-70%, and lymphoid blastic phase responds to ALL-type chemotherapy plus TKIs (complete response ~70%, median survival ~3 years). (Harrison 22e p.834, 838-839)
Unexplained, sustained leukocytosis (with or without splenomegaly) should prompt marrow examination and cytogenetic analysis (Harrison 22e p.837)
Increasing/therapy-resistant leukocytosis, worsening anemia, fever and constitutional symptoms, and rising blasts and basophils signal disease progression (Harrison 22e p.838)
New thrombocytopenia (<100 x 10^9/L unrelated to therapy) suggests worse prognosis or disease acceleration (Harrison 22e p.837-838)
Extramedullary disease (skin/subcutaneous lesions, soft tissue, or lytic bone lesions) with biopsy showing blast predominance indicates transformation (Harrison 22e p.837-838)
Hyperleukocytosis/hyperviscosity or marked thrombocytosis with thrombotic events (priapism, MI, venous thrombosis, visual disturbance, CVA) or bleeding diathesis (Harrison 22e p.836)

CML is staged by clinical phase. Chronic phase: indolent, marrow blasts typically <=5%, where ~90% of patients present. Accelerated phase (historically median survival <2 years): >=15% peripheral blasts, >=30% peripheral blasts plus promyelocytes, >=20% peripheral basophils, cytogenetic clonal evolution (additional chromosomal abnormalities beyond Ph), or thrombocytopenia <100 x 10^9/L unrelated to therapy. Blastic phase: >=30% peripheral or marrow blasts, or sheets of blasts in extramedullary disease (commonly myeloid in ~60%, lymphoid in ~25%). The newest WHO classification suggests eliminating accelerated phase and reclassifying such patients as high-risk CML, but the text argues the accelerated-phase definition should be maintained because their survival is significantly worse than high-risk CML. Risk models (Sokal, Hasford, EUTOS) were used historically. (Harrison 22e p.838)
Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) (non-infective) — Oncology / Hematology Also: CML
Asthma (substantial overlap in older patients; both feature airway hyperresponsiveness and may share genetic/environmental factors)
Bronchiectasis
Interstitial lung disease
Congestive heart failure
Chronic thromboembolic disease / pulmonary hypertension
Lung cancer (especially when new clubbing appears)
Tuberculosis-associated chronic airflow limitation (important in absence of tobacco history)
Pneumonia (frequently found on imaging during presumed exacerbation)
Acute bronchitis
Tuberculosis (can produce chronic airflow limitation with emphysematous and fibrotic change and airway remodeling)
HIV-associated emphysema/COPD (increased risk with lower CD4 counts; often underdiagnosed)
Post-bronchodilator spirometry (FEV1, FVC, FEV1/FVC) for diagnosis and severity grading (GOLD vs ATS/ERS Z-scores)
Lung volumes (TLC, FRC, RV, RV/TLC) and diffusing capacity (DLCO) - DLCO reduced in emphysema
Arterial blood gas and oximetry for resting/exertional hypoxemia, alveolar ventilation and acid-base status (key in exacerbation assessment)
Complete blood count with differential (blood eosinophil count; hematocrit for chronic hypoxemia)
Chest CT (definitive for emphysema pattern/distribution, airway disease, coexisting ILD/bronchiectasis; annual low-dose CT for lung cancer screening in eligible smokers)
Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level with PI-type determination (isoelectric focusing, mass spectrometry/genotyping, or DNA sequencing) when low
6-minute walk distance for exercise capacity and BODE index
C-reactive protein (incorporated into proposed objective criteria for staging exacerbation severity)
Congestive heart failure
Pulmonary embolism (incidence increased during exacerbations; should be considered)
Pneumothorax (asymmetric chest findings can mimic an exacerbation)
Large airway obstruction

Chronic inhaled exposures (most commonly cigarette smoke, also biomass fuels, and increasingly vaping/inhaled cannabis) in genetically susceptible individuals trigger inflammatory and immune cell recruitment in large and small airways and terminal air spaces. Large-airway changes (mucus gland enlargement, goblet cell hyperplasia, squamous metaplasia) produce cough and sputum and define chronic bronchitis. Small airways (<=2 mm) are the major site of increased airflow resistance, narrowed by goblet cell metaplasia replacing surfactant-secreting club cells, smooth-muscle hypertrophy, fibrosis, mucus, edema, and cellular infiltration; small-airway narrowing and drop-out precede emphysematous destruction. Emphysema results from a four-step paradigm: inflammatory/immune recruitment; proteinase release damaging extracellular matrix; oxidant-induced structural cell death, cellular senescence and proteolytic loss of cell-matrix attachments; and disordered repair of elastin. The elastase:antielastase imbalance (epitomized by alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency permitting unopposed neutrophil elastase) plus matrix metalloproteinases (notably MMP12) degrade elastin and collagen, generating chemotactic fragments that fuel a positive-feedback inflammatory loop. Oxidative stress (with NRF2 and SOD3 implicated, and oxidant inactivation of HDAC2 unleashing NF-kB-driven transcription of MMPs, IL-8, TNF-alpha) and impaired macrophage clearance of apoptotic cells and bacteria contribute. Physiologically, airflow obstruction with air trapping causes hyperinflation (raised residual volume, RV/TLC, and total lung capacity); a flattened diaphragm becomes mechanically inefficient. Ventilation-perfusion mismatch accounts for essentially all of the reduction in PaO2 (shunt is minimal), explaining why modest supplemental oxygen corrects hypoxemia. Inflammation can persist even after smoking cessation in susceptible individuals.

COPD is defined by persistent respiratory symptoms with airflow obstruction, and the umbrella term spans emphysema (alveolar destruction with air-space enlargement), chronic bronchitis (chronic cough and phlegm), and small airway disease (narrowing and loss of small bronchioles); these coexist in varying proportions between patients.

Approximately only 1% of COPD patients have severe alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, yet it is the proven monogenic risk factor and demonstrates the powerful role of genetics in susceptibility; PiZ individuals often develop early-onset COPD, accelerated by smoking.
The strongest single predictor of future exacerbations is a prior exacerbation, and the single greatest risk factor for hospitalization with an exacerbation is a history of previous hospitalization.
The BODE index (Body mass index, airflow Obstruction, Dyspnea, Exercise capacity by 6-minute walk) predicts mortality better than FEV1 alone.

Fixed airflow obstruction is the spirometric hallmark: a chronically reduced FEV1/FVC ratio that does not normalize after bronchodilator. The classic threshold is FEV1/FVC <0.7 (GOLD), with the ATS/ERS alternative using Z-scores of FEV1 below the lower limit of normal.

The three cardinal symptoms are cough, sputum production, and exertional dyspnea; many patients have symptoms for months to years before presenting, and a careful history often reveals respiratory symptoms preceding an apparent acute onset.

Activities involving arm work at or above shoulder level are particularly poorly tolerated, whereas activities that let the patient brace the arms and recruit accessory muscles (pushing a shopping cart, treadmill) are better tolerated.

Early disease typically has a normal physical exam; advanced disease shows prolonged expiration, wheeze, barrel chest, poor diaphragmatic excursion, accessory muscle use, the tripod posture, and cyanosis of lips/nail beds.
Digital clubbing is NOT a feature of COPD; its appearance should trigger a search for another cause, most commonly lung cancer in this population.
The blood eosinophil count (on CBC with differential) is used to guide therapy aimed at reducing exacerbation risk; an elevated hematocrit suggests chronic hypoxemia.

Chest CT is the definitive test for establishing presence, pattern, and distribution of emphysema and for medium/large airway disease; chest x-ray may be consistent with COPD (hyperinflation, flat diaphragm, bullae, hyperlucency) but cannot reliably make the diagnosis.

Guidelines recommend testing for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in ALL patients with COPD or with asthma plus chronic airflow obstruction; serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level is the initial test, with PI-type determination for confirmation when levels are low.
Chest x-ray cannot reliably diagnose COPD or establish chronicity; do not rely on it to confirm emphysema.
Pulmonary function testing during an exacerbation has not been shown helpful in diagnosis or management (unlike in asthma exacerbations).
Smokers with normal spirometry are not necessarily spared - many have reduced quality of life, reduced exercise capacity, emphysema/airway disease on CT, and may have exacerbations (pre-COPD).
Attributing new clubbing to COPD itself - it is not a feature and warrants a cancer workup.
Failing to test for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in COPD patients, missing a treatable genetic cause; only a small minority of the ~1 in 3000 with severe deficiency in the US have been identified.
Overlooking pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, heart failure, or pneumothorax during a presumed exacerbation (about 25% of x-rays in moderate/severe distress are abnormal).
Underestimating viral causes of exacerbations - PCR studies show viruses may cause >50% of exacerbations.
Race-specific reference equations for pulmonary function may be inappropriate; race-neutral interpretation may be preferable.

Risk of death from COPD is closely tied to reduced FEV1 and the presence of emphysema. Mortality is predicted better by the multidimensional BODE index than by FEV1 alone. The absolute annual loss of FEV1 is highest in mild COPD and lowest in very severe disease. Cachexia/wasting is an independent poor prognostic factor. Smoking cessation slows the rate of FEV1 decline (greatest benefit when earlier) and improves survival. Among survival-improving interventions are smoking cessation, long-term oxygen in chronically hypoxemic patients, and lung volume reduction surgery in selected emphysema patients. Patients with PRISm (preserved ratio-impaired spirometry) physiology carry increased risk of mortality and respiratory and cardiovascular events. Exacerbations are episodic acute worsenings (usually <14 days) that increase in frequency as obstruction worsens (severe obstruction with FEV1 <50% predicted averages 1-3 episodes per year) and account for most COPD-related health-care costs; there is currently no cure except lung transplantation.
New digital clubbing - investigate for lung cancer, not attributable to COPD
Respiratory acidosis with hypercarbia (PaCO2 >45 mmHg) signaling acute ventilatory failure
New or worsening hypoxemia
Mental status changes (confusion, sleepiness), inability to speak in full sentences, paradoxical abdominal wall motion
Tachycardia, tachypnea, accessory muscle use, perioral/peripheral cyanosis
Cachexia with significant weight loss (independent poor prognostic factor)
Signs of cor pulmonale / right heart failure (lower extremity edema, persistent activity limitation)

Spirometric severity of airflow obstruction (GOLD, post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.7): Mild FEV1 >=80% predicted; Moderate FEV1 50 to <80%; Severe FEV1 30 to <50%; Very severe FEV1 <30% predicted. ATS/ERS alternative uses FEV1/FVC < lower limit of normal with FEV1 Z-scores (borderline zFEV1 > -1.645; mild -1.65 to -2.5; moderate -2.51 to -4; severe < -4.1). The GOLD ABE assessment additionally incorporates respiratory symptom burden (mMRC dyspnea scale or COPD Assessment Test) and annual exacerbation frequency to guide therapy. Multidimensional BODE index (BMI, obstruction, dyspnea, exercise capacity) is used for prognosis. Ventilatory failure is defined as PaCO2 >45 mmHg, classified as acute (with acidemia) or chronic by arterial pH.
Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (non-infective) — Respiratory Also: COPD, Emphysema, Chronic bronchitis, Chronic obstructive lung disease
Pancreatic adenocarcinoma (must be excluded on imaging)
Autoimmune pancreatitis (type 1 AIP / IgG4-related disease; type 2 / idiopathic duct-centric)
Pancreatic pseudocyst
Fecal elastase-1 (random level on a formed stool specimen) to confirm exocrine pancreatic insufficiency
Abdominal CT (initial imaging modality of choice) to show calcifications, dilated pancreatic/biliary ducts, atrophy, and to exclude pseudocyst and cancer
MRI/MRCP, secretin-enhanced MRCP
Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS); five or more of nine endosonographic features considered diagnostic, though not specific for early disease
EUS with endoscopic pancreatic function testing (EUS-ePFT)
Direct pancreatic function test using secretin (best sensitivity; becomes abnormal when >=60% of exocrine function is lost)
Plain abdominal film for diffuse calcifications
Serum amylase/lipase (usually not strikingly elevated), serum bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase (may indicate cholestasis from biliary stricture)
Serum IgG4 (supportive of type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis)

Chronic pancreatitis is characterized by irreversible damage to the pancreas (in contrast to the reversible changes of acute pancreatitis), defined by histologic abnormalities including chronic inflammation, fibrosis, and progressive destruction (atrophy) of both exocrine and endocrine tissue. Irrespective of the mechanism of injury, pancreatic stellate cell activation leads to cytokine expression and production of extracellular matrix proteins contributing to inflammation and collagen deposition. Proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6) and oxidants induce stellate cell activity with new collagen synthesis; TGF-beta-mediated autocrine self-activation pathways may explain disease progression even after removal of noxious stimuli. Etiologies are framed by the TIGAR-O classification (Toxic-metabolic, Idiopathic, Genetic, Autoimmune, Recurrent and severe acute pancreatitis, Obstructive). Heavy alcohol use is the most common clinically apparent cause in U.S. adults, though additional factors are required for disease development (not all heavy drinkers develop disease). Genetic predisposition (e.g., PRSS1 cationic trypsinogen mutations preventing destruction of prematurely activated trypsin; CFTR and SPINK1 disease modifiers) accounts for up to 15% of previously idiopathic cases. Cardinal manifestations are abdominal pain, steatorrhea, weight loss, diabetes mellitus, and, less commonly, pancreatic cancer (p.2750-2752).

Patients typically present with abdominal pain or symptoms of maldigestion; pain is variable in location, severity, and frequency, may be constant or intermittent, and can be exacerbated by eating, leading to fear of eating and weight loss (p.2752).
There is often a disparity between the reported severity of abdominal pain and the physical findings, which mainly consist of nonfocal abdominal tenderness (p.2752).

In contrast to acute pancreatitis, serum amylase and lipase are usually NOT strikingly elevated in chronic pancreatitis; low serum pancreatic enzyme levels are moderately specific but have poor sensitivity (p.2752).
Cumulative prevalence of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency exceeds 80%; overt steatorrhea in a patient with chronic pancreatitis is highly suggestive of this complication (p.2752).
A random fecal elastase-1 level on a formed stool specimen can help confirm exocrine pancreatic insufficiency in patients with milder symptoms (p.2752).

Diffuse calcifications on a plain abdominal film usually indicate significant pancreatic damage and are pathognomonic for chronic pancreatitis; tropical pancreatitis (often SPINK1-associated) characteristically shows bulky calcifications (p.2752).

Lifetime prevalence of chronic pancreatitis-related diabetes exceeds 80%; most develop hyperglycemia from insulin deficiency due to islet cell loss, but diabetic ketoacidosis, diabetic coma, and end-organ damage (retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy) are uncommon (p.2752).

Cigarette smoking is an independent, dose-dependent risk factor for chronic pancreatitis and recurrent acute pancreatitis; continued alcohol and smoking exposure are associated with disease progression including fibrosis and calcifications (p.2750).
Metabolic bone disease is highly prevalent, with about 65% of patients having osteopenia or osteoporosis (p.2752).

Diagnosis of early or mild chronic pancreatitis is challenging because there is no accurate biomarker, and serum amylase/lipase are usually not strikingly elevated (unlike acute pancreatitis) (p.2752).
EUS is not specific enough to diagnose early chronic pancreatitis alone and may show positive features in patients with diabetes, a smoking history, or even normal aging individuals (p.2752).
Elevated serum IgG4 has a low positive predictive value for autoimmune pancreatitis when used in isolation from other clinical findings (p.2751).
Complete correction of steatorrhea with pancreatic enzyme replacement is uncommon, even though enzyme therapy usually controls diarrhea and improves fat absorption (p.2753).
Meta-analyses show no consistent benefit of enzyme therapy at reducing pain; any pain relief may reflect improvement of dyspepsia from maldigestion (p.2753).

Chronic pancreatitis is an irreversible disease; there are currently no therapies to reverse or delay disease progression, so management is focused on screening for and treating complications. Patients have impaired quality of life and significant morbidity with frequent health encounters. Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (cumulative prevalence >80%) and chronic pancreatitis-related diabetes (lifetime prevalence >80%) commonly develop. The 20-year cumulative risk of pancreatic cancer in chronic calcific pancreatitis is 4%, higher in hereditary PRSS1 and tropical forms (p.2752-2754).

Increased risk of pancreatic cancer: cumulative risk is 4% at 20 years after diagnosis of chronic calcific pancreatitis; hereditary PRSS1 and tropical pancreatitis carry an even higher risk than other forms.
Jaundice, cholestasis, and biliary cirrhosis from chronic inflammation around the intrapancreatic common bile duct.

Gastrointestinal bleeding from peptic ulceration, gastritis, a pseudocyst eroding into the duodenum, arterial bleeding into the pancreatic duct (hemosuccus pancreaticus), or ruptured varices from splenic vein thrombosis.

Etiologic classification follows the TIGAR-O system: Toxic-metabolic (alcohol, tobacco smoking, hypercalcemia, hyperlipidemia/hypertriglyceridemia, chronic renal failure), Idiopathic (early onset, late onset, tropical), Genetic (PRSS1 cationic trypsinogen, CFTR, CASR, CTRC, SPINK1), Autoimmune (type 1 IgG4-related; type 2 idiopathic duct-centric), Recurrent and severe acute pancreatitis (postnecrotic, recurrent acute), and Obstructive (pancreas divisum, duct obstruction by tumor, preampullary duodenal wall cysts, posttraumatic duct strictures). Some genetic conditions are disease modifiers requiring additional factors to cause disease (p.2750).

chunks.text: Chronic rhinosinusitis reflects a persistent inflammatory process of the sinonasal mucosa rather than simple ongoing infection. Anatomical narrowing or mucosal swelling at the osteomeatal complex obstructs sinus outflow, disrupting ventilation and mucociliary clearance so that secretions stagnate and mucosal inflammation is perpetuated. Host factors (allergy, asthma, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, immune dysfunction, ciliary disorders) and environmental factors (microbial biofilms, fungi, irritants) drive different inflammatory endotypes; polypoid disease is often eosinophilic and type 2 driven, whereas non-polypoid disease tends to be more neutrophilic. Chronic inflammation causes mucosal oedema, polyp formation and epithelial remodelling that further obstruct drainage, creating a self-sustaining cycle.

chunks.text: Chronic suppurative otitis media is long-standing inflammation of the middle ear cleft with a non-intact tympanic membrane. In the tubotympanic type, persistent Eustachian tube dysfunction and recurrent infection maintain mucosal inflammation and a central perforation, with reversible mucosal changes. In the atticoantral type, retraction pockets or migration of squamous epithelium form a cholesteatoma, an expanding keratinising sac whose enzymatic and pressure effects erode ossicles and surrounding bone. This bony destruction can breach the facial canal, labyrinth, or dural plates, opening routes for intracranial spread.

In chronic venous disease, incompetent (refluxing) or obstructed veins produce sustained venous hypertension with extravasation of fluid and blood elements into limb tissues. Primary varicose veins arise from defective saphenous valves, intrinsic vein-wall weakness, and high intraluminal pressure; secondary varicosities and chronic venous insufficiency result from deep-venous obstruction or valvular incompetence, classically post-thrombotic (valve leaflets thicken and contract after DVT, the vein becomes rigid, and distal valves become incompetent as high pressure distends the vein). Other secondary causes include May-Thurner syndrome, extrinsic compression by tumor/retroperitoneal fibrosis, arteriovenous fistulas, deep-vein agenesis, and venous malformations. Lymphedema results from impaired lymph transport: deficiency, reflux, or obstruction of lymph vessels causes an imbalance between lymph production and absorption (governed by Starling forces), so protein-rich fluid accumulates in the interstitium and raises tissue osmotic load. Persistent lymphedema triggers inflammatory/immune responses with infiltration of mononuclear cells, fibroblasts, and adipocytes, leading to adipose and collagen deposition in skin and subcutaneous tissues (p.2180, 2182-2183).
Chronic venous disease spans a spectrum: telangiectasias and reticular veins, to varicose veins, to chronic venous insufficiency with edema, skin changes, and ulceration (p.2179).
Worldwide, the most common cause of secondary lymphedema is lymphatic filariasis; in developed countries it is surgical excision or irradiation of axillary/inguinal lymph nodes for cancer (p.2183).
Recurrent bacterial lymphangitis, usually streptococcal, is a very common cause of lymphedema, and lymphedema in turn predisposes to recurrent cellulitis/lymphangitis - a vicious cycle (p.2183-2184).

Chronic venous insufficiency arises from incompetent veins with venous hypertension and extravasation of fluid and blood elements into the limb; it may occur with superficial venous disease, but more advanced manifestations are usually caused by deep-vein disease (p.2180).

Secondary deep-venous insufficiency most often follows deep-vein thrombosis (post-thrombotic syndrome): valve leaflets become thickened and contracted, losing the ability to prevent retrograde flow, and the vein wall becomes rigid and thick-walled (p.2180).
Lipodermatosclerosis is the combination of induration, hemosiderin deposition, and inflammation, typically in the lower leg just above the ankle (the gaiter area) (p.2180).
Atrophie blanche is a white patch of scar tissue, often with focal telangiectasias and a hyperpigmented border, usually developing near the medial malleolus (p.2180).
A venous ulcer is typically shallow with an irregular border, a base of granulation tissue, and exudate, and occurs near the medial and lateral malleoli (p.2180).
Venous edema is usually pitting early on, but over time may become less pitting and more indurated, particularly with secondary development of lymphatic dysfunction (phlebolymphedema) (p.2180).

Lymphedema is generally a painless condition; it initially involves the foot and progresses up the leg, with early soft pitting edema that later becomes nonpitting with a woody, indurated, fibrotic texture (p.2183-2184).
Stemmer's sign (inability to tent the skin at the base of the toes) and peau d'orange (orange-peel dimpling), along with squaring of the toes, are characteristic skin findings of lymphedema (p.2184).

Lymphedema is often confused with chronic venous insufficiency, and the two can coexist as phlebolymphedema when venous insufficiency impairs lymphatic function - do not assume a single cause (p.2180).
Distinguish bilateral venous edema and lymphedema from systemic causes (heart failure, hypoalbuminemia, myxedema, drug-induced edema) before attributing swelling to venous disease (p.2180).
Distinguish unilateral leg swelling of chronic venous insufficiency/lymphedema from acute deep-vein thrombosis - the duration of edema helps differentiate them (p.2180, 2183).
Compression garments improve symptoms and aid ulcer healing but are NOT curative and do NOT prevent progression of varicose veins (p.2181).
Antibiotics are NOT indicated for a venous ulcer unless it is infected (p.2181).
Diuretics are contraindicated in lymphedema - they may cause intravascular volume depletion and metabolic abnormalities (p.2184).
No drugs are FDA-approved for chronic venous insufficiency, and there is insufficient evidence to recommend general use of venoactive herbal supplements (p.2182).

Approximately 20% of patients with chronic venous insufficiency develop venous ulcers. Recurrent varicose veins occur in up to 50% of patients by 5 years after ligation and stripping. Endovenous thermal ablation achieves 1- and 5-year occlusion rates exceeding ~90%; sclerotherapy averages ~81% and ~74% at 1 and 5 years. Iliac venous stenting has technical success >85% with long-term patency ~75%; venous bypass long-term patency generally exceeds 60%. Lymphedema is a chronic, generally progressive condition; failure to control limb edema may lead to recurrent infections, progressive trophic skin changes, and rarely the highly lethal complication of lymphangiosarcoma (p.2179, 2182-2184).

Etiologic: Ep primary, Es secondary (Esi intravenous, Ese extravenous), Ec congenital, En none identified. Anatomic: As superficial, Ap perforator, Ad deep, An none. Chronic, repeated hepatocellular injury (toxic, viral, immune, metabolic, cholestatic, or congestive) drives Kupffer cell activation and release of profibrogenic cytokines that activate hepatic stellate cells, producing excess collagen and extracellular matrix. Connective tissue links portal triads to central veins, hepatocytes are lost, and regenerative nodules form, so the liver contracts and loses normal architecture - a process taking years to decades. The resulting distorted vasculature raises intrahepatic resistance, which together with splanchnic arterial vasodilation (driven by mediators such as nitric oxide) produces portal hypertension. Splanchnic vasodilation causes effective arterial underfilling, activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone and sympathetic systems, leading to renal sodium and water retention, plasma volume expansion, and a hyperdynamic circulation; combined with low oncotic pressure from hypoalbuminemia, this generates ascites and edema. Portosystemic shunting plus reduced hepatic mass allows gut-derived neurotoxins (ammonia, false neurotransmitters, mercaptans) to reach the brain and cause encephalopathy (p.2708, p.2713-2717).

Cirrhosis is the end stage of many chronic liver injuries: progressive fibrosis disrupts normal architecture and replaces hepatocytes with regenerative nodules; the main etiologic groups are alcohol-associated, chronic viral hepatitis B/C, biliary, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH, formerly NASH), and miscellaneous (cardiac, cryptogenic) (p.2708).

In hepatic encephalopathy ammonia is usually elevated, but its level correlates poorly with disease severity, so most hepatologists do not rely on ammonia to diagnose or follow the condition; asterixis (liver flap) is a key bedside sign (p.2716-2717).

Standard PT/INR do not reliably measure clotting capacity in cirrhosis because both pro- and anticoagulant factor synthesis fall (rebalanced hemostasis); adequate thrombin generation occurs at platelet counts above ~50,000-60,000/L (p.2717).

Acute-on-chronic liver failure is acute decompensation of cirrhosis with failure of one or more organ systems, behaves like a sepsis-type systemic inflammatory syndrome, and carries 28-day mortality of roughly 20-70% rising with the number of organ failures (p.2717).
Alcohol-associated cirrhosis is classically micronodular (nodules <3 mm); with abstinence larger nodules may form, giving a mixed micronodular/macronodular pattern (p.2708).
In alcohol-related liver disease the AST is typically higher than the ALT, usually in roughly a 2:1 ratio, and aminotransferases are generally <400 IU/mL (p.2708-2709).

Stigmata of chronic liver disease include scleral icterus, palmar erythema, spider angiomas, parotid enlargement, digital clubbing, muscle wasting, and in men decreased body hair, gynecomastia and testicular atrophy; these are often reversible with abstinence (p.2710).

Portal hypertension is defined as a hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) >5 mmHg; clinically significant portal hypertension is an HVPG >=10 mmHg, carrying substantial risk of decompensation (variceal bleeding, ascites, encephalopathy) (p.2713).

A serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) >=1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension as the cause of ascites; cardiac ascites also shows SAAG >=1.1 g/dL but with ascitic protein >2.5 g/dL, whereas SAAG <1.1 g/dL points to infectious or malignant causes (p.2715).
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is diagnosed when the ascitic absolute neutrophil count is >250/uL; ascitic protein <1.5 g/dL marks patients at higher risk for SBP (p.2715-2716).
Most common SBP organisms are Escherichia coli and other gut flora; growth of more than two organisms should raise suspicion for secondary peritonitis from a perforated viscus (p.2716).
Hepatorenal syndrome is functional renal failure without renal histopathology; HRS-AKI (old type 1) is rapidly progressive while HRS-CKD (old type 2) is more stable with a better prognosis (p.2716).

Severity and bleeding risk are stratified by Child-Pugh class and MELD score. Once clinically significant portal hypertension leads to decompensation, median survival is under 2 years. Less than half of patients survive 2 years after the onset of ascites. Patients with complicated cirrhosis who keep drinking have under 50% 5-year survival, whereas abstinence markedly improves outlook. Development of encephalopathy is a poor prognostic sign, and HRS (AKI or CKD type) carries a poor prognosis without transplantation. ACLF 28-day mortality ranges from roughly 20-70%, rising with the number of failing organs. Liver transplantation is the definitive option for end-stage disease and can reverse HRS (p.2709, p.2713, p.2715-2717).
Variceal hemorrhage - immediately life-threatening, with about 20-30% mortality per bleeding episode
New or worsening hepatic encephalopathy, especially with violent agitation or progressive obtundation
Rapidly rising creatinine in a patient with tense ascites suggesting HRS-AKI
Fever, abdominal pain, altered mental status or new AKI in a patient with ascites suggesting SBP
Acute-on-chronic liver failure with multiorgan failure
Refractory ascites failing maximal diuretics

Compensated cirrhosis (HVPG 5-10 mmHg) may be asymptomatic for >=10 years; clinically significant portal hypertension is HVPG >=10 mmHg. Decompensation is marked by variceal bleeding, ascites, or encephalopathy. Overall severity is graded by Child-Pugh class and MELD score, which also predict variceal bleeding risk and guide transplant prioritization. Acute kidney injury is defined as a creatinine rise of 0.3 mg/dL over 48 h or a 50% rise from baseline; SBP is defined by ascitic neutrophils >250/uL (p.2713, p.2715-2716).

chunks.text: CKD results from two overlapping processes: (1) initiating mechanisms specific to the underlying cause (developmental/genetic, immune-complex, inflammatory, metabolic, microvascular, or toxic injury to vascular, glomerular, or tubulointerstitial compartments), and (2) a nonspecific final common pathway in which loss of nephron mass triggers compensatory hyperfiltration and hypertrophy of remaining nephrons. Intrarenal renin-angiotensin activation with blunted tubuloglomerular feedback raises intraglomerular pressure; this adaptation becomes maladaptive, distorting glomerular architecture, impairing podocyte function and the filtration barrier, and producing progressive sclerosis and nephron dropout. The uremic syndrome arises from three spheres of dysfunction: accumulation of retained solutes (urea and creatinine are only readily-measured but incomplete surrogates for many retained toxins), loss of non-excretory kidney functions (fluid/electrolyte homeostasis, hormone production/regulation - EPO, calcitriol, with altered PTH, FGF-23, insulin), and progressive systemic inflammation (elevated CRP, falling albumin/fetuin) feeding a malnutrition-inflammation-atherosclerosis/calcification syndrome (p.2385-2389).

Cardiomyopathy reflects intrinsic disease of the myocardium producing characteristic structural and functional abnormalities. In HCM, abnormal myocyte/sarcomere biology drives increased wall thickness with preserved or supranormal systolic function but impaired filling. In DCM, the ventricle dilates with depressed systolic function (low LVEF). In RCM, the dominant abnormality is impaired ventricular filling from a stiff myocardium causing markedly elevated filling pressures and atrial enlargement, often with relatively preserved EF. Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy involves fibrofatty or fibrotic remodeling that creates a substrate for ventricular arrhythmias with variable RV and/or LV structural change. An expanding catalog of pathogenic genetic variants underlies heritable cardiomyopathy, and inherited differences in immune-response pathways contribute to infectious and noninfectious inflammation that can manifest as myocarditis and cardiomyopathy. Clinical disease often requires a second acquired insult superimposed on a genetic predisposition.

Cardiomyopathy denotes primary disease of the heart muscle itself; strictly it excludes myocardial dysfunction secondary to other cardiovascular disease, though common usage also folds in ischemic, valvular, and hypertensive cardiomyopathy.
Clinical expression frequently follows a two-hit model in which an inherited predisposition is triggered by an acquired insult such as infection, toxic exposure, pregnancy, or tachycardia.

Echocardiography is the initial imaging modality; cardiac MRI adds tissue characterization, with late gadolinium enhancement mapping fibrosis and T1/T2 mapping identifying focal and diffuse inflammation.

Left ventricular noncompaction is a trait (often assessed by a noncompacted-to-compacted myocardium ratio above 2.3) that can accompany HCM, DCM, dystrophies, and syndromes, but can also appear in normal hearts, in pregnancy, and more often in athletes.
The traditional morphologic scheme recognizes three major phenotypes: hypertrophic (HCM), dilated (DCM), and restrictive (RCM) cardiomyopathy.

HCM is characterized by increased left ventricular wall thickness (roughly 13-15 mm depending on context) with a normal or high ejection fraction; LV chamber volume is normal or smaller, and EF is usually above 0.60.

DCM is defined when LVEF is at or below 0.50, although most patients present clinically with LVEF at or below 0.40; an LVEF persistently at or below 0.30-0.35 is the threshold considered for primary-prevention ICD.

RCM is the least common phenotype and is defined more by physiology (moderate-to-severe diastolic dysfunction and/or elevated cardiac filling pressures) than by morphology; wall thickness is often increased but may appear normal, EF is usually only mildly reduced, and marked atrial enlargement with predominant right heart failure is typical.

Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC, originally arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia) is a fourth, predominantly genetic phenotype marked by life-threatening arrhythmias and abnormal RV structure/function with variable LV involvement.

Evolving genotype-driven terminology reframes arrhythmogenic disease as ACM-RV (RV-predominant, formerly ARVC), ACM-LV (LV-predominant), and biventricular arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy; in ACM-LV ventricular arrhythmias can dominate before LVEF is severely reduced, so primary-prevention ICD may be considered even with LVEF above 0.35.

Phenotypes overlap and shift over time: DCM can undergo reverse remodeling toward higher EF and smaller ventricles with recommended therapy, and about 5% of HCM evolves to a reduced-EF, more restrictive state (HCM-rEF).
Mid-range LVEF (0.40-0.50) commonly represents a transition state, either deterioration from early DCM or improvement into DCM remission.

Treating 'congestive heart failure' as a diagnosis or etiology; it is a nonspecific congestion syndrome common to many cardiac conditions (including congenital heart disease, primary pulmonary hypertension, and valve disease) and requires full etiologic evaluation.
Over-relying on morphologic phenotype, since phenotypes overlap and shift over time and many entities (sarcomeric variants, storage diseases) can present as either HCM or RCM.
Missing amyloidosis in older patients, where it can both cause RCM and mimic the asymmetric septal thickening of HCM.
Misclassifying sarcoidosis as restrictive when it more often produces DCM-pattern, regional wall-motion abnormalities, or RV involvement with arrhythmias.
Failing to distinguish PVC-related cardiomyopathy from a genetic arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy that itself causes both the arrhythmias and the muscle disease.
Interpreting LV noncompaction as inherently pathologic, since it can occur in normal hearts, in pregnancy, and in athletes.

Prognosis depends on the specific phenotype and underlying cause rather than on classification alone. DCM may improve substantially with reverse remodeling on guideline-directed therapy, whereas about 5% of HCM deteriorates to a reduced-EF, restrictive state. Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy carries a risk of life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias that can precede heart failure. Persistent severe LV systolic dysfunction (LVEF at or below 0.30-0.35) identifies patients considered for primary-prevention ICD.
Ventricular tachyarrhythmias or nonsustained VT, which may dominate before EF is severely reduced in arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy

Progressive exertional breathlessness, fatigue, orthopnea, edema, and abdominal symptoms indicating the congestion syndrome

Morphologic/functional classification: Hypertrophic (HCM) - septal thickness >=15 mm in men, >=13 mm in women (13-14 mm may suffice in relatives of a proband or with a positive genetic test), LVEF normal or high (usually >0.60), normal/small LV volume. Dilated (DCM) - early: LVEF <=0.50 and/or LV end-diastolic volume >112% of normal for age/sex or LVEDD >95th percentile; LVEF <=0.40 is the threshold for traditionally recommended heart-failure therapy; persistent LVEF <=0.30-0.35 is the threshold for primary-prevention ICD. Restrictive (RCM) - functional diagnosis based on moderate-to-severe diastolic dysfunction and/or elevated filling pressures, usually mildly reduced LVEF, with marked atrial enlargement. Mid-range LVEF (0.40-0.50) represents a transition zone. Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy - ACM-LV (usually DCM morphology), ACM-RV/ARVC (2010 modified task force criteria combining major and minor criteria), and biventricular forms. LV noncompaction trait assessed by noncompacted/compacted ratio >2.3.

Plasma coagulation factor deficiencies impair secondary hemostasis (the coagulation cascade). Inherited hemophilia A and B are X-linked recessive disorders from mutations in F8 and F9 respectively; affected males bleed while carrier women are generally asymptomatic, although a wide range of factor activity from random X-inactivation (lyonization) can produce bleeding in some carriers. FVIII has a very short intrinsic circulating half-life (~25-30 min) that is extended to roughly 12 h when complexed with von Willebrand factor (VWF). VWD reflects quantitative or qualitative defects of VWF, which serves both as the adhesion molecule tethering platelets to exposed subendothelium (function dependent on large VWF multimers) and as the FVIII carrier; loss of high-molecular-weight multimers (e.g., via excessive ADAMTS13 cleavage in type 2A/2B, or shear-induced unfolding) impairs platelet adhesion. Acquired deficiencies (liver disease, DIC, vitamin K deficiency) usually involve multiple factors and perturb both primary (platelet/vessel wall) and secondary (coagulation) hemostasis. (Harrison 22e p.926-930)

The most common inherited factor deficiencies are the hemophilias, X-linked recessive diseases due to deficiency of factor VIII (hemophilia A, ~80% of cases) or factor IX (hemophilia B); hemophilia A and B are clinically indistinguishable (Harrison 22e p.928, 930).

Acquired coagulation factor deficiencies are more frequent than congenital disorders; the most common are the hemorrhagic diathesis of liver disease, DIC, and vitamin K deficiency, each typically involving more than one clotting factor (Harrison 22e p.928).

Disease phenotype correlates with factor activity level: severe (<1%), moderate (1-5%), mild (6-30%). Severe and moderate disease cause bleeding into joints (hemarthrosis), soft tissues, and muscles after minor trauma or spontaneously; mild disease bleeds infrequently and usually only after trauma (Harrison 22e p.930).

Recurrent hemarthroses (knees, elbows, ankles, shoulders, hips) damage a joint to create a chronically affected 'target joint' with synovitis and progressive deformity; deep-muscle hematomas can cause compartment syndrome by compressing arteries, veins, or nerves (Harrison 22e p.930).

Von Willebrand disease (VWD) is the most common inherited bleeding disorder (symptomatic prevalence ~1 in 1000 to 1 in 10,000); VWF tethers platelets to subendothelium and is the carrier protein that prolongs the FVIII half-life (Harrison 22e p.927).

Most VWD symptoms are 'platelet-like' (mucocutaneous: bruising, epistaxis, heavy menstrual bleeding); type 1 (parallel reduction in VWF protein, function, and FVIII) is most common (>=80% of cases) (Harrison 22e p.926-927).
Type 2N VWD ('autosomal hemophilia') is caused by VWF variants that impair FVIII binding, markedly shortening the FVIII half-life and lowering FVIII levels (Harrison 22e p.927).

Screening hemostasis tests: an isolated prolonged PT suggests FVII deficiency; a prolonged aPTT indicates an intrinsic-pathway deficiency, most commonly FVIII, FIX, or FXI; prolongation of both PT and aPTT suggests deficiency of FV, FX, FII, or a fibrinogen abnormality (Harrison 22e p.928).

Mixing study principle: adding normal pooled plasma corrects a prolonged PT/aPTT due to a factor deficiency but fails to correct when an inhibitor (antibody) is present; if it corrects, individual factor activity assays identify the deficient factor (Harrison 22e p.928).

Inhibitor (alloantibody) formation is the major complication of hemophilia treatment, with prevalence ~30% in severe hemophilia A, ~10% in nonsevere hemophilia A, and only 3-5% in hemophilia B; inhibitors increase morbidity and mortality (Harrison 22e p.930-931).

FXII (Hageman factor), high-molecular-weight kininogen, and prekallikrein deficiencies markedly prolong the aPTT but do NOT cause bleeding (no bleeding phenotype; treatment is not indicated) — do not treat the lab abnormality (Harrison 22e p.928).

Not all patients with low VWF levels bleed; mildly decreased VWF should be diagnosed as VWD only with bleeding symptoms and/or a family history, and type O blood physiologically lowers VWF (overlapping the diagnostic range) (Harrison 22e p.926-927).

Bleeding phenotype does not always correlate with factor activity in FXI deficiency, and a negative bleeding history with prior procedures does NOT exclude increased hemorrhage risk (Harrison 22e p.931-932).
Family history of hemophilia is absent in ~30% of cases (de novo mutations), so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.930).
Antifibrinolytic drugs are NOT indicated for hematuria because of the risk of an occlusive clot obstructing the genitourinary tract (Harrison 22e p.931).

Without treatment severe hemophilia may limit life expectancy; with modern recombinant factor concentrates, prophylaxis, and viral-inactivated products, life expectancy of severe hemophilia is now only ~10 years shorter than the general male population and near normal in mild/moderate disease. Since 1998 no new viral hepatitis or HIV infections have been reported in hemophilia patients, though aging patients carry burdens of arthropathy, chronic pain, and prior HCV/HIV infection (hepatocellular carcinoma is the most common cause of death in HIV-negative patients). TTP-related microangiopathy and inhibitors worsen prognosis when present. (Harrison 22e p.930-932)
Bleeding into the oropharyngeal spaces, central nervous system, or retroperitoneum is life-threatening and requires immediate therapy (Harrison 22e p.930)
Retroperitoneal hemorrhage may form a calcified inflammatory mass (pseudotumor syndrome) and damage the femoral nerve; pseudotumors can also form in long bones (Harrison 22e p.930)
Deep-muscle hematomas of the distal limbs can cause compartment syndrome from external compression of arteries, veins, or nerves (Harrison 22e p.930)
Failure to respond to factor replacement at therapeutic doses suggests an inhibitor; early detection is critical (Harrison 22e p.930)
In carriers/women, postpartum hemorrhage risk rises after delivery as the pregnancy-induced rise in clotting factor levels falls rapidly (Harrison 22e p.931)

A discrete or long-segment narrowing of the aortic lumen creates a mechanical obstruction to systemic outflow. Proximal to the obstruction, pressure rises, producing upper-body hypertension and left ventricular pressure overload; distal to it, perfusion pressure falls, causing weak lower-body pulses. In severe neonatal coarctation, lower-body perfusion depends on right-to-left flow through the ductus arteriosus, so ductal closure precipitates hypoperfusion, metabolic acidosis, and circulatory collapse. In slowly progressive disease, collateral arterial channels develop to bypass the obstruction.
A narrowing of the aorta, most often just distal to the left subclavian artery near the ductal region, obstructing flow to the lower body.
The hallmark examination finding is diminished, delayed, or absent femoral pulses compared with the upper limbs, with a blood pressure gradient higher in the arms than the legs.
Severe coarctation may be duct-dependent in the neonate: as the ductus arteriosus closes, lower-body perfusion falls, producing shock, acidosis, and heart failure.
A prostaglandin infusion is used to reopen or maintain ductal patency and restore lower-body perfusion while stabilising a critically ill neonate before repair.
Older children may be asymptomatic and present with an incidentally found murmur, upper-limb hypertension, headaches, or leg claudication.
Coarctation is commonly associated with a bicuspid aortic valve and may occur with other left-sided obstructive lesions and Turner syndrome.
Chest radiograph in older children can show rib notching from collateral vessels and a figure-3 aortic contour.
Echocardiography defines the site and severity of narrowing and associated lesions; CT or MR angiography is useful for detailed anatomy.
Repair by surgery or catheter intervention relieves the obstruction, but lifelong follow-up is needed for recoarctation and persistent hypertension.
