Psychostimulants increase synaptic monoamines. Cocaine binds the dopamine transporter and blocks reuptake of dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin, raising their levels centrally and peripherally; repeated exposure induces long-term neuronal changes including adaptations in glutamate-releasing neurons. Methamphetamine, a cationic lipophilic molecule structurally similar to monoamine transporters, reverses transporter function to dump newly synthesized catecholamines from storage vesicles into the synapse and also inhibits monoamine oxidase, attenuating monoamine metabolism; it is more potent than amphetamine with greater nerve-terminal toxicity. MDMA acts predominantly on serotonin transporters to release serotonin (and norepinephrine/dopamine) and can damage serotonergic nerve endings. Cathinone (from khat) increases dopamine release and reduces its reuptake. Classic hallucinogens disrupt serotonin (affecting mood, perception, sleep, appetite, temperature, sexual behavior, muscle control) and glutamate (affecting pain perception, environmental responses, emotion, learning/memory). The sympathomimetic surge drives the cardiovascular, neurologic, pulmonary, renal, and hyperthermic complications.

Cocaine blocks reuptake at the dopamine transporter, raising synaptic dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin in both CNS and PNS; this monoaminergic excess underlies its euphoric and sympathomimetic effects.

Psychostimulant withdrawal features hypersomnia, increased appetite, and depressed mood; acute withdrawal lasts ~7-10 days but residual symptoms may persist for months. Conditioned (cue-triggered) craving, not physical withdrawal, is considered the primary driver of ongoing use.

Stimulant use disorder is diagnosed by DSM-5 when at least 2 of 11 criteria occur within 12 months; for hallucinogen use disorder only the first 10 criteria apply because the withdrawal criterion does not apply (use is typically not chronic).

Adulterants are a major and underappreciated hazard: cocaine/methamphetamine are increasingly cut with fentanyl-related opioids (overdose deaths), levamisole (agranulocytosis, leukoencephalopathy, cutaneous vasculitis with skin necrosis), clenbuterol (tachycardia, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia), and xylazine (sedation, necrotic soft-tissue lesions).

Smoked or vaporized cocaine (freebase/crack) reaches the brain almost as fast as the IV route because of the large pulmonary vasculature, producing a rapid, intense, transient high that increases addictive potential.

Acute psychostimulant intoxication produces a uniform syndrome regardless of agent: euphoria, increased energy, reduced need for sleep, decreased appetite, heightened alertness, increased libido, plus peripheral tremor, diaphoresis, hypertonia, tachypnea, hyperreflexia, and hyperthermia.

Many psychostimulant effects are biphasic: low doses improve psychomotor performance and increase vagal tone (lowering heart rate), whereas high doses cause tremor/convulsions and raise heart rate and blood pressure.
Combining cocaine with alcohol generates the metabolite cocaethylene, whose cardiovascular toxicity is additive to cocaine's, intensifying pathophysiologic harm.

Methamphetamine is more potent than amphetamine, producing higher synaptic dopamine and greater nerve-terminal toxicity; the dextrorotatory (d-) enantiomer has 3-5 times the CNS activity of the l-form, and smoked bioavailability (~90%) far exceeds oral (~67%).

MDMA acts mainly on serotonin transporters, increasing release of serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine; animal data show moderate-to-high doses can cause loss of serotonergic nerve endings and permanent damage.

Classic (serotonergic) hallucinogens such as LSD, psilocybin, mescaline/peyote, DMT, and ayahuasca disrupt serotonin and glutamate signaling; oral onset is ~20-90 min with duration up to 6-12 h (salvia ~30 min).

Dissociative agents (PCP, ketamine, high-dose dextromethorphan, salvia) distort perception of time, motion, color, sound, and self and can cause respiratory depression, heart-rate abnormalities, and a withdrawal syndrome with craving, confusion, headache, and sweating.

Beta blockers should generally be avoided in cocaine users because unopposed alpha-adrenergic stimulation from beta blockade may cause coronary vasoconstriction, ischemia, and infarction; if essential, mixed alpha/beta agents (e.g., labetalol, carvedilol) are preferred over nonselective beta blockers.
Succinylcholine is relatively contraindicated for rapid-sequence intubation in cocaine use; a nondepolarizing agent (e.g., rocuronium) is the alternative.
Before treating psychomotor agitation, hypoglycemia and hypoxemia must be ruled out first.
Drugs sold as 'Molly'/MDMA frequently contain methylone, ethylone, or other synthetic cathinones rather than MDMA, so the reported drug may not match the actual exposure.
Emerging/new psychoactive substances are often missed on standard drug tests, so a negative screen does not exclude intoxication.
Fentanyl, xylazine, levamisole, and other adulterants can produce effects (and overdose) not anticipated from the intended drug.
MDMA, LSD, and psilocybin remain Schedule I in the United States despite FDA breakthrough-therapy designations; investigational use does not equal approved therapy.

Acute overdose is a medical emergency that can be fatal through cerebral hemorrhage/infarction, cardiac arrhythmia or ischemia, respiratory failure, hyperthermia, or rhabdomyolysis, and management is largely supportive in an ICU/telemetry setting. Co-ingestion of other drugs (especially opioids) markedly increases morbidity and mortality, and overdose deaths involving cocaine and psychostimulants have risen sharply (cocaine-related overdose deaths more than quintupled from 2011 to 2022; psychostimulant-involved deaths reached ~36,000 in 2023). Early abstinence is frequently complicated by depression, guilt, insomnia, and anorexia that can be as severe as a major affective disorder and may persist for months to years. Contingency management has robust evidence of efficacy for stimulant use disorder with benefit lasting up to 2 years after treatment ends; no FDA-approved pharmacotherapy exists for stimulant or hallucinogen addiction. Chronic hallucinogen/dissociative use can leave persistent psychosis, memory loss, anxiety, depression, suicidal ideation, and flashbacks lasting a year or more.
Severe psychomotor agitation, hypertension, tachycardia, headache, and mydriasis indicating sympathetic overactivity / overdose
Hyperthermia (goal to cool to core temperature <39 C within 30 min)
Seizures, coma, or focal neurologic signs
Intracranial hemorrhage or cerebral infarction
Chest pain, cardiac ischemia/arrhythmia, left ventricular dysfunction, aortic dissection/rupture
Respiratory failure, airway burns or bronchospasm from inhaled crack ('crack lung')
Rhabdomyolysis with metabolic acidosis / renal infarction
Concurrent opioid co-ingestion (e.g., fentanyl-adulterated cocaine) precipitating fatal overdose
'Bad trip' with panic, paranoia, or psychosis (hallucinogens), which may persist up to 24 h

No single graded severity scale; DSM-5 stimulant use disorder severity is rated mild (2-3 criteria), moderate (4-5), or severe (>=6) of 11 criteria over 12 months. Acute clinical severity ranges from intoxication to life-threatening overdose marked by sympathetic overactivity (agitation, hypertension, tachycardia), hyperthermia, seizures, intracranial or cardiac events, respiratory failure, and rhabdomyolysis. Complications of psychostimulant use are catalogued in Table 468-1 across cardiovascular, CNS/PNS, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, renal, endocrine, and other organ systems.

Cocaine, Other Psychostimulants, and Hallucinogens (non-infective) — Neurologic / Substance Use (Toxicology) Also: Cocaine intoxication, Methamphetamine use disorder, Stimulant use disorder, MDMA (ecstasy/Molly), Cathinone / bath salts, Hallucinogen use disorder, LSD / PCP / psilocybin / ketamine
Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (primary pulmonary coccidioidomycosis is often misdiagnosed as this) (Harrison 22e p.1697)
Pulmonary malignancy (coccidioidal nodules are difficult to distinguish radiographically and, like malignancies, may enhance on PET) (Harrison 22e p.1697)
Histoplasmosis (can cause false-positive coccidioidal antigen results) (Harrison 22e p.1698)
Blastomycosis (can cause false-positive coccidioidal antigen results) (Harrison 22e p.1698)
Tuberculosis / other chronic granulomatous pulmonary infections (upper lobe infiltrate, cavities, hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy mimic) (Harrison 22e p.1697)
EIA for IgM and IgG antibodies (recommended for initial diagnosis) (Harrison 22e p.1698)
Confirmatory immunodiffusion (IDTP/IDCF) or traditional tube-precipitin and complement-fixation assays with CF titer (CF titer is an important prognostic tool) (Harrison 22e p.1698)
Culture of sputum/respiratory fluids and tissue (grows within 3-7 days at 37 degrees C on artificial media including blood agar) (Harrison 22e p.1698)
Direct microscopy of respiratory specimens (Papanicolaou, Gomori methenamine silver, or calcofluor white) or fixed tissue (H&E or GMS) for spherules (Harrison 22e p.1698)
Coccidioidal antigen test (antigenuria/antigenemia), including CSF assay in suspected meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1698)
CSF examination in suspected meningitis (lymphocytic pleocytosis, profound hypoglycorrhachia, elevated protein, occasional CSF eosinophilia; CF antibody in CSF) (Harrison 22e p.1697)
MRI with gadolinium in meningitis (frequently shows basilar meningeal enhancement; dilated ventricles indicate hydrocephalus) (Harrison 22e p.1697)
Chest imaging/CT for nodules and cavities (multiple nodules and microsatellite lesions favor coccidioidomycosis over malignancy) (Harrison 22e p.1697)
Pulmonary malignancy (solitary or multiple nodules, PET-avid, may require biopsy to distinguish) (Harrison 22e p.1697)

Coccidioides exists as filamentous mold (mycelia) in the environment, producing barrel-shaped airborne spores (arthroconidia, ~2 x 5 microns) that, when inhaled, are small enough to evade mucosal defenses and reach deep into the bronchial tree to initiate infection. Within the host, arthroconidia enlarge into spherules (up to 200 microns, unique to Coccidioides) containing endospores; spherules rupture and release endospores that form new spherules, propagating infection locally. A robust cellular immune response is critical to host control: resolved pulmonary infection shows necrotizing granulomas containing spherules, whereas uncontrolled disseminated disease shows poorly formed or absent granulomas and a polymorphonuclear leukocyte response. In persons with protective cellular immunity, spherules may persist in the lungs for prolonged periods (possibly lifelong) in a latent state, conferring protective immunity but creating a risk of recurrent active disease if that immunity wanes (Harrison 22e p.1696-1697).

Caused by dimorphic soil-dwelling fungi of the genus Coccidioides (C. immitis and C. posadasii), which are clinically indistinguishable; infection follows inhalation of airborne arthroconidia (Harrison 22e p.1696).

A commercial coccidioidal antigen test (antigenuria/antigenemia) is useful in immunosuppressed patients with severe or disseminated disease and when assaying CSF in suspected meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1698).

Coccidioidal meningitis is the most dire disseminated syndrome and is uniformly fatal if untreated; patients present with a persistent dull headache often with lethargy and confusion, and nuchal rigidity, if present, is not severe (Harrison 22e p.1697).

Endemic to the Western Hemisphere between 40 degrees N and 40 degrees S; areas of high endemicity in the US include the southern San Joaquin Valley of California (hence 'Valley fever') and south-central Arizona, with other foci across the southwestern US, northern Mexico, Central America, and parts of South America (Harrison 22e p.1696).

In endemic areas most human cases occur without obvious soil or dust exposure; periods of aridity following rainy seasons are associated with increases in symptomatic infections (Harrison 22e p.1696).

After infection, 60% of individuals are completely asymptomatic; the other 40% have symptoms related primarily to pulmonary infection (fever, cough, pleuritic chest pain) appearing several days to up to 3 weeks after inhalation, with risk of symptomatic illness increasing with age (Harrison 22e p.1697).

Immunologic manifestations of primary pulmonary disease include cutaneous reactions: a diffuse erythematous maculopapular rash ('toxic erythema'), erythema nodosum (typically over the lower extremities), erythema multiforme (often in a necklace distribution), and Sweet syndrome lesions; cutaneous manifestations are especially common in women (Harrison 22e p.1697).
Symmetrical arthralgias ('desert rheumatism'), often involving the ankles, knees, and hips, may occur with or without cutaneous manifestations (Harrison 22e p.1697).

Serology is the most common diagnostic method; EIA for IgM and IgG is recommended for initial diagnosis, with positive results confirmed by immunodiffusion (IDTP/IDCF) or traditional tube-precipitin and complement-fixation assays (Harrison 22e p.1697).

Rising complement-fixation (CF) titers reflect fungal growth and correlate with clinical progression; high CF titers (e.g., 1:32 or greater) suggest unrestrained fungal growth and the possibility of extrathoracic dissemination, while CF antibody in CSF is indicative of coccidioidal meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1698).

Spherules (up to 200 microns) are unique to Coccidioides and can be demonstrated in respiratory specimens after Papanicolaou, Gomori methenamine silver, or calcofluor white staining, or in fixed tissue with hematoxylin-eosin or Gomori methenamine silver (Harrison 22e p.1698).

Primary pulmonary coccidioidomycosis is often misdiagnosed as community-acquired bacterial pneumonia; rash, symmetrical arthralgias, night sweats, marked fatigue, peripheral-blood eosinophilia, failure to improve with antibacterial therapy, or upper lobe infiltrate / hilar or mediastinal adenopathy should suggest the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1697).
Coccidioides poses a significant laboratory hazard if inadvertently inhaled; the clinical laboratory should always be alerted to the possibility of this diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1698).
Coccidioidal pulmonary nodules can be difficult to distinguish radiographically from malignancy and, like malignancies, often enhance on PET; biopsy may be required (Harrison 22e p.1697).
The IgM EIA in particular is occasionally falsely positive; results should be interpreted cautiously when screening asymptomatic individuals (Harrison 22e p.1698).
The EIA IgG optical density does not correlate with the IDCF/traditional CF titer and should not be used as a surrogate for a titer (Harrison 22e p.1698).
Coccidioidal antigen testing may yield false-positive results in histoplasmosis or blastomycosis (Harrison 22e p.1698).
The fungus is isolated from CSF in fewer than one-third of meningitis cases, so a negative CSF culture does not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1697).
Potassium hydroxide preparation of sputum is rarely fruitful for identifying Coccidioides (Harrison 22e p.1698).
PCR genomic detection does not appear to be more sensitive than culture, though it can be more rapid (Harrison 22e p.1698).

In most patients, primary pulmonary coccidioidomycosis resolves without sequelae over several weeks. Clinical dissemination occurs in approximately 1% of infected individuals and, when it occurs, is usually evident within the first 6 months after primary infection. Coccidioidal meningitis is uniformly fatal if untreated; even with treatment, relapse is common after stopping therapy. Antibodies disappear over time in persons whose illness resolves, but the presence of coccidioidal antibodies in serum does not indicate immunity or control of infection (Harrison 22e p.1696-1698).

Disseminated disease (occurs in approximately 1% of infections; defined as fungus found outside the thoracic cavity), more likely in male patients, those of African and perhaps Filipino ancestry, and persons with depressed cellular immunity (Harrison 22e p.1697)

Coccidioidal meningitis: persistent dull headache, lethargy, confusion; uniformly fatal if untreated, may progress to communicating hydrocephalus with declining mental status and gait disturbance (Harrison 22e p.1697)

Immunocompromised hosts at risk for dissemination: HIV-1 infection with CD4 count <250/microL, chronic glucocorticoid therapy, allogeneic solid-organ transplant recipients, and patients on TNF-alpha antagonists or other biological response modifiers (Harrison 22e p.1697)
New coccidioidal infection acquired during the second or third trimester of pregnancy or postpartum (significant risk for disseminated disease) (Harrison 22e p.1697)

Diffuse reticulonodular pneumonia with dyspnea and fever in intense exposure or profoundly suppressed cellular immunity (e.g., untreated HIV with markedly low CD4), associated with unrestrained fungal growth and frequent fungemia (Harrison 22e p.1697)
High serum CF titer (e.g., 1:32 or greater) predicting disease activity and possible extrathoracic dissemination (Harrison 22e p.1698)
Pulmonary cavity rupture into the pleural space causing pyopneumothorax (acute dyspnea, collapsed lung with pleural air-fluid level) (Harrison 22e p.1697)

Clinical presentations and their approximate frequencies (Table 219-1, Harrison 22e p.1698): asymptomatic infection (60%); primary focal pneumonia (40%); diffuse pneumonia (<1%); pulmonary sequelae (~5%: nodule, cavity, chronic pneumonia); and disseminated disease (1% or less, including skin/bone/joint/soft tissue disease and meningitis). High CF titers (e.g., 1:32 or greater) and features such as night sweats >3 weeks, weight loss >10%, CF titer >1:16, and extensive pulmonary involvement indicate greater severity.
Coccidioidomycosis (infective) — Infectious Diseases Also: Valley fever, Coccidioides

chunks.text: A Colles' fracture occurs when a fall onto the dorsiflexed, outstretched hand transmits force through the distal radius, which fails in its metaphyseal cancellous bone. Osteoporosis lowers the threshold for injury, explaining its predominance in postmenopausal women and older adults. The distal fragment tilts and displaces dorsally and radially and impacts proximally, shortening the radius and disrupting the normal volar tilt and radial inclination of the articular surface. Associated soft-tissue swelling or bony displacement may compress the median nerve in the carpal tunnel, and disruption of the distal radioulnar joint or triangular fibrocartilage can affect forearm rotation.

chunks.text: Hemorrhoids or benign anorectal disease as a cause of rectal bleeding (rectal bleeding and altered bowel habits still demand DRE and sigmoidoscopy) (Harrison 22e p.656)
Other causes of iron-deficiency anemia from chronic occult GI blood loss (Harrison 22e p.656)
Inflammatory bowel disease (both a risk factor and a differential for altered bowel habit and bleeding) (Harrison 22e p.655)
Colonoscopy of the entire large bowel (gold standard for detecting cancer and synchronous neoplasms/polyps) (Harrison 22e p.656)
Flexible sigmoidoscopy as a screening modality (Harrison 22e p.655-656)
Stool-based tests: fecal occult blood test, fecal immunochemical test (FIT), and fecal DNA testing (Harrison 22e p.655-656)
Serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) (Harrison 22e p.656)
Complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel (Harrison 22e p.656)
Chest, abdomen, and pelvic CT scan; MRI and PET as dictated by CT findings (Harrison 22e p.656)
Pelvic MRI for rectal cancer to assess mesorectal margin and nodal status (Harrison 22e p.658)
Tumor MMR/microsatellite instability testing (IHC or MSI) and germline genetic testing where indicated (Harrison 22e p.654, 656)
Investigational: plasma circulating tumor DNA as a biomarker for residual/recurrent disease (Harrison 22e p.658)

The majority of colorectal cancers develop through the adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence, in which adenomatous polyps accumulate sequential genetic and epigenetic events involving tumor suppressor genes and oncogenes. Three major sporadic molecular pathways exist: the chromosomal instability (CIN) pathway (the most common), characterized by early loss of the APC tumor suppressor gene followed by sequential MAP-kinase oncogene mutations such as KRAS and BRAF, with loss of p53 as a common final step; the mismatch repair (MMR) pathway, often caused by hypermethylation of MMR gene promoters, producing a microsatellite-instability-high (MSI-high) phenotype; and the CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP), with tumors that are often right-sided and associated with MLH1 methylation. These pathways are not mutually exclusive and can overlap in individual cancers (Harrison 22e p.653-654).

Symptoms vary by tumor location. Right-sided cancers (cecum, ascending colon) can grow large without obstruction because stool is still liquid, and they tend to ulcerate, causing chronic insidious blood loss and presenting as iron-deficiency anemia (Harrison 22e p.656).

Unexplained iron-deficiency anemia in any adult mandates a thorough endoscopic and/or radiographic visualization of the entire large bowel; the possible exception is a premenopausal, multiparous woman (Harrison 22e p.656).

Left-sided (transverse/descending colon) tumors impede passage of more formed stool, producing abdominal cramping, occasional obstruction, and even perforation, classically the annular constricting 'apple-core' lesion on imaging (Harrison 22e p.656).

Rectosigmoid cancers cause hematochezia, tenesmus, and narrowing of stool caliber; these may be mistaken for hemorrhoids, but rectal bleeding and/or altered bowel habits demand prompt digital rectal exam and sigmoidoscopy (Harrison 22e p.656).

Most colorectal cancers arise from adenomatous polyps (not hyperplastic, hamartomatous, or serrated polyps); only a minority of adenomas progress, with risk tied to polyp size and histology, and villous adenomas becoming cancer about threefold more often than tubular adenomas (Harrison 22e p.653).

Universal testing of colorectal tumors for MMR defects is recommended, by immunohistochemistry for MMR proteins or microsatellite instability testing; MSI-high tumors are dramatically sensitive to immune checkpoint inhibition and less sensitive to chemotherapy (Harrison 22e p.653-654, 656).

Serum CEA is used for staging workup and follow-up; some authorities measure plasma CEA at 3-month intervals after curative resection because of its sensitivity as a marker for otherwise undetectable recurrence (Harrison 22e p.656-658).

Liver is the most frequent visceral metastatic site, being the initial site of distant spread in about one-third of recurring cancers and involved in over two-thirds of patients at death; complete resection of metastases isolated to one site (liver, lung, peritoneum) is considered curative (Harrison 22e p.657-658).
Attributing rectal bleeding to hemorrhoids and not pursuing DRE and sigmoidoscopy (Harrison 22e p.656)

Relying on fecal occult blood testing alone: about 50% of patients with documented colorectal cancer have a negative FOBT due to intermittent bleeding, and a colorectal neoplasm is NOT found in most asymptomatic individuals with a positive test (Harrison 22e p.655-656)
Sigmoidoscopy alone misses proximal lesions: about 1.5% of individuals with a normal sigmoidoscopy harbor a high-risk polyp or adenocarcinoma in the proximal colon (Harrison 22e p.656)
Lynch syndrome may not be associated with multiple polyps and is therefore often unrecognized (Harrison 22e p.654)
Disease stage cannot be determined accurately before surgical resection and pathologic analysis unless gross metastatic disease is present (Harrison 22e p.656)

Initial treatment should be delayed until MMR/microsatellite status is known when possible, since MSI-high rectal cancers may be cured with checkpoint inhibitors (PD-1 antibodies) without surgery, radiation, or chemotherapy (Harrison 22e p.656)

Prognosis is stage-related and depends on depth of tumor penetration into the bowel wall, regional lymph node involvement, and distant metastases (TNM). Stage I (T1-2N0M0) confers a high cure rate (>90-95% 5-year survival); 5-year survival declines through stage II (T3-4N0M0), stage III (node-positive), and stage IV (distant metastasis, <5% in colon). Stage I patients are considered cured after complete resection. A minimum of 12 sampled lymph nodes is considered necessary to accurately define stage. Poor-prognosis features include penetration through the bowel wall into pericolic fat, poorly differentiated histology, perforation and/or adherence to adjacent organs, venous invasion, preoperative CEA >5 ng/mL, BRAF mutation, and right-sided primary location. Tumors with MSI/MMR defects have an improved prognosis (enhanced immune response), and left-colon tumors fare better than right-colon tumors. Notably, primary tumor size does not influence prognosis once adjusted for nodal involvement and differentiation. Most recurrences occur within the first 5 years (Harrison 22e p.656-658).
Unexplained iron-deficiency anemia in any adult (mandates evaluation of the entire large bowel)
Change in bowel habit / altered bowel habits
Rectal bleeding (hematochezia) or guaiac-positive stool
Tenesmus and narrowing of the caliber of the stool (rectosigmoid lesions)
Abdominal cramping or obstruction (left-sided lesions)
Strong family history or known hereditary syndrome (FAP, MUTYH-associated polyposis, Lynch syndrome)

TNM classification (American Joint Committee on Cancer / Union for International Cancer Control): T = depth of tumor penetration (T1 submucosa, T2 muscularis, T3 through muscularis, T4 adjacent structures), N = regional lymph node involvement (N1 = 1-3 nodes, N2 = >=4 nodes), M = distant metastasis. Stage I = T1-2N0M0; Stage II = T3-4N0M0; Stage III = any T, N1-2, M0; Stage IV = any T, any N, M1. The older Dukes classification was historically used for colorectal cancer (Harrison 22e p.656).
Colorectal Cancer (non-infective) — Oncology Also: colon cancer, rectal cancer, bowel cancer

chunks.diseaseName: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias
chunks.text: Macroreentrant atrial tachycardia depends on a large anatomic reentry circuit, frequently involving areas of atrial scar with slow conduction. In common (typical) flutter, the wavefront encircles the tricuspid valve annulus, bounded anteriorly by the annulus and posteriorly by the inferior vena cava and Eustachian ridge, passing through the cavotricuspid isthmus between the IVC and tricuspid annulus. The circuit usually rotates counterclockwise as viewed from the ventricular apex; reversed (clockwise) rotation gives reverse typical flutter. AF and typical flutter are mechanistically interrelated: a line of functional block or coalescence of fibrillatory wavelets around barriers such as the crista terminalis and Eustachian valve may convert AF into organized flutter, and conduction-slowing antiarrhythmics promote this reentry. Atypical flutters are macroreentrant circuits not using the cavotricuspid isthmus, almost always associated with atrial scar. MAT arises from triggered automaticity in multiple atrial foci, producing multiple P-wave morphologies (Harrison 22e p.1943-1946).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias
chunks.text: Common (typical) right atrial flutter is a macroreentrant circuit that revolves around the tricuspid valve annulus, passing through the cavotricuspid (sub-Eustachian) isthmus, which is why it is termed cavotricuspid isthmus-dependent flutter and is amenable to interruption at that isthmus (Harrison 22e p.1943).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias
chunks.text: Multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT) is defined by at least three distinct P-wave morphologies with rates typically 100-150 beats/min and is mechanistically attributed to triggered automaticity from multiple atrial foci (Harrison 22e p.1946).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias
chunks.text: Unlike atrial fibrillation, MAT shows clear isoelectric intervals between P waves and a slower atrial rate, helping distinguish the two (Harrison 22e p.1946).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias
chunks.text: MAT is characteristically seen in patients with chronic pulmonary disease during acute illness (Harrison 22e p.1946).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias
chunks.text: Counterclockwise rotation of the typical flutter circuit produces the characteristic negative sawtooth flutter waves in the inferior leads II, III, and aVF and positive flutter (P) waves in V1; clockwise (reverse typical) rotation produces the opposite vectors (Harrison 22e p.1943).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias
chunks.text: The atrial rate in typical flutter is usually 240-300 beats/min but may be slower with atrial disease or antiarrhythmic drugs (Harrison 22e p.1943).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias
chunks.text: Typical flutter often conducts to the ventricle with 2:1 AV block, yielding a regular tachycardia near 140-150 beats/min, where flutter waves can be obscured within the T wave (Harrison 22e p.1943).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias
chunks.text: Maneuvers or AV nodal disease/agents that increase AV block raise the conduction ratio and unmask flutter waves, aiding diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1943).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias
chunks.text: Typical flutter frequently coexists with atrial fibrillation and is associated with atrial scarring from aging or prior cardiac surgery; AF may precede the onset of flutter (Harrison 22e p.1943).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias
chunks.text: Atrial conduction-slowing antiarrhythmics (flecainide, propafenone, amiodarone) can convert a patient's AF presentation into atrial flutter by promoting reentry while suppressing ectopic triggers (Harrison 22e p.1943).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias
chunks.text: Atypical (non-cavotricuspid isthmus-dependent) flutters arise in either atrium, are almost universally tied to atrial scar, and are commonly seen after right atriotomy, extensive left atrial ablation for AF, or mitral valve surgery (Harrison 22e p.1943-1944).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias
chunks.text: Left atrial flutter and perimitral left atrial flutter resemble common flutter clinically but show different P-wave morphologies and can mimic focal atrial tachycardia (Harrison 22e p.1944).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias
chunks.text: In 2:1 conducted flutter, flutter waves hidden in the T wave can be mistaken for another regular narrow-complex tachycardia; failing to use AV-nodal-slowing maneuvers may miss the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1943).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias
chunks.text: Assuming AF and flutter are independent: antiarrhythmics given for AF (e.g., flecainide, propafenone, amiodarone) may unmask or organize the rhythm into flutter (Harrison 22e p.1943).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias
chunks.text: Attempting electrical cardioversion for MAT, which is ineffective for this automatic arrhythmia (Harrison 22e p.1946).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias
chunks.text: Mislabeling atypical/left atrial flutter as focal atrial tachycardia without electrophysiologic confirmation (Harrison 22e p.1944).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias
chunks.text: Assuming MAT carries the same thromboembolic risk as AF or flutter; in MAT this risk remains unclear and is not considered equivalent (Harrison 22e p.1946).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias
chunks.text: Typical flutter is highly treatable, with cavotricuspid isthmus catheter ablation achieving success rates greater than 95% with low complication and recurrence rates; however, up to half of patients undergoing such ablation later develop atrial arrhythmias, most often atrial fibrillation. With antiarrhythmic drug therapy alone, over 70% of patients experience recurrence. MAT prognosis is largely tied to the underlying pulmonary or systemic illness; electrical cardioversion is ineffective for MAT (Harrison 22e p.1944-1946).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias
chunks.text: Hemodynamic instability with rapid ventricular response (may warrant urgent electrical cardioversion)

chunks.diseaseName: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias
chunks.text: Severe symptoms attributable to the arrhythmia

chunks.diseaseName: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias
chunks.text: Difficult-to-control ventricular rate, as rate control in flutter is frequently more challenging than in AF

chunks.diseaseName: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias
chunks.text: Elevated thromboembolic risk by CHA2DS2-VASc requiring attention before rhythm conversion

chunks.diseaseName: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias
chunks.text: No formal severity grading scale; thromboembolic risk in flutter is stratified by the CHA2DS2-VASc score, and hemodynamic stability/symptom severity guides urgency of intervention (Harrison 22e p.1944).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19
chunks.text: Respiratory viruses enter via the respiratory tract and replicate in epithelium whose cell type dictates the resulting syndrome. Purely respiratory viruses (e.g. rhinoviruses) replicate only in respiratory epithelium, whereas systemic viruses (e.g. measles, SARS-CoV) disseminate via the bloodstream and may also injure the airway. Wheezing arises from smooth-muscle contraction plus luminal obstruction by mucus and sloughed epithelium, predominantly at the narrow-caliber bronchioles (bronchiolitis); croup reflects inflammation of larynx, trachea and bronchi causing inspiratory difficulty. Because non-viremic respiratory viruses elicit incomplete or waning immunity, reinfection with the same virus and even the same strain is common across life. Each virus type harbors vast antigenic diversity (e.g. influenza drift/shift, >100 rhinovirus serotypes), limiting durable cross-protection. Influenza pneumonia is notable for a high rate of secondary staphylococcal and streptococcal bacterial superinfection (Harrison 22e p.1531-1534).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19
chunks.text: Respiratory virus infections are the most frequent infections in humans; many agents (rhinovirus, RSV, hMPV, parainfluenza, adenovirus, influenza, non-COVID coronaviruses) produce overlapping syndromes, so epidemiology, season, age, and exposure history narrow the differential more reliably than symptoms alone (Harrison 22e p.1531-1532).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19
chunks.text: RT-PCR (including multiplex panels) is the most sensitive and specific diagnostic, but extreme sensitivity is a pitfall: prolonged genome persistence in secretions for weeks after recovery means a positive result may reflect a recently resolved rather than a currently active infection (Harrison 22e p.1537).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19
chunks.text: Primary infection is generally far more severe than reinfection for the acute respiratory viruses; most primary (and thus many severe) infections occur in the first years of life, yet severe disease rises again in the elderly due to immune senescence (Harrison 22e p.1536).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19
chunks.text: Contact and droplet precautions with rigorous hand hygiene suffice for most respiratory viruses; measles virus and varicella-zoster virus are notable exceptions that require airborne precautions because they spread by small-particle aerosol (Harrison 22e p.1537).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19
chunks.text: The vocal cords mark the boundary between upper and lower respiratory tract; syndrome correlates with the cell types a virus prefers, e.g. rhinitis/common cold, sinusitis, otitis media, pharyngitis and laryngitis above versus tracheitis, bronchitis, bronchiolitis and pneumonia below (Harrison 22e p.1532).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19
chunks.text: Rhinoviruses are the single most common cause of the common cold, account for at least half of cases, and exist as more than 100 serotypes; because most adults develop radiographic sinus changes during a cold that resolve spontaneously, the entity is better termed rhinosinusitis (Harrison 22e p.1534-1535).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19
chunks.text: RSV is among the most transmissible human viruses and a leading cause of severe lower respiratory tract illness and hospitalization in both infants and the frail elderly; it has a single serotype with two antigenic subgroups (A and B) that are only about 25 percent cross-related, partly explaining lifelong reinfection (Harrison 22e p.1533).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19
chunks.text: Human metapneumovirus resembles RSV but is roughly half as likely to cause severe lower-tract disease, attributed to its lack of the nonstructural interferon-antagonist genes RSV uses to blunt innate immunity (Harrison 22e p.1533-1534).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19
chunks.text: Measles is probably the most contagious respiratory virus, spreading by small-particle aerosol; the classic triad is the '3 Cs' (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis) with high fever, a maculopapular rash within days, and pathognomonic Koplik's spots in the setting of typical rash and fever (Harrison 22e p.1534).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19
chunks.text: Coxsackievirus pharyngitis presents as herpangina (palatal vesicles/ulcers with fever, odynophagia and throat pain), and enterovirus A71 outbreaks of hand-foot-and-mouth disease can be complicated by neurologic disease; enterovirus D68 is linked to wheezing and acute flaccid myelitis (Harrison 22e p.1535).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19
chunks.text: Adenovirus species B and C dominate respiratory disease, can establish persistent shedding from tonsils/adenoids for months to years, and classically cause pharyngoconjunctival fever; acute respiratory disease (ARD, types 4 and 7) historically devastated crowded military-recruit settings (Harrison 22e p.1535-1536).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19
chunks.text: Acute bronchitis is a cough of under 3 weeks without pneumonia signs or radiographic infiltrate and is predominantly viral, whereas bacteria figure more prominently in chronic bronchitis; antibiotics do not improve uncomplicated viral respiratory infection in healthy patients (Harrison 22e p.1537).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19
chunks.text: Treating uncomplicated viral respiratory infection with antibiotics, which does not improve outcome in otherwise healthy patients

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19
chunks.text: Over-interpreting RT-PCR positives, since viral genome can persist for weeks post-recovery and asymptomatic individuals (e.g. rhinovirus, bocavirus) frequently test positive

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19
chunks.text: Applying rapid tests indiscriminately, lowering positive predictive value; testing is best targeted to high-risk exposures in the appropriate season

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19
chunks.text: Laboratory PCR contamination from prior reactions producing false positives

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19
chunks.text: Assuming rhinovirus is confined to the upper tract; it is now linked to wheezing, asthma exacerbations and (rhinovirus C) pneumonia/COPD exacerbation

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19
chunks.text: Missing secondary bacterial pneumonia complicating influenza

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19
chunks.text: Most acute viral respiratory infections in immunocompetent hosts are self-limited, with reinfection generally milder than primary infection. Severe and sometimes fatal disease concentrates in infants, the frail/institutionalized elderly, those with underlying lung disease (especially COPD and oxygen-dependent disease) or cardiovascular disease, and immunocompromised patients, in whom conventional viruses may cause chronic and even fatal infection. Selected agents carry high lethality: the 2002-2003 SARS-CoV epidemic (>8000 cases) had mortality approaching 10 percent, and MERS-CoV mortality is approximately 35 percent. Measles, though often milder in immunocompetent children, causes high mortality in low-resource settings, especially with malnutrition (Harrison 22e p.1533-1536).

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19
chunks.text: Hypoxia or respiratory failure requiring oxygen or mechanical ventilation

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19
chunks.text: Exposure history suggesting high-mortality zoonotic agents (avian influenza H5N1/H7N9, MERS-CoV)

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19

chunks.diseaseName: Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19
chunks.text: No formal grading scheme; severity is stratified clinically by anatomic level (upper vs lower respiratory tract), presence of pneumonia or respiratory failure/hypoxia, and host risk (extremes of age, underlying lung/cardiac disease, COPD, obesity, immunocompromise). Accumulation of multiple risk factors markedly increases risk of severe lower respiratory tract disease (Harrison 22e p.1536).

chunks.text: Acute compartment syndrome develops when pressure within a non-compliant osseofascial compartment rises to a level that impedes capillary perfusion. Bleeding, oedema, or external constriction increases compartment volume or reduces its capacity, raising interstitial pressure until it exceeds the perfusion gradient. Ischaemia increases capillary permeability, causing further oedema in a vicious cycle. Muscle and nerve are highly sensitive to ischaemia; sustained pressure elevation for a few hours produces irreversible necrosis. Because arterial inflow pressure is much higher than compartment pressure, distal pulses are often preserved until very late, making them an unreliable marker.

source.ref: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures

chunks.text: A surgical emergency in which raised pressure within a closed fascial compartment compromises tissue perfusion, leading to muscle and nerve ischaemia if not decompressed

source.ref: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures

chunks.text: The cardinal early sign is pain out of proportion to the injury and pain on passive stretch of the muscles in the affected compartment

source.ref: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures

chunks.text: It commonly follows tibial or forearm fractures, crush injuries, reperfusion after vascular occlusion, or tight casts and dressings

source.ref: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures

chunks.text: Pulselessness, pallor, paraesthesia, and paralysis are late signs; waiting for them risks irreversible damage, so a normal distal pulse does not exclude the diagnosis

chunks.text: Diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by compartment pressure measurement, particularly in the unconscious or unreliable patient

source.ref: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures

chunks.text: Definitive treatment is urgent open fasciotomy to decompress all involved compartments; casts and constrictive dressings must be split or removed immediately while preparing for surgery

chunks.text: The limb should be kept at heart level rather than elevated, and hypotension avoided, to maintain perfusion pressure

chunks.text: Missed or delayed treatment leads to Volkmann's ischaemic contracture, permanent deficit, rhabdomyolysis with renal failure, and potential limb loss

source.ref: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures

chunks.text: With prompt fasciotomy, usually within a few hours of onset, muscle and nerve can recover fully; delay leads to ischaemic necrosis, fixed contracture (Volkmann's), sensory and motor deficits, chronic pain, and in severe cases systemic complications or amputation.

source.ref: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures

chunks.text: SURGICAL EMERGENCY: pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch mandate urgent fasciotomy without delay

source.ref: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures

chunks.text: Do not wait for pulselessness or paralysis, which are late and indicate established ischaemic damage

chunks.text: MRI (including gradient-echo/susceptibility-weighted and diffusion sequences) - more sensitive than CT for microhemorrhage and axonal injury; detects intracranial abnormalities in ~27% of CT-negative mild TBI patients and has prognostic value

chunks.diseaseName: Concussion and Other Traumatic Brain Injuries

chunks.diseaseName: Concussion and Other Traumatic Brain Injuries
chunks.text: TBI results from external mechanical force - the head being struck or striking an object, acceleration/deceleration of the brain, penetration, or blast/explosion - producing primary structural lesions and secondary injury. A skull fracture marks the site and severity of impact and, when the arachnoid is torn, opens a pathway for CSF leak and bacterial entry (meningitis risk); basilar fractures may cause CSF leak, pneumocephalus, and delayed cavernous-carotid fistula. Extra-axial hematomas arise from torn meningeal arteries (epidural) or bridging veins (subdural) and exert mass effect that raises intracranial pressure. Cortical surface bruising (contusion) occurs at coup and contrecoup sites with petechial hemorrhage, edema, and tissue destruction. Shearing of axons (traumatic/diffuse axonal injury) at impact, with associated microhemorrhages, disrupts white-matter connectivity. Traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage from rupture of small cortical vessels is common and, when diffuse after severe TBI, increases mortality. In concussion/mild TBI, conventional CT is often normal while higher-resolution 3T MRI may reveal contusion or microhemorrhage; advanced imaging shows reduced cerebral blood flow, altered functional connectivity, and white-matter microstructural change that broadly track injury severity and recovery, though subtle changes may persist after clinical recovery (a neurobiologic recovery 'tail').

chunks.diseaseName: Concussion and Other Traumatic Brain Injuries
chunks.text: TBI is defined as an externally caused alteration in brain function or other evidence of brain pathology, marked by any of the following: loss/decrease in consciousness, retrograde or posttraumatic amnesia, neurologic deficits, or altered mental state at the moment of injury (p.3571).

chunks.diseaseName: Concussion and Other Traumatic Brain Injuries
chunks.text: Second-impact syndrome is a rare, often fatal diffuse cerebral swelling that follows a second minor head injury before the first has resolved - a key reason no athlete should return to play until fully asymptomatic and cleared (p.3575).

chunks.diseaseName: Concussion and Other Traumatic Brain Injuries
chunks.text: Blood biomarkers GFAP (astroglial injury) and UCHL1 (neuronal injury) are now usable at point of care; GFAP in particular discriminates intracranial abnormalities and helps stratify CT+, CT-/MRI+, and CT-/MRI- patients, with both diagnostic and prognostic value (p.3574).

chunks.diseaseName: Concussion and Other Traumatic Brain Injuries
chunks.text: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) - tau deposition in superficial cortical layers, perivascular regions, and the depths of sulci - is linked to repetitive head impacts but remains a postmortem diagnosis; proposed clinical criteria lack specificity and in vivo imaging/biomarker findings have been inconsistent (p.3576-3577).

chunks.diseaseName: Concussion and Other Traumatic Brain Injuries
chunks.text: Incidence shows a bimodal age distribution: motor vehicle crashes predominate in younger persons (more often men), while falls are the leading cause in older adults (more often women); roughly 70-90% (most estimates ~85%) of treated TBIs are mild (p.3570, p.3572).

chunks.diseaseName: Concussion and Other Traumatic Brain Injuries
chunks.text: Severity is graded with the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS): mild 13-15, moderate 9-12, severe 3-8; the individual eye/verbal/motor components (e.g., E3V4M6) are more informative than the summed total, which should only describe groups (p.3571).

chunks.diseaseName: Concussion and Other Traumatic Brain Injuries
chunks.text: In moderate-to-severe TBI, GCS plus the duration of loss of consciousness (LOC) and posttraumatic amnesia (PTA) predict outcome well; in mild TBI, LOC and PTA are far less predictive of recovery time and outcome, and postinjury symptom burden is the most robust predictor (p.3571, p.3574).

chunks.diseaseName: Concussion and Other Traumatic Brain Injuries
chunks.text: Epidural hematoma classically follows tearing of the middle meningeal artery beneath a temporal-bone fracture, evolves rapidly, and may be preceded by a lucid interval; rapid surgical evacuation usually yields a favorable outcome (p.3572).

chunks.diseaseName: Concussion and Other Traumatic Brain Injuries
chunks.text: Acute subdural hematoma is usually venous in origin, can occur without major trauma (especially in the elderly or anticoagulated, or from acceleration/whiplash forces), and carries significant morbidity and mortality when surgery is required - in contrast to the generally better-treated epidural hematoma (p.3572).

chunks.diseaseName: Concussion and Other Traumatic Brain Injuries
chunks.text: Contusions follow coup (under the impact) and contrecoup (antipolar) mechanisms; blunt deceleration typically bruises the orbitofrontal and anterior/basal temporal lobes, and old contusion sites become gliotic scars that are highly epileptogenic (p.3573).

chunks.diseaseName: Concussion and Other Traumatic Brain Injuries
chunks.text: Traumatic axonal injury (TAI) from shearing forces is among the most common TBI lesions; four or more foci constitute diffuse axonal injury (DAI), which when widespread is proposed to underlie prolonged coma and the vegetative state (p.3573).

chunks.diseaseName: Concussion and Other Traumatic Brain Injuries

chunks.text: The typical concussion syndrome has a good prognosis with little risk of subsequent deterioration. After sport-related concussion, recovery is generally favorable: in a large collegiate cohort, median symptom resolution was about 6.4 days and median return to sport 12.8 days, with ~92% symptom resolution and ~85% clearance to return by one month; most athletes across ages fully recover over 1-4 weeks. A subset develop persistent postconcussion symptoms (PPCS) beyond ~3 months; preinjury mental health disorder, migraine, and prior concussion predispose to prolonged recovery. Recovery from severe TBI can take years, and long-term outcome prediction is limited and often incorrect; best practice recommends aggressive therapy for at least 72 h (absent brain death). TBI is now recognized as a chronic, dynamic condition, with meaningful improvement or decline observed 2-7 years post-injury regardless of initial severity. TBI (mild to severe) is associated with a 63-96% increased risk of all-cause dementia, with risk greatest after severe injury; TBI with LOC >1 h has been linked to subsequent Parkinson's disease and Lewy body accumulation.

Mild TBI with CT and/or MRI abnormality is termed 'complicated mTBI' and carries a higher risk of unfavorable outcome. Loss of consciousness and posttraumatic amnesia duration further characterize severity. CTE neuropathology has been proposed to be staged as 'low' or 'high' severity (criteria not yet established).

chunks.text: Conduct disorder arises from an interaction of genetic and temperamental factors, such as difficult temperament and low behavioural inhibition, with adverse environmental influences including harsh or inconsistent parenting, maltreatment, and socioeconomic adversity. Neurobiological correlates include altered function in circuits underlying emotional processing, reward, and threat appraisal, and blunted autonomic responsiveness, particularly in the callous-unemotional subgroup.

A deficiency of an enzyme in the adrenal cortisol synthesis pathway, most often 21-hydroxylase, reduces cortisol production. The resulting loss of negative feedback drives increased ACTH secretion, which stimulates adrenal hyperplasia and diverts steroid precursors into the androgen pathway, causing androgen excess and virilisation. In the severe salt-wasting form, aldosterone synthesis is also impaired, leading to sodium loss, hyperkalaemia, and volume depletion, while accumulation of the precursor 17-hydroxyprogesterone serves as a diagnostic marker.
A group of autosomal recessive disorders of adrenal steroid synthesis, the great majority caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency.
The classic salt-wasting form presents in the first weeks of life with vomiting, poor feeding, weight loss, dehydration, and shock from combined cortisol and aldosterone deficiency.

Female infants with the classic form often show virilisation of the external genitalia (ambiguous genitalia), whereas affected males may appear normal at birth and are at particular risk of unrecognised salt-wasting crisis.
Characteristic biochemistry includes hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, and metabolic acidosis in the salt-wasting crisis, with markedly elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone.
A non-classic (late-onset) form presents later with signs of androgen excess such as premature pubarche, hirsutism, or menstrual irregularity.
Newborn screening measuring 17-hydroxyprogesterone allows early detection before a life-threatening crisis.

Treatment principle is glucocorticoid replacement to correct cortisol deficiency and suppress excess adrenal androgen, with mineralocorticoid replacement (and salt supplementation in infancy) for salt-wasting forms.
Additional stress steroid cover is essential during illness, surgery, or major stress to prevent adrenal crisis.
Management of affected girls includes multidisciplinary care regarding virilised genitalia, and genetic counselling is important for families.
Missing salt-wasting crisis in a male infant with normal genitalia
Failing to provide stress steroid cover during illness or surgery
Over-treating with glucocorticoids, impairing growth, or under-treating, allowing androgen excess
Misattributing a neonatal collapse to sepsis or pyloric stenosis without checking electrolytes and adrenal steroids

With early diagnosis, hormone replacement, and stress dosing, children generally grow and develop well; risks include life-threatening adrenal crises, effects of over- or under-treatment on growth and puberty, and fertility and psychosocial issues in classic disease.
Salt-wasting adrenal crisis with dehydration, hypotension, or shock
Severe hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia

Vomiting and poor feeding in a neonate, particularly a male infant
Intercurrent illness or surgery without adequate stress steroid cover

Failure of the diaphragm to close completely during embryogenesis permits abdominal organs to occupy the thoracic cavity while the lungs are developing. The space-occupying viscera restrict growth of the ipsilateral (and to a lesser extent contralateral) lung, producing pulmonary hypoplasia with fewer alveoli and abnormal, muscularised pulmonary arterioles. After birth these abnormal vessels fail to relax normally, causing persistent pulmonary hypertension with right-to-left shunting, hypoxaemia, and acidosis. The combination of reduced functional lung tissue and elevated pulmonary vascular resistance drives the respiratory failure that dominates the clinical course.

A defect in the diaphragm allows abdominal viscera to herniate into the thorax during fetal development, impairing lung growth; the posterolateral (Bochdalek) defect, more often left-sided, is most common.
The principal problems are pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension rather than the anatomical defect itself.
Many cases are detected on antenatal ultrasound, allowing delivery at a centre with neonatal surgical and intensive care support.
A typical presentation is respiratory distress soon after birth with a scaphoid (sunken) abdomen and a shifted apex or heart sounds, and reduced breath sounds on the affected side.
Bowel sounds may be audible in the chest, and the chest radiograph shows bowel loops in the thorax with mediastinal shift.
Bag-mask ventilation should be avoided because it distends the herniated bowel and worsens lung compression; early endotracheal intubation and gastric decompression are preferred.
Initial management focuses on gentle, lung-protective ventilation, cardiorespiratory stabilisation, and treatment of pulmonary hypertension before surgery.
Surgical reduction and repair of the defect is undertaken after the infant is physiologically stabilised, not as an emergency.
Severe cases may need advanced support such as inhaled pulmonary vasodilators or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation.
Using bag-mask ventilation and inflating herniated bowel, worsening lung compression
Rushing to surgery before stabilising pulmonary hypertension and gas exchange
Attributing neonatal distress to primary lung disease and missing the diagnosis on examination and radiograph
Using aggressive high-pressure ventilation that risks barotrauma to hypoplastic lungs
Overlooking associated cardiac and genetic anomalies that affect management and prognosis

Outcome depends chiefly on the degree of pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension and on associated anomalies. With optimal perinatal care many infants survive, though survivors may have chronic lung disease, feeding and growth problems, and neurodevelopmental sequelae. Severe hypoplasia and refractory pulmonary hypertension carry a poor prognosis.
Severe respiratory distress and hypoxaemia at or shortly after birth
Persistent pulmonary hypertension with right-to-left shunting refractory to therapy
Deterioration after bag-mask ventilation distends intrathoracic bowel

Patent foramen ovale (distinct from ASD; not associated with right heart dilation)
Ventricular septal defect (membranous/perimembranous, muscular, AV-canal/inlet, subpulmonary/conal types)
Patent ductus arteriosus
Partial anomalous pulmonary venous return

Tetralogy of Fallot (most common cyanotic CHD)
Transposition of the great arteries (D-loop and congenitally corrected L-loop)
Coarctation of the aorta (with associated bicuspid aortic valve)
Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography with agitated saline (bubble) contrast — needed to diagnose PFO and non-secundum ASDs; color flow Doppler for VSDs and shunt-ratio estimation
Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging — routine surveillance of RV size, function, and mass in repaired tetralogy of Fallot and other complex CHD; cross-sectional imaging detects PAPVR

Surface ECG — incomplete right bundle branch block in ASD; QRS duration >=180 ms in repaired TOF flags risk of ventricular tachycardia/sudden death; ventricular pre-excitation (WPW) in up to 20% of Ebstein anomaly
Cardiac catheterization — shunt quantification and hemodynamic assessment, particularly when pulmonary hypertension is suspected

Genetic evaluation — testing for 22q11 deletion (DiGeorge) in conotruncal defects (clues: right aortic arch, aberrant subclavian artery); recognition of trisomy 21, Noonan (PTPN11), Williams (7q11.23), and Turner syndromes

Atrial septal defect may be mistaken for mitral stenosis; features favoring ASD over MS include a pulmonary mid-to-upper left sternal border flow murmur, and large left-to-right shunts can produce findings overlapping with MS (Harrison 22e p.2065 / Chap. on MS).
Arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy and Uhl's anomaly are non-shunt myocardial causes of right heart dilation that can mimic the dilated right heart of an ASD.

The normal heart is analyzed segmentally (atria, ventricles, great arteries joined by the atrioventricular canal and conus), with attention to alignment (what drains into what) and connection (how segments are physically linked). The heart forms from the third week of gestation and is nearly complete by 8 weeks; cardiac neural crest cells migrating in weeks 5-6 are essential for outflow septation, semilunar valve formation, and aortic arch patterning, so disturbance of these processes underlies conotruncal defects. Shunt lesions are defined by the relative compliance, pressure, and outflow resistance of the connected chambers/vessels and the defect size. Left-to-right shunts (ASD, VSD, PDA) move oxygenated blood toward the deoxygenated (right) side, volume-loading the pulmonary circulation: ASD/PAPVR (proximal to the tricuspid valve) cause right heart dilation, whereas VSD/PDA (below the tricuspid valve) cause left heart dilation. Sustained high-volume or pressurized left-to-right shunting can raise pulmonary vascular resistance to the point that the shunt reverses (Eisenmenger physiology, right-to-left, cyanosis). Tetralogy of Fallot produces a right-to-left shunt across the VSD because RV outflow obstruction raises right-sided systolic pressure, mixing deoxygenated blood into the LV and causing systemic arterial cyanosis. In transposition of the great arteries the aorta arises from the RV and the pulmonary artery from the LV, creating parallel rather than series circulations that are incompatible with life unless mixing exists (ASD, VSD, or PDA).

At least 1.4 million U.S. adults are living with congenital heart disease (CHD); the majority were diagnosed in childhood, but a substantial percentage have CHD first recognized in adulthood, so lifelong follow-up with ACHD expertise is recommended (Harrison 22e p.2067).

Eisenmenger syndrome is the consequence of a long-standing high-volume or pressurized left-to-right shunt: excessive pulmonary blood flow leads to severely increased pulmonary vascular resistance that eventually REVERSES the shunt, creating bidirectional or right-to-left flow and cyanosis; it can complicate any CHD with an initial left-to-right shunt (Harrison 22e p.2078).

Selective pulmonary vasodilators such as bosentan or sildenafil are efficacious in Eisenmenger syndrome; select patients may be candidates for combined heart-lung transplantation, or preferably lung transplantation with concomitant repair of the intracardiac defect when feasible (Harrison 22e p.2078).

Endocarditis prophylaxis before dental procedures is advised in high-risk CHD lesions: unrepaired cyanotic CHD (including palliative shunts/conduits), completely repaired defects during the first 6 months after repair, and repaired CHD with residual defects adjacent to prosthetic material (Harrison 22e p.745, Table 133-9).

ASD physiology is predominantly a left-to-right shunt; the degree of shunting (and thus right heart volume loading) depends on defect size and the diastolic properties of the heart. As patients age, diabetes, hypertension, and atherosclerosis reduce left-heart compliance and may increase left-to-right shunting and symptoms (Harrison 22e p.2070).

The classic ASD physical finding is a wide, FIXED splitting of the second heart sound, due to prolonged RV ejection and increased pulmonary artery capacitance delaying pulmonary valve closure; the ECG commonly shows incomplete right bundle branch block (Harrison 22e p.2070).

Secundum ASD (defect in the region of the fossa ovalis) is the most common type and can often be closed percutaneously with an occluder device; a patent foramen ovale (PFO) is distinct, is NOT associated with right-sided dilation, and persists in up to 25% of adults (Harrison 22e p.2070).

Surgical closure (not percutaneous) is required for primum ASDs, sinus venosus defects, and coronary sinus septal defects; a sinus venosus defect is not actually a defect of the atrial septum but a communication near the SVC- or IVC-atrial junction with right pulmonary veins (Harrison 22e p.2070-2071).

VSDs are the most common congenital anomaly recognized at birth but account for only ~10% of adult CHD, owing to the high rate of spontaneous closure of small VSDs in early life; the most common location is the membranous (perimembranous/outlet) septum (Harrison 22e p.2071-2072).

Outcome for adults with small VSDs WITHOUT ventricular dilation or pulmonary hypertension is generally excellent; small muscular defects persisting into adulthood are often pressure- and flow-restricted with no significant hemodynamic consequence (Harrison 22e p.2072).

Tetralogy of Fallot is the most common form of cyanotic CHD (~0.5 per 1000 live births) and comprises anterior conal-septal deviation causing RV outflow tract obstruction, a VSD, RV hypertrophy, and an overriding aorta (Harrison 22e p.2073).

In repaired tetralogy of Fallot, pulmonary regurgitation is common and is usually associated with RV dilation; accurate quantification of RV size, function, and mass is particularly important because RV dilation, dysfunction, and hypertrophy are associated with adverse outcomes, and cardiac MRI is routinely used for surveillance (Harrison 22e p.2073-2074).
Confusing a PFO (flap-valve patency, present in up to 25% of adults, no right heart dilation) with a true secundum ASD.

Assuming all ASDs are amenable to percutaneous closure — large defects, inadequate tissue rims, and anomalous draining pulmonary veins make device closure unfavorable, and primum/sinus venosus/coronary sinus defects require surgery.
Overlooking that a sinus venosus defect is not in the atrial septum itself, so it may be missed without dedicated imaging.

Routine phlebotomy in an asymptomatic adult with Eisenmenger syndrome is contraindicated; elevated hematocrit appropriate to the degree of cyanosis should not be lowered reflexively, and iron deficiency should be corrected because it impairs quality of life and function.

Using teratogenic medications (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, direct oral anticoagulants, endothelin receptor blockers) in CHD patients of childbearing potential; estrogen-containing contraception should be avoided in Eisenmenger syndrome due to thrombogenicity.
Failing to test adults with conotruncal defects for 22q11 deletion (DiGeorge) — many were never tested, and unrecognized cognitive/psychiatric disability may go untreated.
Treating an ACHD patient's seemingly minor lesion without recognizing limited hemodynamic reserve and subclinical multi-organ dysfunction before noncardiac surgery.

Outcomes vary widely by lesion. Adults with small VSDs without ventricular dilation or pulmonary hypertension generally have an excellent prognosis. Repaired coarctation patients generally do well but remain at risk for systemic hypertension, premature atherosclerosis, LV failure, and aortic aneurysm/dissection and recoarctation. In repaired tetralogy of Fallot, one prospective cohort of 144 adults showed 72% survival at 40 years but only 25% cumulative event-free survival (events: reintervention, most commonly pulmonary valve replacement; symptomatic arrhythmia; heart failure); LV dysfunction is present in at least 20%. The arterial switch operation for D-loop TGA has produced substantial long-term survival, whereas atrial switch leaves a systemic RV prone to dysfunction. Adults with Eisenmenger syndrome have significant morbidity but generally survive longer than patients with other forms of pulmonary arterial hypertension. In aggregate, adults with CHD have quality-of-life-limiting comorbidities and premature mortality far exceeding age-matched controls, and nearly all can be classified as stage A heart failure or greater; care within a center that has an ACHD specialty program is associated with improved overall survival.
Reversal of a left-to-right shunt to right-to-left flow with cyanosis = Eisenmenger syndrome; develops from severely elevated pulmonary vascular resistance and is a multi-organ condition
Right heart dilation in an unrepaired ASD without other cause signals risk of progression to symptomatic right heart failure, atrial arrhythmias, and pulmonary arterial hypertension
QRS duration >=180 ms on resting ECG in repaired tetralogy of Fallot — associated with increased risk of ventricular tachycardia and sudden cardiac death
Systemic RV dysfunction after atrial switch (Mustard/Senning) for D-loop TGA — the most worrisome long-term complication, with no proven effective medical therapy

Pregnancy in a woman with Eisenmenger syndrome is contraindicated due to high risk of maternal mortality; pulmonary arterial hypertension and severe systemic ventricular dysfunction are WHO class IV (extremely high maternal risk)
New exercise-capacity decline in ACHD may be unrecognized by the patient; by the time symptoms appear, irreversible physiologic changes may already have occurred

The chapter applies the modified World Health Organization (mWHO) classification of maternal risk in heart disease during pregnancy, graded mWHO I (no detectable increased mortality risk, e.g., small/mild lesions) through mWHO IV (extremely high maternal mortality risk; pregnancy generally contraindicated). Examples by class: mWHO II includes unoperated ASD/VSD and repaired tetralogy of Fallot; mWHO III includes mechanical valve, systemic RV, and Fontan circulation; mWHO IV includes pulmonary arterial hypertension, severe systemic ventricular dysfunction (EF <30% or NYHA III-IV), severe aortic dilatation, and Fontan with any complication. The CARPREG II weighted-risk score is also described (highest 3-point factors: prior cardiac event/arrhythmia, NYHA >=III, mechanical valve), stratifying predicted cardiac-event risk from 5% (<=1 point) to 41% (>4 points). For repaired tetralogy of Fallot, potential sequelae are catalogued in Table 280-3 and long-term sequelae of D-loop TGA surgery in Table 280-4.

Thyroid hormone is essential for normal brain growth and myelination, particularly in the first years of life. In congenital hypothyroidism, deficient hormone production results from failure of thyroid gland development, an enzymatic defect in hormone synthesis (dyshormonogenesis), inadequate iodine substrate, or, less commonly, hypothalamic-pituitary (central) dysfunction. In primary disease, low circulating thyroid hormone removes negative feedback on the pituitary, raising TSH. Because maternal thyroid hormone crosses the placenta, the fetus is partly protected in utero, but after birth the untreated infant becomes progressively hypothyroid, and prolonged deficiency during the critical window of brain development produces permanent neurological injury.
One of the most common preventable causes of intellectual disability, resulting from inadequate thyroid hormone at birth or in early infancy.
Most affected newborns appear normal at birth because of transplacental maternal thyroid hormone, so clinical detection is unreliable and newborn screening is essential.
The commonest cause worldwide is thyroid dysgenesis (aplasia, hypoplasia, or an ectopic gland); dyshormonogenesis and, in some regions, iodine deficiency also contribute.
Later clinical features include prolonged jaundice, poor feeding, lethargy, constipation, a large fontanelle, macroglossia, umbilical hernia, hypotonia, and hoarse cry.
Screening measures TSH and/or T4 on a heel-prick sample; a raised TSH with low T4 confirms primary hypothyroidism.
Treatment is early thyroid hormone replacement with levothyroxine, and the key to normal neurodevelopment is starting therapy as early as possible.
Regular monitoring of growth, development, and thyroid function is needed to keep levels in the target range during infancy.
Delay in starting treatment is associated with irreversible loss of cognitive potential, making prompt recognition critical.
Relying on clinical signs, which are usually absent or subtle in the newborn period
Delaying treatment while awaiting further tests once screening is clearly abnormal
Under- or over-treating due to infrequent monitoring during infancy
Missing central hypothyroidism when screening is TSH-based only

With early diagnosis through screening and prompt, adequately dosed replacement, neurodevelopmental outcome is typically normal; delayed or inadequate treatment risks permanent intellectual impairment.

Organisms reach the fetal or newborn lung by several routes: transplacental spread during maternal bloodstream infection, ascending colonisation of amniotic fluid after membrane rupture or with chorioamnionitis, and aspiration of infected amniotic fluid or genital secretions around delivery. Once in the alveoli, pathogens trigger an inflammatory response with exudate, impaired gas exchange, and interference with surfactant function. In early-onset disease this frequently coexists with bacteraemia and systemic sepsis, so lung involvement is often one component of a generalised infection in the vulnerable newborn.
Pneumonia acquired before or during birth typically presents as respiratory distress in the first hours to days of life and often forms part of early-onset neonatal sepsis.
Infection may be acquired transplacentally, by ascending spread from the genital tract (especially with prolonged rupture of membranes or chorioamnionitis), or during passage through the birth canal.
Group B streptococcus and Escherichia coli are leading bacterial causes; other organisms include Listeria, and congenital infections such as certain viruses can also involve the lungs.
Clinical features overlap with other causes of neonatal respiratory distress, so it is often difficult to distinguish pneumonia from surfactant deficiency or transient tachypnoea on presentation.
Maternal and perinatal risk factors, particularly chorioamnionitis, prolonged membrane rupture, and maternal group B streptococcus colonisation, raise the likelihood and guide management.
Chest radiographs may show diffuse or patchy opacities, but findings can mimic respiratory distress syndrome, so imaging is supportive rather than definitive.
Because differentiating infection from non-infectious causes is difficult, empirical antibiotics covering likely organisms are usually started while cultures and the clinical course are followed.
Supportive care to maintain oxygenation, ventilation, temperature, and perfusion is essential alongside antimicrobial therapy.
Attributing respiratory distress solely to surfactant deficiency and delaying antibiotics in an at-risk infant
Underweighting maternal risk factors such as chorioamnionitis or prolonged membrane rupture
Relying on chest radiograph appearance to exclude infection given its overlap with other conditions
Failing to evaluate for accompanying bacteraemia or meningitis

With prompt recognition and appropriate antibiotics and supportive care many infants recover well, but outcome depends on the organism, gestational age, and severity; fulminant early-onset sepsis with pneumonia, particularly from group B streptococcus, can be life-threatening.

chunks.text: Conjunctivitis is inflammation of the conjunctiva, the mucous membrane lining the eyelids and covering the sclera. It arises from infection (bacterial or viral), allergy, or irritation. Inflammatory mediators dilate conjunctival vessels (causing redness) and increase vascular permeability (causing chemosis and discharge), while the cellular response produces follicles in viral and chlamydial disease or papillae in bacterial and allergic disease. Because the process is confined to the conjunctiva and spares the cornea, anterior chamber, and intraocular structures, vision and pupil responses remain normal in uncomplicated cases.

chunks.text: Contact dermatitis has two principal mechanisms. Irritant contact dermatitis results from direct, non-immunological damage to the epidermal barrier by chemical or physical agents, triggering innate inflammation; severity relates to the concentration and duration of exposure. Allergic contact dermatitis is a type IV, T-cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity reaction: after an initial sensitisation phase in which small-molecule haptens bind skin proteins and prime allergen-specific T cells, re-exposure elicits an inflammatory eczematous response over one to several days. Repeated insult impairs the barrier further, perpetuating inflammation and, over time, chronic lichenified changes.
