chunks.text: A range of stimuli converge on a final common pathway of airway inflammation and worsening respiratory symptoms. The underlying COPD substrate is fixed airflow obstruction (chronically reduced, non-normalizing FEV1/FVC) compounded by hyperinflation and air trapping; a flattened diaphragm becomes mechanically disadvantaged, raising the work of breathing during any acute decompensation. Gas exchange is impaired chiefly by ventilation-perfusion mismatching (shunt is minimal), which explains why modest supplemental oxygen usually corrects COPD hypoxemia. Hypoxemia tends not to appear until FEV1 falls below ~50% predicted, and CO2 retention is not expected until FEV1 is below ~25% predicted. Acutely, worsening obstruction and dynamic hyperinflation can precipitate alveolar hypoventilation with rising arterial CO2 and respiratory acidosis (p.2251-2252, p.2255, p.2258).

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

chunks.text: An exacerbation is an episodic acute worsening of respiratory symptoms (increased dyspnea, cough, and/or change in sputum amount or character), typically evolving over less than 14 days; it may or may not be accompanied by fever, myalgias, or sore throat (p.2258).

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

chunks.text: Cor pulmonale (overt right heart failure) is now relatively uncommon since supplemental oxygen became standard, but pulmonary hypertension should be considered in patients with persistent activity limitation or lower-extremity edema; it typically arises with FEV1 <25% predicted and chronic hypoxemia (Pao2 <55 mmHg), though some develop it from vascular destruction independent of obstruction severity (p.2252, p.2254).

chunks.text: COPD exacerbation is fundamentally a clinical diagnosis; spirometry/pulmonary function testing has not been shown to help diagnose or manage an exacerbation, in contrast to its role in asthma (p.2259).

chunks.text: The single strongest predictor of future exacerbations is a prior exacerbation, and the greatest single risk factor for hospitalization is a previous hospitalization for exacerbation (p.2258).

chunks.text: Exacerbation frequency rises as airflow obstruction worsens; patients with severe obstruction (FEV1 <50% predicted) average about 1-3 episodes per year, though some severely obstructed patients exacerbate infrequently (p.2258).

The GOLD ABE assessment further classifies patients using symptom burden (mMRC dyspnea scale or CAT score) and annual exacerbation history: groups A and B for those with 0-1 moderate exacerbations not leading to hospitalization (A = mMRC 0-1/CAT <10, B = mMRC >=2/CAT >=10), and group E for those with >=2 moderate exacerbations or >=1 leading to hospitalization. The ATS/ERS alternative grades obstruction by FEV1 z-scores rather than percent predicted. chunks.text: Because the cord packs nearly the entire motor output and sensory input of the trunk and limbs into a small cross-section, even a small compressive mass causes disproportionately severe, often reversible-if-treated-early, deficits (p.3559). In neoplastic compression, metastases lodge in the vertebral body or pedicle (the axial skeleton is rich in marrow); the enlarging deposit compresses the underlying dura, or a paravertebral mass (lymphoma, myeloma, paediatric tumours) extends through the intervertebral foramen into the canal. Expanding extradural tumour injures axons and myelin mechanically and compromises blood flow, producing ischaemia and infarction (pp.589, 3563). In spinal epidural abscess, as the collection expands it causes additional cord damage through venous congestion and thrombosis, so that once weakness appears deterioration can be rapid and irreversible (p.3606). The thoracic spine is the commonest site of metastatic compression (~70%), followed by lumbosacral (~20%) and cervical (~10%) (p.631).

chunks.text: Outcome is strongly time- and function-dependent: treatment is most successful in patients who are still ambulatory and have intact sphincter control when therapy begins, and a good response is expected in those ambulatory at presentation - treatment usually prevents new weakness and up to a third regain some motor function (pp.632, 3606). Motor deficits fixed for more than 12 h seldom improve, and beyond 48 h substantial recovery is unlikely (p.3606). For spinal epidural abscess, prompt diagnosis and treatment allow significant recovery in up to two-thirds, but surgery is unlikely to reverse deficits fixed for more than a few days (p.3607). Recovery from paraparesis is better after surgery than radiotherapy alone, though survival may be short with widespread metastatic disease (p.768).

chunks.text: A corneal abrasion is a defect in the corneal epithelium, most often from mechanical trauma. Loss of the epithelial barrier exposes richly innervated subepithelial nerve endings, producing intense pain and reflex tearing and blepharospasm. The epithelium normally regenerates rapidly by sliding and mitosis of surrounding cells. Contamination, retained foreign material, or contact lens wear can convert a simple abrasion into a microbial keratitis, and repeated or poorly healing defects may reflect an underlying epithelial basement membrane dystrophy causing recurrent erosions.

chunks.text: Corrosive agents produce tissue destruction on contact. Strong alkalis (e.g. lye, drain cleaner) cause liquefactive necrosis, saponifying fats and dissolving proteins, allowing deep penetration and full-thickness oesophageal injury with risk of perforation and mediastinitis. Strong acids cause coagulative necrosis with eschar formation that can limit depth of penetration but tends to pool in and damage the stomach, risking gastric perforation and peritonitis. Injury severity depends on the agent, concentration, volume, and contact time. Healing of deep circumferential burns leads to fibrosis and stricture, and chronic injury raises long-term malignancy risk.

SARS-CoV-2 (genus Betacoronavirus) is an enveloped positive-sense RNA virus with a ~30,000-nucleotide genome encoding four structural proteins (S spike, E envelope, M membrane, N nucleocapsid) plus a large polyprotein cleaved into 16 nonstructural proteins. The trimeric S protein is a type-1 fusion machine primed by the host transmembrane protease TMPRSS2 and mediates attachment via a receptor-binding domain (RBD) to the human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (hACE2) receptor, allowing viral entry into respiratory epithelium. Infection spreads chiefly by respiratory droplets, with possible short-range airborne and fomite spread. Disease results from direct viral pathogenesis in tissues and the associated immune response. An excessive proinflammatory host response contributes directly to pulmonary pathology; early in infection viral load (peak titer) correlates with severity, whereas later disease is increasingly driven by tissue and systemic inflammatory responses (cytokine storm) rather than direct viral cytopathic effect. The hyperinflammatory and hypercoagulable state drives severe multi-organ complications.

SARS-CoV-2 is an enveloped, positive-sense RNA betacoronavirus; its trimeric spike (S) protein is primed by the host protease TMPRSS2 and attaches via a receptor-binding domain to the human ACE2 receptor (p.1539).

Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C / PMIS) is associated with COVID-19: persistent fever, multi-organ involvement (GI, dermatologic, cardiac, renal, hematologic, neurologic), and elevated inflammatory markers; highest US risk is in Black and Latino children aged 3-12 years. A similar adult syndrome (MIS-A) may rarely occur (p.1540).

Long COVID is a chronic condition occurring after infection, present for at least 3 months, with a wide range of symptoms (respiratory, metabolic, neuropsychiatric, pain) that may improve, worsen, or be ongoing; affected people may have increased suicidal ideation and suicide risk (p.1541).

Vaccination's principal goal is preventing severe COVID-19 (critical illness, death, hospitalization, emergency/urgent-care visits); preliminary data also suggest vaccinated persons with COVID are less likely than unvaccinated persons to develop long COVID (p.1543).

Disease course varies widely: asymptomatic infection, mild disease, moderate disease, or severe disease needing hospitalization, oxygen, intensive care, and mechanical ventilation. Possibly about a third of those infected are asymptomatic yet can still transmit the virus (p.1540).

Onset of disease typically manifests within 4-5 days after exposure and nearly always within 14 days; common symptoms are cough, fever, myalgia, headache, dyspnea, sore throat, and GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea) (p.1541).
Sudden-onset dysgeusia and anosmia (loss of taste and smell) occur in a substantial number of cases and often resolve over weeks to months (p.1541).

Spread is primarily via respiratory droplets between persons in close proximity; airborne transmission by small particles may occur but airborne transmission over long distances is unlikely. Fomite (contaminated-surface) transmission occurs, so hand washing is advised (p.1540).

The basic reproduction number (R0) of SARS-CoV-2 has been estimated to peak around 6, substantially higher than seasonal influenza (typically 1-2); densely populated settings (prisons, cruise ships, nursing homes, airplanes, large indoor gatherings) facilitate high transmission, while outdoor transmission is less common (p.1540).

RNA-dependent RNA polymerases are error-prone, so variants arise frequently; the WHO classifies variants under monitoring (VUMs), of interest (VOIs), and of concern (VOCs). Rapid variant evolution affecting transmission, severity, antigenicity, therapy effectiveness, and diagnostic accuracy is a distinguishing feature of the pandemic (p.1540).

An excessive proinflammatory host response to infection likely contributes directly to pulmonary pathology and disease severity; later in the clinical course pathogenesis is driven more by tissue and systemic inflammation than by direct viral cytopathic effect (p.1541-1542).
Children have lower rates of severe disease than adults, and schools have not been considered a primary driver of population transmission (p.1540).

Antibiotics are NOT generally indicated, as bacterial infection is an uncommon complication of COVID-19; reserve empiric antibiotics for diagnostic uncertainty or proven secondary infection, and deescalate or stop if no evidence of bacterial infection.
Chest CT should NOT be used as a primary diagnostic tool for COVID-19; it is principally for medical management of respiratory disease.
COVID-19-specific therapy is NOT recommended for individuals with asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Antigen (rapid/at-home) tests are less accurate than molecular tests, especially when testing exposed persons without symptoms.
Chest radiographs may be normal despite respiratory compromise, so a normal film does not exclude significant disease.
Possible association between NSAID use and worse outcomes has been raised; acetaminophen is the preferred antipyretic where possible (knowledge point - doses omitted).

Antibody-based therapies and EUAs are repeatedly revoked as new variants escape their activity, so confirm current authorization status before relying on a monoclonal antibody or long-acting antibody product.
Effectiveness of masking in community or health settings has been difficult to assess (most studies observational and confounded), so evidence is uncertain rather than absent.

Symptomatic infection is usually an acute syndrome that resolves within about 2 weeks in roughly 80% of persons, especially after mild or moderate disease. Severe disease often needs several months for recovery. Advanced age is the principal risk factor for severe illness: >95% of deaths occur in persons older than 45 years and >80% in those older than 65; male sex carries higher risk (odds ratio ~1.8), and most who die have preexisting comorbidities. Risk rises markedly with elevated BMI (overweight, obesity, severe obesity). As of September 2024 the virus had caused >700 million cases and >7 million deaths worldwide. A subset progress to recurring or persisting symptoms (long COVID); those with severe acute pulmonary or cardiac injury may have persisting respiratory or cardiac impairment, and adverse long-term mental-health consequences are common.

Spectrum: asymptomatic infection; mild disease (symptomatic, no pneumonia - most symptomatic cases); moderate disease; severe disease (pneumonia with dyspnea, radiographic involvement of more than half the lung, and/or hypoxia with oxygen saturation <=94%, typically requiring hospitalization and oxygen); critical disease (respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation, multiorgan failure, or shock - requires intensive care).

The disorder results from an abnormal immune response to proteins in cow's milk, principally caseins and whey proteins. In IgE-mediated allergy, sensitisation leads to specific IgE that, on re-exposure, triggers mast cell and basophil degranulation with rapid release of histamine and other mediators, producing immediate symptoms. In non-IgE-mediated allergy, cell-mediated and mixed immune mechanisms cause a more delayed inflammatory response in the gastrointestinal tract, resulting in mucosal inflammation, altered motility, and enteropathy. Because the offending proteins can pass into breast milk, exclusively breastfed infants can react to maternal dietary intake.
This is an immune-mediated reaction to cow's milk proteins, distinct from lactose intolerance, which is a non-immune enzyme deficiency.

Reactions are broadly divided into IgE-mediated (rapid onset urticaria, angioedema, vomiting, wheeze, and rarely anaphylaxis) and non-IgE-mediated (delayed gastrointestinal symptoms such as vomiting, diarrhoea, blood or mucus in stool, and colic-like distress).
It is one of the most common food allergies in infancy and can occur in both formula-fed and exclusively breastfed infants exposed to milk protein through maternal diet.
Diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by a compatible history, a trial of milk protein elimination, and improvement followed by recurrence on reintroduction.
For IgE-mediated disease, specific IgE testing or skin prick testing can support the diagnosis, whereas these tests are unhelpful in non-IgE-mediated presentations.
Management centres on strict avoidance of cow's milk protein, using an appropriate hypoallergenic formula in formula-fed infants and maternal dietary exclusion in breastfed infants.
A supervised oral food challenge is the most reliable way to confirm or refute the diagnosis and to assess whether tolerance has developed.
Most children outgrow cow's milk protein allergy during early childhood, so periodic reassessment for acquired tolerance is important to avoid unnecessary long-term restriction.
Confusing cow's milk protein allergy with lactose intolerance and giving inappropriate dietary advice
Relying on IgE tests to diagnose non-IgE-mediated disease
Maintaining prolonged, unnecessary dietary restriction without reassessing for tolerance
Using inadequately hypoallergenic substitutes or overlooking nutritional adequacy of exclusion diets

The prognosis is generally favourable, with the majority of children achieving tolerance during the preschool years; IgE-mediated allergy, particularly with high specific IgE levels, may persist longer than non-IgE-mediated disease.

Viral infection produces inflammation and oedema of the larynx, trachea, and subglottic tissues. Because the subglottis is the narrowest part of a child's airway and is encircled by rigid cricoid cartilage, even modest mucosal swelling markedly narrows the lumen, dramatically increasing airway resistance and producing turbulent airflow heard as inspiratory stridor and the characteristic barking cough. Increased work of breathing follows, and severe obstruction can cause hypoxaemia and fatigue.
A common viral illness of young children, typically 6 months to 3 years, most often caused by parainfluenza viruses, producing upper airway obstruction at the subglottis.
Characterised by a barking (seal-like) cough, inspiratory stridor, and hoarseness, usually preceded by coryza and worse at night.
Diagnosis is clinical; a frontal neck radiograph may show subglottic narrowing (the steeple sign) but is not required.
Corticosteroids are the mainstay and benefit essentially all severities, reducing symptoms and the need for further intervention.
Nebulised adrenaline (epinephrine) provides rapid, temporary relief in moderate to severe cases and mandates a period of observation for rebound.
Keeping the child calm and comfortable is important, as agitation and crying worsen airway obstruction.
Stridor at rest, marked recession, or hypoxaemia indicates significant obstruction requiring active treatment.
Consider alternative diagnoses when the presentation is atypical: sudden toxic appearance suggests epiglottitis or bacterial tracheitis, and drooling with dysphagia is a warning sign.
Distressing the child with unnecessary examination or procedures, worsening obstruction
Withholding corticosteroids in mild cases where they still provide benefit
Discharging a child after nebulised adrenaline without an adequate observation period for rebound
Failing to recognise epiglottitis or bacterial tracheitis presenting with a croup-like picture
Most children have mild, self-limiting illness that resolves within a few days; severe airway compromise is uncommon and the need for intubation is rare with appropriate treatment.

chunks.text: Prolonged compression of muscle causes ischaemic and pressure necrosis (rhabdomyolysis). While compressed, the injury is largely contained, but on release reperfusion washes the accumulated intracellular contents into the systemic circulation. Potassium, myoglobin, phosphate, and organic acids surge, producing hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, and hypocalcaemia. Myoglobin precipitates in the renal tubules, and combined with hypovolaemia from fluid sequestration into damaged muscle, causes acute kidney injury. Massive fluid shifts and the release of vasoactive and inflammatory mediators can cause shock, while swelling within fascial compartments produces compartment syndrome.

Cryptococcal infection is almost always acquired by inhalation of aerosolized particles (small desiccated yeast cells or basidiospores); occasionally by direct skin inoculation. C. neoformans is found in soils contaminated with avian (pigeon) excreta, whereas C. gattii inhabits arboreal species such as eucalyptus and is not found in bird feces. Infection is acquired in childhood and is common, but disease is rare in the absence of impaired immunity, indicating that intact pulmonary defenses effectively contain the fungus. Some infections lead to latency with viable organisms harbored in granulomas. Extrapulmonary dissemination to the CNS may occur via direct fungal migration across endothelium and via macrophage 'Trojan horse' carriage. Virulence factors include the antiphagocytic polysaccharide capsule, melanin production, and enzymes (phospholipase, urease). Copious release of capsular polysaccharide into tissues interferes with local immune responses, and infection may elicit little or no inflammatory response; capsular polysaccharide is the antigen measured diagnostically (p.1704).
Caused by Cryptococcus, a genus of yeast-like fungi; WHO declared C. neoformans a critical priority pathogen in 2022 (p.1703).
Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) can occur after starting ART in HIV; recommended to start ART 4-6 weeks after initiating antifungal therapy (p.1706).
Serum CRAg screening is recommended for asymptomatic people with HIV and CD4+ counts <100-200/uL to identify those at high risk of cryptococcal disease (p.1705-1706).
C. neoformans and C. gattii are now regarded as species complexes; for clinical purposes both cause indistinguishable disease termed cryptococcosis (p.1703-1704).
High-risk hosts for C. neoformans: hematologic malignancy, solid-organ transplant, advanced liver disease, diabetes, glucocorticoid therapy, and advanced HIV with CD4+ counts <200/uL (p.1704).
C. gattii disease is NOT generally associated with specific immune deficits and often occurs in immunocompetent individuals; associated with autoantibodies to GM-CSF (p.1704).
Disease usually presents as pulmonary disease and/or chronic meningoencephalitis, but cryptococcosis can affect any tissue or organ (p.1704-1705).

Cryptococcal meningitis differs from bacterial meningitis: many patients present with symptoms of several weeks' duration and classic meningismus may be absent; indolent cases can present as subacute dementia or depression (p.1705).
In AIDS patients, cryptococcal meningitis is the initial AIDS-defining illness in ~2% and generally occurs with CD4+ counts <100/uL; about one-third also have pulmonary disease (p.1606).

Diagnosis requires demonstration of cryptococcal cells or antigen in normally sterile tissue; India ink of CSF shows encapsulated yeast and CRAg (serum/CSF) is both sensitive and specific with rapid point-of-care lateral flow assays (p.1705).
Increased intracranial pressure in cryptococcal meningoencephalitis is managed by repeated therapeutic lumbar punctures and shunt placement; mannitol and acetazolamide are NOT effective (p.1706).
India ink and Gram stain may be falsely negative with low fungal burden or misread as positive by inexperienced operators (p.1705).
CRAg is often negative in pulmonary cryptococcosis, so it is less useful for diagnosing pulmonary disease and of only limited use in monitoring response to therapy (p.1705).
Cryptococcal cells with negative cultures on CSF staining and persistently elevated CSF/blood cryptococcal antigen long after culture clearance do NOT indicate treatment failure (p.1705).
Categorizing cryptococcosis as 'extrapulmonary without CNS involvement' should be made only after CSF evaluation reveals no evidence of cryptococcal infection (p.1705).

Prophylactic dexamethasone in HIV-associated cryptococcosis is NOT recommended (associated with reduced fungal clearance and increased mortality); glucocorticoids are not helpful for raised ICP unless from a mass lesion with edema (p.1706).
Echinocandins are NOT effective against Cryptococcus species (p.1706).
IRIS can be difficult to distinguish from relapsing/refractory infection (p.1706).

Even with antifungal therapy, cryptococcosis carries high morbidity and mortality. The most important prognostic factors are the extent and duration of the underlying immunologic deficit. Disease is often curable in those with no apparent immune dysfunction, but in irreversible immunosuppression the goal is remission maintained by lifelong suppressive therapy. Before ART, median survival for AIDS patients with cryptococcosis was <1 year. Cryptococcosis with underlying neoplastic disease has a particularly poor prognosis. Poor prognostic markers for CNS disease: positive India ink on initial CSF exam (heavy fungal burden), high CSF pressure, low CSF glucose, low CSF pleocytosis (<2/uL), recovery of yeast from extraneural sites, absence of antibody to capsular polysaccharide, CSF or serum cryptococcal antigen level >=1:32, and concomitant glucocorticoid therapy or hematologic malignancy. Relapse is common even with relatively intact immunity (p.1706).
Raised intracranial pressure in cryptococcal meningoencephalitis requiring serial therapeutic lumbar puncture drainage (and possible shunt placement)
Sudden catastrophic vision loss from meningeal cryptococcosis
Cranial nerve paresis, vision and hearing loss
Altered mental status, headache, and blurred vision as clues to elevated ICP
Refractory cryptococcosis despite antifungal therapy (prompt susceptibility testing)

Nonsevere disease limited to the lungs or other non-CNS sites is distinguished from severe disease or CNS involvement; severe/CNS cryptococcosis is treated with induction, consolidation, and maintenance phases (p.1705).

chunks.text: Ingested Cryptosporidium oocysts release sporozoites that invade the apical surface of intestinal epithelial cells, residing in an intracellular but extracytoplasmic compartment. Infection blunts villi, impairs absorption and increases secretion, producing a watery, non-bloody diarrhoea. In immunocompetent people a robust cellular immune response clears the parasite, but when T-cell immunity is deficient the organism proliferates unchecked, causing high-volume chronic diarrhoea, malabsorption and spread to biliary and respiratory epithelium.

chunks.text: Palindromic rheumatism (Harrison 22e p.2958)
Psoriatic arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2958)
Osteoarthritis - CPPD pseudo-osteoarthritis variant mimics progressive OA, often in atypical joints (MCP, wrist, elbow, shoulder, ankle) (Harrison 22e p.2960-2961)
Rheumatoid arthritis - chronic symmetric CPP synovitis can clinically resemble RA (Harrison 22e p.2961)
Neuropathic (Charcot) arthropathy - severe destructive CPPD may radiographically mimic it (Harrison 22e p.2961)
Cellulitis - acute gout flare with warm, red, swollen periarticular tissue may mimic cellulitis (pseudocellulitis) (Harrison 22e p.2958)

Septic arthritis - crystal arthritis closely mimics it; aspiration with Gram stain and culture is essential, especially as bacterial infection can coexist with crystals in synovial fluid (Harrison 22e p.2958, p.2961)

Polarized light microscopy of synovial fluid - MSU: needle/rod-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent; CPP: rhomboid/rod-shaped, weakly positively or non-birefringent; apatite: non-birefringent (requires alizarin red S staining or electron microscopy); calcium oxalate: bipyramidal, variable/strong birefringence, alizarin red S positive (Harrison 22e p.2959, p.2961-2962)

HLA-B*5801 screening before allopurinol in high-prevalence populations (Southeast Asian, Pacific Islander/Native Hawaiian, Black patients) to reduce risk of severe cutaneous adverse reactions (knowledge point) (Harrison 22e p.2960)
Synovial fluid Gram stain and culture to exclude coexisting septic arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2958, p.2961)

Synovial fluid leukocyte count - gout flare typically 5000-75,000/uL; acute CPPD ~24,000/uL (range several thousand to 100,000); apatite and calcium oxalate usually <2000/uL (Harrison 22e p.2959, p.2961-2962)
Arthrocentesis of an unaffected first MTP joint or knee between flares can still demonstrate MSU crystals (Harrison 22e p.2959)

Plain radiographs - advanced gout: well-defined erosions with sclerotic/overhanging margins, soft tissue tophi; CPPD: punctate/linear chondrocalcinosis in fibrocartilage or hyaline cartilage (Harrison 22e p.2959, p.2961)
Musculoskeletal ultrasound - double-contour sign over articular cartilage indicating MSU deposition; can also reveal chondrocalcinosis in CPPD (Harrison 22e p.2959, p.2961)
Dual-energy CT - identifies MSU crystals by chemical composition (Harrison 22e p.2959)
Baseline labs to assess comorbidities and treatment safety: serum creatinine, liver function tests, hemoglobin, WBC count, HbA1c, lipids (Harrison 22e p.2959)
In CPPD patients under 50, evaluate for metabolic/familial causes: serum calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, magnesium, iron, transferrin (Harrison 22e p.2960)
Acute CPP crystal arthritis (pseudogout) mimics acute gout flares (Harrison 22e p.2960)
Apatite (basic calcium phosphate) deposition disease (Harrison 22e p.2961)
Calcium oxalate arthropathy - acute presentation may be indistinguishable from MSU, CPP, or apatite crystal disease (Harrison 22e p.2962)
Osteoarthritis (pseudo-osteoarthritis pattern of CPPD) (Harrison 22e p.2961)

Gout arises from an increased body urate pool due to chronic hyperuricemia, leading to supersaturation and crystallization of monosodium urate (MSU) within joints and connective tissue. Hyperuricemia is predominantly due to impaired renal urate excretion (~90%) and less often urate overproduction (~10%); a minority (~10%) of cases reflect inherited metabolic disorders (PRPP synthetase superactivity, HPRT deficiency). Crystal shedding from inert synovial deposits, triggered by metabolic factors, diuresis, rapid urate changes (including urate-lowering therapy initiation), local trauma, or medical illness, activates resident synovial phagocytes (monocytes/macrophages, mast cells) and the NLRP3 inflammasome, generating IL-1beta and other proinflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha). Phagocytosis of MSU crystals by neutrophils with a respiratory burst amplifies the acute inflammatory response. Persistent MSU deposition produces tophi (granulomatous inflammation around crystals) and chronic erosive gouty arthritis. In CPPD, increased cartilage inorganic pyrophosphate (largely from extracellular ATP breakdown, regulated by the ANKH transporter) combines with calcium to form CPP crystals; their release similarly drives inflammasome-mediated inflammation, analogous to hyperuricemia in gout. Apatite and calcium oxalate crystals can likewise stimulate synovial cell proliferation and release of proteases, collagenases, and prostaglandin E2, contributing to joint destruction (Harrison 22e p.2956-2962).

Initial gout flares are usually monoarticular; the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra) is involved in 70-90% of cases, followed by tarsal joints, ankles, and knees. Oligo- and polyarticular flares emerge over time (Harrison 22e p.2958).

Apatite (basic calcium phosphate) arthropathy can cause an extremely destructive arthropathy of the elderly, classically the shoulder (Milwaukee shoulder), with low synovial fluid leukocyte counts despite dramatic symptoms (Harrison 22e p.2961).

Hyperuricemia and gout are part of the insulin-resistance syndrome and associate with cardiometabolic-kidney comorbidities: obesity, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, myocardial infarction, stroke, CKD, and urate nephrolithiasis (Harrison 22e p.2956).

Gout flares often begin at night to early morning, are among the most painful conditions humans experience, and the affected joint becomes warm, red, tender, and very swollen, frequently mimicking cellulitis (pseudocellulitis) (Harrison 22e p.2958).
Untreated flares usually subside spontaneously within 1-2 weeks, with symptom-free intervals (intercritical gout) until the next episode (Harrison 22e p.2958).

Serum urate can be normal or low during an acute flare because inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 are uricosuric and can lower urate by about 2 mg/dL; seek historical or post-flare urate values instead (Harrison 22e p.2959).

In CPP crystal arthritis (pseudogout) the knee is most commonly affected, followed by the wrist; the first MTP joint (podagra) is rarely involved, a useful distinguishing clue from gout (Harrison 22e p.2960).
Initial acute CPPD attacks tend to last longer than typical gout flares, sometimes weeks to months (Harrison 22e p.2960).
Acute CPPD can be precipitated by trauma, severe medical illness, or surgery (especially parathyroidectomy, which rapidly lowers serum calcium and magnesium and sheds crystals) (Harrison 22e p.2960).

Women account for only about 5-20% of gout patients; most are postmenopausal, elderly, and often on diuretics with coexisting osteoarthritis, hypertension, or mild renal insufficiency. Premenopausal gout is rare (Harrison 22e p.2958).
Hyperuricemia in a prepubertal boy should prompt consideration of inherited enzyme defects such as HPRT deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan spectrum) or PRPP synthetase superactivity (Harrison 22e p.2958).
Relying on a normal serum urate during an acute flare to exclude gout - urate is often normal or low at flare onset (Harrison 22e p.2959).
Attributing a destructive 'osteoarthritis' in atypical joints (MCP, wrist, elbow, shoulder, ankle) to primary OA rather than recognizing pseudo-osteoarthritis from CPPD (Harrison 22e p.2961).
Assuming chondrocalcinosis on imaging is always CPPD - calcium oxalate deposition in chronic renal failure is an exception (Harrison 22e p.2961).
Missing apatite arthropathy because individual apatite crystals are not visible on routine polarized light microscopy and need alizarin red S staining or electron microscopy (Harrison 22e p.2961).
Overlooking inherited enzyme defects when hyperuricemia/gout presents in a young patient, particularly a prepubertal boy (Harrison 22e p.2958).

Untreated gout flares typically resolve spontaneously within 1-2 weeks, but recurrent flares over years can progress to chronic gouty arthritis with persistent low-grade synovitis, subcutaneous tophi, joint deformity, and erosive bony destruction. Controlling the underlying chronic hyperuricemia (urate-lowering therapy to a subsaturation target) can prevent recurrent flares and dissolve tophi, generally requiring lifelong therapy. For chronic CPPD there is no means to remove established CPP crystal deposits from cartilage and synovium (unlike urate lowering in gout), and progressive destructive large-joint disease may require joint replacement. Apatite-associated destructive arthropathy (e.g., Milwaukee shoulder) progresses indolently and may also lead to joint replacement (Harrison 22e p.2958-2962).

Crystal-proven arthritis does not exclude concurrent septic arthritis - bacterial infection can coexist with MSU or CPP crystals in synovial fluid; always Gram stain and culture (Harrison 22e p.2958, p.2961)

Acute CPPD can produce systemic features (fever, chills, raised acute-phase reactants), with low-grade fever in up to 50% and temperatures occasionally as high as 40C - mandates microbial culture to exclude infection (Harrison 22e p.2960, p.2961)
CPPD onset before age 50 warrants workup for underlying metabolic disease (hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypophosphatasia, hypomagnesemia) or hereditary CPPD (Harrison 22e p.2960)

chunks.text: Cutaneous larva migrans is caused by the larvae of animal hookworms, most often Ancylostoma species from dogs and cats, whose eggs are shed in animal faeces and hatch into infective larvae in warm, moist sand or soil. On contact these larvae penetrate intact human skin but lack the enzymes to cross the basement membrane, so they remain trapped in the epidermis. As the larva migrates it provokes a local eosinophilic inflammatory and hypersensitivity response that produces the itchy, advancing serpiginous track. Because humans are accidental dead-end hosts, the parasite cannot mature or disseminate and eventually dies, giving the self-limiting course.

Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens as an isolated forme fruste of CFTR mutation (p.2247)
Idiopathic/recurrent pancreatitis associated with CFTR mutation in at least one allele (p.2247)
Sweat chloride after pilocarpine iontophoresis (chloride >=60 mEq/L supports diagnosis; highly specific) (p.2246-2247)
CFTR mutation analysis / panels of several hundred variants, or complete CFTR sequencing with splice-junction analysis (p.2246-2247)
Immunoreactive trypsinogen (newborn screening) (p.2246)
Fecal elastase-1 (low in exocrine pancreatic insufficiency) (p.2246)
Sputum culture surveillance for resistant pathogens (Burkholderia cepacia complex, Stenotrophomonas, Achromobacter, mucoid P. aeruginosa, atypical mycobacteria, MRSA) (p.2248)

Mutation of CFTR, an apical epithelial anion channel that conducts chloride and bicarbonate (~1480 amino acids, gated by ATP hydrolysis without active transport against gradient), impairs hydration and clearance of exocrine secretions. In the airway, loss of CFTR-dependent anion secretion depletes the periciliary fluid layer, causing ciliary collapse and failure to clear overlying mucus; mucoobstruction with chronic infection drives an aggressive, unrelenting neutrophilic inflammatory response with proteases and oxidants, leading to airway remodeling and bronchiectasis. Low airway-surface-fluid pH may impair bacterial killing. Similar mechanisms affect pancreatic acini/ducts (fibrotic destruction, cyst formation, exocrine and eventually endocrine insufficiency), hepatobiliary tissue (biliary obstruction, focal/multilobular cirrhosis, portal hypertension), and intestine (meconium ileus, distal intestinal obstructive syndrome). Over 2000 CFTR allelic variants are described and grouped into classes I-VI by molecular mechanism (e.g., F508del is a class II protein-maturation/folding defect degraded in the endoplasmic reticulum; G551D is a class III gating defect).

Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive exocrinopathy affecting multiple epithelial tissues; the gene product CFTR is an apical anion (chloride and bicarbonate) channel that regulates the volume and composition of exocrine secretion (p.2245).

CFTR modulators (ivacaftor potentiator; lumacaftor/tezacaftor/elexacaftor correctors) are highly effective modulator therapy (HEMT); triple combination therapy is projected to benefit >90% of patients and improves FEV1, reduces exacerbations, and lowers sweat chloride (p.2247-2248).

Pulmonary exacerbation poor-prognosis pathogens that are rigorously monitored include Burkholderia cepacia complex, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, Achromobacter, mucoid P. aeruginosa, and atypical mycobacteria; MRSA may also signal worse outcomes (p.2248).
Infection commonly persists despite modulator therapy, so chronic respiratory infection and inflammation continue even after substantial clinical improvement on HEMT (p.2248).

Major morbidity and mortality arise from pulmonary disease: copious hyperviscous adherent secretions obstruct small and medium airways, and a complex flora including Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa is routinely cultured from CF sputum (p.2245).

P. aeruginosa shows stereotypic pathogenesis: an early sentinel colonization often becomes lifelong infection by the same strain, and over years evolves a mucoid (alginate-producing) phenotype that confers selective advantage and poor host prognosis (p.2245).
Radiographic sinusitis occurs in most patients with CF; the sinuses may act as a reservoir for bacterial seeding of the lower airways (p.2245).

Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency causes chronic malabsorption, poor growth, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency; high blood immunoreactive trypsinogen (used in newborn screening) and low fecal elastase-1 are characteristic (p.2245-2246).

CF-related diabetes mellitus occurs in >30% of adults and is multifactorial (endocrine pancreatic destruction plus, in some, insulin resistance); annual diabetes testing is recommended for adults with CF (p.2246, p.2248).
Men typically show complete involution of the vas deferens despite functioning spermatogenesis, and ~99% of males with CF are infertile (unable to conceive without in vitro fertilization) (p.2246).

Diagnosis is confirmed by disease-causing variants on both CFTR alleles and/or sweat chloride >=60 mEq/L together with characteristic exocrine manifestations; sweat electrolyte testing follows pilocarpine iontophoresis (p.2246-2247).

Several severe defects (F508del, G551D, nonsense alleles) predict pancreatic insufficiency, present in ~80% of patients; F508del alone accounts for ~85% of defective CFTR alleles in the United States (p.2247).
Hyperviscosity of eccrine sweat is NOT a feature of CF; the sweat test reflects defective ductal chloride reabsorption, not thick sweat (p.2247).
Anion flux through CFTR does NOT involve active transport against a concentration gradient (p.2245-2246).
Genotype does NOT reliably predict respiratory prognosis or longevity, even though some severe alleles predict pancreatic insufficiency (p.2247).
A subset of patients with F508del respond poorly to triple combination therapy, so modulator benefit is not universal (p.2248).
HEMT may reduce sputum bacterial density but does NOT eradicate infection; chronic respiratory infection and inflammation persist (p.2248).

CF has been underdiagnosed outside historically white populations (Eastern Europe, Latin America, Asia, India, and US minorities), often due to rare/poorly characterized variants and limited access to DNA/sweat testing (p.2249).

Modulator and other therapies have transformed CF from a disease that historically led to death in early childhood to one with frequent survival well into the fifth decade and beyond; US median survival now exceeds 60 years. Genotype is of limited value for predicting respiratory rate of decline or longevity. End-stage pulmonary failure may be treated with lung transplantation (median survival >9 years among adults). Marked geographic disparity exists: median survival is <30 years in much of Latin America versus >60 years in the United States (p.2248-2249).

CFTR mutations are categorized by molecular mechanism into classes I-VI: class I, absent synthesis (e.g., nonsense mutations G542X, R553X, W1282X); class II, defective protein maturation and premature degradation (e.g., F508del, ~85% of US alleles, the most common); class III, disordered gating/regulation (e.g., G551D, ~4% of patients); class IV, defective conductance through the channel pore; class V, reduced transcript number from promoter/splicing abnormality; class VI, accelerated turnover from the cell surface. Severity is not formally graded by stage; FEV1 <30% predicted is used as a lung-transplant referral threshold (p.2246, p.2248).

Mutations in the CFTR gene impair the CFTR chloride and bicarbonate channel at epithelial surfaces. Defective ion transport produces thick, dehydrated secretions across multiple organs. In the airways, viscous mucus impairs mucociliary clearance, promoting chronic infection, neutrophilic inflammation, and progressive bronchiectasis. In the pancreas, ductal obstruction leads to exocrine insufficiency and malabsorption; similar mechanisms affect the intestine, biliary tree, sweat glands (hence high sweat chloride), and reproductive tract.
An autosomal recessive multisystem disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, the most common of which is F508del.
It is a genetic disease, not an infection, though recurrent respiratory infections dominate its course and morbidity.
Suspect it in a child with chronic productive cough, recurrent chest infections, failure to thrive, and greasy, bulky, foul-smelling stools from fat malabsorption.
Meconium ileus in a newborn is highly suggestive and is often the earliest presentation.
Many countries diagnose it through newborn screening, but a positive screen must be confirmed, classically with an elevated sweat chloride test.
Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency is common and requires enzyme replacement and fat-soluble vitamin supplementation, with attention to overall nutrition.
Chronic airway infection, notably with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, drives progressive bronchiectasis and lung function decline.
Care is delivered by a specialist multidisciplinary team, and CFTR modulator therapies have transformed outcomes for eligible genotypes.
Attributing recurrent chest infections and loose stools to common childhood illness and missing the diagnosis
Assuming a negative newborn screen fully excludes CF, since screening can miss some cases
Underestimating nutritional needs and failing to optimise pancreatic enzyme and vitamin replacement
Delaying treatment of new Pseudomonas infection when early eradication is most effective
Overlooking emerging complications such as CF-related diabetes and liver disease

Survival has improved dramatically with multidisciplinary care, aggressive infection and nutrition management, and CFTR modulator therapy, with many people now living well into adulthood; prognosis is largely determined by the rate of progressive lung disease and nutritional status.

chunks.text: When humans ingest Taenia solium eggs, oncospheres hatch in the intestine, penetrate the mucosa and disseminate through the bloodstream to tissues, where they mature into fluid-filled cysticerci. CMV is a beta-herpesvirus with double-stranded DNA, icosahedral symmetry and a lipoprotein envelope; it replicates in the cell nucleus and can establish either lytic/productive or latent infection. After primary infection the virus persists indefinitely in multiple cell types and organs (silent latency). Primary infection in late childhood/adulthood elicits a vigorous CD8+ T-lymphocyte response producing atypical lymphocytes and a mononucleosis-like illness, with polyclonal B-cell activation generating autoantibodies. When host T-cell responses are compromised by disease or iatrogenic immunosuppression, latent virus reactivates; chronic antigenic stimulation under immunosuppression (e.g., post-transplant) is an ideal setting for CMV disease, and potent T-cell suppressants (antithymocyte globulin, alemtuzumab) markedly raise CMV syndrome rates. CMV itself further depresses T-lymphocyte responsiveness, predisposing to superinfection by other opportunists. Congenital disease arises chiefly from primary maternal infection; transmission to transplant/transfusion recipients reflects silent infection in donor tissues (p.1512-1513).

CMV is a beta-herpesvirus carried for life after infection; the infection is usually silent, and reactivation syndromes emerge predominantly when T-lymphocyte-mediated immunity is compromised (organ transplantation, lymphoid neoplasms, HIV, or critical illness in the ICU) (p.1512).

In immunocompetent hosts beyond the neonatal period, the most common manifestation is a heterophile-antibody-negative mononucleosis syndrome; unlike EBV mononucleosis, exudative pharyngitis and cervical lymphadenopathy are rare, though splenomegaly, prolonged high fever, fatigue and malaise are common (p.1513-1514).
The characteristic laboratory finding in CMV mononucleosis is relative lymphocytosis with >10% atypical lymphocytes (predominantly activated CD8+ T cells); heterophile antibodies are absent (p.1514).

Congenital CMV is the commonest congenital infection; most congenital infections are clinically inapparent at birth, yet 7-11% of asymptomatically infected infants develop sensorineural hearing loss over 5 years (p.1512-1513).

Clinical disease in the fetus/newborn is related largely to PRIMARY maternal infection rather than reactivation; primary first-trimester infection carries up to 40-50% risk of sensorineural complications (p.1513).

Preferred diagnosis is detection of virus/antigen/DNA, most commonly quantitative nucleic acid testing (QNAT) by PCR; the pp65 antigenemia immunofluorescence assay is an alternative, and CMV DNA in CSF aids diagnosis of CMV encephalitis or polyradiculopathy (p.1515).

In persons with HIV, end-organ CMV disease (especially retinitis) occurs particularly when CD4+ counts fall below 50/uL; flares of CMV retinitis can occur shortly after starting antiretroviral therapy as an immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) (p.1514).

An immune-complex glomerulopathy has been observed in some CMV-infected patients after renal transplantation, and CMV mononucleosis can produce transient autoantibodies (cryoglobulins, rheumatoid factors, cold agglutinins, antinuclear antibodies) via polyclonal B-cell activation (p.1512-1514).
Pathology shows enlarged 'cytomegalic' cells (2-4x normal) with an eccentric intranuclear inclusion surrounded by a clear halo producing the classic 'owl's eye' appearance (p.1513).

Tissue-invasive CMV disease (e.g., gastrointestinal) may be present despite NEGATIVE blood CMV antigenemia and viral-load testing - diagnosis may require endoscopic biopsy with histopathology, not blood viremia alone (p.1514).

Isolation of CMV from urine, stool, or saliva does NOT by itself prove acute infection, since excretion may persist for months to years; detection of viremia by QNAT or antigenemia is a better predictor (p.1515).
Serology is NOT recommended to diagnose acute disease in immunocompromised patients; IgG may not rise for up to 4 weeks and rheumatoid factor can cause false-positive IgM (p.1515).
CMV detection in blood does not equate to end-organ disease; clinical and tissue correlation is required.
Universal ganciclovir/valganciclovir prophylaxis is bone-marrow suppressive, favoring preemptive strategies in HSCT recipients (p.1515).

Immunocompetent CMV mononucleosis is almost always self-limited (illness lasting 2-6 weeks); most patients recover without sequelae, though postviral asthenia may persist for months and fatal infection is rare. Severely affected congenitally infected infants have a poor prognosis with a mortality of about 5% and few survivors escaping intellectual or hearing impairment; 7-11% of asymptomatically infected neonates still develop sensorineural hearing loss over 5 years. In immunocompromised hosts, untreated CMV may progress to severe end-organ disease; CMV disease is an independent risk factor for both graft loss and death after organ transplantation, and high blood viral loads in HIV predict severe disease and death (p.1513-1514).

Harrison frames CMV by host and syndrome rather than a formal grading scale: (1) congenital CMV - subclinical to severe disseminated cytomegalic inclusion disease; (2) perinatal CMV - usually asymptomatic; (3) immunocompetent CMV mononucleosis - heterophile-negative, self-limited; (4) CMV in the immunocompromised host - asymptomatic infection/viremia, 'CMV syndrome' (febrile leukopenia), and tissue-invasive end-organ disease (pneumonitis, colitis/GI disease, hepatitis, esophagitis, retinitis, encephalitis/polyradiculopathy), stratified by population in Table 200-1 (fetus/neonate, organ transplant recipient, HSCT recipient, person with HIV) (p.1513).

chunks.text: Dacryocystitis is inflammation of the lacrimal sac, almost always resulting from obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct. Obstruction leads to retention and stagnation of tears and mucus within the sac, providing a medium for bacterial overgrowth. Acute infection produces a tense, inflamed sac that may progress to abscess formation, while chronic obstruction causes a mucocele with recurrent low-grade infection and persistent watering. In infants, incomplete canalisation of the duct at the valve of Hasner is the usual cause.

Decompensation is driven by portal hypertension plus renal sodium and water retention. Portal hypertension (elevation of the hepatic venous pressure gradient >5 mmHg) arises from two simultaneous processes: increased intrahepatic resistance from fibrosis disrupting sinusoidal architecture, stellate-cell-mediated smooth-muscle contraction, regenerative nodules, microthrombi, and reduced intrahepatic endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) causing intrahepatic vasoconstriction; and increased splanchnic blood flow from systemic vasodilation. Systemically, raised nitric oxide, VEGF and TNF cause splanchnic arterial vasodilation, pooling blood and reducing effective circulating volume; the kidneys sense this as hypovolemia and activate ADH, the sympathetic nervous system and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, producing free-water and sodium retention (ascites/edema). Encephalopathy results from gut-derived neurotoxins bypassing the liver via portosystemic shunting and reduced hepatic mass. (p.370, p.2756, p.2759)

Compensated cirrhosis can be asymptomatic for a decade or more; the transition to decompensation is marked by the first major event — ascites/edema, variceal hemorrhage, hepatic encephalopathy, or jaundice. (p.2756, p.2754)
Once clinically significant portal hypertension (HVPG ≥5 mmHg, with substantial decompensation risk at ≥10 mmHg) progresses to overt decompensation, median survival is under 2 years. (p.2756)

Encephalopathy in chronic liver disease is almost always triggered by an identifiable precipitant (GI bleeding, infection, volume depletion/overdiuresis, hyponatremia, constipation, uremia, sedatives/narcotics) rather than spontaneous progression. (p.2673, p.2759)

Ammonia levels correlate poorly with the severity of encephalopathy or liver disease; the diagnosis of hepatic encephalopathy is clinical, and most hepatologists do not rely on ammonia to make the diagnosis or follow progress. (p.2759)
A new or worsening encephalopathy episode mandates a search for occult infection — if ascites is present it should be tapped to exclude SBP. (p.2759)
A hyperdynamic circulation (widened pulse pressure, increased cardiac output, reduced peripheral resistance from splanchnic vasodilation) is a hallmark of advanced cirrhosis. (p.2673)

Acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) is acutely decompensating cirrhosis with one or more extrahepatic organ failures, behaves like a sepsis syndrome, and carries 28-day mortality of 20-70% rising with the number of failing organs; it is most often precipitated by bacterial/fungal infection or alcoholic hepatitis. (p.2760)

Decompensation defines a poor-prognosis state: with clinically significant portal hypertension that decompensates, median survival is under 2 years, and fewer than 50% of patients survive 2 years after the onset of ascites. Encephalopathy in chronic liver disease is a poor prognostic sign. HRS (both AKI and CKD types) carries a poor prognosis unless liver transplantation is achieved. ACLF 28-day mortality ranges from 20-70%, rising with the number of organ failures. Severity and transplant priority are graded by Child-Pugh class and the MELD/MELD-Na (MELD 3.0) systems. MELD score uses INR, bilirubin, and creatinine to predict short-term mortality and allocate organs; it was extended with serum sodium and reweighted as MELD-Na / MELD 3.0 for transplant listing. PELD is the pediatric equivalent. Clinically significant portal hypertension is defined by HVPG ≥10 mmHg. (p.2675-2676, p.2756, p.2754)

VTE arises from Virchow's triad of venous stasis, hypercoagulability, and endothelial injury, typically coupled with an inflammatory trigger. Activated platelets release microparticles bearing proinflammatory mediators that recruit neutrophils to form neutrophil extracellular traps; the contained histones drive platelet aggregation and platelet-dependent thrombin generation, and thrombi flourish in conditions of stasis, low oxygen tension, and upregulated proinflammatory genes. Inherited prothrombotic states include factor V Leiden (resistance to protein C) and the prothrombin gene mutation; deficiencies of antithrombin, protein C, and protein S are associated with VTE but rare. Lower-extremity DVT usually begins in the calf and may propagate to the popliteal, femoral, and iliac veins; when thrombi detach they embolize through the vena cava and right heart to lodge in the pulmonary arteries. PE impairs gas exchange, causing arterial hypoxemia and a widened alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient, increased anatomic and physiologic dead space, increased pulmonary vascular resistance (from mechanical obstruction and vasoconstrictors such as serotonin), reflex hyperventilation, increased airway resistance, and reduced pulmonary compliance. Rising pulmonary artery pressure increases RV wall tension, causing RV dilation and dysfunction with BNP release; the interventricular septum bows into and compresses the left ventricle, impairing LV filling; elevated RV wall tension also compresses the right coronary artery, producing RV ischemia/microinfarction with troponin release, and LV underfilling can culminate in falling cardiac output, hypotension, circulatory collapse, and death.

PE is described as the great masquerader; symptoms and signs are nonspecific, and unexplained breathlessness is its most common symptom. Failure to improve despite standard therapy for concurrent heart failure or pneumonia is a clue to coexisting PE.

McConnell's sign on echocardiography (RV free-wall hypokinesis with preserved or hyperkinetic RV apex) is a recognized indirect sign of PE, but most PE patients have a normal echocardiogram, so echo is not a reliable rule-out test.

Many patients with PE have no demonstrable DVT because the leg thrombus has already embolized; paradoxical embolism to the arterial circulation can occur through a patent foramen ovale or atrial septal defect.

Antiphospholipid syndrome is an acquired (not inherited) thrombophilia predisposing to both venous and arterial thrombosis, and patients often warrant lifetime anticoagulation even when the index VTE was provoked.

The most common DVT symptom is a persistent, intensifying calf cramp or 'charley horse'; physical findings may be limited to mild lower-calf tenderness, although massive DVT can produce marked thigh swelling, tenderness, and erythema.
A diffusely edematous leg makes ordinary DVT unlikely, with the important exception of phlegmasia cerulea dolens, the most severe form of DVT.
Recurrent left thigh edema, especially in young women, should raise suspicion for May-Thurner syndrome (right common iliac artery compressing the left iliac vein), which may be associated with DVT.

Wells point scores estimate clinical likelihood of DVT/PE and are validated in ambulatory but not hospitalized patients; low-likelihood DVT or low-to-moderate-likelihood PE can be evaluated with d-dimer alone, while high-likelihood patients should skip d-dimer and go straight to imaging.

Age-adjusted d-dimer (age x 10 ng/mL as the upper limit for patients over 50 with low/intermediate PE probability) reduces unnecessary CT pulmonary angiograms, but it does NOT apply to suspected acute DVT.

Venous ultrasound diagnoses DVT chiefly through loss of vein compressibility; a normal vein collapses with gentle transducer pressure (the 'wink'), whereas an acutely thrombosed vein stays distended and non-compressible.
CT pulmonary angiography is the principal imaging test for PE; an RV-to-LV diameter ratio greater than 1 (RV enlargement) on CT predicts increased 30-day mortality.
ECG S1Q3T3 is relatively specific but insensitive for PE; the most common ECG abnormalities are sinus tachycardia and T-wave inversion in leads V1-V4 from RV strain/ischemia.
Relying on d-dimer in hospitalized patients - levels are frequently elevated by systemic illness, so d-dimer rarely has a useful role in inpatients.
Applying the age-adjusted d-dimer cutoff to suspected acute DVT - it is validated only for ruling out PE in patients over 50 with low/intermediate probability.
Using echocardiography as a rule-out test for PE - most PE patients have normal echocardiograms; echo is better for detecting mimics like MI, tamponade, and aortic dissection.
Assuming absence of DVT excludes PE - the leg thrombus may have already fully embolized.
Treating antiphospholipid syndrome with DOACs - warfarin, not DOACs, is the standard for APS.
Mistaking a diffusely edematous leg for routine DVT and overlooking phlegmasia cerulea dolens; conversely attributing all calf pain to DVT (consider ruptured Baker's cyst) and all dyspnea to PE.
Confusing cellulitis (fever, chills) with DVT.
Overlooking nonthrombotic embolism (fat, tumor, bone marrow, air, amniotic fluid, cement, talc/hair in IV drug users) as a cause of PE.

Prognosis depends on PE severity and RV function. Low-risk PE (about 65-75% of cases) carries an excellent prognosis. Submassive (intermediate-risk) PE (20-25%) with RV dysfunction and biomarker elevation has a high risk of clinical deterioration, and massive (high-risk) PE (5-10%) can cause cardiogenic shock, multisystem organ failure, and death. US PE-related mortality fell from 6 to about 4.5 per 100,000 between 2000 and 2017 but is rising among young and middle-aged adults, with the median age at PE death dropping from 73 (2000) to 68 (2018) and roughly 50% higher mortality in African Americans than Caucasians; mortality is consistently higher in socioeconomically disadvantaged communities. The 30-day all-cause readmission rate after PE hospitalization is about 11% and the 90-day rate about 15%, with recurrent PE the most common readmission cause. Long-term, roughly half of PE patients report persistent dyspnea, fatigue, and reduced exercise capacity and about a quarter have persistent RV dysfunction - the post-PE syndrome; chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) develops in about 2% of acute PE patients. DVT can lead to postthrombotic syndrome (chronic venous insufficiency) with calf/ankle swelling, leg aching, and, in severe cases, deep skin ulceration.

Systemic arterial hypotension with extensive thrombosis - massive (high-risk) PE, accounting for 5-10% of cases, presenting with dyspnea, syncope, hypotension, cyanosis, and possible cardiogenic shock and multisystem organ failure
RV dysfunction on echocardiography or RV enlargement on CT despite normal systemic pressure - submassive (intermediate-risk) PE
Combination of right heart failure with elevated cardiac biomarkers (troponin), indicating high risk of clinical deterioration
Phlegmasia cerulea dolens - the most serious form of DVT with diffuse leg edema
Hemodynamic instability portending high risk of adverse outcomes despite anticoagulation

Pulmonary embolism is stratified into three categories: Massive (high-risk) PE - 5-10% of cases, systemic arterial hypotension with thrombosis involving at least half the pulmonary vasculature, presenting with dyspnea, syncope, hypotension, and cyanosis and capable of causing cardiogenic shock and death. Submassive (intermediate-risk) PE - 20-25% of cases, RV dysfunction despite normal systemic arterial pressure; right heart failure with biomarker (troponin) release marks high risk of deterioration. Low-risk PE - about 65-75% of cases, excellent prognosis. (Wells clinical decision rules in Table 290-2 stratify pretest probability of DVT and PE rather than anatomic severity.)

DLB is a synucleinopathy: the defining neuropathologic lesions are Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites distributed through specific brainstem nuclei, the substantia nigra, amygdala, cingulate gyrus, and ultimately the neocortex. Lewy bodies are intraneuronal cytoplasmic inclusions composed of straight 7-20 nm neurofilaments with surrounding amorphous material; they stain with PAS and ubiquitin and are now identified by antibodies to the presynaptic protein alpha-synuclein. Accumulation of alpha-synuclein aggregates in neurons and glia classifies DLB and PDD molecularly as synucleinopathies, though neuronal and synaptic loss (rather than Lewy pathology itself) best predicts clinical deficits. Pathology progresses through three stages: brainstem-predominant, transitional limbic, and diffuse neocortical. Disease is thought to propagate via a prion-like mechanism in which misfolded alpha-synuclein spreads transneuronally along connection pathways; PD often begins in the enteric nervous system and ascends via the vagus nerve, and/or in the olfactory bulb. A profound cholinergic deficit from basal forebrain and pedunculopontine nucleus loss drives fluctuations, inattention, and hallucinations, while locus coeruleus adrenergic deficits impair arousal and alerting. Both genetic and environmental factors contribute; alpha-synuclein gene duplications/triplications and GBA (glucocerebrosidase) mutations are linked to PDD/DLB presentations, supporting a double-hit hypothesis of toxins acting on a susceptible genetic background (Harrison 22e p.3492).

DLB and Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD) are viewed as points along a single spectrum of Lewy body disease (LBD); LBD is the second most common neurodegenerative dementia after Alzheimer's disease (Harrison 22e p.3491).
Incidence of DLB is roughly 7 per 100,000 person-years; prevalence of both DLB and PDD rises with age and both are more common in men (Harrison 22e p.3491).
About 10% of PD patients develop PDD per year, with most eventually progressing to dementia over time (Harrison 22e p.3491).
A profound cholinergic deficit from basal forebrain and pedunculopontine nucleus involvement underlies the fluctuations, inattention, and visual hallucinations (Harrison 22e p.3492).

The timing between parkinsonism and dementia distinguishes the two: when dementia and neuropsychiatric symptoms precede or emerge alongside parkinsonism, the diagnosis is DLB; when dementia appears in a patient with long-standing PD, it is PDD (Harrison 22e p.3492).
Core diagnostic features of DLB are early psychosis with well-formed visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition, REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and parkinsonism (Harrison 22e p.3491).

The cognitive profile shows severe executive, attentional, and visuospatial deficits with relatively preserved episodic memory; prominent early episodic memory impairment instead suggests comorbid Alzheimer pathology (Harrison 22e p.3491-3492).
Fluctuations in attention and concentration can be marked, with short episodes of confusion or severe lethargy that may resolve rapidly (Harrison 22e p.3492).

Patients are highly sensitive to infectious and metabolic disturbances, and delirium precipitated by infection, a new medication, or systemic illness can be the first manifestation (Harrison 22e p.3492).

RBD, in which dream enactment occurs because normal dreaming muscle atonia is lost (sometimes causing injury to patient or bed partner), is a characteristic and often prodromal feature that may precede the syndrome by years (Harrison 22e p.3492).

A sense of a presence behind the person may precede well-formed hallucinations; delusions are less frequent and usually involve misidentification, infidelity, theft, or persecution (Harrison 22e p.3491-3492).
Autonomic and nonmotor features such as anosmia, constipation, depression, anxiety, orthostatic hypotension, and erectile dysfunction may appear early (Harrison 22e p.3492).
Misclassifying DLB as Alzheimer's disease because frequent AD co-pathology makes prediction of underlying disease challenging; prominent early episodic memory loss points to comorbid AD
Confusing DLB with MSA when autonomic features appear early; MSA autonomic dysfunction is earlier and more severe with relatively preserved cognition
Exposing patients to typical neuroleptics, anticholinergics, or dopamine agonists, which can trigger neuroleptic malignant syndrome or worsen symptoms
Overlooking that scattered Lewy body pathology in substantia nigra, amygdala, or olfactory bulb can be an incidental finding in healthy older individuals
Attributing fluctuating confusion solely to delirium and missing the underlying DLB diagnosis

DLB is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with no currently available disease-modifying therapy; only symptomatic management exists. Severity of behavioral, sleep, and autonomic symptoms correlates with substantial caregiver burden, depression, and reduced caregiver quality of life (Harrison 22e p.3492-3493).
New-onset delirium precipitated by infection, a new medicine, or systemic illness as the presenting feature
Severe sensitivity to dopaminergic medications and to typical neuroleptics, the latter risking neuroleptic malignant syndrome and death
Recurrent falls from early postural instability and orthostatic hypotension causing syncope
Violent dream enactment in RBD causing injury to patient or bed partner

Neuropathologic staging recognizes three stages of LBD progression: (1) brainstem-predominant, (2) transitional limbic, and (3) diffuse neocortical. Both DLB and PDD have a prodromal mild cognitive impairment (MCI) phase; prodromal MCI-Lewy body (MCI-LB) is distinguished from prodromal MCI-AD by clinical and biomarker features (Harrison 22e p.3492).

chunks.text: Following an infective Aedes bite, dengue virus replicates and causes a systemic febrile illness. In severe dengue an intense host immune and cytokine response transiently increases vascular permeability, allowing plasma to leak from the intravascular compartment; this manifests as haemoconcentration, serous effusions and, if severe, hypovolaemic shock. Concurrent thrombocytopenia, platelet dysfunction, coagulopathy and vascular fragility produce the bleeding diathesis. Pre-existing heterotypic antibodies from a prior infection can enhance viral uptake into cells (antibody-dependent enhancement), heightening the risk of severe disease on secondary infection.

chunks.text: Dermatitis herpetiformis is an autoimmune blistering disease driven by gluten sensitivity in genetically predisposed individuals carrying HLA-DQ2 or DQ8. Dietary gluten triggers production of IgA antibodies against tissue transglutaminase and, in the skin, cross-reactivity with epidermal transglutaminase. IgA immune complexes deposit in the dermal papillae, recruiting neutrophils that form the characteristic papillary microabscesses and cause subepidermal separation with vesicle formation. The same gluten-driven autoimmunity produces the small-bowel villous atrophy of coeliac disease, so skin and gut manifestations share a common mechanism and both respond to gluten withdrawal.

chunks.text: Dermatophytosis is caused by dermatophyte fungi of the genera Trichophyton, Microsporum, and Epidermophyton, which possess keratinases enabling them to invade and digest keratin in the stratum corneum, hair, and nails. Infection is acquired from other people (anthropophilic), animals (zoophilic), or soil (geophilic), with zoophilic species often producing more inflammatory reactions. The fungus spreads centrifugally through the stratum corneum, producing the characteristic annular lesion with an active advancing scaly margin. The host inflammatory response accounts for erythema and, in strongly inflammatory infections such as kerion, pustulation and potential scarring. Warmth, moisture, occlusion, and impaired immunity favour infection.

Drug hypersensitivity reactions are classified by timing, mechanism (endotype), and biomarkers. Type I reactions arise from mast cell and basophil activation, either IgE-dependent (requiring prior repeated sensitizing exposures, as with antibiotics, chemotherapy, and some biologics) or IgE-independent (first-exposure reactions via complement activation, COX-1 inhibition, or MRGPRX2 receptor activation by quinolones, vancomycin, icatibant, basic compounds, and certain THIQ-motif general anesthetics). Cytokine release reactions reflect T-cell and other immune-cell activation with transient IL-6 elevation. Delayed type IV reactions are T-cell mediated. Desensitization works because rapid, stepwise delivery of incremental antigen doses recruits inhibitory phosphatases to the IgE receptor, blocking signal transduction and mediator release so that the target dose can be reached without anaphylaxis; desensitized patients show transient conversion of skin tests from positive to negative. Mechanisms for non-IgE phenotypes are less well understood.

Drug desensitization (DD) is a temporary immunotherapy that delivers sequential, incremental small doses of a culprit drug over hours to safely reach the full therapeutic dose, taking advantage of mast cell/basophil inhibitory pathways rather than producing lasting tolerance.

Skin testing reliability falls with greater time since the index reaction and after severe anaphylaxis (mediator depletion can cause false negatives); anaphylaxis to penicillin or carboplatin has not been reported in skin-test-negative patients.

Platinum-drug IgE sensitization usually requires six or more exposures (fewer in BRCA-mutation carriers); skin testing is positive in over 85% of patients with recent reactions, and reexposure of skin-test-positive patients carries high anaphylaxis risk.

Tolerance achieved by DD is transient: it does not produce sustained tolerance and must be repeated for each new course, or when the interval between doses equals two or more drug half-lives; continued exposure (e.g., ongoing antibiotics or aspirin/COX-1 inhibitors) can maintain the desensitized state.

Roughly 10-20% of the health-care-engaged population claims a penicillin allergy, but most labels are unconfirmed; low-risk patients can be delabeled, and single-dose oral challenges have been shown safe in low-risk children and adults.

Serum tryptase is the specific biomarker of anaphylaxis: a level above the normal range (11.4 ng/mL) or above a patient's baseline (a 1.6-fold rise), measured within 30 min to 4 h of symptom onset, supports type I or mixed reactions.

A baseline tryptase of 7.5 ng/mL or higher may signal hereditary alpha tryptasemia (HαT) from TPSAB1 gene duplication on chromosome 16, an autosomal dominant trait in 4-6% of Caucasians that can worsen anaphylaxis severity.

Cytokine release reactions (CRRs) present with fever, chills, and back/chest/pelvic pain and headache with a transient IL-6 rise; mixed reactions combine type I and CRR features with both tryptase and IL-6 elevations.

The most widely used standardized protocol uses three bags (1/100, 1/10, and undiluted target concentration) with 12 doubling steps every 15 min, reaching target dose in about 5.7 h, adaptable to IV, oral, SC, IM, intraperitoneal, intraocular, and intrathecal routes.

Breakthrough reactions occur in roughly 10-30% of protocols, are usually mild and resemble the initial reaction, and do not prevent completion of DD in about 99% of cases; no deaths from DD have been reported.
Corticosteroids do NOT protect against anaphylaxis during desensitization; omalizumab (anti-IgE) has been used as an adjuvant in highly sensitized patients with severe IgE-mediated reactions.
Assuming corticosteroid premedication prevents anaphylaxis during DD - it does not.
Treating SCARS or other contraindicated phenotypes with DD, where even minute drug amounts can trigger severe reactions.
Expecting durable tolerance - DD is temporary and must be repeated each course or after a gap of two or more half-lives.
Relying on a negative skin test performed long after the index reaction or after severe anaphylaxis (false negatives from mediator depletion or time elapsed).
Maintaining unconfirmed penicillin allergy labels, leading to use of less effective, costlier second-line antibiotics.
Overusing one-bag protocols in highly sensitized type I patients, associated with more epinephrine use and failure to complete treatment.
Missing phenotype switching in oxaliplatin DD (type I converting to CRR/mixed reactions).

Rapid multistep desensitization is highly effective and safe across thousands of patients with infections, chronic inflammatory diseases, and malignancies. Protocols are completed in roughly 95-100% of cases (taxane series completed 95-100%), breakthrough reactions occur in about 10-30% and are usually mild, and no deaths attributable to DD have been reported. Drug delivery via DD achieves efficacy equal to standard administration (expected clearance of infection, reduced inflammation, comparable cancer responses); survival of platinum-desensitized cancer patients is noninferior to that of nonallergic patients, and ovarian cancer patients undergoing carboplatin DD have shown a 5-year life-expectancy advantage in one large series.

Hypotension with cardiovascular collapse, throat tightening, oxygen desaturation (grade 3 anaphylaxis)

Hypersensitivity reactions are graded by organ involvement and vital signs: grade 1 (mild, one organ), grade 2 (moderate, two or more organs), grade 3 (severe, with changes in vital signs/cardiovascular collapse). Reactions are also categorized by timing as acute/immediate (during or within 1-6 h of exposure) versus delayed (6 h to days or weeks), and by endotype (type I IgE/non-IgE, cytokine release, mixed, and type II-IV delayed reactions).

Laxity of the hip capsule and abnormal relationship between the femoral head and acetabulum, influenced by maternal hormones, intrauterine packing (as in breech position and oligohydramnios), and genetic factors, allow the femoral head to sit incompletely within or outside a shallow acetabulum. Without a well-seated femoral head, the acetabulum fails to develop its normal depth and shape, perpetuating instability and, over time, leading to secondary degenerative change.
A spectrum of abnormal development of the hip ranging from mild acetabular dysplasia to frank dislocation, present at or developing after birth.
Major risk factors include female sex, breech presentation, oligohydramnios, first-born status, and a positive family history.
Newborn screening uses the Barlow manoeuvre (to dislocate a reducible hip) and the Ortolani manoeuvre (to relocate a dislocated hip).
In older infants, signs include limited hip abduction, asymmetric thigh or gluteal skin creases, and apparent limb-length discrepancy (Galeazzi sign).
Ultrasound is the imaging test of choice in early infancy before the femoral head ossifies; plain radiographs become useful after a few months of age.
Early treatment of a reducible hip with an abduction device such as the Pavlik harness is usually successful and avoids surgery.
The later the diagnosis, the more likely that closed or open reduction and casting, or surgical procedures, will be needed.
Untreated or late-treated dysplasia leads to a limp, gait abnormality, and premature degenerative hip arthritis in adulthood.
Persistent clicks alone are usually benign, whereas a palpable 'clunk' of dislocation or relocation is significant.
Missing dysplasia in bilateral cases where symmetry masks the abnormality
Over-relying on benign hip clicks or reassurance from a single normal newborn examination
Not imaging or closely following high-risk infants (breech, family history) with a normal exam
Applying an abduction device too tightly, risking femoral head avascular necrosis
Failing to recognise late-presenting DDH in a child with a limp or waddling gait

When detected and treated in early infancy, most hips develop normally with excellent long-term function; delayed diagnosis increases the need for surgery and the risk of residual dysplasia, avascular necrosis, and early osteoarthritis.

chunks.text: The nasal septum is formed by the septal cartilage, the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid and the vomer, meeting the maxillary and palatine crests. Deviation arises when these components grow at differing rates or are displaced by trauma, so the septum buckles or angulates away from the midline. The deviation narrows the airway on the concave side and may obstruct the osteomeatal complex, impairing sinus ventilation and mucociliary drainage. Compensatory hypertrophy of the turbinate on the wider side can paradoxically cause obstruction there as well. Mucosa stretched over a spur becomes dry and prone to bleeding, and contact between the deviated septum and the lateral nasal wall can generate pressure-referred headache.
