chunks.text: Monogenic diabetes / MODY (autosomal dominant, onset usually <25 y, impaired secretion; HNF-4alpha, glucokinase, HNF-1alpha/1beta mutations; glucokinase MODY = mild stable hyperglycemia; HNF-1alpha MODY often responds to sulfonylureas) (p.3195-3196, 3203)
Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) - glucose intolerance arising in 2nd/3rd trimester; diabetes in 1st trimester is classified as pre-existing pregestational diabetes (p.3196)

Atypical diabetes (features of both type 1 and type 2, not single-gene; includes ketosis-prone diabetes) and latent autoimmune diabetes of adults (5-10% of phenotypic type 2 have GAD/ICA) (p.3196, 3204)
Pancreatogenic (type 3c) DM from pancreatitis, pancreatectomy, cystic fibrosis (CF-related diabetes prevalence ~50%), hemochromatosis (p.3203)
Endocrinopathy-related hyperglycemia: acromegaly, Cushing's syndrome, glucagonoma, pheochromocytoma, somatostatinoma, hyperthyroidism (p.3196)

Drug/chemical-induced diabetes: glucocorticoids, calcineurin/mTOR inhibitors, pentamidine, nicotinic acid, statins, HIV/protease-inhibitor therapy, thiazides, second-generation antipsychotics, immune checkpoint inhibitors (p.3196, 3203)
Neonatal diabetes (onset <6 months; ATP-sensitive K+ channel subunit mutations may respond to sulfonylureas) (p.3196, 3203)
HbA1c (lab method NGSP-aligned to DCCT reference) for diagnosis and monitoring; affected by hemoglobinopathies and ancestry (p.3196-3197)
Fasting plasma glucose and 75-g OGTT (OGTT mainly for pregnancy/GDM and CF-related diabetes screening) (p.3197)
Islet cell autoantibodies (GAD, IA-2, ZnT8, insulin) to classify type 1 vs type 2 and identify presymptomatic type 1 DM (p.3200-3201, 3204)
C-peptide as a marker of endogenous insulin secretion (distinguishes endogenous vs exogenous insulin) (p.3198)

Spot urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) plus estimated GFR annually for nephropathy (screen 5 y after type 1 onset and at type 2 diagnosis); albuminuria = UACR >30 mg/g, severe >300 mg/g (p.3224)
Annual dilated retinal exam (or retinal photography) - nondilated primary-care exams are inadequate (p.3224)
Annual foot exam with 10-g monofilament, 128-Hz vibration, ankle reflexes, pedal pulses; annual DSPN screening for LOPS (p.3204, 3226)
In DKA/HHS: serum/plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate (preferred over nitroprusside which detects acetoacetate), glucose, electrolytes with corrected sodium, anion gap, bicarbonate, BUN/creatinine (p.3216)

Stress/illness-related transient hyperglycemia from counterregulatory hormone excess (surgery, infection, critical illness) - hyperglycemia in a hospitalized patient need not indicate established DM (p.3217)
Other causes of increased anion-gap acidosis when DKA is suspected: starvation ketosis and alcoholic ketoacidosis (bicarbonate usually >15 meq/L) (p.3216)

Hyperglycemia results from reduced insulin secretion, decreased peripheral glucose utilization, and/or increased hepatic glucose production, with the relative contribution depending on the DM type. Insulin is produced by pancreatic beta cells (from preproinsulin -> proinsulin -> insulin + C-peptide); glucose is the key secretagogue: it enters the beta cell via GLUT transporters, glucokinase phosphorylation is rate-limiting, glycolysis generates ATP that closes the ATP-sensitive K+ channel (target of sulfonylureas/meglitinides), causing depolarization, calcium influx, and insulin release; incretins (GLP-1, GIP) amplify glucose-stimulated secretion only when glucose is above fasting. Type 1 DM arises from interacting genetic (HLA region accounts for ~50% of risk; DR3-DQ2 and DR4-DQ8 predisposing), environmental, and immunologic factors leading to CD8+ T cell-mediated beta cell destruction and absolute insulin deficiency; alpha-cell dysfunction adds fasting/postprandial hyperglucagonemia with impaired glucagon response to hypoglycemia. Type 2 DM combines impaired insulin secretion, insulin resistance (post-receptor defects in skeletal muscle, liver, fat; lipid intermediate accumulation; low-grade metabolic inflammation), excessive hepatic glucose production (failure to suppress gluconeogenesis), abnormal fat metabolism (increased free fatty acids, altered adipokines, reduced adiponectin), giving the characteristic dyslipidemia (high triglycerides, low HDL, small dense LDL); beta cell function is reduced ~50% at onset and declines progressively. Complications stem from chronic hyperglycemia driving advanced glycosylation end products (AGEs), increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, epigenetic changes ("metabolic memory"), and growth factors such as VEGF-A in proliferative retinopathy.

DM is a group of metabolic disorders sharing the phenotype of hyperglycemia; it is defined as the level of glycemia at which a diabetes-specific complication (e.g., retinopathy) occurs, not as a deviation from a population mean (p.3195, 3197).

Distal symmetric polyneuropathy (DSPN) is the most common diabetic neuropathy and occurs in ~50% of long-standing DM; up to 50% are asymptomatic, so annual screening for loss of protective sensation (LOPS) is required - LOPS is a major risk factor for foot ulceration and amputation (p.3226).

Diagnostic criteria (any one, confirmed by repeat testing on a different day unless unequivocal hyperglycemia/acute metabolic decompensation): HbA1c >=6.5% (>=48 mmol/mol); fasting plasma glucose (FPG) >=7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL, fasting = no calories >=8 h); 2-h plasma glucose >=11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) on a 75-g OGTT; or a random plasma glucose >=11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) PLUS classic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss) (p.3197).

Prediabetes (each identifies different individuals via different biologic mechanisms): HbA1c 5.7-6.4%; impaired fasting glucose (IFG) FPG 5.6-6.9 mmol/L (100-125 mg/dL) per ADA; impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) 2-h glucose 7.8-11.0 mmol/L (140-199 mg/dL). WHO defines IFG as FPG >6.1 mmol/L (110 mg/dL). All three confer increased risk of type 2 DM and cardiovascular disease (p.3197).

Type 1 DM = autoimmune beta cell destruction with insulin deficiency; 25-50% present with DKA; ~40% of new type 1 DM now has onset after age 30 and is often initially misdiagnosed as type 2. Islet cell autoantibodies (ICAs: insulin, GAD, IA-2, ZnT8) are present in >85% at new onset and define a 3-stage model: stage 1 = >=2 autoantibodies + normoglycemia, stage 2 = autoimmunity + dysglycemia, stage 3 = overt hyperglycemia (p.3199-3201).

Type 2 DM = heterogeneous: insulin resistance + impaired insulin secretion + increased hepatic glucose production; >=80% of patients are obese (central/visceral). Insulin resistance usually precedes the secretory defect, but diabetes appears only once secretion becomes inadequate for the degree of resistance (p.3195, 3201-3202).
Type 2 DM may be asymptomatic for up to a decade before diagnosis, so some patients already have diabetes-specific complications at the time of diagnosis (p.3198, 3221).
HbA1c can be misleading with hemoglobinopathies and varies by ancestry; OGTT is reserved mainly for pregnancy/GDM and cystic fibrosis-related diabetes screening, not routine care (p.3197).

Symptoms of hyperglycemia: polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, fatigue, weakness, blurred vision (lens water-content change, resolves with control), recurrent superficial infections (vaginitis, fungal skin infections), slow wound healing (p.3203).

Microvascular complications usually do not appear until the second decade of hyperglycemia; macrovascular (ASCVD) risk, driven by insulin resistance and dyslipidemia, may develop before hyperglycemia is established (p.3221).

Do not over-rely on classic features (age of onset, obesity, insulin need) to classify DM - many adult-onset type 1 cases are misdiagnosed as type 2, and many new type 1 patients are now overweight/obese; measure ICAs when type 1 features are present (p.3199, 3204).
Euglycemic DKA can occur (notably with SGLT-2 inhibitors) - a near-normal glucose does not exclude DKA; check ketones and acid-base (p.3216).
In DKA, hyperamylasemia is usually salivary in origin and does NOT diagnose pancreatitis; obtain serum lipase if pancreatitis is suspected (p.3216).
Measured serum sodium is falsely lowered by hyperglycemia (correct ~1.6 mmol/L per 5.6 mmol/L [100 mg/dL] glucose rise); a normal sodium in DKA signals a profound water deficit (p.3216).
Serum potassium may be normal or high at DKA presentation despite a large total-body potassium deficit (acidosis/volume depletion shift) (p.3216).

Nitroprusside ketone tests detect acetoacetate, not the predominant beta-hydroxybutyrate, and give false positives with captopril, penicillamine, or valproic acid - prefer serum beta-hydroxybutyrate (p.3216).

Glycemic control may transiently worsen established retinopathy in the first 6-12 months of improvement, and GLP-1 receptor agonists with marked glycemic improvement have been associated with worsening retinopathy (p.3224).
CKD without retinopathy in type 1 DM should prompt a search for an alternative (non-diabetic) cause of kidney disease (p.3224).
Very strict glycemic control in acutely/critically ill patients (NICE-SUGAR) increased mortality and severe hypoglycemia - avoid overly tight targets in hospital (p.3217).

DM is a major cause of mortality (8th leading cause of death in the US, 2021; likely underreported) and was responsible for ~6.7 million deaths worldwide in 2021 (12.2% of global all-cause mortality in adults 20-79); about one-third of diabetes-related deaths occur before age 60. Cardiovascular disease is the main cause of morbidity and mortality, with ASCVD events and mortality 2-4 times greater in type 2 DM. In the US, DM is the leading cause of end-stage renal disease, nontraumatic lower-extremity amputation, and adult blindness; ~20-40% of patients develop diabetic nephropathy. Intensive glycemic control has durable benefit ("metabolic memory"/legacy effect lasting >=10 years): DCCT/EDIC showed reductions in retinopathy (47%), albuminuria (39%), clinical nephropathy (54%), neuropathy (60%), later a 57% reduction in cardiovascular events and 33% reduction in mortality; UKPDS showed each 1% HbA1c reduction lowered microvascular complications by 35%, and blood pressure control reduced complications even more than glycemic control. Diagnosis at younger age worsens prognosis (~3-4 years of reduced life expectancy per decade of earlier diagnosis).

Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): hyperglycemia (glucose >13.9 mmol/L [250 mg/dL]; may be near-normal = euglycemic DKA, especially on SGLT-2 inhibitors), ketosis, anion-gap metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate <15-18 mmol/L); nausea/vomiting, severe abdominal pain (may mimic acute pancreatitis), Kussmaul respirations, fruity breath, volume depletion, lethargy progressing to coma; cerebral edema is a serious complication mainly in children (p.3216)

Hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state (HHS): older patient, more pronounced dehydration, marked hyperglycemia (often 33.3-66.6 mmol/L [600-1200 mg/dL]) with mental status changes; mortality up to 15% (higher than DKA) (p.3217)

Hypoglycemia (<3.0 mmol/L, <54 mg/dL); hypoglycemia unawareness from autonomic neuropathy raises risk of severe events and can prolong QTc - sudden death has been attributed to cardiac autonomic neuropathy (p.3203, 3226)
New blindness risk: proliferative retinopathy with neovascularization and vitreous hemorrhage; clinically significant macular edema (p.3222-3223)
Loss of protective sensation / foot ulceration predisposing to lower-extremity amputation (p.3226)
Silent (painless) myocardial ischemia is common - absence of chest pain does not exclude coronary disease; consider cardiac evaluation before major surgery (p.3228)

Glucose homeostasis is a spectrum: normal -> impaired (IFG/IGT/HbA1c 5.7-6.4%, i.e., prediabetes) -> diabetes mellitus. DKA severity by ADA: mild (pH 7.25-7.30, bicarbonate 15-18 meq/L, normal mental status), moderate (pH 7.0-7.25, bicarbonate 10-15 meq/L, mildly reduced mental status), severe (pH <7.0). Diabetic retinopathy: nonproliferative (microaneurysms, blot hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots) vs proliferative (neovascularization) +/- clinically significant macular edema. Albuminuria: moderately increased UACR 30-299 mg/g vs severely increased >300 mg/g creatinine. Neuropathy categories: distal symmetric polyneuropathy, autonomic neuropathy, mononeuropathy, and radiculopathy/polyradiculopathy.
Diabetes Mellitus (non-infective) — Endocrine / Metabolic Also: type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes, DM
Diabetic neuropathy is a diagnosis of exclusion - confirm only after excluding other neuropathy causes (e.g., B12/folate deficiency, alcohol, other metabolic/toxic neuropathies)
Chronic kidney disease without retinopathy in type 1 diabetes should prompt investigation for an alternative (non-diabetic) cause of renal disease
Type IV renal tubular acidosis (hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism) as a cause of hyperkalemia/acidemia in diabetic patients
Renovascular hypertension when blood pressure is not readily controlled in type 2 diabetes
Celiac disease in type 1 diabetes presenting with diarrhea/constipation (associated anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies)
Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease, possibly autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome) in type 1 diabetes with orthostatic hypotension
Gas gangrene appearance in a diabetic foot may develop in the absence of clostridial infection
Superficial culture of any foot ulcer yields multiple bacterial species of uncertain significance - infected ulcer is a clinical diagnosis, not a culture diagnosis
Asymptomatic bacteriuria is common with diabetic cystopathy and generally does not require treatment

Dilated retinal examination by optometrist/ophthalmologist or retinal photography with remote reading (nondilated primary-care exams are inadequate); fluorescein angiography and optical coherence tomography to detect macular edema
Spot urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) plus estimated GFR, screening annually (start 5 years after type 1 diagnosis, at diagnosis for type 2)
Annual neuropathy screening with 10-g monofilament and vibration testing to detect loss of protective sensation; begin 5 years after type 1 diagnosis and at diagnosis of type 2
Gastric scintigraphy after a radiolabeled meal to document delayed gastric emptying (may not correlate with symptoms) in suspected gastroparesis
Ankle-brachial index for screening asymptomatic PAD in diabetic patients over 50 with risk factors

Foot ulcer workup: probe-to-bone testing with a blunt sterile instrument, plain radiographs for osteomyelitis in chronic non-healing ulcers, MRI (most specific) with nuclear/labeled-WBC studies as alternatives; cultures from debrided ulcer base or purulent aspirate
Cardiac stress testing in diabetic patients with symptoms (even atypical) suggestive of ischemia (routine screening of asymptomatic patients is not recommended)

Transient worsening of established retinopathy during the first 6-12 months of improved glycemic control (and with GLP-1 receptor agonist-associated rapid glycemic improvement) can mimic disease progression but is temporary

UACR can be falsely elevated by strenuous exercise, fever, infection, congestive heart failure, marked hyperglycemia, marked hypertension, or prostate disease - confirm on 2-3 occasions over 3-6 months
Acute painful diabetic neuropathy may be treatment-related, triggered by improved glycemic control

Chronic hyperglycemia is the principal etiologic driver of microvascular complications, though the precise mechanisms remain incompletely defined and are likely multifactorial. Proposed pathways include hyperglycemia-induced epigenetic changes altering gene expression, formation of advanced glycosylation end products (e.g., pentosidine, glucosepane, carboxymethyllysine) that cross-link proteins and bind cell-surface receptors causing endothelial and glomerular dysfunction and accelerated atherosclerosis, local growth-factor effects (VEGF-A drives proliferative retinopathy), and a unifying hypothesis that hyperglycemia raises mitochondrial reactive oxygen species/superoxide that activate downstream injury pathways. In nephropathy, soluble mediators (angiotensin II, endothelin, AGEs), hemodynamic alterations (glomerular hyperfiltration, increased capillary pressure), and structural changes (basement-membrane thickening, mesangial expansion, fibrosis) lead from early hyperfiltration/renal hypertrophy to irreversible albuminuria and GFR decline. Macrovascular disease additionally reflects insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and inflammation, with insulin failing to suppress adipose lipolysis and causing ectopic lipid accumulation (triglycerides, diacylglycerol, ceramides). In neuropathy both myelinated and unmyelinated fibers are lost; foot ulceration arises from sensory loss removing protective mechanisms, autonomic anhidrosis causing dry/fissured skin, motor changes producing deformity, and PAD impairing healing.

Diabetes-related complications are split into vascular (microvascular: retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy; macrovascular: coronary heart disease, peripheral arterial disease, cerebrovascular disease, heart failure) and nonvascular (infections, dermatologic changes, cheiroarthropathy, hearing loss, cataracts, glaucoma, fractures, cognitive impairment); patterns are similar in type 1 and type 2 disease.

Diabetes is the leading cause of nontraumatic lower-extremity amputation; foot ulcers arise from the interaction of neuropathy, abnormal biomechanics, peripheral arterial disease, and poor wound healing, and a wound that probes to bone is highly likely to harbor osteomyelitis.

Patients have greater frequency and severity of infections; certain severe infections occur almost exclusively in diabetes: rhinocerebral mucormycosis, emphysematous cholecystitis/pyelonephritis/cystitis, and malignant (invasive) otitis externa (usually Pseudomonas aeruginosa).

Characteristic dermatologic findings include xerosis/pruritus, diabetic dermopathy (pigmented pretibial papules), bullosis diabeticorum, necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum (predominantly young women), acanthosis nigricans (severe insulin resistance), and vitiligo/alopecia areata in type 1 disease.

Microvascular complications generally do not become evident until the second decade of hyperglycemia, whereas atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk (driven by insulin resistance and dyslipidemia) may precede frank hyperglycemia, so type 2 patients often have complications already present at diagnosis.

Landmark trials established that chronic hyperglycemia is causative for microvascular disease: in the DCCT, intensive control (HbA1c 7.3% vs 9.1%) reduced retinopathy ~47%, albuminuria ~39%, clinical nephropathy ~54%, and neuropathy ~60%; the UKPDS showed each 1-percentage-point HbA1c reduction lowered microvascular complications by about 35%.

A 'metabolic memory' / legacy effect exists: a period of improved glycemic control yields reduced cardiovascular events and mortality more than a decade later even after glycemic separation between groups disappears (DCCT/EDIC showed ~57% fewer cardiovascular events and ~33% lower mortality long term).

Diabetic retinopathy is staged as nonproliferative (microaneurysms, blot hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, venous caliber change, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities) and proliferative (neovascularization from retinal hypoxemia, risking vitreous hemorrhage and traction retinal detachment); neovascularization is the hallmark of the proliferative stage.

Macular edema can occur at either retinopathy stage and is a key cause of moderate vision loss; duration of diabetes and degree of glycemic control are the strongest predictors of retinopathy, with hypertension, nephropathy, and dyslipidemia as additional risk factors.

Diabetic nephropathy is the leading cause of chronic kidney disease and stage 5 CKD; screening combines a spot urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) and estimated GFR because some patients lose GFR without albuminuria. Albuminuria is a persistently increased UACR >30 mg/g (moderate 30-299 mg/g, severe >300 mg/g).

Diabetic neuropathy affects roughly half of long-standing patients and includes distal symmetric polyneuropathy (DSPN), autonomic neuropathy, and mononeuropathy/radiculopathy; up to 50% of those with DSPN are asymptomatic, so screening for loss of protective sensation (10-g monofilament, vibration) is essential.

Cardiovascular disease (CHD, PAD, cerebrovascular disease, heart failure) is the major cause of death in diabetes; heart failure is about twice as common (HFpEF, HFmrEF, or HFrEF) and 'silent ischemia' with absent chest pain is frequent, warranting a cardiac evaluation before major surgery.
Routine urinalysis does not detect low-level albuminuria - use UACR; and some patients lose GFR without albuminuria, so always assess both eGFR and UACR
Nondilated eye exams by primary providers miss diabetic eye disease - a dilated/photographic retinal exam is required
Once advanced retinopathy or moderate albuminuria is established, improving glycemic control provides less benefit - early detection is critical
Diagnosing diabetic neuropathy without excluding other etiologies; metformin can lower vitamin B12 and pernicious anemia is more common in type 1 disease
Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria unnecessarily; basing diabetic foot infection diagnosis on superficial swab cultures rather than clinical judgment and deep cultures

Failure to hold metformin around iodinated contrast and to monitor creatinine 24-48 h afterward; failing to reassess glucose-lowering drug choice/dose as GFR falls (sulfonylureas and metformin contraindicated in advanced renal insufficiency; SGLT-2 inhibitors ineffective below eGFR 20)
Overlooking silent ischemia given frequent absence of chest pain, and failing to evaluate before major surgery

Complications account for most diabetes-related morbidity and mortality. Diagnosis at a younger age increases lifetime complication burden (one estimate: 3-4 fewer years of life expectancy per decade of earlier diagnosis). Intensive glycemic control substantially improves outcomes: DCCT projections estimated several additional years free of vision loss, end-stage renal disease, and amputation, with overall added life expectancy, and 30-year follow-up showed durable reductions in retinopathy, nephropathy, and cardiovascular events (legacy/metabolic-memory effect). About 20-40% of patients develop diabetic nephropathy, and CKD on dialysis carries a poor prognosis. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death and outcomes after CHD are worse than in nondiabetic patients; CHD tends to involve multiple vessels and revascularization (PCI/CABG) is less durable, though CABG plus optimal medical therapy generally outperforms PCI. Diabetic polyradiculopathies (including amyotrophy) are usually self-limited, resolving over 6-12 months. Foot ulcers carry a substantial amputation risk (about 14-24% with that or subsequent ulceration). Some patients never develop retinopathy or nephropathy despite long-standing disease, suggesting genetic protection.

Neovascularization, vitreous hemorrhage, or traction involving the macula - urgent panretinal laser photocoagulation and/or anti-VEGF; surgical vitrectomy for severe proliferative disease with vitreous hemorrhage
Foot wound that probes to bone (high likelihood of osteomyelitis) or rapidly spreading cellulitis/severe infection requiring IV broad-spectrum coverage and possible surgical debridement

Severe infections seen largely in diabetes: rhinocerebral mucormycosis, malignant (invasive) otitis externa progressing to osteomyelitis/meningitis, emphysematous pyelonephritis/cystitis/cholecystitis - consider especially with severe hyperglycemia

Cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy with resting tachycardia, reduced heart-rate variability, orthostatic hypotension, and QTc prolongation - associated with silent ischemia and reports of sudden death
Hypoglycemia unawareness from autonomic neuropathy/reduced counterregulation, increasing the risk of severe hypoglycemia
Hyperkalemia/acidemia from type IV RTA, potentially exacerbated by ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists
Risk of radiocontrast-induced nephrotoxicity (preexisting nephropathy, volume depletion)

Retinopathy: nonproliferative (mild to severe, with microaneurysms, hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, venous beading, IRMA) versus proliferative (neovascularization), with clinically significant macular edema as a separate sight-threatening category. Albuminuria/CKD: UACR normal (<30 mg/g), moderately increased (30-299 mg/g), severely increased (>300 mg/g), staged alongside eGFR; nephrology referral when eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2, UACR >300 mg/g, or atypical features (hematuria, rapid decline). Diabetic neuropathy categorized as diffuse (distal symmetric polyneuropathy and/or autonomic), focal mononeuropathy, or radiculopathy/polyradiculopathy. Foot infection severity stratified clinically from mild/non-limb-threatening (oral antibiotics) to severe (IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, offloading, debridement).

Diabetes Mellitus: Complications (non-infective) — Endocrine/Metabolic (multisystem) Also: Diabetic complications, Microvascular and macrovascular complications of diabetes, Diabetic retinopathy, Diabetic nephropathy, Diabetic neuropathy, Diabetic foot
Starvation ketosis (bicarbonate typically preserved)
Alcoholic ketoacidosis (bicarbonate usually >15 meq/L)
Other causes of high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis
Acute pancreatitis or surgical abdomen (DKA abdominal pain can mimic these; hyperamylasemia in DKA is usually salivary, so serum lipase is needed)
Lactic acidosis (a small anion-gap acidosis from lactate can accompany HHS)

HbA1c at initial evaluation and at least twice yearly when at goal, every 3 months when control is inadequate or therapy changed (interpret with caution in hemoglobinopathies, anemias, reticulocytosis, transfusion, uremia, G6PD variants, hemodialysis, erythropoietin or HIV therapy)
Continuous glucose monitoring or capillary blood glucose monitoring for short-term control and time-in-range
Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate (preferred over urine nitroprusside ketone assays)
Serum electrolytes with anion gap, potassium, phosphate and magnesium (every 4 h in early DKA), bicarbonate, arterial pH
Serum/plasma glucose every 1-2 h during acute crises
BUN and creatinine (intravascular volume depletion / prerenal azotemia), serum osmolality
Serum lipase if pancreatitis suspected (amylase in DKA is often salivary and nondiagnostic)
Workup for precipitant: cultures, chest x-ray, ECG; corrected sodium calculation
Fructosamine or glycated albumin as alternative measures reflecting glycemia over the prior 2-4 weeks
Acute pancreatitis / acute surgical abdomen presenting with abdominal pain mimicking DKA
Other high-anion-gap metabolic acidoses (starvation, alcohol, toxins)
Alternative causes of altered mental status or coma (stroke, hypoxemia, intoxication) overlapping with severe DKA/HHS presentation

Hyperglycemia in diabetes reflects relative or absolute insulin deficiency with impaired glucose utilization and unrestrained hepatic glucose production. In acute decompensation, severe hyperglycemia drives osmotic diuresis with volume depletion. DKA results from relative or absolute insulin deficiency combined with excess counterregulatory hormones (glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol, growth hormone); the low insulin-to-glucagon ratio promotes hepatic gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, and ketone body formation, while increased lipolysis releases free fatty acids that are shifted toward ketogenesis, producing ketonemia and high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Inflammatory markers (cytokines, C-reactive protein) are elevated in both DKA and HHS. HHS is caused by relative (less severe) insulin deficiency plus inadequate fluid intake; insulin deficiency raises hepatic glucose output and impairs muscle uptake, and osmotic diuresis with poor fluid replacement produces extreme hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, and dehydration. The absence of significant ketosis in HHS is incompletely understood but is attributed to only partial insulin deficiency, lower counterregulatory hormone and free-fatty-acid levels, and an insulin/glucagon balance that does not favor ketogenesis. During exercise or acute illness, surges in counterregulatory hormones and cytokines cause transient insulin resistance and can tip toward hyperglycemia or, with relative hyperinsulinemia, hypoglycemia.

The three overarching goals of diabetes care are to relieve hyperglycemic symptoms, reduce or prevent long-term microvascular and macrovascular complications, and allow as normal a lifestyle as possible; symptoms usually resolve once plasma glucose is below ~200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L), so therapy mainly targets complication prevention. (Harrison 22e p.3205)

In DKA the measured serum sodium is artifactually low; the correction adds ~1.6 mmol/L of sodium for each 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) rise in glucose, and a normal measured sodium in DKA signals a profound free-water deficit. (Harrison 22e p.3217)

Inpatient hyperglycemia predicts worse outcomes, yet very strict glycemic control in the critically ill worsens outcomes; the NICE-SUGAR trial showed higher mortality and more severe hypoglycemia with a target of 81-108 mg/dL versus a moderate goal of <180 mg/dL, supporting a hospital target of roughly 140-180 mg/dL. (Harrison 22e p.3219)

Sliding-scale insulin alone (reactive treatment only when glucose is already high) is inadequate for inpatient management; scheduled basal plus prandial and corrective dosing is preferred, and CGM/automated insulin delivery are not FDA approved for ICU use. (Harrison 22e p.3219-3220)

HbA1c reflects average glycemia over the prior 2-3 months because erythrocytes live ~120 days, with the most recent month contributing roughly half the value; it does not capture short-term variability or recent intercurrent illness the way continuous (CGM) or fingerstick (BGM) monitoring does. (Harrison 22e p.3207-3208)

Continuous glucose monitoring measures interstitial glucose, which is in equilibrium with blood glucose but can lag when glucose changes rapidly or during exercise; an ambulatory glucose profile summarizes time-in-range, time above/below target, the glucose management indicator (correlating with HbA1c), and glucose variability. (Harrison 22e p.3207)

The general HbA1c goal is below 7% (or <=6.5% for selected patients), but a more lenient target of <7.5-8% is appropriate for those with cognitive impairment, hypoglycemia unawareness, or limited life expectancy; about one in four people over 65 has diabetes, so elderly targets must be individualized. (Harrison 22e p.3208)

A consensus CGM time-in-range goal for most patients with type 1 or type 2 DM is >70% of time within 70-180 mg/dL (3.9-10.0 mmol/L), with <4% below 70 mg/dL and <1% below 54 mg/dL. (Harrison 22e p.3208)

Ketones (preferably blood beta-hydroxybutyrate rather than urine nitroprusside assays, which detect only acetoacetate and acetone) should be checked in type 1 DM whenever plasma glucose persistently exceeds 250 mg/dL (13.9 mmol/L) or during intercurrent illness with nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain. (Harrison 22e p.3216)
DKA arises mostly in type 1 DM and HHS mostly in type 2 DM, but the two exist along a continuum of hyperglycemia and up to one-third of patients show features of both. (Harrison 22e p.3216)

Ketosis-prone diabetes can present with DKA at diagnosis in obese young adults of Hispanic or African descent who later recover insulin secretory capacity and can discontinue insulin after weeks to months. (Harrison 22e p.3216)

SGLT-2 inhibitor therapy can precipitate euglycemic DKA in type 2 DM, where glucose is normal or only mildly elevated because of glucosuria, so a normal glucose does not exclude ketoacidosis; resolution should be tracked by bicarbonate correction rather than by glucose. (Harrison 22e p.3216-3217)
Assuming a normal or only mildly elevated glucose excludes ketoacidosis; euglycemic DKA occurs with SGLT-2 inhibitors and resolution must be judged by bicarbonate, not glucose
Relying on urine nitroprusside ketone tests, which miss beta-hydroxybutyrate (the dominant ketone) and give false positives with captopril, penicillamine, or valproic acid
Interpreting hyperamylasemia in DKA as pancreatitis when it is usually salivary in origin; obtain lipase
Failing to correct serum sodium for hyperglycemia, masking a true free-water deficit
Misreading the early/at-presentation serum potassium as adequate; total-body potassium is depleted despite a normal or high initial level, and hypokalemia develops during insulin/fluid therapy
Trusting HbA1c in conditions that alter red-cell turnover (hemoglobinopathy, anemia, reticulocytosis, transfusion, uremia, dialysis, erythropoietin or HIV therapy)
Using sliding-scale insulin alone for inpatients, which is inadequate
Applying overly strict inpatient glucose targets, which increases severe hypoglycemia and can worsen outcomes (NICE-SUGAR)
Substances interfering with glucose sensors/meters (e.g., acetaminophen, ascorbic acid, hydroxyurea, mannitol/sorbitol for CGM; uric acid, galactose, xylose, L-DOPA for BGM)

With appropriate therapy, DKA mortality is low (<1%) and relates more to the underlying or precipitating event (infection/pneumonia, COVID-19, pregnancy, end-stage renal disease, myocardial infarction) than to the metabolic derangement itself; venous thrombosis, upper GI bleeding, ARDS, and cerebral edema (chiefly in children, during resolution) can complicate the course. Even a single DKA episode carries a substantially increased 1-year mortality, and recurrent DKA may signal underlying mental health issues or barriers to care such as insulin cost. HHS carries a substantially higher mortality (up to ~15% in some series) because patients are typically older with serious precipitating illness and comorbidities. Improved glycemic control reduces microvascular complications regardless of baseline level, and early intensive control in type 1 DM (DCCT/EDIC) lowered later cardiovascular events nearly two decades on.
Nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain in a person with type 1 DM (warrants immediate evaluation for DKA)
Kussmaul respirations and a fruity (acetone) breath odor
Lethargy progressing to obtundation or coma; cerebral edema (especially in children during DKA resolution)
Hypotension and tachycardia from volume depletion
Plasma glucose persistently >250 mg/dL or, in HHS, markedly elevated (>1000 mg/dL) with hyperosmolality (>300 mOsm)
Normal measured serum sodium during DKA (indicates profound water deficit)
Hypoglycemia, particularly recurrent, nocturnal, or with hypoglycemia unawareness
Signs of a precipitating event (infection, myocardial infarction, stroke, pancreatitis) even without fever

DKA severity is graded by pH, serum bicarbonate, and mental status: mild (pH 7.25-7.30, bicarbonate 15-18 meq/L, normal mentation); moderate (pH 7.0-7.25, bicarbonate 10-15 meq/L, mildly reduced mentation); severe (pH <7.0, bicarbonate <10-15 meq/L, reduced mental status or coma). Representative presenting laboratory ranges: DKA glucose ~250-600 mg/dL with bicarbonate <18 meq/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate >3.0 mmol/L, and elevated anion gap; HHS glucose ~600-1200 mg/dL (may exceed 1000) with osmolality >300, bicarbonate >18, pH >7.3, and absent/minimal ketones; euglycemic DKA glucose ~100-250 mg/dL with bicarbonate <18 and beta-hydroxybutyrate >3.0.

Diabetes Mellitus: Management and Therapies (non-infective) — Endocrine/Metabolic Also: DM management, comprehensive diabetes care, diabetic ketoacidosis, DKA, hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state, HHS, euglycemic DKA
Hypertensive nephrosclerosis
Glomerulonephritis or other primary glomerular disease
Ischaemic or atheroembolic renal disease
Drug-induced or contrast-associated nephropathy
Obstructive uropathy or recurrent pyelonephritis
Membranous nephropathy or minimal change disease presenting with nephrotic-range proteinuria
Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio for albuminuria
Serum creatinine with estimated GFR
Urinalysis to assess for haematuria or active sediment suggesting an alternative cause
Dilated retinal examination to look for concurrent retinopathy
Renal ultrasound and, in atypical presentations, consideration of renal biopsy

Sustained hyperglycaemia and glomerular hypertension drive haemodynamic and metabolic injury to the kidney. Early glomerular hyperfiltration, mesangial expansion, glomerular basement membrane thickening, and podocyte injury progress to nodular and diffuse glomerulosclerosis, the nodular lesions being the classic Kimmelstiel-Wilson change. Advanced glycation end-products, oxidative stress, and activation of the renin-angiotensin system promote albuminuria, tubulointerstitial fibrosis, and progressive loss of filtration.
Diabetic kidney disease is a leading cause of end-stage renal failure and usually develops after years of diabetes
The earliest clinical marker is moderately increased albuminuria (microalbuminuria), which can progress to overt proteinuria and declining filtration
Screening with an annual urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and estimated GFR allows early detection and intervention
Coexistent diabetic retinopathy supports a diabetic aetiology, and its absence in type 1 diabetes should prompt consideration of an alternative renal diagnosis
Tight control of both blood glucose and blood pressure slows progression, and blockade of the renin-angiotensin system is renoprotective in albuminuric patients
SGLT2 inhibitors reduce progression of diabetic kidney disease and cardiovascular risk and have become central to management
Features such as active urinary sediment, rapid GFR loss, or heavy proteinuria without retinopathy warrant evaluation for a non-diabetic renal disease
Assuming all renal impairment in a diabetic patient is diabetic nephropathy and missing a treatable alternative
Failing to screen for albuminuria and losing the window for early renoprotective therapy
Under-using renin-angiotensin blockade and SGLT2 inhibitors in eligible patients
Neglecting cardiovascular risk, which is the dominant cause of death in these patients

Without intervention diabetic nephropathy progresses to end-stage renal disease and carries a high cardiovascular mortality, but early detection and aggressive control of glucose and blood pressure, renin-angiotensin blockade, and SGLT2 inhibition can substantially slow progression.
Rapidly declining GFR out of proportion to expected diabetic course
Active urinary sediment, red cell casts, or nephrotic syndrome without retinopathy
Uncontrolled hypertension with worsening renal function
Signs of advanced uraemia or fluid overload requiring renal replacement planning
Diabetic nephropathy (non-infective) — Endocrine / Metabolic Also: diabetic kidney disease, diabetic glomerulosclerosis, Kimmelstiel-Wilson disease, diabetic renal disease
Vitamin B12 or other nutritional deficiency neuropathy
Alcoholic neuropathy
Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy
Uraemic neuropathy
Hypothyroid neuropathy
Toxic or drug-induced neuropathy
Lumbosacral radiculopathy or spinal stenosis
Clinical foot examination with monofilament and vibration testing
HbA1c and glucose assessment to gauge control
Serum vitamin B12, thyroid function, and renal function to exclude alternative causes
Nerve conduction studies in atypical or asymmetric presentations
Autonomic function testing including orthostatic blood pressure measurement when indicated

Chronic hyperglycaemia damages peripheral nerves through several linked mechanisms, including accumulation of advanced glycation end-products, activation of the polyol and protein kinase C pathways, oxidative stress, and microvascular ischaemia of the vasa nervorum. These processes injure axons and Schwann cells, producing a length-dependent loss of both small and large fibres. Involvement of autonomic fibres disrupts cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary regulation, while focal ischaemia or entrapment can cause mononeuropathies and radiculopathies.
The most common form is a distal symmetric sensorimotor polyneuropathy that begins in the feet and progresses proximally in a stocking-and-glove distribution
Sensory loss predisposes to unnoticed foot injury, ulceration, and Charcot arthropathy, making regular foot examination essential
Painful neuropathy can coexist with sensory loss, causing burning, tingling, and allodynia that are often worse at night
Autonomic involvement can produce postural hypotension, resting tachycardia, gastroparesis, bladder dysfunction, and erectile dysfunction
It is a diagnosis of exclusion, so other causes of neuropathy such as vitamin B12 deficiency, alcohol, uraemia, and hypothyroidism should be considered
Optimised glycaemic control is central to prevention and slowing progression, particularly in type 1 diabetes
Management of painful neuropathy relies on agents active in neuropathic pain rather than simple analgesics, alongside foot protection strategies
Attributing all neuropathy to diabetes without excluding treatable alternative causes
Neglecting routine foot inspection and patient education, allowing preventable ulcers
Undertreating painful neuropathy or relying on ineffective simple analgesics
Missing autonomic neuropathy as the cause of unexplained postural symptoms or gastrointestinal complaints

Neuropathy tends to progress with duration and poor control of diabetes, and established nerve damage is largely irreversible, so the emphasis is on prevention of ulceration and amputation and on symptom control; autonomic neuropathy carries an adverse cardiovascular prognosis.
Foot ulceration, deformity, or signs of Charcot arthropathy
Rapidly progressive, asymmetric, or predominantly motor deficits suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Severe autonomic features such as symptomatic postural hypotension or gastroparesis
Signs of limb ischaemia or infection complicating a neuropathic foot
Diabetic neuropathy (non-infective) — Endocrine / Metabolic Also: diabetic peripheral neuropathy, distal symmetric polyneuropathy, diabetic autonomic neuropathy, diabetic polyneuropathy
Hypertensive retinopathy

chunks.text: Chronic hyperglycaemia damages retinal capillaries through pathways including accumulation of advanced glycation end-products, oxidative stress, and pericyte loss. This weakens vessel walls (forming microaneurysms), increases permeability (causing exudation and macular oedema), and causes capillary occlusion leading to retinal ischaemia. Ischaemic retina releases vascular endothelial growth factor and other mediators that drive pathological new-vessel formation; these fragile vessels bleed and contract, producing vitreous haemorrhage and tractional detachment in advanced proliferative disease.

chunks.text: DIC arises from uncontrolled thrombin generation triggered by multiple mechanisms, with simultaneous disruption of physiologic anticoagulant pathways and abnormal fibrinolysis. In sepsis and trauma, activation of inflammatory pathways increases tissue factor expression, activates neutrophils and monocytes with cytokine release and neutrophil extracellular trap formation, and releases polyphosphates that cross-talk with the coagulation system (thrombo-inflammation); endothelial damage causes loss of native antithrombotic properties. The result is systemic fibrin deposition in small and mid-size vessels causing microvascular occlusion, ischemic organ damage, and red cell fragmentation/hemolysis. Sustained activation consumes platelets and clotting factors, producing systemic bleeding that is aggravated by secondary hyperfibrinolysis in late stages. Purpura fulminans is a severe form of DIC with extensive cutaneous thrombosis, predominantly in young children after viral or bacterial infection, especially with inherited or acquired protein C pathway deficiency (p.976).

chunks.text: Digoxin inhibits the myocardial sodium-potassium ATPase, raising intracellular sodium and, through sodium-calcium exchange, intracellular calcium, which increases contractility but also enhances automaticity and the tendency to arrhythmia. It also augments vagal tone, slowing sinoatrial and atrioventricular conduction. In acute overdose, widespread inhibition of the pump drives potassium out of cells, producing hyperkalaemia that reflects the degree of poisoning. Electrolyte disturbances (low potassium or magnesium, high calcium) and renal impairment increase myocardial sensitivity and reduce clearance, precipitating chronic toxicity at therapeutic or near-therapeutic levels.

Granulomatous inflammatory disease - sarcoidosis (often regional wall-motion abnormality, DCM phenotype, or RV involvement) and giant cell myocarditis (p.2002, 2016)
Eosinophilic myocarditis / Loeffler endocarditis (can progress to restrictive physiology) (p.2015-2016)
Collagen vascular / connective tissue disease, polymyositis, dermatomyositis, systemic lupus erythematosus (p.2015-2016)
Immune checkpoint-inhibitor myocarditis (most dramatic noninfectious inflammatory myocarditis) (p.2016)

DCM is characterized by decreased LV systolic function, typically with LV chamber dilation (LVEF <=0.50, usually <=0.40 at presentation). Multiple causes (idiopathic, familial/genetic, prior myocarditis, ischaemic, toxic/alcohol, chemotherapy, peripartum, tachycardia-mediated, metabolic/endocrine) converge on a common phenotype resembling post-infarct injury: early myocyte death, later apoptosis, and compensatory hypertrophy of remaining myocytes in response to increased wall stress. Local and circulating neurohormonal factors drive deleterious secondary remodeling; dynamic remodeling of the interstitial scaffold affects diastolic function and the degree of dilation. As the ventricle dilates, the mitral valve apparatus is distorted, producing functional mitral regurgitation. RV dilation/dysfunction develops directly from injury or, more often, secondarily from pulmonary hypertension and ventricular interaction. Chronic inflammation contributes to progression even when not initially implicated, and many 'acute' presentations have progressed silently over months to years (Harrison 22e p.2015).
DCM is defined by decreased left ventricular systolic function, typically with increased LV dimensions, although dilation may be minimal in some cases (p.2015).

Heritability is present in at least 30% of DCM without other clear etiology, and expanded genetic testing reveals pathogenic variants sufficient to cause cardiomyopathy in 20-40% of DCM patients (p.2003, 2013).
Quantitatively, DCM is defined when LVEF is <=0.50, but most clinical presentations occur with LVEF <=0.40; persistent LVEF <=0.30-0.35 is the threshold for primary-prevention ICD (p.2001-2002).

Despite multiple etiologies and variable initial presentations, DCM often progresses into a convergent clinical phenotype similar to that following acute myocardial infarction, with myocyte death, apoptosis, compensatory hypertrophy, and neurohormonal activation (p.2015).
Mitral regurgitation commonly develops as the ventricle dilates and the valvular apparatus is distorted, and is commonly moderate to severe by the time heart failure is advanced (p.2015).

Right ventricular dilation and dysfunction may result directly from the initial injury but more often develop later from elevated afterload due to secondary pulmonary hypertension and mechanical interaction with the failing LV (p.2015).

Alcohol is the most common toxin implicated in chronic DCM, but alcoholic cardiomyopathy is relatively rare and remains a diagnosis of exclusion; atrial fibrillation occurs commonly both early ('holiday heart') and in advanced stages (p.2016).

Truncating variants in TTN and other DCM disease genes can be found in about 10% of patients with presumed alcohol cardiomyopathy and about 15% of peripartum cardiomyopathy, indicating that environmental triggers can unmask genetic predisposition (p.2016-2017).

Chemotherapy agents are the most common drugs implicated in toxic cardiomyopathy; doxorubicin cardiotoxicity generally does NOT cause marked LV dilation, so stroke volume and perfusion can be low with only a modest fall in ejection fraction (p.2016).

Tests of thyroid function are part of the routine evaluation of cardiomyopathy because clinical signs of thyroid disease may be masked; hyperthyroidism should always be considered with new-onset atrial fibrillation or ventricular tachycardia (p.2017).

'Congestive heart failure' should NOT be considered a diagnosis or an etiology of cardiomyopathy - it is a nonspecific syndrome of congestion common to many cardiac diagnoses and requires thorough etiologic evaluation (p.2002).
Phenotypes overlap and evolve over time (DCM can reverse-remodel to higher EF; HCM can evolve to reduced EF), so reliance on a single morphologic phenotype is diminishing (p.2001-2002).
Alcoholic cardiomyopathy is a diagnosis of exclusion, and many patients are fully functional without apparent stigmata of alcoholism (p.2016).
Anthracycline cardiotoxicity can produce low stroke volume/perfusion with only modestly reduced EF because marked LV dilation is usually absent (p.2016).

In peripartum cardiomyopathy, edema and dyspnea may be mistakenly attributed to pregnancy itself; renin-angiotensin system inhibitors should NOT be given before delivery due to adverse fetal effects, and gadolinium should NOT be used on MRI during pregnancy (p.2017-2018).

Detection of anticardiac antibodies and viral genome fragments in chronic cardiomyopathy is of uncertain significance (possible cause vs neutral bystander) and is not in routine clinical use (p.2013).
Immunosuppression for nonspecific chronic lymphocytic myocarditis has not demonstrated convincing benefit (p.2013).

DCM secondary responses are often modifiable or reversible. Almost a third of patients with recent-onset cardiomyopathy without coronary artery disease show substantial spontaneous recovery to normal ejection fraction, and partial recovery to LVEF >0.40 ('heart failure with improved ejection fraction') is common with guideline-directed neurohormonal therapy, CRT for LBBB, and diuretics. Alcoholic cardiomyopathy can improve markedly within 3-6 months of abstinence but has a grim prognosis if heavy drinking continues. In peripartum cardiomyopathy, LVEF improves to >=0.50 in 50-80% of cases (often within 6 months); recovery is less likely with LVEF <0.30, LV end-diastolic dimension >=0.60, black race, and presentation >6 weeks postpartum; U.S. 1-year mortality ranged 4-11% and up to twofold higher in Africa. Takotsubo syndrome has a generally good long-term prognosis (lowest mortality with emotional rather than physical triggers) but in-hospital complications/mortality resemble acute MI, with ~10% recurrence (Harrison 22e p.2002, 2016-2019).
Sudden cardiac death risk: ventricular arrhythmias may be presenting events; persistent LVEF <=0.30-0.35 is the threshold for primary-prevention ICD (p.2001-2002, 2002)
Embolic events from atrial fibrillation or apical LV thrombi can be the first presentation (p.2002)

Peripartum cardiomyopathy with LVEF <0.35 carries higher risk of life-threatening arrhythmias at presentation and early after discharge, and marked dilation/LVEF <0.35 raises LV thrombus and embolic risk (p.2017-2018)

Acute cardiac presentation (elevated troponin, conduction blocks, bizarre arrhythmias) in a patient on immune checkpoint inhibitors warrants immediate coronary-care-unit admission and high-dose glucocorticoids without delay for biopsy (p.2016)
Hyperthyroidism combined with heart failure is a dangerous combination that may decompensate precipitously and fatally during titration of antithyroid therapy (p.2017)

Classification of cardiomyopathies: DCM phenotype - Early: LVEF <=0.50 and/or LVEDV >112% normal for age/sex or LVEDD >95% predicted for sex/height; LVEF <=0.40 is the threshold for traditional heart-failure therapies for low LVEF; persistent LVEF <=0.30-0.35 is the threshold for primary-prevention ICD. Mid-range LVEF 0.40-0.50 is often a transitional state (deterioration from early DCM or improvement into DCM remission). DCM is distinguished from HCM (increased wall thickness, septal >=15 mm men / >=13 mm women, LVEF >=normal usually >0.60), RCM (functional diagnosis from diastolic dysfunction/elevated filling pressures, often marked atrial enlargement), and arrhythmogenic CM (ACM-LV/ACM-RV/ARVC, ventricular arrhythmias dominating). (Harrison 22e p.2001-2002).

Candida (thrush) pharyngitis (p.1223)
Corynebacterium ulcerans / C. pseudotuberculosis, which express the same toxin and cause diphtheria-like disease (p.1222)

Culture of pseudomembrane fragments or submembranous swabs on selective medium (Loffler's or Tinsdale's, tellurite/colistin/nalidixic-acid based) plus nonselective medium such as blood agar (p.1223-1224)
Histopathologic demonstration of compatible gram-positive organisms / characteristic local lesions (p.1223-1224)
Notify the laboratory that diphtheria is being considered so special selective medium and biochemical differentiation from commensal corynebacteria are performed (p.1224)
Toxigenicity testing; report all toxigenic C. diphtheriae isolates to the state health department (reportable disease) (p.1224)
Nasopharyngeal culture in patients with cutaneous diphtheria (p.1224)
Repeat throat culture ~2 weeks after completing antimicrobial therapy to document eradication (p.1224)
Cardiac workup to assess for myocarditis (p.1225)
Antitoxin (antibody) titer measurement after recovery, performed 6 months after antitoxin administration (p.1224)

Disease is driven by diphtheria toxin produced by toxigenic (tox+) strains of C. diphtheriae. The tox structural gene is carried by lysogenic corynebacteriophage beta, and nontoxigenic strains can be converted to the toxigenic phenotype; iron-limiting conditions optimize toxin expression. The toxin is a single-chain 535-amino-acid protein produced in the pharyngeal pseudomembranous lesion, taken up into the bloodstream and distributed to all organs. After binding its receptor (a heparin-binding EGF-like precursor) it is internalized by receptor-mediated endocytosis; the A fragment enters the cytosol and irreversibly inhibits protein synthesis via NAD+-dependent ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor 2, causing cell death. Pseudomembranes consist of an inner fibrin band and a luminal neutrophil band overlying toxin-induced mucosal ulcers with edema, hyperemia, and vascular congestion; initially white and firmly adherent, they turn gray/green/black as necrosis advances and may extend into bronchial airways (p.1221-1223).
Respiratory diphtheria is clinically diagnosed by the constellation of sore throat, adherent tonsillar/pharyngeal/nasal pseudomembranous lesions, and low-grade fever (p.1223).

The diphtheritic pseudomembrane is gray or whitish and sharply demarcated; unlike the exudate of streptococcal pharyngitis it is tightly adherent to underlying tissue, and attempts to dislodge it may cause bleeding (p.1223).
A few patients develop 'bull-neck' diphtheria from edema of the submandibular and paratracheal region, with massive tonsillar swelling, foul breath, thick speech, and stridorous breathing (p.1223).

Diphtheria should be considered in any patient with severe pharyngitis, especially with difficulty swallowing, respiratory compromise, or signs of systemic disease (myocarditis, generalized weakness); a pharyngeal pseudomembrane or extensive exudate should prompt consideration (p.1222-1223).

Toxigenic strains most often cause pharyngeal disease, while nontoxigenic strains commonly cause cutaneous disease; in tropical latitudes cutaneous diphtheria is more common than respiratory diphtheria (p.1221-1222).
Once a clinical diagnosis is made, diphtheria antitoxin should be obtained and administered as rapidly as possible because antitoxin cannot neutralize cell-bound toxin (p.1224).
Hoarseness suggests laryngeal diphtheria, in which laryngoscopy may be diagnostically helpful (p.1223).
Antibiotics in diphtheria are used primarily to prevent transmission to contacts and to halt further toxin production; they are not a substitute for antitoxin (p.1224).

Patients who recover should be vaccinated, since natural infection does not reliably confer protective immunity; antitoxin levels should be measured (6 months after antitoxin administration) (p.1224).
Antitoxin cannot neutralize cell-bound toxin, so delay in administration worsens outcome; do not wait for laboratory confirmation once diphtheria is clinically suspected (p.1224).
Antibiotics are not a substitute for antitoxin; they mainly prevent transmission and further toxin production (p.1224).
Glucocorticoids have NOT been shown to reduce the risk of myocarditis or polyneuropathy (p.1225).

Cutaneous diphtheria lesions are not characteristic and are indistinguishable from other dermatoses, so diagnosis requires laboratory confirmation; the punched-out appearance is only occasional, not consistent (p.1224).
Corynebacterium pseudodiphtheriticum is a nontoxigenic normal throat commensal and does not pose significant risk; it must be differentiated from C. diphtheriae (p.1224).
Drug-resistant and multidrug-resistant C. diphtheriae strains exist and are increasing; consider resistance when eradication efforts fail (p.1224).
Natural infection does not reliably confer immunity, so survivors must be vaccinated (p.1224).

A systematic review of >20 outbreaks found a case-fatality ratio of 29% among unvaccinated, untreated individuals, with children under 5 at 1.5-fold higher mortality risk. Fatal pseudomembranous diphtheria typically occurs in unimmunized patients or those with nonprotective antibody titers. Risk factors for death include bull-neck diphtheria; myocarditis with ventricular tachycardia; atrial fibrillation; complete heart block; age >60 or <6 months; alcoholism; extensive pseudomembrane elongation; and laryngeal/tracheal/bronchial involvement. A key predictor of fatal outcome is the interval between onset of local disease and administration of antitoxin. Cutaneous diphtheria has a low mortality rate and is rarely associated with myocarditis or peripheral neuropathy. Polyneuropathy is typically reversible in patients who survive the acute phase (p.1224-1225).
Neck (submandibular/paratracheal) edema and difficulty breathing in advanced cases carry a poor prognosis (p.1223)

Airway obstruction is a major early risk and accounts for 60-65% of deaths, usually in the first 1-2 weeks; sloughing pseudomembranes may obstruct the airway or extend to larynx/tracheobronchial tree (children especially prone) (p.1224)
Toxic cardiomyopathy/myocarditis (cardiac arrhythmias or congestive heart failure), a late manifestation arising >=1 week after respiratory symptoms, accounting for 20-25% of deaths (p.1223-1224)
Bull-neck diphtheria, ventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, or complete heart block (p.1224)

Polyneuropathy 3-5 weeks after onset: cranial nerve involvement (lingual/facial numbness, dysphonia, dysphagia), then weakness of respiratory and abdominal muscles, limb paresis, sensory ataxia, and autonomic dysfunction with hypotension (~15% of deaths) (p.1224)
Large or extensive pseudomembranes and laryngeal/tracheal/bronchial involvement indicate severe disease and poor prognosis (p.1223-1224)

CDC case definitions: confirmed respiratory diphtheria (laboratory proven or epidemiologically linked to a culture-confirmed case) vs probable respiratory diphtheria (clinically compatible but not laboratory proven or epidemiologically linked). Carriers are individuals with positive C. diphtheriae cultures who are asymptomatic or symptomatic but lack pseudomembranes (p.1223).

chunks.diseaseName: Diseases Caused by Gram-Negative Enteric Bacilli
chunks.text: Enteric GNB are predominantly extracellular pathogens that normally reside in the colonic microbiota and environmental niches. Their outer membrane (lipopolysaccharide and capsule) is central both to virulence and to antimicrobial resistance via permeability barriers and efflux pumps. Disease requires accessory virulence genes: multiple adhesins (e.g., type 1, S, and F1C fimbriae and P pili in E. coli) for attachment; iron-acquisition systems (siderophores) and other nutrient-scavenging tools; capsule and O-antigen to resist complement and phagocytosis in the absence of antibody; and toxins (e.g., E. coli hemolysin) that cause tissue damage facilitating spread. The lipid A moiety of lipopolysaccharide acts as a PAMP that, through pattern-recognition receptors, can trigger an exuberant proinflammatory cascade leading to septic shock, with DAMPs such as HMGB1 propagating injury. Extensive antigenic variation (E. coli alone has more than 150 O, ~80 K, and ~53 H antigens) permits immune evasion and repeated infection and has hampered vaccine development. Host defenses are innate (intact skin/mucosa, complement, antimicrobial peptides, phagocytes, nutrient withholding) and humoral; impairment of these increases both susceptibility and severity. Intestinal pathogenic E. coli use distinct, pathotype-specific mechanisms (Shiga toxin, heat-stable/labile enterotoxins, attaching-and-effacing lesions, epithelial invasion, aggregative adherence).

chunks.diseaseName: Diseases Caused by Gram-Negative Enteric Bacilli
chunks.text: The enteric gram-negative bacilli (GNB) that most often cause extraintestinal infection belong to the order Enterobacterales and include Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterobacter, Serratia, Citrobacter, Morganella, Providencia, Cronobacter, and Edwardsiella; Salmonella, Shigella, and Yersinia are covered separately as mainly enteric pathogens.

chunks.diseaseName: Diseases Caused by Gram-Negative Enteric Bacilli
chunks.text: Pneumonia, sepsis, and septic shock arising from any GNB focus are especially dangerous, carrying reported mortality rates of about 20 to 60 percent.

chunks.diseaseName: Diseases Caused by Gram-Negative Enteric Bacilli
chunks.text: Serratia marcescens is notable for environmental and outbreak associations (contaminated infusates, prefilled syringes, soaps, even chlorhexidine); some strains produce red pigment that can cause distinctive findings such as pink breast milk, pink hypopyon, or pseudohemoptysis.

chunks.diseaseName: Diseases Caused by Gram-Negative Enteric Bacilli
chunks.text: In children with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC/EHEC) infection, antibiotics should be avoided because they may increase the risk of hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS), and adequate volume expansion may help protect the kidneys.

chunks.diseaseName: Diseases Caused by Gram-Negative Enteric Bacilli
chunks.text: Isolation of a GNB from a normally sterile site almost always signifies true infection, whereas recovery from nonsterile sites (open wounds, respiratory tract, catheterized urine) needs clinical correlation because it may represent only colonization.

chunks.diseaseName: Diseases Caused by Gram-Negative Enteric Bacilli
chunks.text: E. coli and, to a lesser extent, Klebsiella are the most virulent of this group and can cause severe disease even in previously healthy ambulatory people; the other genera behave mainly as opportunists in long-term-care and hospitalized patients.

chunks.diseaseName: Diseases Caused by Gram-Negative Enteric Bacilli
chunks.text: The urinary tract is the single most common extraintestinal site infected by extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli (ExPEC), and E. coli is the leading uropathogen across essentially all UTI syndromes and host groups.

chunks.diseaseName: Diseases Caused by Gram-Negative Enteric Bacilli
chunks.text: The urinary tract is also the most common source of E. coli bacteremia (roughly one-half to two-thirds of episodes); the abdomen is the second most common source (about one-quarter), and some abdominal sources such as abscesses can be clinically silent and require imaging.

chunks.diseaseName: Diseases Caused by Gram-Negative Enteric Bacilli
chunks.text: E. coli and group B Streptococcus are leading causes of neonatal meningitis; most neonatal E. coli meningitis strains carry the K1 capsular antigen, and ventriculomegaly is a common complication.

chunks.diseaseName: Diseases Caused by Gram-Negative Enteric Bacilli
chunks.text: Hypervirulent K. pneumoniae (hvKp), first recognized in Taiwan in 1986, classically presents as community-acquired monomicrobial pyogenic liver abscess in patients without prior hepatobiliary disease, often diabetic, with a striking tendency to spread metastatically (e.g., endophthalmitis, brain/splenic/prostatic abscess, meningitis, necrotizing fasciitis).

chunks.diseaseName: Diseases Caused by Gram-Negative Enteric Bacilli
chunks.text: Proteus produces urease, which hydrolyzes urea to ammonia and alkalinizes the urine; this promotes struvite and carbonate-apatite crystals, catheter biofilms, and staghorn calculi, and the organism typically cannot be cleared without removing the stone or catheter.

chunks.diseaseName: Diseases Caused by Gram-Negative Enteric Bacilli
chunks.text: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) are classified by CDC and WHO as an urgent, critical-priority threat and were estimated to cause more than 100,000 deaths globally in 2019, with the heaviest burden in low- and middle-income regions such as the Indian subcontinent.

chunks.diseaseName: Diseases Caused by Gram-Negative Enteric Bacilli
chunks.text: Treating colonization rather than true infection (e.g., asymptomatic bacteriuria or a positive sputum culture without pneumonia), which drives resistance and harm without benefit

chunks.diseaseName: Diseases Caused by Gram-Negative Enteric Bacilli
chunks.text: Relying on third-generation cephalosporins for organisms prone to inducible/derepressed AmpC beta-lactamase (e.g., Enterobacter cloacae, Klebsiella aerogenes, Citrobacter freundii), in which resistance can emerge during therapy and cause clinical failure, particularly in bacteremia

chunks.diseaseName: Diseases Caused by Gram-Negative Enteric Bacilli
chunks.text: Outcomes correlate with severity of illness, underlying host status, and the resistance profile of the infecting organism, which can lead to suboptimal therapy. Pneumonia, sepsis, and septic shock from any GNB focus carry mortality rates of roughly 20 to 60 percent; ExPEC pneumonia specifically has high crude (20-60%) and attributable (10-20%) mortality. Uncomplicated cystitis is largely self-limited and rarely progresses, whereas pyelonephritis can take 5-7 days for fever to resolve even with effective therapy and only uncommonly causes renal parenchymal loss (mainly with obstruction). hvKp infections can be life- and organ-threatening even in young healthy hosts, with survivors often left with catastrophic sequelae such as vision loss or major neurologic deficits. Pandrug-resistant strains exist, and extensive resistance can leave few or no ideal therapeutic options.

chunks.diseaseName: Diseases Caused by Gram-Negative Enteric Bacilli
chunks.text: Disease is stratified clinically rather than by a single formal score: localized/uncomplicated infection (e.g., uncomplicated cystitis with dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain) versus systemic/severe infection (febrile or systemic UTI/urosepsis, pyelonephritis, prostatitis, pneumonia, bacteremia, sepsis syndrome defined as dysfunction of at least one organ/system, and septic shock). Resistance is graded as multidrug-resistant (MDR), extensively drug-resistant (XDR), and pandrug-resistant; resistance mechanisms range from broad-spectrum beta-lactamases through ESBLs and AmpC enzymes to carbapenemases (Ambler class A serine [KPC], class B metallo-beta-lactamases [NDM, VIM, IMP], and class D [OXA-48]).

The esophagus is a muscular tube with a sphincter at each end (UES, LES) that transports food and otherwise remains empty. Disease manifests as impaired function (swallowing disorders, excessive gastroesophageal reflux) or pain. Dysphagia is subclassified by mechanism: structural/mechanical narrowing (lumen <13 mm reliably causes solid-food dysphagia) versus propulsive/motor disorders of peristalsis and deglutitive inhibition. In achalasia, autoimmune-mediated loss of myenteric plexus ganglion cells (involving both excitatory cholinergic and inhibitory nitric-oxide neurons), linked to latent HSV-1 infection plus genetic susceptibility, produces impaired deglutitive LES relaxation and absent peristalsis. GERD results from excessive reflux of gastric acid and pepsin causing a cytokine-mediated (rather than directly caustic) inflammatory mucosal injury; pathologic reflux follows progressive distortion of esophagogastric junction architecture (hiatus widening, loss of intraabdominal esophageal segment/flap valve, axial hiatal hernia, increased junction compliance) compounded by impaired acid clearance from disrupted peristalsis or reduced salivation. Eosinophilic esophagitis is an immunologic disorder driven by antigen (chiefly food allergen) sensitization in susceptible individuals, with eosinophil-predominant inflammation. (Harrison 22e p.2503, p.2506-2510, p.2511)
The major esophageal symptoms are heartburn, regurgitation, chest pain, dysphagia, odynophagia, and globus sensation; the clinical history is central to evaluation (Harrison 22e p.2503).
Erosive esophagitis at the esophagogastric junction is the endoscopic hallmark of GERD but is found in only about one-third of GERD patients (Harrison 22e p.2510).
Eosinophilic esophagitis should be strongly considered in children and adults presenting with dysphagia and food impaction, especially with an atopic history (Harrison 22e p.2511).
EoE is confirmed histologically by esophageal mucosal eosinophilia with a peak density of 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field, in the setting of esophageal symptoms (Harrison 22e p.2512).

Dysphagia for both liquids and solids suggests a motility disorder such as achalasia, whereas dysphagia for solids alone suggests a structural lesion (stricture, web, ring, or tumor) (Harrison 22e p.2504).
Patient localization of where food 'hangs up' is notoriously imprecise; about 30% of distal esophageal obstructions are perceived as cervical (neck) dysphagia (Harrison 22e p.2504).

Intermittent solid-food dysphagia that is unchanged or slowly progressive over years points to a benign process (Schatzki ring or eosinophilic esophagitis), whereas dysphagia progressing over weeks to months raises concern for neoplasia (Harrison 22e p.295).
Odynophagia is uncommon with reflux esophagitis; its presence should raise suspicion of an alternative etiology, particularly pill-induced or infectious esophagitis (Harrison 22e p.2505, p.2513).

Achalasia is diagnosed by barium swallow and/or esophageal manometry; the barium study shows a dilated esophagus with poor emptying, an air-fluid level, and a tapered 'beak-like' narrowing at the LES (Harrison 22e p.2507).

Manometric hallmarks of achalasia are impaired (incomplete) deglutitive LES relaxation plus absent peristalsis; manometry is the most sensitive test as it detects disease before esophageal dilatation (Harrison 22e p.2507-2508).

Endoscopy is a necessary part of the achalasia evaluation to exclude pseudoachalasia from tumor infiltration at the cardia/distal esophagus, which accounts for up to 5% of suspected cases (Harrison 22e p.2507).
The GERD injury spectrum progresses from esophagitis to stricture to Barrett metaplasia to adenocarcinoma; esophageal adenocarcinoma incidence is rising in parallel with GERD (Harrison 22e p.2509).

Treating presumed GERD empirically without recognizing that persistent dysphagia or chest pain may instead reflect eosinophilic esophagitis, peptic stricture, motility disorder, esophageal cancer, or coronary artery disease (Harrison 22e p.2510).
Attributing 'heartburn' to GERD when the term is misused for indigestion or other sensations - clarify the patient's meaning (Harrison 22e p.2503).
Assuming neck-localized dysphagia is oropharyngeal - about 30% of distal esophageal lesions refer pain proximally (Harrison 22e p.2504).
Mistaking pseudoachalasia (tumor infiltration, up to 5% of cases) for primary achalasia - omit endoscopy at peril (Harrison 22e p.2507).
Diagnosing distal esophageal spasm before excluding the more common peptic and infectious esophagitis and, above all, cardiac disease (Harrison 22e p.2509).
Aggressive esophageal dilation in EoE - the stiff-walled esophagus risks deep mural laceration or perforation (Harrison 22e p.2512).
Relying on peripheral blood eosinophilia (present in only 25-50%) or allergy testing (poor sensitivity/specificity) to diagnose EoE or identify trigger foods (Harrison 22e p.2512).

Over-interpreting nonspecific minor manometric findings (hypertensive/hypotensive peristalsis) as a defined motility disorder; reflux and anxiety/depression are common in these patients (Harrison 22e p.2509).

Esophageal cancer carries poor survival even when small because abundant esophageal lymphatics permit early regional nodal metastasis. Barrett metaplasia progresses to adenocarcinoma at an estimated 0.1-0.3% per year through low- and high-grade dysplasia, with greatest risk in obese white males in the sixth decade. Untreated achalasia predisposes to stasis esophagitis and increases squamous cell cancer risk roughly 17-fold; durable therapies (pneumatic dilation, Heller myotomy, POEM) achieve symptom relief in about 80-90% of patients, though peristalsis does not recover and chest pain responds less well than dysphagia. EoE is chronic with nearly universal recurrence on stopping therapy, requiring maintenance treatment. Erosive esophagitis and peptic strictures have become increasingly rare in the era of potent acid suppression. (Harrison 22e p.2507-2508, p.2510-2512)
Progressive solid-food dysphagia with weight loss - classic presentation of esophageal cancer; warrants prompt endoscopy (Harrison 22e p.2507).
Odynophagia (painful swallowing) - usually indicates ulceration; raises suspicion of pill-induced or infectious esophagitis (Harrison 22e p.295, p.2513).
Iron-deficiency anemia / chronic occult GI bleeding accompanying esophageal symptoms.
Hoarseness developing after dysphagia - may indicate recurrent laryngeal nerve compromise by malignancy (Harrison 22e p.295).
Abrupt onset of symptoms (<1 year), advanced age, and weight loss in apparent achalasia - suggests pseudoachalasia from malignancy (Harrison 22e p.2507).
Food impaction with inability to pass a bolus even with liquids - typical of structural dysphagia (Harrison 22e p.295).
Severe cough with swallowing - may signal tracheoesophageal fistula.
Finding of high-grade dysplasia in Barrett esophagus - high rate of progression to and coexisting prevalence of adenocarcinoma; mandates intervention (Harrison 22e p.2511).

GERD esophageal injury spectrum: esophagitis -> stricture -> Barrett metaplasia -> adenocarcinoma; reflux testing defines GERD as esophageal pH <4 for >6% of the day. Barrett progression staged histologically as no dysplasia -> low-grade dysplasia -> high-grade dysplasia -> adenocarcinoma. High-resolution manometry differentiates three achalasia subtypes: type I classic (minimal esophageal-body pressurization), type II with esophageal compression/pressurization, and type III spastic achalasia. EoE histologic threshold: peak >=15 eosinophils per high-power field. (Harrison 22e p.2508-2511)
