Syphilitic aortitis (late luetic infection, typically proximal ascending aorta)
Tuberculous aortic aneurysm (extension from hilar nodes/contiguous abscess)
Mycotic aneurysm from Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Salmonella, or fungi seeding atherosclerotic plaque
Chest x-ray (widened mediastinum, displaced/compressed trachea or left main bronchus; left pleural effusion in dissection)
Contrast-enhanced CT angiography (rapid, most commonly used for dissection; sensitivity/specificity >90%)
MRI/MR angiography (intimal flap, extent, branch involvement, intramural hematoma, penetrating ulcer)
Transthoracic echocardiography (overall sensitivity 60-85%; >80% for proximal ascending dissection)
Transesophageal echocardiography (about 98% sensitivity, ~90% specificity for ascending and descending dissection; less useful for the arch)
Abdominal ultrasound (sizing and surveillance of AAA, detection of mural thrombus; screening tool)
Blood cultures (frequently positive in mycotic aneurysm and infective aortitis)
ESR and C-reactive protein (elevated in active Takayasu and other aortitides)
Genetic testing in ascending thoracic aortic disease with features of Marfan/Loeys-Dietz/vascular Ehlers-Danlos or presentation under age 60
Takayasu arteritis (large-vessel vasculitis, 'pulseless disease')
Giant cell arteritis with aortic involvement
IgG4-related aortitis with retroperitoneal fibrosis
Isolated aortitis
Rheumatic aortitis (rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis and other HLA-B27 spondyloarthropathies, relapsing polychondritis, IBD-associated)
Behcet syndrome and Cogan syndrome
Connective-tissue aortopathies (Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, vascular Ehlers-Danlos) and fibromuscular dysplasia

The aortic wall comprises a thin endothelial intima, a thick smooth muscle/elastin/collagen tunica media, and a connective-tissue adventitia carrying the vasa vasorum. Continuous high pulsatile pressure and shear stress predispose it to injury. Aneurysms result from degradation or abnormal production of structural elastin and collagen; degenerative (most common, atherosclerosis-associated) aneurysms involve inflammation, oxidative stress, proteolysis (B/T lymphocytes, macrophages, cytokines, matrix metalloproteinases) and biomechanical stress, with histology showing elastin/collagen destruction, reduced smooth muscle, neovascularization, and inflammation. Heritable aneurysms reflect medial degeneration: fibrillin-1 deficiency (FBN1 mutation in Marfan) impairs elastic-fiber microfibrils and increases TGF-beta signaling, while Loeys-Dietz arises from mutations in TGF-beta isoforms/receptors and SMAD3; vascular Ehlers-Danlos involves COL3A1 (type III procollagen) mutations. Dissection begins with an intimal tear (often the right lateral ascending aorta or just below the ligamentum arteriosum) or medial hemorrhage, with pulsatile flow splitting the elastic lamellae to create a false lumen that usually propagates distally. Aortitis is inflammation of the wall (vasculitic, rheumatic, or infective) that may produce aneurysmal dilation, aortic regurgitation, or branch occlusion.

The aorta is uniquely prone to aneurysm and rupture because, per Laplace's law, wall tension rises with the product of pressure and radius, so dilation begets further dilation; normal adult diameters are roughly 3.5 cm at origin/ascending, 2.5 cm in descending thoracic, and 1.8-2.0 cm in the abdomen.

Abdominal aortic aneurysms are more common in men, increase with age, and at least 90% of those >4.0 cm are atherosclerotic and infrarenal; they are usually silent and found as a pulsatile, expansile, nontender mass, while new aneurysmal pain is a harbinger of impending rupture.

An ECG without ischemic changes helps distinguish aortic dissection from myocardial infarction in a patient with chest pain; rarely the dissection involves a coronary ostium (usually right) and causes acute MI.

Acute occlusion of the distal abdominal aorta is an emergency threatening limb viability, usually from a cardiac-origin saddle embolus, presenting with rest pain, coolness, pallor, and bilaterally absent distal pulses.

Aortic occlusive disease from atherosclerosis is typically infrarenal and, when extending to the iliacs, can cause Leriche syndrome (buttock/thigh/calf claudication with impotence in men) and absent femoral pulses with an abdominal bruit.

True aneurysms involve all three wall layers; pseudoaneurysms have disrupted intima and media, with the dilated segment contained only by adventitia (and sometimes perivascular clot). Aneurysms are described as fusiform (whole circumference) or saccular (focal outpouching).

A contemporary threshold for an aneurysm of the aortic root/ascending aorta is diameter >=4.5 cm, while 4.0-4.4 cm is termed aortic dilation; descending thoracic and abdominal aneurysms are defined when dilated >=50% beyond the adjacent normal segment.

Medial degeneration (loss of medial smooth muscle and breakdown of collagen/elastin with mucoid/proteoglycan clefts) preferentially affects the proximal aorta and underlies ascending aneurysms in Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, vascular Ehlers-Danlos, bicuspid aortic valve, Turner, and familial thoracic aortic aneurysm syndromes; atherosclerosis is the dominant cause of descending thoracic and abdominal aneurysms.

Thoracic aortic aneurysms grow on average about 0.1-0.2 cm/year and are usually asymptomatic; symptoms (chest pain, dyspnea, cough, hoarseness, dysphagia) arise from compression/erosion, and ascending dilation can cause aortic regurgitation and heart failure.

Aortic dissection classically presents with sudden, severe, tearing chest or interscapular pain with diaphoresis that migrates as the dissection propagates; complications include syncope, pulse deficits, acute aortic regurgitation, pulmonary edema, and end-organ ischemia (stroke, paraplegia, bowel/renal/myocardial ischemia).

Stanford type A dissection involves the ascending aorta; type B is limited to arch and/or descending aorta. The type A/B scheme is more practical for management than the DeBakey I/II/III classification because DeBakey I and II are managed similarly.

Acute aortic regurgitation complicates more than 50% of proximal (type A) dissections, producing bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure, and a diastolic murmur along the right sternal border; retrograde type A dissection can cause hemopericardium and tamponade.

Intramural hematoma (rupture of the vasa vasorum, no intimal flap) and penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer are dissection variants, mostly in the descending thoracic aorta, and either can progress to dissection, false aneurysm, or rupture.
A left pleural effusion in dissection is usually serosanguineous and reactive, NOT necessarily a sign of rupture unless accompanied by hypotension and falling hematocrit.
About 25% of abdominal aortic aneurysms are not calcified and cannot be seen on plain x-ray, so a normal radiograph does not exclude an AAA.
Mural thrombus can reduce the luminal diameter, so contrast aortography may underestimate true aneurysm size.
Isolated direct vasodilators such as hydralazine are contraindicated in acute dissection because they raise hydraulic shear and heart rate and can propagate the dissection.
Transthoracic and even transesophageal echocardiography are relatively poor at imaging the aortic arch, a potential blind spot for dissection.
Serum IgG4 levels may be elevated but are not diagnostic of IgG4-related aortitis.
With adequate collateral flow, complete abdominal aortic occlusion can occur without ischemic symptoms, masking the severity of occlusive disease.
Genetic/heritable aortopathies warrant lower size thresholds for intervention; applying standard atherosclerotic thresholds risks under-treatment.

Rupture risk rises with aneurysm size and symptoms: thoracic aneurysms carry roughly 2-3%/year rupture risk below 4.0 cm rising to about 7%/year above 6 cm; for abdominal aneurysms the 5-year rupture risk is about 1-2% under 5 cm versus 20-40% above 5 cm. Marfan and certain Loeys-Dietz/nonsyndromic familial aortopathies dissect at smaller diameters and expand faster. Elective AAA surgery with careful evaluation carries about 1-2% operative mortality, whereas emergent repair after rupture carries roughly 45-50% mortality. For dissection, in-hospital mortality is about 15-25% after type A surgery and around 12% for medically managed type B; with careful follow-up the 10-year survival after treated dissection is approximately 60%, though Marfan patients remain at high risk for post-dissection complications.
Sudden severe tearing/migrating chest or interscapular pain with diaphoresis (acute dissection)
Acute hypotension or shock suggesting rupture or tamponade
New aortic regurgitation murmur, pulse deficits, or blood-pressure differential between limbs
Neurologic deficits (hemiplegia, paraplegia) indicating carotid or spinal cord ischemia
New or worsening aneurysmal pain (back, flank, scrotum) as a harbinger of AAA rupture
Acute limb ischemia with bilaterally absent distal pulses (acute aortic occlusion)
Fever, sepsis, and aortic/back pain with positive blood cultures (mycotic aneurysm/infective aortitis)

Aortic dissection: Stanford type A (involves ascending aorta, proximal) vs type B (arch and/or descending only, distal); DeBakey type I (ascending with propagation to arch/descending/abdominal), type II (limited to ascending), type III (descending with distal propagation). Type A/B is preferred for management decisions. Acute aortic syndromes encompass aortic rupture, dissection, intramural hematoma, and penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer.
Diseases of the Aorta (non-infective) — Cardiovascular Also: Aortic aneurysm, Aortic dissection, Aortitis, Thoracic aortic aneurysm, Abdominal aortic aneurysm, Acute aortic syndrome
Acute polyneuropathy (e.g., Guillain-Barre) when ascending paresthesias begin in the feet -- bladder dysfunction and a sharp sensory level point instead to the cord
Compressive causes: epidural/intradural/intramedullary neoplasm, epidural abscess, epidural hematoma, herniated disk, cervical spondylosis, post-traumatic vertebral displacement
Vascular: anterior spinal artery infarction, dural arteriovenous fistula/AVM, hematomyelia, antiphospholipid syndrome and hypercoagulable states
Inflammatory/immune: multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica (AQP-4), anti-MOG and anti-GFAP disorders, sarcoidosis, SLE, Sjogren's, Behcet's, vasculitis, CLIPPERS, Erdheim-Chester
Metabolic/nutritional: vitamin B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration), folate deficiency, copper deficiency, nitrous oxide-induced myelopathy
Degenerative/genetic: hereditary spastic paraplegia, primary lateral sclerosis, adrenomyeloneuropathy
Developmental: syringomyelia, tethered cord syndrome, meningomyelocele
Cancer-related: radiation myelopathy, intrathecal methotrexate toxicity, paraneoplastic (anti-amphiphysin, CRMP5, Hu), checkpoint-inhibitor myelopathy
Spinal epidural abscess (most commonly Staphylococcus aureus, including MRSA)
Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott's disease) with epidural extension
Viral myelitis: herpes zoster, HSV-1 and HSV-2 (Elsberg syndrome with recurrent sacral neuritis), EBV, CMV, rabies, Zika
Poliomyelitis and polio-like acute flaccid paralysis (enterovirus A-71, D-68, West Nile and other flaviviruses)
Bacterial/mycobacterial myelitis: Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme), Listeria, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Treponema pallidum (syphilis, tabes dorsalis)
Retroviral myelopathy: HTLV-1 (tropical spastic paraparesis) and HIV vacuolar myelopathy
Parasitic: schistosomiasis (granulomatous), toxoplasmosis (especially in AIDS), cysticercosis
Postinfectious/postvaccinal myelitis (EBV, CMV, mycoplasma, influenza, measles, varicella, mumps, SARS-CoV-2)

MRI of the spinal cord with and without gadolinium, centered on the suspected level, as the initial procedure to exclude compression; imaging the entire spine is often appropriate since up to 40% of patients with cord compression at one level have asymptomatic epidural metastases elsewhere

CSF analysis: cell count, protein, glucose, IgG index/synthesis rate, oligoclonal bands, VDRL, Gram/acid-fast/India ink stains, PCR for VZV/HSV/EBV/CMV/HHV-6/enterovirus/HIV, antibodies for HTLV-1, Borrelia, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia
Serum autoantibodies: anti-aquaporin-4, anti-MOG, anti-GFAP for NMO and related disorders
Serum vitamin B12 with macrocytic indices, and confirmatory elevated homocysteine and methylmalonic acid; serum copper and ceruloplasmin for hypocupric myelopathy

Workup for systemic autoimmune disease: ESR, ANA, dsDNA, rheumatoid factor, anti-SSA/SSB, complement, antiphospholipid/anticardiolipin antibodies, pANCA; serum/CSF ACE, calcium, chest CT, gallium scan for sarcoid
Vascular evaluation: MR/CT angiography and selective spinal angiography (definitive) for suspected AVM or dural fistula; CT myelogram when MRI unavailable
Paraneoplastic antibody panel (amphiphysin, CRMP5, Hu) when malignancy suspected
Diffusion-weighted MRI and recognition of cord-infarction signs (anterior 'pencil-like' T2 signal, 'owl's eyes' axial hyperintensities, adjacent vertebral body infarction)
Multiple sclerosis and neuromyelitis optica presenting as acute or chronic myelitis
Anterior spinal artery infarction mimicking acute transverse myelitis
Dural arteriovenous fistula causing progressive myelopathy that can simulate MS or, with mixed upper/lower motor neuron signs, ALS
Foix-Alajouanine syndrome (subacute necrotic myelopathy from intramedullary vascular malformation)
Subacute combined degeneration and hypocupric myelopathy mimicking each other (B12 normal in copper deficiency)
Primary lateral sclerosis and hereditary spastic paraplegia presenting as slowly progressive spastic paraparesis
Spinal sarcoidosis mimicking tumor or NMO on imaging
Toxic myelopathies: lathyrism (BOAA in chickpeas) and Konzo (cyanogenic cassava)

The spinal cord packs nearly the entire motor output and sensory input of the trunk and limbs into a small cross-sectional area, so focal lesions produce disproportionately severe deficits (quadriplegia, paraplegia, sensory loss). Peripherally located white matter tracts carry ascending sensory (posterior columns for position/vibration, spinothalamic for pain/temperature) and descending motor (corticospinal) pathways, while gray matter contains neuronal cell bodies. The crossing pattern of the spinothalamic tract (decussating anterior to the central canal one to two segments above entry) and the same-side course of the posterior columns and corticospinal tracts generate the characteristic clinical syndromes. The cord is supplied by a single anterior spinal artery (anterior two-thirds) and paired posterior spinal arteries (posterior columns); a watershed zone in the upper thoracic cord makes T3-T4 vulnerable to infarction during hypotension or aortic cross-clamping. Disease mechanisms are grouped into compressive (tumor, abscess, hematoma, disk, spondylosis), vascular/ischemic, inflammatory/immune (MS, NMO, sarcoid, systemic autoimmune), infectious/postinfectious, metabolic/nutritional (B12, copper deficiency), developmental (syringomyelia, tethered cord), and degenerative/genetic categories.

A horizontally defined level below which sensory, motor, and autonomic function is impaired is the hallmark of a spinal cord lesion; the sensory level for pinprick/temperature is sought by moving the stimulus upward and is typically one to two segments below a unilateral cord lesion because second-order spinothalamic fibers ascend before crossing.

Spinal epidural abscess classically presents as the triad of midline back/neck pain, fever, and progressive limb weakness; once myelopathic signs appear progression can be rapid and irreversible, so early recognition is critical.

Spondylotic (degenerative cervical) myelopathy is the most common cause of myelopathy and gait disturbance in the elderly, suspected with progressive spastic paraparesis, foot/hand paresthesias, or wasting of intrinsic hand muscles.

Subacute combined degeneration from vitamin B12 deficiency classically shows the combination of an absent ankle reflex (peripheral neuropathy) with an extensor plantar (Babinski) response, plus loss of vibration/position sense and a positive Romberg sign.

Because the cord segments do not align with the like-numbered vertebrae, lesion localization must account for offset: a sensory level at the umbilicus reflects T10 cord pathology, located adjacent to the seventh or eighth thoracic vertebral body.

Spinal shock can produce flaccid, areflexic paralysis acutely (lasting days, rarely weeks) and may be mistaken for extensive anterior horn cell damage or an acute polyneuropathy; hyperreflexia and spasticity supervene later, but persistent areflexic paralysis with a sensory level usually signifies necrosis across multiple cord segments.

Brown-Sequard (hemicord) syndrome combines ipsilateral weakness and loss of joint position/vibration sense with contralateral loss of pain and temperature one to two levels below the lesion; partial forms are more common than the full syndrome.

Central cord syndrome produces arm weakness out of proportion to leg weakness and a dissociated, suspended cape-distribution sensory loss (loss of pain/temperature with preserved touch, position, and vibration), classically from trauma, syringomyelia, or intrinsic cord tumor.

Anterior cord syndrome (anterior spinal artery territory) abolishes motor, pain/temperature, and autonomic function while strikingly sparing vibration and position sense carried in the posterior columns.

Sacral sparing favors an intramedullary process, reflecting the lamination of the spinothalamic tract with sacral fibers outermost; extramedullary lesions instead tend to cause prominent radicular pain and early sacral sensory loss.

Conus medullaris lesions cause symmetric saddle anesthesia (S3-S5), early prominent bladder/bowel dysfunction with lax anal tone and impotence, and relatively preserved strength; cauda equina lesions instead cause low back and radicular pain, asymmetric leg weakness/sensory loss, areflexia, and relative sparing of bowel/bladder.

A recent onset of persistent thoracic back pain that worsens with movement, coughing, or recumbency and awakens the patient at night should raise concern for vertebral metastasis, since the thoracic spine is uncommonly involved by spondylosis.
Mistaking spinal shock (acute flaccid areflexic paralysis) for a polyneuropathy or for diffuse anterior horn cell disease
Attributing ascending foot paresthesias to peripheral neuropathy and overlooking bladder dysfunction and a sensory level indicating a cord origin
Relying on plain radiographs or radionuclide bone scans, which miss 15-20% of metastatic vertebral lesions and fail to detect paravertebral masses reaching the epidural space through the foramina
Gadolinium contrast can deceptively 'normalize' the appearance of a vertebral metastasis on T1 imaging by raising its signal to that of normal marrow
Failing to image the entire spine when cord compression is found at one level, missing clinically silent additional metastases
Assuming MRI is sensitive for cord infarction early -- it may be normal in the first day
Interpreting HTLV-1 seropositivity alone as proof of causation for a myelopathy in endemic areas
Lumbar puncture in severe thrombocytopenia/coagulopathy (risk of epidural hematoma) or through tissue overlying an epidural abscess (risk of seeding meningitis) -- a high cervical tap may be safer
Overlooking copper deficiency (with normal B12) as a cause of a subacute-combined-degeneration-like myelopathy, particularly after bariatric surgery or with excess zinc intake

Many spinal cord diseases are reversible if recognized and treated early, making them among the most critical neurologic emergencies. For neoplastic compression, ambulatory status at presentation predicts a good outcome; motor deficits established for more than 12 hours rarely improve, and beyond 48 hours the prognosis for substantial motor recovery is poor. With prompt diagnosis and treatment of spinal epidural abscess, up to two-thirds of patients achieve significant recovery, but fixed deficits more than several days old are unlikely to reverse. After cord infarction, severe motor weakness and persistent areflexia predict poor recovery, though more than half of patients in one series regained some ambulation. The prospects for recovery from an acute destructive lesion fade after about 6 months, and there are currently no effective means to repair injured cord tissue. Even complete high cervical lesions can be compatible with a productive life; ultimate disability is determined chiefly by lesion level and whether the deficit is complete or incomplete.
Neck or back pain with progressive limb weakness, bladder disturbance, or a sensory level -- treatable cord compression must be excluded urgently with MRI
Fever with spinal pain and progressive weakness suggesting epidural abscess
New persistent thoracic back pain in a patient with known or suspected malignancy
Hyperextension neck injury in a patient with degenerative cervical stenosis (acute spondylotic myelopathy / central cord syndrome)
Autonomic dysreflexia (paroxysmal hypertension, headache, flushing, diaphoresis, bradycardia) from a noxious stimulus below a lesion at or above T6
Quadriplegic fever and loss of normal somatic/visceral pain signaling masking infection, thrombophlebitis, or intra-abdominal pathology in chronic cord injury
Diaphragmatic weakness with upper cervical lesions

Functional outcome after complete cord lesions is stratified by level (Harrison Table 453-4): high quadriplegia (C1-C4) -- dependent on others, requires respiratory support, motorized wheelchair; low quadriplegia (C5-C8) -- partially independent with adaptive equipment, may use a manual wheelchair and drive with adaptations; paraplegia (below T1) -- independent in self-care and transfers, ambulates short distances with aids. Lesions are also characterized clinically as complete versus incomplete, and intramedullary versus extramedullary (and extradural versus intradural, the former generally malignant and the latter benign).
Diseases of the Spinal Cord (non-infective) — Nervous system Also: Myelopathy, Spinal cord disease, Spinal cord disorders

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Nonvenomous snakebite or 'dry' bite (fang marks without envenomation)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Bite by a harmless species whose saliva causes mild local pain/edema (can mimic mild envenomation)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Cellulitis or other local soft-tissue infection

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Allergic reaction / anaphylaxis (especially scombroid, which mimics food allergy)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Ciguatera differential per Harrison: paralytic shellfish poisoning, eosinophilic meningitis, type E botulism, organophosphate poisoning, tetrodotoxin poisoning, psychogenic hyperventilation

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Cellulitis (rapidly spreading local swelling and erythema after a bite can resemble bacterial cellulitis)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Secondary bacterial wound infection complicating an envenomation (marine wounds: Vibrio in saltwater, Aeromonas in freshwater; Staphylococcus/Streptococcus)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Complete blood count (assess hemorrhage, hemolysis, thrombocytopenia)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Imaging (soft-tissue radiography, ultrasound, or MRI) to locate retained marine spines/foreign bodies

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Repeat coagulation and CBC monitoring for recurrent coagulopathy after discharge

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Blood type and cross-match

chunks.text: Renal and hepatic function panels

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Coagulation studies: prothrombin time and fibrinogen level; fibrin degradation products / D-dimer

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Serial limb circumference measurements at three points every 15 min until local effects stabilize

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: ECG and chest radiography in severe envenomation or significant comorbidity

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Intracompartmental pressure measurement if compartment syndrome suspected (threshold 30-40 mmHg)

chunks.text: Primary cardiac dysrhythmia or shock from non-toxic causes

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Snake venoms are complex mixtures of enzymes, polypeptides, and glycoproteins whose composition varies by species, age, diet, geography, and even within a species. They produce harm through several mechanisms: direct local tissue necrosis, disruption of the coagulation cascade at multiple steps (consumptive coagulopathy, defibrination, thrombocytopenia), organ dysfunction (notably renal), and action at the neuromuscular junction causing paralysis. Early hypotension is partly mediated by bradykinin-potentiating factors causing vasodilation and pooling, compounded by systemic bleeding, hemolysis, and third-spacing of intravascular volume. Renal injury is usually acute tubular necrosis (often reversible), but bilateral cortical necrosis carries a poorer prognosis. Marine envenomations operate by distinct toxins: cnidarian nematocysts inject venom containing phospholipases, metalloproteases, pore-forming toxins, neurotoxins, and bioactive amines (histamine, serotonin); cone snail conotoxins block acetylcholine receptors and ion channels; blue-ringed octopus and pufferfish deliver tetrodotoxin, a potent peripheral sodium-channel blocker. Marine seafood poisonings are ingestion toxidromes: scombroid from bacterial conversion of histidine to histamine in spoiled fish, and ciguatera from ciguatoxins that activate neuronal sodium channels and antagonize voltage-gated potassium channels.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Medically important venomous snakes fall into Viperidae (Old World vipers and New World/Asian pit vipers), Elapidae (cobras, kraits, coral snakes, sea snakes, Australian elapids), the burrowing asps (Atractaspidinae), and a few colubrids; snake envenomation is described as the world's deadliest neglected tropical disease, with roughly 63,000 deaths globally in 2019.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Among marine animals, jellyfish/box jellyfish (Chironex fleckeri), Portuguese man-of-war (Physalia), and the Irukandji jellyfish (Carukia barnesi) cause the most dangerous cnidarian stings; Irukandji syndrome is a catecholamine-excess state with hypertension, tachycardia, severe pain, and risk of pulmonary edema and cardiomyopathy.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Blue-ringed octopus (Hapalochlaena) and pufferfish (order Tetraodontiformes, e.g., fugu) both cause tetrodotoxin toxicity - a sodium-channel blocker producing rapid flaccid paralysis with preserved mentation; consciousness is typically intact even during complete paralysis, so analgesia/sedation matter.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Scombroid (histamine) fish poisoning mimics an allergic reaction (flushing, urticaria, headache, palpitations) and arises when bacteria decarboxylate histidine to histamine in poorly refrigerated fish; the toxin is heat-stable and reactions are more severe in patients on isoniazid (histaminase blockade).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Ciguatera, caused by heat-stable ciguatoxins (Gambierdiscus toxicus) bioaccumulated in large reef fish, classically produces GI symptoms plus neurologic features including reversal of hot/cold temperature sensation and a sensation of 'loose teeth'; neurologic symptoms can persist for weeks.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: A large fraction of bites are 'dry' (no venom injected) - about 20-25% of pit viper bites and up to 75% of sea snake bites - so the presence of fang marks alone does not equal envenomation.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Viperid/cytotoxic patterns produce progressive local pain, soft-tissue swelling, ecchymosis, and hemorrhagic or serum-filled blisters, while neurotoxic elapids (kraits, some cobras, Australian elapids) and certain vipers cause cranial nerve dysfunction (ptosis, dysphagia) progressing to descending paralysis and respiratory failure.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Onset and tempo of symptoms vary with species, bite location, and venom dose; coral snakes, sea snakes, and some non-North American vipers (e.g., hump-nosed pit viper) can have systemic effects delayed by several hours, mandating prolonged observation.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: In resource-limited settings the bedside 20-minute whole-blood clotting test detects venom-induced coagulopathy: 1-2 mL venous blood left undisturbed in a clean dry glass tube that fails to clot at 20 minutes indicates coagulopathy.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Antivenom binds and neutralizes circulating (unbound) venom; it is largely ineffective at reversing damage already established (e.g., fixed paralysis, established renal failure) and offers little cross-protection outside the species it was raised against, so species-appropriate selection is essential.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Compartment syndrome is uncommon after snakebite (fasciotomy needed in under 1% of cases); in North American crotalid bites fasciotomy lacks supporting evidence and may increase morbidity, since effective antivenom lowers compartment pressure.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Recurrent or delayed coagulopathy can appear during the first 2-3 weeks after a bite because venom antigens may outlast antivenom, so patients are warned to avoid elective surgery/high-trauma activity and to have repeat coagulation testing.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Long-term sequelae include permanent limb functional loss from muscle/nerve/vascular injury or scar contracture, and pituitary insufficiency described after Russell's viper (Daboia russelii) envenomation.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Treating fang marks alone as proof of envenomation - many bites are dry and antivenom in such cases is useless and potentially harmful.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Using beta-blockers in Irukandji syndrome hypertension - risks worsening hypertension via unopposed alpha effects.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Relying on color pattern, head shape, or pupil shape to judge whether a snake is venomous - nonvenomous species frequently mimic these features.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Discharging a patient too early: significant toxicity from an apparently 'dry' viperid bite can develop after several hours, and elapid/sea snake/some viper systemic effects are characteristically delayed.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Using outdated first aid (incision, suction, tourniquets/venom-sequestration devices) - these worsen local damage and increase infection risk; pressure-immobilization is reserved for reliably identified primarily neurotoxic species, not viperids.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Relying on antivenom skin testing for hypersensitivity - it is neither sensitive nor specific; prophylactic antihistamines/glucocorticoids have not proven beneficial.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Performing fasciotomy reflexively for limb swelling in North American crotalid bites - evidence does not support it and it may increase morbidity.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Giving blood products before adequate antivenom - this can fuel ongoing consumptive coagulopathy.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: In marine cnidarian stings, applying vinegar indiscriminately - it relieves pain for Indo-Pacific species (C. fleckeri, C. barnesi) but can increase nematocyst discharge in Physalia physalis and Chrysaora quinquecirrha; rubbing the area also worsens stinging.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Mislabeling scombroid poisoning as a seafood allergy, leading to unnecessary lifelong fish avoidance.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: In settings with rapid access to care and appropriate antivenom, mortality is low - under 1% in the United States among victims who receive antivenom. Eastern and western diamondback rattlesnakes account for most U.S. snakebite deaths; globally, major killers include cobras, saw-scaled/carpet vipers (Echis), Russell's vipers, large African vipers (Bitis), lanceheads (Bothrops), and tropical rattlesnakes (Crotalus durissus). Morbidity from permanent limb functional loss is substantial and can be devastating in the developing world; in the U.S. it is more common and severe after rattlesnake bites than after copperhead or water moccasin bites. Renal failure from acute tubular necrosis is frequently reversible, whereas bilateral cortical necrosis carries a worse renal prognosis. For tetrodotoxin/blue-ringed octopus envenomation, recovery usually occurs within 24-48 h and long-term sequelae are uncommon unless hypoxia/hypoperfusion supervened. Most scombroid cases are mild and self-limited (resolving in 8-12 h), and ciguatera GI symptoms typically settle in 24-48 h though neurologic symptoms may persist for days to weeks (and a delayed 'second-phase' syndrome can last 2-6 weeks after parrotfish exposure).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Tetrodotoxin exposure (blue-ringed octopus, pufferfish): oral/facial numbness progressing to flaccid paralysis and respiratory failure

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures
chunks.text: Harrison grades pit viper envenomation severity (U.S./Canada framework) as: None - fang marks only ('dry' bite); Mild - local findings only (pain, ecchymosis, nonprogressive swelling); Moderate - clearly progressing swelling, systemic symptoms/signs, and/or laboratory abnormalities; Severe - neurologic dysfunction, respiratory distress, and/or cardiovascular instability/shock.

Nonceliac gluten sensitivity (Harrison 22e p.2546)
Tropical sprue (Harrison 22e p.2546)

Chronic pancreatitis / exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (Harrison 22e p.2542)
Lactose intolerance from lactase deficiency (Harrison 22e p.2544)

Short-bowel syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2547-2548)

Tropical-environment enteric infections to exclude before diagnosing tropical sprue: Entamoeba histolytica, Cryptosporidium parvum, Cystoisospora (Isospora) belli, Strongyloides stercoralis, Cyclospora cayetanensis, Yersinia enterocolitica, Clostridioides difficile (Harrison 22e p.2547)
72-h quantitative fecal fat collection on a 100-g fat diet (gold standard for steatorrhea); qualitative spot Sudan III stain for fecal fat (Harrison 22e p.2549)
Whipple's disease: tissue PCR for T. whipplei, PAS staining, immunohistochemistry on biopsy (Harrison 22e p.2546)

Labs reflecting site-specific deficiency: iron studies, B12 and folate, fat-soluble vitamins, PT/INR as a functional marker of vitamin K, serum carotene; cross-sectional imaging (MR enterography/CT), video capsule and double-balloon enteroscopy for occult mucosal/lymphatic disease (Harrison 22e p.2549)
24-h stool weight/volume to confirm clinically significant diarrhea; stool osmotic gap (from spot fecal Na and K) to identify osmotic diarrhea (Harrison 22e p.2549)
Tissue transglutaminase IgA (TTG-IgA) with concurrent serum total IgA; TTG-IgG or anti-deamidated gliadin peptide (DGP-IgG) if IgA-deficient (Harrison 22e p.2545)
HLA-DQ2/DQ8 testing chiefly to rule OUT celiac disease (high negative predictive value), especially if gluten was discontinued before testing (Harrison 22e p.2544-2545)
Endoscopy with small-intestinal (duodenal) biopsy; Marsh grading; in celiac, follow-up serology and a follow-up biopsy to document mucosal healing (Harrison 22e p.2545)
Stool elastase for pancreatic insufficiency (Harrison 22e p.2549)
SIBO testing: duodenal aspirate for bacterial titers (gold standard, limited availability) or lactulose/glucose breath hydrogen testing (interpret carefully for false positives) (Harrison 22e p.2543)
Lactose intolerance: lactose-exclusion diet trial, lactose-tolerance test (serum glucose rise <20 mg/L is positive), or breath hydrogen test (>20 ppm rise) (Harrison 22e p.2544-2545)
Protein-losing enteropathy: stool alpha-1 antitrypsin (spot or 24-h) or alpha-1 antitrypsin clearance; lymphopenia with hypoproteinemia supports GI protein loss (Harrison 22e p.2548-2549)
Irritable bowel syndrome (celiac disease can mimic IBS; SIBO and bile-acid malabsorption occur in IBS-D) (Harrison 22e p.2543, 2546)
Microscopic colitis (Harrison 22e p.2546)
Intestinal lymphoma, including enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.2546)
Crohn's disease (Harrison 22e p.2542)
Hyperthyroidism causing rapid-transit diarrhea/malabsorption (Harrison 22e p.2542)
Long-standing diabetes mellitus with enteric autonomic neuropathy (Harrison 22e p.2542)
Scleroderma and other connective-tissue/motility disorders (Harrison 22e p.2542)
Menetrier's disease (hypertrophic gastropathy) as a cause of protein-losing enteropathy (Harrison 22e p.2549)

Malabsorption results from disruption of one or more of the three phases of nutrient assimilation. (1) Luminal/digestive phase: intraluminal hydrolysis by gastric and pancreatic enzymes and solubilization of fat in bile-salt mixed micelles; impaired by postgastrectomy rapid transit, pancreatic insufficiency, hepatobiliary disease, ileal disease interrupting the enterohepatic circulation of bile acids, and small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth (which deconjugates bile acids causing luminal bile-acid deficiency). (2) Mucosal/absorptive phase: brush-border enzymatic digestion (disaccharidases, peptidases, enterokinase) and enterocyte uptake; impaired by isolated brush-border defects (lactase deficiency, glucose-galactose malabsorption, sucrase-isomaltase deficiency) or by diffuse enteropathies (celiac disease, tropical sprue, Whipple's disease, Crohn's, infections). In celiac disease, tissue transglutaminase deamidates gluten-derived peptides, promoting their presentation by antigen-presenting cells in HLA-DQ2/DQ8 individuals, producing proximal villus atrophy with crypt hyperplasia; steatorrhea arises from mucosal malabsorption plus a secretory component from crypt hyperplasia/hypersecretion, and secondary lactase deficiency may develop. (3) Postmucosal/delivery phase: re-esterification of long-chain fatty acids into chylomicrons exiting via lymphatics; impaired by abetalipoproteinemia (failed chylomicron formation) and by lymphatic obstruction/dysfunction (lymphangiectasia, lymphoma, retroperitoneal fibrosis) or circulatory causes (Fontan physiology, constrictive pericarditis, CHF), which also cause protein-losing enteropathy. Specific nutrient deficiencies localize disease: duodenal/proximal disease causes iron and folate deficiency; ileal disease/resection causes B12 deficiency and bile-acid malabsorption; steatorrhea causes fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K) deficiency (Harrison 22e p.2540-2549).

Steatorrhea (fecal fat excretion >7% of dietary fat) is a common manifestation of malabsorption, producing large, bulky, malodorous stools; malabsorptive diarrhea is typically precipitated by eating and lessens or resolves with fasting, which helps distinguish it from secretory (e.g., enterotoxigenic) diarrhea that persists during fasting (Harrison 22e p.2540-2541).

In India, tropical sprue is regarded by some as a postinfectious complication occurring in 8-20% of people after an attack of infectious gastroenteritis, with southern Indian patients often reporting acute enteritis preceding steatorrhea; tropical sprue is rarely seen in Africa, Jamaica, or Southeast Asia, and its overall incidence has declined (Harrison 22e p.2546-2547).

Whipple's disease (Tropheryma whipplei, a PAS-positive non-acid-fast rod) most often affects middle-aged men; arthralgias/arthritis precede GI symptoms by an average of ~6 years (joint disease in >80%), and CNS and cardiac involvement occur later; diagnosis uses biopsy with PCR and PAS-positive macrophages (Harrison 22e p.2546).

Small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth arises from stasis (scleroderma, pseudo-obstruction, blind loops, strictures, diverticulosis) and from hypochlorhydria (chronic PPI use); it causes B12 deficiency (macrocytic anemia, peripheral neuropathy) from bacterial B12 metabolism, yet serum folate may be ELEVATED due to bacterial folate synthesis (Harrison 22e p.2543).

In ileal disease/resection, <100 cm involvement causes bile-acid spillage into the colon and secretory (cholerheic) diarrhea responsive to bile-acid sequestrants, whereas >100 cm exceeds hepatic synthetic capacity to replace lost bile acids, making fat malabsorption (steatorrhea) the dominant mechanism (Harrison 22e p.2542-2543).

Chronic pancreatitis and exocrine pancreatic insufficiency cause voluminous steatorrhea with deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins (most commonly D and K), and stool elastase is helpful for diagnosing pancreatic insufficiency (Harrison 22e p.2542, 2549).

In short-bowel/lipid malabsorption with an intact colon in continuity, luminal fatty acids saponify calcium, freeing oxalate for colonic absorption and increasing the risk of calcium-oxalate renal stones (hyperoxaluria) (Harrison 22e p.2548).

Celiac disease (celiac sprue / gluten-sensitive enteropathy) is a small-intestinal enteropathy from an immune response to gluten (wheat, rye, barley, some oats), characterized by autoantibodies to tissue transglutaminase; it primarily affects the proximal small bowel, so duodenal-limited disease may present as isolated iron-deficiency anemia while diffuse jejunal disease causes severe diarrhea, weight loss, and multinutrient malabsorption (Harrison 22e p.2545).

Tissue transglutaminase IgA (TTG-IgA) is the celiac screening test of choice; serum IgA should be measured concurrently because IgA deficiency causes false-negative TTG-IgA, in which case IgG-based testing (TTG-IgG or anti-deamidated gliadin peptide DGP-IgG) is used (Harrison 22e p.2545).

In adults with positive celiac serology, diagnosis is confirmed by endoscopy with small-intestinal biopsy showing villus blunting, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes; the Marsh classification grades severity (Harrison 22e p.2545).

PITFALL: celiac serologic and histologic testing must be performed while the patient is consuming gluten, since self-discontinuation of gluten before testing produces false-negative results; HLA-DQ2/DQ8 testing is then useful because a negative result rules out celiac disease (negative predictive value >99%) (Harrison 22e p.2544-2545).

HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 are necessary but not sufficient for celiac disease and are present in 25-35% of the general population, so their detection is NOT useful for diagnosis; their value lies in the very high negative predictive value when absent (Harrison 22e p.2544).

Dermatitis herpetiformis, a vesicular rash mediated by IgA skin deposits, is highly associated with celiac disease; celiac disease also carries increased risk of other autoimmune disorders (type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease) and is more frequent in Down and Turner syndromes (Harrison 22e p.2545).

The mainstay of celiac treatment is a strict lifelong gluten-free diet with rigorous dietitian instruction; the most common cause of persistent symptoms or residual disease activity is dietary nonadherence or inadvertent gluten exposure (Harrison 22e p.2545-2546).

Tropical sprue presents with chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea, weight loss, and deficiencies of BOTH folate and vitamin B12; malabsorption of two unrelated substances is required for diagnosis, and it is associated with residence in or travel to specific tropical regions (southern India, Pakistan, Philippines, Puerto Rico, Haiti, Cuba) (Harrison 22e p.2546-2547).

Testing for celiac disease (serology and biopsy) only after the patient has already self-removed gluten gives false-negative results; testing must be done ON a gluten-containing diet, or use HLA-DQ2/DQ8 to exclude disease (Harrison 22e p.2544-2545).

Interpreting HLA-DQ2/DQ8 positivity as diagnostic of celiac disease is wrong, as 25-35% of the general population carry these alleles without disease; only a negative result is clinically useful (rules out) (Harrison 22e p.2544).
Missing IgA deficiency when only TTG-IgA is ordered will produce false-negative celiac screening; order total serum IgA and use IgG-based tests if deficient (Harrison 22e p.2545).

Diagnosing tropical sprue before excluding enteric infection: it should NOT be entertained until cysts and trophozoites are excluded in three stool samples, and a gluten-free diet does NOT improve tropical sprue (unlike celiac disease) (Harrison 22e p.2547).

Breath hydrogen testing for lactose intolerance or SIBO can be inaccurate with abnormal gastric emptying or transit, and SIBO can itself produce false-positive/abnormal breath tests and mimic lactose intolerance (Harrison 22e p.2543, 2545).
In SIBO, expecting low folate is a trap; serum folate may be ELEVATED from bacterial synthesis while B12 is low (Harrison 22e p.2543).

In protein-losing enteropathy, isolated low albumin with normal globulins suggests renal/hepatic disease rather than GI loss; alpha-1 antitrypsin cannot assess gastric protein loss because it is degraded in acid (Harrison 22e p.2548-2549).
Treating the hypoproteinemia of protein-losing enteropathy directly rather than the underlying disease is misdirected; therapy should target the underlying cause (Harrison 22e p.2549).

Most patients with celiac disease respond fully to a strict lifelong gluten-free diet with mucosal healing and symptom resolution; about 10% of those with persistent active disease develop refractory celiac disease, and type 2 refractory disease carries a poor prognosis with enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma in 33-50% of cases at 5 years (requiring intensive chemotherapy and sometimes stem cell transplantation). Tropical sprue is most often curative with broad-spectrum antibiotics plus folic acid, especially if the patient leaves the tropical area and does not return. Whipple's disease requires prolonged antibiotics, but relapses are common. In short-bowel syndrome the intestine adapts over up to 2 years (with reports of continued improvement at 3-5 years); prognosis and parenteral-nutrition dependence relate to the extent of resection, presence of colon in continuity, and retention of the ileocecal valve, with intestinal failure defined by persistent parenteral-nutrition dependence (Harrison 22e p.2542-2548).
Persistent diarrhea, weight loss, and villus atrophy after >=1 year of a strict gluten-free diet with negative serology, indicating refractory celiac disease (Harrison 22e p.2546)

Type 2 refractory celiac disease (clonal CD3+ intraepithelial lymphocytes with monoclonal T-cell receptor gamma-chain rearrangement), which progresses to enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma in 33-50% within 5 years (Harrison 22e p.2546)
New or worsening malabsorption with abdominal mass/imaging lymphadenopathy suggesting small-bowel adenocarcinoma or intestinal lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.2546)
Hypoproteinemia with peripheral edema, diarrhea, and lymphopenia (protein-losing enteropathy) requiring exclusion of cardiac and lymphatic causes (Harrison 22e p.2548)
Severe vitamin K deficiency causing coagulopathy (elevated PT/INR) and significant B12-related peripheral neuropathy (Harrison 22e p.2549)
Whipple's disease relapse, frequently heralding first CNS involvement (Harrison 22e p.2546)

There is no single unified severity scale for malabsorption; severity is assessed by the degree of nutrient deficiency and steatorrhea and by disease-specific schemes. Celiac mucosal injury is graded by the Marsh classification of biopsy lesions (intraepithelial lymphocytosis, crypt hyperplasia, and degrees of villus atrophy). Celiac complications are stratified into refractory celiac disease type 1 (normal intraepithelial lymphocyte population, better prognosis) versus type 2 (clonal CD3+ intraepithelial lymphocytes with monoclonal T-cell receptor gamma rearrangement, worse prognosis with high lymphoma risk). Bile-acid versus fatty-acid diarrhea are distinguished by extent of ileal disease (<100 cm vs >100 cm), degree of steatorrhea, and response to cholestyramine versus a low-fat diet. Short-bowel syndrome is defined as <200 cm of remaining small bowel, and intestinal failure as persistent parenteral-nutrition dependence (generally <100 cm of small bowel with no colon in continuity) (Harrison 22e p.2543, 2545-2548).
Malabsorption (Disorders of Absorption) (non-infective) — Gastroenterology Also: malabsorption, celiac disease, coeliac disease

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: The autonomic nervous system operates as an integrated reflex circuit linking sensory feedback from organs with central processing (insular and prefrontal cortex, limbic system, hypothalamus; brainstem nucleus tractus solitarius, dorsal motor vagal nucleus, nucleus ambiguus) and the spinal intermediolateral cell columns, then to peripheral ganglia and target organs. Dysfunction may arise from decreased activity, overactivity, or dysregulation at the afferent limb, central processor, or efferent limb. In orthostatic hypotension, standing shifts roughly 500-700 mL of blood to the lower limbs and splanchnic bed; the normal compensatory baroreflex (slight tachycardia, veno- and arteriolar constriction) maintains pressure, and neurogenic OH results from inadequate peripheral norepinephrine release with loss of vascular tone. The synucleinopathies (MSA, Parkinson disease with autonomic failure, dementia with Lewy bodies, pure autonomic failure) share aggregation of misfolded, phosphorylated alpha-synuclein in central and peripheral autonomic structures; MSA characteristically shows glial cytoplasmic inclusions in oligodendrocytes (versus neuronal Lewy bodies in PD/LBD), with possible prion-like cell-to-cell transfer. Peripheral autonomic neuropathies damage small myelinated and unmyelinated sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers. POTS pathophysiology is heterogeneous, including distal sympathetic denervation with preserved cardiac sympathetic function (neuropathic POTS), venous pooling, hypovolemia, deconditioning, altered baroreflex regulation, and sympathetic overactivity.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: The autonomic nervous system has parasympathetic (craniosacral), sympathetic (thoracolumbar, T1-L2), and enteric divisions; acetylcholine is the preganglionic transmitter for both arms and the postganglionic parasympathetic transmitter, while norepinephrine is the postganglionic sympathetic transmitter (except eccrine sweat glands, which use acetylcholine).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Cardiac sympathetic innervation imaging (MIBG scintigraphy or fluorodopamine PET) is typically PRESERVED in MSA but reduced in Parkinson disease, Lewy body disease, and pure autonomic failure, aiding differentiation.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy is a treatable cause associated with high-titer antibodies to the alpha-3 ganglionic acetylcholine nicotinic receptor; it may be paraneoplastic (small cell lung cancer, thymoma, lymphoma), so malignancy screening is prudent.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Autonomic dysreflexia is a dramatic BP surge triggered by bladder, bowel, or skin irritation in spinal cord lesions above T6; lesions below T6 permit splanchnic vasodilation and rarely cause it.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Dysautonomia is best classified clinically by organ specificity (heart, vessels, sweat glands, pupils, gastrointestinal, genitourinary) and by time course (acute/subacute/chronic, progressive/static), which helps narrow the differential.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Classical orthostatic hypotension is a sustained fall of systolic BP >=20 mmHg or diastolic BP >=10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing or head-up tilt >=60 degrees; in hypertensive patients the threshold is >=30/15 mmHg.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension is suggested by a blunted compensatory heart-rate rise (<15 beats/min); a heart-rate-rise/systolic-BP-fall ratio below 0.5 beats/min/mmHg after 3 minutes more accurately indicates neurogenic OH and reflects impaired cardiac baroreflex gain.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: POTS is defined as chronic (>3 months) orthostatic intolerance WITHOUT sustained orthostatic hypotension, with a heart-rate rise of >=30 beats/min (>=40 if under age 19) or a rate above 120 beats/min within 10 minutes of standing; it is a sinus-rhythm disorder, four to five times more common in women aged 15-45.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: About half of POTS cases follow a viral illness (notably EBV, coronavirus, enteroviruses); it is the leading manifestation of long COVID, and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome predisposes in up to 25% of patients.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Heart-rate variation to deep breathing tests the vagal (parasympathetic) baroreflex arm; the Valsalva maneuver assesses both parasympathetic (Valsalva ratio) and sympathetic (adrenergic index, BP recovery) arms; both are diminished in most autonomic failure, diabetes, and alpha-synuclein disorders.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Sudomotor localization: a postganglionic lesion shows absent sweating on BOTH QSART and thermoregulatory sweat test (TST), whereas a preganglionic lesion preserves QSART but shows anhidrosis on TST.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Multiple system atrophy (Shy-Drager) combines autonomic failure with parkinsonism (MSA-P) or cerebellar features (MSA-C); the parkinsonism responds poorly/transiently to levodopa and rest tremor is not prominent.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: OH is frequently overlooked because most patients are asymptomatic or only mildly symptomatic, and chronic neurogenic OH may stay mild despite large BP drops due to cerebral autoregulation

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Relying only on the absolute heart-rate rise can misclassify neurogenic OH; cardioactive drugs and intrinsic rhythm disturbances can blunt the expected tachycardia

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Delayed OH may not appear until after 3-5 (sometimes 10) minutes of tilt, so short observation can miss it; postprandial and initial OH have distinct timing and triggers

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Pharmacologic provocation during tilt testing increases sensitivity at the expense of specificity (normal subjects may faint)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Typical MSA MRI findings may appear only in advanced disease, so a normal early scan does not exclude it; the 'hot cross bun' sign is characteristic but not pathognomonic (also seen in some spinocerebellar atrophies)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Failing to screen for occult malignancy in autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy can miss a paraneoplastic small cell lung cancer, thymoma, or lymphoma

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Overlap of preganglionic and postganglionic involvement occurs in autoimmune, paraneoplastic, and neurodegenerative disorders, so localization rules are not absolute

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Attributing POTS symptoms to psychiatric disease; significant psychiatric disorder rates are no higher than in the general population

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Prognosis depends on etiology. Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension carries high mortality, approaching 44% over 30 months and exceeding 60% over 10 years in some series, and OH overall raises risk of falls, coronary disease, heart failure, stroke, and death. MSA progresses relentlessly to death typically 7-10 years after onset, though some survive beyond 10 years; early autonomic and bladder dysfunction, female sex, and rapid disability progression imply worse prognosis. Pure autonomic failure may evolve into a central synucleinopathy (PD, DLB, or MSA) after 5-10 years. Diabetic autonomic neuropathy increases diabetic mortality up to threefold. POTS is often chronic and self-perpetuating through deconditioning, but psychiatric comorbidity rates do not exceed the general population; graded exercise typically needs at least 6 months for benefit. Autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy is important because it is treatable; about one-third of untreated seronegative cases improve spontaneously.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Impaired olfaction, impaired balance, abnormal movements, and dream-enactment sleep behavior (apnea, stridor) signal a degenerative extrapyramidal/synucleinopathy disorder

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Symptomatic orthostatic hypotension within 2 years of parkinsonism onset, early urinary and erectile dysfunction, and rapid disability progression favor MSA over idiopathic Parkinson disease

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Supine hypertension with reverse dipping in autonomic failure predicts end-organ (renal, cardiac, cerebrovascular) damage

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Autonomic dysreflexia BP surges above a T6 cord lesion can precipitate intracranial vasospasm or hemorrhage

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Life-threatening cardiovascular dysautonomia in Guillain-Barre syndrome, especially severe cases

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Subacute autonomic failure after infection, surgery, or with suspected malignancy points to autoimmune/paraneoplastic ganglionopathy requiring workup

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Acroparesthesias/burning feet and hands suggesting autonomic small-fiber neuropathy

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Macroglossia suggesting amyloidosis; angiokeratoma suggesting Fabry disease

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Orthostatic hypotension can be graded into four functional classes: class I, asymptomatic (may still have syncope/falls); class II, weekly-to-monthly symptoms with mild-to-moderate limitation of daily living; class III, more severe and frequent symptoms markedly limiting daily activities; class IV, daily severe symptoms causing significant disability. OH is further distinguished as nonneurogenic (compensatory HR rise >15 beats/min) versus neurogenic (HR rise <15 beats/min, or HR-rise/SBP-fall ratio <0.5 beats/min/mmHg), and by timing as initial, classical, delayed, and postprandial variants.

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System
chunks.text: Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System (non-infective) — Nervous system (autonomic) Also: Dysautonomia, Autonomic failure, Autonomic neuropathy, Orthostatic hypotension, Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), Multiple system atrophy (Shy-Drager syndrome), Pure autonomic failure, Autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Pregnancy (the most common cause of amenorrhea, to be excluded in all cases) (Harrison 22e p.3133)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) - leading cause of oligo-/anovulation (Harrison 22e p.3133)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Premature ovarian insufficiency / gonadal dysgenesis including Turner syndrome (Harrison 22e p.3132, p.3134)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea from undernutrition, excessive exercise, or eating disorders (Harrison 22e p.3132)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Hyperprolactinemia (pituitary lesions or medications) (Harrison 22e p.3134)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Hypothalamic/pituitary tumors and infiltrative disease; Sheehan syndrome and lymphocytic hypophysitis postpartum (Harrison 22e p.3134)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Mullerian agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome) and androgen insensitivity syndrome as causes of primary amenorrhea (Harrison 22e p.3133)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Late-onset (nonclassic) congenital adrenal hyperplasia and androgen-secreting tumors in heterosexual precocity (Harrison 22e p.3131)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Genital tuberculosis as a cause of intrauterine adhesions (Asherman syndrome) in endemic regions, mimicking primary endometrial or ovulatory failure (Harrison 22e p.3133)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: CNS infection as a cause of central precocious puberty (Harrison 22e p.3131)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Pregnancy test (beta-hCG) as the first step in any menstrual disturbance (Harrison 22e p.3133)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: AMH as a marker of ovarian reserve (Harrison 22e p.3126)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Mid-luteal serum progesterone (>3 ng/mL) to confirm ovulation (Harrison 22e p.3130)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Serum FSH and LH to localize the defect (ovarian vs central) (Harrison 22e p.3131, p.3134)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Estradiol and testosterone; DHEAS and 17-hydroxyprogesterone when hyperandrogenism is suspected (Harrison 22e p.3131)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Prolactin in all patients with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (Harrison 22e p.3134)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: TSH and free T4 (Harrison 22e p.3131)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Bone age and assessment of growth velocity in pubertal disorders (Harrison 22e p.3131)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Pelvic ultrasound to assess follicle growth, endometrial thickness, corpus luteum, and reproductive-tract anatomy (Harrison 22e p.3130, p.3131)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Cranial MRI for suspected central/neuroanatomic causes; pelvic MRI to define tract anomalies before surgery (Harrison 22e p.3131, p.3133)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Karyotype in delayed puberty and suspected gonadal dysgenesis (Harrison 22e p.3131)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty mimicking pathologic delayed puberty (Harrison 22e p.3132)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Premature thelarche (isolated breast development before age 2) without progression mimicking true precocious puberty (Harrison 22e p.3131)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Premature adrenarche without progressive pubertal development, to be distinguished from nonclassic CAH and androgen-secreting tumors (Harrison 22e p.3131)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: McCune-Albright syndrome and congenital adrenal hyperplasia, in which initially peripheral precocity may convert to central precocity (Harrison 22e p.3131)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: The female reproductive axis is a tightly regulated hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian system. Pulsatile GnRH from roughly 7000 hypothalamic neurons, coordinated by pulsatile kisspeptin secretion (modulated by stimulatory neurokinin B and inhibitory dynorphin in KNDy neurons), drives pituitary FSH and LH release. FSH recruits secondary follicles from the resting pool (cyclic recruitment), restrained by AMH from small growing follicles. A single dominant follicle is selected within the first week of the cycle through high FSH-receptor density, high aromatase activity, and rising estradiol and inhibin A, which suppress FSH and the growth of competing follicles. Estradiol is produced by the cooperative two-cell mechanism (LH-driven theca androgen synthesis, FSH-driven granulosa aromatization). The mid-cycle estradiol-induced LH surge triggers resumption of oocyte meiosis, induction of COX-2, prostaglandins, and the progesterone receptor, and ovulation, followed by luteinization of theca and granulosa cells to form the progesterone-secreting corpus luteum. Disorders arise from defects at any level: genetic or anatomic GnRH-neuron migration defects, functional hypothalamic suppression from energy deficit, pituitary lesions, ovarian failure (gonadal dysgenesis, premature ovarian insufficiency, mutations in over 50 genes), or outflow-tract obstruction. Over 50 genes have been implicated in premature ovarian insufficiency, reflecting the genetic complexity of follicle endowment and survival (Harrison 22e p.3125-p.3132).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Normal cyclic reproductive function depends on coordinated signaling among the hypothalamus (GnRH), pituitary (FSH and LH), and ovary, producing repeating cycles of follicle growth, ovulation, and endometrial preparation; disruption at any level produces menstrual dysfunction (Harrison 22e p.3124, p.3133).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Menarche occurs late in the pubertal sequence: it is preceded by adrenarche (pubic and axillary hair) and thelarche (breast development), with breast development typically about 2 years before menarche; U.S. average age at menarche is roughly 12.5 years (Harrison 22e p.3130).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Central precocious puberty in girls is idiopathic in about 85% of cases, but a neurogenic cause must be excluded; it shows pulsatile LH and a brisk LH/FSH response to GnRH stimulation, whereas peripheral precocity has suppressed gonadotropins with elevated estradiol (Harrison 22e p.3130, p.3131).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Delayed puberty in girls (absence of secondary sexual characteristics by age 13) is of ovarian origin in 25-40% of cases, with Turner syndrome the leading cause; reversible functional causes such as undernutrition, excessive exercise, eating disorders, and chronic illness account for about 25% (Harrison 22e p.3131, p.3132).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: The ovarian germ cell pool is non-renewable: oogonia peak at roughly 6-7 million by mid-gestation (about 20 weeks) and fall to only 1-2 million primordial follicles at birth, declining further through atresia thereafter (Harrison 22e p.3125, p.3126).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: In a normal ovulatory adult, cycle length averages about 28 days (range 25-35), bleeding lasts about 4-6 days, and the luteal phase is relatively fixed at 12-14 days, so most cycle-length variability reflects differences in follicular phase length (Harrison 22e p.3130).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Cycle-to-cycle variability for a consistently ovulating woman is only about plus or minus 2 days; cycles tend to shorten after age 35 and become more erratic and anovulatory as menopause approaches (Harrison 22e p.3130).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Documentation of ovulation can use a mid-luteal serum progesterone above 3 ng/mL (about 7 days after ovulation), a sustained basal body temperature rise of over 0.5 degrees F from the progesterone thermogenic effect, or a urinary LH surge; an apparent LH surge does not guarantee that ovulation actually occurs (Harrison 22e p.3130).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Estrogen synthesis requires cooperation of two ovarian cell types: theca cells make androgens under LH control, and granulosa cells aromatize these androgens to estradiol under FSH control (the two-cell, two-gonadotropin model) (Harrison 22e p.3127).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Anti-mullerian hormone (AMH), produced by small growing preantral follicles, restrains FSH-driven recruitment, limiting the number of follicles entering the growing pool; AMH is a clinical marker of ovarian reserve and is elevated in PCOS (Harrison 22e p.3126).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: GnRH neurons originate in the olfactory placode and migrate to the hypothalamus alongside olfactory neurons; failure of this migration links anosmia with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (Kallmann phenotype) (Harrison 22e p.3126, p.3127).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: FSH and LH are high in the neonatal period, fall into a quiescent childhood phase, and rise again at puberty; early in puberty gonadotropin secretion is detectable only during sleep before extending across the day (Harrison 22e p.3127).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Failing to exclude pregnancy before any other workup of amenorrhea, since it is the most common cause (Harrison 22e p.3133).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Assuming the absence of premenstrual moliminal symptoms proves anovulation - their absence does not (Harrison 22e p.3130).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Treating a detected urinary LH surge as proof of ovulation when ovulation may still fail to occur (Harrison 22e p.3130).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Overlooking infrequent or absent menses because the patient does not report them, missing an underlying disorder with long-term health consequences (Harrison 22e p.3133).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Not measuring prolactin in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, since hyperprolactinemia from lesions or drugs is a common reversible cause (Harrison 22e p.3134).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Forgetting that peripheral precocious puberty (e.g., McCune-Albright, CAH) can secondarily trigger central precocity, requiring reassessment (Harrison 22e p.3131).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Misattributing irregular cycles in adolescence or perimenopause to pathology when anovulatory irregularity is physiologic in the first few years after menarche and the years before menopause (Harrison 22e p.3130, p.3133).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Many disorders are highly treatable when the level of the defect is identified. Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea from energy deficit is often reversible with restoration of energy balance. Outflow-tract obstruction has a good outcome with timely surgery, but delay increases the risk of endometriosis from retrograde menstruation. Premature ovarian insufficiency and gonadal dysgenesis carry permanent loss of fertility and require attention to long-term estrogen-deficiency consequences for bone and other tissues. In precocious puberty, untreated central precocity risks premature epiphyseal closure and compromised adult height, while appropriate management preserves height and addresses psychosocial impact (Harrison 22e p.3126, p.3131, p.3132, p.3133).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Primary amenorrhea with absent secondary sexual characteristics, short stature, or height below the third percentile suggesting Turner syndrome or another pathologic cause requiring evaluation by age 13 (Harrison 22e p.3133)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Amenorrhea with galactorrhea, headache, visual symptoms, or diabetes insipidus suggesting a hypothalamic-pituitary mass (Harrison 22e p.3134)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Cyclic pelvic pain with primary amenorrhea suggesting outflow-tract obstruction (imperforate hymen, transverse vaginal septum) requiring prompt surgery to limit endometriosis from retrograde flow (Harrison 22e p.3133)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Secondary sexual development before age 8 (or breast/pubic hair before 6-7) warranting evaluation for precocious puberty, including exclusion of CNS tumors (Harrison 22e p.3130, p.3131)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Postpartum amenorrhea raising concern for pituitary necrosis (Sheehan syndrome) or lymphocytic hypophysitis (Harrison 22e p.3134)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Heavy or prolonged bleeding (over 7 days) or markedly irregular intervals (over 35 or under 21 days) prompting evaluation for AUB causes including malignancy/hyperplasia (Harrison 22e p.3133)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Amenorrhea is classified as primary (menses never occurred without hormonal treatment) versus secondary (cessation for 3-6 months). Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) replaces the older term dysfunctional uterine bleeding and is categorized etiologically by the PALM-COEIN system into structural causes (Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy/hyperplasia) and nonstructural causes (Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not yet classified). Precocious puberty is divided into central (GnRH-dependent) and peripheral (GnRH-independent) forms, and delayed puberty into hypergonadotropic (ovarian) and hypogonadotropic (central) forms (Harrison 22e p.3131, p.3133).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System
chunks.text: Disorders of the Female Reproductive System (non-infective) — Reproductive / Endocrine Also: Female reproductive endocrinology, Ovarian function disorders, Disorders of puberty in girls

Mediastinoscopy for sampling of paratracheal and subcarinal lymph nodes

Barium GI studies for posterior mediastinal lesions (hernia, diverticulum, achalasia)
Mediastinal needle aspiration to confirm post-sternotomy mediastinitis
