Disorders of the mediastinum arise from the anatomical structures of its three compartments. Anterior compartment lesions stem from the thymus, lymph nodes, germinal/thyroid tissue, and mammary vessels, giving rise to thymomas, germ cell tumors, lymphomas, and goiter. Middle compartment disease typically reflects embryologic developmental abnormalities producing foregut-derived cysts (bronchogenic, duplication, pericardial), or malignant lymphadenopathy and vascular masses; because central vasculature resides here, compression of structures such as the SVC can produce acute life-threatening physiology. Posterior compartment lesions are predominantly neurogenic, with contributions from diaphragmatic hernia, meningocele, esophageal diverticula, and extramedullary hematopoiesis. Acute mediastinitis is an inflammatory/infectious process driven by esophageal breach, post-sternotomy wound contamination, or descending cervicofacial infection. Chronic and fibrosing mediastinitis represents a spectrum from granulomatous lymph node inflammation to dense fibrosis, usually following granulomatous infection, with progressive encasement and obstruction of mediastinal structures (SVC, large airways, pulmonary vessels, phrenic/recurrent laryngeal nerves). Pneumomediastinum results from alveolar rupture with air dissection into the mediastinum, perforation/rupture of esophagus or airway, or dissection of air from the neck or abdomen.

The mediastinum lies between the pleural sacs, bounded superiorly by the thoracic inlet and inferiorly by the diaphragm, and is divided into anterior, middle, and posterior compartments, each prone to characteristic lesions.

Hamman's sign — a crunching/clicking sound synchronous with the heartbeat, best heard over the anterior chest in the left lateral decubitus position — together with suprasternal subcutaneous emphysema suggests pneumomediastinum.
Most fibrosing mediastinitis follows prior granulomatous infection, commonly histoplasmosis or tuberculosis, though sarcoidosis, silicosis, and fungal disease may also be causative.
Barium gastrointestinal studies are useful in many posterior mediastinal lesions because hernias, diverticula, and achalasia are readily identified this way.
Localizing a mediastinal mass to one of the three compartments is the essential first diagnostic step, since each compartment harbors a distinct set of typical lesions.

The anterior compartment is the source of thymomas, germ cell tumors (including teratomas), lymphomas, and thyroid goiter; thymoma is the most common anterior mediastinal neoplasm and is closely linked to paraneoplastic syndromes, most notably myasthenia gravis.
Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies in serum support a diagnosis of myasthenia gravis in the setting of an anterior mediastinal mass.

Teratomas are the most common germ cell tumor and appear as multilobulated cystic lesions containing fat, soft tissue, and calcium; elevated alpha-fetoprotein and beta-hCG distinguish nonseminomatous from seminomatous germ cell tumors.

Most middle mediastinal masses are benign and developmental in origin, including bronchogenic cysts (abnormal ventral foregut budding), duplication cysts (persistent dorsal foregut diverticulum), and pericardial cysts (abnormal pericardial recess fusion).
Neurogenic tumors are the most common cause of posterior mediastinal masses and are frequently benign, arising from peripheral, autonomic, or paraganglionic nervous tissue.

Superior vena cava syndrome is a medical emergency presenting with severe dyspnea and facial/upper-extremity edema; malignancy causes most cases, with lung cancer (especially small-cell carcinoma) accounting for up to 50%.
Acute mediastinitis most often follows esophageal perforation, median sternotomy for cardiac surgery, or infection descending from the neck, oral cavity, or face.
Failing to compartmentalize a mediastinal mass before working it up, since each compartment has different characteristic lesions.
Overlooking that advanced malignancy may not remain confined to one compartment and can cross borders via hematogenous and lymphatic spread.
Underappreciating SVC compression in the middle mediastinum as an acute, life-threatening emergency.
Missing the link between an anterior mediastinal mass (thymoma) and paraneoplastic myasthenia gravis.
Assuming fibrosing mediastinitis is purely structural without recognizing its common antecedent granulomatous infection and need to exclude malignancy by biopsy.

Prognosis depends on the underlying disorder. Most middle mediastinal masses and posterior neurogenic tumors are benign. Anterior mediastinal neoplasms vary widely, and disease severity across mediastinal masses spans a broad spectrum; clinical symptoms, patient age, and tumor location guide assessment of malignancy and need for intervention. Acute post-sternotomy mediastinitis carries a mortality rate exceeding 20% despite treatment. Fibrosing mediastinitis can be devastating in severe cases owing to obstruction/encasement of vital structures. Pneumomediastinum usually requires no treatment and resolves with absorption of air.
Superior vena cava syndrome (severe dyspnea, facial and upper-extremity edema) — a medical emergency
Acutely ill patient with chest pain and dyspnea suggesting esophageal rupture with mediastinal infection
Post-sternotomy wound drainage with sepsis and a widened mediastinum
Severe substernal chest pain radiating to neck/arms with subcutaneous emphysema (pneumomediastinum)
Hemoptysis, dysphagia, or Horner's syndrome in fibrosing mediastinitis indicating structural invasion/obstruction

No formal grading system; mediastinal disorders are stratified anatomically into anterior, middle, and posterior compartments, and severity is judged by clinical symptoms, patient age, lesion location, likelihood of malignancy, and presence of acute complications such as SVC obstruction or airway compromise.

Disorders of the neurohypophysis arise from deficient or excessive AVP secretion/action. In AVP deficiency (formerly central/neurogenic diabetes insipidus) and AVP resistance (formerly nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), impaired urine concentration increases free-water excretion, causing a small (1-2%) reduction in body water and a rise in plasma osmolality/sodium that stimulates thirst and compensatory drinking; severity ranges from near-complete deficiency unresponsive to maximal stimuli to partial defects in which mild stimuli can still partially concentrate urine, though prior lack of AVP transiently blunts renal concentrating capacity. Central deficiency reflects destruction or dysfunction of AVP-producing neurons (trauma, tumors, vascular, granulomatous, infectious, autoimmune/IgG4 hypophysitis, or genetic AVP-neurophysin II mutations); resistance reflects reduced renal V2-receptor/aquaporin-2 responsiveness from drugs (lithium), hypokalemia, hypercalcemia, infiltrative or vascular disease, or AVPR2/AQP2 mutations. Primary polydipsia is the mirror image: excess intake lowers plasma osmolality, physiologically suppresses AVP, and produces a dilute compensatory diuresis. Hypodipsic/adipsic hypernatremia results from anterior hypothalamic osmoreceptor damage impairing osmotic thirst (occasionally from anti-subfornical-organ autoantibodies), so obligatory renal/insensible losses go unreplaced. In SIAD, AVP is inappropriately elevated when it should be osmotically suppressed, causing water retention, slight volume expansion with renal sodium loss (no edema), and dilutional hypoosmolality with cellular swelling (Harrison 22e p.3014-3019).

The neurohypophysis releases arginine vasopressin (AVP/ADH) and oxytocin from axons whose cell bodies sit in the hypothalamic paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei; AVP conserves water by concentrating urine, while oxytocin drives milk letdown and socioemotional behaviors (Harrison 22e p.3014).

In pregnancy, placental N-terminal aminopeptidase (vasopressinase) accelerates AVP clearance three- to fourfold, producing gestational AVP deficiency that typically remits weeks after delivery; the synthetic analogue DDAVP resists this peptidase (Harrison 22e p.3016-3017).

Hypoosmolality is the hallmark of SIAD; acute or severe hyponatremia can cause headache, confusion, nausea, vomiting, seizures, and coma, while even mild chronic hyponatremia raises the risk of falls, fractures, neurocognitive symptoms, and mortality (Harrison 22e p.3019).

In SIAD, persistent water retention modestly expands total body water and triggers compensatory urinary sodium loss, so edema does not develop; the harm comes from intracellular (notably cerebral) swelling proportional to the speed and degree of the sodium fall (Harrison 22e p.3019).

AVP secretion is governed mainly by an osmotic set point in anteromedial hypothalamic osmoreceptors, with the average threshold near a plasma osmolality of ~275 mosmol/L and sodium ~135 meq/L; only a 2-4% rise above this drives maximum antidiuresis (Harrison 22e p.3015).

Nausea/emetic stimuli are extremely potent AVP releasers, producing 50- to 100-fold increases even without vomiting, far exceeding osmotic stimulation; AVP is also released by a >10-20% fall in blood pressure or volume, hypoglycemia, glucocorticoid deficiency, and smoking (Harrison 22e p.3015).

AVP acts on V2 receptors of collecting-duct principal cells to insert aquaporin-2 water channels, enabling water reabsorption; maximum antidiuresis (urine osmolality up to ~1200 mosmol/L) occurs at plasma AVP of roughly 1-3 pg/mL (Harrison 22e p.3016).
The thirst osmostat is set about 3% higher than the AVP osmostat, so antidiuresis is the first-line defense and thirst/polydipsia only engage once AVP's capacity is exceeded (Harrison 22e p.3016).

Polyuria-polydipsia is defined practically by a 24-h urine volume exceeding ~40-50 mL/kg and/or >3 L/d on unrestricted intake; dehydration and hypernatremia are uncommon in diabetes insipidus unless thirst or access to water is also impaired (Harrison 22e p.3016-3017).

Serum sodium at presentation is a key discriminator: a low sodium (<135 mmol/L) points toward primary polydipsia (patients can drink into hyponatremia), whereas a high sodium suggests AVP deficiency or resistance (Harrison 22e p.3017).

Copeptin, the stable C-terminal fragment of the AVP prohormone, has largely replaced direct AVP assays: a baseline copeptin >21.4 pmol/L without prior water deprivation identifies AVP resistance, and a copeptin >4.9 pmol/L at plasma sodium >=150 mmol/L after hypertonic saline distinguishes AVP deficiency from primary polydipsia with ~96.5% accuracy (Harrison 22e p.3017-3018).

The MRI posterior pituitary bright spot reflects AVP-containing neurosecretory vesicles and is often absent in AVP deficiency, but its absence is not diagnostic since it can persist early or be absent in the elderly (Harrison 22e p.3018).

Low basal AVP/V2 stimulation (e.g., in primary polydipsia) transiently blunts renal concentrating capacity, so the urine osmolality rise after exogenous AVP can falsely suggest a concentrating defect, undermining the traditional indirect water deprivation test (accuracy only ~70%, and ~41% in primary polydipsia) (Harrison 22e p.3016-3017).
Measurement of plasma AVP or copeptin has no diagnostic value in SIAD itself; copeptin is used for the polyuria differential, not for confirming SIAD (Harrison 22e p.3020).
Failing to measure serum osmolality risks misclassifying pseudohyponatremia or translocational hyponatremia as true hypotonic SIAD (Harrison 22e p.3019-3020).
Clinical assessment of volume status is inaccurate, so relying on examination alone to classify hyponatremia can mislead (Harrison 22e p.3020).
Secondary adrenal insufficiency must be excluded before diagnosing SIAD in euvolemic hyponatremia (Harrison 22e p.3020).
Hypertonic saline-stimulated copeptin testing requires close sodium monitoring; absence of the MRI bright spot is not by itself sufficient to diagnose AVP deficiency (Harrison 22e p.3018).
Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia or hypernatremia is dangerous; serum sodium must be corrected slowly with close monitoring (Harrison 22e p.3019-3020).

Uncomplicated AVP deficiency is generally well managed with vasopressin replacement, restoring normal water balance. Hyponatremia is the most common complication of replacement and ranges from mild to severe. AVP resistance is difficult to treat and may respond only partially. Adipsic/hypodipsic hypernatremia carries higher risk because the absent thirst sensation predisposes to recurrent hypertonic dehydration and complications such as rhabdomyolysis, acute renal failure, and thromboembolism; long-term structured fluid-balance management is needed to prevent recurrence. In SIAD, even mild chronic hyponatremia is associated with increased falls, fractures, neurocognitive and neuromuscular symptoms, and increased morbidity and mortality (Harrison 22e p.3017-3019).
Severe or acute hyponatremia with headache, confusion, vomiting, seizures, or coma (cerebral edema)
Hypernatremia with signs of hypovolemia (tachycardia, postural hypotension, azotemia) in adipsic patients
Denial of thirst or failure to drink when conscious and hypernatremic (virtually diagnostic of adipsia)
Rhabdomyolysis, acute renal failure, or thromboembolic disease complicating hypertonic dehydration
Polyuria with rising serum sodium signaling inadequate water replacement
Lithium use with persistent polyuria suggesting drug-induced AVP resistance

Diabetes insipidus is graded as complete versus partial AVP deficiency, and complete versus partial AVP resistance, distinguished by copeptin response, desmopressin response, and the magnitude of urine osmolality change. Hyponatremia severity is gauged by plasma sodium and tempo: severe/acute hyponatremia with neurologic symptoms warrants urgent treatment, whereas gradual or mild hyponatremia may be paucisymptomatic; replacement-related hyponatremia is categorized as mild (sodium 131-134 mmol/L) or more severe (<130 mmol/L). Hypernatremia severity in adipsic patients varies widely and correlates with hypovolemic complications (Harrison 22e p.3017-3019).

Disorders of the Neurohypophysis (non-infective) — Endocrine Also: Posterior pituitary disorders, Diabetes insipidus, AVP deficiency, AVP resistance, Central diabetes insipidus, Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, SIADH, Adipsic hypernatremia
Transudates: congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, peritoneal dialysis, superior vena cava obstruction, myxedema, urinothorax
Exudates from neoplasm: metastatic disease, mesothelioma, lymphoma
Exudates from infection: bacterial (parapneumonic/empyema), tuberculous, fungal, viral, parasitic
Pulmonary embolism
Gastrointestinal causes: esophageal perforation, pancreatic disease, intraabdominal abscess, diaphragmatic hernia, post-abdominal surgery, post liver transplant, variceal sclerotherapy
Collagen vascular disease: rheumatoid pleuritis, SLE, drug-induced lupus, Sjogren syndrome, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, Churg-Strauss

Other: post-CABG, asbestos exposure, sarcoidosis, uremia, Meigs' syndrome, yellow nail syndrome, trapped lung, radiation, post-cardiac injury syndrome, hemothorax, chylothorax, ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, pericardial disease, drug-induced (nitrofurantoin, dantrolene, methysergide, bromocriptine, procarbazine, amiodarone, dasatinib)
Tuberculous pleuritis presenting with fever, weight loss, and pleuritic pain mimicking malignancy or other chronic exudate
Intraabdominal abscess producing a febrile, polymorphonuclear effusion without pulmonary parenchymal abnormality
Hepatic hydrothorax that can be complicated by spontaneous bacterial empyema
Chest imaging: chest x-ray with lateral decubitus films, chest ultrasound, and CT to assess extent, free-flowing versus loculated fluid, and to guide sampling/drainage
Diagnostic thoracentesis with pleural fluid protein and LDH (Light's criteria)
Pleural fluid glucose, differential cell count, Gram stain/culture, and cytology

Disease-specific pleural fluid tests: amylase (pancreatic disease/esophageal rupture), eosinophils (drug-induced), NT-proBNP (heart failure, >1500 pg/mL suggests cardiac origin), cholesterol/triglycerides (chylothorax, triglyceride >110 mg/dL), hematocrit (hemothorax), glucose and pH (rheumatoid disease), Congo red staining (amyloidosis), flow cytometry (lymphoma)
TB markers: pleural fluid adenosine deaminase >40 IU/L or interferon-gamma >140 pg/mL; AFB culture, pleural biopsy
CT/ultrasound-guided pleural biopsy or thoracoscopy when cytology is non-diagnostic
CT angiography for suspected pulmonary embolism; lymphangiogram and chest CT for chylothorax without obvious trauma
Pleural manometry to help confirm trapped lung
Pulmonary embolism mimicking infectious pleuritis with an exudative effusion and pleuritic pain
Malignant effusion (including mesothelioma) mimicking empyema or chronic infection
Rheumatoid or lupus pleuritis mimicking infectious exudate (low glucose in rheumatoid disease)
Pleural effusion ex vacuo / trapped lung mimicking persistent active disease

Pleural fluid normally enters from parietal pleural capillaries and is cleared by parietal pleural lymphatics, which can absorb up to 20 times the normal rate of fluid formation; fluid can also enter from lung interstitium via the visceral pleura or from the peritoneal cavity through diaphragmatic openings. An effusion forms when the hydrostatic-oncotic balance is disturbed and fluid production overwhelms lymphatic removal. Transudates result from altered systemic factors (e.g., elevated left atrial and pulmonary venous pressure in heart failure raising hydrostatic pressure, or low oncotic pressure), whereas exudates result from altered local factors such as inflammation, infection, or malignancy increasing capillary permeability or impairing lymphatic drainage. Parapneumonic effusions begin as a sterile reactive exudate and can progress through exudative, fibrinopurulent, and organizing (pleural peel) phases. Hepatic hydrothorax reflects direct movement of ascitic fluid through small diaphragmatic defects into the pleural space. Pneumothorax results from gas entering the pleural space, abolishing the negative pressure that couples lung to chest wall; in tension pneumothorax a one-way mechanism produces sustained positive pleural pressure.

The pleural space normally holds only a thin film of fluid acting as a coupling system, kept at roughly -3 to -5 cmH2O by the balance between lung elastic recoil (visceral pleura) and chest-wall outward expansion (parietal pleura).

Chylothorax produces milky fluid with a triglyceride level exceeding 110 mg/dL (1.2 mmol/L); prolonged chest-tube drainage should be avoided because chyle loss causes malnutrition and immunologic incompetence.
Hemothorax is defined when pleural fluid hematocrit exceeds half the peripheral blood hematocrit; most are traumatic.
About half of patients with an initial primary spontaneous pneumothorax (from rupture of apical subpleural blebs) will have a recurrence.
Tension pneumothorax is a medical emergency: positive intrapleural pressure throughout the respiratory cycle impairs ventilation and reduces venous return, lowering cardiac output.

The first diagnostic step in any pleural effusion is distinguishing transudate from exudate via thoracentesis; this dictates whether further work-up is needed, since exudates require investigation to define their cause.

Light's criteria define an exudate when at least one is met: pleural fluid/serum protein >0.5, pleural fluid/serum LDH >0.6, or pleural fluid LDH greater than two-thirds the upper normal serum limit; transudates meet none.

Light's criteria misclassify about 25% of transudates as exudates ('pseudoexudates'), often in a diuresed transudate; a serum-to-pleural-fluid protein gradient >3.1 g/dL or albumin gradient >1.2 g/dL helps reclassify these (high sensitivity in heart failure and hepatothorax).
Left ventricular failure is the single most common cause of pleural effusion (a transudate from raised hydrostatic pressure); cirrhosis is the next leading transudative cause in the United States.

Parapneumonic effusions occur in up to 50% of community-acquired pneumonias and are generally the most common exudative effusion in the U.S.; about 10% become complicated or progress to empyema (fibrinopurulent or grossly purulent fluid).

Malignant pleural effusions are the second most common exudate; lung carcinoma, breast carcinoma, and lymphoma together cause roughly 75% of cases, and dyspnea is often out of proportion to effusion size.
Pulmonary embolism is the diagnosis most commonly overlooked in an undiagnosed exudative effusion; the fluid is almost always exudative and dyspnea is the predominant symptom.

Tuberculous pleuritis arises largely as a hypersensitivity reaction to tuberculous protein in the pleural space and yields a lymphocyte-predominant exudate; pleural biopsy culture yield exceeds that of pleural fluid.
Relying on Light's criteria alone can misclassify roughly 25% of transudates as exudates; failing to apply protein/albumin gradients in a clinically transudative setting leads to unnecessary work-up.
Overlooking pulmonary embolism as the cause of an otherwise undiagnosed exudative effusion.
Being overly aggressive in pursuing a diagnosis in a clinically improving patient whose effusion is likely viral and self-limited.

Failing to recognize trapped lung: a thick pleural rind, air on imaging after thoracentesis (pneumothorax ex vacuo), and rapid re-accumulation indicate a lung that will not re-expand without decortication.
Prolonged tube thoracostomy drainage of a chylothorax, which can cause malnutrition and immunologic incompetence.
Not performing diagnostic thoracentesis in a presumed heart-failure effusion that is unilateral, asymmetric, febrile, or pleuritic, or that persists despite therapy.

Prognosis depends on the underlying cause. Transudative effusions from heart failure or cirrhosis improve when the primary condition is treated, and undiagnosed viral effusions usually resolve spontaneously without long-term residua. A malignant pleural effusion usually portends a poor prognosis (often less than 6-month survival) and reflects disseminated disease that is generally not curable with chemotherapy. Untreated complicated parapneumonic effusions can organize into a restrictive pleural peel (trapped lung). Tension pneumothorax is rapidly fatal from inadequate cardiac output or marked hypoxemia if not relieved. Surgical pleurodesis prevents pneumothorax recurrence in nearly 100% of cases.

Tension pneumothorax: enlarged hemithorax with absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, contralateral mediastinal shift, and hypotension; treat as an emergency with immediate needle decompression (large-bore needle in the second anterior intercostal space).
Difficulty ventilating or high peak inspiratory pressures during mechanical ventilation/resuscitation strongly suggest tension pneumothorax.

Complicated parapneumonic effusion/empyema markers indicating need for drainage: loculated fluid, pleural fluid pH <7.20, glucose <60 mg/dL (<3.3 mmol/L), positive Gram stain or culture, gross pus, and elevated pleural fluid LDH (>900 IU/L).
Hemothorax with ongoing pleural hemorrhage exceeding 200 mL/h warrants angiographic embolization, thoracoscopy, or thoracotomy.
Secondary pneumothorax in a patient with underlying lung disease can be more life-threatening because of reduced pulmonary reserve.

Parapneumonic effusions are staged along a continuum from simple (free-flowing, reactive) to complicated (loculated, pH <7.20, glucose <60 mg/dL, positive Gram stain/culture) to empyema (frank pus), with progression through exudative, fibrinopurulent, and organizing (pleural peel) phases guiding the need for escalating intervention. Pneumothorax is categorized as primary spontaneous, secondary, traumatic (including iatrogenic), and tension.
Disorders of the Pleura (non-infective) — Respiratory Also: Pleural effusion, Pneumothorax, Empyema, Hemothorax, Chylothorax, Mesothelioma

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Hemochromatosis (pituitary and/or testicular iron deposition)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Sellar mass lesions / pituitary adenoma impairing gonadotropin secretion

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Functional hypogonadotropic hypogonadism from systemic illness, malnutrition, eating disorders, or opioid use

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Lepromatous leprosy causing testicular atrophy through direct mycobacterial invasion

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Fasting early-morning total testosterone (LC-MS/MS preferred, CDC HoST-certified); repeat if borderline (200-400 ng/dL) and add free testosterone

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Free testosterone by equilibrium dialysis when SHBG is altered (aging, obesity, chronic illness)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: LH and FSH to separate primary (high LH/FSH) from secondary (low/inappropriately normal LH) hypogonadism

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Karyotype in men with low testosterone, elevated LH, and small testes to diagnose Klinefelter syndrome

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Serum prolactin and ferritin/transferrin saturation; pituitary MRI when secondary hypogonadism is found

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Inhibin B (Sertoli cell product) to assess seminiferous tubule integrity

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Semen analysis and Y-chromosome microdeletion testing (AZFa/AZFb/AZFc) in oligo-/azoospermia

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: For gynecomastia: testosterone, estradiol, estrone, androstenedione, LH, hCG (beta), TSH; testicular ultrasound and adrenal/chest imaging if an estrogen- or hCG-secreting tumor is suspected

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Lipomastia (excess adipose) mimicking glandular gynecomastia

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Retractile testis mimicking cryptorchidism

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Age-related decline in testosterone overlapping with symptomatic hypogonadism

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Obesity-related lowering of total testosterone (with often normal free testosterone) due to reduced SHBG

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: The hypothalamic-pituitary-testicular axis governs androgen production and spermatogenesis. Pulsatile hypothalamic GnRH (regulated by kisspeptin, neurokinin B, and dynorphin in KNDy neurons) drives pituitary LH and FSH roughly every 1-3 h. LH stimulates Leydig cell testosterone synthesis (rate-limited by StAR-mediated cholesterol transport into mitochondria and CYP11A1 side-chain cleavage); FSH acts on Sertoli cells to support spermatogenesis and inhibin B production, the latter selectively suppressing FSH. Testosterone is converted by 5-alpha-reductase (SRD5A2) to the more potent DHT (required for external genital virilization and prostate growth) and aromatized by CYP19 to estradiol (mediating effects on bone, epiphyseal closure, libido). Disorders arise from gonadotropin deficiency (secondary/hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, congenital such as GnRH-deficient/Kallmann syndrome or acquired from sellar masses, hyperprolactinemia, hemochromatosis, illness, drugs, obesity) or primary testicular failure (hypergonadotropic), e.g., Klinefelter syndrome, cryptorchidism, orchitis, chemo/radiation, torsion. Resistance syndromes (androgen receptor mutations, 5-alpha-reductase or aromatase deficiency) impair androgen action or conversion. Gynecomastia results from a relative excess of estrogen action on breast tissue (p.3102-3116).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: A low serum testosterone with an elevated LH localizes the defect to the testis (primary/hypergonadotropic hypogonadism), whereas a low or inappropriately normal LH points to a hypothalamic-pituitary defect (secondary/hypogonadotropic hypogonadism) (p.3107, p.3118).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Up to two-thirds of pubertal boys and about half of hospitalized men have benign palpable breast tissue, so not all gynecomastia requires extensive investigation (p.3116).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Kallmann syndrome is the anosmic form of congenital GnRH-deficient hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, arising from defective olfactory bulb morphogenesis and failed migration of GnRH neurons; micropenis and a history of cryptorchidism favor a congenital central defect over self-limited delayed puberty (p.3112, p.3110).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Acquired androgen-deficient men commonly report decreased libido, fewer sexual thoughts and acts, low energy, low mood, and (less often) hot flushes; eunuchoid body proportions (arm span >2 cm greater than height) indicate that deficiency predated epiphyseal fusion (p.3110).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Klinefelter syndrome (classically 47,XXY) is the most common chromosomal cause of testicular dysfunction and male infertility, occurring in about 1 in 600 live-born males, with markedly small testes (often 1-2 mL), azoospermia, low testosterone, raised estradiol, undervirilization, and gynecomastia (p.3110, p.3114).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: True glandular gynecomastia (palpable firm, cord-like tissue >4 cm, often tender) reflects an increased estrogen-to-androgen ratio and must be distinguished from excess adipose (lipomastia); recent rapid onset, tenderness, or occurrence in a lean man warrants workup (p.3115).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Testicular volume is a useful clinical index: normal adult testes are 3.5-5.5 cm long (about 12-25 mL by Prader orchidometer), and very small testes in a hypogonadal man should prompt a karyotype to exclude Klinefelter syndrome (p.3110, p.3119).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Mumps is the classic cause of viral orchitis; orchitis develops in up to one-fourth of affected adult men, is unilateral in about two-thirds, and semen analysis normalizes in three-fourths after unilateral but only one-third after bilateral involvement (p.3114).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Total testosterone can mislead when SHBG is altered (low in obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome; high in aging, hyperthyroidism, estrogen, HIV/hepatitis B and C, some anticonvulsants); measure free testosterone (ideally by equilibrium dialysis) in these settings (p.3106, p.3108).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Cryptorchidism, even when corrected before puberty, carries increased risk of malignancy, infertility, inguinal hernia, and torsion, and is considered part of the testicular dysgenesis syndrome along with hypospadias, impaired spermatogenesis, and testicular cancer (p.3114).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Selective elevation of FSH (with relatively normal LH) suggests seminiferous tubule/Sertoli cell damage, because reduced inhibin B removes the negative feedback restraining FSH (p.3104, p.3107).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Relying on a single random or afternoon testosterone level — values are pulsatile, diurnal, lower in the late afternoon and after meals, and depressed by acute illness, so confirm with a fasting early-morning sample (p.3108, p.3118).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Interpreting total testosterone without accounting for SHBG changes, leading to over- or under-diagnosis in obesity, aging, thyroid disease, or chronic illness (p.3106, p.3108).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Mislabeling the normal aging decline as 'andropause' — there is no discrete andropause and population screening of all older men is not recommended (p.3117).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Subjecting every man with gynecomastia to extensive workup, when most pubertal and many hospitalized men have benign glandular tissue (p.3116).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Confusing retractile testis (no treatment needed) with true cryptorchidism (p.3114).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Assuming corrected unilateral cryptorchidism guarantees normal fertility — sperm counts can remain reduced (p.3114).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Overlooking drug, alcohol, opioid, marijuana, or anabolic-androgenic steroid use as reversible causes of suppressed testosterone (p.3114, p.3119).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Outcomes depend on the underlying disorder. Secondary (hypogonadotropic) hypogonadism is highly amenable to fertility restoration with pulsatile GnRH or gonadotropins, and 10-20% of congenital GnRH-deficient men may have spontaneous reversal in adulthood. In Klinefelter syndrome azoospermia is the rule, though sperm can sometimes be retrieved surgically (including in some non-mosaic men) for ICSI. After mumps orchitis the testis may recover or atrophy. Radiation effects on spermatogenesis are dose-dependent (transient decline below 1 Gy, temporary azoospermia at 1-2 Gy, usually permanent azoospermia above 2 Gy), while Leydig cells are relatively radioresistant (dysfunction generally only above 20 Gy). The age-related testosterone decline is gradual and progressive without a discrete abrupt fall (p.3107, p.3114-3115, p.3117).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Recent-onset, rapidly growing, or tender gynecomastia in a lean man, or breast tissue fixed to underlying tissue (evaluate for tumor/malignancy)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Markedly elevated estradiol with suppressed LH, suggesting a testicular or adrenal estrogen-secreting tumor

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Elevated hCG (beta) prompting search for an hCG-producing germ cell or other tumor

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Very small testes with low testosterone and high LH (consider Klinefelter syndrome and its associated breast cancer risk)

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Diabetes insipidus accompanying hypogonadism, suggesting craniopharyngioma or infiltrative hypothalamic lesion

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Hyperprolactinemia with visual field defects suggesting a pituitary mass

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Diagnostic stratification of male testosterone deficiency (Harrison Fig. 403-8): early-morning total testosterone >350-400 ng/dL makes androgen deficiency unlikely; borderline values 200-350 ng/dL should be repeated with free testosterone; consistently low levels (notably <200 ng/dL) in association with symptoms confirm deficiency. Localization: high LH/FSH = primary (hypergonadotropic) testicular failure; low/inappropriately normal LH = secondary (hypogonadotropic). Harmonized normal total testosterone reference range in healthy young men is 264-916 ng/dL (p.3108, p.3117-3118).

chunks.diseaseName: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System
chunks.text: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System (non-infective) — Endocrine / Male Reproductive Also: Male hypogonadism, Testicular failure, Testosterone deficiency syndrome, Androgen deficiency in men
Parenchymal lung disease (obstructive such as COPD; restrictive such as interstitial lung disease; atelectasis; pulmonary embolus)
Chest wall disorders (kyphoscoliosis, obesity, abdominal distention/ascites)
Neuromuscular disease (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, phrenic nerve injury, spinal cord lesion, myopathy, muscular dystrophy)
Depressed respiratory drive (narcotic/sedative use, brainstem stroke, hypothyroidism, primary alveolar hypoventilation)
Brainstem structural lesions of the pons or medulla (stroke, tumor)
Recurrent pneumonia from ineffective cough in neuromuscular disease can mimic or precipitate acute respiratory deterioration
Arterial blood gas (the diagnostic hallmark): Paco2 >=45 mmHg defines hypoventilation; venous blood gas is an alternative, recognizing venous Pco2 runs a few points higher than arterial

Serum bicarbonate (total CO2) as a sensitive but nonspecific screen: a level <27 mmol/L with normal renal function makes hypoventilation very unlikely, while >=27 mmol/L should prompt Paco2 measurement
Chest x-ray and/or CT to identify lung/chest wall disease
Pulmonary function testing including seated-versus-supine FVC (a 15-25% supine drop suggests diaphragmatic weakness) plus maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures
Polysomnography to demonstrate nocturnal hypercapnia, central versus obstructive apneas/hypopneas, and to screen for OSA
Brain CT or MRI to detect pontine/medullary structural lesions
OSA screening tools (Epworth Sleepiness Scale, Berlin Questionnaire, STOP-Bang) recognizing their limited sensitivity/specificity
Genetic testing for PHOX2b abnormalities in suspected congenital central hypoventilation syndrome

Adequate ventilation depends on a balance between respiratory drive and neuromuscular strength on one side and the elastic plus resistive loads of the respiratory system on the other. Reduced drive, impaired neuromuscular competence, or a markedly increased load lowers effective minute ventilation and produces hypercapnia; conversely, normal muscle strength combined with excessive drive yields hyperventilation and hypocapnia. Diseases reducing minute ventilation or increasing dead space fall into four broad categories: parenchymal lung/chest wall disease, obesity hypoventilation, neuromuscular disease, and respiratory drive disorders. 'Pump failure' encompasses disorders of drive, neural pathways, the neuromuscular junction, and muscle. In OHS the mechanism is multifactorial, combining OSA, increased work of breathing, respiratory muscle impairment against an excess-adiposity load, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and blunted central responsiveness to hypoxemia and hypercapnia. Chronic hyperventilation is conceptualized as having initiating and sustaining factors, with an initial event dropping Paco2 toward ~20 mmHg and resultant symptoms perpetuating overbreathing (Harrison 22e p.2273-2277).
Normal arterial CO2 (Paco2) sits between roughly 37 and 43 mmHg at sea level; all ventilatory disorders manifest as an abnormal Paco2 (Harrison 22e p.2273).

In OHS, the depressed ventilatory responsiveness appears to be a consequence rather than a primary cause, since central drive often improves once sleep-disordered breathing is treated without weight change (Harrison 22e p.2276).

Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (Ondine's curse, CCHS) is linked to PHOX2b gene abnormalities; affected patients lack ventilatory responses to hypoxia/hypercapnia, have mild waking hypercapnia, markedly elevated Paco2 in non-REM sleep, yet can paradoxically normalize Paco2 during exercise and REM sleep (Harrison 22e p.2276).

In chronic hyperventilation, anxiety/panic are not synonymous with the condition; sustaining hypocapnia needs only about a 10% increase in alveolar ventilation, achievable through subtle pattern changes such as occasional sigh breaths or frequent yawning (Harrison 22e p.2277).

Because Paco2 is governed by Paco2 = k(VCO2)/VA, every disturbance reflects altered CO2 production, minute ventilation, or dead-space fraction; a patient can breathe rapidly with a high minute ventilation yet still hypoventilate at the alveolar level if dead space is increased (Harrison 22e p.2273).

Respiratory rhythm is generated in the brainstem (dorsal respiratory group and ventral respiratory column); the pre-Botzinger complex within the VRC is critical for inspiration, and its lesioning abolishes breathing entirely (Harrison 22e p.2273).
Normal sleep brings an attenuated response to hypercapnia and hypoxemia, producing mild nocturnal hypoventilation that corrects on awakening (Harrison 22e p.2273).

New-onset orthopnea is one of the earliest signs of reduced diaphragmatic force generation; 'paradoxical breathing' (abdomen moving inward on deep inspiration while supine) signals significant diaphragmatic weakness or paralysis (Harrison 22e p.2274).

Chronic hypoventilation follows a characteristic sequence: an asymptomatic stage with normal daytime gases, then nocturnal hypoventilation appearing first in REM then non-REM sleep, then falling vital capacity, and finally daytime hypercapnia (Harrison 22e p.2274).

The shared hallmark of all alveolar hypoventilation syndromes is a rise in alveolar and arterial Pco2 with a compensatory increase in plasma bicarbonate; the rising Paco2 displaces alveolar oxygen and commonly causes hypoxemia (Harrison 22e p.2274).

Chronic hypoxemia from hypoventilation can drive secondary erythrocytosis, and the combination of chronic hypoxemia and hypercapnia can cause pulmonary vasoconstriction leading to pulmonary hypertension, right ventricular hypertrophy, and right heart failure (Harrison 22e p.2274).

Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) requires BMI >=30 kg/m2 plus chronic daytime hypoventilation (Paco2 >=45 mmHg) with no other explanation; obstructive sleep apnea coexists in nearly 90% of cases, with about 70% having severe OSA (Harrison 22e p.2275).
Equating high minute ventilation with adequate alveolar ventilation: increased dead space can produce alveolar hypoventilation despite rapid breathing (Harrison 22e p.2273).
Diagnosing primary respiratory drive disorder without excluding far more common secondary causes such as sedatives, chronic narcotics, and significant hypothyroidism (Harrison 22e p.2275).

Misattributing chronic hyperventilation symptoms to cardiopulmonary disease and failing to exclude acute causes (e.g., diabetic ketoacidosis, mild asthma) before labeling it chronic (Harrison 22e p.2276-2277).
Overlooking that supplemental oxygen, even at low concentrations, can worsen hypercapnia in some hypoventilating patients (Harrison 22e p.2276).
Failing to recognize that a serum bicarbonate elevated out of proportion to chronic respiratory acidosis (excess metabolic alkalosis) can itself aggravate hypoventilation (Harrison 22e p.2276).

Chronic hypercapnia in COPD marks more advanced disease and carries worse survival than in equally severe normocapnic patients. Documented daytime hypercapnia treated with nocturnal noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation is associated with improved daytime gas exchange, prolonged survival, and better health-related quality of life. In OHS with severe OSA, both CPAP and NIPPV improve long-term Paco2/bicarbonate and reduce cardiovascular and overall mortality. Progressive neuromuscular disease tends to advance from sleep-only to round-the-clock ventilatory support need, though modern home ventilation can delay tracheostomy and institutionalization (Harrison 22e p.2275-2276).

Diagnostic thresholds rather than a formal grading scale: hypoventilation is defined by Paco2 >=45 mmHg; OHS requires BMI >=30 kg/m2 plus Paco2 >=45 mmHg without another cause; severe OSA is an apnea-hypopnea index >30 events/h; stable chronic hypercapnic COPD considered for home high-intensity ventilation typically has Paco2 >52 mmHg with normal pH (Harrison 22e p.2275-2276).

Effective respiration requires tidal ventilation to freshen alveolar gas, perfusion of each alveolus proportional to its ventilation, and adequate diffusion of O2 and CO2 across the thin alveolar membrane (roughly 70 m2 of surface in about 7 L of thorax via multigenerational airway and vascular branching). Ventilation depends on the volume-related (elastic/static) and flow-related (dynamic) mechanical properties of lung, neuromuscular system, and chest wall; lung recoil rises with inflation while the passive chest wall stiffens at low volume. Disease deranges these properties in a limited number of ways: increased lung elastic recoil restricts volumes (e.g., idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis lowers TLC/FRC/RV/FVC and DLCO but raises flow relative to volume); chest-wall abnormality (e.g., moderate obesity) blunts outward chest recoil and lowers FRC; reduced muscle strength (e.g., myasthenia gravis) lowers TLC and raises RV, reducing FVC/FEV1 as bystanders; decreased airway diameter (e.g., acute asthma) raises resistance and scoops the flow-volume loop; and decreased elastic recoil (e.g., severe emphysema) causes hyperinflation with very elevated TLC/FRC/RV and reduced DLCO. Gas-exchange failure (hypoxemia) results from low inspired oxygen tension, severe alveolar hypoventilation, perfusion of low-V/Q or unventilated (shunt) units, and, rarely, diffusion limitation; shunt blood disproportionately lowers arterial PaO2 because of the nonlinear oxyhemoglobin relationship. Hypercarbia accompanies disorders of ventilation, including severe obstruction and progressive restriction.

The respiratory system can be conceptualized as three functionally independent components: the lung (with its airways), the neuromuscular system (the force generated by respiratory muscles), and the chest wall (everything else, including the muscle mass itself, an obese abdomen, and an enlarged heart).

DLCO interpretation: it falls in diseases that thicken or destroy alveolar membrane (pulmonary fibrosis, emphysema), curtail the pulmonary vasculature (pulmonary hypertension), or reduce capillary hemoglobin (anemia); it can be elevated in asthma, polycythemia, and pulmonary hemorrhage.

In severe airflow obstruction, slowed expiratory flow prevents complete exhalation, raising operating FRC (dynamic hyperinflation / auto-PEEP); at these high volumes the system is less compliant, so the patient senses difficulty INHALING even though the root problem is EXPIRATORY obstruction.

A normal FEV1/FVC ratio does not exclude airflow obstruction: obstruction can raise residual volume and lower FVC, rendering the ratio 'artifactually normal' — lung volumes should scale together (~85-115% predicted) in health, so disproportion is a clue.

Functional residual capacity (FRC) is the passive resting volume where outward recoil of the chest wall is exactly balanced by inward recoil of the lung; at FRC, negative intrapleural pressure offsets positive intrapulmonary pressure giving an airway pressure of 0.

The combined respiratory system pressure-volume relationship is sigmoid: stiffness at high lung volumes is imparted by the lung, stiffness at low volumes by the chest wall (or airway closure), with compliance greatest in the mid-range where normal tidal breathing occurs.

Expiratory airflow limitation is a normal lung property arising from collapsible (not rigid) bronchial airways: as gas accelerates toward the mouth the Bernoulli effect lowers intraluminal and transmural pressure, narrowing the airway, so harder effort yields no net increase in flow.

Inspiratory airflow limitation is rarely caused by diffuse intrathoracic airway disease because more negative pleural pressure during inspiration increases airway transmural pressure and expands airways; instead, inspiratory flow limitation points toward extrathoracic/upper-airway narrowing (e.g., tracheal lesion, post-tracheostomy stricture).

Adequacy of alveolar ventilation is reflected in PaCO2: alveolar and arterial CO2 tensions are equal, the controller normally targets ~40 mmHg, so PaCO2 below 40 indicates hyperventilation and above 40 indicates hypoventilation, with ventilatory failure being extreme hypoventilation.

Only the tidal volume that exceeds the anatomic dead space delivers fresh gas to alveoli; dead space is increased functionally when ventilated lung receives no perfusion (e.g., distal to a large pulmonary embolus), 'wasting' that ventilation.
Oxygen uptake in normal lung is perfusion-limited rather than diffusion-limited: hemoglobin is typically fully saturated by the time blood traverses only about one-third of the alveolar capillary.

Hypoxemia from true shunt (perfusion of nonventilated lung) is refractory to supplemental oxygen, whereas hypoxemia from ventilation/perfusion heterogeneity (low V/Q regions) typically improves with oxygen therapy — a key bedside discriminator.
Interpreting a normal FEV1/FVC ratio as excluding obstruction when raised RV has lowered FVC and made the ratio artifactually normal
Relying on single-breath inert-gas dilution in airflow obstruction, which underestimates true lung volumes because poorly ventilated regions do not receive the inert gas
Assuming alveolar hypoventilation alone explains severe hypoxemia at sea level breathing air — the alveolar gas equation shows this is uncommon unless barometric pressure is reduced (altitude)
Forgetting that a normal chest radiograph does not exclude respiratory disease, especially airway and pulmonary vascular disorders
Attributing a low DLCO to parenchymal disease without considering anemia, while overlooking that DLCO may be elevated in polycythemia or pulmonary hemorrhage
Misreading dyspnea on inhalation in severe obstruction as a primary inspiratory problem when it stems from dynamic hyperinflation due to expiratory flow limitation

Prognosis is determined by the underlying disorder rather than the physiologic pattern itself; the same abnormalities may arise from very different diseases, so pulmonary function testing alone often cannot discriminate among conditions. Many functional disturbances are reversible (e.g., bronchodilator-responsive airflow obstruction in acute asthma), whereas others reflect fixed structural loss (e.g., capillary and alveolar destruction in emphysema or fibrosis) that progressively impairs gas exchange and exercise capacity.
Hypoxemia refractory to supplemental oxygen, suggesting true shunt physiology rather than simple V/Q mismatch
Rising PaCO2 above 40 mmHg indicating alveolar hypoventilation, with extreme elevation signaling impending ventilatory failure
Inspiratory flow plateau on the flow-volume loop, indicating extrathoracic/upper-airway obstruction
Precipitous fall in PaO2 on exertion in emphysema, reflecting inability to raise cardiac output across a destroyed pulmonary vascular bed
Supine FVC decrement greater than about 10-25% (versus the normal 3-8%) indicating significant diaphragmatic/neuromuscular weakness
Isolated reduction in DLCO with preserved spirometry and volumes, prompting evaluation for pulmonary vascular disease

No single formal severity grade applies; physiologic severity is judged by the degree of deviation from predicted values. Most lung-function measures are normal at 85-115% of predicted, and in health volumes scale together. Examples of marked derangement cited include severe emphysema (TLC ~130%, RV ~310%, FEV1 ~35% predicted, low DLCO ~40%) versus pulmonary fibrosis (TLC/FVC/FRC/RV ~60%, low DLCO). Airway resistance (Raw) is normally <2 cmH2O/L/s, and maximal mouth pressures >±60 cmH2O at FRC make significant muscle weakness unlikely.

Diverticula form where the nutrient artery (vasa recta) penetrates the muscularis propria, creating a point of weakness in the colonic wall; most arise in the sigmoid colon, likely reflecting its high-pressure zone where higher-amplitude contractions and firm/constipated stool act on a weak segment. Pathogenesis is now viewed as multifactorial rather than simply low-fiber diet: gut dysbiosis, chronic low-grade inflammation driving neuronal degeneration with resulting dysmotility and high intraluminal pressure, and abnormal collagen cross-linking causing loss of compliance all contribute. Genome-wide association studies (Iceland, Denmark, UK biobanks) link LAMB4 (extracellular-matrix laminin family) and TNFSF15 (TNF family, inflammation) variants to early-onset severe disease. Complications occur when the vasa recta is compressed or eroded (bleeding) or a diverticulum perforates (Harrison 22e p.2578-2579).

Diverticulosis is the most common cause of hematochezia (brisk lower-GI bleed) in patients >60 years; bleeding is abrupt in onset, usually painless, sometimes massive, and often from the right colon. Chronic or occult bleeding is NOT characteristic (Harrison 22e p.2496, 2579).

Routine antibiotics do NOT shorten time to symptom resolution or reduce complications/recurrence in immunocompetent patients with uncomplicated diverticular disease (AVOD and DIABOLO trials, plus meta-analysis) (Harrison 22e p.2580).
Diverticulosis affects about half the population aged >60 years and the majority remain asymptomatic; only ~5% develop acute diverticular disease (Harrison 22e p.2578).

Only ~20% of patients with diverticulosis will ever have GI bleeding; most bleeds are self-limited and stop spontaneously with bowel rest (colonic diverticula stop bleeding spontaneously in >=90% of patients). Lifetime risk of rebleeding is ~25% (Harrison 22e p.2496, 2579).
Acute uncomplicated diverticulitis characteristically presents with fever, anorexia, left lower quadrant abdominal pain, and obstipation (Harrison 22e p.2579).

Diagnosis of diverticulitis is best made on a contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT showing sigmoid diverticula, thickened colonic wall >4 mm, and pericolic fat inflammation WITHOUT extravasation of contrast or fluid (Harrison 22e p.2579).
Diverticula commonly affect the left and sigmoid colon and the rectum is always spared; however in Asian populations 70% of diverticula are in the right colon and cecum (Harrison 22e p.2579).

The pseudodiverticulum (protrusion of mucosa and submucosa only, through the muscularis propria) is the most common type seen in the colon; a true diverticulum is herniation of the entire bowel wall (Harrison 22e p.2578).

Perforated diverticular disease is staged using the Hinchey classification (I: confined paracolic abscess; II: distant/pelvic abscess after spontaneous closure; III: noncommunicating perforation with purulent peritonitis; IV: free perforation with fecal peritonitis); modified to add stage Ia for phlegmon/early abscess (Harrison 22e p.2580).

Pneumaturia or passage of stool/air through the vagina or skin signals a fistula (colovesical, colovaginal, or colocutaneous); colovaginal fistulas are more common in women who have undergone hysterectomy (Harrison 22e p.2579).

Colonoscopy should be considered ~6 weeks AFTER resolution of a first episode, because colon cancer prevalence is low overall (<2%) but higher after complicated diverticulitis (6-8%) (Harrison 22e p.2580).
Do NOT perform colonoscopy during acute diverticulitis (risk of perforation); defer it ~6 weeks until the attack resolves.
Do not reflexively give antibiotics for uncomplicated diverticulitis in immunocompetent patients - trials show no benefit.
The historical advice to avoid nuts, corn, and popcorn rests on anecdotal data only and is not evidence-based; higher intake was actually associated with lower recurrence risk.
Mesalazine appears to help symptoms in SUDD but shows no benefit once objective inflammation (CRP, imaging) is considered.
A systematic review found no benefit to probiotics used alone.
Right-sided diverticula predominate in Asian populations, so a right-colon source should not be dismissed.

Most patients with diverticulosis stay asymptomatic; only ~5% develop acute diverticular disease, and 10-25% of those with diverticular disease have recurrent symptoms with up to 10% requiring surgery. Diverticular bleeds are largely self-limited (spontaneous cessation in >=90%), with lifetime rebleeding risk ~25%. After complicated diverticulitis the risk of underlying colon cancer rises to 6-8% (vs <2% overall). Elective surgical resection for recurrent SUDD improved quality of life and was more cost-effective at 5 years (DIRECT trial) (Harrison 22e p.2578-2581).

Hinchey classification of perforated diverticulitis: Stage I - perforation with confined paracolic abscess (modified stage Ia = phlegmon/early abscess); Stage II - perforation that closed spontaneously with distant (pelvic) abscess; Stage III - noncommunicating perforation with purulent peritonitis (diverticular neck closed off); Stage IV - free perforation communicating with the peritoneum producing fecal peritonitis. Clinically, disease is divided into uncomplicated (~75%) and complicated (~25%: abscess 16%, perforation 10%, stricture 5%, fistula 2%) (Harrison 22e p.2579-2580).

Alcoholic ketoacidosis — high-anion-gap acidosis (predominantly beta-hydroxybutyrate) without hyperglycaemia, usually with preserved renal function, in chronic alcohol use with vomiting and poor intake (p.413).
Starvation ketoacidosis — ketoacidosis with normal or low glucose (p.413).
Other high-anion-gap acidoses: lactic acidosis, toxic ingestions (e.g. salicylates), and renal failure/uraemia (p.413).
Plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate measured directly (more reliable than urine nitroprusside ketones) (p.413).
Anion gap calculation, including assessment for a mixed non-anion-gap / high-anion-gap acidosis when the change in bicarbonate exceeds the change in anion gap (p.413).
Acute pancreatitis can mimic DKA (and vice versa), with overlapping abdominal pain; DKA may itself be accompanied by amylase elevation, complicating the distinction (p.2788).

DKA results from increased fatty acid metabolism with accumulation of the ketoacids acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, producing hyperglycaemia, ketonaemia and a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. It typically occurs in insulin-dependent diabetes when insulin is stopped or when an intercurrent illness (e.g. infection, gastroenteritis, pancreatitis, myocardial infarction) acutely raises insulin requirements. In euglycaemic DKA caused by SGLT2 inhibitors, glycosuria drives an osmotic diuresis and volume depletion while plasma glucose stays in the normal range despite the ketoacidosis (p.413).
An acetone-like fruity odour on the breath is a classic bedside clue to ketoacidosis (p.93).
Urine dipstick (nitroprusside reaction) detects acetoacetate but not beta-hydroxybutyrate, so it can underestimate the true degree of ketosis; measure plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate directly (p.413).

As the circulation is restored with fluids, beta-hydroxybutyrate is converted to acetoacetate, so the nitroprusside ketone reading may paradoxically become more positive during treatment rather than reflecting worsening disease (p.413).
Glucose may be normal or only mildly raised in euglycaemic DKA (SGLT2-inhibitor associated) and in starvation ketoacidosis, so a normal glucose does not exclude ketoacidosis (p.413).
Excretion of ketoacids obligates loss of cations (sodium, potassium), worsening volume depletion and promoting chloride retention (p.413).
Relying on urine ketone dipstick, which misses beta-hydroxybutyrate and underestimates ketosis (p.413).
Interpreting a rising nitroprusside ketone result during fluid resuscitation as deterioration, when it reflects the beta-hydroxybutyrate-to-acetoacetate shift (p.413).
Assuming a normal/near-normal glucose excludes DKA, missing euglycaemic DKA on SGLT2 inhibitors (p.413).
Over-resuscitation with isotonic saline causing volume overload and/or hyperchloraemic acidosis (p.413).

Mucormycosis risk: DKA patients are at high risk of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis; acidosis frees iron from carrier proteins and beta-hydroxybutyrate upregulates fungal adherence/penetration receptors — consider in a DKA patient with sinus/orbital/facial signs (p.1761).
Severe acidaemia (pH <7.00) or shock identifies the small subset where bicarbonate may be considered; cerebral oedema risk limits its use (p.413).
Hyperchloraemic (non-anion-gap) acidosis and volume overload can be precipitated by aggressive isotonic saline during treatment (p.413).

Donovanosis is a chronic granulomatous infection caused by the intracellular gram-negative organism Klebsiella granulomatis (formerly Calymmatobacterium granulomatis). The lesion begins as a papule or subcutaneous nodule that ulcerates, often after trauma. The organism resides within macrophages and the stratum malpighii as intracytoplasmic Donovan bodies inside large mononuclear (Pund) cells; these cysts rupture and release infective organisms. Histology shows chronic inflammation with infiltration by plasma cells and neutrophils, and epithelial changes including ulceration, microabscesses, and elongation of the rete ridges. The organism resisted reproducible culture until the mid-1990s, when isolation in peripheral-blood monocytes and human epithelial cell lines was achieved (Harrison 22e p.1356-1357).
Chronic, progressive bacterial infection that predominantly involves the genital region and is regarded as a sexually transmitted infection of low infectivity (Harrison 22e p.1356).

Donovanosis is a recognized risk factor for HIV infection, and its global decline likely reflects more effective management of genital ulcers given their role in HIV transmission (Harrison 22e p.1357).
The estimated incubation period is approximately 50 days based on experimental human infection, though it remains uncertain (Harrison 22e p.1357).

A diagnostic PCR exploits two unique base changes in the phoE gene that eliminate Hae111 restriction sites, distinguishing K. granulomatis from related Klebsiella species; a multiplex genital-ulcer PCR including K. granulomatis exists (Harrison 22e p.1357).
Caused by Klebsiella granulomatis comb nov; the older name Calymmatobacterium granulomatis is still favored by some authorities based on 16S rRNA gene sequence analysis (Harrison 22e p.1356).

Diagnosis is confirmed by microscopic identification of intracytoplasmic Donovan bodies (about 1.5 x 0.7 micrometers) within large mononuclear Pund cells, where they appear as gram-negative cysts with a characteristic safety-pin appearance (Harrison 22e p.1356-1357).

When donovanosis is suspected clinically, the smear for Donovan bodies should be obtained before swabs for other genital ulcer pathogens so adequate material is collected; smears can be read at the bedside with rapid Giemsa or Wright stain (Harrison 22e p.1357).

An experienced clinician's diagnosis based on lesion appearance has a high positive predictive value, and donovanosis is probably the most readily recognizable cause of genital ulceration (Harrison 22e p.1357-1358).

Four lesion types are described: classic beefy-red ulcerogranulomatous ulcer that bleeds easily on touch, hypertrophic/verrucous ulcer with a raised irregular edge, necrotic foul-smelling destructive ulcer, and sclerotic/cicatricial fibrous lesion (Harrison 22e p.1357).
Genitalia are affected in about 90% of patients and the inguinal region in about 10%; lymphadenitis is uncommon, in contrast to other ulcerative STIs (Harrison 22e p.1357).
Cervical lesions can mimic cervical carcinoma, and in men lesions are associated with lack of circumcision (Harrison 22e p.1357).

Extragenital lesions occur in about 6% of cases and may involve the lip, gums, cheek, palate, pharynx, larynx, and chest; hematogenous spread to liver and bone has been reported (Harrison 22e p.1357).
Collecting other genital-ulcer swabs before the Donovan body smear can leave insufficient material for diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1357).
Serologic tests are only poorly specific and are not currently used, so they should not be relied upon (Harrison 22e p.1357).
Mixed infections with other genital ulcer pathogens are common and may obscure the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1357).
Lymphadenitis is uncommon, so its absence should not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1357).
Cervical lesions can be mistaken for cervical carcinoma and vice versa (Harrison 22e p.1357).
During pregnancy lesions develop more quickly and respond more slowly, so closer monitoring is needed (Harrison 22e p.1357).

Donovanosis is a treatable condition, and reassurance is an important part of care given the embarrassment and low self-esteem many patients experience. It is now confined to a few specific geographic locations, has been almost entirely eliminated in Australia and is close to elimination in South Africa, and its global eradication is considered a distinct possibility. Surgery may be required for very advanced lesions, and patients treated for shorter courses require monitoring until lesions heal completely (Harrison 22e p.1357-1358).

The presence of a third copy of chromosome 21 leads to over-expression of the genes it carries, disrupting normal development across multiple organ systems in a dosage-dependent manner. This gene-dosage imbalance affects neurodevelopment, cardiac and gastrointestinal morphogenesis, immune function, and haematopoiesis. Most trisomy 21 arises from failure of chromosomal separation during meiosis (nondisjunction), while translocation and mosaic forms produce the extra genetic material through other mechanisms.
The most common autosomal chromosomal disorder and a leading genetic cause of intellectual disability, resulting from an extra copy of chromosome 21.
Most cases are due to meiotic nondisjunction, with incidence rising markedly with advancing maternal age; a minority result from translocation or mosaicism.
Recognisable features include hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, a flat nasal bridge, small ears, a single transverse palmar crease, and a sandal gap between the toes.
Congenital heart disease is common, particularly atrioventricular septal defects, so early echocardiography is recommended.
Gastrointestinal anomalies such as duodenal atresia and Hirschsprung disease occur more frequently.
There is increased risk of hypothyroidism, hearing and visual impairment, obstructive sleep apnoea, and atlantoaxial instability, warranting scheduled surveillance.
Children have a higher risk of transient myeloproliferative disorder in the newborn period and of leukaemia in childhood.
Diagnosis is confirmed by karyotype, which also identifies translocations relevant to recurrence risk and family counselling.
Early developmental support and coordinated multidisciplinary care improve developmental and health outcomes.

Overlooking hypothyroidism, which can mimic or worsen developmental delay

Failing to follow structured health surveillance recommendations

Life expectancy has improved substantially with modern medical and surgical care and now commonly extends into adulthood; outcomes depend largely on cardiac disease and other complications, and most individuals have mild to moderate intellectual disability with early-onset Alzheimer-type changes in later life.

chunks.text: Submersion triggers breath-holding, then involuntary aspiration of water or laryngospasm, leading to progressive hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, and acidosis. Aspirated fluid disrupts and washes out pulmonary surfactant and damages the alveolar-capillary membrane, causing atelectasis, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, and potentially acute respiratory distress syndrome. Sustained hypoxia causes global tissue injury, with the brain most vulnerable to hypoxic-ischaemic damage. Cardiac arrhythmias and arrest follow severe hypoxia and acidosis, and coexisting hypothermia alters both the injury and the resuscitation.

chunks.text: Characterise overall physiologic state and toxidrome from vital signs and neuromuscular exam (p.3704)
Anion gap (raised AGMA in methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylate, or any poisoning causing organ failure, seizures or shock; low anion gap with bromide, calcium, iodine, lithium, magnesium) (p.3705)
Osmolal gap (>10 mmol/L suggests a low-molecular-weight solute such as an alcohol or glycol) (p.3705)
Serum lactate (low relative to anion gap in alcohol/glycol intoxication, high and near the anion gap in hypoperfusion) (p.3705)
Glucose, electrolytes, ketones (hypo-/hyperglycaemia and hypo-/hyperkalaemia patterns can implicate specific agents) (p.3705)
ECG (bradycardia/AV block, QRS and QT prolongation, ventricular tachyarrhythmias suggest specific agent classes) (p.3706)
Abdominal/chest radiograph (radiopaque densities suggest heavy metals, drug packets, iron, enteric-coated or salicylate tablets; CXR for pulmonary edema/aspiration) (p.3706)

Quantitative serum levels (acetaminophen, alcohols incl. ethylene glycol/methanol, anticonvulsants, barbiturates, digoxin, iron, lithium, salicylate, theophylline, carboxyhemoglobin, methemoglobin) guide management (p.3706)
Coagulation (PT/INR) for warfarin/rodenticide risk stratification, though unreliable for direct oral anticoagulant overdose (p.3705)
Psychogenic illness / anxiety reaction (mass hysteria, fear of poisoning) producing symptoms inconsistent with the exposure history (p.3705)
Structural CNS lesion - focal neurologic findings are uncommon in poisoning and should prompt evaluation for a structural cause (p.3703)

Poisoning is a dose-related adverse effect from exposure to a chemical, drug or other xenobiotic. Responses to a given dose vary with genetic polymorphism, enzyme induction or inhibition by co-ingestants, and acquired tolerance. Toxicity may be local or systemic depending on route, the agent's physicochemical properties and mechanism, and its severity/reversibility depends on the functional reserve of the patient or target organ (influenced by age and pre-existing disease) (p.3703).

Diagnosis of an unknown poisoning rests on pattern recognition: first classify the overall physiologic state as stimulated, depressed, discordant, or normal, then look for a recognizable toxidrome (p.3704).

Most patients who are or become asymptomatic by 6 h after ingestion are unlikely to develop later toxicity and may be discharged, but longer observation is required after 'toxic time-bomb' ingestions (p.3707).

Core temperature is the single most reliable predictor of poor outcome in stimulant (e.g. cocaine) poisoning or in drug/alcohol/GHB withdrawal, so it must be measured even in difficult or combative patients (p.3704).

Mydriasis is common to all stimulant states but is most marked with anticholinergics (muscarinic loss of pupil reactivity); cocaine and other sympathomimetics enlarge pupils yet retain some light reactivity (p.3704).

The anticholinergic toxidrome is distinguished from other stimulant states by hot, dry, flushed skin, decreased bowel sounds and urinary retention, whereas sympathomimetic states cause diaphoresis and increased bowel activity (p.3704).
Miosis points to a depressed state from opioids or cholinergic agents; muscarinic/nicotinic features separate cholinergic poisoning from opioid poisoning (p.3704-3705).

In opioid and sedative-hypnotic poisoning, vital-sign derangements are secondary to CNS depression and do not appear until consciousness is markedly reduced (grade 3-4 depression); marked cardiovascular depression with preserved consciousness instead suggests a peripherally acting sympatholytic (p.3705).
Rotatory nystagmus among stimulated patients is essentially specific to phencyclidine and ketamine (p.3704).

A near-normal exam may reflect a nontoxic exposure, psychogenic illness, or a 'toxic time-bomb' (slowly absorbed, slowly distributed, requiring metabolic activation, or disrupting metabolism); once-daily reformulations have made these increasingly common (p.3705).
Rapid response of altered mental status to IV dextrose, naloxone or flumazenil is virtually diagnostic of hypoglycemia, opioid poisoning and benzodiazepine intoxication respectively (p.3706).

Rapid hospital urine drug-of-abuse screens are screening tests only, cannot confirm the exact substance, and are not diagnostic or forensic; false positives (e.g. fluoroquinolones triggering false-positive opiate screens) and false negatives are common (p.3706).

A negative drug screen does not exclude poisoning - the agent may be undetectable by the assay (e.g. synthetic cannabinoids/spice, cathinones/bath salts, kratom) or present below the limit of detection at the time of sampling; repeat testing later may turn positive (p.3706).

Qualitative drug screens are not clinically useful or cost-effective when the patient is asymptomatic or the picture fits the reported history; reserve them for severe or unexplained toxicity (coma, seizures, cardiovascular instability, acidosis, nonsinus rhythms) (p.3706).
Blood levels obtained during absorption/distribution may exceed tissue levels and may not correlate with toxicity (p.3707).
In polydrug overdose a clear toxidrome may be obscured when different drug classes counteract each other's physiologic effects (p.3704).
Physostigmine fully reverses anticholinergic poisoning but can also produce some arousal in CNS depression of any cause, so arousal alone is not specific (p.3706).
Overdose effects begin sooner, peak later and last longer than therapeutic-dose effects, and an agent's published (therapeutic) pharmacokinetics differ from its toxicokinetics in overdose (p.3707).

Overall mortality is low (<1% of all poison exposures) but rises to 1-2% among hospitalised patients with intentional (suicidal) overdose or complications of drugs of abuse, who account for most serious poisonings. About 20-25% of exposures need bedside professional evaluation and ~5% need hospitalisation. Acetaminophen is the pharmaceutical most often implicated in fatal poisoning, while carbon monoxide is the leading overall cause of poisoning death (often fatal before discovery). Most patients asymptomatic at 6 h are unlikely to deteriorate (p.3703, p.3707).
Temperature elevation (grade 4 stimulation) - most reliable predictor of poor outcome in stimulant poisoning and withdrawal (p.3704)
Coma, seizures or cardiovascular collapse (grade 4 physiologic stimulation or depression) (p.3705)

Harrison grades physiologic stimulation and depression in poisoning/withdrawal: Stimulation - grade 1 anxious/tremulous with normal vital signs; grade 2 agitated, mildly-moderately raised vitals but can follow commands; grade 3 delirious with motor hyperactivity and markedly raised vitals, possible tachyarrhythmias; grade 4 coma, seizures, cardiovascular collapse. Depression - grade 1 lethargic but arousable to voice/touch; grade 2 responds to pain not voice, brainstem reflexes intact; grade 3 unresponsive to pain, depressed brainstem reflexes, reduced tone/respiration/temperature; grade 4 flaccid, absent brainstem reflexes and respirations, depressed cardiovascular signs (p.3705).

chunks.text: Dry eye disease is a multifactorial disorder of the ocular surface characterised by loss of tear film homeostasis. Reduced aqueous production (as in Sjogren and non-Sjogren lacrimal dysfunction) or excessive evaporation (chiefly from meibomian gland dysfunction with an unstable lipid layer) leads to tear hyperosmolarity. Hyperosmolarity triggers a self-perpetuating cycle of ocular surface inflammation, epithelial damage, and neurosensory dysfunction, which further destabilises the tear film. Goblet cell loss and reduced mucin worsen wetting, sustaining the inflammatory cascade.

Mutations in the DMD gene abolish functional dystrophin, a cytoskeletal protein that links the muscle fibre cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix through the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex. Without it the sarcolemma is unstable and is damaged by contraction, leading to repeated cycles of muscle fibre degeneration and regeneration, calcium influx, inflammation, and eventual replacement of muscle by fat and fibrous tissue. Dystrophin deficiency in cardiac muscle produces cardiomyopathy.
The most common and most severe childhood muscular dystrophy, an X-linked recessive disorder that therefore affects boys, caused by absence of functional dystrophin.
Symptoms usually appear in early childhood with delayed walking, frequent falls, difficulty running and climbing stairs, and a waddling gait.
Gower sign - using the hands to 'climb up' the legs when rising from the floor - reflects proximal, especially pelvic girdle, weakness.
Calf pseudohypertrophy from fatty and fibrous replacement of muscle is a characteristic finding.
Serum creatine kinase is markedly elevated, often into the thousands, even before overt weakness.
Weakness is progressive; most boys lose independent ambulation by around the early teens without disease-modifying therapy.
Cardiomyopathy and respiratory muscle weakness are the main causes of morbidity and death, so cardiac and pulmonary surveillance is essential.
Glucocorticoids slow progression and prolong ambulation and are a mainstay of care; multidisciplinary management improves outcomes.

Diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing for dystrophin gene mutations, with muscle biopsy reserved for uncertain cases; learning and behavioural difficulties are more common than in the general population.

chunks.text: DVT arises from Virchow's triad of venous stasis, hypercoagulability and endothelial injury, now understood to be typically coupled with an inflammatory trigger. Activated platelets release proinflammatory microparticles that recruit neutrophils to form neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs); these histone-rich, web-like networks promote platelet aggregation and platelet-dependent thrombin generation. Thrombi form and propagate in an environment of stasis, low oxygen tension and upregulated proinflammatory genes. Lower-extremity thrombi usually begin in the calf veins and can propagate proximally to the popliteal, femoral and iliac veins; detached thrombi embolize through the vena cava and right heart into the pulmonary circulation, and rarely cross a patent foramen ovale or atrial septal defect to cause paradoxical (arterial) embolism. VTE shares inflammation, hypercoagulability and endothelial injury with arterial atherothrombosis, so VTE patients have more than double the risk of future MI or stroke and vice versa. Common genetic prothrombotic states are factor V Leiden (resistance to protein C) and the prothrombin gene mutation (raised prothrombin level); deficiencies of antithrombin, protein C and protein S also predispose but are rare; antiphospholipid syndrome is an acquired thrombophilia causing both venous and arterial thrombosis (Harrison 22e p.2156-2158).
