chunks.text: Postthrombotic syndrome (chronic venous insufficiency) is the main long-term morbidity: damaged venous valves cause ankle/calf swelling and leg aching after prolonged standing, and in its most severe form deep skin ulceration near the medial malleolus. Notably, graduated compression stockings prescribed for asymptomatic newly diagnosed acute DVT do NOT prevent postthrombotic syndrome (they are used only for symptomatic swelling relief). Recurrence risk after stopping anticoagulation is stratified (ESC 2019) as low (<3%/yr, e.g., major surgery/trauma), intermediate (3-8%/yr, e.g., minor surgery, hospitalization for acute illness, pregnancy/estrogen, long-haul flight, IBD, autoimmune disease, or no identifiable risk factor) and high (>8%/yr, active cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome). Harrison de-emphasizes the 'provoked vs unprovoked' dichotomy because many provoked VTEs recur at rates similar to unprovoked ones, and enduring risk factors (heart failure, chronic lung disease, IBD) raise recurrence risk. The Post-VTE Functional Status scale (grades 0-4) can track functional recovery (Harrison 22e p.2156-2157, 2163).

chunks.text: Wells clinical prediction rule for DVT (Harrison 22e p.2159): low likelihood if score <=0, moderate if 1-2, high if >=3. Points: active cancer +1; paralysis/paresis or recent cast +1; bedridden >3 days or major surgery <12 weeks +1; tenderness along distribution of deep veins +1; entire-leg swelling +1; unilateral calf swelling >3 cm +1; pitting edema +1; collateral superficial nonvaricose veins +1; alternative diagnosis at least as likely as DVT -2. Pretest-probability strategy: patients with low DVT likelihood undergo d-dimer first and need no imaging if it is normal, whereas high-likelihood patients should skip d-dimer and proceed straight to compression ultrasound imaging.

Fasting lipid profile: total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triglycerides (Harrison 22e p.2046).
Lipoprotein(a) measurement, given its role as an independent cardiovascular risk predictor (Harrison 22e p.2017, p.2046).

Screening for secondary contributors: glucose/HbA1c and urinalysis for diabetes and renal disease, and thyroid function testing when indicated (Harrison 22e p.2046).
High-sensitivity C-reactive protein may be considered as an independent cardiovascular risk marker informing therapeutic decisions (Harrison 22e p.2046).

Atherogenic lipoproteins, principally LDL, deposit cholesterol within the arterial wall and disturb normal endothelial functions (control of vascular tone, maintenance of an antithrombotic surface, and regulation of inflammatory cell adhesion and diapedesis), promoting atherosclerosis; LDL, cigarette smoking, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus vary in their relative impact on these endothelial functions. Lipoprotein(a) is thought to add risk through increased cellular lipid accumulation, endothelial dysfunction, and effects on coagulation. Severe hypertriglyceridemia (chylomicron/VLDL accumulation) can precipitate acute pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2017, p.2046).

Elevated plasma LDL cholesterol is a major modifiable driver of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; globally high LDL is estimated to contribute to ~41% of ischemic heart disease deaths and ~9% of stroke deaths (Harrison 22e p.2017).

Lipoprotein(a) appears to be an independent predictor of cardiovascular risk beyond total or LDL cholesterol, and is elevated in roughly 20% of the global population; levels are reported higher in those of African descent and intermediate in East and South Asians (Harrison 22e p.2017).

Tendon xanthomas (e.g., Achilles and extensor finger tendons), xanthelasma, and plane/tuberous xanthomas reflect hypercholesterolemia (hyperlipoproteinemia types II and III); eruptive xanthomas are most commonly associated with hypertriglyceridemia (types I, IV, V) (Harrison 22e p.234, p.1860).
Palmar (palmar crease) xanthomas are specific for type III hyperlipoproteinemia, and severe hypertriglyceridemia can produce eruptive xanthomatosis and lipemia retinalis (Harrison 22e p.1860).

Loss-of-function PCSK9 variants are associated with lower LDL cholesterol and reduced coronary artery disease, which led to development of PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies; rare gain-of-function PCSK9 variants are a cause of familial hypercholesterolemia (Harrison 22e p.260).

Attributing dyslipidemia solely to primary lipid disorders while overlooking secondary causes such as diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, and excess alcohol intake (Harrison 22e p.2046).
Underrecognizing familial hypercholesterolemia in patients with tendon xanthomas and premature coronary disease (Harrison 22e p.234, p.260).

LDL-driven dyslipidemia is a leading contributor to atherosclerotic cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, including ischemic heart disease and stroke; lowering LDL (e.g., a 50% or greater reduction with high-intensity statin therapy in patients with established atherosclerotic disease) reduces the risk of myocardial infarction, stroke, and death (Harrison 22e p.2017, p.2056).
Tendon xanthomas with premature coronary artery disease, suggesting familial hypercholesterolemia (Harrison 22e p.234, p.260).

In primary dysmenorrhoea, the fall in progesterone at the end of the luteal phase triggers release of arachidonic acid and increased endometrial production of prostaglandins, particularly PGF2-alpha. These stimulate intense, poorly coordinated myometrial contractions that raise intrauterine pressure and reduce uterine blood flow, producing ischaemic pain analogous to angina; leukotrienes and vasopressin contribute. In secondary dysmenorrhoea the pain results instead from a structural or inflammatory disorder such as ectopic endometrial tissue, myometrial invasion by endometrium, leiomyomas, or infection.
Primary dysmenorrhoea is painful menstruation without underlying pelvic pathology and typically begins within a year or two of menarche once ovulatory cycles are established
Secondary dysmenorrhoea arises from identifiable pelvic disease, most often endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, or pelvic inflammatory disease, and tends to begin later or change in character
The pain of primary dysmenorrhoea is cramping and suprapubic, often radiating to the back and thighs, and coincides with the onset of menstrual flow
Prostaglandin-driven myometrial contractions and uterine ischaemia underlie primary dysmenorrhoea, which explains the effectiveness of prostaglandin synthesis inhibitors
First-line management combines non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs with hormonal suppression of ovulation such as combined hormonal contraception
Features suggesting secondary causes include pain that starts before bleeding or persists after it, deep dyspareunia, abnormal bleeding, or poor response to standard treatment
A careful history and examination, with pelvic ultrasound and consideration of laparoscopy, help identify secondary pathology when suspected
Symptoms of primary dysmenorrhoea often improve with age and after childbirth
Assuming all menstrual pain is primary and missing endometriosis or adenomyosis
Failing to reassess when standard treatment does not work
Overlooking pelvic inflammatory disease as a treatable secondary cause
Not offering hormonal suppression alongside anti-inflammatory therapy
Attributing new-onset severe pain in an older woman to simple period pain

Primary dysmenorrhoea is benign and commonly improves over time and after childbirth, with most women achieving good symptom control from anti-inflammatory and hormonal treatment. The prognosis of secondary dysmenorrhoea depends on the underlying condition, and outcomes improve when that cause is correctly identified and managed.

chunks.text: Dystonia arises from dysfunction of motor networks centred on the basal ganglia and their connections with the cerebellum, thalamus, and cortex, leading to loss of inhibition, abnormal sensorimotor integration, and maladaptive plasticity. Co-contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles with overflow to adjacent muscles produces the abnormal postures. Causes range from inherited (isolated or combined genetic forms) and idiopathic disease to acquired lesions, drugs, and neurodegenerative or metabolic disorders.

Eclampsia represents the cerebral manifestation of the endothelial dysfunction and vasospasm of pre-eclampsia. Loss of cerebral autoregulation and endothelial injury lead to hyperperfusion, vasogenic and cytotoxic oedema (often in the posterior circulation, akin to posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome), and focal ischaemia, which lower the seizure threshold and provoke generalised convulsions. Cerebral haemorrhage is the most feared and lethal complication.
Defined as new-onset generalised tonic-clonic seizures in a woman with pre-eclampsia that cannot be attributed to another cause
Seizures may occur antepartum, intrapartum, or postpartum, and a substantial proportion arise after delivery
Premonitory features include severe headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain, and hyperreflexia, though seizures can occur without warning
Magnesium sulfate is the treatment of choice for controlling and preventing recurrent seizures and is superior to conventional anticonvulsants in this setting
Immediate priorities are maternal airway protection, oxygenation, and prevention of injury and aspiration during the seizure
Blood pressure must be controlled with antihypertensives to reduce the risk of intracranial haemorrhage
Delivery is undertaken once the mother is stabilised; eclampsia itself is not an indication for immediate caesarean if vaginal delivery is achievable and conditions are favourable
Magnesium toxicity is monitored clinically (loss of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory depression) and calcium gluconate is the antidote
Attributing a peripartum seizure to epilepsy and delaying magnesium therapy
Discontinuing magnesium too early after delivery when postpartum eclampsia remains a risk
Rushing to caesarean during an active seizure rather than stabilising the mother first
Overlooking magnesium toxicity by not monitoring reflexes and respiratory rate
Neglecting ongoing postpartum blood pressure surveillance

With prompt seizure control, blood pressure management, and delivery, most women recover without lasting neurological deficit. However, eclampsia is associated with significant maternal mortality and morbidity worldwide, particularly from intracranial haemorrhage, aspiration, and organ failure, and with increased perinatal loss.

chunks.system: Dermatologic / Skin and Soft Tissue (with neurologic and systemic envenomation involvement)
chunks.text: Ectoparasites are arthropods and organisms of other phyla that infest skin or hair; they may remain superficial (anchored by mouthparts or claws) or penetrate into epidermis, dermis, or subcutaneous tissue. Injury arises through several mechanisms: direct mechanical damage, consumption of blood or nutrients, hypersensitivity reactions to saliva/secretions/excretions, inoculation of toxins or venoms, transmission of pathogens, and creation of skin portals for secondary bacterial infection. In scabies, gravid female mites burrow within the stratum corneum and lay eggs; rash and pruritus result from delayed-type sensitization, with burrows surrounded by infiltrates of eosinophils, lymphocytes, and histiocytes. Lice are obligate blood feeders whose saliva produces a pruritic morbilliform/urticarial reaction in sensitized hosts. Venom-mediated injury is prominent in arachnid and hymenopteran envenomation: widow spider alpha-latrotoxin binds irreversibly to presynaptic terminals causing release then depletion of acetylcholine and norepinephrine; bark scorpion neurotoxins hold sodium channels open producing cranial-nerve and neuromuscular hyperexcitability; some scorpion venoms trigger massive catecholamine release with cardiopulmonary toxicity. Hymenopteran venoms contain amines, kinins, and enzymes (e.g., melittin, phospholipases, hyaluronidase) producing local and systemic effects, with most fatalities due to IgE-mediated type 1 anaphylaxis. Tick salivary secretions are biologically active anticoagulants that can transmit pathogens and provoke sterile inflammatory responses, fever, and toxin-mediated paralysis.

chunks.system: Dermatologic / Skin and Soft Tissue (with neurologic and systemic envenomation involvement)
chunks.text: Of all organisms in this chapter, only the human itch mite (Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis) and human-infesting lice are obligate human parasites; humans are accidental or dead-end hosts for most others.

chunks.system: Dermatologic / Skin and Soft Tissue (with neurologic and systemic envenomation involvement)
chunks.text: Tick paralysis is an acute ascending flaccid Guillain-Barre-like paralysis from a salivary toxin; sensory exam and lumbar puncture are typically normal, and finding/removing the hidden tick (often under scalp hair) reverses it within hours.

chunks.system: Dermatologic / Skin and Soft Tissue (with neurologic and systemic envenomation involvement)
chunks.text: Alpha-gal syndrome (red-meat allergy) follows tick bites that induce IgE against galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose, a carbohydrate present in non-primate mammalian muscle; in the US it is linked to the lone star tick.

chunks.system: Dermatologic / Skin and Soft Tissue (with neurologic and systemic envenomation involvement)

chunks.system: Dermatologic / Skin and Soft Tissue (with neurologic and systemic envenomation involvement)
chunks.text: Scabies affects roughly 250 million people worldwide and is spread mainly by direct skin-to-skin contact; transmission via shared bedding or clothing is less common than widely assumed, and mites usually die within about a day off a suitable host.

chunks.system: Dermatologic / Skin and Soft Tissue (with neurologic and systemic envenomation involvement)
chunks.text: Scabies pruritus reflects a sensitization reaction; an initial infestation can stay asymptomatic for up to about 6 weeks, but reinfestation provokes prompt hypersensitivity. Itch typically worsens at night and after hot showers.

chunks.system: Dermatologic / Skin and Soft Tissue (with neurologic and systemic envenomation involvement)
chunks.text: Crusted (formerly Norwegian) scabies arises in glucocorticoid use, immunodeficiency (including HIV/AIDS), and neuropsychiatric conditions that blunt itching/scratching; it harbors thousands of mites, is highly contagious, often non-pruritic, lacks classic burrows, and can mimic psoriasis.

chunks.system: Dermatologic / Skin and Soft Tissue (with neurologic and systemic envenomation involvement)
chunks.text: Confirmation of louse infestation should rest on finding a live louse, not on nits alone, since hatched/dead eggs (and pseudo-nits of debris/dander/fungi) remain cemented to hair for months and are frequently misread as active disease.

chunks.system: Dermatologic / Skin and Soft Tissue (with neurologic and systemic envenomation involvement)
chunks.text: Body lice (not head lice) are the recognized vectors of epidemic (louse-borne) typhus, louse-borne relapsing fever, and trench fever; outbreaks track societal upheaval, crowding, and inability to launder clothing.

chunks.system: Dermatologic / Skin and Soft Tissue (with neurologic and systemic envenomation involvement)
chunks.text: Furuncular myiasis (e.g., Dermatobia hominis, Cordylobia anthropophaga) presents as a boil-like nodule with a central breathing pore that emits bubbles when submerged in water, and the patient may sense movement within the skin.

chunks.system: Dermatologic / Skin and Soft Tissue (with neurologic and systemic envenomation involvement)
chunks.text: Brown recluse (Loxosceles) envenomation classically produces a painful lesion with central induration, a pale ischemic zone, and surrounding erythema, sometimes evolving to a necrotic black eschar; widow spider (Latrodectus) bites cause minimal local injury but severe neurotoxic muscle cramps via alpha-latrotoxin.

chunks.system: Dermatologic / Skin and Soft Tissue (with neurologic and systemic envenomation involvement)
chunks.text: Removing hard ticks within the first 24 hours of attachment generally prevents transmission of Lyme disease, babesiosis, anaplasmosis, and ehrlichiosis, though tick-borne viruses may transmit faster.

chunks.text: Mistaking widow spider abdominal rigidity for a surgical abdomen and performing unnecessary surgery (the abdomen is not tender on palpation).

chunks.system: Dermatologic / Skin and Soft Tissue (with neurologic and systemic envenomation involvement)

chunks.system: Dermatologic / Skin and Soft Tissue (with neurologic and systemic envenomation involvement)
chunks.text: Most infestations and bites are self-limited or readily treated. Scabies becomes noncommunicable within about a day of proper treatment, though hypersensitivity pruritus may persist for weeks as dead mites and debris are cleared; secondary streptococcal infection can lead to poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis and possibly acute rheumatic fever. Brown recluse lesions usually heal within about 3 months, and verified deaths from North American brown recluse bites have not been confirmed. Widow spider pain typically begins subsiding within the first 12 hours but may recur over days to weeks; fatal outcomes are rare and concentrated in the very young, elderly, or debilitated. Bark scorpion envenomation peaks around 5 hours and subsides over a day or two, with fatal respiratory arrest mainly in young children and the elderly. Tick paralysis generally resolves within hours to days after tick removal but can be fatal from respiratory paralysis or aspiration if untreated. Hymenoptera-related deaths (>=100/year in the US) result almost entirely from anaphylaxis.

chunks.system: Dermatologic / Skin and Soft Tissue (with neurologic and systemic envenomation involvement)
chunks.text: No formal numeric staging is given; severity is graded clinically by host reaction and systemic involvement. Scabies ranges from ordinary (typically <=10-15 burrows) to crusted/hyperinfested (thousands of mites, highly contagious). Arthropod envenomations are stratified from local-only reactions (most scorpion and spider bites: pain, edema) to systemic/life-threatening envenomation (cranial-nerve and neuromuscular dysfunction, cardiopulmonary toxicity, hemolysis, renal failure). Hymenoptera reactions span uncomplicated local stings, large local hypersensitivity reactions spreading >=10 cm over 1-2 days, and systemic type 1 anaphylaxis.

An ectopic pregnancy occurs when the blastocyst implants outside the endometrial cavity, most often in a fallopian tube whose transport function has been impaired by inflammation, scarring, or altered motility. The invading trophoblast erodes the tubal wall, which lacks the capacity to accommodate a growing gestation. This leads to distension and bleeding into the tube, and eventually to tubal rupture with potentially massive intraperitoneal haemorrhage, or to tubal abortion where the products are expelled through the fimbrial end.
Any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain, amenorrhoea, and vaginal bleeding should be assumed to have an ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise
The great majority implant in the fallopian tube; less common sites include the cornua, ovary, cervix, caesarean scar, and abdominal cavity
Risk factors include previous ectopic pregnancy, tubal surgery or damage, pelvic inflammatory disease, endometriosis, assisted reproduction, and intrauterine contraceptive devices
Diagnosis combines serial serum beta-hCG measurement with transvaginal ultrasound; an empty uterus with a beta-hCG above the discriminatory zone raises strong suspicion
Management options are expectant, medical with methotrexate for suitable stable cases, or surgical (usually laparoscopic salpingectomy or salpingotomy)
Rupture causes intraperitoneal haemorrhage and is a life-threatening surgical emergency requiring immediate resuscitation and operative control of bleeding
A pregnancy of unknown location with rising or plateauing beta-hCG and no intrauterine gestation warrants close follow-up and a low threshold for intervention
Anti-D prophylaxis should be given to rhesus-negative women where indicated
Excluding pregnancy on history alone without a beta-hCG test
Falsely reassuring interpretation of a single beta-hCG value rather than the trend
Assuming an intrauterine pregnancy excludes ectopic, missing rare heterotopic pregnancy after assisted conception
Choosing medical management without ensuring reliable follow-up
Delaying surgery in an unstable patient while awaiting investigations

With early diagnosis and treatment the maternal outlook is excellent and fertility is often preserved. Rupture remains an important cause of maternal death, especially where access to care is delayed. Women who have had one ectopic pregnancy carry an increased risk of recurrence and of subtly reduced fertility.

chunks.text: Ectropion is outward rotation of the eyelid margin. Involutional ectropion stems from horizontal lid laxity and weakening of the canthal tendons and retractors with age. Paralytic ectropion follows loss of orbicularis oculi function in facial nerve palsy, so the lid sags and everts. Cicatricial ectropion arises when scarring and contracture of the eyelid skin (anterior lamella) mechanically pull the margin away from the eye. Mechanical ectropion is caused by a mass or oedema everting the lid. Eversion disrupts the normal tear drainage and exposes the cornea and conjunctiva to drying and keratinisation.

chunks.text: Electrical injury results from the passage of current through the body, converting electrical energy to heat and causing direct cellular membrane damage (electroporation). Tissue injury depends on voltage, current type and magnitude, resistance of tissues, current pathway, and contact duration. Current traversing the thorax can disrupt cardiac rhythm, causing ventricular fibrillation or asystole, while passage through the head or chest can arrest respiration centrally or by paralysing respiratory muscles. Deep tissues, especially muscle, sustain extensive thermal and electroporation injury that may exceed the visible cutaneous burn, releasing myoglobin that can precipitate acute kidney injury, and swelling within fascial compartments can compromise perfusion.

chunks.diseaseName: Electrical Storm and Incessant Ventricular Tachycardia
chunks.text: Electrical storm reflects repeated, often rapidly recurring ventricular tachyarrhythmias arising from an unstable myocardial substrate combined with heightened sympathetic drive and acute triggering factors. Substrates vary: in the setting of acute myocardial ischemia/infarction, surviving Purkinje cells within infarcted myocardium can show triggered automaticity, generating recurrent polymorphic VT/VF. PVC-initiated polymorphic VT/VF can also occur without infarction or ischemia (idiopathic VF), where triggering premature ventricular contractions arise from fascicular tissue or papillary muscles, sometimes from scarred myocardium seen on cardiac MRI. Other substrates include acquired or congenital long QT (torsades des pointes from abnormal repolarization), Brugada syndrome (right ventricular outflow tract/epicardial substrate), and inflammatory cardiomyopathies. Incessant VT is usually monomorphic and may be driven or sustained by the proarrhythmic action of antiarrhythmic drugs (Harrison 22e p.1972-1974).

chunks.diseaseName: Electrical Storm and Incessant Ventricular Tachycardia
chunks.text: Electrical storm (VT/VF storm) is defined as three or more episodes of ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation within 24 hours, each requiring intervention to terminate (Harrison 22e p.1972).

chunks.text: Programming VF detection zones above 220 beats/min in primary-prevention ICDs and using longer detection times significantly reduce unnecessary and inappropriate shocks (Harrison 22e p.1972).

chunks.diseaseName: Electrical Storm and Incessant Ventricular Tachycardia
chunks.text: Determining whether the storming rhythm is monomorphic or polymorphic guides management, as does inspecting initiation/termination patterns on stored ICD electrograms for precipitating factors (Harrison 22e p.1973).

chunks.diseaseName: Electrical Storm and Incessant Ventricular Tachycardia
chunks.text: Reducing sympathetic drive is a core management principle: stellate ganglion block and upper thoracic epidural anesthesia can restore stability in some patients (Harrison 22e p.1973).

chunks.diseaseName: Electrical Storm and Incessant Ventricular Tachycardia
chunks.text: It is uncommon in the general population but carries great concern because, untreated, it follows a rapid course that can lead to death; prompt recognition and intervention are essential (Harrison 22e p.1972).

chunks.diseaseName: Electrical Storm and Incessant Ventricular Tachycardia
chunks.text: Storm occurs in about 4% of patients with a primary-prevention ICD but in as many as 20% of patients with prior known VT or resuscitated sudden death (Harrison 22e p.1972).

chunks.diseaseName: Electrical Storm and Incessant Ventricular Tachycardia
chunks.text: VT is termed incessant when it recurs shortly after electrical, pharmacologic, or spontaneous conversion to sinus rhythm; it is typically monomorphic (Harrison 22e p.1972).

chunks.diseaseName: Electrical Storm and Incessant Ventricular Tachycardia
chunks.text: A slow incessant monomorphic VT may rarely escape ICD detection because its rate falls below the programmed detection threshold (Harrison 22e p.1972).

chunks.diseaseName: Electrical Storm and Incessant Ventricular Tachycardia
chunks.text: Antiarrhythmic drugs themselves can be proarrhythmic and render VT incessant (e.g., amiodarone or a sodium-channel blocker such as flecainide) (Harrison 22e p.1972).

chunks.diseaseName: Electrical Storm and Incessant Ventricular Tachycardia
chunks.text: Multiple ICD shocks constitute a medical emergency warranting activation of emergency medical services; patients should never drive themselves to hospital after receiving a shock (Harrison 22e p.1972).

chunks.diseaseName: Electrical Storm and Incessant Ventricular Tachycardia
chunks.text: After any ICD shock, device interrogation is crucial to confirm therapy was delivered for a true ventricular arrhythmia rather than for lead malfunction or an atrial arrhythmia (Harrison 22e p.1972).

chunks.diseaseName: Electrical Storm and Incessant Ventricular Tachycardia
chunks.text: Antitachycardia pacing terminates over 70% of VT episodes—even rapid VT—so appropriate ICD programming markedly reduces shocks and improves quality of life (Harrison 22e p.1972).

chunks.diseaseName: Electrical Storm and Incessant Ventricular Tachycardia
chunks.text: Assuming every ICD shock reflects a true ventricular arrhythmia—lead malfunction or an atrial arrhythmia can trigger inappropriate shocks, so interrogation is required (Harrison 22e p.1972).

chunks.diseaseName: Electrical Storm and Incessant Ventricular Tachycardia
chunks.text: Overlooking that interventions to control the arrhythmia may themselves worsen outcome—most antiarrhythmics can cause bradycardia requiring ICD pacing, which can itself impair ventricular function (Harrison 22e p.1972).

chunks.diseaseName: Electrical Storm and Incessant Ventricular Tachycardia
chunks.text: Failing to recognize antiarrhythmic proarrhythmia as a cause of incessant VT (Harrison 22e p.1972).

chunks.diseaseName: Electrical Storm and Incessant Ventricular Tachycardia
chunks.text: Missing a slow incessant monomorphic VT that falls outside programmed ICD detection parameters (Harrison 22e p.1972).

chunks.diseaseName: Electrical Storm and Incessant Ventricular Tachycardia
chunks.text: Not searching for a treatable substrate (ischemia, long QT, Brugada, inflammatory cardiomyopathy) that dictates specific therapy (Harrison 22e p.1974).

chunks.diseaseName: Electrical Storm and Incessant Ventricular Tachycardia
chunks.text: Spontaneous ventricular arrhythmias—particularly those requiring shock for termination—are associated with an increased subsequent risk of death and hospitalization in patients with depressed ventricular function. Untreated storm progresses rapidly and can be fatal, but catheter ablation, antiarrhythmic drug therapy, and adjunctive measures can be life-saving. An arrhythmic episode should prompt reevaluation for declining cardiac function, ischemia, or intercurrent illness (Harrison 22e p.1972).

VT is classified as monomorphic versus polymorphic, and as sustained versus incessant; substrate-based categories include ischemic, long QT, Brugada, PVC-initiated, and inflammatory (Harrison 22e p.1972-1974).

Type 1 (endometrioid) tumours develop through prolonged oestrogenic stimulation of the endometrium unopposed by progesterone, progressing through endometrial hyperplasia with atypia to invasive carcinoma; they commonly harbour PTEN, PIK3CA, and mismatch repair defects. Type 2 (serous and clear cell) tumours arise in atrophic endometrium independent of oestrogen, frequently carry TP53 mutations, and are more likely to invade deeply and metastasise early. Spread occurs by myometrial invasion, transtubal and peritoneal dissemination, and lymphatic routes to pelvic and para-aortic nodes.
Postmenopausal bleeding is the cardinal presenting symptom and must be investigated to exclude malignancy in every woman
The commonest type is endometrioid adenocarcinoma, which is oestrogen-driven and associated with obesity, nulliparity, late menopause, and unopposed oestrogen exposure
Serous and clear cell carcinomas are less common, oestrogen-independent, tend to occur in older women, and behave more aggressively
Endometrial thickness on transvaginal ultrasound helps triage postmenopausal bleeding, but a normal measurement does not exclude the aggressive non-endometrioid subtypes
Diagnosis rests on endometrial sampling by pipelle biopsy or hysteroscopy with directed biopsy, particularly when bleeding persists despite a thin endometrium
Most cases are diagnosed early because bleeding prompts presentation, and total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is the mainstay of treatment
Lynch syndrome should be considered, especially in younger women, and molecular classification increasingly guides adjuvant therapy and prognosis
Tamoxifen use, polycystic ovary syndrome, and diabetes are additional risk factors reflecting chronic unopposed oestrogen and metabolic influences

The majority of women present with disease confined to the uterus and have an excellent prognosis after surgery, but outcome worsens with deep myometrial invasion, high tumour grade, aggressive histological subtypes, and nodal or distant spread. Molecular subgroups, notably POLE-mutated tumours with favourable and p53-abnormal tumours with adverse outcomes, are refining prognostic estimates and adjuvant treatment decisions.

The most widely cited mechanism is retrograde menstruation, in which viable endometrial cells reflux through the fallopian tubes and implant on peritoneal surfaces. Additional contributions come from coelomic metaplasia, altered immune surveillance that fails to clear ectopic cells, lymphatic or vascular spread, and genetic predisposition. The ectopic tissue is oestrogen-dependent and responds to cyclical hormonal changes, causing local inflammation, repeated microhaemorrhage, fibrosis, adhesion formation, and distortion of pelvic anatomy. Chronic inflammation and nerve involvement generate pain and contribute to subfertility.
Endometriosis is the presence of endometrial-like tissue outside the uterine cavity, most often on the ovaries, uterosacral ligaments, and pelvic peritoneum
Cardinal symptoms are cyclical and chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, and subfertility, though some women are asymptomatic
Symptom severity correlates poorly with the anatomical extent of disease
Ovarian endometriomas (chocolate cysts) contain altered, dark, degenerated blood
Definitive diagnosis has traditionally required laparoscopic visualisation, ideally with histological confirmation, though imaging can identify deep disease and endometriomas
Medical treatment suppresses cyclical ovarian activity to reduce pain, using hormonal therapies that induce a hypo-oestrogenic or progestogen-dominant state
Surgical management aims to excise or ablate deposits and restore anatomy, and can improve both pain and fertility
There is a recognised diagnostic delay of years, so a high index of suspicion in women with chronic cyclical pelvic pain is important
Dismissing severe dysmenorrhoea as normal and delaying diagnosis
Assuming minimal imaging findings exclude significant disease
Overlooking ureteric or bowel involvement in deep infiltrating disease
Relying on symptom severity to gauge disease extent
Neglecting the long-term and psychological impact and the need for a multidisciplinary approach

Endometriosis is a chronic, often relapsing condition. Pain and fertility frequently improve with medical or surgical treatment, but recurrence after stopping hormonal suppression or following surgery is common. Many affected women conceive spontaneously or with assisted reproduction, and symptoms typically regress after the menopause.

chunks.text: Endophthalmitis is infection and severe inflammation of the intraocular contents, involving the aqueous and vitreous. Organisms gain access exogenously through a surgical wound, injection, or penetrating injury, or endogenously by haematogenous seeding from a distant source. Microbial proliferation within the relatively immune-privileged vitreous triggers an intense inflammatory response; bacterial toxins and inflammatory mediators cause rapid retinal necrosis and irreversible photoreceptor damage, which accounts for the poor prognosis when treatment is delayed.

Enterococci are intestinal symbionts that become pathogens when host barriers and colonization resistance are disrupted, most often in hospitalized or chronically ill patients. A higher level of gut colonization is the pivotal step in pathogenesis: suppression of gastric acid, degradation of the protective mucin layer, altered carbon-source availability (e.g., lactose favoring outgrowth, depletion of fructose by Olsenella reducing VRE burden), and especially antibiotic exposure all increase enteric burden. Antibiotic disruption of commensal gram-negative bacteria reduces lipopolysaccharide-driven, NF-kappaB/Toll-like-receptor-mediated production of the antimicrobial lectin RegIIIgamma and of bacteriocins/lantibiotics from organisms such as Blautia producta, impairing clearance of VRE. Three groups of virulence factors are described: (1) secreted factors including hemolysin/cytolysin, the gelatinase and serine proteases (which degrade host tissue and immune components), and a newly described pore-forming toxin Epx targeting HLA class 1; (2) surface components/adhesins (aggregation substance, the collagen adhesins Ace/Acm, pili, Esp, and other MSCRAMM-like proteins) mediating attachment to collagen, fibronectin, and fibrinogen and to biofilm/host tissue; and (3) less-characterized factors such as the stress protein Gls24 (bile-salt resistance, endocarditis), hylEfm-containing transferable plasmids that enhance gut colonization, and the oxidative-stress regulator AsrR. From colonized gut, prostate, intravascular devices, biliary/intraabdominal foci, wounds, or the urinary tract, enterococci enter the bloodstream and can seed heart valves, meninges, bone, and other sites. Genomic plasticity (recombination of core chromosomal DNA plus a malleable accessory genome of plasmids, phages, and mobile elements) drives rising resistance, concentrated in hospital-associated E. faecium clade A, which frequently lacks a functional CRISPR-Cas defense and carries high-expressing PBP5 alleles.

Two species cause the overwhelming majority of human enterococcal disease: E. faecalis (still predominant in nosocomial isolates) and E. faecium (now roughly one-third of species-identified infections and the far more resistant, harder-to-treat species).

E. faecium isolation from blood is associated with worse outcomes and higher mortality than other enterococcal species, largely reflecting more frequent vancomycin and ampicillin resistance and consequently fewer therapeutic options.

Enterococci are normal large-bowel commensals (usually less than 1% of the gut microbiota); antibiotics that are biliary-excreted and broad-spectrum (e.g., certain cephalosporins and anti-anaerobic agents) promote heavy gut overgrowth, the key precursor to infection.

Enterococcal cytolysin (a heterodimeric toxin of some E. faecalis strains) can lyse human and equine but not ovine RBCs as well as neutrophils and macrophages, which is why routine ovine/bovine RBC agar usually reports these strains as nonhemolytic.

Enterococci are gram-positive cocci appearing as single cells, diplococci, or short chains; they were historically grouped with streptococci but reclassified as a distinct genus on the basis of DNA hybridization and 16S rRNA sequencing.

Distinguishing laboratory features: hydrolysis of esculin in 40% bile salts, growth at 6.5% salt and at 46 degrees C, and PYR hydrolysis (the latter helping separate enterococci from the S. gallolyticus/S. bovis group and Leuconostoc).

Urinary tract infection is the most common enterococcal infection and is typically nosocomial, linked to indwelling catheters, instrumentation, or genitourinary anatomic abnormalities; removal of the catheter alone may eradicate the organism without antibiotics.

Enterococci rank second after staphylococci as agents of central line-associated bacteremia in the United States and are the third most common overall isolates from hospital-associated infections (after E. coli and staphylococci).

Enterococci are an important cause of community- and healthcare-associated endocarditis (second after staphylococci in healthcare-associated cases), with the gut or genitourinary tract the presumed bacteremic source; E. faecalis is the leading cause of endocarditis after transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI).

Typical enterococcal endocarditis is subacute (fever, weight loss, malaise, murmur) in elderly debilitated men; classic peripheral stigmata such as petechiae, Osler's nodes, and Roth's spots occur in only a minority.

VRE gut colonization is the critical step preceding invasive enterococcal disease; colonized patients can carry the organism for prolonged periods (sometimes more than a year) and are more likely to develop Enterococcus-related illness such as bacteremia.
Two meta-analyses found that VRE infection independently increases the risk of death compared with infection by a glycopeptide-susceptible strain, irrespective of the patient's clinical status.

Treating enterococcal growth from urine, intraabdominal samples, or surgical wounds as true infection when it often represents colonization, particularly in chronically catheterized or critically ill patients.
Failing to recognize that cephalosporins lack reliable anti-enterococcal activity, so empiric cephalosporin-based regimens leave enterococci uncovered.
Misclassifying E. faecalis as nonhemolytic when some strains carry an acquired hemolysin/cytolysin that lyses human/equine/rabbit RBCs (not the ovine/bovine RBCs in standard plates).
Confusing enterococci with the S. gallolyticus (S. bovis) group or Leuconostoc; PYR hydrolysis aids differentiation.
Underestimating chronic enterococcal prostatitis as an occult source of recurrent bacteremia, especially after urologic manipulation, where the most active agents penetrate prostatic tissue poorly.
Overlooking the markedly different resistance profiles and management implications of E. faecium versus E. faecalis.
Not pursuing echocardiography in enterococcal bacteremia where endocarditis risk is real (DENOVA scoring can guide this decision).

Outcome depends heavily on species, resistance, and host comorbidity. Patients with enterococcal bacteremia are typically chronically ill, long-hospitalized, and previously treated with multiple antibiotics. E. faecium bacteremia carries worse outcomes and higher mortality than other species, largely because of widespread vancomycin and ampicillin resistance; VRE infection independently raises mortality relative to glycopeptide-susceptible strains. For E. faecalis endocarditis, relapse risk is higher with antibiotics alone (about 2-11%) than after surgery (0-3%) and may occur up to a year after treatment. Heart failure is a common endocarditis complication, and valve replacement may be critical for cure when multidrug-resistant organisms or major complications are present. After hospital discharge, gut VRE carriage clears at a median of 2-4 months in patients without ongoing risk factors (continued antibiotics, long-term care residence, hemodialysis).
Persistent or recurrent enterococcal bacteremia, suggesting endocarditis or an undrained deep focus (e.g., chronic prostatitis, abscess)
New or changing cardiac murmur with heart failure in enterococcal bacteremia, signaling endocarditis with valve involvement
E. faecium or VRE bloodstream isolate, predicting higher mortality and limited treatment options
Meningitis after neurosurgery, shunt, CNS trauma, or CSF leak with neutrophilic CSF pleocytosis and low glucose
Enterococcal bacteremia or meningitis in an immunocompromised patient, which has been linked to Strongyloides stercoralis hyperinfection syndrome
Neonatal enterococcal sepsis (often late-onset), especially with prematurity, low birth weight, indwelling devices, or recent abdominal surgery
Infection of prosthetic material/hardware where biofilm reduces antimicrobial efficacy and hardware removal may be required

No single formal severity grading scale for enterococcal infection is given. Severity is stratified clinically by syndrome and resistance: localized/device-related infections (e.g., catheter-associated UTI or bacteremia, often resolved by source removal) are least severe, whereas endovascular infection (endocarditis), meningitis, and multidrug-resistant E. faecium/VRE bloodstream infection represent severe disease. High APACHE (Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation) scores are noted as a risk factor associated with VRE colonization and persistence. Endocarditis severity is influenced by heart failure, multidrug resistance, and the need for valve replacement.

PCR is now the primary diagnostic method; pan-enterovirus reverse-transcription PCR detects all human enteroviruses (CSF PCR ~70-100% sensitive, over 80% specific, faster than culture) but does NOT detect parechoviruses.
CSF PCR is less likely positive if presentation is 3 or more days after meningitis onset or with EV71; in those cases throat or rectal swab PCR (less specific) should be considered.

Serum PCR is highly sensitive/specific for disseminated disease and useful for diagnosis/monitoring in immunodeficient patients on immunoglobulin whose cultures may be negative; antigen detection is less sensitive than PCR.

Viral culture of CSF, serum, body-cavity fluid, or tissue is positive less often but a positive result is diagnostic; throat isolation is more meaningful than stool because shedding is shorter; coxsackievirus A may need special cell lines or suckling-mouse inoculation.

For suspected poliomyelitis: obtain two or more fecal and throat swabs at least 1 day apart for culture; a positive stool culture within the first 2 weeks confirms diagnosis when CSF culture is negative, and any poliovirus isolate must be sent to CDC to distinguish wild-type from vaccine virus.

Serotype identification is mainly for epidemiology; serologic diagnosis (paired acute and ~4-week convalescent neutralizing titers, the most accurate method) is limited by the many serotypes and absence of a common antigen.
Dedicated parechovirus PCR (performed by CDC and research labs; often unavailable commercially) when HPeV is suspected.

In acute flaccid myelitis: spinal-cord MRI may show gray-matter changes; CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and mildly elevated protein; EV-D68 antibodies are most often found in CSF though the virus itself is rarely detected there.

Enteroviruses multiply in the gastrointestinal tract. Based largely on poliovirus studies, after ingestion the virus infects mucosal epithelium and replicates in submucosal lymphoid tissue (tonsils, Peyer's patches), spreads to regional lymph nodes and into a viremic phase with replication in reticuloendothelial organs; a secondary viremia may seed other tissues and cause symptomatic disease. CNS entry is thought to occur via the bloodstream (viremia precedes neurologic disease), but evidence also supports direct neural spread: the poliovirus receptor is an immunoglobulin-superfamily member expressed at the neuromuscular end-plate, and animal/transgenic-mouse studies show that cutting the sciatic nerve prevents spinal-cord involvement after IM virus injection, implying axonal transport from muscle to anterior horn cells. Poliovirus is culturable from blood 3-5 days after infection (before neutralizing antibody); it is shed from the oropharynx up to ~3 weeks and from the GI tract up to ~12 weeks (over 20 years in hypogammaglobulinemia), and attenuated oral vaccine virus can revert toward neurovirulence during GI replication. Capsid protein VP1 is the main neutralizing-antibody target, conferring lifelong serotype-specific protection that does not prevent reinfection or shedding; IgM persists under ~6 months and IgG for life. Mucosal/secretory IgA limits GI replication and shedding, and breast-milk IgA is protective. Acute flaccid myelitis and poliomyelitis both target anterior horn cells of the spinal cord.

Enteroviruses are Picornaviridae with single-stranded RNA and a non-enveloped icosahedral capsid; being non-enveloped they are acid-stable (survive the stomach), resist alcohol and detergent disinfectants, persist for days at room temperature, but are susceptible to chlorine-containing cleansers.

Humoral immunity is critical: patients with agamma-/hypogammaglobulinemia can develop chronic enteroviral meningoencephalitis (often echovirus 11) with a dermatomyositis-like syndrome and chronic hepatitis, and may relapse even while on immunoglobulin; hypogammaglobulinemic patients can shed poliovirus for more than 20 years.

Human parechoviruses (HPeV, also Picornaviridae) mimic enteroviral disease (neonatal generalized disease, aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, seizures, hepatitis, rash) but pan-enterovirus PCR does NOT detect HPeV, so a dedicated PCR is required; infant deaths have been associated with HPeV-1, HPeV-3, and HPeV-6.

Reoviruses are double-stranded RNA viruses; most childhood infection is asymptomatic or causes mild upper respiratory symptoms, and reovirus is only a rare cause of mild gastroenteritis or meningitis, with speculative (unproven) links of reovirus type 3 to neonatal hepatitis and biliary atresia.

More than 50% of nonpolio enterovirus infections and over 90% of poliovirus infections are subclinical; when symptomatic, the most common picture is a nonspecific febrile illness ('summer grippe'), and in temperate climates disease clusters in summer and fall.

In children and young adults enteroviruses account for up to 90% of aseptic meningitis cases with an identifiable agent; CSF shows pleocytosis that shifts from neutrophil to lymphocyte predominance within a day, total cell count usually under 1000/uL, normal glucose, and normal-to-slightly-elevated protein.

A normal CSF glucose in enteroviral meningitis helps distinguish it from mumps meningitis, in which CSF glucose is low; enteroviral meningitis tends to be more severe in adults than children but neurologic sequelae are rare.

Hand-foot-and-mouth disease (most often coxsackievirus A16 or enterovirus 71) is highly infectious with attack rates near 100% in young children; coxsackievirus A6 causes a more extensive atypical form, and a B16/EV71 epidemic in Taiwan (1998) and yearly EV71 epidemics in China since 2008 produced brainstem encephalitis, pulmonary edema/hemorrhage, and deaths, mostly in children 5 years or younger.

Herpangina (usually coxsackievirus A) produces grayish-white papulovesicular ulcerating lesions concentrated in the posterior mouth (soft palate, anterior tonsillar pillars, uvula) and, unlike herpetic stomatitis, is NOT associated with gingivitis.

Pleurodynia (Bornholm disease), usually coxsackievirus B, causes paroxysms of knifelike pleuritic chest or upper-abdominal pain lasting 15-30 minutes with tender muscles and possible pleural rub; WBC and chest x-ray are typically normal.

Enteroviruses cause up to one-third of acute myocarditis cases; patients (over two-thirds male, often neonates/adolescents/young adults) present after a respiratory prodrome with chest pain, arrhythmia, ST/T-wave changes and elevated cardiac enzymes; up to 10% progress to dilated cardiomyopathy.

Acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis (enterovirus 70, coxsackievirus A24) presents with sudden severe eye pain, subconjunctival hemorrhage, chemosis, and preauricular adenopathy; its abrupt onset and short course (recovery in ~10 days) distinguish it from adenoviral or chlamydial eye disease, and EV70 cases have been linked to paralysis during epidemics.
Glucocorticoids are contraindicated in enterovirus infections.

A positive enterovirus culture from stool, nasopharynx, or throat does NOT prove disease causation, since these sites are colonized for weeks during subclinical infection; throat isolation is more meaningful than stool.
Pan-enterovirus PCR does not detect human parechoviruses, so HPeV can be missed unless a dedicated assay is used.
CSF PCR may be falsely negative if obtained 3 or more days into meningitis or in EV71 infection.
Neonatal enteroviral disease can be indistinguishable from bacterial sepsis; a recent viral illness in the mother is a useful clue.
Cultures may be falsely negative due to neutralizing antibody, unsuitable cell lines, or improper specimen handling.

Oral poliovirus vaccine can revert to neurovirulence (vaccine-associated/vaccine-derived poliomyelitis), with risk roughly 2000-fold higher in immunodeficient persons; tonsillectomy predisposes to bulbar polio and IM injections increase paralysis risk in the involved limb.

Most enterovirus infections are mild and self-limited, resolving within about a week. Enteroviral aseptic meningitis carries an excellent prognosis with rare neurologic sequelae (though CSF abnormalities can persist weeks); immunocompetent encephalitis patients generally do well. Pleurodynia resolves in days with rare recurrence; acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis usually recovers completely in ~10 days. Myocarditis in older children and adults usually resolves fully, but neonates often have severe disease and up to 10% progress to chronic dilated cardiomyopathy, with chronic constrictive pericarditis a possible sequela. In paralytic poliomyelitis most patients regain some function over weeks to months but about two-thirds have residual neurologic sequelae; postpolio syndrome has a generally good prognosis with slow progression and plateaus of 1-10 years. Acute flaccid myelitis usually leaves persistent neurologic deficits. EV71 CNS disease can leave lasting dysphagia, cranial-nerve palsies, hypoventilation, limb weakness/atrophy, and impaired cognition. HPeV infection is usually mild (HPeV-1) but has caused infant deaths.

Neonatal enteroviral illness resembling sepsis with myocarditis/hypotension, fulminant hepatitis with DIC, meningoencephalitis, or pneumonia (serious disease most often in the first week of life, up to 3 months).
Rapid onset of flaccid limb paralysis after fever/respiratory symptoms (acute flaccid myelitis or paralytic enteroviral disease).
Brainstem encephalitis with myoclonus, tremor/ataxia, plus pulmonary edema or hemorrhage in young children (severe enterovirus 71 disease).
Bulbar involvement causing dysphagia, dysphonia, or respiratory insufficiency/circulatory collapse in poliomyelitis.
Chest pain, arrhythmia, ST-segment changes, and elevated cardiac enzymes after a respiratory prodrome (enteroviral myocarditis, risk of dilated cardiomyopathy).
Chronic meningoencephalitis or dermatomyositis-like syndrome in an agamma-/hypogammaglobulinemic patient.

Poliovirus infection severity spectrum: asymptomatic (most) -> minor/abortive poliomyelitis (~5%: fever, malaise, sore throat, myalgia, headache, resolving in ~3 days) -> nonparalytic poliomyelitis/aseptic meningitis (~1%) -> paralytic poliomyelitis (least common; asymmetric, proximal-predominant weakness, may be bulbar/respiratory). Paralytic disease is more frequent in older individuals, pregnant women, and those exercising or experiencing trauma at symptom onset. Postpolio syndrome occurs 20-40 years after initial paralytic disease. Vaccine-associated paralytic risk is about 1 per 2.5 million OPV doses.

chunks.text: Entropion is inward rotation of the eyelid margin. Involutional entropion arises from age-related horizontal lid laxity, attenuation or disinsertion of the lower lid retractors, and overriding of the preseptal orbicularis, which together destabilise the lid and allow it to rotate inward. Cicatricial entropion results from contracture of scarred tarsoconjunctiva pulling the margin toward the globe. Spastic entropion is triggered by orbicularis spasm from ocular irritation, and congenital entropion reflects a structural lid defect. In all forms the inturned lashes abrade the ocular surface, causing chronic irritation and potential corneal damage.

chunks.text: Epididymo-orchitis is inflammation of the epididymis, frequently extending to the adjacent testis, usually caused by retrograde ascent of organisms from the urethra or bladder along the vas deferens. In younger men sexually transmitted pathogens predominate, whereas in older men Gram-negative urinary organisms associated with obstruction, catheterisation, or instrumentation are more common. The resulting inflammatory oedema, hyperaemia, and swelling can progress to suppuration, abscess, or testicular infarction from compromised blood supply. Viral causes such as mumps produce orchitis through haematogenous spread.

chunks.text: Episcleritis is inflammation confined to the episclera, the thin vascular layer of connective tissue between the conjunctiva and the sclera. The process is typically a localised, non-granulomatous inflammatory response affecting the superficial episcleral vascular plexus, producing vasodilatation and mild oedema without the deep scleral destruction of true scleritis. It is usually idiopathic and self-limiting, though recurrent or nodular episodes can occasionally be associated with systemic inflammatory disease.

chunks.text: Epistaxis is bleeding from the nasal mucosa, whose rich, superficial vascular supply from branches of both the internal and external carotid systems makes it prone to haemorrhage. Anterior bleeding usually comes from the low-pressure anastomotic vessels of Little's area, provoked by drying, trauma or minor mucosal injury. Posterior bleeding tends to arise from larger branches such as the sphenopalatine artery and is aggravated by hypertension and vascular fragility in older patients. Systemic factors such as bleeding disorders, anticoagulation and platelet dysfunction impair haemostasis and prolong or worsen bleeding.

chunks.text: Penile erection depends on neurally mediated relaxation of cavernosal smooth muscle, increased arterial inflow, and veno-occlusion that traps blood within the corpora cavernosa; nitric oxide and the cyclic GMP pathway are central to this process. Psychogenic factors act through central inhibition of the erectile response. Many patients have a mixed, multifactorial aetiology.

chunks.text: Ethylene glycol is oxidised by alcohol dehydrogenase to glycoaldehyde, then to glycolic acid and finally oxalic acid. Glycolic acid is the main contributor to the profound high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, while oxalic acid combines with calcium to form insoluble calcium oxalate crystals that deposit in renal tubules, causing acute kidney injury, and lower serum calcium. Accumulating toxic metabolites also impair oxidative metabolism, producing lactic acidosis. The parent alcohol raises serum osmolality, giving an early osmolal gap that later falls as the anion gap widens.

Obesity arises from a chronic imbalance in which energy intake exceeds energy expenditure, leading to expansion of adipose depots. It is a highly heterogeneous condition strongly influenced by underlying genetic variation, with environmental factors ubiquitous in developed and developing countries; in some individuals it is attributable entirely to genetic causes. Insulin resistance is one of the earliest complications: muscle (glucose disposal) and liver (glucose production) become less responsive to insulin, prompting compensatory hyperinsulinemia. Two main hypotheses link adiposity to insulin resistance—macrophage- and inflammatory-cell products in obese adipose tissue disturbing insulin action, and the limited storage capacity of adipose tissue causing ectopic lipid deposition in muscle and liver (human data are stronger for the ectopic-fat mechanism). The metabolic, endocrine, and cardiovascular consequences may stem from chronic overnutrition and ectopic fat rather than fat mass per se, whereas certain complications (osteoarthritis, reflux esophagitis, obstructive sleep apnea) relate more directly to mass and volume effects.
More than 70% of U.S. adults are overweight or have obesity, and prevalence is rising in most industrialized nations, with accelerating rates in children and adolescents.

Staging tools such as the AACE/ACE complication-based system (stage 0 with no complications, stages 1-2 with mild-moderate or severe complications) and the Edmonton Obesity Staging System (graded 0-4 across medical, functional, and psychological domains, independent of BMI) help identify high-risk patients beyond BMI alone.
As BMI rises by 5 kg/m2, cancer mortality is estimated to increase by about 10%, and obesity has reportedly overtaken smoking as the leading risk factor for cancer in some countries.
Not every patient meeting a BMI obesity threshold requires treatment, but those with obesity-related complications and comorbidities should be managed proactively.

BMI (weight in kg divided by height in m squared, or weight in lb divided by height in in squared times 703) is used to classify weight status: healthy weight 18.5-24.9, overweight 25.0-29.9, obesity class I 30.0-34.9, class II 35.0-39.9, and extreme/class III obesity 40 or greater.

BMI only reflects body size; it does not capture body composition, fat distribution, or individual health, so it functions as a screening and population tool rather than a direct measure of adiposity.

Waist circumference is a surrogate for visceral adipose tissue and independently predicts metabolic syndrome, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease; it should be measured in the horizontal plane above the iliac crest, particularly when BMI is 35 or below.

Ethnic-specific waist cutpoints differ: for Europeans, greater than 94 cm in men and greater than 80 cm in women; for South Asians and Chinese, greater than 90 cm in men and greater than 80 cm in women.
Lower BMI thresholds for overweight and obesity have been proposed for the Asia-Pacific population because metabolic risk appears at lower body weights.

The obesity-focused history is best approached using neutral language (weight, excess weight, BMI, unhealthy weight) because terms like obesity, morbid obesity, or fatness are perceived as stigmatizing.

Recommended baseline workup for all patients includes a fasting lipid profile (total, LDL, and HDL cholesterol plus triglycerides), a chemistry panel, glycated hemoglobin, and blood pressure measurement.
Physical fitness and sedentary behavior are independent predictors of all-cause mortality regardless of BMI or body composition, underscoring the importance of an activity history.
Relying on BMI alone, which does not measure body composition or fat distribution and can misclassify individual risk.
Using stigmatizing language (obesity, morbid obesity, fatness) that leaves patients feeling judged and can undermine engagement.

Initiating lifestyle change when the patient is not ready, which can cause frustration and hamper future efforts.

Neglecting waist circumference, which adds independent risk information about visceral adiposity.

Obesity is a serious chronic disease associated with increased morbidity and mortality through multiple complications—type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, atherothrombotic cardiovascular disease, stroke, heart failure (often diastolic dysfunction) and atrial fibrillation, obstructive sleep apnea, fatty liver disease that can progress to NASH and cirrhosis, several cancers, osteoarthritis, and gout. Risk generally rises with increasing levels of obesity and with central (visceral) fat distribution. Obesity also worsens outcomes from some infections (notably COVID-19) and raises susceptibility to wound infection and postoperative sepsis. Realistic initial treatment goals (around 8-10% weight loss over 6 months) can meaningfully improve obesity-related complications and quality of life.

Serum liver tests reflect distinct mechanisms rather than overall hepatic function. Aminotransferases (AST, ALT) leak from hepatocytes when cell-membrane permeability increases; ALT is comparatively liver-specific while AST is also present in cardiac and skeletal muscle, kidney, brain, pancreas, lung, leukocytes, and red cells. Cholestasis-associated enzymes (alkaline phosphatase, 5'-nucleotidase, GGT) rise with impaired bile flow; alkaline phosphatase and 5'-nucleotidase localize near the canalicular membrane, whereas GGT, found in endoplasmic reticulum and bile-duct epithelium, is more diffuse and less specific. Bilirubin, the end product of heme catabolism, circulates unconjugated and albumin-bound until hepatocellular uptake, intracellular binding, glucuronide conjugation, and canalicular secretion render it water-soluble and excretable; the rate-limiting step is canalicular transport of conjugated bilirubin. Biosynthetic capacity is reflected by albumin (hepatocyte-synthesized, half-life 18-20 days, so insensitive to acute injury) and the clotting factors (rapid turnover, making PT/INR a sensitive acute marker). Gamma globulins rise in chronic liver disease because the cirrhotic liver fails to clear gut-derived bacterial antigens, increasing antibody synthesis (Harrison 22e p.2634-2636).

Serum biochemical tests labeled 'liver function tests' are useful to detect liver disease, distinguish disorder types, gauge severity, and follow treatment response, but most do not actually measure synthetic liver function; aminotransferases and alkaline phosphatase instead detect hepatocyte damage or impaired bile flow (Harrison 22e p.2633).

Because clotting factors (except factor VIII, made by endothelium) are made only in hepatocytes and turn over rapidly (factor VII half-life ~6 h), the prothrombin time/INR is the single best acute marker of hepatic synthetic function (Harrison 22e p.2636).

Any bilirubin in the urine is conjugated, since unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound and not filtered; bilirubinuria implies liver disease or obstructive jaundice and clears before serum bilirubin during recovery (Harrison 22e p.2634).

Ultrasonography is the first test when cholestasis is suspected (to assess for dilated ducts or gallstones) and is also the first study ordered when Budd-Chiari syndrome is suspected, using Doppler to assess vessel patency and flow direction (Harrison 22e p.2636).

Tests should be used as a battery rather than singly; when more than one is abnormal, or abnormalities persist on serial testing, the probability of liver disease is high, whereas normal results make occult disease unlikely (Harrison 22e p.2633).

Total bilirubin normally runs about 1-1.5 mg/dL (95% of normals 0.2-0.9 mg/dL); if the direct fraction is under 15% of total, the bilirubin is considered essentially all indirect (unconjugated) (Harrison 22e p.2634).

Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia points to hemolysis or genetic conditions such as Gilbert's or Crigler-Najjar syndromes; in an otherwise healthy person without hemolysis it can be attributed to Gilbert's syndrome with no further workup needed (Harrison 22e p.2634).

Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia almost always implies hepatobiliary disease; because the rate-limiting step is canalicular transport rather than conjugation, the conjugated fraction can rise in any liver disease, including fulminant failure (Harrison 22e p.2634).

Aminotransferase elevations above 1000 IU/L occur almost exclusively with extensive hepatocellular injury: viral hepatitis, ischemic/hypoxic injury, or drug/toxin injury; levels up to ~300 IU/L are nonspecific (Harrison 22e p.2635).

The absolute aminotransferase level does not correlate with degree of liver cell damage and has no prognostic significance in acute hepatocellular disease; necrosis is not required for enzyme release, only increased membrane permeability (Harrison 22e p.2635).

An AST:ALT ratio over 2:1 suggests, and over 3:1 strongly suggests, alcohol-related liver disease; AST is rarely above 300 IU/L in alcoholic liver disease and ALT is often normal/low because of pyridoxal phosphate deficiency (Harrison 22e p.2635).

Alkaline phosphatase elevation greater than ~4x normal points to cholestatic disorders, infiltrative diseases (tumor, amyloidosis), or high-turnover bone disease such as Paget's; less than 3x elevation is nonspecific (Harrison 22e p.2635).

Liver tests lack sensitivity and specificity; results can be normal in serious liver disease and abnormal in non-hepatic disease, and rarely indicate a specific diagnosis on their own (Harrison 22e p.2633).
Relying on the absolute aminotransferase value for prognosis is an error, since it does not correlate with the degree of damage in acute hepatocellular disease (Harrison 22e p.2635).
Except with isolated hyperbilirubinemia, fractionating bilirubin rarely identifies the cause of jaundice (Harrison 22e p.2634).
Alkaline phosphatase level does not distinguish intrahepatic from extrahepatic cholestasis (Harrison 22e p.2635).

Albumin is insensitive to acute or mild hepatic dysfunction owing to its long half-life and is not specific for liver disease; it should not be ordered to screen patients without suspected liver disease (Harrison 22e p.2636).

Liver biopsy should not be the first procedure for cholestasis; the biliary tree must first be evaluated for obstruction, and biopsy is subject to sampling error in focal disease (Harrison 22e p.2636).

Blood ammonia correlates poorly with both presence and severity of encephalopathy and with hepatic function, and can be elevated from portal shunting despite near-normal liver function (Harrison 22e p.2636).

Individual tests carry prognostic weight: in viral hepatitis a higher serum bilirubin reflects greater hepatocellular damage, total bilirubin correlates with poor outcome in alcoholic hepatitis and with prognosis in primary biliary cholangitis, and an elevated bilirubin signals more severe drug-induced injury. A prothrombin time prolonged more than 5 seconds above control and not corrected by parenteral vitamin K is a poor prognostic indicator in acute viral and other liver diseases, and elevated arterial ammonia correlates with outcome in fulminant hepatic failure. Bilirubin, INR, creatinine, albumin, and sodium are integrated into the MELD 3.0 score used to gauge hepatic decompensation and prioritize transplant allocation (Harrison 22e p.2634-2636).
Aminotransferases above 1000 IU/L indicating extensive hepatocellular injury (viral, ischemic, or toxin/drug)
Prothrombin time prolonged more than 5 seconds above control and uncorrected by parenteral vitamin K, a poor prognostic sign in acute viral and other liver disease
Albumin below 3 g/dL in apparent hepatitis raising concern for underlying chronic liver disease
Elevated total bilirubin in drug-induced liver injury signaling more severe injury
Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, which nearly always implies hepatobiliary disease and can occur even in fulminant liver failure

Liver test patterns are categorized by pattern recognition (Harrison Table 348-1): hemolysis/Gilbert's (isolated indirect bilirubin, no bilirubinuria, otherwise normal); acute hepatocellular necrosis (aminotransferases often above 500 IU/L with ALT exceeding AST, bilirubinuria, PT prognostic); chronic hepatocellular disorders (aminotransferases usually below 300 IU/L, often low albumin and prolonged PT not corrected by vitamin K); alcoholic hepatitis/cirrhosis (AST:ALT above 2); and intra/extrahepatic cholestasis or infiltrative disease (alkaline phosphatase often above 4x normal). Disease severity in chronic liver disease/cirrhosis is graded by the Child-Pugh classification and, for transplant prioritization, the MELD 3.0 score (bilirubin, INR, creatinine, albumin, sodium) (Harrison 22e p.2636-2637).

Growth requires that energy and nutrient intake exceed the demands of maintenance and activity. Faltering growth arises when this balance is disturbed: intake may be insufficient because of feeding difficulties, poor appetite, incorrect feed preparation, or limited food availability; nutrients may be inadequately absorbed or lost through malabsorption, chronic diarrhoea, or vomiting; or requirements may be raised by chronic illness such as cardiac, respiratory, renal, or inflammatory disease. Prolonged deficits deplete energy stores and, if sustained, can impair linear growth and, in severe or early cases, brain development. Psychosocial and caregiving factors frequently interact with these physiological mechanisms.
Failure to thrive describes inadequate physical growth in a young child, most often identified as weight gain that is poor for age or crosses downward through growth chart percentiles over time.
A single low measurement is less meaningful than the trajectory of serial measurements plotted on an appropriate growth chart.
The traditional split into organic and non-organic causes is artificial; many children have mixed contributors, and inadequate caloric intake is the final common pathway in most cases.
The three broad mechanisms are insufficient intake, inadequate absorption or increased losses, and increased energy requirements, and the history usually distinguishes among them.
A careful feeding, dietary, developmental, social, and psychosocial history plus observation of a feed often yields more than extensive laboratory testing.
Investigations should be guided by clues from the history and examination rather than performed as an indiscriminate panel.
Management prioritises adequate catch-up nutrition while addressing any medical, developmental, feeding, and psychosocial factors, often through a multidisciplinary approach.
Signs of neglect, abuse, or a threatening environment must be considered, but most children with faltering growth are not victims of maltreatment.
Diagnosing failure to thrive from a single measurement rather than the growth trend
Ordering broad laboratory panels instead of history-directed testing
Assuming an organic cause and overlooking feeding technique, caloric adequacy, or psychosocial factors
Mislabelling normal constitutional or genetically small children as failing to thrive

With timely recognition and adequate nutritional rehabilitation most children achieve catch-up growth and do well, but prolonged or severe undernutrition, especially in infancy, can be associated with lasting effects on growth and neurodevelopment.
