chunks.diseaseName: Familial Mediterranean Fever and Other Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases
chunks.text: These disorders reflect dysregulated innate immunity rather than adaptive autoimmunity. In FMF, gain-of-function MEFV mutations lower the activation threshold of the pyrin inflammasome; pyrin (via its PYRIN domain and an adaptor) assembles a macromolecular complex that activates caspase-1, producing IL-1beta and IL-18 and triggering gasdermin-D-mediated pyroptosis. Pyrin normally senses bacterial toxins that inactivate RhoA GTPase as part of host defense. The other syndromes map to specific innate pathways: TRAPS arises from misfolding, aggregation, and retention of mutant TNFR1 with ligand-independent kinase activation, mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, and proinflammatory cytokine release; HIDS/MKD results from mevalonate kinase deficiency that impairs isoprenoid (geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate) synthesis, mislocalizing and inactivating RhoA and thereby activating the pyrin inflammasome; FCAS/MWS/NOMID arise from NLRP3 (cryopyrin) mutations forming an overactive NLRP3 inflammasome with excess IL-1beta and IL-18. Broader categories include interferonopathies driven by aberrant intracellular nucleic-acid sensing (excess type I interferon) and relopathies that dysregulate NF-kB activation or TNF-induced cell death. Untreated chronic inflammation can lead to systemic AA amyloidosis from deposition of a serum amyloid A fragment.

chunks.diseaseName: Familial Mediterranean Fever and Other Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases
chunks.text: FMF is the prototype hereditary autoinflammatory disease: recurrent self-limited fever with serosal, synovial, or cutaneous inflammation, distinguished from autoimmune disease by the relative absence of high-titer autoantibodies or antigen-specific T cells and a predominant role of the innate immune system (Harrison 22e p.2934).

chunks.diseaseName: Familial Mediterranean Fever and Other Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases
chunks.text: About one-third of clinically typical NOMID patients lack germline NLRP3 mutations but are mosaic for somatic NLRP3 mutations; somatic NLRP3 mosaicism has rarely been reported in Schnitzler's syndrome (middle-age recurrent fever, urticaria, monoclonal IgM gammopathy, abnormal bone remodeling) (Harrison 22e p.2936-2937).

chunks.diseaseName: Familial Mediterranean Fever and Other Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases
chunks.text: PFAPA (periodic fever with aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, cervical adenitis) is the most common periodic fever syndrome of childhood, notable for clock-like regularity, familial but non-Mendelian clustering, and a tendency to resolve by early adulthood (Harrison 22e p.2937).

chunks.diseaseName: Familial Mediterranean Fever and Other Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases
chunks.text: Over 60 monogenic autoinflammatory diseases are now recognized, grouped mechanistically into inflammasomopathies (FMF, HIDS, CAPS, PAPA, NLRC4-related), type I interferonopathies (STING-associated vasculopathy, COPA syndrome, Aicardi-Goutieres, CANDLE), and relopathies affecting NF-kB / TNF-induced cell death (Harrison 22e p.2937).

chunks.diseaseName: Familial Mediterranean Fever and Other Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases
chunks.text: Roughly 90% of patients have their first attack by age 20; typical episodes last about 24-72 hours, with arthritic attacks tending to run longer (Harrison 22e p.2934).

chunks.diseaseName: Familial Mediterranean Fever and Other Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases
chunks.text: Over 90% of FMF patients have abdominal (peritoneal) attacks; laparotomy reveals a sterile neutrophil-rich peritoneal exudate, and ascites is rare (Harrison 22e p.2934).

chunks.diseaseName: Familial Mediterranean Fever and Other Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases
chunks.text: Erysipelas-like erythema, a raised erythematous rash typically on the dorsum of the foot, ankle, or lower leg, is the most characteristic skin finding and occurs most often in M694V homozygotes (Harrison 22e p.2934).

chunks.diseaseName: Familial Mediterranean Fever and Other Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases
chunks.text: FMF arthritis is usually monoarticular (knee, ankle, hip) with large sterile neutrophil-rich effusions and little erythema or warmth; radiographic changes are rare even after repeated attacks (Harrison 22e p.2934).

chunks.diseaseName: Familial Mediterranean Fever and Other Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases
chunks.text: The MEFV gene encodes pyrin (~95 kDa); its N-terminal PYRIN domain nucleates the pyrin inflammasome that activates caspase-1, driving IL-1beta and IL-18 secretion and gasdermin-D-mediated pyroptosis (Harrison 22e p.2934).

chunks.diseaseName: Familial Mediterranean Fever and Other Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases
chunks.text: FMF-associated MEFV mutations are gain-of-function, lowering the threshold for pyrin inflammasome activation; severe disease-associated mutations cluster in exon 10, and M694V homozygosity predicts earlier onset and more arthritis, rash, and amyloidosis (Harrison 22e p.2935-2936).

chunks.diseaseName: Familial Mediterranean Fever and Other Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases
chunks.text: The principal hereditary recurrent fever syndromes are differentiated by attack length, ethnicity, and features: TRAPS (TNFRSF1A, dominant, attacks often >7 days, migratory myalgia with overlying erythema, periorbital edema/conjunctivitis), HIDS/MKD (MVK, recessive, painful cervical adenopathy and oral ulcers), and the NLRP3-associated cryopyrinopathies FCAS, MWS, and NOMID (Harrison 22e p.2935-2937).

chunks.diseaseName: Familial Mediterranean Fever and Other Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases
chunks.text: Cryopyrinopathies form a spectrum: FCAS (cold-induced urticaria-like rash, fever, arthralgia, conjunctivitis), MWS (urticarial rash not cold-induced, progressive sensorineural hearing loss), and NOMID/neonatal-onset multisystem inflammatory disease (chronic aseptic meningitis, characteristic arthropathy, rash) (Harrison 22e p.2937).

chunks.diseaseName: Familial Mediterranean Fever and Other Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases
chunks.text: A positive family history can be elicited in only about half of cases (especially where families are small), so its absence does not exclude FMF; FMF can also occur without known Mediterranean ancestry.

chunks.diseaseName: Familial Mediterranean Fever and Other Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases
chunks.text: Only about 70% of clinically typical FMF patients carry two identifiable MEFV mutations in trans, and many clinical cases have only a single demonstrable mutation, so genetic testing cannot rule out the diagnosis.

chunks.diseaseName: Familial Mediterranean Fever and Other Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases
chunks.text: Certain variants are functional polymorphisms rather than disease-causing: E148Q (common in some Asian populations) often affects overall inflammation more than causing clinical FMF, and TNFRSF1A R92Q and P46L may behave as polymorphisms in TRAPS.

chunks.diseaseName: Familial Mediterranean Fever and Other Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases
chunks.text: Serum IgD elevation is neither sensitive nor specific for HIDS/MKD: disease activity does not track IgD levels, some FMF/TRAPS patients have modestly raised IgD, and some MVK-mutation patients have normal IgD (markedly elevated urinary mevalonate during attacks is more reliable).

chunks.diseaseName: Familial Mediterranean Fever and Other Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases
chunks.text: About one-third of NOMID patients lack germline NLRP3 mutations and require testing for somatic mosaicism, which can be missed on standard germline sequencing.

chunks.diseaseName: Familial Mediterranean Fever and Other Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases
chunks.text: FMF attacks are self-limited and recur with variable frequency over a lifetime; episodes may even be associated with remission during pregnancy. The major determinant of long-term outcome is systemic AA amyloidosis, historically a common and serious complication. Amyloidosis risk is increased by the M694V homozygous genotype, positive family history, the SAA1 genotype, male gender, non-adherence to therapy, and national origin (paralleling infant mortality rate). Among the related syndromes, untreated TRAPS leads to amyloidosis in about 15% of cases, MWS in roughly 25%, while amyloidosis is uncommon in FCAS and is a late complication in NOMID. PFAPA generally has a benign course with resolution by early adulthood. NOMID is the most severe cryopyrinopathy.

chunks.diseaseName: Familial Mediterranean Fever and Other Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases

chunks.diseaseName: Familial Mediterranean Fever and Other Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases
chunks.text: No formal numeric severity scale is given; the hereditary recurrent fevers are clinically stratified by syndrome (FMF, TRAPS, HIDS/MKD, and the NLRP3-associated spectrum of FCAS [mildest] -> MWS -> NOMID [most severe]) and by attack length, organ involvement, and genotype. In FMF, M694V homozygosity marks more severe disease (earlier onset; higher frequency of arthritis, rash, and amyloidosis). Development of systemic AA amyloidosis defines the severe end of the disease spectrum.

chunks.text: Fat embolism syndrome typically follows fractures of long bones or the pelvis, or orthopaedic instrumentation, when marrow fat enters the venous circulation. A mechanical component arises as fat globules occlude pulmonary and systemic capillaries, while a biochemical component follows as circulating free fatty acids are released and produce a toxic inflammatory injury to the pulmonary capillary endothelium. The result is impaired gas exchange resembling acute lung injury, cerebral microembolism causing confusion and reduced consciousness, and dermal capillary involvement producing the characteristic petechiae. Symptoms characteristically appear after a latent interval of roughly one to three days.

Febrile seizures reflect the heightened seizure susceptibility of the developing brain when exposed to fever, likely mediated by fever-associated cytokines (such as interleukin-1 beta), the effect of raised temperature on neuronal excitability, and a genetic predisposition, as demonstrated by strong familial clustering. The rate of temperature rise and the immaturity of the young brain contribute, and in most children the tendency resolves with neurological maturation.
A seizure occurring with fever in children roughly 6 months to 5 years of age, without central nervous system infection or a metabolic cause, and not in a child with prior afebrile seizures.
Simple febrile seizures are generalised, last under 15 minutes, and do not recur within 24 hours; complex seizures are focal, prolonged, or recur within a day.
The diagnosis is clinical, and the main task is to exclude meningitis, encephalitis, and other acute causes of the fever.
Routine blood tests, neuroimaging, and EEG are not indicated for simple febrile seizures in an otherwise well child.
Lumbar puncture is considered when meningeal signs are present, in very young or incompletely immunised infants, or when the picture is atypical.
Most febrile seizures are brief and self-terminating; management centres on reassurance, identifying the febrile illness, and safety advice for parents.
Prolonged seizures are treated as status epilepticus with benzodiazepine-based abortive therapy and airway support.
Antipyretics improve comfort but do not reliably prevent recurrence, and daily prophylactic anticonvulsants are generally not recommended for simple febrile seizures.
Assuming fever excludes meningitis and skipping evaluation in a young or unwell infant
Over-investigating a well child after a simple febrile seizure
Reassuring families that antipyretics prevent recurrence
Starting long-term anticonvulsants for simple febrile seizures unnecessarily

The outlook is excellent: most children have normal development and neurological outcome, though about a third experience a recurrence, and the increase in later epilepsy risk is small for simple febrile seizures.

chunks.text: Most urinary tract infections are ascending: bowel-derived uropathogens, chiefly Escherichia coli, colonise the perineum, ascend the urethra, and multiply in the bladder. When bacteria and inflammation reach the kidney, pyelonephritis develops with fever and systemic signs. Bacterial virulence factors and host factors, including urinary stasis, incomplete bladder emptying, and vesicoureteral reflux that carries infected urine toward the kidney, promote upper tract infection. The inflammatory response within the renal parenchyma can injure tissue and, particularly with delayed treatment or recurrent episodes, lead to permanent scarring.

chunks.diseaseName: Febrile Urinary Tract Infection in Children
chunks.text: Fever with a urinary tract infection in a young child usually indicates upper tract involvement (pyelonephritis) and should be taken seriously because of the risk of renal scarring.

chunks.diseaseName: Febrile Urinary Tract Infection in Children
chunks.text: In infants and preverbal children, features are non-specific, so urinary tract infection must be considered in any young child with unexplained fever.

chunks.diseaseName: Febrile Urinary Tract Infection in Children
chunks.text: A properly collected urine specimen is essential; contamination from bag or non-clean-catch samples is a frequent source of misleading results.

chunks.diseaseName: Febrile Urinary Tract Infection in Children
chunks.text: Diagnosis rests on the combination of pyuria and a significant growth of a single uropathogen on culture from an appropriately obtained specimen.

chunks.diseaseName: Febrile Urinary Tract Infection in Children
chunks.text: Escherichia coli is the predominant pathogen, and prompt appropriate antibiotic treatment reduces the likelihood of renal injury.

chunks.diseaseName: Febrile Urinary Tract Infection in Children
chunks.text: Imaging, typically renal and bladder ultrasound, is used to detect structural abnormalities, with further studies such as voiding cystourethrography reserved for selected children.

chunks.diseaseName: Febrile Urinary Tract Infection in Children
chunks.text: Vesicoureteral reflux and other urinary tract abnormalities predispose to recurrent infection and scarring and should be considered, especially after atypical or recurrent infections.

chunks.diseaseName: Febrile Urinary Tract Infection in Children
chunks.text: Recurrent febrile infections and any resulting renal scarring can contribute to later hypertension and reduced renal function, so follow-up matters.

chunks.text: A femoral hernia protrudes through the femoral canal, the medial-most compartment of the femoral sheath, below the inguinal ligament. The canal normally contains fat and a lymph node (node of Cloquet) and has an unyielding boundary. Raised intra-abdominal pressure forces peritoneum and abdominal contents through the femoral ring into this confined space. The rigidity and narrowness of the neck predispose trapped contents to incarceration and rapid compromise of blood supply, causing strangulation and bowel ischaemia. The sac may turn upward over the inguinal ligament, mimicking an inguinal hernia.

FM is regarded as a disorder in which the central nervous system maintains pain and the other core symptoms. Psychophysical testing shows altered afferent pain processing and impaired descending noxious inhibitory control, producing hyperalgesia and allodynia, and functional MRI demonstrates activation of pain-experiencing brain regions in response to stimuli that are innocuous in unaffected individuals. Pain perception is modulated by emotional and cognitive factors such as catastrophizing and perceived control. Genetic susceptibility appears polygenic, involving pathways that control pain and stress responses, including genes for metabolism, transport, and receptors of serotonin and other monoamines, with some genetic underpinnings shared across chronic pain conditions and overlapping with mood disorders. Peripheral pain generators (e.g., arthritis, bursitis, neuropathy, hypermobility) can serve as triggers that alter central pain processing (Harrison 22e p.2964).

Defined by chronic widespread musculoskeletal pain and tenderness, with pain present most of the day on most days for at least 3 months and distributed both above and below the waist, on both sides, and involving the axial skeleton (Harrison 22e p.2963).
Some patients meeting FM criteria have a small-fiber neuropathy, and early reports suggest possible autoimmune changes in the peripheral nervous system in subsets of patients (Harrison 22e p.2964).

Functional assessment across physical, mental, and social domains is central, since improved function (rather than complete pain elimination) is the principal measure of management success (Harrison 22e p.2964).

Beyond pain, patients commonly report fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive dysfunction ("fibro fog"), anxiety, and depression, which may affect function and quality of life as much as or more than the pain itself (Harrison 22e p.2963-2964).

Elevated evoked pain sensitivity may be detected clinically by pain on blood-pressure cuff inflation or skin-roll tenderness; a formal tender-point exam applies ~4 kg/m2 of thumbnail pressure (enough to blanch the nail bed) at defined musculotendinous sites (Harrison 22e p.2963).

Older ACR criteria required 11 of 18 tender points; newer 2016 criteria abandon tender-point counting and instead use a Widespread Pain Index plus Symptom Severity Score (e.g., WPI >=7 and SSS >=5, or WPI 4-6 and SSS >=9, with generalized pain in at least 4 of 5 regions for >=3 months) (Harrison 22e p.2963-2964).
Tenderness is a continuous variable; strict application of a categorical threshold is not required for diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2963).

Peripheral pain generators such as arthritis, bursitis, tendinitis, neuropathies, joint hypermobility, and scoliosis can trigger and perpetuate the centrally maintained widespread pain of FM (Harrison 22e p.2963).

FM is one of the chronic overlapping pain conditions and frequently coexists with myalgic encephalitis/chronic fatigue syndrome, temporomandibular disorder, chronic headaches, irritable bowel syndrome, and interstitial cystitis/painful bladder syndrome, likely sharing central mechanisms (Harrison 22e p.2963).

The lifetime prevalence of mood disorders in FM approaches 80%; depression is neither necessary nor sufficient for diagnosis, but screening for depressed mood and anhedonia is important (Harrison 22e p.2964).

Symptom onset and flares often cluster around periods of perceived stress, and there is a high prevalence of prior interpersonal or other violence exposure; consider posttraumatic stress disorder where relevant (Harrison 22e p.2964).
Failing to consider FM, leading to missed or delayed diagnosis since musculoskeletal pain is so common (Harrison 22e p.2964).
Over-investigating with repeated laboratory tests or, especially, spine MRI in the absence of inflammatory or neurologic features (Harrison 22e p.2964).
Continuing to treat only peripheral or inflammatory pain generators when central FM pain has emerged, instead of addressing central pain processing (Harrison 22e p.2964).
Setting complete pain elimination, rather than improved function and quality of life, as the treatment goal (Harrison 22e p.2965).

FM is a chronic condition with substantial adverse effects on physical and social functioning and on health-related quality of life. Outcomes are best when there is prompt diagnosis, assessment of pain, function, and psychosocial context, patient education, and a partnership-based strategy directed at improving function rather than eliminating pain; illness behaviors such as frequent physician visits are to be discouraged while function-promoting behaviors are encouraged (Harrison 22e p.2964-2965).
Pain extending beyond what a known triggering or inflammatory condition could reasonably explain, signaling emergence of central FM-type pain requiring a different management focus
Objective inflammatory, neurologic, or systemic findings (abnormal ESR/CRP, focal neurologic deficits) that point toward an alternative or comorbid diagnosis rather than FM
Screen-positive major depression with anhedonia, and history suggestive of posttraumatic stress disorder, given high comorbidity and impact on outcome

Severity is captured by the 2016 diagnostic instrument combining the Widespread Pain Index (WPI, range 0-19) and the Symptom Severity Score (SSS, range 0-12, grading fatigue, unrefreshing waking, and cognitive symptoms plus selected somatic items). Diagnosis requires WPI >=7 and SSS >=5, or WPI 4-6 and SSS >=9, with generalized pain in at least 4 of 5 body regions, sustained for at least 3 months; higher WPI and SSS values reflect greater symptom burden (Harrison 22e p.2964).

Filariae are tissue-dwelling nematodes transmitted by mosquitoes or other arthropods; insect-borne infective larvae mature into adult worms that reside in lymphatics (W. bancrofti, Brugia) or subcutaneous tissue (Loa loa, O. volvulus). Adults release microfilariae that circulate in blood or migrate through skin; adults live many years while microfilariae survive 3-36 months. In lymphatic filariasis, pathology results mainly from inflammatory damage caused by ADULT worms (not microfilariae) in afferent lymphatics, with plasma-cell/eosinophil/macrophage infiltration, lymphatic dilation, valve incompetence, and progressive granulomatous reaction and fibrosis (worsened by worm death) leading to obstruction, lymphedema, and elephantiasis; injury is due both to the worm and to host inflammatory response. In contrast, onchocerciasis pathology is elicited by MICROFILARIAE (not adults), causing chronic dermal inflammation/atrophy/fibrosis, fibrous subcutaneous nodules (onchocercomata) around adults, and corneal neovascularization/scarring and intraocular inflammation leading to blindness. In TPE, microfilariae are trapped and cleared by the lungs, provoking allergic/eosinophilic intra-alveolar inflammation that can progress to interstitial fibrosis. Calabar swellings of loiasis are thought to be a hypersensitivity reaction to adult-worm antigens. The Wolbachia endosymbiont contributes to inflammatory reactions (Harrison 22e p.1819-1823).
Eight filarial species infect humans, but four cause most symptomatic disease: Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, Onchocerca volvulus, and Loa loa (Harrison 22e p.1819).

On high-frequency ultrasound, live adult worms in dilated lymphatics show a distinctive motion called the 'filarial dance sign'; worms are seen in the spermatic cord in up to 80% of W. bancrofti-infected men (Harrison 22e p.1821).

Circulating antigen assays (ELISA and rapid lateral-flow) for W. bancrofti have sensitivities of 93-100% and specificity approaching 100% and detect both microfilaremic and cryptic amicrofilaremic infection; there is currently NO circulating-antigen test for brugian filariasis (Harrison 22e p.1821).

Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (TPE) presents with nocturnal paroxysmal cough/wheeze, weight loss, low-grade fever, marked blood eosinophilia (>3000/uL), and very high IgE and antifilarial antibody; microfilariae are cleared from blood by the lungs and are typically NOT found in peripheral blood (Harrison 22e p.1821-1822).

Onchocerciasis ('river blindness'), caused by O. volvulus, primarily affects skin, eyes, and lymph nodes; pruritus and a generalized papular rash are most common, and visual impairment is the most serious complication (Harrison 22e p.1822-1823).

Sclerosing keratitis (in 1-5% of infected persons) is the leading cause of onchocercal blindness; 'snowflake' punctate keratitis around dying microfilariae is common in younger patients and usually resolves (Harrison 22e p.1823).

Onchocercal lymphadenopathy can produce 'hanging groin'; rarely Nakalanga dwarfism and an association with epilepsy/nodding syndrome are seen; blind adults have a 3- to 4-fold higher mortality (Harrison 22e p.1823).

Loiasis (Loa loa, the African eye worm) is suggested by transient subconjunctival worm migration and episodic Calabar swellings (evanescent angioedema); microfilariae have a diurnal periodicity peaking ~10:00 a.m.-2:00 p.m. (Harrison 22e p.1823).
Wolbachia, an intracellular bacterial endosymbiont present in Brugia, Wuchereria, Mansonella, and Onchocerca, is a target for antifilarial (anti-Wolbachia) therapy (Harrison 22e p.1819, 1824).

Filarial disease is characteristically more acute and intense in newly exposed travelers/transmigrants than in lifelong natives of endemic areas; infection usually requires repeated, prolonged exposure to infective larvae (Harrison 22e p.1819).

Lymphatic filariasis (W. bancrofti, B. malayi, B. timori) is widely distributed; W. bancrofti affects ~51 million people and B. malayi occurs primarily in eastern India, Indonesia, Malaysia, and the Philippines; humans are the only definitive host for W. bancrofti (Harrison 22e p.1819-1820).
Most W. bancrofti is nocturnally periodic (microfilariae scarce by day, increasing at night); blood for microfilaria detection must be timed to the regional periodicity (Harrison 22e p.1819-1821).

Common presentations of lymphatic filariasis are asymptomatic/subclinical microfilaremia, hydrocele, acute adenolymphangitis (ADL), and chronic lymphatic disease (lymphedema/elephantiasis) (Harrison 22e p.1820).
Genital lymphatic involvement (funiculitis, epididymitis, hydrocele, scrotal elephantiasis) occurs almost exclusively with W. bancrofti, not Brugia (Harrison 22e p.1820).
ADL lymphangitis is retrograde (spreads peripherally from the draining node), a feature that distinguishes filarial lymphangitis from ascending bacterial lymphangitis (Harrison 22e p.1820-1821).

Dermatolymphangioadenitis (DLA) presents with fever, chills, myalgias, demarcated edematous plaques, and entry lesions (often interdigital) and is frequently misdiagnosed as cellulitis (Harrison 22e p.1820).
Obstruction of retroperitoneal lymphatics can rupture renal lymphatics and produce intermittent chyluria, typically most prominent in the morning (Harrison 22e p.1820).
Seropositivity (antifilarial antibody) cannot be equated with active infection; endemic residents can become sensitized via mosquito exposure without patent infection (Harrison 22e p.1821).
Antifilarial antibody/antigen serology has extensive cross-reactivity with other helminths; W. bancrofti antigen tests can be falsely positive in Loa loa infection (Harrison 22e p.1821).
Many infected individuals are amicrofilaremic, and travelers are often amicrofilaremic, so a negative blood smear does not exclude filariasis (Harrison 22e p.1821, 1823).
Timing of blood collection to the local microfilarial periodicity is critical; mistimed samples miss nocturnally or diurnally periodic microfilariae (Harrison 22e p.1821).
DLA is often misdiagnosed as cellulitis (Harrison 22e p.1820).
Eosinophilia and elevated IgE are nonspecific (common to many parasitic infections) and are not diagnostic by themselves (Harrison 22e p.1823).
For every palpable onchocercal nodule there are an estimated four deeper nonpalpable ones (Harrison 22e p.1823).

Filarial infections are chronic with potential long-term debilitating effects; adult worms live for many years (W. bancrofti/Brugia >2 decades; O. volvulus up to ~18 years, average ~9). Most microfilaremic persons remain clinically asymptomatic for years, and only a minority progress to acute or chronic disease, but lymphatic damage can become permanent (elephantiasis, hydrocele). In onchocerciasis, visual loss is the most serious outcome and blind adults have a 3- to 4-fold increased mortality. Loiasis, historically considered relatively benign in endemic populations, is now linked to chronic morbidity and increased mortality. TPE responds to therapy but relapses in ~12-25% of cases (sometimes years later); untreated TPE can progress to pulmonary fibrosis (Harrison 22e p.1819-1823).
Sclerosing keratitis, anterior uveitis, chorioretinal lesions, or optic atrophy in onchocerciasis (impending/established blindness) (Harrison 22e p.1823)
High Loa loa microfilaremia (>30,000 microfilariae/mL): risk of severe post-treatment encephalopathy with ivermectin or DEC (Harrison 22e p.1822-1823)
Loiasis with CNS involvement during treatment of heavy microfilaremia (coma, encephalitis) (Harrison 22e p.1823)
Chyluria from retroperitoneal lymphatic obstruction in lymphatic filariasis (Harrison 22e p.1820)

Harrison describes lymphatic filariasis along a clinical spectrum rather than a formal grading: asymptomatic/subclinical microfilaremia, hydrocele, acute adenolymphangitis (ADL)/dermatolymphangioadenitis (DLA), and chronic lymphatic disease (lymphedema progressing to elephantiasis). Onchocerciasis severity is gauged by infection burden (skin/eye involvement increasing with moderate-to-heavy microfilarial load). Loa loa microfilaremia is stratified by treatment risk, with >30,000 microfilariae/mL marking high risk of severe post-treatment encephalopathy (Harrison 22e p.1820-1823).

chunks.text: Most anal fistulae are the chronic sequel of a cryptoglandular anorectal abscess. After the abscess drains, the primary infected anal gland at the dentate line persists and an epithelialised or granulation-lined track remains between the internal opening in the anal canal and the external opening on the skin. Ongoing low-grade infection prevents healing. The track's course through the sphincter complex determines its classification and the surgical risk to continence. Secondary causes include Crohn's disease, tuberculosis, radiation, trauma, and malignancy, which produce more complex and refractory fistulae.

chunks.text: When several adjacent ribs are each fractured in two or more places, an isolated segment of chest wall loses its bony connection to the rest of the thoracic cage. This segment then moves according to intrapleural pressure rather than muscular effort, producing paradoxical motion that reduces the efficiency of ventilation. More importantly, the force required to cause the injury bruises the lung beneath, and this pulmonary contusion impairs gas exchange, worsening over the first day or two. Pain from the fractures limits chest expansion and coughing, promoting atelectasis and retained secretions, all of which combine to cause hypoxaemia and, in severe cases, respiratory failure.

Focal AT originates from a single discrete atrial site and is caused by abnormal automaticity, triggered activity, or a small reentry circuit in diseased atrial tissue. It may occur in structurally normal hearts or in association with any condition causing atrial fibrosis, including atrial tissue scarred by prior catheter ablation. Zones of fibrosis serve as a nidus for abnormal automaticity arising from injured but partially viable cells, or for microreentry within and at the border of regions of slow conduction. Sympathetic stimulation is a facilitating factor, and the appearance of AT may signal underlying illness or drug toxicity (digitalis being characteristic). The arrhythmia activates the atria from a focal source through only a small portion of the cycle, producing discrete P waves with isoelectric intervals (p.1937).

Focal AT arises from a discrete atrial site and is driven by one of three mechanisms: abnormal automaticity, triggered activity, or microreentry within diseased atrial tissue; the term 'focal' distinguishes it from typical and atypical (macroreentrant) atrial flutter and does not by itself specify the underlying mechanism (p.1937).
Asymptomatic nonsustained AT seen on monitoring is frequently mislabeled 'SVT' on monitor reports; treatment is NOT recommended for asymptomatic nonsustained AT identified on ECG monitoring (p.1937).
Frequent atrial ectopy and nonsustained AT are often precursors to more significant arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter (p.1937).

Vagal maneuvers, carotid sinus massage, Valsalva, or AV-nodal-blocking agents (e.g., adenosine) are used diagnostically to create transient AV block and unmask P waves when they are buried in the T wave or QRS (p.1937-1938).
It accounts for roughly 10% of paroxysmal SVTs in patients referred for catheter ablation, and may be sustained, nonsustained, paroxysmal, or incessant (p.1937).

Because focal AT is not dependent on AV nodal conduction, it does NOT terminate when AV block is induced and the atrial rate is unaffected by AV-nodal blockade — a key feature separating it from AV-nodal-dependent SVTs such as AVNRT and AVRT (p.1937).

P waves are typically discrete with an intervening isoelectric baseline (because atrial activation from a single focus occupies only a small part of the cycle), in contrast to the continuous undulating activation of atrial flutter / macroreentrant AT (p.1937).

A 'warm-up' phase (gradual acceleration of atrial rate after onset) or a 'cool-down' phase (gradual slowing before termination) favors focal AT with enhanced automaticity over AV-nodal-dependent SVT (p.1937).

Foci tend to cluster in areas of complex atrial anatomy — the crista terminalis, valve annuli, atrial septum, and atrial muscle sleeves extending into the thoracic veins (superior vena cava, coronary sinus, pulmonary veins) — and the focus location can often be approximated from P-wave morphology (p.1937).

P-wave localization clues: septal foci give a narrower P than sinus; left atrial foci give a monophasic positive P in V1 with negative P in I and aVL; superior foci (SVC, superior pulmonary veins) are positive in II, III, aVF; inferior foci (e.g., coronary sinus ostium) are negative in II, III, aVF (p.1937).

Atrial tachycardia WITH AV block is the characteristic arrhythmia of digitalis toxicity, so emergence of AT should prompt consideration of drug toxicity or another underlying illness; sympathetic stimulation promotes AT (p.1937).
Incessant focal AT can cause tachycardia-induced (tachycardia-mediated) cardiomyopathy, which is an important reversible cause of LV dysfunction (p.1937).
Mislabeling asymptomatic nonsustained AT on a monitor as actionable 'SVT' and over-treating it — treatment is not recommended in this setting (p.1937).
Confusing focal AT with sinus tachycardia when the focus is near the sinus node; rely on abrupt onset/offset and subtle P-wave morphology differences (p.1937).

Expecting AV-nodal blockade (adenosine, vagal maneuvers) to terminate the tachycardia — it usually only increases AV block while the atrial rhythm continues, since AT is independent of the AV node (p.1937-1938).
Overlooking digitalis toxicity or another precipitant when AT presents with AV block (p.1937).
Missing reversible tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy as the cause of new LV dysfunction in a patient with incessant AT (p.1937).

Symptoms vary widely and parallel those of other SVTs. Many nonsustained, asymptomatic episodes require no treatment. The principal adverse outcome is tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy from incessant AT, which is typically reversible once rhythm is controlled. Focal AT is frequently a precursor to atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter; however, the stroke risk and the indications for long-term anticoagulation are not considered equivalent to those of AF/flutter and remain unclear. Catheter ablation targeting the focus is successful in more than 80% of patients (p.1937-1938).

When a small object is inhaled it may lodge anywhere from the larynx to the distal bronchi, with the site determining the clinical picture. A large object at the larynx or trachea can cause complete or near-complete obstruction and rapid asphyxia. More commonly the object passes into a bronchus, producing partial obstruction: air may move past on inspiration but be trapped on expiration, causing distal hyperinflation, or the airway may become fully blocked, leading to distal atelectasis. Retained material provokes inflammation and, over time, granulation tissue, mucus retention, and secondary infection, which underlie the chronic complications seen with delayed removal.
Aspiration of a foreign body is most common in toddlers, who explore with their mouths and have immature airway protective reflexes; food items such as nuts and seeds are frequent culprits.
The classic history is a sudden episode of choking, coughing, or gagging in a previously well young child, often while eating or playing with small objects.
Clinical presentation varies with the site and degree of obstruction; a lodged object may produce unilateral wheeze, reduced air entry, or persistent cough.
A witnessed choking event is a strong clue, but the initial episode can be unwitnessed or followed by a symptom-free interval that leads to delayed diagnosis.
Chest radiographs may be normal because most aspirated objects are radiolucent; indirect signs include localised air trapping or hyperinflation, atelectasis, or a persistent infiltrate.
Rigid bronchoscopy is the definitive procedure for both confirming and removing an airway foreign body.
Complete upper airway obstruction is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate basic choking manoeuvres appropriate to the child's age.
Delayed or missed diagnosis can lead to recurrent or persistent pneumonia, bronchiectasis, or chronic lung damage, so a high index of suspicion is important.
Excluding aspiration because the chest radiograph is normal
Being falsely reassured by a symptom-free interval after the initial choking event
Attributing persistent focal respiratory symptoms to recurrent infection or asthma rather than a retained foreign body
Performing blind finger sweeps or inappropriate manoeuvres that may push an object further

With timely recognition and bronchoscopic removal the outlook is generally excellent, whereas complete obstruction can be rapidly fatal and delayed diagnosis may result in chronic pulmonary complications such as bronchiectasis.

chunks.text: Friedreich's ataxia is usually caused by a GAA repeat expansion in the FXN gene, reducing production of frataxin, a mitochondrial protein involved in iron-sulphur cluster assembly and iron handling. Frataxin deficiency impairs mitochondrial energy metabolism and increases oxidative stress, leading to degeneration of the dorsal root ganglia, dorsal columns, spinocerebellar and corticospinal tracts, and the cerebellar dentate nucleus. The same metabolic vulnerability affects the heart and pancreatic islets, explaining the cardiomyopathy and diabetes.

chunks.text: Alzheimer's disease (FTD has relatively preserved memory and parietal function early; a small percentage of FTD syndromes show Alzheimer's pathology at autopsy) (Harrison 22e p.3486-3487)
Progressive supranuclear palsy-Richardson syndrome (PSP-RS) - within the FTD spectrum; falls, vertical supranuclear ophthalmoparesis, axial rigidity (Harrison 22e p.3487)
Corticobasal syndrome (CBS) - asymmetric rigidity, dystonia, myoclonus, apraxia, alien limb phenomena (Harrison 22e p.3488)
Idiopathic Parkinson's disease - PSP is often confused with PD, but PD does not produce downgaze paresis (Harrison 22e p.3488)
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis / motor neuron disease (FTD-MND overlap) (Harrison 22e p.3486)
Structural neuroimaging (MRI) to demonstrate focal frontal/insular/temporal atrophy patterns characteristic of each syndrome (Harrison 22e p.3486)
Genetic testing for C9orf72, GRN, and MAPT mutations in suspected familial cases (Harrison 22e p.3486)
Molecular (tau) PET imaging shows promise but to date binds robustly only to Alzheimer's-related misfolded tau; amyloid PET may help when negative (Harrison 22e p.3487)

Psychiatric disease - depression, idiopathic mania, or acting out: the abulia/blandness of frontal degeneration may be misinterpreted as depression and the disinhibition as mania or acting out; FTD can begin with schizophrenia-like features leading to misdiagnosis of a psychiatric condition (Harrison 22e p.3485, p.209)
Other focal frontal lobe causes: head trauma, ruptured aneurysms, hydrocephalus, tumors (metastases, glioblastoma, meningioma) (Harrison 22e p.208)

FTD is linked to frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD), characterized by focal atrophy of frontal, insular, and/or temporal cortex; atrophy often begins focally in one hemisphere before spreading to anatomically interconnected cortical and subcortical regions. bvFTD shows medial/orbital frontal cortex and anterior insula degeneration, semantic variant PPA the anterior temporal region, and nonfluent/agrammatic PPA the opercular frontal and precentral gyrus of the dominant hemisphere. Microscopically there is gliosis, microvacuolation, and neuronal loss; the disease is subtyped by the protein composition of neuronal and glial inclusions, which contain either tau or TDP-43 in roughly 90% of patients, with the remaining ~10% showing inclusions containing the FET family of proteins (FUS, Ewing sarcoma protein, TAF-15). Loss of cortical serotonergic innervation is common while the cholinergic system is relatively spared. Misfolded proteins are increasingly recognized to have prion-like/corruptive templating properties that may drive network-rooted patterns of disease spread. Autosomal dominant inheritance is seen in only 10-20% of cases, with mutations in C9orf72 (the most common genetic cause, a noncoding GGGGCC hexanucleotide expansion, presenting as bvFTD with or without MND and overlapping with ALS), GRN/progranulin, and MAPT/tau (Harrison 22e p.3485-3487).

FTD is a group of clinical syndromes united by underlying frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) pathology; like other major neurodegenerative diseases it is considered a disorder of abnormal protein aggregation, with either tau or TDP-43 (transactive response DNA-binding protein of 43 kDa) implicated in most cases (Harrison 22e p.3485).
Younger onset than typical Alzheimer's: FTD most often begins in the fifth to seventh decades of life and is nearly as prevalent as Alzheimer's disease in this age group (Harrison 22e p.3485).

Three core clinical syndromes are described: the behavioral variant (bvFTD, the most common) and two forms of primary progressive aphasia (PPA) - the semantic and nonfluent/agrammatic variants (Harrison 22e p.3485-3486).

bvFTD manifests as social and emotional dysfunction - apathy, disinhibition, compulsivity, loss of empathy, and overeating - often but not always accompanied by deficits in executive control (Harrison 22e p.3486).

In semantic variant PPA patients slowly lose the ability to decode word, object, person-specific, and emotion meaning; in nonfluent/agrammatic variant PPA patients develop profound inability to produce words, often with prominent motor speech impairment (Harrison 22e p.3486).

Parietal functions such as visuospatial processing and arithmetic calculation are typically unaffected even late in the FTD syndromes, helping distinguish it from Alzheimer's disease (Harrison 22e p.3486).

Any of the three syndromes, most often bvFTD, may be accompanied by motor neuron disease (MND), in which case the term FTD-MND is applied; corticobasal syndrome (CBS) and progressive supranuclear palsy-Richardson syndrome (PSP-RS) are also considered part of the FTD clinical spectrum (Harrison 22e p.3486).
In contrast to Alzheimer's disease, the cholinergic system is relatively spared in FTD, which accounts for the poor efficacy of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors in this group (Harrison 22e p.3486).
Treatment is symptomatic only; there are currently no therapies known to slow progression or improve symptoms, and no disease-modifying treatments have shown efficacy to date (Harrison 22e p.3487).

Behavioral variant FTD is frequently mistaken for a primary psychiatric disease - the apathy/blandness can be misread as depression and the disinhibition as mania or acting out; FTD may even begin with schizophrenia-like features and be misdiagnosed as a psychiatric condition. Later age of onset, significant cognitive deficits, or abnormal neuroimaging point to a degenerative process (Harrison 22e p.3485, p.209).
Clinical features do not allow reliable prediction of the underlying FTLD molecular subtype (tau vs TDP-43 vs FET) for all syndromes (Harrison 22e p.3487).
Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors are largely ineffective in FTD because the cholinergic system is relatively spared, unlike Alzheimer's disease (Harrison 22e p.3486).
Antipsychotics must be used with caution because FTD is often accompanied by parkinsonism, which they can exacerbate (Harrison 22e p.3487).

Caregivers carry a heavy burden, especially as the illness disrupts core emotional and personality functions. There are currently no therapies known to slow progression or improve symptoms; treatment is symptomatic. For the related PSP-RS within the FTD spectrum, death occurs within 5-10 years of onset (Harrison 22e p.3487).
New-onset disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsivity, or altered dietary preference in a middle-aged adult (Harrison 22e p.3486)
Progressive language breakdown - loss of word/object meaning or inability to produce words (Harrison 22e p.3486)
Emergence of motor neuron disease features in a patient with behavioral or language decline (FTD-MND) (Harrison 22e p.3486)

No formal severity grading is given; FTD is categorized by core clinical syndrome - behavioral variant (bvFTD), semantic variant PPA, and nonfluent/agrammatic variant PPA - and by underlying FTLD molecular class (FTLD-tau, FTLD-TDP, FTLD-FET) (Harrison 22e p.3486-3487).

chunks.text: Frozen shoulder involves inflammation and progressive fibrosis of the glenohumeral joint capsule, particularly the rotator interval and coracohumeral ligament. Fibroblastic proliferation and contracture thicken and tighten the capsule, reducing the intra-articular volume and mechanically limiting movement, with external rotation lost first and most severely. The initial inflammatory, hypervascular stage is painful; as the capsule matures into dense fibrous tissue the pain lessens but stiffness dominates; finally the capsule gradually remodels and mobility returns. The strong association with diabetes and certain endocrine and metabolic states points to a systemic predisposition to abnormal fibrosis.
