Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease
Gastric or oesophageal malignancy
Gastroparesis
Biliary or pancreatic disease
Medication-induced dyspepsia (for example from NSAIDs)
Irritable bowel syndrome with upper gut overlap
Helicobacter pylori testing (breath, stool antigen, or biopsy)
Upper endoscopy when alarm features are present or symptoms are refractory
Full blood count to screen for anaemia
Consideration of gastric emptying study when gastroparesis is suspected
Targeted biliary or pancreatic imaging when the history suggests these

Functional dyspepsia is a disorder of gut-brain interaction without structural disease. Contributing mechanisms include delayed gastric emptying, impaired fundic accommodation to a meal, visceral hypersensitivity to gastric distension and acid, low-grade duodenal inflammation and increased mucosal permeability, and altered central processing of visceral signals. Prior infection, Helicobacter pylori, psychological stress, and genetic predisposition can all contribute, producing symptoms disproportionate to any measurable physiological abnormality.
Functional dyspepsia is chronic epigastric pain, burning, postprandial fullness, or early satiety without an identifiable structural cause on evaluation
It is subdivided into postprandial distress syndrome, dominated by meal-related fullness and early satiety, and epigastric pain syndrome
Diagnosis rests on symptom-based (Rome) criteria after appropriate exclusion of organic disease
Testing for and treating Helicobacter pylori benefits a subset of patients and is a recommended early step
Alarm features such as weight loss, bleeding, dysphagia, persistent vomiting, or older age at onset warrant endoscopy to exclude malignancy and ulcer
Acid suppression is a reasonable first-line therapy, with neuromodulators and prokinetics used for persistent symptoms
There is substantial overlap with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and irritable bowel syndrome, and psychological factors commonly modulate symptoms
Failing to recognise and evaluate alarm features before labelling symptoms as functional
Repeated normal investigations without addressing the gut-brain nature of the disorder
Overlooking Helicobacter pylori as a treatable contributor
Escalating acid suppression indefinitely without considering neuromodulators or psychological factors

Functional dyspepsia is a benign but often chronic and relapsing condition that can substantially impair quality of life; symptoms fluctuate over time and respond variably to treatment, but there is no increase in serious organic disease.
Unintentional weight loss
Gastrointestinal bleeding or iron-deficiency anaemia
Progressive dysphagia or odynophagia
Persistent vomiting or a palpable epigastric mass
New dyspepsia in an older patient
Functional dyspepsia (non-infective) — GI / Hepatology Also: non-ulcer dyspepsia, idiopathic dyspepsia, postprandial distress syndrome, epigastric pain syndrome
Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
Hereditary spherocytosis
Other red cell enzyme defects (e.g. pyruvate kinase deficiency)
Unstable haemoglobin disorders
Drug- or toxin-induced haemolysis from other causes
Neonatal jaundice of other aetiology (ABO/Rh incompatibility, sepsis)
Quantitative G6PD enzyme activity assay (repeat after recovery if measured during crisis)
Full blood count and reticulocyte count
Peripheral blood film for bite cells, blister cells, and Heinz body preparation
Markers of haemolysis: bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin
Urinalysis for haemoglobinuria
Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test to help exclude immune haemolysis

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase is the rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway and generates NADPH, which maintains reduced glutathione in red cells. Deficiency impairs this antioxidant defence, so under oxidative stress haemoglobin is oxidised and denatured, precipitating as Heinz bodies within red cells. These damaged cells are removed by splenic macrophages (producing bite cells) and undergo intravascular haemolysis, resulting in episodic anaemia, jaundice, and haemoglobinuria.
The most common human enzyme defect, inherited in an X-linked pattern so that males are predominantly affected while heterozygous females show variable expression.
Most individuals are asymptomatic between episodes and present only with acute haemolysis triggered by oxidative stress.
Common triggers include certain infections, fava (broad) beans, and oxidant drugs such as some antimalarials, sulphonamides, and nitrofurantoin.
Acute haemolysis produces sudden pallor, jaundice, dark urine, and fatigue, typically 1-3 days after exposure to a trigger.
It is an important cause of neonatal jaundice, which can be severe and lead to kernicterus if unrecognised.
The blood film during a crisis may show bite cells, blister cells, and Heinz bodies, with a rise in reticulocytes.
Enzyme activity assay is diagnostic but can be falsely normal during an acute crisis because young reticulocytes have higher enzyme levels, so retesting after recovery is advised.
Management centres on avoiding known triggers; acute severe haemolysis may require transfusion, and neonatal jaundice is managed with phototherapy or exchange transfusion as needed.
Interpreting a normal enzyme level during acute haemolysis as excluding the diagnosis
Failing to counsel families about drug, food, and infection triggers
Underestimating the risk of severe neonatal jaundice and kernicterus
Prescribing oxidant medications without checking G6PD status in at-risk populations

Most affected individuals lead normal lives with trigger avoidance; haemolytic episodes are usually self-limiting once the trigger is removed, though neonatal jaundice and rare severe crises can cause serious harm if not promptly managed.
Rapidly falling haemoglobin with haemodynamic compromise
Massive haemolysis with haemoglobinuria and acute kidney injury
Severe neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia risking kernicterus
Marked jaundice with lethargy or poor feeding in a neonate
Ongoing exposure to an unrecognised oxidative trigger
Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase Deficiency (non-infective) — Haematological Also: G6PD deficiency, favism, G6PD
Neonatal sepsis of other cause
Other causes of neonatal cholestasis and liver failure
Tyrosinemia and other hepatorenal metabolic disorders
Hereditary fructose intolerance
Neonatal hemochromatosis
Urea cycle disorders presenting with encephalopathy
Newborn screening result and confirmatory GALT enzyme activity assay
Quantitative galactose-1-phosphate and molecular genetic testing
Liver function tests and coagulation studies
Urine for reducing substances (a supportive, non-specific finding)
Blood cultures and sepsis evaluation given the risk of E. coli infection
Ophthalmological examination for cataracts

Deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase blocks the conversion of galactose-1-phosphate to UDP-galactose in the Leloir pathway. Ingested galactose, mainly from lactose in milk, cannot be normally metabolised, so galactose-1-phosphate accumulates in tissues including the liver, kidney, and brain and exerts toxic effects. Excess galactose is also shunted to alternative pathways, generating galactitol, which accumulates in the lens and causes cataract, and galactonate. The metabolite toxicity produces hepatocellular injury, renal tubular dysfunction, and central nervous system effects, and impairs host defences, predisposing to Gram-negative sepsis.
An autosomal recessive disorder of galactose metabolism; the classic and most severe form results from deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT).
Symptoms typically begin in the first days to weeks of life once milk feeding (which contains lactose, a source of galactose) is established.
Presenting features include poor feeding, vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, failure to thrive, and lethargy, often progressing to liver dysfunction and coagulopathy.
Affected neonates are at markedly increased risk of Escherichia coli sepsis, which may be the presenting or dominant feature.
Cataracts can develop early owing to accumulation of galactitol in the lens.
Diagnosis is supported by newborn screening and confirmed by demonstrating reduced GALT enzyme activity and characteristic metabolite abnormalities; a reducing substance may be found in the urine.
The cornerstone of management is strict, lifelong elimination of galactose and lactose from the diet, which reverses the acute toxicity.
Despite early dietary treatment, long-term complications such as speech and cognitive difficulties, ataxia, and ovarian insufficiency in females may still occur.
Milder variant forms (for example some Duarte variants) may have residual enzyme activity and a more benign course.
Treating neonatal sepsis without considering an underlying metabolic disorder such as galactosemia
Delaying dietary galactose elimination while awaiting confirmatory results in a decompensating infant
Assuming that early dietary treatment fully prevents all long-term complications
Overlooking milder variants that may still need dietary attention
Failing to arrange ophthalmological and developmental follow-up

Early diagnosis and strict dietary galactose restriction reverse the life-threatening acute manifestations. However, even with good control, a substantial proportion of children experience long-term neurodevelopmental, speech, and motor difficulties, and most affected females develop primary ovarian insufficiency. Variant forms are generally milder.
Signs of Escherichia coli or other Gram-negative sepsis in a jaundiced neonate
Acute liver failure with coagulopathy and bleeding
Progressive lethargy, poor feeding, and encephalopathy
Severe hypoglycaemia or metabolic decompensation
Continued galactose exposure delaying recognition and worsening toxicity
Galactosemia (non-infective) — Genetic-metabolic Also: classic galactosemia, galactosaemia, GALT deficiency
Acalculous cholecystitis (5-14% of acute cholecystitis; associated with prolonged fasting, severe trauma/burns, postpartum, major nonbiliary surgery, TPN) (p.2733)
Acalculous cholecystopathy / biliary dyskinesia (gallbladder ejection fraction <40% on CCK cholescintigraphy reproducing pain) (p.2733)
Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction (stenosis or dyskinesia) (p.2734)
Choledochal cysts and Caroli's disease / congenital biliary ectasia (recurrent cholangitis, increased cholangiocarcinoma risk) (p.2735)
Benign bile duct strictures (post-surgical, ~1 in 500 cholecystectomies) (p.2737)
Extrinsic bile duct compression (most commonly carcinoma of the head of the pancreas) (p.2737)
IgG4-associated cholangitis (mimics PSC; elevated serum IgG4; steroid-responsive) (p.2737)
Hyperplastic cholecystoses (adenomyomatosis, cholesterolosis/'strawberry gallbladder') (p.2737)
Postcholecystectomy syndrome (overlooked reflux esophagitis, peptic ulcer, IBS, retained stones, bile-salt diarrhea) (p.2734)
Acute (ascending) cholangitis from bacterial superinfection of obstructed bile (p.2735)
Hepatobiliary parasitism (Clonorchis sinensis, Opisthorchis viverrini/felineus, Fasciola hepatica, Ascaris, Echinococcus) causing recurrent pyogenic cholangitis (p.2737)
Emphysematous cholecystitis from gas-producing organisms (Clostridium welchii/perfringens, E. coli) in elderly/diabetic patients (p.2733)
AIDS cholangiopathy (Cryptosporidium, Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare, CMV, Microsporidia, Isospora) mimicking sclerosing cholangitis (p.2737)
Ultrasound - procedure of choice for gallstone detection (>95%), gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, dilated ducts (p.2730, 2733)
MRCP - first choice for choledocholithiasis and the cholangiographic technique of choice in suspected PSC (beaded ducts) (p.2736-2737)
ERCP with endoscopic sphincterotomy - diagnostic and therapeutic for CBD stones and bacterial cholangitis (p.2735-2736)
Cholescintigraphy (HIDA/DISIDA) - confirms cystic duct obstruction / acute cholecystitis; CCK-stimulated for ejection fraction in acalculous cholecystopathy (p.2730, 2733)
Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) - most sensitive for ampullary stones and head-of-pancreas pathology; detects microlithiasis (p.2736)
Plain abdominal film - calcified stones, porcelain gallbladder, limey bile, emphysematous cholecystitis, gallstone ileus (pneumobilia) (p.2730)
Serum bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase - elevation suggests common duct stone; ALP rise often precedes jaundice (p.2731, 2736)

AMA (and sp100/gp210 if AMA-negative) for PBC; IgM elevation; serum IgG4 to exclude IgG4 cholangitis; pANCA in PSC; CA 19-9 for cholangiocarcinoma surveillance in PSC (ch.355 p.2711, ch.357 p.2737, ch.87 p.667)
Endoscopic brushing of biliary strictures (more accurate than bile cytology alone) in suspected neoplastic stricture, especially in PSC (p.2737)
Malignant biliary obstruction (pancreatic head carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, ampullary tumor) - Courvoisier's law: a palpably enlarged gallbladder suggests malignancy rather than stones (p.2736)
Functional/vague dyspepsia, eructation, flatulence after fatty meals - common with or without gallstones but not specific for biliary calculi (p.2731)
Other postcholecystectomy nonbiliary disorders (reflux esophagitis, peptic ulcer, pancreatitis, irritable bowel syndrome) (p.2734)

Bile flow depends on sphincter of Oddi tone and cholecystokinin (CCK)-mediated gallbladder contraction after fatty/amino-acid meals. Gallstones form from abnormal bile composition. Cholesterol stones (>90% in Western countries) require three converging defects: hepatic hypersecretion of cholesterol producing lithogenic/supersaturated bile (driven by obesity, metabolic syndrome, estrogens, rapid weight loss, age, CYP7A1 or MDR3/ABCB4 gene defects, ABCG5/G8 variants), accelerated nucleation of cholesterol monohydrate crystals (excess pronucleating mucin/immunoglobulins vs deficient antinucleating apolipoproteins), and gallbladder hypomotility with stasis (fasting, TPN, pregnancy, octreotide). Pigment stones contain calcium bilirubinate: black stones from chronic hemolysis, cirrhosis, Gilbert's, cystic fibrosis, or ileal disease (enterohepatic bilirubin recycling); brown stones from deconjugation of bilirubin by bacterial beta-glucuronidase in chronically infected/parasitized bile. Symptoms arise when stones obstruct the cystic duct (cholecystitis) or migrate into the CBD (choledocholithiasis) causing biliary obstruction, cholangitis, or gallstone pancreatitis as they pass through the ampulla of Vater. PBC and PSC are chronic cholestatic syndromes from immune-mediated destruction of bile ducts (small/medium ducts in PBC; entire biliary tree in PSC) progressing to biliary cirrhosis and portal hypertension.

Two gallstone types: cholesterol stones (>90% in Western countries, contain >50% cholesterol monohydrate) and pigment stones (mainly calcium bilirubinate, <20% cholesterol, split into 'black' and 'brown' types) (p.2728-2729).

Choledocholithiasis (CBD stones) occurs in ~10-15% of patients with cholelithiasis; incidence rises with age (up to 25% of elderly at cholecystectomy); most are cholesterol stones that migrated from the gallbladder (p.2735).

MRCP is the first choice to assess for choledocholithiasis (comparable sensitivity/specificity to ERCP); ERCP is the cholangiogram of choice when intervention is needed and ERCP with sphincterotomy is preferred for both diagnosis and therapy of bacterial cholangitis (p.2736, 2735).

PBC: female-predominant (~50 yr median age) autoimmune disease with portal inflammation and necrosis of cholangiocytes in small/medium bile ducts; antimitochondrial antibodies (AMA) present in ~95%; key symptoms are fatigue and pruritus (Harrison 22e ch.355 p.2711).

PSC is strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease (60-80%, predominantly ulcerative colitis); cholangiography shows multifocal strictures with intervening normal/dilated segments producing a 'beaded' appearance; pANCA positive in ~65% (ch.357 p.2737; ch.355 p.2712).

Cholangiocarcinoma is classified as intrahepatic (~20-30%), perihilar (~50-60%), and distal (~20-30%); PSC is a clear risk factor for iCCA and pCCA with a 5-10% lifetime incidence, and is a relative contraindication to liver transplantation (ch.87 p.667; ch.355 p.2712).

Gallbladder cancer: cholelithiasis is the major risk factor but <1% of patients with gallstones develop it; polyps >=10 mm are at risk of transformation; early cases are found incidentally at cholecystectomy and symptoms (jaundice, pain, weight loss) indicate advanced disease (ch.87 p.670).

Cholesterol gallstones arise from three defects: (1) bile supersaturation with cholesterol, (2) accelerated nucleation of cholesterol monohydrate crystals, and (3) gallbladder hypomotility/stasis (p.2729).

Black pigment stones associate with chronic hemolysis, alcohol-related cirrhosis, Gilbert's syndrome, cystic fibrosis, and ileal disease/resection/bypass; brown pigment stones form secondary to chronic biliary infection/parasitism with deconjugation of bilirubin (p.2729).

Biliary colic is the most specific symptom: a steady (not intermittent) severe ache or fullness in the epigastrium/RUQ radiating to the interscapular area, right scapula, or shoulder, lasting 30 min to 5 h; the word 'colic' is a misnomer (p.2730-2731).

60-80% of asymptomatic gallstones remain asymptomatic over up to 25 years; symptom development is ~2-4% per year (falling to 1-2% later) and yearly complication rate is ~0.1-0.3%, so prophylactic cholecystectomy is not warranted (p.2731).
Ultrasound is the procedure of choice for detecting gallstones (>95% accuracy) and can identify stones as small as 1.5 mm using acoustic shadowing criteria (p.2730).

Biliary sludge (lecithin-cholesterol liquid crystals, cholesterol monohydrate crystals, calcium bilirubinate, mucin) shifts with posture but does NOT cast an acoustic shadow, distinguishing it from stones; it can be a gallstone precursor (p.2730).

Acute cholecystitis usually follows cystic duct obstruction by a stone; Murphy's sign (inspiratory arrest on RUQ palpation) is characteristic, and the triad of sudden RUQ tenderness, fever, and leukocytosis is highly suggestive (p.2732-2733).

Charcot's triad (biliary pain, jaundice, spiking fevers with chills) characterizes acute cholangitis; suppurative cholangitis with a completely obstructed duct under pressure causes mental confusion, bacteremia, and septic shock (Reynolds' pentad features) (p.2735).
'Biliary colic' is a misnomer - the pain is steady, not intermittent (p.2731)
Vague postprandial dyspepsia, eructation, and flatulence are not specific for gallstones and should not be confused with biliary pain (p.2731)

Pigment stones do NOT respond to UDCA dissolution therapy, and stones >10 mm rarely dissolve - only ~10% of symptomatic patients are dissolution candidates with 30-50% recurrence over 3-5 years (p.2731-2732)
Jaundice is unusual early in acute cholecystitis; its presence (or bilirubin >5 mg/dL) should prompt suspicion of a CBD stone (p.2732, 2736)
Missing Mirizzi's syndrome preoperatively risks CBD injury at surgery (p.2733)
AMA is negative in 5-10% of PBC - liver biopsy and sp100/gp210 are needed, and PSC should be excluded by cholangiography (ch.355 p.2711)
Every patient diagnosed with sclerosing cholangitis should have serum IgG4 checked to exclude IgG4-associated (secondary) cholangitis, especially without IBD (p.2737)
Routine prophylactic cholecystectomy in asymptomatic stones (including young patients and diabetics) is not warranted (p.2731)
The carcinoma risk of porcelain gallbladder has been challenged; cholecystectomy is no longer absolute and surveillance is acceptable (p.2734)

Most asymptomatic gallstones stay silent (60-80% over up to 25 years); cumulative death risk on expectant management is small. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the gold standard with complications ~4%, conversion ~5%, death rate <0.1%, and bile duct injury 0.2-0.6%; it relieves preoperative symptoms in 75-90%. Acute cholecystitis: ~75% remit medically within 2-7 days but ~25% recur within 1 year and 60% within 6 years; free perforation carries ~30% mortality and suppurative cholangitis approaches 100% mortality without drainage. PSC is progressive with a median survival of 12-18 years regardless of therapy and is a common indication for liver transplantation; small-duct PSC has a significantly better prognosis. PBC: UDCA slows but does not reverse disease; transplantation for decompensated cirrhosis. Cholangiocarcinoma has a 5-year survival of ~10%; gallbladder cancer is curable (5-yr survival 60-90%) only when local and resected (~20% of patients), with median survival 10-12 months in advanced disease (ch.357 p.2731-2737; ch.355 p.2711-2712; ch.87 p.667-670).
Biliary pain persisting beyond 5 h - raises suspicion of acute cholecystitis (p.2731)
Fever or chills (rigors) with biliary pain - implies a complication (cholecystitis, pancreatitis, or cholangitis) (p.2731)
Charcot's triad (biliary pain, jaundice, spiking fevers/chills) - acute cholangitis (p.2735)
Mental confusion, bacteremia, septic shock (suppurative cholangitis) - mortality approaches 100% without prompt drainage (p.2735)
Serum bilirubin >=342 micromol/L (20 mg/dL) - suggests neoplastic rather than calculous obstruction (p.2736)
Painless jaundice and/or a palpably enlarged gallbladder (Courvoisier) - points to malignancy (p.2736)
Sudden transient relief of RUQ pain followed by generalized peritonitis - free gallbladder perforation (~30% mortality) (p.2733)
Pruritus preceding jaundice in PBC - indicates severe disease and poor prognosis (ch.355 p.2711)
New/rising bilirubin or dominant stricture in PSC - concern for cholangiocarcinoma (ch.355 p.2712; ch.87 p.667)

Stone-based spectrum: asymptomatic gallstones -> biliary colic (cystic duct/CBD obstruction) -> acute cholecystitis -> complications (empyema, hydrops/mucocele, gangrene, perforation, fistula with gallstone ileus, emphysematous cholecystitis, Mirizzi's syndrome). CBD stone (choledocholithiasis) complications: cholangitis (nonsuppurative vs suppurative), obstructive jaundice, gallstone pancreatitis, secondary biliary cirrhosis. Cholangitis severity by Charcot's triad (pain + jaundice + fever/chills) advancing to suppurative cholangitis (adds confusion + septic shock). PBC has four histologic stages from chronic nonsuppurative destructive cholangitis to cirrhosis. PSC: small-duct (better prognosis) vs classic (large-duct) disease. Cholangiocarcinoma classified anatomically as intrahepatic, perihilar, and distal; gallbladder cancer staged as local vs advanced (ch.357 p.2731-2737; ch.355 p.2711; ch.87 p.667-670).
Gallbladder & Biliary Tract Disease (non-infective) — Hepatobiliary Also: cholelithiasis, gallstones, choledocholithiasis, PSC, PBC
Necrotizing fasciitis (including type I polymicrobial and C. perfringens necrotizing fasciitis); distinction from clostridial myonecrosis is made by muscle biopsy (p.1218/1241)
Other histotoxic clostridial necrotizing soft tissue infections (C. histolyticum, C. septicum, C. novyi, C. sordellii) (p.1241)
Synergistic necrotizing cellulitis / crepitant (crepitus) cellulitis due to mixed anaerobic and aerobic flora (p.gas-forming soft-tissue infections)
Fournier's gangrene (C. perfringens with mixed aerobic/anaerobic microbes can cause aggressive type I necrotizing fasciitis or Fournier's gangrene) (p.1239)
Clostridial sepsis / bacteremia with myonecrosis (grave prognosis when bacteremia accompanies myonecrosis) (p.1240)
Gram stain of a smear of involved tissue (direct examination is of major importance): large gram-positive/gram-variable rods with paucity of leukocytes (p.1242)

Surgical exploration with histopathologic examination (widespread tissue destruction, paucity of leukocytes in infected tissue with accumulation of leukocytes in adjacent vessels, gram-positive rods with or without spores) (p.1242)
Blood cultures (anaerobic) - obtain when spontaneous gas gangrene is suspected, as bacteremia usually precedes cutaneous manifestations by several hours (p.1242)
CT and MRI to define localized vs fascial-plane spread (adjunct only; must not delay surgery) (p.1242)
Needle aspiration or punch biopsy may provide an etiologic diagnosis in at least 20% of cases (p.1242)
In survivors of C. septicum bacteremia/spontaneous gangrene: aggressive diagnostic workup to rule out gastrointestinal pathology (e.g., colonic malignancy) (p.1241)

Gas tracking/dissecting tissue planes from non-clostridial gas-forming processes; note gas gangrene may develop in the ABSENCE of clostridial infection (other gas-producing organisms) (p.crepitus/gas-forming infections)

Development requires an anaerobic environment and wound contamination with clostridial spores or vegetative organisms. Devitalized tissue, foreign bodies, and ischemia lower local oxygen and favor outgrowth. For C. perfringens and C. novyi, trauma must be sufficient to interrupt the blood supply to establish the anaerobic niche; the more aerotolerant C. septicum and C. tertium can seed normal tissue from GI lesions without this. Once established, organisms proliferate and elaborate exotoxins. The major C. perfringens toxins in gas gangrene are alpha toxin (a lethal hemolysin with phospholipase C and sphingomyelinase activity; the major virulence factor) and theta toxin (perfringolysin, a cholesterol-dependent cytolysin). Severe pain, rapid progression, marked tissue destruction, and the characteristic paucity of neutrophils in tissue are largely attributable to alpha-toxin-induced vascular occlusion by heterotypic platelet/neutrophil aggregates (via activation of platelet gpIIb/IIIa). Late cardiovascular collapse reflects theta toxin causing reduced systemic vascular resistance with increased cardiac output ('warm shock') and alpha toxin directly suppressing myocardial contractility, producing profound hypotension (p.1242).

C. perfringens myonecrosis (gas gangrene) is one of the most fulminant gram-positive bacterial infections of humans; it is a true emergency requiring immediate surgical debridement and is invariably fatal if untreated (p.1241).

Emergent thorough surgical debridement with wide resection back to healthy viable muscle and skin is of extreme importance; closure of traumatic wounds or compound fractures should be delayed 5-6 days until sites are certain to be free of infection (p.1242).

Traumatic gas gangrene presents with sudden onset of excruciating pain at the affected site and rapid development of a foul-smelling wound with thin serosanguineous discharge and gas bubbles; brawny edema and induration give way to cutaneous blisters with bluish to maroon-colored fluid (p.1241).

The patient's pain and toxic appearance are characteristically out of proportion to physical findings; the patient may be febrile, apathetic, tachycardic, tachypneic, and may express a feeling of impending doom (p.1218, cross-ref Chap.159).

The margin between healthy and necrotic tissue often advances several inches per hour despite appropriate antibiotic therapy; radical amputation remains the single best life-saving intervention (p.1241).
Incubation period for traumatic gas gangrene can be as short as 6 h and is usually <4 days (p.1241).

Spontaneous (nontraumatic) gas gangrene arises by hematogenous seeding of normal muscle, principally with C. septicum (aerotolerant), C. perfringens, and C. novyi, from a gastrointestinal portal of entry (p.1241).
First symptom of spontaneous gas gangrene may be confusion followed by abrupt onset of excruciating pain in the absence of trauma; with fever, these findings should heighten suspicion (p.1242).

Gram staining of drainage or tissue biopsy is usually definitive in traumatic disease, showing large gram-positive (or gram-variable) rods, an ABSENCE of inflammatory cells, and widespread soft tissue necrosis (p.1241).
CT and MRI help determine whether infection is localized or spreading along fascial planes, but must NOT replace surgical exploration, Gram's staining, and histopathologic examination (p.1242).

Diagnosis depends on clinical signs and symptoms, not solely on bacteriologic findings - 30-80% of open traumatic wounds are contaminated with clostridia and clostridia are isolated equally from suppurative and well-healing wounds (p.1239).
In spontaneous gas gangrene the lack of an obvious portal of entry means the correct diagnosis is frequently delayed or missed (p.1242).
Adjunctive procedures (CT, MRI) or transport to hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) units must NOT delay emergent surgical debridement (p.1243).

The value of HBO remains controversial; HBO inhibits C. perfringens but not the more aerotolerant C. septicum, and blood/macerated muscle inhibit its bactericidal potential in vitro - HBO provides benefit only if surgery and antibiotics precede it (p.1243).
Avoid prolonged tourniquet application and surgical closure of contaminated traumatic wounds; patients with compound fractures are at significant risk if the wound is closed surgically (p.1243).

C. perfringens remains largely penicillin-susceptible but clindamycin resistance has been reported and is increasing in some regions; C. tertium is resistant to penicillin, cephalosporins, and clindamycin - good anaerobic susceptibility testing matters (p.1242-1243).

Invariably fatal if untreated. When patients become bacteremic the mortality rate exceeds 50%. Spontaneous (nontraumatic) gas gangrene mortality ranges from 67-100% in adults and 59% in children (most childhood deaths within 24 h of onset). Prognosis is more favorable when an extremity is involved (easier debridement) than the trunk or visceral organs. Disease is most likely to progress to shock and death in patients with associated bacteremia and intravascular hemolysis; mortality is highest for patients in shock at diagnosis. Gas gangrene associated with bacteremia represents a later stage with the worst outcomes. Survivors may undergo multiple debridements and face prolonged hospitalization and rehabilitation (p.1242-1243).
Pain out of proportion to physical findings - excruciating pain at the affected site (p.1241/1218)
Crepitus and gas in the tissues / gas on imaging with rapidly progressive necrosis (p.1241-1242)
Tissue margin advancing several inches per hour despite antibiotics (p.1241)
Systemic toxaemia: shock, hypotension, multiorgan failure, bacteremia, intravascular hemolysis (p.1241-1242)
Foul-smelling serosanguineous wound discharge with bluish/maroon hemorrhagic bullae and brawny induration (p.1241)
Spontaneous excruciating pain with confusion and fever and NO obvious portal of entry - suggests spontaneous gas gangrene (correct diagnosis frequently delayed or missed) (p.1242)
Feeling of impending doom with apathy, tachycardia, tachypnea (p.1218)
Gas Gangrene (Clostridial Myonecrosis) (infective) — Infectious Diseases Also: clostridial myonecrosis
Melena: distinguish proximal upper-GI bleeding from slow right-colon or small-bowel sources, especially in older patients with slow colonic transit
Hematochezia: colonic source vs brisk upper-GI bleed with rapid transit
Dyspepsia: gastroesophageal reflux vs peptic ulcer disease vs nonulcer (functional) dyspepsia vs uncommon gastric/esophageal malignancy
Colonic dilatation: mechanical obstruction (e.g., malignancy, sigmoid volvulus) vs acute colonic pseudoobstruction
Diverticular hematochezia: exclude vascular ectasias, colitis, and colon cancer before attributing bleeding to a diverticulum
24-hour ambulatory pH and impedance monitoring as the most sensitive test for GERD, capturing nonerosive reflux disease that endoscopy may miss
MRCP and EUS for bile duct stones (>90% accurate), reserving ERCP for cases needing therapy or high pretest probability
Noninvasive H. pylori testing (serology for past/current infection; urea breath test and stool antigen for current infection) before or in lieu of endoscopy in younger patients without alarm features

Capsule endoscopy as the typical next test after negative upper and lower endoscopy in suspected small-bowel bleeding (diagnostic yield ~55%), with a patency capsule beforehand if stricture risk exists

Plain abdominal radiography (and water-soluble contrast enema or CT) to assess colonic dilatation and differentiate obstruction from pseudoobstruction; neck/chest radiographs before endoscopy for esophageal obstruction with fever, >=24-h impaction, or sharp object

Gastrointestinal endoscopy is a diagnostic and therapeutic modality rather than a disease; it directly visualizes mucosal and luminal pathology and adjacent structures (via EUS) and provides access for tissue sampling and intervention. Many of the conditions it manages share a vascular or mechanical basis: peptic ulcers bleed when erosion exposes a submucosal vessel; a Dieulafoy's lesion is an abnormally large-caliber persistent artery running just beneath the epithelium that bleeds through a focal mucosal defect; a Mallory-Weiss tear is a mucosal rent at the gastroesophageal junction caused by retching/vomiting that can disrupt a submucosal arteriole; colonic diverticular bleeding arises from the nutrient artery at the base of a diverticulum; and vascular ectasias are flat mucosal vascular anomalies (e.g., GAVE/watermelon stomach) that cause slow blood loss. Variceal bleeding reflects portal hypertension. Obstructive syndromes (esophageal food impaction, gastric outlet obstruction, colonic obstruction/pseudoobstruction, biliary obstruction by stone) produce luminal blockage that endoscopy can relieve. Barrett's esophagus represents columnar metaplasia of distal esophageal squamous mucosa driven by chronic acid reflux and is a precursor to adenocarcinoma (Harrison 22e p.2464-2491).

Flexible endoscopes generate an electronic video image from a CCD or CMOS chip at the tip, with operator tip-deflection controls, light delivery, and working channels for washing, suction, and accessory passage (Harrison 22e p.2465).

In acute colonic pseudoobstruction (Ogilvie's), the risk of cecal perforation rises when cecal diameter exceeds 12 cm, prompting decompression with intravenous neostigmine or colonoscopy (Harrison 22e p.2487).

Charcot's triad (jaundice, abdominal pain, fever) is present in ~70% of ascending cholangitis; the addition of shock and confusion (Reynolds's pentad) signals high mortality and warrants urgent biliary drainage, typically by ERCP (Harrison 22e p.2489).

Long-standing GERD confers a roughly sixfold increased risk of Barrett's esophagus versus reflux of under one year; screening EGD should be considered after a chronic (>=10-year) GERD history even when symptoms are mild (Harrison 22e p.2490-2491).

Upper endoscopy (EGD) is the best method for examining the upper GI mucosa and is superior to a barium upper-GI series for detecting gastric ulcers and flat lesions such as Barrett's esophagus, while also permitting directed biopsy and therapy (Harrison 22e p.2465).

Colonoscopy is the gold standard for imaging the colonic mucosa, reaching the cecum in over 95% of cases, with greater sensitivity than barium enema for colitis, polyps, and cancer; CT colonography rivals it for many polyps and cancers but is less sensitive for flat serrated lesions (Harrison 22e p.2465).

For obscure small-bowel bleeding, capsule endoscopy visualizes mucosa beyond the reach of a conventional endoscope but is purely diagnostic; push and balloon-assisted enteroscopy allow deeper intubation with biopsy and therapy (Harrison 22e p.2465-2466).

EUS provides the most accurate preoperative local staging of esophageal, pancreatic, and rectal malignancies but does not detect distant metastases beyond its imaging range; it also enables fine-needle aspiration/biopsy and a growing range of therapeutic drainage procedures (Harrison 22e p.2468).

Endoscopic stigmata of a peptic ulcer carry prognostic value: a clean-based ulcer has a low (3-5%) rebleeding risk, flat pigmented spots ~10%, adherent clot ~20%, a visible vessel ~40%, and active spurting ~90% (Harrison 22e p.2478-2479).

Over 90% of patients with melena bleed proximal to the ligament of Treitz and ~85% with hematochezia bleed from the colon, but massive hematochezia can reflect a brisk upper-GI source with rapid transit, warranting urgent upper endoscopy (Harrison 22e p.2476).

Severity of the initial hemorrhage is the most important indicator for urgent endoscopy; falling hematocrit and hemoglobin lag behind the clinical course and are unreliable gauges of acute blood loss (Harrison 22e p.2476).

Acute esophageal obstruction from food impaction or a foreign body is an endoscopic emergency; untreated it can lead to esophageal ulceration, ischemia, and perforation, and an underlying web, ring, or stricture is often present (Harrison 22e p.2484-2485).
Relying on hematocrit/hemoglobin to gauge acute bleeding — these lag behind the clinical course
Assuming melena always means an upper-GI source or hematochezia always a colonic source — exceptions occur with transit-dependent presentations
Performing ERCP indiscriminately in gallstone pancreatitis — only ~20% retain an ampullary/common-bile-duct stone, and initial MRCP/EUS reduces unnecessary ERCP and its adverse events
Using endoscopy to diagnose nonerosive reflux disease — it will miss symptomatic reflux without esophagitis
Treating a Mallory-Weiss tear bearing a nonbleeding sentinel clot like a peptic ulcer — unlike ulcers, such tears rarely rebleed and need no endoscopic therapy
Relying on epinephrine injection alone for ulcer hemostasis — it slows bleeding but is not definitive monotherapy
Obtaining radiographic contrast studies before endoscopy in suspected esophageal obstruction — contrast interferes with the subsequent endoscopic procedure
Proceeding to endoscopy in marked coagulopathy or thrombocytopenia without correction — hemostatic techniques are limited and correction may itself resolve bleeding

Outcomes depend on the underlying condition and endoscopic findings. Most GI bleeding stops spontaneously. Endoscopic therapy of high-risk peptic ulcer stigmata lowers rebleeding to about 5-10%. Endoscopic variceal ligation controls acute esophageal variceal hemorrhage in up to 90% of patients, though chronic eradication therapy prevents long-term rebleeding in only ~50%. A clean-based ulcer carries a low (3-5%) rebleeding risk, permitting early discharge of suitable patients. Post-ERCP pancreatitis is usually mild and self-limited but can be severe. Delayed biliary drainage in ascending cholangitis increases morbidity and mortality (Harrison 22e p.2464-2491).
Resting hypotension, orthostatic vital-sign change, repeated hematemesis, bloody nasogastric aspirate not clearing with lavage, or transfusion requirement — consider urgent endoscopy within 12-24 h
Dyspepsia or reflux with alarm features (weight loss, obstructive symptoms, dysphagia, GI bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia) — perform endoscopy at the outset
Esophageal food/foreign-body impaction with hypersalivation and inability to swallow water — endoscopic emergency
Reynolds's pentad (Charcot's triad plus shock and confusion) in ascending cholangitis — urgent biliary drainage
Cecal diameter exceeding 12 cm in colonic pseudoobstruction — impending perforation
Age >70, cirrhosis, coagulopathy, or respiratory/renal failure with GI bleeding — higher rebleeding risk warranting prompt evaluation

Peptic ulcer rebleeding risk by endoscopic stigmata: clean base 3-5%; flat pigmented spots ~10%; adherent clot ~20%; nonbleeding visible vessel ~40%; active spurting ~90% (Harrison 22e p.2478-2479). Procedural adverse-event risk: bleeding/perforation under 1:1000 for diagnostic EGD, flexible sigmoidoscopy, and colonoscopy, rising to 0.5-5% with therapeutic maneuvers; ERCP carries ~5% pancreatitis risk (up to ~25% in young, anicteric patients with normal ducts) and ~1% post-sphincterotomy bleeding; PEG placement has a 10-15% adverse-event rate (Harrison 22e p.2473-2474).
Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (non-infective) — Gastrointestinal Also: GI endoscopy, EGD, esophagogastroduodenoscopy, colonoscopy, ERCP, endoscopic ultrasound, EUS
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and other nonneuroendocrine pancreatic cancers
Irritable bowel syndrome (small-bowel NETs are frequently misattributed to IBS for months to years)
Psychiatric illness (insulinoma hypoglycemic symptoms may be mistaken for psychiatric disease)
Mixed neuroendocrine-adenocarcinoma tumors (adenocarcinoids) of the appendix
Somatostatin-receptor imaging: gallium-68 dotatate (or DOTATOC, copper-64 dotatate) PET, highly sensitive for primaries and metastases
Cross-sectional imaging with CT or MRI; endoscopic ultrasound especially for small pancreatic primaries such as insulinomas
FDG-PET (often negative in low-grade well-differentiated NETs but positive in higher-grade tumors)
Fasting insulin with proinsulin and C-peptide (elevated in insulinoma; proinsulin/C-peptide normal with exogenous insulin) and serum/plasma sulfonylurea levels
Fasting serum gastrin (interpret with awareness of PPI and achlorhydria effects)
Plasma glucagon (glucagonoma generally >1000 pg/mL), plasma somatostatin, plasma VIP
24-hour urinary or plasma 5-HIAA for carcinoid syndrome (suggestive, not diagnostic; serotonin-rich foods such as salmon and eggs cause false positives)
Chromogranin A (neither sensitive nor specific; falsely elevated in renal impairment and with PPI use)
Histologic grading with mitotic count and Ki-67 plus chromogranin/synaptophysin immunostaining; vitamin B12 and antiparietal evaluation in type 1 gastric NET with atrophic gastritis
Systemic mastocytosis (symptoms can be easily confused with carcinoid syndrome)
Other causes of fasting hypoglycemia: severe liver disease, alcoholism, poor nutrition, post-gastric-bypass postprandial hypoglycemia, surreptitious insulin or sulfonylurea use (mimicking insulinoma)
Causes of secretory diarrhea mimicking VIPoma: inflammatory bowel disease, short-bowel after small-bowel resection, radiation enteritis, surreptitious laxative/diuretic use
Causes of hypergastrinemia other than gastrinoma: proton pump inhibitor use and achlorhydria from chronic atrophic gastritis (mimicking gastrinoma)
Drug-induced valvulopathy mimicking carcinoid heart disease: fenfluramine and ergot-containing dopamine agonists (both act via 5-HT2B receptors)

GI NETs arise from neuroendocrine cells and contain electron-dense neurosecretory granules holding peptides and bioactive amines that can be ectopically secreted. Sporadic pancreatic NETs most frequently harbor MEN1 mutations (about 44%), with frequent mutations in the DAXX/ATRX chromatin-remodeling complex (about 43%) and mTOR-pathway genes (about 15%); recurrent mutations in extrapancreatic NETs are rare, though small-bowel NETs commonly show loss of chromosome 18 and CDKN1B mutations in a minority. In carcinoid syndrome the principal mediator is serotonin (5-HT), synthesized from tryptophan via tryptophan hydroxylase; up to 50% of dietary tryptophan can be diverted into this pathway, which can deplete niacin and produce pellagra-like lesions. Histamine and tachykinins such as substance P also contribute. Serotonin stimulates intestinal secretion and motility and drives fibroblast growth, accounting for mesenteric fibrosis and for valvular fibrosis via activation of 5-HT2B receptors on heart-valve fibroblasts. Right-sided cardiac predominance reflects venous delivery of serotonin from hepatic/retroperitoneal deposits to the right heart, with pulmonary metabolism sparing the left heart. Inherited syndromes (MEN 1, von Hippel-Lindau, neurofibromatosis type 1, tuberous sclerosis) underlie a minority of cases (Harrison 22e p.676-683).

GI NETs are broadly grouped by origin into extrapancreatic NETs (historically called carcinoid tumors) and pancreatic NETs; they typically follow a more indolent course than most malignancies but can synthesize peptides, growth factors, and bioactive amines that are ectopically secreted (Harrison 22e p.676).

More than 90% of NETs express somatostatin receptors, making somatostatin-analogue PET tracers (gallium-68 dotatate, DOTATOC, copper-64 dotatate) highly sensitive for detecting primaries and metastases (Harrison 22e p.681).

Carcinoid heart disease occurs in roughly two-thirds of patients with carcinoid syndrome and is characterized by plaque-like fibrous endocardial thickening classically on the right heart, causing tricuspid regurgitation (nearly universal) plus possible tricuspid stenosis, pulmonary regurgitation, and pulmonary stenosis (Harrison 22e p.683).

A minority of NETs arise within inherited syndromes; MEN 1 (menin gene, 11q13) is the most common, and gastrinoma should prompt a family history and assessment for hyperparathyroidism since up to 25% of ZES patients have MEN 1 (Harrison 22e p.676, 678).

Tumors are classified by differentiation (well vs poorly differentiated) and grade 1-3, which closely correlates with mitotic count and Ki-67 index: grade 1 is <2 mitoses/10 HPF and Ki-67 <3%, grade 2 is 2-20/10 HPF and 3-20%, grade 3 is >20/10 HPF and >20%; poorly differentiated high-grade neuroendocrine carcinomas are the most aggressive category (Harrison 22e p.677).

Only about 20% of pancreatic NETs are functional (hormone-secreting); the majority are nonfunctional and present incidentally or with mass-related symptoms such as abdominal pain and weight loss (Harrison 22e p.677).
The most common functional pancreatic NET is insulinoma, followed by glucagonoma and gastrinoma; somatostatinoma, VIPoma, ACTHoma and others are uncommon (Harrison 22e p.677).

Most gastrinomas actually arise in the gastrinoma triangle (bounded by duodenum, pancreas, and confluence of cystic and common bile ducts) rather than the pancreas, and 50-90% of sporadic gastrinomas arise in the duodenum, where they are often small and hard to localize (Harrison 22e p.678).

Glucagonoma classically presents with necrolytic migratory erythema (often intertriginous, waxing and waning), glucose intolerance and weight loss; a hypercoagulable state is reported in up to one-third of patients (Harrison 22e p.679).

Gastric NETs fall into three types: type 1 (chronic atrophic gastritis, most common, generally benign), type 2 (associated with gastrinoma/ZES), and type 3 (sporadic, normal gastrin, potentially far more aggressive) (Harrison 22e p.680).

Small-bowel NETs (most often terminal ileum) arise within the muscularis/submucosa and are notoriously hard to diagnose early; mesenteric fibrosis from serotonin-driven fibroblast proliferation produces a classic calcified spoke-and-wheel mesenteric mass on CT and can cause intermittent obstruction and bowel ischemia (Harrison 22e p.680).

Carcinoid syndrome (flushing, watery diarrhea, right-sided valvular heart disease, mesenteric fibrosis) is most associated with small intestine or appendiceal primaries and usually develops only after hepatic metastases or retroperitoneal lesions allow serotonin and vasoactive substances to enter systemic circulation (Harrison 22e p.681).
PPIs and achlorhydria can both raise serum gastrin and confound the diagnosis of gastrinoma
Chromogranin A is frequently falsely elevated (renal impairment, PPI use) and is neither sensitive nor specific; assay variability complicates interpretation
Elevated 5-HIAA is suggestive but not diagnostic of carcinoid syndrome, with false positives from serotonin-rich foods

Somatostatin-receptor PET can be falsely positive (physiologic uptake in the pancreatic uncinate process, sarcoidosis, meningiomas, thyroid goiter/thyroiditis) and falsely negative in higher-grade tumors with lower receptor expression
Insulinomas are less reliably avid on somatostatin scintigraphy and are usually small (<2 cm), making EUS the preferred localization tool
Insulinoma may be misdiagnosed as psychiatric illness; surreptitious insulin/hypoglycemic-agent use can mimic it
Small-bowel NETs are easily missed at colonoscopy due to submucosal location beyond the ileocecal valve and may be misattributed to IBS for years
Reduction of serotonin levels does not reverse established carcinoid valvular lesions

NETs are typically more indolent than other malignancies, and both incidence and survival have risen over recent decades (US incidence rose about 6.4-fold from 1973 to 2012; prevalence exceeded 170,000). Prognosis depends strongly on primary site and histologic grade. Median survival for advanced pancreatic NETs rose from roughly 2 years in early SEER analyses to about 4 years more recently, and median survival for well-differentiated advanced small-intestine NETs exceeds 5 years. Appendiceal NETs that are well differentiated and <2 cm have extremely low metastatic risk and excellent prognosis, while metastatic risk rises to about 20-30% for 2-3 cm tumors and is even higher beyond 3 cm. Most rectal NETs are small (<1 cm), well differentiated and rarely metastasize, but up to one-third of 1-2 cm rectal NETs metastasize and >2 cm rectal NETs metastasize in over 70%. Poorly differentiated high-grade neuroendocrine carcinomas carry markedly worse prognosis. The natural history is ultimately progressive (Harrison 22e p.677-682).

Carcinoid crisis: life-threatening profound hypotension or hypertension triggered by tumor manipulation during surgery, hepatic artery embolization, radionuclide therapy, exogenous epinephrine, or anesthesia induction
Right-sided heart failure from carcinoid heart disease, a major source of morbidity and mortality
Severe refractory hypoglycemia from insulinoma causing confusion, coma
Mesenteric fibrosis causing intermittent small-bowel obstruction or bowel ischemia
Profound watery diarrhea with hypokalemia and dehydration in VIPoma (Verner-Morrison/WDHA syndrome)

WHO-type histologic classification used in Harrison: well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor grade 1 (low grade, <2 mitoses/10 HPF, Ki-67 <3%); grade 2 (intermediate, 2-20/10 HPF, Ki-67 3-20%); grade 3 (well-differentiated high grade, >20/10 HPF, Ki-67 >20%); and poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma (high grade, >20/10 HPF, Ki-67 >20%), the most clinically aggressive category (Harrison 22e p.677).

Gastrointestinal Neuroendocrine Tumors (non-infective) — Gastrointestinal/Oncology Also: GI NETs, Carcinoid tumors, Gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, GEP-NETs, Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, Islet cell tumors
Mechanical gastric outlet obstruction
Functional dyspepsia
Cyclic vomiting syndrome or cannabinoid hyperemesis
Rumination syndrome
Small bowel dysmotility or pseudo-obstruction
Peptic ulcer disease or malignancy
Upper endoscopy to exclude mechanical obstruction
Scintigraphic solid-meal gastric emptying study
Wireless motility capsule or breath test as alternatives
Blood glucose and HbA1c assessment in diabetic patients
Review of medications affecting gastric motility
Nutritional and electrolyte assessment in severe or chronic disease

Gastroparesis arises from impaired neuromuscular coordination of gastric emptying. Injury to the vagus nerve, abnormalities of the interstitial cells of Cajal that pace gastric contractions, smooth muscle dysfunction, and autonomic neuropathy disrupt fundic accommodation, antral contractility, and pyloric relaxation. In diabetes, chronic hyperglycaemia and autonomic neuropathy impair motility, and acute hyperglycaemia itself further slows emptying. The result is retained gastric contents, which produce nausea, vomiting, and impaired nutrient and drug absorption.
Gastroparesis is delayed gastric emptying in the absence of mechanical obstruction, presenting with nausea, vomiting, early satiety, bloating, and postprandial fullness
The commonest identifiable causes are diabetes mellitus and prior gastric or vagal surgery, but many cases are idiopathic and some follow a viral illness
Mechanical obstruction must be excluded, typically by endoscopy, before the diagnosis is made
A scintigraphic gastric emptying study of a solid meal is the standard confirmatory test, with wireless motility capsule and breath tests as alternatives
Medications that slow gastric emptying, especially opioids and GLP-1 receptor agonists, can cause or worsen symptoms and should be reviewed
Management combines dietary modification toward small, low-fat, low-fibre meals with prokinetic and antiemetic therapy
Refractory disease may require enteral feeding beyond the stomach, gastric electrical stimulation, or endoscopic pyloric procedures
Diagnosing gastroparesis without first excluding mechanical obstruction
Overlooking opioids or GLP-1 receptor agonists as reversible contributors
Ignoring hyperglycaemia, which acutely delays emptying and undermines treatment
Missing alternative diagnoses such as rumination or cyclic vomiting that mimic gastroparesis

Gastroparesis is often a chronic, fluctuating condition; many patients achieve reasonable symptom control with diet and medication, but a subset have refractory, disabling symptoms with recurrent hospitalisation and nutritional compromise.
Intractable vomiting with dehydration and electrolyte disturbance
Significant weight loss or malnutrition
Features suggesting mechanical obstruction or malignancy
Marked or unstable glycaemic control complicating diabetic gastroparesis
Gastroparesis (non-infective) — GI / Hepatology Also: delayed gastric emptying, gastric stasis, diabetic gastroparesis, gastroparetic syndrome
Acute myelopathies, especially with prolonged back pain and sphincter disturbance (p.3620)
Diphtheria with early oropharyngeal disturbance (p.3620)
Porphyria (clues: abdominal pain, seizures, psychosis) (p.3620)
Vasculitic neuropathy (check ESR) (p.3620)
Critical illness neuropathy or myopathy (p.3620)
Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) in patients with late or recurrent relapses (p.3622)
Poliomyelitis and acute flaccid myelitis (wild-type poliovirus, West Nile virus, enterovirus D68, enterovirus A71, Japanese encephalitis virus) (p.3620)
Lyme polyradiculitis and other tick-borne paralyses (p.3620)
CMV polyradiculitis in immunocompromised patients (p.3620)
Botulism (a neuromuscular junction disorder; pupillary reactivity lost early) (p.3620)
CSF protein may be normal when symptoms have been present <=48 h and usually rises only by the end of the first week, so a normal early CSF does not exclude GBS (p.3619).

A sustained CSF pleocytosis (or counts above the GBS range) should prompt a search for an alternative or concurrent diagnosis such as viral myelitis, HIV, leukemia/lymphoma infiltrating nerves, or neurosarcoidosis (p.3619).
Electrodiagnostic abnormalities are mild or absent early and lag behind the clinical course; earliest AIDP findings are prolonged F-wave and distal latencies and reduced CMAP amplitudes (p.3619).
Antiganglioside antibodies (e.g., anti-GM1 in AMAN/AMSAN, anti-GQ1b in Miller Fisher) can support specific subtypes (p.3618-3619).
Test for HIV in patients with risk factors or CSF pleocytosis (p.3620).
Myasthenia gravis (neuromuscular junction disorder) (p.3620)
Poisoning with organophosphates, thallium, or arsenic (p.3620)
Paralytic shellfish poisoning (p.3620)
Severe hypophosphatemia (rare) (p.3620)

GBS is an acute, often fulminant autoimmune polyradiculoneuropathy thought to arise from immune responses to non-self antigens (infections, vaccines) that cross-react with peripheral nerve via molecular mimicry, with gangliosides (glycosphingolipids concentrated at sites such as nodes of Ranvier) as likely targets. In AIDP, the demyelinating and most common form, both cellular and humoral mechanisms operate: complement deposits on the outer Schwann cell surface, triggering membrane-attack-complex formation, vesicular myelin disintegration, and macrophage-mediated removal of myelin. The resulting conduction block (with axons left intact) explains the flaccid paralysis and the potential for rapid recovery once remyelination occurs; secondary axonal degeneration in severe cases slows recovery and worsens residual deficit. In the axonal variants (AMAN/AMSAN), IgG and complement deposit at the nodes of Ranvier of motor axons, with anti-GD1a antibodies preferentially targeting motor over sensory roots; low CMAP amplitudes often reflect reversible nodal/paranodal conduction block rather than true axon loss, though severe cases show axonal degeneration (p.3617-3620).

About 70% of cases follow an acute infection (usually respiratory or GI) by 1-3 weeks; roughly 20-30% are preceded by Campylobacter jejuni, with a similar share after herpesvirus infection (often CMV or EBV) (p.3617).
Weakness usually evolves over hours to a few days and is classically ascending (legs more than arms), often first noticed as 'rubbery legs', with tingling dysesthesias in the extremities (p.3617).

Facial diparesis occurs in ~50% of patients and lower cranial nerve/bulbar involvement is common; bulbar weakness with difficulty handling secretions can initially be mistaken for brainstem ischemia (p.3617).
Pain (neck, shoulder, back, or diffuse spinal pain) is common early, in ~50% of patients, and deep aching muscle pain plus dysesthetic limb pain also occur (p.3617).
Large-fiber functions (deep tendon reflexes, proprioception) are affected more severely than cutaneous pain/temperature sensation (p.3617).

AMAN and AMSAN are axonal variants associated with anti-GD1a/anti-GM1 antibodies and preceding C. jejuni; AMAN can occur in seasonal outbreaks (e.g., rural China) and is prevalent in China and Mexico (p.3617-3619).
Miller Fisher syndrome (~5% of cases) presents with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia without limb weakness and carries anti-GQ1b antibodies in >90% (p.3617, p.3619).
If diagnosis is strongly suspected, treatment should not wait for the characteristic CSF or electrodiagnostic findings to evolve (p.3620).
Corticosteroids have NOT been found effective in GBS and should not be relied on as treatment (p.3621).

Treatment timing matters: each day counts, and by ~2 weeks after the first motor symptoms it is unknown whether immunotherapy is still effective; if a patient has reached the plateau, treatment is probably no longer indicated unless severe weakness suggests ongoing immune attack (p.3620).
Lack of improvement after a course of IVIg or plasmapheresis is NOT an indication to switch to the other modality, and combining the two is not significantly better than either alone (p.3621).
Early CSF and electrodiagnostic studies can be normal/minimal; relying on them to confirm before treating can cause harmful delay (p.3619-3620).
Acute flaccid myelitis can closely mimic GBS because sphincter disturbances may be absent (p.3620).

About 85% of patients reach full functional recovery within several months to a year, though minor signs (e.g., persistent areflexia) and complaints such as fatigue may remain. Mortality is <5% in optimal settings, usually from secondary pulmonary complications. The outlook is worst with severe proximal motor and sensory axonal damage; other adverse factors are advanced age, a fulminant or severe attack, and delayed treatment. Elevated serum neurofilament light chains and high anti-GM1 titers both correlate with greater axonal involvement and poorer recovery. Between 5 and 10% of typical GBS patients have one or more late relapses, many later reclassified as CIDP (p.3621-3622).

Rapid tempo of progression and severe weakness on admission, plus facial and/or bulbar weakness in the first week, predict the need for mechanical ventilation (up to ~30% of patients require ventilatory support) (p.3617).
Bulbar weakness with difficulty handling secretions threatens the airway (p.3617).
Autonomic instability — wide blood pressure swings, postural hypotension, and cardiac dysrhythmias — can be fatal and may occur even when limb weakness is otherwise mild (p.3617).
Presence of fever or constitutional symptoms at onset casts doubt on the diagnosis and should prompt reconsideration (p.3617).
Prominent or early bladder dysfunction, or a sensory level, should raise suspicion for spinal cord disease rather than GBS (p.3617).

Brighton Collaboration case definitions (2011) grade diagnostic certainty in three levels. Level 1 (highest certainty) requires bilateral flaccid limb weakness, decreased/absent reflexes in weak limbs, a monophasic course with onset-to-nadir of 12 h to 28 days followed by plateau, electrophysiology consistent with GBS, cytoalbuminologic dissociation (elevated CSF protein with CSF white cell count <50/microL), and no alternative diagnosis. Lower levels relax the laboratory/electrophysiologic requirements. Parallel criteria exist for Miller Fisher syndrome (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia without limb weakness) (p.3620-3621).
Nerve conduction studies
CSF (albuminocytologic dissociation)
Serial vital capacity / NIF
Guillain-Barré syndrome (non-infective) — Neurology
Progressive ascending weakness with areflexia and no fever suggests Guillain-Barré; watch respiratory function.
Red flags: Respiratory failure & autonomic instability — monitor FVC, may need ventilation

[guideline] management → Intravenous immunoglobulin First-line immunotherapy — equivalent efficacy to plasma exchange and usually more practical. Corticosteroids are ineffective and should not be used.
[guideline] adjunct → Pharmacological VTE prophylaxis Immobile patients are at high venous-thromboembolism risk; give prophylactic LMWH unless contraindicated.

chunks.text: Generalized anxiety disorder involves dysregulation of fear and worry circuitry, particularly heightened amygdala reactivity with insufficient prefrontal regulation, alongside imbalances in gamma-aminobutyric acid, serotonin, and noradrenaline signalling. Genetic predisposition, temperamental traits such as behavioural inhibition, and chronic stress interact to produce a persistent state of anticipatory apprehension and autonomic arousal.

chunks.text: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (sarcomeric)
Dilated cardiomyopathy (e.g., TTN truncating variant)
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy / arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy
Restrictive cardiomyopathy (inherited, including DES-related and transthyretin amyloidosis)
Left ventricular noncompaction
Conduction disease with dilated cardiomyopathy (e.g., LMNA, SCN5A)
Inherited metabolic/storage cardiomyopathies (Fabry's, Danon, PRKAG2, carnitine and fatty-acid oxidation defects, mitochondrial syndromes)

Detailed multigenerational family history (heart failure, cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy, conduction disease, tachyarrhythmias, sudden death, early atrial fibrillation/pacemaker, muscular dystrophy)
Two-dimensional and Doppler echocardiography (central to HCM/DCM diagnosis; physical exam and ECG are insensitive for HCM)
Electrocardiogram
Cardiac MRI for myocardial fibrosis (late gadolinium enhancement) and inflammation
Genetic counseling and multigene cardiomyopathy panel testing, with confirmatory variant testing in relatives

Endomyocardial biopsy with electron microscopy when a specific diagnosis with therapeutic implications is suspected (e.g., Fabry's lamellar inclusions; not used to diagnose HCM but can exclude infiltrative/metabolic disease)
Enzyme activity assay and/or GLA sequencing when Fabry's disease suspected
Ambulatory ECG monitoring and exercise testing for nonsustained ventricular tachycardia and outflow gradient provocation
Athlete's heart (physiologic hypertrophy that regresses with detraining, with supernormal VO2max >50 mL/kg/min, mild dilation, and normal diastolic function)
Hypertensive or aortic valve disease causing secondary LV hypertrophy
Infiltrative/storage disease mimicking HCM via pseudohypertrophy (often with short PR interval)
Cardiac amyloidosis, particularly transthyretin-variant amyloid causing restrictive physiology

Many distinct genes are implicated (locus heterogeneity), each with numerous pathogenic variants (allelic heterogeneity). Mutant proteins can interfere with the normal allele via a dominant-negative mechanism, while nonsense/frameshift variants may yield truncated or unstable proteins whose absence causes disease through haploinsufficiency; some genetic DCM combines both effects. Functional gene groups include sarcomeric proteins, Z-disk/cytoskeletal proteins, nuclear membrane proteins, excitation-contraction coupling proteins, metabolic enzymes, mitochondrial DNA, sarcolemmal membrane proteins, and desmosomal proteins. In HCM, sarcomere variants enhance calcium sensitivity, maximal force generation, and ATPase activity, producing abnormal energetics and impaired relaxation; myofibril and myocyte misalignment/disarray occurs, with interstitial fibrosis appearing before overt hypertrophy and focal replacement fibrosis providing arrhythmic substrate, plus microvascular ischemia from thickened intramural vessels. In DCM and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, cytoskeletal, sarcolemmal (dystrophin), nuclear membrane (lamin A/C, emerin), and desmosomal protein defects impair force transmission, mechanical/electrical coupling, and cell survival; desmosomal disruption activates Wnt/beta-catenin and proinflammatory signaling with replacement of myocytes by fat and fibrous tissue, creating arrhythmogenic, sometimes aneurysmal regions.

Each traditional morphologic form of cardiomyopathy (hypertrophic, dilated, restrictive) can be caused or modified by underlying genetic factors; heritability is well recognized in HCM and present in at least 30% of dilated cardiomyopathy without another clear etiology (p.2003-2004).

DCM is considered present when LVEF is <=0.50 and/or LV diastolic dimension exceeds the 95th percentile predicted for age and sex; some patients have reduced LVEF with minimal dilation (nondilated/minimally dilated cardiomyopathy) (p.2008).

Inherited metabolic and storage disorders can mimic HCM by thickening the myocardium with abnormal products ('pseudohypertrophy'), classically with a short PR interval; most are diagnosed in childhood (p.2010).

Fabry's disease (X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency from GLA variants) can affect female carriers; endomyocardial biopsy shows diagnostic concentric lamellar inclusions on electron microscopy, and diagnosis matters because enzyme replacement can reduce deposits (p.2010).

Most familial cardiomyopathies are autosomal dominant, with occasional autosomal recessive, matrilineal (mitochondrial), and X-linked inheritance; missense and truncating variants are the commonest abnormalities (p.2003).

Genetic cardiomyopathy shows age-dependent and incomplete penetrance: the phenotype is rarely present at birth and in some carriers may never manifest; relatives carrying the same variant can differ markedly in severity and progression (p.2004).
Penetrance and clinical severity tend to be greater in men for most cardiomyopathies; current therapy is based on phenotype rather than the genetic defect (p.2004).

The greatest current utility of genetic testing is to focus and inform family evaluations; it can also provide risk stratification and occasionally identify a treatable disorder such as Fabry's or Gaucher's disease (p.2004).

A sarcomere gene variant is found in roughly 40-50% of HCM patients, more often with familial disease and asymmetric septal hypertrophy; about 80% of these involve MYH7 or MYBPC3 encoding the thick myofilament (p.2005).

HCM is defined as left ventricular hypertrophy developing without a causative hemodynamic factor (e.g., hypertension, aortic valve disease) or infiltrative/storage disease; prevalence is about 1:500 (p.2005).

Outflow tract obstruction is present at rest in about 30% of HCM patients and provoked by exercise in another ~30%; systolic anterior motion of an enlarged anterior mitral leaflet against the hypertrophied septum produces obstruction and posteriorly directed mitral regurgitation (p.2006).

Truncating variants in TTN (titin) are the commonest genetic cause of dilated cardiomyopathy, accounting for up to 25% of familial DCM; men with TTN truncating variants typically develop disease about a decade before women (p.2008-2009).
Identifying a variant in a proband to focus family screening requires high certainty the variant is truly pathogenic and not a benign DNA variant.

Most identified variants are 'private' to individual families, complicating interpretation; growing recognition that multiple intermediate-effect alleles and polygenic risk influence penetrance and expression.
Athlete's heart can mimic mild HCM; distinguishing features include regression with detraining, supernormal exercise capacity, mild dilation, and normal diastolic function.
Late gadolinium enhancement on MRI, once attributed to prior viral myocarditis, is now recognized as common in genetic cardiomyopathy.
Cardiac glycosides should be avoided in HCM with obstruction because they increase contractility and worsen obstruction.
The positive predictive value of most HCM sudden-death risk factors is low, so many patients receiving a defibrillator never receive appropriate device therapy.
Endomyocardial biopsy is not used to diagnose HCM itself but may exclude infiltrative/metabolic disease.

HCM prognosis is better than in early referral-population studies but mortality remains higher than in age-matched individuals without cardiomyopathy; sudden death risk is under 1% per year (about 0.5% per year baseline). Up to 1 in 20 HCM patients progress to overt systolic dysfunction (EF <50%) with or without dilation ('burned out'/end-stage HCM), with increased risk of death from progressive heart failure and sudden death unless transplanted. In DCM and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, prognosis is driven by disease stage and sudden-death risk, which is higher for variants in DES, DSP, DSC2, FLNC, LMNA, PKP2, PLN, RBM20, SCN5A, and TMEM43; progression rate is also gene-dependent, and patients with TTN truncating variants frequently recover with medical therapy.
History of cardiac arrest or spontaneous sustained ventricular tachycardia
Syncope, particularly nonvagal and occurring with or after exertion
Family history of sudden cardiac death at early ages
Maximal LV wall thickness >30 mm
LV systolic dysfunction with ejection fraction <50% in HCM
LV apical aneurysm (especially with apical hypertrophy)
Spontaneous nonsustained ventricular tachycardia (>3 beats at rate >120)
High late gadolinium enhancement burden on cardiac MRI
Pathogenic LMNA or FLNC variants, or right-ventricular cardiomyopathy progressing to LV dysfunction (higher arrhythmic/adverse-event risk)

HCM sudden-death risk stratification uses major risk factors (prior cardiac arrest or sustained VT, exertional/nonvagal syncope, family history of sudden cardiac death, LV apical aneurysm, maximal wall thickness >30 mm, LVEF <50%) plus modifying factors (late gadolinium enhancement burden, spontaneous nonsustained VT). The externally validated European Society of Cardiology HCM Risk-SCD calculator integrates age, LV outflow tract gradient, left atrial diameter, maximal wall thickness, syncope, family history, and nonsustained VT to estimate 5-year cardiac-arrest risk: ICD generally advised at >=6%, considered at 4-6%, and not advised at <4%. DCM is defined by LVEF <=0.50 and/or LV diastolic dimension >95th percentile for age and sex.

chunks.text: Pathologic reflux arises from anatomic and physiologic failure of the oesophagogastric junction valve - widening of the diaphragmatic hiatus with diminished crural diaphragm function, loss of the intra-abdominal oesophageal segment disabling the flap valve, axial (sliding) hiatus hernia causing LES hypotension, and increased junctional compliance allowing liquid to escape during transient LES relaxations (the belch reflex). Some reflux is physiologic and intertwined with belching, but esophagitis follows excessive reflux plus impaired acid clearance, which depends on peristalsis returning fluid to the stomach and bicarbonate in swallowed saliva neutralising residual acid; impaired peristalsis and reduced salivation therefore prolong acid contact. Mucosal injury is driven by a cytokine-mediated inflammatory pathway rather than purely direct caustic injury. Gastric acid hypersecretion is usually NOT the dominant factor (exceptions: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, severe esophagitis in ~50%); chronic H. pylori gastritis may even be protective by inducing hypoacidity. Pepsin, bile, and pancreatic enzymes also injure the epithelium, and bile persists in refluxate despite acid suppression and is implicated as a cofactor in Barrett's metaplasia and adenocarcinoma. Exacerbating factors include abdominal obesity, pregnancy, gastric hypersecretory states, delayed gastric emptying, disrupted peristalsis, and overeating. Esophageal chest pain itself reflects a shared nerve plexus with the heart and poor discriminative ability of oesophageal afferents (p.2503-2504, p.2509-2510).

source.page: Harrison 22e: Chest Discomfort ch.15 p.104-109; Diseases of the Esophagus ch.334 p.2503-2511; Nausea, Vomiting, and Indigestion ch.48 p.300-301

chunks.text: Esophageal pain shares a nerve plexus with the heart and esophageal afferents discriminate stimuli poorly, so distention or acid (chemostimulation) is often perceived as pressure-type mid-chest pain radiating to back, arms, or jaw - closely mimicking angina (p.2503-2504).

chunks.text: Most patients in whom an acute cardiopulmonary cause is excluded have a favourable prognosis; in low-risk patients the 30-day major cardiovascular event rate is about 2.5%. However, historically 2-6% of presumed-nonischaemic chest pain patients discharged from the ED were later found to have had a missed myocardial infarction, underscoring the cost of misclassification. For GERD itself, erosive esophagitis and peptic strictures have become rare with potent acid suppression, but Barrett's metaplasia and oesophageal adenocarcinoma have increased; progression of Barrett's to adenocarcinoma is estimated at roughly 0.1-0.5% per year, with obese white men in their sixth decade at greatest risk. High-grade dysplasia in Barrett's carries a high rate of progression and a high prevalence of coexisting unrecognised cancer (p.104, p.2510-2511, ch.85 p.92).

Pregnancy is a progressively insulin-resistant state driven by placental hormones such as human placental lactogen, progesterone, and cortisol. Gestational diabetes develops when maternal pancreatic beta-cell insulin secretion cannot compensate for this physiological resistance, leading to maternal hyperglycaemia. Glucose crosses the placenta freely and stimulates fetal insulin secretion; the resulting fetal hyperinsulinaemia acts as a growth factor causing macrosomia and, after cord clamping removes the maternal glucose supply, predisposes the neonate to hypoglycaemia.
Defined as carbohydrate intolerance first recognised during pregnancy, distinguishing it from pre-existing diabetes detected in early pregnancy
Diagnosis rests on an oral glucose tolerance test, usually performed around 24 to 28 weeks, or earlier in high-risk women
Risk factors include obesity, advanced maternal age, prior GDM, macrosomic infant, family history of diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome, and certain ethnic backgrounds
First-line management is medical nutrition therapy, glucose self-monitoring, and physical activity, with pharmacotherapy added if glycaemic targets are not met
Fetal complications include macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, birth trauma, neonatal hypoglycaemia, and polycythaemia
Maternal hyperglycaemia drives fetal hyperinsulinaemia, which promotes excessive fetal growth and adiposity
Most women return to normal glucose tolerance after delivery, but there is a substantially increased lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes
Postpartum glucose testing is essential to detect persistent diabetes and to guide long-term risk reduction
Missing overt pre-existing diabetes by not testing high-risk women in early pregnancy
Relying on symptoms, which are usually absent, rather than screening
Assuming a normal-sized fetus excludes risk of neonatal hypoglycaemia
Failing to arrange postpartum glucose reassessment and long-term follow-up
Neglecting neonatal glucose monitoring after delivery

Well-controlled gestational diabetes has an excellent outcome, approaching that of the non-diabetic population. Poor control raises risks of macrosomia, operative delivery, birth trauma, and neonatal metabolic problems. Long term, affected women have a markedly increased risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, and their offspring have higher rates of obesity and glucose intolerance.
Marked fetal macrosomia or polyhydramnios increasing risk of shoulder dystocia and stillbirth

Pregnancy alters thyroid physiology through oestrogen-driven increases in thyroxine-binding globulin, rising total hormone levels, and hCG-mediated stimulation of the TSH receptor that transiently lowers TSH in the first trimester. Increased renal iodide clearance and placental deiodinase activity raise iodine and hormone demand. Autoimmune thyroid disease may worsen or improve with the shifting immune state of pregnancy, and transplacental passage of TSH-receptor antibodies or antithyroid drugs can affect the fetal thyroid.
Pregnancy raises thyroxine-binding globulin and total thyroid hormone levels, so trimester-specific reference ranges for free hormones and TSH must be used to interpret results correctly

High levels of hCG in early pregnancy weakly stimulate the TSH receptor, producing a physiological fall in TSH and sometimes transient gestational thyrotoxicosis, often linked to hyperemesis gravidarum
Gestational thyrotoxicosis from hCG is usually self-limiting and must be distinguished from Graves' disease, which typically has orbitopathy and positive TSH-receptor antibodies
Maternal thyroid hormone is critical for early fetal neurodevelopment, so overt hypothyroidism requires prompt and adequate replacement
Levothyroxine requirements commonly increase during pregnancy, so women on replacement need dose adjustment and monitoring
TSH-receptor antibodies cross the placenta and can cause fetal or neonatal thyroid dysfunction, so antibody levels help assess fetal risk in Graves' disease
When antithyroid drugs are needed, the choice and timing consider the differing teratogenic profiles of the agents across trimesters

With appropriate monitoring and treatment, most women with thyroid disease have good maternal and fetal outcomes, but poorly controlled disease increases the risk of miscarriage, pre-eclampsia, growth restriction, and impaired fetal neurodevelopment.
