Gestational trophoblastic disease results from abnormal fertilisation and proliferation of trophoblastic tissue. A complete mole typically arises when an anucleate ovum is fertilised and the paternal chromosomes duplicate, giving a diploid androgenetic genome with swollen avascular chorionic villi and no fetus, while a partial mole usually results from dispermic fertilisation producing a triploid conceptus with focal villous change and a nonviable fetus. Excessive trophoblast produces very high hCG. In gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, trophoblast invades the myometrium and vasculature, and choriocarcinoma disseminates haematogenously, favouring the lungs, brain, and liver.

Gestational trophoblastic disease is a spectrum of proliferative disorders of placental trophoblast ranging from benign hydatidiform mole to malignant gestational trophoblastic neoplasia including choriocarcinoma
A complete mole usually arises from fertilisation of an ovum lacking maternal genetic material and contains no fetal tissue, whereas a partial mole is typically triploid with some fetal parts

Classic presentation includes irregular vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy, a uterus large for dates, markedly elevated hCG, and sometimes early or severe hyperemesis or pre-eclampsia before twenty weeks
Ultrasound may show a vesicular or snowstorm appearance with absent or abnormal fetal development, and diagnosis is confirmed histologically
Uterine evacuation by suction curettage is the treatment for molar pregnancy, followed by structured monitoring of serial hCG to detect persistent disease
Persistently elevated or rising hCG after evacuation indicates gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, which is highly chemosensitive and generally curable even when metastatic
Reliable contraception during hCG surveillance is essential because a new pregnancy would obscure the marker used to detect persistent disease
Choriocarcinoma can follow any pregnancy, including normal or ectopic, and may present with metastatic symptoms such as haemoptysis or neurological signs

Most hydatidiform moles are cured by evacuation alone, and even when gestational trophoblastic neoplasia develops it is one of the most curable malignancies, with excellent survival when managed in specialist centres using chemotherapy guided by prognostic scoring. Outcome depends on prompt diagnosis, adherence to hCG surveillance, and risk stratification, with high-risk and heavily metastatic disease requiring more intensive multi-agent treatment.

chunks.text: Ingested Giardia cysts excyst in the small intestine and release trophozoites that attach to the duodenal and jejunal mucosa via a ventral adhesive disc. Colonisation causes villous shortening, disruption of the brush-border enzymes and a mucosal inflammatory response, impairing absorption of fats, carbohydrates and other nutrients. This produces the characteristic malabsorptive, non-inflammatory diarrhoea. Trophozoites encyst as they pass down the gut, and the environmentally hardy cysts are excreted to continue the cycle.

chunks.text: Acute nephritic syndrome: poststreptococcal GN, subacute bacterial endocarditis-associated GN, lupus nephritis, anti-GBM disease, IgA nephropathy, ANCA small-vessel vasculitis (GPA, MPA, EGPA), IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura), cryoglobulinemia, MPGN, C3 glomerulopathy, mesangioproliferative GN (Harrison 22e p.2414-2415).

Nephrotic syndrome: minimal change disease, FSGS, membranous glomerulonephritis, diabetic nephropathy, AL/AA amyloidosis, light-chain deposition disease, fibrillary-immunotactoid disease, Fabry's disease (Harrison 22e p.2415).
Pulmonary-renal syndromes: Goodpasture's/anti-GBM disease, ANCA vasculitis, IgA vasculitis, cryoglobulinemia (Harrison 22e p.2414-2415).
Basement membrane syndromes: anti-GBM disease, Alport's syndrome, thin basement membrane disease, nail-patella syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2415).
Glomerular vascular syndromes: atherosclerotic and hypertensive nephropathy, cholesterol emboli, sickle cell disease, thrombotic microangiopathies, antiphospholipid syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2415).

Microscopic hematuria with minimal proteinuria can also reflect non-glomerular causes: urinary tract malignancy (especially older men), BPH, interstitial nephritis, papillary necrosis, hypercalciuria, kidney stones, cystic kidney disease, or renal vascular injury (Harrison 22e p.2414).
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis after nephritogenic streptococcal pharyngitis (1-3 weeks) or skin infection (2-6 weeks) (Harrison 22e p.2417-2418).

Subacute bacterial endocarditis-associated and other persistent-infection (shunt, abscess, infected prosthesis; often Staphylococcus) glomerulonephritis, which can mimic or coexist with ANCA vasculitis (Harrison 22e p.2417).

Hepatitis B and C (membranous, MPGN, cryoglobulinemic patterns), HIV-associated nephropathy (collapsing FSGS), syphilis, leprosy, malaria, and schistosomiasis - globally, malaria and schistosomiasis may be the most common causes of glomerulonephritis (Harrison 22e p.2416, 2459).
IgA-dominant Staphylococcus-associated infectious glomerulonephritis can mimic primary IgA nephropathy (Harrison 22e p.2419).

Urinalysis with microscopy for dysmorphic red cells, red blood cell casts, pyuria; quantify proteinuria by spot urine albumin/creatinine ratio (UACR >30 mg/g abnormal) or 24-h collection; distinguish selective (albumin-predominant, childhood MCD) from nonselective proteinuria (Harrison 22e p.2414).

Serologies: ASO/anti-DNase/antihyaluronidase and streptozyme; ANA and anti-dsDNA; complement C3 and C4 (low C3 with normal C4 in poststreptococcal GN and C3 glomerulopathy; hypocomplementemia in active lupus nephritis); ANCA (anti-PR3, anti-MPO); anti-GBM antibody to the alpha3 NC1 domain specifically; cryoglobulins and rheumatoid factor; antiphospholipid antibodies; HIV and hepatitis B/C serologies (Harrison 22e p.2416).
Target-antigen antibodies in nephrotic disease: anti-PLA2R and anti-THSD7A (membranous nephropathy); DNAJB9 (fibrillary GN) (Harrison 22e p.2416-2417, 2422-2423).
Kidney ultrasound to assess kidney size (small kidneys suggest chronicity) and exclude obstruction (Harrison 22e p.2416).

Kidney biopsy with light microscopy (H&E, PAS, Jones silver, Congo red, Masson trichrome), immunofluorescence (IgG/IgM/IgA, C3/C4, PLA2R/THSD7A/DNAJB9), and electron microscopy to localize deposits and assess the GBM (Harrison 22e p.2416-2417).
C3 nephritic factor, factor H, soluble C5b-9, paraprotein screening, and CFHR genetic testing (with family screening) when C3 glomerulopathy is suspected (Harrison 22e p.2420).
Diabetic nephropathy and amyloidosis both thicken the GBM and can mimic membranous nephropathy on light microscopy (Harrison 22e p.2422-2423).

Secondary FSGS (adaptive hyperfiltration/obesity, reflux, hypertension, drugs such as heroin/interferon/bisphosphonates, viruses) and genetic/familial podocytopathies must be excluded before diagnosing primary FSGS, as immunosuppression is not indicated in secondary/genetic forms (Harrison 22e p.2421-2422).
Secondary membranous nephropathy from malignancy (breast, lung, colon), infection, lupus or other autoimmune disease, IgG4 disease, or drugs (gold, penicillamine, NSAIDs) (Harrison 22e p.2422).
Membranous lupus nephritis (subendothelial deposits/tubuloreticular inclusions) may precede extrarenal lupus and mimic primary MGN (Harrison 22e p.2423).
C3 glomerulopathy can be morphologically indistinguishable from resolving postinfectious glomerulonephritis (Harrison 22e p.2420).
Mesangioproliferative pattern is shared by IgA nephropathy, P. falciparum malaria, resolving postinfectious GN, and lupus class II (Harrison 22e p.2421).

Each kidney holds ~0.9 million glomerular tufts whose fenestrated endothelium, GBM, and podocyte foot processes with slit-pore membranes form a size- and charge-selective filtration barrier; glomerular injury allows gram quantities of protein (mainly albumin) to escape (Harrison 22e p.2411-2412). Disease arises through genetic mutations (e.g., NPHS1/nephrin, NPHS2/podocin, TRPC6, APOL1 risk variants for FSGS; type IV collagen alpha3/4/5 in Alport's; complement-pathway/CFHR mutations in MPGN and C3 glomerulopathy/aHUS), infection, toxins, autoimmunity, hypertension/atherosclerosis, thrombosis/emboli, and diabetes; many cases remain idiopathic (Harrison 22e p.2411-2412). Inflammation of glomerular capillaries (glomerulonephritis) is typically immune-mediated: preformed circulating immune complexes deposit on the subendothelial side or mesangium, while in-situ formation produces subepithelial deposits; anti-GBM antibodies bind linearly to the GBM. Deposits and Toll-like receptor activation recruit neutrophils, macrophages, and T cells, activate complement to C5-9 membrane-attack complexes, and release proteases and oxidants that damage the mesangium, capillaries, and GBM and efface podocytes; early CD4/CD8 T-cell activation is important. Depending on antigen location and host genetics, injury produces endocapillary or extracapillary (crescentic) proliferation. Progression to chronic kidney failure tracks with downstream tubulointerstitial nephritis and fibrosis, driven by proteinuria-laden filtrate, inflammatory mediators carried from inflamed glomeruli, and fibroblast/myofibroblast expansion (TGF-beta, FGF-2, HIF-1alpha, PDGF) laying down collagen (Harrison 22e p.2412-2414).

Glomerular disease is grouped into six clinical syndromes that overlap and are not mutually exclusive: acute nephritic, pulmonary-renal, nephrotic, basement membrane, glomerular-vascular, and infectious disease-associated (Harrison 22e p.2414-2416).

IgA nephropathy is defined by dominant/codominant mesangial IgA deposits and is one of the most common glomerulonephritides worldwide; the two classic presentations are persistent asymptomatic microscopic hematuria and recurrent gross hematuria during/just after an upper respiratory infection (synpharyngitic) (Harrison 22e p.2419).

Membranoproliferative GN (MPGN) is now viewed as a pattern of injury (mesangial/subendothelial immune complexes, complement, or monoclonal deposits) producing GBM double contours ('tram-tracking'), rather than a single disease; classify by underlying immune-complex, complement, or monoclonal cause (Harrison 22e p.2420-2421).

C3 glomerulopathy (dense deposit disease and C3 glomerulonephritis) shows sole/dominant glomerular C3 with little or no immunoglobulin and is driven by alternative-complement-pathway dysregulation (e.g., CFHR mutations, C3 nephritic factor) (Harrison 22e p.2420).

RPGN is the clinical picture of acute nephritis with serum creatinine rising over days; crescentic glomerulonephritis is its pathologic equivalent and warrants urgent biopsy and treatment (Harrison 22e p.2414, 2419).
When RPGN presents with lung hemorrhage it is a pulmonary-renal syndrome; consider anti-GBM/Goodpasture disease, ANCA small-vessel vasculitis, lupus, and cryoglobulinemia (Harrison 22e p.2414, 2418).

ANCA small-vessel vasculitis (GPA, MPA, EGPA, renal-limited) causes a pauci-immune (little/no immune-complex deposition) segmental necrotizing/crescentic glomerulonephritis; anti-PR3 is more common in GPA and anti-MPO in MPA/EGPA (Harrison 22e p.2419-2420).

Anti-GBM disease targets the alpha3 NC1 domain of type IV collagen; biopsy shows linear IgG staining along the GBM (versus the granular 'lumpy-bumpy' deposits of immune-complex disease); 10-15% also have anti-MPO ANCA (Harrison 22e p.2418-2419).

Poststreptococcal GN classically shows subepithelial 'humps' on electron microscopy, low C3/CH50 with normal C4 in the first week, and a positive streptozyme test; it rarely requires biopsy and has a good prognosis in children (Harrison 22e p.2417-2418).

Lupus nephritis is classified ISN/RPS class I-VI; proliferative class III/IV lesions (and class IV with crescents) carry the worst prognosis, while mesangial class I/II need little therapy and class V is a membranous pattern (Harrison 22e p.2418).

Kidney failure in glomerulonephritis correlates histologically with the degree of tubulointerstitial nephritis and interstitial fibrosis rather than with the specific glomerular lesion; interstitial fibrosis is an ominous sign of irreversibility (Harrison 22e p.2413-2414, 2416).

Nephritic syndrome = inflammatory pattern: hematuria with red blood cell casts, dysmorphic red cells, pyuria, hypertension, fluid retention, only mild-to-moderate (1-2 g/24 h) proteinuria, and a falling GFR (Harrison 22e p.2414, 2416).

On biopsy, <50% glomerular involvement is focal and >50% diffuse; injury within a tuft is segmental (part) or global (most); endocapillary proliferation is within the tuft and extracapillary proliferation (crescents) extends into Bowman's space (Harrison 22e p.2417).

Nephrotic syndrome = heavy proteinuria (>3.0-3.5 g/24 h) with hypoalbuminemia, hypercholesterolemia, edema/anasarca, hypertension, and only minimal/microscopic hematuria; isolated heavy proteinuria without these features is termed nephrotic-range proteinuria (Harrison 22e p.2414, 2420).
Red blood cell casts or dysmorphic red cells in the sediment make glomerulonephritis likely; as few as 3-5 red cells in spun first-morning urine is suspicious (Harrison 22e p.2414).
Gross hematuria is rare in glomerular disease except in IgA nephropathy and sickle cell disease; most glomerular hematuria is asymptomatic and microscopic (Harrison 22e p.2414).

Kidney biopsy is the key diagnostic step in most glomerulonephritis; it identifies the lesion and often directs treatment, but is reserved for clinically stable patients with adequate clotting who can receive therapy (Harrison 22e p.2416-2417).

Minimal change disease (MCD) causes 70-90% of childhood nephrotic syndrome but only 10-15% in adults; light microscopy is normal, immunofluorescence negative (or scant mesangial IgM), and electron microscopy shows foot-process effacement; childhood proteinuria is selective (mostly albumin) (Harrison 22e p.2420-2421).

FSGS is the most common cause of primary glomerular disease leading to ESKD in the US; lesions are focal and segmental and concentrated at the corticomedullary junction, so a superficial biopsy can miss them and be misread as MCD (Harrison 22e p.2421-2422).

Membranous glomerulonephritis (MGN) accounts for ~25% of adult nephrotic syndrome; 70-80% of primary cases have circulating IgG4 anti-PLA2R antibodies, and biopsy may no longer be required when anti-PLA2R is positive with normal creatinine and no secondary cause (Harrison 22e p.2422-2423).

A superficial kidney biopsy that fails to sample deeper corticomedullary glomeruli can miss the focal/segmental lesions of FSGS and be misdiagnosed as minimal change disease - suspect FSGS in steroid-resistant 'MCD' (Harrison 22e p.2421-2422).

Test serum specifically against the alpha3 NC1 domain of collagen IV: non-nephritic anti-alpha1 NC1 antibodies in paraneoplastic syndromes cannot be distinguished by assays using whole basement-membrane fragments (Harrison 22e p.2419).
ANCA-associated vasculitis can accompany or be confused with subacute bacterial endocarditis-associated GN; it must be ruled out because the treatments differ (Harrison 22e p.2417).
There is no role for immunosuppression in poststreptococcal GN even when crescents are present, nor in secondary or genetic FSGS (Harrison 22e p.2418, 2422).

Glomerular hematuria is usually microscopic and asymptomatic, so the diagnosis is often delayed; isolated microscopic hematuria in older men still requires exclusion of urinary tract malignancy (Harrison 22e p.2414).

Nephrotic-range proteinuria without edema or hypoalbuminemia is not necessarily full nephrotic syndrome, and transient/orthostatic proteinuria (fever, exercise, obesity, CHF, upright posture) must be distinguished from sustained pathologic proteinuria (Harrison 22e p.2414, 2420).

Prognosis is lesion-specific and tracks with the degree of tubulointerstitial fibrosis. Poststreptococcal GN resolves in most children within 3-6 weeks with rare progression to ESKD, but is worse in the elderly (up to 60% azotemia) (Harrison 22e p.2418). Minimal change disease responds to steroids in 90-95% of children and 80-90% of adults though relapse is common (70-75% of children) (Harrison 22e p.2421). Primary FSGS with nephrotic-range proteinuria reaches ESKD in ~50% by 10 years and rarely remits spontaneously, but treatment-induced remission improves outcome (Harrison 22e p.2421-2422). In membranous nephropathy roughly one-third remit spontaneously, one-third have relapsing nephrotic syndrome with preserved function, and one-third progress to kidney failure or die of complications (Harrison 22e p.2423). IgA nephropathy progresses to ESKD in only 25-30% over 20-25 years; persistent proteinuria >=6 months is the strongest adverse predictor (Harrison 22e p.2419). Dense deposit disease progresses to ESKD in ~50%. Untreated RPGN/crescentic disease and ANCA vasculitis carry high mortality, but ANCA vasculitis achieves remission in 75-90% with treatment (relapse 25-50%) (Harrison 22e p.2419-2420).
RPGN / crescentic glomerulonephritis - serum creatinine rising over days is a nephrologic emergency requiring urgent biopsy and immunosuppression (Harrison 22e p.2414, 2419).

Pulmonary-renal syndrome (glomerulonephritis with lung hemorrhage/hemoptysis and falling hemoglobin) - consider anti-GBM/Goodpasture, ANCA vasculitis, lupus, cryoglobulinemia; lung hemorrhage responds to plasmapheresis (Harrison 22e p.2414, 2418-2419).
Anti-GBM disease with oliguria, serum creatinine >5-6 mg/dL, need for acute dialysis, or >50% crescents on biopsy - markers of a poor prognosis requiring prompt treatment (Harrison 22e p.2419).
ANCA small-vessel vasculitis - high mortality without treatment; virtually all patients need urgent induction therapy (Harrison 22e p.2419).
Malignant hypertension can rapidly complicate glomerulosclerosis with fibrinoid arteriolar necrosis, thrombotic microangiopathy, and acute kidney failure (Harrison 22e p.2412).
Nephrotic syndrome is a hypercoagulable state - membranous nephropathy carries the highest risk of renal vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and deep-vein thrombosis (Harrison 22e p.2423).

Glomerular disease is organized into six clinical syndromes (acute nephritic, pulmonary-renal, nephrotic, basement membrane, glomerular-vascular, infectious disease-associated) graded semiquantitatively by proteinuria, hematuria, and vascular injury (Table 326-2, Harrison 22e p.2414-2416). Biopsy descriptors: focal (<50% of glomeruli) vs diffuse (>50%); segmental (part of a tuft) vs global; endocapillary vs extracapillary (crescentic) proliferation (Harrison 22e p.2417). Lupus nephritis uses the ISN/RPS class I-VI scheme (I minimal mesangial, II mesangial proliferative, III focal, IV diffuse, V membranous, VI sclerotic) (Table 326-3, Harrison 22e p.2418). IgA nephropathy uses the Oxford MEST-C score (mesangial/endocapillary hypercellularity, segmental sclerosis, tubular fibrosis, crescents) (Harrison 22e p.2419). Albuminuria is staged normal (8-10 mg/24 h), microalbuminuria (30-300 mg/24 h), and frank proteinuria (>300 mg/24 h) (Table 326-1, Harrison 22e p.2414).
Glomerular Diseases (Spectrum) (non-infective) — Nephrology Also: glomerulopathy, IgA nephropathy, FSGS, membranous nephropathy, minimal change disease

chunks.text: GN reflects glomerular inflammation producing hypertension, volume expansion (edema, sometimes ascites), and an abnormal (nephritic) urinalysis; intense cellular proliferation reduces filtering surface area, causing oliguria/anuria, sodium and water retention, and concentrated low-sodium urine. Three mechanistic categories underlie RPGN: (1) ANCA-associated pauci-immune vasculitis (anti-proteinase-3/cANCA, anti-myeloperoxidase/pANCA) where autoantibodies recruit complement and drive inflammatory vasculitis of kidney and peripheral vessels; (2) anti-GBM disease, where circulating IgG directed at an epitope in the alpha-3 chain of the non-collagenous domain of type IV collagen binds in situ with C3; and (3) immune-complex disease with low circulating C3 from subendothelial deposits (post-infectious/PIGN, endocarditis, SLE, cryoglobulinemia, hepatitis B/C, syphilis). In PIGN, antibody-bacterial antigen complexes form ~10 days-3 weeks after pharyngeal or skin (impetigo) infection by nephritogenic group A strep, activate complement causing hypocomplementemia and subendothelial deposits, with later subepithelial 'humps'. Pathologically, RPGN shows parietal epithelial and inflammatory cell proliferation forming cellular crescents that compress capillaries; crescents progress to fibrosis and global glomerulosclerosis. IgA nephropathy results from mesangial deposition of C3 binding galactose-deficient IgA-1. (p.2354-2356)

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.319 (Approach to Renal Disease) p.2353-2356; Ch.55 (Azotemia/Urinary Abnormalities) p.341-343

chunks.text: The nephritic urinalysis is the foundation of diagnosis: dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, pyuria, and proteinuria; always examine a freshly spun sediment to confirm active GN (p.2353-2354).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.319 (Approach to Renal Disease) p.2353-2356; Ch.55 (Azotemia/Urinary Abnormalities) p.341-343

chunks.text: Dysmorphic ('acanthocyte') RBCs on phase-contrast microscopy point to a glomerular bleeding source; RBC casts are highly specific but very insensitive for GN, so their absence does not exclude glomerular disease (p.341-342).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.319 (Approach to Renal Disease) p.2353-2356; Ch.55 (Azotemia/Urinary Abnormalities) p.341-343

chunks.text: The triad of dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, and proteinuria >500 mg/day is essentially diagnostic of glomerulonephritis and warrants serologic workup plus biopsy even when creatinine is still normal (p.343).

chunks.text: Outcome depends on acuity vs chronicity: early reversible inflammatory/proliferative/necrotizing lesions can respond to prompt treatment, whereas sclerotic and atrophic biopsy findings indicate chronicity. Untreated RPGN capillaritis leads to complete, irreversible loss of kidney function; crescents that become fibrotic and atrophic cause global glomerulosclerosis, and when >50% of glomeruli are involved (diffuse) the process usually progresses to global glomerulosclerosis. Anti-GBM disease is usually a single acute fulminant event, while ANCA vasculitides may relapse (even subclinically) over time. IgA nephropathy can show rapid GFR decline to end-stage disease, especially in those of African ancestry with high-risk APOL1 alleles. Early diagnosis is critical. (p.2354-2356)

chunks.text: RPGN crescent burden on biopsy stratifies severity: focal and segmental necrotizing GN when <50% of glomeruli are acutely and only segmentally involved (better preserved), versus diffuse involvement when >50% of glomeruli are affected, which usually progresses to global glomerulosclerosis. Healed focal segmental lesions yield secondary FSGS, distinct from primary podocytopathic FSGS. RPGN is mechanistically triaged into three serologic categories: ANCA-associated (pauci-immune), anti-GBM, and low-C3 immune-complex disease. (p.2355-2356)

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: Glycogen is the branched storage polymer of glucose, formed from alpha-1,4 chains branched by alpha-1,6 linkages. Inherited enzyme defects along glycogen synthesis, glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, and the linked galactose/fructose pathways disrupt glucose homeostasis. In GSD I, deficient glucose-6-phosphatase (Ia) or its translocase (Ib) blocks the final conversion of glucose-6-phosphate to glucose, impairing both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis and causing fasting hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis and secondary hyperuricemia and hyperlipidemia. In disorders of glycogenolysis with intact gluconeogenesis (GSD III debrancher, GSD VI liver phosphorylase, GSD IX phosphorylase kinase), incomplete glycogen breakdown causes hepatomegaly and milder, often ketotic hypoglycemia. GSD IV (brancher deficiency) produces poorly soluble abnormal glycogen (polyglucosan) injuring liver, heart, muscle, and nervous system. Pompe disease (GSD II) results from lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency causing lysosomal glycogen accumulation in cardiac and skeletal muscle. Muscle-energy GSDs (V/McArdle myophosphorylase, VII/Tarui phosphofructokinase, and rarer defects of phosphoglycerate mutase, LDH-A, aldolase A, beta-enolase) limit ATP generation from glycogenolysis/glycolysis, producing exercise intolerance, cramps, and rhabdomyolysis. In galactosemia, deficiency along the Leloir pathway (most commonly GALT) leads to accumulation of toxic galactose-1-phosphate injuring liver, kidney, brain, lens, and ovary. In hereditary fructose intolerance, aldolase B deficiency causes fructose-1-phosphate accumulation and ATP depletion that inhibits gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis.

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: Glycogen storage diseases (GSDs) are inherited defects of glycogen metabolism producing glycogen that is abnormal in structure and/or quantity; collectively their prevalence is estimated at roughly 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 25,000 live births, with most being autosomal recessive and a minority X-linked or autosomal dominant.

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: Classic galactosemia (GALT deficiency) presents after milk feeding with vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice, hepatomegaly, aminoaciduria, and a notable susceptibility to gram-negative (especially E. coli) sepsis that may precede diagnosis; even with early dietary galactose elimination, long-term outcomes remain poor (speech/learning disorders, cataracts, primary ovarian insufficiency in females).

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: Hereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B deficiency) patients are asymptomatic until fructose/sucrose/sorbitol is ingested, then develop postprandial hypoglycemia, jaundice, hepatomegaly, vomiting, and convulsions; affected children characteristically develop an aversion to sweets.

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: Genetic/molecular testing has largely replaced invasive tissue biopsy for diagnosis and subtyping of many GSDs; Pompe disease is now on the U.S. recommended uniform newborn screening panel.

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: GSDs are grouped by the predominant organ affected (liver vs muscle). The most common childhood forms are glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (GSD I), acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency (GSD II/Pompe), debrancher deficiency (GSD III), and liver phosphorylase kinase deficiency (GSD IX); the most common adult form is myophosphorylase deficiency (GSD V/McArdle).

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: GSD I (von Gierke) classically presents around 3-4 months with hepatomegaly, doll-like facies with round cheeks, thin extremities, short stature, and a protuberant abdomen; lab hallmarks are fasting hypoketotic hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and elevated LDL with low HDL producing milky/cloudy serum.

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: A key distinction of GSD III from GSD I is that lactate and uric acid are normal in GSD III, whereas aminotransferases and urine glucose tetrasaccharide (Glc4) are markedly elevated early then decline with age; GSD III hypoglycemia is typically ketotic and gluconeogenesis remains intact (unlike GSD I, which impairs both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis).

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: GSD I type Ib differs from Ia by additional neutropenia and impaired neutrophil function, causing recurrent bacterial infections, mucosal ulceration, inflammatory-bowel-disease-like findings, and periodontal disease.

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: Pompe disease (GSD II) is unique in storing glycogen primarily within lysosomes rather than cytoplasm; classic infantile-onset disease presents with hypotonia, generalized weakness, macroglossia, and rapidly progressive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with death usually before age 2 if untreated, whereas late-onset disease is defined by absence of cardiomyopathy in the first year and slowly progressive proximal/respiratory (diaphragm) weakness.

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: McArdle disease (GSD V) is a prototypical muscle-energy disorder with exercise-induced cramps, myalgia, weakness, and myoglobinuria; the characteristic 'second wind' phenomenon (continuing exercise pain-free after a brief rest, as fatty-acid oxidation takes over) is unique to GSD V and there is no rise in blood lactate with exercise.

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: Tarui disease (GSD VII, phosphofructokinase-M deficiency) mimics GSD V but shows an 'out of wind' phenomenon worsened by carbohydrate-rich meals and exercise, no spontaneous second wind, plus compensated hemolysis and hyperuricemia; giving IV dextrose or pre-exercise simple carbohydrates is detrimental in GSD VII (opposite to GSD V).

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: In a young male with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) pattern on ECG strongly suggests Danon disease (X-linked LAMP2), where the WPW prevalence is about five times that in idiopathic/familial HCM.

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: Normal serum creatine kinase does not exclude muscle involvement, including in late-onset Pompe disease, and normal muscle histology or EMG can occur due to disease heterogeneity.

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: GSD VI and hepatic GSD IX were historically considered benign but show clinical heterogeneity, with reported fibrosis, cirrhosis, HCA, and HCC, including in the X-linked form.

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: Giving IV dextrose or pre-exercise simple carbohydrates worsens GSD VII (Tarui), the opposite of the beneficial effect of pre-exercise carbohydrate in GSD V (McArdle).

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: PRKAG2 syndrome can be misdiagnosed as infantile-onset Pompe disease due to phenotypic similarity of severe hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: Diagnosing galactokinase (type II) deficiency is often missed because many newborn screening programs measure GALT activity rather than galactose directly, so it requires excluding GALT deficiency.

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: Complete galactose elimination is NOT recommended in GALE deficiency (type III), because galactose is needed for nervous-system structural proteins and these patients cannot synthesize UDP-galactose from glucose; dietary restriction rather than elimination is used.

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: The traditional discrete hepatic versus neuromuscular subtyping of GSD IV is now viewed as an oversimplification; it is better conceptualized as a multidimensional clinical continuum.

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: McArdle disease may mimic inflammatory myopathy/polymyositis on EMG, risking misdiagnosis.

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: Prognosis varies widely by disorder and treatment. GSD I requires lifelong fasting avoidance; survivors face long-term gout, osteopenia/osteoporosis, hepatocellular adenoma with potential HCC, progressive renal disease/proteinuria advancing to end-stage renal disease, and increased pancreatitis and cardiovascular risk. GSD III liver disease often appears to improve in childhood but can progress to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and HCC, while GSD IIIa muscle and cardiac disease may worsen after the third-fourth decade with risk of sudden death from arrhythmia. Classic infantile Pompe disease is fatal within about 2 years untreated, but enzyme replacement therapy has substantially improved survival in both infantile and late-onset forms; CRIM-negative patients fare worse without immunomodulation. McArdle disease has a generally good prognosis with lifestyle measures, and physically active patients do better than inactive ones. Andersen disease (GSD IV) classic hepatic form is often fatal before age 5 without liver transplantation. Danon disease carries a poor prognosis with progressive end-stage heart failure in early adulthood. Classic galactosemia has poor long-term neurodevelopmental and ovarian outcomes despite early diet, whereas clinical-variant galactosemia and well-treated hereditary fructose intolerance generally have good prognoses; benign fructosuria and biochemical-variant (Duarte) galactosemia are essentially benign.

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: Neonatal/infant hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis (GSD I) or with sepsis-like presentation

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: Rapidly progressive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and heart failure in infancy (infantile Pompe; congenital PRKAG2; massive myocardial glycogen deposition)

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: WPW pattern with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in a young male (Danon disease)

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: Burgundy/dark urine with myoglobinuria after strenuous exercise (rhabdomyolysis) risking acute renal failure and acute compartment syndrome in muscle GSDs

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: Respiratory insufficiency/failure as a presenting or progressive feature of late-onset Pompe disease

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: Easy bruising, epistaxis, and prolonged bleeding time from platelet dysfunction/acquired von Willebrand-like disease in GSD I

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: Hepatocellular adenoma with hemorrhage or malignant transformation to hepatocellular carcinoma in liver GSDs (I, III, IV, VI, IX)

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: Risk of malignant hyperthermia with halogenated anesthetics/muscle relaxants in GSD V and VII

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: Several GSDs are stratified by clinical severity and onset. Pompe disease (GSD II): classic infantile-onset (cardiomyopathy at/near birth, fatal within ~2 years untreated, GAA typically <1%), nonclassic infantile-onset (less severe cardiomyopathy, slower progression), and late-onset (no cardiomyopathy in first year, slowly progressive proximal/respiratory weakness, GAA ~2-35%); CRIM-positive versus CRIM-negative status further guides immunomodulation. GSD III is subclassified IIIa (~85%, liver plus cardiac/skeletal muscle) versus IIIb (~15%, liver only). GSD I is divided into Ia (~80%) and Ib (~20%, with neutropenia/neutrophil dysfunction). GSD IV/Andersen spans a continuum from lethal perinatal/congenital neuromuscular forms through classic progressive and nonprogressive hepatic forms to adult polyglucosan body disease (APBD). Galactosemia type I is graded as classic (absent/barely detectable GALT, severe), clinical variant (residual activity, milder, common in African Americans), and biochemical/Duarte variant (asymptomatic).

chunks.diseaseName: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism
chunks.text: Glycogen Storage Diseases and Other Inherited Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism (non-infective) — Endocrine/Metabolic Also: Glycogenoses, GSD, von Gierke disease (GSD I), Pompe disease (GSD II), Cori/Forbes disease (GSD III), Andersen disease (GSD IV), McArdle disease (GSD V), Hers disease (GSD VI), Tarui disease (GSD VII), Galactosemia, Hereditary fructose intolerance

Nongonococcal urethritis (C. trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma urealyticum, Trichomonas vaginalis, HSV) - clinically often impossible to distinguish from gonococcal urethritis (p.1255-1256)
Bacterial cystitis/urinary tract infection versus the urethral syndrome in women presenting with dysuria (p.1256)

For the bacteremic stage of DGI: reactive arthritis, acute rheumatoid arthritis, sarcoidosis, erythema nodosum, drug-induced arthritis, and viral infections including hepatitis B and acute HIV infection (p.1257)
Suppurative gonococcal arthritis in the absence of symptomatic genital infection cannot be distinguished from septic arthritis caused by other pathogens (p.1257)
Meningococcemia, which can produce a dermatitis-arthritis syndrome, purulent monoarthritis, and reactive polyarthritis similar to DGI (p.1058)
Acute HIV infection and hepatitis B (viral causes mimicking the bacteremic arthritis-dermatitis stage of DGI) (p.1257)
Gram stain of urethral discharge for gram-negative intracellular monococci/diplococci - highly sensitive in symptomatic men, only ~50% sensitive for cervicitis (p.1255, 1257)

NAAT (e.g., Aptima Combo 2, Xpert CT/NG, BD ProbeTec, COBAS) on urine, urethral, cervical or self-collected vaginal swabs - more sensitive than culture and co-detects C. trachomatis; point-of-care NAAT with ~30-minute turnaround available (p.1257)
Culture on modified Thayer-Martin/selective medium with prompt processing (gonococci do not tolerate drying); single endocervical culture ~80-90% sensitive (p.1257)
In MSM, screen rectum and pharynx in addition to urine, since urine alone will miss the majority of cases (p.1257)

Blood cultures (Isolator tubes may improve yield; positivity falls after 48 h of illness) and synovial fluid (inoculate into blood culture broth and chocolate agar) in suspected DGI; organisms are seldom recovered from blood and synovial fluid in the same patient (p.1257)
Standardized culture is the preferred legal-evidence method in children for suspected sexual abuse; two NAATs targeting different sequences may substitute (p.1257)

Reactive arthritis (joint distribution differs from DGI; skin and genital manifestations also differ) (p.1257)

N. gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative, nonmotile, non-spore-forming, oxidase-positive diplococcus and an exclusively human pathogen; it carries on average three genome copies per coccal unit, and this polyploidy supports a high level of antigenic variation that aids host survival. Pili (fimbriae) mediate initial adherence to nonciliated columnar epithelial cells and enable invasion, transcytosis, genetic competence and transformation; pilus expression is switched off on subculture as a basis for antigenic variation. Opacity-associated protein (Opa) mediates intergonococcal and epithelial adhesion and binds CEACAM receptors, promoting invasion, suppressing CD4+ T-cell activation, and enabling nonopsonic neutrophil phagocytosis. Porin (the most abundant surface protein) forms the basis of serotyping; PorB.1A strains are associated with disseminated infection, resist normal human serum killing, bind complement-inhibitory molecules and may not cause local symptoms, whereas PorB.1B strains usually cause local genital infection. Lipooligosaccharide (LOS) has marked endotoxic activity; sialylation of LOS inhibits classical and alternative complement pathways and reduces neutrophil killing. Iron/zinc scavenging proteins (transferrin-, lactoferrin-, hemoglobin-binding proteins) and IgA1 protease promote survival. Host entry into nonphagocytic cells involves phospholipase C and sphingomyelinase activation with ceramide-mediated apoptosis, and inflammation is driven by LOS and peptidoglycan-induced cytokine release (p.1254-1255).

Gonorrhea is a sexually transmitted infection of the epithelium that commonly presents as cervicitis, urethritis, proctitis, or conjunctivitis; if untreated it can cause local complications including endometritis, salpingitis, tuboovarian abscess, bartholinitis, peritonitis, and perihepatitis in women, and periurethritis and epididymitis in men (p.1253).
Quinolone-containing regimens and cefixime are no longer recommended as first-line treatment in the United States because of widespread quinolone resistance and rising cefixime MICs (p.1259).
Because co-infection with C. trachomatis occurs frequently, concurrent treatment for chlamydia (doxycycline) is recommended whenever chlamydial infection cannot be excluded (p.1259).

In men, acute urethritis is the most common manifestation, typically after a 2-7 day incubation, with discharge that is initially scant and mucoid but becomes profuse and purulent within a day or two; however, a reservoir of infected men remains asymptomatic (p.1255).

About half of women infected with N. gonorrhoeae develop symptoms; many have only minor symptoms (scant cervical discharge, dysuria) and may delay care, so the asymptomatic/minimally symptomatic reservoir is key to ongoing transmission (p.1256).

Gram stain of urethral exudate showing gram-negative intracellular monococci and diplococci is highly specific and sensitive in symptomatic men, but is only about 50% sensitive for gonococcal cervicitis, so women should be diagnosed by culture or a nonculture (NAAT) method (p.1257).

Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) are now widely used, are more sensitive than culture for both N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis, allow urine and self-collected vaginal swab testing, and simultaneously detect chlamydial co-infection (p.1257).

Disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) results from gonococcal bacteremia and most commonly presents as an arthritis-dermatitis syndrome with fever, chills, tenosynovitis, polyarthralgias, and characteristic skin lesions (papules/pustules with a hemorrhagic component, ~5-40, on the extremities) seen in about 75% of patients (p.1257).
Menstruation is a risk factor for dissemination and roughly two-thirds of DGI cases occur in women; in about half of affected women symptoms begin within 7 days of onset of menses (p.1257).

Persons deficient in terminal complement components (C5-C9) and those receiving the C5-blocking monoclonal antibody eculizumab are predisposed to recurrent neisserial bacteremia; anyone with more than one episode of DGI should be screened for complement deficiency (p.1255, 1260).

Ceftriaxone is the recommended first-line agent for uncomplicated gonococcal infection, now at twice the previously recommended dose because mean inhibitory concentrations of current strains have doubled relative to 20 years ago (p.1259).

Because co-infection with C. trachomatis is frequent, treatment of gonorrhea must include concurrent therapy for chlamydia (doxycycline) whenever chlamydial infection cannot be excluded - omitting this is a key pitfall (p.1259).
Azithromycin is no longer recommended as part of the first-line regimen because U.S. gonococcal resistance to azithromycin rose more than sevenfold to 4.7% in 2021 (p.1259).
A presumptive diagnosis of gonorrhea cannot be made from gram-negative diplococci on a pharyngeal Gram stain, because commensal Neisseria species are normal pharyngeal flora (p.1257).
Gram stain is only ~50% sensitive for gonococcal cervicitis; relying on it in women risks missed diagnoses, so culture or NAAT is required (p.1257).
DGI strains often do not incite a local genital inflammatory response and may not cause genital symptoms, so disseminated disease can occur without an obvious mucosal source (p.1254, 1257).
Quinolones and cefixime are no longer first-line in the United States due to resistance and rising MICs - using them empirically risks treatment failure (p.1259).

Persistent symptoms after a recommended regimen should prompt evaluation for reinfection, a drug-resistant strain, or an alternative diagnosis rather than simple re-treatment; culture and susceptibility testing should be performed (p.1259).
Because of high reinfection rates within 6-12 months, persons treated for gonorrhea should be retested at 3 months (p.1259).

A single recommended ceftriaxone regimen almost always cures uncomplicated urethral, cervical, rectal, or pharyngeal infection, and true treatment failure with a recommended regimen is rare. Symptomatic pharyngeal gonorrhea is harder to eradicate than genital infection. In the preantibiotic era untreated urethritis persisted about 8 weeks. DGI incidence has fallen (from ~0.5-3% of untreated mucosal infections in the 1970s) likely due to a decline in disseminating strains. A dramatic alleviation of arthritis-dermatitis symptoms within 12-24 h of appropriate antibiotics supports a clinical diagnosis of DGI even when cultures are negative. Rising worldwide resistance, including reduced ceftriaxone susceptibility, threatens future treatment efficacy (p.1257-1260).
Disseminated gonococcal infection with the joint-localized suppurative arthritis stage - hospitalization indicated, may need joint aspiration and higher/longer therapy (p.1259)
Gonococcal meningitis - rare complication of DGI requiring high-dose IV ceftriaxone for 10-14 days (p.1257, 1260)
Gonococcal endocarditis - rare today but historically accounted for about one-quarter of endocarditis cases; requires at least 4 weeks of IV therapy (p.1257, 1260)
Ophthalmia neonatorum and adult ocular gonorrhea - prompt recognition and treatment essential, as corneal ulceration may progress to perforation, panophthalmitis and blindness (p.1256-1257)
Pelvic inflammatory disease should be considered when cervical infection extends to cause dyspareunia or lower abdominal/back pain (p.1256)

Clinical manifestations span uncomplicated mucosal infection (urethritis, cervicitis, proctitis, pharyngitis, conjunctivitis) versus complicated/disseminated disease. DGI has historically been described in two overlapping stages: a bacteremic stage (higher fever, chills, polyarthralgias, tenosynovitis, and skin lesions) and a joint-localized stage with suppurative (septic) arthritis, though a clear-cut progression is usually not evident (p.1257).

Palindromic rheumatism
Psoriatic arthritis

Acute septic arthritis can closely resemble an acute crystal flare, and bacterial infection can coexist with MSU or CPP crystals in synovial fluid, so joint fluid should be Gram-stained and cultured
Acute flares with overlying erythema, warmth, and swelling can mimic cellulitis (pseudocellulitis)
Synovial fluid aspiration with polarized light microscopy to identify and distinguish crystal type (MSU vs CPP); apatite is not identifiable by polarized light alone

Serum urate (interpreting with awareness it may be transiently normal during a flare)

Plain radiography (erosions with overhanging margins in gout; chondrocalcinosis in CPPD; periarticular calcification in apatite disease)
Musculoskeletal ultrasound (double-contour sign) and dual-energy CT for MSU detection

In CPPD patients under 50: serum calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, magnesium, iron, and transferrin, plus screening for familial aggregation and metabolic disease (hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypophosphatasia, hypomagnesemia)
Serum creatinine, liver function tests, hemoglobin, WBC count, HbA1c, and lipids at baseline to assess comorbidities and treatment risk

Chronic hyperuricemia is a prerequisite for gout but not sufficient alone, since only a minority of hyperuricemic individuals ever develop disease. Humans uniquely develop gout spontaneously because of an evolutionary species-wide loss of uricase, the enzyme that converts urate to highly soluble allantoin; at physiologic pH uric acid (pKa about 5.8) exists mainly as ionized urate. An increased urate body pool leads to MSU supersaturation (favored above roughly 6.85 mg/dL) and crystal formation/deposition in joints and connective tissue, modulated by temperature, pH, intra-articular dehydration, cation concentration, and matrix proteoglycans/collagen. Hyperuricemia stems predominantly from impaired renal excretion (about 90%) and less often overproduction (about 10%); overproduction relates to increased cell turnover (hematologic malignancy, psoriasis), chemotherapy, tissue hypoxia, or inherited defects such as PRPP synthetase superactivity or HPRT deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan spectrum). Renal handling involves sodium-dependent apical reabsorption via URAT1/OAT10, basolateral GLUT9 efflux, and intestinal excretion via ABCG2. Acute flares are triggered when MSU crystals are shed from inert deposits and activate resident synovial macrophages, mast cells, and the NLRP3 inflammasome, generating IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-alpha; neutrophil phagocytosis of crystals amplifies inflammation via a respiratory burst. Untreated, growing tophaceous MSU deposits with granulomatous inflammation produce chronic gouty arthritis with erosive deformity. In CPPD, increased cartilage inorganic pyrophosphate (largely from extracellular ATP breakdown, regulated by the ANKH transporter) combines with calcium to form CPP crystals that, like MSU, activate phagocytes and the inflammasome. Apatite deposition occurs in tissue damage (dystrophic), hypercalcemic/hyperparathyroid states (metastatic), connective tissue disease (calcinosis), and chronic renal failure (tumoral calcinosis, calciphylaxis). CaOx deposits accumulate in cartilage, synovium, bone, and viscera in chronic renal failure and primary oxalosis (Harrison 22e p.2956-2962).

Gout is a hyperuricemic metabolic disorder in which chronic hyperuricemia leads to supersaturation and deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in joints and connective tissue; it typically presents with episodic, intensely painful inflammatory arthritis in middle-aged-to-elderly men and postmenopausal women (Harrison 22e p.2956-2957).

Chondrocalcinosis (punctate/linear radiodense deposits in fibrocartilage or hyaline cartilage) supports CPPD; definitive diagnosis requires rhomboid or rod-shaped weakly positively birefringent or nonbirefringent crystals in synovial fluid or tissue (Harrison 22e p.2961).

Apatite (basic calcium phosphate) crystals are extremely small and individually visible only by electron microscopy; clumps appear as nonbirefringent globules staining bright red with alizarin red S, and apatite underlies the destructive 'Milwaukee shoulder' of the elderly (Harrison 22e p.2961).

Calcium oxalate (CaOx) arthropathy is largely a disease of patients on long-term dialysis, especially with ascorbic acid supplementation, since ascorbate is metabolized to oxalate that is poorly cleared in uremia; the readily recognized crystals are bipyramidal with strong birefringence (Harrison 22e p.2962).

The first metatarsophalangeal joint of the great toe (podagra) is involved in 70-90% of cases; other early targets are tarsal joints, ankles, and knees, while finger, wrist, and elbow involvement is more typical of elderly patients or advanced disease (Harrison 22e p.2958).

Flares often begin at night or in the early morning and are among the most painful conditions humans experience; affected joints rapidly become warm, red, tender, and swollen, sometimes mimicking cellulitis (pseudocellulitis), and usually subside spontaneously within 1-2 weeks (Harrison 22e p.2958).

Definitive diagnosis rests on demonstrating needle-shaped MSU crystals (intracellular and extracellular) showing strong negative birefringence under compensated polarized light; synovial fluid is cloudy with leukocyte counts roughly 5000-75,000/uL (Harrison 22e p.2958-2959).

Serum urate may be normal or even low during an acute flare because inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 are uricosuric and can lower it by about 2 mg/dL, so a normal level during a flare does not exclude gout; historical or postflare values are more diagnostically useful (Harrison 22e p.2959).

Musculoskeletal ultrasound (double-contour sign over articular cartilage) and dual-energy CT (chemical identification of MSU) aid early diagnosis; plain radiographs in advanced tophaceous gout show well-defined erosions with sclerotic, overhanging margins and soft-tissue masses, though these are absent early (Harrison 22e p.2959).

Hyperuricemia is most often due to impaired renal urate excretion (about 90%) rather than overproduction (about 10%); roughly two-thirds of daily uric acid is eliminated renally and one-third through the gut (intestinal uricolysis by gut bacteria) (Harrison 22e p.2957).

Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD) is strongly age-related, with prevalence in articular tissues roughly doubling each decade after 60 and reaching nearly 50% in those over 85; most deposition is asymptomatic (Harrison 22e p.2960).

Acute CPP crystal arthritis (pseudogout) most often affects the knee, then the wrist, and rarely the first MTP joint; episodes tend to last longer than gout flares (weeks to months) and may be accompanied by fever, chills, and elevated acute-phase reactants (Harrison 22e p.2960).
Assuming a normal serum urate during an acute attack excludes gout; cytokine-mediated uricosuria (e.g., IL-6) can lower it by about 2 mg/dL during flares
Failing to exclude infection: bacterial sepsis can coexist with crystals, and crystals do not rule out a septic joint
Relying on polarized light microscopy to detect apatite, whose individual crystals require electron microscopy and special stains/techniques
Overlooking a secondary metabolic cause when CPPD presents before age 50
Confusing intra-/periarticular apatite calcifications with the linear calcifications of CPPD on radiographs
Diagnosing chondrocalcinosis as CPPD without considering calcium oxalate deposition in chronic renal failure as an alternative

Typical acute gout flares are self-limited, resolving spontaneously within 1-2 weeks, with symptom-free intercritical intervals; however, untreated recurrent flares over years can progress to chronic gouty arthritis with persistent low-grade synovitis, subcutaneous tophi, deformity, and erosive bony destruction. Gout is associated with multiple cardiometabolic-kidney comorbidities (obesity, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, myocardial infarction, stroke, chronic kidney disease, urate nephrolithiasis). Apatite-associated destructive arthropathy (e.g., Milwaukee shoulder) tends to progress indolently but can cause severe pain, instability, and disability requiring joint replacement, and CaOx and chronic CPP arthropathies may progressively destroy joints (Harrison 22e p.2956-2962).
Acutely hot, swollen joint where septic arthritis cannot be excluded clinically, mandating synovial fluid Gram stain and culture
Fever, chills, and elevated acute-phase reactants during a crystal flare (seen in up to 50% of acute CPPD episodes, occasionally to 40 C), which overlap with infection
Hyperuricemia in prepubertal boys, which should prompt evaluation for inherited enzyme defects (HPRT deficiency, PRPP synthetase superactivity)
CPPD arthritis in patients under 50, raising concern for an underlying metabolic disorder (e.g., hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypophosphatasia, hypomagnesemia)
Progressive destructive large-joint disease (e.g., Milwaukee shoulder) signaling severe apatite-associated joint destruction

Gout is described as a clinical continuum rather than by a formal grading scale: asymptomatic hyperuricemia; acute (episodic) gout flares with intercritical symptom-free intervals; and chronic (tophaceous) gouty arthritis with persistent synovitis, tophi, deformity, and bony destruction. Crystal-induced disease is categorized by pattern as acute (episodic) mono-, oligo-, or polyarthritis; periarticular inflammation (bursitis, tendinitis, enthesitis); tophaceous deposits; chronic destructive or chronic inflammatory arthropathy; a peculiar osteoarthritis-like form; spinal arthritis; and carpal tunnel syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2956-2957).

Normal intrauterine or ectopic pregnancy versus molar pregnancy

Dysfunctional or anovulatory uterine bleeding versus endometrial carcinoma
Pelvic inflammatory disease / tubo-ovarian abscess mimicking an adnexal malignancy
HPV-related cervicitis or low-grade transient HPV infection mimicking high-grade cervical dysplasia
Serum CA-125 (and HE-4, mesothelin) for ovarian cancer; trends used to monitor relapse
Transvaginal/pelvic ultrasonography to characterize adnexal masses; CT for carcinomatosis and adenopathy
Serum and serial beta-hCG (and AFP) for germ cell and gestational trophoblastic tumors
Pap (cytology) smear plus HPV PCR testing for cervical screening
Endometrial biopsy for postmenopausal or abnormal bleeding
MRI for cervical uterine/paracervical extension; CT for hydronephrosis
Germline BRCA1/2 and Lynch syndrome (MSH2, MLH1, MSH6, PMS1, PMS2) testing; tumor microsatellite instability and homologous recombination deficiency testing

Ovarian cancer arises from epithelial, stromal/sex-cord, or germ cell lineages; high-grade (type 2) serous cancers begin in fallopian tube epithelium with BRCA1/2 loss and TP53 mutation producing intraepithelial cancer, then shed and disseminate across the peritoneum aided by MUC16 expression and mesothelin binding, whereas indolent type 1 cancers carry KRAS/BRAF/PTEN/PIK3CA mutations. Cervical cancer follows persistent high-risk HPV infection near the cervical transformation zone, where viral E6/E7 inactivate p53 and RB to immortalize epithelium; HPV genome integration plus APOBEC-pattern mutagenesis and further hits drive progression from dysplasia to invasive squamous cell carcinoma or adenocarcinoma. Endometrial type 1 (endometrioid) cancers are driven by relative estrogen excess unopposed by progesterone, with secondary PI3K mutation or PTEN loss; type 2 (serous, clear cell) cancers show TP53 loss and behave like high-grade serous ovarian cancer. Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia results from outgrowth/persistence of placental trophoblast, with complete moles being androgenetic diploid tumors and partial moles triploid.

Epithelial tumors are the most common ovarian neoplasm; ovarian cancers are split into indolent type 1 (low-grade, KRAS/BRAF/PTEN/PIK3CA mutations) and aggressive type 2 high-grade serous cancers, the latter driven by TP53 loss (about 95%) and BRCA1/2 dysfunction, with growing evidence that many high-grade serous cancers actually originate in the fallopian tube epithelium.

Gestational trophoblastic disease spans benign hydatidiform mole to choriocarcinoma; complete moles are diploid with entirely paternal genetic material (uniparental disomy, no fetal development), while partial moles are triploid (egg fertilized by two sperm) and may show early fetal development.
Trophoblastic disease is exquisitely chemosensitive and monitored by serial serum beta-hCG; even very advanced disease is almost uniformly curable when managed by an expert.

Gardasil-9 protects against HPV types 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58; vaccination before sexual activity dramatically lowers high-risk infection and dysplasia, but vaccinated women remain at residual risk and still need Pap screening.

Germline BRCA1/2 testing is recommended for all incident epithelial ovarian cancers; lifetime ovarian cancer risk is roughly 39 to 63 percent for BRCA1 and 16.5 to 27 percent for BRCA2, and risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy after childbearing (ideally before age 40) is highly protective and also lowers subsequent breast cancer risk by about 50 percent.
About 70 percent of ovarian cancer patients present at stage III; a markedly elevated serum CA-125 (shed MUC16) is characteristic but not specific, and PET is generally not required for evaluation.

Bilateral ovarian masses from metastatic mucin-secreting gastrointestinal cancers are termed Krukenberg tumors; metastatic disease to the ovary also arises from colon, appendix, stomach, and breast primaries, so other malignancies must be considered in the workup.

High-risk HPV infection (especially types 16 and 18, also 31, 33, 35, 52, 58) is the primary initiating event in the vast majority of invasive cervical cancers; viral E6 and E7 proteins inactivate p53 and RB respectively, but full transformation requires additional acquired mutations over years.

Cervical cancer staging is fundamentally clinical: stage I confined to cervix, stage II into upper vagina/paracervical tissue, stage III to lower vagina or pelvic sidewall, stage IV invading bladder/rectum or distant; MRI better estimates uterine and paracervical soft-tissue extension while CT detects hydronephrosis indicating sidewall disease.

Endometrioid endometrial adenocarcinoma is the most common gynecologic malignancy in the United States; unopposed estrogen exposure is the principal risk factor, so obesity, postmenopausal estrogen therapy, estrogen-producing tumors, and tamoxifen (weakly estrogenic in uterine epithelium) all increase risk while progestins are protective.

Most women with uterine corpus cancer present with postmenopausal bleeding (or atypical intermenstrual bleeding premenopausally), leading to early-stage detection and high cure rates; about 75 percent are stage I.

Routine microsatellite instability (MSI) testing of all endometrial cancers is now standard, because MSI/mismatch-repair-deficient tumors that recur or present advanced are likely to respond to PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint therapy.
Nonspecific GI symptoms (bloating, early satiety, change in bowel/urinary pattern) of ovarian cancer are frequently dismissed until late stages
Needle biopsy of an adnexal mass is contraindicated because it risks seeding malignant cells into the peritoneal cavity
HPV-negative cervical cancers (more common in older women, with KRAS/ARID1A/PTEN mutations) may behave differently
Endocervical canal or glandular cervical lesions may be invisible on inspection and missed by Pap smear
Adding HPV PCR increases sensitivity but lowers specificity, flagging many transient infections needing no intervention
Minimally invasive surgery for early cervical cancer gives inferior outcomes compared with open hysterectomy
Suboptimally debulked ovarian cancer (residual >1 cm) derives very little benefit from surgery
Late relapse (>2 years) of germ cell tumors tends to be chemoresistant and is best approached surgically

Ovarian epithelial cancer 5-year survival correlates strongly with stage: roughly 90 to 95 percent stage I, 70 to 80 percent stage II, 25 to 40 percent stage III, and 10 to 15 percent stage IV; prognosis improves with lower histologic grade and BRCA1/2 germline mutation, and complete (R0) cytoreduction yields median survival beyond 60 months versus 28 to 42 months with macroscopic residual disease. Endometrial cancer is usually localized (about 75 percent stage I) with high cure; cervical cancer 5-year survival declines from about 85 percent (stage I) to roughly 7 percent (stage IV). Borderline (low malignant potential) ovarian tumors and ovarian germ cell tumors (including dysgerminoma) are highly curable. Gestational trophoblastic disease is almost uniformly curable, with single-agent therapy curing about 90 percent of low-risk cases.
Rapidly increasing abdominal girth from ascites with nausea, early satiety, bloating, and abdominal pain suggesting advanced ovarian cancer
Postmenopausal vaginal bleeding (must exclude endometrial carcinoma)
Postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding or foul/persistent discharge suggesting cervical cancer
Flank pain/hydronephrosis or sacral/pelvic nerve pain indicating advanced cervical pelvic sidewall disease
Persistent or rising beta-hCG after molar evacuation indicating persistent gestational trophoblastic disease
Preeclampsia/eclampsia, hyperthyroidism, or very high beta-hCG in pregnancy raising concern for molar pregnancy
Acute pelvic pain from ovarian torsion, intratumoral hemorrhage, or rupture

Staging per Table 94-1: Ovarian - I confined to ovary (88-95%), II confined to pelvic organs (70-80%), III intra-abdominal spread to omentum/diaphragm/nodes (20-40%), IV spread outside abdominal cavity/parenchymal/pleural (10-20%); most present as stage IIIC (bulky intraperitoneal or positive nodes). Endometrial - I confined to corpus (>90%), II corpus and cervix (~75%), III outside uterus but within true pelvis (45-60%), IV beyond true pelvis or bladder/rectum (~20%). Cervix - 0 carcinoma in situ (100%), I confined to uterus (85%), II beyond uterus not to pelvic wall (65%), III to pelvic wall and/or lower third vagina or hydronephrosis (35%), IV invading bladder/rectal mucosa or beyond true pelvis (7%). Gestational trophoblastic disease is risk-stratified (low/intermediate/high) by scoring algorithms guiding single- versus multiagent therapy.

Other clotting factor deficiencies (e.g. factor XI)
Vitamin K deficiency or liver disease
Disseminated intravascular coagulation
Platelet function disorders or thrombocytopenia
Non-accidental injury when bruising pattern is unexplained
aPTT, prothrombin time, and platelet count as initial screen
Specific factor VIII and factor IX activity assays
Mixing study to demonstrate factor deficiency versus inhibitor
Inhibitor (Bethesda) assay when replacement therapy is failing
Von Willebrand factor studies to exclude von Willebrand disease
Genetic testing for carrier detection and prenatal diagnosis

Deficiency of factor VIII or factor IX impairs the intrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade, reducing generation of activated factor X and thereby the thrombin burst required for a stable fibrin clot. Primary haemostasis (platelet plug formation) is intact, so initial bleeding may stop, but the fibrin clot is inadequate and delayed or recurrent bleeding follows, characteristically into joints and muscles. Repeated haemarthroses cause iron deposition, synovial hypertrophy, and cartilage destruction leading to chronic arthropathy.
An X-linked recessive bleeding disorder affecting mainly males; haemophilia A results from factor VIII deficiency and haemophilia B from factor IX deficiency.
The two types are clinically indistinguishable and are separated by specific factor assays.
Disease severity correlates with residual factor activity: severe disease often presents with spontaneous bleeding, while milder forms bleed mainly after trauma or surgery.
Hallmark manifestations are deep bleeding into joints (haemarthrosis) and muscles rather than mucocutaneous bleeding.
Screening typically shows a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) with a normal prothrombin time and platelet count.
Recurrent joint bleeds lead to chronic synovitis and progressive haemophilic arthropathy if not prevented.
Management centres on replacing the deficient clotting factor, with prophylactic regimens preventing bleeds in severe disease and on-demand treatment for acute bleeds.
Development of inhibitory antibodies against the replaced factor is a major complication that reduces treatment efficacy.
Intracranial haemorrhage is a life-threatening event that warrants immediate factor replacement, and newer therapies such as non-factor agents and gene therapy are changing management.
Delaying factor replacement while awaiting imaging in suspected serious bleeding
Attributing bleeding solely to trauma and missing an underlying disorder
Using aspirin or NSAIDs and intramuscular injections that increase bleeding risk
Overlooking inhibitor development when a previously effective factor dose stops working

With modern factor replacement and prophylaxis, life expectancy and quality of life approach normal; outcomes worsen with inhibitor development, chronic arthropathy, and delayed treatment of major bleeds.
Suspected intracranial haemorrhage (headache, vomiting, altered consciousness, focal signs)
Bleeding into the neck, throat, or retroperitoneum threatening the airway or causing large occult loss
Compartment syndrome from muscle bleeding
Poor response to factor replacement suggesting an inhibitor
Significant bleeding after trauma or before surgery without prophylaxis

For H. ducreyi cutaneous ulcers: yaws (Treponema pallidum subsp. pertenue)

Culture from a normally sterile site (blood, CSF, joint, pleural, pericardial fluid, or subdural effusion) is the most reliable means of diagnosing invasive H. influenzae and is needed for susceptibility testing
Gram stain of CSF showing gram-negative coccobacilli supports Hib meningitis; predominant gram-negative coccobacilli among abundant neutrophils in sputum suggests nontypeable H. influenzae pneumonia
PCR and other DNA-based detection methods, now common in clinical labs
Genotypic markers (16S rRNA, superoxide dismutase, outer-membrane protein P6, protein D, fuculose kinase) and whole-genome sequencing to distinguish H. influenzae from H. haemolyticus
Pneumatic otoscopy detects middle-ear fluid; tympanocentesis with culture gives etiologic diagnosis of otitis media but is not routine

For chancroid: culture of H. ducreyi (requires selective/supplemented media) from the lesion or node aspirate, and PCR; dark-field exam and syphilis serology to exclude T. pallidum and HSV testing of exudate

Hib strains produce systemic disease by invading the respiratory mucosa and spreading hematogenously to distant sites such as meninges, bones, and joints; the type b polysaccharide capsule (ribosyl-ribitol phosphate) is a key virulence factor that resists opsonization. Nontypeable strains lack a capsule and cause disease by local mucosal invasion (e.g., otitis media via the eustachian tube, lower respiratory infection in COPD), persisting in airways both extracellularly and intracellularly and forming biofilms in the middle ear that resist host clearance and antibiotics; they vary expression of virulence genes by slipped-strand mispairing and phase-variable DNA methylases. M. catarrhalis colonizes the upper airway and infects by contiguous spread, often following a viral upper respiratory infection (e.g., rhinovirus promotes adhesion); it uses multiple adhesins, invades several cell types with an intracellular lymphoid reservoir, and sheds outer-membrane vesicles that deliver beta-lactamase and induce inflammation, potentially protecting co-pathogens such as group A streptococci and H. influenzae. H. ducreyi infects through an epithelial break during sexual contact, producing ulcers with predominantly T-cell infiltrate.
H. influenzae is a small, pleomorphic gram-negative coccobacillus that often stains only faintly with safranin in CSF and sputum, so it is easily overlooked on Gram stain.

Moraxella catarrhalis is an unencapsulated gram-negative diplococcus of the respiratory tract; its colonies can be slid intact across the agar surface (the hockey puck sign) and turn pink after 48 h, distinguishing them from commensal Neisseria.

M. catarrhalis is the second most common bacterial cause of COPD exacerbations after H. influenzae and accounts for roughly 15-20 percent of acute otitis media cases by middle-ear culture (30-50 percent by molecular detection).

Haemophilus ducreyi causes chancroid, a painful genital ulcer disease; prior chancroid does not confer protection, and H. ducreyi is also an important cause of non-sexually transmitted cutaneous ulcers in children in the South Pacific and Africa.

Aerobic growth of H. influenzae requires both hemin (X factor) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (V factor) and needs preheated blood, so it grows on chocolate agar but not on ordinary (unheated) blood agar.

Six capsular serotypes (a-f) exist plus unencapsulated nontypeable strains; type b (Hib) and nontypeable strains are the most clinically important, with Hib being invasive (hematogenous spread) and nontypeable being primarily mucosal pathogens.

Maternally acquired anticapsular (anti-PRP) antibody declines from birth to about 6 months; the antibody nadir corresponds to the peak age of type b disease, and systemic Hib disease is unusual after age 6 owing to acquired protective antibody.

Hib meningitis primarily affects children under 2 years; subdural effusion is the most common complication and should be suspected when seizures, hemiparesis, or persistent obtundation follow 2-3 days of appropriate therapy.

Hib epiglottitis is a life-threatening cellulitis of the epiglottis and supraglottic tissues occurring in an older age group (2-7 years) than other Hib infections; in countries with childhood Hib vaccination it now occurs mainly in adults.
Nontypeable H. influenzae is the most common bacterial cause of COPD exacerbations and, in recent years, has caused community-acquired pneumonia more frequently than S. pneumoniae.

Nontypeable H. influenzae is one of the three most common causes of childhood otitis media (with S. pneumoniae and M. catarrhalis); clinical clues include recurrent episodes, treatment failure, concomitant conjunctivitis, and bilateral disease.

Invasive nontypeable strains causing neonatal/puerperal sepsis after colonizing the female genital tract have been provisionally named Haemophilus quentini (related to but distinct from H. haemolyticus).
H. influenzae may be missed on Gram stain because it stains only faintly with safranin in CSF and sputum.
Ordinary (unheated) blood agar fails to grow H. influenzae, which can lead to false-negative cultures if chocolate agar is not used.
Distinguishing H. influenzae from the commensal H. haemolyticus is difficult because they share growth requirements and many H. haemolyticus isolates are now nonhemolytic.
M. catarrhalis has historically been overlooked as a pathogen because its colonies resemble those of commensal Neisseria species on respiratory cultures.

Approximately 30-40 percent of nontypeable H. influenzae produce beta-lactamase (conferring ampicillin/amoxicillin resistance), and a second mechanism, altered penicillin-binding proteins (beta-lactamase-negative ampicillin-resistant strains), is increasing in Europe and common in Japan.
Over 90 percent of M. catarrhalis strains now produce beta-lactamase and are resistant to amoxicillin; macrolide and fluoroquinolone resistance is emerging, notably in Asia.
Clinical diagnosis of chancroid is often inaccurate, so laboratory confirmation should be attempted; in HIV-positive patients apparent treatment failure may reflect HSV co-infection.
Isolation of M. catarrhalis from expectorated sputum during an exacerbation is suggestive but not diagnostic of it as the cause.

The overall mortality of Hib meningitis is about 5 percent with a high morbidity rate; about 6 percent of survivors have permanent sensorineural hearing loss, roughly one-fourth have a significant disability, and up to half have some neurologic sequela such as partial hearing loss or delayed language development when sought carefully. Hib epiglottitis is life-threatening due to risk of acute upper-airway obstruction. Glucocorticoids reduce the incidence of neurologic sequelae in Hib meningitis. Nontypeable strains tend to cause recurrent otitis media and recurrent COPD exacerbations because immunity is strain-specific. M. catarrhalis otitis media and exacerbations are clinically milder (less fever, less red bulging tympanic membrane) than pneumococcal disease, and invasive M. catarrhalis infection is rare. Repeated H. ducreyi infections can occur because infection confers no protection; in HIV-positive patients chancroid healing may be slow and require longer therapy.
Sore throat and fever rapidly progressing to dysphagia, drooling, and airway obstruction (epiglottitis) - a medical emergency requiring airway maintenance
Fever with altered CNS function and nuchal rigidity (which may be absent) in a young child suggesting Hib meningitis
Seizures, hemiparesis, or persistent obtundation after 2-3 days of appropriate antibiotics, suggesting subdural effusion
Underlying immunosuppression, HIV, cardiopulmonary disease, alcoholism, or cancer in a patient with H. influenzae bacteremia

Salivary gland tumors (mucoepidermoid, adenoid cystic carcinoma, adenocarcinoma)
Sarcoma, including radiation therapy-induced sarcoma after prior radiotherapy
Metastasis to supraclavicular nodes from a primary site in the chest or abdomen
Thorough otolaryngologic examination including inspection of all visible mucosal surfaces and palpation of the floor of mouth, tongue, and neck
CT or MRI of the head and neck to define disease extent (comparably accurate, 65-90%, for cervical nodal metastases)
CT of chest and upper abdomen for patients with lymph node involvement to screen for distant metastases; chest CT also screens for second lung primary in heavy smokers
PET scan to identify or exclude distant metastases and assess treatment response
Endoscopic examination under anesthesia (panendoscopy) with multiple biopsies
Fine-needle aspiration or excisional lymph node biopsy when no primary is visible
