TNM staging per AJCC (varies by anatomic subsite)
Premalignant mucosal lesions (leukoplakia, erythroplakia) representing hyperplasia, dysplasia, or carcinoma in situ

Squamous cell carcinomas arise from the mucosal surfaces of the upper aerodigestive tract. The entire pharyngeal mucosa is exposed to alcohol- and tobacco-related carcinogens, producing field cancerization with risk of premalignant lesions (erythroplakia, leukoplakia) progressing through hyperplasia, dysplasia, and carcinoma in situ to invasive carcinoma. In HPV-negative tumors, p53 mutations are frequent along with mitotic-signaling and Notch pathway alterations and dysregulated cell-cycle control. HPV oncogenes drive carcinogenesis by directly inhibiting the p53 and RB tumor-suppressor genes; HPV-positive tumors carry a distinct mutational signature with frequent PI3K pathway alteration. EGFR is frequently overexpressed and correlates with poor prognosis. EBV is associated with undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma (lymphoepithelioma) (Harrison 22e p.610-611).
Most head and neck cancers are squamous cell carcinomas arising from the mucosal surfaces of the paranasal sinuses, oral cavity, nasopharynx, oropharynx, hypopharynx, and larynx (Harrison 22e p.610).
Alcohol and tobacco are the most significant environmental risk factors and act synergistically when used together; smokeless tobacco is an etiologic agent for oral cancers (Harrison 22e p.610).

In Western countries, HPV (predominantly HPV-16) causes over 50% of oropharyngeal cancers (tonsillar bed and base of tongue); these occur in younger patients and carry a better prognosis, especially in nonsmokers (Harrison 22e p.610-611).

EBV infection is frequently associated with nasopharyngeal cancer, especially in endemic areas (East Asia, some Mediterranean countries); EBV antibody titers can be used to screen high-risk populations (Harrison 22e p.610).

HPV testing should be performed at diagnosis for all patients with oropharyngeal tumors; HPV-related disease has a more favorable AJCC 8th-edition staging (advanced nodal stage can still be equivalent to overall early stage) (Harrison 22e p.611-613).

Panendoscopy under anesthesia (laryngoscopy, esophagoscopy, bronchoscopy) with multiple directed biopsies is the definitive staging procedure to establish diagnosis, define extent, and identify second primaries (Harrison 22e p.611).

When a head and neck lesion treated initially with antibiotics does not resolve in a short period, further workup is indicated; simply continuing antibiotics may lose the chance for early diagnosis of a malignancy (Harrison 22e p.611).

For an enlarged cervical node with no visible primary, diagnose by fine-needle aspiration or lymph node excision; if squamous cell carcinoma, perform panendoscopy with directed biopsies of nasopharynx, tonsil, tongue base, and pyriform sinus (Harrison 22e p.611-612).

Most parotid tumors are benign, but about half of submandibular and sublingual tumors and most minor salivary gland tumors are malignant; adenoid cystic carcinoma tends to recur along nerve tracks and metastasize as late as 10-20 years (Harrison 22e p.610-611, 613).
Continuing antibiotic treatment for a non-resolving head and neck lesion rather than pursuing workup may delay diagnosis of malignancy (Harrison 22e p.611).

Fine-needle aspiration should not be the first diagnostic procedure for a suspicious cervical node when a head and neck primary is suspected; perform a careful ENT exam and biopsy any suspicious mucosal lesion first (Harrison 22e p.4012-type cross-reference, p.611).

EGFR overexpression does not reliably predict response to EGFR inhibitors (active in only ~10-15% as single agents); substituting cetuximab for cisplatin in HPV-related cancers has shown inferior survival (Harrison 22e p.611, 613).
Retinoid supplements (e.g., cis-retinoic acid) have not been shown to prevent head and neck (or lung) cancer and may increase risk in active smokers (Harrison 22e p.610).
About 50% of patients develop hypothyroidism after treatment; thyroid function should be monitored (Harrison 22e p.613).

Poorly differentiated tumors have a worse prognosis than well-differentiated tumors. Overt distant metastases are present in <10% at diagnosis. HPV-related oropharyngeal cancers consistently carry a better prognosis (reflected in a separate, more favorable AJCC 8th-edition staging system), especially in nonsmokers. For localized disease (about one-third of patients), overall 5-year survival is 60-90%, with most recurrences occurring within the first 2 years and usually local. For locally/regionally advanced disease (>50% of patients at presentation), 5-year survival exceeds 50% in many trials (partly due to the increasing fraction of HPV-related tumors); advanced nasopharyngeal cancer treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by concomitant chemoradiotherapy has achieved 5-year survival exceeding 80% in a Southeast Asian study. Patients cured of early-stage tobacco/alcohol-related disease are at greater risk of dying from a second malignancy than from recurrence of the primary (Harrison 22e p.611-613).

Clinically categorized into three groups: (1) localized disease (T1-T2 / stage I-II without nodal or distant spread), (2) locally or regionally advanced disease (large primary and/or cervical nodal metastases, lymph-node positive), and (3) recurrent and/or metastatic disease below the neck. chunks.text: HFrEF is a progressive disease in which an index injury (e.g. acute MI, chronic pressure/volume overload, genetic or congenital disease) triggers months-to-years of structural and functional cardiovascular remodelling; patients may stay asymptomatic for long periods because compensatory mechanisms are activated that ultimately drive further deterioration. Pressure overload produces concentric hypertrophy and volume overload produces eccentric (dilated) hypertrophy, accompanied by myocyte hypertrophy, interstitial fibrosis, apoptosis and re-expression of fetal genes. Sustained activation of the sympathetic nervous system and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system initially supports cardiac output but becomes maladaptive, causing excessive vasoconstriction, sodium/water retention, electrolyte and renal disturbance, direct myocardial toxicity and arrhythmias; counter-regulatory natriuretic peptides, prostaglandins, bradykinin and nitric oxide are upregulated but inadequate. Therapies that antagonise RAAS and the sympathetic system (RAAS inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, beta blockers) attenuate or reverse remodelling and improve outcomes. Secondary mitral regurgitation arises from ventricular dilatation, sphericity and annular changes, perpetuating a vicious cycle. HFpEF reflects multiple mechanisms beyond diastolic dysfunction (impaired calcium reuptake, vascular stiffness, renal dysfunction, sodium avidity, inflammation related to adiposity, oxidative/nitrosative stress, insulin resistance). The cardiorenal syndrome is driven not only by low forward flow but importantly by systemic venous congestion and raised intra-abdominal/splanchnic pressure, so relief of congestion improves renal function (p.1977-1982).

HFrEF is a progressive disorder in which an index event (acute myocardial infarction, chronic pressure or volume overload, inherited or congenital disease) is followed by months to years of cardiovascular remodeling. Concentric hypertrophy reduces wall stress in pressure overload, while eccentric hypertrophy (chamber dilation) occurs in volume overload; remodeling involves myocyte hypertrophy, interstitial fibrosis, altered calcium handling, fetal gene reexpression, necrosis, apoptosis, and autophagy. Maladaptive activation of the sympathetic nervous system and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system initially supports cardiac output but ultimately produces excessive vasoconstriction, volume retention, electrolyte and renal abnormalities, baroreceptor dysfunction, direct myocardial toxicity, and arrhythmias, with antagonism of these systems shown to attenuate or reverse remodeling and reduce mortality. Counterregulatory vasodilatory hormones (ANP, BNP, prostaglandins, bradykinin, adrenomedullin, nitric oxide) are upregulated; neprilysin inactivates natriuretic peptides and bradykinin, the rationale for angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibition. Endothelin, inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6), and reactive oxygen species contribute to remodeling, and the cardiorenal syndrome reflects both reduced forward flow and systemic venous/abdominal congestion. HFpEF pathophysiology is less defined and involves diastolic dysfunction together with vascular stiffness, renal dysfunction, sodium avidity, comorbidity-driven microvascular inflammation, and impaired nitric oxide/cGMP/protein kinase G signaling causing myocardial stiffening (Harrison 22e p.1978-1982, 1989).

Management is driven by clinical phenotype and by left ventricular ejection fraction: HFrEF (LVEF <=40%), HFmrEF (41-49%), and HFpEF (>=50%); the older terms systolic and diastolic heart failure have been abandoned because most patients have both systolic and diastolic abnormalities (Harrison 22e p.1987, 1978).

Approximately one-half of patients with HF have reduced EF and one-half have preserved or mildly reduced EF; classifying by EF matters because of differences in demographics, comorbidities, and treatment response (Harrison 22e p.1978).

Acute heart failure (formerly acute decompensated HF) refers to rapid onset or worsening of symptoms; most episodes are decompensations of chronic HF, but roughly 20% are new-onset, occurring with acute coronary syndrome, acute valvular dysfunction, hypertensive urgency, or postcardiotomy syndrome (Harrison 22e p.1976).

HF with recovered EF (HFrecEF) is a subgroup whose EF normalizes on therapy; predictors include younger age, shorter HF duration, nonischemic etiology, smaller ventricular volumes, and absence of fibrosis, and withdrawal of disease-modifying therapy can cause recurrence in up to half of patients within 6 months (Harrison 22e p.1977).

The disease is staged along the ACC/AHA framework: stage A (at risk), stage B (asymptomatic structural/ventricular dysfunction), stage C (symptomatic HF), and stage D (advanced/refractory HF); approach to therapy escalates across these stages (Harrison 22e p.1987).

Stage B asymptomatic ventricular dysfunction is treated to facilitate ventricular recovery and prevent progression to clinical HF, whereas stage D carries a high risk of death from sudden death or end-stage pump failure and may prompt consideration of transplant, mechanical circulatory support, or palliative care (Harrison 22e p.1987).

The robust randomized-trial evidence base supporting disease-modifying therapy applies to HFrEF (LVEF <=40%); historically HFmrEF and HFpEF management was symptom-focused owing to lack of outcome-improving therapies (Harrison 22e p.1987).

Even with effective therapy, patients across all EF categories remain at risk for clinical deterioration, typically from progressive sodium and fluid retention that drives congestive symptoms and acute decompensated HF (Harrison 22e p.1987).

Trials of agents that improve outcomes in HFrEF (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta blockers, digoxin, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists) have generally been unsuccessful when exported to HFpEF, with several large trials showing reduced HF hospitalizations but no all-cause mortality benefit (Harrison 22e p.1987-1988).

Management of HFpEF has centered on lifestyle modification, control of congestion, rhythm stabilization (especially atrial fibrillation), blood pressure control to guideline targets, and treatment of comorbidities such as obesity, obstructive lung disease, sleep apnea, diabetes/insulin resistance, anemia, iron deficiency, and chronic kidney disease (Harrison 22e p.1987).

A favorable signal for spironolactone in HFpEF emerged mainly from the subgroup randomized in the Americas in the TOPCAT trial, supporting only a weak guideline recommendation in selected patients at low risk for hyperkalemia and worsening renal function (Harrison 22e p.1988).

The microvascular endothelial inflammation paradigm proposes that comorbidity-driven inflammation impairs nitric oxide signaling and increases myocardial stiffness in HFpEF; trials enhancing NO bioavailability (sildenafil in RELAX, nitrates in NEAT-HFpEF, inorganic nitrite in INDIE-HFpEF) failed to improve functional capacity or quality of life (Harrison 22e p.1988-1989).
Signs and symptoms of HF are neither sensitive nor specific, so a high index of suspicion is needed, especially in older patients with hypertension, diabetes, or CKD (Harrison 22e p.1985).
Right HF with hepatic congestion can elevate transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin and be misdiagnosed as biliary tract disease (Harrison 22e p.1984).
Cardiac asthma (wheezing and rhonchi from bronchial congestion) can be mistaken for asthma or COPD and treated inappropriately (Harrison 22e p.1983).
Rales may be absent in longstanding HF with chronically elevated wedge pressures because of increased lymphatic drainage, so their absence does not exclude congestion (Harrison 22e p.1983).
NYHA functional class correlates poorly with objective measures of cardiac structure (LV size, EF) and function (peak VO2) (Harrison 22e p.1982).
Natriuretic peptide levels may be falsely low in obesity and elevated by noncardiac factors (age, female sex, CKD) and other cardiac conditions, limiting interpretation (Harrison 22e p.1985).

Lower extremity edema may be absent in acute HF or in younger adults despite marked systemic venous hypertension; unilateral edema suggests DVT, prior trauma, or vein harvest rather than HF (Harrison 22e p.1984).
Drugs causing salt/water retention (NSAIDs) or negative inotropy (calcium channel blockers) can precipitate decompensation and should be recognized as provider-related triggers (Harrison 22e p.1983).
Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, RAAS inhibitors, and potassium supplements can cause hyperkalemia, particularly with reduced GFR, requiring monitoring (Harrison 22e p.1984-1985).

Overall 5-year survival after a primary-care diagnosis of HF is about 50%, and 1-year mortality may reach 40% in severe HF. After an HF admission, mortality ranges from 8-14% at 30 days to 26-37% at 1 year and up to 75% at 5 years, with readmission rates of 20-25% at 60 days approaching 50% at 6 months; risk of death rises with each subsequent admission. Most deaths are cardiovascular, from progressive pump failure or sudden cardiac death. Independent predictors of adverse outcome include older age, male sex, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, coronary disease, advanced NYHA class, presence of an S3 or elevated JVP, reduced LV/RV ejection fraction, elevated wedge pressure, low cardiac index, reduced peak VO2, pulmonary hypertension, worsening renal function, hyponatremia, hyperuricemia, elevated troponin and natriuretic peptides, raised neurohormones, tachycardia, wide QRS/LBBB, atrial fibrillation, and ventricular ectopy. Black patients have higher case-fatality rates and there is regional variation (highest in the US Midwest and rural areas). HFrecEF generally carries a better prognosis than HFrEF or HFpEF. Overall outcomes are improving with guideline-directed therapy and risk-factor control (Harrison 22e p.1976-1977).

Two complementary frameworks are used. The NYHA functional classification grades symptom-limiting activity: class I (no limitation), class II (mild; symptoms with ordinary activity), class III (moderate; symptoms with less-than-ordinary activity), and class IV (severe; symptoms at rest worsening with any activity). The ACC/AHA staging is progressive and irreversible: stage A (at risk, no structural disease or symptoms), stage B (structural disease/asymptomatic ventricular dysfunction without symptoms), stage C (structural disease with current or prior symptoms), and stage D (advanced/refractory HF requiring specialized interventions). Patients are additionally phenotyped by ejection fraction: HFrEF (LVEF <=40%), HFmrEF (41-49%), and HFpEF (>=50%) (Harrison 22e p.1982-1983, 1987).

HFrEF is a progressive disease in which an index event (acute MI, chronic pressure/volume overload, genetic or congenital disease) triggers months to years of cardiovascular remodeling. Pressure overload produces concentric hypertrophy and volume overload produces eccentric hypertrophy; both involve myocyte hypertrophy, interstitial fibrosis, altered calcium-handling and cytoskeletal proteins, reexpression of fetal genes, and myocyte necrosis, apoptosis, and autophagy, completing a vicious cycle of pump dysfunction and rising wall stress. Compensatory neurohormonal activation of the sympathetic nervous system and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system initially supports output but becomes maladaptive, causing vasoconstriction, sodium and water retention, baroreceptor dysfunction, direct myocardial toxicity, arrhythmia, and adverse remodeling of heart, vessels, and kidneys. Counterregulatory vasodilators (ANP, BNP, prostaglandins, bradykinin, adrenomedullin, nitric oxide) are upregulated and act via guanylate cyclase to promote vasodilation and natriuresis; bradykinin and natriuretic peptides are degraded by neprilysin. Endothelin, inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1 beta, IL-6), and reactive oxygen species contribute to remodeling. HFpEF mechanisms are less defined but extend beyond diastolic dysfunction to vascular stiffness, renal dysfunction, sodium avidity, adiposity-related inflammation, oxidative/nitrosative stress, and insulin resistance. Electrical dyssynchrony (LBBB/IVCD), secondary mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, cardiorenal and splanchnic/hepatic congestion, gut microbiome alterations with endotoxemia, and high-output states further drive progression.

Heart failure is a clinical syndrome of symptoms and signs arising from any structural or functional impairment of ventricular filling or ejection; it is the common final pathway for most chronic cardiovascular diseases including hypertension, coronary artery disease, and valvular disease (p.1975).

High-output HF is rare and usually requires underlying structural heart disease; consider it with severe anemia (often hemoglobin less than or equal to 8 g/dL), arteriovenous fistula, severe obesity, cirrhosis, thyrotoxicosis, end-stage renal disease, or beriberi (p.1982).
Iron deficiency (with or without anemia) is common in chronic HF; IV iron (not oral) improves symptoms, exercise capacity, and reduces hospitalizations, though survival benefit is uncertain (p.1985).

Q waves with reduced QRS voltage (pseudo-infarct pattern) suggest infiltrative or restrictive cardiomyopathy such as amyloid, and conduction system disease should raise suspicion for cardiac sarcoid or Chagas in the right setting (p.1985).

Roughly half of patients with HF have reduced ejection fraction (EF less than or equal to 40%, HFrEF) and about half have preserved (greater than or equal to 50%, HFpEF) or mildly reduced (41-49%, HFmrEF) EF; because most patients have both systolic and diastolic abnormalities, the older terms 'systolic' and 'diastolic' heart failure have been abandoned (p.1977).

An EF that recovers to normal on guideline-directed therapy defines HF with recovered EF (HFrecEF); predictors include younger age, shorter HF duration, nonischemic etiology, smaller ventricular volumes, and absence of fibrosis, and withdrawal of therapy can cause symptom and EF recurrence in up to half of patients within 6 months (p.1977).

Dyspnea progresses in severity as exertional dyspnea, then orthopnea, then paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, then dyspnea at rest; bendopnea (breathlessness when bending forward) reflects elevated filling pressure, especially with low cardiac output (p.1982).

Orthopnea typically occurs within 1-2 minutes of lying down, whereas paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea occurs after prolonged recumbency and may require 30 minutes or more upright for relief; cardiac asthma (wheezing) can mimic primary lung disease (p.1982).

An S3 gallop indicates volume overload, suggests severe hemodynamic compromise, and carries negative prognostic significance, whereas an S4 is nonspecific and often reflects hypertensive HFpEF (p.1984).

Pulmonary rales may be ABSENT in longstanding HF despite chronically elevated wedge pressures because increased lymphatic drainage prevents alveolar spillage, so a clear chest does not exclude congestion (p.1983, p.1985).

Natriuretic peptides (BNP, NT-proBNP) rise with wall stress and aid diagnosis when uncertain, but levels are falsely LOW in obesity and falsely elevated by age, female sex, chronic kidney disease, atrial fibrillation, pulmonary embolism, and pulmonary arterial hypertension (p.1985).

Cardiorenal syndrome is driven not only by reduced forward cardiac output but importantly by systemic and abdominal venous congestion; relieving congestion (diuretics or ultrafiltration) often improves renal function (p.1981).
Relying on signs and symptoms alone, which are neither sensitive nor specific for HF; maintain a high index of suspicion in high-risk patients (older, hypertension, diabetes, CKD).
Excluding HF because the lung exam is clear; rales can be absent in chronic HF with chronically elevated wedge pressures.
Misreading right-HF hepatic congestion (elevated transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin) as biliary tract disease.

Attributing diuretic-refractory nonpitting edema to HF when it represents lymphedema needing different workup.

Failing to seek precipitating factors (identifiable in 50-90% of admissions), such as nonadherence, excess salt/fluid, NSAIDs, negative inotropes, ischemia, arrhythmia, infection, anemia, thyroid disease, or sleep apnea.

Overall 5-year survival after HF diagnosis in primary care is about 50%, and 1-year mortality may reach 40% in severe HF. Post-admission mortality ranges from 8-14% at 30 days to 26-37% at 1 year and up to 75% at 5 years, with readmission of 20-25% at 60 days and nearly 50% at 6 months; risk of death rises with each subsequent admission. Most deaths are cardiovascular, from progressive HF or sudden cardiac death. Black patients have higher case-fatality, men higher age-adjusted mortality than women. Independent predictors of adverse outcome include older age, male sex, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, coronary disease, advanced NYHA class, S3 or elevated JVP, reduced LV/RV EF, elevated wedge pressure, low cardiac index and peak VO2, pulmonary hypertension, worsening renal function, hyponatremia, hyperuricemia, elevated troponin and natriuretic peptides, elevated neurohormones, widened QRS/LBBB, atrial fibrillation, and ventricular arrhythmias. HFrecEF carries a better prognosis than HFrEF or HFpEF. Overall outcomes are improving with risk-factor treatment and guideline-directed therapies.

The central thermostat in the preoptic nucleus of the anterior hypothalamus orchestrates heat dissipation via autonomic-driven cutaneous vasodilation and diaphoresis. Heat is lost through evaporation, radiation, conduction, and convection; skin blood flow can rise 25-30 fold with compensatory splanchnic and renal vasoconstriction. When heat load overwhelms dissipation, illness results. Heat cramps reflect relative intracellular deficiency of sodium, potassium, and fluid, compounded by copious hypotonic fluid replacement that produces hyponatremia and hypochloremia. Heat exhaustion arises from water depletion, sodium depletion, or both. Heatstroke begins when maintaining perfusion forces peripheral vasoconstriction, which halts cutaneous heat radiation and causes core temperature to rise sharply. Above 42C (107.6F) direct cellular injury occurs: thermosensitive enzymes fail, oxidative phosphorylation uncouples irreversibly, heat-shock proteins and cytokines drive a systemic inflammatory response, and endothelial damage activates the coagulation cascade. Splanchnic shunting causes gut ischemia with endotoxin release that further impairs thermoregulation, potentially progressing to hepatic dysfunction, renal failure, DIC, and fulminant multisystem organ failure.
Heat-related illnesses span a spectrum from minor syndromes (heat edema, prickly heat, heat syncope, heat cramps) through heat exhaustion to heatstroke, a true medical emergency.
Heatstroke commonly produces a thermal cardiomyopathy with potentially elevated CVP despite dehydration, plus deceptive noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and basilar rales in a hypovolemic patient.

The wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT) is a superior environmental heat-load index to the simple heat index because it incorporates radiant heat and wind speed in addition to air temperature and humidity.

Acclimatization to heat develops over one to several weeks (lowered sweat threshold, increased sweat volume with lower salt content, plasma volume expansion, lower heart rate with higher stroke volume) and dissipates rapidly within weeks after leaving the hot environment.

Heatstroke is distinguished by the historical/physical triad of heat-stress exposure, CNS dysfunction, and a core temperature above 40.5C (104.9F); some patients with impending heatstroke may initially appear lucid.
In contrast to heatstroke, fever reflects intact thermoregulation, whereas heatstroke represents total loss of thermoregulatory control.

Heat exhaustion is characterized by preserved thermoregulatory control and CNS function with core temperature usually below 40.5C (105F); more profound CNS impairment should raise concern for heatstroke or another cause.

Two clinical forms of heatstroke exist: classic (epidemic) heatstroke (CHS) in older or chronically ill, often medicated, sedentary patients during heat waves (skin frequently hot and dry from ceased sweating), and exertional heatstroke (EHS) in young healthy exercising individuals who are often profusely diaphoretic despite dehydration.

Evaporation of skin moisture is the single most efficient mechanism of heat loss but becomes progressively ineffective once relative humidity exceeds 70%; conduction and convection fail once ambient temperature exceeds skin temperature.

Many patients are unaware that their medications impair heat tolerance: anticholinergics, phenothiazines, and heterocyclic antidepressants blunt sweating and central thermoregulation, while beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, and various stimulants reduce cutaneous perfusion or increase heat production.
Hepatocytes are highly heat sensitive: AST is routinely elevated on presentation in heatstroke, and both AST and ALT can eventually rise to over 100 times normal values.
Core-temperature elevation duration directly drives morbidity and mortality; peripheral (non-core) temperature measurement is unreliable, and continuous core monitoring is needed.
Treating heat edema with diuretics, which are ineffective and predispose to volume depletion and more serious heat illness.
Failing to recognize that heat exhaustion can progress to heatstroke after the patient is removed from heat stress.
Relying on peripheral temperature measurements, which are unreliable in heatstroke.
Mistaking cold-induced tonic-clonic muscular rigidity during cooling for seizure activity.
Misinterpreting an elevated CVP as adequate volume status, since thermal cardiomyopathy and a hyperdynamic circulation can elevate CVP despite significant dehydration.

Minor heat syndromes (heat edema, prickly heat, heat syncope, hyperventilation tetany, heat cramps) and heat exhaustion generally resolve favorably with removal from heat, cooling, and fluid/electrolyte repletion; younger, previously healthy heat-exhaustion patients without major laboratory abnormalities often do well, while older patients with comorbidities frequently require inpatient management. Heatstroke prognosis is closely tied to the duration of core-temperature elevation: delayed cooling can lead to severe hepatic dysfunction, permanent renal failure, DIC, and fulminant multisystem organ failure. Heat-related cardiac biomarker elevations and thermal cardiomyopathy may be reversible. Heat waves substantially increase mortality, especially among the elderly and malnourished, and secondary vascular events (strokes, myocardial infarctions) occur at least ten times more often during extreme heat.

Severity ladder of heat-related illness: minor heat-emergency syndromes (heat edema, prickly heat/miliaria rubra, heat syncope, hyperventilation tetany) and heat cramps are mild and self-limited; heat exhaustion is intermediate with core temperature usually below 40.5C (105F) and preserved CNS function; heatstroke is the most severe with core temperature above 40.5C (104.9F), CNS dysfunction, and loss of thermoregulation. Heatstroke is further classified as classic (epidemic) heatstroke (CHS - older/chronically ill, sedentary, anhidrotic, milder coagulopathy and lactic acidosis, mild CK rise) versus exertional heatstroke (EHS - younger/healthy, exercising, diaphoretic, with rhabdomyolysis, marked lactic acidosis, acute renal failure, DIC, hypoglycemia/hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia, and hyponatremia).

Metals enter the body chiefly by inhalation of dusts/fumes, ingestion of contaminated food or water (especially via hand-to-mouth activity in children), and sometimes vapor (e.g., mercury) or dermal absorption (organic lead, thallium). Gastrointestinal absorption varies markedly with the chemical form of the metal and host nutritional status. Once absorbed, metals are transported in blood and sequestered in organs such as bone, liver, and kidney, sometimes for years, then excreted mainly by renal and gastrointestinal routes (with minor losses via sweat, saliva, breath, milk, skin, hair, and nails). Toxicity arises from enzyme inhibition, damage to subcellular organelles and DNA, covalent protein modification, generation of reactive oxygen species, and displacement of essential metals from metal-dependent proteins; metals also alter DNA methylation and other epigenetic marks, dysregulating gene and microRNA expression. Many metals bind sulfhydryl (thiol) groups; cadmium and mercury both bind cellular sulfhydryls, cadmium competing with zinc and calcium, and lead interferes with mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, ATPases, and calcium-dependent messengers while enhancing oxidation and apoptosis. Genetic polymorphisms affecting metal binding/transport and nutritional/comorbid factors modify individual susceptibility (Harrison 22e p.3699-3700).

The U.S. ATSDR ranks arsenic, lead, mercury, and cadmium as the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 7th most hazardous substances at toxic waste sites; the WHO lists all four among the 10 chemicals of greatest public-health concern globally (Harrison 22e p.3699).
Dimethylmercury is 'supertoxic' -- a few drops absorbed through skin or inhaled can cause fatal cerebellar degeneration (Harrison 22e p.3701).

Manganese overexposure (miners, welders, dry-battery workers) causes a parkinsonian syndrome within 1-2 years that, unlike idiopathic Parkinson disease, is nonresponsive to L-dopa (Harrison 22e p.3702).
The single most important treatment is recognizing and stopping the exposure; activated charcoal does not bind metals and is of limited value in acute metal ingestion (Harrison 22e p.3699).
Lead and mercury are xenobiotic metals with no clear safe threshold, whereas copper and selenium are essential trace elements that become toxic only at high exposure (Harrison 22e p.3699).

Acute arsenic poisoning produces hemorrhagic gastroenteritis with intestinal mucosal necrosis, fluid loss and hypotension, plus delayed cardiomyopathy, acute tubular necrosis, and hemolysis; chronic exposure causes peripheral neuropathy, hyperkeratosis/hyperpigmentation, and cancers of skin, lung, liver (angiosarcoma), bladder, and kidney (Harrison 22e p.3700).
Classic arsenic signs include a garlicky breath odor and Mees' lines (transverse white striae on the fingernails); arsenic is radiopaque and may be visible on abdominal x-ray (Harrison 22e p.3700).

Cadmium has a biologic half-life of 10-30 years; severe food/water contamination in Japan caused itai-itai (ouch-ouch) disease with painful bone fractures from cadmium-induced bone toxicity (Harrison 22e p.3699-3700).

Lead in blood is 95-99% sequestered in red cells, so lead must be measured in whole blood rather than serum; about 15% of an absorbed dose is stored in bone with a half-life >20 years, making bone (KXRF) levels a marker of cumulative exposure (Harrison 22e p.3700).

Impairment of childhood IQ from lead occurs with no measurable threshold down to the assay limit of detection (~1 ug/dL); the CDC recommends screening children at about 6 months and intervening if blood lead exceeds 3.5 ug/dL (Harrison 22e p.3700).

Chronic metallic mercury vapor exposure produces an intention tremor and mercurial erethism (excitability, memory loss, insomnia, timidity, delirium) -- the historical 'mad as a hatter' picture (Harrison 22e p.3701).

Children exposed to mercury in any form may develop acrodynia ('pink disease'): flushing, itching, swelling, tachycardia, hypertension, excessive salivation/perspiration, irritability, weakness, and desquamation of palms and soles (Harrison 22e p.3701).
Measuring lead in serum instead of whole blood (95-99% of lead is in red cells) (Harrison 22e p.3700).

Relying on activated charcoal for metal ingestion -- charcoal does not bind metals (Harrison 22e p.3699); however thallium is an exception, where charcoal interrupts enterohepatic circulation (Harrison 22e p.3702).
Attributing high urinary beta-2-microglobulin solely to cadmium -- it also rises in other renal diseases such as pyelonephritis (Harrison 22e p.3700).
Misreading elevated total arsenic from recent seafood (nontoxic organic arsenobetaine/arsenocholine) as toxic inorganic arsenic -- test after 24 h without seafood (Harrison 22e p.3700).
Attempting chelation for cadmium poisoning -- chelation is not useful and dimercaprol can worsen cadmium nephrotoxicity (Harrison 22e p.3700).
Expecting chelation to improve outcomes in asymptomatic childhood lead exposure -- a large randomized trial showed no benefit on intelligence at BPb 20-40 ug/dL (Harrison 22e p.3700).
Mistaking manganese parkinsonism for idiopathic Parkinson disease and expecting an L-dopa response (Harrison 22e p.3702).

Outcome depends on the metal, dose, acuity, and promptness of exposure termination. Acute high-dose poisoning can be fatal (e.g., lead encephalopathy at BPb >120 ug/dL; inorganic mercury ingestion at 10-42 mg/kg; cadmium or mercury-vapor pulmonary edema; dimethylmercury exposure). Many effects of chronic exposure are irreversible or only partly reversible, including peripheral neuropathy, cognitive decline, manganese parkinsonism (L-dopa nonresponsive), itai-itai bone disease, and cadmium-related chronic renal failure for which no effective chelation exists. Cumulative lead burden is an established risk factor for chronic disease, including hypertension, cardiovascular morbidity/mortality, and chronic kidney disease, and prenatal exposure carries lasting offspring neurodevelopmental risk (Harrison 22e p.3699-3702).
Acute encephalopathy with convulsions and coma at very high blood lead (>80-120 ug/dL) -- risk of death
Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema after acute cadmium or mercury-vapor inhalation
Hemorrhagic gastroenteritis with hypotension and delayed cardiomyopathy in acute arsenic poisoning
Cardiovascular collapse after acute ingestion of inorganic mercury (lethal dose 10-42 mg/kg)
Garlicky breath, Mees' lines, or a gingival 'lead line' indicating significant metal exposure
Skin or inhalational exposure to dimethylmercury (supertoxic; minute amounts fatal)
Pregnancy exposure to mercury or high maternal bone lead -- risk of severe fetal neurodevelopmental injury

No single unified grading; severity is metal- and level-specific. Lead: subclinical childhood effects at BPb ~25-60 ug/dL, with IQ impairment down to ~1 ug/dL; clinically apparent neurodevelopmental delay at BPb 40-80 ug/dL; acute impaired neurotransmission/neuronal death at BPb >60-80 ug/dL; acute encephalopathy with convulsions/coma at BPb >80-120 ug/dL. Adult occupational removal at BPb >40 ug/dL (proposed newer target <10 ug/dL, removal if >20 ug/dL). Arsenic lethal dose 120-200 mg in adults, 2 mg/kg in children. Inorganic mercury ingestion lethal at 10-42 mg/kg; organic mercury CNS lesions at >1.7 mg/kg. Thallium severe poisoning after single dose >1 g or >8 mg/kg (Harrison 22e p.3700-3702).

Urea breath test (noninvasive) for active infection and for confirming eradication.
Stool (fecal) antigen test (noninvasive) for active infection and eradication confirmation.
Endoscopic biopsy with histopathology, including for gastric lymphoma staging.
PCR or FISH for the t(11;18) translocation in gastric MALT lymphoma to predict responsiveness to eradication therapy (p.649).

H. pylori is a flagellated gastric bacterium whose colonization triggers chronic mucosal inflammation. The flagellum lets the organism access the gastric epithelium and is essential for virulence; H. pylori evades innate immunity by producing a flagellin epitope that does not bind TLR5 and tetra-acylated LPS that does not activate TLR4 (p.1009-1010). Adhesion and gastric tropism are mediated by bacterial outer-membrane proteins BabA and SabA interacting with epithelial GM1 ganglioside (p.1009). Chronic H. pylori inflammation, partly via generation of carcinogenic nitrites from dietary nitrates, drives the gastritis-to-cancer sequence and is a recognized cause of peptic ulcer disease, gastric adenocarcinoma (intestinal subtype), and gastric MALT lymphoma; certain higher-virulence strains carry greater cancer risk (p.646).
H. pylori has a proven etiologic role in peptic ulcer disease; together with NSAID use it is one of the two most common causes of gastroduodenal ulcers (p.302).

In dyspeptic patients under 60 with no alarm features, test-and-treat is the recommended initial strategy: assess H. pylori status by fecal (stool) antigen or urea breath testing, and treat those who are positive (p.303).
Eradication of H. pylori in patients with bleeding ulcers lowers rebleeding rates to under 5% (p.272).
H. pylori is a known driver of gastric cancer; the intestinal subtype of gastric adenocarcinoma is associated with H. pylori infection and atrophic/atopic gastritis (p.646, p.647).
Although H. pylori is extremely common (present in roughly half of all humans), gastric cancer develops in only a small subset of those infected, so infection alone is not sufficient (p.646).

Treating H. pylori reduces future gastric cancer risk: eradication lowered gastric cancer incidence in people with a first-degree relative who had gastric cancer, and reduced second cancers in patients with prior early-stage gastric cancer (p.646).
All patients with gastric lymphoma should have H. pylori status evaluated; if histopathology is negative, confirm with a stool antigen test or urea breath test (p.649).

For gastric MALT lymphoma, antibiotic eradication of H. pylori alone is highly effective and is the initial therapy when H. pylori is positive and the t(11;18) translocation assay is negative, producing high response and complete-remission rates (p.649-650).
PITFALL: PPIs and other acid-suppressing drugs can cause false-negative urea breath and stool antigen tests; acid suppression must be stopped before testing for active H. pylori infection.
Confirmation of eradication should be performed 4-6 weeks after completing therapy, not immediately (p.303).
Do not rely on a single negative histopathology result in gastric lymphoma; confirm with noninvasive stool antigen or urea breath testing (p.649).

NEGATION: Even H. pylori-negative MALT tumors may respond to anti-H. pylori therapy, so a negative test does not preclude a trial of eradication; the t(11;18) translocation identifies a subgroup less likely to respond (p.649-650).
NEGATION: H. pylori eradication does NOT worsen GERD symptoms, despite H. pylori infection being associated with a reduced prevalence of GERD (p.302).

Eradication markedly improves ulcer outcomes (rebleeding falls below 5%). In gastric MALT lymphoma, H. pylori eradication yields high response rates with complete remission in the majority, though time to remission can be prolonged (averaging ~15-16 months in some studies), requiring patient monitoring before declaring non-response (p.272, p.650). Benefit in functional dyspepsia is limited but statistically significant (about a 9% risk reduction vs placebo) (p.302).

Dyspepsia with alarm features (dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding/anemia, jaundice, palpable mass or adenopathy, family history of gastroesophageal malignancy) or age over 60 warrants upper endoscopy to exclude malignancy rather than test-and-treat alone (p.302-303).
Failure to respond to eradication, or recurrent/refractory symptoms, should prompt further evaluation.

Acute GVHD versus conditioning regimen toxicity, drug eruption, or infection as a cause of post-transplant rash, diarrhea, and hepatic dysfunction (biopsy of skin, liver, or gut often needed for confirmation) (Harrison 22e p.917)
Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome versus other causes of tender hepatomegaly, jaundice, and fluid retention early after transplant (Harrison 22e p.916)
Transplant-associated thrombotic microangiopathy versus other microangiopathic processes (schistocytes, elevated LDH, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury) (Harrison 22e p.916-917)
Idiopathic/diffuse interstitial pneumonia from conditioning toxicity can mimic infectious pneumonia early post-transplant (Harrison 22e p.916)
Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia and bronchiolitis obliterans (late, often GVHD-associated) can mimic chronic respiratory infection (Harrison 22e p.916)
HLA typing of HLA-A, -B, -C, and -D (and DRB1) to assess donor-recipient matching; AML/ALL candidates should be HLA-typed soon after diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.915, 919)
Screening recipients for donor-directed anti-HLA antibodies before transplant, since their presence predicts poor engraftment (Harrison 22e p.917)

Chimerism/engraftment documentation by fluorescence in situ hybridization of sex chromosomes (sex-mismatched pairs) or short tandem repeat polymorphism analysis after DNA amplification (Harrison 22e p.916)
CD34 antigen quantification or colony-forming unit assays to gauge stem cell dose adequacy (Harrison 22e p.915)
PCR monitoring of blood for CMV (and other viral) DNA to guide preemptive therapy (Harrison 22e p.918)
Minimal residual disease assessment by multidimensional flow cytometry or molecular methods to refine transplant candidacy in acute leukemia (Harrison 22e p.919)
GVHD severity biomarkers including ST2, REG3a, and TNF R1 (Harrison 22e p.917)
Many noninfectious conditions can mimic acute GVHD, so histologic confirmation is usually required (Harrison 22e p.917)
Post-transplant autoimmune phenomena (autoimmune hemolytic anemia, immune thrombocytopenia) in 3-5% can mimic relapse-related or drug-induced cytopenias (Harrison 22e p.918)

A single hematopoietic stem cell can regenerate the entire lympho-hematopoietic system, including red cells, granulocytes, B and T lymphocytes, platelets, and fixed-tissue macrophages (Kupffer cells, alveolar macrophages, osteoclasts, Langerhans cells). Infused cells home to the marrow via selectin/integrin adhesion and CXCL12-CXCR4 signaling. In allogeneic transplant, the central immunologic axis is HLA matching: HLA molecules present antigenic peptides to T cells, so mismatched 'major antigens' provoke strong T-cell reactions while even HLA-matched pairs can react against 'minor' endogenous antigens. Donor T cells reacting against host tissue cause graft-versus-host disease, whereas residual immunocompetent host cells can mediate graft rejection if conditioning is insufficiently immunosuppressive. The same alloreactivity underlies the beneficial graft-versus-tumor effect. Conditioning regimens combine antineoplastic activity, myelosuppression, and (for allogeneic) immunosuppression to eradicate disease and prevent rejection (Harrison 22e p.914-916).

Hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) is the umbrella term that has replaced 'bone marrow transplantation,' reflecting that hematopoietic stem cells can be sourced from marrow, growth-factor-mobilized peripheral blood, or umbilical cord blood (Harrison 22e p.914).

Reduced-intensity and nonmyeloablative conditioning rely heavily on the graft-versus-tumor effect; they carry higher relapse but lower transplant-related mortality, favoring older patients and those with comorbidities, whereas high-dose conditioning is preferred when measurable disease is present and the patient can tolerate it (Harrison 22e p.915-916).

Evidence for the graft-versus-tumor effect: relapse is lowest in patients who develop acute and chronic GVHD, higher without GVHD, and highest after T-cell-depleted allogeneic or syngeneic grafts; donor lymphocyte infusions can induce remission in post-transplant relapse (Harrison 22e p.916).
Worldwide more than 100,000 transplants were performed in 2022, with frequency closely tracking gross national income per capita (Harrison 22e p.914).

It is used both to replace a defective but non-malignant lympho-hematopoietic system with a normal donor system and to treat malignancy, the latter by permitting higher myelosuppressive doses and, in allogeneic transplant, by adding an immunologic graft-versus-tumor effect (Harrison 22e p.914).

Transplant categories are syngeneic (identical twin, ~1% of cases, no GVHD and no tumor contamination), allogeneic (genetically non-identical donor, risk of GVHD and graft rejection), and autologous (patient's own stored cells, no GVHD/rejection but lacks a graft-versus-tumor effect and may carry contaminating tumor cells) (Harrison 22e p.914-915).
The chance any one full sibling is HLA-matched is 1 in 4; the probability a patient has an HLA-identical sibling is 1 - (0.75)^n where n is the number of siblings (Harrison 22e p.915).

With registries exceeding 40 million volunteer donors, an HLA-matched unrelated donor can be found for about 60% of patients, with higher rates in Caucasians and lower rates in minorities and people of mixed ancestry; a search and scheduling typically takes 3-4 months (Harrison 22e p.915).

Autologous engraftment is reliable when more than 2.5 x 10^6 CD34+ cells/kg are infused; the 5-10% of patients who mobilize poorly with growth factor alone may benefit from plerixafor, a CXCR4 antagonist that releases stem cells from the marrow niche (Harrison 22e p.915).

Stem cell homing depends on P- and E-selectin/integrin (e.g., VLA-4) interactions and on niche-derived CXCL12 binding CXCR4 on the stem cell; human HSCs tolerate cryopreservation, enabling autologous storage (Harrison 22e p.914-915).

After marrow grafting, granulocytes recover to ~100/uL by about day 16 and ~500/uL by day 22; mobilized peripheral blood speeds recovery by ~1 week while cord blood delays it by ~1 week (Harrison 22e p.916).

Innate immunity recovers quickly, but adaptive (T- and B-cell) immunity may take 1-2 years; early T-cell recovery is dominated by infused donor CD8+ T cells with a limited repertoire, with diverse de novo CD4+/CD8+ cells emerging months later (Harrison 22e p.916).

Premedication is not a reliable solution: in transfusion-related GVHD analogies aside, here the key pitfall is assuming infectious causes for early rash/diarrhea/hepatic dysfunction; acute GVHD typically needs biopsy because many conditions mimic it (Harrison 22e p.917)
Grade I acute GVHD is clinically minor, does not affect survival, and does not require treatment; over-treating it adds unnecessary immunosuppression (Harrison 22e p.917)
Mobilized peripheral blood gives faster engraftment but, in matched-unrelated-donor transplant, increases chronic GVHD without a compensatory survival advantage (Harrison 22e p.916)
No prospective randomized trial has shown that purging autologous grafts of tumor cells reduces relapse or improves survival (Harrison 22e p.915)

Standard high-dose conditioning is poorly tolerated if given within 100 days of a first transplant due to cumulative toxicity; reduced-intensity regimens may be needed for graft failure salvage (Harrison 22e p.917)
Patients with Fanconi anemia are abnormally sensitive to alkylating agents, so less intensive conditioning must be used (Harrison 22e p.918)
Vaccine-preventable antibody titers wane after transplant unless recipients are revaccinated; live vaccines (MMR/MMR-V) are generally avoided until 2 years post-transplant (Harrison 22e p.918)
Reinfusing donor stem cells into a patient with immunologic graft rejection is usually futile unless preceded by a second immunosuppressive conditioning regimen (Harrison 22e p.917)

Outcomes are highly disease- and stage-dependent (CIBMTR estimates, transplants 2010-2020). Reported approximate 3-year survival: severe combined immunodeficiency ~95% allogeneic; aplastic anemia ~98% allogeneic; thalassemia ~95% allogeneic; AML 57% (first remission) and 53% (second remission); ALL 64% (first remission) and 45% (second remission); CML 71% (chronic phase), 67% (accelerated), 28% (blast crisis); CLL ~64%; myelodysplasia ~50%; multiple myeloma ~80% autologous as initial therapy; non-Hodgkin lymphoma 45% allogeneic / 55% autologous (first relapse/second remission); Hodgkin disease 68% allogeneic / 89% autologous (first relapse/second remission). Matched-unrelated-donor survival now essentially equals matched-sibling survival. Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome carries ~30% mortality; chronic GVHD mortality averages ~15% (range 5-50% by severity). HLA-matched sibling allogeneic transplant carries roughly a 1-3% graft rejection risk and ~15% risk of severe acute GVHD (Harrison 22e p.915-920).

Tender hepatomegaly, jaundice, ascites, and fluid retention within the first month (peak ~day 16) suggest sinusoidal obstruction syndrome, which carries ~30% mortality and can progress to fatal hepatorenal syndrome (Harrison 22e p.916)

Erythematous maculopapular rash, persistent anorexia or diarrhea, and rising bilirubin/transaminases/alkaline phosphatase in the first 3 months point to acute GVHD; grades II-IV require aggressive therapy (Harrison 22e p.917)
Schistocytes, elevated LDH, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury about a month post-transplant indicate transplant-associated thrombotic microangiopathy (Harrison 22e p.916-917)
Diffuse fluffy pulmonary infiltrates with alveolar hemorrhage on lavage suggest conditioning-related diffuse alveolar damage rather than infection (Harrison 22e p.916)
Failure of marrow function to return, or loss after initial engraftment, signals graft failure/rejection; persistence of host-origin lymphocytes indicates immunologic rejection (Harrison 22e p.917)
Fever once the granulocyte count falls below 500/uL prompts broad-spectrum empiric antibacterial therapy because infection risk is so high (Harrison 22e p.918)
Community respiratory viruses (RSV, parainfluenza, influenza, metapneumovirus) can be life-threatening or fatal in transplant recipients (Harrison 22e p.918)

Acute GVHD is staged per organ and combined into an overall grade (Harrison 22e p.917). Skin stage 1-4 (rash <25% body surface up to generalized desquamation/bullae); liver stage by bilirubin from 34-51 umol/L [2-3 mg/dL] up to >257 umol/L [>15 mg/dL]; gut stage by diarrhea volume from 500-1000 mL/d up to ileus. Overall grade I (skin 1-2 only) is clinically insignificant; grades II-IV reflect progressively greater organ involvement, worse survival, and need for aggressive therapy. Myelodysplasia transplant timing uses the International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS), with transplant generally reserved for Int-2 or higher (or selected Int-1 with poor features) (Harrison 22e p.919).

Deep/next-generation sequencing to detect somatic mutations and clonal hematopoiesis (e.g., DNMT3a, TET2, ASXL1 variant allele fractions)
Surface immunophenotyping of stem/progenitor markers (CD34, CD90/Thy-1, CD117/c-Kit, CD133, CD164, CD110/c-Mpl) as described in murine-based studies

Hematopoiesis originates from a small self-renewing HSC pool. During development, blood production shifts sequentially from the yolk sac (embryonic-hemoglobin red cells and tissue-resident macrophages) to the placenta and intraembryonic sites near the aorta-gonad-mesonephros region, then to fetal liver, and in the second trimester to bone marrow and spleen; HSCs reach marrow via bloodborne transit from fetal liver after long-bone calcification, and proliferation falls sharply soon after birth. HSCs reside in a specialized perivascular/endosteal marrow niche where mesenchymal, endothelial, neural, and other cells provide regulatory signals (kit ligand, CXCL12) governing survival, expansion, and constraint. Trafficking depends on selectins binding CD162/CD44, integrin-mediated firm adhesion (VCAM-1/VLA-4), and CXCL12-CXCR4 plus calcium-sensing receptor signaling. Most HSCs are deeply quiescent and cytokine-resistant, dividing on the order of months to years; quiescence is enforced by high cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors (e.g., p57/CDKN1c blocking the G1-S transition) and niche signals such as angiogenin, IL-18, and angiopoietin 1. Self-renewal preserves any acquired mutation in the durable stem pool, whereas progenitor mutations are largely lost through terminal differentiation; epigenetic regulators (DNMT3a, TET2, ASXL1) are critical for pool homeostasis and for restraining outgrowth of potentially pathogenic clones.

Every blood cell type and certain tissue-resident cells (e.g., microglia, some macrophages) arise from hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs); catastrophic loss of HSC function leaves a person able to survive only about 2-4 weeks without extraordinary support.
Maturation of progenitors into mature cells takes roughly 10-14 days in humans, clinically reflected in the lag between cytotoxic chemotherapy and blood count recovery.
HSCs are heterogeneous: individual stem cells can be biased toward particular lineages and differ in proliferation and death responses, so the population behaves as an aggregate.

Clonal hematopoiesis: HSCs accumulate roughly 17 somatic mutations per year of life; variant alleles contributing to over 1% of blood cells become nearly universal by age 70, with an inactivating TET2 mutation able to worsen outcomes of some chronic inflammatory conditions.

Genetically modifying long-lived HSCs underlies curative cell therapies for cerebral adrenoleukodystrophy and the hemoglobinopathies, including a CRISPR gene-edited approach that suppresses BCL11A to reactivate fetal hemoglobin in beta thalassemia and sickle cell anemia.
The HSC pool is estimated at only about 20,000-200,000 cells, yet it generates hundreds of billions of mature blood cells daily and sustains this output over decades.

Stem cells are defined by two cardinal properties: self-renewal (dividing while staying undifferentiated) and differentiation into mature effector cells; loss of either leads to pool exhaustion or to organ failure/neoplasia.

A dividing HSC can yield two stem cells, two differentiating cells (symmetric division), or one of each (asymmetric division); this asymmetry lets a small pool produce roughly seven orders of magnitude more mature cells daily.
Mature blood cell lifespans vary widely, from hours for neutrophils to a few months for red cells to years for memory lymphocytes, but the durable source is the persistent stem cell pool.
HSCs circulate in blood throughout life, but free-circulating time is brief (minutes in the mouse); circulating HSCs remain functional and usable for transplantation.

The bone marrow niche (notably perivascular regions near trabecular bone) is both nurturing and constraining: mesenchymal and endothelial cells supply kit ligand and CXCL12, and the niche limits how many stem cells are produced.

CXCR4/CXCL12 (SDF1) signaling retains HSCs in marrow; disrupting it (via CXCR4 blockade, CXCL12 cleavage, or receptor downregulation) mobilizes stem cells into blood, enabling collection by leukapheresis rather than operative marrow harvest.

Differentiation proceeds along a branching hierarchy (stem cell to multipotent progenitor to lineage-committed precursor to mature cell), with progressive loss of plasticity and, in most lineages, loss of proliferative capacity.

Regulators of mature/progenitor cells do not predict HSC behavior: erythropoietin and G-CSF drive precursor proliferation but do not directly cycle stem cells (G-CSF instead mobilizes HSCs by altering CXCL12 tethering).
Deep HSC quiescence and resistance to cytokines make robust in vitro expansion of human HSCs difficult.
Assuming leukemia must arise only from normal stem cells is an oversimplification, since less self-renewing mature populations can also be transformed and self-renewal can be acquired by mutation.
The classic differentiation hierarchy diagram is a simplification; lineage-biased and intermediate cell states are increasingly recognized.
Progenitor (transient amplifying) cells are short-lived and largely lack durable self-renewal, so gene-modifying progenitors rather than true stem cells fails to give lasting benefit.

In the absence of disease the HSC pool is essentially inexhaustible: serial murine transplants can reconstitute several animals in succession and allogeneic transplant recipients never run out of blood cells over decades, indicating even limiting stem cell numbers suffice. With aging, clonal diversity declines as a small number of expanded clones (estimated 10-20 clones supplying 30-60% of blood cells by age 70) dominate; most such clones are benign, but some carry driver mutations with a low risk of progression to myeloid malignancy.
Complete failure of HSC function (e.g., after a nuclear/radiation accident) predicts survival of only about 2-4 weeks without extraordinary support
Expansion of clones carrying 'driver' mutations seen in myelodysplasia and myeloid leukemias, with low-frequency progression to overt neoplastic disease
Acquired self-renewal via oncogenic mutation in stem or more mature populations, providing a substrate for leukemia

Secondary (acquired) iron overload from chronic transfusion in hemoglobinopathies/thalassemia (Harrison 22e p.2062, p.821)
Other metabolic causes of skin hyperpigmentation: porphyria cutanea tarda, vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, pellagra, malabsorption/Whipple's disease (Harrison 22e p.443)
Transferrin saturation (serum iron / total iron-binding capacity) as a key screening test for iron overload (Harrison 22e p.2062, p.805)
Serum ferritin to assess body iron stores (Harrison 22e p.805)
MRI quantitation of hepatic and cardiac iron stores (Harrison 22e p.2062)
Genetic testing for HFE mutations (the gene underlying the common autosomal recessive form) (Harrison 22e p.2062, p.702)
Endomyocardial biopsy with Prussian blue iron stain (reserved; not usually needed when MRI is available) (Harrison 22e p.2062)
Other causes of restrictive or dilated cardiomyopathy; hemochromatosis is listed among restrictive cardiomyopathies but often presents clinically as a dilated cardiomyopathy (Harrison 22e p.2062)
Other chronic liver diseases progressing to cirrhosis (alcohol, viral hepatitis, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis) (Harrison 22e p.702)

Systemic iron homeostasis is controlled by hepcidin, a hepatocyte-derived peptide that blocks the iron exporter ferroportin, limiting iron flux from duodenal enterocytes, recycling macrophages, and storing hepatocytes. High plasma/liver iron normally raises hepcidin via the BMP-SMAD pathway, with HFE, transferrin receptor 2, and hemojuvelin contributing to hepcidin upregulation. Mutations in these genes (most commonly HFE) lead to inappropriately low hepcidin, increased iron absorption, and rising transferrin saturation. Because no regulated route of iron excretion exists, iron accumulates progressively. When transferrin saturation exceeds ~60%, non-transferrin-bound iron (NTBI) appears in the circulation and is taken up by liver, pancreas, and heart, driving parenchymal injury. In the heart, excess iron deposits in the perinuclear compartment of cardiomyocytes, disrupting intracellular architecture and mitochondrial function (Harrison 22e p.805, p.2062).
Hemochromatosis is variably classified as a metabolic or storage disease; the common autosomal recessive form is related to the HFE gene (Harrison 22e p.2062).

Up to 10% of the population is heterozygous for one HFE mutation, so clinical prevalence might be as high as 1 in 500, though observed rates are lower because of limited (incomplete) penetrance (Harrison 22e p.2062).
Increased iron in the skin in types 1 and 2 hemochromatosis stimulates melanin pigment production and leads to the classic bronze color (Harrison 22e p.443).

Systemic iron overload is diagnosed from serum iron and transferrin saturation, with thresholds noted around >60% in men and >45-50% in women; ferritin and transferrin saturation are the main usable laboratory biomarkers of iron status (Harrison 22e p.2062, p.805).

MRI is used to quantitate iron stores in the liver and heart; for cardiac iron overload the diagnosis is made principally by MRI, and endomyocardial biopsy (Prussian blue stain) is not usually needed (Harrison 22e p.2062).
When diagnosed early, hemochromatosis can often be managed by repeated phlebotomy to remove iron (Harrison 22e p.2062).

Hepcidin-regulating proteins HFE, transferrin receptor 2, and hemojuvelin, whose mutations cause different forms of hemochromatosis, normally contribute to hepcidin upregulation; impaired hepcidin signaling allows excess iron entry into plasma (Harrison 22e p.805).

There is no regulated mechanism for iron excretion; physiologic iron loss occurs only through cell desquamation and menses, which is why unregulated absorption produces progressive overload (Harrison 22e p.805).

Incomplete penetrance: many HFE mutation carriers never develop clinical iron-overload disease, so genotype does not equal phenotype, and additional genetic and environmental factors (e.g., alcohol) modify expression (Harrison 22e p.2062).
Hemochromatosis may present clinically as a dilated cardiomyopathy even though it is categorized among restrictive cardiomyopathies (Harrison 22e p.2062).

Iron chelation therapy itself (e.g., desferrioxamine) can supply accessible iron to Yersinia and impair neutrophil function, precipitating Yersinia septicemia in iron-overloaded patients (Harrison 22e p.1392).

If diagnosed early, iron overload can often be removed by repeated phlebotomy, and cardiac function can improve with iron removal provided myocyte loss and replacement fibrosis are not too severe. Late disease carries the burden of established cirrhosis (with hepatocellular carcinoma risk) and irreversible cardiac and endocrine damage (Harrison 22e p.2062, p.702).
Hemochromatosis (HFE germline mutations) is a recognized risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, typically via cirrhosis (Harrison 22e p.702)
Progression to cirrhosis from hepatic iron loading (Harrison 22e p.2062)
Cardiomyopathy from cardiac siderosis, which may cause heart failure or arrhythmia (Harrison 22e p.2062)
Markedly increased susceptibility to Vibrio vulnificus sepsis (primary sepsis develops most often in patients with cirrhosis or hemochromatosis) (Harrison 22e p.1373)

Increased susceptibility to Yersinia (Y. enterocolitica / Y. pseudotuberculosis) septicemia, with iron overload providing accessible iron; iron chelators such as desferrioxamine can precipitate Yersinia infection (Harrison 22e p.1392)

Inherited intracorpuscular defects: hemoglobinopathies (sickle cell, thalassemia; Chap. 103), enzymopathies (G6PD deficiency, pyruvate kinase deficiency, pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase deficiency), membrane-cytoskeleton defects (hereditary spherocytosis) (p.791-792, Table 105-1)

Malaria - the most frequent infectious cause of HA in endemic areas (p.801)
Shiga toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7 causing HUS, more common in children (p.801)
Clostridium perfringens sepsis - life-threatening intravascular hemolysis from lecithinase toxin (open wounds, septic abortion, contaminated blood unit) (p.801, Table 105-7)
Babesia, and Mycoplasma infection (associated with paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria); viral triggers (EBV, CMV, parvovirus B19, HIV, HCV) of secondary autoimmune HA (p.801-802, Table 105-8)
Reticulocyte count - corrected percentage and absolute count (often neglected in initial anemia workup) (p.791)
Unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin, AST, LDH, haptoglobin (p.791, Table 105-2)
Urine for hemoglobinuria/hemosiderinuria and stool/urine urobilinogen when intravascular hemolysis suspected (p.791)
Peripheral blood smear for schistocytes (microangiopathy/fragmentation), spherocytes (AIHA, hereditary spherocytosis), bite cells (G6PD), basophilic stippling (lead/P5N deficiency) (p.799-804)
Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test - broad-spectrum then specific anti-Ig/anti-C reagents (p.801)
Quantitative G6PD assay (screening tests can miss deficiency soon after a hemolytic attack because young high-G6PD reticulocytes mask it); DNA testing and point-of-care tests available (p.799-800)
Flow cytometry for CD59-negative red cell population in PNH (p.801, Table 105-7)
Donath-Landsteiner antibody for paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria; blood cultures for clostridial septicemia (p.801, Table 105-7)
Red cell survival study (51Cr or nonradioactive 15N) as the gold standard for shortened life span; bone marrow (if done) shows erythroid hyperplasia, usually not required (p.791-792)
Compensated hemolysis presenting without anemia, mimicking a non-hemolytic state until it decompensates (p.792)
Reticulocytosis-driven macrocytosis that can be mistaken for a megaloblastic process (p.791)
Parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis causing a precipitous hemoglobin fall in a chronic hemolytic patient, mimicking acute worsening of hemolysis (p.792)
Coombs-negative AIHA, which can still be severe when a high-affinity antibody opsonizes red cells with few molecules (p.802)

The mature red cell loses mitochondria and ribosomes, leaving anaerobic glycolysis (Embden-Meyerhof pathway) as the sole source of ATP and the hexose-monophosphate shunt (via G6PD-generated NADPH and reduced glutathione) as defense against oxidant stress; damaged proteins cannot be replaced, so any metabolic failure ultimately damages the membrane or the cation pump and shortens the ~120-day life span. Senescent or damaged red cells expose band-3 neoantigens, become opsonized, and are phagocytosed by splenic, hepatic, and other macrophages (extravascular hemolysis); this senescence process is accelerated in many HAs. The essential common feature is increased red-cell turnover; when destruction outpaces marrow production, anemia results. Chronic intravascular hemolysis causes iron loss via hemoglobinuria, whereas chronic extravascular hemolysis (especially if transfused) tends toward iron overload and, untreated, secondary hemochromatosis (p.791-792).

Hemolytic anemia (HA) is anemia from increased red-cell destruction with a normal (usually increased) marrow supply; unlike acute blood loss, cells are destroyed within the body rather than physically lost (p.791).

Classify by primary etiology (inherited vs acquired), tempo (acute vs chronic), severity, site of hemolysis (intravascular vs extravascular), and mechanism (intracorpuscular vs extracorpuscular defects) (p.791, Table 105-1).

Inherited HA generally reflects intracorpuscular defects (hemoglobinopathies, enzymopathies such as G6PD, membrane-cytoskeleton defects); acquired HA generally reflects extracorpuscular factors (autoimmune, microangiopathic/mechanical, toxins, drugs, infection). Exceptions: PNH (inherited-like somatic mutation but acquired) and familial/atypical HUS (p.791-792, Table 105-1).

Core clinical sign is jaundice; patients may report dark urine; splenomegaly is common as a preferential site of hemolysis, the liver may enlarge, and pigment gallstones are common with chronic hemolysis (p.791).

Laboratory hallmarks: increased reticulocytes (both percentage and the more definitive absolute count), raised MCV with macrocytes/polychromasia on smear, increased unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin and AST, raised LDH, and reduced-to-absent haptoglobin (p.791, Table 105-2).

Extravascular hemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin and urobilinogen; intravascular hemolysis is signalled by hemoglobinuria (often with hemosiderinuria), free plasma hemoglobin, markedly raised LDH (up to ~10x), and low haptoglobin, with bilirubin only mildly elevated (p.791, Table 105-2).

A positive broad-spectrum direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is on its own almost diagnostic of autoimmune HA; the broad reagent detects bound immunoglobulin and/or complement (C3 fragments) on red cells (p.801).

Warm AIHA (mostly IgG, optimal 37C) causes predominantly extravascular hemolysis with spherocytes; cold agglutinin disease (mostly IgM anti-I, optimal 4-30C) activates complement causing intravascular hemolysis with hemoglobinuria plus Kupffer-cell extravascular destruction in the liver (p.801-803, Fig. 105-9, Table 105-8).

Compensated hemolysis: a brisk EPO-driven erythropoietic response can fully offset red-cell destruction so an inherited hemolytic condition may present without anemia; it can decompensate in pregnancy, folate deficiency, or renal failure (p.792).
Neglecting the reticulocyte count, a key early clue to a hemolytic mechanism (p.791)

Screening (semiquantitative) G6PD tests give falsely normal results immediately after a hemolytic attack because the oldest deficient cells are destroyed and young reticulocytes have higher G6PD - use a quantitative assay; female heterozygotes may also be missed (p.799-800)

Dismissing Coombs-negative AIHA as not serious - high-affinity antibody can cause severe disease with few bound molecules; false-positive Coombs can follow transfusion, organ transplant, or Ig/anti-lymphocyte products (p.801-802)
Assuming an inherited hemolytic disorder always causes anemia - compensated hemolysis can be normo-hemoglobinemic until decompensation (p.792)

In cold agglutinin disease, prednisone and splenectomy are ineffective (unlike warm AIHA), and transfused (I-positive) red cells survive no longer than the patient's; the blood bag and patient extremities must be kept warm (p.803)
Misattributing favism to fava bean pollen inhalation (it does not cause favism) or to other beans (which are safe) (p.799)

Transient hemolysis usually has no long-term consequences beyond increased erythropoietic (folate) requirement; recurrent or persistent hemolysis predisposes to pigment gallstones, splenomegaly with hypersplenism (neutropenia/thrombocytopenia), and, with chronic extravascular hemolysis or repeated transfusion, iron overload progressing to secondary hemochromatosis affecting liver and heart. Warm AIHA carries ~5-10% mortality even with appropriate management; predictors of worse outcome/relapse include Evans syndrome, hemoglobin <6 g/dL, acute renal failure, infection, and high-affinity antibody. G6PD-related acute hemolysis generally resolves fully once the trigger is removed and in the absence of comorbidity, with full recovery from renal failure the rule when there is no prior kidney disease (p.792, 799, 801).
Schistocytes (fragmented/helmet cells) on smear indicating microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) - consider TTP, HUS, and DIC; an emergency requiring urgent evaluation (p.799, 801, Table 105-7)
Abrupt severe drop in hemoglobin (to as low as 4 g/dL within days) in warm AIHA with jaundice and splenomegaly - a medical emergency (p.801)
Acute renal failure - the most serious threat from acute hemolytic attacks in adults (e.g., G6PD-related), and a predictor of poor AIHA outcome (p.799, 801)
Hemoglobinuria signalling intravascular hemolysis (mismatched transfusion, PNH, clostridial sepsis, march hemoglobinuria, favism) (p.801, Table 105-7)
Evans syndrome (AIHA plus autoimmune thrombocytopenia) signals high-risk disease and may indicate underlying immune deficiency (p.801)
Mismatched (usually ABO-incompatible) blood transfusion causing abrupt intravascular hemolysis (p.801, Table 105-7)
Clostridium perfringens sepsis causing life-threatening intravascular hemolysis (p.801)

No single formal grading. Severity is gauged clinically by the hemoglobin level and tempo (mild compensated hemolysis without anemia through to abrupt severe drops to ~4 g/dL in AIHA) and by the site of hemolysis: intravascular hemolysis is signalled by hemoglobinuria, free plasma hemoglobin, LDH up to ~10x normal, and absent haptoglobin, whereas extravascular hemolysis chiefly raises unconjugated bilirubin and urobilinogen. High-risk markers in AIHA include hemoglobin <6 g/dL, acute renal failure, infection, and Evans syndrome (p.791-792, 801, Tables 105-2, 105-7).

When fetal red cells carrying a paternally inherited antigen absent in the mother enter the maternal circulation, the mother may form IgG alloantibodies. These IgG antibodies cross the placenta, bind fetal red cells, and cause their destruction, chiefly in the fetal spleen. The resulting anaemia stimulates extramedullary haematopoiesis and, when severe, causes high-output cardiac failure, hepatic dysfunction, hypoalbuminaemia, and hydrops. After birth, loss of placental clearance means the newborn must conjugate the large bilirubin load from continuing haemolysis with an immature liver, producing rapidly rising unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia that risks bilirubin neurotoxicity.
Immune-mediated haemolysis of fetal or neonatal red cells caused by maternal antibodies crossing the placenta and targeting fetal red cell antigens inherited from the father.
Rhesus (anti-D) disease was historically the most severe form; ABO incompatibility is now a more common but generally milder cause, and other minor blood-group antibodies can also be responsible.
Rh disease typically requires prior maternal sensitisation, so it usually spares the first pregnancy and worsens with subsequent affected pregnancies, whereas ABO disease can affect a first-born.
Severe fetal anaemia can cause hydrops fetalis with generalised oedema, effusions, hepatosplenomegaly, and heart failure.
In the newborn the dominant problem is rapidly rising unconjugated bilirubin from ongoing haemolysis, which can appear within the first day of life.
A positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test on the infant supports immune haemolysis, along with anaemia, reticulocytosis, and a rising bilirubin.
Rh disease is largely preventable by giving anti-D immunoglobulin to at-risk Rh-negative mothers to prevent sensitisation.
Management ranges from monitoring and phototherapy for hyperbilirubinaemia to exchange transfusion for severe or rapidly rising bilirubin, and intrauterine transfusion for severe fetal anaemia.
Late anaemia can develop over the following weeks as haemolysis and marrow suppression continue, so follow-up haemoglobin monitoring is important.
Underestimating ABO disease because it can affect a first-born and cause significant jaundice
Failing to monitor bilirubin closely and intervene before it reaches neurotoxic levels
Overlooking late anaemia in the weeks after birth once early jaundice has settled
Missing an opportunity for anti-D prophylaxis in an at-risk mother
Attributing early jaundice to physiological causes when haemolysis is occurring

With antenatal surveillance, intrauterine transfusion for severe fetal anaemia, and neonatal phototherapy or exchange transfusion, outcomes are generally good. Prophylactic anti-D has dramatically reduced severe Rh disease. Prognosis worsens if severe hyperbilirubinaemia progresses to kernicterus or if profound fetal anaemia and hydrops are untreated.

chunks.text: Haemorrhoids result from abnormal engorgement and downward displacement of the normal anal cushions, which are vascular submucosal structures that contribute to continence. Chronic straining, constipation, and raised intra-abdominal pressure disrupt the supporting connective tissue, allowing the cushions to enlarge, congest, and prolapse. The classical sites are the left lateral, right anterior, and right posterior positions. Bleeding is arteriovenous in origin, giving the characteristic bright red colour. Thrombosis of external components or prolapsed internal haemorrhoids produces acute pain, and long-standing prolapse can cause mucous discharge and pruritus.

chunks.text: Haemothorax is accumulation of blood in the pleural space, usually from injury to the chest wall vessels (such as intercostal or internal mammary arteries), the lung, or the great vessels. The pleural cavity can hold a large proportion of the circulating blood volume, so bleeding into it causes hypovolaemic shock. At the same time, the collected blood compresses the ipsilateral lung and can shift the mediastinum, impairing ventilation and, when large, venous return. Thus a massive haemothorax produces the dual insult of haemorrhage and respiratory compromise, and the blood must be evacuated while the circulation is restored.

Henoch-Schonlein purpura is an immune-complex mediated small-vessel vasculitis characterised by deposition of IgA1-containing immune complexes in the walls of small vessels of the skin, gut, joints, and kidney. This triggers a leukocytoclastic vasculitis with neutrophilic infiltration and vessel wall inflammation, producing the palpable purpura and visceral manifestations. In the kidney, mesangial IgA deposition causes a glomerulonephritis histologically similar to IgA nephropathy. A preceding infection or other antigenic trigger is thought to initiate the abnormal IgA response in susceptible children.
The most common small-vessel vasculitis of childhood, typically affecting children 3-10 years, often following an upper respiratory infection.
The classic tetrad is palpable purpura (predominantly on the buttocks and lower limbs), arthritis/arthralgia, abdominal pain, and renal involvement.
The rash is non-thrombocytopenic palpable purpura, distinguishing it from bleeding disorders; platelet count and coagulation are normal.
Gastrointestinal involvement causes colicky abdominal pain and can be complicated by intussusception, which is typically ileo-ileal.
Renal involvement ranges from isolated microscopic haematuria to nephritis; it is the main determinant of long-term prognosis.
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by palpable purpura plus at least one of abdominal pain, arthritis, or renal involvement; biopsy shows IgA deposition when needed.
Most cases are self-limiting; management is largely supportive with analgesia and hydration, and corticosteroids are considered for severe abdominal or other significant organ involvement.
Prolonged urinalysis and blood pressure monitoring are needed after recovery to detect delayed or progressive nephritis.

Most children recover completely within weeks, though relapses can occur; long-term outcome is dictated by renal involvement, with a small proportion developing chronic kidney disease, so renal follow-up is essential.
