chunks.text: Hepatic encephalopathy is an alteration of mental status and cognition resulting from liver failure, in which gut-derived neurotoxins are not cleared because of portosystemic vascular shunting and decreased functional hepatic mass and thus reach the brain. Ammonia is the principal candidate toxin: high ammonia concentrations are thought to drive increased synthesis of glutamine within astrocytes, causing osmotic astrocyte swelling, mitochondrial energy failure, and generation of reactive nitrogen and oxygen species, together with increased levels of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA and synthesis of putative 'false' neurotransmitters. No single one of these mechanisms fully explains the confusion and stupor, and which is mainly responsible for hepatic coma is not known. Other contributing compounds include certain false neurotransmitters and mercaptans. Chronic HE is characteristically accompanied by diffuse astrocytosis. In acute liver failure (but not chronic liver disease) cerebral edema with gray-matter swelling can occur and carries a risk of cerebral herniation (Harrison 22e p.230-231, p.2716).

Connective tissues (skin, bone, cartilage, ligament, tendon, vessel wall) are built from an extracellular matrix of fibrillar collagens, proteoglycans, elastin/fibrillin microfibrils and noncollagenous glycoproteins. Fibrillar collagen monomers are triple helices of alpha chains with a repeating Gly-X-Y motif; glycine at every third position is sterically required, and proline/hydroxyproline confer rigidity. Procollagen undergoes extensive post-translational processing (prolyl/lysyl hydroxylation requiring ascorbate, glycosylation, triple-helix folding aided by chaperones, secretion, N- and C-propeptide cleavage, then self-assembly into fibrils stabilized by lysyl-oxidase cross-links). Mutations may be quantitative (null alleles giving reduced normal collagen, generally milder) or structural (glycine substitutions, splice defects, charged/branched residue substitutions in X/Y positions) that disrupt folding, fibril assembly and mineralization. OI arises mainly from dominant type I collagen defects, plus rarer recessive defects in collagen modification, processing, folding/cross-linking and osteoblast differentiation. EDS reflects defects in collagen types I/III/V, in processing enzymes (ADAMTS2), cross-linking (PLOD1/lysyl hydroxylase 1), glycosaminoglycan biosynthesis, or matrix glycoproteins (tenascin X). Marfan/HTAD reflects fibrillin-1 microfibril dysfunction with secondary dysregulation of TGF-beta signaling; Loeys-Dietz reflects primary mutations in the TGF-beta pathway. Chondrodysplasias reflect intrinsic cartilage/growth-plate abnormalities (e.g., FGFR3 gain-of-function in achondroplasia, COL2A1 in type II collagenopathies).

This is an umbrella group of several hundred genetic disorders affecting bone, cartilage, skin, tendons and other connective tissues; mutations in over 550 genes underlie 771 defined skeletal disorders, so classification by either clinical phenotype or causative gene remains a continuing challenge.

FBN1 defects impair not only microfibril structure but also TGF-beta bioavailability; reduced/altered fibrillin-1 releases sequestered TGF-beta in the aortic wall, driving remodeling, excess MMP-2/MMP-9, and the aneurysmal phenotype.

Loeys-Dietz syndrome (TGFBR1/2, TGFB2/3, SMAD2/3) overlaps with MFS but is distinguished by arterial tortuosity and aneurysms beyond the aortic root, hypertelorism, and cleft palate or bifid uvula; ectopia lentis is typically absent.
Achondroplasia, the common short-limb dwarfism, is caused by a gain-of-function FGFR3 mutation; most cases are sporadic, and the homozygous form is more severe and may be lethal in the neonate.

Connective tissue strength comes from fibrillar collagens (types I, II, III) whose alpha chains have a repeating Gly-X-Y sequence; glycine, the smallest amino acid, must occupy every third position, so substitution of glycine by a bulkier residue is a frequent disease-causing mechanism.

Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) is dominated by bone fragility, deformity and growth deficiency; ~80-85% of cases stem from heterozygous COL1A1/COL1A2 mutations, and secondary features include blue sclerae, dentinogenesis imperfecta, hearing loss, basilar invagination and cardiac-valve abnormalities.

OI bone is paradoxically hypermineralized: DXA returns a reduced density value, yet quantitative backscattered electron imaging and 3D CT show the bone is over-mineralized, making it both weak and brittle so that it snaps like chalk.

Null COL1A1 mutations (about half-normal but structurally normal collagen) produce mild type I OI, whereas structural glycine-substitution defects produce the more severe types II-IV; type II causes in-utero fractures and perinatal death.

The Ehlers-Danlos syndromes (EDS) share soft hyperextensible skin, abnormal wound healing with atrophic/papyraceous scarring, easy bruising and joint hypermobility; the current classification recognizes 13 clinical types across roughly 20 genes.

Vascular EDS (COL3A1, type III collagen) is the dangerous form: medium- and large-vessel arterial rupture, sigmoid colon perforation without prior colon disease, and uterine rupture in the third trimester can occur, often in skin that is thin and translucent rather than velvety hyperextensible.
Classic EDS is most often due to COL5A1/COL5A2 (type V collagen) mutations in ~90% of patients; hypermobile EDS has no identified gene, so it remains a clinical diagnosis of exclusion.

Marfan syndrome (MFS) classically combines a tall marfanoid habitus with arachnodactyly, ectopia lentis (lens dislocation, ~60%), and aortic root dilation at the sinuses of Valsalva; ~95% of cases are due to fibrillin-1 (FBN1) mutations.
DXA underestimates true bone mineral in OI - a low DXA value coexists with actual hypermineralization, so bone is brittle despite the reading.
Marfan-like presentation may actually be homocystinuria; always check plasma amino acids before settling on MFS.
Hypermobile EDS has no confirmed gene; it is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion and cannot be confirmed by genetic testing.
Same clinical OI subtype may be assigned different type labels over a patient's lifetime or among family members under clinical (versus genetic) classification.
Blue sclerae are not specific to OI - they occur in EDS, MFS and even healthy individuals; conversely severe neonatal OI with white sclerae suggests recessive prolyl 3-hydroxylation defects.
In infants, OI fractures may be mistaken for non-accidental injury (battered child syndrome).
Tissues in MFS/LDS and EDS are friable, complicating surgical repair.

Highly variable, even within a single disorder type and among family members carrying the same mutation. In OI, type I is mild and fractures often decline after puberty, while type II is lethal in the perinatal period; pulmonary disease is the leading cause of death in OI. In Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes, cardiovascular disease (aortic dilation, dissection, rupture; mitral valve disease) is the major source of morbidity and mortality, and dilation rate is unpredictable and accelerated by exertion, emotional stress and pregnancy. Vascular EDS carries serious risk from arterial, intestinal and uterine rupture. Milder phenotypes across these disorders may go undiagnosed and have near-normal life expectancy.

Osteogenesis imperfecta is classified by the Sillence system (clinical/radiologic types I-IV: type I mildest with normal-quality but reduced collagen; type II perinatal lethal; type III progressively deforming; type IV mild-to-moderate) extended to genetic types V-XXII grouped by causative gene and mechanism. Ehlers-Danlos syndromes are classified into 13 clinical types (e.g., classic, vascular, hypermobile, arthrochalasia, dermatosparaxis, kyphoscoliotic) by clinical features, inheritance and molecular defect. Marfan syndrome diagnosis uses the revised Ghent nosology, emphasizing aortic root dilation/dissection and ectopia lentis as cardinal features plus a systemic score. Heritable thoracic aortic disease is divided into syndromic and nonsyndromic (familial thoracic aortic aneurysm) forms.

HSV-1 and HSV-2 are neurotropic DNA herpesviruses that establish lifelong latency in sensory ganglia after primary mucocutaneous infection; periodic reactivation produces recurrent localized disease (e.g., recurrent herpes labialis with HSV-1 and herpes genitalis with HSV-2). Virus enters and replicates within the epidermis at the site of inoculation. In HSV encephalitis there is characteristic unilateral temporal-lobe involvement. The virus can disseminate, particularly in the setting of disrupted skin (eczema herpeticum) or impaired cell-mediated immunity; visceral dissemination may occur even with only localized mucocutaneous disease (Harrison pp.1050, 1010 App. A1, p.747).

Primary HSV infection produces erythema followed by hallmark painful grouped vesicles that may evolve into pustules and ulcerate, especially on mucosal surfaces; lesions appear at the site of inoculation (Harrison p.~1010, App. A1).
HSV-1 classically causes orolabial disease (cold sores, herpes labialis) and HSV-2 causes genital lesions, but either type can infect either site (Harrison p.1050).
Non-genital cutaneous presentations include herpes gladiatorum (head and neck of young wrestlers) and herpetic whitlow (digits of health care workers) (Harrison p.1050).

Primary acute herpetic gingivostomatitis (usually HSV-1) presents with labial vesicles that rupture and crust plus intraoral vesicles that quickly ulcerate; it is extremely painful, with acute gingivitis, fever, malaise, foul odor, and cervical lymphadenopathy, occurring primarily in infants, children, and young adults (Harrison p.~325, Table 38-1).
Recurrent disease is milder than primary infection, and there is typically no fever in recurrent infection; herpes labialis recurrences typically do not involve the oral mucosa (Harrison App. A1).
Sexually transmitted HSV causes most genital ulcer disease worldwide, and there is a documented positive-feedback loop between HSV and HIV transmission (Harrison p.1096).
Although the HSV–HIV epidemiologic link is consistent, randomized trials of antiviral suppression of HSV showed no protective effect against HIV acquisition or transmission (Harrison p.1096).
CSF HSV PCR may be falsely negative early in the course of encephalitis, so a negative early result does not exclude the diagnosis and should not delay empiric aciclovir (Harrison p.747)
Tzanck smear cannot distinguish HSV from VZV; type-specific identification requires culture, immunofluorescence, or genetic testing (Harrison p.~480)
HSV visceral dissemination can occur with only localized mucocutaneous disease, so absence of widespread skin lesions does not exclude serious systemic infection (Harrison App. A1)
Oral lesions lasting more than 3 weeks should prompt consideration of an alternative diagnosis rather than primary HSV (Harrison Table 38-1)

Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis heals spontaneously in 10-14 days; lesions persisting beyond 3 weeks (unless secondarily infected) are not due to primary HSV infection. Recurrent disease is generally milder than primary infection. Approximately 25% of patients with herpes simplex encephalitis subsequently develop an autoimmune (anti-NMDAR) encephalitis weeks after the viral infection resolves - in children often with choreoathetosis and in adults with cognitive/psychiatric symptoms (Harrison pp.325, 821).

Fever with decreased level of consciousness and unilateral temporal-lobe involvement on imaging suggests HSV encephalitis - start empiric aciclovir promptly because CSF PCR may be falsely negative early (Harrison p.747)

chunks.text: Herpes simplex keratitis is caused by herpes simplex virus, usually type 1, which after primary infection establishes latency in the trigeminal ganglion. Reactivation, precipitated by stress, illness, ultraviolet light, or immunosuppression, sends the virus along sensory nerves to the cornea. Active viral replication in the epithelium produces the dendritic ulcer. Persisting viral antigen and the host immune response drive stromal inflammation (immune stromal keratitis) and endothelial disease (disciform keratitis), which can cause oedema, scarring, neovascularisation, and thinning. Repeated episodes and antiviral toxicity contribute to reduced corneal sensation and a neurotrophic cornea.

chunks.text: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus is caused by reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus residing in the trigeminal ganglion after childhood chickenpox. Declining cell-mediated immunity, with age or immunosuppression, allows the virus to travel down the ophthalmic division, causing a dermatomal vesicular eruption and neuritis. Direct viral cytopathic effect, immune-mediated inflammation, and an occlusive vasculitis of ocular vessels together produce the diverse anterior and posterior segment complications. Sensory nerve damage leads to reduced corneal sensation, neurotrophic keratopathy, and chronic neuropathic pain (post-herpetic neuralgia).

chunks.text: Diabetic ketoacidosis (and the DKA/HHS overlap presentation) (p.3216).
Other causes of an altered/hyperosmolar sensorium - the differential for hyperosmolar coma includes uremia, nonketotic hyperosmolar states and other metabolic derangements (p.3216, general).
Plasma glucose - typically markedly elevated, may be >55.5 mmol/L (1000 mg/dL) (p.3219).
Serum osmolality - characteristically >300 mOsm/L (p.3219).
Corrected serum sodium - measured Na may be normal or low, but corrected Na (add ~1.6 meq/L for each 5.6 mmol/L [100 mg/dL] rise in glucose) is usually elevated (p.3219).
Renal function (BUN/creatinine) - prerenal azotaemia from volume depletion; creatinine typically moderately raised (p.3219).
Ketones/beta-hydroxybutyrate - absent or only mild; serum beta-hydroxybutyrate <1.0 mmol/L; any moderate ketonuria is usually due to starvation (p.3219).
Acid-base status - acidosis absent or mild; a small anion-gap metabolic acidosis may reflect raised lactic acid (p.3219).

HHS arises from RELATIVE insulin deficiency combined with inadequate fluid intake. Insulin deficiency drives hepatic glucose overproduction (glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis) and impairs glucose uptake by skeletal muscle. The resulting hyperglycaemia causes an osmotic diuresis with intravascular volume depletion that is worsened by inadequate fluid replacement. The reason ketosis is absent is not fully understood; the insulin deficiency is presumed to be only relative and less severe than in DKA, and some studies show lower counterregulatory hormone and free-fatty-acid levels in HHS than in DKA, with possibly reduced hepatic ketone synthesis or an insulin/glucagon ratio that does not favour ketogenesis. Inflammatory markers (cytokines, C-reactive protein) are elevated in both HHS and DKA (p.3217-3219).
Typical patient is an older adult with type 2 diabetes presenting after a several-week prodrome of polyuria, weight loss and falling oral intake, progressing to confusion, lethargy or coma (p.3219).
Examination reflects profound dehydration and hyperosmolality: hypotension, tachycardia and altered mental status (p.3219).
Features classically ABSENT in HHS that are seen in DKA: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and Kussmaul respirations (p.3219).
HHS and DKA lie on a continuum of hyperglycaemia; up to one-third of patients have overlapping features of both (p.3216).
Plasma glucose in HHS is usually markedly higher than in DKA and may exceed 55.5 mmol/L (1000 mg/dL) (p.3219).
A debilitating condition (e.g. prior stroke, dementia) or a social situation that limits access to water frequently contributes to HHS by impairing water intake (p.3218-3219).
Worldwide reported cases of both HHS and DKA are rising for reasons that are not clear (p.3216).
A normal or low measured serum sodium can be falsely reassuring - it must be corrected for hyperglycaemia, after which it is usually elevated and reveals a profound water deficit (p.3219).
Mild ketonuria may be present but is typically from starvation, not from ketoacidosis - it should not redirect the diagnosis away from HHS (p.3219).
Fever may be absent even when infection is the precipitant; signs of infection should be sought regardless (p.3217, DKA section, applicable to acute hyperglycaemic crises).

Even with appropriate treatment, HHS has a substantially higher mortality rate than DKA, reported up to about 15% in some clinical series. The worse outlook reflects that HHS patients are usually older, have more profound fluid losses and dehydration (developed over days to weeks), are more likely to have mental status changes, and more often have a life-threatening precipitating event with accompanying comorbidities (p.3219).
HHS carries a substantially higher mortality than DKA (up to ~15% in some series), reflecting older patients, more pronounced dehydration and serious precipitating events with comorbidities (p.3219).
Hyperosmolar state must be reversed gradually - too-rapid correction risks worsening neurologic function (p.3219).
Precipitant is often a serious concurrent illness - myocardial infarction, stroke, sepsis, pneumonia or other severe infection - which must be actively sought (p.3219).

Harrison does not give a graded severity classification specific to HHS (unlike DKA, which is graded mild/moderate/severe by pH, bicarbonate and mental status). HHS is instead defined by marked hyperglycaemia, hyperosmolality (>300 mOsm/L) and the relative absence of ketosis/acidosis, on a continuum with DKA (p.3218-3219).

chunks.text: Hidradenitis suppurativa is a chronic inflammatory disorder centred on the hair follicle in apocrine-bearing skin. The primary event is follicular occlusion by hyperkeratosis, leading to follicular dilatation, rupture, and release of keratin and bacteria into the surrounding dermis. This provokes an intense inflammatory response with nodules and abscesses; recurrent inflammation drives formation of epithelialised sinus tracts and progressive scarring. Genetic predisposition, dysregulated innate immunity, hormonal influences, obesity, and smoking all contribute. Although bacteria colonise lesions and secondary infection occurs, the disease is fundamentally inflammatory rather than a primary infection.

chunks.text: Hip fractures usually result from a fall onto the greater trochanter in bone weakened by osteoporosis, though high-energy trauma or pathological lesions can cause them at any age. The proximal femur is supplied largely by the medial femoral circumflex artery via retinacular vessels ascending the femoral neck beneath the capsule. Intracapsular fractures may tear these vessels, threatening viability of the femoral head and predisposing to avascular necrosis and non-union, especially when displaced. Extracapsular fractures occur through well-vascularised cancellous bone and heal reliably but can bleed substantially. Immobility after fracture drives systemic decompensation in frail patients.

Failure of the craniocaudal migration of neural crest-derived enteric ganglion cells leaves the distal bowel without submucosal (Meissner) and myenteric (Auerbach) plexuses. The aganglionic segment cannot relax and remains tonically contracted, while abnormal cholinergic and other innervation adds to the dysmotility. This creates a functional obstruction with proximal dilatation (megacolon) and predisposes to stasis, bacterial overgrowth, and enterocolitis.
Caused by absence of ganglion cells in the distal bowel, producing a tonically contracted, non-relaxing aganglionic segment and functional obstruction.
Most neonates present with delayed passage of meconium beyond 48 hours, abdominal distension, and bilious vomiting.
The aganglionic segment extends proximally from the anus for a variable distance; short-segment disease confined to the rectosigmoid is most common and it is more frequent in boys.
Associated with Down syndrome and other congenital conditions, and there can be a positive family history.
Contrast enema may show a transition zone between the narrow distal aganglionic bowel and dilated proximal colon, but a normal study does not exclude the diagnosis.
Anorectal manometry shows failure of the internal anal sphincter to relax with rectal distension.
Rectal suction biopsy demonstrating absent ganglion cells with hypertrophied nerve trunks is the diagnostic gold standard.
Definitive treatment is surgical resection of the aganglionic segment with a pull-through procedure connecting normally innervated bowel to the anus.
Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis is the most serious complication and can present with fever, distension, foul explosive diarrhoea, and sepsis.

Androgens drive differentiation of pilosebaceous units, transforming vellus hairs into terminal hairs and stimulating sebaceous gland development; the total number of follicles is fixed for life, but follicle size and hair type change with androgen exposure and local growth factors. Testosterone, secreted roughly equally by ovaries (LH-driven) and adrenals (ACTH-driven), is a precursor that is converted within the pilosebaceous unit by 5-alpha-reductase to the more potent dihydrotestosterone, the chief local mediator. End-organ sensitivity, genetic and ethnic background, and local growth factors explain why androgen levels correlate only modestly with the amount of hair. Excess androgen also shortens the scalp-hair anagen phase, producing thinning/androgenic alopecia. Hyperinsulinemia and androgen excess suppress hepatic SHBG, raising bioavailable free testosterone. In nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (usually 21-hydroxylase deficiency), impaired cortisol synthesis reduces negative feedback, driving compensatory ACTH-mediated adrenal hyperplasia and accumulation of steroid precursors that are shunted to androgens (Harrison 22e p.3138-3141).
Hirsutism is defined as excessive growth of terminal (long, coarse, pigmented) hair in an androgen-dependent distribution and affects roughly 10% of reproductive-age women (Harrison 22e p.3137).
Acanthosis nigricans and skin tags are cutaneous markers of associated insulin resistance in hyperandrogenic women (Harrison 22e p.3138).
A BMI >25 kg/m2 (and especially >30) is frequently associated with hirsutism, partly via increased peripheral conversion of androgen precursors to testosterone (Harrison 22e p.3138).

After menopause, ovarian estrogen production falls more than androgen production and SHBG declines, increasing the relative proportion of unbound testosterone, which can exacerbate hirsutism (Harrison 22e p.3140).
Most cases are idiopathic or due to androgen excess from polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS); PCOS is the single most common cause of ovarian androgen excess (Harrison 22e p.3137-3140).

Hirsutism must be distinguished from hypertrichosis, which is androgen-independent generalized excess vellus/terminal hair often caused by medications such as phenytoin, minoxidil, and cyclosporine (Harrison 22e p.3138).

Virilization (deepened voice, breast atrophy, increased muscle bulk, clitoromegaly, increased libido) signals markedly elevated androgens and raises concern for an ovarian or adrenal neoplasm, or hyperthecosis (Harrison 22e p.3138).
Sudden onset and rapid progression of hirsutism, especially with virilization, suggests an androgen-secreting tumor and warrants urgent evaluation (Harrison 22e p.3138).

The modified Ferriman-Gallwey scale grades nine androgen-sensitive sites from 0 to 4; a normal score is <8, and scores >=8 in most non-Hispanic white and African American women indicate excess androgen-mediated hair growth (Harrison 22e p.3138-3139).
Asian and Native American women are less likely to manifest hirsutism even with androgen excess; pustular acne and scalp hair thinning may be the only cutaneous clues (Harrison 22e p.3138).

Free (unbound) testosterone is often more informative than total testosterone, because hyperinsulinemia and androgen excess lower SHBG, keeping total testosterone high-normal while unbound testosterone is substantially elevated (Harrison 22e p.3139-3140).

Dihydrotestosterone (DHT), formed from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase within the pilosebaceous unit, is the principal mediator of androgen action on the hair follicle; type 2 isoenzyme predominates in hair follicles and type 1 in sebaceous glands (Harrison 22e p.3139).
Relying on total testosterone alone can miss hyperandrogenism, since low SHBG can keep total levels high-normal while free testosterone is elevated.
Assuming shaving increases hair rate or density; it does not.

Over-interpreting ovarian ultrasound: polycystic-appearing ovaries also occur in hypothalamic amenorrhea and in women without PCOS, so ultrasound has low specificity and is often unnecessary to diagnose PCOS.
Random LH/FSH measurements are unreliable for PCOS because of pulsatile gonadotropin secretion.
Mild DHEAS elevations are common in PCOS and do not by themselves indicate an adrenal tumor.

Most hirsutism is benign and chronic, reflecting underlying functional androgen excess (commonly PCOS) or idiopathic causes; with treatment, hair growth typically progresses slowly. Even effective therapy yields only modest reduction in hair, with attenuation usually not evident until 4-6 months and maximal effect requiring 9-12 months because of the length of the hair growth cycle. By contrast, rapidly progressive hirsutism with virilization may herald a malignant or otherwise serious neoplasm and carries a prognosis tied to that underlying tumor (Harrison 22e p.3138-3141).

Infection follows inhalation of microconidia, the naturally infectious mycelial form; particles 2-4 micrometers reach terminal bronchioles and alveoli where alveolar macrophages engulf them and they transform into small (2-5 micrometer) narrow-budding yeasts, a calcium- and iron-dependent process central to pathogenesis. Yeasts evade the immune system and multiply within resting macrophages, then translocate via phagosomes to draining lymph nodes and spread hematogenously throughout the reticuloendothelial system. Effective cellular immunity develops about 2 weeks after infection, with T-cell interferon-gamma helping macrophages kill the organism; IL-12 and TNF-alpha are essential to cellular immunity. In immunocompetent hosts, organized granulomas contain the organisms and typically fibrose and calcify (calcified lung nodules, mediastinal nodes, hepatosplenic calcifications), and infection confers protective immunity to reinfection. With impaired cellular immunity, infection is not contained and disseminates as progressive disseminated histoplasmosis. Structural lung disease such as emphysema impairs clearance and leads to chronic pulmonary disease with progressive inflammation, necrosis and fibrosis mimicking cavitary tuberculosis (p.1693-1694).

Caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, a thermal dimorphic fungus; H. capsulatum var. capsulatum predominates in North America, while var. duboisii in Africa produces larger yeasts and a clinically distinct disease with frequent skin and bone involvement (p.1692-1693, 1695).

Detection of Histoplasma antigen in body fluids is extremely useful for PDH and acute diffuse pulmonary disease (sensitivity >95% in PDH, >80% in severe acute pulmonary disease when both urine and serum are tested); urine is often positive in disseminated disease (p.1694-1695, 1693).
Antigen levels correlate with severity in PDH, fall with effective therapy, and a stable or rising level predicts relapse or treatment failure (p.1695-1696).

Serology (immunodiffusion, complement fixation, IgG/IgM EIA) is especially useful in immunocompetent patients and for chronic pulmonary disease; IgM appears first and declines, IgG appears later and rises (p.1695).

Most prevalent endemic mycosis in North America, classically the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys, with foci in Mexico, Central/South America (Brazil), Africa and Asia; soil enriched with bird or bat droppings promotes growth, and disruption aerosolizes microconidia (p.1693).
High-exposure, high-attack-rate activities include spelunking (cave exposure), excavation, cleaning chicken coops, demolition/remodeling of old buildings and cutting dead trees (p.1693).
Clinical spectrum spans asymptomatic infection to life-threatening illness; severity depends on intensity of exposure, host immune status and underlying lung architecture (p.1693-1694).

Acute pulmonary disease appears 1-4 weeks after exposure as a flulike illness (fever, chills, sweats, headache, myalgia, anorexia, dry cough, dyspnea, chest pain), often with hilar/mediastinal adenopathy on chest radiograph (p.1694).
Arthralgia/arthritis with erythema nodosum occurs in 5-10% of acute cases and represents an inflammatory response, not extrapulmonary spread; pericarditis may also develop (p.1694).

Chronic cavitary pulmonary histoplasmosis occurs in smokers with structural lung disease (e.g., bullous emphysema), with productive cough, dyspnea, low-grade fever, night sweats, weight loss and upper-lobe cavitary infiltrates resembling tuberculosis (p.1694).

Progressive disseminated histoplasmosis (PDH) involves the reticuloendothelial system - lungs, bone marrow, spleen, liver, adrenal glands and mucocutaneous membranes; common findings are fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly and thrombocytopenia, with possible meningitis, oral/GI ulceration and adrenal insufficiency (p.1694).
Fungal culture is the diagnostic gold standard but may take up to 1 month and is often negative in less severe cases; in PDH yield is highest from BAL fluid, bone marrow aspirate and blood (p.1694).

Chronic cavitary histoplasmosis closely mimics cavitary tuberculosis radiographically (upper-lobe infiltrates, cavitation, pleural thickening) and may be misdiagnosed as TB, sarcoidosis, lymphoma or malignancy.
Asymptomatic calcified nodules from controlled prior infection may be mistaken for malignancy on screening CT in smokers from endemic areas.
Fungal stains may misidentify staining artifacts or other fungal elements as Histoplasma yeasts.
Persistent antibodies for several years after infection can cause a false misdiagnosis of active histoplasmosis in a patient with another disease process.
ID and CF serology are insensitive early in infection and have reduced sensitivity in immunosuppressed patients, especially organ transplant recipients.
Antigen testing cross-reacts with African histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis, paracoccidioidomycosis, talaromycosis and rarely aspergillosis.
Fibrosing mediastinitis is a chronic fibrotic reaction to past infection, not active disease, and does NOT respond to antifungal therapy.
Unlike latent tuberculosis, inactive histoplasmosis does NOT reactivate.

Most immunocompetent individuals with low-level exposure are asymptomatic or have a mild, self-limited illness that resolves without therapy; up to 75% of adults in endemic areas have evidence of prior infection without clinical disease. Untreated chronic cavitary disease is slowly progressive. Progressive disseminated histoplasmosis ranges from an acute, rapidly fatal course to a subacute/chronic one and is a devastating illness requiring prompt recognition, particularly in AIDS or anti-TNF therapy. Fibrosing mediastinitis is fatal in up to one-third of cases. Antigen levels track severity and response, with stable or rising levels signaling treatment failure or relapse (p.1693-1696).

Severity is graded by intensity of exposure, host immune status and underlying lung architecture (p.1693-1695).

HIV is a human retrovirus that infects cells bearing the CD4 receptor together with a chemokine co-receptor (CCR5 or CXCR4), leading to progressive depletion and dysfunction of CD4+ T lymphocytes (Harrison 22e ch.208, p.1556; co-receptor role cross-ref ch.61 p.448, ch.63). Reverse transcriptase copies the viral RNA genome into DNA that integrates into the host genome, establishing lifelong infection and a latent reservoir. Primary infection produces a burst of high-level viremia (the acute retroviral syndrome) followed by partial immune control and a viral set point, then a prolonged clinically latent phase during which CD4+ T cells are gradually lost. Once CD4+ T-cell counts fall sufficiently, the profound cellular immunodeficiency permits opportunistic infections and AIDS-defining illnesses. The mononuclear phagocyte system can also be infected and serves as a reservoir (cross-ref ch.63 p.461).

HIV is a retrovirus whose hallmark is progressive depletion of CD4+ T lymphocytes; the resulting immunodeficiency underlies the susceptibility to opportunistic infections and AIDS-defining illnesses (Harrison 22e ch.208, p.1556).

Consider acute (primary) HIV infection in a patient presenting with a mononucleosis-like illness: sore throat is reported by roughly half of patients with acute HIV infection, often together with fever, headache, myalgias, lymphadenopathy, anorexia and rash (p.1556; cross-ref ch.38 p.293).

The acute retroviral syndrome rash is typically a nonspecific diffuse macular/papular eruption favouring the upper thorax, face and collar region; less commonly urticarial or vesicular lesions occur, and oral or genital ulcers may accompany it (p.1556; cross-ref Appendix A1).
After primary infection there is HIV seroconversion, then a usually asymptomatic phase, and ultimately progression to symptomatic HIV disease/AIDS if untreated (cross-ref ch.38 p.297).

Three diagnostic markers appear sequentially in primary infection: HIV viral load (RNA) first, then p24 antigen, then HIV antibody; modern fourth-generation Ag/Ab combination assays shorten the window period by detecting p24 antigen before antibody is present (cross-ref ch.126, Fig.126-1).

The CD4+ T-cell count stratifies opportunistic-infection risk: as the count falls (notably below ~200 cells/uL) the risk of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, cerebral toxoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex and CMV end-organ disease rises, guiding prophylaxis decisions (p.1556; cross-ref ch.62, ch.108).

A nondetectable (suppressed) HIV viral load on antiretroviral therapy is the goal of treatment; sustained viral suppression is the basis of the Undetectable = Untransmittable (U=U) principle and of treatment-as-prevention (cross-ref ch.108 p.745).

Antiretroviral therapy is recommended for essentially all people with HIV regardless of CD4 count; in patients with concurrent malignancy or other illness, ART should run concurrently with the primary treatment together with appropriate antimicrobial prophylaxis (cross-ref ch.108 p.745).
Doses and specific drug regimens are deliberately omitted here; ART is presented only as a principle (combination antiretroviral therapy to achieve durable viral suppression).

Failing to consider acute HIV in a mononucleosis-like illness: although about half of patients with acute HIV infection have a sore throat, in most U.S. settings only about 1% of patients with viral or mononucleosis-like symptoms actually have acute HIV — a negative antibody test early does not exclude it, so check viral load/p24 (cross-ref ch.38 p.293).

Relying on antibody testing alone during the window period can miss acute infection before seroconversion; the dashed limit-of-detection and marker sequence (VL, then p24, then Ab) explain false-negative antibody results (cross-ref ch.126, Fig.126-1).
Attributing post-ART clinical deterioration to treatment failure rather than recognising IRIS, particularly in patients with a treated or unmasked opportunistic infection (cross-ref ch.205 p.1490).
Overlooking subclinical adrenal insufficiency in advanced HIV, which may be unmasked by stress or by drugs that inhibit steroidogenesis (cross-ref ch.49 p.379).

Untreated HIV infection is progressive and ultimately fatal once advanced immunodeficiency and AIDS-defining illnesses supervene. Effective antiretroviral therapy that achieves a durable nondetectable viral load markedly improves survival and restores immune function; for example, in HIV-positive patients with PML, institution of ART enhances survival, and those with higher CD4 counts (>300/uL) and low or nondetectable HIV viral loads have a better prognosis (cross-ref ch.205, p.1490).

HL is of B-cell origin. The malignant Reed-Sternberg (HRS) cells are large bilobed/multinucleate cells that constitute <1% of the tumor mass; the bulk of the tumor is a surrounding polyclonal inflammatory infiltrate, probably a reaction to cytokines produced by the tumor cells. Immunoglobulin genes in the neoplastic cells are rearranged but not expressed. HRS cells interact with their microenvironment via cell-cell contact and elaboration of growth factors and cytokines, producing a cellular milieu that protects them from host immune attack while supporting their proliferation and survival. 97% of HRS cells in cHL harbor genetic aberrations in the PD-L1 locus on chromosome 9p24.1, causing overexpression of PD-L1 (ligand for the inhibitory PD-1 receptor on immune cells), a mechanism for immune evasion that may also contribute to generalized immune suppression in HL patients. An association with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is suggested: monoclonal/oligoclonal EBV-infected cells are found in 20-40% of HL patients, but a definitive etiologic role is not settled. Viral oncogenesis appears greater in HIV-related cHL, where EBV is detectable in nearly all cases (versus only one-third of non-HIV-associated cHL) and HRS cells express EBV latent membrane protein 1 (LMP-1) with episomal, clonal EBV genomes suggesting direct involvement in early lymphomagenesis (p.868-869).

Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL) is a malignancy of mature B lymphocytes and accounts for ~10% of all lymphomas diagnosed each year; most are classical HL (cHL), with nodular lymphocyte-predominant HL (NLPHL) a distinct second subtype (p.868).
Cure rates now exceed 85%, and the new central challenge in HL care is late therapy-related toxicity, including a high rate of secondary malignancies and cardiovascular disease (p.868).

Reed-Sternberg (HRS) cells are diagnostic of cHL: large cells with abundant cytoplasm and bilobed and/or multiple nuclei, comprising <1% of tumor cellularity within a surrounding polyclonal inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes, eosinophils, neutrophils, macrophages, plasma cells, fibroblasts, and collagen (p.868-869).

By immunohistochemistry HRS cells are often PAX-5 positive but have low to no expression of other B-cell antigens such as CD19 and CD20; they express CD15 and CD30 in 85% and 100% of cases, respectively (p.868).

Most patients present with nontender palpable lymphadenopathy, typically in the neck, supraclavicular area, and axilla; more than half have mediastinal adenopathy at diagnosis, sometimes as the initial manifestation (p.869).

About one-third of patients present with B symptoms (fevers, night sweats, and/or weight loss); HL can occasionally present as a fever of unknown origin, more common in older patients with mixed-cellularity HL in an abdominal site (p.869).
Pel-Ebstein fever describes a pattern of fevers persisting for days to weeks, followed by afebrile intervals and then recurrence (p.869).
Pain in lymph nodes on alcohol ingestion and severe unexplained itching (pruritus) are recognized unusual manifestations of HL (p.869).

Staging is anatomically based using the Ann Arbor staging system because the disease tends to march from one lymph node group to the next, often contiguous group; staging guides therapy duration and intensity (p.869).
PET/CT is used for staging and is more accurate than bone marrow biopsy for assessing bone marrow involvement, which in cHL tends to be patchy and may be missed on a unilateral marrow biopsy (p.869).

The late age peak in the bimodal distribution may be artifactual, attributable to confusion with similar-appearing entities such as anaplastic large-cell lymphoma and T-cell/histiocyte-rich B-cell lymphoma (p.868).
Bone marrow involvement in cHL is patchy and can be missed on a unilateral marrow biopsy; PET/CT is more accurate (p.869).

Combined-modality therapy in early-stage disease reduces relapse only slightly while increasing late toxicity, with minimal or no improvement in long-term survival; much of the excess risk is attributable to radiotherapy (p.869-870).

NLPHL is biologically distinct from cHL and resembles indolent B-cell NHL; its 'popcorn'/L&H cells are CD30- and CD15-negative (unlike HRS cells), so it should not be managed identically to cHL (p.868, 871).
Alternative regimens (Stanford V, escalated BEACOPP) have not improved survival over standard therapy in early- or advanced-stage disease and are associated with increased toxicity (p.870).
Subdiaphragmatic presentation of cHL is unusual; it is more common in older males (p.869).

cHL is highly curable and a success story of modern oncology, with cure rates now >85%; the overwhelming majority of patients are cured with chemotherapy alone or combined chemotherapy and radiation. Patients are stratified into early-stage (I/II) versus advanced-stage (III/IV) disease. Early-stage patients have a better prognosis overall and are further classified as favorable or unfavorable. In advanced-stage disease, prognosis is best predicted by the International Prognostic Score (IPS), which assigns 1 point each for male sex, age >45 years, stage IV disease, serum albumin <4 g/dL, hemoglobin <10.5 g/dL, white blood cell count >=15,000/uL, and lymphocyte count <600/uL and/or <8% of WBC count; 5-year progression-free survival ranges from 88% (no risk factors) to 62% (four or more factors), though very few patients carry multiple risk factors. NLPHL tends to have a chronic, relapsing course resembling indolent B-cell NHL, with a 15-year nonrelapse survival of 82% for early-stage disease treated with definitive radiotherapy. A major concern is that in some early-stage series more patients died from late treatment complications than from HL itself (p.868-871).

Ann Arbor Staging System: Stage I = single lymph node region or lymphoid structure (e.g., spleen, thymus, Waldeyer's ring); Stage II = two or more node regions on the same side of the diaphragm (mediastinum counts as one site; bilaterally involved hilar nodes constitute stage II); Stage III = node regions/lymphoid structures on both sides of the diaphragm (III1 limited to spleen, splenic hilar, celiac, or portal nodes; III2 adds paraaortic, iliac, or mesenteric nodes); Stage IV = extranodal involvement beyond 'E', more than one extranodal deposit at any location, or any liver/bone marrow involvement. Suffix A = no symptoms; B = unexplained weight loss >10% over 6 months, persistent/recurrent fever >38°C in the previous month, or recurrent drenching night sweats in the previous month; E = localized solitary extralymphatic involvement (excluding liver and bone marrow). Patients are further grouped clinically as early-stage (I/II) versus advanced-stage (III/IV), with early-stage subclassified favorable vs unfavorable and advanced-stage risk-scored by the International Prognostic Score (p.869).

chunks.text: Severe, rapidly progressive BP elevation produces mechanical/pressure-related vascular injury that overwhelms protective vascular tone. In malignant hypertension the characteristic lesion is fibrinoid necrosis of small vessels — breakdown of the vessel wall with deposition of eosinophilic fibrin-containing material and a perivascular cellular infiltrate; larger interlobular arteries may show a hyperplastic 'onionskin' proliferative lesion. These changes can obliterate glomeruli and tubular structures, driving progressive kidney failure. Multiple pathways can generate this pressure injury, including activation of the renin-angiotensin system and intense vasospasm from catecholamine release; when endothelial injury is severe enough it triggers microangiopathic hemolysis. Cerebral involvement reflects failure of cerebral blood-flow autoregulation: at extreme pressures autoregulatory limits are exceeded, producing hyperperfusion, vasogenic edema and the encephalopathy/PRES picture — which is also why too-rapid lowering below the autoregulatory range can cause cerebral or optic ischemia (p.2153-2154, p.192, p.227).

chunks.text: Hypertensive urgency = markedly elevated BP (e.g., SBP/DBP >=180/100 mmHg) in an asymptomatic patient WITHOUT evidence of acute ongoing end-organ damage — manage with oral agents as outpatient. Hypertensive emergency = comparably high BP WITH evidence of active end-organ injury (encephalopathy, acute LV failure/pulmonary edema, acute kidney failure, retinal hemorrhage/papilledema, dissection, eclampsia, pheochromocytoma crisis) — requires immediate, carefully supervised IV therapy in ER/inpatient setting. chunks.text: Human papillomaviruses are DNA viruses that, like other papillomaviruses, gain entry through breaks in the skin and infect epithelial cells, producing benign cutaneous neoplasms (warts). Keratinized cells are not viable hosts for replication, so the virus targets viable epithelium at cutaneous and mucosal surfaces. More than 100 HPV types exist; certain oncogenic types (notably 16 and 18) integrate into host epithelium and drive intraepithelial neoplasia and squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix, anus, vulva, and penis, and persistent oral HPV-16 promotes oropharyngeal carcinoma. Histology of affected sites may show changes of typical warts and/or features of intraepidermal carcinoma (Bowen's disease). The oncogenic potential is markedly amplified in immunosuppressed hosts (Harrison 22e p.1525, p.1601).

chunks.system: Dermatologic / Mucocutaneous (with anogenital and aerodigestive involvement)
chunks.text: Warts are cutaneous neoplasms caused by human papillomaviruses (HPVs), of which more than 100 distinct types have been described (Harrison 22e p.1525).

chunks.system: Dermatologic / Mucocutaneous (with anogenital and aerodigestive involvement)
chunks.text: A highly effective HPV vaccine for selected types is FDA-approved and reduces the incidence of anogenital and cervical carcinoma (Harrison 22e p.1525).

chunks.system: Dermatologic / Mucocutaneous (with anogenital and aerodigestive involvement)
chunks.text: The available nonavalent HPV vaccine covers strains 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58; types 6 and 11 cause genital papillomas while the remaining types drive cervical and anal cancer, and reduction of types 16 and 18 alone could theoretically prevent more than 70% of cervical cancers worldwide (Harrison 22e p.1601).

chunks.text: Verruca vulgaris, the common wart, is typically a sessile, dome-shaped lesion roughly a centimeter across with a hyperkeratotic surface made up of many fine filamentous projections (Harrison 22e p.1525).

chunks.text: Genital warts start as small papillomas that can enlarge into large fungating lesions; in women they may involve the labia, perineum, perianal skin, and the vaginal, urethral, anal, and cervical mucosa, while in men they often begin in the coronal sulcus and may extend to the penile shaft, scrotum, perianal skin, or urethra (Harrison 22e p.1525).

chunks.text: Most warts in normal (immunocompetent) individuals resolve spontaneously within 1-2 years. However, oncogenic HPV types, especially 16 and 18, can lead to intraepithelial neoplasia and squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix, anus, vulva, penis, and oropharynx, with higher risk in immunosuppressed patients. chunks.text: Huntington disease results from an expanded CAG repeat in the HTT gene encoding a polyglutamine tract in the huntingtin protein. The mutant protein exerts a toxic gain of function, causing progressive neuronal loss most marked in the medium spiny neurons of the striatum (caudate and putamen), with later cortical involvement. Disruption of basal ganglia circuitry underlies the chorea and other movement abnormalities, while cortical and striatal degeneration drives cognitive and psychiatric decline.

chunks.text: A hydrocele results from an imbalance between secretion and absorption of fluid within the tunica vaginalis surrounding the testis. Congenital (communicating) hydroceles occur when the processus vaginalis fails to obliterate, allowing peritoneal fluid to track into the scrotum. Non-communicating hydroceles arise from excess fluid production or impaired reabsorption by the tunica. Secondary hydroceles develop as a reactive effusion in response to underlying testicular or epididymal disease such as tumour, infection, torsion, or trauma. Chronic large hydroceles may occasionally impair testicular perfusion or spermatogenesis.

Hyperbaric oxygen exerts effects through both physical mechanisms and biochemical cell signaling. Physically, raising ambient pressure shrinks gas bubbles per Boyle's law and steepens inert-gas diffusion gradients from bubble to tissue to blood and lungs, the basis for treating decompression sickness and arterial gas embolism. The markedly elevated arterial Po2 fully saturates hemoglobin and greatly increases dissolved plasma oxygen, improving diffusion into hypoxic and irradiated tissue. Beyond simple oxygen delivery, intermittent hyperoxia generates reactive oxygen species (superoxide, hydrogen peroxide) and reactive nitrogen species (nitric oxide) that drive cytokine and angiogenic growth-factor production, stimulate fibroblast activity, enhance macrophage bacterial killing, mobilize vasculogenic progenitor cells from marrow, and paradoxically produce anti-inflammatory effects such as reduced leukocyte beta-2 integrin adhesion. Hyperoxia also causes vasoconstriction and an osmotic gradient that reduce tissue edema and is directly toxic or bacteriostatic to anaerobes. In late radiation tissue injury, irradiation produces fibrosis and obliterative endarteritis leaving hypovascular hypoxic tissue (an alternative model emphasizes cytokine-driven fibrosis from oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction); HBO2T's most important benefit is promoting angiogenesis and increasing microvascular density. In carbon monoxide poisoning, CO impairs oxygen carriage, acts as an anesthetic, disrupts cellular oxidative processes, binds heme proteins including cytochrome a/a3, and peroxidizes brain lipids, with brain and heart most vulnerable. In diving, breathing gas at elevated ambient pressure loads inert gas (usually nitrogen) into tissues; if washout during ascent lags the falling ambient pressure, tissues become supersaturated and bubbles form, causing mechanical distortion of tissues and, in the venous circulation, inflammatory and coagulation cascades, endothelial injury, capillary leak, hemoconcentration, and pulmonary vascular obstruction. Barotrauma arises when noncompliant gas-filled spaces fail to equalize with changing ambient pressure.

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBO2T) means breathing physician-prescribed medical-grade oxygen while the whole body is enclosed in a chamber pressurized to at least 2.0 ATA; most regimens use 2-2.8 ATA for roughly 90-120 minutes per session.

Cerebral arterial gas embolism (CAGE) from pulmonary barotrauma presents within minutes of surfacing with loss of consciousness, confusion, hemiplegia, visual or speech disturbance, and can be mistaken for stroke or TIA by clinicians unfamiliar with diving.

Decompression sickness occurs in roughly 1 in 5000-10,000 recreational dives; most cases are mild (limb pain, fatigue, patchy paresthesias), and serious DCS usually appears within 60 min of surfacing.
Symptoms beginning more than 24 h after a dive are very unlikely to be DCS unless the diver was subsequently exposed to reduced ambient pressure such as air travel or higher-altitude surface travel.

About 25% of adults have a patent foramen ovale; right-to-left shunting (PFO, atrial septal defect, intrapulmonary shunt) lets venous bubbles 'arterialize' and raises the risk of cerebral, spinal cord, inner ear, and skin DCS manifestations.

At 2.8 ATA, arterial Po2 can theoretically rise above ~2025 mmHg and dissolved plasma oxygen to ~60 mL/L, enough to sustain life without hemoglobin in animal studies, which sharply improves oxygen diffusion through tissues.

Even a single HBO2T exposure produces durable cell-signaling effects (on fibroblasts, leukocytes, angiogenesis, antioxidant defenses) that persist for hours after oxygen levels return to baseline, mediated by reactive oxygen and nitrogen species.

The UHMS recognizes 15 accepted indications, including air/gas embolism, carbon monoxide poisoning, gas gangrene, crush injury, decompression sickness, problem wounds, intracranial abscess, necrotizing soft tissue infection, refractory osteomyelitis, delayed radiation injury, and sudden sensorineural hearing loss.

For chronic problem wounds, candidate selection is often guided by transcutaneous oximetry around the wound while breathing air and oxygen at pressure; in diabetic patients a transcutaneous Po2 threshold of <50 mmHg may be more appropriate than the usual <40 mmHg cutoff.

Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin with more than 200 times the affinity of oxygen and shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve leftward; HBO2T shortens the COHb half-life to about 21 min at 2.0 ATA versus roughly 5.5 h breathing air at sea level.
Admission carboxyhemoglobin levels confirm CO exposure but do NOT reliably predict severity or prognosis; delayed neuropsychological sequelae can appear after days to months of apparent recovery.
Ambient pressure increases by 1 atmosphere (101.3 kPa) for every 10.1 m of seawater, so a diver at 20 m experiences about 3 ATA.

In diving, the maximum acceptable inspired Po2 is generally considered 1.6 ATA (lower than therapeutic HBO2T pressures) because immersion and exercise raise the risk of oxygen-toxic seizures; helium replaces nitrogen at depth to cut narcosis and gas density.

Misdiagnosing CAGE as a typical stroke or TIA when the clinician is unfamiliar with diving medicine.
Relying on admission carboxyhemoglobin level to judge severity or prognosis of CO poisoning.
Assuming there is a confirmatory diagnostic test for DCS — diagnosis rests on dive profile, symptom timing, and examination.
Treating CAGE/DCS distinction as clinically critical — first aid and definitive management are the same for both.
Compressing a patient with an untreated pneumothorax or with gas-trapping lesions such as bullae without careful risk assessment and, for pneumothorax, a patent chest drain.

Overstating the risk of pulmonary oxygen toxicity from remote bleomycin exposure; published experience suggests the relationship may have been exaggerated, though recent bleomycin or mitomycin C with pneumonitis warrants careful evaluation.
Promoting HBO2T (sometimes with air) as a panacea for unproven indications, general well-being, or anti-aging — practice should be confined to accepted, periodically updated indications.

Most HBO2T adverse events are mild and self-limiting, and the therapy is generally safe. For late radiation tissue injury pooled data suggest improved tissue healing and reduced wound dehiscence in jaw osteoradionecrosis. About 70% of indolent problem ulcers are substantially improved or healed 6 months after a course, and meta-analyses report increased complete healing and reduced amputation of diabetic foot ulcers. In CO poisoning the most rigorous trial showed fewer cognitive sequelae at 6 weeks (25% vs 46%) and 12 months (18% vs 32%) with HBO2T, though a Cochrane review found overall evidence insufficient. Survivors of CO poisoning may develop delayed neuropsychological sequelae; risk factors for poor outcome are age over 35, exposure beyond 24 h, acidosis, and loss of consciousness. In diving, CAGE often shows substantial or complete early resolution as bubbles involute, but secondary deterioration or re-embolization can occur. Most DCS cases are mild, but spinal cord DCS frequently causes permanent disability and pulmonary/cardiovascular forms can be fatal.

Decompression sickness manifestations (Harrison Table 476-2) are grouped by organ system: musculoskeletal (limb pain); neurologic cerebral (confusion, visual and speech disturbances), spinal (weakness, paralysis, upper motor neuron signs, bladder/sphincter dysfunction, dermatomal sensory disturbance, abdominal/girdle pain), vestibulocochlear (hearing loss, vertigo, ataxia, nausea/vomiting), and peripheral (patchy nondermatomal sensory disturbance); pulmonary (cough, dyspnea); cardiovascular (hemoconcentration, coagulopathy, hypotension); cutaneous (rash, itch); lymphatic (localized soft tissue edema); and constitutional (fatigue, malaise). Most cases are mild; serious DCS usually manifests within 60 min of surfacing.

Calcium balance is governed by PTH and the vitamin D metabolites 1,25(OH)2D and 25(OH)D acting across parathyroid, kidney, intestine and bone. Hypercalcaemia of malignancy arises mainly through three mechanisms. (1) PTHrP overproduction by solid tumours (squamous head/neck, lung, skin; breast; genitourinary; gastrointestinal) — PTHrP mimics PTH at the PTH receptor, raising bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption. (2) Local osteolysis from skeletal metastases (breast, myeloma), where metastatic deposits secrete PTHrP and chemokines driving bone breakdown. (3) Excess 1,25(OH)2D production, notably by lymphomas (and granulomatous disease) via macrophage CYP27B1 converting 25(OH)D to active 1,25(OH)2D, enhancing intestinal calcium absorption. PTHrP induction is linked to PTHLH hypomethylation, hedgehog/Gli signalling, TGF-beta, oncogene activation (e.g. Ras) and p53 loss. In all these malignant mechanisms, the high serum calcium activates the parathyroid CaSR and appropriately suppresses endogenous PTH (p.363, 737).

Humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HHM) occurs in up to ~20% of cancer patients; the typical picture is a patient with known malignancy found hypercalcaemic on routine labs, though occasionally hypercalcaemia is the presenting feature of an undiagnosed cancer (p.737).
Most malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia runs a relatively acute course, in contrast to the chronic, fluctuating high-normal pattern of primary hyperparathyroidism or occasionally myeloma (p.363).
An elevated PTHrP level confirms HHM and is raised in roughly 80% of hypercalcaemic cancer patients; PTH should be suppressed in true HHM (p.738).
Features favouring HHM over primary hyperparathyroidism: known malignancy, recent onset, and very high serum calcium levels (p.738).
PTHrP shares homology with the first ~13 amino acids of PTH and binds the PTH receptor, explaining the PTH-like biochemical effects on bone and kidney (p.363, 737).
Serum free light chains should be checked when myeloma is suspected, since ~3% of myeloma is missed by serum/urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation (p.364).

Hypercalcaemia of malignancy is one of the few clinical settings where measuring serum 1,25(OH)2D is genuinely useful — it is elevated or inappropriately normal in lymphoma- and granulomatous-mediated hypercalcaemia (p.364).
Always confirm true hypercalcaemia first by correcting for albumin (add ~0.8 mg/dL to total calcium per 1.0 g/dL fall in albumin below 4.0 g/dL) to exclude pseudohypercalcaemia (p.363).
Failing to correct calcium for albumin can produce pseudohypercalcaemia or pseudohypocalcaemia and a false diagnosis (p.363).
FHH may present with mildly elevated PTH and hypercalcaemia and be mistaken for primary hyperparathyroidism — parathyroid surgery is ineffective in FHH and must be excluded (p.363).
Mild hypercalcaemia (10.5-11.9 mg/dL) is often asymptomatic or causes only vague neuropsychiatric or constitutional symptoms, so it may be overlooked (p.363).
Ionised calcium measurement is easily distorted by collection technique (e.g. prolonged tourniquet); corrected total calcium is generally preferable (p.363).

The cause is multifactorial. Rising human chorionic gonadotrophin and oestrogen are strongly implicated, explaining the peak in the first trimester and the higher frequency in molar and multiple pregnancies where hCG is elevated. Genetic factors, including variants affecting the appetite-regulating hormone GDF15, and altered gut motility contribute. Protracted vomiting leads to loss of fluid, hydrogen, chloride, and potassium ions, producing dehydration, hypokalaemia, and a hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis, while starvation drives ketosis and depletes thiamine stores.

Plasma K+ rises when efflux of intracellular K+ outpaces clearance or when renal excretion falls. Acidaemia drives K+ out of cells via effective K+-H+ exchange to buffer extracellular pH — but this shift is seen mainly with non-anion-gap (mineral) and respiratory acidoses; it does NOT occur with the organic anion-gap acidoses (lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis). Hyperosmolality (mannitol, hypertonic saline, IVIG, hypertonic glucose without insulin in diabetics) shifts K+ out by solvent drag. Cationic amino acids (lysine, arginine, epsilon-aminocaproic acid) and Na+/K+-ATPase inhibitors (digoxin and related cardiac glycosides from yellow oleander, foxglove, cane-toad bufadienolide; fluoride) cause efflux. Succinylcholine depolarises muscle via upregulated acetylcholine receptors (contraindicated after burns, neuromuscular injury, disuse atrophy, prolonged immobilisation). Impaired excretion arises from blockade of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, reduced distal Na+/flow delivery, hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism, mineralocorticoid resistance, and reduced functioning nephron mass. Cardiotoxicity reflects altered cardiac membrane excitability: mild rises alter repolarisation (T-wave changes), higher levels depress intracardiac conduction (PR/QRS prolongation, P-wave loss, QRS widening, sine wave). (p.401-403)
Hyperkalaemia (plasma K+ ≥5.5 mM) occurs in up to 10% of hospitalised patients; severe hyperkalaemia (>6.0 mM) in ~1% and carries significantly increased mortality (p.401).
Reduced renal K+ excretion is the single most common underlying cause; transcellular shift and reduced tissue uptake act mainly as acute contributors (p.401).

Excess dietary intake alone is a rare cause because the kidney can normally upregulate secretion — but small intake increments can provoke severe hyperkalaemia in susceptible patients (e.g. diabetics with hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism and CKD); occult sources include K+-containing salt substitutes (p.401-402).
The ECG changes of hyperkalaemia are notoriously INSENSITIVE, particularly in CKD/ESRD patients — a normal ECG does NOT exclude dangerous hyperkalaemia (p.403).

Hyperkalaemia per se impairs renal acid excretion (K+ competes with NH4+ for TALH reabsorption), so it can itself contribute to metabolic acidosis; restoring normokalaemia often corrects this hyperkalaemic acidosis (p.403).

Hyperkalaemia can produce a type I Brugada ECG pattern (pseudo-RBBB with coved ST elevation in precordial leads); the hyperkalaemic Brugada sign is distinguished from genetic Brugada syndrome by absent P waves, marked QRS widening and an abnormal QRS axis (p.403).
A urine Na+ concentration <20 mM signals that low distal Na+ delivery is limiting K+ excretion, suggesting volume repletion or a loop diuretic may help lower K+ (p.403).
Treating a falsely high K+: failing to exclude pseudohyperkalaemia before intervening (haemolysed sample, fist clenching, extreme thrombo/leuko/erythrocytosis, cold storage) (p.401-402).
Relying on a normal/near-normal ECG to exclude dangerous hyperkalaemia — ECG changes are notoriously insensitive, especially in CKD/ESRD (p.403).

Forgetting drug and dietary causes: ACEi/ARB/renin inhibitors and mineralocorticoid-receptor blockers (spironolactone, eplerenone, drospirenone) — additive in combination; K+-sparing diuretics and the structurally similar antibiotics trimethoprim and pentamidine block ENaC; NSAIDs/COX-2 inhibitors, calcineurin inhibitors and beta-blockers cause hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism; heparin/LMWH inhibit aldosterone synthesis (p.402).
Drugs blocking the RAA axis also blunt the adrenal aldosterone response to a rising K+, compounding the effect (p.402).

Anion-gap acidoses (lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis) do NOT shift K+ out by the acidosis mechanism, unlike non-anion-gap and respiratory acidoses — so attributing hyperkalaemia to acidosis in these settings can mislead (p.402).

Severe hyperkalaemia (>6.0 mM) is associated with a significantly increased risk of mortality. Cardiac toxicity can progress rapidly to fatal arrhythmia, but is reversible with prompt treatment; hyperkalaemic metabolic acidosis frequently corrects once normokalaemia is restored. (p.401, p.403)
Hyperkalaemia is a medical emergency because of its cardiac effects — arrhythmias include sinus bradycardia, sinus arrest, slow idioventricular rhythms, VT, VF and asystole (p.402-403).

ECG progression as a severity cue: tall peaked T waves (5.5-6.5 mM) -> loss of P waves (6.5-7.5 mM) -> widened QRS (7.0-8.0 mM) -> sine-wave pattern (>8.0 mM), heralding impending VF/asystole (p.403).
ECG manifestations mandate urgent treatment; but K+ ≥6.5 mM WITHOUT ECG changes should still be managed aggressively, because ECG findings are an unreliable predictor of cardiac toxicity (p.403-404).

Management principle (knowledge): a three-stage sequence — (1) immediately antagonise cardiac effects (IV calcium stabilises the myocardium by raising the action-potential threshold), (2) shift K+ into cells, (3) remove K+ from the body (p.403-404).
Secondary hyperkalaemic paralysis — ascending paralysis that can include diaphragmatic paralysis and respiratory failure (p.403).

HP is an immune-mediated reaction to inhaled antigens small enough to deposit in distal airways and alveoli, characterized by dysregulated TH1 and TH17 responses. Precipitating IgG antibodies indicate adaptive immunity, but innate mechanisms also contribute, with Toll-like receptors and downstream MyD88 signaling driving neutrophil recruitment. No clear genetic basis is established, though polymorphisms in antigen-processing genes (TAP1, MHC class II) occur in some cohorts. In chronic HP, bone marrow-derived fibrocytes may contribute to inflammation and fibrosis, and chronic HP shares the MUC5B promoter polymorphism with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. In the pulmonary eosinophilic syndromes, the eosinophil is central; pathology shows tissue eosinophil infiltration, and in EGPA extravascular granulomas and necrotizing vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis/thrombosis may involve lung, heart, skin, muscle, liver, spleen and kidney. These syndromes are thought to arise from dysregulated eosinophilopoiesis or autoimmunity (elevated IgE, IgG4, rheumatoid factor; heightened T-cell immunity); IL-5 is hypothesized to be etiologic, and ANCAs binding vascular walls likely contribute to vascular injury in EGPA (p.2229, 2231).

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP, extrinsic allergic alveolitis) results from inhalational exposure to a wide range of antigens, producing an inflammatory response of the alveoli and small airways; systemic symptoms such as fever and fatigue can accompany the respiratory complaints (p.2228).

Characteristic HP histology is loose, poorly defined NONcaseating granulomas near small airways—contrasting with the well-formed granulomas of sarcoidosis—plus a patchy lymphocyte-predominant interstitial infiltrate and bronchiolitis with organizing exudate (p.2230).

HP Study Group clinical prediction rule: six significant predictors, the strongest being exposure to a known HP antigen; others are serum precipitins, recurrent symptoms, symptoms 4-8 h after exposure, inspiratory crackles, and weight loss (p.2230).

Pulmonary eosinophilic syndromes share pulmonary infiltrates plus increased eosinophils in tissue, sputum and/or BAL; the first classifying step is distinguishing PRIMARY disorders from eosinophilia SECONDARY to a drug, infection, malignancy, or another pulmonary condition such as asthma (p.2231).

Acute eosinophilic pneumonia (AEP): acute febrile illness <1 month with hypoxemic respiratory failure (often needing ventilation), diffuse infiltrates and BAL eosinophilia >25%; typically affects men aged 20-40 with NO asthma history and is often linked to recent tobacco initiation, vaping, or dust from indoor renovation (p.2231).

AEP is often initially mistaken for acute lung injury/ARDS until BAL reveals >25% eosinophils; peripheral eosinophilia is often ABSENT at presentation but appears 7-30 days later; it is distinguished by absence of organ failure beyond the lungs, high corticosteroid responsiveness, excellent prognosis, and recovery without relapse (p.2231-2232).

Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia (CEP): indolent illness, mostly female nonsmokers (mean age 45), many with asthma; the 'photographic negative of pulmonary edema' (peripheral/pleural-based opacities) is pathognomonic but seen in <25% of patients; ~90% have peripheral eosinophilia and >50% relapse, often needing prolonged corticosteroids (p.2232).

EGPA (formerly Churg-Strauss): eosinophilic vasculitis with asthma and multi-organ involvement (lung, heart, skin, GI, nerve, kidney); peripheral eosinophilia >1000/uL (or >10% WBC) and ANCA (perinuclear/anti-MPO) in about one-third of patients; cardiac, GI and renal involvement portend a poorer prognosis (p.2232-2233).

ABPA is an eosinophilic disorder from allergic sensitization to Aspergillus, presenting asthmatically with brownish mucus plugs; it features prominent peripheral eosinophilia, IgE >500 (often >1000) IU/mL, and Aspergillus sensitivity—central bronchiectasis is a classic finding but is NOT required for diagnosis; consider ABPA in refractory asthma and as a complication of cystic fibrosis (p.2233-2234).

Loffler syndrome is transient pulmonary infiltrates with eosinophilia from helminthic larvae passing through the lung, most commonly Ascaris (also hookworm); symptoms are generally self-limited (p.2234).
Sensitization to an inhaled antigen (specific circulating IgG) is necessary but NOT sufficient to define HP, because many sensitized individuals never develop disease (p.2228-2229).
There is an as-yet-unexplained DECREASED risk of developing HP in smokers (p.2229).

US risk groups include farmers (farmer's lung: thermophilic actinomycetes/Aspergillus from grain, moldy hay, silage), bird owners (bird fancier's lung: feather, dropping and serum-protein antigens), industrial workers (chemical worker's lung: diphenylmethane and toluene diisocyanate), and hot tub users; mycobacteria can cause HP rather than frank infection in hot tub lung and metalworking-fluid HP (p.2229).

Recent guidelines advocate ABANDONING the acute/subacute/chronic terminology in favor of categorizing HP as either nonfibrotic or fibrotic; cluster analysis splits patients into a recurrent-systemic-symptom group and a more-severe-respiratory group (p.2229).
Antigen avoidance generally results in resolution of symptoms; acute symptoms may resolve within hours to days, while a more subacute course resolves over weeks to months (p.2229).

Chronic/fibrotic HP can present insidiously with progressive dyspnea, cough, fatigue, weight loss and digital clubbing, and—unlike other forms—can have an irreversible respiratory component NOT responsive to antigen removal; bird-antigen exposure tends toward a fibrotic phenotype while farmer's lung may show an emphysematous phenotype (p.2229).

Diagnosis depends foremost on a history of exposure to an offending antigen that correlates with symptoms; a careful occupational and home exposure history is essential and may be supplemented by a clinician visit to the work or home environment, with reexposure sometimes used to confirm the diagnosis (p.2229).
BAL lymphocytosis is characteristic of HP though not specific; most cases have a CD4+/CD8+ ratio <1, but a lower lymphocyte threshold should be applied in active smokers (p.2230).
Failing to obtain a detailed exposure history - the single most important step, as the strongest HP predictor is exposure to a known antigen
Relying on specific IgG/precipitins alone: asymptomatic exposed individuals (farmers, pigeon breeders) can be IgG positive, and limited antigen panels often yield false negatives
Expecting a particular PFT pattern - HP can be restrictive OR obstructive, so PFTs do not establish the diagnosis
Misdiagnosing AEP as ARDS/acute lung injury because peripheral eosinophilia is often absent at presentation (BAL eosinophilia is the key)
Treating EGPA-prone severe asthma with corticosteroids can mask systemic eosinophilia and vasculitis and delay the EGPA diagnosis
Confusing fibrotic HP with IPF/NSIP even on biopsy (basal sparing favors HP)

HP that has not progressed to chronic lung disease has a favorable outcome with likely resolution if antigen avoidance is achieved; chronic HP with lung fibrosis has a poorer prognosis, with chronic pigeon breeder's lung showing mortality similar to IPF. Acute eosinophilic pneumonia has an excellent prognosis with near-complete recovery and no recurrence. Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia responds rapidly to corticosteroids but >50% of patients relapse. In EGPA, up to 50% of untreated patients die within 3 months of diagnosis whereas treated patients have >70% six-year survival; clinical remission is achievable in >90% with ~25% relapsing, and myocardial, GI and renal involvement portend a poor prognosis. HES respond less reliably to corticosteroids (<50% first-line responders) (p.2229, 2232, 2233).
Hypoxemic respiratory failure with diffuse infiltrates in a previously healthy young man - consider acute eosinophilic pneumonia
Progressive dyspnea, weight loss and digital clubbing with honeycombing - chronic/fibrotic HP that may be irreversible and IPF-like

Asthma with neuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex), purpura, cardiac or renal involvement and eosinophilia - EGPA; cardiac involvement portends worse prognosis and up to 50% of untreated EGPA die within 3 months
Refractory asthma with brownish mucus plugs and very high IgE - evaluate for ABPA
Eosinophilia in an immunocompromised or steroid-treated patient - risk of fatal Strongyloides hyperinfection

Current guidance categorizes HP as nonfibrotic versus fibrotic (replacing the older acute/subacute/chronic scheme). Acute eosinophilic pneumonia diagnostic criteria: acute febrile respiratory illness <1 month, hypoxemic respiratory failure, diffuse infiltrates on chest x-ray, BAL eosinophilia >25%, absence of parasitic/fungal/other infection, absence of drugs known to cause pulmonary eosinophilia, quick corticosteroid response, and failure to relapse after stopping corticosteroids.

TRAb (TSH-receptor antibodies) - confirms Graves' when goitre/ophthalmopathy absent; useful for monitoring pregnant Graves' patients (high TSI crosses placenta -> neonatal thyrotoxicosis) (p.3033-3034)
Radionuclide (99mTc, 123I or 131I) scan and uptake - diffuse high uptake in Graves' vs LOW uptake in destructive thyroiditis, iodine excess, and factitious thyrotoxicosis (p.3034)

Pituitary MRI/CT and alpha-subunit if TSH inappropriately non-suppressed (suspect TSH-secreting adenoma) (p.3034, 3037)
