Depression (especially apathetic thyrotoxicosis in the elderly) (p.3033)

Graves' hyperthyroidism is caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSIs, detected as TSH-receptor antibodies/TRAb) that activate the TSH receptor. Susceptibility involves genetic (HLA-DR, CTLA-4, CD25, CD40, PTPN22, TSH-R gene) and environmental factors; concordance is 20-30% in monozygotic vs <5% in dizygotic twins. Triggers/risk factors include stress, smoking (moderate for Graves', major for ophthalmopathy), sudden iodine intake increases, the postpartum period (threefold rise), and immune reconstitution after HAART, alemtuzumab, or immune checkpoint inhibitors. Coexisting lymphocytic thyroiditis and TPO/Tg antibodies (up to 80%) mean there is no direct correlation between TSI level and hormone levels. Ophthalmopathy is driven by cytokine-mediated (IFN-gamma, TNF, IL-1) infiltration of extraocular muscles by activated T cells, fibroblast activation, glycosaminoglycan deposition trapping water, and aberrant IGF-1R signalling; the TSH-R is expressed in orbital tissue (p.3032-3033).

Thyrotoxicosis (state of thyroid hormone excess) is NOT synonymous with hyperthyroidism (excessive thyroid gland function); destructive thyroiditis and ingestion of exogenous hormone cause thyrotoxicosis without true hyperthyroidism (p.3032).

Graves' ophthalmopathy specific signs (proptosis, periorbital oedema, conjunctival injection, diplopia) occur in ~one-third of Graves' patients clinically; ~10% of ophthalmopathy is unilateral (p.3033-3034).
Graves' ophthalmopathy can occur in the absence of hyperthyroidism in ~10% (euthyroid ophthalmopathy); onset is within a year before/after thyrotoxicosis diagnosis in 75% (p.3034).
A diffuse, firm (non-nodular) goitre with a thrill or bruit at the inferolateral margins points to Graves' disease (p.3033).
Thyrotoxic hypokalaemic periodic paralysis is a recognised association, particularly common in Asian males (p.3033).

Mild hypercalcaemia occurs in up to 20% of patients (hypercalciuria more common) from thyroid-hormone-driven bone resorption; long-standing disease causes osteopenia and a small increased fracture rate (p.3033).
Graves' disease accounts for 60-80% of thyrotoxicosis; affects up to 2% of women, ~10x less common in men, typically ages 20-50 (p.3032).
In the elderly, features may be subtle or masked, presenting mainly with fatigue and weight loss ('apathetic thyrotoxicosis'), and may be mistaken for depression (p.3033).
Weight loss occurs despite increased appetite due to raised metabolic rate, but ~5% of patients GAIN weight due to increased food intake (p.3033).
Atrial fibrillation is more common in patients >50 years; treating the thyrotoxic state alone reverts AF to sinus rhythm in up to 75% of those without underlying cardiac disease (p.3033).

Symptoms in descending frequency: hyperactivity/irritability, heat intolerance/sweating, palpitations, fatigue/weakness, weight loss with increased appetite, diarrhoea, polyuria, oligomenorrhoea/loss of libido (p.3033 Table 396-2).
Signs: tachycardia (AF in elderly), fine tremor, goitre, warm moist skin, proximal myopathy, lid retraction/lag (p.3033 Table 396-2).
Fine tremor is best elicited by having the patient stretch out the fingers while feeling the fingertips with the palm (p.3033).
Lid retraction (staring appearance) results from sympathetic overactivity and occurs in ANY form of thyrotoxicosis; it is distinct from the specific eye signs of Graves' ophthalmopathy (p.3033).

Do NOT assume thyrotoxicosis means hyperthyroidism - low radionuclide uptake indicates destructive thyroiditis, iodine excess or factitia rather than gland overactivity, which changes management (p.3032, 3037).

T3 toxicosis: 2-5% have suppressed TSH with elevated T3 but normal T4, so a normal T4 does not exclude thyrotoxicosis; conversely iodine-induced T4 toxicosis can show elevated T4 with normal T3 (p.3034).
Diagnostic confusion: thyrotoxicosis can elevate bilirubin, liver enzymes and ferritin, and cause microcytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia (p.3034).

Antithyroid drug agranulocytosis (<1%) is idiosyncratic and abrupt - routine prospective blood-count monitoring is NOT useful; instead warn patients to stop the drug and obtain an urgent FBC for sore throat, fever or mouth ulcers (p.3036).

Suppressed TSH may persist for several months after starting antithyroid drugs, so TSH is not a reliable early index of response - titrate on unbound T4; euthyroidism is usually not reached until 6-8 weeks (p.3035).
Thyroid acropachy/clubbing without coincident dermopathy and ophthalmopathy in a Graves' patient should prompt a search for an alternative cause of clubbing (p.3034).
A normal TSH with normal unbound T4/T3 excludes thyrotoxicosis and excludes Graves' as the cause of a diffuse goitre (p.3034).

Untreated, clinical features generally worsen; historical mortality was 10-30% before effective therapy. Mild Graves' may show spontaneous relapses and remissions, and rarely fluctuates between hypo- and hyperthyroidism with changing TRAb activity. About 15% of treated patients in remission develop hypothyroidism 10-15 years later from the destructive autoimmune process. Ophthalmopathy runs an independent course: typically worsens over 3-6 months, plateaus over 12-18 months, then partially improves (soft-tissue changes especially); fulminant in up to 5% requiring acute intervention. Thyrotoxic crisis carries 4-17% mortality even with treatment (p.3034-3036).
Optic nerve compression at the orbital apex -> papilloedema, peripheral field defects and permanent vision loss; sight-threatening ophthalmopathy is an emergency (p.3034, 3036)
Corneal exposure/ulceration when lids fail to close during severe proptosis (p.3034)
Atrial fibrillation or worsening angina/heart failure, especially in elderly or pre-existing cardiac disease - high cardiac output can precipitate high-output failure (p.3033)
Features suggesting thyroid storm: fever, delirium, seizures, coma, vomiting, diarrhoea, jaundice (p.3036)

Subclinical hyperthyroidism = low TSH with normal free T3 and free T4; treatment is increasingly recommended in the elderly to reduce atrial fibrillation and bone-loss risk (p.3034, 3041). Graves' ophthalmopathy severity is graded by the NO SPECS mnemonic (0 no signs/symptoms; 1 only signs e.g. lid retraction/lag; 2 soft tissue involvement; 3 proptosis >22 mm; 4 extraocular muscle involvement/diplopia; 5 corneal involvement; 6 sight loss), though activity-based systems such as EUGOGO are preferred for monitoring/treatment decisions (p.3034).

Palpitations, weight loss and tachycardia with appetite preserved suggest thyrotoxicosis.
Red flags: Escalation to thyroid storm if fever/altered sensorium

[guideline] management → Beta-blocker for adrenergic symptoms / Antithyroid drug (first-line) / Antithyroid drug (first-trimester pregnancy) Rapidly controls adrenergic symptoms (tremor, palpitations, anxiety) while antithyroid therapy takes effect; non-selective and also reduces peripheral T4→T3 conversion at higher doses.

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: Graves' disease results from a combination of genetic susceptibility (HLA-DR and immunoregulatory genes such as CTLA-4, CD25, CD40, PTPN22, plus the TSH-R gene) and environmental triggers (smoking, stress, sudden iodine excess, the postpartum period, and immune reconstitution after HAART, alemtuzumab, or immune checkpoint inhibitors). Hyperthyroidism is caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins that bind and stimulate the TSH receptor; coexisting lymphocytic thyroiditis (TPO and thyroglobulin antibodies in up to 80%) means there is no direct correlation between TSI level and hormone levels. Ophthalmopathy reflects activated T-cell infiltration of extraocular muscles with cytokine-driven (IFN-gamma, TNF, IL-1) fibroblast activation, glycosaminoglycan accumulation that traps water and causes muscle swelling, increased orbital fat, and late irreversible fibrosis; the TSH-R is an orbital autoantigen and aberrant IGF-1 receptor signaling on orbital fibroblasts contributes. In destructive thyroiditis, follicular disruption releases preformed hormone (low radionuclide uptake). Toxic multinodular goiter reflects acquired functional autonomy of nodules, while toxic adenoma reflects constitutive cyclic AMP signaling from activating TSH-R or GSalpha mutations.

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: Thyrotoxicosis means a state of thyroid hormone excess and is not synonymous with hyperthyroidism, which specifically denotes excessive thyroid gland function; the major hyperthyroid causes are Graves' disease, toxic multinodular goiter, and toxic adenoma (Harrison 22e p.3032).

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: Toxic multinodular goiter typically affects elderly patients with subclinical or mild overt hyperthyroidism, often presenting with atrial fibrillation; iodine exposure (e.g., contrast dye) can precipitate thyrotoxicosis, and the scan shows heterogeneous patchy uptake (Harrison 22e p.3042).

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: A toxic (hyperfunctioning) adenoma usually causes only mild thyrotoxicosis, generally detectable when the nodule exceeds about 3 cm, and over 90% harbor activating somatic mutations in the TSH receptor or GSalpha (Harrison 22e p.3043).

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: Mild hypercalcemia occurs in up to 20% of thyrotoxic patients (hypercalciuria is more common), and longstanding thyrotoxicosis causes osteopenia with a small increase in fracture rate due to direct stimulation of bone resorption (Harrison 22e p.3033).

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: Graves' disease accounts for roughly 60-80% of thyrotoxicosis, occurs in up to 2% of women (about one-tenth as frequent in men), and typically presents between 20 and 50 years of age (Harrison 22e p.3032).

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: Graves' hyperthyroidism is driven by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins acting on the TSH receptor; TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb) can be measured and, because they cross the placenta, are useful for monitoring pregnant Graves' patients for neonatal thyrotoxicosis (Harrison 22e p.3033).

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: Symptoms in descending frequency include hyperactivity/irritability, heat intolerance with sweating, palpitations, fatigue and weakness, weight loss with increased appetite, and diarrhea; signs include tachycardia (atrial fibrillation in the elderly), tremor, goiter, warm moist skin, and proximal myopathy (Harrison 22e p.3033).

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: Apathetic thyrotoxicosis in the elderly may present mainly with fatigue and weight loss and can be mistaken for depression; features may be subtle or masked in older patients (Harrison 22e p.3033).

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: Treating the thyrotoxic state alone converts atrial fibrillation to normal sinus rhythm in up to about 75% of patients without underlying cardiac disease (Harrison 22e p.3033).

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: Graves' ophthalmopathy (thyroid eye disease) is specific to Graves'; about one-third of patients have clinical eye disease, it can occur without hyperthyroidism in ~10%, and onset is within the year before or after thyrotoxicosis diagnosis in 75% (Harrison 22e p.3033).

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: Destructive (subacute or silent) thyroiditis causes a transient thyrotoxic phase from release of preformed hormone with characteristically LOW radionuclide uptake and elevated thyroglobulin; true hyperthyroidism is absent (Harrison 22e p.3035).

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: Subacute (de Quervain's) thyroiditis classically evolves through three phases over about 6 months: thyrotoxic, then hypothyroid, then recovery; it is supported by a high ESR and a tender goiter, and the T4/T3 ratio is higher (T3 less disproportionately elevated) than in Graves' or thyroid autonomy (Harrison 22e p.3038).

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: Equating thyrotoxicosis with hyperthyroidism: destructive thyroiditis, factitia, and iodine excess cause hormone excess without true gland hyperfunction (low uptake)

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: Missing apathetic thyrotoxicosis in the elderly, where it can present as fatigue/weight loss or be mistaken for depression or malignancy

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: Overlooking that there is no direct correlation between TSI level and hormone levels because coexisting thyroiditis affects function

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: Interpreting thyroid function tests during acute severe illness (sick euthyroid/nonthyroidal illness) as true thyroid disease; routine testing in acutely ill patients should be avoided, though an undetectable TSH (<0.01 mIU/L) makes primary thyroid disease more likely

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: Failing to recognize that radioiodine therapy can worsen ophthalmopathy in a small proportion of patients, especially smokers

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: Attributing clubbing to thyroid acropachy in a Graves' patient who lacks coincident dermopathy and ophthalmopathy, where another cause should be sought

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: Untreated, clinical features generally worsen and mortality was historically 10-30% before effective therapy. Some patients with mild Graves' disease have spontaneous relapses and remissions, and about 15% of those who enter remission develop hypothyroidism 10-15 years later from ongoing autoimmune destruction. Ophthalmopathy follows an independent course, typically worsening over 3-6 months, plateauing over the next 12-18 months, then partially improving, though up to ~5% have a fulminant course. Subacute thyroiditis usually resolves completely, with late permanent hypothyroidism in about 15%. Thyrotoxic crisis carries a high mortality (about 4-17%) even with treatment, due to cardiac failure, arrhythmia, or hyperthermia. Toxic multinodular goiter and toxic adenoma do not remit spontaneously and require definitive therapy.

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: Thyrotoxic crisis (thyroid storm): fever, delirium, seizures, coma, vomiting, diarrhea, and jaundice with a high mortality (about 4-17% even with treatment)

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: New or worsening atrial fibrillation or high-output heart failure, particularly in the elderly or those with preexisting cardiac disease

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: Sight-threatening ophthalmopathy from optic nerve compression (papilledema, peripheral field defects, loss of vision) or corneal ulceration/exposure

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: Thyrotoxic hypokalemic periodic paralysis (notably in Asian males)

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: Diplopia or severe proptosis with corneal exposure during sleep

chunks.diseaseName: Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
chunks.text: Graves' ophthalmopathy is graded by the NO SPECS mnemonic (0 no signs/symptoms; 1 only signs such as lid retraction/lag; 2 soft tissue involvement/periorbital edema; 3 proptosis >22 mm; 4 extraocular muscle involvement/diplopia; 5 corneal involvement; 6 sight loss), although activity-based systems such as EUGOGO are preferred for monitoring and treatment decisions. Thyrotoxicosis itself ranges from subclinical (low TSH, normal free T4/T3) to overt disease and may escalate to thyrotoxic crisis/thyroid storm.

chunks.text: Hyphema results from disruption of iris or ciliary body vessels, most often by blunt trauma that causes rapid globe compression and a sudden shift of intraocular structures, tearing vessels at the iris root or angle. Red cells settle inferiorly under gravity. Clot formation and subsequent fibrinolysis create a window of rebleeding risk. Blood and inflammatory debris obstruct the trabecular meshwork, raising intraocular pressure; in sickle cell disease, red cells sickle in the low-oxygen, acidotic aqueous, further impairing outflow and increasing susceptibility to optic nerve damage. Prolonged high pressure with an intact endothelial insult leads to corneal blood staining.

chunks.text: Insulinoma (endogenous hyperinsulinism) — fasting hypoglycemia with elevated insulin, proinsulin, C-peptide (p.721)
Surreptitious/factitious insulin or sulfonylurea use (suppressed C-peptide with exogenous insulin; serum sulfonylurea assay if suspected) (p.721)
Non-islet-cell tumor hypoglycemia from IGF-II excess (mesenchymal tumors, hepatomas, adrenocortical and other large tumors) (p.635-636, p.782)
Severe liver disease, alcoholism, and poor nutrition causing fasting hypoglycemia (p.721)
Post-gastric-bypass postprandial hypoglycemia (p.721)

Severe falciparum malaria — hypoglycemia is a common complication and its neurologic effects are indistinguishable from cerebral malaria; usual adrenergic signs (sweating, gooseflesh, tachycardia) are often absent (p.1807)
Fasting insulin level (p.721)
Proinsulin level (p.721)
C-peptide level — helps separate endogenous from exogenous insulin (p.721)
Serum/plasma sulfonylurea assay when surreptitious agent use suspected (p.721)
IGF-II level and IGF-II/IGF-I ratio (ratio >10:1 suggestive of non-islet-cell tumor hypoglycemia; standard IGF-II assays may miss precursors) (p.782)
Endoscopic ultrasound for localization of insulinoma (typically small, <2 cm) (p.721)
Syncope and seizure — hypoglycemia-related loss of consciousness can be mistaken for either (p.204)
Psychiatric illness — neuroglycopenic behavioral symptoms of insulinoma can be misdiagnosed as psychiatric disease (p.721)

Pseudohypoglycemia — artifactually low glucose from in vitro glucose consumption by markedly elevated leukocytes (hyperleukocytosis in leukemia, myeloproliferative disease, leukemoid reaction, or after colony-stimulating factor) (p.635-636)

Falling glucose triggers counterregulatory autonomic activation (catecholamines) producing adrenergic warning symptoms, while inadequate glucose supply to the brain produces neuroglycopenia. Endogenous hyperinsulinism (insulinoma) drives fasting hypoglycemia with elevated insulin, proinsulin, and C-peptide. Non-islet-cell tumors can cause hypoglycemia chiefly through secretion of incompletely processed IGF-II ('big' IGF-II), which weakly activates insulin receptors and more strongly IGF-I receptors; reduced IGFBP-3 and acid-labile subunit increase IGF-II bioavailability to target tissues, and large tumors may also impair hepatic gluconeogenesis or consume glucose. In severe malaria, hypoglycemia arises from failed hepatic gluconeogenesis combined with increased host (and to a lesser extent parasite) glucose consumption, and may be worsened by quinine-induced insulin secretion (p.204, p.635-636, p.721, p.782, p.1807).

Symptoms fall into two groups: autonomic/adrenergic features (tremor, palpitations, anxiety, sweating, hunger, paresthesias) driven by counterregulatory activation, and neuroglycopenic features (fatigue, weakness, dizziness, confusion, behavioral change, cognitive impairment) from impaired neuronal function (p.204).
Hypoglycemia can cause transient loss of consciousness and may mimic syncope or seizure; hunger as a premonitory symptom and absence of immediate reorientation help distinguish it (p.204).
Insulinoma may first be misattributed to psychiatric illness, with symptoms (confusion, irrational behavior, visual difficulty, coma) recognized as neuroglycopenic only in retrospect (p.721).

Distinguish endogenous insulin excess (insulinoma) from surreptitious exogenous insulin use: C-peptide and proinsulin are elevated with insulinoma but suppressed with exogenous insulin injection (p.721).

A non-islet-cell tumor cause is suggested by hypoglycemia with suppressed insulin and C-peptide plus an elevated IGF-II/IGF-I ratio (>10:1) and inappropriately low GH and beta-hydroxybutyrate (p.635-636, p.782).
Repeated hypoglycemia produces hypoglycemia unawareness by impairing the counterregulatory response, so the absence of adrenergic warning symptoms does not exclude dangerous hypoglycemia (p.204).

In severe malaria the clinical signs of hypoglycemia (sweating, gooseflesh, tachycardia) are typically absent and its neurologic effects mimic the underlying disease, so it is easily missed without glucose measurement (p.1807).
Failing to measure C-peptide/proinsulin can miss surreptitious exogenous insulin use, which mimics insulinoma (p.721).
Circulating IGF-II may not be overtly elevated in tumor-induced hypoglycemia, so a normal IGF-II level does not exclude it; the IGF-II/IGF-I ratio is more informative (p.635-636, p.782).
A markedly raised leukocyte count can cause artifactual low glucose (pseudohypoglycemia) if the sample is not processed promptly (p.635-636).
Hypoglycemia is rapidly reversible with glucose, but in severe malaria it independently signals a poor prognosis, particularly in children and pregnant women (p.1807).
Hypoglycemia complicating severe malaria carries a poor prognosis, especially in children and pregnant women, and the usual warning signs may be absent (p.1807)
Recurrent hypoglycemia blunts counterregulation, causing hypoglycemia unawareness — loss of the warning symptoms that normally prompt correction (p.204)
Coma or seizures from neuroglycopenia indicate severe, potentially irreversible CNS compromise (p.721, p.782)
Capillary & lab glucose
Give IV dextrose
Hypoglycemia (non-infective) — Endocrine
Altered sensorium with low glucose is rapidly reversible and must be excluded first.
Red flags: Rapidly reversible — check glucose first in any altered patient

[guideline] management → Oral fast-acting carbohydrate (conscious) / IV glucose (impaired consciousness / NBM) / IM glucagon (no IV access) First-line if the patient is conscious and able to swallow; follow with longer-acting carbohydrate once recovered.

[guideline] adjunct → Somatostatin analogue (sulfonylurea overdose) Suppresses sulfonylurea-driven insulin secretion and reduces recurrent hypoglycaemia; use alongside glucose with prolonged monitoring and admission.
Hypovolaemic: GI losses (vomiting, diarrhoea, tube drainage) and insensible loss (sweating, burns) with inadequate replacement — urine Na+ typically <20 mM (p.390).
Hyperglycaemia-related ('true') hyponatraemia — plasma Na+ falls ~1.6-2.4 mM per 100 mg/dL rise in glucose; resolves after correcting hyperglycaemia (p.393).

Hypovolaemic renal: thiazide diuretics, mineralocorticoid/aldosterone deficiency (primary adrenal insufficiency, hypoaldosteronism), salt-losing nephropathies (reflux nephropathy, interstitial nephropathies, post-obstructive uropathy, medullary cystic disease, recovery phase of ATN) — urine Na+ typically >20 mM (p.390-391).
Osmotic/solute-driven hypovolaemic: glycosuria, ketonuria (starvation, diabetic or alcoholic ketoacidosis), bicarbonaturia (RTA, metabolic alkalosis) (p.391).
Cerebral salt wasting (subarachnoid haemorrhage, traumatic brain injury, craniotomy, encephalitis, meningitis) (p.391).
Hypervolaemic: congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, and acute or chronic renal failure (the latter uniquely with raised urine Na+) (p.391).
Euvolaemic: SIAD, moderate-to-severe hypothyroidism, secondary adrenal insufficiency from pituitary disease (glucocorticoid deficiency) (p.391).
Low solute intake: beer potomania (alcoholics whose sole nutrient is beer) and nutrient-restricted/extreme vegetarian diets — urine osmolality <100-200 mOsm/kg, urine Na+ <10-20 mM (p.391-392).

SIAD causes: malignancy (especially small-cell lung carcinoma — 75% of malignancy-associated SIAD; ~10% present with Na+ <130 mM), pulmonary disease (pneumonia, TB, abscess, pleural effusion), CNS disease (tumour, subarachnoid haemorrhage, meningitis, encephalitis, head trauma, hydrocephalus), drugs, and transient causes (pain, nausea, stress, endurance exercise, general anaesthesia) (p.391-392).
Pseudohyponatraemia — hyponatraemia coexisting with normal/increased plasma tonicity, from extreme hyperlipidaemia or hyperproteinaemia (p.393).

Serum osmolality, converted to effective osmolality/tonicity by subtracting urea (in mg/dL divided by 2.8) — true hyponatraemia has effective osmolality <275 mOsm/kg; this also excludes pseudohyponatraemia (p.393).
Imaging — chest CT in smokers/high-risk patients (screening CXR can miss small-cell lung carcinoma); CNS imaging where a central cause is suspected (p.393).
Serum glucose — to identify and correct hyperglycaemic (translocational) hyponatraemia (p.393).
Serum uric acid — low (<4 mg/dL) in SIAD physiology, often high in volume depletion (p.393).
Serum K+, BUN/creatinine — hyperkalaemia suggests adrenal insufficiency/hypoaldosteronism; raised urea/creatinine suggests renal cause (p.393).
Thyroid, adrenal and pituitary function testing, including a cosyntropin (ACTH) stimulation test to assess primary adrenal insufficiency, in the appropriate setting (p.393).
Urine osmolality — <100 mOsm/kg suggests primary polydipsia; >400 mOsm/kg indicates dominant AVP excess; intermediate values suggest multifactorial physiology (p.393).
Urine Na+ — <20-30 mM suggests hypovolaemia; >30 mM suggests SIAD, but values overlap, especially in the elderly (p.393).
Urine K+ — to calculate the urine-to-plasma electrolyte ratio, useful for predicting response to fluid restriction (p.393).
Demonstration that plasma Na+ corrects after isotonic saline hydration is the diagnostic gold standard for hypovolaemic hyponatraemia (p.393).
Pseudohyponatraemia from severe hyperlipidaemia/hyperproteinaemia: measured Na+ is low but plasma tonicity is normal or high; exclude by measuring serum osmolality (p.393).
Hyperglycaemic hyponatraemia: a translocational, true hyponatraemia driven by glucose-induced water efflux that corrects once glucose is lowered (p.393).

Hyponatraemia reflects a relative excess of body water to sodium, almost always from increased circulating AVP (or heightened renal AVP sensitivity) together with free-water intake. Volume status modulates AVP release: hypovolaemia raises AVP at any given osmolality, and 'hypervolaemic' arterial underfilling (heart failure, cirrhosis) triggers neurohumoral activation that likewise elevates AVP, causing water retention. In hypovolaemia, AVP-mediated V2-receptor water reabsorption plus free-water intake lowers Na+. In hypervolaemic oedematous states (CHF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome), total-body Na+ rises but water rises proportionally more; reduced arterial filling drives the AVP response. In euvolaemic hyponatraemia, SIAD is the commonest cause: free-water intake persists at osmolalities below the normal thirst threshold, with patients subclinically volume-expanded (so-called 'AVP escape' limits distal tubular transport, preserving a modestly hypervolaemic steady state). Four AVP-secretion patterns occur in SIAD: erratic unregulated secretion (~1/3 of patients), failure to suppress at low osmolality, a 'reset osmostat', and a subset with undetectable AVP (gain-of-function V2-receptor mutations causing 'nephrogenic' SIAD). At the brain level, hyponatraemia causes water to move down the osmotic gradient from hypotonic ECF into cells, producing cellular swelling and cerebral oedema within the rigid skull; acute encephalopathy results when volume-regulatory mechanisms (CSF shunting, efflux of Na+/K+/Cl-) are overwhelmed. In chronic hyponatraemia, brain cells extrude organic osmolytes (creatine, betaine, glutamate, myoinositol, taurine), a process largely complete within 48 h, which mitigates but does not abolish symptoms (p.390-392).
Hyponatraemia (plasma Na+ <135 mM) is very common, affecting up to ~22% of hospitalised patients (p.390).
The absolute plasma Na+ concentration says nothing about a patient's volume status, which must be assessed separately for both diagnosis and management (p.390).

Hyponatraemia is almost always driven by excess circulating AVP and/or increased renal sensitivity to AVP combined with free-water intake; the main exception is hyponatraemia from low solute intake (p.390).
Diagnostically subdivide by ECF volume into hypovolaemic, euvolaemic, and hypervolaemic groups based on clinical history and volume status (p.390).
In hypovolaemic patients, a urine Na+ <20 mM predicts a brisk rise in plasma Na+ with isotonic saline, because AVP falls and a water diuresis ensues (p.391).
Serum uric acid helps discriminate: SIAD is typically associated with low uric acid (<4 mg/dL), whereas hypovolaemic hyponatraemia is often hyperuricaemic (p.391, p.393).
Thiazides can mimic SIAD and do not impair urinary concentrating ability, so AVP retains full effect; defer diagnosing SIAD until 1-2 weeks after stopping the thiazide (p.391, p.393).
The 48-hour mark distinguishes acute from chronic hyponatraemia and is decisive for how aggressively/cautiously sodium may be corrected (p.392).

Cerebral salt wasting (a rare hypovolaemic cause linked to intracranial disease) responds to aggressive salt-and-water repletion, so distinguishing it from SIAD is critical because their management diverges (p.391).
Hypovolaemic patients may appear clinically euvolaemic, with only a low urine Na+ to reveal the cause (p.390).
Hyponatraemia is frequently multifactorial, especially when severe — evaluate every source of excess AVP (volume status, drugs, nausea, pain) rather than settling on one (p.393).
Failing to exclude pseudohyponatraemia/hyperglycaemia before correcting; check serum osmolality and glucose first (p.393).
The 93%-water assumption used by ion-sensitive electrodes makes plasma Na+ falsely low in extreme hyperlipidaemia/hyperproteinaemia (p.393).
Urine Na+ values overlap substantially between SIAD and hypovolaemia (particularly in the elderly); the saline-challenge response is the definitive discriminator (p.393).
Diagnosing SIAD in a patient on thiazides — defer the SIAD label until 1-2 weeks after stopping the drug (p.393).
Distinguishing cerebral salt wasting from SIAD is critical because management differs (salt repletion vs fluid restriction) (p.391).

Acute symptomatic hyponatraemia carries high risk of severe neurological injury and death; encephalopathy is more severe in premenopausal women. The degree of hyponatraemia is an important prognostic indicator in hypervolaemic states, reflecting the intensity of neurohumoral activation. Chronic hyponatraemia, even when judged 'asymptomatic', is associated with subtle gait and cognitive deficits (reversible with correction), increased risk of falls, and an increased fracture risk due to neurological dysfunction and reduced bone density — so safe correction is warranted even without overt symptoms. Osmotic demyelination from overcorrection can produce permanent disabling neurological deficits (p.392-393).
Acute symptomatic hyponatraemia is a medical emergency: nausea/headache/vomiting can rapidly progress to seizures, brainstem herniation, coma and death (p.392).

Acute hyponatraemia can cause normocapnoeic or hypercapnoeic respiratory failure, typically from non-cardiogenic 'neurogenic' pulmonary oedema with normal wedge pressure; resulting hypoxia amplifies neurological injury (p.392).
Premenopausal women are far more likely than men to develop encephalopathy and severe neurological sequelae (p.392).

Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia (>8-10 mM in 24 h or >18 mM in 48 h) risks osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS), classically central pontine myelinolysis — presenting days later with para-/quadriparesis, dysphagia, dysarthria, diplopia, 'locked-in' syndrome, or reduced consciousness (p.393).
ODS can occur even with appropriately slow correction in high-risk patients: alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalaemia, and liver transplantation (p.393).
Plasma Na+ <125 mM is the threshold at which chronic hyponatraemia commonly becomes overtly symptomatic (nausea, vomiting, confusion, seizures) (p.392).

Iatrogenic settings for acute hyponatraemia: postoperative premenopausal women given hypotonic fluids, glycine irrigation (TURP/uterine surgery), colonoscopy prep, recent thiazide initiation (Table 56-2, p.392).
MDMA ('Ecstasy'/'Molly') causes potent thirst and AVP induction leading to severe acute hyponatraemia; exercise-associated (endurance/marathon) hyponatraemia is another acute setting (p.392).

By volume status: hypovolaemic (total body water down, total body Na+ down more), euvolaemic/no oedema (total body water up, Na+ near-normal), and hypervolaemic (total body water up markedly, Na+ up) — Fig. 56-5, p.391. By chronicity: acute hyponatraemia is <48 h (osmolyte extrusion incomplete, higher cerebral-oedema risk) and chronic is >48 h (osmolytes largely extruded, lower acute symptom risk but higher ODS risk on correction), p.392. By tonicity: true hypotonic hyponatraemia has effective osmolality <275 mOsm/kg, distinct from pseudohyponatraemia (normal/high tonicity) and hyperglycaemic translocational hyponatraemia, p.393. Symptomatic threshold for chronic disease is generally plasma Na+ <125 mM (p.392). SIAD diagnostic features include euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia, inappropriately concentrated urine (urine osmolality typically >400 mOsm/kg / not maximally dilute), urine Na+ >30 mM, low serum uric acid (<4 mg/dL), and absence of thyroid/adrenal dysfunction, diuretics, hypovolaemia or hypervolaemia (p.391, p.393).

Hypoparathyroidism results from deficient secretion or action of parathyroid hormone, most often after surgical injury to the glands but also from autoimmune destruction, genetic syndromes, infiltration, or severe magnesium disturbance. Lack of PTH reduces renal calcium reabsorption and phosphate excretion, decreases bone resorption, and impairs conversion of vitamin D to its active form, together producing hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia. Low ionised calcium increases neuromuscular excitability, causing the characteristic clinical features.
The hallmark is hypocalcaemia with an inappropriately low or undetectable parathyroid hormone level, usually accompanied by hyperphosphataemia
Neck surgery is the most common cause, from inadvertent removal of or damage to the parathyroid glands
Symptoms of hypocalcaemia range from perioral and acral paraesthesiae and muscle cramps to tetany, laryngospasm, and seizures
Chvostek and Trousseau signs are useful bedside indicators of neuromuscular irritability from low calcium
Severe symptomatic or acute hypocalcaemia is a medical emergency requiring intravenous calcium and cardiac monitoring
Long-term management uses calcium and active vitamin D (calcitriol) analogues, aiming to relieve symptoms while avoiding hypercalciuria and renal complications
Autoimmune, genetic, and magnesium-related causes should be considered when there is no surgical history, as hypomagnesaemia impairs PTH secretion and action
Overlooking coexisting hypomagnesaemia, which must be corrected before hypocalcaemia will respond
Interpreting calcium without correcting for albumin or measuring the ionised fraction
Aiming for fully normal serum calcium and inducing hypercalciuria and renal damage
Failing to anticipate and monitor for hypocalcaemia after thyroid or parathyroid surgery

With appropriate calcium and active vitamin D therapy most patients maintain adequate calcium and lead normal lives, though lifelong treatment and monitoring are needed and chronic therapy carries risks of hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis, and renal impairment.
Tetany, laryngospasm, seizures, or carpopedal spasm
Prolonged QT interval or cardiac arrhythmia from acute hypocalcaemia
Rapidly falling calcium in the early postoperative period after neck surgery
Altered mental status or stridor accompanying severe hypocalcaemia

Low target-organ hormone with low or inappropriately normal trophic hormone (e.g., low free thyroxine with low/inappropriately normal TSH = secondary hypothyroidism; low testosterone without elevated gonadotropins = hypogonadotropic hypogonadism)

ACTH/cortisol reserve: most reliably assessed during insulin-induced hypoglycemia; CRH stimulation and cosyntropin (synthetic ACTH) testing also used

Impaired synthesis or secretion of one or more anterior pituitary trophic hormones (GH, FSH, LH, TSH, ACTH, PRL), and sometimes posterior pituitary AVP. Causes are developmental/genetic (transcription factor mutations such as PROP1, PIT-1, TPIT, midline defects) or, more commonly in adults, acquired from compressive mass effect of tumors or from local pituitary/hypothalamic traumatic, autoimmune, inflammatory, infiltrative, or vascular damage. The same processes may impair hypothalamic hormone production with secondary pituitary failure. With progressive compression/destruction, hormone loss is typically sequential (GH > FSH > LH > TSH > ACTH) (Harrison 22e p.2992).
Deficient production of one or more anterior pituitary trophic hormones produces the clinical features of hypopituitarism; most adult cases are acquired (Harrison 22e p.2992).

With pituitary compression or destruction, trophic hormone failure usually occurs sequentially: GH first, then FSH, LH, TSH, and ACTH last; in children growth retardation is often the presenting feature, in adults hypogonadism is the earliest symptom (Harrison 22e p.2992).

Clinical manifestations depend on which hormones are lost and the degree of deficiency: GH deficiency causes growth disorders in children and abnormal body composition in adults; gonadotropin deficiency causes menstrual disorders/infertility/loss of secondary sexual characteristics; TSH deficiency causes hypothyroidism; ACTH deficiency causes secondary adrenal insufficiency; PRL deficiency causes failure of lactation (Harrison 22e p.2996).
Secondary adrenal insufficiency from ACTH deficiency causes hypocortisolism with relative preservation of mineralocorticoid production (unlike primary adrenal failure) (Harrison 22e p.2996).

Pituitary apoplexy is an endocrine emergency: acute intrapituitary hemorrhage/infarction presenting with severe headache, meningeal signs, bilateral visual changes, ophthalmoplegia, and in severe cases cardiovascular collapse and loss of consciousness (Harrison 22e p.2993).

Lymphocytic hypophysitis occurs most often in postpartum women, presents with hyperprolactinemia and an MRI mass resembling an adenoma, and may be transient or permanent; it should be considered before unnecessary surgery in a postpartum woman with a new pituitary mass (Harrison 22e p.2993).

Up to 20% of patients receiving CTLA-4 inhibitor immunotherapy (e.g., ipilimumab) develop hypophysitis; PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors (pembrolizumab, nivolumab) can also cause it, sometimes with delayed presentation (Harrison 22e p.2993).
Patients on glucocorticoid replacement require careful dose escalation (stress dosing) during acute illness, dental procedures, trauma, and hospitalization (Harrison 22e p.2996).

Critical sequencing pitfall: in suspected combined deficiency, glucocorticoid replacement must be started BEFORE thyroid hormone, because giving thyroxine first can accelerate cortisol clearance and precipitate an adrenal crisis in a patient with unrecognized secondary adrenal insufficiency (Harrison 22e p.3133).

Insulin-induced hypoglycemia testing must be performed cautiously in suspected adrenal insufficiency (enhanced susceptibility to hypoglycemia/hypotension) and is contraindicated in active coronary artery disease or known seizure disorders (Harrison 22e p.2996).

Lymphocytic hypophysitis may be radiologically indistinguishable from a pituitary adenoma and should be considered in a postpartum woman with a new pituitary mass before surgery is undertaken (Harrison 22e p.2993).

Radiation-induced and brain-injury-related hypopituitarism develops insidiously over 5-15 years (and in 25-40% after brain injury), so long-term periodic endocrine follow-up is required even after apparently successful treatment (Harrison 22e p.2993).
Empty sella patients usually have normal pituitary function, but hypopituitarism may develop insidiously (Harrison 22e p.2994).

Hormone replacement is usually safe and effective at maintaining homeostasis when it mimics physiologic secretion. However, long-standing pituitary damage carries an increased mortality rate, primarily from cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease; adult hypopituitarism is associated with an approximately threefold increase in cardiovascular mortality versus age- and sex-matched controls. Prior head/neck irradiation is an additional determinant of increased mortality, especially from cerebrovascular disease. Lymphocytic hypophysitis may resolve with recovery of pituitary function after glucocorticoid treatment depending on extent of damage; hypopituitarism is common after apoplexy (Harrison 22e p.2996).

Pituitary apoplexy: an endocrine emergency that may cause severe hypoglycemia, hypotension/shock, CNS hemorrhage, and death; severe ophthalmoplegia or progressive visual loss indicates need for urgent surgical decompression
Secondary adrenal insufficiency / adrenal crisis: hypocortisolism that can precipitate life-threatening shock, especially during stress, illness, surgery, or trauma

Heat is lost by radiation (55-65%), conduction (10-15%, markedly increased in cold water), convection (increased with wind), respiration, and evaporation. The preoptic anterior hypothalamus orchestrates thermoregulation: the immediate autonomic defense releases norepinephrine, raises muscle tone, and triggers shivering to increase the basal metabolic rate, while cutaneous cold reception drives reflex vasoconstriction; prolonged cold also stimulates the thyroid axis. When these defenses are overwhelmed, hypothermia first stimulates and then progressively depresses every organ system. In peripheral freezing injury, tissue freezing causes ice-crystal formation that destroys cellular architecture; endothelial damage leads to stasis and microvascular thrombosis, and after thawing progressive dermal ischemia, arteriovenous shunting, rising tissue pressures, edema, and necrosis develop. Nonfreezing injuries (chilblain, trench/immersion foot) arise from neuronal and endothelial damage caused by repetitive cold exposure above the freezing point.

Accidental hypothermia is defined as an unintentional fall in core temperature below 35C (95F); at this threshold the compensatory mechanisms that conserve heat begin to fail. Primary hypothermia follows direct cold exposure of a previously healthy person, while secondary hypothermia complicates a systemic illness or injury and carries a much higher mortality.

Frostbite always produces a sensory deficit (light touch, pain, or temperature); superficial frostbite causes anesthesia and erythema without tissue loss, whereas vesiculation with surrounding edema/erythema indicates deeper injury and hemorrhagic vesicles signal severe microvascular damage that may lead to amputation.

Chilblain (pernio) is a nonfreezing injury from repetitive damp-cold exposure above freezing, most common in young women with a history of Raynaud phenomenon, producing erythema, edema, pruritus, then plaques, blue nodules, and ulcerations on the dorsa of hands and feet.

Trench foot / immersion foot results from repetitive wet-cold exposure above freezing; feet are initially cyanotic, cold, and edematous, with bullae progressing to ulceration and liquefaction gangrene, and survivors may have hyperhidrosis, cold sensitivity, and painful ambulation for years.

Core temperature cannot be reliably predicted from the clinical picture, so confirmation requires direct measurement; a probe in the lower third of the esophagus with continuous monitoring is preferred because rectal and bladder readings lag behind true core changes.

Severity grading by core temperature: mild 35C to 32.2C (initial tachycardia then bradycardia, shivering, apathy, dysarthria, impaired judgment, cold diuresis); moderate 32.2C to 28C (declining consciousness, pupillary dilation, paradoxical undressing, atrial/ventricular arrhythmias, J-wave changes, loss of protective airway reflexes); severe below 28C (coma, loss of cerebrovascular autoregulation, maximal risk of ventricular fibrillation and asystole, apnea, poikilothermia).

Vital signs are difficult to interpret without the core temperature: respiratory rate should be low because CO2 production declines, so persistent hyperventilation suggests a CNS lesion or organic acidosis, and tachycardia out of proportion to temperature suggests secondary causes such as hypoglycemia, hypovolemia, or toxin overdose.

Paradoxical undressing (inappropriate removal of clothing in response to cold stress) is a classic maladaptive behavior; cold-induced ileus and rectus abdominis spasm can mimic or mask an acute abdomen, and confusion or combativeness resolves faster with rewarming than with chemical or physical restraint.
The J (Osborn) wave at the QRS-ST junction supports the diagnosis and is frequently misread by automated ECG software as an injury current.

Laboratory values are systematically distorted by cold: hematocrit rises about 2% per 1C drop (masking anemia), white-cell sequestration and marrow suppression can mask infection, and coagulation tests run at 37C appear deceptively normal despite a genuine in-vivo coagulopathy, so platelet and fresh-frozen-plasma transfusion is ineffective for the cold-induced coagulopathy.

Arterial blood gases should NOT be temperature-corrected; an uncorrected pH of 7.42 and PCO2 of 40 mmHg reflect appropriate ventilation and acid-base balance at any core temperature, and overzealous hyperventilation is a common error given depressed CO2 production.

Frostbite occurs when tissue temperature falls below 0C (32F): ice-crystal formation distorts cellular architecture, endothelial damage produces microvascular thrombosis, and after thawing there is progressive dermal ischemia, arteriovenous shunting, edema, and superficial necrosis, with mummification and demarcation taking weeks to months.

Repeated dosing of drugs (e.g., digoxin, insulin) that are ineffective while cold but become toxic during rewarming

Outcome depends heavily on whether hypothermia is primary or secondary, the precipitating cause, and the presence of asphyxia. Secondary hypothermia complicating systemic illness carries much higher mortality, and hypothermia with sepsis is a poor prognostic sign. Because cold itself is protective, survival has been reported after cardiac arrest times exceeding 7 hours, and intact neurologic recovery has occurred at extremely low core temperatures; the patient is not dead until warm and dead. Markers of a grave prognosis during resuscitation include potassium >12 mmol/L (cell lysis), pH <6.5, fibrinogen <0.5 g/L, and core temperature <10-12C, while preceding asphyxia (avalanche) is the most important negative predictor. The HOPE score uses six covariates to predict which arrested hypothermic patients may benefit from extracorporeal life support. Frostbite sequelae often persist as paresthesia, thermal misperception, and hyperhidrosis, with delayed nail deformities, cutaneous carcinomas, and epiphyseal damage in children.

Hypothermia is graded by core temperature: Mild = 35C (95F) to 32.2C (90F); Moderate = below 32.2C (90F) to 28C (82.4F); Severe = below 28C (82.4F). Frostbite is classified as superficial (anesthesia and erythema, no tissue loss) versus deep (vesiculation, hemorrhagic vesicles, possible amputation); an alternative scheme grades by the proximal extent of presenting cyanosis: grade 1 none, grade 2 distal phalanx, grade 3 to the metacarpophalangeal joint, grade 4 proximal to the MP joint.

Hypothyroidism is deficient thyroid hormone action, most often from primary thyroid failure. In autoimmune (Hashimoto's) disease, T cell-mediated lymphocytic infiltration with germinal-center formation, follicular atrophy, oxyphil metaplasia, and fibrosis progressively destroy the gland; atrophic thyroiditis represents its fibrotic end stage. As function declines there is a compensated phase in which a rising TSH maintains hormone levels (subclinical hypothyroidism); later free T4 falls and TSH rises further, producing overt disease. Susceptibility reflects genetic factors (HLA-DR3/DR4/DR5, PTPN22, CTLA-4) and environmental factors including high iodine intake. TPO and thyroglobulin antibodies are markers; up to 20% of patients have TSH-receptor-blocking antibodies that prevent TSH binding and can cause thyroid atrophy and, by transplacental passage, transient neonatal hypothyroidism. Increased dermal glycosaminoglycan deposition traps water, producing nonpitting myxedema (Harrison 22e p.3029-3030).

In iodine-sufficient regions the most common causes are autoimmune disease (Hashimoto's thyroiditis) and iatrogenic injury (treatment of hyperthyroidism); iodine deficiency remains a leading cause worldwide (p.3027).
Biochemical hallmark of primary hypothyroidism is an elevated TSH with a low unbound (free) T4; a normal TSH excludes primary, but not secondary/central, disease (p.3030-3031).

Subclinical hypothyroidism is biochemical thyroid hormone deficiency (raised TSH, usually still-normal free T4) with few or no symptoms; overt hypothyroidism typically corresponds to TSH >10 mIU/L with a low free T4 (p.3029, p.3032).

Symptoms (descending frequency) include tiredness/weakness, dry skin, cold intolerance, hair loss, poor concentration and memory, constipation, and modest weight gain with poor appetite (the weight gain is mainly fluid retention in myxedematous tissue) (p.3028-3029).

Signs include dry coarse skin, cool extremities, nonpitting puffiness of face/hands/feet (myxedema), diffuse alopecia with thinning of the outer eyebrow, bradycardia, peripheral edema, and delayed relaxation of tendon reflexes (p.3028-3029).
TPO and thyroglobulin antibodies are present in >95% of autoimmune hypothyroidism and confirm the etiology once hypothyroidism is established (p.3030).

Onset is usually insidious, so patients may only recognize symptoms once euthyroidism is restored; Hashimoto's patients may present with goiter (irregular, firm) rather than hypothyroid symptoms (p.3029-3030).

Associated laboratory abnormalities include raised creatine phosphokinase, elevated cholesterol and triglycerides, and a normocytic or macrocytic anemia, which generally resolve with thyroxine replacement (p.3030).

Autoimmune hypothyroidism clusters with other autoimmune disorders, particularly vitiligo, pernicious anemia, Addison's disease (Schmidt's syndrome), type 1 diabetes, and the autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes (p.3030).

Central (secondary) hypothyroidism is missed if TSH is used alone: in pituitary/hypothalamic disease TSH may be low, normal, or even slightly raised, so a low free T4 is needed to make the diagnosis and TSH cannot be used to monitor therapy.
A normal TSH excludes primary but NOT secondary/central hypothyroidism.
T4 alone is an inferior screening test because it will not detect subclinical hypothyroidism; T3 is normal in ~25% of patients and is not indicated.
An elevated TSH with normal/high free T4 in a patient on adequate levothyroxine usually reflects poor adherence (taking medication only shortly before testing), not a TSH-secretion disorder.
Confirm that a raised TSH is sustained over ~3 months before treating subclinical hypothyroidism.
TSH should not be relied on in the months immediately after radioiodine for Graves' disease (it stays suppressed); use unbound T4 instead.
External rewarming in myxedema coma can precipitate cardiovascular collapse, and hypotonic fluids can worsen hyponatremia.

With levothyroxine replacement and dose titration to a normal TSH, prognosis is excellent and most laboratory and clinical abnormalities resolve, though full symptomatic relief may take months and about 10-15% report persistent symptoms despite biochemical euthyroidism. Untreated congenital hypothyroidism causes permanent neurologic damage, and myxedema coma still carries a 20-40% mortality independent of T4 and TSH levels (Harrison 22e p.3031-3032).

Myxedema coma — the severe end of untreated hypothyroidism: reduced level of consciousness (sometimes seizures), hypothermia (can reach 23 C), with 20-40% mortality despite treatment; almost always in the elderly and often precipitated by infection, cold, sedatives, or acute cardiopulmonary events.
Hypoventilation with hypoxia and hypercapnia, plus hypoglycemia and dilutional hyponatremia, in profound hypothyroidism.
Impaired adrenal reserve in profound hypothyroidism (consider co-existing adrenal insufficiency before/with thyroid replacement).

Significant pericardial or other serous effusions, conductive deafness, or carpal tunnel/entrapment syndromes as manifestations of severe disease.

Spectrum from subclinical hypothyroidism (raised TSH, normal free T4, few/no symptoms) to overt/clinical hypothyroidism (raised TSH usually >10 mIU/L with low free T4 and symptoms); myxedema coma represents the severe, life-threatening end. chunks.text: Hypovolemic shock arises when a fall in intravascular volume reduces preload, lowering stroke volume and cardiac output and therefore systemic oxygen delivery; CVP and PCWP are low and systemic vascular resistance rises as a compensatory response (p.2311). Inadequate oxygen delivery forces cells into anaerobic metabolism, so pyruvate is converted to lactate with markedly less ATP generation; failure of ATP-dependent ion pumps disrupts ionic and pH homeostasis, and calcium influx activates phospholipases/proteases causing cell swelling and death, with leaked intracellular contents driving inflammation and microvascular injury (p.2310). In acute haemorrhage, hypovolaemia dominates first and threatens high-flow organs (brain, kidneys); the haemoglobin is initially normal and only falls over hours as fluid shifts from the extravascular to the intravascular space (haemodilution), so the haematocrit does not reflect the volume lost early on (pp.850-851).

IBD is a chronic idiopathic inflammatory disease of the GI tract regarded as a dysregulated, inappropriate immune response to the endogenous commensal microbiota (with or without an autoimmune component) in a genetically susceptible host. Homeostasis among the gut microbiota, intestinal epithelial cells, and mucosal immune system is normally maintained by regulatory pathways (e.g., FoxP3 T-regulatory cells); environmental factors (smoking, antibiotics, enteropathogens, diet) acting on genetic susceptibility (>240 GWAS loci, ~20% of risk explained; rare single-gene defects such as IL10/IL10R in very-early-onset disease) disrupt this balance and produce sustained inflammation. UC is a mucosal/superficial-submucosal disease, while Crohn's is transmural with fissuring and fistula/stricture formation (p.2551-2556).

UC inflammation is continuous from the rectum proximally without skip areas, whereas Crohn's is segmental with skip lesions and frequently spares the rectum; this distribution difference is a key way to separate the two (p.2555-2556).

Granulomas (noncaseating, in all bowel-wall layers) are characteristic of Crohn's but are found less often on mucosal biopsy than on surgical resection specimens, so their absence does not exclude Crohn's (p.2556).
On biopsy, distorted/branching crypt architecture and basal plasmacytosis/lymphoid aggregates indicate chronicity and help distinguish IBD from acute self-limited or infectious colitis (p.2556).

Faecal calprotectin and lactoferrin correlate with histologic inflammation, help predict relapse, and can detect pouchitis; they are used to distinguish active inflammation from IBS or bacterial overgrowth (p.2556-2557).
Distinguishing UC from Crohn's is not possible initially in up to ~15% of cases (indeterminate colitis), though the true type usually declares itself later (p.2559).
Only ~15% of UC patients present initially with severe disease (p.2557).
Distal/proctitis-limited UC can paradoxically present with constipation due to slowed proximal transit despite distal inflammation (p.2557).
In severely ill UC patients serum albumin falls quickly; leukocytosis can occur but is not a specific marker of disease activity (p.2557).

Before escalating immunosuppression in a presumed flare, exclude superimposed infection - C. difficile and CMV colitis can mimic or complicate IBD; diagnosis requires negative stool studies (culture, C. difficile toxin, ova and parasites) and, for CMV, identification of intranuclear inclusions on mucosal biopsy (p.2557, p.2560).

A first 'flare' of bloody diarrhoea may actually be an infectious colitis (e.g., Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, C. difficile, amoebic) - infection should be excluded before diagnosing IBD; Campylobacter and others can also reactivate established UC (p.2559-2560).
Granulomas are frequently absent on mucosal biopsy even in Crohn's, so their absence does not rule it out (p.2556).
Effective medical therapy can normalise mucosal appearance and create apparent skip areas in UC, mimicking Crohn's distribution; biopsy normal-appearing mucosa (p.2555-2556).
Extensive perianal lesions in a patient labelled UC should raise suspicion for Crohn's instead (p.2557).
In patients on glucocorticoids, peritoneal signs of perforation may be blunted/absent (p.2557).
An impassable colonic stricture should be presumed malignant rather than benign inflammatory (p.2557).

Toxic megacolon occurs rarely; about 50% of acute dilations resolve with conservative management, but those that do not require urgent colectomy. Perforation complicating toxic megacolon carries ~15% mortality. Risk of colorectal cancer rises with duration and extent of colitis (historically ~2% at 10 yr, 8% at 20 yr, 18% at 30 yr, though rates have fallen with better inflammation control and surveillance; still ~1.5-2x the general population). Extensive long-standing colitis carries the highest cancer risk. Strictures occur in ~5% of UC patients. Up to one-third of IBD patients develop at least one extraintestinal manifestation (p.2557-2563, p.2570).

IBS is a multifactorial functional bowel disorder with no structural lesion. Proposed mechanisms include altered GI motor activity (e.g., exaggerated postprandial and distention-evoked colonic contractions, increased high-amplitude propagating contractions with rapid transit in IBS-D), visceral hypersensitivity (lower thresholds to rectal balloon distention with sparing of somatic pain pathways), and disordered brain-gut interaction with central neural dysregulation (greater activation of mid-cingulate and prefrontal cortices on functional imaging). Psychological factors (anxiety, depression, somatization, prior physical/sexual abuse) modulate pain thresholds, and genetic factors such as serotonin transporter (SERT) polymorphisms are implicated. Peripheral contributors include low-grade mucosal immune activation with mast cells, lymphocytes and proinflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-1beta, TNF), upregulated TRPV1 sensory channels, increased intestinal permeability ('leaky gut', chiefly in IBS-D and post-infectious IBS), gut dysbiosis (reduced microbial diversity, fewer Bifidobacterium/Faecalibacterium, more Enterobacteriaceae), abnormal serotonin pathways with increased enterochromaffin-cell serotonin in IBS-D, and bile acid malabsorption in up to ~25% of IBS-D.

Rome IV makes IBS a positive symptom-based diagnosis, not purely one of exclusion: recurrent abdominal pain on average at least 1 day/week over the prior 3 months plus at least two of being related to defecation, a change in stool frequency, or a change in stool form, with onset at least 6 months earlier.
Rome IV is stricter than Rome III: it requires pain at least weekly and dropped 'discomfort' as a qualifying symptom; painless diarrhoea or constipation alone does NOT meet criteria.
Abdominal pain is mandatory for the diagnosis; it is typically episodic and crampy, often worsened by eating or emotional stress and relieved by passing flatus or stool.

Subtype by predominant stool form: IBS-C (constipation), IBS-D (diarrhoea), and IBS-M (mixed) — but subtypes are unstable, with about three-quarters of patients changing subtype and ~29% switching between IBS-C and IBS-D over a year.
Onset is usually before age 45 and IBS is two to three times more common in women, who make up ~80% of severe cases.

Symptoms commonly overlap with other functional disorders (fibromyalgia, headache, backache, genitourinary symptoms) and with functional dyspepsia, suggesting a shared, more extensive digestive disorder.

Bloating and a subjective sense of excess gas are common, but most patients actually generate a normal volume of intestinal gas and instead have impaired gas transit/tolerance and proximal reflux of gas.
Malnutrition is exceedingly rare in IBS and the pain almost always occurs only during waking hours, so sleep disruption from pain is unusual.

Treating IBS as a diagnosis of exclusion only and over-investigating: few tests are needed when symptoms are typical and alarm features are absent, and unnecessary investigations may be costly and even harmful.

Missing organic disease in higher-risk patients: older age, rapidly progressive symptoms, or alarm features should prompt a thorough work-up to exclude IBD, coeliac disease and colorectal cancer rather than labelling as IBS.
Attributing bloating to excess gas when most patients produce a normal gas volume but have impaired gas transit.
Over-interpreting an abnormal hydrogen breath test, which can be positive simply from rapid small-bowel transit and does not reliably predict treatment response.

Hypertensive ICH usually results from spontaneous rupture of a small (~30-100 microns) penetrating artery deep in the brain, with chronic hypertension producing vascular injury preferentially at the basal ganglia (especially putamen), thalamus, cerebellum and pons. The clot may stay small or enlarge to compress adjacent tissue and cause herniation; dissection into the ventricles markedly increases morbidity and can produce hydrocephalus. Most hypertensive bleeds evolve over 30-90 minutes, whereas anticoagulant-related bleeds may keep expanding for 24-48 h. By ~48 h macrophages begin phagocytosing the haemorrhage at its surface, and over 1-6 months it resolves to a slit-like glial-scarred cavity with haemosiderin-laden macrophages. In cerebral amyloid angiopathy, arteriolar degeneration with amyloid deposition in cortical vessel walls causes single and recurrent lobar haemorrhages, the commonest cause of lobar bleeding in the elderly (p.3453-3454).
ICH typically presents as abrupt-onset focal deficit; compared with ischaemic stroke, headache is more common, but imaging is still required to distinguish the two (p.3453).
Putaminal haemorrhage damages the adjacent internal capsule, so contralateral hemiparesis is the sentinel sign, often with the eyes deviated away from the side of the weakness (p.3454).

Thalamic haemorrhage produces a prominent all-modality contralateral sensory deficit and characteristic ocular signs from inferior extension into the upper midbrain (e.g. eyes deviated down-and-in 'looking at the nose', poorly reactive unequal pupils, vertical-gaze palsy) (p.3454).
Pontine haemorrhage causes rapid deep coma with quadriplegia, decerebrate rigidity and reactive 'pinpoint' (~1 mm) pupils (p.3454).
Cerebellar haemorrhage classically gives occipital headache, repeated vomiting and gait ataxia; in mild cases gait ataxia may be the only sign (p.3454).
Lobar haemorrhage symptoms mirror the lobe involved: occipital → hemianopia, left temporal → aphasia and confusion, parietal → hemisensory loss, frontal → arm weakness (p.3454).
Seizures are uncommon at presentation but occur in roughly 6-15% of patients within the first 3 days (p.3453).
Lumbar puncture is generally unnecessary and should usually be avoided in ICH because focal signs and raised ICP make it potentially herniation-inducing (p.3455).
ICH accounts for about 10% of all strokes, with disproportionately high incidence in Asian and Black populations (p.3453).

Cerebellar haemorrhage can deteriorate precipitously from brainstem compression or obstructive hydrocephalus; immediate surgical evacuation before severe brainstem compression may be lifesaving, and hydrocephalus from a cerebellar haematoma should generally be managed by definitive evacuation rather than ventricular drainage alone (p.3454).

Haemorrhage outside the typical deep hypertensive sites, or in a non-hypertensive patient, should prompt a search for other causes (amyloid angiopathy, tumour, vascular malformation, vasculitis, coagulopathy) rather than being assumed hypertensive (p.3454).
Conflating hypertensive encephalopathy/PRES with hypertensive ICH leads to inappropriately aggressive BP lowering - hypertensive encephalopathy warrants less aggressive reduction (p.3455).
ICP is often normal even with large ICHs, so it cannot be assumed; conversely induced hyperventilation can cause ischaemia and should be limited to acute resuscitation only (p.3456).
Glucocorticoids are not recommended for treating ICH (p.3456).
In ICH on antiplatelet drugs without thrombocytopenia, platelet transfusion showed no benefit and possible harm (p.3456).
Despite the presence of haemorrhage, venous sinus thrombosis is an indication for anticoagulation to relieve venous hypertension (p.3455).

Overall, about 35-45% of patients die within the first month, and roughly 40% with a hypertensive ICH die, though survivors can achieve good to complete recovery because peri-haematoma tissue is displaced rather than infarcted and often regains function as the clot resorbs over months. The validated ICH Score stratifies mortality and outcome but should not be used to precisely prognosticate an individual, since withholding early aggressive care risks a self-fulfilling prophecy of poor outcome. Deep pontine haemorrhage with coma usually ends in death or a locked-in state, but small bleeds are compatible with survival; in cerebellar haemorrhage, full recovery is common if the deep cerebellar nuclei are spared (p.3453-3456).

IgG4-RD is characterized by a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate rich in IgG4-positive plasma cells, a distinctive storiform (woven-mat / basket-weave) pattern of fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis reflecting vascular tropism, and a mild-to-moderate tissue eosinophilia. The infiltrate combines B cells (organized in germinal centers, with IgG4+ CD19/CD138 plasma cells radiating outward) and a more diffusely distributed, predominant population of CD4+ T cells. Despite the disease's name, the IgG4 molecule itself is not thought to directly drive injury in most organs: IgG4 undergoes Fab-arm exchange, binds antigen weakly, and has low affinity for Fc receptors and C1q, making it a generally noninflammatory immunoglobulin that may even play a counterregulatory role. A unique oligoclonally expanded CD4+ cytotoxic T cell, abundant at tissue sites, secretes interferon-gamma, TGF-beta, and interleukin-1 (driving storiform fibrosis) as well as perforin, granzymes A/B, and granulysin (mediating cytotoxicity), and appears to be a major disease driver. Oligoclonal plasmablast expansions in blood, with continuous B-cell/plasmablast antigen presentation, are thought to support these profibrotic, tissue-injuring CD4+ cytotoxic T cells.
A fibroinflammatory disorder whose hallmark is a tendency to form tumefactive (mass-like) lesions that frequently mimic malignancy; initial misdiagnosis as cancer is extremely common.

Renal involvement (tubulointerstitial nephritis) is strongly associated with hypocomplementemia; membranous glomerulonephropathy is a less common renal manifestation that must be distinguished from idiopathic disease.
Clinical course is variable: disease may relapse and remit within a given organ, accumulate new organ involvement over time, or be found incidentally on imaging.
Disease can evolve over months, years, or even decades before an organ becomes symptomatic enough to prompt medical attention.

Protean and multisystem: can affect virtually any organ, with predilection for pancreas, biliary tree, major salivary glands (submandibular, parotid), periorbital/lacrimal tissues, kidneys, lungs, lymph nodes, and retroperitoneum; meninges, aorta, prostate, thyroid, pericardium, and skin are also described.
Regarded as a variable-vessel vasculitis because it can target arteries and veins of any size, with venous involvement (obliterative phlebitis) being a particular hallmark.

Typical patient is a middle-aged to elderly man (male-to-female ratio about 2:1), contrasting with classic autoimmune diseases that favor young women; head-and-neck (orbit, lacrimal, salivary) disease has a sex ratio closer to 1:1.
Usually presents subacutely; most patients lack fever or marked C-reactive protein elevation even with multiorgan disease. Substantial weight loss can occur, often from exocrine pancreatic failure.
Mikulicz's disease (lacrimal, parotid, and submandibular gland enlargement), once thought to be a Sjogren's subset, is one of the most common presentations of IgG4-RD.
Allergic features are common: atopy, eczema, asthma, nasal polyps, sinusitis, and modest peripheral eosinophilia.

Type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis classically shows a diffusely enlarged 'sausage-shaped' pancreas with loss of normal lobularity; 20-50% of patients present with acute glucose intolerance and a pancreatic mass mimicking adenocarcinoma.
Diagnosis requires correlation of clinical, serologic, radiologic, and pathologic findings; pathology alone is never sufficient, and biopsy is often done mainly to exclude malignancy.
Treating the disease as purely IgG4-antibody-mediated; the IgG4 molecule is largely noninflammatory and may be counterregulatory rather than a primary driver.

Excluding the diagnosis because serum IgG4 is normal: ~30% of histologically proven cases have normal levels, and retroperitoneal fibrosis (often advanced/fibrotic at presentation) frequently shows normal IgG4.
Missing markedly elevated IgG4 because of the prozone effect on nephelometry; suspect this when results are normal despite strong clinical features and re-test with dilution.
Relying on pathology alone for diagnosis; histopathology, while characteristic, is essentially never diagnostic by itself and must be interpreted with clinical, serologic, and radiologic data.
Mistaking tumefactive lesions for malignancy and proceeding to major resections (e.g., Whipple procedure, thyroidectomy) before the correct diagnosis is recognized.

Histologic features such as intense neutrophilic infiltration, leukocytoclasis, granulomatous inflammation, multinucleated giant cells, or fibrinoid necrosis are uncommon in IgG4-RD and argue against the diagnosis.
Assuming serum IgG4 reliably tracks disease activity; correlations are imperfect, levels often do not fully normalize, and remissions can occur with persistently elevated levels.

Course is generally subacute but can cause major morbidity and organ failure. Aggressive disease may rapidly produce end-stage liver disease, permanent pancreatic exocrine and endocrine (diabetes) impairment, renal atrophy, aortic dissection or aneurysm, and destructive sinonasal lesions. Some manifestations (e.g., IgG4-related lymphadenopathy) can remain indolent and asymptomatic for years. Even with apparently effective immunosuppression, renal atrophy is a frequent sequel to tubulointerstitial nephritis, and end-organ fibrotic damage may be irreversible if diagnosis is delayed. Relapses are common, including in patients with persistently normal IgG4 levels.
New tumefactive mass mimicking cancer in pancreas, salivary gland, orbit, lung, or other organ.
Obstructive jaundice from pancreatic or biliary involvement (undiagnosed/undertreated sclerosing cholangitis can lead to hepatic failure within months).
Ureteral entrapment, hydronephrosis, postobstructive uropathy, and renal atrophy from retroperitoneal fibrosis.
Aortic involvement causing aneurysm or dissection.
Anterior pituitary hormone deficiency and/or central diabetes insipidus from hypothalamic-pituitary involvement.
Spinal cord compression, cranial nerve palsies, or radiculopathy from hypertrophic pachymeningitis.
Destructive bone lesions of sinuses, head, and middle ear mimicking granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
Persistently rising serum IgG4 concentrations signaling risk of clinical flare and serious organ involvement.
Coronary arteritis (wall thickening, periarterial encasement, stenosis, calcification, aneurysm/ectasia) in longstanding disease with high IgG4 and biomarker levels.

No formal numeric severity score is given. Practical stratification distinguishes vital/organ-threatening involvement (e.g., pancreas, biliary tree/liver, kidneys, aorta, sinonasal destruction, pituitary, meninges) requiring prompt treatment from indolent manifestations (e.g., asymptomatic lymphadenopathy) amenable to watchful waiting with close monitoring; classification of disease itself relies on correlation of clinical, serologic, radiologic, and pathologic findings (ACR/EULAR classification criteria are referenced).

chunks.text: ILDs are characterised by remodelling of the interstitium with variable degrees of inflammation and fibrosis, but alveolar epithelial and endothelial cell injury is also central to pathogenesis. The idiopathic interstitial pneumonias (IIPs) are the most common group. In IPF the histologic hallmark is a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern: subpleural reticulation with honeycomb change and fibroblast foci (subepithelial collections of myofibroblasts and collagen) alternating with preserved normal alveolar architecture, producing temporal and spatial heterogeneity. NSIP shows more uniform interstitial inflammation and fibrosis with honeycombing usually absent and fibroblast foci rare. Genetic studies show that a substantial fraction of familial and even sporadic/idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis has a genetic basis: a MUC5B promoter variant (present in ~20% of Caucasians, 35-45% of IPF patients) confers an approximately sixfold risk, and variants in telomere-length genes (TERT, TERC, RTEL1) and surfactant protein genes (SFTPA2) are also implicated. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is an immune-mediated response to inhaled antigens small enough to reach distal airways and alveoli, driven by dysregulated TH1/TH17 responses with precipitating IgG and innate (Toll-like receptor/MyD88) signalling; chronic HP shares the MUC5B variant with IPF (pp.2259-2266; 2228-2229).

chunks.text: Prognosis varies widely by ILD subtype and disease extent. IPF carries a poor prognosis (~50% survival at 3-5 years; pre-antifibrotic-era life expectancy 3-5 years from diagnosis). Idiopathic NSIP is comparatively favourable (>80% 5-year survival), with cellular NSIP doing better than fibrosing NSIP. Reported subtype mortality includes RB-ILD ~25% at 7 years and systemic sclerosis-associated ILD ~20-30% at 10 years; sarcoidosis mortality is generally low but state-dependent. RB-ILD usually has prolonged survival with death from progressive ILD rare. AIP has >50% 6-month mortality with frequent recurrences, though survivors can recover substantial lung function. Acute exacerbations of fibrotic ILD carry very high mortality (>85%). In CTD-ILD, a UIP pattern and more extensive fibrosis (e.g. in RA) predict reduced survival. Chronic fibrotic HP can mirror IPF in radiology and prognosis (pp.2260, 2262-2266; 2229).

chunks.text: Harrison frames ILD pattern recognition rather than a single numeric severity score. ILDs are first split into known cause (occupational e.g. asbestosis/silicosis; drug-induced e.g. amiodarone, nitrofurantoin, methotrexate, bleomycin; systemic/CTD-associated; granulomatous including HP) versus unknown cause (idiopathic interstitial pneumonias, plus rarer entities such as LAM, PAP, PLCH, sarcoidosis). The idiopathic interstitial pneumonias are further classified (per the ATS/ERS consensus) into chronic fibrosing (IPF, idiopathic NSIP), smoking-related (RB-ILD, DIP), and acute/subacute (COP, acute interstitial pneumonia, lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia). The UIP pattern (subpleural, basal reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis) defines IPF, while NSIP shows more ground-glass and rare honeycombing. HP is now classified as nonfibrotic versus fibrotic (replacing the older acute/subacute/chronic terminology). Disease severity is gauged by extent of fibrosis/honeycombing on HRCT, degree of PFT (FVC/DLCO) impairment and its rate of decline, and presence of pulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale (pp.2259-2266; 2229).

chunks.text: Impetigo is a superficial bacterial infection of the epidermis caused predominantly by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes, alone or together. Organisms colonise and then invade skin whose barrier has been breached by minor trauma, bites, or pre-existing dermatoses. In bullous disease, staphylococcal exfoliative toxins cleave desmoglein-1 in the superficial epidermis, causing intraepidermal separation and blister formation. The host inflammatory response and serous exudate dry to form the typical crusts. Certain nephritogenic streptococcal strains can trigger immune-complex-mediated post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

chunks.text: An incisional hernia develops when the musculo-aponeurotic layers of a healed surgical wound fail to maintain their integrity, allowing peritoneum and abdominal contents to protrude beneath the intact skin. Impaired wound healing, whether from infection, ischaemia, raised intra-abdominal pressure, technical factors, or patient factors such as obesity, diabetes, and malnutrition, weakens the fascial repair. Over time the defect enlarges and the sac expands, sometimes housing much of the abdominal contents. Narrow-necked defects can trap and strangulate bowel, while very large defects lead to loss of domain and altered abdominal wall mechanics.
