Gastro-oesophageal reflux occurs when gastric contents pass back into the oesophagus, largely through transient relaxations of the lower oesophageal sphincter. Reflux is especially common in infancy because of a short oesophagus, a predominantly liquid and high-volume diet, frequent recumbency, and immaturity of the antireflux barrier. In most infants this is physiological and self-resolving. Reflux disease develops when refluxate causes oesophageal mucosal injury and pain, impairs feeding and growth, or reaches the airway to provoke respiratory symptoms. Contributing factors include delayed gastric emptying and, in some infants, cow's milk protein allergy that produces overlapping symptoms.

It is essential to distinguish physiological gastro-oesophageal reflux, which is common and benign in healthy infants, from reflux disease, in which reflux causes troublesome symptoms or complications.
Effortless regurgitation or posseting in a thriving, comfortable infant (the happy spitter) is normal and typically improves as the infant matures and begins to sit and take solids.
Reflux disease is suggested by poor weight gain, feeding refusal or distress, persistent irritability, back-arching with feeds, or respiratory symptoms attributable to reflux.
Diagnosis is largely clinical from the history and examination; investigations are reserved for atypical presentations, complications, or diagnostic uncertainty.
First-line management uses conservative measures such as optimising feeding volume and technique, thickened feeds where appropriate, and positioning advice consistent with safe sleep guidance.
A trial of cow's milk protein elimination is reasonable when allergy is suspected, since it can mimic or coexist with reflux disease.
Acid-suppressing medication is not appropriate for uncomplicated physiological reflux and should be limited to infants with clear evidence of reflux disease.
Warning features such as bilious or forceful vomiting, gastrointestinal bleeding, or onset of vomiting after six months point away from simple reflux and toward an alternative diagnosis.
Treating benign physiological reflux with acid suppression or unnecessary investigation
Missing an alternative diagnosis such as pyloric stenosis or malrotation presenting with vomiting
Overlooking cow's milk protein allergy as a mimicking or coexisting cause
Recommending positioning that conflicts with safe sleep advice

Physiological reflux resolves in the great majority of infants during the first year to eighteen months as the infant matures; reflux disease also generally improves with time and appropriate management, though some infants with underlying conditions require more prolonged treatment.

Infantile colic does not have a single established mechanism and is best understood as excessive crying at the upper end of the normal developmental crying curve, which peaks in early infancy. Proposed contributors include transient gastrointestinal factors such as immature motility, gas, or feeding-related discomfort, alterations in the gut microbiome, cow's milk protein sensitivity in a subset of infants, heightened infant sensitivity or difficult temperament, and stress within the infant-caregiver relationship. In most infants no pathological process is identified, and the self-limited course paralleling normal maturation supports a developmental rather than a disease-based explanation.
Infantile colic describes recurrent, prolonged episodes of inconsolable crying and fussiness in an otherwise healthy, well-fed, and thriving young infant.

It is often characterised by the rule of threes: crying for more than about three hours a day, on more than three days a week, for more than three weeks, though clinical judgement matters more than strict criteria.
Episodes commonly cluster in the late afternoon and evening and may be accompanied by drawing up of the legs, a flushed face, and clenched fists.
It is a diagnosis of exclusion, established when a careful history and thorough examination reveal no underlying organic cause and growth is normal.
Typical onset is in the first few weeks of life, with peak intensity around six weeks and spontaneous resolution by around three to four months of age.
The cause is not fully understood and is likely multifactorial, involving normal developmental crying, gut and feeding factors, and infant-caregiver interaction.
Management centres on parental reassurance, education about the benign and self-limiting nature, soothing techniques, and support for exhausted caregivers.
Because the crying is intense and distressing, clinicians should assess caregiver stress and coping and be alert to the risk of frustration-related harm such as abusive head trauma.

Missing a serious acute condition such as intussusception or infection presenting as excessive crying
Overmedicalising a benign condition or making unnecessary formula changes
Neglecting caregiver distress and the associated risk of abusive head trauma
Infantile colic is benign and self-limiting, resolving spontaneously by around three to four months of age in most infants, with no adverse effect on long-term growth or development.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Hospitalized patients are exposed to pathogens from other patients, visitors, staff, and the inanimate environment. Health care personnel carry multidrug-resistant organisms between patients on hands or shared equipment (stethoscopes, portable imaging machines); spread also occurs via contaminated plumbing, person-to-person respiratory routes, or contamination of food, water, and medications. Antibiotic exposure disrupts the host microbiota, permitting colonization with resistant organisms; colonized but immunocompromised patients, or those whose barriers are breached by surgery or invasive devices, then develop infection either from their own flora or from cross-transmitted pathogens. Invasive devices (urinary catheters, central venous catheters, endotracheal tubes) create direct portals of entry, bypassing normal defenses. Resistant organisms frequently colonize the gastrointestinal and respiratory tracts and can establish enduring environmental reservoirs, with potential horizontal transfer of resistance genes between co-colonizing strains.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Infections appearing within the first 48-72 hours of admission are generally regarded as community-acquired (or attributed to a transferring institution); those arising afterward are considered health care-associated (nosocomial).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Candida auris is a multidrug-resistant, environment-adapted pathogen that survives long periods on surfaces and is resistant to some standard disinfectants, requiring select agents and strict contact precautions.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Tap water is not sterile; waterborne organisms such as Legionella pneumophila and nontuberculous mycobacteria colonize plumbing biofilm, favored by low disinfectant levels, warm temperatures, and stagnation.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Apart from pregnant patients, asymptomatic bacteriuria in catheterized patients should generally not be cultured or treated; in the elderly nonspecific symptoms like confusion are often unrelated to bacteriuria, and overtreatment drives a cycle of escalating antimicrobial use and resistance.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Surveillance infection rates are expressed as standardized infection ratios (observed infections divided by predicted infections), benchmarked through the CDC National Healthcare Safety Network.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Patient-related vulnerabilities to nosocomial infection include indwelling invasive devices, immune deficiency (congenital or acquired), renal insufficiency, diabetes, and other major comorbidities.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Disruption of a patient's own microbiota by antibiotics or other drugs promotes colonization with multidrug-resistant organisms; colonized patients then act as silent reservoirs for transmission to others and to the environment.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Colonization pressure (the proportion of patients on a ward who are colonized) is itself a risk factor for the spread of resistant organisms.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Catheter-associated bloodstream infections roughly triple the risk of in-hospital death; central lines are foreign objects in direct contact with the bloodstream and each handling is a potential contamination event.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Ventilator-associated pneumonia occurs in up to 10% of mechanically ventilated patients and can prolong ventilation and ICU stay or be fatal.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Clostridioides difficile infection is both the most frequent cause of health care-associated diarrhea and the most frequent hospital-acquired infection in the United States; recent antibiotic exposure is the most common precipitant.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Alcohol-based hand gel and standard hospital cleaners do NOT kill C. difficile spores or inactivate norovirus, so handwashing with soap and water plus sporicidal (e.g., bleach) cleaning is required.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Candida species account for the vast majority of health care-associated fungal infections; antifungal prophylaxis can select for non-albicans species such as Candida glabrata.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Culturing and treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in catheterized patients, then re-testing for 'clearance', fueling a cycle of escalating antimicrobial use and resistance.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Relying on alcohol-based hand gel against C. difficile spores or norovirus, which it does not eliminate.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Failing to remove indwelling urinary catheters and central lines promptly when no longer needed, the principal driver of these preventable device infections.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Overlooking that patients already colonized with C. difficile on admission are by far the most likely to develop infection during the stay.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Missing exogenous transmission of Candida auris because it resists some standard disinfectant cleaners and recontaminates surfaces rapidly.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Treating commercial multiplex respiratory PCR results as adequate to exclude or identify novel influenza strains such as H5N1.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Health care-associated infections are a substantial source of morbidity and mortality in hospitalized patients, frequently caused by antimicrobial-resistant organisms that prolong hospital stays and worsen outcomes. Catheter-associated bloodstream infections triple in-hospital mortality risk, and ventilator-associated pneumonia can be fatal or prolong ICU stay. Multidrug-resistant organism infections are associated with higher morbidity, higher mortality, and added costs; globally about 1.27 million deaths were attributed to antibiotic-resistant infections in 2019. After years of decline from prevention efforts, device-related and other nosocomial infection rates rose during the COVID-19 pandemic.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: New bloodstream infection in a patient with a central venous catheter (markedly elevated in-hospital mortality)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Nosocomial diarrhea progressing toward toxic megacolon in C. difficile colitis

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: A single case of nosocomial Legionnaires disease, which should trigger a full investigation

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Suspected active tuberculosis requiring immediate airborne precautions

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Identification of Candida auris, carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, or other high-priority multidrug-resistant organisms requiring coordinated containment

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: Presentation of a returning traveler with possible viral hemorrhagic fever (Ebola, Marburg)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
chunks.text: C. difficile colitis spans a clinical spectrum from mild diarrhea to life-threatening toxic megacolon. Pathogen transmission risk is operationally classified by route into contact, droplet, and airborne precautions (per WHO and CDC); some conditions (e.g., concurrent varicella and SARS-CoV-2) warrant combined precautions. Airborne isolation requires a negative-pressure room with at least 12 air changes per hour, exhausted outdoors or through a HEPA filter, with respirator use; protective (positive-pressure, HEPA-filtered) isolation is used for highly susceptible patients such as those with prolonged neutropenia or stem cell transplants to exclude mold spores.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms
chunks.text: Campylobacters survive in the gastrointestinal mucous layer of food animals and pets and reach humans mainly via undercooked/contaminated food or animal contact. In C. jejuni enteritis the jejunum, ileum, and colon are injured; biopsy shows a nonspecific acute inflammatory reaction with neutrophils, monocytes, and eosinophils in the lamina propria plus epithelial damage, mucus loss, glandular degeneration, and crypt abscesses. Strain motility and adherence favor disease, whereas classic entero- and cytotoxins (including cytolethal distending toxin) seem not to drive tissue injury; tissue invasion and occasional bacteremia indicate clinically significant invasion. C. fetus pathogenesis is better defined: nearly all clinical isolates bear a proteinaceous S-layer capsule-like structure conferring resistance to complement and opsonization, allowing bacteremia and seeding of extraintestinal sites, while antigenic switching of S-layer proteins contributes to chronicity and recurrence in compromised hosts. Protective immunity is incompletely understood but appears antibody-dependent and may be short-lived without continuous exposure (Harrison 22e p.1304-1305).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms
chunks.text: Campylobacters are motile, non-spore-forming, curved (vibrio-like) gram-negative rods that are microaerophilic, and the genus was split off from Vibrio in 1973; over 20 species now span the genera Campylobacter, Arcobacter, and Helicobacter (Harrison 22e p.1304).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms
chunks.text: Sialylated lipopolysaccharide on certain C. jejuni strains drives molecular mimicry against axonal cell-surface molecules; Campylobacter is estimated to trigger 20-40% of all Guillain-Barre cases despite occurring in only ~1 per 1000-2000 infections (Harrison 22e p.1305).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms
chunks.text: Diagnosis rests on culture on Campylobacter-selective fastidious media (the gold standard), with species-specific real-time PCR being more sensitive; MALDI-TOF identifies species, and Gram/Wright fecal smears or dark-field microscopy may reveal vibrioid forms with characteristic darting motility (Harrison 22e p.1305-1306).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms
chunks.text: Infection with C. jejuni in low- and middle-income countries, even when asymptomatic, is associated with childhood stunting (short stature) and a distinctive microbiome signature (Harrison 22e p.1304).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms
chunks.text: C. jejuni is the dominant diarrheal pathogen, accounting for roughly 80-90% of recognized illness in this group, while C. fetus is the principal cause of extraintestinal/systemic disease (Harrison 22e p.1304).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms
chunks.text: Undercooked poultry is the leading source in developed countries (30-70% of cases); other routes include unpasteurized milk, untreated water, infected pets, contaminated seafood, foreign travel, and oral-anal sexual contact (Harrison 22e p.1304).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms
chunks.text: Enteritis typically begins 2-4 days after exposure (range 1-7 days) and is often preceded 12-48 h by a prodrome of fever, headache, myalgia, and malaise (Harrison 22e p.1304-1305).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms
chunks.text: Visibly bloody stool occurs in about 10% of adult cases; most patients presenting for care have 10 or more bowel movements on the worst day, and cramping abdominal pain may be the most prominent feature (Harrison 22e p.1305).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms
chunks.text: C. jejuni can produce pseudoappendicitis, and isolated fever can be the only early sign, mimicking the onset of typhoid fever; myocarditis and pericarditis have been seen, especially in young men, and febrile young children may have convulsions (Harrison 22e p.1305).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms
chunks.text: C. fetus has a tropism for vascular sites, causing endocarditis, mycotic aneurysm, and septic thrombophlebitis; its protective S-layer resists complement-mediated killing and opsonization, enabling bacteremia and antigenic variation (Harrison 22e p.1305).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms
chunks.text: About 90% of bacteremic cases are due to C. jejuni and C. fetus in roughly equal numbers, despite C. jejuni being far more common overall (Harrison 22e p.1305).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms
chunks.text: The two major postinfectious sequelae are reactive arthritis (up to 2.5% of cases, no HLA-B27 association, averaging about 3.2 joints, knees most often) and Guillain-Barre syndrome (Harrison 22e p.1305).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms
chunks.text: Labeling inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis or Crohn's) before excluding Campylobacter and related infections, since presentations and biopsy findings can overlap and Campylobacter enteritis is far more common in young adults (Harrison 22e p.1306).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms
chunks.text: Assuming a negative stool culture excludes Campylobacter, as these fastidious organisms are missed without selective media or techniques (Harrison 22e p.1306).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms
chunks.text: Over-interpreting culture-independent test positivity, which may reflect nonviable bacteria and can be falsely positive, unlike culture which usually implies active or recent infection (Harrison 22e p.1306).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms
chunks.text: Treating commensal oral organisms (C. sputorum, C. concisus) as pathogens, since they rarely have pathogenic significance (Harrison 22e p.1306).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms
chunks.text: Missing C. fetus bacteremia because of its low metabolic activity in standard blood culture media (Harrison 22e p.1306).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms
chunks.text: Overlooking that not every patient with enteritis benefits from antimicrobials, and that antimotility agents can prolong symptoms and have been associated with toxic megacolon and death (Harrison 22e p.1306).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms
chunks.text: Almost all patients recover fully from Campylobacter enteritis, spontaneously or with therapy; the rare deaths are linked largely to volume depletion. Symptoms persist beyond one week in 10-20% of patients seeking care, and clinical relapses occur in 5-10% of untreated patients. Some patients develop reactive arthritis or Guillain-Barre syndrome. Systemic C. fetus infection is far more often fatal than infection with related species, with overall reported bacteremia mortality around 12%; outcome depends on how promptly appropriate therapy begins. Otherwise healthy hosts usually survive C. fetus infection without sequelae, whereas compromised hosts often suffer recurrent and/or life-threatening disease (Harrison 22e p.1306).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms
chunks.text: Septic thrombophlebitis (suggests C. fetus)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms
chunks.text: Immunocompromise, diabetes, liver disease, or extremes of age (risk of severe/recurrent extraintestinal disease)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms
chunks.text: Neurologic symptoms suggesting Guillain-Barre syndrome or its Miller Fisher variant following infection

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms
chunks.text: Three patterns of extraintestinal infection are described: (1) transient bacteremia in a normal host with enteritis, which is benign and needs no specific treatment; (2) sustained bacteremia or focal infection in a normal host, arising from enteritis and responding well to antimicrobials; and (3) sustained bacteremia or focal infection in a compromised host, in which enteritis may not be apparent and prompt, possibly prolonged, therapy is required (Harrison 22e p.1305).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Pneumococcal pneumonia with parapneumonic effusion

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Gram stain of pus/sputum showing a mixed bacterial population, especially when routine culture is negative or grows only streptococci or a single aerobe such as E. coli

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Anaerobic culture from normally sterile sites (blood, pleural/peritoneal fluid, CSF, sterile-site aspirates or biopsies); samples from mouth, nose, vagina, or feces are unacceptable due to commensal contamination

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Air-free syringe collection capped and placed in anaerobic transport media with rapid transport; liquid/tissue specimens preferred over swabs

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Pleural fluid analysis (WBC count, LDH, pH) to distinguish empyema from a simple parapneumonic effusion

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Imaging (chest x-ray/CT) showing dependent-segment consolidation or cavitary abscess; cross-sectional imaging for intraabdominal/pelvic abscess and for typhlitis bowel-wall thickening (>4 mm)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Referral to a reference laboratory for susceptibility testing in serious, refractory, or prolonged-therapy infections (brain abscess, meningitis, joint infection, osteomyelitis, prosthetic joint infection, endocarditis)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Chemical pneumonitis from gastric acid aspiration (Mendelson syndrome)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Foreign-body airway obstruction

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Malignancy or granulomatous disease mimicked by chronic actinomycotic 'lumpy jaw'

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Anaerobic infection requires an anaerobic microenvironment with a lowered oxidation-reduction potential, which arises directly from tissue ischemia, trauma, surgery, or a perforated viscus, or is established and maintained by co-infecting facultative organisms that consume local oxygen. Disease typically follows breakdown of a mucosal barrier (intestinal perforation, ischemia, surgery) or direct inoculation (bite wounds, trauma), seeding normally sterile tissue with commensal organisms. The resulting infections are usually polymicrobial, with facultative and obligate anaerobes acting synergistically: facultative organisms create and sustain the reduced-oxygen environment, short-chain fatty acids and succinic acid impair phagocyte clearance, certain organisms supply growth factors to others (e.g., oral diphtheroids producing vitamin K needed by P. melaninogenica), and tissue damage promotes spread. Virulence factors include adhesins/fimbriae (P. gingivalis, B. fragilis pili, F. nucleatum as a bridging coaggregator), exoproteins such as P. gingivalis collagenase, and capsular polysaccharides. The B. fragilis capsular polysaccharide complex, particularly the zwitterionic PSA, is the most studied factor; its charged repeating-unit motif drives abscess formation by stimulating peritoneal macrophages (via TLR2) to release IL-8, IL-17, and TNF-alpha, recruiting PMNs that adhere to ICAM-1-upregulated mesothelial cells to form the abscess nidus, with T-cell IL-17/IFN-gamma also required (Harrison 22e p.1372-1373).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Most clinically relevant anaerobes (Bacteroides fragilis, Prevotella melaninogenica, Fusobacterium nucleatum) are relatively aerotolerant rather than strict obligate anaerobes; obligate anaerobes are killed by oxygen at or above roughly 0.5%, whereas facultative anaerobes grow with or without oxygen (Harrison 22e p.1371).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Empyema fluid characteristics (mean WBC ~55,000 cells/mL, LDH >1000 IU/L, pH <7.2, loculations, thick pleural peel) contrast sharply with a simple parapneumonic effusion (mean WBC ~5000 cells/mL, LDH >200 IU/L, pH ~7.4) (Harrison 22e p.1376).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Aspiration pneumonia/lung abscess localizes to dependent segments: basilar lower-lobe segments if aspiration occurred upright, and posterior upper-lobe (usually right) or superior lower-lobe segments if supine (Harrison 22e p.1375-1376).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Clostridium septicum bacteremia, often arising via neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis), is strongly associated with underlying malignancy, particularly colon cancer (Harrison 22e p.1376).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Anaerobes dominate the normal mucocutaneous microbiota, accounting for about 99.0-99.9% of cultivable organisms, with concentrations ranging from ~10^3/mL in the nose to ~10^12/mL in gingival crevices and colon; the lower GI tract is the major reservoir (anaerobe-to-aerobe ratio ~1000:1) (Harrison 22e p.1371-1372).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Infections are typically polymicrobial, commonly yielding three to six species, and occasionally more than 10 species from a single suppurative site; the etiologic organisms mirror the neighboring resident microbiota (Harrison 22e p.1372-1373).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Bacteroides fragilis, though only ~0.5-1% of the colonic microbiota, is the anaerobe most often isolated from intraabdominal infections and bacteremia; its zwitterionic capsular polysaccharide A (PSA) is the principal virulence factor driving abscess formation via a TLR2-dependent cytokine/chemokine response (IL-8, IL-17, TNF-alpha) (Harrison 22e p.1373).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Anaerobic gram-negative endotoxin (lipid A) is roughly 100-1000 times less biologically potent than aerobic gram-negative endotoxin, which helps explain why DIC, purpura, and septic shock are less frequent in anaerobic gram-negative bacteremia; Fusobacterium LPS is an exception and contributes to the severity of Lemierre's syndrome (Harrison 22e p.1373).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: A putrid/foul-smelling discharge is considered suggestive of anaerobic infection but is a late finding present in only about 30-50% of cases, so its absence does not exclude anaerobes (Harrison 22e p.1374).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Sterile pus paradox: an abscess that yields no growth on routine culture but shows teeming organisms on Gram stain strongly suggests anaerobes that failed to grow because of inadequate transport/culture technique (Harrison 22e p.1373-1378).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Anaerobes are recovered in up to ~30% of brain abscesses, ~20% of epidural abscesses, and ~10% of subdural empyemas, but rarely cause meningitis; brain abscesses from contiguous (otogenic, odontogenic, sinus) spread are the most likely to involve anaerobes (Harrison 22e p.1375).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Bacterial aspiration pneumonia evolves indolently over days to weeks, distinguishing it from chemical pneumonitis (e.g., Mendelson syndrome from acid aspiration), which develops within 4-6 hours and can produce a bilateral chest x-ray 'whiteout' within 8-24 hours (Harrison 22e p.1375).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Submitting specimens from heavily colonized sites (mouth, nose, vagina, feces) or expectorated sputum for anaerobic culture, which yields uninterpretable results from commensal contamination

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Dismissing an infection as 'sterile' when routine culture is negative despite a Gram stain teeming with organisms, missing inadequate anaerobic transport/culture

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Prior antibiotic therapy reducing the cultivability of anaerobes and masking the diagnosis

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Using agents with no useful anaerobic activity (aminoglycosides, monobactams, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) and attributing nonresponse to other causes; failure to respond to such agents itself suggests an anaerobic etiology

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Treating gas in tissue or a putrid odor as pathognomonic for anaerobes; gas can be produced by aerobes and putrid odor appears in only 30-50% of cases

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Overlooking that right-lower-quadrant pain and tenderness are absent in nearly half of typhlitis cases (and may be absent entirely in patients on glucocorticoids)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Relying on antibiotics alone without surgical debridement of devitalized tissue and drainage of large abscesses

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Manifestations of severe sepsis and DIC are unusual in purely anaerobic infection, and septic shock is less common with B. fragilis than with aerobic gram-negative bacillary bacteremia. Nonetheless, isolation of a B. fragilis-group organism from blood indicates serious underlying infection with an untreated mortality rate of about 60%; case-fatality rises with advancing age (reported >66% in patients over 60), with isolation of multiple species, and with failure to surgically remove the focus. Reported relative mortality has been suggested to vary by species (B. thetaiotaomicron > P. distasonis > B. fragilis). Anaerobic endocarditis, though rare, carries significant mortality (~21-43%). Noma is highly lethal without treatment (70-90%). Recovery from empyema may take several months, particularly without surgical intervention (Harrison 22e p.1374, 1377-1378).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Ludwig's angina from molar dental infection: submandibular/sublingual/submental swelling with trismus and posterior-superior tongue displacement causing swallowing impairment and airway obstruction (tracheotomy may be lifesaving)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Noma (cancrum oris): gangrenous orofacial destruction in malnourished young children with untreated mortality of 70-90%

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Lemierre's syndrome: oropharyngeal infection with septic internal jugular vein thrombophlebitis and septic emboli, usually due to Fusobacterium necrophorum

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Necrotizing fasciitis / synergistic necrotizing cellulitis / Fournier gangrene: subcutaneous gas, foul discharge, cutaneous anesthesia preceding skin necrosis, fever and systemic toxicity

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis) with bowel-wall thickening, fever, and bacteremia; Clostridium septicum bacteremia signaling possible occult colon malignancy

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: B. fragilis-group bacteremia indicating underlying colonic pathology (neoplasia, diverticulitis) and carrying high untreated mortality

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: No single formal grading scheme; severity is judged by anatomic site, extent, and systemic involvement. Localized/indolent processes (chronic sinusitis, periodontal disease, indolent anaerobic cellulitis) contrast with severe, life-threatening forms (Ludwig's angina with airway compromise, noma, Lemierre's syndrome, necrotizing fasciitis/Fournier gangrene, brain abscess, B. fragilis-group bacteremia, endocarditis). Antibiotic selection is guided empirically by infection location, severity, and local resistance patterns; reference-laboratory susceptibility testing is reserved for serious, refractory, or prolonged-therapy infections (Harrison 22e p.1374-1379).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms
chunks.text: Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms (infective) — Infectious Diseases (multisystem) Also: Anaerobic bacterial infections, Mixed aerobic-anaerobic infection, Polymicrobial anaerobic infection, Bacteroides fragilis infection, Non-clostridial anaerobic infection

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Other gram-negative bacterial pneumonia and sepsis (clinically often indistinguishable from P. aeruginosa)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia (can also produce ecthyma-gangrenosum-like lesions)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Tuberculosis (chronic cavitary melioidosis mimic)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Pyogenic meningitis of other bacterial etiology (CSF profile of Pseudomonas meningitis is nonspecific)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Polymicrobial osteomyelitis from trauma or decubitus ulcers

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Aspergillosis and mucormycosis (can produce ecthyma-gangrenosum-like lesions)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus species causing malignant/necrotizing otitis externa

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Tuberculosis mimicked by chronic pulmonary melioidosis

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Other gram-negative enterocolitis mimicked by Pseudomonas enterocolitis / Shanghai fever

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Sputum Gram stain showing predominant polymorphonuclear leukocytes plus culture positive for P. aeruginosa supports acute pneumonia rather than colonization

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Multiplex PCR platforms on respiratory and blood samples identify P. aeruginosa earlier than classical culture

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Technetium-99 bone scan as the gold standard for malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: MRI and bone scan for puncture-wound foot osteomyelitis; needle aspiration usually yields the diagnosis

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Deep bone biopsy before treating presumed P. aeruginosa osteomyelitis in trauma or decubitus settings to confirm its causative role

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Blood cultures plus echocardiographic/clinical signs for endocarditis (blood cultures often negative in vertebral osteomyelitis unless endocarditis coexists)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Mandatory laboratory susceptibility testing before using newer beta-lactam/beta-lactamase-inhibitor agents or cefiderocol against MDR/XDR strains

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Fluid overload mistaken for pneumonia on CT in ventilated patients (contributes to overdiagnosis of HAP/VAP)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: P. aeruginosa possesses an unusually large arsenal of putative virulence factors, yet few are individually proven to drive human disease, and there is great redundancy. Adhesins (pili, flagellin/flagellar cap binding mucins, LPS outer core binding CFTR to aid internalization, and alginate in mucoid strains) mediate colonization, with adhesion strongest to injured cell surfaces. A type III secretion system injects toxins (ExoS or ExoU, ExoT, ExoY) into host cells, allowing evasion of phagocytes; strains secreting ExoU are associated with higher mortality. A type II secretion system releases diffusible toxins including exotoxin A, multiple proteases (which degrade host cytokines and chemokines), and phospholipases. Rhamnolipids, pyocyanin, and hydrocyanic acid further injure tissue and can cause neutrophil death. Inflammatory responses to lipid A and flagellin via Toll-like receptors (principally TLR4 and TLR5) are required for defense but, when florid, contribute to sepsis and septic shock. In chronic infection (cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis, diffuse panbronchiolitis) defective mucociliary clearance and mucus stasis select for P. aeruginosa, which adapts over time by losing pili and flagella, losing the O side chain of LPS (becoming complement-sensitive), and overproducing mucoid exopolysaccharide, dampening the host response and enabling decades of persistence with attenuated virulence factor production. B. pseudomallei survives within neutrophils and macrophages, aided by a polysaccharide capsule and a type III secretion system, and provokes a florid inflammatory response. B. cepacia complex organisms bind lung mucus and possess potent LPS that drives lung inflammation. S. maltophilia virulence is limited, with disease largely a host inflammatory response to LPS and flagellin; its hallmark is broad intrinsic antibiotic resistance via efflux pumps and the L1 and L2 beta-lactamases.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: The pseudomonads are a heterogeneous group of non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative bacteria now split across three medically important genera: Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas; most cause disease opportunistically, the exceptions being the primary pathogens B. pseudomallei and B. mallei.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Melioidosis can mimic tuberculosis with chronic cough, fever, hemoptysis, night sweats, and cavitary upper-lobe disease, and may also present as skin ulceration with lymphangitis and regional lymphadenopathy or as high-mortality septicemia.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Burkholderia cepacia complex can cause the rapidly fatal cepacia syndrome (respiratory distress plus septicemia) in cystic fibrosis; B. cenocepacia in particular is a barrier to lung transplantation, with relatively high one-year mortality.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia is an opportunist whose emergence requires major disruption of host flora, classically broad-spectrum cephalosporin or carbapenem therapy; distinguishing colonization from true infection in ventilated, non-neutropenic patients is a recurring clinical dilemma.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: P. aeruginosa rarely causes infection without a breach in host defenses; disease typically requires compromised immunity, mucosal trauma, physiologic derangement, or antibiotic-mediated suppression of normal flora, so most infections cluster in intensive care units.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: On primary culture P. aeruginosa is identified by a yellow to dark-green or bluish pigment, a shiny gun-metal colony sheen, a characteristic fruity odor, failure to ferment lactose on MacConkey agar, and a positive oxidase reaction; cystic fibrosis isolates may appear mucoid from overproduction of alginate.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Ecthyma gangrenosum is the distinctive skin lesion of P. aeruginosa bacteremia, occurring almost exclusively in markedly neutropenic patients and those with AIDS; lesions begin pink, darken to purple, then become black and necrotic, and histologically are due to vascular invasion teeming with bacteria.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: P. aeruginosa keratitis is a medical emergency because it can progress over roughly 48 hours to involve the entire cornea with opacification and even perforation; it is strongly associated with contact lenses, especially the extended-wear type.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa most often occurs in elderly diabetics and can extend to cranial nerve palsies (most commonly cranial nerve VII) or cavernous sinus thrombosis; the ESR is invariably elevated, often 100 mm/h or more.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Hot-tub folliculitis, toe-web infection, and the green-nail syndrome (pyocyanin diffusing into the nail bed of a Pseudomonas paronychia) are characteristic community skin manifestations; whirlpools, spas, and pools are common sources, and folliculitis is usually self-limited.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Vertebral osteomyelitis and sternoclavicular septic arthritis are uncommon but characteristic complications in people who inject drugs; Pseudomonas osteomyelitis of the foot typically follows a puncture wound through a sneaker, mainly in children, often with negative blood cultures.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Melioidosis (B. pseudomallei) is geographically restricted chiefly to Southeast Asia and northern Australia (with cases in India and China); the organism is a facultative intracellular pathogen acquired from soil and water that can cause latent infection presenting long after exposure.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Overdiagnosing HAP/VAP: positive sputum, endotracheal aspirate, or PCR results may reflect tracheobronchial colonization, endotracheal-tube biofilm, or simple tracheobronchitis rather than true pneumonia; clinical judgment is essential.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: In trauma- or decubitus-associated osteomyelitis, infection is often polymicrobial and the causative role of P. aeruginosa can be overstated without a deep bone biopsy.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Treating S. maltophilia or P. aeruginosa pulmonary cultures as infection when they may represent colonization, especially in non-neutropenic patients; unnecessary therapy promotes resistance.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Assuming community sputum cultures prove community-acquired P. aeruginosa pneumonia in patients prone to airway colonization by multiple bacterial strains.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Empirically relying on first-line antipseudomonal agents in settings where susceptibility is below 80%, or on the newer agents/cefiderocol without susceptibility testing given unpredictable resistance mechanisms.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Failing to remove indwelling foreign bodies (urinary catheters, stents, stones, central lines) — relapse of UTI or bacteremia may be due to the retained device or ongoing obstruction rather than antibiotic resistance.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Not recognizing that melioidosis can present long after travel to an endemic area due to latent intracellular infection.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: P. aeruginosa carries high attributable mortality and is among the most feared pathogens in neutropenic patients. Historical crude bacteremia mortality exceeded 50%, with more recent attributable mortality of about 28 to 44% depending on adequacy and timing of treatment and underlying disease severity. Pneumonia mortality has been reported at 40 to 80%, though the fraction attributable to underlying disease is uncertain, and VAP outcomes are poor. Chronic airway infection (e.g., cystic fibrosis) is rarely eradicated and is the leading contributor to respiratory failure and death in CF. Pseudomonas endovascular infection in people who inject drugs is more indolent than S. aureus endocarditis and is more often curable when right-sided. Melioidosis septicemia carries high mortality, with rates as high as 44% reported in Thailand. B. cenocepacia infection has relatively high one-year mortality after lung transplantation. S. maltophilia pneumonia/bacteremia can cause septic shock, with a severe high-mortality form described in neutropenic patients.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Ecthyma gangrenosum in a neutropenic or AIDS patient suggesting P. aeruginosa bacteremia

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Rapidly progressive corneal opacification/perforation indicating sight-threatening Pseudomonas keratitis (medical emergency)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Severe lancinating ear pain with granulation tissue in a diabetic, plus cranial nerve palsy, signaling malignant otitis externa

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Hypothermia or shock in P. aeruginosa bacteremia (marker of severe illness)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Cepacia syndrome: rapidly fatal respiratory distress with septicemia in cystic fibrosis

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Hemoptysis, night sweats, and cavitary disease in a patient from an endemic region suggesting melioidosis with systemic spread

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: No single formal severity score is presented. Resistance is graded as multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) P. aeruginosa, with extremely high MDR rates reported from eastern/southern Europe, Latin America, India, and China, especially in ICUs. Carbapenemase production is highlighted as the most threatening resistance mechanism. The B. cepacia cepacia syndrome denotes a rapidly fatal severe phenotype. Melioidosis spans a clinical spectrum from asymptomatic infection through localized abscesses and pneumonia to high-mortality disseminated septicemic disease.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species
chunks.text: Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species (infective) — Multisystem / Infectious Diseases Also: Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, Burkholderia cepacia complex infection, Melioidosis, Glanders, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia infection, Pseudomallei infection, Ecthyma gangrenosum (Pseudomonas)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Viridans group streptococcal endocarditis (also subacute, culture-positive, common in dental-source disease)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Enterococcal endocarditis

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Culture-negative endocarditis (Bartonella, Coxiella burnetii, Tropheryma whipplei) when blood cultures are sterile

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis when the course is more acute

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Septic arthritis/osteomyelitis from Staphylococcus aureus in children (where K. kingae may have surpassed S. aureus as a leading cause)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection when ecthyma gangrenosum-like skin lesions are present (Aeromonas)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Neisseria meningitidis sepsis (K. kingae bacteremia can produce a similar petechial rash)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection (Aeromonas can cause indistinguishable ecthyma gangrenosum)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Other gram-negative bacteremic pneumonias (Achromobacter xylosoxidans bacteremia, similar high mortality)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Other causes of culture-negative or slow-growing endocarditis

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Blood cultures with notification of the laboratory that a HACEK organism is suspected; modern automated systems (e.g., BACTEC) usually yield growth within the first week

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: 16S rRNA gene amplification (PCR) of blood or cardiac valve specimens for culture-negative or fastidious cases

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry performed directly on colonies for rapid, accurate species identification

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Echocardiography to detect valvular vegetations (seen in up to 85% of HACEK endocarditis)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Real-time PCR of blood or joint fluid for Kingella kingae; inoculation of synovial fluid into aerobic blood culture bottles to improve recovery

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: In vitro antimicrobial susceptibility testing, including Etest, given slow growth and possible undetected beta-lactamase; susceptibility testing is essential for the miscellaneous multidrug-resistant gram-negative organisms

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Noninfective embolic disease and vasculitis (HACEK endocarditis frequently presents with embolic, vascular, and immunologic phenomena such as cerebrovascular accidents, mycotic aneurysms, and immune-complex glomerulonephritis that may mimic primary vasculitic or thromboembolic disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Hemolytic-uremic syndrome (rare HUS following bloody diarrhea has been linked to Aeromonas, but HUS itself is the differential)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: HACEK organisms are commensals of the human oral cavity. Disruption of the oral mucosa (dental procedures, nasopharyngeal infection, periodontal disease) allows transient bacteremia; in patients with damaged native valves or prosthetic material, the slow-growing organisms seed and form valvular vegetations, producing a typically subacute, indolent endocarditis. Their fastidious, CO2-dependent slow growth accounts for delayed culture positivity and difficulty in susceptibility testing (including underdetection of beta-lactamase). The remaining fastidious and miscellaneous gram-negative organisms in this chapter act largely as opportunists: animal-mouth flora (Pasteurella multocida, Capnocytophaga canimorsus) inoculated through bites/scratches/licking, environmental and waterborne organisms (Aeromonas, Shewanella, Chromobacterium violaceum, Achromobacter xylosoxidans) introduced through wounds or contaminated fluids, and nosocomial nonfermenters (Elizabethkingia/Chryseobacterium, Rhizobium radiobacter, Alcaligenes faecalis) associated with contaminated fluids, indwelling devices, and immunocompromised hosts.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: HACEK is an acronym for a group of fastidious, slow-growing gram-negative bacteria that require a carbon-dioxide-enriched atmosphere and do not grow on routine enteric media such as MacConkey agar: Haemophilus species, Aggregatibacter (formerly Actinobacillus) species, Cardiobacterium species, Eikenella corrodens, and Kingella kingae.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Diagnostic recovery of HACEK organisms is improved by alerting the microbiology laboratory; most cultures turn positive within the first week with modern systems (e.g., BACTEC), and prolonged incubation has not been shown to increase recovery of clinically significant isolates.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Molecular methods aid diagnosis: 16S rRNA gene amplification (PCR) on blood or cardiac valve tissue and MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry on colonies increase the accuracy and speed of HACEK identification; real-time PCR and inoculation of synovial fluid into aerobic blood culture bottles enhance recovery of K. kingae in culture-negative cases.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Chromobacterium violaceum causes rare but often fatal soft tissue infections and metastatic abscesses, occurring especially in children with defective neutrophil function such as chronic granulomatous disease.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: These organisms normally colonize the oral cavity; invasive disease characteristically follows a recent dental procedure or nasopharyngeal infection in a patient with underlying valvular heart disease or prosthetic valves.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: A positive HACEK blood culture is strongly predictive of underlying infective endocarditis, with an overall positive predictive value around 60%, though this varies sharply by organism (e.g., 62-100% with Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans bacteremia versus only 0-6% with Eikenella bacteremia).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: HACEK organisms cause roughly 0.8-6% of infective endocarditis cases, most often due to Aggregatibacter species, Haemophilus species, and Cardiobacterium hominis; the aortic and mitral valves are most commonly affected.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Compared with non-HACEK endocarditis, HACEK endocarditis occurs in younger patients and is more frequently associated with embolic, vascular, and immunologic manifestations; systemic embolization is common (major emboli in roughly 28-71% of cases) and vegetations are seen on echocardiography in up to 85% of patients.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Kingella kingae behaves differently from the other HACEK organisms: more than half of K. kingae infections are bone and joint infections, oropharyngeal colonization peaks in the first 3 years of life and is higher in daycare-attending children, and it can be transmitted child-to-child and cause outbreaks; K. kingae bacteremia can present with a petechial rash resembling Neisseria meningitidis sepsis.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Capnocytophaga canimorsus and C. cynodegmi are endogenous to the dog and cat mouth; infection often follows a dog or cat bite (or exposure without a bite), and asplenia, glucocorticoid use, and alcohol abuse predispose to severe sepsis with shock and DIC, classically with a petechial rash progressing to purpura and gangrene.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Pasteurella multocida colonizes the respiratory and GI tracts of domestic animals (oropharyngeal colonization 50-90% in cats, 50-70% in dogs) and is transmitted by bites, scratches, or licking; most human infections are skin and soft tissue, and almost two-thirds are caused by cats.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Aeromonas can produce ecthyma gangrenosum (hemorrhagic vesicles with a rim of erythema and central necrosis/ulceration) resembling lesions of Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, and is associated with water exposure, floods, and other hydrologic disasters (along with Shewanella and Chromobacterium).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Because of slow growth, antimicrobial susceptibility testing may be difficult and beta-lactamase production may go undetected; resistance is most common in Haemophilus and Aggregatibacter species.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Prolonged blood-culture incubation has not been shown to improve recovery of clinically significant HACEK isolates, so relying on extended incubation alone may delay diagnosis—molecular methods may be needed.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Failing to alert the microbiology laboratory that a fastidious HACEK organism is suspected can compromise recovery and identification.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Eikenella corrodens is resistant to clindamycin, metronidazole, and aminoglycosides, so empirical regimens chosen for typical gram-negatives may fail.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Many miscellaneous gram-negative organisms (Achromobacter, Elizabethkingia/Chryseobacterium, Chromobacterium, Aeromonas) are frequently multidrug-resistant—Elizabethkingia/Chryseobacterium are typically resistant to carbapenems while Aeromonas can produce carbapenemases—so therapy must be guided by susceptibility testing rather than assumptions.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Capnocytophaga canimorsus infection may be missed when there is exposure without an obvious scratch or bite, and severe disease can occur in patients without an apparent wound.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Overall prognosis in both native-valve and prosthetic-valve HACEK endocarditis is excellent and significantly better than endocarditis caused by non-HACEK pathogens; one case-control study found significantly lower 1-year mortality than viridans group streptococcal endocarditis. Mortality associated with HACEK endocarditis in older series ranged from about 28 to 71% depending on the cohort. By contrast, several miscellaneous organisms carry high mortality: Pasteurella multocida invasive disease up to ~30% despite therapy, Achromobacter xylosoxidans bacteremia up to ~67%, Aeromonas sepsis ~25% in immunocompromised adults and >90% with myonecrosis, Chryseobacterium indologenes up to ~50%, and Elizabethkingia anophelis bloodstream infection ~18%.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Systemic embolization (cerebral and other major emboli are common in HACEK endocarditis)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Congestive heart failure complicating endocarditis (reported in roughly 19-50% of Haemophilus HACEK cases)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Mycotic aneurysm formation

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Petechial/purpuric rash with sepsis after a dog or cat bite in an asplenic, alcohol-abusing, or glucocorticoid-treated patient (Capnocytophaga canimorsus, may progress to shock, DIC, and gangrene)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Petechial rash with bacteremia mimicking meningococcemia (Kingella kingae)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Necrotizing fasciitis or myonecrosis after water/wound exposure (Aeromonas; very high mortality with myonecrosis)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: Sepsis with metastatic abscesses in a child with defective neutrophil function (Chromobacterium violaceum)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
chunks.text: No formal grading system; clinical severity is stratified by site and host factors. HACEK endocarditis runs a typically subacute course (more aggressive with Kingella kingae) with severity marked by embolic, vascular, and immunologic complications, heart failure, and mycotic aneurysm. For the miscellaneous organisms, severity escalates with immunocompromise, asplenia, cirrhosis, malignancy, diabetes, neutrophil dysfunction, and extremes of age, and with deep/invasive presentations such as bacteremia, necrotizing fasciitis, myonecrosis, and septic shock with DIC.

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Bullous: staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome, necrotizing fasciitis, gas gangrene, halophilic Vibrio (V. vulnificus)

chunks.text: Crusted: impetigo contagiosa/bullous impetigo, ringworm (dermatophytes), sporotrichosis, blastomycosis, disseminated coccidioidomycosis, cutaneous TB, M. chelonae nodules in HIV
