chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Ulcers/eschars: cutaneous anthrax, ulceroglandular tularemia, bubonic plague, Buruli ulcer (M. ulcerans), leprosy, cutaneous TB, chancroid, primary syphilis

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Sebaceous cysts blocked at the follicular duct can resemble or become secondarily infected like staphylococcal abscesses

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Hidradenitis suppurativa (sweat-gland inflammation, especially axillary) can mimic hair-follicle infection

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Crusted primary infections with Blastomyces dermatitidis or Sporothrix schenckii can initially resemble ringworm

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Gram stain and culture of drainage, open wound, or obvious portal of entry give a definitive cellulitis diagnosis when present

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Needle aspiration of the leading edge or punch biopsy (positive in only ~20% of cellulitis and ~80% negative in deep infections)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Punch biopsy with frozen section to distinguish SSSS from TEN and to evaluate necrotizing fasciitis

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: KOH staining of skin scrapings for dermatophyte (ringworm) infection

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Soft-tissue plain radiography, CT, and MRI to assess depth, localize abscess, and detect tissue gas

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Serum creatine phosphokinase, which may be markedly elevated in concomitant myositis/myonecrosis

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Open surgical inspection with debridement as the best means of determining extent/severity and obtaining material for Gram stain and culture

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Biopsy and culture of crusted lesions in patients from endemic areas (e.g., for Coccidioides immitis)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Toxic epidermal necrolysis (drug-induced, adult, higher mortality) versus staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome; distinguished by frozen-section cleavage plane (stratum germinativum in TEN vs stratum corneum in SSSS)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Pyoderma gangrenosum on the anterior shins, distinguished from infectious ulcers by biopsy histology

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Decubitus (pressure) ulcers from pressure-induced vascular insufficiency, which may become secondarily infected

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Early necrotizing fasciitis misdiagnosed as thrombophlebitis or a simple muscle strain/bruise

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Infection localizes according to skin anatomy. The epidermis is avascular and relies on the stratum corneum as a mechanical barrier; disruption permits bacterial entry, and hair follicles act as portals for normal flora (Staphylococcus) or exogenous organisms (Pseudomonas in hot-tub folliculitis). The rich subpapillary capillary plexus mediates inflammatory signs and allows metastatic seeding (Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, palpable purpura in endocarditis; cutaneous lesions of disseminated fungal, gonococcal, Salmonella, Pseudomonas/ecthyma gangrenosum, meningococcal, and staphylococcal infection) and access to the bloodstream. Bacteria such as S. pyogenes spread laterally via lymphatics, producing rapidly extending erysipelas, and subsequent lymphatic obstruction causes flaccid epidermal edema. Excess cytokines or bacterial toxins amplify these responses, causing leukostasis, venous occlusion, and edema; loss of vascular integrity produces purple bullae and cutaneous anesthesia indicative of deep necrotizing infection. In necrotizing fasciitis, infection extends along fascial planes and through venous channels and lymphatics, with dermal-papillary vessel thrombosis and progression to friable, bluish/black skin and systemic toxicity. Group A streptococcal and clostridial muscle infection can produce acute rhabdomyolysis with markedly elevated creatine phosphokinase. Toxin biology drives several syndromes: exfoliatin (phage group II S. aureus) cleaves the stratum corneum in staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome, while PVL-producing MRSA can cause necrotizing fasciitis and pyomyositis, and TSST-1/enterotoxins underlie shock in toxic shock syndrome (Harrison 22e p.1049-1053).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: An anatomic approach is the key to diagnosis: the level and physical appearance of the lesion (epidermis, dermis, subcutaneous fat, fascia, or muscle) together with location, time course, travel/animal-bite history, age, comorbidities, and lifestyle narrow the differential (Harrison 22e p.1049-1052).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Imaging (plain films, CT, MRI) helps localize abscess or detect gas in tissue but may show only nonspecific soft-tissue swelling; notably, gas is usually absent in necrotizing fasciitis and myonecrosis caused by group A Streptococcus or MRSA, so a negative gas finding does not exclude fulminant infection (Harrison 22e p.1053).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Hospital admissions for skin and soft tissue infections rose ~27% from 2000-2004, largely due to emergence of the USA300 MRSA clone (Harrison 22e p.1049).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Pyomyositis (usually S. aureus, common in the tropics) typically has no portal of entry and begins at the exact site of blunt trauma or muscle strain; PVL-producing MRSA pyomyositis has occurred in U.S. children (Harrison 22e p.1053).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Because the avascular epidermis is protected mainly by the stratum corneum, any breach (burns, bites, abrasions, foreign bodies, ulcers, surgery, primary dermatologic disease) lets bacteria reach deeper structures (Harrison 22e p.1049).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Edema with purple bullae, ecchymosis, and cutaneous anesthesia signals loss of vascular integrity and mandates exploration of deep structures for necrotizing fasciitis or myonecrosis (Harrison 22e p.1049).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Unexplained fever plus disproportionate soft-tissue pain and tenderness, even without overt cutaneous inflammation, should raise high suspicion for a deep necrotizing infection and prompt early diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1049).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Vesicular lesions reflect viral proliferation within the epidermis (e.g., varicella with crops of 'dewdrop' vesicles, dermatomal herpes zoster preceded by pain, HSV around lips or genitals, coxsackievirus A16 hand-foot-mouth); rickettsialpox produces a crusted black eschar after mite-bite inoculation of Rickettsia akari (Harrison 22e p.1049-1050).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Crusted golden-brown lesions suggest impetigo: impetigo contagiosa from S. pyogenes (linked to poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis but NOT rheumatic fever) and bullous impetigo from S. aureus; MRSA impetigo epidemics have been reported (Harrison 22e p.1051).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: A focused exposure history points to the organism in cellulitis: cat/dog bites (Pasteurella multocida, also S. intermedius, Capnocytophaga), freshwater lacerations (Aeromonas hydrophila), Gulf of Mexico/Atlantic saltwater or raw seafood in cirrhosis (Vibrio vulnificus), fish/swine handling (Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae), and aquariums/swimming pools (Mycobacterium marinum) (Harrison 22e p.1050-1052).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Cultures are frequently unrevealing in cellulitis: even needle aspiration of the leading edge or punch biopsy is positive in only about 20% of cases, suggesting low bacterial numbers and a toxin/inflammatory-mediator effect (Harrison 22e p.1052).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Erysipelas (S. pyogenes) shows abrupt fiery-red swelling with sharply demarcated indurated margins (classically along the nasolabial fold), rapid spread, and intense pain; desquamation follows at 5-10 days (Harrison 22e p.1052).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Relying on absence of gas to exclude necrotizing fasciitis/myonecrosis - gas is usually absent with group A Streptococcus or MRSA

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Sending home patients with severe pain and fever after misdiagnosing early necrotizing fasciitis as thrombophlebitis and giving only analgesia

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Trusting negative imaging or biopsy (negative in ~80% of deep infections) to rule out fulminant infection

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Using empirical vancomycin against Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, which is unusually vancomycin-resistant among gram-positive organisms

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Confusing SSSS with TEN without frozen-section evaluation of the cleavage plane

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Letting hyperbaric oxygen delay or substitute for surgical debridement when debridement is indicated

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Outcome ranges from benign and self-limited (e.g., hot-tub folliculitis, though rare bacteremia and shock have occurred) to rapidly fatal. Necrotizing fasciitis with no defined portal of entry carries high mortality, and survivors often require repeated surgery including amputation. Clostridium sordellii infection (postpartum, post-abortion, or black-tar-heroin injection) is often fatal with rapid death. Mpox case-fatality (1-10%) is lower than smallpox, and TEN carries higher mortality than SSSS. Delay in surgical debridement significantly increases mortality in fulminant infections (Harrison 22e p.1050-1053).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Disproportionate pain and tenderness with unexplained fever and minimal skin findings

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Edema with purple/violaceous bullae, ecchymosis, skin sloughing, or cutaneous anesthesia

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Rapidly progressing lesion with brawny edema, dark-red or bluish/maroon/black skin discoloration

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Systemic toxicity, shock, multiorgan failure, or renal impairment preceding shock (streptococcal necrotizing fasciitis/TSS)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Scrotal/perineal swelling extending to abdominal wall or legs (Fournier gangrene)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Postpartum or post-abortion woman with little/no fever, no purulent discharge, refractory hypotension, marked edema/effusions, hemoconcentration, and a very high WBC count (Clostridium sordellii infection - often rapidly fatal)

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Halophilic Vibrio infection that is as fulminant as necrotizing fasciitis with seawater/raw-seafood exposure, especially in cirrhosis

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Clinically stratified by depth and aggressiveness rather than a single formal score: (1) superficial epidermal/follicular infections (vesicular, crusted, folliculitis); (2) dermal/lymphatic spread (erysipelas, cellulitis - subdivided into purulent cellulitis [MSSA/MRSA, focal abscess source] versus nonpurulent cellulitis [S. pyogenes, rapidly spreading, lymphangitis/fever]); and (3) deep, life-threatening necrotizing infections of fascia and muscle (necrotizing fasciitis, gas gangrene/myonecrosis, pyomyositis), signaled by systemic inflammatory response, shock, and multiorgan failure (Harrison 22e p.1052-1053).

chunks.diseaseName: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues
chunks.text: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues (infective) — Skin / Soft Tissue / Musculoskeletal (Infectious Diseases) Also: Skin and soft tissue infections, SSTI, Soft tissue infections
Crystal-induced arthritis (gout, pseudogout) - can clinically mimic and may coexist with septic arthritis
Cellulitis
Bursitis
Acute osteomyelitis

Reactive/postinfectious arthritis
Acute rheumatic fever
Osteoarthritis
Gonococcal disseminated infection presenting as arthritis-dermatitis (versus true septic monoarthritis)
Meningococcemia with dermatitis-arthritis or purulent monoarthritis
Poncet's disease (reactive polyarthritis of disseminated tuberculosis, with no organisms in the joint)
Viral arthritides (parvovirus B19, rubella, hepatitis B, arboviruses)
Postinfectious/reactive arthritis following enteric or chlamydial infection
Arthrocentesis with synovial fluid cell count, differential, Gram stain, and culture (obtain before antibiotics)
Synovial fluid examination for crystals to exclude/identify coexistent gout or pseudogout
Blood cultures (positive in up to 50-70% of S. aureus infections)
Inoculation of synovial fluid into blood-culture bottles to improve yield for fastidious organisms
Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT) and MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry for partially treated or culture-negative cases
Sonication of explanted prosthetic material to disrupt biofilm and improve culture yield
Plain radiographs; ultrasound for hip effusion; CT/MRI for sacroiliac, sternoclavicular, and spinal joint infection
Mucosal cultures (endocervical/urethral, rectal, oropharyngeal) and urine NAAT when gonococcal arthritis is suspected
Synovial tissue biopsy and culture for suspected mycobacterial or fungal arthritis
Crystal-induced arthritis (gout, pseudogout)
Rheumatoid arthritis flare
Reactive arthritis / serum sickness
Hemarthrosis, fracture, or foreign body
Ischemic necrosis and osteoarthritis

Bacteria reach the joint hematogenously, from a contiguous bone or soft-tissue focus, or by direct inoculation during surgery, injection, bite, or trauma. In hematogenous infection, organisms escape from synovial capillaries, which lack a limiting basement membrane, and within hours provoke neutrophilic infiltration of the synovium. Neutrophils and bacteria enter the joint space and bacteria adhere to articular cartilage. Cartilage degradation begins within about 48 hours owing to increased intraarticular pressure, release of proteases and cytokines from chondrocytes and synovial macrophages, and invasion of cartilage by bacteria and inflammatory cells. Synovial proliferation forms a pannus over the cartilage, and thrombosis of inflamed synovial vessels develops; abscesses may extend into synovium, cartilage, and subchondral bone. S. aureus surface adhesins promote cartilage adherence and endotoxins drive chondrocyte-mediated cartilage breakdown. Gonococcal arthritis-dermatitis and viral arthritides are believed to be largely immune-mediated, reflecting reaction to circulating organisms and immune-complex deposition rather than direct joint invasion.
Staphylococcus aureus, streptococci, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae are the most common causes of infectious arthritis, though mycobacteria, spirochetes, fungi, and viruses can also seed joints.

Tuberculous arthritis is usually a chronic granulomatous monoarthritis of large weight-bearing joints (hips, knees, ankles); synovial fluid acid-fast staining is positive in under one-third of cases but synovial tissue culture is positive in about 90%.

Parvovirus B19 causes polyarthritis or polyarthralgia in about 60% of infected women and 10% of children; rubella, mumps, hepatitis B, and arboviruses (Zika, chikungunya, Ross River) are other notable viral causes.

Prosthetic joint infection complicates roughly 0.5-2% of total joint replacements and is more common after knee than hip arthroplasty; indolent infection with coagulase-negative staphylococci, Cutibacterium, enterococci, or diphtheroids may persist for months to years without constitutional symptoms.
Acute bacterial infection can rapidly destroy articular cartilage, so every inflamed joint warrants prompt evaluation; cartilage degradation can begin within about 48 hours.
Roughly 90% of acute septic arthritis presents in a single joint, most often the knee, then the hip, and less often shoulder, wrist, or elbow.
In IV drug users, infections of the spine, sacroiliac joints, and sternoclavicular joints are more common than those of the appendicular skeleton.

Acute bacterial infection typically causes mono- or oligoarthritis; subacute/chronic monoarthritis suggests mycobacterial or fungal disease, and acute polyarthritis suggests viral, immunologic (endocarditis, rheumatic fever, DGI), or underlying rheumatoid disease.

Synovial fluid Gram stain is positive in roughly 30-50% of cases overall; organisms are seen on smear in nearly three-quarters of S. aureus and streptococcal infections but only 30-50% of gram-negative and other bacterial infections.

Synovial fluid cultures are positive in over 90% of nongonococcal bacterial arthritis cases, but in gonococcal arthritis synovial cultures are frequently negative and blood cultures positive in fewer than 45%.

Disseminated gonococcal infection most commonly presents as an arthritis-dermatitis syndrome with fever, chills, hemorrhagic pustular rash, tenosynovitis, and migratory arthritis; women are 2-3 times more likely than men to develop DGI, with peak risk during menses and pregnancy.

Lyme disease causes arthritis in up to 60% of untreated persons; serologic IgG to B. burgdorferi is positive in over 90% of Lyme arthritis, and NAAT detects Borrelia DNA in synovial fluid in about 85%.
Serum procalcitonin is only about 50% sensitive and must not be used to rule out infectious arthritis.
Elevated synovial protein and lactate dehydrogenase with depressed glucose are nonspecific and not required for diagnosis.
Failing to test synovial fluid for crystals can miss coexisting infection and crystal disease, which can occur together.
Relying on synovial fluid culture in suspected gonococcal arthritis is misleading, since cultures are often negative; mucosal-site cultures and NAAT are needed.

Coagulase-negative staphylococci, Cutibacterium, or diphtheroids in a prosthetic joint may represent indolent true infection rather than contamination, so semiquantitative culture and careful aspiration technique are important.
Cellulitis, bursitis, and osteomyelitis can mimic septic arthritis; preserved passive range of motion and less-than-circumferential swelling help distinguish them.
Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) are typically elevated but nonspecific.

Prompt systemic antibiotics with timely joint drainage can prevent cartilage destruction, postinfectious degenerative arthritis, joint instability, and deformity, so outcome depends heavily on early recognition and adequate decompression. Radiographic joint-space narrowing and bony erosions indicate advanced disease and a poorer outcome. Gonococcal and Lyme arthritis generally respond well to therapy, and most reactive arthritis resolves within about 6 months, though recurrent disease is more common after chlamydial urethritis. Untreated Lyme arthritis leaves about 10% with chronic erosive synovitis, and certain viral arthropathies (e.g., parvovirus B19) occasionally become chronic.
Acutely inflamed joint - treat as a medical emergency given rapid cartilage destruction
Narrowing of joint space and bony erosions on radiographs indicate advanced infection and poor prognosis
Septic arthritis of the hip, especially in young children, threatens viability of the femoral head and is best managed surgically
Polyarticular involvement or absent fever in rheumatoid, renal, hepatic, or immunosuppressed patients can mask infection
Failure of repeated needle aspiration to clear effusion, lower synovial WBC, and sterilize cultures signals need for arthroscopic or open drainage

No single formal grading system; synovial fluid cell count guides likelihood and severity. Normal synovial fluid contains fewer than 180 cells/uL (predominantly mononuclear). Acute bacterial infection averages about 100,000 cells/uL (range roughly 25,000-250,000/uL) with over 90% neutrophils. Crystal-induced, rheumatoid, and other noninfectious inflammatory arthritides usually show under 30,000-50,000 cells/uL. Mycobacterial and fungal infections typically show 10,000-30,000 cells/uL with 50-70% neutrophils. Gonococcal DGI synovial fluid usually contains only 10,000-20,000 leukocytes/uL, whereas true gonococcal septic arthritis contains over 50,000/uL.
Infectious Arthritis (infective) — Musculoskeletal Also: septic arthritis, bacterial arthritis, pyogenic arthritis, joint infection

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Rat-bite fever versus Rocky Mountain spotted fever, Lyme disease, leptospirosis, and secondary syphilis (p.1143)

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Localized bite-wound cellulitis versus tissue damage from snake envenomation, which can mimic infection (p.1145)

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae) as a late consequence of cat bites/scratches (p.1143)

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Inflammatory tissue necrosis from venomous snake envenomation, which can be difficult to distinguish from secondary infection (p.1145)

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Gram's stain and aerobic culture of all infected wounds; anaerobic cultures when abscess, devitalized tissue, or foul-smelling exudate is present (p.1144)

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Notify the microbiology laboratory when fastidious organisms such as Eikenella corrodens are suspected in human bites (p.1144)

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: White blood cell count, and blood cultures if systemic infection is suspected (p.1144)

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Radiographs of penetrating wounds to assess fracture or retained foreign body such as a tooth fragment (p.1144)

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Hand-surgery consultation for hand injuries to evaluate tendon, nerve, and muscular involvement (p.1144)

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: For suspected Capnocytophaga sepsis, prolonged blood-culture incubation (up to 14 days); organisms may be seen within polymorphonuclear leukocytes on Wright-stained peripheral smears (p.1143)

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Traumatic soft-tissue injury, crush injury, and laceration without infection

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Local envenomation reaction

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Bite injuries inoculate the victim's tissues with the biting animal's oral flora plus environmental and cutaneous organisms, producing a typically polymicrobial mix of aerobes and anaerobes. Deep puncture wounds (cat canines, clenched-fist injuries) drive organisms into joints, tendons, and bone, predisposing to septic arthritis and osteomyelitis. Local spread produces cellulitis with purulent discharge, while seeding can lead to systemic disease (bacteremia, meningitis, brain abscess, endocarditis). Impaired lymphatic drainage (e.g., post-mastectomy limb) or immunocompromise (glucocorticoids, SLE, leukemia, cirrhosis, splenectomy) facilitates dissemination, and Capnocytophaga can incite DIC and renal failure in such hosts (p.1142-1144).

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Bite-wound flora generally mirrors the oropharyngeal flora of the biting animal, though organisms from soil, the victim's and animal's skin, and animal feces may also contribute (p.1142).

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Aquatic exposures matter: alligator or piranha bites may harbor Aeromonas hydrophila, while shark, moray eel, and barracuda bites are associated with marine Vibrio species (p.1143).

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Old World monkey (Macaca) bites can transmit B virus (Macacine herpesvirus 1), a cause of serious CNS infection; nonhuman primate bites otherwise resemble human bites (p.1143).

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Seal, walrus, and polar bear bites can cause 'seal finger,' a chronic suppurative infection attributed to Mycoplasma species such as M. phocacerebrale (p.1143).

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Dogs account for about 80% of animal bites; roughly 15-20% of dog bites become infected, whereas more than half of cat bites and scratches become infected (p.1142-1143).

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Cat bites carry a higher infection risk than dog bites because narrow sharp canine teeth inoculate deeply, predisposing to septic arthritis and osteomyelitis, especially with punctures over or near a joint of the hand (p.1143).

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Dog-bite infection typically appears 8-24 h after injury with pain and cellulitis plus purulent, sometimes foul-smelling discharge; the bite-to-symptom interval is notably shorter for cat bites (p.1143).

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Pasteurella multocida, a small gram-negative coccobacillus from feline oral flora, causes the majority of cat-bite infections and tends to advance rapidly, sometimes within hours (p.1143).

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Capnocytophaga canimorsus following dog bites (or licking of open wounds) can cause fulminant sepsis, DIC, and renal failure, particularly in asplenic, immunosuppressed, or hepatically impaired hosts; this thin gram-negative rod is hard to grow on solid media and may need up to 14 days to grow on blood culture (p.1143).

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Human bites become infected more often than other animal bites (~10-15%); clenched-fist ('fight bite') injuries are especially serious because deep hand structures including bone, joint, and tendon are inoculated (p.1144).

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Eikenella corrodens is a fastidious organism particularly associated with clenched-fist injuries; the microbiology laboratory should be alerted when it is suspected (p.1144).

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Rat-bite fever (Streptobacillus moniliformis in the US; Spirillum minor 'sodoku' mainly in Asia) characteristically manifests after the initial wound has healed; streptobacillary disease causes fever, migratory arthralgias, and a maculopapular rash involving the palms and soles (p.1143).

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Underestimating infection risk in cat bites, whose deep punctures seed joints and bone despite small surface wounds (p.1143)

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease

chunks.text: Primary closure of high-risk wounds (e.g., cat puncture wounds, wounds >12 h old on a limb or >24 h old on the face), which raises infection risk (p.1144)

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Most localized bite-wound infections resolve with appropriate wound care and treatment, but a significant minority become severe or life-threatening. Septic arthritis and osteomyelitis prolong the course. Capnocytophaga sepsis can be fulminant in susceptible hosts. Streptobacillary rat-bite fever was frequently fatal in the preantibiotic era and may be complicated by endocarditis, myocarditis, meningitis, pneumonia, and multi-organ abscesses (p.1142-1145).

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Bites posing rabies risk, requiring contact with public-health authorities (p.1144)

chunks.system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease
chunks.text: Human-bite wound infection risk stratifies by depth: approximately 2% for superficial wounds versus over 25% for deep wounds such as clenched-fist injuries. Human bites are categorized as occlusional injuries (from actual biting) or clenched-fist ('fight bite') injuries (fist striking teeth), the latter being more common and more serious owing to inoculation of deep hand structures (p.1144).

Heterophile antibody test (titer >=40 diagnostic with compatible symptoms and atypical lymphocytes), or the more sensitive commercial Monospot test (~75% sensitive, ~90% specific vs EBV-specific serology) (Harrison 22e p.1511)
EBV-specific serology: IgM and IgG anti-VCA, anti-EBNA, and (less useful for routine diagnosis) anti-early antigen (EA-D, EA-R) (Harrison 22e p.1511)
Peripheral blood examination for atypical lymphocytes and CBC (leukocytosis, possible neutropenia/thrombocytopenia) (Harrison 22e p.1509)
Liver function tests (aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin) (Harrison 22e p.1509)

EBV DNA detection by PCR in blood or CSF (useful when serology is equivocal, in CNS lymphoma in AIDS, and for monitoring lymphoproliferative disease); throat or blood culture is NOT helpful because EBV persists for life in the oropharynx and B cells (Harrison 22e p.1511)
Lymphoma (fixed, nontender nodes; atypical lymphocytes) (Harrison 22e p.1511)
Drug-induced mononucleosis-like reaction (phenytoin, carbamazepine, sulfonamides, minocycline) (Harrison 22e p.1511)

EBV, a herpesvirus, is transmitted in saliva and infects oropharyngeal and salivary epithelium plus B lymphocytes (including tonsillar-crypt lymphocytes directly), then disseminates via the bloodstream. Proliferation of EBV-infected B cells alongside reactive T cells enlarges lymphoid tissue. During acute IM up to 1 in 100 peripheral B cells is infected (falling to 1-50 per million after recovery), and there is an inverted CD4+/CD8+ ratio with large clonal CD8+ T-cell expansions (up to 40% directed against EBV antigens). The EBV receptor on B cells is CD21 (the C3d complement receptor); HLA class II is a co-receptor for B-cell entry, while epithelial entry uses ephrin A2. Memory B cells (not epithelial cells) are the lifelong reservoir. Cellular immunity (NK cells, cytotoxic T cells recognizing EBNAs and LMPs) is more important than humoral immunity in control; if T-cell immunity is impaired, infected B cells may proliferate, and in EBV-associated tumors LMP-1 mimics TNF-receptor-family signaling (e.g., CD40) to drive growth (Harrison 22e p.1508-1509).

Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is the cause of heterophile-positive infectious mononucleosis (IM), classically marked by the triad of fever, sore throat (pharyngitis), and lymphadenopathy, together with atypical lymphocytosis (Harrison 22e p.1508).

EBV-specific serology pattern: IgM antibody to viral capsid antigen (VCA) is most useful for acute IM (present only during the first 2-3 months); IgG anti-VCA persists for life and indicates past exposure; antibodies to EBNA appear late (3-6 weeks after symptom onset) and persist for life (Harrison 22e p.1511).
Most cases of IM are self-limited; most patients have symptoms for 2-4 weeks, but nearly 10% have fatigue persisting for 6 months or more (Harrison 22e p.1509).

EBV is associated with several malignancies, including Burkitt's lymphoma (~90% of African cases, ~15% of US cases), anaplastic nasopharyngeal carcinoma (uniformly EBV-associated in southern China), gastric carcinoma (the most common EBV-associated malignancy worldwide), Hodgkin's lymphoma (especially mixed-cellularity type), and various T-/NK-cell and CNS lymphomas; EBV-driven lymphoproliferative disease occurs in immunodeficient and transplant patients (Harrison 22e p.1509-1511).

Large epidemiologic data show a strong association of EBV with multiple sclerosis; one study of over a million military personnel found a 32-fold higher MS risk after primary EBV infection, though the causal role still requires further research (Harrison 22e p.1508, 1511).

EBV is spread mainly by contact with oral secretions (saliva); by adulthood >90% of individuals are seropositive. IM is typically a disease of young adults, while in young children primary infection is usually asymptomatic or a mild pharyngitis (Harrison 22e p.1508-1509).

The incubation period in young adults is about 4-6 weeks, often preceded by a 1-2 week prodrome of fatigue, malaise, and myalgia before fever, sore throat, and lymphadenopathy appear (Harrison 22e p.1509).

Lymphadenopathy (most often posterior cervical, tender, symmetric, not fixed) and pharyngitis are most prominent in the first 2 weeks, whereas splenomegaly is more prominent during the second and third weeks (Harrison 22e p.1509).

Lymphadenopathy and fever are the most common signs (each in >90%), with pharyngitis/tonsillitis in ~82% and splenomegaly in ~51%; tonsillar exudate can resemble streptococcal pharyngitis (Harrison 22e p.1509).

Characteristic laboratory features: leukocytosis peaking at the second-to-third week with >10% atypical lymphocytes (enlarged cells with abundant cytoplasm, predominantly CD8+ T cells), often with mild neutropenia and thrombocytopenia (Harrison 22e p.1509).
Abnormal liver function (mildly elevated aminotransferases and alkaline phosphatase) occurs in >90% of cases, with hyperbilirubinemia in about 40% (Harrison 22e p.1509).

The heterophile (and the somewhat more sensitive Monospot) test is the standard diagnostic test in children and adults; heterophile antibodies do not interact with EBV proteins. Tests are positive in ~40% in week 1 and 80-90% by week 3, so repeat testing may be needed if performed early (Harrison 22e p.1511).
Heterophile antibodies are often absent in children under 5 years, the elderly, and patients with atypical presentations; in these cases EBV-specific serology should be used (Harrison 22e p.1511).

Ampicillin/penicillin rash pitfall: about 95% of patients with infectious mononucleosis given ampicillin develop a rash; classically a macular rash followed penicillin-derivative use, although more recent studies suggest EBV-associated rashes may occur at similar frequency with or without penicillin exposure, and these rashes are not predictive of future penicillin reactions (Harrison 22e p.1509, 1513).

Heterophile/Monospot tests are often falsely negative early in illness (positive in only ~40% during week 1) and are unreliable in children under 5, the elderly, and atypical presentations - repeat testing or EBV-specific serology may be required (Harrison 22e p.1511).
False-positive Monospot results are more common in connective tissue disease, lymphoma, viral hepatitis, and malaria (Harrison 22e p.1511).
Culture of EBV from throat washings or blood does NOT diagnose acute infection because the virus persists lifelong in the oropharynx and B cells (Harrison 22e p.1511).
Glucocorticoids are NOT indicated for uncomplicated IM and may predispose to bacterial superinfection (Harrison 22e p.1512).
Acyclovir has had no significant clinical impact on IM in controlled trials (Harrison 22e p.1512).

Persistent EBV infection is NOT a cause of chronic fatigue syndrome; antibody titers in such patients are not significantly different from healthy seropositive adults and EBV DNA is not elevated (Harrison 22e p.1510-1511).

Most cases of IM are self-limited and resolve over 2-4 weeks; deaths are very rare and are most often due to CNS complications, splenic rupture, upper-airway obstruction, or bacterial superinfection. Nearly 10% of patients have fatigue persisting for 6 months or more. Disease severity correlates with blood CD8+ T-cell and EBV DNA levels. Most neurologic complications resolve without sequelae. The risk of EBV-positive Hodgkin's lymphoma is significantly increased in young adults for several years after EBV-seropositive IM (Harrison 22e p.1509-1511).

Splenic rupture (occurs in <0.5% of cases, more common in males; may present as abdominal pain, referred shoulder pain, or hemodynamic compromise) - a leading cause of the rare deaths from IM (Harrison 22e p.1510)
Upper-airway obstruction from tonsillar/adenoidal hypertrophy or epiglottic/pharyngeal/uvular edema (Harrison 22e p.1510)

CNS complications (meningitis, encephalitis, cerebellar ataxia, cranial nerve palsies especially CN VII, Guillain-Barre syndrome, transverse myelitis) - usually within the first 2 weeks (Harrison 22e p.1510)
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (Coombs-positive, cold agglutinins to red-cell i antigen, ~2% of cases) (Harrison 22e p.1510)
Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, severe cytopenias (red-cell aplasia, severe granulocytopenia, thrombocytopenia, pancytopenia) (Harrison 22e p.1510)
Fulminant hepatitis, myocarditis/pericarditis, pneumonia with pleural effusion (Harrison 22e p.1510)
Fatal IM in patients with X-linked lymphoproliferative disease or other primary immunodeficiencies - and rarely in patients with no obvious preexisting immune defect (Harrison 22e p.1510)

Conception requires ovulation of a competent oocyte, patent fallopian tubes, a receptive uterus, and adequate sperm delivery and function; disruption at any step causes infertility. Female causes include tubal damage (often from pelvic inflammatory disease, endometriosis, prior surgery, or salpingitis isthmica nodosum), uterine factors (fibroids distorting the cavity, congenital mullerian anomalies, intrauterine scarring), ovulatory dysfunction (PCOS, diminished ovarian reserve, premature ovarian insufficiency), and endocrine disturbance (hypothyroidism, hyperprolactinemia). Age-related decline reflects accumulating meiotic chromosomal errors in the oocyte after 35. Male causes include anatomic/obstructive problems (vasectomy, infection, congenital absence of the vas), endocrine causes (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, hypothyroidism, hyperprolactinemia, morbid obesity, certain drugs and exogenous testosterone suppressing spermatogenesis), sexual dysfunction, and primary testicular/genetic defects (Klinefelter syndrome, Y-chromosome microdeletions). Hormonal contraception works through negative feedback: continuous estrogen suppresses FSH and follicular development while continuous progestin suppresses the LH surge and ovulation, thickens cervical mucus, thins/alters the endometrium, and impairs tubal motility; progestin-only and levonorgestrel-IUD effects rely mainly on cervical mucus thickening and endometrial thinning. Copper IUDs act as a spermicide that also impairs fertilization and implantation (Harrison 22e p.3149-3154).
Infertility is defined as failure to conceive after 12 months of unprotected intercourse; global prevalence is roughly 17.5%, affecting an estimated 48-72 million couples (Harrison 22e p.3149).

Emergency contraception should be offered to any woman who requests it up to 5 days after unprotected intercourse and should NOT be delayed for a pregnancy test or exam; the copper IUD is the most effective option and ulipristal acetate the most effective oral agent (Harrison 22e p.3154).

Lactation can provide effective contraception during the first 6 postpartum months only if breastfeeding is exclusive and menses have not resumed, with failure rates as low as 0.5-1.5 per 100 women-years (Harrison 22e p.3154).

Primary infertility describes couples who have never conceived, whereas secondary infertility follows at least one prior pregnancy; about 85% of couples conceive within 12 months and 95% within 24 months (Harrison 22e p.3149).

Female-only factors account for roughly 30-40% of cases, male-only factors 40-50%, combined factors 20-30%, and unexplained infertility up to about 30% - so a complete workup of BOTH partners is recommended (Harrison 22e p.3149-3150).

Fecundability falls steeply with maternal age: compared with women aged 30-31, it is reduced about 14% at 34-35, 53% at 40-41, and 59% at 42-44 years, largely from oocyte meiotic chromosomal errors; a comparable decline is NOT seen in men under 50 (Harrison 22e p.3149).
Evaluation is generally started after 12 months of trying, but after only 6 months if the female partner is over 35 and immediately if she is over 40 (Harrison 22e p.3150).

The fertile window is about 5-6 days before ovulation; intercourse every 1-2 days during this interval maximizes the chance of conception. A basal body temperature rise confirms ovulation has already occurred and therefore cannot be used prospectively to time intercourse (Harrison 22e p.3151).

Long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARC; IUDs and subdermal implants) are the most effective reversible methods, rivaling sterilization, with high continuation and satisfaction rates, making them a good choice even for adolescents and nulliparous women (Harrison 22e p.3153-3154).

Combined estrogen-progestin contraceptives reduce the risk of endometrial cancer (about 50%) and ovarian cancer (about 40%) and help regulate cycles and reduce menorrhagia, dysmenorrhea and hyperandrogenism (Harrison 22e p.3153).

Unintended pregnancies arise mainly from non-use or inconsistent use rather than method failure; methods requiring daily or coitus-related use fail more often than LARC and permanent methods (Harrison 22e p.3152-3153).
Treating only one partner - both must be evaluated because male, female, and combined factors are common.
Using basal body temperature to time intercourse prospectively; the temperature rise only confirms ovulation has already happened.
Over-relying on HSG positive findings - its positive predictive value for tubal occlusion is low even though its negative predictive value is high.

Performing routine sperm-antibody testing, scrotal ultrasound, diagnostic laparoscopy, postcoital test, endometrial biopsy, thrombophilia, immunologic testing, or karyotype as part of the initial infertility workup - these are NOT indicated routinely.
Attempting tubal repair/reconstruction with hydrosalpinx or prior tubal infection - low success and increased ectopic risk; salpingectomy of hydrosalpinges actually improves subsequent IVF outcomes.
Routine screening for familial thrombotic disorders before prescribing hormonal contraception is not recommended.
Withholding or delaying emergency contraception to obtain a pregnancy test or exam, or withholding it from overweight/obese women.
Assuming individual abnormal semen parameters predict infertility - none alone is predictive; risk rises with multiple abnormalities.

About 85% of couples not using contraception conceive within one year and 95% within two years, but success of fertility treatment depends strongly on the female partner's age, ovarian reserve, smoking, BMI, and race; advanced maternal age (>35) raises aneuploidy risk and advanced paternal age (>40) is linked to adverse offspring outcomes. IVF carries an overall low complication risk, with multiple pregnancy being the main hazard and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome reduced by careful monitoring and GnRH (rather than hCG) triggering. Infertility causes substantial psychological stress, but the condition and its treatment do not appear to produce long-term psychological sequelae (Harrison 22e p.3149-3152).
Female partner over 40 years - evaluate immediately rather than waiting
Azoospermia or severe oligospermia (<5 million/mL) - requires genetic and endocrine evaluation
Smoker aged 35 or older using >=15 cigarettes/day - USMEC category 4 contraindication to estrogen-containing contraception
History of venous thromboembolism, known thrombogenic mutations, stroke, or ischemic heart disease - avoid estrogen-containing contraceptives
Migraine with aura - contraindication to combined hormonal contraception
Current breast cancer - contraindication to hormonal contraception
Recurrent pregnancy loss - consider sperm DNA fragmentation assay

Contraceptive choice is guided by the U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria (USMEC, adapted from WHO): Category 4 = unacceptable health risk (e.g., smoker >=35 years with >=15 cigarettes/day, acute DVT or prior VTE at high recurrence risk, stroke or thrombogenic mutations, complicated valvular disease, current breast cancer, migraine with aura, uncontrolled hypertension >=160/100); Category 3 = theoretical/proven risks outweigh benefits (e.g., smoker >=35 with <15 cigarettes/day, controlled or moderate hypertension, certain enzyme-inducing anticonvulsants, rifampin/rifabutin, some HIV regimens, bariatric malabsorptive surgery); Category 2 = benefits generally outweigh risks (e.g., obesity alone). Method effectiveness ranges from highly effective sterilization and LARC (>99%) to less reliable barrier and fertility-awareness methods (Harrison 22e p.3152-3153).

IBD is regarded as an inappropriate, dysregulated mucosal immune response to the endogenous commensal microbiota (with or without an autoimmune component) in a genetically susceptible host, shaped by environmental factors. Homeostasis among the commensal microbiota, intestinal epithelial cells and mucosal immune cells is disrupted, producing chronic inflammation. More than ~240 genetic loci (e.g. NOD2, ATG16L1, IL23R, IL12B, IL10, XBP1) contribute incrementally and affect pathways of innate immunity, autophagy/unfolded-protein response, adaptive immunity and inflammation/healing; ~two-thirds are shared between CD and UC. Dysbiosis (e.g. expansion of adherent/invasive E. coli, loss of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii) and defective oral (mucosal) tolerance lead to unrestrained CD4+ T-cell (TH1/TH2/TH17) and innate immune activation, with a self-perpetuating cytokine cascade (IL-1, IL-6, IL-12, IL-23, TNF) driving fibrogenesis, leukocyte recruitment and tissue damage. TH1-driven transmural granulomatous inflammation resembles CD; TH2-type superficial mucosal inflammation resembles UC. Roughly 5-10% of patients have familial disease and only ~20% of disease risk is currently explained by known genetics (Harrison 22e p.2551-2555).
IBD is a chronic, idiopathic inflammatory disease of the GI tract; ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn's disease (CD) are its two major types (Harrison 22e p.2551).

Up to one-third of IBD patients have at least one extraintestinal manifestation; some parallel bowel activity (erythema nodosum, peripheral arthritis, episcleritis) while others run an independent course (pyoderma gangrenosum, ankylosing spondylitis, sacroiliitis, uveitis, PSC) (Harrison 22e p.2561-2563).

Smoking has opposite associations in the two diseases: it may be protective in UC (OR 0.58) but is a risk factor for CD (OR 1.76); prior appendectomy with confirmed appendicitis is protective against UC but not CD (Harrison 22e p.2551-2552).

Patients with long-standing extensive colitis (UC or Crohn's colitis) have an increased risk of colonic dysplasia and carcinoma; surveillance colonoscopy with multiple biopsies is the standard of care (Harrison 22e p.2612-2613).

UC is a mucosal disease that almost always involves the rectum and extends proximally in continuity, without intervening areas of uninvolved (skip) mucosa; ~40-50% have disease limited to rectum/rectosigmoid and ~20% have pancolitis (Harrison 22e p.2555).

CD can affect any part of the GI tract from mouth to anus, is segmental with skip areas, and characteristically spares the rectum (unlike UC); the terminal ileum is involved in ~90% of those with small-intestinal disease (Harrison 22e p.2556).

CD is a transmural process producing fistulas, strictures, abscesses and an endoscopic/radiographic 'cobblestone' appearance, whereas UC inflammation is limited to mucosa and superficial submucosa except in fulminant disease (Harrison 22e p.2555-2556).

Noncaseating granulomas are a characteristic histologic feature of CD but are found less often on mucosal biopsy than on surgical resection specimens; UC shows crypt distortion, basal plasmacytosis, cryptitis and crypt abscesses (Harrison 22e p.2556).

Major UC symptoms are diarrhoea, rectal bleeding, tenesmus, mucus passage and crampy abdominal pain; severe pain is not prominent in UC, whereas CD ileocolitis classically causes right-lower-quadrant pain and diarrhoea, sometimes mimicking acute appendicitis (Harrison 22e p.2556-2557).

Perianal disease (perirectal fistulas, fissures, abscesses, anal stenosis, skin tags) occurs in about one-third of CD patients and points away from UC; extensive perianal lesions in apparent UC should suggest CD (Harrison 22e p.2556, p.2557).

Faecal calprotectin and faecal lactoferrin are neutrophil-derived markers that correlate with histologic inflammation, help distinguish IBD from irritable bowel syndrome, predict relapse and detect pouchitis; calprotectin is more sensitive for ileocolonic/colonic than isolated ileal inflammation (Harrison 22e p.2557, p.2558).
Distinguishing UC from CD is impossible initially in up to 15% of cases (indeterminate colitis); ~5% of resection specimens cannot be classified due to overlapping features (Harrison 22e p.2559).

Failing to exclude infective colitis (especially C. difficile, Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, E. coli, CMV) and amebiasis before diagnosing or escalating treatment of IBD - infection can both mimic IBD and trigger relapse (Harrison 22e p.2559-2561).

In UC, biopsies of normal-appearing mucosa are usually abnormal, so multiple biopsies should be taken from apparently uninvolved proximal and distal mucosa; effective medical therapy can also create pseudo-skip areas (Harrison 22e p.2555).
Peritoneal signs of perforation may be absent or subtle in patients on glucocorticoids (Harrison 22e p.2557).
A colonic stricture impassable with the colonoscope should be presumed malignant until proven otherwise (Harrison 22e p.2557).
Extensive perianal lesions in apparent UC should raise suspicion for Crohn's disease (Harrison 22e p.2557).
Wireless capsule endoscopy must be avoided when a small-bowel stricture is suspected because of the risk of capsule retention (Harrison 22e p.2558).
Serologic tests (ASCA, pANCA) have variable predictive value and unclear clinical usefulness for distinguishing or predicting IBD (Harrison 22e p.2559).
Pyoderma gangrenosum and ankylosing spondylitis run a course independent of bowel disease and do not reliably improve with colectomy (Harrison 22e p.2561-2562).

IBD is a lifelong chronic disease with a relapsing-remitting course; only ~15% of UC patients present initially with severe disease. Massive haemorrhage occurs in ~1% of UC patients and toxic megacolon is rare (about 50% of acute dilations resolve with conservative management, the remainder requiring urgent colectomy). In CD the inflammatory process tends to evolve toward a fibrostenotic obstructing pattern or a penetrating fistulous pattern; intestinal obstruction occurs in ~40%, intraabdominal/pelvic abscesses in 10-30%, and free perforation in 1-2%. Long-standing extensive colitis carries an increased colorectal cancer risk (UC meta-analysis figures of ~2% at 10 years, 8% at 20 years, 18% at 30 years, though rates have fallen with better inflammation control and surveillance; overall colorectal cancer rates remain ~1.5-2 times the general population). CD and UC cancer risks are probably equivalent for similar extent and duration. Associated PSC carries a 7-10% risk of cholangiocarcinoma (Harrison 22e p.2557-2563, p.2612-2613).
Toxic megacolon (transverse or right colon diameter >6 cm with loss of haustration in a severe attack) - may be precipitated by electrolyte abnormalities and narcotics; risk of perforation
Perforation - most dangerous local complication; peritoneal signs may be masked by glucocorticoids; mortality of perforation complicating toxic megacolon is ~15%

Ulcerative colitis is graded by the Montreal classification of extent (E1 proctitis; E2 left-sided/distal UC, distal to splenic flexure; E3 extensive/pancolitis, proximal to splenic flexure) and severity (S0 clinical remission; S1 mild: <=4 stools/day with or without blood, no systemic illness, normal ESR; S2 moderate: >=4 stools/day with minimal systemic toxicity; S3 severe: >=6 bloody stools/day, pulse >=90/min, temperature >=37.5C, haemoglobin <10.5 g/100 mL, ESR >=30 mm/h). Crohn's disease is classified by the Vienna and Montreal systems by age at diagnosis (A1/A2/A3), location (L1 ileal, L2 colonic, L3 ileocolonic, L4 upper/foregut) and behaviour (B1 nonstricturing-nonpenetrating, B2 stricturing, B3 penetrating), with a 'p' modifier for perianal disease (Harrison 22e p.2557-2558).

The inflammatory myopathies are immune-mediated muscle diseases with distinct mechanisms by subtype. DM microvasculopathy and skin/muscle damage are increasingly attributed to type I interferon (IFN)-mediated toxicity, most likely IFN-beta, rather than the older model of antibody/complement-mediated capillary destruction with watershed ischemia; immunoglobulin deposition on endothelium is largely absent and complement deposition may be secondary, and there is increasing evidence MSAs are directly pathogenic (e.g. anti-Mi-2 entering myonuclei to inhibit the CHD4/NuRD complex). PM is heterogeneous with poorly understood pathogenesis; its infiltrate is predominantly CD8+ T cells and macrophages in endomysial, perimysial, and perivascular regions. IMNM shows multifocal necrotic and regenerating fibers with few inflammatory cells; it does not appear primarily complement-driven (complement inhibition failed in anti-HMGCR and anti-SRP disease), anti-HMGCR antibodies may bind sarcolemmal receptor causing acetyl-CoA and lipid accumulation, and anti-SRP antibodies appear directly causal. ASyS resembles DM histologically but with more perifascicular necrosis and HLA-DR (MHC-II) expression suggesting gamma-IFN rather than type I IFN drive. IBM combines adaptive immune attack (highly differentiated CD8+CD57+ KLRG1+ T cells invading non-necrotic MHC-I/II-expressing fibers, plus a relatively specific autoantibody) with degenerative features including rimmed vacuoles, beta-sheet amyloid inclusions, p62/LC3 aggregates and ER stress/autophagy, mitochondrial abnormality (ragged-red and COX-negative fibers), and extrusion of TDP-43 from myonuclei; whether damage is primarily immune or a secondary neurodegenerative process is unclear.

Major idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IMs) are dermatomyositis (DM), polymyositis (PM), immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM), antisynthetase syndrome (ASyS), and inclusion body myositis (IBM); idiopathic PM without an overlap syndrome is quite rare, while DM, ASyS, IBM, and IMNM occur in roughly similar frequencies (Harrison 22e p.2909).

DM, PM, ASyS, and IMNM are typically responsive to immunotherapy with high-dose glucocorticoids as first-line; IBM does NOT typically respond to any known immunotherapy and is managed with physical/occupational and swallowing therapy (Harrison 22e p.2915-2916).

Most IMs (DM, PM, IMNM, ASyS) present with symmetric proximal-greater-than-distal weakness; DM additionally has a characteristic rash and PM/IMNM/ASyS do not (DM rash, ASyS rash sometimes) (Harrison 22e p.2909-2910).

Serum creatine kinase (CK) is the most sensitive laboratory marker of muscle destruction; a markedly elevated CK (e.g. >2000 U/L) is almost always due to a myopathy, and CK is always elevated in uncontrolled PM and markedly elevated (usually >10x normal) in IMNM (Harrison 22e p.2910-2912).

DM rash includes the heliotrope rash (violaceous eyelid discoloration with periorbital edema), Gottron sign and Gottron papules over extensor joint surfaces, V-sign (anterior neck/chest), shawl sign (posterior neck/shoulders), nail-bed telangiectasias, and subcutaneous calcium deposits; a heliotrope rash with Gottron papules and dilated nailfold capillaries is diagnostic for DM (Harrison 22e p.2910-2911).

Myositis-specific antibodies (MSAs) help define subtypes: DM (anti-Mi-2, anti-TIF1-gamma, anti-MDA5, anti-NXP-2, anti-SAE); IMNM (anti-HMGCR, anti-SRP); ASyS (antisynthetase antibodies, most commonly anti-Jo-1); IBM (anti-cN-1A) (Harrison 22e p.2909-2914).

EMG/nerve conduction studies help localize the lesion to muscle but are nonspecific for cause; muscle MRI shows edema, atrophy, or fatty replacement and can show subtype-specific patterns (e.g. IBM spares the rectus femoris while involving vastus medialis/lateralis) (Harrison 22e p.2910-2914).

A muscle biopsy is often required to distinguish myopathies when there is no characteristic DM rash or MSA, and should be performed in every case of suspected PM to exclude IBM and other causes; biopsy a clinically affected but not too-weak muscle (e.g. MRC grade 4/5) to avoid sampling only end-stage muscle (Harrison 22e p.2910-2911).

Patients with severe muscle pain, subjective weakness, and fatigue but normal strength/function on exam are not likely to have an IM; consider polymyalgia rheumatica in older patients with raised ESR/CRP but normal CK and EMG, and fibromyalgia when the lab workup is normal (Harrison 22e p.2911).

Overlap syndrome describes an IM associated with another connective tissue disease (scleroderma, MCTD, Sjogren syndrome, SLE, rheumatoid arthritis); overlap syndromes are usually responsive to immunotherapy, except Sjogren syndrome with coexisting IBM (Harrison 22e p.2912).

IBM is frequently misdiagnosed and is distinguished from PM by distal/asymmetric weakness with predilection for finger/wrist flexors and quadriceps in patients >50, normal or only mildly elevated CK, and being essentially steroid-refractory and unresponsive to any known immunotherapy - so a normal CK should alert clinicians to the possibility of IBM
Many older series of 'PM' likely actually included patients with IBM, IMNM, or muscular dystrophies with inflammation, biasing reported treatment response and cancer-risk data
Perifascicular atrophy (the classic DM biopsy finding) is present in perhaps only 50% of DM patients; MxA immunostaining is diagnostically more sensitive and highly specific
Rimmed vacuoles may be absent in up to 20-30% of IBM biopsies; mitochondrial abnormality (ragged-red/COX-negative fibers) and p62 inclusions help distinguish IBM from PM in such cases
Anti-HMGCR myopathy does NOT improve when statins are stopped (unlike common toxic statin myopathy) and can occur in statin-naive children/young adults, mimicking limb-girdle muscular dystrophy
IBM EMG can show large-amplitude long-duration motor units that may be misinterpreted as neurogenic but actually reflect chronicity of the myopathy
Muscle biopsy should sample a clinically affected but not too-weak muscle (e.g. MRC 4/5); biopsying an end-stage muscle yields non-diagnostic tissue

In the absence of malignancy, DM prognosis is generally favorable with 5-year survival of 70-93%; poor prognostic features (DM and PM) are increased age, associated ILD, cardiac disease, and late or previously inadequate treatment. Most PM patients improve with immunotherapy but usually require lifelong treatment. IMNM varies by subtype: anti-HMGCR myopathy is often responsive to IVIG monotherapy, whereas anti-SRP and seronegative IMNM are much harder to treat and need aggressive immunotherapy; increased cancer incidence may exist in anti-HMGCR myopathy. ASyS patients mostly respond but disease can be difficult to treat (especially with ILD, where early rituximab is warranted) with no apparent increased malignancy risk. IBM is slowly progressive and not typically responsive to immunotherapy; most patients require a scooter or wheelchair within ~10-15 years of symptom onset, with no known increased malignancy risk.

Dermatomyositis rash (heliotrope rash, Gottron sign/papules) - adult-onset DM carries ~15% malignancy risk within the first 2-3 years; enhanced cancer vigilance especially with anti-TIF1-gamma (89% specificity, 70% sensitivity for cancer-associated DM)
Anti-MDA5 antibodies - palmar rash, severe ischemic skin ulceration, and rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease (also frequent in amyopathic DM)
Dyspnea from ILD, bronchopneumonia, alveolitis, or ventilatory muscle weakness
Dysphagia and dysarthria (aspiration risk; common in IBM and seen in DM/IMNM)
Myocarditis / cardiac disease (poor prognostic feature)
Markedly elevated CK (e.g. >2000 U/L) - almost always indicates a myopathy

Harrison does not provide a formal numeric severity grading scale for the inflammatory myopathies. Disease is characterized instead by clinical subtype (DM, PM, IMNM, ASyS, IBM), pattern and degree of weakness (graded clinically, e.g. MRC strength), serum CK elevation, presence of organ involvement (ILD, myocarditis, dysphagia), associated malignancy, and responsiveness to immunotherapy. Treatment intensity (first-line high-dose glucocorticoids; early second-line agents for severe weakness, organ involvement such as myocarditis/ILD, steroid-complication risk, or IMNM) reflects severity stratification in practice.

Influenza is a single-stranded, segmented, negative-sense RNA genome virus of the family Orthomyxoviridae, with four (sero)types: A, B, C, and D. Influenza A and C infect multiple species; B infects humans almost exclusively; D primarily infects cattle and is not known to infect humans. Influenza A is subdivided into 18 hemagglutinin (H) and 11 neuraminidase (N) surface-protein subtypes. Two distinct mechanisms drive antigenic variation: antigenic drift (accumulation of point mutations in the HA and NA molecules) produces the gradual divergence underlying annual epidemics and requires new vaccines each year; antigenic shift, enabled by the segmented genome allowing reassortment between two viruses co-infecting one host, can produce a major novel virus and a pandemic. Type B viruses mutate less frequently than type A, probably reflecting their near-exclusive human host range. Many highly pathogenic strains circulate in aquatic birds; pigs, which carry both avian and human receptors, can serve as a mixing vessel for reassortment that makes zoonotic viruses more fit for human replication (Harrison 22e p.1576).
Influenza presents with an abrupt febrile illness: fever, myalgias, fatigue, sore throat, headache, and cough (Harrison 22e p.1576).

Influenza A viruses are the most virulent for humans and cause most severe disease, though type B viruses (Victoria lineage) also cause substantial morbidity; type A is subdivided by hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N) surface protein subtypes (Harrison 22e p.1576).
Two type A subtypes (H1N1 and H3N2) and one type B lineage (Victoria) cause annual seasonal epidemics, which occur in winter in temperate regions (Harrison 22e p.1576, p.1579).

Influenza pneumonia has an unusually high rate of complication by bacterial superinfection, with staphylococcal and streptococcal pneumonia occurring in as many as 10% of cases in some series (Harrison 22e p.1576).

Antiviral treatment of influenza is effective only when given early in the course of illness; baloxavir marboxil is approved for acute uncomplicated flu when started within 2 days of onset (Harrison 22e p.1537, p.1580).

Antibiotics do NOT improve the outcome of uncomplicated viral respiratory infection in otherwise healthy people, but influenza can be complicated by secondary bacterial infection that does warrant antibacterials (Harrison 22e p.1537).

Annual vaccine reformulation is required because antigenic drift (point mutations in HA and NA) causes antigenic divergence; an occasional antigenic mismatch can render a vaccine component of negligible efficacy (Harrison 22e p.1538).

RT-PCR is extremely sensitive: viral genome can persist in nasal secretions for weeks after an infection resolves, so a positive test may reflect a recently resolved rather than a currently acute infection, and laboratory contamination can produce false positives (Harrison 22e p.1537).
Rapid diagnostic tests have the highest positive predictive value when applied to high-risk, appropriately seasonal samples; indiscriminate testing lowers predictive value (Harrison 22e p.1537).
Adamantanes (amantadine, rimantadine) should not be relied upon: widespread resistance has occurred in many currently circulating influenza A viruses (Harrison 22e p.1580).
Antiviral therapy started late is of limited benefit, as it is effective mainly when given early in the course (Harrison 22e p.1537).

Uncomplicated influenza in otherwise healthy adults is generally self-limited, and antiviral therapy started early shortens illness. Severe and even fatal pneumonia occurs particularly in elderly patients, nursing-home residents, immunocompromised persons, and very young children. Bacterial superinfection complicates as many as 10% of influenza pneumonia cases in some series. Pandemics caused by novel viruses occur on average every 20-30 years (Harrison 22e p.1576, p.1538).

chunks.text: An inguinal hernia is protrusion of abdominal contents through the inguinal canal. Indirect hernias pass through the deep (internal) inguinal ring into the canal, often through a patent processus vaginalis, and may descend into the scrotum. Direct hernias bulge forward through an attenuated posterior wall of the canal (Hesselbach's triangle) as a result of acquired weakness of the transversalis fascia. Raised intra-abdominal pressure and weakened abdominal wall connective tissue promote herniation. As a hernia enlarges the neck may narrow relative to the sac, predisposing to incarceration (irreducibility) and strangulation, in which the blood supply to trapped bowel is compromised, leading to ischaemia and, if untreated, perforation.

Membrane transporters of the solute-carrier (SLC) superfamily move amino acids, peptides, sugars, ions, vitamins, water, and other molecules across plasma membranes and organelle membranes. Inherited loss of a transporter produces disease whose organ pattern depends on the transporter's tissue distribution and whether redundant transporters exist. In cystinuria, defective apical proximal-tubule and intestinal transport of dibasic amino acids leads to massive cystine excretion; because cystine is poorly soluble, it precipitates and forms stones. In lysinuric protein intolerance, a basolateral transport defect traps arginine inside cells and secondarily impairs the urea cycle, with proposed nitric-oxide-mediated immune dysfunction. In citrin deficiency, the mitochondrial aspartate-glutamate carrier defect limits cytoplasmic aspartate for argininosuccinate synthesis and impairs the malate-aspartate NADH shuttle, so a cytoplasmic NADH excess (worsened by carbohydrate) drives metabolic decompensation and hyperammonemia. In Hartnup disease, loss of the neutral amino acid transporter B0AT1 causes renal and intestinal malabsorption of tryptophan, producing functional niacin deficiency and pellagra-like features. In cystinosis, a defective lysosomal cystine/proton transporter causes intralysosomal cystine accumulation and crystal deposition throughout tissues, with the kidney (Fanconi syndrome, progressive renal failure) and cornea most prominently affected.

These disorders arise from defects in solute-carrier (SLC) family transporters; tissue distribution of the affected transporter and presence or absence of redundant transporters determine which organs (notably brain and sensory organs) are involved.

Cystinosis has three forms graded by residual transporter function: classic nephropathic (renal Fanconi syndrome with rickets in infancy, progressing to renal failure), juvenile nephropathic (proteinuria leading slowly to kidney failure), and ocular nonnephropathic (photophobia from corneal crystals as the only manifestation).

Citrin deficiency can present in infancy as neonatal intrahepatic cholestasis with failure to thrive and dyslipidemia, or in adulthood (typically ages 20-50) with recurrent hyperammonemic neuropsychiatric episodes resembling hepatic encephalopathy.

Most inherited amino acid transport defects are autosomal recessive; exceptions include certain neuronal/synaptic-vesicle glutamate transporter disorders (e.g., SLC1A2, SLC1A3, SLC17A8) that are autosomal dominant.

Cystinuria is an autosomal recessive defect of apical brush-border transport in the proximal renal tubule and small intestine, impairing reabsorption of the dibasic amino acids cystine, lysine, arginine, and ornithine; only poorly soluble cystine causes clinical disease through stone formation.

Cystine stones account for roughly 1-2% of all urinary calculi and about 4-5% of stones in children; suspect cystinuria when typical hexagonal crystals appear in acidified, concentrated, chilled urine or with a positive nitroprusside test.

Two cystinuria variants exist: type A (SLC3A1, a membrane glycoprotein) and type B (SLC7A9, the b0,+ transporter); the SLC3A1 glycoprotein aids correct processing of the b0,+ transporter, explaining why two different genes cause similar disease.

Lysinuric protein intolerance is a basolateral (not luminal) transport defect (SLC7A7, y+LAT transporter) affecting lysine, arginine, and ornithine but sparing cystine, with secondary impairment of the urea cycle and characteristic episodic hyperammonemia after protein loads or infection.

Citrullinemia type 2 (citrin deficiency, SLC25A13) reduces cytoplasmic aspartate available for the urea cycle and impairs the malate-aspartate NADH shuttle; affected individuals often spontaneously prefer protein/fat-rich foods and avoid carbohydrates, since carbohydrate-driven cytoplasmic NADH worsens the defect.

Hartnup disease is an autosomal recessive defect of the neutral/aromatic amino acid transporter B0AT1 (SLC6A19), which requires collectrin in kidney and ACE2 in intestine for surface expression; symptoms reflect tryptophan and consequent niacin deficiency.
In Hartnup disease only a minority of carriers of the transport defect become symptomatic, indicating that clinical expression depends on additional environmental and nutritional factors.

Cystinosis (CTNS gene; lysosomal cystine/proton transporter cystinosin) causes intralysosomal cystine accumulation and crystal formation; cystine crystals in the cornea on slit-lamp examination are an important diagnostic clue.
Attributing pellagra solely to dietary niacin deficiency and missing Hartnup disease; neutral aminoaciduria distinguishes the two and does not occur in dietary deficiency.
Expecting elevated glutamine as in classic urea cycle defects in citrin deficiency, where glutamine is often low or normal during attacks.
Failing to recognize that cystinuria heterozygotes (especially type B) can have increased cystine excretion and may form stones, so quantitative measurement is needed.
Overlooking that only a minority of individuals with the Hartnup transport defect become symptomatic, so genotype does not equal disease.
Missing the carbohydrate-driven decompensation in citrin deficiency, where high sugar intake (and triggers such as acetaminophen, surgery, or alcohol) precipitates attacks.

Prognosis is disorder-specific. Cystinuria can cause recurrent stones and occasional progression to renal failure requiring transplantation. Citrin deficiency, untreated, leads to death from cerebral edema within a few years in most symptomatic patients, but liver transplantation halts progression and normalizes biochemistry. In nephropathic cystinosis, life span was under 10 years before cystine-depleting therapy and transplantation; with current management affected individuals can survive into their late forties with satisfactory quality of life, though many still progress to end-stage renal disease and develop late multisystem complications.
Episodic hyperammonemia with altered mental status, seizures, or coma in lysinuric protein intolerance or citrin deficiency (risk of cerebral edema and death)
Recurrent urolithiasis progressing to obstructive uropathy and renal insufficiency in cystinuria
Infantile renal Fanconi syndrome with rickets in nephropathic cystinosis (progression to renal failure by about age 10 without treatment)
Pellagra-like rash with neurologic relapse in Hartnup disease provoked by fever, sunlight, stress, or sulfonamides
Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, severe osteoporosis, or pancreatitis as adult presentations of lysinuric protein intolerance

Cystinosis is graded by residual transporter function into classic nephropathic (most severe, infantile Fanconi syndrome and early renal failure), juvenile nephropathic (proteinuria with slower decline to renal failure), and ocular nonnephropathic (photophobia from corneal crystals only). Cystinuria homozygotes excrete 2400-7200 micromol (600-1800 mg) cystine daily versus the maximum urinary solubility of roughly 1200 micromol/L (300 mg/L) at physiologic pH 4.5-7.0.
