chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: Each amino acid has a unique degradative pathway that recycles its nitrogen and carbon for synthesis of other amino acids, carbohydrates, and lipids. An enzymatic block causes accumulation of compounds upstream of the lesion; what accumulates depends on the site of the block, reversibility of proximal reactions, and availability of alternative metabolic runoff pathways. In phenylketonuria, accumulated phenylalanine competitively inhibits transport of other amino acids needed for protein and neurotransmitter synthesis, reduces myelin synthesis while increasing its degradation, impairs norepinephrine and serotonin formation, and inhibits tyrosinase causing hypopigmentation. In homocystinuria, defective cystathionine beta-synthase or impaired remethylation of homocysteine to methionine raises homocysteine, which produces endothelial dysfunction and acts as an atherogenic and thrombophilic agent. In urea cycle defects, ammonia generated from protein nitrogen cannot be cleared, so ammonia and glutamine accumulate causing direct neuronal toxicity and brain edema. In alkaptonuria, deficient homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase leads to urinary excretion of homogentisic acid and deposition of its oxidized pigment in connective tissue (ochronosis).

chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: Disorders of amino acid metabolism are individually rare (roughly 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 200,000) but collectively affect around 1 in 4000 newborns, and nearly all are inherited as autosomal recessive traits.

chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: Diagnosis relies on plasma amino acid analysis, urine organic acid analysis (GC/MS), and plasma acylcarnitine profile (tandem MS), confirmed by enzyme assay or DNA testing.

chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: Some metabolic disorders remain asymptomatic until adulthood, declaring themselves only when fasting or severe stress demands full activity of the affected pathway.

chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: In maternal phenylketonuria, uncontrolled maternal phenylalanine levels before and during pregnancy increase fetal risk of congenital defects, microcephaly, intellectual disability, and growth retardation regardless of fetal genotype.

chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: Conditions are generally named for the compound that accumulates to highest concentration: aminoacidopathies show excess of the parent amino acid, whereas organic acidemias accumulate downstream catabolic products.

chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: Some defects (e.g., sarcosinemia, cystathioninuria, hyperlysinemia) are clinically benign, while at the opposite extreme complete ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency is lethal in the untreated neonate.

chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: Classic phenylketonuria results from deficient phenylalanine hydroxylase activity; untreated infants are normal at birth but develop microcephaly, progressive intellectual disability, seizures, hypopigmentation, eczema, and a characteristic mousy odor from phenylacetate.

chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: Classic homocystinuria (cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency) typically presents at 3-5 years with dislocated optic lenses, intellectual disability in about half, marfanoid habitus, and osteoporosis, with total plasma homocysteine usually above 100 micromol/L.

chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: Alkaptonuria (homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency) may be unrecognized until midlife; urine darkens on standing or with alkali, and ochronotic pigment deposits cause degenerative arthritis, scleral and ear pigmentation, and later aortic stenosis.

chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency is X-linked and the most common urea cycle defect; heterozygous females can become symptomatic when mutant hepatocytes predominate due to random X-inactivation.

chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: Plasma citrulline helps localize urea cycle defects: it is low or undetectable in proximal defects (NAGS, CPS-1, OTC) and markedly elevated in citrullinemia type 1 (argininosuccinate synthase deficiency).

chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: Urine orotic acid is increased only in ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency among the proximal urea cycle defects, distinguishing it from CPS-1 and N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency.

chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: Milder variants of homocystinuria may be missed by newborn methionine screening.

chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: Heterozygous females with X-linked OTC deficiency can be overlooked because symptoms depend on the proportion of mutant hepatocytes from random X-inactivation.

chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: Adult-onset metabolic decompensation can be triggered by involuntary fasting, severe stress, corticosteroids, or chemotherapy and may be mistaken for primary GI, allergic, behavioral, or hepatic disease.

chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: Hyperhomocysteinemia has many acquired causes (B6/folate/B12 deficiency, aging, smoking, renal failure, hypothyroidism, leukemias, and certain drugs such as methotrexate, nitrous oxide, and isoniazid) that must be distinguished from inherited homocystinuria.

chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: An abnormal newborn screen in an infant may actually reflect a maternal metabolic disorder (e.g., glutaric acidemia type 1, methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency, primary carnitine deficiency, fatty acid oxidation defect).

chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: Clinical manifestations of many of these conditions can be prevented or mitigated when diagnosis is early and appropriate management (e.g., dietary protein/amino acid restriction or vitamin supplementation) is started promptly; for phenylketonuria, treatment must begin before 2 weeks of age to prevent intellectual disability, and children detected and treated at birth show none of the classic abnormalities. Untreated classic disorders carry severe outcomes, including lethality of complete neonatal OTC deficiency and early vascular morbidity/mortality in homocystinuria. Alkaptonuria progresses slowly to disabling ochronotic arthritis and later cardiac valve disease.

chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: Neonate with refusal to feed and lethargy progressing to coma (classic urea cycle defect presentation at 1-4 days of life)

chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: Hyperammonemia precipitated by systemic corticosteroids or chemotherapy, which can be fatal in previously asymptomatic individuals of any age

chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: Postpartum behavioral change, stupor, or coma in a female (possible decompensated OTC deficiency from fasting and stress)

chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: Life-threatening coronary, renal, or cerebral arterial thrombosis in a young patient with homocystinuria

chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: Aortic stenosis developing in alkaptonuria, especially after age 60, from pigment deposition in heart valves

chunks.diseaseName: Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults
chunks.text: Severity is largely biochemical and enzyme-activity dependent: complete enzyme deficiencies (e.g., classic urea cycle defects) present catastrophically in the neonatal period, whereas partial/residual-activity variants may remain asymptomatic until adulthood and declare during fasting or stress. For phenylketonuria, dietary restriction is generally instituted when blood phenylalanine exceeds 360 micromol/L, with a target maintenance range of 120-360 micromol/L for life.

chunks.text: Insomnia disorder is conceptualised through a model of hyperarousal, in which heightened cognitive, emotional, and physiological arousal impairs the normal sleep process. Predisposing traits, precipitating stressors, and perpetuating behaviours and beliefs (such as excessive time in bed and worry about sleep) interact, with dysregulation of arousal and sleep-wake regulatory systems maintaining the condition over time.

source.ref: Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry; DSM-5-TR

source.ref: Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry; DSM-5-TR

chunks.text: Strongyloides midepigastric pain resembles peptic ulcer disease, except it is aggravated by food ingestion (p.1816)
Heavy trichuriasis with bloody/mucoid diarrhea may resemble inflammatory bowel disease (p.1818)
Intestinal/biliary ascariasis may present as a surgical acute abdomen mimicking acute appendicitis in endemic areas (p.1815)
Strongyloides hyperinfection-associated gram-negative sepsis, pneumonia, or meningitis can dominate or be mistaken for primary bacterial infection (p.1817)
Hookworm rhabditiform larvae in non-fresh stool must be differentiated from Strongyloides larvae (p.1816)

Stool microscopy for characteristic ova and parasites: Ascaris eggs (~65 x 45 um), hookworm eggs (~40 x 60 um, species indistinguishable by light microscopy), Trichuris lemon-shaped eggs (~50 x 20 um) (p.1815-1818)

Strongyloides: rhabditiform larvae (~250 um, short buccal cavity) on stool microscopy; single stool detects only ~one-third of uncomplicated cases, so serial examinations and agar plate method improve sensitivity; duodenojejunal aspirate/biopsy; ELISA serum antibody serology (sensitive for uncomplicated infection); in dissemination, filariform larvae in stool, sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage, or surgical drainage fluid (p.1817)
Enterobius: eggs are NOT found in stool - diagnose with morning cellulose acetate tape applied to the perianal region (eggs oval, ~55 x 25 um, flattened on one side) (p.1818)
Ascaris lung phase: larvae detectable in sputum or gastric aspirates before eggs appear in stool; chest imaging showing transient rounded infiltrates (Loffler's syndrome) (p.1815)
PCR of stool worm DNA (increasing use, mostly research/some clinical) for species-level diagnosis (p.1815-1818)
Abdominal imaging: plain film for masses of worms in obstruction; ultrasound and ERCP for pancreaticobiliary Ascaris (ERCP can also extract worms) (p.1815)
Hookworm disease bloodwork: hypochromic microcytic anemia, sometimes eosinophilia or hypoalbuminemia (p.1816)
Inflammatory bowel disease (heavy trichuriasis) (p.1818)
Peptic ulcer disease (strongyloidiasis epigastric pain) (p.1816)
Acute appendicitis / surgical acute abdomen (intestinal or biliary ascariasis) (p.1815)

Intestinal nematodes are nonsegmented roundworms ranging from ~1 mm to many centimeters. Ascaris and the hookworms have life cycles involving migration through the heart and lungs before maturing in the intestine (larvae penetrate alveoli, ascend the bronchial tree, are swallowed, and reach the small bowel). Ascaris adults live in the small-intestinal lumen and females are extraordinarily fecund (>200,000 eggs/day); eggs are highly environmentally resistant and become infective after maturation in warm, moist soil. Hookworm adults attach to the small-bowel mucosa using buccal teeth (Ancylostoma) or cutting plates (Necator), invade submucosa, and ingest blood and villous tissue, producing iron-deficiency anemia; filariform larvae penetrate skin. S. stercoralis filariform larvae penetrate skin or mucous membranes, migrate via blood to the lungs and then the small intestine, where parthenogenetic adult females embed in the mucosa; rhabditiform larvae can transform directly into filariform larvae that re-penetrate the colonic wall or perianal skin to drive ongoing autoinfection - which can amplify into hyperinfection and dissemination under immunosuppression. Trichuris adults embed their thin anterior portions in colonic/cecal mucosa with no pulmonary larval passage. Enterobius adults dwell in the cecum; gravid females migrate nocturnally to the perianal skin to deposit eggs, which become infective within hours and spread by hand-to-mouth (autoinfection from scratching) and retroinfection. (p.1814-1818)

More than one billion people worldwide are infected with one or more intestinal nematode species; they are most common where sanitation and fecal-waste disposal are inadequate, especially resource-limited tropical and subtropical regions, but are seen with increasing frequency among immigrants and refugees to developed countries (p.1814).

Hookworm larvae may cause a pruritic maculopapular rash (ground itch) at the skin penetration site; hypochromic microcytic anemia, sometimes with eosinophilia or hypoalbuminemia, is characteristic of hookworm disease (p.1816).

S. stercoralis is distinguished by its ability - unique among helminths except Capillaria - to complete its life cycle and replicate within a human host (autoinfection), so infection can persist for decades without further exogenous exposure (p.1816).

Larva currens, a rapidly advancing (up to ~10 cm/h) pruritic serpiginous skin eruption, is pathognomonic of strongyloidiasis; recurrent urticaria, often on the buttocks, is the most common cutaneous manifestation (p.1816).

Impaired cell-mediated immunity - especially high-dose glucocorticoid therapy, and less commonly other immunosuppressants or HTLV-1 infection - can trigger Strongyloides hyperinfection with massive larval numbers, leading to colitis/enteritis/malabsorption and disseminated disease (CNS, skin, peritoneum, liver, kidneys) (p.1817).

Disseminated strongyloidiasis is often complicated by gram-negative bacteremia, pneumonia, or meningitis from enteric flora translocating through disrupted mucosal barriers; eosinophilia is often ABSENT in severely infected patients (p.1817).

Even asymptomatic strongyloidiasis must be treated because of the potential for later hyperinfection and fatal dissemination; Strongyloides serology should be performed before starting glucocorticoids or solid-organ transplantation in patients with prior potential exposure, especially with eosinophilia (p.1817).

Most Trichuris (whipworm) infections are asymptomatic, but heavy infections may cause anemia and bloody/mucoid diarrhea resembling inflammatory bowel disease; massive infection in children can cause rectal prolapse from protracted tenesmus (p.1818).

Enterobius (pinworm) is more common in temperate climates than the tropics; perianal pruritus, worse at night when gravid females emerge, is the cardinal symptom, and eosinophilia is uncommon (p.1818).

The major intestinal roundworms are Ascaris lumbricoides, the hookworms (Necator americanus, Ancylostoma duodenale, A. ceylanicum), Strongyloides stercoralis, Trichuris trichiura (whipworm), and Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) (p.1815).
Ascaris, Trichuris, and the hookworms require a soil phase for development, whereas S. stercoralis and E. vermicularis can be transmitted directly from person to person (p.1814).

Because most helminths cannot fully complete their life cycle within the same human host, heavy adult-worm burdens require repeated exposure; clinical disease (versus asymptomatic/subclinical infection) generally develops only with repeated exposure and is typically related to infection intensity (p.1814).
Eosinophilia and elevated serum IgE are features of many helminth infections, the latter particularly when the life cycle involves tissue migration (Ascaris, Strongyloides, hookworms) (p.1814).

Ascaris larval migration through the lungs (~9-12 days after egg ingestion) can cause an irritating nonproductive cough, substernal discomfort, eosinophilia, and transient rounded pulmonary infiltrates - eosinophilic pneumonitis (Loffler's syndrome) (p.1815).

Heavy Ascaris infection can cause small-bowel obstruction by a bolus of entangled worms (more common in children with narrow lumens), sometimes complicated by perforation, intussusception, or volvulus; an adult worm migrating into the biliary tree can cause biliary colic, cholecystitis, cholangitis, pancreatitis, or rarely intrahepatic abscess (p.1815).
In highly endemic areas, intestinal and biliary ascariasis can rival acute appendicitis as a cause of surgical acute abdomen (p.1815).

The major consequence of chronic hookworm infection is iron deficiency; symptoms are minimal if iron stores are adequate, but undernourished individuals develop progressive iron-deficiency anemia and hypoproteinemia (fatigue, weakness, dyspnea). Hookworm disease requires the combination of heavy worm burden, prolonged duration, and inadequate iron intake (p.1816).

Failing to screen for and treat asymptomatic strongyloidiasis before glucocorticoids or solid-organ transplantation - asymptomatic infection must still be treated because of the risk of later hyperinfection and fatal dissemination (p.1817)
Relying on eosinophilia to exclude strongyloidiasis - it is often absent in severe/disseminated disease (p.1817)
Using routine stool ova-and-parasite microscopy to diagnose pinworm - Enterobius eggs are not passed in feces; perianal cellulose acetate tape is required (p.1818)
Single stool examination for Strongyloides detects only about one-third of uncomplicated cases (p.1817)
Misidentifying hookworm rhabditiform larvae (in non-fresh stool) as Strongyloides (p.1816)

Intestinal nematode infections are not usually fatal but contribute to malnutrition, impaired physical and cognitive development, and diminished work capacity, particularly in children with marginal nutritional status. Significant protective immunity does not appear to develop in humans. The major exception is strongyloidiasis: autoinfection allows decades-long persistence, and in immunocompromised hosts hyperinfection and dissemination can be fatal (high mortality, especially with unrecognized infection on glucocorticoids). (p.1814, p.1816-1817)
Disseminated strongyloidiasis - particularly in patients with unsuspected infection who are taking glucocorticoids - has a HIGH mortality rate (p.1817)
Strongyloides hyperinfection with gram-negative sepsis, pneumonia, or meningitis from enteric flora translocation (p.1817)
Eosinophilia is often ABSENT in severe/disseminated strongyloidiasis, removing a reassuring marker (p.1817)
Complete intestinal obstruction with perforation, intussusception, or volvulus from a heavy Ascaris worm bolus (p.1815)
Biliary Ascaris causing cholangitis, pancreatitis, or intrahepatic abscess (p.1815)

Harrison does not provide a formal severity classification for intestinal nematode infections; severity correlates with infection intensity (worm burden) and host factors. Disease ranges from asymptomatic/subclinical light infection to clinical disease with heavy burden (e.g., Ascaris bowel/biliary obstruction; hookworm iron-deficiency anemia/hypoproteinemia; Trichuris dysentery and rectal prolapse). For Strongyloides, the spectrum is uncomplicated strongyloidiasis vs. hyperinfection (amplified autoinfection, larvae confined largely to the normal migration route) vs. disseminated strongyloidiasis (larvae in CNS, skin, peritoneum, liver, kidneys). (p.1814-1817)

Primary versus secondary peritonitis (single organism without source versus mixed flora with an identifiable viscus source)
Pancreatitis versus its infectious complications (infected pseudocyst, pancreatic abscess, infected pancreatic necrosis) - fever, leukocytosis, and abdominal pain alone do not distinguish them
Diverticular abscess versus simple diverticulitis
Tuboovarian abscess and other female genital tract infection extending into the pelvis
Perinephric/renal abscess versus uncomplicated pyelonephritis when fever persists beyond 4-5 days of therapy
Hemoperitoneum (especially in trauma) mimicking infective peritonitis

Amebic liver abscess (cross-reference Chap. 230) - positive amebic serology in over 95% of cases
Candidal liver or renal abscess following fungemia, often unmasked when PMNs recover after neutropenia
Diagnostic paracentesis of any cirrhotic with ascites and fever, with PMN count (>250/uL diagnostic of PBP) and culture of fluid in blood-culture bottles plus simultaneous blood cultures
Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT to exclude or identify a primary intraabdominal source (highest yield for abscess localization)
Chest and abdominal radiography to exclude free air signaling perforation (pneumoperitoneum) and to suggest liver abscess via raised right hemidiaphragm, basilar infiltrate, or pleural effusion
Ultrasonography (particularly useful for right upper quadrant, kidneys, and pelvis) and MRI for abscess characterization
Indium-labeled WBC scan or gallium scan to localize occult collections (indium preferred near bowel); PET scanning for resolution and availability

Serum alkaline phosphatase (elevated in about 70% of liver abscess - the single most reliable laboratory finding), bilirubin (elevated in ~50%), AST (~48%); leukocytosis, normochromic normocytic anemia (~50%), hypoalbuminemia (~33%)
Amebic serology and PCR to exclude amebic liver abscess

In CAPD-associated peritonitis, dialysate cell count with differential (cloudy fluid with >100 WBC/uL, >50% neutrophils, or >50% PMN with shortened dwell time) and concentrated dialysate culture in blood-culture bottles
Needle aspiration under CT guidance for culture in suspected infected pancreatic necrosis
Acute pancreatitis without infected necrosis (sterile inflammation producing fever and leukocytosis)
Chemical peritonitis from a ruptured gastric ulcer in the absence of significant bacterial load
Malignant ascites or metastatic intraabdominal malignancy
Congestive heart failure, systemic lupus erythematosus, and lymphedema as noncirrhotic settings reported with PBP

Intraperitoneal infection begins when a normal anatomic barrier is breached and organisms normally contained within the bowel or another organ enter the sterile peritoneal cavity. Inflammation triggers an early influx of polymorphonuclear leukocytes followed by a prolonged phase of mononuclear cell migration, with the leukocyte phenotype shaped by resident-cell chemokine synthesis. In primary (spontaneous) bacterial peritonitis, a diseased liver with altered portal circulation impairs the normal filtration function, allowing hematogenous organisms to seed ascites; cirrhosis-related defects (low peritoneal complement, diminished PMN opsonic and phagocytic capacity, gut dysbiosis with overgrowth of Enterobacteriaceae, reduced Paneth cell defensins, decreased motility, and portal-hypertensive enteropathy) promote bacterial translocation. Secondary peritonitis follows direct viscus spillage; an early containment phase produces a fibrin- and PMN-rich exudate, and severity reflects whether spillage is chemically irritant (acidic gastric contents) or heavily bacterial (colonic contents). If overt gram-negative sepsis does not prove fatal, the host walls off persisting organisms and PMNs in a fibrous capsule to form an abscess; B. fragilis is uniquely able to induce abscesses, with its zwitterionic capsular polysaccharide A stimulating peritoneal macrophages (TNF-alpha, ICAM-1) and CD4+ T lymphocytes that secrete leukoattractant cytokines, while the alternative complement pathway and fibrinogen also participate.

Intraperitoneal infection follows disruption of a normal anatomic barrier (ruptured appendix, diverticulum, or ulcer; ischemic, tumor-related, or inflammatory bowel wall weakening; or leakage from adjacent pancreatitis or pelvic inflammatory disease), and evolves in two sequential stages: peritonitis first, then abscess formation if the patient survives untreated.

Of all intraabdominal abscesses, about 74% are intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal (non-visceral); most intraperitoneal abscesses arise from fecal spillage (e.g., an inflamed appendix), and diverticular abscesses are the least likely to rupture.

The liver is the organ most subject to abscess; biliary tract disease is now the most common source (formerly ruptured appendicitis), and pylephlebitis (suppurative portal vein thrombosis) is another route of seeding. Half of liver-abscess patients lack hepatomegaly, right-upper-quadrant tenderness, or jaundice, so liver abscess can present as fever of unknown origin, especially in the elderly.

Hypermucoviscous (hypervirulent) Klebsiella pneumoniae causes a distinctive community-acquired syndrome of liver abscess with bacteremia and metastatic infection of the eye(s) and lung(s), originally described in Southeast Asia and now emerging in North America and elsewhere.

Splenic abscess is rare but frequently fatal if untreated and often diagnosed late (at autopsy in about 37% of one series); hematogenous spread predominates, with bacterial endocarditis the most common associated infection and streptococci then S. aureus the usual isolates.

More than 75% of perinephric and renal abscesses now arise from ascending urinary tract infection rather than hematogenous seeding; concomitant obstructing nephrolithiasis is the most important risk factor (renal stones in 20-60% of perinephric abscess cases).

Primary (spontaneous) bacterial peritonitis (PBP) in adults occurs chiefly with cirrhotic ascites, develops in up to about 10% of cirrhotic patients, and is thought to arise from hematogenous spread when impaired hepatic filtration and altered portal flow allow organisms to seed and multiply in ascitic fluid.

A peritoneal-fluid count of more than 250 polymorphonuclear leukocytes/uL is diagnostic of PBP; this threshold does not apply to secondary peritonitis. Normal peritoneal fluid contains under 300 WBC/uL (mainly mononuclear) and protein under 30 g/L.

PBP is typically caused by a single organism (often enteric gram-negative bacilli such as E. coli, but increasingly gram-positive cocci and ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae); recovery of multiple organisms including anaerobes should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis and a search for a secondary source.

Fever is the most common manifestation of PBP (up to 80%), but abdominal pain and peritoneal signs may be absent; nonlocalizing features such as malaise, encephalopathy, jaundice, or unexplained acute kidney injury in a cirrhotic with ascites should also trigger diagnostic paracentesis.

Yield of peritoneal-fluid culture is improved by inoculating about 10 mL directly into a blood-culture bottle, and simultaneous blood cultures should be drawn because bacteremia frequently accompanies PBP; samples are best obtained before antibiotics.

Secondary peritonitis results from spillage from an intraabdominal viscus and yields a mixed flora dominated by facultative gram-negative bacilli and anaerobes, especially with a colonic source; early death is driven by gram-negative bacillary sepsis and circulating endotoxin.

The bacterial burden of a perforation depends on site: a ruptured gastric ulcer (if not achlorhydric) causes mainly low-pH chemical irritation with a low bacterial load, whereas leaked colonic contents (pH 7-8, ~10^11 anaerobes/g feces) cause intense infection from heavy bacterial load.

Bacteroides fragilis, though only about 0.5% of normal colonic flora, is the anaerobe most frequently isolated from intraabdominal infections and abscesses and the most common anaerobic bloodstream isolate; its zwitterionic capsular polysaccharide (polysaccharide A) drives abscess localization via a CD4+ T-cell-dependent host response.
Failing to perform diagnostic paracentesis in a febrile cirrhotic with ascites, as PBP is often subtle and abdominal pain/peritoneal signs may be absent
Misclassifying secondary peritonitis as PBP - the >250 PMN/uL threshold and single-organism rule apply only to PBP; mixed flora or anaerobes indicate a secondary source
Relying on cultures from chronic drain sites, which are not reliable for defining infection etiology
Attributing fever, leukocytosis, and pain in pancreatitis to the inflammation itself and overlooking an infected pseudocyst, pancreatic abscess, or infected necrosis
Most clinical treatment failures in abscesses result from failure to achieve source control (drainage), not antibiotic selection
Injecting barium when perforation is suspected (contraindicated), even though barium enema may occasionally reveal a diverticular abscess
Missing splenic or perinephric abscess because of nonspecific presentation and frequently delayed diagnosis
Overlooking polymicrobial urine culture, known renal stones, or sterile pyuria as clues to perinephric/renal abscess

PBP carries substantial morbidity and mortality, reflecting its concentration among patients with advanced liver disease; reported in-hospital mortality was about 17.6% in a 2018 US cohort, and another series found 23% mortality at 30 days and 37% at 90 days. PBP recurs frequently, with up to 70% of patients experiencing recurrence within 1 year. Patients with PBP usually respond to appropriate antibiotics within 72 h, and delayed therapy increases mortality. In secondary peritonitis, early death is attributable to gram-negative bacillary sepsis and endotoxemia, and the urgency and success of source control - rather than the choice of empiric antibiotics - drive survival odds. Pyogenic liver abscess mortality averaged about 15% despite treatment. Splenic and perinephric abscesses are frequently fatal when diagnosis is delayed, so early diagnosis is the most important determinant of outcome.
Free air under the diaphragm on upright chest film indicating bowel perforation with peritonitis requiring urgent intervention
Hemodynamic instability in suspected secondary peritonitis warranting surgery without delay for imaging
Persistent fever after 4-5 days of treatment for pyelonephritis suggesting perinephric or renal abscess
Polymicrobial growth in PBP-suspected peritoneal fluid signaling missed secondary peritonitis source
Liver abscess presenting only as fever of unknown origin, especially in the elderly
Hypervirulent K. pneumoniae liver abscess with metastatic eye and lung involvement
Splenic abscess with underlying endocarditis or hemoglobinopathy given high untreated fatality

No single formal severity score is given; the text frames disease along the peritonitis-to-abscess continuum and stratifies risk by setting. PBP is graded operationally by ascitic-fluid PMN count (>250/uL diagnostic) and by markers of advanced liver disease (serum creatinine, BUN, total bilirubin, Child-Turcotte-Pugh score) that identify highest-risk and worst-prognosis patients. Secondary and abscess-related infection severity is stratified clinically as community-acquired mild-to-moderate disease versus critically ill or health care-associated infection, which guides anticipated flora and management intensity.

The commonest pathway is uteroplacental insufficiency, in which inadequate trophoblastic remodelling of the spiral arteries produces a poorly perfused placenta with reduced capacity to deliver oxygen and nutrients. The fetus adapts by redistributing cardiac output to preserve the brain, heart, and adrenals at the expense of the abdominal viscera and peripheral tissues, producing asymmetrical growth and oligohydramnios from reduced renal perfusion. Progressive hypoxaemia and acidaemia manifest as deteriorating Doppler indices and, ultimately, cardiovascular decompensation. Other cases stem from fetal chromosomal or structural abnormalities, congenital infection, or maternal disease reducing substrate supply.
Intrauterine growth restriction describes a fetus that fails to achieve its genetically determined growth potential, and it should be distinguished from constitutionally small but healthy fetuses
It is broadly divided into placental (uteroplacental insufficiency), maternal, and fetal causes, with placental insufficiency the commonest mechanism in developed settings

Symmetrical restriction, in which head and body are proportionally small, often reflects early insults such as chromosomal abnormality or congenital infection, whereas asymmetrical restriction with relative head sparing suggests later placental insufficiency
Accurate dating early in pregnancy is essential, as growth restriction cannot be assessed reliably without a correct gestational age
Surveillance combines serial ultrasound biometry, amniotic fluid assessment, and umbilical artery Doppler to detect deterioration
A progression of Doppler abnormalities, from raised umbilical artery resistance to absent or reversed end-diastolic flow and abnormal ductus venosus, reflects worsening fetal compromise
Management balances the risks of prematurity against those of continued exposure to a hostile intrauterine environment, and antenatal corticosteroids are given when early delivery is anticipated
Growth-restricted fetuses have higher risks of stillbirth, intrapartum compromise, and neonatal complications, and later cardiovascular and metabolic disease
Confusing a constitutionally small healthy fetus with pathological growth restriction, or vice versa
Relying on a single scan rather than serial measurements to judge growth
Neglecting accurate early dating, which undermines all subsequent assessment
Delivering too early for prematurity risk or too late with ongoing fetal hypoxia
Overlooking congenital infection or aneuploidy in early symmetrical restriction

Outcome depends on the underlying cause, the severity and gestation at onset, and the timeliness of surveillance and delivery. Early-onset severe placental disease carries the greatest risk of stillbirth and neonatal morbidity, whereas late-onset restriction is often milder but still increases perinatal risk. Survivors have higher rates of neurodevelopmental impairment and of adult cardiovascular and metabolic disease, underscoring the importance of careful monitoring and appropriately timed birth.

Abnormal ductus venosus flow or a non-reassuring cardiotocograph signalling impending fetal decompensation
Reduced or absent fetal movements
Static or falling growth on serial scans with oligohydramnios

A proximal segment of bowel (the intussusceptum) invaginates into the lumen of the adjacent distal segment (the intussuscipiens), dragging its mesentery with it. This compromises venous and lymphatic drainage, producing bowel wall oedema and engorgement; the mixture of sloughed mucosa, blood, and mucus produces the characteristic red currant jelly stool. Progressive swelling obstructs the lumen and, if unrelieved, arterial compromise leads to ischaemia, necrosis, and perforation. In infants a lead point is usually hypertrophied lymphoid tissue, whereas older children more often have a pathological lead point such as a Meckel diverticulum or polyp.
The most common cause of intestinal obstruction in infants and toddlers, typically between 6 months and 3 years, in which one segment of bowel telescopes into the adjacent distal segment.
The classic triad is intermittent colicky abdominal pain (with drawing up of the legs), vomiting, and red currant jelly stool, but all three are present in only a minority.
Between painful episodes the infant may appear well or lethargic; lethargy can be a prominent and misleading feature.
A sausage-shaped mass may be palpable, often in the right upper quadrant, with an empty right lower quadrant.
Most cases are ileocolic and idiopathic, sometimes following a viral illness with hypertrophied Peyer patches acting as a lead point.
Ultrasound is the diagnostic investigation of choice, showing a target or doughnut sign on cross-section.
In a stable child without peritonitis or perforation, non-operative reduction with an air or contrast enema is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
Surgery is required when enema reduction fails, or when there is perforation, peritonitis, shock, or a pathological lead point.
Waiting for the full classic triad, which is often incomplete, and delaying diagnosis
Attributing marked lethargy to another cause and missing intussusception
Attempting enema reduction in a child with peritonitis, perforation, or shock
Failing to consider a pathological lead point in older children or recurrent cases
With early diagnosis and reduction the outlook is excellent; delay increases the risk of ischaemia, resection, and complications, and a proportion recur after non-operative reduction.

Anemia of inflammation (anemia of chronic disease) - the second most common anemia worldwide, due to functional iron deficiency; a diagnosis of exclusion usually occurring with an inflammatory disorder such as cancer or infection (Harrison 22e p.765, p.450).
Thalassemia trait - microcytosis with normal-to-high ferritin and serum iron; red cells are more homogeneous in volume with a low/normal RDW (Harrison 22e p.450, p.767).
Mixed forms (combined absolute and functional iron deficiency) (Harrison 22e p.767).
Other nutritional anemias - vitamin B12 and folate deficiency (megaloblastic, macrocytic); may coexist with and mask iron deficiency in malabsorption (Harrison 22e p.765).
Sideroblastic anemia (rare) as a cause of microcytic hypochromic red cells (Harrison 22e p.~).
Serum ferritin (mainstay; <30 µg/L diagnostic, sensitivity 92% / specificity 98%); note ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and may rise severalfold in inflammation (Harrison 22e p.765, p.450).
Transferrin saturation (serum iron/TIBC); iron-restricted erythropoiesis at <15-20% (Harrison 22e p.765).
Serum iron (reduced, but diurnal fluctuation prevents use as a single test) (Harrison 22e p.765).
MCV and RDW from the CBC (MCV <80 fL when established; RDW often elevated reflecting anisocytosis) (Harrison 22e p.765).
Soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR) - increased in iron deficiency; sTfR/log ferritin ratio >2 favors iron deficiency (Harrison 22e p.766, p.767).
Reticulocyte hemoglobin content (CHr, reduced) and percentage of hypochromic red cells (%HYPO, increased >6%), reflecting iron availability days to months before testing (Harrison 22e p.766, p.767).
Serum hepcidin (low/undetectable in absolute deficiency; not routinely measured, reference values not standardized) (Harrison 22e p.766, p.767).
Absence of stainable iron in bone marrow remains the gold standard, although it is rarely needed and unacceptably invasive (Harrison 22e p.765).
Endoscopy and/or radiographic imaging to identify the cause - essential in males and postmenopausal females to rule out malignancy or other severe bleeding sources (Harrison 22e p.765, p.~).
Anemia of inflammation / chronic disease (functional iron deficiency from high hepcidin: low serum iron and transferrin saturation with NORMAL-to-HIGH ferritin) (Harrison 22e p.764, p.767).
Thalassemia trait (microcytic but with normal-to-high ferritin and iron, and a low/normal RDW) (Harrison 22e p.450, p.767).

Iron supply becomes inadequate for needs through excessive demand, insufficient intake, defective absorption, or blood loss; multiple causes frequently co-occur, especially in the elderly and in multimorbidity (Harrison 22e p.764). In ISOLATED iron deficiency, stores are depleted while hemoglobin is still normal; when iron remains sufficient for erythropoiesis, red cells are normochromic/normocytic with decreased ferritin (<15-30 µg/L). As transferrin saturation falls <15-20%, iron supply to erythropoiesis is insufficient and cells become hypochromic and microcytic, the classic feature of iron-deficiency anemia (Harrison 22e p.764). Iron deficiency is ABSOLUTE when stores are exhausted and FUNCTIONAL when erythropoiesis is iron-restricted but stores are adequate or even increased. Low hepcidin in iron deficiency maximizes dietary absorption; TMPRSS6 mutations cause hereditary iron-refractory IDA (IRIDA) with reduced absorption and oral-iron refractoriness. In inflammation, high hepcidin sequesters iron into stores, producing functional iron deficiency with low serum iron and transferrin saturation despite elevated ferritin; absolute and functional deficiency often coexist (IBD, CKD, aging). Beyond anemia, heart, muscle, and brain are affected; immune response may be blunted as lymphocytes require iron during the metabolic burst (Harrison 22e p.764).

Classic blood picture is a microcytic, hypochromic anemia (MCV <80 fL in established disease), but microcytosis can be ABSENT in early iron deficiency or masked by liver disease or concomitant folate/B12 deficiency (Harrison 22e p.765, p.450).

Low serum ferritin is the mainstay of absolute iron deficiency, reflecting depleted stores; ferritin <30 µg/L has high sensitivity and specificity (92% and 98%) and can be used as a single diagnostic test (Harrison 22e p.765).
Transferrin saturation (serum iron/TIBC) measures iron available for erythropoiesis; erythropoiesis becomes iron-restricted at values <15-20% (Harrison 22e p.765).

Anemia develops only in the LATE stage because the erythron is relatively spared compared with heart and skeletal muscle, which become iron-depleted earlier; slow progression plus compensation means anemia is often undetected, especially in the young, until hemoglobin falls below ~8 g/dL (Harrison 22e p.765).

Clinical clues include pica (compulsive ingestion of nonnutritive substances such as ice, soil, or clay), nail fragility and koilonychia, hair loss, cheilosis, atrophic glossitis, and dysphagia from esophageal webs (Plummer-Vinson syndrome) (Harrison 22e p.765; Koilonychia association noted p.~).

Even symptomatic isolated iron deficiency WITHOUT anemia matters: suboptimal myocyte, cardiomyocyte, and neuron function can cause fatigue, irritability, poor concentration, restless legs syndrome, and reduced exercise capacity (Harrison 22e p.765).

Severe iron-deficiency anemia may be accompanied by thrombocytosis, due to prevalent megakaryocyte commitment of the common erythroid-platelet progenitor when iron is insufficient (Harrison 22e p.766).
Serum hepcidin is low/undetectable in absolute iron deficiency (maximizing dietary iron absorption) but elevated in inflammation and in IRIDA (TMPRSS6 mutations) (Harrison 22e p.766).

Inadequate therapeutic response (no reticulocytosis after 1 week, or <1 g/dL hemoglobin rise after 2 weeks of iron therapy) should prompt a search for the cause: noncompliance, ongoing blood loss, or malabsorption (Harrison 22e p.766).

Classic microcytosis/hypochromia can be ABSENT in early iron deficiency, in elderly patients, or when masked by concomitant folate/B12 deficiency or liver disease - do not exclude IDA on a normal MCV alone (Harrison 22e p.765, p.450).
Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant; normal or high ferritin during inflammation can mask coexisting iron deficiency (Harrison 22e p.450).
Serum iron alone is unreliable as a single test due to diurnal variation (Harrison 22e p.765).
Treating IDA without investigating the cause can miss occult GI malignancy; isolated symptomatic iron deficiency without anemia should not be underestimated (Harrison 22e p.764, p.765).
Biomarkers other than ferritin and transferrin saturation are limited by poor standardization and accessibility (Harrison 22e p.766).

Iron deficiency and IDA are highly treatable with iron replacement. Oral iron usually requires at least ~3 months of therapy to restore hemoglobin and replenish stores and prevent early recurrence; inadequate response (no reticulocytosis at 1 week or <1 g/dL hemoglobin rise at 2 weeks) should prompt a search for noncompliance, ongoing blood loss, or malabsorption. Prognosis ultimately depends on the underlying cause (e.g., occult GI malignancy) rather than the anemia itself (Harrison 22e p.766).

Unexplained iron-deficiency anemia in any adult (with the possible exception of a premenopausal, multiparous woman) MANDATES thorough endoscopic and/or radiographic visualization of the entire large bowel - right (ascending) colon cancer causes insidious blood loss and often presents as IDA (Harrison 22e p.~, colorectal cancer chapter).
Imaging and endoscopy to trace the cause are essential in males and postmenopausal females to rule out malignancy or other severe causes of bleeding (Harrison 22e p.765).
Hemoglobin falling below ~8 g/dL or otherwise severe anemia (Harrison 22e p.765).

Myelophthisic blood smear (nucleated red cells, teardrop cells, immature white cells) suggesting marrow infiltration mandates marrow examination - a competing cause of anemia to recognize (Harrison 22e p.450).

Harrison describes a continuum rather than a formal grading scale: (1) isolated/absolute iron deficiency with depleted stores (ferritin <15-30 µg/L) but NORMAL hemoglobin and normochromic-normocytic cells; (2) iron-restricted erythropoiesis once transferrin saturation falls <15-20%, with hypochromic microcytic cells; (3) overt iron-deficiency anemia. Severe anemia is generally taken as hemoglobin <=8 g/dL (the threshold at which anemia commonly becomes detectable and at which rapid IV correction is considered) (Harrison 22e p.764-766).

chunks.text: In overdose, free iron overwhelms the body's binding capacity (transferrin) and circulates unbound. It is directly corrosive to the gastrointestinal mucosa, causing haemorrhagic gastroenteritis and fluid loss. Absorbed free iron is a potent catalyst of free-radical formation and disrupts mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, causing cellular injury most prominently in the liver, along with a high anion-gap metabolic (lactic) acidosis. Iron-induced vasodilatation, increased capillary permeability, and myocardial depression produce shock. Healing of the corrosive gastric injury can later cause strictures and gastric outlet obstruction.

Myocardial oxygen demand (MVO2) is governed by heart rate, contractility, and wall tension, while supply depends on oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood and coronary blood flow (predominantly diastolic). Coronary resistance resides mainly in prearteriolar (R2) and arteriolar/capillary (R3) microvascular beds, which normally dilate to match demand (metabolic regulation and autoregulation). Atherosclerosis of epicardial arteries, driven by endothelial dysfunction from high LDL, smoking, hypertension, and diabetes, produces subintimal plaques; plaque rupture or erosion exposes contents to blood, triggering platelet activation/aggregation and the coagulation cascade with fibrin deposition and thrombus formation. As proximal stenoses worsen, distal resistance vessels dilate maximally and flow becomes pressure-dependent, so increased demand (exertion, emotion, tachycardia) precipitates ischemia. Ischemia causes regional contractile dysfunction (hypokinesis to dyskinesis), impaired relaxation, a metabolic shift to anaerobic lactate production with falling intracellular pH and high-energy phosphate depletion, membrane dysfunction with potassium leak and cytosolic calcium rise, characteristic ECG repolarization changes, and electrical instability. The subendocardium is most vulnerable to underperfusion (Harrison 22e p.2090-2092).

IHD reflects an imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand; the dominant cause is atherosclerotic narrowing of one or more epicardial coronary arteries reducing regional myocardial perfusion (Harrison 22e p.2090).

An ischemic stress-ECG response is flat or downsloping ST depression >0.1 mV lasting >0.08 s; upsloping or junctional ST changes are not diagnostic, and a test failing to reach 85% of age/sex-predicted maximal heart rate is nondiagnostic (Harrison 22e p.2094-2095).
Chest wall tenderness, pain reproduced by palpation, or pain localizable with a single fingertip makes a myocardial ischemic origin unlikely (Harrison 22e p.2093-2094).
Most patients who die suddenly from IHD do so from ischemia-induced ventricular tachyarrhythmias (Harrison 22e p.2092).

Anginal discomfort is classically described as heaviness, pressure, squeezing, smothering or choking rather than frank pain, is crescendo-decrescendo, typically lasts 2-5 minutes, and may be signaled by a clenched fist over the sternum (Levine's sign) (Harrison 22e p.2092).

Anginal pain may radiate to either shoulder, both arms (especially the ulnar forearm/hand), back, interscapular region, neck, jaw, teeth, or epigastrium; it is rarely localized below the umbilicus or above the mandible (Harrison 22e p.2092).
Radiation to the trapezius muscles is NOT typical of myocardial ischemia and points more toward pericarditis; this is a useful discriminating feature (Harrison 22e p.2092).

Anginal equivalents (dyspnea, nausea, fatigue, faintness) and atypical presentations are more common in women, the elderly, and patients with diabetes mellitus, in whom angina may not relate strictly to provoking factors (Harrison 22e p.2093).

A resting 12-lead ECG may be entirely normal in typical angina; ST-T and LVH changes are suggestive but nonspecific, whereas dynamic ST-T changes appearing with an anginal episode and resolving afterward are more specific (Harrison 22e p.2094).

A stenosis must reduce epicardial luminal diameter by about 50% to limit flow augmentation on demand, and by roughly 80% before resting flow falls; beyond that, small further reductions cut flow dramatically (Harrison 22e p.2091).
Reversible ischemic injury occurs within roughly 20 minutes of total occlusion (without collaterals); occlusion beyond 20 minutes leads to myocardial necrosis (Harrison 22e p.2091).
The Canadian Cardiovascular Society class grades angina severity and the New York Heart Association class grades functional limitation (Harrison 22e p.2093).
Relying on coronary artery calcium as the primary screening test or sole basis for therapeutic decisions; it is adjunctive only (Harrison 22e p.2092).

Interpreting a stress ECG without accounting for pretest probability; false positives rise in low-probability patients (e.g., asymptomatic men <40, premenopausal women without risk factors) and in those on digitalis/antiarrhythmics, with conduction disturbances, LVH, resting ST-T abnormalities, or abnormal potassium (Harrison 22e p.2095).
Assuming a negative stress ECG excludes CAD; sensitivity is only about 75%, though it makes three-vessel or left main disease unlikely (Harrison 22e p.2095).
Circumflex-territory disease may yield a false-negative stress test because the posterolateral wall is poorly represented on the surface 12-lead ECG (Harrison 22e p.2095).
Coronary arteriography images only the lumen and can miss severe non-luminal (remodeled, outwardly bulging) atherosclerosis (Harrison 22e p.2097).
Missing atypical/anginal-equivalent presentations in women, the elderly, and patients with diabetes (Harrison 22e p.2093).
Overlooking that about 25% of acute MI survivors never come to medical attention yet share the same adverse prognosis (Harrison 22e p.2092-2093).

Principal prognostic determinants are age, left ventricular function, the location and severity of coronary stenoses, and the severity/activity of ischemia. Recent-onset or unstable angina, early post-MI angina, angina poorly responsive to therapy, and angina with heart failure all carry increased risk. Elevated LV end-diastolic pressure/volume and reduced ejection fraction signal poor prognosis. Left main (>50% diameter) or proximal LAD obstruction carries greater risk than right or circumflex lesions because more myocardium is jeopardized. With any obstructive disease, mortality rises sharply when LV function is impaired; the larger the established necrosis, the poorer the prognosis. Conversely, patients with chest discomfort but normal LV function and normal coronary arteries have an excellent prognosis, as do those completing stage III of the Bruce protocol with a normal perfusion scan or negative stress echo. Greater number/severity of risk factors (advanced age >75, hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, morbid obesity, peripheral/cerebrovascular disease, prior MI), elevated CRP, extensive coronary calcification, and increased carotid intimal thickening all worsen prognosis (Harrison 22e p.2097).
Angina occurring with less exertion than before, at rest, or awakening the patient from sleep (features of an unstable syndrome) (Harrison 22e p.2093)
Angina accompanied by symptoms or signs of heart failure, pulmonary edema, transient third heart sound, or mitral regurgitation (Harrison 22e p.2092, 2097)
Inability to exercise beyond 6 minutes / stage II of the Bruce protocol (Harrison 22e p.2097)
Ischemia at low workload, >=0.2 mV ST depression, or ST depression persisting >5 minutes after exercise (Harrison 22e p.2097)
A fall in systolic blood pressure >10 mmHg during exercise or exercise-induced ventricular tachyarrhythmia (Harrison 22e p.2096-2097)
Large or multiple perfusion defects, increased lung tracer uptake, or a fall in LV ejection fraction during stress imaging (Harrison 22e p.2097)
Reduced resting LV ejection fraction (<0.40) (Harrison 22e p.2097)
Sudden cardiac death may be the unheralded presenting manifestation of IHD (Harrison 22e p.2092)

Angina severity is graded by the Canadian Cardiovascular Society (CCS) functional classification (Class I: angina only with strenuous/rapid/prolonged exertion; Class II: slight limitation of ordinary activity; Class III: marked limitation with ordinary activity such as walking 1-2 blocks; Class IV: inability to perform any physical activity without discomfort, angina may be present at rest). Functional impact is described by the New York Heart Association (NYHA) classification (Classes I-IV) (Harrison 22e p.2093).

chunks.text: Acute occlusion of an intracranial artery reduces regional cerebral blood flow; the resulting deficit depends on collateral supply, occlusion site, and systemic pressure. Energy failure from loss of glucose and oxygen halts ATP-dependent ion pumps, causing depolarization, sodium and calcium influx, excess synaptic glutamate, and excitotoxicity with reactive oxygen species that damage membranes and DNA, followed by an innate inflammatory response. Fever and hyperglycaemia (glucose >200 mg/dL) worsen the injury. Mechanistically, ischemic stroke arises by three routes (the basis of TOAST-style classification): (1) embolic occlusion of a large intracranial vessel - either cardioembolic (e.g., atrial fibrillation, mural thrombus, valvular disease) or artery-to-artery from carotid/aortic-arch plaque; (2) in-situ thrombosis of small penetrating arteries from lipohyalinosis or microatheroma, producing lacunar (small-vessel) infarcts; and (3) hypoperfusion from flow-limiting stenosis of a major extracranial or intracranial vessel, producing watershed/border-zone ischemia. Cardioembolism causes ~20%, large-artery/carotid atherosclerosis ~10%, and small-vessel disease ~20% of ischemic strokes (p.3439, p.3443-3446).

chunks.text: Stroke is a clinical diagnosis: abrupt-onset focal neurologic deficit from a vascular cause; imaging is used to support it and to separate ischemia from hemorrhage (p.3427).

chunks.text: Time-is-brain: with complete arterial occlusion, neurons die within roughly 4-10 minutes; flow <16-18 mL/100 g/min infarcts within an hour, while 18-20 mL/100 g/min causes reversible ischemia unless prolonged (p.3439).

chunks.text: The ischemic penumbra is reversibly dysfunctional tissue around the infarct core; it is the target of reperfusion and can be visualized as a perfusion-diffusion (or CT-perfusion) mismatch (p.3439).

chunks.text: A useful triage rule of thumb is that a deficit maximal at onset (or one that remits) favors ischemia, whereas a depressed conscious level, very high initial blood pressure, or progressive worsening favors hemorrhage - though no clinical feature reliably separates them, so CT is required (p.3440).

chunks.text: Stroke is the second leading cause of death worldwide; outcome hinges on time to reperfusion ('time-is-brain'). For large-vessel occlusion, the chance of a good outcome falls steeply with delay - the odds of a good result exceed 3 if groin puncture for thrombectomy is within 2 h but fall to about 2 by 8 h, and over 80% do well if the vessel opens within 1 h of arrival versus about one-third at 6 h. In pooled thrombectomy trials ~46% achieved functional independence (modified Rankin 0-2) versus ~26.5% with medical care, with a mortality benefit. Small-vessel (lacunar) strokes generally recover more rapidly and completely than large-vessel strokes, though some stutter or leave severe disability. Without secondary prevention the annual risk of a further stroke after atherothrombotic stroke/TIA is about 8-10%; symptomatic intracranial atherosclerosis and untreated symptomatic carotid stenosis each carry ~15% per year. Care in a dedicated stroke unit followed by rehabilitation improves neurologic outcome and reduces mortality (p.3427, p.3441-3442, p.3445-3446).

chunks.text: Severity is graded clinically by the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS). A disabling deficit (NIHSS >5) flags potential eligibility for thrombolysis/endovascular therapy, whereas minor non-disabling stroke (NIHSS 0-5) may be managed with aspirin or short-term dual antiplatelet therapy. Mechanism-based (TOAST-style) classification - cardioembolic, large-artery atherosclerosis (carotid/intracranial), small-vessel/lacunar, other defined cause, and cryptogenic (~30%) - drives secondary prevention. Carotid disease is further classed as symptomatic vs asymptomatic and by degree of stenosis, with risk rising with stenosis severity except for near-occlusions, which carry lower risk (p.3440-3441, p.3443, p.3445).

chunks.text: ITP results from immune-mediated destruction of antibody-coated platelets by the reticuloendothelial system, and possibly impaired platelet release from megakaryocytes. Primary ITP has no identifiable cause; secondary ITP is associated with an underlying disorder such as autoimmune disease (notably SLE) or infection (HIV, hepatitis C). Childhood ITP commonly follows a viral infection through immune mechanisms and usually resolves spontaneously (Harrison 22e p.922, p.924).

chunks.text: Japanese encephalitis virus is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus maintained in an enzootic cycle between Culex mosquitoes and amplifying vertebrate hosts, chiefly pigs and water birds. Humans are incidental dead-end hosts. Following a mosquito bite the virus replicates locally and in regional lymph nodes, producing a viraemia that may seed the central nervous system across the blood-brain barrier. Neuronal infection and the accompanying inflammatory response cause neuronal death particularly in the thalamus, basal ganglia, brainstem and cerebral cortex, accounting for the movement disorders and depressed consciousness seen clinically.

Juvenile dermatomyositis is an immune-mediated systemic vasculopathy affecting small vessels of skeletal muscle, skin, and other organs. Complement-mediated injury to the capillary endothelium leads to capillary dropout, ischaemia, and perifascicular muscle fibre atrophy. Interferon-driven inflammation and immune complex deposition contribute to ongoing muscle and skin damage, producing the characteristic weakness and rash.
The most common inflammatory myopathy of childhood, characterised by proximal muscle weakness together with distinctive skin changes.
Look for the heliotrope rash (violaceous discolouration of the upper eyelids) and Gottron papules over the knuckles, elbows, and knees.
Weakness is typically symmetrical and proximal, so children struggle to climb stairs, rise from the floor, or lift their arms overhead.
Nailfold capillary changes (dilated, dropout, or tortuous loops) are a useful bedside clue and correlate with disease activity.
Calcinosis of skin and soft tissues is a late complication, more likely when treatment is delayed or inadequate.
Unlike adult dermatomyositis, an underlying malignancy is rarely associated in children.
A small vessel vasculopathy can affect the gastrointestinal tract, potentially causing ulceration, bleeding, or perforation.
Early diagnosis and adequate immunosuppression improve outcomes and reduce the risk of chronic disability and calcinosis.

With prompt, adequate immunosuppression many children achieve remission and regain function; delayed or insufficient treatment increases the risk of chronic disease, calcinosis, and long-term disability. A monocyclic course carries the best prognosis.

JIA results from immune dysregulation leading to chronic inflammation of the synovium. In most subtypes, an aberrant adaptive immune response with T-cell activation and autoantibody production drives synovial proliferation (pannus), which can erode cartilage and bone and disturb the growth of nearby physes. Systemic JIA is instead an autoinflammatory condition driven predominantly by the innate immune system and proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1 and interleukin-6, accounting for its prominent systemic features and its predisposition to macrophage activation syndrome.
The most common chronic rheumatic disease of childhood, defined by arthritis beginning before 16 years of age and persisting for at least 6 weeks, with other causes excluded.
It is a heterogeneous group of subtypes, including oligoarticular, polyarticular, systemic, enthesitis-related, and psoriatic forms, each with distinct features and prognosis.
Arthritis presents with joint swelling, morning stiffness or gelling, and limited movement, often with less pain than expected; young children may present with limp or refusal to use a limb.
Oligoarticular JIA is the most common subtype, typically affecting large joints in young girls and carrying a significant risk of chronic anterior uveitis.
Uveitis is frequently asymptomatic, so regular ophthalmological slit-lamp screening is essential to prevent visual loss, particularly in young ANA-positive children.
Systemic JIA features prominent extra-articular disease with quotidian high fever, an evanescent salmon-coloured rash, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and serositis.
The diagnosis is clinical and one of exclusion; laboratory tests support rather than confirm it, and inflammatory markers may be normal in oligoarticular disease.
A serious complication of systemic JIA is macrophage activation syndrome, a form of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis that can be rapidly fatal.
Management principles combine anti-inflammatory therapy, disease-modifying agents, and increasingly biologic therapy, alongside physiotherapy to preserve joint function and growth.

Outcome varies by subtype; many children with oligoarticular disease do well, while polyarticular and systemic forms may follow a more persistent course, and modern therapy has substantially improved remission rates and reduced long-term joint damage. Uveitis and macrophage activation syndrome remain important causes of morbidity.

chunks.text: Sandfly bites inoculate Leishmania promastigotes, which are taken up by macrophages and transform into amastigotes that multiply within the mononuclear phagocyte system. The parasite disseminates to the spleen, liver and bone marrow, driving reticuloendothelial hyperplasia that produces organomegaly and, through hypersplenism and marrow infiltration, the characteristic pancytopenia. A vigorous but non-protective humoral response causes hypergammaglobulinaemia, while impaired cell-mediated immunity permits unchecked parasite proliferation and progressive, potentially fatal systemic disease.

chunks.text: Keloids arise from dysregulated wound healing in which the normal resolution of the proliferative phase fails and fibroblasts remain persistently activated. Overexpression of profibrotic mediators, notably transforming growth factor-beta, drives excessive and disorganised deposition of thick, hyalinised collagen bundles that extend into surrounding normal dermis. Reduced apoptosis of fibroblasts, altered mechanotransduction from wound tension, and a genetic predisposition all contribute. Unlike hypertrophic scars, keloids do not remodel and regress over time, reflecting a sustained imbalance between collagen synthesis and breakdown.

chunks.text: Keratoconus is a progressive, non-inflammatory ectasia in which the cornea thins and steepens into a conical shape, producing irregular astigmatism and myopia. The stromal thinning reflects disorganisation of collagen lamellae and altered enzyme activity with increased degradation of the corneal matrix. Mechanical stress from chronic eye rubbing and an association with atopy and certain systemic syndromes are recognised contributors. As the cone advances, the apex scars and Descemet membrane may rupture, precipitating acute hydrops with corneal oedema.

Unconjugated bilirubin is normally tightly bound to albumin and does not enter the brain. When the bilirubin load overwhelms albumin binding capacity, or binding is reduced by acidosis, hypoalbuminaemia, prematurity, or competing substances, free unconjugated bilirubin crosses the blood-brain barrier. It is neurotoxic, being preferentially deposited in and damaging the basal ganglia (notably the globus pallidus and subthalamic nuclei), the brainstem auditory and oculomotor nuclei, hippocampus, and cerebellum. Bilirubin impairs mitochondrial function and neuronal signalling, causing acute dysfunction and, if sustained, permanent neuronal loss and gliosis with the characteristic clinical sequelae.
Kernicterus refers to the neurological injury caused by deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in the brain, classically in the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei.
It is a preventable complication of severe neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and represents the chronic, permanent form of bilirubin neurotoxicity.

Acute bilirubin encephalopathy evolves through phases: early lethargy, hypotonia, and poor feeding, followed by hypertonia with backward arching (retrocollis and opisthotonus), high-pitched cry, and fever, and later apnoea, seizures, and coma.
The classic chronic tetrad includes choreoathetoid cerebral palsy, high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss (or auditory neuropathy), impaired upward gaze, and dental enamel dysplasia.
Only unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin that is not bound to albumin can cross the blood-brain barrier, so free bilirubin and factors lowering albumin binding increase risk.
Prematurity, haemolysis, sepsis, acidosis, hypoalbuminaemia, and certain drugs that displace bilirubin heighten vulnerability at any given bilirubin level.
Prevention rests on identifying and monitoring at-risk newborns, timely phototherapy, and exchange transfusion when bilirubin approaches neurotoxic thresholds.
Once established, chronic bilirubin encephalopathy is largely irreversible, underscoring the importance of early recognition and treatment of hyperbilirubinaemia.
Structured predischarge risk assessment and follow-up of jaundiced newborns reduce the incidence of this now-rare but devastating condition.
Interpreting bilirubin values without reference to the infant's age in hours and risk factors
Underestimating neurotoxic risk in preterm, acidotic, hypoalbuminaemic, or septic infants at lower bilirubin levels
Delaying phototherapy or exchange transfusion while bilirubin rises
Missing early, subtle neurological signs of acute encephalopathy
Discharging a jaundiced newborn without adequate follow-up and risk assessment

Acute bilirubin encephalopathy may be partly reversible if bilirubin is lowered promptly, but progression to chronic kernicterus produces permanent, often severe disability including movement disorder, hearing loss, and gaze abnormalities. Because the condition is largely preventable, prognosis hinges on timely detection and treatment of severe hyperbilirubinaemia.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis is now understood as a myeloid neoplasm driven by activating mutations of the MAPK/ERK signalling pathway, most often BRAF V600E, in dendritic cell precursors. Constitutive pathway activation causes accumulation of pathological CD1a-positive, langerin-positive histiocytes that, together with eosinophils and other inflammatory cells, form granulomatous infiltrates. These lesions destroy local tissue (such as lytic bone lesions) and, when disseminated, impair function of organs including the liver, spleen, marrow, and pituitary.
A clonal proliferative disorder of Langerhans-type dendritic cells that can range from a single isolated lesion to widespread multisystem disease.
Bone is the most commonly involved site, often presenting as a painful lytic lesion, classically in the skull but also in other flat and long bones.
Skin involvement can mimic seborrhoeic dermatitis or a persistent scaly, petechial rash, particularly in infants.
Diabetes insipidus from pituitary or hypothalamic involvement is a characteristic endocrine manifestation and may be the presenting feature.
Risk organ involvement (liver, spleen, and bone marrow) identifies higher-risk multisystem disease with greater mortality.
Diagnosis rests on biopsy showing characteristic cells expressing CD1a and CD207 (langerin); Birbeck granules may be seen on electron microscopy.
Many cases harbour activating mutations in the MAPK pathway, most commonly BRAF V600E, which has therapeutic implications.
Treatment ranges from observation or local therapy for single-system disease to systemic chemotherapy for multisystem or risk-organ disease.
Mistaking the infantile skin rash for simple seborrhoeic dermatitis and delaying diagnosis
Overlooking diabetes insipidus as an early or isolated manifestation
Assuming a solitary lytic bone lesion is infection or a benign cyst without biopsy
Failing to assess for risk-organ involvement, which changes treatment intensity and prognosis

Single-system disease, especially isolated bone lesions, often has an excellent prognosis and may even regress; multisystem disease with risk-organ involvement carries higher mortality. Survivors are at risk of long-term sequelae such as diabetes insipidus, other endocrinopathies, orthopaedic problems, and neurodegeneration.

Cytopenias suggesting marrow infiltration

Rapidly progressive multisystem disease in an infant

chunks.text: Laryngitis is inflammation of the laryngeal mucosa, especially the vocal folds. In acute laryngitis, viral (or sometimes bacterial) infection produces mucosal hyperaemia and oedema that increase the mass and stiffness of the vocal folds, disturbing their vibratory pattern and causing hoarseness. In chronic laryngitis, sustained irritation from voice overuse, tobacco smoke, gastric reflux or persistent infection leads to ongoing mucosal changes such as oedema, thickening and keratosis. In children, the narrow subglottis means that inflammatory swelling can significantly compromise the airway.

In laryngomalacia the supraglottic tissues, including the epiglottis and aryepiglottic folds, are excessively soft and poorly supported, and there is often associated neuromuscular immaturity affecting airway tone and coordination. During inspiration the negative airway pressure draws these floppy structures inward, causing dynamic collapse over the laryngeal inlet and producing turbulent airflow and inspiratory stridor. The obstruction is worse when airflow demand or negative pressure increases, such as with crying, feeding, or agitation, and lessens with maturation as the tissues become firmer and neuromuscular control improves. Coexisting reflux can worsen supraglottic oedema and symptoms.
Laryngomalacia is the most common cause of chronic stridor in infants and results from collapse of soft, immature supraglottic structures during inspiration.
The typical presentation is inspiratory stridor that begins in the first weeks of life, worsens with feeding, crying, agitation, or lying supine, and improves when the infant is calm or prone.
In most infants the condition is mild and self-limiting, with symptoms peaking in the early months and resolving as the airway matures, usually within the first one to two years.
Flexible laryngoscopy in the awake infant is the diagnostic gold standard, demonstrating the characteristic dynamic supraglottic collapse.
Gastro-oesophageal reflux commonly coexists and can aggravate symptoms, so it is often addressed as part of management.
Feeding difficulty, choking or coughing with feeds, and poor weight gain indicate more significant disease and warrant closer evaluation.
Severe disease with significant obstruction, apnoea, or failure to thrive may require surgical intervention such as supraglottoplasty.
Persistent or atypical stridor should prompt evaluation for additional or synchronous airway lesions.
Assuming all infant stridor is laryngomalacia and missing another airway lesion
Underestimating severity by not assessing feeding, growth, and oxygenation
Overlooking a synchronous second airway abnormality
Failing to recognise and manage contributing gastro-oesophageal reflux
The outlook is excellent for the majority, in whom mild laryngomalacia resolves spontaneously as the airway matures; a minority with severe disease require surgery, which is generally effective.
