Other atypical-pneumonia pathogens, notably Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Chlamydia pneumoniae (Harrison 22e p.1272)
In immunocompromised patients, Legionella can present as pulmonary nodules with or without cavitation that mimic fungal infection, or as lung abscesses (Harrison 22e p.1273)

Lower-respiratory culture (sputum, BAL fluid, lung tissue, or extrapulmonary sites) on cysteine-supplemented buffered charcoal yeast extract (BCYE) agar is the gold standard and is essential for epidemiologic typing; growth is slow (typically 3-5 days, longer for non-pneumophila species) (Harrison 22e p.1273-1274)

Polymerase chain reaction / nucleic acid amplification (including LAMP and multiplex respiratory panels) on lower-tract specimens is more sensitive than culture and remains useful during antibiotic therapy, but does not provide serotype information and most assays target only L. pneumophila (Harrison 22e p.1274-1275)
Bronchoscopy when urinary antigen is negative and the patient cannot produce adequate sputum, or in severe disease requiring ICU care (Harrison 22e p.1273)
Serology (paired acute/convalescent titers; fourfold rise to L. pneumophila serogroup 1 confirms) has limited acute sensitivity but aids outbreak investigation (Harrison 22e p.1274)
Direct fluorescent antibody testing of sputum has low and variable sensitivity (~20-70%) and is not recommended for low-risk screening due to false positives (Harrison 22e p.1274)

Legionellae are aerobic gram-negative bacteria ubiquitous in aquatic environments, damp soil, and compost. Their natural hosts are amoebae and other free-living protozoa, within which they replicate intracellularly; humans are accidental hosts. They have a biphasic life cycle (a nutrient-rich replicative phase and a transmissive phase under resource scarcity) and persist in biofilms within natural and engineered water systems, including building premise plumbing where temperature and nutrients support protozoal hosts. After inhalation or aspiration of small aerosol particles, the organisms are phagocytized by alveolar macrophages and monocytes; pathogenic species evade intracellular defenses (forming Legionella-containing vacuoles, downregulating cytokine receptors, inhibiting host protein synthesis, and avoiding lysosomal degradation) and replicate. Innate pattern-recognition receptors (Toll-like and NOD-like receptors) together with adaptive CD4 and CD8 T-cell responses drive interferon-gamma, TNF, and neutrophil recruitment, which can clear the pathogen but may also produce immunopathology. L. pneumophila is more cytopathogenic than most non-pneumophila species, which may underlie its association with severe disease (Harrison 22e p.1269).

Legionella species cause two distinct illnesses collectively termed legionellosis: Legionella pneumonia (Legionnaires' disease) and Pontiac fever; most clinical disease is driven by L. pneumophila, predominantly serotype 1 (Harrison 22e p.1269).

Almost all cases trace to waterborne exposure; aerosolizing or aspiration sources include cooling towers, fountains, water misters, HVAC systems, hot tubs/spas, ice machines, and showerheads/sinks in large premise-plumbing systems (Harrison 22e p.1270-1271).

Legionella pneumonia presents as an 'atypical pneumonia' with nonspecific onset of fever, myalgias, headache, breathlessness, and dry or productive cough; accompanying neurologic or gastrointestinal symptoms (anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, confusion) raise the likelihood of legionellosis (Harrison 22e p.1272).

A characteristic laboratory cluster supports the diagnosis: hyponatremia and/or renal dysfunction are frequent, with elevated liver enzymes, and leukocytosis or leukopenia plus thrombocytopenia (Harrison 22e p.1272).

Per CDC, a single confirmed Legionella case in a patient who did not leave a health care facility/campus for the 10 days before onset should trigger an outbreak investigation, because nosocomial cases may signal water-system contamination (Harrison 22e p.1270-1273).

Pontiac fever is a milder, self-limited influenza-like illness defined by the ABSENCE of pneumonia, with fever, headache, myalgias, chills, vertigo, nausea/vomiting and diarrhea; antibiotics are not required (Harrison 22e p.1273).

Urinary antigen testing detects ONLY L. pneumophila serotype 1; it gives false-negative results in most cases caused by non-serotype 1 L. pneumophila and non-pneumophila species, so a negative result does not exclude legionellosis (sensitivity for serotype 1 is ~70%, though specificity is high) (Harrison 22e p.1274).

Urinary antigen can be falsely negative very early in disease yet remain positive for months after infection (especially in immunosuppressed patients), and it cannot be used in anuric patients (Harrison 22e p.1274).

Because community-acquired pneumonia guidelines recommend empirical coverage active against Legionella, specific testing is often skipped and cultures are frequently collected only after antibiotics, reducing yield (Harrison 22e p.1273-1274).

Diagnosis on clinical grounds alone is unreliable; clinical-prediction tools (e.g., Winthrop-University Hospital Criteria, Legionella Score) are more useful for their negative than their positive predictive value (Harrison 22e p.1272).
Routine testing is less common in children, so pediatric cases may be underreported; immunosuppressed patients may present without fever or pulmonary exam findings (Harrison 22e p.1271-1272).

Legionella pneumonia carries significant morbidity and mortality, with most patients hospitalized and many requiring ICU admission. The reported case-fatality rate is about 10%, rising to roughly 25% in health care-associated L. pneumophila pneumonia and to approximately 30-50% in immunocompromised hosts. Delayed antibiotic treatment is associated with about a threefold higher mortality. More than a quarter of survivors of severe disease have lasting complications, including recurrent hospitalizations, acute renal failure, respiratory sequelae, and recurrent pneumonias. By contrast, Pontiac fever is self-limited, usually resolving within 3-5 days, with hospitalization, complications, and death extremely rare (Harrison 22e p.1275).
Severe pneumonia with acute respiratory failure or a sepsis-like presentation warrants testing for Legionella (Harrison 22e p.1272)
Pneumonia developing during hospitalization, after recent travel, or during a known or possible outbreak should prompt Legionella testing (Harrison 22e p.1272)
Immunosuppressed patients may lack typical features such as fever and may show radiographic progression during early therapy (Harrison 22e p.1272-1273)

Treatment is stratified by severity: Pontiac fever requires no antibiotics (supportive care only), whereas Legionella pneumonia is managed as mild versus moderate/severe disease. All immunosuppressed patients are considered to have moderate or severe disease and should receive IV therapy where possible; all patients needing inpatient care should receive IV therapy until improving before switching to an oral agent. CDC distinguishes health care-associated cases as presumptive (Legionella pneumonia after >=10 days continuous stay in a health care facility during the 14 days before symptom onset) versus possible (some health care exposure in that window but insufficient to meet presumptive criteria) (Harrison 22e p.1272-1275).

Sandflies inoculate flagellate promastigotes into the skin; neutrophils first take up the organisms, then macrophages and dendritic cells engulf them, and parasites multiply as nonflagellate amastigotes within macrophages, rupturing cells and invading new macrophages. Acquired resistance depends on a T helper 1 (TH1) response driven by IL-12, IFN-gamma, and TNF-alpha; most infected individuals control infection and never develop symptomatic disease. In active VL there is markedly elevated IL-10, which conditions macrophages for parasite survival, downregulates TNF-alpha and nitric oxide, and suppresses antigen presentation, so patients lack a positive leishmanin (Montenegro) skin test. In VL the reticuloendothelial organs (spleen, liver, lymph nodes, tonsils, intestinal submucosa) are heavily parasitized, and bone marrow dysfunction produces pancytopenia. Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis reflects an absent cell-mediated/DTH response with high IL-10, TGF-beta, and IL-4, allowing unchecked parasite multiplication (p.1781-1786).

Caused by obligate intracellular protozoa of the genus Leishmania (~20 species), transmitted by phlebotomine sandflies (Phlebotomus in the Old World, Lutzomyia in the New World); syndromes fall into three categories: visceral (VL), cutaneous (CL), and mucosal (ML) (p.1781).

Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) develops in 2-50% of patients during or after cure of VL on the Indian subcontinent and in East Africa, presenting as hypopigmented macules, papules, nodules, or diffuse skin infiltration (p.1785).
Visceral leishmaniasis is a recognized cause of secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH); Leishmania is the most common parasite associated with HLH (p.1369-1370).

Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar, Hindi for 'black fever') is caused by the L. donovani complex (L. donovani, L. infantum); classic presentation is abrupt moderate-to-high fever with rigors, progressive massive splenomegaly, moderate hepatomegaly, weight loss/wasting, and skin hyperpigmentation (p.1782-1783).
Lymphadenopathy is common in most VL-endemic regions but is rare on the Indian subcontinent (p.1783).

VL causes pancytopenia from bone marrow dysfunction and reticuloendothelial infiltration: leukopenia and anemia appear early, followed by thrombocytopenia; there is a marked polyclonal increase in serum immunoglobulins (hypergammaglobulinemia) (p.1782-1783).
Fever with neutropenia or pancytopenia in a patient from an endemic region strongly suggests VL; hypergammaglobulinemia in long-standing illness strengthens the diagnosis (p.1784).
Demonstration of amastigotes in tissue aspirate smears is the gold standard for VL: splenic smear sensitivity is >95%, bone marrow 60-85%, lymph node aspirate ~50% (p.1783).
The rK39 rapid immunochromatographic antibody test is used worldwide for VL field diagnosis (sensitivity ~98%, specificity ~90% in immunocompetent individuals; both lower in East Africa) (p.1783).

Cutaneous leishmaniasis: a sandfly bite is followed days-to-weeks later by a papule that becomes a nodule and ulcerates over weeks-to-months, with raised, indurated margins and a usually painless base; most lesions heal spontaneously over 2-15 months, leaving a scar (p.1786).

Mucosal leishmaniasis (espundia) is typically caused by L. (Viannia) braziliensis and is almost entirely confined to the Americas; it presents with nasal stuffiness and bleeding followed by destruction of nasal cartilage, septal perforation, and collapse of the nasal bridge (p.1787-1788).
VL is easily mistaken for malaria and other tropical febrile illnesses; a careful travel history is essential in nonendemic countries.
Antibody detection tests (rK39, ELISA, IFAT) remain positive for years after cure, so they cannot be used to assess cure or detect relapse, and positive serology does not help diagnose PKDL.
In HIV/VL co-infection serodiagnostic tests may be negative in up to 50% of patients, and parasites may be found in unusual sites (e.g., bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, buffy coat).
Splenic aspiration, though most sensitive, is invasive and may be dangerous in untrained hands.
In PKDL, parasites are scanty and skin smear sensitivity is low, especially in hypopigmented macules (parasites are more readily found in nodular lesions).
Patients with active VL and IL-10-mediated suppression do not have a positive leishmanin (Montenegro) skin test.
In ML the strongly positive DTH response fails to distinguish past from present infection.

Untreated visceral leishmaniasis is fatal in most patients, including 100% of those with HIV co-infection. With effective treatment, recovery is quick: defervescence, regression of splenomegaly, weight gain, and hematologic recovery occur within a week, and continued improvement over 12 months suggests cure; a small percentage relapse (usually within 6-12 months) but respond to retreatment. Cutaneous lesions heal spontaneously in most cases (2-15 months), leaving a scar, but may cause permanent scarring and social stigma. Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis does not heal spontaneously and is difficult to treat. Mucosal leishmaniasis does not heal spontaneously despite strong TH1/DTH immunity; the more extensive the disease, the worse the prognosis (p.1782-1788).
Massive (hugely enlarged) splenomegaly with fever and pancytopenia in a patient from or returning from an endemic region
Severe anemia, which may cause congestive heart failure
Bleeding (epistaxis, retinal hemorrhages, gastrointestinal bleeding) from thrombocytopenia
Hypoalbuminemia with pedal edema and ascites in advanced illness
HIV co-infection (untreated VL is fatal in 100% of HIV-co-infected patients)
Secondary infections (pneumonia, tuberculosis, dysentery, gastroenteritis)
In ML: destruction of nasal cartilage/septal perforation; aspiration pneumonia may be fatal

Harrison does not give a formal grading system; leishmaniasis is classified clinically by syndrome: visceral leishmaniasis (VL/kala-azar), cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL, with Old World and New World forms, plus leishmaniasis recidivans and diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis [DCL]), and mucosal leishmaniasis (ML). Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) is a sequel of VL.

Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, especially mycosis fungoides (p.1410)
Lupus erythematosus (p.1410)
Granuloma annulare (p.1410)
Diabetic, amyloid, or myxedema-related mononeuropathy (p.1410)

Leprosy is caused by Mycobacterium leprae, an obligate intracellular, acid-fast, rod-shaped bacterium with a preferred growth temperature of 27-30 degrees C, explaining its predilection for cooler surface tissues (skin, peripheral nerves, testes, upper airways) and relative sparing of inner viscera. After entry (assumed mainly via the respiratory tract, sometimes through damaged skin), the pathogenic process usually begins in peripheral nerves once bacilli are engulfed by Schwann cells. The histopathologic outcome - and thus the type of leprosy - depends on the host cell-mediated immune (CMI) response. The Ridley-Jopling spectrum (TT, BT, BB, BL, LL, with indeterminate IL as an early form) reflects this: at the tuberculoid pole, strong CMI produces epithelioid/giant-cell granulomas that destroy nerves (causing anaesthesia and muscle weakness) but contain few bacilli; toward the lepromatous pole, weak CMI permits unrestricted multiplication of bacilli within macrophages (lepra cells) as clumps/globi, with widespread dissemination and high bacterial load. Tissue damage is largely due to delayed hypersensitivity. M. leprae carries the species-specific phenolic glycolipid PGL-1, used in serodiagnosis. M. lepromatosis is a related species associated with diffuse leprosy of Lucio and Latapi.

Leprosy is a chronic infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae, with manifestations largely confined to skin, peripheral nerves, eyes, and the upper respiratory tract; M. leprae has a predilection for peripheral nerves (p.1404).

Diagnosis rests on three cardinal signs, of which at least one establishes the diagnosis: (1) a hypopigmented or erythematous skin lesion with definite loss/impairment of sensation, (2) involvement of peripheral nerves shown by definite thickening with sensory impairment, and (3) a positive result for acid-fast bacilli on slit-skin smear or biopsy, or a positive biopsy PCR (p.1409-1410).
The differing immune responses to M. leprae produce a clinical spectrum; immunologic resistance is strong at the tuberculoid end and weakest at the lepromatous end (p.1404, p.1406).
Skin surfaces in tuberculoid lesions are dry, hairless, and anaesthetic owing to destruction of underlying cutaneous nerves, plus autonomic damage causing loss of sweating (p.1407).
Slit-skin smear bacteriologic index runs from negative (tuberculoid) up to 4+ to 6+ with globi (lepromatous), and falls an average of ~1 log unit per year on multidrug therapy (p.1404, p.1407-1408).

Leprosy is the principal treatable cause of peripheral neuropathy worldwide in some settings; nerve enlargement is often palpable (e.g., greater auricular, ulnar, median, radial, lateral popliteal, posterior tibial, sural, superficial peroneal) (p.1409-1410).

Treatment principle: WHO-recommended multidrug therapy (a combination of rifampin, dapsone, and clofazimine) is the standard of care and cures the disease; paucibacillary disease uses two drugs and multibacillary disease uses three, with the cure rate ~99% (no doses given here) (p.1410, p.1412).
M. leprae has never been grown in artificial media; it is propagated only in animal models (mouse footpad, armadillo), which underlies the difficulty of culture-based diagnosis (p.1404).

Leprosy is frequently diagnosed late - in non-endemic countries it is often misdiagnosed simply because it is not considered - increasing the risk of irreversible nerve damage and disability (p.1404, p.1410)

On the face, sensory impairment may be difficult to demonstrate because of generous bilateral sensory innervation, which can compensate for damage to certain nerve branches and obscure the indeterminate stage (p.1407, p.1409)

'Silent neuritis' / 'quiet nerve paralysis': nerve function can be lost progressively without pain, paresthesia, tenderness, or other signs of reaction - regular nerve function assessment is needed during and after therapy (p.1409, p.1411)

Distinguishing relapse from a type 1 reaction in paucibacillary disease can be difficult; a therapeutic glucocorticoid trial helps - improvement within 4 weeks favors T1R, lack of response favors relapse (p.1412)

Patients often equate cure with absence of symptoms, but in leprosy bacteriologic cure does not eliminate established nerve-impairment sequelae - this must be explained at completion of therapy (p.1412-1413)
Multidrug therapy for clinical leprosy has apparently not interrupted transmission, and subclinical/undiagnosed multibacillary cases are likely a main source of ongoing spread (p.1405)

Leprosy can be cured effectively: the cure rate with multidrug therapy is ~99% and treatment-failure rates are very low when therapy is completed. Relapse rates are well below 1% except in patients with a very high baseline bacillary load (bacteriologic index >=4), and relapses usually occur within 5 years of finishing therapy; antimicrobial resistance is rare, so relapsed multibacillary patients can be re-treated with the same regimen. The major determinant of long-term outcome is nerve damage and resulting disability, which drives stigma and social exclusion. Highest risk of (additional) nerve damage is in multibacillary patients with nerve impairment already present at diagnosis (up to ~65%); intermediate risk (~16%) in multibacillary patients without impairment or paucibacillary patients with impairment at diagnosis; and lowest (~3%) in paucibacillary patients without impairment. Leprosy reactions and new nerve damage can occur even after completing therapy, up to 3 years afterward. Cure (cessation of bacterial activity) must be distinguished from sequelae (nerve impairment, reactions, disabilities such as claw hand or neuropathic foot) that may persist and require chronic care.

Type 1 (reversal) reaction: delayed-hypersensitivity reaction with sudden upgrading of CMI; acute swelling and redness of existing lesions, painful/tender nerves with neuritis; can cause silent neuritis and irreversible sensory/motor nerve damage - a medical urgency to prevent disability (p.1407, p.1408-1409)

Type 2 reaction / erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL): immune-complex-mediated syndrome with crops of painful red nodules, fever, malaise, and possible neuritis, iridocyclitis, orchitis, nephritis/renal failure, and (late) amyloidosis (p.1408-1409)

Neuritis with nerve function impairment, including 'silent neuritis' (progressive sensory/motor loss without pain or tenderness) - requires prompt treatment to avoid permanent disability and blindness (p.1409, p.1410-1411)
Lucio's phenomenon in diffuse leprosy of Lucio and Latapi: vasculitis and thrombosis causing hemorrhagic skin infarction and necrotic ulcers (p.1409)
Eye involvement (corneal anaesthesia, iridocyclitis, lagophthalmos, corneal ulceration) threatening sight (p.1408)

Ridley-Jopling classification (1962) defines five overlapping categories along the immunologic spectrum: tuberculoid (TT), borderline tuberculoid (BT), mid-borderline (BB), borderline lepromatous (BL), and lepromatous (LL), with indeterminate leprosy (IL) as an early form; immunologic resistance is strongest at TT and weakest at LL, with TT and LL relatively stable and BT/BB/BL unstable. For operational/treatment purposes the WHO simplified classification is used: paucibacillary disease = negative slit-skin smears at all sites (or, on clinical criteria, one to five skin lesions and no/only one involved nerve), and multibacillary disease = positive smear at any site (or six or more lesions and/or more than one involved nerve). The WHO disability grading system scores eyes, hands, and feet (grades 0-2), summed into the Eye-Hand-Foot (EHF) score as an overall impairment indicator (p.1405-1406).

chunks.diseaseName: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies
chunks.text: These entities are individually rare clonal neoplasms of the lymphoid or myeloid lineages. Rare lymphoid tumors are mature B-cell, T-cell, or NK-cell neoplasms; several B-cell variants of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma have distinctive biology, such as intravascular large B-cell lymphoma (confined to vessel lumens, postulated to reflect defective adhesion molecule and homing function with absent beta-1 integrin and ICAM-1), primary effusion lymphoma (HHV-8/KSHV-driven, frequently EBV co-infected), and lymphomatoid granulomatosis (an angiodestructive EBV-infected monoclonal B-cell proliferation outnumbered by reactive T cells). Many T/NK entities are EBV-associated and angiocentric. On the myeloid side, distinct molecular drivers define the entities: activating CSF3R mutations in chronic neutrophilic leukemia, GM-CSF hypersensitivity from dysregulated RAS/MAPK signaling (mutually exclusive RAS, PTPN11, NF1 mutations) in juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia, somatic GATA1 mutations in transient myeloproliferative disorder of Down syndrome, and constitutively active tyrosine kinase gene fusions (involving PDGFRA such as FIP1L1-PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, ABL1, JAK2, FLT3) in eosinophilic myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms. Mastocytosis reflects neoplastic mast cell proliferation typically driven by KIT D816V. Dendritic/histiocytic neoplasms arise from antigen-presenting or antigen-processing cell lineages; Langerhans cell histiocytosis cells are S100+/CD1a+ with Birbeck granules and about 55% carry BRAF V600E.

chunks.diseaseName: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies
chunks.text: This chapter covers the uncommon hematologic neoplasms, each individually accounting for under 1% of hematologic malignancies; the rare lymphoid tumors are all mature B-cell, T-cell, or NK-cell neoplasms (Harrison 22e p.871).

chunks.diseaseName: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies
chunks.text: Chronic neutrophilic leukemia is a clonal proliferation of mature neutrophils molecularly defined by activating CSF3R mutations (most commonly the membrane-proximal T618I, found in about 90% of cases); diagnosis requires excluding reactive neutrophilia and other myeloid neoplasms (Harrison 22e p.875-876).

chunks.diseaseName: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies
chunks.text: Systemic mastocytosis diagnosis rests on a major criterion (multifocal aggregates of >=15 mast cells) or three minor criteria including >25% atypical mast cells, aberrant mast cell expression of CD25/CD2/CD30, KIT D816V or other activating KIT mutation, and serum tryptase >20 ng/mL (Harrison 22e p.881).

chunks.diseaseName: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies
chunks.text: Transient myeloproliferative disorder occurs in about 10% of infants with Down syndrome, carries somatic GATA1 mutations, and either regresses spontaneously (about 75%) or progresses to acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (about 25%) (Harrison 22e p.879).

chunks.diseaseName: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies
chunks.text: Splenic marginal zone lymphoma cells express surface immunoglobulin and CD20 but are negative for CD5, CD10, CD43, and CD103; absence of CD5 separates it from CLL and absence of CD103 separates it from hairy cell leukemia, and circulating cells are villous lymphocytes (Harrison 22e p.872).

chunks.diseaseName: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies
chunks.text: Hairy cell leukemia is a frequent cause of a 'dry tap' on marrow aspiration because of increased reticulin fibers; it shows profound monocytopenia (predisposing to atypical mycobacterial infection), strong CD22/CD25/CD103 expression, tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase positivity, and the activating BRAF V600E mutation in most cases (Harrison 22e p.872-873).

chunks.diseaseName: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies
chunks.text: Mediastinal (thymic) large B-cell lymphoma typically remains confined to the mediastinum, affects women more than men (ratio about 1:2-3) at a median age of 35-40 years, is CD20 positive and CD45 positive (unlike classical Hodgkin's), and may lack surface immunoglobulin and HLA class I/II expression (Harrison 22e p.873).

chunks.diseaseName: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies
chunks.text: Primary effusion lymphoma presents with effusions usually without a tumor mass, is caused by HHV-8/KSHV (often EBV co-infected), occurs mainly in immunodeficiency such as AIDS, and follows a rapidly fatal course (Harrison 22e p.873).

chunks.diseaseName: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies
chunks.text: T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia is aggressive with very high WBC counts often exceeding 100,000/uL, hepatosplenomegaly, and adenopathy; chromosome 14 inversion between q11 and q32 occurs in about 80% of patients (Harrison 22e p.874).

chunks.diseaseName: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies
chunks.text: T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukemia is dominated by severe neutropenia and is frequently associated with systemic autoimmune disease such as rheumatoid arthritis; pure red cell aplasia occurs in 15-20% and the course is generally indolent (Harrison 22e p.874).

chunks.diseaseName: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies
chunks.text: Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type, is an EBV-related angiocentric/angiodestructive CD56-positive lesion prevalent in Asia, Mexico, and Central/South America; historic names include lethal midline granuloma and polymorphic reticulosis (Harrison 22e p.874).

chunks.diseaseName: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies
chunks.text: Enteropathy-type T-cell lymphoma is a rare complication of longstanding celiac disease, usually arising in jejunum or ileum, with most patients carrying the celiac-associated HLA DQA1*0501 or DQB1*0201 genotype (Harrison 22e p.874).

chunks.diseaseName: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies
chunks.text: Misclassifying nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin's lymphoma as classical Hodgkin's; the L&H 'popcorn' cell is a clonal B cell expressing CD45/CD79a/CD20/CD19/BCL2 and lacking CD30/CD15, behaving more like indolent B-cell NHL

chunks.diseaseName: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies
chunks.text: Confusing B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia with leukemic mantle cell lymphoma, since both can express CD5 and t(11;14) and no reliable distinguishing criteria have emerged

chunks.diseaseName: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies
chunks.text: Overlooking that a dry tap on marrow aspiration may signal hairy cell leukemia, myelofibrosis, metastatic carcinoma, CML, or acute leukemia rather than a technical failure

chunks.diseaseName: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies

chunks.diseaseName: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies

chunks.diseaseName: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies

chunks.diseaseName: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies

chunks.diseaseName: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies
chunks.text: Outcomes vary widely by entity. Indolent disorders include splenic marginal zone lymphoma (median survival over 10 years), T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukemia, and primary cutaneous CD30+ T-cell lymphoma (5-year survival over 90%). Aggressive entities carry poor outcomes: T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (median survival about 12 months), enteropathy-type T-cell lymphoma (median 7-11 months), hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma (median about 2 years), primary effusion lymphoma (death typically within 6 months), and intravascular large B-cell lymphoma. Mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma is potentially curable with good multi-year survival. In extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type, survival tracks with the number of risk factors (B symptoms, advanced stage, elevated LDH, regional node involvement), with 5-year survival ranging from 81% (zero risk factors) down to 7% (three to four factors). Chronic neutrophilic leukemia has a median survival of about 2 years, atypical CML around 10-25 months, and CMML survival ranges by Mayo Molecular Model risk from about 16 to 97 months. Histiocytic sarcoma has a poor prognosis with median survival measured in months to about 2 years.

chunks.diseaseName: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies
chunks.text: Aggressive NK cell leukemia presenting with fever, pancytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, hemophagocytosis, coagulopathy, or multiorgan failure

chunks.diseaseName: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies

chunks.diseaseName: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies
chunks.text: Several entities have formal staging/risk schemes. Myeloid neoplasms are classified by the ICC and WHO systems using blood counts, smear, marrow morphology, and cytogenetic/molecular tests. CMML is graded as CMML-1 (<10% marrow and <5% blood blasts) and CMML-2 (10-19% marrow or 5-19% blood blasts), with the Mayo Molecular Model assigning low to high risk by truncating ASXL1 mutation, absolute monocytes >10 x10^9/L, hemoglobin <10 g/dL, platelets <100 x10^9/L, and circulating immature myeloid cells. Systemic mastocytosis is subclassified into indolent, smoldering (requires two or more B findings), aggressive, SM with associated myeloid/hematologic neoplasm, and mast cell leukemia (>=20% mast cells in marrow aspirate); advanced SM is defined by an associated neoplasm or organopathy (C findings). Hypereosinophilia is defined as absolute eosinophil count >=1500 x10^9/L, with hypereosinophilic syndrome requiring eosinophil-mediated organ damage. Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma nasal type uses a four-factor risk model (B symptoms, advanced stage, elevated LDH, regional node involvement).

chunks.text: Lichen planus is a T-cell-mediated inflammatory disorder in which cytotoxic CD8 T lymphocytes target basal keratinocytes, apparently in response to an altered self-antigen. The resulting band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermo-epidermal junction produces the characteristic histological features of basal cell degeneration, a saw-tooth epidermal profile, hypergranulosis, and apoptotic keratinocytes (Civatte bodies). Pigment released from damaged basal cells accounts for the post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation often seen, particularly in darker skin. Triggers can include certain drugs (lichenoid reactions) and, in some populations, hepatitis C infection.

L. monocytogenes is a ubiquitous, nonsporulating, facultatively anaerobic gram-positive rod (showing small zones of beta-haemolysis and characteristic tumbling motility) that lives in soil and decaying vegetation and can grow at refrigerator temperatures as low as 4 C and tolerate low-pH/high-salt environments. Infection follows ingestion of contaminated food; the infectious dose is likely very low in the severely immunocompromised, and raised gastric pH (e.g. from proton-pump inhibitors) probably promotes gut survival. After transcytosis across the intestinal epithelium the organism spreads via mesenteric lymph nodes and bloodstream to its target organs (liver and spleen) and can cross the blood-brain barrier and the placenta. Virulence factors include internalins (InlA, InlB) for invasion of nonphagocytic cells, listeriolysin O and phospholipases for escape from the phagocytic vacuole, and ActA for actin-based cell-to-cell spread that evades antibodies and complement. Iron promotes growth, explaining the association of listeriosis with iron-overload states such as haemochromatosis. Host defence is predominantly cell-mediated (interferon-gamma, TNF-alpha, and CD8+ T cells), accounting for the predilection for those with impaired cellular immunity. (p.1227)

Listeriosis is acquired almost always via foodborne transmission; implicated foods are refrigerated ready-to-eat items (deli/delicatessen meats, hot dogs), soft cheeses made with raw/unpasteurised milk, unpasteurised dairy, raw produce (packaged salad, sprouts, enoki mushrooms, cantaloupe, caramel apples, frozen vegetables) and pate/meat spreads (p.1227-1228).

Pregnant women usually have only mild flulike illness and rarely develop neurolisteriosis or death, yet transmit infection transplacentally to the fetus with high fetal morbidity; prepartum antibiotics started >=1 day before delivery improve the chance of a healthy infant (p.1228-1229).

In invasive disease virtually all patients are hospitalised and 18% die; consider listeriosis acquired in hospital and investigate hospital-provided food when a hospitalised (especially immunocompromised) patient develops new symptoms (p.1227-1228).
TMP-SMX given as Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis (e.g. in HIV or transplant recipients) also helps prevent listeriosis (p.1229).

Major risk groups for invasive disease are pregnant women and their neonates, older adults (risk rises with each decade over age 59), and immunocompromised persons (impaired cellular immunity from haematologic malignancy, transplant, HIV, glucocorticoids/immunosuppressants, or TNF-alpha inhibitors) (p.1227-1228).
Bacteraemia without a focus is the most common manifestation of invasive listeriosis; presents with fever, chills, myalgias and arthralgias sometimes preceded by nausea/diarrhoea (p.1228).

Neurolisteriosis is the second most common invasive manifestation; in a French cohort 84% of neurolisteriosis cases presented as meningoencephalitis (meningitis plus altered mental status, seizures, or focal findings) (p.1228).

Compared with other bacterial meningitides, CSF pleocytosis and neutrophil predominance are typically LESS pronounced; ~60-75% have CSF WBC <1000/uL and only ~30-40% have low CSF glucose, so normal-ish CSF does not exclude Listeria (p.1228).

Empiric bacterial-meningitis cover (ceftriaxone + vancomycin) does NOT cover Listeria; add ampicillin for Listeria coverage in patients >50 years old or with comorbid/immunocompromising disease (Chap.143, p.140372 / p.1122).

Rhombencephalitis (brainstem/cerebellar encephalitis) disproportionately affects otherwise healthy older adults, classically biphasic (fever and headache, then asymmetric cranial nerve palsies, ataxia, tremor, hemiparesis or hemisensory deficits); nearly half develop respiratory failure (p.1228).
MRI is superior to CT for diagnosis of neurolisteriosis, including rhombencephalitis (p.1228).

Diagnosis is by isolation from a normally sterile site (blood, CSF, amniotic fluid, placental or fetal tissue); blood cultures are positive only about half the time in pregnant women, and CSF multiplex PCR panels and MALDI-TOF aid rapid identification (p.1229).

Cephalosporins are NOT effective against L. monocytogenes; standard empiric meningitis cover (ceftriaxone +/- vancomycin) misses Listeria, so ampicillin must be added empirically in patients >50 years or with comorbid/immunocompromising disease (p.1229, Chap.143 p.140372).

Febrile gastroenteritis form is rarely diagnosed because Listeria is not detected by routine stool cultures or rapid stool tests, and stool culture is NOT indicated in evaluating invasive listeriosis (p.1227, p.1229).
Gram-variable appearance as cocci, diplococci or diphtheroids can obscure the diagnosis; Listeria must be distinguished from other gram-positive rods, especially diphtheroids (p.1227, p.1229).

Relatively bland CSF (WBC often <1000/uL, frequently no organisms on Gram stain, only ~30-40% with low glucose) can falsely reassure - do not exclude Listeria meningitis on CSF profile alone (p.1228).
Brain abscess due to Listeria may be misdiagnosed as primary or metastatic malignancy; CSF can be normal when abscess occurs without concurrent meningitis (p.1228).
Adjunctive dexamethasone is associated with reduced survival in neurolisteriosis and should be avoided; it is also not recommended for established Listeria meningitis (p.1229, Chap.143).
Treatment failures have been reported with meropenem despite in vitro susceptibility, and TMP-SMX resistance occurs - perform susceptibility testing if TMP-SMX is considered (p.1229).
Testing/treatment is NOT indicated for an asymptomatic person who ate a recalled product, even if they have risk factors (p.1229).

Invasive listeriosis carries substantial mortality: 18% of reported cases die and virtually all are hospitalised. In a large French (MONALISA) cohort the 3-month mortality was 46% for bacteraemia and 30% for neurolisteriosis; death was associated with multiorgan failure, neoplasia, worsening of preexisting comorbidities, monocytopenia (<200 cells/uL), older age and female sex, and (for neurolisteriosis) a positive blood culture and adjunctive dexamethasone use. Nearly half of neurolisteriosis survivors have long-term neurologic impairment. In pregnancy-associated disease, fetal/neonatal outcomes are poor: in a cohort of 107 pregnancies 24% ended in fetal loss, 45% in premature birth and only ~5% had a normal delivery and postpartum course; overall 3% of 189 live-born infants died. (p.1228-1229)

No formal severity score. Harrison frames the clinical spectrum from non-invasive self-limited febrile gastroenteritis in healthy persons to invasive listeriosis (bacteraemia without a focus, neurolisteriosis [meningoencephalitis, cerebritis, focal abscess, rhombencephalitis], focal infections, and pregnancy-associated/neonatal disease [granulomatosis infantiseptica, early-onset sepsis, late-onset meningitis]). Severity is judged clinically by syndrome, with prognostic markers including multiorgan failure and monocytopenia. (p.1227-1229)

chunks.text: Lithium is a monovalent cation handled by the kidney similarly to sodium, so states that reduce renal perfusion or increase sodium reabsorption (volume depletion, diuretics, renal impairment) reduce its clearance and raise levels. It moves slowly across cell membranes, accumulating intracellularly and particularly in the central nervous system, which explains the delay between serum levels and clinical effect and the persistence of neurotoxicity. Intracellularly it interferes with neurotransmission and second-messenger systems. Lithium also impairs renal concentrating ability, causing nephrogenic diabetes insipidus that promotes dehydration and a vicious cycle of rising concentration.

chunks.text: Posttransplant graft dysfunction: rejection vs biliary obstruction vs primary graft nonfunction vs vascular compromise (portal vein or hepatic artery thrombosis) vs drug hepatotoxicity vs recurrent primary disease vs viral hepatitis/CMV — these are clinically and biochemically difficult to distinguish, often requiring biliary imaging and percutaneous liver biopsy.
Recurrent primary biliary cholangitis vs chronic rejection (histologically nearly indistinguishable; a florid inflammatory bile duct lesion favors recurrent PBC but is not specific).
Recurrent autoimmune hepatitis or sclerosing cholangitis vs rejection or posttransplant bile duct injury.
MELD/MELD-Na/MELD-3.0 score calculation (bilirubin, albumin, sodium, creatinine, INR) for allocation and prognosis; PELD for children under 12.
Serum bilirubin and aminotransferases — most reliable, though nonspecific, indicators of allograft rejection.
Percutaneous liver biopsy and radiographic visualization of the biliary tree to differentiate causes of graft dysfunction.

Donor screening: hemodynamic stability, oxygenation, absence of infection/abdominal trauma/hepatic dysfunction; serologic testing for HBV, HCV, HIV (infected organs now used selectively with matching and informed consent).
Recipient cardiopulmonary evaluation (especially age >70) to exclude ischemic cardiac disease; assessment of pulmonary artery pressure and intrapulmonary shunting.
anti-HBs titer monitoring (threshold ~100 mIU/mL) to guide HBIg dosing in hepatitis B recipients.

End-stage liver disease produces portal hypertension, coagulopathy (prolonged prothrombin time, thrombocytopenia), and a hyperdynamic high-cardiac-output circulatory state; transplantation replaces the failing organ and rapidly reverses the hyperdynamic state. The graft is vulnerable to immunologic and ischemic injury. Acute cellular rejection arises 1-2 weeks postoperatively from a T-cell-mediated response, with histology showing a mixed portal infiltrate, bile duct injury, and endothelialitis. Chronic rejection produces progressive cholestasis, vascular lesions (intimal fibrosis, subintimal foam cells, fibrinoid necrosis), and ductopenia (vanishing bile duct syndrome). Calcineurin inhibitors act on the calcium-dependent T-cell signal transduction pathway to block lymphokine (IL-2/3/4, TNF-alpha) gene activation. Ischemic injury during harvesting underlies primary graft nonfunction; preservation in University of Wisconsin solution (rich in lactobionate and raffinose) extends tolerable cold-ischemic time. ABO-mismatched grafts (e.g., group O liver into a group A or B recipient) can cause transient passenger-lymphocyte autoimmune hemolytic anemia that resolves once recipient marrow repopulates the graft.

Orthotopic transplantation (native liver removed, donor organ placed in the same anatomic site) is the preferred and technically most advanced approach; 1-year survival has risen from roughly 30% in the 1970s to over 90% today, attributed more to better patient selection and timing than to technical or immunologic advances alone.

Infection timing follows a predictable pattern: conventional postoperative infections (pneumonia, wound, urinary, line, intraabdominal) dominate the first month, after which opportunistic pathogens (CMV, herpesviruses, Aspergillus, Candida, Cryptococcus, mycobacteria, Pneumocystis, Toxoplasma, Nocardia, Legionella, Listeria) predominate as immunosuppression takes its toll.

Long-term HBIg prophylaxis transformed transplantation for chronic hepatitis B; without prophylaxis hepatitis B almost always recurs, but indefinite/long-term HBIg (often combined with high-barrier oral antivirals such as entecavir or tenofovir) reduces reinfection and mortality, yielding outcomes indistinguishable from non-HBV indications.

Direct-acting antiviral (DAA) agents against HCV have markedly improved both pre- and posttransplant outcomes, allowing pretransplant clearance of viremia (sometimes delaying or obviating transplant) and high sustained virologic response rates in allograft HCV infection.

Optimal timing matters: the disease should be advanced enough that medical options are exhausted, yet the procedure performed early enough to allow success. Better pretransplant clinical status predicts higher posttransplant survival.

Allocation of deceased-donor organs is driven by the MELD score (bilirubin, albumin, sodium, creatinine, INR, plus a female adjustment), a continuous scale from 6 to 40 in which higher values indicate greater illness severity; it replaced the older Child-Turcotte-Pugh-based scheme and reduced waiting-list mortality.
Status 1 (highest priority) is reserved for acute liver failure and for early posttransplant catastrophes such as primary graft nonfunction and hepatic artery thrombosis, superseding the MELD score.
Liver recipients with MELD scores below 15 have higher posttransplant mortality than comparable patients who remain on the waiting list, so transplant at very low MELD offers limited benefit.

HLA tissue typing is NOT required for liver transplantation, and preformed cytotoxic HLA antibodies do not preclude the procedure; ABO compatibility and organ size are the key matching considerations.

Tacrolimus has supplanted cyclosporine as primary immunosuppression; it is 10-100 times more potent, but nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity (tremor, seizures, hallucinations, psychosis, coma) are its principal adverse effects. Cyclosporine and tacrolimus should not be combined because of overlapping nephrotoxicity.

Both calcineurin inhibitors are metabolized by cytochrome P450 IIIA: enzyme inducers (phenytoin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, rifampin) lower drug levels, while inhibitors (azoles, macrolides, verapamil, diltiazem, ritonavir) raise them.

Sirolimus is avoided early posttransplant because it impairs wound healing and is associated with increased hepatic artery thrombosis in the first 30 days; its antiproliferative effect makes it attractive in recipients with prior or current malignancy such as HCC.
Treating acute rejection with pulse glucocorticoids in HCV-infected recipients risks triggering severe recurrent allograft hepatitis C (though DAAs now mitigate this concern).
Cyclosporine and tacrolimus must not be co-administered because of overlapping nephrotoxicity and because tacrolimus reduces cyclosporine clearance.
Prior extensive biliary/hepatobiliary surgery complicates transplantation and is a relative contraindication, so biliary diversion has been largely abandoned in sclerosing cholangitis candidates.
Cholangiocarcinoma recurs almost invariably; only highly selected stage I/II patients after neoadjuvant chemoradiation should be considered.
Eradicating HCV before transplant can lower the MELD score and paradoxically reduce allocation priority in patients who still need a graft for ongoing decompensation.
Advanced age alone is no longer an absolute contraindication, but in patients over 70 a thorough cardiac and comorbidity workup is mandatory.
Relying on short-term (2 months or less) HBIg, preoperative vaccination, or interferon alone is ineffective for preventing hepatitis B recurrence; long-term prophylaxis is required.

One-year survival is now about 85-90%, and 5-year survival exceeds 60%. Outcome correlates strongly with pretransplant status: patients still working or only partially disabled achieve roughly >85% 1-year survival; those needing continuous in-hospital care about 70%; those requiring ICU life support about 50%. High pretransplant disease severity (MELD >25) and high-risk features (malignancy, fulminant hepatitis, age >65, concurrent renal failure, respirator dependence, portal vein thrombosis, prior portacaval shunt or multiple right-upper-quadrant operations) reduce survival to about 60% at 1 year and 35% at 5 years. Survival after retransplantation for primary graft nonfunction is about 50%. Failures within the first 3 months are mainly technical, infectious, or hemorrhagic; later failures stem from infection, rejection, or recurrent disease (malignancy, viral hepatitis, return to alcohol use). Renal failure (18% at 5 years, 25% at 10 years) and cardiovascular disease are leading causes of late mortality.
Acute liver failure with impending cerebral edema — a transplant emergency requiring rapid donor identification before life-threatening complications set in.
Fever, right upper quadrant pain, and falling bile pigment/volume with rising bilirubin and aminotransferases — suggest acute allograft rejection.

Fibrosing cholestatic hepatitis (marked hyperbilirubinemia and prolonged prothrombin time out of proportion to modest aminotransferase rises) in recurrent hepatitis B — rapidly progressive liver failure.
Postoperative intraperitoneal bleeding raising intraabdominal pressure and reducing renal blood flow — reversible with laparotomy to evacuate clot and ligate the bleeding site.
New opportunistic infection beyond the first postoperative month in an immunosuppressed host demands prompt recognition and treatment.

Severe portopulmonary hypertension (mean pulmonary artery pressure >35 mmHg) or severe hypoxemia from right-to-left intrapulmonary shunts (PO2 <50 mmHg) — relative contraindications signaling high operative risk.

Allocation and prognosis use the Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score, a continuous scale from 6 to 40 (values above 40 counted as 40) derived from serum bilirubin, albumin, sodium, creatinine, and INR with a female adjustment; higher scores indicate greater illness severity. Variants include MELD-Na (2016) and MELD-3.0 (2023). PELD is used for candidates under 12. Status 1 (acute liver failure, primary graft nonfunction, hepatic artery thrombosis) supersedes MELD. The older Child-Turcotte-Pugh score (encephalopathy, ascites, bilirubin, albumin, prothrombin time) has been replaced for allocation. MELD exception points are granted (e.g., for HCC) via the National Liver Review Board.

chunks.text: Ludwig angina begins most often as an odontogenic infection of the mandibular molars. Because the roots of the second and third molars lie below the attachment of the mylohyoid muscle, infection spreads into the submandibular space and then communicates with the sublingual and submental spaces, involving all three bilaterally. The result is a rapidly advancing cellulitis of the floor of the mouth with dense inflammatory oedema rather than a localised abscess. Swelling of the sublingual tissues elevates and displaces the tongue posteriorly, while induration of the submandibular region narrows the oropharyngeal airway. Untreated, infection can extend along fascial planes to the parapharyngeal and retropharyngeal spaces and into the mediastinum, and airway obstruction or sepsis can be fatal.

chunks.text: The intervertebral disc comprises a gelatinous nucleus pulposus contained by the fibrous annulus fibrosus. With age and repetitive loading the annulus weakens and fissures, allowing nuclear material to bulge or herniate, usually posterolaterally where the annulus is thinnest and the posterior longitudinal ligament offers least support. The herniated fragment compresses and inflames the traversing or exiting nerve root, producing radicular pain, and inflammatory mediators from the nucleus contribute to root irritation. A large central herniation can compress the cauda equina. Over time herniated material often shrinks through dehydration and resorption, correlating with symptom resolution.

chunks.text: Lung cancer arises from respiratory epithelium (bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli). Environmental carcinogens, chiefly tobacco smoke, drive transformation of bronchoepithelial cells, modulated by polymorphisms in carcinogen-metabolising genes (e.g. CYP1A1). Cancers accumulate gain-of-function oncogene mutations and loss-of-function tumour-suppressor mutations; allelic loss on chromosome 3p occurs very early, even in histologically normal smoke-damaged epithelium. NSCLC adenocarcinomas are frequently driven by targetable oncogenic alterations (EGFR ~10-35%, KRAS ~15-25%, ALK rearrangement 3-7%, plus BRAF, HER2, MET, RET, ROS1, NTRK), whereas nearly 90% of SCLCs carry TP53 and RB1 mutations. Clinical manifestations stem from the primary lesion, local/regional invasion, distant metastases, or paraneoplastic syndromes. Paraneoplastic endocrine effects reflect ectopic hormone secretion: PTH-related peptide (squamous cell) causing hypercalcaemia, ADH or atrial natriuretic peptide (SCLC) causing hyponatraemia, and ectopic ACTH (SCLC, pulmonary carcinoids) causing Cushing-type biochemistry. (p.615-619)

chunks.text: Outcome is closely tied to stage at diagnosis, but over half of patients present with locally advanced or metastatic disease. In NSCLC, about 15% have localised disease amenable to curative surgery or radiotherapy, roughly a quarter have local/regional disease that may or may not be curable, and about half have metastatic disease at diagnosis. SEER data (2022) show a 5-year survival of about 63% for localised disease. Extrathoracic metastases are found at autopsy in >50% of squamous, ~80% of adenocarcinoma/large-cell, and >95% of SCLC cases. SCLC is highly likely to present extensive-stage (60-70%). Adenocarcinoma pattern carries prognostic weight: lepidic-predominant is favourable, acinar/papillary intermediate, and solid or micropapillary poor; adenocarcinoma in situ and minimally invasive adenocarcinoma achieve essentially 100% 5-year disease-free survival after complete resection. Weight loss >10%, and thrombotic disease complicating cancer, are poor prognostic signs. (p.616, p.619, p.621-622)

B. burgdorferi is a fastidious microaerophilic spirochete with an unusually small genome and more than 100 predicted lipoproteins, mostly plasmid-encoded and displayed on the outer membrane to interact with host and tick. It expresses outer-surface protein A (OspA) in the tick midgut and upregulates OspC during migration to the salivary gland, where OspC binds the tick salivary protein Salp15 (required for mammalian infection). After injection into skin the organism downregulates OspC and upregulates the antigenically variable VlsE lipoprotein, then may migrate outward to produce EM and spread hematogenously or via lymphatics to skin, nervous system, heart, and joints. Its only known virulence factors are surface proteins that attach to host proteins, integrins, glycosaminoglycans, or glycoproteins (e.g., plasminogen binding aids tissue spread; complement regulators such as Factor H protect against lysis; decorin-binding proteins bind collagen-associated decorin, possibly explaining alignment with collagen fibrils). The host mounts innate and adaptive responses producing proinflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IFN-gamma) and opsonizing antibodies; immune mechanisms eventually control disseminated infection even without antibiotics, though spirochetes may persist in localized niches for years. Postinfectious (antibiotic-refractory) Lyme arthritis is not due to persistent infection (culture and PCR of synovium are uniformly negative after antibiotics) but to a dysregulated, excessive proinflammatory response with very high IFN-gamma, host genetic factors (HLA-DRB1*0401, TLR1 1805GG polymorphism), and autoimmune responses to vascular and extracellular matrix autoantigens.

Caused by spirochetes of the Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato group (also called Borreliella spp.), transmitted by Ixodes ricinus complex ticks; B. burgdorferi sensu stricto is the predominant cause in the United States, while B. afzelii, B. garinii, and B. bavariensis also occur in Europe and Asia. (p.1448-1449)

Lyme disease is the most common vector-borne infection in the United States and Europe; in the U.S. more than 30,000 cases are reported annually but true cases are estimated at about 476,000 per year. (p.1450)

Posttreatment Lyme disease syndrome (PTLDS) affects roughly 10% of treated patients (reported figures vary widely) with persistent subjective pain, neurocognitive symptoms, or fatigue; there is NO evidence these symptoms reflect active infection, and randomized trials show repeated antibiotic courses do not help and are not recommended. (p.1451-1453)

Reinfection can occur after EM treated with antibiotics because the immune response after early infection is not protective; however, patients who develop an expanded immune response over months (e.g., those with Lyme arthritis) have protective immunity for years and rarely become reinfected. (p.1454)
Maternal-fetal transmission of B. burgdorferi appears to occur rarely if at all; standard therapy is recommended for pregnant women. (p.1453)
No Lyme disease vaccine is currently commercially available; the previously marketed vaccine was discontinued by its manufacturer. (p.1454)

Staged illness: stage 1 (early localized) presents with erythema migrans (EM); stage 2 (early disseminated) may follow with secondary skin lesions, neurologic involvement (meningitis, cranial neuritis, radiculoneuritis), carditis with atrioventricular block, and migratory musculoskeletal pain; stage 3 (late/persistent) typically manifests as intermittent arthritis and, rarely, chronic encephalopathy, polyneuropathy, or acrodermatitis. (p.1448-1449)

EM begins after an incubation period of roughly 3-32 days as a red macule or papule at the bite site that expands into a large annular lesion, often with a bright red outer border and partial central clearing; common sites include the thigh, groin, and axilla, and the lesion is warm but usually not painful. (p.1451)
Approximately 20% of patients do NOT develop the characteristic EM skin lesion, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis. (p.1451)

Cardiac involvement occurs in about 8% of patients within weeks of onset; the most common abnormality is fluctuating atrioventricular block (first-degree, Wenckebach, or complete heart block), and most cardiac involvement lasts only a few weeks. (p.1451)

About 15% of untreated patients develop frank neurologic abnormalities after weeks to months; the typical U.S. pattern is fluctuating meningitis with facial palsy (cranial neuritis, often the facial nerve, sometimes bilateral) and peripheral radiculoneuropathy. CSF in U.S. neuroborreliosis shows lymphocytic pleocytosis (~100 cells/uL) with elevated protein and normal or slightly low glucose. (p.1451)

In Europe and Asia the characteristic first neurologic sign is radicular pain followed by CSF pleocytosis (meningopolyneuritis or Bannwarth's syndrome), often without meningeal or encephalitic signs. (p.1451)

Lyme arthritis (stage 3) develops in about 60% of untreated U.S. patients months after onset; the typical pattern is intermittent oligoarticular attacks in large joints, especially the knees. Joint fluid white cell counts range widely (500-110,000/uL, average ~25,000/uL), mostly neutrophils, and rheumatoid factor and ANA tests are usually negative. (p.1451)

Most patients experience early symptoms during summer, reflecting transmission by nymphal Ixodes ticks; the tick must usually remain attached for at least about 24 hours for transmission of B. burgdorferi. (p.1449-1450)
Assuming a negative serologic test excludes acute Lyme disease - serology may be negative during the first several weeks (early seronegativity), so diagnosis of early Lyme disease is clinical
Missing the diagnosis because of atypical EM morphology or because ~20% of patients never develop EM
Relying on a positive IgM result alone in illness lasting more than 2 months - such an isolated IgM is likely false-positive and should not support the diagnosis
Misusing or misinterpreting IgM Western blots, a recognized cause of incorrect Lyme diagnoses in patients with other illnesses
Using serology as a screening test in patients with nonspecific pain or fatigue (low pretest probability), where a false-positive result is more likely than a true-positive
Interpreting persisting seropositivity (including VlsE C6 and IgM responses, which can persist for years after therapy) as evidence of active, recent, or recurrent infection

Treating persistent subjective symptoms as active infection - 'chronic Lyme disease' equated with chronic B. burgdorferi infection is a misnomer, and repeated/prolonged antibiotic courses lack benefit and carry documented harm
Using PCR positivity in joint fluid to judge active infection or adequacy of therapy, since DNA may persist for weeks after spirochetal killing

Response to treatment is best when given early in the disease; later treatment remains effective but the convalescent period may be longer. Eventually most patients recover with minimal or no residual deficits. Even without antibiotics, innate and adaptive immunity usually control disseminated infection within weeks to months, though untreated spirochetes may persist in localized niches for years. A small percentage develop persistent postinfectious arthritis or, rarely, chronic encephalopathy or polyneuropathy, and about 10% have PTLDS, which usually improves over months but may last years.
High-degree (third-degree) atrioventricular block or PR interval >0.3 s in carditis, warranting IV therapy and cardiac monitoring
Severe objective neurologic abnormalities (e.g., meningitis, encephalitis, severe neuroborreliosis)
Optic nerve involvement in children from inflammation or raised intracranial pressure, which may lead to blindness
Borrelial encephalomyelitis/leukoencephalitis (rare, mainly B. garinii in Europe) with spastic paraparesis and bladder dysfunction
Rare fatal pancarditis or cardiomegaly
Suspected tick-borne co-infection (e.g., babesiosis, anaplasmosis, Powassan virus), which can cause severe or fatal illness, especially in the very young or elderly

Staged clinical classification per Harrison: Stage 1 - early localized infection (erythema migrans at the bite site). Stage 2 - early disseminated infection (secondary annular skin lesions, neurologic involvement such as meningitis/cranial neuritis/radiculoneuritis/peripheral neuritis, carditis with atrioventricular nodal block, and migratory musculoskeletal pain). Stage 3 - late/persistent infection (intermittent or persistent arthritis, and rarely chronic encephalopathy, polyneuropathy, or acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans). For diagnostic/testing purposes, the American College of Physicians algorithm stratifies by pretest probability: high (EM - treat empirically without serology), intermediate (e.g., oligoarticular arthritis - test and treat if positive), and low (nonspecific symptoms - neither test nor treat).

Idiopathic hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (about 1-3% have Fabry disease)
Idiopathic stroke at 35-50 years (about 2-5% carry GLA mutations)
Idiopathic renal failure in males (about 5% have GLA mutations)
Cryptogenic cirrhosis / nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (childhood/adult-onset LALD)
Familial hyperlipidemia (LALD)
Parkinson disease (associated with GBA1 carriage)
Acute appendicitis or renal colic (Fabry abdominal pain can mimic these)
Enzyme assay in nucleated cells, serum/plasma, or leukocytes specific to the suspected disorder
Molecular/genetic testing: whole GBA1 sequencing is the standard for Gaucher (enzyme testing has poor sensitivity for heterozygote detection)
Slit-lamp examination for corneal and lenticular lesions to support a Fabry diagnosis
Decreased acid beta-glucosidase activity (0-20% of normal) in nucleated cells establishes Gaucher disease; the enzyme is normally absent from bodily fluids
Markedly reduced acid sphingomyelinase activity (1-10% of normal) in nucleated cells confirms Niemann-Pick A/B
Confirmation of specific enzyme deficiency in Morquio (GALNS vs acid beta-galactosidase) before therapy
Gene sequencing to confirm CLN2 given overlap among the neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses
Newborn screening (now includes MPS I and, in many states, Pompe disease)
Bone imaging / nuclear scan in Gaucher bone crises (localized absent uptake of pyrophosphate agents indicates acute bone infarction)
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (Fabry cardiac variant)

Cryptogenic/idiopathic cirrhosis (childhood/adult-onset LALD)

Lysosomal biogenesis requires ongoing synthesis of lysosomal hydrolases, membrane proteins and new membranes; lysosomes form by fusion of trans-Golgi network vesicles with late endosomes, and progressive acidification creates a pH gradient that drives pH-dependent dissociation of receptors from ligands and activates the hydrolases. Lysosomes are part of the lysosome/autophagy/mitophagy system regulated by mTORC1-mediated phosphorylation of transcription factors TFEB/TFE3, which balances anabolic and catabolic pathways; this regulation is disrupted to varying degrees in tissues affected by specific LSDs. Defects at any biosynthetic step can impair enzyme function: oligosaccharide remodeling in the Golgi (including the mannose-6-phosphate lysosomal targeting ligand), membrane sorting signals, phosphorylation, sulfation, additional proteolysis and heteromer assembly are all critical, and abnormalities in these shared processes can produce multiple simultaneous enzyme/protein deficiencies. The final common pathway is accumulation of specific macromolecules within tissues and cells that normally carry a high flux of those substrates; most deficiencies arise from point mutations or rearrangements at a single hydrolase/subunit locus, though some mutations affecting targeting, active sites, macromolecular assembly or trafficking impair several hydrolases at once. Substrate buildup distorts lysosomes and may exert pharmacologic effects, notably activation of innate immune responses. Some substrates are made within the tissue of pathology, while others are delivered exogenously (LDL receptor-mediated uptake in Fabry and LALD; phagocytosis in Gaucher type 1). The threshold hypothesis holds that disease emerges below a certain level of residual enzyme activity, and that activity can be challenged by changes in substrate flux from genetic background, cell turnover, recycling or metabolic demand, so a given residual level may suffice in some tissues but not others.

Lysosomes are subcellular organelles holding specific hydrolases that process or degrade proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates and lipids; there are more than 50 distinct lysosomal storage diseases (now also called lysosomal system diseases), grouped by the predominant accumulated material.

Lysosomal acid lipase deficiency (LIPA mutations) spans infantile Wolman syndrome (failure to thrive, vomiting, hepatosplenomegaly; median death about 3.7 months) and childhood/adult-onset cholesterol ester storage disease (elevated liver enzymes, microvesicular fatty liver, cryptogenic cirrhosis); neither variant causes primary CNS disease and statins do not halt the underlying tissue pathology.

CLN2 (neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis type 2, TPP1/tripeptidyl peptidase 1 deficiency) usually begins at age 2-4 years with seizures, ataxia, myoclonus and vision loss, progressing to severe disability and death around age 12; it is the only NCL with a specific approved treatment.

Alpha-mannosidosis (MAN2B1 biallelic loss of function) accumulates mannose-rich oligosaccharides and causes intellectual disability, incapacitating skeletal changes, immunodeficiency, ataxia, hearing loss, neurodegeneration and psychosis.

Consider an LSD in the differential when a patient has unexplained neurologic, renal or muscular degeneration, or unexplained hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, cardiomyopathy, or skeletal dysplasias/deformities; physical findings are disease-specific and diagnosis is confirmed by enzyme assay or genetic testing.

Nearly all LSDs are autosomal recessive, with notable exceptions: Hunter disease (MPS II), Danon disease and Fabry disease are X-linked, and two autosomal dominant conditions exist (Parry-type CLN from DNAJC5 mutations, and frontotemporal dementia/CLN11 from GRN/progranulin mutations).

Tay-Sachs disease (total hexosaminidase A deficiency) is carried by roughly 1 in 30 Ashkenazi Jews; the infantile form features macrocephaly, loss of motor skills, an exaggerated startle reaction and a macular cherry-red spot, with carrier screening recommended in this population.

Fabry disease (X-linked, alpha-galactosidase A deficiency) presents with angiokeratomas, hypohidrosis, corneal and lenticular opacities, debilitating episodic burning pain of the hands and feet (acroparesthesia), and progressive renal, cardiac and cerebrovascular disease; angiokeratomas are punctate, dark red to blue-black, do not blanch and cluster in the 'bathing suit area' between umbilicus and knees.

Gaucher disease (acid beta-glucosidase deficiency, GBA1) is classified by CNS involvement: type 1 is nonneuronopathic with hepatosplenomegaly and bone disease, type 2 is a severe progressive CNS disease causing death by about 2 years, and type 3 has variable CNS and visceral disease; early CNS signs in type 3 may be limited to supranuclear lateral gaze palsy.
GBA1 mutations, whether heterozygous or homozygous, substantially raise the lifetime risk of Parkinson disease.

Niemann-Pick types A and B reflect acid sphingomyelinase deficiency: type A has early onset with rapid CNS deterioration, while type B is later/variable with hepatosplenomegaly, cirrhosis, and lethal progressive pulmonary disease (foam cells in alveoli, lymphatics and pulmonary arteries); Niemann-Pick C is a separate disorder from NPC1/NPC2 defects in cholesterol/sphingolipid transport.

Pompe disease (acid alpha-glucosidase/acid maltase deficiency, GAA) is the only LSD causing primary glycogen storage; the classic infantile form has hypotonia, cardiomyopathy and hepatosplenomegaly with near-total enzyme deficiency, whereas late-onset forms resemble a limb-girdle myopathy and may not have cardiomyopathy.
Treating the disease nosology as fixed discrete entities is misleading: each LSD is heuristic and clinically expresses a continuous spectrum from severe to attenuated forms.
Angiokeratomas of Fabry disease can be easily overlooked and also occur in several other rare LSDs, so they are not specific.
Fabry abdominal pain may be mistaken for appendicitis or renal colic, delaying diagnosis.
Enzyme testing has poor sensitivity for Gaucher heterozygote detection; molecular GBA1 sequencing is required.

In Niemann-Pick, hepatic or bone marrow transplantation has produced more complications than expected (recurrent hepatic disease from ASM-deficient myeloid repopulation after liver transplant, or failure to clear hepatocyte sphingomyelin after BMT/HSCT).
Enzyme replacement therapy does not cross the blood-brain barrier and does not directly treat CNS disease (e.g., MPS I, MPS II); HSCT has not succeeded against CNS disease in MPS II.
Statins lower hypercholesterolemia in LALD but do not alter the underlying progressive tissue (e.g., liver) pathology.
Late cardiac and respiratory complications of MPS I (obstructive breathing, cardiomyopathy, valve disease) can emerge even after successful HSCT, so lifelong follow-up is required.
Morquio variants A and B require confirmation of the specific enzyme deficiency because approved enzyme therapy (elosulfase alfa) applies only to MPS IVA.

Prognosis varies enormously across and within disorders, each spanning a spectrum from severe to attenuated forms. Infantile Tay-Sachs is fatal in infancy; juvenile-onset Tay-Sachs causes death by 10-15 years. In Fabry disease, death results from cardiovascular, renal or cerebrovascular disease; renal insufficiency, cardiac fibrosis and stroke are irreversible, so early therapy offers the best chance to slow life-threatening complications, and heart disease is the most common life-threatening manifestation in females while renal then cardiovascular disease predominates in males. Gaucher type 2 leads to death by about 2 years, while type 1 and type 3 are highly variable. Niemann-Pick type B can progress to death in adolescence or early adulthood from hepatic or pulmonary disease. Infantile Pompe is rapidly progressive with death typically in the first year without treatment. Infantile-onset LALD is fatal by about 1 year (median 3.7 months) untreated, and untreated childhood/adult-onset LALD progresses to early cirrhosis (mean about age 13) and early-adulthood atherosclerosis. Early infantile Krabbe presents around 4 months and progresses rapidly to death at a mean of about 18 months. CLN2 progresses to severe disability with most children wheelchair-bound in late childhood, death at a mean of about 12 years, and survival beyond adolescence rare.
Macular cherry-red spot with macrocephaly and exaggerated startle in an infant (infantile Tay-Sachs)
Splenic infarction in Gaucher disease that can present as an acute abdomen
Gaucher 'bone crisis' with excruciating localized pain, sometimes erythema, fever and leukocytosis, representing acute bone infarction
Pulmonary hypertension or alveolar Gaucher cell accumulation (uncommon but life-threatening, more common in splenectomized females)
Vertebral collapse and avascular necrosis (femoral head) with potential spinal cord involvement in Gaucher disease
Infantile-onset LALD presenting as a medical emergency with severe failure to thrive, vomiting and hepatosplenomegaly
Fetal hydrops in severe MPS VII (Sly), which can cause stillbirth or perinatal demise
Progressive pulmonary disease with dyspnea and hypoxemia in Niemann-Pick type B
Respiratory insufficiency requiring ventilation in late-onset Pompe disease

Within individual diseases, severity is typically stratified by age of onset and CNS involvement. Examples: Tay-Sachs is divided into infantile, juvenile-onset and adult-onset forms. MPS I is graded as Hurler (MPS I H, severe with neurodegeneration), Hurler-Scheie (MPS I H/S, intermediate, severe somatic disease without major neurologic decline), and Scheie (MPS I S, later-onset without neurologic involvement). Gaucher disease is classed as type 1 (nonneuronopathic), type 2 (acute severe CNS), and type 3 (variable subacute/chronic CNS). Niemann-Pick distinguishes type A (early-onset, progressive CNS), type B (later, variable, with an A/B variant having slowly progressive CNS involvement), and the separate type C. LALD ranges from infantile-onset (Wolman) to childhood/adult-onset (cholesterol ester storage disease). Pompe and Krabbe are divided into early/infantile and later-onset variants.
