chunks.text: Hodgkin lymphoma (classical) - nontender cervical/supraclavicular/axillary nodes, frequent mediastinal involvement (Harrison 22e p.869)
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma - nodal and extranodal disease; B symptoms part of staging (Harrison 22e p.860)
Acute or chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (can produce generalised adenopathy and constitutional symptoms) (Harrison 22e p.476)
Richter transformation of CLL - rapidly progressive focal adenopathy with night sweats, fever, weight loss and high LDH (Harrison 22e p.897)
Metastatic carcinoma to nodes (head/neck, lung, breast, thyroid, GI primaries) (Harrison 22e p.477)
Germ-cell tumour (retroperitoneal nodes in young men) (Harrison 22e p.477)
Occult solid tumours presenting with involuntary weight loss - GI/hepatobiliary, lung, breast, genitourinary, ovarian, prostate (Harrison 22e p.317)
Infectious mononucleosis (EBV or CMV) - generalised adenopathy with constitutional symptoms (Harrison 22e p.476)
Tuberculosis - can cause unilateral mediastinal adenopathy and mesenteric lymphadenitis mimicking lymphoma, with night sweats and weight loss (Harrison 22e p.477)
Histoplasmosis - unilateral paratracheal node involvement that can mimic lymphoma in endemic regions (Harrison 22e p.477)
Toxoplasmosis - generalised reactive adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.476)
HIV / AIDS - generalised lymphadenopathy and a recognised lymphoma risk factor (Harrison 22e p.476, p.903)

Excisional biopsy of the largest abnormal node is preferred; fine-needle aspiration should NOT be the first procedure as it usually yields insufficient tissue and delays diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.478)
Age/sex/risk-appropriate cancer screening (e.g. faecal occult blood, colonoscopy, mammography) and abdominal ultrasound in occult-malignancy weight-loss workup (Harrison 22e p.318)
Serum protein electrophoresis to detect a monoclonal paraprotein (Harrison 22e p.903)
Serum beta2-microglobulin and LDH - independent prognostic markers in NHL (Harrison 22e p.903)
CBC with differential, comprehensive metabolic/liver panel, uric acid and calcium (Harrison 22e p.317, p.904)
ESR and CRP as part of the constitutional-symptom / weight-loss workup (Harrison 22e p.316, p.869)
Contrast CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis for staging; FDG-PET/CT preferred for aggressive lymphomas and Hodgkin lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.904)
Bone marrow biopsy where indicated; lumbar puncture if CNS-risk histology or neurologic features (Harrison 22e p.903-904)
HIV and hepatitis B and C serology - risk factors for NHL and relevant to hepatitis B reactivation risk (Harrison 22e p.904)
Cervical node ultrasound long-to-short axis ratio (<2.0 favours malignancy) where head/neck cancer is suspected (Harrison 22e p.478)
Sarcoidosis - mediastinal/hilar adenopathy and constitutional symptoms (Harrison 22e p.477)
Systemic lupus erythematosus and mixed connective tissue disease - generalised adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.476)
Drug-induced (phenytoin/diphenylhydantoin and others) lymphadenopathy, including DRESS/DIHS with eosinophilia and extensive adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.193, p.476)
Castleman disease, Kikuchi histiocytic necrotizing lymphadenitis, Rosai-Dorfman disease, angioimmunoblastic lymphadenopathy, IgG4-related disease (Harrison 22e p.476)

B symptoms in lymphoma are cytokine-mediated systemic effects of the tumour rather than direct mass effects. In classical Hodgkin lymphoma the malignant Hodgkin/Reed-Sternberg cells are rare within a tumour mass that is largely a polyclonal inflammatory infiltrate reacting to tumour-derived cytokines; this inflammatory milieu drives constitutional symptoms and contributes to the generalised immune suppression seen in these patients. Involuntary weight loss in malignancy reflects a combination of anorexia, sarcopenia and a cytokine-driven cachexia syndrome. (Harrison 22e p.316, p.869)

B symptoms are formally defined for lymphoma staging (the Ann Arbor 'B' suffix) as unexplained fever (>38C), drenching night sweats, and/or unexplained weight loss exceeding 10% of body weight over the 6 months before diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.861, p.869).

Half of all cancer patients lose some weight and up to 20% of cancer deaths are attributable directly to cachexia; malignancy that declares itself through marked weight loss generally carries a poor prognosis (Harrison 22e p.317).
The tempo of symptoms helps separate aggressive from indolent lymphoma: rapid symptomatic progression and the presence of B symptoms suggest a more aggressive process (Harrison 22e p.903).
Among malignancies, lymphoma is by far the commonest cause of malignancy-related fever of unknown origin, and the fever can precede any palpable lymphadenopathy (Harrison 22e p.193).

About one-third of patients with classical Hodgkin lymphoma present with B symptoms; Hodgkin disease can even present as a fever of unknown origin, more often in older patients with abdominal mixed-cellularity disease (Harrison 22e p.869).
Pel-Ebstein fever (cyclical fever lasting days to weeks alternating with afebrile intervals) is a rare but classic Hodgkin lymphoma presentation (Harrison 22e p.869).

Node character matters: lymphomatous nodes tend to be large, firm, rubbery, mobile, symmetric and non-tender, whereas metastatic carcinoma nodes are typically hard, non-tender and fixed to surrounding tissue (Harrison 22e p.477).

Supraclavicular and scalene node enlargement is always abnormal and warrants prompt evaluation; a left supraclavicular node (Virchow node) classically reflects a gastrointestinal primary, but lung, breast, testis and ovarian cancers also seed these nodes (Harrison 22e p.477).

Examination in suspected lymphoma should systematically cover all peripheral nodal sites plus Waldeyer ring, liver and spleen size, effusions/ascites, and testicular, breast or skin involvement, since any of these can change staging and management (Harrison 22e p.903).

Enlarged intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal nodes are usually malignant (lymphoma, or germ-cell tumour in young men), in contrast to the largely benign causes of cervical adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.477).

Do NOT give glucocorticoids for undiagnosed lymphadenopathy - their lympholytic effect can obscure lymphoma, leukaemia and Castleman disease and delay/disrupt diagnosis (the rare exception is life-threatening pharyngeal obstruction from Waldeyer-ring tissue in mononucleosis) (Harrison 22e p.521).

Fine-needle aspiration is inadequate for an initial lymphoma diagnosis - obtain an excisional/core biopsy; FNA is reserved for thyroid nodules and confirming relapse of a known cancer (Harrison 22e p.478).
Antibiotics are NOT indicated for lymphadenopathy unless there is strong evidence of bacterial infection (Harrison 22e p.521).
Localized-versus-generalized adenopathy has limited discriminatory value because many causes produce either pattern; do not over-rely on it (Harrison 22e p.476).

In primary care most lymphadenopathy is benign (>two-thirds nonspecific/URI, <1% malignant) and needs only short-interval follow-up - but persistent or enlarging nodes must be re-evaluated and biopsied (Harrison 22e p.476, p.521).
If a head-and-neck primary is suspected behind a solitary cervical node, perform a careful ENT exam and biopsy any suspicious mucosal lesion first before excising the node (Harrison 22e p.478).

Lymphoma prognosis is stage- and biology-dependent. For NHL the International Prognostic Index uses five factors (age >=60, elevated LDH, ECOG performance status >=2, Ann Arbor stage III/IV, and >1 extranodal site); for DLBCL treated with R-CHOP, 0 factors gives ~94% 4-year survival versus ~53% with 3-5 factors. Across lymphomas, decreased outcome is associated with B symptoms, advanced stage, elevated LDH and bulky disease (e.g. lymph-node mass >7 cm). In occult solid malignancy, presentation through significant involuntary weight loss generally carries a very poor prognosis, whereas when no cause is found after thorough workup the prognosis is comparatively favourable. (Harrison 22e p.317, p.861, NHL prognosis section)
Supraclavicular or scalene adenopathy - always abnormal, biopsy promptly (Harrison 22e p.477-478)
Solitary hard non-tender cervical node in an older tobacco user - prompt biopsy after ENT mucosal assessment (Harrison 22e p.478)
Node size >2 cm with an abnormal chest x-ray in younger patients - predicts malignant/granulomatous biopsy yield (Harrison 22e p.521)
Hard fixed nodes, or firm mobile generalised adenopathy suggestive of lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.478)
Airway, oesophageal or SVC compression from thoracic adenopathy (cough/wheeze, hoarseness, dysphagia, facial/arm/neck swelling) (Harrison 22e p.520)
Enlarged intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal nodes (usually malignant) (Harrison 22e p.477)
Involuntary weight loss >=5% over 6 months prompting structured malignancy workup (Harrison 22e p.358)

Ann Arbor staging (stages I-IV) with suffix A (no systemic symptoms) or B (presence of B symptoms: fever >38C, drenching night sweats, or weight loss >10% body weight over preceding 6 months); suffix E for localized extralymphatic extension. B-symptom status (the A/B designation) and stage drive prognosis and therapy. (Harrison 22e p.861, p.869)

Validated risk-screening tools: Malnutrition Screening Tool, Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST), Nutritional Risk Screening 2002, Mini Nutritional Assessment, Subjective Global Assessment
Anthropometrics: serial body weight (without shoes/heavy garments), BMI, calf circumference, mid-upper arm circumference; height estimated by arm span or knee-height caliper when needed
Body composition: bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA, portable), dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA), air displacement plethysmography, and opportunistic CT/MRI muscle measurement
Laboratory: complete blood count with differential (screen for iron, B12, folate, vitamin C deficiencies), C-reactive protein for inflammation, specific micronutrient levels
Indirect calorimetry for resting energy expenditure; 24-h urine urea nitrogen and nitrogen balance to gauge catabolism and protein adequacy (normal renal/hepatic function required)

Nutrition-focused physical examination for edema, subcutaneous fat and muscle loss; diet history including oral supplements, enteral and parenteral intake

Hypocholesterolemia related to acute illness rather than malnutrition per se

Malnutrition arises from an imbalance between nutrient intake/assimilation and metabolic demand, and acute or chronic inflammation is now recognized as central to its pathophysiology. Inflammatory mediators raise resting energy expenditure, promote anabolic resistance and muscle catabolism, and cause anorexia that further reduces intake. Severe acute inflammation (e.g., critical illness, sepsis, burns, trauma, closed head injury) may be superimposed on a mild-to-moderate chronic inflammatory state (e.g., malignancy, COPD, congestive heart failure, chronic renal disease, chronic GI disease). The resulting deficits impair wound healing, immune function, and organ function. Because albumin and prealbumin behave as negative acute-phase reactants, the inflammatory milieu also distorts these traditional nutrition biomarkers (Harrison 22e pp.2615-2617).
Malnutrition affects roughly 30-50% of hospitalized patients, with the exact prevalence varying by clinical setting, underlying diagnosis, and the diagnostic criteria applied (Harrison 22e p.2615).

Calf circumference is a practical, valid estimate of skeletal muscle mass that requires less training than mid-upper arm circumference, with ethnicity-specific reference ranges that should be adjusted for BMI extremes (Harrison 22e p.2618).
When inflammation is severe, nutrition care tends to be supportive only; at low-to-moderate inflammation, nutrition care may be therapeutic and improve clinical outcomes (Harrison 22e pp.2615-2616).
Calf circumference, BMI, and other GLIM parameters make malnutrition diagnosis feasible even in the outpatient/ambulatory setting where dietitian access may be limited (Harrison 22e p.2617).

The 2019 GLIM (Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition) consensus requires at least one phenotypic criterion (nonvolitional weight loss, low BMI, or reduced muscle mass) PLUS at least one etiologic criterion (reduced food intake/assimilation, or disease burden/inflammation) to diagnose malnutrition (Harrison 22e p.2616).

Severity grading in GLIM is determined by the phenotypic criterion: moderate (stage 1) malnutrition is 5-10% weight loss within 6 months (or 10-20% beyond 6 months), and severe (stage 2) is >10% within 6 months (or >20% beyond) (Harrison 22e p.2616).

Patients at any BMI can be malnourished; overweight or obese individuals may have sarcopenic obesity from muscle loss, and conversely being underweight does not by itself equal malnutrition (Harrison 22e p.2617).

Handgrip strength is among the more clinically useful functional measures because it is easy to perform and helps identify which patients are most likely to benefit from individualized nutritional support (Harrison 22e p.2617).
Patients with apparently adequate oral intake may still be at risk of malnutrition when chronic gastrointestinal disease compromises nutrient assimilation or absorption (Harrison 22e p.2617).
A 5-10% loss of body weight over 6 months is clinically relevant, while >10% loss over the same period is considered severe (Harrison 22e p.2617).

Albumin and prealbumin are negative acute-phase reactants and fall with injury, disease, or inflammation; they have poor sensitivity and specificity for malnutrition, though they retain value for predicting clinical outcomes (Harrison 22e pp.2617-2618).

C-reactive protein is a positive acute-phase reactant useful for confirming inflammation, with the chapter noting supportive thresholds of mild 3.0-9.9 mg/L, moderate 10-50 mg/L, and severe >50 mg/L (Harrison 22e p.2616).

Relying on albumin or prealbumin to diagnose malnutrition or judge response to nutrition therapy; they reflect inflammation, hepatic/renal status, hydration, and other factors and have poor specificity (Harrison 22e pp.2617-2618).
Assuming a normal or high BMI excludes malnutrition; sarcopenic obesity and muscle loss can occur at any BMI (Harrison 22e p.2617).
Overlooking edema, which can mask true weight loss unless dry weight is estimated (Harrison 22e p.2617).

Using BUN/creatinine, total lymphocyte count, cholesterol, creatinine-height index, cytokines, ECG, recall-antigen skin testing, or urine 3-methylhistidine as malnutrition indicators; the chapter lists these as NOT recommended for diagnosis (Harrison 22e pp.2618-2619).
Comparing malnutrition prevalence across studies without accounting for differences between diagnostic tools, which yield incomparable rates (Harrison 22e p.2616).
Failing to recognize prolonged pre-admission decreases in intake when an acute event is superimposed on chronic disease (Harrison 22e p.2617).

Malnutrition is associated with poor wound healing, compromised immunity, and impaired organ function, leading to longer hospital stays, more readmissions, higher mortality, and increased health care costs. Severe inflammation may limit nutritional interventions to a supportive rather than therapeutic role, and the associated malnutrition can diminish the effectiveness of medical therapies. Robust evidence indicates that a multipronged approach to malnutrition intervention reduces mortality and holds promise for improving quality of life, so timely diagnosis and treatment are important (Harrison 22e pp.2615, 2618).

A defect in the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex blocks the oxidative decarboxylation of the ketoacids derived from leucine, isoleucine, and valine. As a result these branched-chain amino acids and their corresponding ketoacids accumulate in blood, urine, and tissues. Leucine and its ketoacid are particularly neurotoxic, disturbing neurotransmitter balance, cerebral amino acid transport, and cellular osmolarity, which produces cerebral oedema and encephalopathy. During catabolic states, endogenous protein breakdown releases further branched-chain amino acids, precipitating acute, potentially life-threatening metabolic decompensation.
An autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, impairing breakdown of the branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine, and valine.
The classic severe form presents in the first week of life with poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, and worsening encephalopathy after protein feeding begins.
Neurological signs may include fluctuating tone, dystonic posturing, a boxing or bicycling movement pattern, and progression to seizures and coma.
The urine, sweat, or cerumen may carry a characteristic sweet, maple-syrup or burnt-sugar odour.
Leucine and its ketoacid accumulation is the principal driver of neurotoxicity and cerebral oedema.

Newborn screening detects elevated branched-chain amino acids; diagnosis is confirmed by the plasma amino acid pattern (notably raised leucine and the presence of alloisoleucine) and molecular testing.
Acute management centres on halting protein intake, promoting anabolism with adequate energy, and rapidly lowering branched-chain amino acid levels, with dialysis or haemofiltration in severe crises.
Long-term treatment is a carefully monitored diet restricting branched-chain amino acids while providing enough protein and energy for growth.
Intercurrent illness, fasting, or catabolic stress can precipitate metabolic crises even in previously stable, treated children.
Mistaking early presentation for neonatal sepsis and delaying metabolic evaluation
Not recognising the characteristic sweet odour as a diagnostic clue
Continuing protein feeds during an acute crisis instead of stopping them and driving anabolism
Underestimating how rapidly catabolic stress can trigger dangerous decompensation
Failing to establish sick-day plans and long-term dietary monitoring

Outcome depends on how quickly the diagnosis is made and metabolic control is achieved; early treatment and avoidance of crises support near-normal development, whereas repeated or severe decompensations and prolonged high leucine levels risk permanent neurological damage. Lifelong dietary management and prompt sick-day protocols are essential.

Mastocytosis is a clonal mast cell disorder driven by somatic gain-of-function mutations in the KIT (stem cell factor receptor) gene, with KIT D816V present in >90% of patients. The mutation produces ligand-independent KIT activation and clonal mast cell proliferation/accumulation in skin, bone marrow, liver, spleen, and gut. KIT mutations occur across all forms of SM and in lesional skin of some children with cutaneous disease; additional mutations (TET2, SRSF2, ASXL1, RUNX1) seen in other hematologic neoplasms can appear in advanced SM variants. Disease manifestations arise from release of bioactive mast cell mediators acting locally and distally, tissue infiltration by mast cells, and the tissue response to that infiltrate; mast cell-mediated fibrosis may affect liver, spleen, and bone marrow but not gastrointestinal tissue or skin (p.2819-2820).

Mastocytosis is defined by accumulation of clonally expanded mast cells in tissues (skin, bone marrow, liver, spleen, gut); mast cell expansion is most readily identified in skin and/or bone marrow (p.2819).

Patients with recurrent mast cell activation (especially anaphylaxis with hypotensive syncope) who carry KIT D816V but do not meet full SM criteria are termed monoclonal mast cell activation syndrome (p.2821).
More than 90% of patients carry a somatic gain-of-function KIT D816V mutation in the stem cell factor receptor gene (p.2819).

Classification recognizes cutaneous mastocytosis (with variants), systemic mastocytosis (SM, five variants), and mast cell sarcoma; cutaneous mastocytosis is the most common diagnosis in children and is usually diagnosed within the first year of life (p.2819-2820).

Systemic mastocytosis denotes involvement of an extracutaneous site, most often bone marrow; indolent systemic mastocytosis (ISM) accounts for >70% of adult patients and is associated with a normal life expectancy (p.2820).

Cutaneous lesions of maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis (MPCM, also called urticaria pigmentosa) are reddish-brown macules, papules, or plaques that urticate and become erythematous on rubbing or trauma (Darier's sign) (p.2820).

Clinical manifestations of SM reflect release of bioactive mast cell mediators plus tissue infiltration: intermittent urticaria, flushing, tachycardia and vascular collapse, gastric acid hypersecretion, crampy lower abdominal pain, and diarrhea (p.2820).

Anaphylaxis in mastocytosis is most commonly triggered by Hymenoptera stings and NSAIDs; symptom flares may also follow alcohol, temperature change, stress, and mast cell-interactive opioids (p.2820).
A basal serum tryptase level is a useful noninvasive test to consider before bone marrow biopsy; total serum tryptase >20 ng/mL is a minor diagnostic criterion for SM (p.2821).

Diagnosis of SM requires tissue confirmation (lesional/bone marrow biopsy): one major plus one minor, or three minor criteria. Major = multifocal dense mast cell aggregates (>15 mast cells per aggregate) in extracutaneous tissue; minor = spindled/atypical morphology, aberrant CD25/CD2/CD30 phenotype, activating KIT mutation, or tryptase >20 ng/mL (p.2821).
Atopy is not increased in mastocytosis compared with the general population (p.2819).
Imatinib is not effective in most cases because the KIT D816V mutation confers resistance (p.2821).
Osteoporosis alone without osteolytic lesions does not satisfy the C-finding skeletal criterion for aggressive SM (p.2821).
SM cannot be confirmed on clinical and laboratory grounds alone; tissue diagnosis is required (p.2821).
Anaphylaxis in SM typically lacks the urticaria, angioedema, and bronchospasm seen in IgE-mediated or idiopathic anaphylaxis (p.2821).
Baseline serum tryptase elevation must be interpreted with caution where hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (extra TPSAB1 copies) coexists (p.2821).

Prognosis is variant-dependent. Life expectancy is normal for cutaneous mastocytosis and most ISM; progression from ISM to a more advanced form is uncommon (~5% lifetime risk). In SM-AHNMD, outcome is determined by the associated non-mast cell hematologic disorder. SSM carries an intermediate prognosis. Aggressive SM and mast cell leukemia have a poor prognosis, and mast cell leukemia is invariably fatal at present. In infants and children with cutaneous disease, visceral involvement is usually absent and spontaneous resolution before adolescence is common; progression from cutaneous mastocytosis to ISM occurs in ~10% of children, especially with high mast cell burden or hematologic abnormalities (p.2820).
Anaphylaxis with rapid, life-threatening vascular collapse (most often after Hymenoptera stings or NSAIDs)

Consensus classification: Cutaneous mastocytosis (CM) - maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis (MPCM/urticaria pigmentosa), solitary mastocytoma of skin, diffuse cutaneous mastocytosis. Systemic mastocytosis (SM) - indolent SM (ISM, >70% of adults, normal life expectancy), smoldering SM (SSM; >=2 B findings, no C findings: high mast cell burden with marrow infiltration >30%, basal tryptase >200 ng/mL, and/or KIT D816V VAF >10%, dysmyelopoiesis, organomegaly), SM with associated clonal hematologic non-mast cell lineage disease (SM-AHNMD), aggressive SM (ASM; >=1 C finding - cytopenias, hepatic dysfunction with ascites, hypersplenism, malabsorption with weight loss, osteolytic fractures), mast cell leukemia (MCL, rarest, invariably fatal). Mast cell sarcoma (MCS) is a rare invasive solid mast cell tumor (Tables 366-1, 366-2; p.2820).

chunks.text: The mastoid air cells are continuous with the middle ear, so mucosal inflammation accompanies most episodes of acute otitis media. Mastoiditis develops when purulent material is trapped because the aditus ad antrum becomes blocked by oedema, allowing pressure and infection to build within the air cells. Persistent suppuration decalcifies and destroys the thin bony septa between cells, which fuse into an abscess cavity (coalescent mastoiditis). Pus may then track outward through the cortex to form a subperiosteal abscess, along fascial planes into the neck (Bezold abscess), or inward toward the dura, sigmoid sinus and posterior/middle cranial fossae, producing serious intracranial complications.

Measles virus is deposited in the respiratory tract, oropharynx, or conjunctivae, then proliferates locally in dendritic cells and lymphocytes and spreads to draining lymph nodes. It enters the bloodstream by budding from infected lymphocytes, producing a viremia that disseminates infection throughout the body (respiratory epithelium, lymphatic tissue, spleen, lung, thymus, liver, skin). Signs and symptoms appear 8-12 days after infection as virus replicates in target organs and the host immune response develops; the characteristic rash is itself a consequence of the cellular immune response. TH1 (interferon-gamma) responses are essential for viral clearance and later TH2 (interleukin-4) responses drive protective antibody. Paradoxically, measles induces a state of immunosuppression lasting weeks to months that depresses responses to unrelated antigens, reduces the magnitude and diversity of pre-existing antibody ("immune amnesia"), and increases susceptibility to secondary bacterial and viral infections, accounting for much measles-related morbidity and death.

Caused by measles virus, a paramyxovirus; transmitted primarily by respiratory droplets and, less commonly, by small-particle aerosols that can remain suspended in air, making it highly transmissible (Harrison 22e p.1639).
Incubation is ~10 days to fever onset and ~14 days to rash onset; this period may be shorter in infants and longer (up to 3 weeks) in adults (Harrison 22e p.1640).
Classic prodrome is fever and malaise beginning ~10 days after exposure, followed by the three Cs: cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis, increasing in severity over ~4 days (Harrison 22e p.1640).

Koplik's spots (bluish-white ~1 mm dots surrounded by erythema on the buccal mucosa opposite the lower molars) are pathognomonic, appear ~2 days before the rash, and fade with rash onset (Harrison 22e p.1641).

The exanthem is an erythematous maculopapular rash beginning behind the ears and on the neck/hairline, spreading cephalocaudally to face, trunk, arms, and then legs/feet by the end of the second day; it fades in the same order and may desquamate, especially in undernourished children (Harrison 22e p.1641).
Care is largely supportive; vitamin A is recommended for children with measles and can markedly reduce morbidity and mortality (Harrison 22e p.1641).
Two doses of live attenuated measles vaccine (commonly as MMR or MMRV) are highly protective; ~85% develop protective antibody after one dose at 9 months and ~95% at 12 months (Harrison 22e p.1642).

Post-exposure human immunoglobulin within 72 h usually prevents infection and, given up to 6 days after exposure, can still prevent or modify disease in susceptible high-risk contacts (Harrison 22e p.1642).

Endemic transmission was eliminated in the United States in 2000, but outbreaks recur from imported cases amplified in under- and unvaccinated communities; vaccine hesitancy and pandemic-related disruption of immunization programs have driven a global resurgence (Harrison 22e p.1638, p.1369).
Patients are contagious before recognizable disease appears, which undermines isolation measures; nosocomial transmission in waiting rooms, hospitals, and physicians' offices is well recognized.

Clinical diagnosis is difficult during the prodrome, when the rash is attenuated by passively acquired antibody or prior immunization, when the rash is absent/delayed in immunocompromised or severely undernourished children, and in low-incidence regions.
Measles virus-specific IgM may be falsely negative if serum is obtained too early (within the first few days of rash onset).
Persons with impaired cellular immunity may not develop the characteristic rash, may develop giant cell pneumonitis, and have a high case-fatality rate.
There is no specific antiviral therapy; ribavirin benefit has not been conclusively demonstrated in trials.
The 1998 report hypothesizing an MMR-autism link was a misinterpreted temporal association, has been refuted by numerous studies, and was retracted - there is no causal link.

Most persons recover and develop long-term (generally lifelong) protective immunity. Case-fatality varies with age at infection, nutritional and immunologic status, vaccine coverage, and access to care. In most developed countries the case-fatality rate is 0.01-0.1%, but in endemic areas of sub-Saharan Africa it may be 5-10% or higher, and in refugee camps and internally displaced populations rates have reached 20-30%. Previously vaccinated persons who become infected have less severe disease and significantly lower mortality. Measles still causes more than 100,000 deaths per year worldwide.

Pneumonia - secondary bacterial bronchopneumonia or measles giant cell pneumonitis (the latter in immunocompromised persons); recurrence or persistence of fever after the rash suggests secondary bacterial infection
Acute laryngotracheobronchitis (croup) with risk of airway obstruction, particularly in young children

Intrauterine stress and hypoxia can provoke passage of meconium into the amniotic fluid and gasping that draws it into the airways. Aspirated meconium causes mechanical airway obstruction with a ball-valve effect producing air trapping and air leaks, a chemical pneumonitis with inflammation, and inactivation of surfactant. These changes cause ventilation-perfusion mismatch and hypoxaemia, and, combined with hypoxia-driven pulmonary vasoconstriction, promote persistent pulmonary hypertension with right-to-left shunting.
Respiratory distress in a newborn born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid, when meconium is aspirated into the airways around the time of birth.
It occurs mainly in term and post-term infants and is associated with fetal distress and intrauterine hypoxia.
Affected infants may be meconium-stained, have distress from birth with tachypnoea and recession, and show a barrel-shaped, hyperinflated chest.
The chest radiograph typically shows patchy or coarse infiltrates with areas of hyperinflation and atelectasis, and air leaks are common.
Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn frequently complicates the syndrome and contributes to severe hypoxaemia.
Routine intrapartum suctioning of the airway and routine tracheal suction of vigorous meconium-stained infants are no longer recommended.
Non-vigorous infants born through meconium may need resuscitation, and management is largely supportive with oxygen and respiratory support.
Severe cases may require mechanical ventilation, surfactant, inhaled nitric oxide for pulmonary hypertension, and occasionally extracorporeal membrane oxygenation.
Air leaks such as pneumothorax and pneumomediastinum are important and potentially sudden complications.
Performing routine intrapartum or tracheal suctioning that is no longer recommended
Underestimating the risk of pneumothorax and missing a sudden air leak
Failing to recognise coexisting persistent pulmonary hypertension
Overlooking associated hypoxic-ischaemic injury to other organs
Delaying escalation of respiratory support in rapidly deteriorating infants

Most infants with mild to moderate disease recover with supportive care, but severe disease complicated by persistent pulmonary hypertension or air leaks carries significant morbidity and mortality; survivors may have transient respiratory sequelae.

Macrocytosis without true megaloblastic change: alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, pregnancy, myelodysplasia, myeloma/paraproteinemia, aplastic anemia, smoking (Harrison 22e p.790)
Serum cobalamin (ELISA or competitive-binding luminescence assay); note IF antibodies can cause falsely normal results in up to 50% of pernicious anemia cases (Harrison 22e p.788)
Serum methylmalonic acid (raised in cobalamin deficiency sufficient for anemia/neuropathy; fluctuates in renal failure) (Harrison 22e p.788, p.789)
Serum homocysteine (raised in early cobalamin and folate deficiency but nonspecific) (Harrison 22e p.789)
Serum folate and red cell folate (red cell folate reflects body stores; false-normal after transfusion or with high reticulocytes) (Harrison 22e p.789)
Serum gastrin (raised in pernicious anemia) and pepsinogen I (low) (Harrison 22e p.785, p.789)
Intrinsic factor and parietal cell antibodies; gastric endoscopy/biopsy (Harrison 22e p.786, p.789)
Bone marrow examination in selected severely anemic patients (Harrison 22e p.784)
Transglutaminase antibodies to exclude gluten-induced enteropathy in folate deficiency (Harrison 22e p.789)
Myelodysplasia (megaloblastoid marrow may mimic megaloblastic anemia and, in severe cases, accumulation of blasts may mimic acute myeloid leukemia) (Harrison 22e p.785)
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (a weakly positive direct antiglobulin test due to complement from ineffective erythropoiesis can lead to a false diagnosis) (Harrison 22e p.785)
Other causes of macrocytosis: alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, pregnancy (Harrison 22e p.790)

The common defect is impaired DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells. In folate or cobalamin deficiency, conversion of deoxyuridine monophosphate (dUMP) to deoxythymidine monophosphate (dTMP) fails because the folate coenzyme 5,10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate, needed for this step, becomes scarce. The shortage of dTTP precursor slows DNA replication, leaving single-stranded breaks; an alternative theory invokes misincorporation of uracil into DNA. Cobalamin is a cofactor for two reactions: methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and the methionine-synthase-mediated methylation of homocysteine to methionine, which also requires 5-methyl-THF. In cobalamin deficiency, 5-methyl-THF accumulates in plasma while intracellular THF (the substrate for folate polyglutamate formation) falls — the methylfolate trap (THF starvation) — explaining high serum folate but low cell folate, and why the anemia of cobalamin deficiency can respond to large folic acid doses. Death of nucleated red cells in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis) produces unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, raised LDH, raised urine urobilinogen, and reduced haptoglobins (Harrison 22e p.782, p.783, p.785).

Megaloblastic anemias share a defect in DNA synthesis affecting rapidly dividing marrow cells, producing characteristic morphology with a hypercellular marrow and ineffective erythropoiesis (Harrison 22e p.780).

Older patients with iron deficiency should also be assessed for cobalamin deficiency and vice versa, since coexistence is common (15-20% over age 60) and iron deficiency may blunt the macrocytosis (Harrison 22e p.789).

Removal of 1.2 m or more of terminal ileum, total gastrectomy, fish tapeworm (Diphyllobothrium latum) infestation, and intestinal stagnant-loop syndrome are recognized malabsorptive causes of cobalamin deficiency (Harrison 22e p.786, p.787).

The usual cause is deficiency of cobalamin (vitamin B12) or folate, but the picture can also arise from genetic or acquired abnormalities of their metabolism or from DNA-synthesis defects unrelated to either vitamin (Harrison 22e p.780).

Body cobalamin stores (about 2-3 mg) are large enough to last 3-4 years if intake stops, whereas folate stores (about 10 mg total, mostly hepatic) suffice for only 3-4 months, so severe folate deficiency can develop rapidly (Harrison 22e p.780, p.781).
Cobalamin is made only by microorganisms; the sole human source is animal-derived food, so strict vegans are at risk of dietary deficiency (Harrison 22e p.781, p.786).

Pernicious anemia, the dominant cause of severe cobalamin deficiency in Western countries, is gastric atrophy with severe lack of intrinsic factor; median onset is age 70-80, it clusters with other organ-specific autoimmune diseases (thyroid disease, vitiligo, type 1 diabetes, Addison disease), and gastric output of acid, pepsin, and intrinsic factor is severely reduced with raised serum gastrin and low pepsinogen I (Harrison 22e p.785, p.786).

Cobalamin deficiency can cause neurologic disease (subacute combined degeneration) with demyelination of posterior and lateral spinal columns, peripheral neuropathy, optic atrophy, and cerebral changes including dementia and psychosis; patients (more often male) present with paresthesias, weakness, or gait difficulty, often with positive Romberg and Lhermitte signs (Harrison 22e p.783).

Peripheral blood shows oval macrocytes with marked aniso-poikilocytosis, an MCV usually >100 fL (unless coexisting microcytosis), and hypersegmented neutrophils (more than five nuclear lobes) (Harrison 22e p.784).

In a nonanemic patient, a few macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils may be the only clue to underlying deficiency, and serum cobalamin may be borderline; supporting tests include MMA, IF/parietal-cell antibodies, and serum gastrin (Harrison 22e p.783, p.784).

Periconceptional folic acid reduces neural tube defects (anencephaly, meningomyelocele, encephalocele, spina bifida) by roughly 80%; the lower the maternal folate, the greater the fetal risk (Harrison 22e p.783).

Intrinsic-factor antibodies can produce falsely normal serum cobalamin in up to 50% of pernicious anemia patients tested by certain assays — a normal level does not exclude pernicious anemia when clinical suspicion is strong (Harrison 22e p.788).
Giving large doses of folic acid before excluding/correcting cobalamin deficiency can allow cobalamin neuropathy to progress despite hematologic response (Harrison 22e p.789, p.790).
Serum folate falls with recent poor diet but rises in severe cobalamin deficiency (methylfolate trap) and in stagnant-loop syndrome, so it can mislead (Harrison 22e p.789).
Mildly elevated MMA and/or homocysteine occur in up to 30% of healthy volunteers and in 15% of elderly with normal cobalamin, so cutoffs and clinical significance are uncertain (Harrison 22e p.789).
Coexisting iron deficiency may mask macrocytosis; the term 'megaloblastoid' is best avoided as it refers to myelodysplastic change refractory to vitamin therapy (Harrison 22e p.785, p.789).
A weakly positive direct antiglobulin test from ineffective erythropoiesis can be misread as autoimmune hemolytic anemia (Harrison 22e p.785).

With regular treatment of pernicious anemia, life expectancy is normal in women; men historically had slightly reduced life expectancy due to a higher incidence of gastric carcinoma, with current data unavailable. Neurologic recovery depends on duration before treatment, and a therapeutic trial of at least 3 months may be needed to judge improvement in neuropsychiatric cases. Untreated severe deficiency causes progressive anemia, neurologic deterioration, and infertility (Harrison 22e p.783, p.786).
Neurologic signs of subacute combined degeneration: loss of proprioception/vibration, positive Romberg and Lhermitte signs, ataxic/spastic gait, hyperreflexia (Harrison 22e p.783)
Cerebral involvement: dementia, depression, psychosis, cognitive impairment, visual impairment from optic atrophy (Harrison 22e p.783)
Nonanemic patient with neurologic/psychiatric features and low or borderline serum cobalamin (deficiency must be actively confirmed) (Harrison 22e p.783)
Severe thrombocytopenia (rarely <40 x 10^9/L) with bruising (Harrison 22e p.783, p.784)
Marked marrow blast accumulation in severe cases mimicking acute leukemia (Harrison 22e p.785)

Severity is gauged by the degree of anemia and parallels the morphologic changes; marrow involvement is described as severe, intermediate, mild, or early. In megaloblastic anemia due to cobalamin deficiency the serum cobalamin is usually <74 pmol/L (100 ng/L), with 74-148 pmol/L (100-200 ng/L) regarded as borderline; the more severe the deficiency, the lower the level, and very low levels occur with spinal cord involvement even without anemia (Harrison 22e p.785, p.788).

chunks.text: Melasma reflects an acquired disorder of localised hyperpigmentation in which functionally hyperactive melanocytes deposit excess melanin in the epidermis, dermis, or both. Ultraviolet and visible light, hormonal influences (pregnancy, oestrogen), and a genetic predisposition upregulate melanogenic signalling, while an altered dermal environment with solar elastosis, increased vascularity, and a disrupted basement membrane allows pigment to drop into the dermis. This basement-membrane damage helps explain the chronic, relapsing nature and the resistance of dermal pigment to topical therapy.

chunks.text: Meniere's disease is attributed to endolymphatic hydrops, an abnormal accumulation of endolymph that distends the membranous labyrinth. Impaired production, circulation or absorption of endolymph, potentially involving the endolymphatic sac, raises pressure within the scala media. Episodic rupture or dysfunction of the membranes allows mixing of endolymph and perilymph, disturbing the ionic environment of the sensory hair cells and producing acute vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus. Repeated insults cause progressive damage to cochlear and vestibular structures, leading to permanent hearing loss and vestibular hypofunction.

chunks.text: Other causes of bacterial meningitis (presentation of meningococcal meningitis is indistinguishable unless an associated petechial/purpuric rash or gram-negative diplococci are present) (p.1248-1249)

Differential of chronic meningococcemia: bacterial endocarditis, acute rheumatic fever, Henoch-Schonlein purpura, infectious mononucleosis, disseminated gonococcal infection, immune-mediated vasculitis (p.1248-1249)

Viral infections (enteroviruses, influenza and other respiratory viruses, measles, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, parvovirus) - most patients presenting with a petechial/purpuric rash have a viral infection (p.1248)
Pneumococcal, streptococcal, staphylococcal, or other gram-negative bacterial sepsis (p.1248)

Blood culture for confirmation and public health investigation (positive in up to ~75% of cases); avoid media containing sodium polyanethol sulfonate, which may inhibit meningococcal growth, and avoid delay in transport (p.1249)
Real-time PCR of whole blood increases diagnostic yield by more than 40% and may remain positive for several days after antibiotics (p.1249)

Lumbar puncture for CSF in suspected meningitis (unless contraindicated); CSF Gram stain is up to ~80% sensitive, CSF culture sensitivity ~90%, plus PCR where available; CSF latex agglutination antigen testing is insensitive and should be replaced by molecular diagnosis (p.1249)
Inflammatory markers (WBC count, C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, ESR) may support the diagnosis but can be normal or low in rapidly progressive disease and do not exclude it (p.1249)
Severe septicemia laboratory findings: hypoglycemia, acidosis, hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hypophosphatemia, anemia, coagulopathy (p.1249)
Measure total hemolytic complement activity to assess for complement deficiency in patients with recurrent disease, particularly non-B capsular groups (p.1247)
Protein C or S deficiency (including post-varicella protein S deficiency) (p.1248)
Platelet disorders (e.g., idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, drug effects, bone marrow infiltration) (p.1248)
Henoch-Schonlein purpura, connective tissue disorders, and trauma (including nonaccidental injury in children) (p.1248)

N. meningitidis colonizes the human nasopharynx, then in a susceptible individual may invade the mucosa into the bloodstream, usually within a few days of acquisition. The polysaccharide capsule is a key virulence factor providing resistance to phagocytosis; acapsular strains rarely cause invasive disease. During growth meningococci shed outer-membrane blebs containing lipopolysaccharide (LPS, endotoxin), which binds CD14/TLR4 to trigger an inflammatory cascade (TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, PAI-1 and others). Disease severity relates to both endotoxin levels and the magnitude of the inflammatory response. Endothelial injury is central to meningococcemia, causing increased vascular permeability (capillary leak with hypovolemia, tissue and pulmonary edema), altered vascular tone, loss of thromboresistance, intravascular coagulation, and myocardial dysfunction. Procoagulant activation with tissue factor upregulation, downregulation of anticoagulant pathways (loss of thrombomodulin/protein C receptors; reduced antithrombin III, protein C, protein S, tissue factor pathway inhibitor) and impaired thrombolysis from high PAI-1 produce purpura fulminans and skin/limb infarction. Shock results from hypovolemia plus myocardial depression (hypoxia, metabolic derangements such as hypocalcemia, cytokines). Bacteria reaching the meninges provoke a local cytokine-driven inflammatory response that can cause cerebral edema and raised intracranial pressure (p.1247-1248).

Neisseria meningitidis most commonly causes asymptomatic nasopharyngeal colonization; invasive disease is rare and usually presents as either bacterial meningitis or meningococcal septicemia (p.1244).
Immunization is regarded as the only rational approach to prevention at a population level; chemoprophylaxis of close contacts aims to eradicate carriage of the invasive strain (p.1250-1253).

A nonblanching petechial or purpuric rash develops in over 80% of cases, but it is often absent early in the illness and may begin as a blanching maculopapular or urticarial eruption indistinguishable from common viral rashes before becoming petechial/purpuric over hours; some patients, including those with overwhelming sepsis, have no rash at all (p.1248).
In the most severe cases large purpuric lesions develop (purpura fulminans) with signs of peripheral ischemia (p.1248).

Roughly 30-50% present with a meningitis syndrome alone, up to 40% of meningitis patients also have features of septicemia, and meningococcal septicemia alone accounts for up to 20% of cases (p.1248).
In fulminant disease death may occur within hours of the first symptoms; early septicemic symptoms are nonspecific and influenza-like (fever, headache, myalgia, vomiting, abdominal pain) (p.1248).
In children, hypotension is a late sign; they more commonly present with compensated shock (tachycardia, poor peripheral perfusion, normal blood pressure) (p.1248).

Terminal complement component (C5-9), properdin or factor D deficiency, and treatment with complement inhibitors such as eculizumab, increase the risk of meningococcal disease (up to ~600-fold) and may cause recurrent attacks (p.1247).

Chronic meningococcemia is rarely recognized and presents as recurrent episodes of petechial rash with fever, joint pain/arthritis, and splenomegaly, with bacteremia that characteristically clears without treatment then recurs (p.1248-1249).
Tobacco smoking (and passive smoke exposure) is an important risk factor that damages the nasopharyngeal epithelium and increases both carriage and invasive disease (p.1247).
A normal or low WBC count and inflammatory markers do not exclude meningococcal disease and may occur in rapidly progressive disease (p.1249)
The rash may be absent early or absent altogether (including in overwhelming sepsis), and may initially appear blanching/viral before becoming petechial or purpuric (p.1248)

Most patients with a petechial/purpuric rash and fever do NOT have meningococcal disease - fewer than 10% of children (and in some settings under 1%) with this presentation are found to have it, so most have a viral cause (p.1248)

Lumbar puncture should generally be avoided in meningococcal septicemia because positioning may critically compromise circulation in hypovolemic shock; it is also contraindicated with raised intracranial pressure, uncorrected shock, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, respiratory insufficiency, local infection, or ongoing convulsions (p.1249)
A normal CT brain scan does not exclude raised intracranial pressure in meningococcal meningitis (p.1249)

CSF latex agglutination antigen testing and urinary antigen testing are insensitive; throat-swab identification has limited diagnostic value because N. meningitidis is normal nasopharyngeal flora (p.1249)

Postmeningococcal reactive (immune-complex) disease arising ~4-10 days after onset (rash, arthritis, iritis, pericarditis/polyserositis with fever) can be mistaken for relapse and lead to unnecessarily prolonged antibiotics; it resolves spontaneously (p.1249)
Aggressive fluid resuscitation with unbuffered electrolyte solutions was found to increase mortality in febrile African children (p.1249-1250)

About 10% of patients with meningococcal disease die despite antimicrobial therapy and intensive care. Fulminant meningococcemia is more likely to cause death or ischemic skin loss than meningitis alone. Factors associated with poorer prognosis include shock; extremes of age (infancy and old age) and adolescence; coma; purpura fulminans; disseminated intravascular coagulation; thrombocytopenia; leukopenia; absence of meningitis; metabolic acidosis; low antithrombin and protein S/C levels; high PAI-1; and a low ESR or C-reactive protein. The Glasgow Meningococcal Septicaemia Prognostic Score (GMSPS) performs well for severity assessment, though scoring systems do not direct specific interventions; the management priority remains recognition and urgent treatment of compromised airway, breathing, or circulation. Most patients improve rapidly with appropriate antibiotics and supportive care. Complications include scarring after purpuric skin necrosis (~10%, sometimes requiring skin grafting), amputation in 1-2% of survivors after peripheral ischemia or compartment syndrome, hearing loss (~5%), neurologic complications (~7%), chronic pain, and psychological/psychosocial sequelae (p.1249-1250).
A nonblanching (petechial or purpuric) rash in a febrile patient should be treated as a medical emergency suggestive of meningococcal disease (p.1248)
Purpura fulminans / large purpuric lesions with peripheral ischemia (p.1248)
Signs of shock: tachycardia, poor peripheral perfusion, tachypnea, oliguria, cold mottled extremities, limb pain (hypotension is a late sign in children) (p.1248)
Reduced level of consciousness, agitation, or confusion (decreased cerebral perfusion or raised intracranial pressure) (p.1248)
Features of raised intracranial pressure: reduced consciousness, relative bradycardia and hypertension, focal neurologic signs, abnormal posturing, unequal/dilated/poorly reactive pupils (p.1248)
Rapid progression - death may occur within hours of first symptoms in fulminant cases (p.1248)

Clinical spectrum spans asymptomatic nasopharyngeal carriage, occult bacteremia, localized/focal infection (pneumonia, arthritis, osteomyelitis, pericarditis, conjunctivitis), meningitis, and meningococcal septicemia, with chronic meningococcemia as a relapsing form. The Glasgow Meningococcal Septicaemia Prognostic Score (GMSPS) is used for severity assessment. Fulminant meningococcemia with purpura fulminans and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (overwhelming meningococcal sepsis) represents the most severe end of the spectrum (p.1244, p.1248-1249).

chunks.text: The menisci are fibrocartilaginous, wedge-shaped structures that deepen the tibial articular surface, distribute load, absorb shock, and contribute to joint stability and lubrication. A twisting force on a weight-bearing flexed knee shears the meniscus between the femoral and tibial condyles, producing longitudinal, radial, horizontal, or complex tears; a longitudinal tear whose free fragment displaces into the notch forms a bucket-handle lesion that can block extension. With age the meniscal tissue degenerates and tears more readily under low loads. Only the peripheral third has a blood supply capable of healing, so the location of a tear largely determines whether repair or excision is appropriate. Loss of meniscal tissue raises articular contact pressures and predisposes to degenerative change.

chunks.text: Pregnancy as a cause of amenorrhea in perimenopausal women (unintentional pregnancy rate in the forties rivals that of adolescents)
Premature ovarian insufficiency / primary ovarian insufficiency when ovarian failure occurs well before the usual age
Thyroid dysfunction or other endocrine causes of menstrual irregularity and vasomotor-like symptoms
Uterine structural lesions (leiomyomata, endometrial polyps, hyperplasia or carcinoma) presenting as abnormal/heavy bleeding
Other age-related conditions causing midlife mood, sleep, cognitive, or sexual complaints not attributable to ovarian senescence
Menstrual cycle history as the principal STRAW+10 criterion for staging reproductive aging, with biomarkers as supportive criteria
FSH measurement: random level >25 IU/L is characteristic of the late menopausal transition; day-3 levels <20, 20 to <30, and >=30 IU/L indicate good, fair, and poor pregnancy likelihood respectively
Estradiol levels, recognizing that FSH and estradiol are imperfect diagnostic indicators in still-menstruating perimenopausal women due to marked intraindividual variability
Anti-mullerian hormone and inhibin B as additional markers of reproductive aging
Transvaginal ultrasound (with saline enhancement) to detect leiomyomata or polyps when bleeding is abnormal
Endometrial aspiration/biopsy to identify hyperplastic or premalignant changes when menorrhagia or abnormal bleeding occurs
Bone mineral density assessment and FRAX 10-year fracture risk estimation to guide osteoporosis decisions; 25-hydroxyvitamin D level >=50 nmol/L considered sufficient for bone maintenance
Thyroid disease producing vasomotor-like flushing and menstrual change
Anxiety or panic disorder mimicking hot flashes
Endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma presenting as abnormal bleeding rather than physiologic transition
Medication effects or other causes of secondary amenorrhea

Ovarian mass and fertility decline sharply after age 35 and more steeply during perimenopause as the pool of primary follicles, depleting since before birth, runs down. Altered folliculogenesis and reduced inhibin secretion cause FSH to rise; the propensity for anovulatory cycles produces a relatively hyperestrogenic, hypoprogestagenic milieu that may underlie the increased perimenopausal incidence of endometrial hyperplasia/carcinoma, uterine polyps, and leiomyomata. With transition into menopause, estradiol falls markedly while estrone is comparatively preserved through peripheral aromatization of adrenal and ovarian androgens; FSH rises more than LH owing to loss of inhibin plus estrogen feedback. Exogenous estrogen lowers LDL and raises HDL cholesterol by about 10-15% and favorably affects lipoprotein(a), LDL oxidation, and endothelial function, but it also raises triglycerides, promotes coagulation (factor VII, prothrombin fragments, fibrinopeptide A), and elevates C-reactive protein, providing a mechanistic basis for both potential benefits and thrombotic/inflammatory harms.

Menopause is the permanent cessation of menstruation from loss of ovarian follicular function and is diagnosed retrospectively after 12 months of amenorrhea; the average age in U.S. women is about 51 years.
A 1-year absence of spontaneous menses reliably indicates ovulation has ceased, but natural menstrual pattern cannot be assessed while a woman is taking oral contraceptives.

Estrogen reduces bone turnover and resorption; postmenopausal estrogen (with or without a progestogen) increases spine bone density by about 4-6% and hip density by about 2-3%, with WHI showing roughly a 33% reduction in hip fractures.

Unopposed estrogen markedly raises endometrial cancer risk; adding a progestogen opposes this effect and can even reduce endometrial cancer risk, which is why estrogen-only therapy is reserved for women without a uterus.

Perimenopause is the transition preceding menopause when fertility wanes and cycles become irregular, typically beginning 2-8 years before the final menses (mean duration about 4 years); smoking advances the transition by roughly 2 years.

Perimenopause is marked by 'irregularly irregular' hormone levels rather than the consistently high FSH and low estradiol of established menopause; intermenstrual intervals often shorten (by about 3 days) due to an accelerated follicular phase.

FSH rises before LH during the transition, attributed to loss of inhibin and estrogen feedback; after menopause estradiol falls markedly while estrone is relatively preserved through peripheral aromatization of adrenal and ovarian androgens.

Vasomotor symptoms (hot flashes, night sweats), irregular bleeding, and vaginal dryness are strongly attributable to the transition; sleep disturbance has moderate supporting evidence, while mood swings, memory/concentration changes, incontinence, and sexual dysfunction are not clearly caused by ovarian aging alone.
Nearly 60% of women in one U.S. study reported hot flashes in the 2 years before their final menses; symptom intensity, frequency, duration, and quality-of-life impact are highly variable.
Estrogen therapy is the most effective treatment for vasomotor and genitourinary symptoms; randomized trial data suggest hormone therapy reduces menopausal symptoms by roughly 65-90%.

The 'timing hypothesis' holds that estrogen may slow early atherosclerosis but adversely affect advanced lesions, so women initiating hormone therapy early after menopause may differ in cardiovascular outcome from those starting many years later.
Primary prevention of cardiovascular disease should NOT be considered an expected benefit of hormone therapy; an increased stroke risk and a small early increase in coronary risk should be weighed.

Observational studies overstated cardiovascular benefit because women choosing hormone therapy tend to be healthier and more health-conscious (healthy-user confounding); randomized trials did not confirm the benefit.
Relying on a single FSH or estradiol value to diagnose perimenopause in a menstruating woman is unreliable given extreme intraindividual variability.
Prescribing unopposed estrogen to a woman with an intact uterus markedly raises endometrial cancer and atypical hyperplasia risk; a progestogen is needed for endometrial protection.
Attributing midlife mood, cognitive, urinary, or sexual complaints to menopause when evidence does not support ovarian aging as the principal cause.
Counseling should emphasize absolute rather than relative risk measures, since absolute risks rise with age even when relative risks are similar.
Apparent excess breast cancer detection in early hormone therapy users may partly reflect more frequent screening mammography rather than a true biologic effect.
Assuming the cardiovascular and other effects of one formulation/route apply to all, since transdermal estrogen may carry lower thrombotic and gallbladder risk than oral estrogen.

Most peri- and postmenopausal symptoms are self-limited though variable in duration and intensity. In the WHI, many risks and benefits of hormone therapy dissipated within 5-7 years after stopping, though some persisted: with estrogen-progestin an elevated breast cancer risk continued over long follow-up and a reduced hip fracture risk and reduced endometrial cancer risk persisted; with estrogen alone the breast cancer risk reduction became significant on extended follow-up. Estrogen-progestin carried an overall unfavorable global benefit-risk profile that did not vary by 10-year age group, whereas estrogen-only therapy had a roughly neutral profile overall with a more favorable balance in younger women (relative risks for the global index of about 0.84, 0.99, and 1.17 in ages 50-59, 60-69, and 70-79). Over extended follow-up estrogen alone was associated with reduced all-cause mortality in women aged 50-59 (notably those with bilateral oophorectomy), while estrogen-progestin showed elevated breast cancer risk and a suggestion of increased breast cancer mortality.
Unexplained or undiagnosed vaginal bleeding requires evaluation to exclude endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma before attributing it to the transition
An acute coronary event or stroke while on hormone therapy mandates immediate discontinuation of therapy
New or worsening vasomotor symptoms accompanied by features suggesting thromboembolism, given the increased VTE risk with oral estrogen
Heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia) in perimenopause warrants evaluation for uterine disorders rather than assumption of benign cause
Symptoms or signs of estrogen-dependent malignancy in a woman considering or using hormone therapy

The Stages of Reproductive Aging Workshop +10 (STRAW+10) system stages reproductive aging using menstrual cycle characteristics as principal criteria (e.g., persistent >=7-day differences in consecutive cycle length in the early transition; an interval of amenorrhea of >=60 days in the late transition) with endocrine markers (FSH, AMH, inhibin B, antral follicle count) as supportive criteria, spanning reproductive, menopausal transition (perimenopause), and postmenopause stages around the final menstrual period.

Menstrual function depends on coordinated signaling among four compartments - hypothalamus, pituitary, ovary, and uterus/outflow tract - linked by feedback loops involving GnRH, the gonadotropins FSH and LH, and the ovarian products estradiol, progesterone, and the inhibins (inhibin A and B). Disorders divide into outflow-tract/uterine problems and ovulatory disorders. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism arises when anatomic, genetic, or functional disturbances impair hypothalamic GnRH output or pituitary responsiveness, producing low estrogen with normal or low LH/FSH; in functional hypothalamic amenorrhea, energy deficit and stress raise CRH, suppress GnRH, and lower TRH input, with leptin and hypothalamic kisspeptin/neurokinin B/dynorphin signaling transducing metabolic and stress cues to the GnRH pulse generator. Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (ovarian insufficiency) removes negative feedback, raising FSH and LH. In PCOS, abnormal GnRH pulsatility elevates LH and drives ovarian androgen output, and insulin resistance in muscle and fat further augments insulin-stimulated ovarian androgen production; frequent anovulation yields irregular menses and unopposed estrogen effect on the endometrium. Pelvic pain shares mechanisms with abdominal pain - parietal peritoneal inflammation, hollow-viscus obstruction, vascular compromise (e.g., ovarian torsion), and abdominal-wall pain - and may be referred from extrapelvic sources. Primary dysmenorrhea is mediated chiefly by prostaglandin pathways causing intense uterine contractions, reduced blood flow, and peripheral nerve hypersensitivity, with PG-independent mediators such as platelet-activating factor also contributing. Endometriosis reflects ectopic endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus that respond to hormonal stimulation.

Amenorrhea is the absence of menses: primary when bleeding has never occurred without hormonal treatment, secondary when established cycles stop for 3-6 months; primary amenorrhea is rare (<1% of women), whereas roughly 3-5% of women have at least 3 months of secondary amenorrhea in a given year.

Up to 60% of pelvic pain is attributable to gastrointestinal causes (appendicitis, cholecystitis, infection, obstruction, diverticulitis, inflammatory bowel disease); urinary and musculoskeletal disorders are also common, so pelvic pain is frequently not gynecologic in origin.

Beta-hCG normally roughly doubles every 48 h in the early first trimester, and 99% of viable intrauterine pregnancies show at least a 53% rise over 2 days; the discriminatory zone (about 1500-3000 IU/mL) is the level above which a normal intrauterine pregnancy should be visible on ultrasound.

Dysmenorrhea begins with menstrual flow and eases over 12-72 h; primary dysmenorrhea is largely prostaglandin-mediated, while secondary dysmenorrhea reflects underlying pelvic pathology such as endometriosis or adenomyosis.
Pregnancy is the single most common cause of amenorrhea and must be excluded in every case with a beta-hCG, regardless of the history offered.

A normal cycle recurs every 21-35 days, lasts 4-7 days, and involves up to about 80 mL of blood loss; the term abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) has replaced dysfunctional uterine bleeding and is categorized by the PALM-COEIN scheme (structural: polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, malignancy/hyperplasia; non-structural: coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, endometrial, iatrogenic, not yet classified).
Evaluation of ovulatory disorders rests on three initial tests: a pregnancy test, an FSH level (to localize the problem to the ovary versus a central cause), and assessment for hyperandrogenism.

FSH is a better marker of ovarian failure than LH because it reflects loss of negative feedback from both estradiol and the inhibins and is less variable; anti-mullerian hormone (AMH) is also low in primary ovarian insufficiency.

Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea is a diagnosis of exclusion, typically driven by a mismatch between energy expenditure and intake and/or significant stress, with suppressed GnRH, low gonadotropins, and normal prolactin; eating disorders, excessive exercise, and chronic disease must be specifically ruled out.
Isolated hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (IHH) is three times more common in men; about half of affected women have anosmia (Kallmann syndrome), and roughly half have an identifiable genetic cause.

Primary ovarian insufficiency (POI) - the preferred term over premature menopause/ovarian failure - denotes ovarian failure before age 40, accounts for about 10% of secondary amenorrhea, and can wax and wane so serial measurements may be needed.
Roughly up to one-third of women between menarche and menopause experience abnormal uterine bleeding at some point.
Failing to exclude pregnancy before pursuing an amenorrhea or pelvic-pain work-up.
Overlooking infrequent or absent menses because the patient does not volunteer it - a focused menstrual history is needed at every encounter.
Attributing pelvic pain to the reproductive tract when up to 60% of cases are gastrointestinal and urinary/musculoskeletal causes are common.
Waiting for positive microbiology before treating suspected PID - a presumptive clinical diagnosis is sufficient to begin treatment, and negative tests do not exclude it.
Confusing androgen insensitivity syndrome with mullerian agenesis - absent pubic/axillary hair and a male-range testosterone distinguish AIS.

Diagnosing PCOS without excluding mimics (hypothyroidism, hyperprolactinemia, adrenal hyperandrogenism); it is a diagnosis of exclusion, and in adolescents one should wait at least 3 years after menarche and not rely on ultrasound/AMH criteria.
Performing ovarian biopsy in POI - it is not indicated; routine genetic testing beyond FMR1 is also not currently recommended.
Assuming endometriosis severity at laparoscopy correlates with pain - it does not always; a normal CA-125 does not exclude endometriosis.
Delaying surgery for outflow-tract obstruction - early correction reduces the risk of endometriosis from retrograde menstruation.

Outcome depends on cause. Many causes of functional hypothalamic amenorrhea are reversible with restoration of energy balance, though bone density may not fully recover with hormone replacement alone. Amenorrhea of any cause is usually associated with chronically low estrogen, carrying risk to bone and cardiovascular health if untreated. PID untreated risks infertility and ectopic pregnancy, and subclinical PID remains a major worldwide cause of these complications. PCOS carries elevated long-term risk of metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, obstructive sleep apnea, steatotic liver disease, and a two- to sixfold increase in endometrial hyperplasia/cancer from chronic anovulation; symptoms often improve with age, with most women regaining regular menses and normal androgens by the fourth decade. POI is associated with additional health problems and infertility, though oocyte donation has high success. Ectopic pregnancy with tubal rupture can be fatal.
Shock or peritoneal signs in a woman with pelvic pain - identify life-threatening conditions first as they may need emergent surgery
Reproductive-age woman with abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding - maintain high suspicion for ectopic pregnancy regardless of contraceptive use; tubal rupture is a life-threatening emergency
Severe pain with fever and peritoneal signs in PID suggests tubo-ovarian abscess or peritonitis
Right upper quadrant pain in PID suggests perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome)
Acute unilateral intermittent pain raising concern for ovarian torsion (confirm by absent Doppler flow)
Atypical amenorrhea history with headache, signs of hypothalamic dysfunction, short stature, diabetes insipidus, or galactorrhea - evaluate for a neuroanatomic lesion
Heavy or prolonged bleeding warrants prompt attention, but infrequent or absent bleeding is often under-reported and should be actively elicited

Abnormal uterine bleeding is categorized etiologically by the PALM-COEIN system (structural causes: Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy/hyperplasia; non-structural: Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not yet classified). PCOS is diagnosed by the updated Rotterdam criteria (2023 international guidelines): two of three among irregular menses (fewer than 8 per year), clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound (>=20 antral follicles or ovarian volume >=10 cm3 in one ovary) or elevated AMH, yielding hyperandrogenic and non-hyperandrogenic phenotypes. Pelvic pain is classified as acute versus chronic and cyclic versus noncyclic to guide evaluation. Endometriosis is staged by laparoscopy.

Gastrointestinal malignancy (must be excluded in chronic presentations)

Thin-cut (1 mm or thinner) CT angiography is the gold standard for detecting mesenteric arterial occlusive (embolic/thrombotic) disease and for assessing bowel; venous-phase imaging detects mesenteric venous thrombosis with diffuse bowel-wall thickening and splanchnic thrombus (p.2588-2589).

Mesenteric duplex ultrasound is a sensitive/specific screening tool; a high SMA peak flow velocity carries ~80% positive predictive value, and a negative duplex virtually excludes mesenteric ischaemia (test must be done fasting) (p.2588).

Leukocytosis, metabolic acidosis and lactic acidosis support advanced ischaemia but may be absent in reversible ischaemia and cannot reliably distinguish reversible ischaemia from frank necrosis (p.2589).
ECG and echocardiogram may help identify an embolic cardiac source but must not delay surgical therapy (p.2588).
Hypercoagulability workup in suspected mesenteric venous thrombosis (e.g. factor V Leiden, prothrombin mutation, protein C/S or antithrombin deficiency, antiphospholipid syndrome) (p.2587, 2589).
Colonoscopy if ischaemic colitis is suspected, to grade mucosal injury (p.2589).
Acute intestinal obstruction (mechanical or strangulated bowel)
Other noninflammatory causes of abdominal pain such as biliary colic and neoplasia
Inflammatory abdominal conditions: pancreatitis, cholecystitis, appendicitis, diverticulitis, peptic ulcer, inflammatory bowel disease

Intestinal ischaemia occurs when splanchnic perfusion fails to meet the bowel's metabolic demand, producing ischaemic tissue injury. The gut is supplied by the celiac artery, SMA and IMA with extensive collateralisation between major trunks and mesenteric arcades; protective responses include this collateral network, autoregulation of flow and the ability to increase oxygen extraction. Watershed colonic zones with inherently lower flow are Griffiths' point (splenic flexure) and Sudeck's point (descending/sigmoid colon), the commonest sites of colonic ischaemia. The splanchnic bed can receive up to 30% of cardiac output. Occlusive ischaemia results from an embolus or progressive thrombosis in a major mesenteric artery (over 75% of emboli are cardiac in origin and lodge in the SMA distal to the middle colic artery). Chronic intestinal angina generally requires progressive stenosis of two of the three major vessels. Non-occlusive ischaemia is driven by disproportionate mesenteric arteriolar vasospasm in response to severe physiological stress such as shock; untreated, early mucosal stress ulceration progresses to full-thickness injury. Mesenteric venous thrombosis is usually precipitated by a hypercoagulable state. (p.2587-2588)

Severe, acute, non-remitting abdominal pain that is strikingly out of proportion to physical findings is the most common complaint in arterial acute mesenteric ischaemia, present in about 95% of cases; pain precedes signs because ischaemia begins in the mucosa and progresses outward to the serosa (p.2588).

About half of acute mesenteric ischaemia cases are embolic, lodging in the mid-to-distal SMA just past the middle colic artery origin; emboli commonly arise from atrial fibrillation, recent MI, soft atherosclerotic plaque, infective endocarditis, valvular heart disease, or recent cardiac/vascular catheterisation (p.2587).

Acute-on-chronic thrombotic ischaemia (about 25-30% of cases) occurs at sites of severe atherosclerotic narrowing of the SMA or celiac artery, typically in patients with pre-existing mesenteric atherosclerosis who may have had prior chronic mesenteric ischaemia (p.2587, 2588).

Embolic disease is suggested by older patients with a predisposing cardiac source (AF, prior embolic event, recent infective endocarditis), whereas thrombotic disease suggests underlying atherosclerosis with possible prior intestinal angina (p.2588).

Chronic mesenteric ischaemia classically presents as recurrent dull, crampy, postprandial epigastric pain ('intestinal angina') with fear of eating and weight loss; chronic diarrhoea may occur and symptoms typically last 6-12 months before diagnosis (p.2587-2588).

Mesenteric venous thrombosis tends to present more vaguely and subacutely with non-specific abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, distension, mild-to-moderate tenderness and dehydration, making it easy to under-recognise (p.2589).
The decision to operate in suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia is often based on a high index of suspicion from history and examination despite normal laboratory results (p.2588).
Treating pain out of proportion to examination as benign — early ischaemia produces severe pain with deceptively unremarkable abdominal signs because injury starts in the mucosa (p.2588).

Waiting for abnormal labs before acting — lactate and acidosis are late and may be normal in reversible ischaemia or even necrosis; the operative decision is often made on clinical suspicion despite normal results (p.2588-2589).
Overlooking non-occlusive ischaemia in obtunded/critically ill patients where examination findings are absent or obscured by the underlying illness (p.2589).
Missing the vaguer, subacute presentation of mesenteric venous thrombosis (non-specific pain, nausea, distension) (p.2589).
Failing to perform mesenteric duplex while fasting — bowel gas obscures flow and the post-prandial vasodilatory response (p.2588).

Acute mesenteric ischaemia carries a high mortality, roughly 50-80% at presentation (with the acute arterial form quoted at over 50%); it is one of the most challenging diagnoses, and the single most important determinant of survival is the timeliness of diagnosis and treatment. Endovascular stenting for chronic mesenteric ischaemia has about an 80% long-term success rate. (p.2587-2588)
Pain out of proportion to examination with a high-risk cardiac source (AF, recent MI, endocarditis) — embolic acute mesenteric ischaemia until proven otherwise
Later signs of peritonitis and cardiovascular collapse indicate established transmural infarction
Blood per rectum, marked distension or obtundation in a critically ill/shocked patient (suggests non-occlusive ischaemia)
Rising lactate / metabolic acidosis is a late marker and its absence does not exclude ischaemia

Harrison classifies intestinal ischaemia into chronic mesenteric ischaemia (CMI) and acute mesenteric ischaemia (AMI). Acute mesenteric vascular insufficiency is subdivided into (1) arterio-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia — further split into arterial embolus (~50%) and arterial thrombosis (~25-30%, often acute-on-chronic), (2) non-occlusive/vasospastic mesenteric ischaemia (~20%, vasospasm or hypoperfusion), and (3) mesenteric venous thrombosis (<10%). Ischaemic colitis mucosal injury is graded as mild (minimal erythema), moderate (pale ulceration extending into muscularis), or severe (black/green discoloration with full-thickness necrosis). (p.2587-2589)
