The intestine is perfused by the celiac artery, superior mesenteric artery (SMA), and inferior mesenteric artery (IMA), with extensive collateralization through the mesenteric arcades; small-bowel collaterals converge at the duodenum and pancreatic bed, while colonic collaterals meet at the splenic flexure (Griffiths' point) and the descending/sigmoid colon (Sudeck's point), the watershed zones most prone to colonic ischemia. The splanchnic bed can receive up to ~30% of cardiac output, and protective mechanisms include abundant collaterals, autoregulation of flow, and the capacity to increase oxygen extraction. Occlusive ischemia results from embolic or thrombotic interruption of a major mesenteric artery (emboli, originating from the heart in >75% of cases, preferentially lodge in the SMA distal to the middle colic origin); development of chronic intestinal angina generally requires significant stenosis of two of the three major vessels, with SMA involvement most concerning. CMI reflects failure to mount the normal postprandial hyperemic increase in intestinal blood flow, analogous to cardiac angina, due to atherosclerotic narrowing of the SMA and/or celiac origins. Nonocclusive ischemia represents disproportionate mesenteric arteriolar vasospasm in response to severe physiologic stress such as shock; if untreated, early mucosal stress ulceration progresses to full-thickness injury. Mesenteric venous thrombosis arises from inherited or acquired hypercoagulable states (p.2587).

Intestinal ischemia arises when splanchnic perfusion cannot meet the metabolic demands of the gut; it is broadly divided into chronic mesenteric ischemia (CMI) and acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI), with the latter carrying a high mortality (~50-80%) and depending critically on early diagnosis and prompt intervention (p.2586).
Mesenteric venous thrombosis (<10% of cases) tends to be associated with hypercoagulable states; documented inherited thrombophilia warrants long-term anticoagulation (p.2587, p.2588-2589).

Severity of ischemic colonic mucosal injury is graded by colonoscopy from mild (minimal erythema) to moderate (pale ulcerations extending into muscularis) to severe (black/green discoloration indicating full-thickness necrosis) (p.2589).
AMI is mechanistically categorized into three patterns: arterio-occlusive (embolic or thrombotic), nonocclusive (vasospastic/hypoperfusion), and mesenteric venous thrombosis (p.2587).

Roughly half of AMI cases are embolic, with emboli typically lodging in the mid-to-distal superior mesenteric artery (SMA) just beyond the origin of the middle colic artery; about 25-30% are acute-on-chronic thrombosis on preexisting mesenteric atherosclerosis (p.2586-2587).

The hallmark of acute arterial mesenteric ischemia is severe, abrupt, nonremitting abdominal pain that is strikingly out of proportion to physical examination findings, present in roughly 95% of cases (p.2588).
Pain is disproportionate to exam because ischemia begins in the mucosal layer and advances outward toward the serosa, so peritoneal signs and cardiovascular collapse are late developments (p.2588).

CMI classically presents with insidious, recurrent dull crampy postprandial epigastric pain ('intestinal angina'), fear of eating, and consequent weight loss, often over 6-12 months, in a malnourished patient with other signs of atherosclerosis (p.2587).

CT angiography with 1-mm or thinner cuts is the gold-standard diagnostic test for both acute and chronic mesenteric arterial occlusive disease; a venous-phase study aids detection of mesenteric venous thrombosis (p.2587-2588).

Fasting mesenteric duplex ultrasound is a useful screening tool: a high SMA peak flow velocity carries about an 80% positive predictive value, and a negative duplex study virtually excludes mesenteric ischemia (p.2587).

In suspected AMI the decision to operate is frequently driven by a high index of suspicion from history and exam despite normal laboratory values, and surgical consultation should not be delayed (p.2588).
Anchoring on a benign cause and underestimating severity because abdominal pain is markedly out of proportion to a relatively unremarkable exam (p.2588).
Waiting for abnormal laboratory values before acting; lactate, leukocytosis, and acidosis may be normal early or fail to distinguish reversible ischemia from necrosis (p.2588-2589).
Performing mesenteric duplex without fasting, since bowel gas obscures flow and the postprandial vasodilation response (p.2587).
Mistaking ischemic colitis for inflammatory bowel disease (p.2589).
Overlooking nonocclusive ischemia in obtunded, critically ill patients in whom physical findings are obscured by the underlying illness (p.2589).

Failing to recognize that the proximal jejunum may be spared in SMA embolism while the rest of the small bowel to the transverse colon becomes ischemic, leading to incomplete bowel assessment (p.2589).

Acute mesenteric ischemia carries a mortality rate exceeding 50% and is among the most challenging diagnoses; the timeliness of diagnosis and treatment is the single most important determinant of survival. Chronic mesenteric ischemia managed with revascularization has favorable long-term outcomes, with endovascular stenting associated with about an 80% long-term success rate. Outcomes hinge on early recognition before progression to full-thickness bowel necrosis and peritonitis (p.2587-2588).
Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical findings
Blood per rectum / bloody stools
Peritonitis and cardiovascular collapse (late findings indicating advanced ischemia)
Leukocytosis with metabolic/lactic acidosis suggesting advanced ischemia or necrosis
Black or green colonic mucosal discoloration on colonoscopy indicating full-thickness necrosis
Atrial fibrillation, recent myocardial infarction, or infective endocarditis in a patient with acute abdominal pain (embolic source)

Ischemic colonic mucosal injury is graded by colonoscopy: mild = minimal mucosal erythema; moderate = pale mucosal ulcerations with extension into the muscular layer; severe = severe ulcerations with black or green mucosal discoloration consistent with full-thickness bowel-wall necrosis. Mechanically, mesenteric ischemia is classified as chronic (CMI) versus acute (AMI), and AMI is subclassified as arterio-occlusive (embolic or thrombotic), nonocclusive (vasospastic/hypoperfusion), or mesenteric venous thrombosis (p.2587, p.2589).

chunks.text: Delirium reflects diffuse rather than focal brain dysfunction; the attentional deficit localizes broadly to brainstem, thalamus, prefrontal cortex and parietal lobes, and most cases arise from widespread cortical and subcortical disturbance rather than a single lesion. Acetylcholine deficiency is thought to be central (explaining the potency of anticholinergic drugs), with additional roles for excess dopamine, proinflammatory mediators and individual susceptibility. The concept is that of an insult acting on a vulnerable, low-reserve brain. For most metabolic causes (hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperosmolarity, hypercapnia, hypercalcaemia, hepatic and renal failure) the brain shows little or no structural damage and the effects are largely reversible, attributed to impaired energy supply, altered ion fluxes across neuronal membranes and neurotransmitter abnormalities. In hepatic encephalopathy, raised ammonia is proposed to drive astrocytic glutamine synthesis and osmotic swelling, mitochondrial energy failure, reactive nitrogen/oxygen species, increased inhibitory GABA tone and 'false' neurotransmitters, with chronic disease producing diffuse astrocytosis. Uraemic encephalopathy is multifactorial (urea itself is not the cause): accumulated neurotoxins, catecholamine depletion, altered glutamate/GABA tone, raised brain calcium and blood-brain-barrier disruption. Importantly, the degree of neurologic change in metabolic encephalopathies depends heavily on the rapidity with which the serum derangement develops, not just its absolute level. In sepsis-associated encephalopathy, circulating inflammatory mediators (TNF, IL-1, IL-2, IL-6) appear to cause diffuse cerebral dysfunction that is not simply explained by the metabolic derangements of organ failure (p.183, p.188-189, p.2348-2349).

chunks.text: Once viewed as benign and transient, delirium is now recognized as a marker of serious illness with substantial morbidity and mortality: in-hospital mortality is roughly 25-33% (similar to sepsis), and delirious patients have about a fivefold higher mortality in the ensuing months versus matched non-delirious inpatients, plus longer stays, more nursing-home discharge, higher readmission and recurrent episodes. Most metabolic and toxic encephalopathies are reversible with no or minimal structural brain damage, and drug/toxin-induced coma typically resolves fully provided hypoxia or severe hypotension has not occurred. However, some episodes persist for weeks to months or longer, delirium can cause lasting cognitive decline, and lingering effects (ranging from amnesia for the episode to PTSD-like re-experiencing) are common. Sepsis-associated encephalopathy severe enough to cause coma carries a mortality approaching 50%, though this mainly reflects severity of the underlying critical illness rather than the encephalopathy itself (p.182, p.188-189, p.2349).

chunks.text: Methanol is oxidised by alcohol dehydrogenase to formaldehyde, which is rapidly converted by aldehyde dehydrogenase to formic acid. Formic acid is the principal toxin: it inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase, causing cellular hypoxia and lactate accumulation, and produces a profound high anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Formate is directly toxic to the retina and optic nerve, causing oedema and demyelination that can lead to irreversible blindness, and can injure the basal ganglia (putaminal necrosis). Because the parent alcohol elevates serum osmolality, an early osmolal gap precedes the later anion-gap acidosis.

chunks.text: Migraine is understood as a brain disorder of sensory processing rather than a primary vascular disease. The characteristic sensory sensitivity is attributed to dysfunction of monoaminergic and other sensory-control systems in the brainstem and hypothalamus. The key nociceptive pathway is the trigeminovascular system: trigeminal innervation of large intracranial vessels and dura, with terminals that, when activated, release vasoactive neuropeptides - notably calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP) - at vascular terminals and within the trigeminal nucleus. Second-order neurons of the trigeminocervical complex (caudal trigeminal nucleus extending into the upper cervical dorsal horns, receiving C1-C2 input) decussate and project via the quintothalamic tract to ventrobasal and posterior thalamic nuclei, with additional projections to periaqueductal gray and hypothalamus that exert descending antinociceptive modulation; the dorsal raphe nucleus, locus coeruleus, parabrachial nucleus and rostroventromedial medulla are implicated in this modulation. Serotonin (5-HT) is involved - triptans are 5-HT1B/1D agonists (some also 5-HT1F) and ditans are selective 5-HT1F agonists - and dopamine contributes, with dopamine-receptor hypersensitivity in migraineurs. Functional imaging shows hypothalamic activation in the premonitory phase and persistent dorsolateral pontine (including locus coeruleus) activation during attacks and in chronic migraine, with lateralization correlating with the side of head pain. Genetic study of familial hemiplegic migraine implicates ion channels (CACNA1A/Cav2.1 P/Q calcium channel in FHM1 ~50%; ATP1A2 Na-K ATPase in FHM2 ~20%; SCN1A sodium channel in FHM3), suggesting altered membrane excitability predisposes to aura. The slowly advancing visual scotoma with luminous (fortification) edges is recognized as a marker of spreading cortical depression associated with migraine (p.3462-3464, p.3379).

chunks.text: Patients should understand that migraine is an inherited tendency to headache that can be modified and controlled by lifestyle measures and medication but not eradicated. Except on some occasions in women taking oral estrogens or contraceptives, migraine is not associated with serious or life-threatening illness (p.3464). Migraine is nonetheless the most common neurologic cause of disability worldwide (p.3462). Recognized complications (ICHD-3) include status migrainosus, persistent aura without infarction, migrainous infarction, and migraine aura-triggered seizure; migraine may also progress to chronic migraine (Table 441-1, p.3463). Overuse of acute analgesics can transform episodic migraine into refractory medication-overuse headache; many patients improve after withdrawal, though residual headache often persists reflecting the underlying primary disorder (p.115-116).

chunks.text: Miliaria results from obstruction of the eccrine sweat ducts, which causes sweat to leak into the surrounding skin rather than reach the surface. Keratin plugging of the duct, often aggravated by an overgrowth of skin flora producing occlusive material, blocks flow at varying levels. The level of the block determines the clinical form: obstruction within the stratum corneum causes the superficial vesicles of crystallina, blockage within the epidermis produces the inflammatory papulovesicles of rubra, and obstruction at the dermo-epidermal junction gives the deeper papules of profunda. The extravasated sweat provokes local inflammation and the sensation of prickling, while widespread duct blockage can compromise thermoregulation.

Post-infectious or membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
Lupus nephritis
Congenital nephrotic syndrome (in infants)
Secondary nephrotic syndrome (e.g. Henoch-Schonlein, infection-related)
Urinalysis and quantification of proteinuria (protein:creatinine ratio or 24-hour protein)
Serum albumin, lipid profile, and renal function
Serum complement (C3, C4)
Autoimmune serology when secondary causes are suspected
Assessment for infection and, in selected cases, screening for thrombosis
Renal biopsy in atypical presentations or steroid resistance

A poorly understood immune dysregulation, involving circulating permeability factors and T-cell mediated signalling, injures the glomerular podocytes. On light microscopy the glomeruli appear normal, but electron microscopy reveals diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes. Loss of the size- and charge-selective filtration barrier permits massive albumin leakage into the urine, producing hypoalbuminaemia, reduced oncotic pressure, oedema, and compensatory hepatic lipoprotein synthesis causing hyperlipidaemia.
Minimal change disease accounts for the large majority of idiopathic nephrotic syndrome in children, most commonly presenting between about 1 and 6 years of age.
The defining features are heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, and hyperlipidaemia.
Oedema is typically dependent and periorbital and can progress to generalised swelling with ascites and pleural effusions.
Most children are steroid-responsive, and a favourable response to corticosteroids is both diagnostic and therapeutic in the typical age group.

Renal biopsy is generally reserved for atypical features such as age under 1 or over 10 years, persistent hypertension, gross haematuria, low complement, impaired renal function, or steroid resistance.
Children are at increased risk of infection, particularly spontaneous bacterial peritonitis from encapsulated organisms, because of urinary immunoglobulin losses.
A hypercoagulable state develops from urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins, increasing the risk of venous and arterial thrombosis.
Relapses are common, and some children become frequent relapsers or steroid-dependent, requiring steroid-sparing agents.
Missing spontaneous bacterial peritonitis because ascitic signs can be subtle in an oedematous child
Overlooking thrombosis risk during periods of heavy proteinuria and diuresis
Assuming all childhood nephrotic syndrome is minimal change and delaying biopsy in atypical cases
Over-diuresing and precipitating hypovolaemia in a child with low intravascular volume

Children with steroid-sensitive minimal change disease generally have an excellent long-term renal prognosis, though many experience relapses over several years before remitting; steroid-resistant disease, often reflecting focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, carries a higher risk of progression to chronic kidney disease.
Signs of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (fever, abdominal pain, tenderness)
Features of venous or arterial thrombosis, including limb swelling, respiratory compromise, or neurological signs
Hypovolaemic shock during aggressive diuresis
Severe respiratory distress from large pleural effusions or ascites
Steroid resistance or deteriorating renal function suggesting a more aggressive lesion

Aortic stenosis (basally-radiating MR murmur from posterior leaflet prolapse/flail can be confused with AS) (p.2054)
Mitral stenosis (a brief early-diastolic LA-LV gradient with rapid filling sound and mid-diastolic rumble in pure severe MR can masquerade as MS) (p.2053-2054)
Ventricular septal defect and other causes of a holosystolic murmur

Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) with Doppler to define mechanism and severity (jet width/area, regurgitant volume, regurgitant fraction, effective regurgitant orifice area, LV volumes/EF, LA/LV size, chordal integrity, annular calcification) (p.2053)
Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) for greater anatomic detail (p.2053-2054)
Estimation of pulmonary artery systolic pressure from the tricuspid regurgitation jet velocity (p.2053)
Exercise (stress) echocardiography to assess exercise capacity and dynamic change in MR severity, PA pressures, and biventricular function when clinical and resting findings disagree (p.2053)
Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) for quantitative regurgitant measures when TTE is discordant or insufficient (noted as not widely available) (p.2052-2053)
ECG (LA enlargement, possible RA enlargement with pulmonary hypertension, AF, eccentric LVH) (p.2053)
Chest X-ray (LA/LV enlargement, pulmonary venous congestion, Kerley B lines, mitral/annular calcification; asymmetric pulmonary edema possible in acute MR) (p.2053-2054)
Left and right heart catheterization with contrast ventriculography and coronary angiography when noninvasive findings are discrepant or to identify coronary disease before surgery (p.2053, p.2056)

MR can arise from disease of any of the five components of the mitral apparatus: leaflets, annulus, chordae tendineae, papillary muscles, and subjacent myocardium (p.2052). MR reduces resistance to LV emptying (lowers afterload); the LV decompresses into the LA during ejection, so initial compensation is more complete LV emptying. Over time LV volume rises as regurgitation worsens and contractile function deteriorates, and forward cardiac output falls; LV compliance is often increased so LV diastolic pressure does not rise until late (p.2052-2053). The regurgitant volume varies directly with LV systolic pressure and the size of the regurgitant orifice (influenced by LV and annular dilation and leaflet morphology). LA compliance governs the clinical picture: in acute severe MR the regurgitant volume enters a normal-sized, noncompliant LA so LA and pulmonary venous pressures rise sharply with a prominent v wave and pulmonary edema is common; in chronic severe MR the LA enlarges and becomes more compliant, buffering pressure so pulmonary congestion is initially less prominent and fatigue from low forward output predominates (p.2053). Chronic secondary MR results from annular dilation, ventricular remodeling, papillary muscle displacement, and leaflet tethering (e.g., after MI, in dilated cardiomyopathy once LV end-diastolic dimension reaches ~6 cm, or atrial functional MR from chronic AF with annular dilation) (p.2052).

Distinguish primary (degenerative) MR, where the leaflets and/or chordae are themselves abnormal, from secondary (functional) MR, where leaflets and chordae are usually normal and regurgitation is driven by LV/LA remodeling, annular dilation, papillary muscle displacement, dyssynchrony, or leaflet tethering; assessment, treatment, and prognosis differ significantly between the two (p.2052).
With post-MI papillary muscle rupture the posteromedial papillary muscle is involved far more often than the anterolateral muscle because of its single blood supply (p.2052).
The characteristic murmur of chronic severe MR is a holosystolic, plateau-configuration systolic murmur of at least grade III/VI, most prominent at the apex and radiating to the axilla (p.2053-2054).

Murmur radiation reflects jet direction: with posterior leaflet prolapse/flail the eccentric anteriorly-directed jet strikes the LA wall near the aortic root and the murmur radiates to the base (can mimic aortic stenosis), whereas anterior leaflet prolapse/flail directs the jet and murmur toward the axilla (p.2054).
Ruptured chordae tendineae may give the systolic murmur a cooing or 'seagull' quality; a flail leaflet may produce a musical murmur (p.2054).
The murmur of chronic MR not due to MVP is intensified by isometric handgrip and reduced during the strain phase of Valsalva (decreased LV preload) (p.2054).

In acute severe MR the murmur is early in timing and decrescendo, ending well before S2, reflecting the rapidly rising LA pressure and diminishing LV-LA gradient — in contrast to the holosystolic plateau murmur of chronic MR (p.2053-2054).
Because EF rises in severe MR when LV function is normal, even a modest fall in EF (below 60%) reflects significant contractile dysfunction (p.2052-2053).
Atrial fibrillation is almost invariably present once the LA dilates significantly in chronic severe MR; LA enlargement and AF support the diagnosis on ECG (p.2053).
'MR begets MR': LA enlargement tensions the posterior leaflet pulling it away from the orifice, and LV dilation increases regurgitation, enlarging LA and LV further in a vicious cycle (p.2052).
In secondary MR the severity can be underappreciated by echocardiographic/Doppler techniques, and lesser degrees of regurgitation may carry relatively greater prognostic weight (p.2053).
An S3 in MR may reflect rapid LV filling, but in ischemic or dilated cardiomyopathy an S3 may instead signify ventricular dysfunction (p.2054).
Because EF is artifactually elevated in severe MR with normal myocardium, a 'low-normal' EF may already represent meaningful contractile dysfunction (p.2052-2053).

Routine surgical valve repair for significant secondary MR due to dilated cardiomyopathy has NOT been shown to improve long-term survival versus optimal guideline-directed medical therapy, especially in the era of quadruple HFrEF therapy (p.2056).
Direct oral anticoagulants should NOT be used if moderate or severe rheumatic mitral stenosis coexists, and are NOT approved for mechanical prosthetic valves (p.2055).
A presystolic murmur is not ordinarily heard with isolated MR (p.2054).

Chronic mild-to-moderate isolated MR is well tolerated and usually asymptomatic. Chronic severe MR tends to be progressive ('MR begets MR') and, when secondary, severity correlates inversely with prognosis, with adverse outcome tied to the degree of LV remodeling and myocardial dysfunction (p.2052-2053). With surgery, repair carries substantially lower risk than replacement; a 2023 STS database analysis reported mean perioperative mortality of about 1.16% (under 0.5% in patients younger than 65) for repair of primary MR, durable repair is feasible in up to 95% of degenerative cases at high-volume centers, and reoperation runs about 1% per year over the first 10 years. In ischemic MR with severely impaired LV function (EF below 30%), surgical risk is higher, recovery of LV performance is incomplete, and long-term survival is reduced (p.2055-2056).

Acute severe MR is a surgical emergency: papillary muscle rupture post-MI or leaflet destruction/perforation in infective endocarditis can cause sudden pulmonary edema and hemodynamic collapse, requiring urgent stabilization and emergent surgery (p.2052, p.2055-2056)
Acute pulmonary edema, hypotension with narrow pulse pressure, and prominent signs of pulmonary congestion with a non-displaced apex point to acute severe MR (p.2053)
Onset of palpitations or atrial fibrillation in chronic severe MR (p.2053)

Late-onset right heart failure with hepatic congestion, ankle edema, distended neck veins, ascites, and secondary tricuspid regurgitation, indicating pulmonary vascular disease and pulmonary hypertension (p.2053)
Falling LVEF (to 60% or below) or rising LV end-systolic dimension (40 mm or more), even when asymptomatic, signals contractile dysfunction warranting surgical referral (p.2053, p.2056)

Chronic severe MR (Doppler/CMR quantitative criteria) is defined by a regurgitant volume of at least 60 mL/beat, regurgitant fraction of at least 50%, and effective regurgitant orifice area of at least 0.40 cm2 (p.2053). ACC/AHA disease staging (Stages B, C1, C2, D) is applied: Stage C is asymptomatic severe MR (C1 normal LV systolic function with LVEF above 60% and ESD below 40 mm; C2 LV systolic dysfunction with LVEF at or below 60% or ESD at or above 40 mm) and Stage D is symptomatic severe MR (p.2054-2055).
Mitral Regurgitation (non-infective) — Cardiology Also: MR
Mitral regurgitation (may have an apical diastolic flow murmur, but it begins slightly later, S1 is soft or absent, and there is no opening snap; LV enlargement is common) (p.2049)
Severe aortic regurgitation with an Austin Flint murmur (apical mid-diastolic murmur not intensified in presystole and softened by amyl nitrite/arterial vasodilators) (p.2049)
Tricuspid stenosis (rare without MS; its diastolic murmur increases with inspiration and the jugular venous y descent is delayed) (p.2049-2050)
Atrial septal defect (RV enlargement and increased pulmonary vascularity, but no LA enlargement or Kerley B lines, with fixed splitting of S2) (p.2050)
Left atrial myxoma (obstructs LA emptying causing a positional diastolic murmur; often with systemic features such as weight loss, fever, anemia, emboli, elevated IgG/IL-6) (p.2050)
Infective endocarditis with large vegetations is itself a recognized (uncommon) cause of left ventricular inflow obstruction mimicking MS (p.2048)

Transthoracic echocardiography with color flow and spectral Doppler for mitral inflow velocities, peak/mean gradients, mitral orifice area, leaflet calcification and restriction, and suitability for percutaneous mitral balloon commissurotomy (p.2049)
Transesophageal echocardiography when TTE is inadequate, and specifically to exclude left atrial thrombus before commissurotomy (p.2049)
Exercise (stress) echocardiography to assess mean mitral diastolic gradient, PA pressures, and RV function when clinical and resting hemodynamic findings are discrepant (p.2049)
ECG showing left atrial enlargement (P-wave changes), and right axis deviation/RV hypertrophy when severe pulmonary hypertension supervenes (p.2049)

Chest X-ray showing straightening of the left cardiac border, prominent main PAs, upper-lobe pulmonary venous dilation, an enlarged LA, and Kerley B lines when mean LA pressure exceeds about 20 mmHg (p.2049)
Left and right heart catheterization when clinical and noninvasive findings are discrepant; CT coronary angiography to screen for coronary disease before valve surgery (p.2050)
Congenital mitral valve stenosis (parachute valve, cor triatriatum) (p.2048)
Severe mitral annular calcification with extension onto the leaflets (p.2048)
Systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis involving the valve (p.2048)
Left atrial myxoma (p.2048)

In normal adults the mitral valve orifice area is 4-6 cm2. Significant obstruction occurs when the orifice is reduced to less than about 2 cm2, so blood can only flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle if propelled by an abnormally elevated left atrioventricular pressure gradient, the hemodynamic hallmark of MS. When the orifice is below 1.5 cm2 (severe MS), an LA pressure of about 25 mmHg is required to maintain normal cardiac output. Elevated pulmonary venous and PA wedge pressures reduce pulmonary compliance and cause exertional dyspnea. Because tachycardia shortens diastole proportionately more than systole, an increased heart rate (including rapid AF) augments the transvalvular gradient and further elevates LA pressure. Chronic LA pressure elevation leads to LA enlargement, predisposing to AF and to thrombus formation (particularly in the LA appendage) with risk of systemic embolization. Pulmonary hypertension develops from passive backward transmission of elevated LA pressure, reactive pulmonary arteriolar constriction (the so-called second stenosis), interstitial edema of small pulmonary vessels, and, at end stage, obliterative pulmonary vascular changes; severe pulmonary hypertension produces RV enlargement, secondary tricuspid and pulmonic regurgitation, and right-sided heart failure (p.2048-2049).
Rheumatic fever is the leading cause of mitral stenosis; pure or predominant MS occurs in roughly 40% of patients with rheumatic heart disease and a history of rheumatic fever (p.2048).
Although declining in temperate, middle- to high-income climates, MS remains a major problem in low-income countries, especially sub-Saharan Africa, India, Southeast Asia, and Oceania (p.2048).

Auscultation classically reveals an accentuated first heart sound (S1), an opening snap (OS) of the mitral valve heard best in expiration at or just medial to the apex, followed by a low-pitched rumbling diastolic murmur heard best at the apex in the left lateral recumbent position (p.2049).
The A2-to-opening-snap interval varies inversely with severity of MS: a shorter interval indicates more severe stenosis (p.2049).
In patients in sinus rhythm, the diastolic murmur often reappears or becomes louder during atrial systole (presystolic accentuation) (p.2049).
Development of persistent atrial fibrillation often marks a turning point in the patient's course and is associated with acceleration of symptom progression (p.2048).

Echocardiography (TTE with Doppler) provides mitral orifice area, transvalvular gradients, leaflet calcification/restriction, and suitability for percutaneous mitral balloon commissurotomy; TEE is especially indicated to exclude LA thrombus before intervention (p.2049).
Mitral valve area 1-1.5 cm2 denotes severe MS; an LA pressure of about 25 mmHg is needed to maintain normal cardiac output when the orifice falls below 1.5 cm2 (p.2048-2049).
When cardiac output is markedly reduced, the typical auscultatory findings including the diastolic rumble may be undetectable (silent MS) and may reappear only as compensation is restored (p.2049)
Systemic embolization may be the presenting feature in otherwise asymptomatic patients with only mild MS (p.2049)
The Graham Steell murmur of pulmonic regurgitation can be indistinguishable from aortic regurgitation, though it may increase with inspiration and is accompanied by a loud, often palpable P2 (p.2049)
A history of rheumatic carditis is increasingly rare and often cannot be elicited (p.2048)

In temperate climates the latent period between the initial attack of rheumatic carditis and symptomatic MS is generally about two decades, with disability typically beginning in the fourth decade. Historical studies before surgical valvotomy showed that once a patient became seriously symptomatic, the disease progressed inexorably to death within 2-5 years. Onset of persistent AF generally marks acceleration of symptom progression (p.2048).
Atrial fibrillation, which accelerates symptom progression and markedly increases thromboembolic risk (p.2048)
Systemic embolization (incidence 10-20%), more frequent with AF, age over 65, and reduced cardiac output; may be the presenting feature even in mild MS (p.2049)
Hemoptysis from rupture of pulmonary-bronchial venous connections due to pulmonary venous hypertension (p.2048)
Pulmonary hypertension and right-sided heart failure (hepatomegaly, ankle edema, ascites, pleural effusion) (p.2048-2049)
Recurrent pulmonary emboli, sometimes with infarction, an important late cause of morbidity and mortality (p.2048)
Decompensation precipitated by tachycardia, fever, severe anemia, paroxysmal AF, thyrotoxicosis, exertion, or pregnancy (p.2048)

In pregnancy, increased blood volume, cardiac output, and tachycardia can raise the transmitral gradient and cause pulmonary edema or tachyarrhythmias, with the immediate postpartum period a time of particular concern due to rapid volume shifts (p.3900)

Severity is graded by mitral valve area. The normal orifice is 4-6 cm2; significant obstruction begins below about 2 cm2. A valve area below 1.5 cm2 is termed severe MS (with an LA pressure of about 25 mmHg required to maintain normal cardiac output), and an area below 1 cm2 is very severe, at which cardiac output is subnormal at rest. Echocardiographic measurement of mitral orifice area and transvalvular gradient is the basis for grading; commissurotomy is generally indicated for symptomatic patients with valve area below about 1 cm2/m2 body surface area or below 1.5 cm2 in normal-sized adults (p.2048-2051).
Mitral Stenosis (non-infective) — Cardiology Also: MS
Other causes of primary mitral regurgitation
Rheumatic mitral valve disease (chordae thickened but not fused in MVP, unlike rheumatic disease)
Innocent or functional systolic murmurs
Angina pectoris (when atypical chest pain is present)
ECG (often normal; may show biphasic or inverted T waves in leads II, III, aVF and supraventricular or ventricular premature beats)
Transthoracic echocardiography to identify abnormal leaflet position and prolapse and define the >=2 mm displacement criterion
Color flow and continuous-wave Doppler to assess associated MR and estimate severity
Three-dimensional echocardiography and cardiac MRI for more precise LV volumes and detection of papillary muscle fibrosis/late gadolinium enhancement
Transesophageal echocardiography when detailed anatomy is needed and for intraoperative or transcatheter procedural guidance
Exercise testing (often with rest and immediate poststress TTE) to assess functional capacity, LV/RV function, dynamic MR, and pulmonary pressures
Left ventriculography during catheterization (rarely necessary)

MVP results from myxomatous degeneration of the mitral valve apparatus with excessive or redundant leaflet tissue and markedly increased glycosaminoglycan content. In many cases the cause is unknown, but some forms are genetically determined; reduced type III collagen production has been implicated, and electron microscopy shows fragmentation of collagen fibrils. Genome-wide association work has identified multiple genetic loci (candidate genes include LMCD1, SPTBN1, LTBP2, TGFB2, NMB, and ALPK3), and associations with LMNA, FLNC, and FLNA that are often expressed as cardiomyopathies. The posterior leaflet is typically more affected, the annulus is often dilated, and elongated, redundant, or ruptured chordae contribute to regurgitation. Prolapse may impose excessive stress on the papillary muscles, producing localized ischemia, infarction, and replacement fibrosis that can serve as a nidus for ventricular arrhythmias (visible as late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac MRI even without coronary disease). Chordal rupture along with progressive annular dilation and calcification worsen regurgitation, placing further stress on the diseased apparatus in a self-perpetuating cycle (p.2057-2058).

MVP is a clinically variable syndrome arising from diverse pathologic mechanisms affecting the mitral valve apparatus, commonly excessive or redundant leaflet tissue associated with myxomatous degeneration and increased glycosaminoglycan concentrations (p.2057).
Most patients are asymptomatic and remain so for life; the disease may progress slowly over years to decades or worsen abruptly from chordal rupture or endocarditis (p.2058).
MVP can occur as a rare sequel to acute rheumatic fever, in ischemic heart disease, in various cardiomyopathies, and in about 20% of patients with ostium secundum atrial septal defect (p.2058).

It is the most common abnormality leading to primary mitral regurgitation and to mitral valve repair surgery, and in North America is now the most common cause of isolated severe MR requiring surgery (p.2057-2058).

MVP is more common in women than men and typically presents between ages 15 and 30 with a generally benign course; in older patients (>50 years, often men) MR tends to be more severe because of chordal rupture (p.2058).

The posterior leaflet is usually more affected than the anterior, the annulus is often dilated, and elongated, redundant, or ruptured chordae tendineae frequently cause or contribute to regurgitation (p.2058).

The hallmark auscultatory finding is a mid- or late nonejection systolic click occurring 0.14 s or more after S1, often followed by a high-pitched mid-late systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur best heard at the apex, sometimes described as whooping or honking (p.2058).

Dynamic auscultation aids diagnosis: standing, the strain phase of Valsalva, and any maneuver decreasing LV volume make the click and murmur occur earlier, whereas squatting and isometric exercise (increasing LV volume) delay the click-murmur complex and may make it disappear (p.2058).

Murmur radiation depends on the leaflet involved: posterior leaflet prolapse directs the jet anteriorly with radiation toward the base, while anterior leaflet involvement directs the jet posteriorly with radiation to the axilla and back (p.2058).

A useful echocardiographic definition is systolic displacement of the belly of the mitral leaflets by at least 2 mm into the left atrium above the plane of the mitral annulus in the parasternal long-axis view (p.2058).
Chest pain in MVP is often substernal, prolonged, and unrelated to exertion, and only rarely resembles angina pectoris (p.2058).
Relying on a static exam can miss MVP; the click and murmur are dynamic and shift with maneuvers that alter LV volume (Valsalva/standing exaggerate, squatting/isometrics diminish them).
Presentations vary: some patients have a mid-systolic click without a murmur, others a murmur without a click, and still others both at different times.
The eccentric MR jet typical of MVP makes effective regurgitant orifice area and regurgitant volume difficult to assess with standard techniques.
Atypical, prolonged, non-exertional chest pain may be misattributed to coronary disease and is often difficult to evaluate.
Sudden death and significant arrhythmias can occur even in patients with normal LV size and function, so apparently low-risk patients are not entirely without risk.

The clinical course is most often benign, and the majority of patients remain asymptomatic for their entire lives. In many the condition progresses gradually over years to decades, while in others it worsens rapidly from chordal rupture or endocarditis. Sudden death is a very rare complication, occurring most often with severe MR and depressed LV systolic function but possible even with normal LV size and function; a small high-risk subset has high-grade ventricular ectopy with characteristic imaging features, and patients with a flail leaflet carry an excess sudden-death risk (p.2058).
Severe MR with depressed LV systolic function (highest risk for sudden death)
Flail leaflet, which carries an excess risk of sudden death and usually accompanies severe MR
High-grade ventricular ectopy with inferior-apical T-wave abnormalities, high-density premature ventricular complexes at rest, mitral annular disjunction, and papillary muscle fibrosis on cardiac MRI
Syncope or light-headedness from arrhythmias
Transient ischemic attacks from emboli due to endothelial disruption on the valve
Features suggesting infective endocarditis in patients with MR and/or leaflet thickening

Severity is anchored on the associated mitral regurgitation, ranging from a benign isolated systolic click with mild posterior-leaflet prolapse to severe MR from chordal rupture and leaflet flail. Echocardiographic prolapse is defined as >=2 mm systolic displacement of the leaflet belly into the left atrium above the annular plane (parasternal long-axis), with Doppler used to grade MR severity (p.2058).

chunks.text: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a poxvirus (molluscum contagiosum virus) that replicates within epidermal keratinocytes. The virus induces localised proliferation of the epidermis and produces large intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies (Henderson-Paterson bodies) packed with viral particles, which form the soft core expressed from the umbilicated centre. The virus encodes proteins that dampen the local host immune response, allowing lesions to persist; eventual immune recognition produces the inflammatory reaction that precedes clearance. Transmission is by direct contact, fomites, and autoinoculation, and impaired cell-mediated immunity permits widespread or atypical disease.

Nucleic acid (molecular) testing is the most common diagnostic tool: PCR assays for non-variola orthopoxvirus (NVO), orthopoxvirus generic, generic mpox, and mpox clade II; sequencing for full isolate characterization (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Multiplex assays combining NVO- and MPXV-specific targets, and clade-specific testing (U.S. Government and Public Health Laboratories), are available (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Viral culture: orthopoxviruses grow well in standard clinical tissue culture; parapoxviruses are difficult to isolate (primary cells best); MCV cannot be cultured (Harrison 22e p.1519).

Electron microscopy: characteristic large brick-shaped particles on negative stain for orthopoxvirus, yatapoxvirus, or MCV; parapoxviruses show an ovoid structure with crisscross spicules (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Histopathology of biopsy: MCV shows classic Henderson-Patterson bodies (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Serology can demonstrate orthopoxvirus reactivity but most assays cannot distinguish between orthopoxvirus species due to broad antigenic similarity (Harrison 22e p.1519).

Poxviruses are large double-stranded DNA viruses that replicate entirely in the cytoplasm. Orthopoxvirus infection (variola, MPXV) is thought to involve systemic spread from the inoculation site to local lymph nodes, seeding of lymphoreticular tissue, and then symptomatic (febrile) viremia with viral skin tropism; disease severity reflects how well innate immune and interferon responses control early infection. Immunocompetent hosts develop lesions (often at the exposure site) about 1 week after exposure, progressing through staged phases over 7-14 days with scabbing and resolution by 14-21 days after rash onset. In severe immunocompromise (e.g., advanced HIV with CD4 <200 cells/mm3, organ transplantation), MPXV spread/growth goes unchecked, producing wide dissemination with large confluent lesions persisting for months and additional organ involvement. Most other poxvirus infections (e.g., parapoxviruses, MCV) involve only local viral growth at the inoculation site; yatapoxvirus (tanapox) pathogenesis is poorly understood (Harrison 22e p.1518).
Classic mpox/smallpox prodrome: fever first, followed days later by rash; other prodromal features include malaise, sore throat, and headache (Harrison 22e p.1519).

Two distinct MPXV clades exist: Clade I (formerly Congo Basin, Central Africa) causes a higher proportion of severe disease than Clade II (formerly West African); Clade II subdivides into IIa (endemic West Africa) and IIb (spread worldwide in 2022) (Harrison 22e p.1517).
Lymphadenopathy is a key historical feature distinguishing mpox (present) from smallpox (absent) in endemic countries (Harrison 22e p.1519).

Classic systemic orthopoxvirus rash evolves through macular, papular, vesicular, and pustular phases (the pustular stage with central umbilication), each stage lasting 2-3 days, with lesions in the same anatomic location typically at the same stage of development (Harrison 22e p.1519).

Classic distribution is diffuse, well-circumscribed, and centrifugal: lesions more prominent on face and extremities (including palms and soles) than on the trunk; lesions are painful as they emerge and become pruritic in later stages (Harrison 22e p.1519).

In the 2022 clade IIb outbreak, transmission was primarily through close, intimate (e.g., sexual) contact and predominantly affected gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (MSM) (Harrison 22e p.1518).

Clade IIb mpox often departed from the classic picture: rash was frequently the first or only sign (prodrome absent or concurrent), lesions were often localized to the anogenital region, smaller, fewer (often <10), and could be at different stages at the same anatomic site (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Up to 50% of those diagnosed during the 2022 outbreak in the U.S. context were also living with HIV (Harrison 22e p.1518).

Molluscum contagiosum (MCV) has a classic pearly appearance that may umbilicate as it matures, with little surrounding inflammation and painless lesions that persist for months but gradually regress over 6-12 months (Harrison 22e p.1519).

The infectious period for orthopoxvirus infections lasts from symptom onset until all lesions have crusted, the crusts have separated, and fresh healthy skin has formed underneath; lesion scabs contain viable virus (Harrison 22e p.1518).

Do not assume a classic systemic presentation: during the 2022 clade IIb outbreak rash was often the first/only sign with prodrome absent, lesions localized to the anogenital area, smaller, fewer (<10), and could be at different stages at the same site - contrary to the classic rule that lesions in the same location are at the same stage (Harrison 22e p.1519).

Anogenital mpox lesions can be mistaken for common STIs (gonorrhea, chlamydia, syphilis); up to 10% of mpox patients may be coinfected with an STI, so a positive STI test does not exclude mpox (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Characteristic lesions plus exposure history narrow the differential, but laboratory testing is required to confirm the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Distinguish mpox from varicella (VZV), herpes simplex, and syphilis - overlapping vesiculopustular/anogenital presentations are a recognized diagnostic trap (Harrison 22e p.1519).
MCV cannot be cultured, so reliance on culture for diagnosis of molluscum is futile; biopsy (Henderson-Patterson bodies) or clinical/EM findings are needed (Harrison 22e p.1519).

In immunocompetent hosts most poxvirus infections are self-limited, resolving in weeks (or months for molluscum contagiosum). Exceptions are the generalized orthopoxvirus infections caused by MPXV and variola, which carry higher case-fatality. In unvaccinated individuals smallpox mortality is up to 30%; MPXV mortality is approximately 1.4-10% (clade I), ~1% (clade IIa), and <1% (clade IIb). Immunocompromised hosts may have more severe orthopoxvirus and parapoxvirus disease (severe mpox, progressive vaccinia, eczema vaccinatum, severe borealpox) with higher mortality, or atypical presentations (e.g., giant orf). In advanced HIV, effective antiretroviral therapy is essential to favorable outcomes. MCV can be diffuse in the immunocompromised, and immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) has been associated with recrudescence of MCV. Poxvirus reinfections are seldom reported (Harrison 22e p.1521).

Severe immunocompromise (advanced HIV with CD4 <200 cells/mm3, especially <50; organ transplantation) predisposes to severe, disseminated, prolonged mpox with numerous large coalescing or necrotic lesions and multi-organ involvement (GI tract, liver, lungs, brain) (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Ocular involvement: eye pain, redness, vision changes/loss, periorbital swelling, blepharitis, conjunctivitis, keratitis - can result in vision loss (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Neurologic complications: encephalitis, myelitis - severe headache, neck pain, altered mentation, focal deficits (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Myopericarditis: dyspnea or palpitations with elevated cardiac biomarkers and ECG changes (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Mucosal complications affecting alimentation, urination, or defecation due to painful or obstructive lesions; may lead to strictures, edema, and severe lymphadenopathy (Harrison 22e p.1519).
Most deaths have occurred predominantly among people with advanced HIV and CD4 <50 cells/mm3 (Harrison 22e p.1519).

Mpox ranges from typical self-limited disease (immunocompetent, including HIV with CD4 >200 cells/mm3, generally without increased severity) to severe mpox. Severe manifestations include ocular infection, neurologic complications (encephalitis, myelitis), myopericarditis, obstructive mucosal disease, and uncontrolled viral replication with disseminated/necrotic lesions and multi-organ involvement, occurring chiefly in severely immunocompromised patients (advanced HIV, organ transplantation). Clade I causes a higher proportion of severe disease than clade II (Harrison 22e p.1519).

Movement disorders arise predominantly from dysfunction of the basal ganglia (striatum = caudate plus putamen) and their cortical and thalamic connections, which modulate motor output rather than directly generating it; disruption of these circuits yields either hypokinetic syndromes (parkinsonism) or hyperkinetic syndromes (chorea, dystonia, tremor). Huntington's disease is caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat (autosomal dominant) with degeneration of the striatum. Wilson's disease results from impaired copper excretion with copper accumulation in liver and brain. Tardive dyskinesia reflects chronic blockade of striatal D2 dopamine receptors (Harrison 22e p.3508; basal ganglia/striatum anatomy p.~199-200 ch.31).

Movement disorders are classified as hypokinetic (poverty of movement, e.g. parkinsonism with rest tremor, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia) versus hyperkinetic (excess movement, e.g. chorea, dystonia, tremor); the rest tremor and cogwheel rigidity of Parkinson's disease are extrapyramidal signs distinct from the action tremor of essential tremor (Harrison 22e p.3508; cf. p.197 ch.31).

Essential tremor is an action/postural tremor; a key pitfall is mislabeling it as Parkinson's disease, but Parkinson tremor is characteristically a rest tremor accompanied by cogwheel rigidity and bradykinesia, whereas essential tremor lacks these and worsens with sustained posture or movement (Harrison 22e p.3508).

Huntington's disease is an autosomal dominant degenerative disorder producing the triad of chorea, psychiatric/behavioral disturbance (mood, anxiety, psychosis), and progressive dementia; the unpredictable choreic movements give the gait a characteristic dancing quality (Harrison 22e p.3508; gait described p.~3535 ch.32; HD as autosomal-dominant dementia p.198 ch.31).

Dystonia is defined as sustained muscle contractions producing repetitive twisting movements and abnormal posture; it often has a genetic basis, but new asymmetric dystonia—particularly involving gait—in a younger adult may be an early sign of Parkinson's disease (Harrison 22e p.3508; cf. gait chapter p.~3535).

Sydenham's chorea (a manifestation of acute rheumatic fever after group A streptococcal infection) is the prototypical post-infectious chorea: it occurs mainly in females after a prolonged latent period, affects especially the head (darting tongue movements) and upper limbs, may be generalized or hemichoreic, and is frequently accompanied by emotional lability or obsessive-compulsive traits; >50% of patients presenting with chorea have carditis, so echocardiography is warranted (Harrison 22e p.3508; ch. on rheumatic fever p.~2992).

Tardive dyskinesia is a drug-induced hyperkinetic disorder seen with chronic exposure to antipsychotics and other agents that block the D2 dopamine receptor, and is a common cause of stereotypic movement and gait disturbances (Harrison 22e p.3508).
Misdiagnosing essential (action) tremor as Parkinson's disease, or vice versa — Parkinson tremor is a rest tremor with cogwheel rigidity and bradykinesia
Failing to test for Wilson's disease in a young patient with new movement disorder; Wilson's may present with chronic hepatitis long before neurologic signs or Kayser-Fleischer rings appear
Overlooking carditis in a patient presenting with chorea (Sydenham's), since chorea may be the sole or delayed manifestation of rheumatic fever
Not recognizing drug-induced/tardive movements from D2-blocking medications

Prognosis is disorder-specific. Essential tremor is typically slowly progressive and non-degenerative. Huntington's disease is relentlessly progressive and degenerative. Wilson's disease can improve substantially with prompt diagnosis and copper-chelating treatment before end-stage manifestations become irreversible. Sydenham's chorea is usually self-limited, with choreiform movements resolving within about 6 weeks, occasionally up to 6 months, though associated obsessive-compulsive or emotional symptoms may persist longer (Harrison 22e p.3508; Wilson p.~2713 ch.355; chorea p.~2992).

New chorea, dystonia, tremor or parkinsonism in an adolescent or young adult — exclude Wilson's disease (treatable; look for Kayser-Fleischer rings, low ceruloplasmin, high urinary copper) before manifestations become irreversible
Chorea with autosomal dominant family history plus psychiatric change and cognitive decline — consider Huntington's disease
Acute chorea (especially in a young female) — evaluate for acute rheumatic fever and carditis with echocardiography
Abnormal movements in a patient on long-term antipsychotics/D2 blockers — recognize tardive dyskinesia and acute dystonic reactions

No single unified severity scale spans all movement disorders; assessment is disorder-specific and functional. Chorea, for example, ranges from movements evident only on careful examination in mild cases to inability to perform activities of daily living in severe cases (Harrison 22e p.3508).

chunks.text: MS is an autoimmune CNS disease producing chronic inflammation, demyelination, gliosis (sclerotic plaques) and neuronal/axonal loss (p.3577). New lesions begin with perivenular cuffing by T cells and macrophages and blood-brain-barrier (BBB) disruption with a preserved vessel wall (unlike vasculitis); cytotoxic CD8 cells line the leading edge, B cells infiltrate, myelin-specific autoantibodies coat degenerating myelin, and complement is activated (p.3581). Sharply demarcated demyelination is the hallmark; axons are relatively spared early but can be destroyed in highly inflammatory lesions, and partial remyelination produces 'shadow plaques' (p.3581). Cumulative axonal/neuronal loss drives irreversible disability (up to ~70% of corticospinal axons lost in MS paraplegia) via demyelination-related loss of trophic support, ion-channel redistribution, and dying-back axonopathy (p.3581). Progressive MS features more diffuse microglial activation, chronic active (slowly expanding) plaques with microglia at a leading edge behind an intact BBB, cortical/subpial plaques poorly seen on MRI, and meningeal ectopic lymphoid follicles linked to subpial cortical demyelination (p.3581-3582). Physiologically, demyelination causes conduction block (hyperpolarization from exposed potassium channels) and conduction slowing; temperature and metabolic changes worsen block, explaining heat- and fever-related fluctuations (p.3582-3583). Susceptibility is polygenic with the strongest signal at HLA-DRB1*1501 (~10% of risk), and EBV seroconversion appears a near-universal prerequisite, plausibly via molecular mimicry between EBV peptides and myelin autoantigens (p.3580-3581).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Even relapse-free RRMS patients undergo subtle 'silent progression,' and disability accumulation is now attributed mainly to progression independent of relapse activity (PIRA) rather than incomplete recovery from relapses (RAW), across RRMS, SPMS, and PPMS (p.3578-3580).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: A radiologically isolated syndrome (RIS) is incidental MRI evidence of MS in an asymptomatic person; clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) is a first demyelinating event at high risk for MS (p.3577-3580).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Typical onset is age 20-40 (slightly later in men); women are affected roughly three times as often as men (p.3577).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: The most common presenting symptoms are sensory loss (~37%) and optic neuritis (~36%), followed by limb weakness (~35%) and paresthesias (p.3577).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Optic neuritis usually causes monocular reduced acuity, dimness, and color desaturation, with periorbital pain worsened by eye movement and an afferent pupillary defect; uveitis is uncommon and should prompt thought of sarcoidosis or lymphoma (p.3577).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: A bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia (impaired adduction with nystagmus of the abducting eye, from a medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion) is particularly suggestive of MS; related gaze findings include horizontal gaze palsy and the 'one-and-a-half' syndrome (p.3578).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Lhermitte's symptom is a neck-flexion-induced electric-shock sensation radiating down the spine/legs; it is not specific to MS and can occur with other cervical cord disease such as spondylosis (p.3578).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Uhthoff's symptom (heat sensitivity) is transient worsening of neurologic symptoms with elevated core temperature (hot shower, exercise, fever) and reflects temperature-dependent conduction block rather than a true new lesion (p.3578).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Exercise-induced weakness is characteristic; weakness is of upper-motor-neuron type with spasticity, hyperreflexia, and extensor plantar responses, though a tendon reflex can occasionally be lost if a plaque disrupts the afferent reflex arc (p.3578).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Paroxysmal symptoms (tonic spasms, paroxysmal dysarthria/ataxia, sensory bursts) are brief (10 s-2 min), frequent (5-40/day), without altered consciousness, and self-limited; they arise from spontaneous discharges at the edges of demyelinated plaques (p.3578).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Do not over-diagnose MS from a single isolated event or from MRI white-matter lesions alone - the diagnosis requires dissemination in space and time (clinical, MRI, or CSF evidence) per the McDonald criteria, and there is no single confirmatory test (p.3582-3583).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: A pseudoexacerbation from heat/fever/infection (Uhthoff phenomenon) can mimic a relapse but reflects transient conduction block, not a new lesion; treating it as a relapse with steroids is inappropriate (p.3578, 3585).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Failing to distinguish NMOSD, MOGAD, and GFAP autoimmunity from MS - clues are bilateral/severe optic neuritis, severe longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (>=3 vertebral segments), brain MRI lesions that are non-destructive/cloud-like and can fully resolve, and CSF pleocytosis greater than in MS with neutrophils/eosinophils and oligoclonal bands in <20% (p.3584, 3590).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: ADEM should be considered for hyperacute or postinfectious demyelinating presentations rather than assuming a first MS attack (p.3584).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: MS-associated genetic variants (including HLA-DRB1*1501) lack the sensitivity and specificity to be used for diagnosis (p.3581).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Highly restricted CNS oligoclonal antibodies are characteristic of MS but their specific antigenic targets differ between patients and their pathogenic role is uncertain - they aid diagnosis, not mechanistic certainty (p.3581).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Lhermitte's symptom and trigeminal neuralgia are not specific to MS and occur with other cervical cord/cranial nerve pathology (p.3578).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: The clinical course is highly variable. RRMS accounts for ~90% of cases with attacks evolving over days to weeks and substantial early recovery; PPMS (~10%) declines steadily from onset, begins later (mean ~40 years), has a more even sex ratio, and accrues disability faster (p.3578-3580). In the pretreatment era, by 15 years after onset only ~20% had no functional limitation and one-third to one-half of relapsing patients had progressed to SPMS needing ambulatory assistance, with ~80% reaching that level by 25 years; the prior RRMS-to-SPMS conversion rate of ~3%/year has fallen to <1%/year in the high-efficacy-therapy era (p.3579, 3588). Favorable prognostic features (pretreatment data): optic neuritis or sensory onset, fewer than two relapses in the first year, and minimal impairment at 5 years; adverse predictors: older onset age, male sex, greater disability, and motor signs in the first year. About <10% have a benign variant that never produces disability even untreated (p.3588). Pregnancy: fewer attacks during gestation (especially the third trimester) but more in the first 3 months postpartum, with the overall pregnancy-year course unchanged (p.3588).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Distinguish a true relapse from a pseudoexacerbation driven by raised ambient temperature, fever, or infection - glucocorticoids are inappropriate for a pseudoexacerbation (p.3585).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Features atypical for MS that should prompt an alternative diagnosis: symptoms confined to posterior fossa/craniocervical junction/spinal cord; onset <15 or >60 years; progressive course from onset; never any visual, sensory, or bladder symptoms; or atypical MRI/CSF/EP findings (p.3584).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Symptoms rare/uncommon in MS that favor another diagnosis: aphasia, parkinsonism, chorea, isolated dementia, severe muscle atrophy, peripheral neuropathy, episodic loss of consciousness, fever, headache, seizures, or coma (p.3584).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Bilateral and/or severe optic neuritis or severe transverse myelitis should raise NMOSD, MOGAD, or GFAP autoimmunity rather than MS (p.3584).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Uveitis is uncommon in MS and should suggest sarcoidosis or lymphoma (p.3577).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Intense inflammatory swelling can produce a mass lesion mimicking tumor (tumefactive MS), sometimes requiring brain biopsy (p.3584, 3589).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Course-based subtypes: relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS, ~90%), secondary progressive MS (SPMS, always evolves from RRMS), and primary progressive MS (PPMS, ~10%); 'relapsing MS (RMS)' covers all relapsing patients and 'active progressive MS' denotes SPMS/PPMS with ongoing relapses or new MRI lesions (p.3578-3579). Neurologic impairment is graded with the Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS), 0 (normal) to 10 (death), built from Functional Status (FS) subscores; EDSS <3.5 generally indicates normal walking and little disability, whereas EDSS >4.0 indicates gait-impaired progressive (SPMS/PPMS) disease. An EDSS >=4 plus a motor FS score >=2 supports an SPMS diagnosis (p.3579-3580, 3585). Fulminant clinical variants include Marburg's (acute fulminant) MS, tumefactive MS, and Balo's concentric sclerosis (p.3589).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

Mucorales are ubiquitous environmental fungi to which humans are constantly exposed; they cause invasive, angioinvasive infection primarily in hosts with uncontrolled diabetes, phagocytic defects (neutropenia or high-dose corticosteroids), and/or elevated free iron, which supports fungal growth in serum and tissue. Iron-overloaded end-stage renal failure patients treated with the iron chelator deferoxamine had high risk of rapidly fatal disseminated disease, because deferoxamine acts as a fungal xenosiderophore that delivers iron directly to the Mucorales. In diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), acidosis dissociates iron from sequestering proteins (enhancing fungal survival/virulence) and the ketoacid beta-hydroxybutyrate upregulates host and fungal receptors that increase fungal adherence and tissue penetration; however the majority of diabetic patients with mucormycosis are NOT acidotic on presentation. Even without acidosis, hyperglycemia raises risk via hyperglycation of iron-sequestering proteins, upregulation of the host receptor GRP78 (which binds Mucorales and enables tissue penetration), poorly characterized phagocytic defects, and enhanced expression of the Mucorales-specific invasin CotH (which binds GRP78). Blood vessel thrombosis and tissue necrosis impair antifungal penetration to the site of infection. (Harrison 22e p.1717-1718)

Mucormycosis is a group of life-threatening infections caused by fungi of the order Mucorales (subphylum Mucoromycotina); it is highly invasive and relentlessly progressive, with morbidity/mortality higher than many other infections (Harrison 22e p.1717).

Rhizopus oryzae and R. delemar (family Mucoraceae) are by far the most common causes in the Western Hemisphere; Apophysomyces elegans is a notable cause in India and Mucor irregularis in China (Harrison 22e p.1718).

Five well-defined clinical syndromes: rhino-orbital-cerebral, pulmonary, cutaneous, gastrointestinal, and disseminated; specific host defects predispose to specific syndromes (diabetes/DKA to rhino-orbital-cerebral; leukemia/HSCT to pulmonary) (Harrison 22e p.1718).

Rhino-orbital-cerebral disease is the most common form worldwide; early symptoms are nonspecific (eye/facial pain, facial numbness) progressing to conjunctival suffusion, blurry vision, proptosis, and chemosis (Harrison 22e p.1718-1719).

Biopsy with histopathology is the most sensitive and specific modality: wide (>=6-30 microm), thick-walled, ribbon-like, ASEPTATE hyphae branching at RIGHT angles, in contrast to thinner, septate, acute-angle-branching Aspergillus/Fusarium/Scedosporium (Harrison 22e p.1719).
Mucorales are best visualized with periodic acid-Schiff or H&E; methenamine silver may NOT stain them optimally (Harrison 22e p.1719).

Tissue for culture should be cut into sections and placed in the center of culture media, NOT homogenized, because homogenization kills the long filamentous hyphae and lowers culture yield; the lab should be alerted when mucormycosis is suspected (Harrison 22e p.1720).

It is important to distinguish mucormycosis from aspergillosis because treatments differ: polyenes for Mucorales versus expanded-spectrum triazoles for most septate molds; voriconazole is the first-line treatment for aspergillosis but EXACERBATES mucormycosis in animal models (Harrison 22e p.1719-1720).
Misperception that mucormycosis is always rapidly progressive; rate of progression is in fact highly variable (days to a year or more).
Cultures are positive in fewer than half of cases, and up to half of cases are diagnosed only at autopsy; a negative culture does NOT exclude the diagnosis.
Standard tissue homogenization for culture kills the filamentous Mucorales and lowers yield; tissue must be sectioned and not homogenized, and the lab alerted.
Imaging underestimates disease: sinus CT may look like ordinary bacterial sinusitis, and bony erosion into the orbit is rarely seen on CT even when clinically present.

Treating with voriconazole (first-line for aspergillosis) can exacerbate mucormycosis; distinguish the two molds because preferred treatments differ, and consider dual infection in highly compromised patients.

Delaying treatment of the underlying malignancy until mucormycosis is 'cured' is a common error; antifungals provide only a holding action until near-normal immunity is restored, and untreated underlying disease is the typical primary driver of death.
Iron administration and liberal blood transfusion (free iron from hemolysis) should be avoided as iron exacerbates infection.
Therapy should not be delayed for diagnostic confirmation: when suspicion is reasonable, empirical lipid polyene therapy should be started early because earlier polyene therapy improves survival.

Overall mortality remains high though it has declined with earlier initiation of effective antifungal therapy; outcome is often driven by progression of the underlying predisposing condition. Necrotizing fasciitis from cutaneous disease carries mortality approaching 80%, gastrointestinal disease progressing to perforation has extremely high mortality, and widely disseminated disease exceeds 90% mortality. In contrast, isolated nonnecrotizing cutaneous mucormycosis treated with prompt aggressive surgical debridement has a favorable prognosis and low mortality. Rate of progression is highly variable (days to a year or more), not invariably rapid. (Harrison 22e p.1717-1720)

Rhino-orbital-cerebral involvement with a black necrotic eschar and/or painful necrotic ulceration of the hard palate (late finding indicating extensive, well-established angioinvasive infection) is a surgical emergency requiring urgent debridement.
Bilateral proptosis, chemosis, vision loss, and ophthalmoplegia (contralateral eye involvement) suggest cavernous sinus thrombosis and are ominous.

Hyperglycemia or DKA with sinusitis and possible orbital extension, even without a known diabetes history, should raise high suspicion (presentation may be the first recognition of diabetes, often unmasked by recent glucocorticoids).
Necrotizing fasciitis from cutaneous mucormycosis (mortality approaching 80%) and necrotic skin lesions from hematogenous dissemination.
Disseminated disease (most lethal form), seen with antifungal prophylaxis breakthrough and in highly immunocompromised patients.

Harrison classifies mucormycosis by clinical syndrome rather than a numeric severity score: rhino-orbital-cerebral, pulmonary, cutaneous (ranging from isolated nonnecrotizing cutaneous disease with favorable prognosis to necrotizing fasciitis), gastrointestinal, and disseminated/miscellaneous disease, with mortality rising steeply from localized cutaneous disease to disseminated disease (>90%). (Harrison 22e p.1718-1720)
