chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: In multivalvular heart disease the hemodynamic effects of a proximal valve lesion can mask those of a more distal lesion. With combined rheumatic mitral and aortic disease, the reduced cardiac output imposed by mitral disease lessens the apparent severity of the aortic lesion, while AF arising during mitral stenosis can abruptly worsen previously silent aortic disease. Reactive pulmonary vascular disease acts as a secondary obstructive lesion in series, and as cardiac output falls with progressive tricuspid disease, associated mitral or aortic disease may be underestimated. Functional TR follows right ventricular and annular dilation with morphologically normal leaflets, producing large systolic c-v waves in the RA pressure pulse whose height depends on RA compliance and regurgitant volume; advanced chronic severe TR ventricularizes the RA waveform. In MS with concomitant AR, enhanced LV filling raises diastolic pressure depending on chamber compliance. Secondary MR in severe AS arises from LV remodeling and leaflet tethering under high systolic pressures. In mixed AS/AR, augmented transvalvular systolic velocities inflate the Doppler gradient and murmur intensity relative to true orifice size, and the Gorlin formula is inaccurate. In mixed mitral disease, the elevated mitral E-wave velocity in severe MR may not reflect any contribution of associated MS to LA hypertension. Noncompliant, nondilated, concentrically hypertrophied ventricles (as in significant AS, radiation heart disease, cardiac amyloid, or obesity/diabetes cardiomyopathy) tolerate acute volume loads poorly, so sudden AR causes rapid rise in LV diastolic pressure and severe heart failure.

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: Multiple acquired and congenital lesions can produce stenosis and/or regurgitation across one or more valves; rheumatic disease classically affects mitral, aortic, and tricuspid valves alone or in combination.

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: An early ejection click, typical of bicuspid aortic valve in young adults, is often absent in congenital mixed AS and AR.

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: Patients with multiple or mixed valve disease may become symptomatic earlier than those with isolated single-valve lesions, sometimes even with only moderate individual lesions.

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: Palpitations suggesting AF can flag clinically unsuspected mitral valve disease as an important component of the presentation.

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: In multivalvular disease, derangements from the more proximal valve lesion can mask the full hemodynamic expression of a more distal lesion.

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: Reduced cardiac output from mitral valve disease lowers transaortic flow and can lead to underestimation of the severity of a coexisting aortic lesion.

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: Functional tricuspid regurgitation accompanying significant mitral valve disease is one of the most common forms of multivalve disease; the tricuspid leaflets are morphologically normal and TR arises from right ventricular and annular dilation.

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: Onset of atrial fibrillation can be especially deleterious in rheumatic mitral plus aortic disease: loss of atrial systole can critically reduce cardiac output and raise left atrial and LV diastolic pressures.

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: When AR or MR is the dominant lesion in mixed aortic or mitral disease, the LV is dilated; when AS or MS predominates, LV chamber size is normal or small.

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: Secondary (functional) MR complicating severe AS reflects altered LV geometry and systolic leaflet tethering with normal leaflets and chordae; it may improve after relief of afterload with valve replacement.

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: Persistent significant secondary MR after aortic valve replacement is associated with impaired functional outcomes and reduced survival.

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: Severe mitral annular calcification can cause both regurgitation (reduced systolic annular shortening) and mild-to-moderate stenosis (calcium extending onto the leaflets restricting opening).

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: The Gorlin formula is inaccurate in mixed aortic valve disease because augmented transvalvular flow from AR inflates the gradient relative to true orifice size.

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: Doppler-derived LV-aortic gradients and systolic murmur intensity overestimate true valve orifice severity in mixed AS/AR with preserved LV function.

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: A high mitral E-wave velocity in severe MR may be misread as indicating significant MS contribution to LA hypertension.

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: Low cardiac output from a proximal lesion (or AF) can mask the true severity of a more distal aortic or tricuspid lesion, leading to underestimation.

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: A mid-systolic outflow murmur is common in significant AR even without valve sclerosis/stenosis, so other signs of AS must be sought rather than assuming combined disease.

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: Combined aortic and mitral valve replacement carries significantly higher perioperative mortality than single-valve surgery, so the decision must be made carefully.

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: Natural history is usually driven by the dominant valve lesion; for moderate mixed AS/AR in which stenosis dominates, the course tends to parallel isolated severe AS. Patients with multiple or mixed disease may develop limiting symptoms or physiologic impairment even with only moderate lesions. Persistent significant secondary MR after AVR carries worse functional outcomes and survival, and significant paravalvular regurgitation after transcatheter AVR is a notable risk factor for short- to intermediate-term death.

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: Abrupt development of acute aortic regurgitation (e.g., from IE or paravalvular leak after AVR/TAVI) in a noncompliant, nondilated, hypertrophied LV, causing rapid rise in diastolic pressure and severe heart failure

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: New atrial fibrillation in moderate mitral disease precipitating heart failure when severe aortic disease coexists

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: Significant paravalvular regurgitation after transcatheter AVR (risk factor for short- to intermediate-term death)

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: Symptoms of right heart failure (abdominal fullness/bloating, edema, ascites) signaling advanced disease

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: ECG or chest x-ray signs of pulmonary hypertension or RA hypertension in a patient with left-sided valve disease

chunks.diseaseName: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease
chunks.text: No discrete severity grading scheme for combined disease; severity is determined by an integrated clinical and noninvasive assessment that identifies the dominant lesion, whose grading and management recommendations are then applied, with attention to lesion severity, ventricular remodeling, functional capacity, and PA pressures.

Germline RET mutation testing in all patients with medullary thyroid carcinoma, with cascade screening of relatives (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397).
MEN1 (menin) gene testing in patients with the parathyroid/pancreatic-islet/pituitary tumor pattern or relevant family history (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.392/ch.376).
Biochemical screening for pheochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism in RET-mutation carriers identified as at risk for MEN2 (Harrison 22e p.3079).

Other familial pituitary tumor / endocrine neoplasia syndromes: MEN 4 (CDKN1B mutation; hyperparathyroidism and pituitary adenomas), Carney complex (PRKAR1A; spotty skin pigmentation, myxomas, endocrine tumors), McCune-Albright syndrome, and familial isolated pituitary adenomas (AIP) (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.392).
Other inherited predispositions to pheochromocytoma that overlap with MEN2: von Hippel-Lindau disease, neurofibromatosis, and hereditary paraganglioma syndromes (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.247).

MEN1 follows the two-hit tumor-suppressor paradigm: the affected individual inherits a mutant copy of the MEN1 gene (menin, chromosome 11q13), and tumorigenesis follows a somatic 'second hit' (deletion or point mutation) that inactivates the remaining normal allele. In contrast, MEN2 is caused by activating point mutations in a single allele of the RET protooncogene, encoding a receptor tyrosine kinase; constitutive RET activity leads to thyroid C-cell hyperplasia in childhood that precedes the development of medullary thyroid carcinoma (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.388/ch.397).
MEN1 is characterized primarily by the triad of parathyroid, pancreatic islet, and pituitary tumors (the '3 Ps'); it is an autosomal dominant syndrome (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.392/ch.388).
MEN2 predisposes to medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), pheochromocytoma, and hyperparathyroidism (Harrison 22e p.3079).

There are three familial forms of MTC: MEN 2A, MEN 2B, and familial MTC without other features of MEN; MTC is more aggressive in MEN 2B than in MEN 2A, and familial MTC is more aggressive than sporadic MTC (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397).

MEN1 is caused by inactivating germline mutations of the MEN1 (menin) tumor-suppressor gene on chromosome 11q13; about half of affected patients develop prolactinomas, while acromegaly and Cushing's disease are less common (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.392).

MEN2 is caused by activating point mutations of the RET protooncogene (a receptor tyrosine kinase) in a single allele, in contrast to the tumor-suppressor loss-of-function mechanism of MEN1 (Harrison 22e p.3079).

Early genetic screening for RET mutations identifies individuals at risk for MEN2 who may benefit from prophylactic thyroidectomy and biochemical screening for pheochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism (Harrison 22e p.3079).

All patients with MTC should be tested for RET mutations, because genetic counseling and cascade testing of family members can then be offered to those who test positive (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397).
Proceeding to surgery (e.g., thyroidectomy or parathyroid surgery) without first excluding an unsuspected pheochromocytoma in a RET-mutation carrier (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397).
Failing to perform RET testing in all MTC patients and thereby missing cascade screening opportunities for at-risk family members (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397).

Prognosis is driven by the component tumors and genotype. MTC is more aggressive in MEN 2B than in MEN 2A, and familial MTC is more aggressive than sporadic MTC; early genetic identification permits prophylactic thyroidectomy before malignant transformation, improving outcome (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397).

Exclude pheochromocytoma BEFORE any surgery: prior to surgery, pheochromocytoma should be excluded in all patients with a RET mutation (failure to do so risks an intraoperative hypertensive crisis) (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397).
MTC in the context of MEN 2B carries a more aggressive course than MEN 2A and warrants early/prophylactic intervention (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397).

Caused by mumps virus, a single-stranded negative-sense enveloped RNA paramyxovirus (Rubulavirus genus, Paramyxoviridae); there is only one serotype (p.1646). Humans are the only known natural reservoir; transmission is via direct contact with respiratory droplets or saliva of an infected person. Incubation averages 16-18 days (range 12-25). A person is most infectious from 2 days before until 5 days after onset of parotitis (virus detected in saliva as early as 7 days before to as late as 9 days after onset) (p.1647). Primary replication likely occurs in the nasal/upper respiratory mucosal epithelium, with spread to regional lymph nodes and infection of mononuclear cells facilitating viremia lasting ~3-5 days. Viremia produces acute inflammatory reactions most commonly in the salivary glands (parotitis) and testes (orchitis), with dissemination also to kidneys, CNS, pancreas, heart, ovaries, mammary glands, cochlear perilymph, and (in pregnancy) the fetus. Mumps encephalitis in many cases appears to be a para- or postinfectious demyelinating process rather than direct viral cytotoxicity, though rare primary encephalitis with viral isolation from brain tissue does occur (p.1647-1648).

Acute, self-limited systemic viral illness typically characterized by parotitis or other salivary gland swelling; suspect in any patient with parotitis or mumps complications regardless of age, vaccination status, or travel history (p.1646).

Parotitis is generally bilateral but may not be synchronous on both sides; unilateral involvement occurs in about one-third of cases, with tenderness and obliteration of the space between the earlobe and angle of the mandible (p.1647).

Parotitis is often preceded by a several-day prodrome of low-grade fever, malaise, myalgia, headache, and anorexia; it typically lasts ~5 days (range 3-7) with most cases resolving within 10 days (p.1647).
Infection is asymptomatic in ~20% of unvaccinated patients; it can also present as nonspecific respiratory symptoms (p.1647).
Fully vaccinated persons can still contract mumps, but are at lower risk for mumps and for mumps complications (p.1647).

Buccal swabs are the best specimens for virus detection; the parotid gland should be massaged for 30 s before collection, and specimens collected as close to parotitis onset as possible (maximal shedding within 5 days of symptom onset) (p.1649).
Complications can occur in the absence of parotitis and are more common in adults than children and in males than females (largely due to orchitis) (p.1648).
A negative virologic or serologic result does NOT rule out mumps in a person with clinical signs, especially in vaccinated patients (p.1649).
Failure to detect mumps IgM is very common in vaccinated patients (IgM response often undetectable, transient, or delayed); IgM can also yield false positives from cross-reactions (p.1649).
Presence of parotitis, orchitis, or oophoritis supports a mumps diagnosis but their absence does NOT exclude it; complications can occur without parotitis (p.1648).

A positive IgG titer indicates only prior exposure (vaccination or natural infection) and does NOT predict protection; IgG titers should NOT be used to infer immunity in close contacts since they may instead reflect acute infection (p.1649).
Elevated serum amylase can arise from parotitis OR pancreatitis; lipase is needed to distinguish (p.1648).
Mumps reinfection and recurrent infection can occur and may be more common than previously thought (p.1648).

MMR vaccine has NOT been shown to prevent illness or alter severity in persons already infected and is NOT recommended as postexposure prophylaxis; mumps immune globulin is also NOT recommended for postexposure prophylaxis or treatment (p.1649).

Generally a benign, self-resolving illness; death due to mumps is exceedingly rare (p.1648). Aseptic meningitis is self-limited without significant risk of death or long-term sequelae. Encephalitis carries a mortality of ~1.5%, may leave permanent sequelae, and has poorer outcomes in adults than children. Orchitis can cause testicular atrophy in ~30-50% of affected testicles and temporary sterility/subfertility, but no studies have assessed the risk of permanent infertility. Mumps-related hearing loss is usually transient; bilateral permanent loss is rare. Mumps in pregnancy is generally benign and no more severe than in non-pregnant women, and evidence for an association with increased spontaneous abortion or fetal death is inconclusive (p.1648).
Orchitis (most common complication; up to 30% of unvaccinated and 6% of vaccinated postpubertal males) with possible testicular atrophy and temporary subfertility
Aseptic meningitis (up to 10% of unvaccinated, <=1% of vaccinated patients)
Encephalitis (<=1% of patients; high fever, altered consciousness, seizures, focal neurologic signs; mortality ~1.5%)
Sensorineural hearing loss / deafness (usually sudden, unilateral, transient; bilateral and permanent loss are rare)
Oophoritis (~7% unvaccinated, <=1% vaccinated postpubertal women)
Pancreatitis (~4% unvaccinated, <1% vaccinated)
Supraglottic edema (rare, life-threatening) from obstructed lymphatic drainage
Other CNS complications: cerebellar ataxia, facial palsy, transverse myelitis, hydrocephalus, Guillain-Barre syndrome, flaccid paralysis
Myocarditis and endocardial fibroelastosis (rare but potentially severe)

No formal severity classification in the source. Spectrum ranges from asymptomatic infection (~20% of unvaccinated) through classic self-limited parotitis to complicated disease (orchitis, oophoritis, pancreatitis, hearing loss, aseptic meningitis, encephalitis); subclinical CNS involvement (CSF pleocytosis) occurs in up to 55% of patients.

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Myopathies reflect structural or functional impairment intrinsic to muscle, distinguishing them from anterior horn cell, peripheral nerve, and neuromuscular junction disorders. In the dystrophies, the molecular defect lies in proteins linking the sarcolemma to the cytoskeleton and extracellular matrix: dystrophin (DMD/BMD) connects the actin cytoskeleton through the dystroglycan complex to the matrix, and mutations in sarcoglycans, dysferlin, calpain-3, anoctamin-5, glycosylation enzymes of alpha-dystroglycan, and sarcomeric/Z-disk and nuclear-envelope proteins underlie the limb-girdle, distal, and Emery-Dreifuss phenotypes. Nuclear-membrane protein defects (emerin, lamin A/C, nesprin-1/2, LUMA) destabilize the inner nuclear envelope and cause EDMD with prominent contractures and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy. Myotonic dystrophies arise from non-coding repeat expansions (CTG in DMPK for DM1, CCTG in CNBP for DM2) acting through a toxic RNA gain of function: mutant RNA forms nuclear inclusions that sequester splicing regulators, causing widespread aberrant splicing and the multisystem phenotype, with anticipation as repeat length grows across generations. FSHD results from hypomethylation at 4q35 (contracted D4Z4 repeats in FSHD1; SMCHD1/DNMT3B/LRIF1 mutations in FSHD2) that permits toxic expression of the DUX4 transcription factor. Energy-metabolism disorders impair glycolysis (e.g., myophosphorylase/McArdle), glycogen handling (acid maltase/Pompe), or fatty-acid transport into mitochondria via carnitine palmitoyltransferase, producing either exertional cramping with rhabdomyolysis/myoglobinuria or progressive weakness. Mitochondrial myopathies stem from maternally inherited mtDNA point mutations or deletions, or nuclear-gene defects of mtDNA maintenance/replication, impairing oxidative phosphorylation. Channelopathies of the sarcolemma (calcium CACNA1S, sodium SCN4A, potassium Kir2.1, chloride CLCN1) disturb membrane excitability to produce periodic paralysis and/or myotonia. Endocrine and toxic myopathies act through hormonal or pharmacologic injury, often producing fiber atrophy rather than destruction.

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Most myopathies cause persistent, symmetric, proximal (limb-girdle) weakness with preserved reflexes and intact sensation; associated sensory loss instead points toward a peripheral neuropathy or CNS (myelopathy) process rather than primary muscle disease.

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Episodic weakness beginning after age 25 is almost never due to a periodic paralysis, with thyrotoxic periodic paralysis being the notable exception (favoring men of Asian descent despite higher thyrotoxicosis rates in women).

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: In McArdle disease, a slow warm-up or brief rest produces a 'second-wind' phenomenon as the muscle shifts to fatty acid utilization; the forearm exercise test shows a blunted venous lactate rise with a normal ammonia rise.

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Ragged red fibers and cytochrome-oxidase (COX)-negative fibers on muscle biopsy, often with elevated serum lactate, FGF-21, and GDF-15, point toward a mitochondrial myopathy.

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: The pattern of muscle involvement is the single most useful clue for narrowing the differential: facial weakness with scapular winging suggests FSHD, facial/distal weakness with grip myotonia is virtually diagnostic of myotonic dystrophy type 1, ptosis/ophthalmoparesis suggests oculopharyngeal dystrophy or mitochondrial myopathy, and asymmetric flexor-forearm plus quadriceps weakness suggests inclusion body myositis.

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Creatine kinase (CK) is the most sensitive marker of muscle damage; the MM isoenzyme predominates in skeletal muscle while CK-MB marks cardiac muscle. CK can be elevated in healthy people after strenuous activity, trauma, prolonged cramp, or seizure.

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Elevated AST, ALT, aldolase, and LDH can originate from muscle and be misattributed to liver disease; a normal gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) helps confirm a muscle (rather than hepatic) source because GGT is not present in muscle.

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: The Gower sign (using the arms to climb up the legs to rise from the floor) and a waddling or hyperlordotic toe-walking gait reflect proximal hip, thigh, and trunk weakness.

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Calf enlargement in many limb-girdle dystrophies represents true muscle hypertrophy that stays strong late in the disease, so the term 'pseudohypertrophy' is best avoided; by contrast, early medial gastrocnemius atrophy characterizes Miyoshi myopathy (dysferlin/anoctamin-5).

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Cardiac and ventilatory muscle involvement are the leading causes of mortality across the dystrophies, so cardiology follow-up, ECG monitoring, and surveillance for respiratory insufficiency are central to care.

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Genetic testing is the gold standard for hereditary myopathies, but next-generation panels can miss large deletions/duplications and intronic mutations and frequently return variants of uncertain significance; muscle imaging (MRI/ultrasound) can support a specific diagnosis by showing characteristic involvement patterns.

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is multisystem: hatchet facies, frontal balding, distal weakness, cataracts, cardiac conduction block, insulin resistance, gonadal atrophy, hypersomnia, and cognitive impairment; congenital DM1 occurs almost exclusively in infants of affected mothers.

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Attributing isolated fatigue to primary muscle disease: fatigue without abnormal clinical or laboratory findings almost never indicates a myopathy, and asthenia must be distinguished from true pathologic fatigability.

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Misreading muscle-derived transaminase/aldolase/LDH elevations as liver disease; checking GGT clarifies the source.

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Diagnosing myositis in FSHD when biopsy shows an inflammatory infiltrate, leading to incorrect immunosuppressive treatment.

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Overlooking immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (a treatable autoimmune cause) in apparent LGMD without an identified pathogenic mutation; antibody screening is warranted.

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Calling calf enlargement 'pseudohypertrophy' when it is true hypertrophy in many LGMDs.

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Assuming hyperkalemia in hyperkalemic periodic paralysis; patients are often normokalemic during attacks, and the disorder is defined by precipitation with potassium loading.

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Misattributing exertional cramps: cramps follow short intense bursts in glycolytic defects, whereas CPT2-deficiency pain appears only after prolonged exercise once muscle breakdown has begun.

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Preferring muscle biopsy over imaging in suspected diabetic muscle infarction, where hemorrhage into the biopsy site can occur.

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Relying solely on next-generation sequencing panels, which can miss large deletions/duplications and intronic mutations and may yield variants of uncertain significance.

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: The dystrophies generally follow a slowly progressive course, though severity varies between and within subtypes. Life expectancy is reduced in DMD and BMD, with most BMD patients surviving into the fourth or fifth decade; death is often attributable to associated cardiomyopathy. FSHD usually spares the heart, but about 20% of patients progress to pelvic-girdle involvement and possible wheelchair dependence. In Kearns-Sayre syndrome, death from heart block occurs in roughly 20% of patients, underscoring the value of cardiac surveillance and prophylactic pacing for conduction defects. MELAS in full expression can lead to dementia, a bedridden state, and a fatal outcome. Most endocrine myopathies respond to treatment of the underlying disorder. For many hereditary myopathies no specific disease-modifying therapy exists, and care centers on preserving function and managing cardiac and respiratory complications.

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Cardiac conduction abnormalities or arrhythmias (atrial fibrillation, atrioventricular/complete heart block, atrial standstill) in EDMD and myotonic dystrophy carrying risk of sudden death

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Dilated cardiomyopathy or heart failure in DMD/BMD, LGMD, and myofibrillar myopathies

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Ventilatory/diaphragmatic muscle weakness causing respiratory insufficiency (may be the presenting feature in adult Pompe disease and LGMD)

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Myoglobinuria with CK rising to over 100 times normal, signaling rhabdomyolysis

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Life-threatening hypokalemia-related arrhythmias during hypokalemic periodic paralysis attacks; potentially serious long-QT and ventricular arrhythmias in Andersen-Tawil syndrome

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Dysphagia with aspiration risk in oculopharyngeal dystrophy/OPDM and myotonic dystrophy

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: Complete heart block and cardiac arrest in Kearns-Sayre syndrome; stroke-like episodes in MELAS

chunks.diseaseName: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases
chunks.text: No single unifying grading system; severity is assessed disease-specifically. Functional milestones (Gower sign, gait pattern, ambulatory status, wheelchair dependence) and manual muscle testing (e.g., biopsy is best taken from a muscle around grade 4/5) gauge weakness. Mortality risk is stratified by cardiac (conduction disease, cardiomyopathy) and respiratory (ventilatory insufficiency) involvement. In rhabdomyolysis, CK over 100 times normal accompanies myoglobinuria, and for statin myotoxicity, marked CK elevation (more than 3 to 5 times baseline) with severe myalgia, weakness, or myoglobinuria is an indication to stop the drug.

ME/CFS is understood as a complex disorder involving alterations across multiple interrelated homeostatic systems rather than a single mechanism. A wide range of infectious agents (viral and nonviral) can trigger a postinfectious fatiguing illness resembling ME/CFS, and noninfectious stressors - toxins, physical trauma, adverse life events, and cumulative allostatic load ('wear and tear') - are also associated. Twin and family studies suggest contributions from shared environment and genetic factors. Evidence for immunologic dysfunction is inconsistent and not established in most patients; reported findings include modest antinuclear antibody elevations, reduced immunoglobulin subclasses, impaired mitogen-driven lymphocyte proliferation, decreased natural killer cell activity, altered cytokine production, and altered T-cell metabolism. A hypothesis that excess cytokines such as interleukin-1 or interferon-alpha drive the fatigue and flulike symptoms lacks compelling supporting data. Other inconsistent and nondiagnostic findings include nonspecific regional brain MRI changes, autonomic nervous system dysfunction, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis abnormalities, altered metabolism, and gut microbiome dysbiosis. Unifying multisystem models integrate infection, immune, central and autonomic nervous system, metabolic, genetic, lifestyle, and stress factors.
ME/CFS is a chronic, complex, multisystem illness whose functional impact on daily functioning has been compared to that of multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, and congestive heart failure.
An estimated 80% or more of people who meet ME/CFS criteria have never been diagnosed by a health care provider.
Patients are reported to be more medication-sensitive than the general population, so any drug should begin at lower-than-usual doses and be increased slowly.
Patients may appear well during an office visit and then relapse afterward from the exertion of attending the consultation.

The defining feature is persistent, unexplained fatigue causing substantial functional impairment, together with postexertional malaise (PEM) - worsening of symptoms after physical, mental, or emotional exertion that would not have been a problem before the illness.
PEM relapses last longer than a day and can persist for weeks; the relationship between a relapse and the preceding activity is often not apparent to the patient, so PEM may go unrecognized.

Common accompanying symptoms include pain, cognitive dysfunction (patient-described 'brain fog'), unrefreshing sleep, headache, sore throat, tender lymph nodes, muscle and joint aches, feverishness, and orthostatic intolerance.
There is no diagnostic test; diagnosis rests on a characteristic profile of patient-reported symptoms, requiring evaluation by an experienced clinician.

The 2015 Institute of Medicine criteria require substantial activity reduction with profound new-onset fatigue not relieved by rest, plus PEM, plus unrefreshing sleep, plus either cognitive impairment or orthostatic intolerance.
Routine laboratory tests are typically within normal limits in ME/CFS; their value lies in identifying alternative or contributing illnesses rather than confirming the diagnosis.

Roughly 10% of patients remain ill for 6 months or more after a variety of infections (e.g., Epstein-Barr virus, Ross River virus, Q fever, Ebola, SARS-CoV-1, Giardia); recovery is otherwise the rule.
Recognition of ME/CFS as a diagnosable component of Long COVID has increased clinical awareness, but patients still encounter stigma and misunderstanding from clinicians.
Trivializing the illness or dismissing patients, contributing to stigma and underdiagnosis (most who meet criteria are never diagnosed).
Failing to recognize PEM because patients do not connect relapses to preceding exertion, and may appear well in clinic only to crash afterward.
Attributing a continued functional decline to ME/CFS rather than investigating an alternative diagnosis.
Standard-dose medication initiation in patients who are unusually drug-sensitive, increasing toxicity risk.
Encouraging overexertion on 'good days' that leads to the 'push and crash' cycle and negates functional gains.
Relying on laboratory tests for diagnosis - results are usually normal and serve only to exclude other conditions.

Severity ranges from mild or moderate (retaining varying degrees of pre-illness function) to severe (essentially homebound). Most patients experience some improvement and stabilize, but a return to the prior level of function is unusual. A continued functional decline is atypical and should trigger evaluation for other illnesses. Because of social isolation and loss of hope, serious depression and an increased risk of suicide are reported, warranting active screening and referral.
Continued decline in function (should prompt evaluation for another illness rather than being attributed to ME/CFS)
New, worsening, or unusual symptoms warranting further workup for a new illness

Severity is described clinically as mild/moderate (patients retain varying degrees of pre-illness function) versus severe (patients essentially homebound). Diagnostically, the 2015 IOM criteria require substantial activity reduction lasting more than 6 months with profound new-onset fatigue not relieved by rest, plus postexertional malaise, plus unrefreshing sleep, plus either cognitive impairment or orthostatic intolerance, with symptoms present at least half the time and of at least moderate intensity.

MG is an autoimmune NMJ disorder in which the number of available postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) is reduced and the postsynaptic folds are flattened ('simplified'), decreasing the efficiency of neuromuscular transmission so that normally released ACh produces small end-plate potentials that may fail to trigger muscle action potentials. Anti-AChR antibodies (IgG, T-cell dependent) act by three mechanisms: accelerated AChR turnover via cross-linking and endocytosis, complement-mediated damage to the postsynaptic membrane, and blockade of the ACh-binding site. Anti-MuSK antibodies (IgG4, do not activate complement) impair MuSK-LRP4 interaction and AChR clustering; anti-LRP4 antibodies (IgG1) cause complement-mediated destruction. The normal decline in ACh release on repeated activity (presynaptic rundown) combined with reduced transmission efficiency produces myasthenic fatigue and the decremental response to repetitive nerve stimulation. The thymus is abnormal in ~75% of AChR antibody-positive patients (~65% hyperplastic, ~10% thymoma) (Harrison 22e p.3624-3626).
Cardinal features are fatigable, fluctuating skeletal muscle weakness that worsens with repeated use or late in the day and improves with rest or sleep (Harrison 22e p.3625-3626).

Ocular and eyelid muscles are commonly involved early; diplopia and ptosis are frequent initial symptoms, and facial weakness can produce a 'snarling' expression on attempted smiling (Harrison 22e p.3626).
Bulbar involvement causes nasal/dysarthric 'mushy' speech, dysphagia with nasal regurgitation or aspiration, and chewing weakness; neck extensor weakness can cause head drop (Harrison 22e p.3626).
If weakness stays confined to ocular muscles for 3 years, later generalization is unlikely (ocular MG), though rare patients generalize beyond 5 years (Harrison 22e p.3626).
Bulbar, neck, and ventilatory weakness can be especially prominent in MuSK antibody-positive MG (Harrison 22e p.3626).

Ice-pack test: applying ice over a ptotic eye for 2 min produces a lid rise of 2 mm or more (positive) when ptosis is due to an NMJ defect; it is a quick, very sensitive bedside test (Harrison 22e p.3626-3627).
Approximately 10-15% of MG patients have a thymoma, so chest CT or MRI to evaluate the thymus is performed at diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.3628).
A negative anti-AChR antibody test does not exclude MG, and the antibody level does not correlate well with disease severity (Harrison 22e p.3627).

Distinguish LEMS from MG: LEMS is presynaptic (P/Q-type calcium channel antibodies), preferentially affects proximal lower-limb muscles, typically spares prominent ocular/bulbar onset, and shows depressed/absent reflexes plus autonomic features (dry mouth, orthostasis, impotence); unlike MG, strength and CMAP amplitude increase (incremental response) after brief exercise or high-rate (20-50 Hz) stimulation. In older adults LEMS is associated with malignancy, most commonly small-cell lung cancer (Harrison 22e p.3628).
Anti-striated muscle (titin) antibodies are not pathogenic and do not confirm MG or a thymoma (Harrison 22e p.3627).

Aminoglycoside, quinolone, and macrolide antibiotics, IV magnesium, procainamide, and penicillamine can exacerbate myasthenic weakness; botulinum toxin injections should be avoided in MG patients (Harrison 22e p.3627).

Anti-MuSK MG generally responds less to anticholinesterase agents (and may worsen) and does not respond to complement inhibition because MuSK antibodies are IgG4 and do not activate complement (Harrison 22e p.3626, p.3628-3629).
Diagnosis must be confirmed definitively before treatment because other treatable conditions mimic MG and treatment carries surgical/drug risks (Harrison 22e p.3626).

Prognosis has improved strikingly with modern treatment, and nearly all myasthenic patients can be returned to full productive lives with proper therapy. The course is variable, with exacerbations and remissions, particularly in the first 1-3 years; in ~85% of patients weakness becomes generalized. A cure remains elusive (Harrison 22e p.3625-3628).

Myasthenic crisis: ventilatory weakness requiring intubation or noninvasive ventilation to avoid intubation, managed in intensive care (treat respiratory infection, attend to fluids); requires rescue therapy with IVIg or plasmapheresis (Harrison 22e p.3626, p.3628-3629).
Dysphagia with nasal regurgitation or aspiration of liquids/food (bulbar involvement) (Harrison 22e p.3626).
Enlargement of the thymus in a patient older than 40 years is highly suspicious for thymoma (Harrison 22e p.3628).
Infection or tapering of MG therapy can precipitate myasthenic exacerbation or crisis (Harrison 22e p.3626).
ICI-related MG with concurrent myocarditis carries a high fatality rate in fulminant disease (Harrison 22e p.3627).

Weakness is classified as ocular versus generalized (the latter affecting facial, bulbar, axial, or limb muscles in ~85% of patients). Worsening requiring intubation or noninvasive ventilation defines myasthenic crisis; all other worsening is termed exacerbation. Standardized measures referenced include the Myasthenia Gravis Activities of Daily Living (MGADL) and Quantitative MG (QMG) scores (Harrison 22e p.3626, p.3631).

Mycoplasmas are prokaryotes of the class Mollicutes, the smallest organisms capable of independent replication; they lack a cell wall and are bound only by a cell membrane, which explains the inactivity of beta-lactam antibiotics (penicillins and cephalosporins) against them. M. pneumoniae is generally an extracellular pathogen that attaches to ciliated respiratory epithelial cells via a complex terminal organelle using interactive adhesins and accessory proteins. Tissue injury is thought to be mediated by production of hydrogen peroxide and an ADP-ribosylating and vacuolating cytotoxin similar to pertussis toxin. Lacking a cell wall, mycoplasmas lack cell-wall-derived innate immune stimulators (lipopolysaccharide, lipoteichoic acid, peptidoglycan), but membrane lipoproteins act through Toll-like receptors (primarily TLR2). Innate immunity provides most lung defense, cellular immunity may be immunopathogenic, and humoral immunity protects against dissemination; patients with humoral immunodeficiency are prone to disseminated disease (arthritis, meningitis, osteomyelitis). Extrapulmonary manifestations may arise from disseminated infection, postinfectious autoimmune phenomena (e.g., Guillain-Barre syndrome), or possibly an ADP-ribosylating toxin (Harrison 22e p.1464-1466).
M. pneumoniae pneumonia is also called Eaton agent pneumonia, primary atypical pneumonia, and 'walking' pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.1465).
M. pneumoniae has been implicated as a likely etiologic agent in 5-7% of cases of encephalitis (Harrison 22e p.1465).
Diagnosis is most sensitively and rapidly made by combining PCR of respiratory tract secretions with serologic testing of paired acute- and convalescent-phase samples (Harrison 22e p.1466).

M. pneumoniae is the most frequently detected 'atypical' organism in adult community-acquired pneumonia; older pooled data gave a prevalence of about 22.7%, and more recent (2002-2015) analyses gave about 7.2% (Harrison 22e p.1465).

Onset of pneumonia is usually gradual over several days; the most common presenting symptom is cough, which is typically nonproductive, though headache, malaise, chills, and fever are noted in the majority of patients (Harrison 22e p.1465).
Pneumonia develops in only 3-13% of infected individuals; upper respiratory illness is far more common, with an estimated incidence up to 20 times that of pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.1465).
Wheezes or rales are detected in about 80% of patients with M. pneumoniae pneumonia, but in many patients pneumonia can be diagnosed only by chest radiography (Harrison 22e p.1465).

The most common radiographic pattern is peribronchial pneumonia with thickened bronchial markings, streaks of interstitial infiltration, and subsegmental atelectasis; segmental or lobar consolidation is not uncommon (Harrison 22e p.1465).
Clinical presentation does not reliably distinguish M. pneumoniae pneumonia from other causes of community-acquired pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.1465).
Many patients with extrapulmonary M. pneumoniae disease do not have respiratory disease (Harrison 22e p.1465).

Hematologic manifestations include hemolytic anemia, aplastic anemia, cold agglutinins, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and hypercoagulopathy; when anemia occurs it generally develops in the second or third week of illness (Harrison 22e p.1466).

Erythema multiforme major (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) is the most clinically significant skin eruption associated with M. pneumoniae and appears to occur more commonly with M. pneumoniae than with other infectious agents; in M. pneumoniae-induced rash and mucositis (MIRM)/reactive infectious mucocutaneous eruption (RIME) there may be minimal cutaneous involvement with prominent mucosal disease (Harrison 22e p.1466, p.591).

Because mycoplasmas lack a cell wall, beta-lactam antibiotics (penicillins and cephalosporins) are ineffective; consider M. pneumoniae particularly when community-acquired pneumonia fails to respond to these agents (Harrison 22e p.1464-1465).
M. pneumoniae lacks a cell wall and is therefore not visible on Gram stain (Harrison 22e p.1466).
Measurement of cold agglutinin titers is no longer recommended for diagnosis because the findings are nonspecific and specific M. pneumoniae assays are now available (Harrison 22e p.1466).

A single acute-phase serum sample is not adequate for diagnosis, and IgM antibody can persist for up to 1 year, so its presence may indicate recent rather than acute infection - paired samples are needed (Harrison 22e p.1466).
Little evidence supports the commonly held belief that M. pneumoniae is an important cause of otitis media, with or without bullous myringitis (Harrison 22e p.1465).
A test of cure for eradication is not suggested, because appropriate antibiotics do not appear to shorten the duration of detection by culture or PCR (Harrison 22e p.1466).
Ciprofloxacin and ofloxacin are not recommended for M. pneumoniae owing to high MICs and poor experimental performance, in contrast to respiratory fluoroquinolones (Harrison 22e p.1466).

M. pneumoniae pneumonia is generally self-limited, with symptoms usually resolving within 2-3 weeks of onset even without treatment; appropriate antimicrobial therapy significantly shortens the duration of clinical illness. Infection uncommonly results in critical illness and only rarely in death. Long-term recurrent wheezing or reactive airway disease may follow resolution of acute pneumonia, and a possible link to asthma is under investigation. Immunity following severe infection is more protective and longer-lasting than after mild infection, and genuine second attacks of pneumonia are reported infrequently (Harrison 22e p.1465).

Neurologic manifestations: meningoencephalitis, encephalitis, Guillain-Barre syndrome, aseptic meningitis, transverse myelitis, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, cerebrovascular thromboembolic events, acute psychosis, cerebellar ataxia, cranial neuropathy
Severe mucocutaneous disease: erythema multiforme major / Stevens-Johnson syndrome / MIRM

No formal severity classification is given for Mycoplasma infection; M. pneumoniae illness is generally graded clinically from mild self-limited upper respiratory illness through pneumonia to severe/refractory or critical disease, with macrolide resistance and extrapulmonary involvement marking more severe courses (Harrison 22e p.1464-1466).

chunks.text: Multiple myeloma is a malignant proliferation of a single plasma-cell clone. Myeloma cells adhere to bone marrow stromal cells and extracellular matrix, triggering cytokine loops (IL-6, IGF-1, VEGF) and signaling (Ras/Raf/MAPK, PI3K/Akt, PKC) that drive growth, survival, drug resistance, and migration. Osteoclast-activating factors (RANK ligand, MIP-1alpha, IL-1, lymphotoxin, TNF, VEGF) increase bone resorption while DKK-1 suppresses osteoblasts, producing purely lytic bone disease, hypercalcemia, fractures, and cord compression. The immune microenvironment is remodeled (expansion of MDSCs, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, TH17; suppression of effective antimyeloma T/B/NKT responses). Recurrent cytogenetic events include hyperdiploidy (trisomies) in ~half, and 14q32 IGH translocations [t(11;14), t(4;14), t(14;16)] in the rest, plus del13q, 1q amplification/1p deletion, and del17p; KRAS/NRAS are the most frequently mutated genes (~20% each), with TP53, DIS3, FAM46C, BRAF in 5-10%. No single unifying mutation exists; subclonal heterogeneity present at diagnosis drives genomic evolution. All myeloma is preceded by MGUS (p.883-885).

chunks.text: Serum beta-2-microglobulin is the single most powerful survival predictor; combined with albumin it defines the 3-stage International Staging System (ISS): Stage I (b2M <3.5 mg/L, albumin >=3.5 g/dL) median survival ~62 months; Stage II ~44 months; Stage III (b2M >5.5 mg/L) ~29 months. High LDH, circulating plasma cells, high labeling index, and poor performance status indicate worse outcome. Cytogenetic risk: high-risk = del(17p) (>=20% clonality)/TP53 mutation, t(4;14)/t(14;16)/t(14;20) with 1q gain or 1p deletion, biallelic/del1p with 1q gain, and high b2M with normal creatinine (~20-25% of patients, expected survival 3-4 years); standard-risk includes t(11;14), del(13), hyperdiploidy (~75-80%, survival 8-10+ years). del(13q) and t(11;14) are NOT high-risk markers. MGUS progresses ~1%/yr; SMM higher (high-risk SMM ~76% at 5 years). Solitary plasmacytomas carry median survival >=10 years. The Durie-Salmon system is no longer used (p.888-889).

chunks.text: Diagnosis (IMWG, Table 116-1): clonal marrow plasma cells (or biopsy-proven plasmacytoma) PLUS >=1 myeloma-defining event. CRAB end-organ damage: hyperCalcemia (>2.75 mmol/L or >0.25 mmol/L above ULN); Renal insufficiency (CrCl <40 mL/min or creatinine >177 micromol/L [>2 mg/dL]); Anemia (Hb <100 g/L or >20 g/L below LLN); Bone lesions (>=1 lytic lesion on radiograph/CT/PET-CT). SLiM biomarkers of malignancy (any one): clonal marrow plasma cells >=60%; involved:uninvolved serum free light chain ratio >=100; >1 focal lesion (>=5 mm) on MRI. Staging severity: International Staging System (ISS) I-III by serum beta-2-microglobulin and albumin; cytogenetic high-risk vs standard-risk further stratifies (R-ISS combines ISS with high-risk cytogenetics and LDH). MGUS = M protein <30 g/L, marrow plasma cells <10%, no myeloma-defining events; smoldering myeloma = M protein >=30 g/L (or urine >=500 mg/24h) and/or marrow plasma cells 10-60%, no myeloma-defining events (p.887-889).

chunks.text: Myoclonus results from abnormal, excessive neuronal discharge that can arise at several levels of the nervous system. Cortical myoclonus reflects hyperexcitability of the sensorimotor cortex and often coexists with epilepsy; subcortical and brainstem forms arise from deeper generators; and spinal and peripheral forms originate in the cord or nerve. Loss of normal inhibitory control, frequently involving impaired GABAergic and serotonergic mechanisms, allows brief synchronous muscle discharges. Underlying processes include metabolic derangement, drugs and toxins, neurodegeneration, hypoxia, and epilepsy.

Hashimoto's encephalopathy - a steroid-responsive syndrome with TPO antibodies, myoclonus and EEG slow-wave activity (relationship to hypothyroidism not established) (p.3030).
Sepsis should be actively suspected as a precipitant; hypothermia obscures fever and leukocytosis, and infectious rigors may be mistaken for shivering (p.3032, p.3769).
Pneumonia as a respiration-impairing precipitant (p.3032).
Arterial blood gas to detect hypoxia and hypercapnia from hypoventilation (p.3032).
Glucose to detect contributing hypoglycemia (p.3032).
Septic screen / cultures, since infection is a common precipitant and is masked by hypothermia (p.3032, p.3769).
Core temperature measurement (may be very low, down to ~23 degrees C) (p.3032).
Environmental / accidental hypothermia from cold exposure, drugs (ethanol, sedatives, antipsychotics, antidepressants), or malnutrition (p.3768).
Hypoglycemia from insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents, which itself causes hypothermia via neuroglycopenic hypothalamic effects (p.3768).

Long-standing thyroid hormone deficiency depresses the metabolic rate and thermogenesis, producing hypothermia, bradycardia, and reduced myocardial contractility. Dermal accumulation of glycosaminoglycans traps water, giving nonpitting myxedematous swelling. In myxedema coma, hypoventilation is central to pathogenesis: it leads to hypoxia and hypercapnia (CO2 retention). Dilutional hyponatremia (reduced renal perfusion with inappropriate vasopressin) and hypoglycemia further contribute. There is impaired adrenal reserve in profound hypothyroidism, and impaired peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion (p.3032; p.3768).
Myxedema coma carries a 20-40% mortality despite intensive care, and outcome does not correlate with the degree of T4 or TSH abnormality (p.3032).
It occurs almost exclusively in the elderly, often in winter, and may arise either in a known hypothyroid patient with poor treatment adherence or in someone not previously diagnosed (p.3032).
Hypothermia in myxedema can be profound, reaching as low as 23 degrees C (74 degrees F) (p.3032).
Reduced consciousness is the hallmark and may be accompanied by seizures, alongside the usual signs of hypothyroidism (p.3032).
A distinguishing examination clue in hypothyroidism is a deep tendon reflex (e.g., Achilles) whose relaxation phase is prolonged out of proportion to the contraction phase (p.3769).
Hypothyroidism, especially extreme as in myxedema coma, is a recognised endocrine cause of hypothermia by reducing metabolic rate and impairing thermogenesis and behavioural responses (p.3768).

Bradycardia, reduced myocardial contractility and stroke volume, and pericardial effusion (up to ~30% of hypothyroid patients) reflect the cardiac depression that underlies the haemodynamic picture (p.3030).
Carotene accumulation can give the skin a yellow tinge, and nonpitting (myxedematous) tissue swelling distinguishes the oedema from pitting fluid overload (p.3029-3030).
Sedatives, anesthetics, and antidepressants can precipitate or worsen myxedema coma, and impaired drug metabolism means standard doses may accumulate (p.3032).
Hypothermia masks fever and leukocytosis, so infection can be missed; rigors may be misread as shivering (p.3769).
Giving parenteral levothyroxine to a euthyroid hypothermic patient is potentially hazardous, so clinical/historical evidence of hypothyroidism should be sought first (p.3769).
Sick euthyroid syndrome can confound thyroid function tests in the acutely ill patient (p.3769).

Mortality remains 20-40% even with intensive treatment, and prognosis is independent of the measured T4 and TSH levels. Hypothermia associated with concurrent sepsis is a poor prognostic sign (p.3032, p.3769).

MASLD arises from imbalance between energy intake and expenditure: excess caloric intake, reduced physical activity, and limited peripheral adipose expansion drive visceral adiposity, insulin resistance, and metabolic dysfunction. Hepatocyte triglyceride accumulates from increased free fatty acid delivery (dietary uptake, adipose lipolysis, de novo lipogenesis), impaired fatty acid disposal, or impaired triglyceride export; triglyceride storage itself is relatively safe, so steatosis per se does not damage the liver but is a biomarker of metabolic dysfunction. When adaptive mechanisms are overwhelmed, lipotoxicity from dysfunctional lipid handling injures and kills hepatocytes, producing steatohepatitis (MASH) with inflammation and ballooned hepatocytes. Repeated/protracted MASH triggers regenerative responses that become maladaptive, promoting progressive fibrosis (replacement of functional parenchyma by scar) and primary liver cancer; cirrhosis represents futile repair. Heritable factors (e.g., PNPLA3, TM6SF2, MBOAT7 variants), epigenetic influences, gut microbiota alterations, and environmental factors (high-fat/high-sugar diets) modify susceptibility (Harrison 22e p.2701-2702).

Steatotic liver disease (SLD) is the most common cause of chronic liver disease in the US and worldwide; metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and steatohepatitis (MASH) now replace the older terms NAFLD and NASH, with ~98% population overlap (Harrison 22e p.2700-2701).

Diagnosis of MASLD requires hepatic steatosis plus little/no alcohol intake (<20 g/d women, <30 g/d men) and at least one cardiometabolic risk factor (overweight/obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia, insulin resistance/T2DM) (Harrison 22e p.2700, 2703).
Most patients are asymptomatic; MASLD is typically detected incidentally via raised ALT or steatosis on imaging done for other reasons (Harrison 22e p.2702-2703).

Disease spans a dynamic, potentially reversible spectrum: simple steatosis (MASL) -> steatohepatitis (MASH) -> fibrosis -> cirrhosis/HCC; chronic steatohepatitis is the primary driver of fibrosis, and fibrosis severity is the chief predictor of liver-related morbidity/mortality (Harrison 22e p.2700-2701, 2704).

FIB-4 (age, AST, ALT, platelets) is the recommended first-line noninvasive score with excellent negative predictive value: FIB-4 <1.3 = low risk (manage in primary care), >=2.67 = moderate/high risk warranting a secondary test (elastography or ELF) (Harrison 22e p.2704-2705).

T2DM is the strongest risk factor for MASLD acquisition, fibrosis progression, and HCC; the MASLD-T2DM relationship is bidirectional, so patients with MASLD should be screened for T2DM (Harrison 22e p.2703).

Foundational treatment is lifestyle modification with weight loss: ~5% weight loss improves steatosis, while >10% improves MASH and can reverse fibrosis; cardiovascular risk reduction and treatment of metabolic comorbidities apply to all patients (Harrison 22e p.2706).
Statins are safe across the MASLD spectrum and indicated for dyslipidemia given high cardiovascular risk; reluctance to use them is not supported by evidence of liver harm (Harrison 22e p.2707).
Failing to exclude significant alcohol intake and other chronic liver diseases (viral, autoimmune, iron/copper overload, alpha-1 antitrypsin) before attributing steatosis to MASLD.
Assuming normal liver enzymes exclude MASLD - they do not; normal ALT 'reference ranges' are inflated by including people with undiagnosed liver disease.
Relying on liver tests for staging - aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, albumin, and PT may all be completely normal even with significant disease.
MASLD can occur in lean individuals (BMI <25, or <23 in Asians), especially with truncal/visceral adiposity, so a normal BMI does not exclude it.
FIB-4 has reduced accuracy in patients >65 and <35 years and is a less robust predictor in T2DM, so a secondary noninvasive test is needed in these groups.
Liver biopsy is limited by sampling error, inter/intraobserver variability (worse with cores <2 cm), and gives only a static snapshot of disease activity.

Variable and stage-dependent. The 10-year probability of liver-related morbidity/mortality is negligible with steatosis alone, so this group is managed conservatively. Fibrosis severity is the primary predictor of outcome: average fibrosis progression is roughly one stage every 14 years in steatosis versus one stage every 7 years in MASH; once at stage >=F2 ('at-risk MASH') the risk of further progression and bad outcomes rises. Once MASLD-related cirrhosis develops, progression to decompensation runs 3-20% per year and annual primary liver cancer incidence can reach 1-2% per year, prompting biannual HCC surveillance and variceal screening. Cirrhosis can regress, and MASLD outcomes after liver transplantation are generally good in well-selected patients, though comorbid diabetes, obesity, and CVD limit candidacy and disease may recur post-transplant. MASLD is also a premalignant condition increasing risk of primary and extrahepatic malignancy even in noncirrhotic livers (Harrison 22e p.2701, 2704, 2708).

chunks.text: Narcolepsy type 1 results from selective loss of hypocretin (orexin)-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus, most likely through an autoimmune process in genetically susceptible individuals carrying HLA-DQB1*06:02. Hypocretin normally stabilises wakefulness and suppresses inappropriate REM sleep; its deficiency destabilises the sleep-wake switch, producing daytime sleepiness and the intrusion of REM features such as cataplexy into wakefulness. Type 2 has preserved hypocretin levels and a less well-defined mechanism.

chunks.text: Nasal polyps are pedunculated masses of oedematous, chronically inflamed sinonasal mucosa, most often stemming from persistent inflammation in the ethmoid region. Ongoing mucosal inflammation, frequently eosinophil-rich, causes fluid accumulation within the lamina propria, and gravity together with impaired lymphatic drainage encourages the mucosa to prolapse into the nasal cavity as polyps. Contributing factors include chronic rhinosinusitis, allergy, aspirin sensitivity and, in children, cystic fibrosis. The antrochoanal polyp arises from maxillary sinus mucosa, passes through its ostium and enlarges into the choana and nasopharynx.

chunks.text: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma develops in the epithelial lining of the nasopharynx, typically in the recess of the fossa of Rosenmuller near the Eustachian tube opening. Malignant transformation is closely linked to latent Epstein-Barr virus infection, together with genetic susceptibility and environmental exposures such as diets rich in preserved salted foods and nitrosamines. The tumour tends to spread submucosally and infiltrate early, obstructing the Eustachian tube to cause middle ear effusion, and eroding through the skull base foramina to involve cranial nerves and the cavernous sinus. Its rich lymphatic drainage leads to early and often bilateral cervical lymph node metastasis, and distant spread to bone, lung and liver can occur.

Necrotizing enterocolitis reflects a multifactorial injury to the immature intestine. An excessive inflammatory response of the immature gut mucosa, altered microbial colonisation, ischaemia or impaired mucosal perfusion, and enteral substrate combine to cause mucosal injury, bacterial translocation, and gas production within the bowel wall. Progression leads to full-thickness necrosis, perforation, peritonitis, and systemic inflammatory response with sepsis and shock.
The most common acquired gastrointestinal emergency of the newborn, occurring mainly in preterm, low-birth-weight infants and usually within the first weeks after birth.
Presentation ranges from feeding intolerance, abdominal distension, and bloody stools to systemic signs such as lethargy, temperature instability, apnoea, and shock.
The pathognomonic radiographic sign is pneumatosis intestinalis (intramural gas); portal venous gas and free intraperitoneal air are more ominous findings.
Prematurity is the dominant risk factor; enteral feeding, particularly with formula, and intestinal dysbiosis are contributory, while human milk is protective.
Initial management is medical: stop enteral feeds, decompress the bowel with a nasogastric tube, give intravenous fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics, and provide supportive care.
Serial abdominal radiographs and clinical review guide progression; free air on imaging indicates perforation and the need for surgery.
Surgical options include peritoneal drainage or laparotomy with resection of necrotic bowel, sometimes with a stoma.
The Bell staging system grades severity from suspected to advanced disease with perforation and is used to guide management.
Extensive resection can leave short bowel syndrome with long-term dependence on parenteral nutrition.

After the cord is cut, the newborn loses its steady maternal glucose supply and must mobilise hepatic glycogen, activate gluconeogenesis, and use alternative fuels such as ketones and lactate, processes driven by a surge in counter-regulatory hormones and a fall in insulin. When glycogen stores are limited (prematurity, growth restriction), glucose demand is high (stress, sepsis, hypothermia), or insulin secretion is excessive (infant of a diabetic mother, hyperinsulinism), this adaptation fails and blood glucose falls. Because the neonatal brain depends heavily on glucose, inadequate supply combined with immature ketogenesis in some infants places the brain at risk.
Low blood glucose is common in the transitional period after birth as the newborn adapts from continuous placental glucose supply to intermittent feeding.
Infants at highest risk include those of diabetic mothers, large- or small-for-gestational-age babies, preterm infants, and any newborn who is stressed, cold, or septic.
Signs are often subtle and non-specific: jitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy, hypotonia, temperature instability, apnoea, or seizures; many affected infants appear asymptomatic.
At-risk and symptomatic infants should be screened with bedside glucose testing, with low values confirmed on a laboratory sample given the imprecision of point-of-care meters.
Early and frequent feeding is the first-line measure; infants who cannot maintain adequate glucose or who are symptomatic require intravenous dextrose.
Symptomatic hypoglycaemia with a documented low glucose that resolves when glucose is normalised (Whipple triad) warrants investigation and treatment.
Persistent or recurrent hypoglycaemia beyond the first days of life suggests an underlying disorder such as hyperinsulinism, endocrine deficiency, or an inborn error of metabolism.
The clinical concern is that prolonged or severe low glucose can injure the developing brain, so prevention and prompt correction are priorities.

Newborns have increased bilirubin production from a high red cell mass with shorter red cell lifespan, combined with immature hepatic conjugation (low UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity) and enhanced enterohepatic recirculation of bilirubin. These factors produce transient physiological unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Pathological jaundice arises when production is excessive (haemolysis, extravasated blood), conjugation or uptake is impaired, or excretion is obstructed (cholestasis). Unbound unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and can cross the blood-brain barrier, depositing in the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei to cause neurotoxicity.
Visible yellow discolouration of skin and sclerae from raised serum bilirubin, extremely common in newborns and usually due to unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinaemia.
Physiological jaundice appears after the first 24 hours, peaks around days 3-5 in term infants, and resolves without harm; it reflects normal neonatal bilirubin handling.
Jaundice in the first 24 hours of life is always pathological and demands urgent evaluation, commonly for haemolysis.
Key pathological causes include blood-group incompatibility (Rh, ABO), G6PD deficiency, sepsis, and other haemolytic conditions.
Conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinaemia is never physiological and requires investigation for cholestasis, notably biliary atresia, which needs early surgery.
Breastfeeding-associated (early, from inadequate intake) and breast-milk (later, prolonged) jaundice are common benign patterns once other causes are excluded.
Management depends on bilirubin level plotted against age in hours and risk factors; phototherapy is first-line and exchange transfusion is reserved for dangerously high or rapidly rising levels.
The feared complication is bilirubin-induced neurological dysfunction (acute encephalopathy progressing to kernicterus), which is preventable with timely treatment.
Dismissing jaundice in the first 24 hours as physiological
Failing to fractionate bilirubin and missing cholestasis / biliary atresia
Assessing jaundice by clinical appearance alone rather than measured bilirubin against age-specific thresholds
Overlooking dehydration from inadequate feeding as a contributor in early breastfeeding jaundice
Not investigating jaundice that persists beyond the expected period

Immature type II pneumocytes produce insufficient pulmonary surfactant, so alveolar surface tension is high. This causes progressive diffuse atelectasis, reduced lung compliance, and ventilation-perfusion mismatch. Hypoxaemia and hypercapnia with acidosis follow, and pulmonary vascular resistance may remain elevated with right-to-left shunting. Epithelial injury and protein-rich exudate form the hyaline membranes that give the disease its historical name, further impairing gas exchange.
A disease of surfactant deficiency affecting mainly preterm infants; incidence rises steeply as gestational age falls, being greatest below about 28 weeks.
Distress typically begins at or soon after birth with tachypnoea, grunting, nasal flaring, intercostal and subcostal recession, and cyanosis that worsen over the first hours to days.
Chest radiograph classically shows a diffuse fine reticulogranular (ground-glass) pattern with air bronchograms and low lung volumes.
Antenatal maternal corticosteroids given before anticipated preterm delivery accelerate lung maturation and markedly reduce incidence and severity.
Exogenous surfactant replacement, delivered into the airway, is a cornerstone of treatment and improves oxygenation and survival.
Early nasal continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) helps maintain functional residual capacity and can reduce the need for intubation and mechanical ventilation.

Maternal diabetes, male sex, second-born twins, caesarean delivery without labour, and perinatal asphyxia increase risk, whereas chronic intrauterine stress and prolonged rupture of membranes may reduce it.
Untreated disease tends to worsen for about 2-3 days before recovery begins, often heralded by a spontaneous diuresis.

Over-oxygenation, which increases the risk of retinopathy of prematurity and oxidative lung injury

With antenatal steroids, surfactant, and modern respiratory support, survival is high, particularly in more mature preterm infants; outcome worsens with decreasing gestational age and with complications such as air leak, intraventricular haemorrhage, and progression to bronchopulmonary dysplasia.

The immature neonatal brain is intrinsically more excitable because excitatory glutamatergic circuits mature earlier than inhibitory GABAergic systems, and GABA can be depolarising early in development. An acute insult, most often hypoxia-ischaemia, disrupts energy metabolism and ion gradients, leading to neuronal depolarisation and synchronised, excessive electrical discharges. Metabolic derangements, structural lesions, infection, or genetic and metabolic disorders lower the seizure threshold further. Frequent dissociation between electrical seizures and visible clinical signs reflects this immaturity and underlies the need for electrographic monitoring.
Seizures in the newborn period are usually a symptom of an acute underlying brain insult rather than a chronic epilepsy, so the priority is to find and treat the cause.
Presentations are often subtle: repetitive eye deviation or blinking, lip-smacking or chewing, cycling or boxing limb movements, and apnoea, in addition to clonic or tonic activity.
Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy is the most common cause; other important causes include stroke, intracranial haemorrhage, infection, metabolic disturbances, and inborn errors of metabolism.
Because clinical signs are unreliable and electroclinical dissociation is common, EEG or amplitude-integrated EEG monitoring is central to accurate diagnosis.
Immediate workup should exclude readily treatable causes such as hypoglycaemia and electrolyte abnormalities, correcting these before escalating anticonvulsant therapy.
Non-epileptic movements like jitteriness can mimic seizures but are stimulus-sensitive, suppressible by gentle restraint, and lack autonomic or ocular features.
Neuroimaging and, where appropriate, lumbar puncture and metabolic or genetic testing help establish aetiology and guide prognosis.
Pyridoxine-dependent and other vitamin-responsive epilepsies should be considered when seizures are refractory to standard agents.

Outcome depends largely on the underlying cause and the severity of any brain injury; seizures due to transient metabolic disturbances often resolve well, whereas those from severe hypoxic-ischaemic injury, major structural lesions, or certain genetic-metabolic disorders carry a higher risk of epilepsy and neurodevelopmental impairment.

Neonates are relatively immunocompromised, with immature innate and adaptive defences, low immunoglobulin levels, and impaired neutrophil function. Organisms reach the infant by ascending or intrapartum transmission from the maternal genital tract in early-onset disease, or from the postnatal environment and invasive devices in late-onset disease. Once bloodstream invasion occurs, bacterial products trigger a systemic inflammatory response with cytokine release, endothelial injury, capillary leak, and impaired perfusion that can progress to septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and multi-organ dysfunction. The immature blood-brain barrier and limited containment of infection predispose to meningitis.

A systemic bacterial (occasionally fungal or viral) infection in the first 28 days of life, conventionally split into early-onset (within roughly the first 72 hours, often maternally acquired) and late-onset (after 72 hours, frequently nosocomial or community-acquired).
Signs are notoriously nonspecific: temperature instability (fever or hypothermia), poor feeding, lethargy or irritability, respiratory distress, apnoea, tachycardia, and abdominal distension.

Group B Streptococcus and Escherichia coli dominate early-onset disease; coagulase-negative staphylococci, Staphylococcus aureus, and Gram-negative organisms are common in late-onset disease, especially in preterm infants with indwelling lines.
Maternal risk factors include prolonged rupture of membranes, chorioamnionitis, maternal fever, and GBS colonisation without adequate intrapartum prophylaxis.
Blood culture is the diagnostic gold standard; a lumbar puncture should be considered because meningitis frequently coexists and may be missed.
Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics must be started promptly after cultures because deterioration can be rapid; the regimen is later narrowed to culture results.
Supportive care (thermoregulation, respiratory and haemodynamic support, glucose management) is as important as antimicrobials.
A low threshold for treatment is appropriate given nonspecific signs, but antibiotics are stopped early when cultures remain negative and the infant is well.

Outcome depends on gestational age, organism, and speed of treatment; prompt therapy usually leads to recovery, but meningitis, shock, and prematurity carry higher mortality and risk of neurodevelopmental sequelae.
