Inhaled environmental carcinogens, principally those in tobacco smoke, drive transformation of bronchoepithelial cells to a malignant phenotype. Susceptibility is modulated by polymorphisms in carcinogen-metabolizing genes (e.g., CYP1A1) and by genetic loci affecting nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and telomerase (5p15, 6p21, 15q25). Tumorigenesis reflects accumulation of gain-of-function mutations in oncogenes and loss-of-function mutations in tumor-suppressor genes, with the sequence differing by histologic type. Adenocarcinomas frequently harbor targetable driver alterations: activating receptor tyrosine kinase mutations (EGFR, HER2/ERBB2, MET), intracellular signaling mutations (KRAS, BRAF), and chromosomal rearrangements activating ALK, ROS1, RET, and NTRK. Squamous tumors may show FGFR1 amplification, DDR2 mutations, PIK3CA mutations/PTEN loss, and BRAF/MET alterations. Inactivated tumor suppressors include TP53, RB1, RASSF1A, CDKN2A/B, LKB1 (STK11), and FHIT; allelic loss on chromosome 3p occurs very early, even in histologically normal smoke-damaged epithelium. Clinical manifestations arise from central/endobronchial growth (cough, hemoptysis, wheeze, postobstructive pneumonia), peripheral growth (pleural/chest-wall pain, dyspnea, cavitation), regional intrathoracic spread (recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy with hoarseness, phrenic nerve palsy, Horner syndrome, Pancoast syndrome, superior vena cava syndrome, pericardial/lymphatic involvement), distant metastasis, or paraneoplastic mechanisms.
Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death worldwide and in the United States; over half of patients present with locally advanced or metastatic disease at diagnosis.
Hypercalcemia from ectopic PTH-related peptide is the most common life-threatening metabolic complication of malignancy and occurs primarily with squamous cell carcinoma.

On FDG PET, a standardized uptake value (SUV) above 2.5 is highly suspicious for malignancy, but PET must never be used alone to diagnose cancer, nodal involvement, or metastasis because of false positives (infection, granulomatous disease such as tuberculosis) and false negatives (lesions under 8 mm, slow-growing tumors, diabetes).

Adenocarcinoma in situ and minimally invasive adenocarcinoma (solitary lesions 3 cm or less with pure or predominant lepidic growth and 5 mm or less invasion) achieve near 100% 5-year disease-free survival after complete resection.

Tobacco smoking accounts for roughly two-thirds of lung cancer deaths globally, but about 65% of new U.S. diagnoses are now in former smokers or never-smokers; one in five women and one in twelve men diagnosed have never smoked.

The WHO divides epithelial lung cancers into four major types: small-cell carcinoma (SCLC) and three non-small-cell types (adenocarcinoma, squamous cell, large-cell). Together these account for about 90% of epithelial lung cancers; adenocarcinoma is now the most common subtype.

Separating SCLC from NSCLC and, within NSCLC, squamous from nonsquamous histology is essential because natural history and management differ markedly; a generic diagnosis of 'non-small-cell carcinoma, not otherwise specified' is no longer acceptable.

A chronic cough with or without hemoptysis in a current or former smoker with COPD aged 40 or older warrants thorough evaluation for lung cancer even with a normal chest x-ray; a persistent pneumonia unresponsive to repeated antibiotics also requires workup.
Tissue sampling is required to confirm diagnosis in all suspected cases; a core biopsy is preferred over fine-needle aspiration to provide adequate material for molecular and PD-L1 testing.

Central, endobronchial lesions (squamous cell, small-cell, carcinoid) are more readily reached by bronchoscopy, whereas peripheral lesions (adenocarcinoma, large-cell) are more amenable to transthoracic biopsy.
Driver oncogenes (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, RET, NTRK, BRAF, MET, HER2, KRAS) are enriched in nonsquamous NSCLC and define distinct molecular cohorts; nearly 90% of SCLCs carry TP53 and RB1 mutations.

Paraneoplastic syndromes are common, especially with SCLC, and may be the presenting feature or first sign of recurrence; they can mimic metastatic disease and lead to inappropriately palliative rather than curative management.
A normal chest x-ray does not exclude lung cancer in a high-risk symptomatic smoker.
Negative TTF-1 does not exclude a pulmonary primary; TTF-1 is also positive in neuroendocrine and thyroid tumors.

PET-CT cannot establish a tissue diagnosis: false positives occur with tuberculosis/granulomatous and infectious disease and false negatives with sub-8 mm, slow-growing, or carcinoid/well-differentiated tumors.
Paraneoplastic syndromes may be mistaken for metastatic disease, risking inappropriate palliative rather than curative treatment.
A single negative thoracentesis does not exclude a malignant effusion; repeat sampling is essential.
Diagnosing on small biopsy/cytology specimens may blur squamous-versus-nonsquamous distinction; repeat biopsy is advised in advanced disease for adequate molecular and PD-L1 testing.

Low-dose CT screening carries a high false-positive rate (false-positive rate about 96% among positive screens in NLST), with attendant risks of overdiagnosis, unnecessary procedures, and radiation exposure.

Outcome is strongly stage-dependent. For NSCLC by the eighth-edition TNM system, 5-year overall survival ranges from roughly 90% for the earliest (stage IA1) disease down to about 10% for stage IVB; SEER data report a 5-year survival of about 63% for localized NSCLC. Lepidic-predominant adenocarcinoma has a favorable prognosis, acinar and papillary intermediate, and solid-predominant and micropapillary patterns poor. SCLC is more aggressive: 60-70% present with extensive-stage disease, and even in limited-stage SCLC median survival is roughly 12-20 months historically. Weight loss over 10% of body weight and thrombotic complications of malignancy are poor prognostic signs. Extrathoracic metastases are found at autopsy in over 50% of squamous, about 80% of adenocarcinoma/large-cell, and over 95% of SCLC cases.

NSCLC is staged with the eighth-edition (2018) TNM system: T1 (3 cm or less; subdivided T1a 1 cm or less, T1b over 1 to 2 cm, T1c over 2 to 3 cm), T2 (over 3 to 5 cm or visceral pleura/main bronchus involvement/atelectasis; T2a over 3 to 4 cm, T2b over 4 to 5 cm), T3 (over 5 to 7 cm or invasion of chest wall/pericardium/phrenic nerve or satellite nodule in same lobe), T4 (over 7 cm or invasion of mediastinum, heart, great vessels, trachea, recurrent laryngeal nerve, esophagus, vertebra, carina, or separate nodule in a different ipsilateral lobe). Nodes: N0 none, N1 ipsilateral peribronchial/hilar/intrapulmonary, N2 ipsilateral mediastinal/subcarinal, N3 contralateral mediastinal/hilar or scalene/supraclavicular. Metastasis: M1a contralateral nodule or pleural/pericardial nodule/malignant effusion, M1b single extrathoracic metastasis, M1c multiple extrathoracic metastases. SCLC is commonly classified by the two-stage Veterans Administration system: limited-stage (confined to ipsilateral hemithorax within a tolerable radiation port) versus extensive-stage (overt metastatic disease). Physiologic operability thresholds: FEV1 over 2 L or over 80% predicted suggests tolerance of pneumonectomy; FEV1 over 1.5 L suggests adequate reserve for lobectomy; VO2max under 15 mL/kg/min predicts higher postoperative risk; contraindications to thoracic surgery include FEV1 under 1 L, resting PCO2 over 45 mmHg, DLCO under 40%, severe pulmonary hypertension, and recent myocardial infarction.

Stones form when urine becomes supersaturated with lithogenic solutes, i.e., when the concentration product exceeds the solubility product. Most people's urine is supersaturated for one or more crystal types, but crystallization inhibitors (notably urine citrate) prevent continuous stone formation. Recent biopsy data have shifted the paradigm for stone initiation: calcium phosphate deposits in the renal interstitium, hypothesized to begin at the thin limb of the loop of Henle, then extends to and erodes through the papillary epithelium, forming Randall's plaque on which most calcium oxalate stones grow. Tubular plugs of calcium phosphate may initiate calcium phosphate stones. Thus stone formation can begin years before a stone is clinically detectable. Higher urine calcium (from greater GI absorption and/or bone turnover) and higher urine oxalate (largely dietary, with higher dietary calcium reducing GI oxalate absorption) raise calcium oxalate/phosphate risk, while low urine citrate removes a key inhibitor (Harrison 22e p.2448-2450).

Calcium oxalate stones are by far the most common type (~75%), followed by calcium phosphate (~15%), uric acid (~8%), struvite (~1%), and cystine (<1%); many stones are mixtures and contain protein matrix (Harrison 22e p.2448).

Two 24-h urine collections on the patient's usual diet are the cornerstone of preventive evaluation, measuring volume, calcium, oxalate, citrate, uric acid, sodium, potassium, phosphorus, magnesium, pH, and creatinine; two collections are needed because of substantial day-to-day variability (Harrison 22e p.2451-2452).

Urinary risk factors (calcium, oxalate, citrate) are continuous variables with no valid normal/abnormal cutoff; dichotomizing them is misleading and arbitrary thresholds should be avoided (Harrison 22e p.2449, 2452).
Pure uric acid stones can be recognized by their low Hounsfield units on CT, helping distinguish stone composition non-invasively (Harrison 22e p.2452).

Identifying the stone type is clinically important because it informs prognosis and the choice of preventive strategy; patients should be encouraged to retrieve and submit passed stones for composition analysis (Harrison 22e p.2451-2452).

The two classic acute presentations are renal colic and painless gross hematuria; symptom onset reflects a stone moving into the ureter and gives no clue as to when the stone actually formed, since stone growth is typically clinically silent over weeks to years (Harrison 22e p.2450).

Pain radiation depends on stone location: an upper ureteral stone may radiate anteriorly, while a lower ureteral stone may radiate to the ipsilateral testicle (men) or labium (women); a ureterovesical-junction stone can cause urinary urgency and frequency (Harrison 22e p.2450).
Absence of hematuria does not exclude a stone, particularly when urine flow is completely obstructed (Harrison 22e p.2450).

Noncontrast helical CT is the gold-standard imaging test: it detects stones as small as 1 mm and visualizes uric acid stones that are traditionally considered radiolucent on plain films (Harrison 22e p.2450).

Urine pH governs solubility of several stone types: uric acid stones form at pH consistently <=5.5, calcium phosphate stones are favored at pH >=6.5, and cystine is more soluble at higher pH; calcium oxalate stone risk is not influenced by urine pH (Harrison 22e p.2450).

Urine citrate is the most clinically important natural inhibitor of calcium-containing stones; metabolic acidosis (including from high animal-flesh intake) lowers citrate excretion by enhancing its tubular reabsorption (Harrison 22e p.2448, 2449).

Dietary calcium restriction is counterproductive: higher dietary calcium intake lowers stone risk by binding intestinal oxalate and reducing urinary oxalate, whereas low calcium intake increases stone risk and may lower bone density (Harrison 22e p.2449).

Recommending low dietary calcium, which actually increases stone risk and harms bone density

Basing the preventive regimen on a single 24-h urine collection despite large day-to-day variability

Failing to recognize that symptom onset does not indicate when the stone formed

Although renal colic is reported as among the worst pain patients experience, nephrolithiasis is rarely fatal. More than half of first-time stone formers have a recurrence within 10 years, but recurrence of most or all stone types can be prevented with careful evaluation and targeted, often lifelong, intervention. Untreated infection (struvite) stones can have devastating consequences and progress to end-stage renal disease, and repeated obstruction and instrumentation (e.g., in cystinuria) can reduce GFR. Primary hyperoxaluria can cause intraparenchymal calcium oxalate deposition leading to renal failure (Harrison 22e p.2448, 2450, 2451).
UTI in the setting of an obstructing stone is a urologic emergency ('pus under pressure') requiring urgent restoration of drainage via ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy

chunks.text: Nephrotic syndrome reflects increased glomerular permeability to plasma proteins. Minimal change disease causes diffuse fusion (effacement) of podocyte foot processes producing predominantly 'selective' albumin loss, whereas immune-complex disruption of the basement membrane and slit diaphragms yields 'nonselective' loss of albumin and larger proteins. Hypoalbuminaemia results from urinary loss plus increased proximal-tubule catabolism of filtered albumin, exceeding hepatic synthesis (a hypercatabolic, negative-nitrogen-balance state). Oedema arises from renal sodium retention and reduced plasma oncotic pressure; perceived reduction in effective intravascular volume activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, AVP and the sympathetic nervous system, and filtered proteases can directly activate the epithelial Na channel (ENaC) in principal cells, promoting further salt/water retention. Hyperlipidaemia/hypercholesterolaemia reflect increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis. Notably, hypertension is uncommon in primary kidney diseases causing nephrotic syndrome (p.385). Hereditary nephrotic syndrome can result from podocyte slit-diaphragm gene mutations (nephrin NPHS1, podocin NPHS2); APOL1 risk variants predispose to FSGS, with disease expression triggered by a 'second hit' of infection/inflammation damaging podocytes and glomerular endothelium (p.2357-2358).

chunks.text: Glomerular proteinuria in diabetes typically appears after years of small-vessel disease (hence frequent coexistent retinopathy) and predicts progression to nephrotic syndrome and renal failure; the rate of progression is faster with hypertension, obesity and poor glucose control. Diffuse glomerular involvement (most glomeruli) makes nephrotic syndrome likely, whereas focal disease (<50% of glomeruli) tends to give subnephrotic albuminuria. In membranous nephropathy, ~70% of primary cases are anti-PLA2R associated. Collapsing glomerulopathy (HIVAN) is a severe, treatment-resistant FSGS variant. Quartan malarial nephropathy responds poorly to therapy (p.2356-2358).

Injury to the glomerular filtration barrier, particularly the podocytes and their slit diaphragms, increases permeability to plasma proteins, producing heavy albuminuria. In minimal change disease, light microscopy is near-normal and electron microscopy shows diffuse podocyte foot process effacement, implicating a circulating permeability factor and immune dysregulation. Urinary protein loss lowers serum albumin, reducing plasma oncotic pressure and, together with secondary sodium retention, causing oedema. The liver increases lipoprotein synthesis in response to low oncotic pressure, producing hyperlipidaemia. Loss of immunoglobulins and complement factors predisposes to infection, and loss of anticoagulant proteins with raised procoagulants predisposes to thrombosis.
Defined by the tetrad of heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, and hyperlipidaemia.
In children it is most often idiopathic, and minimal change disease is the predominant histology, especially in preschool children.
Oedema is the usual presenting feature, typically starting periorbitally and becoming generalised with dependent swelling and sometimes ascites.
Most childhood cases are steroid-responsive, so an empirical corticosteroid trial is standard first-line therapy without initial biopsy in the typical age group.
Renal biopsy is reserved for atypical features: older or very young age, gross haematuria, hypertension, impaired renal function, or steroid resistance.
Children are at increased risk of infection (notably pneumococcal peritonitis) from urinary immunoglobulin loss, and of thromboembolism from a hypercoagulable state.
Supportive care includes sensible salt restriction, careful management of oedema, and attention to nutrition and infection prevention including vaccination.
Relapses are common; the pattern of response guides classification into steroid-sensitive, frequently relapsing, steroid-dependent, or steroid-resistant disease.
Attributing oedema to another cause and missing proteinuria on urinalysis
Overlooking infection or thrombosis, the major acute complications
Missing atypical features that warrant biopsy rather than empirical steroids
Aggressive diuresis precipitating hypovolaemia and thrombosis in an intravascularly depleted child

Children with steroid-sensitive minimal change disease generally have a good long-term renal outcome despite frequent relapses; steroid resistance, often from focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, carries a higher risk of progression to chronic kidney disease.
Fever with abdominal pain suggesting spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
Signs of thromboembolism (limb swelling, respiratory distress, neurological signs)
Hypertension, gross haematuria, or reduced renal function suggesting a nephritic process
Severe hypovolaemia from rapid fluid shifts, or tense ascites and respiratory compromise
Steroid resistance prompting reassessment and biopsy

chunks.diseaseName: Nervous System Disorders in Critical Care
chunks.text: Life-threatening neurologic illness in the critically ill arises from primary lesions anywhere along the neuraxis or as a consequence of systemic disorders (hepatic failure, multiorgan failure, cardiac arrest). The unifying goal is preventing secondary brain injury from ischemia, hemorrhage, edema, herniation, and elevated ICP. Brain edema is vasogenic (fluid crossing an incompetent blood-brain barrier) and/or cytotoxic (cellular swelling and death); clinically significant edema usually combines both and can raise ICP and cause tissue shifts. Inadequate oxygen/glucose delivery triggers the ischemic cascade: excitatory amino acid (glutamate) release, calcium and sodium influx, protease/lipase activation, lipid peroxidation, free-radical membrane injury, cytotoxic edema, and necrotic cell death; an alternative apoptotic pathway occurs without edema and is often not seen on imaging. Penumbra denotes still-salvageable ischemic tissue. Secondary insults (hypotension, hypoxia, fever, seizures, hyperglycemia) worsen the cascade. The skull tolerates little added volume, so once intracranial compliance is exhausted, small volume increases sharply raise ICP, lower CPP, and provoke ischemia; ischemia-driven autoregulatory vasodilation can paradoxically further raise blood volume and ICP, creating a vicious cycle.

chunks.diseaseName: Nervous System Disorders in Critical Care
chunks.text: Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) equals mean arterial pressure (MAP) minus intracranial pressure (ICP); the general targets in neurocritical care are ICP below 20 mmHg and CPP at or above 60 mmHg (Harrison 22e p.2345).

chunks.diseaseName: Nervous System Disorders in Critical Care
chunks.text: Critical illness polyneuropathy is the most common PNS complication of prolonged critical illness and sepsis; it is a distal axonal sensorimotor neuropathy and should be suspected when a patient fails to wean from the ventilator despite resolving sepsis (Harrison 22e p.2351).

chunks.diseaseName: Nervous System Disorders in Critical Care
chunks.text: Persistent neuromuscular junction weakness in the ICU is almost always drug-related, most often from nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents (pancuronium, vecuronium, rocuronium, cisatracurium) and potentiated by aminoglycosides; recovery is full once the drug is cleared (Harrison 22e p.2351-2352).

chunks.diseaseName: Nervous System Disorders in Critical Care
chunks.text: In PNS weakness, intubation should be considered when maximal inspiratory force falls below -25 cmH2O or vital capacity is under 1 L, and the decision should be clinical rather than waiting for oxygen desaturation or CO2 retention (Harrison 22e p.2351).

chunks.diseaseName: Nervous System Disorders in Critical Care
chunks.text: Cerebral autoregulation normally keeps cerebral blood flow constant across a wide MAP range, but in severe brain injury it can be lost, making flow directly pressure-dependent so that hypotension causes ischemia and hypertension causes hyperperfusion (Harrison 22e p.2343-2344).

chunks.diseaseName: Nervous System Disorders in Critical Care
chunks.text: Cerebral blood flow rises with hypercapnia/acidosis and falls with hypocapnia/alkalosis, which is the basis for short-term hyperventilation to lower ICP; the effect is short-lived (hours) due to interstitial buffering, and abrupt discontinuation can cause rebound ICP elevation (Harrison 22e p.2344, p.2345).

chunks.diseaseName: Nervous System Disorders in Critical Care
chunks.text: In altered consciousness, the first task is to separate a diffuse/metabolic process from a focal/structural one; prominent focal signs such as pupillary asymmetry, hemiparesis, gaze palsy, or visual field deficit suggest a structural lesion and mandate urgent neuroimaging (Harrison 22e p.2344).

chunks.diseaseName: Nervous System Disorders in Critical Care
chunks.text: After cardiac arrest, poor-prognosis indicators include absent pupillary light reflex or extensor/absent motor response to pain at days 5-7, bilateral absence of the N20 somatosensory evoked potential component, a burst-suppression or nonreactive EEG, and a markedly elevated neuron-specific enolase (NSE), but sedation, metabolic derangements, and hypothermia confound these signs (Harrison 22e p.2346).

chunks.diseaseName: Nervous System Disorders in Critical Care
chunks.text: Osmotic demyelination syndrome (formerly central pontine myelinolysis) is typically precipitated by rapid correction of hyponatremia or hyperosmolar states, presenting days later with quadriplegia and pseudobulbar palsy; corrective sodium changes should be limited to roughly 8 mmol/L per 24 h and 15 mmol/L per 48 h (Harrison 22e p.2348-2349).

chunks.diseaseName: Nervous System Disorders in Critical Care
chunks.text: Wernicke's disease is a thiamine-deficiency emergency; only about one-third of patients show the classic triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and global confusion, and IV glucose can precipitate or worsen it, so thiamine must precede glucose in at-risk patients (Harrison 22e p.2349).

chunks.diseaseName: Nervous System Disorders in Critical Care
chunks.text: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) reflects hyperperfusion/vasogenic edema favoring posterior (occipital) regions; the rate of blood pressure rise rather than the absolute value is the key risk factor, and the syndrome is not always reversible or strictly posterior (Harrison 22e p.2349-2350).

chunks.diseaseName: Nervous System Disorders in Critical Care
chunks.text: Sepsis-associated encephalopathy is a diffuse brain dysfunction without focal findings, occurs in the majority of patients with sepsis and multiorgan failure, and is not simply explained by metabolic derangements; cytokines such as TNF and interleukins are implicated (Harrison 22e p.2348).

chunks.diseaseName: Nervous System Disorders in Critical Care
chunks.text: Outcome depends heavily on the underlying disorder and on prevention of secondary injury. After hypoxia-ischemia, recovery may be full if circulation is restored within 3-5 minutes, while longer insults often cause permanent damage; the brain tolerates pure hypoxia better than combined hypoxia-ischemia. Reliable post-arrest prognostication requires sufficient observation time, and hypothermia/sedation delay when predictors become valid; some patients awaken after a week or longer, so premature withdrawal risks a self-fulfilling prophecy. Sepsis-associated encephalopathy carries roughly 50% mortality when severe enough to cause coma, though this mainly reflects underlying illness severity; the encephalopathy usually improves substantially with successful treatment, but long-term cognitive dysfunction is increasingly recognized, especially in older survivors. Critical illness polyneuropathy and thick-filament critical illness myopathy generally recover spontaneously if the patient survives, though recovery may take weeks to months and some residual weakness can persist. Prolonged neuromuscular blockade causes no permanent damage and resolves once the agent clears.

Neuroblastoma develops from neural crest-derived precursors of the sympathetic nervous system, giving rise to a spectrum from undifferentiated neuroblastoma to more mature ganglioneuroblastoma and benign ganglioneuroma. Tumour behaviour is strongly governed by biology: MYCN amplification, segmental chromosomal changes, and DNA ploidy correlate with aggressiveness, while some infant tumours undergo differentiation or apoptosis and regress spontaneously.
The most common extracranial solid tumour of childhood and the most common malignancy of infancy, arising from primitive sympathetic neural crest cells.
It can occur anywhere along the sympathetic chain; the adrenal medulla and paraspinal abdomen are the most frequent primary sites.
An abdominal primary often presents as a firm, irregular mass that crosses the midline, distinguishing it from Wilms tumour.
Presentation is highly variable and may include systemic upset, bone pain, proptosis with periorbital bruising ('raccoon eyes') from orbital metastases, or a paraspinal mass causing cord compression.
Distinctive paraneoplastic features include opsoclonus-myoclonus (dancing eyes, dancing feet) and secretory diarrhoea from vasoactive intestinal peptide.
Most tumours secrete catecholamines, so urinary homovanillic acid (HVA) and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) are useful markers.
Behaviour spans a remarkable spectrum, from spontaneous regression in infants (including stage MS/4S disease) to aggressive, widely metastatic disease.
MYCN amplification is a key adverse biological marker that upstages risk and intensifies therapy.
Risk stratification integrating age, stage, histology, and genetics guides treatment ranging from observation or surgery to intensive multimodal therapy.
Confusing it with Wilms tumour when it presents as an abdominal mass

Outcome is extremely variable: low-risk and infant disease (including 4S/MS) often has excellent survival and may regress, whereas high-risk disease with MYCN amplification or widespread metastases has a much poorer prognosis despite intensive therapy.

chunks.text: Ingested Taenia solium eggs release oncospheres that reach the brain and develop into cysticerci. Viable cysts in the parenchyma may remain quiescent, but immune-mediated degeneration releases antigens that provoke perilesional inflammation and oedema, generating seizures and focal deficits. As cysts die they may calcify, and these calcified foci can remain epileptogenic. In the ventricles and subarachnoid space, cysts and the associated inflammation can block cerebrospinal fluid pathways, producing raised intracranial pressure and hydrocephalus, while subarachnoid (racemose) disease may cause arachnoiditis and vasculitis.

chunks.text: Normal micturition depends on coordinated control between the pontine micturition centre, spinal pathways, and sacral (S2-S4) reflexes governing the detrusor and urethral sphincter. Neurological lesions disrupt this coordination in patterns determined by lesion level. Upper motor neuron lesions above the sacral cord release the sacral reflex from higher inhibition, producing detrusor overactivity and often detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia, in which the sphincter contracts against a contracting bladder, generating dangerously high pressures. Lower motor neuron or peripheral lesions abolish the reflex arc, producing an acontractile, flaccid bladder with retention and overflow. Sustained high intravesical pressure and incomplete emptying threaten the upper tracts and predispose to infection and stones.

Neuroimaging techniques exploit differing physical tissue properties. CT reconstructs a cross-sectional map of x-ray attenuation: dense tissue (bone, acute clot) attenuates heavily and appears bright, while water and air appear dark. MRI maps the distribution and relaxation behavior of (mainly hydrogen) protons placed in a strong static magnetic field and excited by radiofrequency pulses; T1 relaxation is the time for ~63% of protons to return toward equilibrium and T2 the time for ~63% to dephase. Manipulating pulse timing (TR and TE) yields T1-weighted images (fat and subacute hemorrhage bright; CSF/edema dark) or T2-weighted images (CSF/edema/demyelination/infarct bright). Gray matter contains roughly 10-15% more water than white matter, providing intrinsic contrast. Pathology such as infarction, abscess, and dense tumor restricts microscopic water motion, producing high DWI signal. Iodinated and gadolinium contrast agents reveal blood-brain barrier breakdown by tumor, infarct, or infection. Flow phenomena underlie MR angiography, and regional changes in oxy/deoxyhemoglobin underlie the BOLD signal of functional MRI (Harrison 22e p.3383-3392).

MRI is generally more sensitive than CT for lesions of the central and peripheral nervous system, whereas CT is faster and the pragmatic first choice for uncooperative patients and for suspected acute stroke, hemorrhage, or acute intracranial/spinal trauma (Harrison 22e p.3383).
CTA and gadolinium-enhanced MRA have largely replaced catheter angiography, which is now reserved for cases needing fine small-vessel detail or planned interventional therapy (Harrison 22e p.3383).

Vessel wall MR imaging is a high-resolution technique that interrogates the arterial wall itself and helps distinguish atherosclerosis, primary CNS vasculitis, and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (Harrison 22e p.3390).

Amyloid PET can be positive in up to about 25% of cognitively normal older adults, so a positive scan does not by itself diagnose Alzheimer disease; tau PET appears more specific (Harrison 22e p.3392).

Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) is the single most sensitive technique for detecting acute cerebral or spinal cord ischemia, with restricted diffusion (high DWI signal) appearing in infarction of less than about 7 days; it also lights up encephalitis, abscess, and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (Harrison 22e p.3383, 3389).

CT is superior to MRI for fine osseous detail and is preferred for the initial workup of conductive hearing loss and skull/spine bone lesions, while MRI better detects bone-marrow infiltrative processes that CT may miss (Harrison 22e p.3383).

On unenhanced CT, denser structures such as bone or acute blood appear bright (high attenuation), whereas water, air, and soft tissue appear dark; this is why acute hemorrhage and bone are well seen on noncontrast CT (Harrison 22e p.3383-3384).

Iodinated contrast highlights vascular structures and blood-brain barrier defects; in the normal CNS only vessels and structures lacking a blood-brain barrier (pituitary, choroid plexus, dura) enhance (Harrison 22e p.3384).

Susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) is highly sensitive to blood, calcium, and air and is the sequence of choice for microhemorrhages seen in amyloid angiopathy, hypertension, hemorrhagic metastases, traumatic brain injury, and thrombotic states (Harrison 22e p.3387-3388).

FLAIR suppresses the bright CSF signal of T2 imaging, improving detection of edematous/water-containing lesions adjacent to CSF spaces such as periventricular plaques and cortical lesions (Harrison 22e p.3387).

Gadolinium-based contrast does not cause contrast-induced nephropathy, but linear (group 1/3) agents can cause nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in patients with severe renal impairment; macrocyclic (group 2) agents are far safer and preferred in at-risk patients (Harrison 22e p.3388-3389).

Perfusion imaging that shows a region of prolonged mean transit time with preserved cerebral blood volume identifies tissue at risk (ischemic penumbra) that may be salvageable, distinct from infarcted core where blood volume and flow are reduced (Harrison 22e p.3390).

Reliance on shellfish or iodine allergy to predict contrast reactions is unreliable; the strongest predictor is a prior contrast reaction (about fivefold risk), plus atopy/asthma and other drug/food allergies (Harrison 22e p.3385).
Premedication regimens shorter than 4-5 hours have no demonstrated efficacy and do not guarantee prevention of contrast reactions (Harrison 22e p.3387).
Bicarbonate and acetylcysteine have not shown protection over normal saline against contrast-associated AKI in recent meta-analyses (Harrison 22e p.3385).

MRA has lower spatial resolution than catheter angiography, is insensitive to slow flow, and may not distinguish near-complete from complete occlusion or detect small-vessel vasculitis/distal vasospasm (Harrison 22e p.3390).

Brain gadolinium deposition (dentate nuclei, globus pallidus) occurs even with normal renal/hepatic function, is dose-dependent and greater with linear agents, but to date has no proven neurotoxic histologic correlate (Harrison 22e p.3387-3388).
The MR magnet is always on; ferromagnetic missile injuries and torqued implants can be fatal, so rigorous screening of patients and staff is mandatory (Harrison 22e p.3389).
Patient motion degrades MRI; uncooperative patients should be sedated or imaged with CT, and children under ~8 years often require monitored anesthesia (Harrison 22e p.3389).
Iodinated contrast should be avoided before planned radioactive iodine thyroid therapy because it reduces radioisotope uptake (Harrison 22e p.3387).

As a diagnostic modality, neuroimaging itself is generally safe. Contrast-associated acute kidney injury from iodinated contrast is rare, usually transient with creatinine returning toward baseline within 1-2 weeks, and most strongly associated with preexisting severe renal insufficiency; gadolinium does not cause it. Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis from linear gadolinium agents in severe renal failure is rare (reported incidence ~0.19-4% in GFR <30) but can be severely disabling with multiorgan fibrosis. Severe allergic reactions are uncommon (~0.04% with nonionic iodinated agents; gadolinium severe reactions exceedingly rare). Radiation-induced malignancy from diagnostic CT is felt to be minimal but is dose-dependent (Harrison 22e p.3384-3389).

Contrast-associated acute kidney injury is defined per KDIGO criteria within 48 h of contrast: absolute serum creatinine rise >=0.3 mg/dL (>26.4 micromol/L), a >=50% (>=1.5-fold) increase over baseline, or urine output <=0.5 mL/kg per h for at least 6 h. Renal-risk stratification for contrast uses eGFR, with <30 mL/min per 1.73 m2 carrying the greatest evidence for risk (normal >=90 mL/min per 1.73 m2) (Harrison 22e p.3384-3386).

NMO is an autoimmune astrocytopathy driven by autoantibodies against the water channel aquaporin-4 (AQP4), which is concentrated on astrocyte foot processes apposed to endothelium and at paranodal regions near nodes of Ranvier. Pathology shows loss of AQP4 staining with antibody and complement deposition, astrocyte cytolysis, thickened vessel walls, demyelination, and inflammation. AQP4 antibodies are likely pathogenic, since passive transfer reproduces disease features in animals; both complement fixation and antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity contribute to astrocyte injury, and TH17 proinflammatory T cells recognizing an immunodominant AQP4 epitope may also participate. A thymic B-cell population that constitutively expresses AQP4 normally interacts with AQP4-specific T cells to maintain tolerance, and impairment of this interaction may contribute. During acute myelitis attacks, CSF levels of IL-6 and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) are markedly elevated, reflecting active inflammation and astrocyte injury (Harrison p.3590-3591).

NMO is an aggressive antibody-mediated inflammatory CNS disorder defined by recurrent attacks of optic neuritis and myelitis; the broader term NMOSD captures partial forms and cases with additional CNS involvement (Harrison p.3590).

Up to 40% of NMO patients have a coexisting systemic autoimmune disorder (e.g., SLE, Sjögren's syndrome, p-ANCA vasculitis, myasthenia gravis, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, mixed connective tissue disease) - a feature distinguishing it from MS (Harrison p.3591).
Symptomatic onset may follow acute infection with varicella-zoster virus, Epstein-Barr virus, HIV, or tuberculosis; rare cases are paraneoplastic (breast, lung, or other cancers) (Harrison p.3592).
Asian and African ancestry populations are disproportionately affected, with the highest reported prevalence in Martinique; among white populations MS is far more common than NMO (Harrison p.3591).
Strongly female-predominant (women:men roughly 9:1), with a mean onset around age 40 but possible at any age (Harrison p.3590).

Optic neuritis in NMO can be bilateral and cause severe vision loss, a pattern uncommon in MS; myelitis is often severe, transverse, and longitudinally extensive spanning three or more contiguous vertebral segments (Harrison p.3590).
Unlike MS, NMO rarely follows a progressive course; accumulated disability results from attack-related injury rather than progression (Harrison p.3590).

Brain MRI is not invariably normal: lesions may involve the area postrema (intractable hiccups or vomiting), hypothalamus (sleep disorder or endocrinopathy), or cerebral hemispheres; large hemispheric lesions can be asymptomatic, show a 'cloud-like' appearance, be non-destructive, and resolve completely (Harrison p.3590).
Spinal cord lesions are focal enhancing areas of swelling and tissue destruction over three or more segments and are centered on the gray matter on axial imaging (Harrison p.3590).

CSF typically shows greater pleocytosis than MS, sometimes with neutrophils and eosinophils in acute cases, while oligoclonal bands are uncommon (present in fewer than 20% of patients) (Harrison p.3590-3591).

A highly specific serum autoantibody against the water channel aquaporin-4 (AQP4) is present in about 90% of patients and is diagnostic when paired with a typical clinical presentation (Harrison p.3590).
In a subset of AQP4-negative cases, autoantibodies against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) are found (Harrison p.3591).
Assuming a normal brain MRI excludes NMO - characteristic area postrema, periependymal brainstem, diencephalic, and cloud-like hemispheric lesions can be present (Harrison p.3590).
Conflating NMO with MS: bilateral severe optic neuritis, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, marked CSF pleocytosis, and frequent absence of oligoclonal bands favor NMO (Harrison p.3590).
Relying on oligoclonal bands, which are present in fewer than 20% of NMO patients (Harrison p.3590-3591).
Overlooking that NMO frequently coexists with systemic autoimmune disease, unlike MS (Harrison p.3591).

Failing to recognize AQP4-negative disease, where MOG antibodies may be present and where seronegative NMOSD requires both optic neuritis and longitudinally extensive myelitis to meet criteria (Harrison p.3591-3592).

NMO is typically a relapsing disease; a monophasic course occurs in fewer than 10% of patients and is somewhat more likely in AQP4-antibody-negative individuals. Untreated disease is severely disabling: historically about one-third of patients developed respiratory failure from cervical myelitis, and by 8 years roughly 60% were blind and more than half had permanent limb paralysis. AQP4-seropositive patients carry a high relapse risk (more than half relapse within 1 year if untreated). Long-term outcomes have substantially improved with the advent of attack and relapse therapies, with reported 5-year survival rising from about 68-75% around 1999 to 91-98% by 2017 (Harrison p.3590-3591).
Bilateral simultaneous optic neuritis with severe vision loss
Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis spanning three or more vertebral segments
Intractable hiccups, nausea, or vomiting (area postrema syndrome)

No formal severity grading; diagnosis follows the 2015 International Consensus Diagnostic Criteria for NMOSD, which stratify by AQP4-IgG status. AQP4-IgG-positive disease requires at least one core clinical characteristic, a positive AQP4-IgG test, and exclusion of alternatives. AQP4-IgG-negative or unknown-status disease requires at least two core characteristics (one of which must be optic neuritis, acute myelitis with longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, or area postrema syndrome), dissemination in space, fulfillment of additional MRI requirements, a negative or unavailable AQP4-IgG test, and exclusion of alternatives. Core clinical characteristics: optic neuritis, acute myelitis, area postrema syndrome, acute brainstem syndrome, symptomatic narcolepsy/acute diencephalic syndrome with typical MRI lesions, and symptomatic cerebral syndrome with typical brain lesions (Harrison p.3591, Table 456-1).

Structured history of total daily frequency of all nicotine products used (cigarettes, cigars, roll-your-own, vaping, oral pouches/snuff)
Duration of regular use, prior quit experiences, and current interest in quitting
Markers of addiction intensity: episodes per day, spacing through the day, and use within 30 minutes of waking
Biomarkers of smoke-toxicant exposure (markedly lower in exclusive e-cigarette users than in cigarette smokers)

Nicotine reaching the brain reversibly binds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors that are highly active in networks mediating mood, reward, joy, and excitement. With sustained high exposure, nicotinic receptors are upregulated on brain cells, so that for most people daily use is required to maintain the addicted state. As blood nicotine falls between doses, nicotine detaches from receptors and addicted individuals no longer feel 'normal,' producing a compulsive drive for the next dose. The strength and speed of addiction depend on dosing frequency and on the arterial nicotine concentration reaching the brain, which varies by product. Unprotonated (freebase) nicotine, favored at alkaline pH, is absorbed readily across mucosa but is airway-irritating at high concentration; addictive products use mildly acidic aerosols in the mouth to limit irritation and permit deep inhalation, after which alveolar pH shifts toward blood pH (~7.4), rapidly liberating absorbable unprotonated nicotine and driving fast arterial rises to the brain.

Addiction is established when nicotine in any form (combusted or heated tobacco, oral pouches, or vaped nicotine/nicotine salt) is used with sufficient intensity for a sufficient duration; addicted users self-titrate the frequency and intensity of use to achieve psychoactive effects and avoid withdrawal.

About 40% of cigarette smokers die prematurely from smoking unless they quit; the population still smoking has shifted toward socially disadvantaged groups, and prevalence has declined more slowly in those over 40 who are most likely to develop disease.

'Lower tar/nicotine' filtered cigarettes do not reduce real exposure because smokers compensate by altering puffing behavior or number smoked; ventilation-hole designs lower only machine-measured yields, not delivered toxicants.

Several genes are associated with nicotine addiction (some reducing nicotine clearance, others increasing dependence likelihood or depression risk), but the large declines in smoking since the mid-1950s indicate non-genetic factors dominate population trends.

The diagnosis is clinical and hinges on loss of control over the next use of a nicotine product, evidenced by daily use, high number of episodes per day, use shortly after waking, craving during abstinence, and prior failed quit attempts.

The clinically important metric is the cumulative frequency of any nicotine dosing across all products used, not the specific product source, because it is dosing frequency that creates and sustains addiction.

Nicotine itself causes relatively little disease (notably pregnancy complications); the majority of disease burden comes from repetitive exposure to the carcinogens and toxicants carried with nicotine in various products, which addiction drives by compelling multiple daily exposures.
Withdrawal symptoms intensify with longer abstinence as blood nicotine falls and detaches from receptors, and these symptoms can persist for roughly 4-6 weeks.

Acidic aerosols (cigarettes and nicotine salt vaping devices) reduce airway irritation, permit deep inhalation, and produce rapid arterial nicotine rises reaching the brain, making them more addictive than products with slower delivery.
Cancer risk rises linearly with the number of cigarettes per day and logarithmically with duration of smoking; relative risk of lung cancer in current smokers ranges roughly 13-28 across age groups.

Cigarette smoking accounts for about 80% of COPD, about 90% of peripheral vascular disease in nondiabetics, about 50% of aortic aneurysms, about 24% of coronary artery disease, and about 11% of strokes.

Smoking induces the cytochrome P450 system, which can lower serum levels of drugs such as warfarin; conversely, levels may rise during hospitalization when a patient stops smoking, an important consideration for narrow-therapeutic-index agents.

Assuming cigars or pipe tobacco are lower-risk: most cigars are now made like cigarettes and most pipe tobacco is used for roll-your-own, so risks are similar; clinicians should ask about and not recommend them.
Treating 'low tar/nicotine' cigarettes as safer; compensatory smoking negates any benefit and design changes have raised adenocarcinoma rates.
Focusing only on cigarettes and missing cumulative nicotine intake from vaping, oral pouches, and other products when assessing addiction intensity.
Overlooking smoking-induced cytochrome P450 changes when adjusting drug doses around hospitalization or discharge.
Dismissing patients not currently interested in quitting; many still attempt cessation in the subsequent year and benefit from a clear personalized message.
Equating exclusive e-cigarette use (lower toxicant exposure) with cessation of addiction, since persistent nicotine dependence and relapse risk remain.

Cessation produces substantial reversible benefit: risk of a second coronary event falls within 6-12 months, and first myocardial infarction and coronary death rates decline within 2-4 years; after about 15 years of abstinence cardiovascular risk approaches that of never-smokers. Cancer risk declines relative to continued smoking after about 4 years, but a roughly three- to fourfold excess lung cancer risk persists even 20 years after quitting. Small-airway changes in young smokers reverse after 1-2 years of abstinence; in established airflow obstruction cessation mainly slows further decline rather than restoring lung function. Quitting is typically cyclical with multiple attempts: about 70-80% of smokers want to quit and over half try in a given year, but only about 6% remain abstinent at 6 months and about 3% at 2 years; systemwide tracking and assistance can raise 12-month abstinence to as high as 25%.
Continued smoking during chemotherapy or radiation, associated with poorer outcomes and reduced survival
Smoking in pregnancy: premature rupture of membranes, abruptio placentae, placenta previa, preterm delivery, small-for-gestational-age, increased perinatal mortality and sudden infant death syndrome
Dual use of e-cigarettes and combusted cigarettes, which negates toxicant-reduction benefits
High-frequency use of noncombusted inhaled nicotine products in patients who never used combusted tobacco
Multiplicative cardiac risk when smoking is combined with hypertension or elevated lipids
Higher vascular graft occlusion rates in smokers after bypass surgery

No formal grading is presented; addiction intensity is gauged clinically by cumulative daily dosing frequency across all products, spacing of use through the day, use within 30 minutes of waking, craving during abstinence, and history of failed quit attempts.

chunks.text: Nipah virus is an enveloped RNA henipavirus that infects endothelium and neurons. After spillover from fruit bats (directly, via contaminated food, or from intermediate hosts such as pigs), the virus causes a systemic vasculitis with endothelial infection, syncytium formation, thrombosis and microinfarction, particularly in the central nervous system. This vasculitic and direct neuronal injury produces the severe encephalitis, while pulmonary endothelial and epithelial infection can cause acute respiratory distress. The capacity of the virus to persist may underlie relapsing or delayed-onset encephalitis in some survivors.

chunks.text: Lymphocutaneous (sporotrichoid) presentation overlaps with Sporothrix schenckii and Mycobacterium marinum infection (p.1360).

Mycetoma differential: actinomycetoma (filamentous bacteria, e.g., Nocardia), eumycetoma (fungal), and botryomycosis (cocci/bacilli, often Staphylococcus aureus) are difficult to separate clinically and require granule microscopy, culture, or biopsy (p.1361).
Ocular nocardiosis (keratitis, scleritis, endophthalmitis) cannot be distinguished from other ocular infections by signs and symptoms alone (p.1360).
Sporothrix schenckii (sporotrichosis) for lymphocutaneous disease
Mycobacterium marinum for lymphocutaneous disease
Eumycetoma (fungal mycetoma) for actinomycetoma
Botryomycosis (often Staphylococcus aureus) for actinomycetoma
Other causes of pulmonary nodules/cavitation and ring-enhancing brain lesions in immunocompromised hosts (e.g., fungi, mycobacteria, toxoplasmosis as discussed in brain abscess context)
Sputum or pus microscopy for branching beaded Gram-positive filaments plus modified (weak-acid) acid-fast staining; organisms may also take up silver stains (p.1360-1361).
Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid or lung biopsy when sputum smears are negative, as they frequently are in pulmonary nocardiosis (p.1361).

Selective media (colistin-nalidixic acid agar, modified Thayer-Martin agar, or buffered charcoal-yeast extract agar) for mixed-flora specimens; avoid mycobacterial decontamination procedures, which can kill nocardiae; alert the laboratory to incubate cultures for prolonged periods (up to 2-4 weeks) (p.1361).

Species/complex identification by MALDI-TOF or genomic sequencing (16S rRNA, secA1, hsp65, or gyrB), with antimicrobial susceptibility testing (ideally CLSI broth dilution); susceptibility testing requires experience because nocardiae grow slowly and clump (p.1361).
Granule examination in mycetoma: wash suspect particles in saline, examine microscopically, and culture; culture is the most reliable way to identify the causative organism (p.1361).
Contrast-enhanced CNS imaging (MRI preferred, with IV gadolinium more sensitive than CT) in all patients with non-cutaneous/non-ocular nocardiosis to detect occult brain abscess (p.1360-1362).

Testing for underlying immunodeficiency in patients lacking typical risk factors, including HIV testing; test for chronic granulomatous disease in children and adults with nocardiosis who have no major risk factor (p.1359, p.1362).
Pulmonary or cerebral malignancy/metastases presenting as nodules, masses, or ring-enhancing lesions

Nocardia species are saprophytic, filamentous, aerobic Gram-positive bacteria ubiquitous in soil, water, and decaying organic matter; their cell walls contain mycolic acids and trehalose (Mycobacteriales order), and they are weakly (modified) acid-fast and catalase positive. Pulmonary and systemic disease follow inhalation of fragmented bacterial mycelia, while primary cutaneous and ocular disease follow direct inoculation. Most immunocompetent people clear inhaled nocardiae without disease; invasive infection is favored by impaired host defenses. Innate and adaptive responses, with neutrophils and macrophages central to antinocardial defense (underscored by the frequency of nocardiosis in chronic granulomatous disease), normally control the organism. Nocardiae have evolved mechanisms to survive within phagocytes, including neutralization of oxidants and prevention of phagosome-lysosome fusion and phagosome acidification; neutrophils limit but do not efficiently kill them. The characteristic pathology is an abscess with neutrophilic infiltration and prominent necrosis, with little fibrosis/encapsulation, whereas actinomycetoma shows granulomatous inflammation with sinus tract formation. (p.1358-1359)

Nocardiosis is usually an opportunistic infection occurring primarily in hosts with impaired defenses, especially defects in cell-mediated immunity and specific phagocyte function; typical risk factors include solid organ or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, systemic corticosteroids or Cushing syndrome, other immunosuppressive therapy, and HIV infection (p.1358-1359).

Pulmonary disease is the usual portal after inhalation of fragmented mycelia; onset is typically subacute over days to weeks (more acute in the severely immunocompromised), with prominent cough producing thick non-malodorous purulent sputum, fever, anorexia, and malaise (p.1359).

Typical chest imaging shows infiltrates, nodules, and masses in one or more lobes, and nodules frequently cavitate; pleural effusion or empyema occurs in about one-third of cases, occasionally without lung involvement (p.1359).
Dissemination occurs in up to one-third of patients with pneumonia, most often to the CNS and to skin/subcutaneous tissues; virtually any organ can be involved (p.1359-1360).

CNS involvement occurs in up to two-thirds of disseminated cases; brain imaging classically shows one or more ring-enhancing, multilobulated lesions, and multiple abscesses are seen in two-thirds of patients (p.1360).

Diagnosis starts with examining sputum or pus for branching, beaded, Gram-positive filaments (~1 um wide, up to 50 um long) that fragment into apparent cocci/coccobacilli; most nocardiae are modified (weak) acid-fast (e.g., modified Kinyoun, modified Ziehl-Neelsen, Fite-Faraco) (p.1360-1361).

Primary cutaneous nocardiosis follows transcutaneous inoculation (often thorn/gardening injury) and takes three forms: cellulitis, lymphocutaneous (sporotrichoid) syndrome, or actinomycetoma; N. brasiliensis is the usual cause of skin-limited and lymphocutaneous disease and of actinomycetoma (p.1358, p.1360).

Nocardiosis tends to remit and relapse; without definitive treatment, pulmonary disease characteristically follows a course of remissions and exacerbations over weeks to months, and prolonged therapy (months) is required (p.1359, p.1362-Table 179-1).

Failing to image the brain: because brain abscess may be asymptomatic, all patients with pulmonary or systemic nocardiosis should have contrast-enhanced CNS imaging (MRI preferred) regardless of neurologic symptoms (p.1360, p.1362).

Missing the diagnosis on smear: sputum smears are frequently negative in pulmonary nocardiosis, and the modified (weak) acid-fast technique must be used or organisms may be overlooked; standard mycobacterial decontamination can kill nocardiae (p.1360-1361).

Cultures lost to short incubation: nocardiae grow slowly (colonies up to 2 weeks, characteristic appearance up to 4 weeks), so the laboratory must be informed to incubate cultures for prolonged periods (p.1361).

Overcalling colonization or contamination: Nocardia can colonize the respiratory tract in bronchiectasis/structural lung disease, and isolation from a respiratory specimen does not always indicate infection; blood culture isolates may be contaminants in low-risk patients without clinical disease (p.1361).
Adjunctive topical corticosteroids should NOT be given to patients with nocardial keratitis (p.1362).

With appropriate treatment, mortality for localized pulmonary nocardiosis is less than 10%. Disseminated disease carries a higher mortality, especially with CNS involvement. Primary cutaneous and ocular disease often respond to therapy. Mortality from actinomycetoma is exceedingly low, but patients often suffer substantial morbidity, disfigurement, disability, and/or stigmatization. Prolonged therapy is required and disease tends to relapse, so secondary prophylaxis is considered by some experts for patients who remain at high risk after completing antimicrobial therapy. (p.1362)

CNS dissemination: brain abscess may be clinically silent, so absence of neurologic symptoms does not exclude it - one-third of patients with CNS involvement have no CNS symptoms and one-fourth have no apparent pulmonary disease at presentation (p.1360).
Disseminated nocardiosis carries a higher mortality than localized pulmonary disease, especially with CNS involvement (p.1362).
Nocardiosis in a patient without a major risk factor should prompt evaluation for an undiagnosed immunologic defect, including HIV and chronic granulomatous disease (p.1359, p.1362).

Disease is categorized clinically and by host status to guide therapy duration: pulmonary/systemic disease in hosts with intact defenses versus deficient defenses, CNS disease, primary cutaneous disease (cellulitis, lymphocutaneous), osteomyelitis/arthritis/laryngitis/sinusitis, actinomycetoma, and keratitis - longer courses for immunocompromised and CNS disease, with indefinite therapy considered in some AIDS patients with CD4 below 200/uL or chronic granulomatous disease (p.1362). [Durations noted as classification context only; not dosing guidance.]
Nocardiosis (infective) — Infectious Diseases Also: Nocardia infection, Actinomycetoma (Nocardia)

Night-time continence depends on the balance between overnight urine production, bladder storage capacity, and the ability to either suppress bladder contractions during sleep or wake in response to a full bladder. Enuresis arises when this balance fails: some children produce a relatively large volume of urine at night, some have a smaller functional bladder capacity or overactive bladder, and many have a high arousal threshold so a full or contracting bladder does not wake them. These factors, strongly influenced by genetic predisposition and developmental maturation, often coexist. Constipation can reduce functional bladder capacity and provoke bladder overactivity, and secondary enuresis may reflect an acquired medical or psychosocial trigger.
Nocturnal enuresis is involuntary voiding during sleep in a child old enough to be expected to have night-time bladder control, generally around five years and older.
It is classified as primary when the child has never achieved a sustained period of night-time dryness and secondary when wetting returns after at least six months of dryness.
Monosymptomatic enuresis involves night-time wetting alone, whereas non-monosymptomatic enuresis is accompanied by daytime lower urinary tract symptoms such as urgency, frequency, or daytime wetting.
Common contributing factors include a family history, delayed maturation of arousal and bladder control, reduced overnight bladder capacity, and relative overnight excess of urine production.
Most primary monosymptomatic enuresis is not caused by serious disease, and evaluation is mainly history, examination, and urinalysis to exclude infection and glycosuria.
Secondary enuresis or associated daytime symptoms warrant closer evaluation for causes such as urinary tract infection, constipation, diabetes, or psychosocial stress.
First-line management emphasises reassurance, education, and behavioural measures, with the enuresis alarm being the most effective long-term intervention for motivated families.
Constipation frequently coexists and, when treated, wetting often improves, so bowel habits should always be assessed.
Treating the child punitively or blaming the child for an involuntary problem
Overlooking coexisting constipation as a contributor
Failing to distinguish monosymptomatic from non-monosymptomatic enuresis before choosing therapy
Missing an underlying cause of secondary enuresis such as infection or diabetes

Primary monosymptomatic enuresis has a high rate of spontaneous resolution with age, and treatment can accelerate dryness; the outlook is generally excellent, though relapses can occur and cases with daytime symptoms may need more prolonged management.

NHLs arise from mature B, T, or NK lymphocytes, with ~90% being B-cell neoplasms; transformation typically requires several genetic events. Characteristic chromosomal translocations create fusion or deregulated oncogenes: t(14;18) with BCL2 overexpression in follicular lymphoma (>85% of cases, necessary but not sufficient for transformation); MYC rearrangement at 8q24 in >95% of Burkitt's lymphoma (most often t(8;14) fusing MYC to IgH); and t(11;18) (API2-MLT) in MALT lymphoma. Gene-expression profiling subdivides DLBCL into germinal-center B-cell (GCB)-like and activated-B-cell (ABC)-like subtypes with differing prognoses. Several NHLs are linked to chronic antigenic stimulation or infection-driven immune dysregulation, and immunodeficiency states strongly predispose to (often EBV-associated) lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.857-863).

NHLs are cancers of mature B, T, and NK cells; ~90% are of B-cell origin. They are distinguished from Hodgkin's lymphoma by the absence of the Reed-Sternberg cell and differ from HL in biology, natural history, and the more variable prognosis (Harrison 22e p.857).

Clinically, NHL is grouped by behavior: indolent/slow-growing (e.g., follicular lymphoma, the most common indolent NHL), aggressive (DLBCL, the most common subtype overall, ~one-third of cases), and highly aggressive/most rapidly growing (Burkitt's lymphoma, doubling time <24 h). Mantle cell lymphoma is intermediate-grade (Harrison 22e p.857, 862).

The duration and pace of symptoms help distinguish aggressive from indolent disease, as does the presence or absence of 'B' symptoms — fevers, drenching night sweats, and unexplained weight loss (>10% of body weight over the 6 months before diagnosis) (Harrison 22e p.860-861).

Most common presentation of follicular lymphoma is new, painless lymphadenopathy at multiple sites; most patients lack elevated LDH or B symptoms. Asymptomatic indolent disease should be observed, as treating asymptomatic patients does not improve survival (Harrison 22e p.863-864).
Serum LDH and serum beta-2-microglobulin are important independent prognostic factors in NHL and should be measured at diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.860).

Aggressive lymphomas (DLBCL, Burkitt's) are potentially curable with combination chemotherapy, whereas most indolent lymphomas are very responsive to therapy but not ultimately curable in the vast majority of cases except in localized early-stage disease (Harrison 22e p.862-863).

Diagnosis requires an adequate tissue sample interpreted by an expert hematopathologist; an inadequate or unrepresentative specimen risks misclassification (e.g., missing coexisting DLBCL within follicular lymphoma or confusing lymphoma with reactive follicular hyperplasia) (Harrison 22e p.860, 863).

The Ann Arbor anatomic staging system is less useful in NHL than in Hodgkin's lymphoma because NHL disseminates widely rather than in an ordered stepwise fashion; histology and the IPI matter more than stage (Harrison 22e p.861).
Treating asymptomatic indolent (follicular) lymphoma does not improve survival — appropriate patients should be observed rather than treated immediately (Harrison 22e p.864).
Failing to anticipate and prevent tumor lysis syndrome before treating rapidly proliferating Burkitt's lymphoma can be life-threatening (Harrison 22e p.862).

A residual mass on CT after therapy may represent treated fibrosis rather than active disease; PET can help distinguish, but end-of-treatment PET should be delayed (preferably 6-8 weeks after chemotherapy) to avoid false positives (Harrison 22e p.861).

Prognosis is highly variable and driven more by histology and clinical parameters than by anatomic stage. Overall 5-year survival for NHL is ~74%. The International Prognostic Index (IPI; age >=60, elevated LDH, ECOG performance status >=2, Ann Arbor stage III/IV, and >1 extranodal site) is the best predictor for aggressive NHL: 5-year overall survival ~73%, 51%, 43%, and 26% for 0-1, 2, 3, and 4-5 risk factors. With R-CHOP, ~65-70% of DLBCL patients are cured. The FLIPI predicts follicular lymphoma outcome; most FL patients live 15-20 years but the disease is generally not curable (except localized early-stage), and Burkitt's lymphoma is curable in ~80-90% when treated promptly and correctly (Harrison 22e p.857, 861-862).

Burkitt's lymphoma is highly aggressive (doubling time <24 h) — treatment must be initiated quickly and the tumor carries a high risk of tumor lysis syndrome; TLS is most often associated with treatment of Burkitt's lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.862, 1014)
Rapid growth of lymph nodes with new B symptoms in known indolent (follicular) lymphoma suggests histologic transformation to DLBCL (~3% per year) (Harrison 22e p.864)

Disease involving paranasal sinuses, testes, breast, kidneys, adrenal glands, or epidural space — and highly aggressive histologies like Burkitt's — carries increased risk of CNS dissemination (Harrison 22e p.861)
Concerning neurologic signs/symptoms warrant lumbar puncture for CNS involvement (Harrison 22e p.860)
'Double-hit' high-grade B-cell lymphoma (concurrent MYC and BCL2 rearrangements) has an extremely poor prognosis (median OS ~12-18 months) (Harrison 22e p.862-863)

WHO (WHO-HAEM5) classification of lymphoid malignancies categorizes NHL by cell of origin (mature B-cell vs mature T/NK-cell neoplasms) and entity. Anatomic extent is described by the Ann Arbor staging system (Stage I-IV, with suffix A/B for absence/presence of B symptoms). Prognostic stratification uses the International Prognostic Index (IPI) for aggressive NHL and the FLIPI for follicular lymphoma; follicular lymphoma is also graded I-III by centroblasts per high-power field (Harrison 22e p.857-862).

NTM are ubiquitous environmental organisms (soil and water) with specific niches (e.g., M. simiae in aquifers, M. fortuitum in pedicure baths, M. immunogenum in metalworking fluids). Because exposure is essentially universal yet disease is rare, normal host defenses are strong and significant disease implies a specific susceptibility. Mycobacteria are phagocytosed by macrophages, which release IL-12; IL-12 activates T and NK cells (via STAT4) to secrete IFN-gamma, which activates macrophages/neutrophils (via STAT1) and upregulates TNF-alpha, forming a positive IFN-gamma/IL-12 feedback loop critical for mycobacterial control. Disseminated NTM correlates with declining CD4+ T cells (advanced HIV, idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia), TNF-alpha inhibitors (which impair granuloma formation), Mendelian mutations in the IFN-gamma/IL-12 pathway (IFNG, IFNGR1, IFNGR2, STAT1, GATA2, ISG15, IRF8, IL-12A, IL-12RB1, IL-12RB2, CYBB, IKBKG/NEMO and others), or neutralizing anti-IFN-gamma autoantibodies. Only ~70% of non-HIV disseminated cases have a genetic diagnosis. In contrast, the best-recognized substrate for pulmonary NTM is bronchiectasis (cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, STAT3 hyper-IgE/Job's syndrome, idiopathic), but the mechanism by which bronchiectasis predisposes to locally destructive yet non-systemic disease is unknown (p.1414-1415).

NTM (also termed atypical, environmental, or mycobacteria other than tuberculosis) are ubiquitous in soil and water and refer to mycobacteria other than M. tuberculosis and its close relatives and M. leprae; over 199 species are recognized (p.1414).

Isolated cervical lymphadenopathy is the most common form of NTM infection in young children in North America (usually MAC); the swelling is firm and relatively painless with few systemic signs and is often diagnosed inadvertently at biopsy for suspected malignancy (p.1416).
Children with isolated cervical or intrathoracic NTM infection do NOT commonly have underlying immune defects and usually do NOT go on to develop other opportunistic infections (p.1416).

Cutaneous NTM usually requires a break in the skin; rapidly growing NTM (M. abscessus, M. fortuitum, M. chelonae) cause outbreaks via contaminated surgical instruments/injections, with painful erythematous draining subcutaneous nodules typically WITHOUT fever or systemic symptoms (p.1416).

M. marinum (fish tanks, pools, fish handling) causes 'fish-tank granuloma' and can spread up the arm in a sporotrichoid pattern; M. ulcerans causes painless Buruli ulcer via the toxin mycolactone (p.1416).
'Hot-tub lung' is a pulmonary hypersensitivity reaction to NTM (most often MAC) growing in underchlorinated water, distinct from true pulmonary or disseminated infection (p.1415).

For susceptibility testing, only MAC testing for clarithromycin and M. kansasii testing for rifampin is indicated; few data support other in vitro susceptibility tests, and MAC isolates not previously exposed to macrolides are almost always susceptible (p.1417).

Most NTM cause human disease only when host defense is impaired (e.g., bronchiectasis) or breached by inoculation (liposuction, trauma, cardiac surgery); human-to-human transmission is rare and occurs almost exclusively in cystic fibrosis (p.1414).

Pulmonary disease is by far the most common form in North America and is highly associated with pulmonary epithelial defects but NOT with systemic immunodeficiency; disseminated disease instead denotes significant immune dysfunction such as advanced HIV (p.1414, 1416).

Pulmonary MAC most commonly presents in the 6th-7th decade in women with months to years of nagging intermittent cough and fatigue; pulmonary NTM in a tall, thin woman with chest-wall abnormalities is termed 'Lady Windermere syndrome' (p.1416).

Pulmonary MAC affects older nonsmoking white women more than men (onset ~60 years); such patients tend to be taller and thinner with high rates of scoliosis, mitral valve prolapse, and pectus anomalies (p.1416).

Male smokers with upper-lobe cavitary disease tend to carry the same single MAC strain indefinitely, whereas nonsmoking women with nodular bronchiectasis carry several MAC strains simultaneously that change over the disease course (p.1416).
M. kansasii can produce a clinical syndrome strongly resembling tuberculosis with hemoptysis, chest pain, and cavitary lung disease (p.1416).

Disseminated MAC (or M. kansasii) in advanced HIV is now uncommon in North America owing to effective prophylaxis and improved HIV treatment; when common, the portal of entry was the bowel with spread to bone marrow and bloodstream (p.1415).

Disseminated NTM is often indolent and progressive over weeks to months with malaise, fever, weight loss, organomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and anemia; blood cultures may be negative even though involved organs carry heavy organism burdens, sometimes with grossly impaired granulomatous response (p.1415).

Not all NTM isolations, especially from the lung, reflect disease or require treatment; distinguishing colonization/contamination from true infection requires an appropriate clinical and radiographic setting (nodules, bronchiectasis, cavities) plus repeated isolation per American Thoracic Society criteria (p.1417).

The single most critical and sensitive step in diagnosis is simply to suspect NTM and request the correct, separately processed mycobacterial smears, cultures, and dedicated blood culture media; many cases go undiagnosed because the appropriate test was never ordered (p.1416-1417).
M. gordonae is frequently recovered from respiratory samples but is almost never a pathogen (p.1417).
PPD does not differentiate NTM from M. tuberculosis well; intermediate (~10 mm) reactions overlap, BCG cross-reacts, but large reactions (>15 mm) most commonly signify TB (p.1416-1417).

Slow-growing NTM typically do NOT proliferate in routine blood culture media, so suspicion and correct bottles are essential; biopsy isolation is strong evidence but laboratory contamination does occur (confirm with organisms on stained sections) (p.1417).

NTM cause chronic infections evolving slowly over weeks to years, so emergent therapy before diagnosis and speciation is rarely needed. Treatment is complex, often poorly tolerated, and potentially toxic; inadequate single-drug therapy is almost always associated with emergence of resistance and relapse. Pulmonary MAC therapy is prolonged, generally continued for 12 months after culture conversion (typically at least 18 months total). The typical lag between symptom onset and diagnosis is about 5 years in older women (p.1416-1418).
Disseminated involvement of two or more organs without an iatrogenic cause (prompts IFN-gamma/IL-12 pathway genetic investigation)
Disseminated NTM with bacterial/viral infections plus conical/peg/missing teeth or abnormal hair pattern in males (suggests NEMO/IKBKG NF-kB defect, possibly with immunoglobulin defects)

American Thoracic Society criteria for pulmonary NTM diagnosis: growth of NTM from two of three sputum samples (regardless of smear), OR a positive bronchoalveolar lavage sample (regardless of smear), OR a lung parenchymal biopsy with granulomatous inflammation or mycobacteria on section plus NTM on culture, in an appropriate clinical and radiographic setting. Isolation of NTM from blood or organ biopsy in a compatible clinical setting is considered diagnostic. NTM are categorized as rapidly growing (<7 days) versus slowly growing (>=7 days) (p.1417).

Vitamin D deficiency reduces intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate, lowering their availability for bone mineralisation. The falling calcium stimulates parathyroid hormone secretion (secondary hyperparathyroidism), which mobilises calcium from bone and promotes renal phosphate wasting. The combination of low calcium-phosphate product and PTH-driven bone resorption leaves the expanding cartilage of the growth plate and newly formed osteoid unmineralised, producing the soft, deformable bones and characteristic metaphyseal changes of rickets.
A disorder of defective mineralisation of growing bone, most commonly due to deficiency of vitamin D and/or dietary calcium.
Risk factors include exclusive breastfeeding without vitamin D supplementation, darker skin pigmentation, limited sun exposure, and prematurity.

Skeletal signs include widening of the wrists and ankles, a rachitic rosary at the costochondral junctions, frontal bossing, delayed fontanelle closure, and bowing of the legs once weight-bearing begins.
Non-skeletal features can include delayed motor milestones, hypotonia, growth faltering, and increased susceptibility to fractures.
Severe hypocalcaemia may present with tetany, carpopedal spasm, or seizures, especially in infants.
Biochemistry classically shows low or low-normal calcium and phosphate, elevated alkaline phosphatase, raised parathyroid hormone, and low 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
Radiographs of the wrist or knee reveal metaphyseal cupping, fraying, and widening of the growth plate.
Treatment replaces vitamin D and ensures adequate dietary calcium, with biochemical and radiological healing confirming response.
Prevention through routine vitamin D supplementation in infancy is highly effective, and failure to respond should prompt evaluation for inherited or renal forms.
Attributing bowed legs solely to physiologic causes and missing biochemical rickets
Overlooking dietary calcium deficiency as a cause even when vitamin D is adequate
Failing to investigate inherited or renal rickets when there is no response to treatment
Not providing routine vitamin D supplementation to exclusively breastfed infants

With adequate treatment, biochemical recovery occurs within weeks and radiographic healing over months; most deformities remodel in young children, though severe or late-treated cases may leave residual bowing.
Hypocalcaemic seizures, tetany, or laryngospasm
Cardiomyopathy associated with severe hypocalcaemia or vitamin D deficiency
Pathological fractures

Progressive deformity or signs suggesting an inherited or renal cause
