Hypothyroidism — may cause weight gain but is rarely the sole cause of severe obesity; check TSH (and free thyroxine for rare secondary hypothyroidism) in any patient presenting with obesity (Harrison 22e p.3185, 3188)

Cushing's syndrome / endogenous hypercortisolism — suggested by spontaneous bruising, livid striae, myopathy and marked centripetal fat distribution; confirmed via 24-h urinary free cortisol or dexamethasone suppression (Harrison 22e p.3185)

Hypothalamic obesity — from tumors (e.g., craniopharyngioma), inflammatory masses, or severe head injury disrupting hypothalamic energy-balance centres, often with anterior/posterior pituitary dysfunction and short history of hyperphagia (Harrison 22e p.3185)
Insulinoma — weight gain driven by frequent eating to avoid hypoglycemia (Harrison 22e p.3185)
Polycystic ovarian syndrome — secondary cause/association meriting evaluation (Harrison 22e p.3188)

Monogenic / syndromic obesity — leptin or leptin-receptor deficiency, POMC, PCSK1, MC4R, SIM1, BDNF/TrkB, SH2B1 mutations; syndromes such as Prader-Willi, Bardet-Biedl, Albright's hereditary osteodystrophy/pseudohypoparathyroidism, Cohen's, Carpenter's, Alström's, Tubby (Harrison 22e p.3183–3185)

Drug-induced weight gain — insulin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones, glucocorticoids, antipsychotics (clozapine, olanzapine, risperidone), lithium, antidepressants (tricyclics, MAOIs, paroxetine, mirtazapine), antiepileptics (valproate, gabapentin, carbamazepine) (Harrison 22e p.3188)
BMI calculation plus waist circumference (surrogate for visceral fat; measure horizontally above the iliac crest, particularly when BMI ≤35) and/or waist-to-hip ratio (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187)
Fasting lipid profile (total, LDL, HDL cholesterol and triglycerides), chemistry panel, glycated haemoglobin, and blood pressure in all patients (Harrison 22e p.3187)
TSH ± free thyroxine to evaluate for hypothyroidism (Harrison 22e p.3185, 3188)
24-h urinary free cortisol or dexamethasone suppression test when Cushing's syndrome is suspected (Harrison 22e p.3185)
Genetic testing in severe early-onset obesity (up to ~20% of children with severe obesity have chromosomal abnormalities or highly penetrant mutations) (Harrison 22e p.3183)
Very muscular body habitus — BMI may overestimate body fat (Harrison 22e p.3181)
Peripheral edema from NSAIDs or calcium channel blockers — increases weight without increasing body fat (Harrison 22e p.3188)

Adipose tissue evolved to store excess calories as triglyceride in unilocular lipid droplets and release free fatty acids and glycerol when needed. In an obesogenic environment (abundant energy-dense palatable food, larger portions, reduced physical activity), chronic energy intake exceeding expenditure — even by as little as ~7 kcal/day sustained over years — produces a cumulative excess of adipose triglyceride. Genetic factors strongly determine individual susceptibility (twin studies show adiposity tracks with biological, not adoptive, family), acting largely through the brain's control of food intake. Body weight is homeostatically defended by the hypothalamus, which integrates the adipose hormone leptin (whose fall below an individual's habitual level is a powerful drive to eat) with gut hormones (GLP-1, CCK, GIP, PYY, oxyntomodulin, ghrelin) and pancreatic insulin/amylin. Within the arcuate nucleus, leptin stimulates POMC neurons (whose products α-/β-MSH act via MC4R in the paraventricular nucleus to reduce intake and raise energy expenditure) and inhibits orexigenic AGRP/NPY/GABA neurons. Leptin defends strongly against fat loss but responds weakly to fat excess ("leptin resistance"), explaining why rising leptin does not prevent obesity. As obesity develops, the earliest abnormality is insulin resistance with compensatory hyperinsulinemia, worse with central fat; this arises from adipose-tissue inflammation and/or ectopic lipid deposition in liver and muscle once safe adipose storage capacity is exceeded (the human data favouring the ectopic-fat mechanism, as illustrated by lipodystrophy). Insulin resistance/hyperinsulinemia then predisposes to the metabolic, endocrine, and cardiovascular complications of obesity (Harrison 22e p.3181–3186).

Obesity is defined as a state of excess adipose tissue mass that adversely affects health; because direct measurement of fat mass is impractical in routine clinical practice, the body mass index (BMI = weight/height² in kg/m²) is used as a proxy (Harrison 22e p.3181).

WHO BMI classes: underweight <18.5; normal 18.5–24.9; overweight 25–29.9; obesity ≥30 kg/m². AACE/ACE management staging further subdivides obesity into class I (30.0–34.9), class II (35.0–39.9), and class III / extreme obesity (≥40) with correspondingly higher disease risk (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187).

BMI-based cutoffs were derived largely from white Western populations; adverse outcomes occur at lower BMI in other ethnic groups, so lower thresholds and ethnic-specific waist-circumference cutpoints (e.g., South Asians/Chinese, Japanese) are recommended (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187).

Fat distribution matters independent of overall BMI: a waist-to-hip ratio >0.9 in women and >1.0 in men, and excess abdominal (visceral) adiposity, are independently associated with type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, metabolic syndrome, and cardiovascular disease (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187).

Energy balance is under homeostatic control by the hypothalamus, which integrates the adipose-derived hormone leptin (rises with fat stores, falls fast with caloric restriction) with gut signals — GLP-1, CCK, GIP, PYY, oxyntomodulin, ghrelin — plus pancreatic insulin and amylin (Harrison 22e p.3181–3182).

Insulin resistance with compensatory hyperinsulinemia is one of the earliest and most prominent biochemical abnormalities of obesity, is worse with central adiposity, and underlies/precedes many adverse cardiometabolic consequences (Harrison 22e p.3186).

Two leading (not mutually exclusive) hypotheses link obesity to insulin resistance: adipose-tissue inflammation (macrophage accumulation around dying adipocytes), and ectopic lipid deposition once safe adipose storage capacity is exceeded — with stronger human data supporting the ectopic-fat / limited-storage mechanism (Harrison 22e p.3186).

Obesity care begins with sensitive, non-stigmatizing language and an obesity-focused history covering diet, physical activity, sleep, stress, contributing factors, complications, and the patient's readiness/motivation to change (Harrison 22e p.3187–3188).

Treating BMI alone: BMI only reflects body size, not body composition, fat distribution, health, or quality of life — not all patients with a high BMI need treatment, and BMI overestimates fat in very muscular individuals (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187, 3190).

Applying white-Western-derived BMI cutoffs uniformly: adverse outcomes occur at lower BMI in other ethnic groups, and ethnic-specific (e.g., Asia-Pacific) thresholds should be used (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187).
Overlooking that severe hypothyroidism is rarely the sole cause of severe obesity, yet thyroid function should still always be checked (Harrison 22e p.3185).
Mistaking the lower GH response to provocative testing in common obesity for a structural hypothalamic-pituitary lesion (Harrison 22e p.3186).
Assuming a specific macronutrient ratio is key: weight loss depends primarily on total caloric reduction and adherence, not on the proportion of carbohydrate, fat, or protein (Harrison 22e p.3190).

Using stigmatizing language ('obesity', 'morbid obesity', 'fatness') rather than neutral terms ('weight', 'excess weight', 'unhealthy weight'), which leaves patients feeling judged (Harrison 22e p.3188).
Initiating lifestyle change before assessing readiness, which leads to frustration and may hamper future efforts (Harrison 22e p.3188).

Obesity is a serious, highly heterogeneous chronic disease that increases morbidity and mortality across many organ systems. The number and severity of complications generally rise with increasing BMI, and excess abdominal/visceral fat confers added cardiometabolic risk. As BMI rises by 5 kg/m², cancer mortality increases by ~10%; in some countries obesity has overtaken smoking as the leading risk factor for cancer. People with obesity have increased morbidity and mortality from atherothrombotic vascular disease (coronary artery disease, stroke) even without diabetes, and are at increased risk of heart failure (especially diastolic dysfunction) and atrial fibrillation. Modest, sustained weight loss (an initial goal of ~8–10% over 6 months) improves obesity-related complications and quality of life; some complications, including type 2 diabetes (e.g., the DiRECT trial showed remission in nearly half of participants with intensive low-energy dietary intervention), can substantially improve or remit with weight loss (Harrison 22e p.3186–3187, 3190).
Short history of hyperphagia and rapid weight gain with signs of anterior/posterior pituitary dysfunction — suggests hypothalamic damage from tumor, inflammation, or head injury (Harrison 22e p.3185)
Spontaneous bruising, livid striae, proximal myopathy, marked centripetal fat — suggests Cushing's syndrome rather than common obesity (Harrison 22e p.3185)
Severe early-onset obesity in childhood with intense hyperphagia/food-seeking — prompts screening for monogenic/syndromic causes (Harrison 22e p.3183–3185)
Severe hypertriglyceridemia secondary to insulin resistance — risk of pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.3186)

BMI-based (kg/m²): underweight <18.5; healthy/normal weight 18.5–24.9; overweight 25.0–29.9; obesity class I 30.0–34.9 (high disease risk); obesity class II 35.0–39.9 (very high risk); extreme/class III obesity ≥40 (extremely high risk). Risk is refined by excess abdominal fat (ethnic-specific waist-circumference cutpoints; waist-to-hip ratio >0.9 women / >1.0 men). Disease-staging systems augment BMI: the AACE/ACE staging (stage 0 = no complications; stage 1 = mild-moderate complications; stage 2 = at least one severe complication) and the Edmonton Obesity Staging System (EOSS, grades 0–4 across medical, functional, and psychological domains, independent of BMI) (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187–3188).

chunks.text: Obsessive-compulsive disorder is typically chronic with waxing and waning severity, but many patients achieve substantial improvement with exposure and response prevention and adequate pharmacotherapy. Early onset, poor insight, and comorbidity are associated with a more persistent course.

chunks.text: Physiological pruritus of pregnancy without cholestasis
Pregnancy-specific skin conditions such as polymorphic eruption or pemphigoid gestationis
Pre-eclampsia or HELLP syndrome with liver involvement
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
Viral hepatitis or other intrinsic liver disease
Gallstone disease or biliary obstruction
Serum bile acid measurement, ideally with serial monitoring of peak levels
Liver function tests including transaminases and bilirubin
Coagulation studies where cholestasis is prolonged or severe
Viral hepatitis screen and liver autoantibodies to exclude other liver disease
Liver ultrasound to exclude biliary obstruction
Fetal surveillance, recognising that routine monitoring poorly predicts sudden stillbirth

Obstetric cholestasis reflects impaired hepatocellular secretion and enterohepatic circulation of bile acids in genetically susceptible women, in whom the high oestrogen and progesterone levels of pregnancy reduce the function of bile acid transport proteins. This leads to accumulation of bile acids in the maternal circulation, causing pruritus, and their transfer across the placenta is thought to underlie the fetal risks, with high concentrations having arrhythmogenic and vasoconstrictive effects that may contribute to sudden fetal death. Cholestasis can also impair absorption of fat-soluble vitamins including vitamin K.
Obstetric cholestasis is a pregnancy-specific liver disorder characterised by pruritus and raised bile acids, typically presenting in the second half of pregnancy
The hallmark symptom is generalised itching, often severe and worse at night, classically involving the palms and soles, in the absence of a primary skin rash
Diagnosis rests on elevated serum bile acids with or without raised transaminases once other causes of itch and abnormal liver function are excluded
The main concern is fetal rather than maternal, as high bile acid concentrations are associated with an increased risk of stillbirth, preterm birth, and meconium-stained liquor
The risk of stillbirth rises with the degree of bile acid elevation, so severity is graded on peak bile acid levels and guides timing of delivery
Ursodeoxycholic acid is commonly used to relieve maternal itching, though its effect on fetal outcome is limited, and vitamin K may be considered if there is prolonged clotting from fat malabsorption
Symptoms and biochemistry resolve after delivery, but the condition recurs in a high proportion of future pregnancies and with oestrogen-containing contraception
Persistent abnormal liver function after delivery should prompt investigation for underlying hepatobiliary disease
Dismissing severe pruritus in pregnancy without checking bile acids and liver function
Failing to exclude pre-eclampsia, HELLP, and acute fatty liver in a woman with abnormal liver tests
Over-reliance on cardiotocography to predict a sudden stillbirth it cannot reliably foresee
Not grading severity by bile acid level to guide timing of delivery
Overlooking persistent postpartum liver dysfunction that signals underlying disease

For the mother the condition is usually self-limiting and resolves promptly after birth, though it recurs frequently in later pregnancies and with oestrogen exposure. The principal concern is the fetus, and careful monitoring of bile acid levels with timely delivery reduces perinatal risk; failure of liver function to normalise postpartum should prompt further hepatological assessment.
Markedly elevated bile acids indicating higher stillbirth risk and need for planned delivery
Coexisting features of pre-eclampsia or HELLP suggesting an alternative or additional diagnosis
Jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, or systemic upset suggesting significant hepatic pathology
Reduced fetal movements or other signs of fetal compromise
Prolonged clotting from vitamin K deficiency increasing bleeding risk
Obstetric Cholestasis (non-infective) — Obstetrics / Gynaecology Also: intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, ICP, cholestasis of pregnancy, pruritus gravidarum with cholestasis
Asbestosis vs other causes of diffuse interstitial fibrosis (IPF/UIP) (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Chronic beryllium disease vs sarcoidosis (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Silicosis (complicated/PMF) vs coal worker's pneumoconiosis and progressive massive fibrosis (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Acute silicosis vs pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Acute farmer's lung (hypersensitivity pneumonitis) vs influenza or community-acquired pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Occupational asthma / RADS vs nonoccupational asthma and COPD (Harrison 22e p.2234)

Acute farmer's lung (hypersensitivity pneumonitis from thermophilic actinomycete spores) presenting 4-8 h after exposure with fever, chills, malaise, cough, and dyspnea can mimic influenza or pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Acute silicosis with profuse miliary infiltration may radiographically resemble miliary infectious processes (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Pre- and post-shift spirometry (change in FEV1) to detect acute bronchoconstriction (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Chest radiograph graded by the ILO International Classification of Radiographs of Pneumoconioses (Harrison 22e p.2234)
CT and high-resolution CT (HRCT) - more sensitive than radiograph for lung opacities, pleural thickening, and interstitial change (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Pulmonary function testing (restrictive pattern with reduced lung volumes and diffusing capacity in fibrosing disease) (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Skin prick testing or specific IgE for immediate hypersensitivity (e.g., flour antigens in bakers) (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Specific IgG precipitating antibody titers for hypersensitivity pneumonitis agents (e.g., pigeon antigen in bird handlers) (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test (BeLPT) for beryllium sensitization (Harrison 22e p.2234)

Fiberoptic bronchoscopy with transbronchial lung biopsy (e.g., to diagnose chronic beryllium disease); occasionally video-assisted thoracoscopic surgical biopsy for definitive diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Chronic beryllium disease closely mimics sarcoidosis (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Aluminum and titanium dioxide exposure can produce a sarcoid-like reaction in lung tissue (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Asbestosis mimics idiopathic and other diffuse interstitial fibroses (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Hard-metal (tungsten carbide/cobalt) exposure can cause giant cell interstitial pneumonitis (Harrison 22e p.2234)

Disease depends on the chemical/physical properties of the inhaled agent, which determine dose and site of deposition: water-soluble gases (ammonia, SO2) are absorbed in proximal airways causing irritation/bronchoconstriction, while less-soluble gases (NO2, phosgene) reach bronchioles/alveoli causing chemical pneumonitis. Particles >10-15 micrometres deposit in the nose/throat; particles <10 micrometres reach below the larynx, with coarse-mode (~2.5-10 micrometres, crustal elements like silica) depositing high in the tracheobronchial tree, fine-mode (<2.5 micrometres, from combustion/high-temperature processes) dominating surface area for toxin delivery to lower airways, and ultrafine (<0.1 micrometres, nanoparticles) potentially entering the circulation. Asbestos fibers induce fibrosis through oxidative injury from reactive oxygen species generated by surface transition metals and by phagocytosing cells. Silica causes alveolar macrophage dysfunction (predisposing to infection) and has immunoadjuvant properties (predisposing to autoimmune connective tissue disease). Beryllium drives a CD4+ T-cell-mediated granulomatous inflammation, with susceptibility strongly linked to HLA-DP alleles bearing glutamic acid at position 69 of the beta chain. (Harrison 22e p.2234)

A detailed occupational and environmental exposure history is the single most important step; include hobbies, home characteristics, secondhand smoke, and proximity to traffic/industry, plus short- and long-term exposures in the distant past (Harrison 22e p.2234).

Acute (accelerated) silicosis from very heavy exposure (e.g., sandblasting in confined spaces, denim sandblasting, artificial-stone countertop fabrication) can resemble pulmonary alveolar proteinosis with a 'crazy paving' HRCT pattern and may progress despite stopping exposure (Harrison 22e p.2234).

Chronic beryllium disease mimics sarcoidosis (noncaseating granulomas); the distinguishing feature is a beryllium-specific cell-mediated (delayed hypersensitivity) immune response demonstrated by the beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test (BeLPT) (Harrison 22e p.2234).
Caplan syndrome is the combination of pneumoconiotic nodules and seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, first described in coal miners and later in silicosis (Harrison 22e p.2234).
Documented mesothelioma in a patient with occupational/environmental asbestos exposure may be compensable, as >80% of mesotheliomas are associated with asbestos exposure (Harrison 22e p.2234).

Inorganic/organic dust exposure characteristically causes interstitial lung disease with a restrictive pattern and reduced diffusing capacity, whereas dusts/chemicals causing occupational asthma or COPD produce airway obstruction (Harrison 22e p.2234).
A drop in FEV1 measured before vs after a work shift can detect an acute occupational bronchoconstrictive response (Harrison 22e p.2234).
Radiographic pattern hints at etiology: small rounded opacities suggest silicosis or coal worker's pneumoconiosis, while small linear/irregular opacities suggest asbestosis (Harrison 22e p.2234).

Asbestos exposure causes a spectrum of disease: pleural plaques and benign effusions (marking exposure only), asbestosis (interstitial fibrosis), bronchogenic lung cancer, and pleural/peritoneal mesothelioma (Harrison 22e p.2234).
Pleural plaques indicate past asbestos exposure but, by themselves, imply only exposure and not pulmonary impairment (Harrison 22e p.2234).
Smoking and asbestos exposure interact more than additively, producing lung cancer risk greater than the sum of each factor; mesothelioma risk is NOT associated with smoking (Harrison 22e p.2234).

Silicosis raises the risk of mycobacterial (including M. tuberculosis), atypical mycobacterial, and fungal infection because silica impairs alveolar macrophage function; treatment of latent TB is given for a longer duration in these patients (Harrison 22e p.2234).
Eggshell calcification of hilar nodes (seen in up to ~20% of cases) is a characteristic radiographic clue to silicosis (Harrison 22e p.2234).

Failing to take an occupational/environmental exposure history is the cardinal pitfall - the etiologic link to occupation is missed unless specifically sought, e.g., asking about beryllium exposure in a patient labeled as having sarcoidosis (Harrison 22e p.2234)

The ILO radiographic classification, though useful for screening populations, is problematic for the individual worker: rounded-opacity disease may look extensive on film with minimal functional impairment, whereas linear/irregular opacities (asbestosis) may lead to underestimation of impairment until late (Harrison 22e p.2234)
In early chronic beryllium disease both chest imaging and pulmonary function tests may be normal (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Attributing dust-related chronic bronchitis/COPD solely to occupation without accounting for cigarette smoking, whose effect is generally additive (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Overlooking that talc and vermiculite may be contaminated with asbestos, conferring fibrosis, lung cancer, and mesothelioma risk (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Combat-related embedded metal fragments (shrapnel) in veterans may contain beryllium and serve as an unrecognized exposure source (Harrison 22e p.2234)

Outcome varies by exposure and disease. Pleural plaques alone do not imply impairment. Simple silicosis and simple CWP are often present without significant functional impairment, but nodular fibrosis can progress even after exposure ceases, coalescing into complicated disease and PMF, which carries severe functional deficits and premature mortality. Acute silicosis may be severe and progressive despite stopping exposure. No specific therapy exists for asbestosis (supportive care as for any diffuse interstitial fibrosis); newly diagnosed cases usually reflect exposures from many years earlier. Asbestos exposure carries excess lung cancer risk (latency ~15-19 years) and mesothelioma risk (latency up to ~40 years). (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Mesothelioma may follow relatively short asbestos exposures (<=1-2 years) with latency up to ~40 years - a thorough exposure history is essential (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Lung cancer after asbestos exposure has a minimum latency of ~15-19 years from first exposure (Harrison 22e p.2234)

Progressive massive fibrosis (PMF), occurring in complicated silicosis and CWP, causes severe lung function deficits and is associated with premature mortality; PMF is rising at an alarming rate in the Appalachian coal belt (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Active tuberculosis risk is increased in silicosis (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Acute silicosis can be severe and progressive even after exposure ceases (Harrison 22e p.2234)

Silicosis and coal worker's pneumoconiosis are categorized as simple (small rounded opacities, usually without functional impairment) versus complicated (nodules >=1 cm) which can progress to progressive massive fibrosis (PMF, conglomerate masses >1 cm with restrictive and obstructive impairment). Acute (accelerated) silicosis is distinguished from chronic silicosis by very heavy short-duration exposure and an alveolar-proteinosis-like presentation. Occupational asthma is divided into immunologic (high- vs low-molecular-weight stimuli, with a latency period) and irritative (reactive airway dysfunction syndrome, RADS) forms. (Harrison 22e p.2234)
Occupational and Environmental Lung Disease (non-infective) — Respiratory Also: pneumoconiosis, silicosis, asbestosis
SVCS in a young man with a mediastinal mass: lymphoma versus primary mediastinal germ cell tumor (Harrison 22e p.585)

Cauda equina syndrome: low back pain, saddle sensory loss, rectal/bladder dysfunction, sexual impotence and absent reflexes from compression of nerve roots forming the cauda equina (Harrison 22e p.589)

Abrupt stroke-like onset of headache, nausea, vomiting and focal deficit in brain metastasis usually indicates hemorrhage into the metastasis (melanoma, germ cell and renal cell tumors bleed readily) (Harrison 22e p.590)
Pyogenic epidural abscess or vertebral tuberculosis can mimic malignant spinal cord compression (Harrison 22e p.589)

SVCS: chest radiograph (superior mediastinal widening, usually right-sided), CT thorax (most reliable mediastinal view; 'hot quadrate' hepatic hotspot sign suggests SVC obstruction), MRI (100% sensitivity/specificity but supine positioning may be difficult in dyspneic patients) (Harrison 22e p.586)

Spinal cord compression: neurologic exam and plain spine films first (earliest finding is the 'winking owl' sign of pedicle erosion; plain films are insensitive), then full-length spinal MRI (procedure of choice); myelography reserved for poor or unobtainable MRI (Harrison 22e p.589)
Brain metastases/raised ICP: gadolinium-enhanced MRI is superior to CT and more sensitive for meningeal involvement and small posterior-fossa lesions (Harrison 22e p.590)

TLS pretreatment evaluation in at-risk patients: complete blood count, serum chemistry (electrolytes, creatinine, calcium, phosphate, uric acid) and urinalysis; follow plasma rather than serum potassium when pseudohyperkalemia is suspected; sonography/CT of kidneys and retroperitoneum if baseline renal function is abnormal (Harrison 22e p.593)
A urinary uric acid to urinary creatinine ratio >1 supports acute hyperuricemic nephropathy; <1 suggests renal failure of other cause (Harrison 22e p.593)

Spinal cord compression mimics: osteoporotic vertebral collapse, disk disease, radiation myelopathy, neoplastic leptomeningitis, benign tumors, epidural hematoma and spinal lipomatosis (Harrison 22e p.589)
About 20% of vertebral collapse (especially in older patients and postmenopausal women) is due to osteoporosis rather than cancer (Harrison 22e p.589)
Benign causes of SVCS: aortic aneurysm, thyromegaly, thrombosis, and fibrosing mediastinitis from prior irradiation, histoplasmosis or Behcet's syndrome (Harrison 22e p.585)
Pseudohyperkalemia from high leukocyte/platelet counts (cell lysis after blood draw) can falsely elevate potassium in TLS; no ECG abnormalities are present (Harrison 22e p.593)
Pseudohypoglycemia from glucose consumption in the test tube with hyperleukocytosis, myeloproliferative disease or CSF treatment (Harrison 22e p.593)

Oncologic emergencies arise by three mechanisms (Harrison 22e p.585). Structural-obstructive emergencies result from a space-occupying lesion: in SVCS, malignant tumor or thrombosis obstructs the superior vena cava, reducing venous return from head, neck and upper limbs; in malignant spinal cord compression, an expanding extradural tumor (usually metastasis to vertebral body or pedicle, or paravertebral extension through the intervertebral foramen) mechanically injures axons and myelin and compromises blood flow, causing ischemia/infarction; raised intracranial pressure results from brain metastases and surrounding edema, sometimes with hemorrhage or CSF obstruction causing hydrocephalus and herniation (Harrison 22e p.585-590). Metabolic/hormonal (paraneoplastic) emergencies include hypercalcemia, SIADH-related hyponatremia, lactic acidosis and hypoglycemia (Harrison 22e p.592-593). Treatment-related TLS occurs when cytotoxic killing of a large rapidly proliferating tumor releases intracellular contents: nucleic acid turnover raises uric acid which precipitates in the acidic renal tubules; released phosphate causes hyperphosphatemia with reciprocal hypocalcemia and calcium-phosphate nephrocalcinosis; and massive cell destruction releases potassium causing hyperkalemia, which in renal failure can cause fatal ventricular arrhythmias (Harrison 22e p.593).

Emergencies in cancer fall into three groups: pressure/obstruction from a space-occupying lesion (structural-obstructive), metabolic or hormonal problems (paraneoplastic), and treatment-related complications (Harrison 22e p.585).
Full-length spinal MRI is the imaging procedure of choice for cord compression and is as good as or better than myelography plus post-myelogram CT (Harrison 22e p.589).

About 25% of cancer patients die with intracranial metastases; lung and breast cancer and melanoma metastasize to brain most often, and brain metastases present features of an expanding intracranial lesion: headache, nausea, vomiting, behavioral change, seizures and focal progressive deficits (Harrison 22e p.589-590).
Dexamethasone is the best initial treatment for all symptomatic patients with brain metastases and raised intracranial pressure (Harrison 22e p.590).
Hypercalcemia is the most common paraneoplastic syndrome, and SIADH is the most common cause of hyponatremia among cancer patients (both detailed in Chaps. 98 and 422/393) (Harrison 22e p.592).

Tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) is characterized by hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia and hypocalcemia from destruction of large numbers of rapidly proliferating cells; acidosis may develop and acute renal failure occurs frequently (Harrison 22e p.593).

TLS is most often associated with treatment of Burkitt's lymphoma, ALL, AML and other rapidly proliferating lymphomas, and usually occurs during or shortly (1-5 days) after chemotherapy; risk correlates with tumor burden and high LDH (>1500 U/L) (Harrison 22e p.593).
Recognition of risk and prevention are the most important steps in TLS management; the standard preventive approach is allopurinol plus aggressive hydration (Harrison 22e p.593).
Febrile neutropenia is the clinical presentation of fever with <1500 granulocytes/uL; it is a key treatment-related emergency in cancer patients (Harrison 22e p.575).

Superior vena cava syndrome (SVCS) reflects SVC obstruction with severe reduction of venous return from head, neck and upper extremities; lung cancer (especially small-cell and squamous) accounts for ~85% of malignant cases, and in young adults lymphoma is a leading cause (Harrison 22e p.585).
Benign causes of SVCS are increasing with intravascular device use (central catheters, pacemaker/defibrillator leads) and now account for at least 40% of cases (Harrison 22e p.585).

SVCS typically presents with neck and facial swelling (especially periorbital), dyspnea, cough, dilated neck veins, collateral chest-wall veins, cyanosis and facial plethora that worsens when supine; bending forward or lying down aggravates symptoms (Harrison 22e p.585).

The diagnosis of SVCS is clinical; the most significant chest radiograph finding is widening of the superior mediastinum (most often right-sided), and CT provides the most reliable mediastinal anatomy (Harrison 22e p.586).

Malignant spinal cord compression (MSCC) is compression of cord and/or cauda equina by an extradural tumor mass; spinal cord compression occurs in 5-10% of cancer patients and is the first manifestation of malignancy in ~10% (Harrison 22e p.588).

Localized back pain and tenderness is the most common initial symptom of spinal cord compression, often present for days to months before neurologic findings; it characteristically worsens when supine, unlike disk-disease pain (Harrison 22e p.588-589).

The thoracic spine is the most common site of cord compression (70%), followed by lumbosacral (20%) and cervical (10%); lung, breast and prostate cancers are the most frequent offenders (Harrison 22e p.588).

Treatment of spinal cord compression is more often successful in patients still ambulatory and with sphincter control at initiation; patients whose exam suggests compression should receive dexamethasone immediately and undergo MRI (Harrison 22e p.589).
A normal chest radiograph is still compatible with the diagnosis of SVCS if other characteristic findings are present (Harrison 22e p.586)
A normal appearance of plain spine films does not exclude cancer; plain films are insensitive for cord compression (Harrison 22e p.589)
Vertebral collapse is not a reliable indicator of tumor since ~20% of collapses are osteoporotic (Harrison 22e p.589)
After SVC stenting, the prompt increase in venous return may precipitate heart failure and pulmonary edema (Harrison 22e p.586)

Urinary alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate is no longer recommended in TLS: although it increases uric acid solubility, a high pH decreases solubility of xanthine, hypoxanthine and calcium phosphate, potentially increasing intratubular crystallization (Harrison 22e p.593)

Rasburicase is contraindicated in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, and it causes ex vivo degradation of uric acid in the test tube giving spuriously low levels unless samples are cooled immediately (Harrison 22e p.594)
Pseudohyperkalemia in TLS shows no ECG abnormalities; plasma rather than serum potassium should be followed (Harrison 22e p.593)
Arterial blood gas oxygen tension can be spuriously low in hyperleukocytosis due to oxygen consumption by white cells; pulse oximetry is the most accurate measure of oxygenation (Harrison 22e p.591)

In SVCS, mortality relates to the underlying cause rather than to caval obstruction itself, and clinical improvement occurs in most patients (sometimes via collateral circulation); SVCS recurs in 10-30% (Harrison 22e p.586). For spinal cord compression, tumor histology is an important determinant of recovery and survival, and rapid onset/progression of signs and symptoms are poor prognostic features; treatment is more often successful in ambulatory patients who retain sphincter control (Harrison 22e p.589). Brain metastases frequently cause major symptoms, disability and early death (Harrison 22e p.590). Lactic acidosis in cancer carries a poor prognosis regardless of treatment, and cancer patients with malignant cells on pericardial cytology have very poor survival (Harrison 22e p.587, 592). Despite aggressive prophylaxis, TLS with oliguric/anuric renal failure may still occur and often requires renal replacement therapy (Harrison 22e p.594).

SVCS with cerebral and/or laryngeal edema, proptosis, glossal/laryngeal edema, obtundation or postural hypotension carries poorer prognosis and requires urgent evaluation and early stenting (Harrison 22e p.585-586)

Tracheal obstruction from a superior mediastinal mass is the one potentially life-threatening complication of SVCS and demands emergent therapy; cardiac arrest or respiratory failure can occur, particularly with sedatives or general anesthesia (Harrison 22e p.585-586)

Cancer patient with back pain plus a crescendo pain pattern, Lhermitte's sign, or pain aggravated by cough/Valsalva/recumbency should be evaluated for cord compression as quickly as possible (Harrison 22e p.589)

Loss of bowel or bladder control, autonomic dysfunction (decreased anal tone, distended bladder, absent anal wink/bulbocavernosus reflex) signals significant cord involvement and is an unfavorable prognostic feature (Harrison 22e p.588)
Hyperkalemia in TLS with renal failure can rapidly become life-threatening, causing ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death (Harrison 22e p.593)
Acute adrenal insufficiency (adrenal crisis) is potentially lethal and may be masked by nonspecific symptoms attributed to cancer or therapy (Harrison 22e p.593)
Febrile neutropenia (fever with <1500 granulocytes/uL) is a treatment-related emergency requiring prompt management (Harrison 22e p.575)

Spinal cord compression management uses the NOMS framework (Memorial Sloan Kettering): Neurologic assessment (degree of epidural compression, myelopathy, functional radiculopathy), Oncologic assessment (tumor radiosensitivity), Mechanical assessment (spinal stability), and Systemic factors (extent of disease and comorbidities determining tolerance of therapy) (Harrison 22e p.589-590). TLS risk is stratified by tumor burden, renal function, hyperuricemia and high LDH (>1500 U/L); a high-risk management algorithm escalates from hydration and allopurinol to recombinant urate oxidase/rasburicase and hemodialysis based on serum uric acid, creatinine, potassium, phosphate and symptomatic hypocalcemia thresholds (Harrison 22e p.593-594).
Oncologic Emergencies (non-infective) — Oncology / Emergency Also: tumor lysis syndrome, superior vena cava syndrome
Cholinergic (muscarinic/nicotinic) poisoning — also causes miosis plus a depressed physiologic state (p.3748)
Sedative-hypnotic / GABAergic poisoning (alcohols, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, GHB) — depressed state, distinguished as naloxone-unresponsive (p.3748)
Sympatholytic poisoning (alpha-2 agonists e.g. clonidine, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, cardiac glycosides) (p.3747)
Other causes of coma including hypoglycemia (reversed by dextrose) (p.3748)
Blood/urine toxicology can confirm a suspected diagnosis but must not delay clinical management (p.3690)
ECG to detect QT prolongation (e.g. methadone), which can cause sudden death (p.3733)
Chest imaging for noncardiogenic pulmonary edema / ARDS, a recognized complication of opioid poisoning (p.3749)
In IV users, screen for blood-borne infection (hepatitis B, HIV) and bacterial complications (meningitis, osteomyelitis, abscesses, endocarditis) (p.3733)
Hypoglycemia (responds to dextrose, mimics opioid coma) (p.3748)
Benzodiazepine intoxication (responds to flumazenil) (p.3748)

Opioids act mainly through the mu receptor (also kappa, delta, nociceptin/orphanin), all G protein-coupled, inhibiting the cAMP system and opening GIRK potassium channels to hyperpolarize and silence neurons. Life-threatening respiratory depression results from opioid-induced insensitivity of brainstem (medullary) respiratory neurons to rising carbon dioxide; analgesia and respiratory depression are mediated by receptors in the periaqueductal grey and medulla oblongata. Untreated, progression goes to respiratory and then cardiovascular collapse and death (p.3733, p.3690).
The classic overdose picture is shallow/slow respirations, miosis, bradycardia, hypothermia, and stupor or coma; toxicology can confirm but immediate management is clinical (p.3690).

Pinpoint pupils are characteristic, BUT mydriasis (dilated pupils) appears once significant cerebral anoxia supervenes — dilated pupils do not exclude opioid toxicity in a deteriorating patient (p.3690).

Hypoxia, not the drug itself, is what kills: in opioid and sedative-hypnotic poisoning, vital-sign changes are secondary to CNS depression or consequent hypoxemia and do not appear until consciousness is markedly reduced (grade 3-4 depression) (p.3748).
Aspiration pneumonia is common in overdose because of loss of the gag reflex (p.3733).
Opioids generally do NOT cause seizures, except in polydrug use, with meperidine, with high-dose tramadol, or in the newborn (p.3690).

Fentanyl and its derivatives may require severalfold higher reversal doses than other opioids, and adulteration of illicit fentanyl with xylazine markedly worsens respiratory suppression (p.3689, p.3733).

Prompt reversal of altered mental status and vital signs within minutes of IV naloxone is virtually diagnostic of opioid poisoning (alongside dextrose for hypoglycemia and flumazenil for benzodiazepine intoxication) (p.3748).
Fluoroquinolones commonly cause false-positive opiate urine screens; rapid urine drug screens are screening-only, prone to false results, and miss agents such as kratom (p.3748).
When naloxone has only a limited effect, suspect a co-ingested sedative — most commonly a benzodiazepine, which has caused fatal overdoses in combination with buprenorphine (p.3691).
Do not assume normal-sized or dilated pupils exclude opioids — mydriasis does NOT occur until significant brain anoxia supervenes (p.3690).
Significant vital-sign abnormalities do NOT occur in opioid poisoning until there is a marked decrease in level of consciousness, so early near-normal vitals are falsely reassuring (p.3748).

A negative urine drug screen does NOT rule out opioid toxicity (concentration too low, or agent such as kratom not detected); opiate screens also give false positives (e.g. fluoroquinolones) (p.3748).

Primary buprenorphine overdose is nearly impossible because it is a partial agonist with increasing antagonist activity at higher doses; failure to respond to naloxone should prompt search for a co-ingested sedative (p.3690-3691).
Be sure a patient is not also withdrawing from alcohol or sedatives, which may be more dangerous to manage than opioid withdrawal (p.3733).

Potentially lethal but rapidly reversible if respiratory depression is recognized and supported; untreated overdose progresses to respiratory and cardiovascular collapse and death. Opioid use disorder is chronic and relapsing, and most patients relapse during or after detoxification (p.3690, p.3691). Some opioid intoxications can leave delayed diffuse white-matter injury producing a persistent coma syndrome (p.232).
Dilated pupils in a suspected opioid overdose suggest cerebral anoxia has already occurred (p.3690)
Re-sedation: naloxone lasts only a few hours while most opioids (especially methadone, sustained-release/'toxic time-bomb' formulations) last far longer (p.3691, p.3747)
Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema / ARDS (p.3749)
Methadone-associated QT prolongation and sudden death (p.3733)
Necrosis and limb-loss risk with fentanyl-xylazine injection (p.3733)

Harrison frames poisoning severity by physiologic state (Tables 470-1/470-2): opioids produce a 'depressed' physiologic state (decreased pulse, BP, respiratory rate, temperature, neuromuscular activity, with miosis). Severity is graded by depth of CNS/physiologic depression (grades 1-4); marked vital-sign abnormalities indicate grade 3-4 depression (p.3747-3748). Note: opioid WITHDRAWAL is a separate 'stimulated' syndrome — onset 8-10 h after the last dose with lacrimation, rhinorrhea, yawning and sweating, progressing to gooseflesh, nausea/vomiting, myalgia, hyperpnea, hyperthermia, hypertension, mydriasis over a 7-10 day acute course (p.3690).
Clinical (pinpoint pupils, ↓RR)
Trial of naloxone
Opioid overdose (non-infective) — Toxicology
Reduced consciousness with depressed respiration and pinpoint pupils is opioid toxicity until proven otherwise.
Red flags: Respiratory depression — naloxone + airway support

[guideline] management → IV naloxone (titrated) Competitive opioid antagonist reversing respiratory depression. Titrate to respiration, not full arousal, to avoid precipitating acute withdrawal. Fentanyl/analogues may need severalfold higher doses.

[guideline] adjunct → IV naloxone infusion Naloxone lasts only 30–90 min while methadone and sustained-release opioids last far longer, so a bolus alone risks re-sedation. Continue with prolonged observation after discontinuation.

Opioid receptors (mu, kappa, delta, nociceptin/orphanin) are G protein-linked and coupled to the cyclic AMP (cAMP) second-messenger system and to G protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium channels (GIRKs); receptor binding increases potassium permeability, hyperpolarizes neurons, and inhibits action potentials, producing analgesia, sedation, and reinforcement. Reinforcing euphoria is mediated through the mesolimbic dopaminergic pathway from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens, where opioids indirectly raise dopamine by inhibiting GABAergic interneurons; the subjective high requires a fast rate of dopamine change. Tolerance and withdrawal arise from adaptive upregulation of the cAMP-PKA-CREB cascade in locus coeruleus noradrenergic neurons after chronic mu-receptor inhibition: sustained inhibition triggers compensatory increases in cyclic AMP enzyme activity, so abrupt opioid cessation produces unopposed noradrenergic overactivity and withdrawal symptoms; this model underlies the use of alpha2-agonists to suppress that activation. PKA-driven phosphorylation of CREB also induces genes such as tyrosine hydroxylase and BDNF, the latter implicated in long-term neuroplastic changes (Harrison 22e pp.3689-3690).

DSM-5 (2022) replaced the older terms dependence and addiction with opioid use disorder, opioid intoxication, and opioid withdrawal; the disorder is defined as repeated use over a 12-month period causing problems in two or more domains (tolerance, withdrawal, using larger amounts than intended, craving, and continued use despite adverse consequences) (Harrison 22e p.3688).

Heroin users are frequently polydrug users (alcohol, sedatives, cannabinoids, stimulants); none substitute for opioids but they have additive effects, so concurrent alcohol or sedative withdrawal (which can be more dangerous) must be excluded before managing opioid withdrawal (Harrison 22e p.3690).

Buprenorphine's partial agonism means escalating doses shift toward antagonist activity, so primary buprenorphine overdose is nearly impossible, but high doses can precipitate withdrawal in patients on full agonists such as morphine or methadone (Harrison 22e pp.3690-3691).
Most opioid-using individuals meet more than three diagnostic criteria, so reducing the DSM threshold from three to two problem areas did not change measured disease rates (Harrison 22e p.3688).

The mu receptor is the receptor most clinically relevant to opioid effects; mu actions include analgesia, euphoric reinforcement, cough and appetite suppression, decreased respiration, decreased GI motility, sedation, and hormonal changes, while kappa activation tends to produce dysphoria and psychotic symptoms (Harrison 22e p.3689).

An opioid 'high' occurs only when the rate of rise in dopamine is fast, so rapid routes such as smoking and intravenous injection produce a 'rush' whereas oral and transdermal routes give analgesia/sedation without the euphoric high (Harrison 22e p.3689).

Opioid overdose is recognized clinically by shallow, slow respirations, pupillary miosis (mydriasis appears only after significant brain anoxia), bradycardia, hypothermia, and stupor or coma; immediate management is based on clinical criteria rather than waiting for toxicology (Harrison 22e p.3690).

Fentanyl overdose may require roughly twice the reversal-agent dose needed for other opioids, and reversal antagonists are short-acting relative to most opioids, so re-sedation can occur after an initial response (Harrison 22e pp.3688, 3690).

Adding xylazine (a nonopioid veterinary sedative) to illicit fentanyl markedly worsens respiratory suppression and is associated with tissue necrosis and increased risk of limb amputation in people who inject (Harrison 22e p.3690).
Opioids generally do not cause seizures except in unusual situations: polydrug use with meperidine, high-dose tramadol, or the newborn (Harrison 22e p.3690).

Withdrawal risk has a strong genetic component (up to ~50% related to functional polymorphisms), including a mu-opioid receptor variant conferring threefold higher affinity for opioids and beta-endorphin; epigenetic methylation may compensate by reducing mu-receptor numbers (Harrison 22e p.3689).

Methadone can prolong the QT interval (rates reported as high as ~16% above non-methadone injecting patients) and has caused sudden death; QT monitoring is relevant during overdose and maintenance (Harrison 22e pp.3690, 3691).
Administering so much antagonist that opioid withdrawal is precipitated, rather than targeting reversal of respiratory depression
Assuming a single antagonist dose is sufficient, since antagonists last only a few hours while most opioids persist longer, risking re-sedation (close monitoring/continuous antagonism often needed)
Overlooking concurrent benzodiazepine or alcohol/sedative involvement when reversal has only limited effect
Misjudging dose in naive or infrequent users because actual ingested potency is hard to estimate, especially with fentanyl derivatives
Forgetting that buprenorphine and methadone themselves can be misused and that buprenorphine can precipitate withdrawal in fentanyl- or high-dose-methadone-dependent patients

Opioid use disorder is a chronic, relapsing condition; most patients tend to relapse during or after detoxification, and stopping use is far easier than preventing relapse. Long-term relapse prevention requires combined pharmacologic and psychosocial approaches. Medication-free inpatient/outpatient programs have poor 1- to 5-year outcomes compared with pharmacotherapy, except for residential programs lasting roughly 6-18 months. Untreated potentially lethal overdose progresses to respiratory and cardiovascular collapse and death. Globally the World Drug Report attributes the greatest burden of drug-related morbidity and mortality to opioid misuse; in 2022 over 76,000 US overdose deaths involved opioids, with rates accelerating due to high-potency fentanyl derivatives and stimulant co-use (Harrison 22e pp.3688, 3691-3692).
Shallow/slow respirations with pinpoint miosis, bradycardia, hypothermia, and stupor or coma indicating life-threatening overdose
Mydriasis in a suspected overdose suggesting significant brain anoxia has supervened
Limited or absent response to standard reversal dosing, prompting suspicion of fentanyl, high antagonist requirement, or concurrent benzodiazepine overdose
Loss of gag reflex with aspiration pneumonia risk
Skin necrosis or limb compromise suggesting xylazine-adulterated fentanyl use
Septic complications of injection use such as meningitis, osteomyelitis, or organ abscesses

Withdrawal time course (heroin): symptoms begin ~8-10 h after the last dose, with early lacrimation, rhinorrhea, yawning, and sweating; later stages bring restless sleep, weakness, chills, piloerection ('cold turkey'), nausea/vomiting, muscle aches, involuntary movements, hyperpnea, hyperthermia, and hypertension. Acute withdrawal lasts ~7-10 days, followed by a protracted abstinence phase of ~26-30 weeks (hypotension, bradycardia, hypothermia, mydriasis, blunted respiratory CO2 responsiveness). Tolerance/withdrawal can develop within ~6-8 weeks of chronic daily use. Plasma half-lives vary widely: ~2.5-3 h for morphine, >22 h for methadone, minutes for fentanyl-related opioids, and longest for buprenorphine/metabolites (Harrison 22e pp.3689-3690).

chunks.text: Optic neuritis is inflammation and demyelination of the optic nerve, most commonly immune-mediated and associated with multiple sclerosis. An inflammatory, often T-cell-driven process attacks the myelin sheath of optic nerve axons, disrupting conduction and causing loss of visual acuity, colour vision, and contrast. Because conduction rather than the axon itself is initially affected, remyelination allows substantial recovery, though repeated or severe attacks cause axonal loss and permanent deficits with optic atrophy. Antibody-mediated variants (aquaporin-4 in neuromyelitis optica, MOG antibody disease) and infective or granulomatous causes produce similar inflammation through different mechanisms.

chunks.text: Orbital cellulitis is infection of the soft tissues posterior to the orbital septum. Infection most commonly extends directly from the paranasal sinuses (particularly the ethmoid, separated from the orbit only by the thin lamina papyracea), but can also arise from trauma, dacryocystitis, dental infection, or haematogenous spread. Inflammation and oedema within the confined bony orbit raise pressure, displace the globe forward (proptosis), impair extraocular muscle function, and can compress or ischaemically injure the optic nerve. Spread posteriorly risks cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, and intracranial abscess.

Organophosphate (and carbamate) insecticides, and nerve agents such as sarin, soman, tabun and VX, inhibit acetylcholinesterase, leading to accumulation of synaptic acetylcholine at both muscarinic and nicotinic cholinergic receptor sites; the resulting overstimulation produces the combined muscarinic, nicotinic and CNS toxidrome. Organophosphates are 'toxic time-bombs' in that they may require metabolic activation, so onset of toxicity can be delayed. Separately, organophosphates bind and inhibit neuropathy target esterase, with axonal degeneration of the gracile fasciculus and corticospinal tracts producing a delayed sensorimotor polyneuropathy. (p.3610, p.3712, p.3704)

Belongs to the depressed physiologic state / cholinergic toxidrome; miosis is common and is most pronounced in opioid and cholinergic poisoning, distinguished from other depressant syndromes by muscarinic and nicotinic signs (p.3705).

Muscarinic features: seizures, excessive secretions (lacrimation, salivation, bronchorrhoea and wheezing, diaphoresis), and increased bowel/bladder activity with nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, and incontinence of faeces and urine (p.3712).
Nicotinic features: hypertension, tachycardia, muscle cramps, fasciculations, weakness, and paralysis — note these oppose the muscarinic picture, so vital signs can be mixed (p.3712).
Death is usually due to respiratory failure (p.3712).
Organophosphates and carbamates can produce bradycardia and atrioventricular block on ECG (p.3706).
Organophosphate (and amanita/mushroom) poisoning can present as acute, often systemic-compromising diarrhoea (p.46/Acute Diarrhea chapter).
Organophosphates can cause a delayed organophosphate-induced neuropathy: early generalised weakness from neuromuscular blockade, then an axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy ensues (p.3610).

Vital signs may be discordant: muscarinic effects cause bradycardia while nicotinic stimulation can cause hypertension and tachycardia, so a 'normal' or mixed heart rate does not exclude poisoning (p.3712).
Organophosphates are 'toxic time-bombs' requiring metabolic activation, so a patient may be initially well or minimally symptomatic and deteriorate later (p.3704).
Cholinesterase activity is <50% of normal in acetylcholinesterase-inhibitor poisoning — a key confirmatory threshold not to overlook (p.3712).

Death is usually due to respiratory failure (p.3712). Outcome and reversibility of any poisoning depend on the functional reserve of the individual or target organ, influenced by age and preexisting disease (p.3704).

No blood tests are routinely indicated unless symptoms or signs suggest inflammatory arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2953).

Radiographs are not routinely indicated; order only when pain and findings are atypical of OA or when pain persists after effective treatment. Imaging findings correlate poorly with pain, and x-rays may be normal in early disease (insensitive to cartilage loss) (Harrison 22e p.2953).

MRI is not indicated in the diagnostic workup; meniscal tears and cartilage/bone lesions are common both in OA and in older persons without joint pain, and MRI findings rarely warrant a change in therapy (Harrison 22e p.2953).

OA is joint failure in which all joint structures undergo pathologic change. The pathologic hallmark is focal, initially nonuniform loss of hyaline articular cartilage, accompanied by thickening and sclerosis of the subchondral bony plate, marginal osteophyte outgrowth, stretching of the articular capsule, variable synovitis, and weakness of muscles bridging the joint (meniscal degeneration occurs in knees). Disease begins with joint injury when protective mechanisms (joint capsule/ligaments, bridging muscle, sensory afferents, underlying bone, and synovial-fluid lubrication via hyaluronic acid and lubricin) fail. Cartilage shows depletion of aggrecan and loss/unfurling of type 2 collagen, losing compressive stiffness; chondrocytes shift toward catabolism, producing matrix-degrading enzymes (MMPs, ADAMTS-5). Local inflammation (including mechanoinflammation), with cytokines, alarmins/DAMPs, and growth factors (BMP-2, TGF-beta drive osteophytes; VEGF drives vascular invasion), accelerates progression. Risk reflects the balance between joint vulnerability (age, female sex, genetics such as GDF5, prior damage, malalignment, bridging-muscle weakness, high bone density) and joint loading (obesity, occupational/repetitive use, major injury) (Harrison 22e pp.2949-2952).

OA is the most common type of arthritis and a leading cause of disability in the elderly; prevalence rises strikingly with age, being uncommon before 40 and highly prevalent after 60 (Harrison 22e p.2949).

Joint involvement is characteristic: hips, knees, first MTP joint, cervical/lumbosacral spine, and in the hands the DIP, PIP, and thumb base; the wrist, elbow, and ankle are usually spared (Harrison 22e p.2949).

Joint pain is primarily activity-related early on, coming on during or just after use and resolving with rest; as disease progresses pain becomes continuous and may be bothersome at night (Harrison 22e p.2952).
Morning stiffness, when present, is usually brief (<30 min), in contrast to the prolonged stiffness (hours) of inflammatory arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2952).
Hand OA produces bony enlargement of the DIP joints (Heberden's nodes) and PIP joints (Bouchard's nodes) (Harrison 22e p.2949).
On hip examination, OA can be detected by loss of internal rotation on passive movement (Harrison 22e p.2953).
Mechanical symptoms (buckling, catching, locking) are common in knee OA and need further evaluation for internal derangement only when they follow an acute knee injury (Harrison 22e p.2952).
Osteophytes are an important radiographic hallmark of OA, along with joint-space narrowing reflecting cartilage loss (Harrison 22e pp.2952-2953).

Distinguish OA from rheumatoid (and other inflammatory) arthritis, crystal arthritis (gout/pseudogout), and septic arthritis; prolonged morning stiffness, systemic features, and an inflammatory synovial fluid white count point away from OA.
Do not rely on radiographs to gauge symptom severity: x-ray changes correlate poorly with pain, and films may be normal in early disease.
Many persons with x-ray or MRI evidence of OA have no joint symptoms, so structural findings alone do not establish symptomatic OA.
Back pain and neck pain are not tied to x-ray findings of spinal OA and are evaluated separately.

OA is a chronic, generally progressive disorder of the elderly whose high prevalence and impact on physical function make it a leading cause of disability. Severely malaligned knees may be destined to progress regardless of other risk factors, whereas weight loss greater than 10% of body weight reduces cartilage loss and, in most affected persons, alleviates pain (Harrison 22e pp.2949-2952).
Prominent nocturnal pain in the absence of end-stage OA merits a distinct workup (Harrison 22e p.2953).
Prolonged morning stiffness with many joints affected suggests inflammatory arthritis rather than OA (Harrison 22e p.2952).
Mechanical symptoms (buckling, catching, locking) developing after an acute knee injury warrant evaluation for internal derangement (Harrison 22e p.2952).

Harrison's chapter 383 does not present a single formal grading scale; OA is characterized clinically along a spectrum from early, episodic activity-related pain with brief morning stiffness to advanced/end-stage disease with continuous and nocturnal pain. The chapter references the WOMAC index as a patient-reported outcome measure of pain, stiffness, and function (Harrison 22e p.2952).

Osteomyelitis is infection of bone reached by microorganisms via one of three routes. In hematogenous disease, circulating organisms seed the metaphyses of long bones in children and the vertebral column in adults; because the adult intervertebral disk is avascular, organisms enter through the segmental arteries supplying the adjacent endplates and then spread into the disk, producing the characteristic involvement of two contiguous vertebrae and the intervening disk. Alternative routes include retrograde seeding through the prevertebral venous plexus and direct inoculation during spinal surgery, epidural procedures, or trauma. Contiguous-focus disease follows bone trauma or surgery, with wound infection after sternotomy, open-fracture repair, or prosthetic-joint placement. Vascular-insufficiency/neuropathic disease, most often in poorly controlled diabetes, arises from progressively deep foot infection driven by ischemia of skin, soft tissue, and bone combined with motor, sensory, and autonomic neuropathy. Foreign material is highly vulnerable: host proteins such as fibronectin coat the device, favoring staphylococcal adherence and biofilm formation that resists phagocytosis and antibiotics. Failure of timely or adequate therapy leads to bone necrosis (sequestra) and progression to chronic osteomyelitis with sinus tracts and soft-tissue destruction (Harrison 22e p.1061-1066).

Three mechanisms underlie osteomyelitis: hematogenous spread, contiguous spread after surgery or trauma, and secondary infection due to vascular insufficiency or neuropathy; in adults hematogenous disease most often involves the vertebral column, whereas in children long bones are seeded (Harrison 22e p.1061).

Subacute or chronic vertebral disease is typically caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis or Brucella in endemic regions, and by low-virulence organisms (coagulase-negative staphylococci, Cutibacterium acnes) in implant-associated infection; tuberculous spondylitis preferentially involves the thoracic spine (about two-thirds of cases) (Harrison 22e p.1062).

Synovial fluid analysis is central to diagnosing periprosthetic joint infection: leukocyte thresholds of ~1700/uL (knee) and ~4200/uL (hip) are about 90% sensitive and specific, and alpha-defensin is highly specific but limited by cost and sensitivity, so it should confirm rather than screen (Harrison 22e p.1066).

Chronic osteomyelitis can reactivate decades later; recurrence after a symptom-free interval exceeding 70 years has been described, most often in elderly patients with S. aureus disease acquired in the preantibiotic era (Harrison 22e p.1063-1064).

The clinically decisive distinction is not a fixed duration but the presence or absence of bone necrosis (sequestra): acute osteomyelitis without necrosis can generally be cured with antimicrobials alone, while chronic osteomyelitis with sequestra requires combined surgical debridement (Harrison 22e p.1062).

Back pain is the leading symptom of vertebral osteomyelitis (>85%), and the location maps to the level of infection (lumbar ~60%, thoracic ~30%, cervical ~10%); only about half of patients are febrile, partly because of analgesic use (Harrison 22e p.1062).

ESR and CRP are markedly more useful than the leukocyte count for screening: CRP is elevated in essentially all and ESR in ~98% of vertebral osteomyelitis cases, whereas leukocytosis and neutrophilia have sensitivities of only ~65% and ~40% (Harrison 22e p.1062).

In patients without sepsis syndrome, antibiotics should be withheld until a pathogen is documented (by blood culture, bone biopsy, or aspirated pus), because pretreatment markedly lowers culture yield and an established microbiologic diagnosis guides therapy (Harrison 22e p.1062-1063).

MRI is the diagnostic gold standard for vertebral osteomyelitis and should be obtained urgently when neurologic impairment is present to detect epidural abscess or exclude disk herniation; 18F-FDG PET is the alternative when MRI is contraindicated or implants/multifocal disease are suspected (Harrison 22e p.1062).

A primary focus is found in only about half of hematogenous cases; common sources are the urinary tract, skin/soft tissue, intravascular catheters, and the endocardium, and endocarditis is identified in roughly 10% overall (and in ~50% of viridans streptococcal cases) (Harrison 22e p.1061-1062).

Implanted foreign material creates a zone of local immunodeficiency and a host-protein-coated surface that promotes staphylococcal adherence and biofilm formation, so device-related bone and joint infection generally cannot be cured by antimicrobials alone (Harrison 22e p.1062, 1066).

Brodie's abscess is a subacute form occurring mainly in young males, presenting with pain (~98%) and swelling (~53%) in the tibia or femur, with a median diagnostic delay of about 3 months; localized unexplained tibial/femoral pain in a young patient warrants imaging (Harrison 22e p.1064).
Starting empiric antibiotics before obtaining cultures in a non-septic patient, which markedly lowers culture yield and obscures the microbiologic diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1062-1063).
Relying on plain radiographs or the leukocyte count in acute disease, both of which have low sensitivity; normal radiographs do not exclude acute osteomyelitis (Harrison 22e p.1062).

Using follow-up MRI to judge treatment response in uncomplicated cases, since radiologic improvement correlates poorly with clinical healing; imaging follow-up is reserved for pyogenic complications (Harrison 22e p.1063).
Misinterpreting a three-phase bone scan or 18F-FDG PET within ~1 year of surgery, when ongoing bone remodeling produces nonspecific uptake (Harrison 22e p.1064, 1066).
Assuming antimicrobials alone will cure device-associated osteomyelitis or PJI; without appropriate surgery such therapy is generally only suppressive (Harrison 22e p.1061, 1067).

Dismissing coagulase-negative staphylococci or Cutibacterium acnes as contaminants, when in the setting of an implant or prolonged bacteremia they may be the true low-virulence pathogens (Harrison 22e p.1062).
Failing to consider tuberculous or brucellar disease in patients from or traveling to endemic regions, where subacute/chronic vertebral osteomyelitis predominates (Harrison 22e p.1063-1065).

Prognosis depends on early diagnosis, presence of bone necrosis, and whether an implant is involved. Acute hematogenous vertebral and long-bone osteomyelitis without sequestra or hardware can usually be cured with antimicrobials alone; a randomized trial in pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis reported ~91% cure at one year with no difference between 6- and 12-week regimens. Failure of adequate treatment, open fractures, and unaddressed implant infection drive progression to chronic osteomyelitis with sinus tracts and soft-tissue damage. In fracture-related infection, implant-retention success falls with chronicity (about 86-100% in early, 82-89% in delayed, and ~67% in late infection). In periprosthetic joint infection, implant retention offers >80% infection-free survival only when the infection is acute, the implant is stable, the pathogen is susceptible to a biofilm-active agent, and the soft tissues are intact; in patients with severe comorbidity, lifelong suppressive therapy may be the chosen goal rather than cure (Harrison 22e p.1063-1067).

No single accepted comprehensive scheme exists. Osteomyelitis is categorized by pathogenesis (hematogenous, contiguous, vascular insufficiency/neuropathic), by course (acute versus subacute/chronic, with the presence or absence of sequestra being the decisive feature), and by location (long bone, vertebral, periarticular). The Cierny-Mader staging system classifies long-bone disease by anatomic extent, host physiologic class (systemic and local compromise of immunity, metabolism, and vascularity), and radiographic findings, and is used mainly to guide surgical management. Implant-associated disease is further classified by timing relative to surgery (e.g., early/acute, delayed, late), and periprosthetic joint infection is grouped for therapeutic decisions as acute hematogenous, early postinterventional, or chronic (Harrison 22e p.1061, 1066).

Osteoporosis is reduced bone strength leading to skeletal fragility and fractures; BMD alone underestimates fragility because microarchitectural deterioration and component misalignment also contribute. A low peak bone mass (genetic, hormonal, nutritional) may underlie disease, with superimposed age-related and extrinsic changes in bone remodeling. In adults remodeling (not modeling) predominates and serves to repair microdamage and supply calcium. Estrogen deficiency drives bone loss by (1) activating new remodeling sites and (2) creating an imbalance favoring resorption over formation: loss of estrogen increases RANKL and reduces osteoprotegerin, increasing osteoclast formation/recruitment, while shortening osteoblast life span and prolonging osteoclast longevity/activity. Trabecular bone (80% of surface area) is preferentially affected, so vertebral fractures are the earliest skeletal consequence. Estrogen also regulates remodeling in men. Heritability of BMD is ~50-80%; LRP5 activating mutations cause high bone mass and inactivating mutations cause osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome (Harrison 22e p.3293-3295).

WHO operationally defines osteoporosis as a bone density T-score of -2.5 or below (>=2.5 SD below the young-adult mean for same sex/race), measured at lumbar spine, total hip, or femoral neck; osteopenia (low bone density) is a T-score of -1.0 to -2.5 and is a risk factor for developing osteoporosis (Harrison 22e p.3291).

A fragility fracture (hip or vertebral) by definition establishes osteoporosis and warrants treatment, regardless of the T-score; patients presenting with hip or spine fractures by definition have osteoporosis (Harrison 22e p.3291, p.3298).
Osteoporosis is most common among postmenopausal women, but ~30% of fragility fractures occur in men; secondary osteoporosis arises from other underlying diseases (Harrison 22e p.3291).

>50% of fractures, including hip fractures, among postmenopausal women occur in individuals with osteopenia rather than densitometric osteoporosis, because that population is much larger - hence the shift toward absolute fracture-risk assessment (Harrison 22e p.3291).

FRAX and the Garvan Fracture Risk Calculator estimate 10-year probability of hip or major osteoporotic fracture by combining age, sex, and clinical risk factors with or without BMD, and inform country-specific intervention thresholds distinct from diagnostic thresholds (Harrison 22e p.3291, p.3298).
Glucocorticoids are the most common cause of medication-induced osteoporosis (Harrison 22e p.3296).
Any fracture (excluding fingers, toes, face, skull) in a woman aged >50 or a man aged >60 should trigger investigation for osteoporosis (Harrison 22e p.3293).

Failing to exclude secondary causes of osteoporosis (e.g. myeloma, hyperparathyroidism, thyrotoxicosis, Cushing's, malabsorption/celiac, hypogonadism, mastocytosis) before attributing low bone mass to primary disease, particularly in patients with fractures or unexpectedly low Z-scores.

Excluding a patient from osteoporosis evaluation simply because a fracture was traumatic - patients with osteoporosis are also more likely to sustain traumatic fractures, and any fracture warrants skeletal assessment.

Relying solely on BMD, which can underestimate fragility (microarchitectural deterioration not captured) and is falsely elevated in the spine by osteoarthritic bone spurs/spondylosis; small slim people show falsely low DXA values.
Fewer than 20% of fracture patients are investigated or treated for osteoporosis within 6 months; postfracture care remains fragmented.
Drug holidays are appropriate to consider for oral/IV bisphosphonates but should be avoided for denosumab and anabolic agents because of more rapid offset.

Lifetime osteoporotic fracture risk for a 50-year-old Caucasian woman is ~50% and ~25% for a man; lifetime hip fracture probability ~14% (women) and ~5% (men), roughly half for African Americans. Hip fractures carry high morbidity and mortality with 20-25% of patients dying within the year (higher among men and African Americans), and ~30% of survivors requiring long-term care, many never regaining prior independence. A first fracture exponentially increases risk of further fracture, especially in the first year; almost 20% of women sustain a second fracture within 2 years (Harrison 22e p.3291-3293).
Vertebral fracture (even asymptomatic) is a major sign of skeletal fragility and markedly increases risk of subsequent fracture, especially within the first 12-24 months (imminent fracture risk)
Significant height loss (>4 cm) suggesting occult vertebral fracture
Hip fracture - high mortality (20-25% die within the year) and major loss of independence
More chronic severe pain after vertebral fracture should raise suspicion of multiple myeloma or other underlying bone condition

WHO densitometric categories: normal (T-score >= -1.0), osteopenia/low bone density (T-score -1.0 to -2.5), osteoporosis (T-score <= -2.5 at lumbar spine, femoral neck, or total hip). Presence of a fragility fracture (notably hip or vertebral) defines established/clinical osteoporosis regardless of T-score. Absolute fracture risk (FRAX/Garvan 10-year hip and major osteoporotic fracture probability) is increasingly used alongside or instead of T-score for treatment decisions (Harrison 22e p.3291, p.3297-3298).

chunks.text: Osteosarcoma is a malignant tumour of mesenchymal cells that produce osteoid or immature bone. It typically arises in the metaphysis of rapidly growing long bones, explaining its predilection for the knee region in adolescence during the growth spurt. The tumour destroys normal bone while laying down disorganised neoplastic osteoid, lifts and stimulates the periosteum, and breaks through the cortex to form a soft-tissue mass. It spreads haematogenously, with a strong tendency to metastasise to the lungs, and micrometastases are often present at diagnosis even when not radiologically evident. Predisposing factors include prior radiation, Paget's disease of bone, and genetic conditions such as hereditary retinoblastoma and Li-Fraumeni syndrome.

chunks.text: Otitis externa is inflammation of the skin lining the external auditory canal. Breakdown of the canal's protective barrier, through excess moisture, mechanical trauma, cerumen removal, or altered pH, allows bacterial or fungal overgrowth. In malignant otitis externa, infection (typically Pseudomonas) spreads from the soft tissue into the temporal bone and skull base, causing progressive osteomyelitis and potential cranial nerve involvement.

chunks.text: Otitis media with effusion results from prolonged Eustachian tube dysfunction that impairs middle ear ventilation. Persistent negative pressure encourages transudation of fluid and metaplasia of the middle ear mucosa toward a secretory epithelium, producing a serous or mucoid (glue-like) effusion. The retained fluid dampens ossicular movement and causes a conductive hearing loss. Contributing factors include adenoid hypertrophy, recurrent upper respiratory infections, allergy, cleft palate and, in adults, nasopharyngeal masses obstructing the tube.

chunks.text: Otosclerosis is a primary disorder of endochondral bone of the otic capsule in which foci of normal lamellar bone are resorbed and replaced by irregular, highly cellular and vascular spongy bone that later matures into dense sclerotic bone. The commonest site is the region of the fissula ante fenestram just anterior to the oval window; as the focus enlarges it invades and fixes the stapes footplate, producing progressive conductive hearing loss. Extension of foci into the cochlear endosteum can damage the neural elements and cause sensorineural loss. The condition is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with incomplete penetrance, and hormonal factors appear to modulate its activity.

High-grade serous ovarian cancer is now believed to originate frequently from serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma in the fimbrial end of the fallopian tube, with early TP53 mutation and genomic instability, often in the context of homologous recombination deficiency from BRCA pathway defects. Malignant cells exfoliate and disseminate across the peritoneal cavity, seeding the omentum, bowel serosa, and diaphragm, producing ascites through increased vascular permeability and lymphatic obstruction. Other histological types arise from ovarian surface epithelium, germ cells, or sex cord-stromal cells with distinct biology.
Most cases are epithelial in origin, and high-grade serous carcinoma, now thought largely to arise from the distal fallopian tube, is the commonest and most aggressive subtype

Symptoms are frequently vague and persistent, including abdominal bloating, early satiety, pelvic or abdominal discomfort, and urinary urgency, so a high index of suspicion is needed particularly in women over fifty
Because there is no reliable early symptom or screening test, the majority present with advanced intra-abdominal disease
Inherited mutations in BRCA1 and BRCA2 and Lynch syndrome markedly increase lifetime risk and should prompt genetic assessment
A pelvic mass combined with ascites and a raised CA-125 in a postmenopausal woman is highly suggestive and warrants specialist referral
Management centres on maximal cytoreductive surgery to remove all visible tumour combined with platinum-based chemotherapy
Risk assessment tools that combine ultrasound features, menopausal status, and CA-125 help triage women to gynaecological oncology
Germ cell and sex cord-stromal tumours are important in younger women and can produce hormonal effects or tumour markers such as AFP, hCG, or inhibin

Failing to refer suspicious masses to a gynaecological oncology centre before intervention

Overall survival is dominated by stage at presentation and by the completeness of surgical cytoreduction; disease confined to the ovary is potentially curable, whereas widespread peritoneal disease carries a poorer outlook despite platinum sensitivity. Tumour grade, histological subtype, and BRCA/homologous recombination status influence response to chemotherapy and to maintenance agents such as PARP inhibitors, and relapse is common in advanced disease.
