When the ovary or adnexa rotates about the infundibulopelvic and utero-ovarian ligaments, the lower-pressure venous and lymphatic drainage is occluded first, producing congestion and marked ovarian oedema and enlargement. Continued or tightening rotation eventually compromises arterial inflow, leading to ischaemia, haemorrhagic infarction, and necrosis. Because arterial flow may persist longer than venous outflow owing to the thicker arterial wall and dual blood supply, viability can be maintained for a variable period, defining a window in which detorsion can salvage the ovary.
Torsion is a gynaecological emergency in which the ovary, often with the fallopian tube, twists on its pedicle and compromises its blood supply, threatening ovarian viability
It classically presents with sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain, often colicky and associated with nausea and vomiting, sometimes provoked by exertion or a change in position
An enlarged ovary or an ovarian mass, particularly cysts around five centimetres or larger, predisposes to torsion, so it is uncommon in a normal-sized ovary
Doppler ultrasound may show reduced or absent flow, but preserved arterial flow does not exclude torsion because dual blood supply and intermittent twisting can maintain signals
Torsion can occur in pregnancy, especially after ovulation induction with enlarged ovaries, and in premenarchal girls in whom the diagnosis is easily missed
Prompt surgical intervention, usually laparoscopic detorsion with conservation of the ovary, is preferred over oophorectomy even when the ovary looks dusky, as tissue often recovers
The classic error is delay: repeated observation while awaiting imaging or normalisation of pain risks irreversible ischaemic loss of the ovary
Intermittent torsion produces recurrent self-limiting episodes of pain and warrants evaluation before a definitive infarction occurs
Excluding torsion because Doppler shows preserved arterial flow
Delaying surgery for repeated imaging or observation while ischaemia progresses
Performing oophorectomy on a dusky ovary that would recover after simple detorsion
Failing to consider torsion in premenarchal girls and pregnant women
Missing intermittent torsion by attributing recurrent pain to functional cysts

When detorsion is performed promptly the ovary usually recovers function even if it appeared ischaemic at surgery, and future fertility is generally preserved. Delayed diagnosis leads to infarction requiring oophorectomy and loss of that ovary's function; recurrence can occur, and oophoropexy may be considered in selected cases such as recurrent torsion or a normal ovary in a child.

The principal abnormality is increased number and activity of osteoclasts, which are large, increased 10- to 100-fold in number, and contain many nuclei (up to 100 vs 3-5 in normal osteoclasts), creating a sevenfold rise in resorptive surfaces. Contributing mechanisms include osteoclast precursor hypersensitivity to 1,25(OH)2D3, hyperresponsiveness to RANK ligand (RANKL), increased RANKL expression by marrow stromal cells, increased IL-6 (raising precursor recruitment), increased c-fos expression, and overexpression of the antiapoptotic oncogene Bcl-2. Osteoblasts are recruited to resorption sites and lay down large amounts of new bone matrix, so turnover is high and bone mass is normal or increased (not reduced) unless there is concomitant calcium/vitamin D deficiency. The process passes through an initial osteolytic phase (prominent resorption and hypervascularization, seen radiographically as an advancing lytic wedge or 'blade of grass' lesion), an active mixed phase replacing lamellar bone with haphazard woven bone (marrow may be replaced by fibrous tissue), and a final sclerotic ('burned-out') phase of hard, dense, less vascular mosaic bone; all three phases may coexist at different sites. Etiology remains unknown but evidence supports both genetic (family history in 15-25%; familial syndromes linked to TNFRSF11B/osteoprotegerin, TNFRSF11A/RANK, profilin 1, valosin-containing protein, and the common SQSTM1/p62 mutation) and viral (paramyxovirus-like inclusions and viral mRNA in osteoclasts) contributions (p.3311-3313).

A localized bone-remodeling disorder affecting widespread, noncontiguous areas of the skeleton; initiated by overactive osteoclastic resorption followed by compensatory osteoblastic new bone formation, producing a disorganized mosaic of woven and lamellar bone (p.3311).

Most patients are asymptomatic; diagnosis is often made incidentally from an elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP) on routine blood chemistry or an abnormal skeletal radiograph obtained for another indication (p.3311, p.3312-3313).
Serum calcium and phosphate levels are normal in Paget's disease; isolated/raised ALP with normal calcium is the characteristic biochemical picture (p.3314).
Sites most commonly involved are the pelvis, vertebral bodies, skull, femur, and tibia; familial early-onset cases often have numerous active sites (p.3313).

The most common presenting symptom is pain, which may arise from increased bony vascularity, expanding lytic lesions, fractures, bowing, or deformity; long-bone bowing causes gait abnormalities and secondary osteoarthritis of hip or knee (p.3313).

Skull involvement may cause headaches, frontal bossing, increased head size, and narrowing of cranial foramina leading to hearing loss (cochlear nerve damage from temporal bone involvement), cranial nerve palsies, and platybasia with risk of brainstem compression (p.3313).

For most patients, serum total ALP remains the test of choice for both diagnosis and assessing response to therapy; bone resorption markers (N-telopeptide, C-telopeptide) fall more rapidly with treatment than ALP (p.3313).
Radionuclide 99mTc bone scans are less specific but more sensitive than standard radiographs for identifying sites of active skeletal lesions (p.3313).
Assuming an isolated raised ALP is benign - it can be the only clue to asymptomatic Paget's disease and warrants workup (radiograph plus bone scan).
A symptomatic patient with progression at a single site may have a normal total ALP but an increased bone-specific ALP.
Using serum osteocalcin to diagnose or monitor disease - it is not always elevated and is not recommended.
Attributing hypercalcemia to Paget's disease/immobilization - normal calcium and phosphate are expected, so hypercalcemia should prompt a search for another cause.

Starting bisphosphonate therapy without ensuring adequate calcium and vitamin D intake first - very active bone formation with rapid resorption suppression can precipitate hypocalcemia or mild secondary hyperparathyroidism.

Most patients are asymptomatic and have a benign course; for unclear reasons the prevalence and severity are decreasing and the age of diagnosis is increasing. Effective potent antiresorptive (bisphosphonate) therapy can normalize bone turnover and is associated with an apparently decreasing incidence of sarcoma. Serious complications - fractures, deformity, secondary osteoarthritis, neurologic compromise (hearing loss, cranial nerve palsies, cord/brainstem compression), high-output cardiac state, and rare (<0.5%) malignant transformation (usually osteosarcoma) - drive morbidity. Whether early therapy prevents late complications remains to be determined; deformities may take many years to manifest (p.3312-3314).
New pain in a long-standing pagetic lesion - suggests sarcomatous (most often osteosarcoma) transformation, although neoplasms arising from pagetic bone are rare (<0.5%)

High-output cardiac state and cardiac enlargement from extensive arteriovenous shunting when large portions (15-35%) of the skeleton are involved with high disease activity (e.g., ALP four times above normal); overt high-output heart failure is relatively rare and usually requires concomitant cardiac pathology
Platybasia (softening of the skull base) with risk of brainstem compression; spinal cord compression from bone enlargement or vascular steal syndrome
Fractures, typically in long bones at areas of active or advancing lytic lesions (common at femoral shaft and subtrochanteric regions)
Discovery of hypercalcemia (even with immobilization) should prompt a search for another cause of hypercalcemia

Harrison does not give a formal staging system. Disease activity is gauged by the extent of skeletal involvement and the degree of bone-turnover marker elevation (notably total ALP, with ALP roughly four times above normal cited as marking high activity and cardiovascular risk when 15-35% of the skeleton is involved). Pathologically the disease evolves through three phases that may coexist: an osteolytic phase, an active mixed (woven-bone) phase, and a final sclerotic 'burned-out' phase (p.3313-3314).

Ductal adenocarcinoma is the most common and most lethal exocrine pancreatic neoplasm, characterized by infiltrating desmoplastic stromal reaction and arising in the head, body, or tail. Most cancers arise from pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN, graded 1-3 in a progression model), with genetic alterations accumulating as PanIN grade increases; some arise from noninvasive cystic precursors (e.g., IPMN). The mutational landscape is dominated by four commonly altered genes: KRAS (mutated in 90-95%, primarily codon 12), p16/CDKN2A (inactivated in >90% of invasive tumors), TP53 (~75%), and DPC4/SMAD4 (~50%); BRCA2 is mutated in 3.5-10%. A 'KRAS wildtype' subset (more common in patients under 55) may harbor actionable BRAF mutations, oncogenic fusions (NRG-1, NTRK1-3), or microsatellite instability (p.672).

The classic presentation of cancer arising in the head of the pancreas is 'painless' jaundice; jaundice is visually detectable once bilirubin exceeds ~2 mg/dL and may be accompanied by pruritus from bile salt skin deposition (p.672).

Pain, when present, is typically mid-epigastric and 'boring' with radiation to the back (from retroperitoneal invasion of the splanchnic nerve plexus) and may be worsened by eating or lying flat (p.672).
A palpable, non-tender gallbladder in the setting of biliary obstruction is Courvoisier's sign (p.672).

Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis and combined deep venous plus arterial thromboses (Trousseau's syndrome) can occur; metastatic disease is frequently associated with a hypercoagulable state requiring anticoagulation (p.672-674).

New-onset diabetes (especially with concomitant weight loss) or unexplained worsening of type 2/type 3c diabetes, or rising HbA1c/hyperglycemia in the preceding 1-2 years, may signal underlying pancreatic cancer (p.671-672).

CA19-9 is best drawn after the bilirubin has normalized because biliary obstruction itself elevates CA19-9; CA125 can help in the 8-15% of Lewis-antigen non-secretors who have undetectable CA19-9 (p.674).
Cigarette smoking is the greatest environmental risk factor, accounting for an estimated 25-30% of cases, with risk persisting at least 10 years after cessation (p.671).

Histologic/cytologic tissue diagnosis is essential and also enables molecular testing (next-generation sequencing for KRAS and other alterations) and microsatellite status determination, which increasingly guide therapy (p.674).
Signs of late-stage disease include a left supraclavicular Virchow's node and a periumbilical Sister Mary Joseph's nodule indicating peritoneal metastases (p.672-673).
Drawing CA19-9 while bilirubin is elevated falsely raises the level, since biliary obstruction itself elevates CA19-9 (p.674).
8-15% of patients are Lewis-antigen non-secretors with undetectable CA19-9, so a normal CA19-9 does not exclude disease; CA125 may help in this group (p.674).
Even high-grade PanIN precursor lesions are not detectable by current imaging, limiting early detection (p.672).
For average-risk individuals with no predisposing factors there is currently no recommended screening (p.671).
Whether diabetes causes or is caused by pancreatic cancer is not clearly established (p.671).
Fine-needle aspiration cytology is acceptable but less preferred than core (Tru-Cut) biopsy, which yields adequate tissue for molecular testing (p.674).
Biliary stenting is not necessarily warranted if upfront surgery is planned, but is required (where medically indicated) before neoadjuvant systemic therapy (p.674).

Pancreatic cancer is the most lethal human cancer, with an overall 5-year survival of about 13% (up from 3% in 1975). SEER estimates 5-year survival of ~44% for localized disease, ~16% for regional disease, and ~3.2% for metastatic disease. Late presentation is common, only about 10-20% of tumors are resectable, and the disease is the third leading cause of cancer mortality in the U.S. and projected to become the second by 2030 (p.671-672).

Acute pancreatitis is thought to begin with autodigestion: intracellular premature activation of trypsin (via lysosomal cathepsin B colocalising with digestive zymogens) within acinar cells, which then activates other proteolytic and lipolytic enzymes (chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, phospholipase A2). A second phase recruits and sequesters leukocytes/macrophages, amplifying intrapancreatic inflammation, and a third phase results from activated enzymes and cytokines acting on distant organs, producing edema, hemorrhage, vascular damage, fat necrosis and coagulation/cellular necrosis. Release of bradykinin, vasoactive substances and histamine drives vasodilation, increased vascular permeability and edema, and can culminate in SIRS, ARDS and multiorgan failure. Pathologically the spectrum runs from interstitial (perfusion preserved, self-limited) to necrotizing pancreatitis (perfusion interrupted). Genetic susceptibility/modifier variants include PRSS1 (cationic trypsinogen), SPINK1, CFTR, CTRC, CASR and CLDN2, all converging on control of intrapancreatic trypsin activity (Harrison 22e p.2744-2745).
Diagnosis requires 2 of 3: typical epigastric pain radiating to the back, serum lipase/amylase >=3x ULN, or characteristic findings on cross-sectional imaging (Harrison 22e p.2745).

Lipase is more pancreas-specific than amylase and is the single best enzyme to measure; it stays elevated longer (7-14 days) whereas amylase often normalises by 3-7 days (Harrison 22e p.2740, p.2745).
Gallstones and alcohol together account for ~80-90% of cases; gallstones are the single most common cause (30-60%), alcohol the second (15-30%) (Harrison 22e p.2744).
ALT >3x ULN strongly points to a gallstone aetiology in acute pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2745).

Abdominal ultrasound is the recommended initial imaging study, chiefly to assess for gallstones and bile-duct dilation; contrast CT is best deferred to ~3-5 days if the patient is not improving and is usually not needed in the first 48-72 h (Harrison 22e p.2745-2746).
Persistent organ failure (>48 h) is the most important determinant of severity; if SIRS has resolved by 24 h, organ failure or necrosis is unlikely to develop (Harrison 22e p.2746, p.2748).
Hemoconcentration (hematocrit >44%) and a rising BUN are early warning signs of more severe disease and higher mortality (Harrison 22e p.2745-2748).
Cullen's sign (periumbilical bruising) and Grey Turner's sign (flank discoloration) are rare but signal severe necrotizing/hemorrhagic disease (Harrison 22e p.2745).
Enzyme magnitude does NOT track severity - degree or serial trend of lipase/amylase does not correlate with how severe the pancreatitis is (Harrison 22e p.2745).
Serum amylase can be falsely normal or low in hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis, masking the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2739, p.2745).

Amylase is non-specific - raised in salivary, tubo-ovarian, pulmonary, malignant and other conditions, and spuriously high in acidemia/DKA (arterial pH <=7.32) without true pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2740, p.2745).

Lipase can be mildly elevated in renal failure, and >3x ULN can occur in hepatobiliary/GI malignancy, sepsis, cirrhosis, SLE, head injury, chronic alcoholism, diabetes and post-ERCP without pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2740).
Routine/early CT (within 72 h) is overused and usually unnecessary, especially in mild disease; necrosis may not be visible until several days in (Harrison 22e p.2746-2747).
Prophylactic antibiotics are NOT recommended, even in severe or necrotizing pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2746, p.2749).
Enzyme levels may be normal if blood is drawn 2-5 days after onset or if the underlying problem is chronic rather than acute pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2740).

Overall mortality is low (~1%) and median hospital stay ~4 days; most cases are mild and self-limited within 3-7 days. Interstitial pancreatitis (90-95% of admissions) carries low mortality, whereas necrotizing pancreatitis (5-10%) drives most deaths. In necrotizing disease the median prevalence of organ failure exceeds 50% (slightly higher with infected vs sterile necrosis); mortality is 3-10% with single-organ failure but approaches 50% with multiorgan failure. Patients with only extrapancreatic necrosis fare better than those with pancreatic parenchymal necrosis. About 25% of patients have a recurrence, most commonly from alcohol or gallstones (Harrison 22e p.2747, p.2749).

Revised Atlanta classification (Banks et al., Gut 2013). PHASES: early (<2 weeks; severity judged clinically, not by morphology) and late (>2 weeks; imaging for local complications). SEVERITY: (1) Mild - no local complications and no organ failure (most interstitial cases; self-limited 3-7 days); (2) Moderately severe - transient organ failure (resolves <48 h) and/or local or systemic complications without persistent organ failure; (3) Severe - persistent organ failure >48 h in >=1 organ system (respiratory, cardiovascular, renal; defined by modified Marshall score >=2). MORPHOLOGY: two types - interstitial (parenchymal enhancement, no necrosis) vs necrotizing (lack of parenchymal enhancement and/or peripancreatic necrosis); local collections - acute pancreatic fluid collection and pseudocyst (interstitial, pseudocyst usually >4 wk) vs acute necrotic collection (ANC) and walled-off necrosis (WON, usually >4 wk, encapsulated). SEVERITY SCORES/MARKERS: BISAP >=3 (BUN >25 mg/dL, Impaired mental status/GCS<15, SIRS >=2/4, Age >60, Pleural effusion); APACHE II >=8 at 24 h; SIRS >=2 of 4 (temp <36 or >38C, HR >90, RR >20 or PCO2 <32, WCC >12,000 or <4000 or >10% bands); hematocrit >44%; admission BUN >20 mg/dL; persistent organ failure >=48 h, and pancreatic/extrapancreatic necrosis as in-hospital markers. Ranson criteria are a traditional severity index (referenced contextually).

chunks.text: Panic disorder is thought to arise from dysregulation of fear-processing circuits, particularly hypersensitivity of the amygdala and brainstem structures involved in the alarm and respiratory response, with contributions from serotonergic, noradrenergic, and GABAergic dysfunction. chunks.text: Papilloedema is passive swelling of the optic nerve head produced by raised intracranial pressure transmitted along the subarachnoid space surrounding the optic nerve. The elevated pressure impedes axoplasmic flow within the retinal ganglion cell axons at the optic disc, causing them to become distended, along with venous congestion and leakage that produce the characteristic disc appearance. Because the mechanism is mechanical rather than primarily ischaemic or inflammatory, central acuity is often spared until late. Persistently raised pressure eventually causes axonal loss and secondary optic atrophy.

Eosinophilia with pulmonary infiltrates resembling infectious or hypersensitivity pneumonitis
Serum calcium with PTH (suppressed in HHM) and PTHrP level; 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D in suspected lymphoma
Serum sodium and osmolality with paired urine osmolality and urine sodium for SIADH

Plasma ACTH, urine-free cortisol, high-dose (8 mg) dexamethasone suppression test, and inferior petrosal sinus sampling with CRH stimulation (>3:1 central:peripheral ACTH ratio suggests pituitary source)
Serum glucose with insulin, IGF-II, and IGF-II/IGF-I ratio (>10:1 suggestive) for tumor hypoglycemia
Serum phosphorus, FGF23, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D for oncogenic osteomalacia; octreotide scan to localize tumor
Hematocrit, red cell mass, and serum erythropoietin for erythrocytosis
Compression ultrasonography/impedance plethysmography (venography if equivocal) for DVT; ventilation-perfusion scan, chest radiograph, ECG, and ABG for suspected pulmonary embolism

Insulinoma or factitious hypoglycemia (vs IGF-II tumor hypoglycemia)

Neoplastic cells, particularly those of neuroendocrine origin (SCLC, carcinoids), secrete peptide hormones, cytokines, and growth factors or induce antibody production, altering endocrine, hematologic, and other systems independently of tumor bulk. Most ectopic hormone production reflects cellular dedifferentiation with derepression of developmental gene programs (epigenetic changes, altered microRNA expression); genetic rearrangements bringing a hormone gene under aberrant regulatory control are a rare alternative mechanism. HHM arises chiefly from tumor PTHrP, which binds the PTH receptor to mimic hyperparathyroidism (driven by PTHLH hypomethylation, hedgehog/Gli, TGF-beta, Ras activation, p53 loss); lymphomas may instead convert 25-OH vitamin D to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. SIADH results from ectopic vasopressin (often with co-expressed oxytocin) causing water retention and dilutional hyponatremia. Ectopic ACTH comes from unregulated POMC expression, with release of large biologically inactive fragments plus small amounts of active ACTH; very high cortisol overwhelms renal 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type II, allowing cortisol to act at mineralocorticoid receptors and produce severe hypokalemia. IGF-II precursor (from loss of 11p15 imprinting) causes hypoglycemia by acting on insulin/IGF-I receptors and suppressing GH and insulin. FGF23 forms a ternary complex with klotho and renal FGF receptors to reduce phosphate reabsorption and inhibit 1-alpha-hydroxylation. Hematologic syndromes are mediated by ectopic erythropoietin (erythrocytosis); G-CSF, GM-CSF, IL-6 (granulocytosis); IL-6/thrombopoietin (thrombocytosis); IL-5 (eosinophilia); and poorly defined procoagulants/cytokines (hypercoagulability).

Paraneoplastic syndromes are disorders accompanying benign or malignant tumors that are NOT due to direct mass effect, invasion, or metastasis; neuroendocrine tumors such as small-cell lung carcinoma (SCLC) and carcinoids are especially common sources, and these syndromes are more common than generally appreciated (Harrison 22e p.736).

Non-islet-cell tumor hypoglycemia is driven by IGF-II precursor; serum IGF-II may not be markedly elevated, but an IGF-II/IGF-I ratio greater than 10:1 is suggestive, and the responsible tumor is usually large (>10 cm) and clinically apparent (Harrison 22e p.739-740).

Oncogenic (tumor-induced) osteomalacia from FGF23 (phosphatonin) presents with low serum phosphorus, renal phosphate wasting, low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, but NORMAL serum calcium and PTH; it is usually caused by benign mesenchymal tumors and reverses with tumor resection (Harrison 22e p.739-741).

Among paraneoplastic hematologic syndromes (erythrocytosis, granulocytosis, thrombocytosis, eosinophilia), red/white/platelet elevations are usually self-limited and asymptomatic; by far the most consequential hematologic abnormality in cancer patients is hypercoagulability (Harrison 22e p.740).

Migratory or recurrent thrombophlebitis can be the initial manifestation of cancer; peripheral venous thrombosis coexisting with visceral carcinoma, especially pancreatic cancer, is termed Trousseau's syndrome (Harrison 22e p.741).

Hormones may be eutopic (from normal tissue of origin) or ectopic (atypical source); ectopic expression is often quantitative rather than absolute and is characterized by defective feedback regulation (e.g., ectopic ACTH) and release of large, unprocessed precursor peptides such as POMC (Harrison 22e p.736).

The three most common paraneoplastic endocrine syndromes are hypercalcemia from PTHrP overproduction, hyponatremia from excess vasopressin (SIADH), and Cushing's syndrome from ectopic ACTH (Harrison 22e p.737).

Humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy (HHM) occurs in up to 20% of cancer patients, is most often caused by PTHrP, and favoring features over primary hyperparathyroidism are known malignancy, recent onset, and very high calcium; PTH is suppressed and an elevated PTHrP is raised in roughly 80% of hypercalcemic cancer patients (Harrison 22e p.737-738).

HHM produces hypercalciuria and hypophosphatemia like hyperparathyroidism, but is typically accompanied by metabolic alkalosis rather than the hyperchloremic acidosis of hyperparathyroidism; lymphomas can cause hypercalcemia via 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D rather than PTHrP (Harrison 22e p.737-738).

Ectopic vasopressin causes SIADH in at least half of SCLC patients; hyponatremia with low serum osmolality occurs alongside an inappropriately normal or high urine osmolality, and intake of free water (oral or IV) can rapidly worsen the hyponatremia (Harrison 22e p.738).

Ectopic ACTH accounts for 10-20% of Cushing's syndrome; SCLC is the leading cause, followed by bronchial and thymic carcinoids; plasma ACTH is usually >22 pmol/L (>100 pg/mL) and urine-free cortisol is typically more than 2-4 times normal (Harrison 22e p.738-739).

Ectopic ACTH Cushing's differs from pituitary disease: less weight gain/centripetal fat (brief exposure plus cachexia), but prominent fluid retention, hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, glucose intolerance, and hyperpigmentation from MSH within the POMC precursor (Harrison 22e p.739).

Most ectopic ACTH sources fail to suppress with high-dose dexamethasone (8 mg suppresses ~80% of pituitary adenomas but fails in ~90% of ectopic cases), though bronchial and other carcinoids are notable exceptions that may show pituitary-like feedback (Harrison 22e p.739).
Attributing atypical metabolic or neurologic findings to the malignancy or its treatment and overlooking a paraneoplastic syndrome
Confusing HHM with primary hyperparathyroidism; PTH should be suppressed and acid-base pattern differs (alkalosis in HHM vs hyperchloremic acidosis in hyperparathyroidism)
Rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia, which can precipitate central pontine myelinolysis; correction should be gradual (about 0.5-1 meq/L per hour)

Excluding ectopic ACTH on the basis of high-dose dexamethasone suppression alone, since bronchial/thymic carcinoids can suppress like pituitary adenomas; conversely a suppressed ACTH indicates an ACTH-independent cause
Relying on serum IGF-II levels, which may be normal in tumor hypoglycemia because assays may miss IGF-II precursors (use the IGF-II/IGF-I ratio)
Over-relying on D-dimer in cancer patients, where it is less predictive of DVT and rises with age without thrombosis

Pursuing extensive cancer work-up after a first unprovoked thrombophlebitis or PE in a patient without cancer; targeted evaluation is reserved for refractory, unusual-site, or migratory/recurrent clots

Endocrine paraneoplastic syndromes can cause substantial morbidity and may be the presenting clue to an occult malignancy; treatment of the underlying tumor is the mainstay but rarely alters overall survival or cancer progression. Hematologic cell-count syndromes are generally self-limited and asymptomatic, but thrombocytosis can mark advanced-stage disease and poorer prognosis. Hypercoagulability is the most consequential hematologic complication, and oncogenic osteomalacia and several endocrinopathies can reverse with successful tumor resection; checkpoint-inhibitor-associated endocrinopathies are generally irreversible and require lifelong hormone replacement.
Markedly elevated calcium (>3.5 mmol/L [>14 mg/dL]) with fatigue, altered mentation, polyuria, dehydration, or arrhythmias (short ST/QT, bundle branch block, bradyarrhythmia)
Severe hyponatremia (Na <115 meq/L) or any hyponatremia with confusion, depressed mental status, or seizures
Profound hypokalemia with metabolic alkalosis and hypertension in ectopic ACTH; opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis, mycoses) are a frequent cause of death
Increased venous thromboembolism risk in ectopic ACTH and in cancer generally; migratory/recurrent thrombophlebitis or clot in an unusual site
New atypical clinical or metabolic findings in a known cancer patient should prompt consideration of a paraneoplastic syndrome
Markedly elevated eosinophils (>5000/uL) causing dyspnea, wheezing, and diffuse pulmonary infiltrates

No single formal severity scale; severity is gauged by the magnitude and acuity of the biochemical derangement (e.g., calcium level and rate of rise, sodium level [Na <115 meq/L denotes severe hyponatremia], eosinophil count >5000/uL). For venous thromboembolism risk during chemotherapy, the Khorana risk score (Harrison Table 98-3) stratifies patients using cancer type, therapy, blood counts, and body mass index.

chunks.text: Paraquat undergoes cyclical reduction and oxidation (redox cycling), generating large amounts of superoxide and other reactive oxygen species that deplete NADPH and cause lipid peroxidation and cell death. It is actively taken up and concentrated by alveolar epithelial (type I and II) cells, making the lung the primary target: an early destructive phase of alveolitis and haemorrhagic oedema is followed by an obliterative pulmonary fibrosis. The kidneys and liver, which also accumulate the compound, sustain acute injury, and high oxygen tensions worsen the oxidative damage.

Extracellular calcium is held in a narrow range (~8.5-10.5 mg/dL) by feedback among the parathyroids, kidney, bone, and intestine. A fall in ECF calcium is sensed by the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) on parathyroid chief cells, triggering PTH release; PTH increases bone calcium resorption, distal-tubule reabsorption of filtered calcium, and renal proximal-tubule 1,25(OH)2D production, and 1,25(OH)2D in turn raises intestinal calcium absorption. Hypercalcemia arises from derangements of this loop: PTH-dependent overproduction (pHPT due to adenoma/hyperplasia, rarely carcinoma; tertiary hyperparathyroidism; ectopic PTH; FHH and CaSR-altering states such as lithium), or PTH-independent mechanisms (PTHrP-secreting tumors, lytic skeletal metastases, extrarenal 1,25(OH)2D production in granulomatous disease/lymphoma, vitamin D intoxication, increased bone resorption from thyrotoxicosis/Paget's/immobilization, and calcium overload e.g. milk-alkali). Hypocalcemia results from low PTH (hypoparathyroidism: surgical, autoimmune, infiltrative, genetic, CaSR-activating, or magnesium-related) or high PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism from vitamin D deficiency, renal failure, intestinal malabsorption, or PTH resistance/pseudohypoparathyroidism). Low calcium increases neuromuscular irritability (Harrison 22e p.3271).
Primary hyperparathyroidism (pHPT) and malignancy are the two most common causes of hypercalcemia; the diagnostic split hinges on the PTH level (Harrison 22e p.3271).

Neuromuscular irritability of hypocalcemia is detected by Chvostek's sign (perioral twitch on tapping the facial nerve) and the more specific Trousseau's sign (carpal spasm after inflating a BP cuff above systolic for 3 min); paresthesias of fingers, toes, and circumoral region are typical (Harrison 22e p.3271).

Because PTH is the main minute-by-minute defense against hypocalcemia, hypoparathyroidism can produce profound, life-threatening hypocalcemia, whereas vitamin D deficiency causes less severe hypocalcemia since the parathyroids mount a compensatory PTH rise (at the expense of bone) (Harrison 22e p.3271).
Impaired PTH secretion may be secondary to magnesium deficiency (via intracellular effects); hypomagnesemic hypocalcemia will not correct until magnesium is repleted (Harrison 22e p.3271).
Hungry bone syndrome after parathyroidectomy is a recognized cause of post-operative hypocalcemia with high PTH (Harrison 22e p.3271).

pHPT is almost always a benign neoplastic disorder of the parathyroids (adenoma or hyperplasia) producing PTH that is not appropriately suppressed by the elevated calcium; parathyroid carcinoma is a rare cause (Harrison 22e p.3271).

In hypercalcemia, an elevated or 'inappropriately normal' PTH with elevated calcium and low/low-normal phosphorus is almost always pHPT; because of PTH's phosphaturic action, pHPT hypercalcemia is often accompanied by low/frankly low serum phosphate (Harrison 22e p.3271).

A suppressed PTH in the face of hypercalcemia means the process is independent of the parathyroid glands and is most often malignancy; many solid tumors secrete PTHrP, which mimics PTH at its receptor on bone and kidney (Harrison 22e p.3271).

Hypercalcemia from lymphoma or granulomatous disease (e.g., sarcoidosis, tuberculosis) is driven by extrarenal macrophage CYP27B1 conversion of 25(OH)D to 1,25(OH)2D; in such cases 1,25(OH)2D is increased or inappropriately normal (Harrison 22e p.3271).

Classic chronic hypercalcemia (months to years, fluctuating between high-normal and just above normal) is most often pHPT or FHH, occasionally multiple myeloma; malignancy-associated hypercalcemia usually has a more acute course (Harrison 22e p.3271).

Mild hypercalcemia (10.5-11.9 mg/dL) is largely asymptomatic; symptoms ('stones, bones, groans') include nephrolithiasis, reduced bone density / bone pain or pathologic fractures with long-standing hyperparathyroidism, constipation/nausea/vomiting/anorexia/peptic ulcer/pancreatitis, plus fatigue, proximal weakness, hyporeflexia, and neuropsychiatric changes (Harrison 22e p.3271).

Hypocalcemia is differentiated by whether PTH is low (hypoparathyroidism) or high (secondary hyperparathyroidism); a low or 'inappropriately low' PTH with hypocalcemia establishes hypoparathyroidism, whereas an elevated PTH points to the vitamin D axis or primary small-bowel calcium malabsorption (Harrison 22e p.3271).

In adults, hypoparathyroidism most commonly results from inadvertent damage to all four parathyroid glands during thyroid or parathyroid surgery; autoimmune endocrinopathy accounts for about a quarter of cases (Harrison 22e p.3271).
Failing to correct calcium for albumin before launching a workup - low albumin can mask true hypercalcemia and falsely suggest hypocalcemia (Harrison 22e p.3271).

Mistaking FHH for pHPT: FHH can present with mildly elevated PTH and hypercalcemia, but parathyroid surgery is ineffective; a calcium/creatinine clearance ratio <0.01 and family history of mild asymptomatic hypercalcemia or repeated failed neck surgeries should prompt CASR/GNA11/AP2S1 testing (Harrison 22e p.3271).
Overlooking lithium therapy, which raises the CaSR set point and can cause hyperparathyroidism (Harrison 22e p.3271).
Not repleting magnesium in hypocalcemia: hypomagnesemia impairs PTH secretion and the hypocalcemia will not correct until magnesium is restored (Harrison 22e p.3271).
Chvostek's sign is nonspecific - present in ~10% of normal individuals; Trousseau's sign is the more definitive marker of neuromuscular irritability (Harrison 22e p.3271).

Attributing hypercalcemia of immobilization solely to bed rest - an unrecognized resorptive process (pHPT, Paget's, myeloma) may be the real driver, especially in older patients (Harrison 22e p.3271).
When tetany accompanies alkalosis, a second cause of impaired calcium homeostasis is usually present (Harrison 22e p.3271).
Ectopic PTH secretion, unlike pHPT, does not fluctuate with correction of calcium because it is not under CaSR control (Harrison 22e p.3271).

Mild, asymptomatic hypercalcemia (commonly pHPT detected incidentally in settings with routine calcium screening) carries a benign short-term course, whereas advanced pHPT can cause severe skeletal disease (osteitis fibrosa cystica). Hypoparathyroidism, because PTH is the chief minute-by-minute defense against hypocalcemia, can be profound, debilitating, and life-threatening, while vitamin D-deficiency hypocalcemia is typically milder owing to compensatory PTH secretion (at the expense of bone). Severe hypercalcemia (coma, renal failure, arrhythmia) and severe hypocalcemia (seizures, laryngospasm, Torsade) are medical emergencies (Harrison 22e p.3271).
Moderate-to-severe hypercalcemia (>=12-14 mg/dL) with progressive lethargy, stupor, or coma
Hypercalcemia with acute renal failure and volume depletion from polyuria
Hypercalcemic ECG changes: bradycardia, AV block, QRS widening, short QTc
Severe hypocalcemia causing seizures, carpopedal spasm, bronchospasm, or laryngospasm

Pathologic hallmarks are degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), reduced striatal dopamine, and intraneuronal alpha-synuclein-staining inclusions in cell bodies and axons (Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites; collectively Lewy pathology). Lewy pathology can also affect cholinergic neurons of the nucleus basalis of Meynert, noradrenergic neurons of the locus coeruleus, serotonergic raphe neurons, and the olfactory system, cerebral hemispheres, spinal cord, and peripheral autonomic nervous system, accounting for nonmotor features. Pathology may begin in the peripheral autonomic nervous system, GI tract, olfactory system, or dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus and spread sequentially (Braak staging), giving rise to 'body-first' versus 'brain-first' concepts. In the basal-ganglia network, dopamine denervation leads to increased firing of the subthalamic nucleus (STN) and globus pallidus interna (GPi), excessive inhibition of the thalamus, reduced cortical motor activation, and the emergence of parkinsonian features. Pathogenesis involves an interacting network of oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, protein aggregation, excitotoxicity, and inflammation; a 'double hit' of genetic susceptibility plus an environmental insult has been proposed (p.3493-3494, p.3498-3500).

PD is the second most common age-related neurodegenerative disease after Alzheimer's; mean age of onset ~60 years, lifetime risk ~3% in men and ~2% in women, though cases can occur in the twenties or younger, particularly with a pathogenic gene mutation (p.3493).

Cardinal motor features are bradykinesia, rest tremor, rigidity, and gait dysfunction with postural instability; additional motor features include freezing of gait, micrographia, masked facies (hypomimia), reduced eye blinking, drooling, soft voice (hypophonia), and dysphagia (p.3493-3494).

Parkinsonism (bradykinesia with rigidity and/or tremor) combined with rest tremor, asymmetry of motor impairment, and a good levodopa response is much more likely to predict the correct pathologic diagnosis; with these U.K. Brain Bank Criteria, PD can be confirmed pathologically in >90% of patients (p.3495).
Levodopa is the gold standard symptomatic therapy; almost all PD patients improve, and failure to respond to an adequate trial of levodopa should cause the diagnosis to be questioned (p.3501).

Dopamine-system imaging (PET/SPECT) typically shows reduced, asymmetric striatal uptake, most pronounced in the posterior putamen with relative sparing of the caudate; it is useful when the diagnosis is uncertain but is not routinely required (p.3495-3496).
Among forms of parkinsonism, PD is the most common (~75% of cases) (p.3495).
Diagnosing PD on two of three cardinal features alone carries a ~24% postmortem error rate; rest tremor, motor asymmetry, and a good levodopa response markedly improve diagnostic accuracy (p.3495).

Drug-induced parkinsonism is the most common secondary parkinsonism and is easily missed - remember that metoclopramide, used for GI symptoms, is a neuroleptic, and that calcium channel blockers (flunarizine, cinnarizine), tetrabenazine, amiodarone, and lithium can also be responsible (p.3497).
Wilson's disease must be actively excluded because progression can be prevented with copper chelators (p.3497).
Dopamine-system imaging cannot separate PD from atypical parkinsonism, since striatal dopamine depletion occurs in both (p.3496).
Some genetic forms of PD (e.g., certain LRRK2 cases) may occur without Lewy bodies, and MPTP toxicity causes parkinsonism typically without Lewy bodies (p.3496, p.3498).

PD is progressive. Levodopa prolongs independence and employability, improves quality of life, and increases life span, but chronic treatment with ongoing disease progression is associated in most patients with motor complications - response fluctuations ('on'/'off', wearing-off, on-off phenomenon) and dyskinesias. As the disease advances, nondopaminergic features that respond poorly to levodopa emerge - falling, freezing, autonomic dysfunction, sleep disorders, and dementia - and these (especially falls and dementia) are the primary source of disability and the main reason for hospitalization and nursing home placement in advanced PD. Atypical parkinsonisms generally follow a more aggressive course than classic PD (p.3496-3497, p.3501).

Harrison does not present a single formal severity grading; clinical diagnostic confidence is staged by the MDS Clinical Diagnostic Criteria into 'clinically established PD' and 'clinically probable PD', which combine core motor parkinsonism with supportive criteria, absolute exclusion criteria, and red flags. Disease evolution is commonly framed by the emergence of levodopa-related motor complications and levodopa-unresponsive nondopaminergic features in advanced PD (p.3495-3496, p.3501).

PSVTs in this group are AV node-dependent. AVNRT is a reentrant circuit within the compact AV node and perinodal atrium enabled by dual pathways: a slowly conducting pathway (usually the right inferior nodal extension running toward the coronary sinus floor) and a faster pathway near the His bundle, allowing a self-sustaining loop. Accessory pathways are congenital muscular connections that bridge atrium and ventricle across the fibrous AV rings owing to incomplete partitioning during development; they most often lie at the left free wall, followed by posteroseptal, right free wall, and anteroseptal sites. Antegrade conduction over an AP produces ventricular preexcitation (short PR, delta wave, wide QRS), with QRS/delta morphology determined by pathway location. AVRT reentry circulates between the AV node/His-Purkinje system and the AP (orthodromic when antegrade over the node and retrograde over the AP, antidromic when reversed). Junctional ectopic tachycardia is due to abnormal automaticity within the AV node rather than reentry (Harrison 22e pp.1938-1942).

PSVT here refers to sustained supraventricular tachycardias that depend on the AV node: AVNRT, junctional tachycardia, AV reciprocating tachycardia (AVRT) using an accessory pathway, and preexcited tachycardias (Harrison 22e p.1938).
Concealed accessory pathways conduct only retrograde (ventricle to atrium), so no preexcitation is seen in sinus rhythm, yet SVT can still occur (Harrison 22e pp.1940-1941).

Antidromic AVRT and bystander AP conduction produce preexcited (wide-complex) tachycardias that can be indistinguishable from monomorphic VT; the presence of preexcitation in sinus rhythm suggests the diagnosis (Harrison 22e pp.1941-1942).

Junctional ectopic tachycardia arises from automaticity within the AV node, is rare in adults, and is more often seen as an incessant tachycardia in children, especially perioperatively after congenital heart surgery (Harrison 22e p.1940).

AVNRT is the most common form of PSVT, accounting for roughly 60% of cases referred for catheter ablation, typically presenting in the second to fourth decades and more often in women (Harrison 22e p.1939).

AVNRT mechanism is reentry within the AV node and perinodal atrium, made possible by dual conduction pathways; the typical form uses a slowly conducting pathway (right inferior nodal extension) for the antegrade limb and the fast pathway as the exit (Harrison 22e p.1939).

In typical AVNRT atrial and ventricular activation are near-simultaneous, so the P wave falls during, just before, or just after the QRS and is hard to see — often appearing as a pseudo-r' in V1 and pseudo-S waves in leads II, III, and aVF (Harrison 22e p.1939).

Simultaneous atrial and ventricular contraction drives atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve, producing cannon A waves and a fluttering neck sensation; elevated venous pressure can release natriuretic peptides causing post-tachycardia diuresis (Harrison 22e p.1939).
Unlike atrial tachycardias, maneuvers or drugs that block the AV node terminate AVNRT and orthodromic AVRT, because the AV node is part of the reentry circuit (Harrison 22e p.1939).

Accessory pathways occur in about 1 in 1500-2000 people; most patients have structurally normal hearts, but APs are associated with Ebstein's anomaly and certain hypertrophic cardiomyopathies including PRKAG2 mutations, Danon's disease, and Fabry's disease (Harrison 22e p.1940).
Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome is defined as ventricular preexcitation during sinus rhythm (short PR <0.12 s, delta wave, widened QRS) plus episodes of PSVT (Harrison 22e p.1940).

Orthodromic AVRT is the most common AP-mediated PSVT: the wavefront goes antegrade down the AV node/His-Purkinje and returns retrograde up the AP, giving a narrow (or aberrant) QRS with the P wave always following the QRS, never simultaneous with it (Harrison 22e p.1941).

Administering AV nodal-blocking agents (verapamil, diltiazem, beta blockers, adenosine, amiodarone) during preexcited AF is contraindicated, as slowing the AV node without slowing the AP can accelerate ventricular rate and precipitate ventricular fibrillation (Harrison 22e p.1942).

Gradual loss of AP conduction with rising sympathetic tone on exercise testing does not reliably indicate a low-risk pathway, because it can simply reflect shortening AV nodal conduction time (Harrison 22e p.1942).
Adenosine itself can precipitate atrial fibrillation in up to ~15% of patients, which is hazardous in WPW where AF may cause hemodynamic instability (Harrison 22e p.1942).
Adenosine is contraindicated after cardiac transplantation due to denervation hypersensitivity and may aggravate bronchospasm (Harrison 22e p.1942).
Negative delta waves from left-sided or diaphragmatic/paraseptal APs can mimic Q waves of lateral or inferior myocardial infarction (Harrison 22e p.1940).
Left free wall APs may show minimal or absent preexcitation on the 12-lead ECG because of the distance from the sinus node, so preexcitation can be missed (Harrison 22e p.1940).
PJRT and atypical AVNRT both produce long R-P tachycardias that can be difficult to distinguish from atrial tachycardia without an invasive EP study (Harrison 22e p.1941).

In patients without structural heart disease, AVNRT is not life-threatening though it may cause significant symptoms. Catheter ablation of the slow AV nodal pathway is curative in over 95% of cases, with a risk of AV block requiring permanent pacing in under 1%. For accessory pathways, ablation efficacy is around 95% (varies by location) with serious complications in under 3% and procedural mortality under 1 in 1000. Risk of cardiac arrest in symptomatic preexcitation patients is roughly 2 per 1000 adults and likely higher in children. Adults with asymptomatic preexcitation have an estimated sudden death risk of about 1 per 1000 patient-years, while children carry a higher risk of around 2 per 1000 patient-years (Harrison 22e pp.1939-1942).

B19V is a small nonenveloped single-stranded DNA virus (genus Erythroparvovirus) that replicates in erythroid progenitor cells. Cell entry depends on the unknown primary receptor recognized by VP1u and, at a later step, the blood group P antigen (globoside); people lacking P antigen are naturally resistant. Infection produces high-titer viremia (up to ~10^12-10^14 particles/mL at the peak) and virus-induced cytotoxicity that halts red cell production. In immunocompetent hosts with normal hematopoiesis the arrest of erythropoiesis is transient with only a minimal fall in hemoglobin, resolving as neutralizing antibody is produced. In hosts with increased erythropoiesis (e.g., hemolytic anemia) the same arrest precipitates a transient aplastic crisis; in those who fail to mount neutralizing antibody (immunocompromised hosts or the fetus) lytic infection persists and chronic anemia/PRCA develops. The classic rash and arthropathy of erythema infectiosum are immune-mediated, beginning 2-3 weeks after infection as the IgM response peaks. B19V can also enter nonpermissive cells (B cells, monocytes, endothelial cells) by antibody-dependent enhancement and persist as DNA for life in many tissues (heart, liver, kidney, synovium, brain, bone), generally without disease.
Parvovirus B19 (B19V) has a narrow tropism for erythroid progenitor cells in the bone marrow, which underlies most of its clinical effects on red cell production.
Detection of B19V DNA in tissue by PCR alone does not establish causation, since viral DNA can persist in healthy tissues for decades; quantitative PCR and serologic correlation are needed.
Human bocavirus 1 (HBoV1) is a separate human parvovirus causing upper and lower respiratory tract infection in young children (peak ~2 years) and infecting nearly all children before age 5.
An immune-mediated rash can appear in chronically infected immunocompromised patients after immunoglobulin administration, due to antigen-antibody complexes in skin.

Most B19V infections are asymptomatic or cause only a mild nonspecific illness; the characteristic disease, erythema infectiosum (fifth disease, slapped-cheek disease), occurs mainly in children 3-12 years old.
Transmission is primarily respiratory and occurs before the onset of rash or arthralgia; once the rash appears the child is no longer infectious and can return to school.
In adults the classic slapped-cheek appearance is usually absent; instead they often present with arthralgia, with or without a macular rash.

Arthropathy occurs in roughly 50% of infected adults, is more common in women, tends to be symmetrical and involves small joints of the hands (sometimes ankles, knees, wrists), and can mimic rheumatoid arthritis with detectable rheumatoid factor.

In patients dependent on rapid red cell turnover (hemolytic disorders, hemoglobinopathies, red cell enzymopathies, autoimmune hemolytic anemia), B19V is the predominant cause of transient aplastic crisis (TAC).

Bone marrow in TAC and pure red cell aplasia shows characteristic giant pronormoblasts with absent or scarce erythroid precursors; in a sickle-cell patient, reticulocytopenia with acute worsening anemia is diagnostic without marrow examination.

Chronic B19V infection causing pure red cell aplasia (PRCA)/persistent anemia is a treatable cause of anemia in immunocompromised hosts and is important to recognize because effective immunoglobulin therapy exists.
Individuals genetically lacking the blood group P antigen (globoside) are naturally resistant to B19V infection because that antigen is a required receptor.
Interpreting tissue B19V DNA detected by PCR as proof of active disease - viral DNA persists in healthy tissues for decades, so PCR alone in tissue should not establish a B19V etiology.
Presence of B19V DNA in synovium does not prove a causal role in arthritis, since healthy individuals also harbor viral DNA in synovia.
In TAC and chronic infection, classic immune-mediated symptoms (rash, arthralgia) are often absent, making the diagnosis easy to miss in immunocompromised or hemolytic patients.
Relying on qualitative PCR for HBoV1 in respiratory secretions can misattribute etiology, since HBoV1 DNA may persist for weeks to months after acute infection.
Serology may be negative or only weakly positive in immunodeficient patients with PRCA, so quantitative serum DNA is needed.

Most B19V infections are self-limited. Erythema infectiosum and B19V-associated arthropathy generally resolve spontaneously, though joint symptoms may recur for weeks to months. Transient aplastic crisis is, by definition, transient: anemia resolves once cytopathic infection of erythroid progenitors ceases, and lifelong immunity follows. Chronic anemia/PRCA in immunocompromised hosts is treatable and can be cured or ameliorated with immunoglobulin. Risk of fetal loss is highest (excess risk roughly 9%) when maternal infection occurs before gestational week 20 and is very low thereafter; most fetal infections resolve spontaneously, B19V does not appear to be teratogenic, and rare reports of eye damage, CNS abnormalities, and congenital anemia exist.

The ductus arteriosus normally constricts and closes after birth in response to rising oxygen tension and falling circulating prostaglandins. When it remains patent, the postnatal fall in pulmonary vascular resistance establishes a left-to-right shunt from the aorta to the pulmonary artery throughout the cardiac cycle. This increases pulmonary blood flow and volume-loads the left atrium and left ventricle, while diastolic runoff from the aorta lowers diastolic pressure and can compromise systemic and coronary perfusion. A large chronic shunt raises pulmonary pressures and can lead to pulmonary vascular remodelling and shunt reversal over time.
Persistence of the fetal ductus arteriosus beyond the normal postnatal closure period allows shunting between the aorta and pulmonary artery; it is especially common in preterm infants.
Because aortic pressure exceeds pulmonary pressure once pulmonary resistance falls, the shunt is left-to-right, increasing pulmonary blood flow and left heart volume load.
The classic sign is a continuous machinery murmur beneath the left clavicle, though in neonates only a systolic component may be audible.
A large shunt produces bounding peripheral pulses and a wide pulse pressure from diastolic runoff into the pulmonary circulation.

In preterm infants a significant ductus can worsen respiratory distress, contribute to heart failure, and is associated with complications such as necrotising enterocolitis and intraventricular haemorrhage.
In some duct-dependent congenital heart lesions the ductus is essential for survival, and a prostaglandin infusion is used to keep it open until definitive intervention.
Closure of an isolated symptomatic ductus may use pharmacological prostaglandin inhibitors in preterm infants or transcatheter/surgical closure in others.
Echocardiography confirms the ductus, estimates shunt size, and assesses left heart dilation and pulmonary pressures.
A large, longstanding, unrepaired ductus risks pulmonary vascular disease and eventual shunt reversal.

This foundational chapter frames nervous-system disease around several converging mechanisms rather than a single illness. (1) Neuroimmunology/neuroinflammation: microglia and brain macrophages (yolk-sac-derived innate immune cells) and astrocytes are active, non-passive participants that prune synapses through complement, present antigen, secrete cytokines and trophic factors, and can shift between homeostatic and tissue-damaging states; crosstalk among microglia, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes produces non-cell-autonomous pathology in MS, AD, PD, and ALS. (2) Myelin biology: oligodendrocytes maintain saltatory conduction and provide metabolic/neuroprotective support to axons, with activity-dependent (adaptive) myelination. (3) Waste clearance: the glymphatic system and meningeal lymphatic-like vessels clear interstitial solutes and aggregated proteins, with sleep-dependent and age-dependent modulation via aquaporin-4. (4) The microbiome can influence brain disease through molecular mimicry, immune modulation, circulating bacterial metabolites, enteric neural signaling, and possible prion-like seeding (e.g., the unproven hypothesis that E. coli Curli templates alpha-synuclein). (5) Protein aggregation and prion biology: misfolded, self-propagating proteins (Abeta, tau, alpha-synuclein, PrP, SOD1, TDP-43, expanded-polyglutamine huntingtin) spread trans-synaptically; toxic oligomers, defective ubiquitin-proteasome and autophagy-lysosome clearance, mitochondrial dynamics (fission/fusion via Drp1, MFN1/2, OPA1; mitophagy via PINK1/parkin), and retromer (VPS35/VPS26/VPS29) dysfunction all contribute to neuronal death. (6) Stem cell biology: iPSCs and cerebral organoids reproduce early human brain-development disorders and enable disease modeling and drug screening.

Microglia, the brain's resident innate immune and antigen-presenting cells, arise from primitive yolk-sac macrophages that seed the CNS before the blood-brain barrier forms and are sustained largely by self-renewal rather than by replenishment from the circulation; under some conditions peripherally derived macrophages can become microglia-like and replace damaged cells.

Toxic small oligomers, rather than the mature plaques, tangles, and inclusion bodies, are increasingly viewed as the harmful species; visible aggregates may represent a relatively protective sequestration of toxic protein.

Impaired autophagy and lysosomal handling are central to neurodegeneration; GBA (glucocerebrosidase) mutations underlie about 5% of Parkinson's disease and 8-9% of dementia with Lewy bodies, with bidirectional inhibition between alpha-synuclein and glucocerebrosidase.

Induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons and 3D cerebral organoids model human neurodevelopmental disease (microcephaly, lissencephaly/Miller-Dieker, fragile X, Rett, Timothy syndrome) and confirmed Zika virus tropism for human neural progenitor (radial glia) cells as the cause of congenital microcephaly.

Microglia sculpt and prune synapses via classical complement proteins (C1q, C3) and complement receptors; in Alzheimer's disease, excess beta-amyloid drives C1q/C3 tagging of synapses that are then eliminated by CR3-expressing microglia, and knockout of C1q or C3 can rescue some neurodegenerative pathology in models.

Genetic data link innate immunity to neurodegeneration: more than half of genes implicated in Alzheimer's GWAS involve innate immune/microglial processes, and loss-of-function mutations in the microglial receptor TREM2 increase Alzheimer's risk up to roughly fourfold.

Around 10% of frontotemporal degeneration cases are due to heterozygous granulin (GRN) mutations causing progranulin haploinsufficiency; progranulin is a neurotrophic factor essential for lysosomal function and microglial homeostasis.

Activated microglia (via IL-1alpha, TNF, and C1q) can convert astrocytes to a reactive, neurotoxic (A1) phenotype that loses phagocytic capacity and damages neurons and oligodendrocytes through complement, nitric oxide, and free radicals; astrocytes are non-cell-autonomous contributors across MS, AD, PD, and ALS.

The glymphatic system uses periarterial CSF inflow through aquaporin-4-rich astrocyte foot processes to clear interstitial solutes and debris; clearance accelerates during sleep, and in models sleep deprivation increased beta-amyloid plaque accumulation while aquaporin-4 knockout reduced interstitial flow.

Harrison proposes a prion-based reclassification of neurodegenerative disease in which host proteins (PrP, Abeta, tau, alpha-synuclein, SOD1, possibly huntingtin) adopt self-propagating, beta-sheet-rich conformations that template normal precursor protein and spread between synaptically connected neurons.

The prion concept holds that the transmissible agents of kuru, CJD, scrapie, and BSE are devoid of nucleic acid and composed of host-encoded protein; AD is framed as a 'double-prion' disease in which both Abeta and tau prions coexist.

Late onset of inherited neurodegenerations, despite lifelong expression of the mutant protein, is attributed to age-dependent decline in protein quality-control/clearance mechanisms, consistent with the view that these are disorders of the aging nervous system.
Assuming that macroscopic aggregates (plaques, tangles, inclusion bodies) directly cause neuronal dysfunction; toxic soluble oligomers may be the harmful species and sequestration may be protective.
Viewing microglia and astrocytes as merely secondary scavengers; genetic evidence places them as primary drivers of many neurodegenerative conditions.
Treating the resting-versus-activated microglial dichotomy as adequate; single-cell data reveal extensive, functionally heterogeneous states.

Over-extrapolating from rodent models; several human organoid findings (e.g., outer radial glia defects in Miller-Dieker syndrome) were not seen in mice, and some iPSC findings require replication before confidence.
Accepting unproven microbiome-seeding hypotheses (e.g., bacterial Curli triggering Parkinson's) as established; no proven microbiome-modulating therapy yet exists for any brain disease.
Therapeutic targeting of broadly acting systems (e.g., complement) risks off-target toxicity and loss of homeostatic functions such as physiologic synaptic pruning.

As a mechanistic overview the chapter does not give a single prognosis. It frames many neurodegenerative diseases as relentlessly progressive disorders of the aging nervous system driven by self-propagating prion-like proteins, while emphasizing that emerging understanding of complement, microglial, lysosomal/autophagy, mitochondrial, and prion-clearance pathways offers new and rational therapeutic targets (e.g., anti-C1q and anti-TREM2 antibody trials, progranulin-directed and gene/protein-replacement strategies) and new hope for prevention, treatment, and repair.
Progressive, age-related cognitive or motor decline suggesting an underlying self-propagating proteinopathy
Family history with high penetrance (e.g., GRN mutations highly penetrant for FTD) prompting genetic evaluation
Rapidly progressive dementia raising concern for a transmissible prion disease
Microcephaly with developmental delay and intractable epilepsy in neurodevelopmental disorders

chunks.text: Sarcoidosis and other granulomatous conditions in patients predisposed to cryptococcosis (Harrison 22e p.1688)

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: Fungi are eukaryotes classified morphologically as yeasts (round/budding single cells), molds (filamentous hyphae at both room temperature and in tissue, e.g., Aspergillus, Mucorales, dermatophytes), and dimorphic fungi (yeast or spherical structures in tissue but filamentous forms in the environment). Candida produces both yeast and pseudohyphal forms in tissue except C. glabrata and C. auris, which form only yeasts; Cryptococcus exists only as yeast. Deep-organ infection by molds and endemic dimorphic fungi follows inhalation, whereas commensal Candida invades from mucocutaneous colonization in the gut or skin. Antifungal immunity centers on the C-type lectin receptor/SYK/CARD9 signaling pathway, which recognizes fungal polysaccharides and drives proinflammatory mediator release, leukocyte recruitment, inflammasome activation, and Th17 differentiation. Protection is site- and pathogen-specific: at mucosa, IL-17A/IL-17F and IL-22 from Th17, Tc17, gamma-delta T, and innate lymphoid cells stimulate epithelial antimicrobial peptide production and barrier repair (STAT3-dependent); against invasive molds and Candida, recruited neutrophils assemble the six-subunit NADPH oxidase to generate superoxide for fungal killing; against intramacrophagic fungi, IL-12-producing macrophages activate STAT4 in T cells to release IFN-gamma, which signals through STAT1 (with TNF-alpha and GM-CSF) to enable intracellular killing. Defects at any node, whether inherited (e.g., IL17F/IL17RA/IL17RC/TRAF3IP2, STAT3, STAT1, CARD9, NADPH oxidase subunits, IL12RB1, IFNGR1/2, IRF8, GATA2) or pharmacologic/acquired (IL-17/IL-23 biologics, BTK inhibitors, glucocorticoids, anti-TNF agents, JAK inhibitors, anti-IFN-gamma or anti-GM-CSF autoantibodies), produce predictable, compartment-specific fungal susceptibility (Harrison 22e pp.1687-1689).

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: Human fungal disease has risen sharply with the AIDS pandemic, broad antibacterial use, cytotoxic chemotherapy, biologic/precision-medicine immunosuppressants, and solid-organ or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (Harrison 22e p.1687).

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: AIDS predisposes to mucosal but not invasive candidiasis (reflecting IL-17 dependence), whereas vaginal candidiasis arises with antibiotic use rather than AIDS or IL-17-targeted biologics, highlighting the protective role of the vaginal microbiota (Harrison 22e p.1689).

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: Chronic granulomatous disease, caused by NADPH-oxidase subunit mutations impairing neutrophil superoxide generation, carries roughly a 40% lifetime risk of invasive aspergillosis; Aspergillus nidulans is seen almost exclusively in this condition (Harrison 22e pp.1688-1689).

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: Early initiation of appropriate antifungal therapy is a key determinant of outcome in candidemia, aspergillosis, and mucormycosis, alongside source control (catheter removal in candidemia, abscess drainage, surgical debridement in mucormycosis) and immune reconstitution (Harrison 22e p.1691).

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: Mycoses are categorized clinically as mucocutaneous versus deep-organ disease, and epidemiologically as endemic versus opportunistic; mucocutaneous disease causes morbidity but is rarely fatal, whereas deep-organ disease is often severe with high mortality (Harrison 22e p.1687).

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: Endemic fungi are environmentally acquired and not part of normal flora, typically causing self-limited disease in immunocompetent hosts but severe illness when immunity is impaired; opportunistic fungi such as Candida and Aspergillus are commensal or ubiquitous and invade when host defenses fail (Harrison 22e p.1687).

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: Definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic demonstration of the fungus invading tissue together with culture from the specimen; a positive culture from blood or tissue can instead reflect colonization or laboratory contamination depending on organism and site (Harrison 22e p.1690).

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: PAS and Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) are the principal fungal stains; Candida (unlike most fungi) is visible on Gram-stained tissue, and a positive India ink stain of CSF is diagnostic for cryptococcosis (Harrison 22e p.1690).

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: The most reliable antigen/serologic tests are Coccidioides antibody, Histoplasma antigen, and cryptococcal polysaccharide antigen; galactomannan (best in BAL fluid) aids aspergillosis diagnosis but has frequent false negatives during antifungal prophylaxis and false positives with other fungi (Harrison 22e p.1691).

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: The serum beta-D-glucan assay has a high negative predictive value for invasive candidiasis but lacks specificity, and T2 magnetic resonance is FDA-approved for detecting Candida in blood (Harrison 22e p.1691).

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: Inherited CARD9 deficiency is the only known primary immunodeficiency that produces fungus-specific susceptibility without predisposition to other infections, autoimmunity, allergy, or cancer, causing chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, CNS Candida/Aspergillus/phaeohyphomycete infection, and deep dermatophytosis (Harrison 22e p.1688).

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: Antifungal host defense is compartmentalized: IL-17-producing lymphoid cells protect mucosal surfaces against Candida invasion, neutrophils control invasive Aspergillus and Candida, and the IL-12/IFN-gamma axis with activated macrophages controls intramacrophagic fungi such as Cryptococcus, Pneumocystis, and endemic dimorphic fungi (Harrison 22e pp.1688-1689).

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: Treating a positive fungal culture as proof of infection when it may represent colonization or contamination, depending on organism and anatomic site (Harrison 22e p.1690)

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: Relying on galactomannan for aspergillosis without accounting for frequent false negatives under antifungal prophylaxis and false positives from other fungi (Harrison 22e p.1691)

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: Interpreting a beta-D-glucan result without recognizing its lack of specificity despite a high negative predictive value (Harrison 22e p.1691)

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: Attempting to identify fungi reliably on H&E alone, which defines tissue reaction but is insufficient for speciation (Harrison 22e p.1690)

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: Overlooking that fluconazole and echinocandins lack activity against molds (and echinocandins against Cryptococcus and endemic dimorphic fungi), and that voriconazole/echinocandins do not cover Mucorales (Harrison 22e pp.1691-1692)

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: Failing to monitor drug levels where pharmacokinetics are variable (e.g., itraconazole capsules, voriconazole with CYP2C19 polymorphism) (Harrison 22e pp.1691-1692)

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: Not recognizing that emerging immunomodulatory biologics (IL-17/IL-23 inhibitors, BTK inhibitors, JAK inhibitors, anti-TNF, SYK inhibitors) create predictable, compartment-specific fungal risk (Harrison 22e pp.1688-1689)

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: Outcome hinges on host immune status, the fungus and site involved, timeliness of appropriate therapy, source control, and immune reconstitution. Mucocutaneous mycoses cause morbidity but are rarely fatal, whereas deep-organ infections are frequently severe with high mortality. Before amphotericin B, cryptococcal meningitis and other disseminated mycoses were nearly always fatal. A favorable prognosis in opportunistic mycoses depends substantially on restoring host immunity, for example neutrophil recovery, tapering of immunosuppression, or starting combination antiretroviral therapy in AIDS (Harrison 22e pp.1687, 1691).

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: Profound or prolonged neutropenia, allogeneic HSCT, or high-dose glucocorticoids portend invasive mold disease (aspergillosis, mucormycosis) and invasive candidiasis (Harrison 22e pp.1688-1689)

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: Diabetic ketoacidosis as a setting for rhinocerebral/sinopulmonary mucormycosis (Harrison 22e p.1688)

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: Advanced AIDS with low CD4 counts predisposing to intramacrophagic and mucosal mycoses (Harrison 22e p.1689)

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: Delay in appropriate antifungal therapy in candidemia, aspergillosis, or mucormycosis, which worsens outcome (Harrison 22e p.1691)

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: Failure to achieve source control (retained central venous catheter in candidemia, undrained abscess, undebrided necrotic sinus tissue in mucormycosis) (Harrison 22e p.1691)

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: Emerging drug-resistant species: azole/echinocandin-resistant Candida glabrata, Candida auris, and azole-resistant Aspergillus fumigatus (Harrison 22e p.1687)

chunks.diseaseName: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections
chunks.text: Classified by anatomic depth (mucocutaneous infections, which are rarely fatal, versus deep-organ infections, which are severe and often highly fatal) and by epidemiologic category (endemic versus opportunistic). Severity within these groups is further modulated by host immune competence, the implicated fungus, and the involved tissue (Harrison 22e p.1687).

chunks.text: Virchow's triad of venous stasis, hypercoagulability, and endothelial injury, typically with an inflammatory trigger, recruits activated platelets that release microparticles and drive neutrophil extracellular trap formation, promoting thrombin generation; venous thrombi flourish in stasis, low oxygen tension, and proinflammatory gene upregulation. Detached lower-limb thrombi embolize through the vena cava and right heart to lodge in the pulmonary arteries (rarely paradoxically to the arterial circulation via a patent foramen ovale or atrial septal defect). The dominant gas-exchange defects are arterial hypoxemia and a widened alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient with increased dead space; additional mechanisms include raised pulmonary vascular resistance from obstruction and vasoconstrictors (e.g., serotonin), ventilation-perfusion mismatch remote from the embolus, reflex hyperventilation, increased airway resistance, and reduced compliance. Pulmonary-artery obstruction plus neurohumoral mediators raise pulmonary pressure and resistance; rising RV wall tension produces RV dilation, stretch and dysfunction (releasing BNP), septal bowing that impairs LV filling, and compression of the right coronary artery causing RV ischemia/microinfarction (releasing troponin), ultimately reducing LV output and systemic pressure, leading to circulatory collapse and death. Prothrombotic states include factor V Leiden, the prothrombin gene mutation, and deficiencies of antithrombin/protein C/protein S (rare); antiphospholipid syndrome is an acquired thrombophilia predisposing to both venous and arterial thrombosis. (p.2156-2158)

chunks.text: Low-risk PE (about 65-75% of cases) with normal blood pressure and normal RV carries an excellent prognosis; submassive (intermediate-risk) PE (~20-25%) has RV dysfunction despite normal pressure with raised cardiac biomarkers and a high risk of deterioration; massive (high-risk) PE (5-10%) presents with hypotension/shock and can lead to multisystem organ failure and death. A high-probability V/Q scan confers ~90% diagnostic certainty for PE. Roughly half of survivors report persistent dyspnea, fatigue, and reduced exercise capacity, and about one-quarter have persistent RV dysfunction on echo ('post-PE syndrome'); CTEPH is a less frequent late complication. Risk of recurrent VTE after stopping anticoagulation ranges from low (<3%/yr, e.g., major surgery/trauma) to intermediate (3-8%/yr) to high (>8%/yr, e.g., active cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome) (ESC 2019). (p.2154-2155, 2158, 2161, 2163-2164)

Acute severe asthma results from intense airway inflammation, bronchial smooth muscle constriction, mucosal oedema, and mucus plugging, producing widespread airflow obstruction that is worse on expiration. Air trapping and dynamic hyperinflation increase the work of breathing and impair gas exchange, causing ventilation-perfusion mismatch and hypoxaemia. Early tachypnoea drives off carbon dioxide, but as the child fatigues and obstruction worsens, alveolar ventilation falls, carbon dioxide rises, and respiratory acidosis develops, heralding respiratory failure. Hyperinflation also impairs venous return and can compromise cardiac output.
A severe, sustained asthma exacerbation that does not respond adequately to initial bronchodilator therapy and constitutes a medical emergency.
Assessment combines clinical signs (work of breathing, accessory muscle use, air entry, mental state) with objective measures such as oxygen saturation and, where feasible, peak flow.
A quiet chest with poor air entry is ominous, indicating severe airflow limitation rather than improvement.
Rising carbon dioxide on blood gas in a tiring child signals impending respiratory failure; early in an attack hypocapnia is expected, so a normalising or high CO2 is a warning sign.
First-line treatment uses inhaled short-acting beta-agonists, often with inhaled anticholinergic agents, and early systemic corticosteroids, alongside oxygen to maintain saturations.
Escalation options for refractory cases include intravenous magnesium sulfate, continuous nebulised bronchodilator, and intravenous beta-agonist, with careful monitoring.
Agitation, drowsiness, exhaustion, cyanosis, or a silent chest indicate life-threatening disease requiring intensive care and possible ventilatory support.
Mechanical ventilation carries particular risks in asthma (air trapping and barotrauma) and is reserved for refractory respiratory failure using lung-protective, permissive strategies.
Identifying and addressing triggers, ensuring correct inhaler technique, and providing a written action plan help prevent recurrence.
Misreading a quiet chest or a normalising carbon dioxide as improvement rather than deterioration
Delaying systemic corticosteroids or under-treating a severe exacerbation
Over-relying on oxygen saturation alone without assessing work of breathing and mental state
Instituting mechanical ventilation without anticipating air trapping and barotrauma

Most children with severe exacerbations recover fully with prompt, escalating treatment. A minority progress to respiratory failure requiring intensive care and ventilation, which carries higher risk. Poor prognostic factors include delayed treatment, prior life-threatening attacks, and inadequate preventive management; good discharge planning reduces relapse.
