PID arises when micro-organisms ascend from the vagina and cervix through the endometrial cavity to the fallopian tubes and adjacent structures. Sexually transmitted pathogens, chiefly Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae, disrupt the cervical barrier and facilitate co-infection with endogenous aerobic and anaerobic vaginal flora. The resulting inflammation damages the tubal epithelium and cilia, leading to scarring, adhesions, and tubal occlusion. Progression can produce pyosalpinx, tubo-ovarian abscess, and pelvic peritonitis; spread to the hepatic capsule causes perihepatitis.
PID is infection and inflammation of the upper female genital tract, encompassing endometritis, salpingitis, oophoritis, tubo-ovarian abscess, and pelvic peritonitis
It is usually an ascending infection, most commonly caused by Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae, often with anaerobes and other vaginal flora
The clinical picture is variable and often subtle; classic findings are lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia, abnormal discharge, and cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness
Because sequelae are serious and diagnosis is imprecise, a low threshold for empirical treatment in at-risk women is recommended
Antibiotic regimens are broad-spectrum to cover gonococcus, chlamydia, and anaerobes; sexual partners should be evaluated and treated to prevent reinfection
Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (perihepatitis) causes right upper quadrant pain and can mimic hepatobiliary disease
Intrauterine device users, recent instrumentation, and multiple sexual partners increase risk
Long-term consequences include tubal-factor infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain, and risk rises with each recurrent episode
Withholding treatment while awaiting definitive confirmation, allowing tubal damage to progress
Missing an ectopic pregnancy by not performing a pregnancy test
Neglecting to test for and treat sexual partners, leading to reinfection
Failing to recognise or drain a tubo-ovarian abscess
Assuming an absence of fever or normal inflammatory markers excludes PID

Prompt, adequate antibiotic treatment usually resolves acute infection, but even treated PID carries appreciable risk of long-term tubal damage. Each recurrent episode further increases the likelihood of infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain, so prevention and partner treatment are central to a good outcome.

Inability to tolerate oral therapy, pregnancy, or failure of outpatient treatment requiring admission
Severe right upper quadrant pain raising concern for perihepatitis or an alternative surgical diagnosis

chunks.text: Pemphigus vulgaris is an autoimmune disease in which IgG autoantibodies target desmoglein 3 (and desmoglein 1 in mucocutaneous disease), transmembrane desmosomal cadherins that mediate keratinocyte adhesion. Antibody binding disrupts desmosomal function and triggers intracellular signalling that causes loss of cell-to-cell adhesion (acantholysis). This produces a suprabasal split within the epidermis, giving rise to fragile flaccid blisters and erosions. Because desmoglein 3 is expressed strongly in mucosa, mucosal disease often predominates; involvement of both desmogleins produces combined mucosal and cutaneous lesions. Extensive erosions lead to fluid loss, protein depletion, and susceptibility to secondary infection and sepsis.

chunks.text: A penetrating object breaches the abdominal wall and can lacerate solid organs (liver, spleen), causing haemorrhage, or hollow viscera (bowel, stomach), causing spillage of contents and peritoneal contamination. Vascular injury may produce rapid exsanguination into the peritoneal cavity or retroperitoneum. Low-energy stab wounds injure tissue along a relatively predictable track, whereas high-energy gunshot wounds transfer energy widely, causing cavitation and injury beyond the visible path. The result is a combination of haemorrhagic shock from bleeding and, later, peritonitis and sepsis from contamination.

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: Peptic ulcers are mucosal breaks >5 mm extending into the submucosa, occurring in the stomach (gastric ulcer, GU) or duodenum (duodenal ulcer, DU); >95% of DUs lie in the first part of the duodenum, within about 3 cm of the pylorus. The disease reflects an imbalance between aggressive factors (acid, pepsin) and mucosal defence. H. pylori and NSAIDs cause the majority of ulcers but act differently: H. pylori-associated benign GUs show antral gastritis, whereas NSAID-related GUs typically lack chronic active gastritis and instead show a chemical gastropathy (foveolar hyperplasia, lamina propria oedema). Duodenal ulcer patients tend to have increased basal and nocturnal acid secretion (with substantial overlap with controls) and reduced duodenal bicarbonate, both potentially influenced by H. pylori; gastric acid output in GU patients is usually normal or reduced, implying impaired mucosal defence. H. pylori is a gram-negative microaerophilic urease-producing rod living in the gastric mucous layer; virulence factors such as the cag pathogenicity island (delivering CagA), VacA, and urease determine the clinical outcome among colonisation, PUD, MALT lymphoma, and gastric adenocarcinoma (pp.2518-2520).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: Endoscopy detects an ulcer in fewer than 30% of patients investigated for dyspepsia, reflecting how poorly symptoms predict an actual ulcer (p.2522).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: Every gastric ulcer must be biopsied (multiple samples) at discovery because a GU may be malignant, and healing on therapy does not exclude cancer - about 70% of GUs ultimately found malignant show significant (usually incomplete) healing; repeat endoscopy with biopsy at 8-12 weeks is needed if the ulcer persists (pp.2519, 2531-2532).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: Abdominal pain has poor predictive value for an ulcer, and a normal exam or absent pain does not exclude PUD - many patients, especially the elderly or those on NSAIDs, present first with a complication (pp.2522-2523).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: Right-sided epigastric tenderness in about 20% of patients can mislead the examiner; epigastric tenderness overall has low predictive value (p.2522).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: Widespread PPI use can mask and delay the diagnosis of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and increase false-positive gastrin results (p.2534).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: Consider gastrinoma/ZES when ulcers occur in unusual locations (second part of duodenum or beyond), are multiple, are refractory, recur after acid-reducing surgery, present with frank complications, or arise without H. pylori or NSAID use (p.2535).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: More than 90% of both gastric and duodenal ulcers heal with conventional therapy; a GU not healed by 12 weeks or a DU not healed by 8 weeks is considered refractory. Eradicating H. pylori has cut duodenal ulcer recurrence by >80%. GI bleeding complicates roughly 15% of PUD with a 30-day mortality of about 2.5-10% (most deaths from non-bleeding causes such as multiorgan failure, pulmonary complications, and malignancy). Perforation occurs in ~6-7% of patients with 30-day mortality >20%, and penetration carries comparable mortality; gastric outlet obstruction is least common (~1-2%). Complications and mortality rise in patients over 60, partly reflecting greater NSAID use (pp.2522-2523, 2532).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: Alarm features warranting prompt endoscopy rather than empirical test-and-treat - nausea, vomiting, weight loss, evidence of GI bleeding, or age >=60 years with new dyspepsia (pp.2523, 2531).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: Constant pain no longer relieved by food/antacids and radiating to the back suggests a penetrating ulcer (e.g. into the pancreas) (p.2522).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: Sudden severe generalised abdominal pain with a board-like, rigid abdomen (the triad of acute pain, tachycardia, and rigidity) suggests perforation (pp.2522-2523).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: Pain worsening with meals plus vomiting of undigested food, early satiety, weight loss, or a succussion splash suggests gastric outlet obstruction (pp.2522-2523).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: Tarry stools or coffee-ground emesis indicate bleeding; tachycardia and orthostasis suggest hypovolaemia from blood loss or vomiting (p.2522).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
chunks.text: Ulcers result from an imbalance between mucosal aggressive factors (gastric acid secreted by parietal-cell H+,K+-ATPase, pepsin from chief cells) and mucosal defense/repair (a preepithelial mucus-bicarbonate-phospholipid layer, epithelial restitution and tight junctions, and a subepithelial microvascular bed), with prostaglandins, nitric oxide, and mucosal blood flow central to protection. H. pylori, a gram-negative microaerophilic urease-producing rod, colonizes gastric mucus, causes chronic active gastritis in nearly all infected individuals, and produces frank ulceration in only 10-15%; virulence factors include urease (generating ammonia), CagA delivered by a type IV secretion system from cag-PAI-positive strains, VacA, and adhesins. Antral-predominant gastritis raises acid and promotes duodenal ulcer, whereas corpus-predominant pangastritis lowers acid and favors gastric ulcer and carcinoma. NSAIDs injure mucosa both systemically (COX-1 inhibition depletes protective prostaglandins) and topically (weak acids that become trapped and ionized intracellularly), with neutrophil adherence to the gastric microcirculation initiating injury; H. pylori and NSAIDs act as independent and synergistic risk factors. In Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, autonomous gastrin secretion from a neuroendocrine tumor drives acid hypersecretion, parietal-cell hyperplasia, ulceration, esophagitis, and diarrhea (Harrison 22e p.2514-2521, p.2534).

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
chunks.text: A peptic ulcer is a break in the mucosa larger than 5 mm that extends into the submucosa; more than 90% of patients with the classic dyspepsia symptom complex have no ulcer, and many patients with true ulcers are asymptomatic (Harrison 22e p.2514, p.2522).

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
chunks.text: A fasting serum gastrin above ten times normal strongly suggests Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, but two-thirds of ZES patients have gastrin levels that overlap with commoner causes; a secretin-stimulated rise of 120 pg/mL or more within 15 minutes is over 90% sensitive and specific (Harrison 22e p.2535-2536).

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
chunks.text: Suspect gastrinoma with ulcers in unusual locations (second part of duodenum or beyond), refractory or recurrent ulcers, ulcers with complications, or ulcers without H. pylori or NSAID use; about 25% of gastrinomas arise in MEN 1 (Harrison 22e p.2534-2535).

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
chunks.text: Stress-related mucosal injury (Cushing's ulcer after head injury, Curling's ulcer after burns) histologically lacks inflammation and H. pylori, so 'gastritis' is a misnomer; bleeding typically appears 48-72 h after the insult with mechanical ventilation and coagulopathy as key risk factors (Harrison 22e p.2536).

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
chunks.text: Burning/gnawing epigastric pain typically occurs 90 minutes to 3 hours after eating in duodenal ulcer and is relieved by food or antacids; pain that wakes the patient between midnight and 3 A.M. is the most discriminating symptom (about two-thirds of DU patients), though it also occurs in roughly one-third with non-ulcer dyspepsia (Harrison 22e p.2522).

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
chunks.text: In gastric ulcer the pain may instead be precipitated by food, and nausea and weight loss are more common than in duodenal ulcer (Harrison 22e p.2522-2523).

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
chunks.text: H. pylori and NSAIDs are the two dominant risk factors (US odds ratios about 3.7 and 3.3); idiopathic and non-Hp/non-NSAID ulcers are rising as H. pylori prevalence falls (Harrison 22e p.2518, p.2522).

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
chunks.text: Gastric ulcers can be malignant and must be biopsied at discovery; duodenal ulcers are almost never malignant (Harrison 22e p.2518).

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
chunks.text: NSAID toxicity correlates poorly with symptoms: over 80% of patients with serious NSAID-related complications had no preceding dyspepsia, and even 75 mg/day of aspirin can cause serious ulceration, so no NSAID dose is completely safe (Harrison 22e p.2520-2521).

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
chunks.text: About two-thirds of PUD patients have no abdominal pain, and up to 87% of those with NSAID-induced disease present with a complication without prior symptoms; more than 50% of ulcer hemorrhages occur without warning (Harrison 22e p.2522).

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
chunks.text: Antral-predominant H. pylori gastritis predisposes to duodenal ulcer, whereas corpus-predominant gastritis predisposes to gastric ulcer, atrophy, and ultimately gastric carcinoma (Harrison 22e p.2519-2520).

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
chunks.text: Endoscopy is the most sensitive and specific test; it detects an ulcer in fewer than 30% of patients presenting with dyspepsia, allows biopsy to exclude malignancy and detect H. pylori, and barium studies are now rarely used (Harrison 22e p.2523).

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
chunks.text: Treating dyspepsia as PUD: abdominal pain has poor predictive value and most dyspeptic patients have no ulcer, so empiric assumptions can miss alternative diagnoses.

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
chunks.text: Relying on symptoms to gauge NSAID risk: serious complications usually occur without preceding dyspepsia.

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
chunks.text: Failing to biopsy a gastric ulcer to exclude malignancy.

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
chunks.text: Misinterpreting an elevated fasting gastrin: PPIs, hypochlorhydria/achlorhydria, pernicious anemia, H. pylori, renal insufficiency, retained antrum, and G-cell hyperplasia all raise gastrin, and PPIs must be stopped (about 7 days, bridged with an H2 antagonist) before ZES testing to avoid false positives.

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
chunks.text: Assuming serology proves active H. pylori infection, when it cannot distinguish current from prior infection and is unreliable for follow-up.

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
chunks.text: Abruptly stopping PPIs in gastrinoma patients, which can precipitate severe acid-related complications.

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
chunks.text: Calling stress-related mucosal injury 'gastritis' despite the absence of inflammation, or labeling endoscopic erythema as gastritis without histology.

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
chunks.text: Eradication of H. pylori reduces duodenal ulcer recurrence by more than 80%, and improving sanitation has steadily lowered ulcer incidence, surgery rates, and physician visits over the past decades. Complications still carry meaningful mortality: GI bleeding (the commonest, ~15% of patients) has a 30-day mortality of about 2.5-10% and is more frequent in those over 60; perforation occurs in about 6-7% of patients with 30-day mortality over 20%; gastric outlet obstruction is the least common (1-2%). Approximately 15,000 deaths per year in the US are attributed to complicated PUD. For gastrinoma, overall 5- and 10-year survival is about 62-75% and 47-53%; complete resection or negative laparotomy yields survival over 90%, while hepatic metastasis drops 5-year survival below 20% (Harrison 22e p.2514, p.2516, p.2522-2523, p.2536).

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
chunks.text: PUD severity is framed clinically by the presence and type of complication: uncomplicated ulcer versus bleeding (commonest, ~15%, 30-day mortality ~2.5-10%), perforation/penetration (~6-7%, 30-day mortality >20%; DU penetrates posteriorly into pancreas, GU into left hepatic lobe), and gastric outlet obstruction (1-2%, may be inflammatory/reversible or fixed scar). For gastrinoma, prognosis is stratified by resectability and metastatic burden rather than a formal stage in this chapter (Harrison 22e p.2522-2523, p.2536).

chunks.text: Perforation occurs when a peptic ulcer erodes through the full thickness of the gastric or duodenal wall, allowing gastric and duodenal contents to spill into the peritoneal cavity. Mucosal breakdown is driven by an imbalance between aggressive factors (acid, pepsin, Helicobacter pylori, NSAIDs) and mucosal defence. Escaped acidic contents first cause a sterile chemical peritonitis, followed within hours by bacterial contamination and generalised bacterial peritonitis. The resulting inflammatory cascade produces fluid sequestration, sepsis, and, if untreated, septic shock and multi-organ failure. Duodenal and pyloric ulcers most often perforate anteriorly.

These are disorders of the soft tissues surrounding joints rather than the synovial joint itself. Bursitis is synovial inflammation of a bursa from frictional overuse, trauma, systemic inflammatory/crystal disease, or infection. Tendinopathies (rotator cuff, bicipital, patellar, epicondylar, De Quervain's) result from mechanical impingement and repetitive resisted loading producing microtears, inflammation, and degeneration at tendon insertions; the supraspinatus is uniquely vulnerable to impingement beneath the acromion. Calcific tendinitis is caused by hydroxyapatite deposition within tendon substance through poorly understood phases of calcification that can incite acute inflammation. Adhesive capsulitis features a thickened shoulder capsule with mild chronic inflammatory infiltrate and fibrosis, often after a period of immobility. Plantar fasciitis arises at the fascial origin on the medial calcaneal tuberosity from cumulative loading. Drug-induced tendinopathies have an unknown mechanism but are linked to specific drug classes.

Periarticular disorders are common soft-tissue musculoskeletal problems affecting people of any age, arising from structures around (rather than within) the joint such as bursae, tendons, fascia, and connective-tissue bands.

Plantar fasciitis classically causes severe heel pain with the first steps in the morning or after rest, easing with initial activity then worsening with prolonged weight-bearing; tenderness localizes to the medial calcaneal attachment of the fascia.

Drug-induced tendinopathy is increasingly recognized, with quinolones, glucocorticoids, aromatase inhibitors, and statins implicated; the Achilles tendon is most often affected and rupture can be the presenting event.

Yergason's test (pain on resisted forearm supination with the elbow at 90 degrees) supports bicipital tendinitis; biceps tendon rupture in older patients may be painless and recognized by a retracted bulge of the long head.

Bursitis is inflammation of a synovial-lined sac; adults have over 150 bursae that ease gliding of tendons and muscles over bony prominences, and overuse, trauma, systemic disease (rheumatoid arthritis, gout), or infection can trigger inflammation.
Subacromial (subdeltoid) bursitis is the most common bursitis and frequently coexists with rotator cuff tendinitis, presenting with anterolateral shoulder pain.

Acutely inflamed olecranon or prepatellar bursitis with warmth/redness warrants aspiration with Gram stain, culture, and crystal examination to exclude infection or gout before assuming a mechanical cause.

Rotator cuff tendinitis (impingement syndrome) is the leading cause of a painful shoulder; the supraspinatus tendon is most often affected due to impingement between the humeral head and the anterior acromion/coracoacromial ligament, classically producing a painful abduction arc of 60-120 degrees.

Calcific tendinitis reflects hydroxyapatite (calcium salt) deposition within a tendon, most often the supraspinatus (involved in about 63% of cases), typically after age 40, and may be asymptomatic or cause sudden severe shoulder pain.

De Quervain's tenosynovitis involves the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis at the radial styloid; a positive Finkelstein test (thumb tucked in fist with ulnar wrist deviation) reproduces radial styloid pain.

Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) causes painful, globally restricted active and passive shoulder motion, usually without intrinsic joint disease, and is associated with diabetes, thyroid disease, chronic pulmonary disease, and prior myocardial infarction.

Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) arises from repetitive resisted wrist extension/supination; most patients are injured by activities other than tennis such as pulling weeds, carrying briefcases, or using a screwdriver.
Anserine bursitis is a frequently overlooked periarticular cause of knee pain.
Assuming inflamed olecranon or prepatellar bursitis is mechanical without excluding infection or gout by aspiration.
Mislabeling globally restricted shoulder motion as simple tendinitis when it is adhesive capsulitis.
Attributing heel pain to a radiographic heel spur, which is of little diagnostic significance in plantar fasciitis.
Overlooking medication as a cause of tendon pain or rupture (drug-induced tendinopathy), and reintroducing the offending agent.
Confusing iliopsoas bursitis pain with pain originating within the hip joint itself.

Most periarticular disorders are self-limited and respond to conservative measures. Adhesive capsulitis usually improves spontaneously over 1-3 years, though many patients retain some residual loss of shoulder motion. More than 80% of plantar fasciitis cases resolve within 12 months. Calcific tendinitis is largely self-limited. Rotator cuff tears vary in outcome depending on tear size, chronicity, pain, functional loss, and coexisting osteoarthritis.
Acutely warm, red, tender bursa suggesting septic bursitis or gout requiring aspiration
Weakness of abduction/external rotation or a positive drop-arm test suggesting a rotator cuff tear
Acute tendon rupture (e.g., Achilles in drug-induced tendinopathy, biceps in active patients)
Globally restricted active and passive shoulder motion suggesting adhesive capsulitis rather than a focal tendinitis
Periarticular pain in the setting of systemic disease (rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, thyroid disease) prompting evaluation of the underlying condition

No formal grading system; rotator cuff tears are clinically characterized as acute, subacute, or chronic and as partial- or full-thickness, with management guided by tear severity, symptom duration, pain, functional loss, and coexisting osteoarthritis.

Parasitic/protozoal and syphilitic pericarditis (amebiasis, toxoplasmosis, echinococcosis, trichinosis) (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2083)

Transthoracic echocardiography: most widely used, sensitive, specific, bedside-capable; localizes and estimates pericardial fluid and shows late-diastolic collapse of the RV free wall and right atrium in tamponade (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2082)

Doppler echocardiography: in tamponade and constriction, inspiratory increase in tricuspid/pulmonic flow velocities with decrease in pulmonary venous/mitral/aortic velocities and a leftward septal shift (respirophasic variation) (Harrison 22e p.2082, p.2084)

CT and MRI: superior for loculated effusions, pericardial thickening, pericardial masses, calcification, and detecting pericardial inflammation; more accurate than echocardiography for confirming or excluding constriction (MRI assesses myocardial involvement) (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2084)

ECG: stage 1-4 evolution in acute pericarditis; low QRS voltage and electrical alternans with large effusion/tamponade; low voltage and diffuse T-wave changes with atrial fibrillation in constriction (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2081, p.2083)
Chest radiograph: enlarged cardiac silhouette with a 'water bottle' configuration in large effusion; pericardial calcification (most common in tuberculous constriction) (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2084)

Laboratory: elevated C-reactive protein and white blood cell count in viral/idiopathic pericarditis (Harrison 22e p.2082)

The pericardium is a double-layered sac (visceral and parietal layers) separated by 15-50 mL of plasma ultrafiltrate; it restrains sudden cardiac chamber dilation and fixes cardiac position. In acute pericarditis, inflammation produces fibrinous or effusive disease. Cardiac tamponade occurs when fluid accumulates in the pericardial space in quantity sufficient to obstruct ventricular inflow, raising intrapericardial pressure and limiting diastolic filling throughout diastole, reducing stroke volume, cardiac output, and arterial pressure. As little as 200 mL can cause tamponade when fluid develops rapidly, versus >2000 mL when it accumulates slowly and the pericardium stretches. In chronic constrictive pericarditis, healing of fibrinous/serofibrinous pericarditis or resorption of effusion produces granulation tissue that contracts into a rigid, sometimes calcified scar encasing the heart; ventricular filling is unimpeded early in diastole then abruptly halts at the pericardium's elastic limit. End-diastolic pressures in both ventricles and mean atrial, pulmonary venous, and systemic venous pressures equalize within ~5 mmHg, while resting systolic function is typically normal or only mildly impaired (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2081, p.2083).
Acute pericarditis has four principal diagnostic features: chest pain, a pericardial friction rub, characteristic ECG changes, and pericardial effusion (Harrison 22e p.2078).

Constrictive pericarditis produces an M-shaped atrial pressure contour with prominent x and y descents; the y descent (diminished/absent in tamponade) is the most prominent deflection, and the ventricular pressure pulse shows a 'square root' sign in diastole (Harrison 22e p.2083).

In developing nations a high percentage of chronic constrictive pericarditis is tuberculous, but TB is now an uncommon cause in North America and Western Europe; other causes include prior viral/idiopathic pericarditis, cardiac surgery, mediastinal irradiation, and neoplasm (Harrison 22e p.2083).

Pericarditic chest pain is typically retrosternal/left precordial, often pleuritic, may radiate to the trapezius ridge, and is characteristically intensified by lying supine and relieved by sitting up and leaning forward (Harrison 22e p.2079).

A pericardial friction rub is audible at some point in approximately 85% of patients with acute pericarditis; it may have up to three components per cycle and is best heard at end expiration with the patient upright and leaning forward (Harrison 22e p.2079).

The ECG of acute pericarditis classically evolves through four stages: stage 1 widespread upwardly-concave ST elevation with PR-segment depression, stage 2 normalization of ST, stage 3 T-wave inversion, and stage 4 return to normal (Harrison 22e p.2079).
Beck's triad of cardiac tamponade is hypotension, soft or absent heart sounds, and jugular venous distention with a prominent x descent but an absent y descent (Harrison 22e p.2081).

Pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory fall in systolic pressure >10 mmHg) is an important clue to tamponade, but also occurs in about one-third of constrictive pericarditis cases and in hypovolemic shock, obstructive airway disease, and pulmonary embolism (Harrison 22e p.2081-2082).

In constrictive pericarditis the rigid thickened pericardium limits ventricular filling only after early diastole (unimpeded in early diastole, then abruptly reduced), whereas in tamponade filling is impeded throughout diastole (Harrison 22e p.2083).

Kussmaul's sign (failure of venous pressure to decline, or a rise, during inspiration) is common in chronic constrictive pericarditis but is also seen in tricuspid stenosis, right ventricular infarction, and restrictive cardiomyopathy; it is negative in cor pulmonale (Harrison 22e p.2083-2084).
A pericardial knock, an early third heart sound at the apex from abrupt cessation of ventricular filling, is often conspicuous in constrictive pericarditis (Harrison 22e p.2083).

Distinguishing constrictive pericarditis from restrictive cardiomyopathy is critical because constriction is surgically correctable; their hemodynamics overlap (square-root sign and equalized diastolic pressures occur in both) and echocardiography alone cannot definitively establish or exclude constriction, so MRI/CT is needed (Harrison 22e p.2083, p.2084).

Acute pericarditis is commonly mistaken for AMI and vice versa; in pericarditis the ST elevations are upwardly concave, reciprocal depression is limited to aVR/V1, and biomarker rises (from epi-myocarditis) are modest relative to AMI (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2083).
Pericardial calcification may occur without constriction, and constriction may occur without calcification, so calcification neither confirms nor excludes the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2084).
Acute idiopathic pericarditis is a diagnosis of exclusion with no specific test; all other causes of fibrinous pericarditis must be considered (Harrison 22e p.2082-2083).

Constrictive pericarditis with hepatomegaly, jaundice, and intractable ascites can be misdiagnosed as hepatic cirrhosis unless the distended neck veins with characteristic waveform are recognized (Harrison 22e p.2084).
Pain is often absent in slowly developing tuberculous, postirradiation, neoplastic, and uremic pericarditis, so its absence does not exclude pericardial disease (Harrison 22e p.2079).
Anticoagulants should be avoided in acute pericarditis because they could cause bleeding into the pericardial cavity and tamponade (Harrison 22e p.2080).

Viral or idiopathic acute pericarditis usually runs its course in a few days to 4 weeks; recurrent (relapsing) pericarditis occurs in approximately one-fourth of patients, and both tamponade and constriction are possible but infrequent complications. Most patients with acute pericarditis can be managed as outpatients with careful follow-up. Untreated cardiac tamponade may be rapidly fatal. Purulent pericarditis generally has a poor prognosis. Without treatment, tuberculous pericardial disease may progress to constriction. Pericardial resection is the only definitive treatment of constrictive pericarditis, with benefits accruing progressively over months; operative mortality is in the range of 5-10% even at experienced centers, highest in the most severe disease, especially radiation-induced (Harrison 22e p.2080, p.2082, p.2083, p.2084).

Cardiac tamponade: hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure, and unexplained sudden enlargement of the cardiac silhouette; may be rapidly fatal if not recognized and treated promptly (Harrison 22e p.2081)
Reduced QRS amplitude with electrical alternans of P, QRS, or T waves raises suspicion of tamponade (Harrison 22e p.2081)

Predictors of poor prognosis warranting hospitalization in acute pericarditis: fever >38C, subacute onset, large pericardial effusion, immunosuppression, or evidence of tamponade (Harrison 22e p.2080)
Purulent (pyogenic) pericarditis carries a poor prognosis and requires immediate drainage and antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.2083)
Without treatment, tuberculous pericardial disease can progress to constriction; constriction should be treated surgically (Harrison 22e p.2084)

Clinical classification: I. Acute pericarditis (<6 weeks) - A. Fibrinous, B. Effusive (serous or sanguineous); II. Subacute pericarditis (6 weeks to 6 months) - A. Effusive-constrictive, B. Constrictive; III. Chronic pericarditis (>6 months) - A. Constrictive, B. Adhesive (nonconstrictive). Etiologic classification: infectious, noninfectious, and presumed autoimmune. A hypoxic-ischaemic insult around the time of birth causes an initial phase of energy failure with cellular depolarisation, excitotoxic glutamate release, and calcium influx. After partial recovery of cerebral metabolism, a delayed (secondary) phase of energy failure ensues over hours to days, driven by mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, inflammation, and apoptotic and necrotic cell death. This latent window is the rationale for early therapeutic hypothermia, which slows the destructive secondary cascade.
Brain injury in the newborn resulting from a perinatal event that reduces cerebral oxygen delivery and blood flow, producing an evolving encephalopathy.
It is a leading cause of neonatal mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental disability, including cerebral palsy.
Severity is graded clinically using the Sarnat stages (mild, moderate, severe) based on level of consciousness, tone, reflexes, autonomic function, and seizures.
Supportive evidence of a hypoxic-ischaemic insult includes fetal distress, low Apgar scores, the need for resuscitation, and a low umbilical cord arterial pH with metabolic acidosis.
Therapeutic hypothermia, started within the first hours of life for eligible term and near-term infants with moderate to severe encephalopathy, reduces death and disability.
Seizures are common and may be subtle; EEG or amplitude-integrated EEG assists detection and monitoring.
The injury frequently involves other organs, causing renal, cardiac, hepatic, and haematological dysfunction that also require support.
MRI in the first week helps define the pattern and extent of injury and informs prognosis.
Important mimics, including infection, metabolic disorders, and stroke, should be considered rather than assuming every encephalopathy is purely hypoxic-ischaemic.

HIV crosses to the infant transplacentally, through exposure to maternal blood and genital secretions during delivery, or via breast milk. The virus infects CD4 T lymphocytes and other immune cells, integrating into host DNA and causing progressive depletion and dysfunction of CD4 cells. In infants the immune system is immature and the initial viral burden relative to immune capacity is high, so without treatment immunodeficiency and disease progression can occur faster than in adults, predisposing to opportunistic and recurrent infections and end-organ involvement.
Most childhood HIV infection is acquired from the mother during pregnancy, around delivery, or through breastfeeding, and transmission is largely preventable with effective interventions.

Maternal antiretroviral therapy that suppresses viral load, appropriate mode of delivery, infant antiretroviral prophylaxis, and safe infant feeding practices dramatically reduce vertical transmission.

Infected infants are frequently asymptomatic at birth, so diagnosis relies on virological (nucleic acid) testing rather than antibody tests, because maternal antibodies cross the placenta and persist for months.
Untreated perinatal infection can progress rapidly in infancy, with failure to thrive, recurrent or severe infections, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and developmental regression.
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is a serious early opportunistic infection, so prophylaxis is important in at-risk and infected infants.
Early initiation of antiretroviral therapy in infected infants improves survival and outcomes and is recommended as soon as diagnosis is confirmed.
A definitive diagnosis of infection or its exclusion requires a defined schedule of repeat virological testing over the first months of life.
Comprehensive care includes immunisations adapted to immune status, growth and developmental monitoring, and support for the whole family.
Using antibody testing rather than virological testing to diagnose infection in young infants
Interpreting a single negative early test as excluding infection without completing the testing schedule
Delaying antiretroviral therapy or Pneumocystis prophylaxis in an at-risk or infected infant
Overlooking co-infections such as tuberculosis or hepatitis

With early diagnosis, prompt antiretroviral therapy, and prophylaxis against opportunistic infections, children can achieve viral suppression, immune recovery, and near-normal life expectancy; untreated perinatal infection carries high morbidity and mortality in early childhood.

HIV infection - distal symmetric polyneuropathy, AIDP/CIDP, progressive polyradiculopathy, multiple mononeuropathies, sensory ganglionopathy (Harrison 22e p.3606)

Leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae) - most common cause of peripheral neuropathy in Southeast Asia, Africa, and South America; mononeuropathies or symmetric sensorimotor polyneuropathy (Harrison 22e p.3606)
Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi) - facial neuropathy (bilateral in ~half, unlike idiopathic Bell's palsy), polyradiculoneuropathy, multiple mononeuropathies (Harrison 22e p.3606)
Diphtheria (Corynebacterium diphtheriae) - toxin-mediated neuropathy 3-4 weeks after infection (Harrison 22e p.3606)

Baseline labs: CBC, electrolytes, renal and hepatic function, fasting glucose and HbA1c, thyroid function, B12, folate, ESR, rheumatoid factor, ANA, SPEP with immunofixation, and serum/urine free light chains (Harrison 22e p.3597)
Oral glucose tolerance test in painful sensory neuropathy even when fasting glucose and HbA1c are normal (abnormal in ~one-third) (Harrison 22e p.3597)

Vasculitis workup for mononeuropathy multiplex: ANCA, cryoglobulins, hepatitis serology, Lyme Western blot, HIV, occasionally CMV titer (Harrison 22e p.3598)
Lumbar puncture in suspected GBS/CIDP for elevated CSF protein (pleocytosis should be absent in idiopathic cases) (Harrison 22e p.3598)

Antibodies to SS-A/Ro, SS-B/La, and antineuronal nuclear (anti-Hu) antibodies in sensory ataxia/ganglionopathy; nerve biopsy reserved mainly for suspected amyloid or vasculitis and only when NCS are abnormal; skin biopsy for small-fiber neuropathy (Harrison 22e p.3598)

Multifocal motor neuropathy - treatable mimic of motor neuron disease (Harrison 22e p.3596)
Radiculopathy, plexopathy, and compressive/entrapment mononeuropathy (Harrison 22e p.3596)

Peripheral nerves contain mixed sensory, motor, and autonomic fibers grouped as large myelinated, small myelinated, and small unmyelinated classes; motor axons are usually large myelinated fast-conducting (~50 m/s) fibers, large-diameter sensory fibers carry proprioception and vibration, and small myelinated/unmyelinated fibers carry pain, temperature, and autonomic signals. Disease may target the neuronal cell body (neuronopathy/ganglionopathy), the myelin sheath (myelinopathy/demyelination), or the axon (axonopathy), each producing distinct clinical and electrophysiologic features. Most generalized polyneuropathies are length-dependent axonopathies producing distal (glove-and-stocking) deficits, whereas ganglionopathies produce non-length-dependent loss. Demyelination slows or blocks conduction; axonal loss reduces response amplitudes (Harrison 22e p.3594).

Three goals in the patient with neuropathy: localize the lesion, identify the cause, and determine treatment; the assessment is structured around seven key questions covering systems involved, distribution of weakness, nature of sensory loss, upper motor neuron signs, temporal evolution, hereditary clues, and associated medical conditions (Harrison 22e p.3595).

Pattern recognition is central: length-dependent symmetric distal sensory loss (Pattern 2) points to diabetes/metabolic, drugs, toxins, alcohol, hereditary causes; symmetric proximal AND distal weakness with sensory loss (Pattern 1) is the hallmark of acquired immune demyelinating polyneuropathy (GBS and CIDP); asymmetric/multifocal deficits (Pattern 3, mononeuropathy multiplex) suggest vasculitis, cryoglobulinemia, amyloid, sarcoid, or infection (Harrison 22e p.3596).

Nerve conduction studies and needle EMG distinguish axonal degeneration (low-amplitude potentials, relatively preserved distal latencies and conduction velocities, fibrillations on EMG) from segmental demyelination (slow conduction velocities, prolonged distal latencies, relatively preserved amplitudes, no fibrillations) (Harrison 22e p.3597).

Nonuniform slowing, conduction block, or temporal dispersion on NCS suggests an ACQUIRED demyelinating neuropathy (GBS or CIDP), whereas uniform slowing suggests a HEREDITARY demyelinating neuropathy (e.g., CMT type 1) (Harrison 22e p.3597).

Pure loss of pain and temperature with preserved vibration/position sense, normal strength and reflexes, and normal NCS indicates a small-fiber neuropathy; the most commonly identified causes are diabetes mellitus or glucose intolerance, with amyloid neuropathy also to be considered (Harrison 22e p.3596).

Dramatic proprioceptive/vibratory loss with normal strength, especially when non-length-dependent (arms more than legs or asymmetric), points to a sensory neuronopathy/ganglionopathy (Pattern 9) rather than a typical length-dependent polyneuropathy (Harrison 22e p.3597).

Diabetes mellitus is the most common cause of peripheral neuropathy in developed countries; distal symmetric sensory/sensorimotor polyneuropathy (DSPN) is the most common form, beginning in the toes and ascending (Harrison 22e p.3604).
Diabetic third nerve palsies are characteristically pupil-sparing (Harrison 22e p.3604).

Missing a treatable cause - acquired demyelinating neuropathy (GBS/CIDP) and multifocal motor neuropathy are treatable and should be distinguished from untreatable mimics such as ALS (Harrison 22e p.3596)
Overlooking treatable systemic/metabolic causes such as B12 deficiency, thyroid disease, or a paraprotein/monoclonal gammopathy in an apparently idiopathic polyneuropathy (Harrison 22e p.3597)

B12-deficiency neuropathy can occur with only peripheral findings and without anemia or macrocytosis (lacking in up to 40%); check methylmalonic acid and homocysteine when suspicion is high (Harrison 22e p.3612)

Routine antiganglioside autoantibody panels have no proven added value beyond a complete clinical exam and detailed EDx, and a heavy metal screen is not a useful blind screening test without exposure history or suggestive findings (Harrison 22e p.3598)
Nerve biopsy rarely distinguishes one neuropathy from another beyond clinical exam and NCS; reserve it for suspected amyloid or vasculitis and only when NCS are abnormal (Harrison 22e p.3598)

A hereditary neuropathy can be missed when patients have marked sensory signs but few sensory symptoms plus slowly progressive distal weakness and skeletal clues (high/flat arches, hammer toes, scoliosis); examining family members may be needed (Harrison 22e p.3597)

Most neuropathies are insidious and slowly progressive; course may be monophasic, progressive, or relapsing (e.g., CIDP, porphyria). Despite extensive evaluation, about half of patients have no etiology identified (cryptogenic/idiopathic sensory polyneuropathy). Outcome depends heavily on cause: treatable acquired demyelinating neuropathies (GBS, CIDP) and treatable systemic causes can respond to therapy, whereas axonal degeneration tends to recover slowly and incompletely. Even with adequate cobalamin replacement, treatment of B12-deficiency neuropathy usually does not fully reverse deficits and at least 50% of patients retain some permanent neurologic deficit (Harrison 22e p.3595, p.3612).

Rapidly progressive symmetric proximal and distal weakness with sensory loss (Pattern 1) - acute (GBS) or chronic (CIDP) demyelinating neuropathy; GBS can require respiratory support, so identifying this treatable pattern is critical (Harrison 22e p.3596)
Acute/subacute course (days to weeks) - GBS, vasculitis, diabetic or Lyme radiculopathy require prompt evaluation (Harrison 22e p.3597)
Autonomic dysfunction without diabetes (orthostatic drop without compensatory tachycardia, bowel/bladder/sexual dysfunction) - should raise concern for amyloid polyneuropathy (Harrison 22e p.3595)
Mononeuropathy multiplex pattern - suggests vasculitis and warrants an urgent vasculitis workup (Harrison 22e p.3596)

Severe sensory ataxia from a ganglionopathy - consider paraneoplastic (anti-Hu, often small-cell lung cancer); the neuropathy can precede detection of malignancy and should prompt a cancer search (Harrison 22e p.3598)

No formal numeric severity score is used; characterization is by anatomic/electrophysiologic classification rather than a grading scale - by fiber type affected (motor, sensory, autonomic, or combined; large- vs small-fiber), by distribution (mononeuropathy, mononeuropathy multiplex, polyneuropathy, radiculopathy, plexopathy; ten clinical patterns in Table 457-2), by underlying pathology (axonal degeneration vs segmental demyelination on NCS/EMG, Table 457-3), and by temporal course (acute: days to 4 weeks; subacute: 4-8 weeks; chronic: >8 weeks) (Harrison 22e p.3595, p.3597).

chunks.text: Peritonsillar abscess develops when infection extends beyond the tonsillar capsule into the loose peritonsillar space between the tonsil and the superior constrictor muscle, typically as a progression of acute tonsillitis or from obstructed minor salivary (Weber) glands. Cellulitis in this space evolves into a localised collection of pus, most often at the upper pole. The expanding abscess pushes the tonsil and soft palate medially, irritates the pterygoid muscles to cause trismus, and can dissect into adjacent deep neck spaces, threatening the airway and vascular structures.

chunks.text: Perthes' disease results from a temporary interruption of the blood supply to the immature femoral head epiphysis, causing avascular necrosis. The precise trigger is unknown but the epiphysis undergoes a sequence of ischaemic necrosis, followed by fragmentation and resorption of dead bone, then reossification and remodelling as revascularisation occurs. During the biologically 'plastic' necrotic and fragmentation phases the softened femoral head is vulnerable to deformation under load, and can flatten and enlarge (coxa magna) or become incongruent if not well contained within the acetabulum. The ultimate shape of the healed head, and hence long-term function, depends on how well sphericity and containment are preserved through this self-limiting but prolonged process.

Infection begins with attachment of B. pertussis to ciliated epithelial cells of the nasopharynx, mediated by surface adhesins (pertactin, filamentous hemagglutinin) binding integrin-family proteins, probably with pertussis toxin. The organism multiplies locally and produces toxins causing mucosal damage (tracheal cytotoxin, dermonecrotic toxin); host defense is impaired by pertussis toxin and adenylate cyclase-hemolysin toxin. There is local cellular invasion with intracellular persistence, but systemic dissemination does NOT occur; systemic manifestations such as lymphocytosis result from the toxins. The cause of the hallmark paroxysmal cough is not known; a pivotal role for pertussis toxin has been proposed but not confirmed. Neurologic events (seizures, encephalopathy) are thought to result from hypoxia due to coughing paroxysms or apnea rather than from specific bacterial products. Deaths in young infants are frequently associated with very high leukocytosis and pulmonary hypertension (p.1278).
Acute respiratory tract infection caused by Bordetella pertussis; 'pertussis' means 'violent cough' and the inspiratory whoop at the end of a paroxysm gives the disease its common name (p.1276).
Highly communicable: attack rates of 80-100% among unimmunized household contacts; cyclical outbreaks occur every 3-5 years despite widespread immunization (p.1277).
Severe morbidity and high mortality are restricted almost entirely to infants; in the US (2000-2017) infants under 2 months accounted for 84% of pertussis deaths (p.1278).

Classic course runs through three stages: catarrhal phase (1-2 weeks of coryza, lacrimation, mild cough, low-grade fever, malaise, indistinguishable from a common cold), then paroxysmal phase (frequent spasmodic bursts of 5-10 coughs within a single expiration), then convalescent phase (p.1278-1279).
Paroxysms may end in an audible whoop produced by rapid inspiration against a closed glottis; post-tussive vomiting is frequent and a mucous plug may be expelled (p.1279).

During a coughing spasm there may be neck-vein distension, bulging eyes, tongue protrusion, and cyanosis; paroxysms can be precipitated by noise, eating, or physical contact and are often worse at night (p.1279).
Between attacks the patient looks normal but shows increasing fatigue; fever is uncommon and, when present, suggests bacterial superinfection (p.1279).
The convalescent phase lasts 1-3 months with gradual resolution; for 6-12 months afterward, intercurrent viral infections may trigger a recrudescence of paroxysmal cough (p.1279).
Incubation period averages 7-10 days (p.1279).
The whoop is variable: uncommon in infants 6 months of age or younger and frequently absent in older children and adults (p.1276).
Lymphocytosis (absolute lymphocyte count >108-109/L) is common in young children and unusual with other infections, but is not a feature in adolescents and adults (p.1279).

In adolescents and adults the presentation is often atypical -- frequently no paroxysmal cough or whoop -- so pertussis is a commonly missed cause of prolonged cough; B. pertussis may be the agent in 12-30% of adults whose cough does not improve within 2 weeks (p.1278).
Antibiotic therapy aims to eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage; it does NOT substantially alter the clinical course unless given early in the catarrhal phase (p.1279).
Cough suppressants are NOT effective and have no role in management; beta-adrenergic agonists and glucocorticoids have been advocated but are NOT proven effective (p.1280).
Lymphocytosis is helpful in young children but is NOT a reliable feature in adolescents and adults (p.1279).
There is only a small window for culture/PCR diagnosis because much of the period of organism recovery is during the catarrhal phase when pertussis is not yet suspected (p.1279).
Cross-reactivity of antigens such as filamentous hemagglutinin and pertactin among Bordetella species makes diagnosis based on seroconversion of a single antibody type unreliable (p.1279).

Suspect pertussis in any patient with a cough not improving within 14 days, a paroxysmal cough of any duration, cough followed by vomiting (adolescents/adults), or respiratory symptoms after contact with a laboratory-confirmed case (p.1280).
Waning vaccine-derived immunity (faster with acellular vaccines) underlies resurgent outbreaks even in fully immunized older children, adolescents, and adults (p.1278).

With universal childhood immunization, reported cases fell by >90% and mortality declined even more dramatically. Severe morbidity and high mortality remain almost entirely restricted to infants; WHO estimates ~40 million cases and ~400,000 deaths globally each year, mostly among infants under 3 months. Immunity after natural infection is NOT lifelong; immunity after whole-cell vaccination is short-lived (little protection after 10-12 years) and wanes even faster (within 2-4 years of the fifth or sixth dose) in those immunized with acellular vaccines (p.1277-1278).

Infants, especially those under 2-3 months, carry the highest risk of complications and death and should generally be hospitalized (p.1278, 1279).

Deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (or, less commonly, of its tetrahydrobiopterin cofactor) blocks the conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine. Phenylalanine therefore accumulates in blood and tissues and is diverted to alternative metabolites such as phenylketones. High phenylalanine levels are neurotoxic to the developing brain, interfering with amino acid transport across the blood-brain barrier, neurotransmitter synthesis, and myelination, producing the intellectual disability and neurological features of untreated disease. Reduced tyrosine availability also limits synthesis of melanin, contributing to hypopigmentation.
An autosomal recessive inborn error of amino acid metabolism caused most often by deficiency of the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase.
Untreated, accumulation of phenylalanine causes progressive and irreversible intellectual disability, seizures, and behavioural problems.
Affected infants are typically normal at birth, so detection relies on newborn screening rather than clinical signs.
Classic untreated features can include a musty or mousy body odour, eczema, and reduced pigmentation with fair hair and skin.
Early diagnosis through screening and prompt dietary treatment prevent the neurological damage almost entirely.
Treatment centres on a lifelong low-phenylalanine diet with a special protein substitute, guided by regular monitoring of blood phenylalanine levels.
A subset of patients respond to the cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (sapropterin), and disorders of biopterin metabolism must be excluded as a separate cause of high phenylalanine.

Maternal PKU with poorly controlled phenylalanine during pregnancy can damage the fetus, causing microcephaly, congenital heart disease, and developmental delay, so strict control is essential before and during pregnancy.
Lifelong follow-up in a metabolic service supports adherence and long-term neurocognitive outcomes.
Assuming a normal newborn appearance excludes the diagnosis
Failing to exclude tetrahydrobiopterin deficiency as a treatable alternative cause
Relaxing dietary control in older children and adults, risking cognitive and neuropsychiatric effects
Overlooking the need for strict preconception and pregnancy control in affected mothers

With early diagnosis and consistent dietary control, cognitive development is normal or near-normal; delayed treatment or poor lifelong control leads to irreversible neurocognitive impairment, and maternal control critically affects offspring.

chunks.text: Excess production of catecholamines, usually by a benign neuroendocrine tumour of chromaffin cells in the adrenal medulla (80-85%) or in extra-adrenal paraganglion tissue (paraganglioma). The catecholamine surge drives paroxysmal hypertension, headache, sweating and cardiac arrhythmias, and produces a hyperdynamic catecholaminergic state. Chronic/episodic catecholamine exposure can cause microvascular myocardial ischaemia (microinfarcts similar to those seen with stimulant toxicity) and a catecholamine-mediated cardiomyopathy; the same mechanism of sudden catecholamine release underlies stress (takotsubo / apical ballooning) cardiomyopathy (hypertension, cardiomyopathy and cardiac-tumour chapters).

PPGLs are well-vascularized neuroendocrine tumors derived from chromaffin cells of the sympathetic and parasympathetic paraganglial system. They synthesize and store catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine), and tumoral release drives the clinical syndrome; the name pheochromocytoma reflects the dark staining produced by chromaffin oxidation of catecholamines. The etiology of sporadic tumors is unknown, but 25-33% carry germline mutations. Susceptibility genes fall into three pathogenetic clusters: cluster 1 (pseudohypoxia: SDHx, FH, VHL, HIF2A), cluster 2 (kinase signaling: RET, NF1, TMEM127, MAX, HRAS, KIF1B-beta, PDH), and cluster 3 (Wnt signaling: CSDE1, MAML3). Most genes act as tumor suppressors with biallelic inactivation, while RET is a protooncogene whose mutations activate receptor tyrosine kinase activity; SDH is a Krebs-cycle/mitochondrial respiratory chain enzyme, and the VHL protein is part of a ubiquitin E3 ligase whose loss upregulates cell-cycle, glucose metabolism, and oxygen-sensing pathways.

Pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas (PPGLs) are catecholamine-producing tumors arising from sympathetic (adrenal medulla, sympathetic trunk) or parasympathetic (carotid body, glomus tympanicum/jugulare/vagale) paraganglia; by WHO usage pheochromocytoma denotes the adrenal tumor and paraganglioma denotes tumors at all other sites.
About 25-33% of patients have an inherited syndrome (MEN 2, VHL, NF1, paraganglioma syndromes, TMEM127, MAX); these patients present on average about 15 years younger than those with sporadic tumors.

Universal germline panel testing is the gold standard and identifies a genetic cause in up to about 30% of cases, with higher yield in early onset, extra-adrenal, multiple, or metastatic tumors or a family history.
Pheochromocytoma in pregnancy may produce adrenergic crises, possibly via hCG/LHCG-receptor-mediated stimulation of epinephrine production, and is challenging to manage.

The classic triad is episodic palpitations, headache, and profuse sweating, present in roughly one-third of patients; the combination of this triad with hypertension makes pheochromocytoma a likely diagnosis, though tumors can remain asymptomatic for years.
Hypertension is the dominant sign and may be paroxysmal (classic) or sustained (also common); paroxysms generally last under one hour.
The classic 'rule of tens' states that about 10% are bilateral, 10% extra-adrenal, and 10% metastatic.
Diagnosis rests on two equally important pillars: biochemical documentation of catecholamine excess and imaging localization of the tumor.

Plasma free metanephrines are the most sensitive biochemical test and are less prone to false-positive elevation from stress including venipuncture; most tumors continuously leak O-methylated metabolites even when catecholamine secretion fluctuates.

Values three times the upper limit of normal make the diagnosis highly likely regardless of assay; because the tumor is rare, borderline elevations are more likely to be false positives, so drug/dietary confounders should be excluded and testing repeated.
On unenhanced CT, an adrenal mass with attenuation below 10 Hounsfield units makes pheochromocytoma unlikely; about 5% of adrenal incidentalomas prove to be pheochromocytomas on endocrine evaluation.

Histology classically shows a 'Zellballen' pattern of neuroendocrine chief cell nests with peripheral sustentacular cells; chief cells stain for chromogranin and synaptophysin, sustentacular cells for S-100, and loss of SDHB staining suggests an underlying germline SDH mutation.

Borderline biochemical elevations are frequently false positives given tumor rarity; failing to exclude dietary/drug confounders (sympathomimetics, diuretics, tricyclics, alpha/beta blockers, levodopa withdrawal) and repeat testing leads to overdiagnosis.
Serial catecholamine levels vary widely due to fluctuating secretion, so reliance on a single catecholamine measurement can miss the diagnosis; metanephrines are continuously leaked.
Starting a beta blocker before adequate alpha blockade can precipitate severe hypertension.
FNA of a presumed adrenal mass that is actually a pheochromocytoma can provoke a crisis.
Standard histologic atypia, mitoses, and local invasion do not reliably establish malignancy.
Symptoms can be misattributed to a primary psychiatric/panic disorder.
NF1 germline mutations are essentially never found in sporadic pheochromocytoma, so NF1 testing is unnecessary without other neurofibromatosis features.
Sequencing protocols may miss large single- or multi-exon deletions.

Complete tumor removal is potentially curative and can prevent lethal hypertensive crises. About 5-10% of PPGLs are metastatic; histologic criteria alone are insufficient to define malignancy, and the WHO now uses 'metastatic' (lymph node or distant spread, commonly to lung, bone, or liver) rather than 'malignant.' The prognosis of metastatic disease is variable with 5-year survival of roughly 30-60%. Hereditary syndromes influence risk: about one-third of PGL4 (SDHB) patients develop metastases, the highest rate among the associated syndromes, and metastatic disease also occurs notably with VHL, NF1, and PGL1.
Catecholamine crisis causing heart failure, pulmonary edema, arrhythmias, or intracranial hemorrhage
Paroxysms precipitated by surgery, anesthesia/intubation, positional change, exercise, micturition (bladder paraganglioma), pregnancy, or drugs (tricyclics, opiates, metoclopramide)
Paradoxical hypertensive response to antihypertensive drugs

Hypertensive crisis or adrenergic crisis during pregnancy
Features suggesting a hereditary syndrome (early onset, bilateral/multifocal, extra-adrenal, family history, MTC, retinal/CNS/renal tumors)

Malignancy/recurrence risk is assessed by markers including tumor size >5 cm, the Pheochromocytoma of the Adrenal gland Scaled Score (PASS), the Grading system for Adrenal Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma (GAPP), and SDHB status, although these remain controversial. Disease is now categorized by the WHO as localized versus metastatic (regional lymph node or distant metastasis) rather than benign versus malignant.

chunks.text: In physiological phimosis the foreskin is non-retractile simply because natural adhesions between the inner prepuce and glans have not yet separated and the preputial opening is developmentally narrow. Pathological phimosis results from fibrosis and scarring of the preputial ring, most often due to chronic or recurrent inflammation (balanoposthitis), repeated trauma from forced retraction, or lichen sclerosus (balanitis xerotica obliterans), an inflammatory dermatosis that causes progressive sclerosis. The scarred, inelastic ring restricts retraction and may obstruct the urinary stream.

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: The cardiovascular examination derives diagnostic and prognostic information from the mechanical and hemodynamic consequences of cardiac and vascular disease. The jugular venous waveform reflects right atrial pressure dynamics: the a wave is presystolic right atrial contraction, the x descent is atrial relaxation, the c wave is the systolic bulging of the closed tricuspid valve, the v wave is atrial filling during ventricular systole, and the y descent is right atrial emptying after tricuspid opening. Reduced right ventricular compliance accentuates the a wave; tricuspid regurgitation accentuates the v wave with a rapid y descent and progressively 'ventricularizes' the waveform; obstruction to right ventricular inflow (tricuspid stenosis, tamponade) blunts or prolongs the y descent. Arterial pulse contour depends on stroke volume, ejection velocity, vascular compliance, and systemic vascular resistance, so fixed outflow obstruction blunts and delays the upstroke while wide pulse pressure states produce a bounding collapsing pulse. Heart sound intensity reflects valve leaflet excursion and mobility, ventricular contractility, and the PR interval, while the distance between the stethoscope and the cardiac event (obesity, lung disease, effusion) attenuates all sounds. Splitting of S2 depends on the relative timing of aortic and pulmonic valve closure, which is altered by conduction delays, shunts, and outflow obstruction.

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: The jugular venous pressure is the single most important bedside measurement for estimating volume status; the internal jugular vein is preferred over the external because the latter is valved and not directly in line with the superior vena cava and right atrium.

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Lower extremity edema with an elevated JVP indicates volume overload (heart failure or constrictive pericarditis), whereas edema without jugular venous hypertension suggests hypoalbuminemia (nephrotic syndrome, liver failure), venous insufficiency, or dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker use.

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Janeway lesions (nontender hemorrhagic macules on palms and soles) and Osler's nodes (tender nodules on finger/toe pads), along with splinter hemorrhages in the mid-nail bed, are peripheral signs of infective endocarditis.

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: An ankle-brachial index (ankle systolic pressure divided by the higher brachial systolic pressure) is a powerful predictor of long-term cardiovascular mortality; a >2% finger-to-toe oxygen saturation difference on pulse oximetry performs comparably for detecting lower extremity peripheral arterial disease.

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Using the sternal angle (angle of Louis) as the reference point systematically underestimates central venous pressure, so it is better used to separate normal from elevated CVP than to quantify it; venous pulsations above the clavicle in the sitting position are clearly abnormal since the clavicle-to-right-atrium distance is at least 10 cm.

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: The venous waveform is biphasic in sinus rhythm whereas the carotid pulse is monophasic; the venous pulse is not easily obliterated by palpation and changes with posture and inspiration, helping distinguish it from the arterial pulse.

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: A cannon a wave occurs with atrioventricular dissociation when the right atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve; in a wide-complex tachycardia, cannon a waves identify the rhythm as ventricular in origin. The a wave is absent in atrial fibrillation.

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Kussmaul's sign (a rise or lack of fall of the JVP with inspiration) is classically associated with constrictive pericarditis but also occurs with restrictive cardiomyopathy, massive pulmonary embolism, right ventricular infarction, and advanced left ventricular systolic heart failure, and is common after cardiac surgery.

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Pulsus parvus et tardus (weak and delayed carotid pulse) suggests severe aortic stenosis, whereas a sharp rapidly collapsing carotid upstroke (Corrigan's or water-hammer pulse) points to chronic severe aortic regurgitation.

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory fall in systolic pressure >10 mmHg) is seen in pericardial tamponade but also occurs with massive pulmonary embolism, hemorrhagic shock, severe obstructive lung disease, and tension pneumothorax; it reflects exaggerated interventricular dependence.

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Fixed splitting of S2 (a wide A2-P2 interval that does not vary with respiration) is characteristic of a secundum atrial septal defect, while reversed (paradoxical) splitting occurs with left bundle branch block, right ventricular pacing, severe aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, and acute myocardial ischemia.

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: The mitral valve prolapse click-murmur complex moves away from S1 with maneuvers that increase preload (squatting) and closer to S1 on standing, a dynamic behavior that helps distinguish it from other systolic events.

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Using an inappropriately small blood pressure cuff overestimates pressure, while an oversized cuff underestimates it; the bladder should be about 80% of arm length and 40% of arm circumference.

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Examining the carotid upstrokes simultaneously, or before auscultating for a bruit, and applying heavy pressure can precipitate carotid hypersensitivity and syncope in susceptible elderly patients.

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: A cervical bruit correlates poorly with the degree of carotid stenosis, and its absence does not exclude significant obstruction.

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Palpation alone is insufficiently accurate to diagnose an abdominal aortic aneurysm, and sensitivity falls with increasing body size.

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Homans' sign is neither sensitive nor specific for deep venous thrombosis.

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Arcus senilis lacks specificity as a marker of coronary heart disease risk.

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Physician-measured blood pressures tend to be higher than nurse- or self-recorded values, contributing to white coat hypertension; conversely masked hypertension can be missed when clinic pressures are normal despite target organ damage.

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Heart and pulse findings can be misleading in low cardiac output states and in stiffened arteries from aging, hypertension, or peripheral arterial disease.

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Bedside findings carry independent prognostic weight. In heart failure, an elevated JVP and a third heart sound predict the pulmonary artery wedge pressure and are associated with higher risk of heart failure hospitalization and death; an estimated right atrial pressure >10 mmHg predicted a wedge pressure >22 mmHg with high positive value in advanced heart failure. The ankle-brachial index is a powerful predictor of long-term cardiovascular mortality, and higher ambulatory systolic pressures independently predict cardiovascular events and all-cause death. Pulsus alternans indicates severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction, and when accompanied by electrocardiographic T-wave alternans the arrhythmic risk appears increased.

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Markedly elevated JVP that does not pulsate with a dusky cyanotic head and neck, suggesting superior vena cava syndrome

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Pulsus paradoxus with elevated JVP and blunted y descent, suggesting pericardial tamponade

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: Orthostatic hypotension without compensatory tachycardia, suggesting autonomic insufficiency

chunks.diseaseName: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
chunks.text: No formal grading scale; specific findings convey severity within individual conditions (e.g., pulsus parvus et tardus and a soft A2 indicate severe aortic stenosis; the A2-opening snap interval in mitral stenosis is inversely proportional to the left atrial-left ventricular gradient; a JVP distance >4.5 cm above the sternal angle at 30 degrees, or any venous pulsation above the clavicle in the sitting position, is abnormal; orthostatic hypotension is a fall in systolic pressure >20 mmHg or diastolic >10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing).

Sinus rhythm originates from spontaneous depolarization of pacemaker cells in the sinus node at the right atrium-SVC junction within the crista terminalis. Heart rate is modulated by the autonomic balance between sympathetic input (which accelerates and shifts the activation focus) and parasympathetic (vagal) input (which slows the node). Sinus arrhythmia reflects normal beat-to-beat shifts in autonomic tone, classically respiratory-linked vagal modulation. Sinus tachycardia results from increased sympathetic drive and/or vagal withdrawal raising the rate of spontaneous nodal depolarization; when this is an appropriate response to exercise, stress, or illness it is physiologic. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is thought to stem from an imbalance between sympathetic and parasympathetic input to the node, altered membrane automaticity of sinus node cells, or both, though the precise mechanism remains poorly defined. POTS reflects orthostatic autonomic dysfunction, sometimes postviral.

The sinus node sits at the lateral-superior junction of the right atrium and superior vena cava, within the upper portion of the crista terminalis where the smooth posterior wall (from the sinus venosus) meets the trabeculated anterior right atrium.
POTS can follow a viral illness and may resolve spontaneously over 3-12 months; a POTS-like autonomic picture has been described in prolonged post-COVID-19 (long COVID) syndromes.
Distinguishing IST from POTS is clinically critical because they require fundamentally different management approaches; conflating them risks worsening symptoms.
Asymptomatic sinus arrhythmia is physiologic, is not considered pathogenic, and does not warrant further cardiac evaluation.

Normal sinus rhythm runs between roughly 60 and 100 beats/min, with a sinus P wave that is upright in leads II, III, and aVF, negative in aVR, and initially positive/biphasic in V1, reflecting an inferiorly and leftward-directed frontal-plane axis.

Sinus arrhythmia is a common, usually asymptomatic finding defined as a sinus-origin rhythm with P-P interval variation greater than 120 ms; when P-wave morphology also varies, premature atrial contractions rather than true sinus arrhythmia are the likely cause.

Three patterns of sinus arrhythmia are described: respirophasic (vagal tone reflexively falls in inspiration and is restored in expiration), ventriculophasic (seen with heart block or after a PVC, where an interposed ventricular beat shortens the P-P interval), and nonphasic (P-P variation unrelated to cardiac or respiratory cycle).

Sinus tachycardia (>100 beats/min) arises from sympathetic stimulation and/or vagal withdrawal; the earliest activation focus shifts more leftward toward the superior septal crista terminalis, producing taller inferior-lead P waves than in resting sinus rhythm.
Sinus bradycardia is defined as a rate <60 beats/min but can be entirely normal during sleep and in physically fit individuals.
A gradual rate rise with an identifiable trigger (such as exertion) favors sinus tachycardia, whereas abrupt onset and offset favor focal atrial tachycardia originating near the sinus node.

Inappropriate sinus tachycardia (IST) is an uncommon disorder of autonomic dysregulation in which the sinus rate climbs at rest or out of proportion to physiologic demand; it most often affects women in their third or fourth decade.
POTS is defined by symptomatic sinus tachycardia on standing, with a rate increase of at least 30 beats/min or to >120 beats/min within 10 minutes of standing in the absence of hypotension.
Mislabeling rhythm irregularity with varying P-wave morphology as sinus arrhythmia when it is actually premature atrial contractions.
Diagnosing nonphysiologic sinus tachycardia before excluding reversible drivers such as anemia, thyroid disease, and pulmonary embolism.

Failing to separate inappropriate sinus tachycardia from POTS, since blood-pressure-raising strategies appropriate for POTS are inappropriate for IST, and sinus node modification is ineffective for POTS and may worsen its nontachycardia features.

Pursuing catheter-based sinus node modification for IST, which often yields poor long-term symptom control and can lead to symptomatic sinus bradycardia, sinus arrest, or chronotropic incompetence requiring a permanent pacemaker.
Overtreating an asymptomatic, constitutionally elevated resting or exercise sinus rate with no identifiable underlying cause.

Sinus arrhythmia is benign and physiologic, requiring no treatment. Physiologic sinus tachycardia resolves with correction of the underlying condition and often needs no specific therapy. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia tends to be a chronic, often disabling condition that responds poorly to therapy and may be difficult to control long term. POTS frequently improves over time, and postviral POTS may resolve spontaneously within 3-12 months.
Sinus tachycardia accompanied by hypotension, impaired consciousness, angina, or heart failure, suggesting a serious underlying cause requiring urgent attention
Unexplained or persistent sinus tachycardia mandating exclusion of pulmonary embolism, myocardial ischemia, and structural/functional cardiac disease before labeling it nonphysiologic
Syncope or disabling palpitations accompanying tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia as a possible marker of underlying systemic illness (e.g., infection, malignancy, endocrine disorder) or drug toxicity

Sinus tachycardia is rate-defined as >100 beats/min and sinus bradycardia as <60 beats/min, with normal sinus rhythm spanning 60-100 beats/min. POTS is defined diagnostically by an orthostatic heart-rate rise of >=30 beats/min (or to >120 beats/min) within 10 minutes of standing without hypotension. Sinus arrhythmia is defined by P-P interval variability >120 ms of sinus origin.

chunks.text: Pilonidal disease is now regarded as an acquired condition in which loose hairs are driven into the skin of the natal cleft, provoking a foreign-body inflammatory reaction and forming midline pits. The pits become epithelialised sinuses that trap further hair and debris, leading to chronic infection, abscess formation, and secondary tracks extending laterally. Friction, sweating, deep natal clefts, hirsutism, and prolonged sitting promote hair insertion and infection. Recurrent cycles of infection and incomplete healing perpetuate the disease.
