Pituitary adenomas are benign, almost always monoclonal neoplasms derived from a single anterior pituitary cell lineage, implying acquisition of somatic mutation(s) conferring a growth advantage. Hormonally active tumors secrete autonomously with reduced responsiveness to physiologic feedback. Several molecular events are implicated: about 35% of GH-secreting tumors carry activating Gs-alpha mutations that lower GTPase activity, raise cyclic AMP, and drive somatotrope proliferation; growth factors (bFGF, EGFR signaling, the latter linked to USP8 mutation in some ACTH tumors), activated oncogenes (RAS, PTTG), loss of suppressors (e.g., MEG3), and loss of negative feedback (as in primary hypothyroidism/hypogonadism) also contribute. Hypothalamic hormones GHRH and CRH can additionally stimulate mitotic activity, so ectopic GHRH/CRH-producing chest or abdominal tumors can cause somatotrope or corticotrope hyperplasia. Familial settings include MEN 1 (MENIN, 11q13), MEN 4 (CDKN1B), Carney complex (PRKAR1A), McCune-Albright (mosaic Gs-alpha), and familial acromegaly (AIP). Clinical effects arise both from hormone hyper-/hyposecretion and from local mass effect: dorsal expansion lifts the optic chiasm, stalk compression disrupts dopaminergic inhibition of lactotropes (hyperprolactinemia) and portal hormone delivery, and lateral extension into the cavernous sinus impairs cranial nerves III, IV, VI and trigeminal branches.

Pituitary adenomas are benign monoclonal neoplasms arising from one of the five anterior pituitary cell types; the secreted hormone (PRL, GH, ACTH, TSH, or LH/FSH) determines the clinical syndrome. About one-third are clinically nonfunctioning, most of these originating from gonadotrope or null cells (p.3003-3004).
Iatrogenic glucocorticoid use remains the most common overall cause of cushingoid features and must be excluded by history before pursuing an endogenous workup (p.3010).

ACTH-secreting adenomas retain partial suppressibility by high-dose glucocorticoids, distinguishing them from ectopic ACTH sources; inferior petrosal sinus sampling with CRH (central:peripheral ratio >2 basal, >3 post-CRH) has >95% sensitivity for localizing a pituitary source (p.3011-3012).

Nonfunctioning/gonadotrope adenomas are the most common adenoma type at presentation and are usually macroadenomas discovered through mass effect or as incidentalomas; mildly elevated PRL from stalk compression must not be mistaken for a true prolactinoma since these tumors do not shrink with dopamine agonists (p.3012-3013).

Most pituitary glands harbor an unsuspected microadenoma at autopsy (up to one-quarter), and imaging detects clinically inapparent lesions (incidentalomas) in at least 10% of people; small nonsecretory intrasellar lesions can be safely followed with serial MRI (p.2999, p.3003).

Hormone output does not reliably track tumor size: small secretory microadenomas can be highly symptomatic, whereas large adenomas producing little hormone may stay clinically silent until mass effects appear (p.3003).

Suprasellar extension classically compresses the optic chiasm to produce bitemporal hemianopia, often worse superiorly, because crossing nasal ganglion-cell fibers in the ventral chiasm are most vulnerable; loss of red color perception can be an early sign (p.2998-2999).

The 'stalk section' phenomenon: any sellar mass that compresses the pituitary stalk and portal vessels causes early hyperprolactinemia (typically 30-100 ug/L) with later loss of other anterior pituitary hormones, even when the mass itself is not a prolactinoma (p.2998-2999).

Hyperprolactinemia is the most common pituitary hypersecretion syndrome; PRL levels above 200 ug/L almost always indicate a prolactin-secreting adenoma, while milder elevations are more often drug-induced, stalk-related, or due to hypothyroidism or renal failure (p.3004-3005).

Microprolactinomas show a marked female predominance (~20:1) and present early with amenorrhea/galactorrhea/infertility, whereas macroprolactinomas have a near 1:1 sex ratio and men tend to present later with larger, invasive tumors and mass effects (p.3005-3006).

Acromegaly is typically indolent and may go undiagnosed for a decade or more; acral and soft-tissue overgrowth (frontal bossing, prognathism, enlarged hands/feet, coarse features) plus visceromegaly are characteristic, and GH excess before epiphyseal closure causes gigantism (p.3008-3009).

Random single GH measurement is not diagnostic for acromegaly because of GH pulsatility; an age- and sex-matched IGF-1 is the screening test, and diagnosis is confirmed by failure of GH to suppress below threshold after an oral glucose load (p.3009).

Cushing's disease (corticotrope adenoma) accounts for ~70% of endogenous Cushing's syndrome, is 5-10 times more common in women, and the tumors are usually small microadenomas, about half undetectable on MRI (p.3010-3011).

Assuming PRL suppression by a dopamine agonist proves a prolactinoma: stalk-compression hyperprolactinemia from a nonfunctioning mass also falls with dopamine agonists even though the mass does not shrink.
Very high prolactin levels (>1000 ug/L) may be reported falsely low due to assay 'hook' artifact unless the sample is diluted, leading to underestimation of macroprolactinoma.
Falsely elevated PRL from biologically inactive macroprolactin can prompt unnecessary evaluation.
Diagnosing acromegaly on a single random GH level is unreliable because of GH pulsatility; IGF-1 and a glucose-suppression test are required.
Attributing every small pituitary lesion to a secretory tumor: incidental microadenomas are very common, and ~50% of ACTH adenomas are MRI-occult, so imaging cannot reliably localize the ACTH source.
Overlap in basal ACTH levels between pituitary and ectopic ACTH sources means ACTH measurement alone cannot distinguish them; dynamic testing or petrosal sampling is needed.
Mistaking iatrogenic glucocorticoid excess for endogenous Cushing's syndrome.
Headache severity correlates poorly with adenoma size; a small intrasellar tumor can cause significant headache while a large tumor may not.

Pituitary tumors are overwhelmingly benign and slow growing; true carcinomas with extracranial metastases are exceedingly rare. Outcomes depend on tumor type and size and require lifelong follow-up. Prolactinomas respond well to dopamine agonists with normoprolactinemia and gonadal recovery in roughly 80% of microadenomas and tumor shrinkage in most macroadenomas; about 20% (especially men) are dopamine-resistant, and hyperprolactinemia may resolve spontaneously in up to 30% of hyperprolactinemic patients without a visible adenoma. Surgical PRL normalization reaches ~70% for microprolactinomas but only ~40% for macroadenomas, with substantial long-term recurrence (>50% for macroadenomas). In acromegaly, untreated GH excess roughly triples mortality and shortens survival by about 10 years, driven by cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and respiratory disease and increased colon cancer risk; transsphenoidal remission is ~70% for microadenomas and under 50% for macroadenomas. Cushing's disease has a microadenoma surgical remission of ~80% (<50% for macroadenomas), with ~5% biochemical recurrence and a postoperative period of ACTH deficiency. Untreated hypercortisolism carries excess mortality, chiefly cardiovascular, plus increased infection and suicide risk.
Progressive visual field loss or new bitemporal hemianopia (chiasmal compression)
Cranial nerve III/IV/VI palsy, diplopia, ptosis, or facial numbness indicating cavernous sinus invasion
Severe sudden headache with visual loss or ophthalmoplegia suggesting pituitary apoplexy (intratumoral hemorrhage/infarction)
Signs of raised intracranial pressure: headache, vomiting, papilledema, hydrocephalus
Arginine vasopressin deficiency (polyuria) as a presenting feature, which suggests posterior pituitary involvement or a non-adenomatous lesion such as metastasis or germ cell tumor
Rapid-onset hypercortisolism with hyperpigmentation, severe myopathy, and hypokalemic alkalosis suggesting an ectopic ACTH source
Features of acute adrenal insufficiency from coexisting hypopituitarism

Pituitary adenomas are conventionally classified by size into microadenomas (<10 mm) and macroadenomas (>=10 mm, often locally invasive with parasellar extension), and by secretory phenotype into functioning (lactotrope/PRL, somatotrope/GH, corticotrope/ACTH, thyrotrope/TSH, gonadotrope/FSH-LH, or plurihormonal) versus clinically nonfunctioning (frequently gonadotrope or null-cell). Sellar mass severity is further graded by anatomic impact in Table 392-1 (compression of pituitary, optic chiasm, hypothalamus, cavernous sinus, frontal lobe, or brain), as larger/invasive tumors carry higher surgical risk and lower cure rates.

chunks.text: Pityriasis rosea is widely regarded as a self-limiting exanthem linked to reactivation of human herpesviruses 6 and 7, supported by the viral prodrome, seasonal clustering, and detection of viral markers in some patients. The eruption reflects a T-cell-mediated inflammatory response in the skin producing spongiotic dermatitis with focal parakeratosis, which accounts for the fine collarette of scale. The alignment of lesions along Langer's cleavage lines gives the distinctive distribution. A clinically indistinguishable pityriasis rosea-like eruption can be triggered by certain drugs and vaccines through a similar hypersensitivity mechanism.

Vasa praevia
Local causes such as cervical ectropion, polyp, or cervical carcinoma
Bloody show of labour
Uterine rupture
Transabdominal and confirmatory transvaginal ultrasound to localise the placenta relative to the os
Colour Doppler or MRI to evaluate for placenta accreta spectrum, especially with prior caesarean

Coagulation studies if haemorrhage is significant
Cardiotocography to assess fetal wellbeing during bleeding episodes

In placenta praevia the placenta implants in the lower uterine segment overlying or adjacent to the internal os. As the lower segment stretches and the cervix effaces in later pregnancy and labour, the inelastic placental attachment is disrupted from the underlying decidua, tearing maternal vessels and causing painless bleeding. Because the lower segment contracts poorly after delivery, the placental bed is prone to continued haemorrhage. Prior uterine scarring predisposes to abnormally adherent or invasive placentation (accreta spectrum).
Placenta praevia is placental implantation over or very close to the internal cervical os, classically presenting as painless bright-red vaginal bleeding in the second half of pregnancy
Digital vaginal examination must be avoided when praevia is suspected because it can provoke catastrophic haemorrhage; ultrasound is the diagnostic tool
Many low-lying placentas identified early in pregnancy migrate upward as the lower segment develops, so diagnosis is confirmed on later transvaginal scanning
Risk factors include previous caesarean section, prior praevia, multiparity, advanced maternal age, multiple pregnancy, and assisted conception
Prior caesarean scars raise the risk of associated placenta accreta spectrum, which should be actively sought on imaging
The fetus often lies in an abnormal (transverse or breech) presentation because the placenta occupies the lower segment
Delivery is by caesarean section for significant praevia; timing and setting are planned to allow for major haemorrhage
Management of bleeding episodes includes resuscitation, blood availability, corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity when preterm, and anti-D for rhesus-negative women
Performing a digital vaginal examination before excluding praevia
Labelling an early low-lying placenta as definitive praevia without rescanning later
Overlooking placenta accreta spectrum in women with previous caesarean and anterior praevia
Underestimating blood loss and failing to prepare adequate transfusion support
Attributing painless antepartum bleeding to a benign local cause without imaging

With antenatal diagnosis, planned caesarean delivery, and ready access to blood products, maternal and perinatal outcomes are generally good. Uncontrolled haemorrhage, particularly with coexisting accreta spectrum, remains a major cause of maternal morbidity, massive transfusion, and peripartum hysterectomy.
Heavy or recurrent vaginal bleeding causing maternal haemodynamic instability
Signs of hypovolaemic shock requiring urgent resuscitation and delivery
Imaging features of placenta accreta, increta, or percreta
Non-reassuring fetal heart pattern during a bleed
Bleeding with uterine contractions suggesting onset of labour with praevia

Uterine rupture
Preterm labour
Vasa praevia

Acute abdomen from a non-obstetric cause
Continuous cardiotocography to detect fetal compromise and uterine hypertonicity
Full blood count and serial haemoglobin
Coagulation screen including fibrinogen to identify disseminated intravascular coagulation
Group and cross-match for transfusion
Ultrasound mainly to exclude praevia rather than to confirm abruption
Kleihauer test in rhesus-negative women to quantify fetomaternal haemorrhage

Abruption begins with rupture of maternal decidual vessels, causing bleeding into the decidua basalis that splits the placenta from the uterine wall. The expanding retroplacental clot further separates the placenta, reducing the functional area for maternal-fetal exchange and provoking uterine irritability and contraction. Thromboplastins released from the disrupted placenta and decidua enter the maternal circulation and can trigger consumptive coagulopathy (disseminated intravascular coagulation), while extravasation of blood into the myometrium (Couvelaire uterus) impairs contractility and postpartum haemostasis.
Abruption is premature separation of a normally sited placenta before delivery, classically presenting with painful vaginal bleeding and a tender, firm, or hypertonic uterus
Bleeding may be concealed behind the placenta, so the degree of vaginal blood loss can badly underestimate the true haemorrhage
Risk factors include hypertension and pre-eclampsia, trauma, cocaine or tobacco use, prior abruption, polyhydramnios with rapid decompression, and thrombophilia
Fetal compromise or death can occur rapidly because the separated placenta cannot support gas exchange
It is largely a clinical diagnosis; ultrasound is insensitive and a normal scan does not exclude abruption
Disseminated intravascular coagulation is an important complication, particularly with large abruptions or fetal demise
Management depends on maternal and fetal status: resuscitation, and prompt delivery (often by caesarean) when there is fetal distress or maternal instability
Anti-D should be given to rhesus-negative women and blood products used to correct coagulopathy
Being falsely reassured by minimal external bleeding when concealed haemorrhage is severe
Relying on ultrasound to rule out abruption
Underestimating and undertreating evolving coagulopathy
Delaying delivery in the face of fetal distress or maternal instability
Failing to consider abruption after seemingly minor abdominal trauma in pregnancy

Small abruptions with a stable mother and reassuring fetus may allow expectant management with good outcomes. Large abruptions carry high risks of fetal death, maternal haemorrhage, coagulopathy, and organ injury, and abruption is a leading cause of perinatal mortality and antepartum stillbirth. Recurrence risk in future pregnancies is increased.
Maternal haemodynamic instability or shock, which may be disproportionate to visible blood loss due to concealed haemorrhage
Non-reassuring or absent fetal heart activity
Developing coagulopathy with falling fibrinogen and abnormal clotting
A rigid, exquisitely tender uterus with frequent contractions
Rapid clinical deterioration requiring emergency delivery

Acute focal lymphadenopathy of other etiologies (for bubonic plague): streptococcal or staphylococcal infection, tularemia, cat-scratch disease, tick typhus, infectious mononucleosis, lymphatic filariasis (p.1343).
Tuberculosis (in differential of fever and hemoptysis in plague-endemic areas, as a small-airborne-particle-transmitted infection) (p.1347).
Tonsillitis with peritonsillar abscess (resembles plague pharyngitis) (p.1344).
Tularemia (Francisella tularensis) (p.1343)
Cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae) (p.1343)
Tick typhus (rickettsial) (p.1343)
Infectious mononucleosis (p.1343)
Lymphatic filariasis (p.1343)
Streptococcal or staphylococcal lymphadenitis (p.1343)

Bubo aspirate (bubonic), bronchoalveolar lavage fluid or sputum (pneumonic), and blood (septicemic) are the appropriate specimens; culture of postmortem organ biopsy can also be diagnostic. Transport medium such as Cary-Blair preserves viability (p.1345).

Direct microscopy: Gram-negative coccobacilli with characteristic bipolar 'closed safety pin' appearance on Wayson or Wright-Giemsa stain; bipolar bacilli may be visible on direct blood smear in septicemic plague, indicating very high circulating bacterial numbers and a poor prognosis (p.1345).

Culture on nutrient-rich media (sheep blood agar, brain-heart infusion broth) and selective agar (MacConkey, EMB, or Yersinia-specific CIN agar); optimal growth at <37 degC (25-29 degC). Y. pestis is oxidase-negative, catalase-positive, urease-negative, indole-negative, lactose-negative, and nonmotile (distinguishing it from other Yersinia species) (p.1345).

F1 antigen detection: direct immunofluorescence and rapid immunochromatographic test strip (F1RDT), effective on bubo aspirates and sputum and widely used in endemic countries; a Pla antigen strip can detect F1-negative strains (p.1345).
PCR/RT-PCR requiring positivity for at least two Y. pestis-specific targets (e.g., caf1, pla, and chromosomal genes); FDA-authorized BioFire FilmArray panels include Y. pestis (p.1346).
Serology: rising hemagglutinating antibody titer to F1 antigen, or seroconversion/fourfold rise in paired sera; ELISA for IgG and IgM to F1 antigen (p.1345-1346).
WHO case definitions (suspected/probable/confirmed) guide presumptive diagnosis followed by reference laboratory confirmation (p.1345).

Y. pestis is a gram-negative bacterium of the order Enterobacterales that recently evolved from the enteric pathogen Y. pseudotuberculosis. It has a two-stage life cycle alternating between arthropod (flea) and a wide range of mammalian hosts. In the flea, the organism multiplies and forms biofilm-embedded aggregates in the midgut; some fleas become 'blocked' at the proventriculus and regurgitate bacteria into the bite site, while early-phase unblocked transmission also occurs. In the mammalian host, dissemination from the inoculation site is initially dependent on plasminogen activator (Pla), which activates plasminogen, degrades complement, and binds laminin, and is essential for high-level virulence and bubo formation. Bacteria are rapidly transported to regional lymph nodes where Y. pestis replicates extracellularly with full expression of antiphagocytic systems (type III secretion machinery and effectors encoded by pYV plus the F1 capsule), producing a bubo (hemorrhagic/necrotic node with thrombosed vessels, replaced architecture, and abundant bacteria). LcrV targets phagocytes and exerts an anti-inflammatory effect, and modified lipopolysaccharide minimizes Toll-like receptor 4 stimulation, prolonging high-grade bacteremia. Spread via efferent lymphatics to the thoracic duct produces high-grade bacteremia and hematogenous seeding of spleen, liver, secondary buboes, lungs (secondary plague pneumonia), and meninges, with uncontrolled septicemia leading to death; the septicemic phase can occur without an obvious prior bubo (p.1342-1343).

Plague is a systemic zoonosis caused by Yersinia pestis, predominantly affecting small rodents in rural areas of Africa, Asia, and the Americas and usually transmitted to humans by an arthropod (flea) vector; less often via contact with animal tissues or respiratory droplets (p.1341).

Three principal clinical forms: bubonic, septicemic, and pneumonic. Worldwide, bubonic plague is the predominant reported form; a minority (10-20%) present as primary septicemic or pneumonic disease (p.1343).

Bubonic plague: after a 2-6 day incubation, sudden onset of fever (>38 degC), malaise, myalgia, dizziness, and increasing pain from progressive regional lymphadenitis. The bubo is a tense, tender swelling with a boggy consistency and underlying hard core, usually solitary and erythematous with periganglionic edema, most commonly inguinal but may be crural, axillary, cervical, or submaxillary depending on bite site (p.1343).
Children most commonly present with cervical or axillary buboes; abdominal pain from intraabdominal node involvement can occur without other visible signs (p.1343).

Primary pneumonic plague follows inhalation of infectious droplets from another person or animal with plague pneumonia; short incubation (a few hours to 2-3 days, range 1-7 days) with abrupt fever, headache, myalgia, weakness, nausea, vomiting, dizziness; respiratory signs (cough, dyspnea, chest pain, sputum with hemoptysis) typically appear after 24 h (p.1344).

Primary pneumonic plague is generally the least common but most fatal of the main presentations; treated pneumonic plague has an estimated death rate of about 17% versus 98% for untreated pneumonic plague (p.1343).

Primary septicemic plague (10-25% of infections) presents as gram-negative septicemia (hypotension, shock) WITHOUT preceding lymphadenopathy; occurs in all age groups but risk is elevated in persons over 40 (p.1344).

WBC count is generally raised (10,000-20,000/uL) with neutrophilic leukocytosis and left shift; counts can be very high in children (>100,000/uL), but in some cases the WBC is normal or leukopenia develops. DIC occurs in a significant minority (p.1346).
Appropriate treatment of bubonic plague resolves fever within 2-5 days, but buboes may remain enlarged for more than a week after initial treatment and can become fluctuant (p.1344).
The term 'septicemic plague' can be confusing because most patients with buboes have detectable bacteremia at some stage, with or without systemic sepsis signs (p.1344).
Automated biochemical or mass-spectrometry identification systems can misidentify Y. pestis as Y. pseudotuberculosis or other species (p.1345).
Meningeal plague may be associated with suboptimal antimicrobial therapy (delayed treatment, penicillin use, or low-dose tetracycline) (p.1344).

A single negative rapid antigen test is insufficient to exclude plague; WHO exclusion requires two negative F1RDT tests on specimens collected 24 h apart when confirmatory tests are unavailable (p.1345-1346).

F1RDT specificity for culture-confirmed pneumonic plague was only 71%, so a positive sputum test in an endemic area identifies a probable case requiring treatment but needs additional confirmatory testing (p.1345-1346).
Culture yield can be low after prehospital antimicrobial use (as observed in the 2017 Madagascar outbreak) (p.1345).

Untreated plague carries high mortality, but it is treatable with antimicrobials. Treated pneumonic plague has an estimated death rate of about 17% compared with 98% for untreated pneumonic plague. In the United States, case-fatality fell from 66% in 1900-1941 to 16% in the post-antibiotic era (1942 onward); in 2000-2018, mortality was 8% in patients receiving any antimicrobial and 4% in those receiving currently recommended high-efficacy agents. The global case-fatality rate notified to WHO for 2013-2018 was 17%. Visible bipolar bacilli on direct blood smear signal very high bacteremia and poor prognosis (p.1343, 1345).
Pneumonic plague is transmissible person-to-person via respiratory droplets (productive cough), making it a public-health emergency requiring immediate isolation and notification (p.1344, 1347).

Aerosolized Y. pestis is a recognized potential bioterrorism agent (Tier 1 select agent); an outbreak of primary pneumonic plague in a nonendemic region or urban setting should raise concern for intentional release (p.1342, 1344, 1345).
Rapid progression of primary pneumonic plague from segmental pneumonitis to lobar and bilateral involvement with hemoptysis and ARDS within hours to days (p.1344).
Bipolar bacilli visible on direct blood smear indicate very high circulating bacterial numbers and a poor prognosis (p.1345).
Disseminated intravascular coagulation with shock in septicemic disease (p.1346).

WHO case classification of plague: Suspected case (clinical presentation suggestive of plague plus an epidemiologic context of possible exposure within 10 days of onset); Probable case (suspected case plus one of: F1 antigen detected by rapid test or immunofluorescence, a single anti-F1 serology without prior infection/immunization, or direct microscopy showing bipolar-staining gram-negative coccobacilli); Confirmed case (suspected case plus one of: isolation of Y. pestis, seroconversion or fourfold anti-F1 titer change in paired sera, or species-specific PCR positivity); Not a case (suspected case with negative confirmatory testing) (p.1345).

Autoimmune conditions: rheumatoid arthritis, myasthenia gravis, cold agglutinin disease
Post organ-transplant immunosuppression (and rarely allogeneic transplant)
Skin diseases with monoclonal gammopathy: lichen myxedematosus (papular mucinosis), necrobiotic xanthogranuloma (~10% progress to myeloma)
Mixed cryoglobulinemia (IgM/IgA complexed with IgG) seen in rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune disease, usually not associated with malignancy

In normal B-cell maturation, antigen exposure drives differentiation of mature B lymphocytes into antibody-secreting plasma cells; in plasma cell disorders this control is lost, producing a monoclonal expansion that secretes a single (monoclonal) immunoglobulin or fragment (M component). Clinical manifestations arise from neoplastic cell expansion, from the secreted products (intact immunoglobulin, free light/heavy chains, lymphokines), and from the host response. In multiple myeloma, recurrent chromosomal lesions include hyperdiploidy and 14q32 translocations (e.g., t(11;14), t(4;14), t(14;16)), with errors in immunoglobulin switch recombination implicated in early transformation. Waldenström's macroglobulinemia arises from a post-germinal-center IgM-bearing memory B cell, driven by MYD88 L265P (TLR/IL-1R IRAK and NF-kB signaling, plus BTK/HCK signaling) and frequently CXCR4 mutations. In AL amyloidosis, clonal plasma cells produce a monoclonal light chain (lambda predominates) that misfolds into insoluble amyloid fibrils deposited extracellularly in tissues (Harrison 22e p.883-884, 893; ch.117 p.896-897).

Plasma cell disorders are monoclonal neoplasms of late B-lymphocyte lineage; the group includes multiple myeloma (MM), Waldenström's macroglobulinemia, primary (AL) amyloidosis, and the heavy chain diseases, also termed monoclonal gammopathies, paraproteinemias, plasma cell dyscrasias, or dysproteinemias (Harrison 22e p.883).

In WM the IgM may have specificity for myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG); a peripheral neuropathy may precede the neoplasm and about half of these patients are anti-MAG positive (Harrison 22e p.893).

POEMS syndrome = Polyneuropathy, Organomegaly, Endocrinopathy, M-protein, and Skin changes; patients typically have a severe progressive sensorimotor polyneuropathy with sclerotic bone lesions, and polyneuropathy occurs in only ~1.4% of myelomas with POEMS being a rare subset (Harrison 22e p.893).

AL (primary) amyloidosis is a plasma cell disorder most often caused by clonal bone marrow plasma cells secreting a misfolding monoclonal light chain; it can coexist with multiple myeloma, Waldenström's macroglobulinemia, or non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (Harrison 22e ch.117 p.896-897).
Macroglossia and periorbital ('raccoon-eye') ecchymoses are pathognomonic but uncommon signs of AL amyloidosis, each seen in only ~10% of patients (Harrison 22e ch.117 p.897).

MGUS is vastly more common than myeloma, occurring in ~1% of the population aged >50 and up to ~10% of those aged >75; no specific intervention is indicated and annual (or less frequent) follow-up is adequate, with closer monitoring only for higher-risk MGUS (Harrison 22e p.887-890).
About ~1% of MGUS patients per year progress to myeloma, but essentially all cases of myeloma are preceded by MGUS (Harrison 22e p.887).

Higher-risk MGUS features are non-IgG subtype, abnormal kappa/lambda free light chain ratio, and serum M-protein >15 g/L (1.5 g/dL); absence of all three predicts ~5% progression while presence of all three predicts ~60% progression over 20 years (Harrison 22e p.887).

Diagnostic workup for a monoclonal protein uses serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) for quantitation and immunoelectrophoresis/immunofixation for confirmation of a single heavy and/or light chain; serum free light chain assay and urine studies (UPEP) detect light-chain-only and Bence Jones disease (Harrison 22e p.883-884).

An M component must be present at ~5 g/L (0.5 g/dL) to be accurately quantitated by electrophoresis; the serum M-protein level is a reliable measure of tumor burden but is not specific enough to screen asymptomatic patients (Harrison 22e p.883-884).

MGUS diagnostic criteria: serum monoclonal protein (non-IgM) <30 g/L, clonal bone marrow plasma cells <10%, and absence of myeloma-defining events or amyloidosis attributable to the plasma cell disorder (Harrison 22e p.888, Table 116-1).

Waldenström's macroglobulinemia (WM) is a malignancy of IgM-secreting lymphoplasmacytoid cells; unlike myeloma it presents with lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly and its major manifestation is hyperviscosity syndrome (Harrison 22e p.893).

A distinct MYD88 L265P somatic mutation is present in >90% of WM patients and the majority of IgM MGUS, and is used as a diagnostic test to discriminate WM from marginal zone lymphoma, IgM-secreting myeloma, and CLL with plasmacytic differentiation (Harrison 22e p.893).

Do not equate a monoclonal protein with malignancy: distinguish MGUS (clonal marrow plasma cells <10%, M-protein <30 g/L, no myeloma-defining events/amyloidosis) from multiple myeloma, which requires marrow plasmacytosis and myeloma-defining events / CRAB end-organ damage (Harrison 22e p.887-888).

SPEP/UPEP are useful in myeloma but are NOT adequate screening tests for AL amyloidosis, because the clonal light chain is often insufficient to produce an M-spike; use serum/urine immunofixation and free light chain assay (>90% positive) (Harrison 22e ch.117 p.897).

A monoclonal protein alone is not diagnostic of amyloidosis since MGUS is common in older patients; when MGUS coexists with biopsy-proven amyloidosis, AL type must be ruled out and 'smoldering myeloma' patients should be screened for AL (Harrison 22e ch.117 p.897).

WM does not cause bone lesions or hypercalcemia (unlike myeloma); large IgM paraprotein causes little renal excretion so renal disease is uncommon (~20% excrete light chains)—reserve the diagnosis of IgM myeloma for lytic bone lesions with CD138+ plasma cells and t(11;14) (Harrison 22e p.893).
Suspected cryoglobulin: draw blood into a warm syringe and transport in warm water to avoid errors in quantitation (Harrison 22e p.893).
Rituximab can produce an IgM flare in WM—use plasmapheresis first or initially withhold rituximab in patients with high IgM levels (Harrison 22e p.894).
Pseudohyponatremia and a decreased anion gap can occur in myeloma because the cationic M component retains chloride and displaces serum water (Harrison 22e p.887).

MGUS carries a low malignant potential, with ~1% per year progression to myeloma (risk stratified by IgG vs non-IgG subtype, free light chain ratio, and M-protein level: ~5% at 20 years with no risk features vs ~60% with all three). Smoldering myeloma progresses to symptomatic MM in ~25% at 5 years with one risk feature and ~76% with all three high-risk features. Waldenström's macroglobulinemia is often indolent and may not require therapy; median survival is reported as ~50 months, with older age, male sex, general symptoms, and cytopenias defining a high-risk group. AL amyloidosis is often rapidly progressive and fatal if untreated (occurs after age 40); very low dFLC (<50 mg/L) predicts significantly better outcome (Harrison 22e p.887-888, 893-894; ch.117 p.896-898).

Hyperviscosity syndrome in Waldenström's macroglobulinemia / IgM gammopathy: headache, visual disturbance, retinal vein segmentation and dilation, epistaxis, altered consciousness, paresis (most IgM is intravascular and responds to plasmapheresis)
Myeloma-defining end-organ damage (CRAB): hyperCalcemia, Renal insufficiency, Anemia, Bone lytic lesions
Spinal cord compression: new lower-extremity neurologic deficit, severe localized back pain, or loss of bowel/bladder control requiring emergency MRI and radiation/decompression
Acute renal failure from light chain cast nephropathy, especially with dehydration
Cardiac involvement in AL amyloidosis (70-80%) is the leading cause of death; low-voltage ECG with pseudo-infarct pattern and thickened ventricles on echo
MGUS with severe polyneuropathy (consider causal IgM/anti-MAG neuropathy)

MGUS vs smoldering (asymptomatic) myeloma vs symptomatic multiple myeloma per IMWG criteria (Harrison Table 116-1). MGUS: non-IgM serum M-protein <30 g/L, clonal marrow plasma cells <10%, no myeloma-defining events/amyloidosis. Smoldering MM: serum M-protein (IgG/IgA) >=30 g/L or urine M-protein >=500 mg/24h and/or clonal marrow plasma cells 10-60%, without myeloma-defining events. Symptomatic MM: clonal plasma cells (or plasmacytoma) plus a myeloma-defining event—CRAB end-organ damage (hyperCalcemia, Renal insufficiency, Anemia, Bone lesions) or a biomarker of malignancy (clonal marrow plasma cells >=60%, involved:uninvolved serum free light chain ratio >=100, or >1 focal MRI lesion). POEMS requires polyneuropathy + monoclonal plasma cell disorder + (sclerotic bone lesions / Castleman's / elevated VEGF) + an additional system feature.

Hemostasis depends on platelets and the vessel wall. Platelets are activated on adhesion to von Willebrand factor (VWF) and collagen in exposed subendothelium after injury; adhesion (primarily via VWF) generates signals activating the GpIIb/IIIa (alphaIIb-beta3) receptor and aggregation, with release of granule contents and stabilization by a fibrin mesh. Normal platelet count is 150,000-450,000/uL; thrombopoietin (TPO), made in the liver, is the major regulator, and roughly one-third of platelets reside in the spleen. Thrombocytopenia results from decreased production, splenic sequestration, and/or increased destruction. In HIT, antibodies form to a complex of platelet factor 4 (PF4) and heparin/glycosaminoglycans; the anti-heparin/PF4 antibody activates platelets via the FcgammaRIIa receptor and also activates monocytes, endothelium, and coagulation, producing a prothrombotic state. ITP is immune-mediated platelet destruction with possible inhibition of platelet release from megakaryocytes. In TTP, deficiency of or antibodies to the metalloprotease ADAMTS13 leave ultra-large VWF multimers uncleaved, driving pathogenic platelet adhesion/aggregation and microvascular thrombosis. HUS features acute renal failure with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia; atypical HUS arises from genetic complement-regulatory defects or anti-complement-regulator antibodies causing chronic complement activation.

Thrombocytopenia arises from one or more of three mechanisms: decreased bone marrow production, sequestration (usually in an enlarged spleen), and/or increased platelet destruction (Harrison 22e p.921).

In thrombotic microangiopathies (TTP/HUS) the PT and aPTT are characteristically normal, which helps distinguish them from DIC, where a coagulopathy predominates with elevated PT and often aPTT (Harrison 22e p.924-925).
An ADAMTS13 activity level of <10% is diagnostic of TTP (Harrison 22e p.925).

Markedly elevated platelet counts (>1.5 million), usually in a myeloproliferative disorder, carry an increased risk of bleeding rather than thrombosis, due in part to acquired von Willebrand disease (Harrison 22e p.926).
First step in evaluating thrombocytopenia is reviewing the peripheral blood smear and ruling out pseudothrombocytopenia, especially when there is no apparent cause (Harrison 22e p.921).

Petechiae are pinpoint, nonblanching hemorrhages that usually signify a decreased platelet number rather than platelet dysfunction; they first appear in areas of increased venous pressure (ankles/feet in ambulatory patients) (Harrison 22e p.921-922).

Wet purpura (blood blisters on the oral mucosa) and retinal hemorrhages are thought to denote an increased risk of life-threatening hemorrhage in the thrombocytopenic patient (Harrison 22e p.922, 924).

Drugs are the most common cause of thrombocytopenia; in a patient with no apparent cause, all drugs (including herbal and OTC preparations) should be suspect and stopped or substituted if possible (Harrison 22e p.922).

Infection is the most common noniatrogenic cause of thrombocytopenia; viral and bacterial infections can affect both platelet production and survival, and immune mechanisms may also contribute (Harrison 22e p.921-922).
In HIT, thrombocytopenia is usually not severe (nadir rarely <20,000/uL) and is not associated with bleeding; instead it markedly increases the risk of thrombosis (Harrison 22e p.923).
Most patients develop HIT 5-14 days after heparin exposure; onset before 5 days suggests prior heparin exposure within ~100 days with circulating anti-heparin/PF4 antibodies (Harrison 22e p.923).
ITP is characterized by mucocutaneous bleeding and a low, often very low, platelet count with an otherwise normal peripheral blood smear and cell counts (Harrison 22e p.924).
Pseudothrombocytopenia: EDTA-induced platelet agglutination is an in vitro artifact and not true thrombocytopenia; confirm with a smear and a count in citrate/heparin or fresh fingerstick blood.
Anti-heparin/PF4 antibodies are common without clinical disease (e.g., ~50% after cardiopulmonary bypass), so the HIT immunoassay has low specificity; HIT remains a clinical diagnosis.
The 4T score is very useful for excluding HIT but overdiagnoses it in settings (e.g., ICU) where thrombocytopenia and thrombosis from other causes are common.
LMWH cross-reacts with HIT antibodies and must not be used to treat HIT.
Starting warfarin alone in HIT/HITT may precipitate thrombosis and venous gangrene; overlap with a DTI, fondaparinux, or DOAC and start only after thrombocytopenia resolves.
Serologic (antibody) testing in ITP is generally unhelpful due to low sensitivity and specificity.
Plasma infusion/exchange has not been shown to alter the overall course of HUS or atypical HUS (except aHUS with antibodies to factor H).
Petechiae indicate decreased platelet number, not platelet dysfunction -- excessive bruising can occur with disorders of either number or function.

ITP: in children usually acute, post-infectious, and self-limited; in adults more chronic, though some remit spontaneously within months. Patients with platelet counts >30,000/uL appear not to have increased mortality from the thrombocytopenia. TTP: introduction of plasma exchange reduced mortality from 85-100% to 10-30%; however 25-45% relapse within 30 days of remission and 12-40% have late relapses, with relapses more frequent in those with severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. HUS: diarrhea-associated HUS has overall mortality <5% (about 40% of children need dialysis), whereas non-diarrhea-associated HUS mortality is higher (~26%). VITT is fatal in about 20%.
HIT: thrombosis (venous and/or arterial) despite a falling platelet count -- stop all heparin immediately (including LMWH, which cross-reacts) and start a non-heparin anticoagulant
Wet purpura (oral mucosal blood blisters) and retinal hemorrhages herald life-threatening, including CNS, bleeding
VITT: high D-dimer with thrombosis in unusual sites such as cerebral venous sinuses (fatal in ~20%)
New thrombocytopenia with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes) suggesting TTP -- a devastating disease if not promptly diagnosed and treated
Severe thrombocytopenia (<5000/uL) or signs of impending bleeding in ITP requiring urgent inpatient combined-modality therapy
Introducing warfarin alone in HIT/HITT may precipitate thrombosis (e.g., venous gangrene) due to reduced protein C and S

No single formal grading scale is given; clinically meaningful thresholds noted: ~5000-10,000/uL platelets needed to maintain microvascular integrity; severe ITP thrombocytopenia <5000/uL (or impending bleeding) warrants inpatient combined-modality therapy; ITP counts >30,000/uL not associated with increased mortality; HIT nadir rarely <20,000/uL; ADAMTS13 activity <10% diagnostic of TTP; platelet counts >1.5 million (myeloproliferative) carry bleeding risk. The 4Ts score is used for HIT pretest probability.

Cirrhosis / hepatic hydrothorax (often right-sided) (Harrison 22e p.366, p.373)
Nephrotic syndrome and other hypoalbuminemic states (Harrison 22e p.422)
Parapneumonic effusion / empyema complicating pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.1235)
Malignant effusion (e.g., lung cancer, metastatic disease) (Harrison 22e p.662)
Tuberculous pleurisy (Harrison 22e p.1430)
Pulmonary embolism (Harrison 22e p.314)
Tuberculous pleural effusion — straw-colored (sometimes hemorrhagic) lymphocyte-predominant exudate that can mimic a parapneumonic or malignant effusion (Harrison 22e p.1430).
Tuberculous empyema, usually from rupture of a cavity into the pleural space, sometimes with a bronchopleural fistula and air in the pleural space (Harrison 22e p.1431).
Spontaneous bacterial empyema complicating hepatic hydrothorax in cirrhosis (Harrison 22e p.373).
Diagnostic thoracentesis to determine whether the fluid is a transudate or an exudate and to identify the underlying cause (Harrison 22e p.1430).
Pleural fluid pH — a value of ≤7.1 in a parapneumonic setting indicates empyema requiring drainage (Harrison 22e p.1235).

Pleural fluid protein, glucose, and cell count/differential; in TB the fluid is an exudate with protein >50% of serum (often ~4-6 g/dL), normal-to-low glucose, pH ~7.3 (occasionally <7.2), and 500-6000 WBC/uL, with neutrophils early and lymphocyte predominance later (Harrison 22e p.1430).
Pleural fluid adenosine deaminase (ADA) — an elevated level is consistent with TB and a very low level helps exclude it (Harrison 22e p.1430).
Pleural fluid IFN-gamma and lysozyme as adjuncts for suspected tuberculous effusion (Harrison 22e p.1430).
Pleural fluid cytology for malignancy, with repeat thoracentesis if the first sample is negative (Harrison 22e p.663).
Needle (closed) pleural biopsy for suspected TB, which reveals granulomas and/or yields positive culture in up to ~80% of cases and is favored over fluid analysis (Harrison 22e p.1430).
Xpert MTB/RIF on pleural biopsy tissue (positive in ~75%); testing pleural fluid itself with this assay is not recommended owing to low sensitivity (Harrison 22e p.1430).
Serum-to-pleural-fluid albumin gradient — a value >=1.1 g/dL suggests hepatic hydrothorax (Harrison 22e p.373).
Heart-failure transudate, which can be unilateral and be mistaken for a localized pathologic effusion (Harrison 22e p.314).
Hepatic hydrothorax from cirrhosis, mimicking other right-sided effusions (Harrison 22e p.366, p.373).
Malignant effusion, which may be exudative or bloody and can coexist with or be confused for a parapneumonic effusion (Harrison 22e p.663).

Fluid abnormally accumulates in the pleural space when the balance of hydrostatic and oncotic forces, lymphatic drainage, or capillary permeability is disturbed. Transudates arise from systemic forces (raised hydrostatic pressure or low plasma oncotic pressure) as in the sodium-avid edematous states of heart failure, cirrhosis, and nephrotic syndrome (Harrison 22e p.422). Exudates result from local pleural or capillary processes such as infection, malignancy, or inflammation. In hepatic hydrothorax, ascitic fluid migrates through diaphragmatic fenestrae into the pleural space (Harrison 22e p.373). Tuberculous effusion typically reflects a hypersensitivity reaction to mycobacterial antigens after recent primary infection, or contiguous spread from parenchymal disease (Harrison 22e p.1430). Malignant effusions arise from pleural involvement or from lymphatic obstruction by tumor (Harrison 22e p.662).

On examination an effusion gives dullness to percussion, reduced or absent breath sounds, and decreased tactile fremitus over the fluid; this contrasts with consolidation, where fremitus is increased (Harrison 22e p.2243).
Percussion helps separate the two causes of a quiet hemithorax: an effusion is dull, whereas a pneumothorax is hyper-resonant (Harrison 22e p.2243).
Skodaic resonance, a band of hyper-resonance just above the dull effusion, is a classic percussion sign (Harrison 22e p.89).

Bilateral effusions are characteristic of congestive heart failure (and some collagen-vascular disorders), whereas a unilateral effusion should raise suspicion of malignancy or pulmonary embolism, though heart failure and parapneumonic effusion can also be unilateral (Harrison 22e p.314).
A right-sided pleural effusion can occur in advanced cirrhosis even when no ascites is clinically detectable (Harrison 22e p.366).
In a malignant effusion an initially negative thoracentesis does not exclude cancer; repeating the tap is essential because cytologic yield improves with repeat sampling (Harrison 22e p.663).
Avoid attributing every quiet, dull hemithorax to effusion — confirm with percussion and fremitus, since pneumothorax and consolidation differ (Harrison 22e p.2243).
A negative initial pleural cytology does not rule out malignancy; failing to repeat the tap is a diagnostic pitfall (Harrison 22e p.663).
Do not assume a unilateral effusion is benign heart failure — it may be malignant or embolic (Harrison 22e p.314).
Testing pleural fluid (rather than biopsy tissue) with Xpert MTB/RIF is unreliable for TB because of low sensitivity (Harrison 22e p.1430).
AFB smears are rarely positive and cultures are often falsely negative in tuberculous effusions, so a negative smear/culture does not exclude pleural TB (Harrison 22e p.1430).
In hepatic hydrothorax, chest-tube placement should be avoided (Harrison 22e p.373).

Tuberculous pleural effusion responds rapidly to antituberculous chemotherapy and may even resolve spontaneously; concurrent glucocorticoids may shorten fever and chest pain but are of unproven benefit (Harrison 22e p.1430). Parapneumonic effusions are usually a self-limited inflammatory response, whereas a true empyema requires drainage and carries a worse course if undrained (Harrison 22e p.1235).

Frank pus, organisms on microscopy, or pleural fluid pH <=7.1 in a parapneumonic effusion — diagnostic of empyema and mandates aggressive complete drainage, usually via chest tube (Harrison 22e p.1235).
New or persistent fever and leukocytosis after 4-5 days of appropriate antibiotics for pneumonia — suspect empyema (Harrison 22e p.1235).
Exudative or bloody effusion — raises concern for malignancy (Harrison 22e p.663).
Unilateral effusion without an obvious cause — investigate for malignancy or pulmonary embolism (Harrison 22e p.314).

Parapneumonic effusions are distinguished from empyema by their character: an uncomplicated parapneumonic effusion is a self-limited reaction to adjacent pneumonia, whereas frank pus, visible organisms, or a pleural fluid pH <=7.1 defines empyema (a complicated/infected collection) that requires complete drainage (Harrison 22e p.1235).

chunks.text: PMR sits on the same disease spectrum as giant cell arteritis, an antigen-driven panarteritis of medium- and large-sized vessels with mononuclear infiltrates and frequent giant cell formation. Activated CD4+ T lymphocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells are central; restricted clonal T-cell receptor expansion suggests an antigen residing in the arterial wall. Two CD4 T-cell lineages (IFN-gamma-producing TH1 and IL-17-producing TH17) participate in vascular inflammation, with IL-6 signaling driving hepatic acute-phase protein (CRP, and effects on ESR) production. Familial aggregation and HLA-DR4 / HLA-DRB1*04 associations have been reported for the GCA end of the spectrum (p.2945).

Pneumococci are encapsulated gram-positive diplococci that colonise the human nasopharynx from an early age; colonisation is common while disease is rare. All pneumococcal infection ultimately stems from nasopharyngeal acquisition. The anti-phagocytic polysaccharide capsule is the key virulence determinant, resisting complement deposition in the absence of type-specific antibody. The organism dynamically modulates capsule expression: it downregulates capsule in the nasopharynx (rough colonies) to evade immune recognition and upregulates it on tissue invasion (smooth colonies). From the nasopharynx, organisms spread haematogenously to distant sites (brain, joints, bone, peritoneum) or locally to mucosal surfaces (otitis media, pneumonia). Intercurrent viral respiratory infection increases susceptibility by upregulating epithelial adhesion factors, permitting adhesion via surface adhesins (PsaA, PspA, CbpA/PspC, pneumolysin, neuraminidases). Disease pathology is driven by host inflammation: cell-wall teichoic acids and peptidoglycan induce IL-1, IL-6, and TNF and activate the alternative complement pathway, and pneumolysin drives proinflammatory cytokine release. Host defence depends on intact respiratory epithelium, the cough reflex and mucociliary escalator, splenic function, complement, neutrophils/macrophages, CRP binding of cell-wall phosphorylcholine, and TLR2/TLR4 recognition, together with acquired anticapsular IgG (Harrison 22e p.1190-1191).
S. pneumoniae can infect nearly any tissue; the four most common syndromes are otitis media, pneumonia, bacteraemia, and meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1191).

There is no pathognomonic presentation of pneumococcal disease, and a microbiologically confirmed diagnosis is made in only a minority of cases, so empirical therapy covering S. pneumoniae is often indicated (Harrison 22e p.1191).

In the elderly, pneumococcal pneumonia may present non-specifically with confusion or malaise without fever or cough; a high index of suspicion is required because delayed treatment leads to rapid, severe deterioration (Harrison 22e p.1192).

Pneumococcal pneumonia can mimic an acute abdomen (upper abdominal pain from diaphragmatic pleural involvement); clinicians should remember to keep this non-abdominal process in the differential (Harrison 22e p.1192).

Now that H. influenzae type b vaccine is in routine childhood use, S. pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis are the most common bacterial causes of meningitis in both adults and children (Harrison 22e p.1193).

Pneumococcal meningitis can be a primary presentation or a complication of skull fracture, otitis media, mastoiditis, or bacteraemia; most cases arise from haematogenous spread rather than direct extension (Harrison 22e p.1191, 1193).

A positive urinary pneumococcal antigen test is useful for etiologic attribution in adults (low nasopharyngeal colonization) but is generally uninformative in children and in high-colonization low-income settings (Harrison 22e p.1192-1193).
Most pneumococcal pneumonia is non-bacteraemic; only ~5-20% of cases are accompanied by bacteraemia, and blood cultures are positive in fewer than 30% of cases (Harrison 22e p.1190, 1192).

Empyema is the most common focal complication of pneumococcal pneumonia (<5% of cases); pleural fluid with frank pus, visible bacteria, or pH <=7.1 indicates empyema and demands complete drainage (Harrison 22e p.1192).
Treating an apparent acute abdomen while overlooking pneumococcal lower-lobe pneumonia causing referred abdominal pain (Harrison 22e p.1192).
Relying on a normal early chest radiograph to exclude pneumonia; an infiltrate may be absent early or with dehydration and appear after rehydration (Harrison 22e p.1192).
Over-interpreting a positive urinary pneumococcal antigen in children or in high-colonization settings, where it does not reliably attribute etiology (Harrison 22e p.1192-1193).
Diagnosing otitis media from tympanic-membrane redness alone, which is insufficient (Harrison 22e p.1193).
Attributing round/spherical consolidation solely to pneumococcus without considering other causes, especially cancer (Harrison 22e p.1192).

Assuming PPSV23 reliably prevents non-bacteraemic pneumococcal pneumonia, particularly in the elderly and immunodeficient, where effectiveness is reduced and protection wanes after ~5 years (Harrison 22e p.1194).

Case-fatality varies with age, comorbidity, disease severity at presentation, and access to care. For pneumococcal pneumonia, CFR ranges from <5% in hospitalised patients aged 18-44 to >12% in those over 65, even with timely management; severity at presentation (rather than the presence of bacteraemia) drives mortality, and early deaths reflect a rapidly progressive cascade that often unfolds irrespective of antibiotic administration. Pneumococcal meningitis carries a mortality of ~20%, and up to 50% of survivors have acute or chronic sequelae (deafness, hydrocephalus, and cognitive impairment in children; diffuse brain swelling, subarachnoid bleeding, hydrocephalus, cerebrovascular complications, and hearing loss in adults) (Harrison 22e p.1190, 1193).

Pneumococcal syndromes are classified as invasive (a normally sterile site is infected or bacteraemia is present, e.g., bacteraemic pneumonia, meningitis, bacteraemia) versus noninvasive (contiguous spread, e.g., otitis media, sinusitis, bronchitis); whether non-bacteraemic pneumonia counts as invasive is debated. In children, WHO IMCI algorithms stratify illness by danger signs (very severe disease: inability to drink, convulsions, lethargy, severe malnutrition) and by cough with tachypnoea plus lower chest-wall indrawing to guide antibiotics and referral; no equivalent validated algorithm exists for adults (Harrison 22e p.1191).

Pneumocystis jirovecii is a fungus with unique tropism for the lung. Organisms are inhaled into the alveolar space, presumably after being exhaled by another human; most people are exposed and infected early in life. Disease may arise from primary infection, reinfection, or reactivation of latent infection. Clinically apparent pneumonia occurs only in immunocompromised hosts, where defects in cellular and/or humoral immunity (congenital, HIV-related, or drug-induced) permit proliferation. CD4+ T cells are critical for host defence. The organism proliferates in the lung provoking a mononuclear cell response; alveoli fill with proteinaceous material and alveolar-capillary injury with surfactant abnormalities develops. Stained sections show foamy, vacuolated alveolar exudates of viable and nonviable organisms, with interstitial oedema and fibrosis. Much of the clinical deterioration after starting specific therapy is attributed to enhanced inflammation from dying organisms, the rationale for adjunctive glucocorticoids (Harrison 22e p.1731-1734).
Caused by the fungus Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly P. carinii); the organism cannot be cultured and is host-specific to humans, infecting only via other humans (Harrison 22e p.1730-1731).

Since the organism cannot be cultured, diagnosis relies on staining of cyst or trophozoite forms in lung tissue/secretions with methenamine silver, toluidine blue O, Giemsa, or specific immunofluorescent antibody (Harrison 22e p.1733).

An induced sputum sample, when obtained and interpreted by an experienced provider, can be highly sensitive and specific, but sensitivity is widely variable (55-90%); expectorated sputum and throat swabs have very low sensitivity (Harrison 22e p.1733).

Adjunctive glucocorticoids improve survival in moderate-to-severe disease (initial room-air PaO2 <70 mmHg or alveolar-arterial gradient >=35 mmHg) by reducing the inflammation that follows organism die-off once specific therapy begins; they should be started when PCP therapy is initiated, even if the diagnosis is only suspected (Harrison 22e p.1734).

Prophylaxis is the cornerstone of prevention; for HIV, CD4+ counts <200/uL (or CD4 percentage <15) are an indication to start or continue chemoprophylaxis, alongside prior PCP, unexplained prolonged fever, or recent oropharyngeal candidiasis (Harrison 22e p.1734).
PCP now occurs more often from non-HIV-related immunosuppression than from HIV infection in many health care systems (Harrison 22e p.1731).

An opportunistic pathogen of immunocompromised hosts: HIV infection, organ transplantation, haematologic malignancy, and those on high-dose glucocorticoids or certain immunosuppressive monoclonal antibodies (Harrison 22e p.1730).
Among people with HIV, PCP incidence is inversely related to CD4+ T-cell count: at least 80% of cases occur at counts <200/uL and most actually develop at counts <100/uL (Harrison 22e p.1731-1732).

Classic presentation is acute or subacute pneumonia, often beginning with a vague sense of dyspnoea alone, then progressing to fever, nonproductive cough, and progressive shortness of breath (Harrison 22e p.1731).
Decreased oxygen saturation at rest or with exertion is characteristic; untreated it progresses to severe hypoxaemia (Harrison 22e p.1731).
Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is often elevated from pulmonary damage (Harrison 22e p.1731).
Classic chest radiograph shows diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates that are perihilar and symmetric, which can progress to alveolar filling (Harrison 22e p.1731).
High-resolution chest CT shows diffuse ground-glass opacities in virtually all PCP patients, often before the plain chest radiograph becomes abnormal (Harrison 22e p.1731).
Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) is the most common sampling method; demonstration of organisms in BAL fluid is almost 100% sensitive and specific for PCP (Harrison 22e p.1733).
A normal LDH does not rule out PCP, and an elevated LDH is not specific for PCP (Harrison 22e p.1731).
PCP can occur at CD4+ counts >200/uL in HIV (uncommon, especially at counts well above 200), and in non-HIV immunosuppression a CD4+ count >200/uL does not imply protection (Harrison 22e p.1731).

PCR is so sensitive that it cannot reliably distinguish colonization from true pneumonia; there is no validated PCR threshold, so a positive result does not definitively attribute disease to Pneumocystis (Harrison 22e p.1733).
Serum/BAL (1->3)-beta-D-glucan and serum PCR are not sufficiently sensitive or specific to establish or exclude PCP (Harrison 22e p.1733).
If treated with specific therapy but without corticosteroids, patients of any severity often deteriorate during the first few days from inflammation induced by dying organisms (Harrison 22e p.1733).
Initial chest radiograph may be normal in mild disease, and the classic dense perihilar infiltrate is unusual in AIDS; relying on plain film can delay diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1730-1731).
Extrapulmonary pneumocystosis is rare and nonspecific; when present, the priority is to look for another concurrent infectious or neoplastic process (Harrison 22e p.1733).

Untreated, PCP is invariably fatal. HIV-associated disease is often indolent, presenting early as mild exercise intolerance or chest tightness without fever or cough and a normal or near-normal chest radiograph, then progressing over days to months to fever, cough, diffuse alveolar infiltrates, and profound hypoxaemia; non-HIV immunosuppressed patients more often have acute disease progressing over days to respiratory failure. Mortality is influenced by age, degree of immunosuppression, preexisting lung disease, need for mechanical ventilation, and development of pneumothorax. With advances in critical care, prognosis for those requiring intubation has improved and depends largely on comorbidities and the underlying disease (Harrison 22e p.1733).

Severity is staged largely by oxygenation. Moderate-to-severe disease is defined by an initial room-air PaO2 <70 mmHg or an alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient >=35 mmHg; this threshold identifies patients (with HIV, and probably other immunodeficiencies) who benefit from adjunctive glucocorticoids in addition to specific antimicrobial therapy. Arterial blood-gas measurement both aids diagnosis and directs treatment by staging severity (Harrison 22e p.1731, 1734).

Pneumothorax is the accumulation of gas in the pleural space. In primary spontaneous pneumothorax, apical subpleural blebs rupture, allowing air to enter the pleural space without preceding trauma and in the absence of underlying lung disease. Secondary pneumothorax occurs when the same process complicates established lung disease, where loss of pulmonary reserve makes the event more dangerous. Traumatic pneumothorax results from penetrating or non-penetrating chest injury, and iatrogenic pneumothorax (a traumatic subtype) follows procedures such as transthoracic needle aspiration, thoracentesis, or central venous catheter insertion. In a tension pneumothorax, a one-way valve effect produces pleural pressure that remains positive across the whole respiratory cycle; this both severely compromises ventilation and transmits positive pressure to the mediastinum, reducing venous return to the heart and thereby cardiac output (Harrison 22e p.2313, p.2314).

Pneumothorax is simply gas within the pleural space; classify it as spontaneous (no preceding trauma) versus traumatic, and spontaneous further as primary (no underlying lung disease) versus secondary (underlying lung disease present) (Harrison 22e p.2313).
A tension pneumothorax is defined physiologically as one in which pleural pressure stays positive throughout the entire respiratory cycle (Harrison 22e p.2313).

Tension pneumothorax should be treated as a clinical emergency on the basis of bedside findings; do not wait for a confirmatory chest radiograph before relieving the pressure, because untreated tension leads to death from inadequate cardiac output or severe hypoxemia (Harrison 22e p.2314).

When a tension pneumothorax is suspected, decompression precedes imaging: a large-bore needle is placed into the pleural space and a rush of escaping gas confirms the diagnosis (knowledge principle; no dose/technique detail) (Harrison 22e p.2314).
Primary spontaneous pneumothorax typically results from rupture of small apical subpleural blebs (cystic spaces within or just beneath the visceral pleura) (Harrison 22e p.2313).
Classic primary spontaneous pneumothorax patient is a young, tall, thin man; smoking, male sex, family history, and Marfan syndrome are recognized risk factors (Harrison 22e p.104, p.105).
Symptom onset in primary spontaneous pneumothorax is usually sudden but dyspnea can be mild, so presentation to care is sometimes delayed (Harrison 22e p.104).

Tension pneumothorax most often arises during mechanical ventilation or resuscitation; difficulty ventilating during resuscitation or high peak inspiratory pressures on the ventilator should strongly raise suspicion (Harrison 22e p.2314).
Persistent air leak is a recognized entity, defined as a non-resolving pneumothorax with an air leak lasting longer than about 5-7 days (Harrison 22e p.2273).
Waiting for a chest radiograph to confirm a suspected tension pneumothorax instead of decompressing immediately — tension is a clinical diagnosis and delay can be fatal (Harrison 22e p.2314).
Underestimating a secondary pneumothorax in a patient with COPD, asthma, or cystic fibrosis; because of poor reserve it can be far more dangerous than a primary event (Harrison 22e p.104, p.2313).
Mild dyspnea in primary spontaneous pneumothorax can lead to delayed presentation, so a benign-seeming history does not exclude it (Harrison 22e p.104).
Forgetting iatrogenic pneumothorax after thoracentesis, transthoracic needle aspiration, or central line placement (Harrison 22e p.2314).
Attributing absent or diminished breath sounds to effusion when percussion (hyper-resonant in pneumothorax, dull in effusion) would distinguish them (Harrison 22e respiratory-examination chapter).
Overlooking tension pneumothorax as a reversible cause of PEA arrest and obstructive shock (Harrison 22e shock and cardiac-arrest chapters).

Roughly half of patients with an initial primary spontaneous pneumothorax experience a recurrence. Secondary pneumothorax carries a worse outlook than pneumothorax in otherwise normal lungs because the underlying lung disease leaves little pulmonary reserve, making the event potentially more life-threatening. Untreated tension pneumothorax is rapidly fatal from inadequate cardiac output or severe hypoxemia (Harrison 22e p.2313, p.2314).

Tracheal/mediastinal shift to the contralateral side, absent breath sounds over an enlarged hemithorax, hyperresonant percussion, and hypotension — the bedside signs of tension pneumothorax (Harrison 22e p.2314).
Hemodynamic collapse from trapped intrathoracic air defines tension pneumothorax as a medical emergency (Harrison 22e p.104).

Tension pneumothorax is a cause of obstructive shock and of pulseless electrical activity (PEA) arrest, and is a reversible cause to consider during resuscitation (Harrison 22e shock and cardiac-arrest chapters).
Pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory systolic fall greater than 10 mmHg) can accompany tension pneumothorax and signals significant hemodynamic compromise (Harrison 22e p.1813).
Tachycardia and hypotension in a patient with chest discomfort should trigger rapid evaluation for the most lethal causes, including tension pneumothorax (Harrison 22e p.105).
Difficulty ventilating during resuscitation or rising peak inspiratory pressures on mechanical ventilation should prompt urgent suspicion of tension pneumothorax (Harrison 22e p.2314).

Harrison classifies pneumothorax by mechanism and risk rather than a numeric score: (1) primary spontaneous (no underlying lung disease, often young tall thin smokers, frequently manageable conservatively if asymptomatic/minimally symptomatic); (2) secondary spontaneous (underlying lung disease present, e.g., COPD, asthma, cystic fibrosis — more life-threatening because of limited reserve); (3) traumatic, including the increasingly common iatrogenic subtype; and (4) tension pneumothorax, defined by positive pleural pressure throughout the respiratory cycle and treated as a medical emergency. Persistent air leak is a recognized complication defined as a non-resolving pneumothorax with air leak beyond about 5-7 days (Harrison 22e p.2313, p.2314, p.2273).
CXR (or POCUS)
Decompress if tension

Sudden pleuritic pain with breathlessness and reduced breath sounds suggests pneumothorax.
Red flags: Tension pneumothorax → immediate needle decompression

[guideline] management → Supplemental oxygen Relieves hypoxia and accelerates reabsorption of pleural air in conservatively managed pneumothorax. Definitive management is procedural (needle decompression/aspiration/chest drain).
