Poisoning is the development of dose-related adverse effects from exposure to chemicals, drugs, or other xenobiotics. Effects may be local (skin, eyes, lungs) or systemic depending on the route of exposure and the chemical's physical properties and mechanism of action. Toxidromes reflect the net effect on autonomic and neuromuscular function: stimulated states arise from sympathetic, anticholinergic, or hallucinogen activity or from drug withdrawal; depressed states from functional sympatholytics, cholinergic agents, opioids, and sedative-hypnotic GABAergic agents; discordant states from asphyxiants, CNS syndromes, membrane-active agents, and anion-gap metabolic acidosis inducers. In opioid and sedative-hypnotic poisoning, vital-sign derangement is secondary to depression of central cardiovascular and respiratory centers (or resulting hypoxemia) and is seen only with marked depression of consciousness, whereas direct/peripheral sympatholytics can cause prominent cardiovascular depression without comparable CNS depression. Some agents (acetaminophen, ethylene glycol, methanol) owe their toxicity to metabolites more toxic than the parent compound.

Poisoning severity is dose-related, but individual responses to a given dose vary with genetic polymorphisms, enzyme induction or inhibition from co-ingested xenobiotics, and acquired tolerance; the functional reserve of the target organ (influenced by age and preexisting disease) also shapes severity and reversibility.
Symptomatic patients (e.g., apnea from opioids) should be managed on the basis of history, examination, and the observed toxidrome without waiting for laboratory confirmation.

Effects after overdose typically begin sooner, peak later, and last longer than after a therapeutic dose, and the toxicokinetic profile differs from the published therapeutic pharmacokinetics in standard references.

Most patients who are asymptomatic 6 h after ingestion are unlikely to develop later toxicity and can be discharged safely, but longer observation is mandatory after suspected toxic time-bomb ingestions.

Diagnosis of an unknown poisoning rests on pattern recognition: first characterize the overall physiologic state as stimulated, depressed, discordant, or normal, then look for a toxidrome and finally for agent-specific clues.

Core temperature must be measured and reassessed frequently even in combative patients, because temperature elevation is the single most reliable predictor of poor outcome in stimulant poisoning (e.g., cocaine) and in withdrawal states (e.g., alcohol, GHB).

Mydriasis is characteristic of all stimulant states but is most marked in anticholinergic poisoning because pupillary reactivity is muscarinic; sympathomimetic poisoning also dilates pupils but some light reactivity persists, whereas the anticholinergic toxidrome adds hot, dry, flushed skin, decreased bowel sounds, and urinary retention.
Rotatory nystagmus points specifically to phencyclidine or ketamine, the only physiologic stimulants that produce this sign.
Miosis is most pronounced in opioid and cholinergic poisoning; cholinergic poisoning is distinguished by accompanying muscarinic and nicotinic features.

A normal exam can be deceptive: 'toxic time-bombs' (slowly absorbed, slowly distributed, requiring metabolic activation, or disrupting metabolism) and the proliferation of once-daily extended-release formulations mean delayed, severe toxicity is increasingly common.

A rapid response to a diagnostic antidote can confirm the cause: improvement within minutes of IV dextrose, naloxone, or flumazenil is essentially diagnostic of hypoglycemia, opioid poisoning, and benzodiazepine intoxication respectively.

Qualitative urine drug-of-abuse screens are screening tests only: false positives and negatives are common (e.g., fluoroquinolones cause false-positive opiate screens), and newer agents such as synthetic cannabinoids (spice), cathinones (bath salts), and kratom are not detected at all.
Relying on the gag reflex as an indicator of the need for intubation; it is not reliable, and a patient may protect the airway while stimulated but not when left alone.
Treating a negative qualitative drug screen as exclusion of poisoning; the agent may be undetectable by the assay or present below the limit of detection, and repeat testing later may turn positive.
Treating a positive qualitative screen as diagnostic or forensic; cross-reacting drugs cause false positives and confirmatory GC/MS may take weeks.

Assuming blood levels correlate with toxicity during absorption/distribution (levels can exceed tissue concentrations) or during resolution (levels fall below tissue concentrations); rebound increases (e.g., lithium) can occur after extracorporeal removal stops.

Discharging too early after ingestion of a toxic time-bomb (slow-absorption, slow-distribution, metabolic-activation, or metabolism-disrupting agents) on the basis of an initially benign presentation.
Failing to consider all medications available in the home (including pet medications) when the history is unclear in a suspected poisoning.
Overlooking intentional self-harm: failing to maintain continuous observation and self-injury precautions in patients who have attempted suicide.

Using class IA, IC, or III antiarrhythmics, or beta blockers driven by sympathetic hyperactivity, for toxin-induced ventricular arrhythmias; sodium bicarbonate is the preferred first agent for membrane-active toxicity.

Overall mortality is low at less than 1% of all poisoning exposures, with most being minor or non-toxic and involving children under 6 years. Mortality is substantially higher (1-2%) among hospitalized patients with intentional (suicidal) overdose or complications from drugs of abuse, who account for most serious poisonings. Acetaminophen is the pharmaceutical most often implicated in fatal poisoning. Carbon monoxide is the overall leading cause of poisoning death, although it is underrepresented in hospital and poison-center statistics because such patients are typically dead when found and referred directly to medical examiners. Drug overdose deaths have risen steadily since 1999 (over 106,600 U.S. deaths in 2021; age-adjusted rate 32.4 per 100,000), driven largely by synthetic opioids such as fentanyl and emerging agents such as xylazine. Once the offending agent is eliminated, maintaining tissue perfusion is critical to complete recovery.
Coma or progressively decreasing level of consciousness
Respiratory depression, apnea, or hypoxemia
Hypotension or cardiovascular collapse
Cardiac conduction abnormalities or arrhythmias (QRS/QT prolongation, ventricular tachyarrhythmias)
Seizures
Hyperthermia or hypothermia (temperature elevation is the most reliable predictor of poor outcome in stimulant/withdrawal states)
Suspected ingestion of a toxic time-bomb or an agent with toxic metabolites (acetaminophen, ethylene glycol, methanol)
Body packing or body stuffing (concealment of illicit drug packets)
Intentional (suicidal) overdose requiring continuous observation and self-injury precautions

Harrison grades physiologic stimulation and depression on a 1-4 scale. Stimulation: Grade 1 - anxious, irritable, tremulous with normal vital signs; Grade 2 - agitated, possible confusion/hallucinations but still able to converse and follow commands, mildly-to-moderately elevated vital signs; Grade 3 - delirious, unintelligible speech, uncontrollable motor hyperactivity, markedly raised vital signs, possible tachyarrhythmias; Grade 4 - coma, seizures, cardiovascular collapse. Depression: Grade 1 - lethargic/sleeping but arousable, able to converse; Grade 2 - responds to pain not voice, brainstem reflexes intact; Grade 3 - unresponsive to pain, depressed brainstem reflexes, decreased tone/respiration/temperature; Grade 4 - flaccid paralysis, absent brainstem reflexes and respirations, decreased cardiovascular vital signs.
Poisoning and Drug Overdose (non-infective) — Toxicology / Multisystem Also: xenobiotic poisoning, drug overdose, intoxication, toxic ingestion, acute poisoning

Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD, PKHD1) - distal/collecting-duct cysts, oligohydramnios if severe, hypertension, congenital hepatic fibrosis and Caroli disease; absence of renal cysts in either parent >40y on ultrasound helps distinguish ARPKD from ADPKD (p.2430, p.2434)
ADPKD-like disease (GANAB, DNAJB11) - normal-to-smaller kidneys with fewer cysts, variable liver cysts (p.2430-2432)
Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease (ADTKD; UMOD, MUC1, REN, HNF1B, SEC61A1) - small fibrotic kidneys, medullary cysts, gout in adults (p.2430)

Tuberous sclerosis (TSC1/TSC2) - renal cysts (20-30%), angiomyolipomas, increased risk of renal cell carcinoma, facial angiofibromas, CNS hamartomas; TSC2 is adjacent to PKD1 so a contiguous gene deletion can cause both ADPKD and TS (p.2430, p.2434)
Von Hippel-Lindau disease (VHL) - renal cysts, renal cell carcinoma, retinal angiomas, CNS hemangioblastomas, pheochromocytomas (p.2430)
Nephronophthisis and other ciliopathies (e.g., Bardet-Biedl, Meckel-Gruber, Senior-Loken) - cystic kidney phenotypes with syndromic features (p.2430)
Renal cysts and diabetes syndrome (HNF1B) - kidney cysts with aberrant nephrogenesis and diabetes (p.2430)
Acquired simple renal cysts (increase in frequency with age and can confound diagnostic cyst counts) (p.2432-2433)
Renal ultrasonography - first-line for presymptomatic screening and donor evaluation; age-stratified cyst-count criteria for diagnosis (p.2432-2433)

CT and T2-weighted MRI (with/without contrast) - more sensitive than ultrasound, detect smaller cysts (MRI with gadolinium can detect 2-3 mm cysts); useful to distinguish malignancy from a complex cyst (p.2432-2433)
Magnetic resonance angiography for presymptomatic intracranial aneurysm screening in patients with a positive family history of aneurysm (p.2432)
CT scan as first diagnostic test for suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage, with lumbar puncture to confirm (p.2432)

Genetic testing by linkage and mutational analysis for ambiguous cases; PKD1 analysis is difficult and costly owing to gene size and homologous pseudogenes (paired-end next-generation sequencing may improve this) (p.2433)

ADPKD results from mutations in PKD1 and PKD2, encoding polycystin-1 (PC1, a large 11-transmembrane G-protein-coupled-receptor-like protein) and polycystin-2 (PC2, a calcium-permeable six-transmembrane TRP-family cation channel). PC1 and PC2 bind via their C-terminal tails to form a receptor-channel complex (proposed 1:3 PC1:PC2 stoichiometry) located on the primary cilium and at cell membranes and cell-cell junctions of tubular epithelium, functioning as a mechano-/chemosensor regulating calcium and G-protein signaling. Every cell carries a germline mutant allele, but cysts develop in only a small fraction of nephrons, thought to arise from clonal growth of cells sustaining a somatic 'second hit' in the normal allele; a 'third hit' such as renal injury or an additional genetic/epigenetic event may accelerate cyst formation. Loss of ciliary PC1/PC2 function is hypothesized to cause aberrant calcium signaling, increased adenylyl cyclase and decreased phosphodiesterase activity, raising cellular cAMP; increased cAMP promotes protein kinase A activity, driving cyst growth through proliferation and chloride/aquaporin-mediated fluid secretion. Cellular defects include increased proliferation and fluid secretion, decreased differentiation, and abnormal extracellular matrix; affected signaling pathways include Wnt, mTOR, STAT3, cMET, PI3K/Akt, GPCR, EGFR, and CFTR. Rarer ADPKD-associated genes GANAB and DNAJB11 affect PC1 trafficking and cause milder cystic disease.

Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the most common life-threatening monogenic disease, affecting ~12 million people worldwide (estimated prevalence 1:1000 to 1:400), and is a leading cause of kidney failure; it is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with complete penetrance but variable expressivity (p.2430-2431).

Infection is the second most common cause of death; up to half of patients have one or more renal infections, most commonly an infected cyst or acute pyelonephritis due to gram-negative bacteria, with fever and flank pain (p.2432).

ADPKD is caused by mutations in PKD1 (chromosome 16p13, ~85% of cases, encodes polycystin-1) and PKD2 (chromosome 4q21-q23, ~15% of cases, encodes polycystin-2); PKD2 patients tend to have milder disease and may be underdiagnosed. Polycystins are localized on the primary cilium, and defective ciliary function places ADPKD among the ciliopathies (p.2430-2431).

It is characterized by progressive bilateral formation of epithelial-lined renal cysts; cysts arise in only ~5% of tubules but their enormous growth destroys surrounding tissue. Enlarged kidneys can reach a fourfold increase in length and up to 20 times the normal weight (p.2430-2431).

Back or flank pain is a frequent symptom in ~60% of patients and may result from cyst infection, hemorrhage, or nephrolithiasis; gross hematuria from cyst rupture occurs in ~40% during the disease course, often recurrently (p.2432).

Hypertension is common and typically occurs before any reduction in GFR; it is a risk factor for both cardiovascular and kidney disease progression. Cardiovascular complications are the major cause of mortality in ADPKD (p.2432).

Intracranial (berry) aneurysm occurs four to five times more frequently than in the general population and causes high mortality; about 20-50% of patients may have 'warning headaches' preceding subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured aneurysm (p.2432).

Liver (biliary epithelial) cysts are the most common extrarenal complication; massive polycystic liver disease occurs almost exclusively in women, particularly those with multiple pregnancies. Mitral valve prolapse occurs in up to 30% of patients, and colonic diverticulae and abdominal wall hernias are also increased (p.2432).

Diagnosis is typically made from a positive autosomal dominant family history plus bilateral kidney cysts on ultrasonography; in at-risk subjects aged 15-29 years, two renal cysts (unilateral or bilateral) suffice (sensitivity 96%, specificity 100%), with higher cyst counts required at older ages because simple cysts increase with age (p.2432-2433).

Tolvaptan, a vasopressin V2-receptor (V2R) antagonist, inhibits the cAMP pathway in collecting ducts and reduces cell proliferation by lowering renal cAMP, slowing the decline of renal function; the FDA has indicated it only for patients at risk of rapidly progressing disease (p.2433).
Proteinuria is usually only a MINOR feature of ADPKD, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis (p.2432).

Renal cell carcinoma is NOT increased in frequency compared with the general population, but when it does occur in ADPKD it is more often bilateral, multicentric, and sarcomatoid; radiologic imaging is often unable to distinguish cyst infection from cyst hemorrhage due to their complexity (p.2432).
Diagnostic cyst-count thresholds rise with age because simple renal cysts increase with age; criteria have lower sensitivity for PKD2 patients owing to late onset (p.2432-2433).

No specific FDA-approved treatment prevents cyst growth or the decline of renal function; more rigorous blood pressure control does not equal greater benefit, and targeting systolic pressure to 110 mmHg in moderate/advanced disease may worsen progression by reducing renal blood flow (p.2433).

Most renal cysts are not connected to glomerular filtration, so cyst infection requires lipid-soluble antibiotics that penetrate cyst walls (e.g., trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, quinolones, chloramphenicol), often for 4-6 weeks (p.2433).
Polycystic liver disease in ADPKD is distinct from isolated autosomal dominant polycystic liver disease (ADPLD; PRKCSH/SEC63), which does NOT progress to renal failure (p.2432).

ADPKD progression shows striking inter- and intrafamilial variability; disease can present as early as in utero, but end-stage renal disease typically occurs in late middle age. Risk factors for progression include early diagnosis, hypertension, gross hematuria, multiple pregnancies, and large kidney size; PKD2 disease is generally milder with later onset. More than half of patients eventually require peritoneal dialysis, hemodialysis, or kidney transplantation. Cardiovascular complications are the major cause of mortality, and renal infection is the second most common cause of death (p.2431-2433).
Sudden severe headache or 'warning headache' suggesting subarachnoid hemorrhage from ruptured intracranial (berry) aneurysm (p.2432)
Positive family history of intracranial aneurysm - a risk factor for aneurysm rupture warranting presymptomatic MRA screening (p.2432)
Fever and flank pain indicating infected cyst or acute pyelonephritis (with or without bacteremia); infection is the second most common cause of death (p.2432)
Gross hematuria from cyst rupture (p.2432)
Diffuse arterial dolichoectasia of the cerebral circulation predisposing to arterial dissection and stroke (p.2432)

Harrison does not provide a formal stage-based severity classification for ADPKD. Genotype broadly stratifies severity (PKD1 disease ~85% of cases is more severe with earlier onset than PKD2 disease ~15%; GANAB/DNAJB11 mutations cause milder cystic disease). Risk of rapid progression - used to select patients for tolvaptan - is estimated by combining genotypic and imaging (kidney growth rate) information; recognized clinical risk factors for progression include early diagnosis, hypertension, gross hematuria, multiple pregnancies, and large kidney size (p.2431-2433).
Polycystic Kidney Disease (non-infective) — Nephrology Also: ADPKD, PKD

PCOS reflects a complex interplay of hormonal and metabolic disturbances. Insulin resistance with compensatory hyperinsulinaemia stimulates ovarian theca cells to overproduce androgens and reduces hepatic sex hormone-binding globulin, raising free androgen levels. Altered gonadotrophin secretion, with a relatively high luteinising hormone drive, further promotes androgen production and disrupts follicular maturation, so multiple small antral follicles accumulate without a dominant follicle emerging, causing anovulation. Chronic unopposed oestrogen exposure from anovulation places the endometrium at risk of hyperplasia.

PCOS is diagnosed using the Rotterdam criteria, requiring at least two of oligo- or anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound, after excluding mimics
Common presentations include irregular or absent periods, hirsutism and acne, subfertility, and difficulty with weight
Insulin resistance is central to the syndrome and is often present regardless of body weight, though obesity worsens it
It is the leading cause of anovulatory infertility
Unopposed oestrogen from chronic anovulation increases the long-term risk of endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma, so regular endometrial protection is important
Lifestyle modification with weight management is the first-line intervention and can restore ovulation and improve metabolic profile
Management is symptom-directed: cycle regulation and endometrial protection, treatment of hyperandrogenic features, and ovulation induction when fertility is desired
Screening for and managing metabolic complications, including impaired glucose tolerance, type 2 diabetes, and dyslipidaemia, is an essential part of long-term care
Diagnosing PCOS without excluding thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia, and other mimics
Relying on ultrasound alone, since polycystic ovarian morphology can occur in healthy women
Overlooking endometrial protection in women with prolonged amenorrhoea
Focusing only on fertility and neglecting long-term metabolic and cardiovascular risk
Attributing severe or rapidly progressive virilisation to PCOS

PCOS is a lifelong condition whose reproductive symptoms often improve with weight management and targeted therapy, and many women conceive with or without ovulation induction. The main long-term concerns are metabolic, with increased risks of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and, through chronic anovulation, endometrial cancer; proactive metabolic surveillance improves outcomes.
Rapid onset or severe virilisation suggesting an androgen-secreting tumour rather than PCOS
Prolonged amenorrhoea with abnormal bleeding raising concern for endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma
Markedly elevated androgens beyond the range typical of PCOS
Features of Cushing syndrome
Severe metabolic derangement such as newly diagnosed diabetes

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: These chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms originate in a single hematopoietic stem cell and produce overabundant mature blood elements without significant dysplasia, together with a tendency toward extramedullary hematopoiesis, myelofibrosis, and eventual leukemic transformation. PV, PMF, and ET share constitutive activation of the nonreceptor tyrosine kinase JAK2, the cognate kinase and chaperone for the erythropoietin and thrombopoietin receptors. The JAK2 V617F mutation in the autoinhibitory pseudokinase domain causes ligand-independent kinase activation, explaining erythropoietin hypersensitivity, erythropoietin-independent erythroid colony growth, increased Bcl-XL expression, and apoptosis resistance in PV progenitors. Loss of heterozygosity on chromosome 9p (uniparental disomy) leads to JAK2 V617F homozygosity, common in PV, less so in PMF, and rare in ET. JAK2 V617F alone does not account for the entire phenotype and is probably not the initiating lesion: the same mutation yields different phenotypes in ET versus PMF, familial PV can occur without it, and leukemia may arise in a JAK2-negative progenitor, implying an ancestral precursor. PMF and ET may instead carry MPL (thrombopoietin receptor) or CALR (calreticulin) mutations; mutant CALR binds and activates MPL at the cell surface. In PMF, marrow fibrosis is a reactive, polyclonal fibroblast response driven by cytokines from the clone (TGF-beta, thrombopoietin), with extramedullary hematopoiesis in liver and spleen. Megakaryocyte genome reduplication is endomitotic and thrombopoietin-driven; paradoxically, MPL expression is reduced and plasma thrombopoietin is increased across these MPNs despite the expanded megakaryocyte/platelet mass.

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: The classic chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms covered here (PV, PMF, ET) all arise from a hematopoietic stem cell and share constitutive activation of JAK2 through driver mutations in JAK2, MPL, or CALR; their natural histories are usually measured in decades, and leukemic transformation is uncommon in the absence of chemotherapy or radiation (Harrison 22e p.818).

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: In ET the large platelet mass can cause spurious (test-tube) hyperkalemia from platelet potassium release on clotting, with no electrocardiographic correlate, and can make arterial oxygen measurements inaccurate unless blood is collected on ice (Harrison 22e p.823).

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: Very high platelet counts (above about 1 million/microL) are associated primarily with bleeding from acquired von Willebrand disease due to proteolysis of high-molecular-weight von Willebrand multimers, not with thrombosis; tobacco use is the most important thrombotic risk factor in ET (Harrison 22e p.823-824).

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: PMF and ET diagnoses are largely diagnoses of exclusion: significant splenomegaly in apparent ET suggests another MPN, and FISH for BCR-ABL is preferred to exclude CML in JAK2-negative thrombocytosis because reverse-transcriptase PCR for BCR-ABL is prone to false positives (Harrison 22e p.823-824).

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: JAK2 V617F is expressed in more than 95% of PV patients and in roughly 50% of PMF and ET patients; most JAK2-negative PV patients carry a JAK2 exon 12 mutation, while a few have LNK or calreticulin mutations (Harrison 22e p.818-819).

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: In PV the plasma volume is expanded, unlike other causes of true erythrocytosis, so an elevated red cell mass can be masked, especially in women; below a hemoglobin of about 20 g/dL (hematocrit 60%) one cannot reliably separate true erythrocytosis from plasma-volume contraction without red cell mass and plasma volume measurement (Harrison 22e p.819-820).

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: PV should be suspected in any woman presenting with hepatic vein (Budd-Chiari) thrombosis, since this is the type of thrombosis particularly associated with JAK2 V617F; portal vein thrombosis is more common in male PV patients (Harrison 22e p.819).

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: Aquagenic pruritus and erythromelalgia are the symptoms that can suggest PV over other causes of erythrocytosis; pruritus may reflect JAK2 V617F-driven mast cell activation, and Helicobacter pylori incidence is increased in PV (Harrison 22e p.819-820).

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: Only three conditions cause microcytic erythrocytosis: beta-thalassemia trait, hypoxic erythrocytosis, and PV; the red cell distribution width is typically normal in thalassemia trait but may be elevated in hypoxic erythrocytosis or PV when iron deficiency coexists (Harrison 22e p.820).

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: In a PV patient with massive splenomegaly, a 'normal' hematocrit or hemoglobin should be regarded as indicating an elevated red cell mass until proven otherwise, because the associated plasma volume increase masks the true red cell mass (Harrison 22e p.820).

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: In PMF the peripheral smear shows a leukoerythroblastic picture with teardrop-shaped red cells, nucleated red cells, myelocytes, and promyelocytes; marrow is usually inaspirable ('dry tap') owing to fibrosis, and bone x-rays may show osteosclerosis (Harrison 22e p.821-822).

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: PMF marrow fibroblasts are polyclonal and not part of the neoplastic clone; fibrosis is driven by overproduction of transforming growth factor beta, tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases, and thrombopoietin, while osteosclerosis relates to osteoprotegerin and angiogenesis to vascular endothelial growth factor (Harrison 22e p.821).

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: Treating the platelet count rather than the patient in ET: a high platelet count alone does not establish thrombotic risk, and the cause of any symptom must be confirmed to be platelet-related before therapy

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: Assuming a high platelet count causes thrombosis when very high counts more often cause hemorrhage via acquired von Willebrand disease; aspirin can promote bleeding in this setting

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: Interpreting a normal hematocrit/hemoglobin as excluding elevated red cell mass in a PV patient with massive splenomegaly (plasma volume expansion masks it)

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: Relying on a low-level JAK2 V617F allele burden (VAF 5% or less) to diagnose a blood disease, since not everyone with low burden has one

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: Assuming a normal serum erythropoietin excludes PV (it does not), or overlooking that an elevated level points to a secondary cause

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: Diagnosing ET in a JAK2 V617F-positive patient without red cell mass/plasma volume studies, since many such patients actually have PV

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: Misreading spurious hyperkalemia or inaccurate arterial oxygen values caused by the large platelet mass in ET

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: Mistaking secondary myelofibrosis/myelophthisis for PMF and missing a treatable underlying disorder

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: Using leukemogenic agents (alkylating agents, radioactive phosphorus-32) and prolonged hydroxyurea, which is itself mutagenic and antagonizes TP53, in disorders with otherwise long survival

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: PV is generally indolent, with a clinical course measured in decades; most patients live long lives without functional impairment when red cell mass is controlled, and the incidence of acute leukemia is very low in those not exposed to chemotherapy or radiation. Myelofibrosis is part of the natural history of PV but is usually reactive and reversible without prognostic significance, although about 15% develop hematopoietic stem cell failure with extramedullary hematopoiesis and transfusion-dependent anemia. PMF has the shortest survival of the three: it follows a course of progressive marrow failure and organomegaly, can evolve to an accelerated phase, and about 10% transform spontaneously to a treatment-refractory acute leukemia. PMF survival is stratified by IPSS, DIPSS, and DIPSS-Plus risk factors (anemia, leukocytosis, peripheral blasts, constitutional symptoms, age over 65, unfavorable karyotype, thrombocytopenia, transfusion dependence); ASXL1, EZH2, SRSF2, and IDH1/2 mutations and complex cytogenetics independently predict early death or leukemic transformation, and triple-negative PMF carries the worst prognosis. ET is more benign than previously thought; survival is comparable to the general population regardless of driver mutation, and leukemic evolution is more often a consequence of therapy than of the disease.

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: Hepatic vein thrombosis (Budd-Chiari) in a young woman, or portal/mesenteric vein thrombosis, as a presenting feature of PV

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms

chunks.text: Sudden splenic enlargement with painful splenic infarction (fever, pleuritic chest pain)

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: Development of transfusion-dependent anemia, increasing organomegaly, or peripheral blood blasts signaling marrow failure or accelerated/blastic transformation in PMF

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: Constitutional symptoms (night sweats, fatigue, weight loss) suggesting a myeloproliferative rather than reactive process

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: Spinal cord compression, pericardial tamponade, or ureteral/intestinal obstruction from exuberant extramedullary hematopoiesis in PMF

chunks.diseaseName: Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
chunks.text: For primary myelofibrosis, prognostic risk is estimated by the IPSS (2009), DIPSS (2010), and DIPSS-Plus (2011) scoring systems. Risk factors include anemia (hemoglobin <10 g/dL), leukocytosis (>25,000/microL), peripheral blood blasts (>=1%), constitutional symptoms, and age over 65; DIPSS-Plus adds unfavorable karyotype, platelet count <100,000/microL, and transfusion dependence. In DIPSS, anemia is weighted as 2 points. Categories run Low, Intermediate-1, Intermediate-2, and High by number/weight of factors. These systems are not accurate for risk assessment of PV or ET patients who have developed secondary myelofibrosis.

chunks.text: Brugada pattern ST elevation must be distinguished from LV hypertrophy, pericarditis, myocardial ischemia/MI, hyperkalemia, hypothermia, right bundle branch block, and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (p.1970)

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: Polymorphic VT arises from a continually changing ventricular activation sequence. Proposed mechanisms include reentry with variable paths, spiral wave reentry, and multiple automatic foci, often near fibrotic myocardium and potentiated by damaged Purkinje cells or ventricular hypertrophy. Abnormal transmural dispersion of repolarization can drive it in the setting of channelopathies or antiarrhythmic drugs even without structural disease. In acute MI/ischemia, reentry through the infarct border zone is implicated, and surviving automatic Purkinje cells can initiate it. Torsades des pointes is associated with abnormal QT prolongation and pause-dependent initiation. Congenital LQTS reflects mutations in ion-channel genes governing repolarization (potassium channels in LQTS-1/-2, sodium channel in LQTS-3, and calcium channels in others). Short QT syndrome reflects a gain of function of the IKr potassium channel or reduced inward depolarizing currents. Brugada syndrome reflects dispersion of repolarization across the ventricular wall, with epicardial and M cells more affected than endocardial cells, localized to the right ventricular outflow tract; sodium channel mutations (SCN5A, SCN1B, SCN10A) are found in about 25% of cases. Catecholaminergic polymorphic VT results from cardiac ryanodine receptor (and less often calsequestrin 2) mutations causing abnormal sarcoplasmic calcium handling. Ventricular fibrillation represents disordered activation without organized QRS, frequently as degeneration of sustained polymorphic or monomorphic VT (p.1968-1971).

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: Sustained polymorphic VT shows a QRS configuration that changes continuously beat to beat, reflecting an ever-changing ventricular activation sequence; unlike monomorphic VT it does not necessarily imply a fixed structural abnormality or single automatic focus (p.1968).

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the most common genetic cardiovascular disorder (about 1 in 500), is a prominent cause of sudden death before age 35, typically via polymorphic VT/VF (p.1971).

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: Ventricular fibrillation shows disordered electrical ventricular activation with no identifiable QRS complexes; spiral wave reentry and multiple circulating reentry wavefronts are proposed mechanisms (p.1971).

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: After surviving acute MI and revascularization, poorly coupled but surviving Purkinje fibers (which tolerate ischemia owing to glycogen stores and oxygenation from the LV cavity) can trigger PVCs and ventricular fibrillation (p.1971).

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: Sustained polymorphic VT commonly degenerates into ventricular fibrillation (p.1969).

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: Acute myocardial infarction or ischemia is a frequent cause and should be the first consideration; roughly 10% of acute MI patients develop VT that degenerates to VF, with greatest risk in the first hour (p.1969).

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: Polymorphic VT/VF occurring within the first 48 hours of acute MI carries higher in-hospital mortality, but survivors to discharge are not at increased risk of later arrhythmic sudden death (p.1969).

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: Torsades des pointes is the polymorphic VT linked to QT prolongation and classically begins in a pause-dependent fashion: a PVC induces a pause, the following sinus beat has a longer QT, and a PVC interrupting that T wave starts the run (p.1969).

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: Congenital long QT syndrome stems from ion-channel gene mutations; LQTS-1, -2, and -3 account for roughly 80-90% of cases, with LQTS-1/-2 involving potassium channels and LQTS-3 involving the sodium channel (p.1969-1970).

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: Genotype influences triggers: LQTS-1 events tend to occur during exertion (notably swimming), LQTS-2 with sudden auditory stimuli or emotional upset, and LQTS-3 sudden death tends to occur during sleep (p.1970).

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: Brugada syndrome causes syncope or cardiac arrest from polymorphic VT in the absence of structural heart disease; arrest may occur during sleep or be provoked by febrile illness, and males are more commonly affected (p.1970).

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: Catecholaminergic polymorphic VT is a rare familial disorder of abnormal sarcoplasmic calcium handling producing arrhythmias resembling digitalis toxicity, often with bidirectional (alternating QRS morphology) VT, presenting in childhood with exertion- or emotion-induced events (p.1971).

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: Assuming polymorphic VT implies a fixed structural focus as monomorphic VT does (p.1968)

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: Overlooking ongoing ischemia/inadequate reperfusion when polymorphic VT/VF recurs after MI (p.1969)

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: Failing to recognize numerous noncardiac QT-prolonging drugs and drug interactions that raise levels of an offending agent as precipitants of torsades (p.1969)

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: Re-exposing a patient who had QT-prolongation-induced polymorphic VT to QT-prolonging medications; such patients should be considered susceptible and avoid all future exposure (p.1969)

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: Misinterpreting benign J-point elevation (a common normal variant) as pathologic early repolarization syndrome (p.1971)

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: Confusing the asymptomatic Brugada ECG pattern with true Brugada syndrome (p.1970)

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: Polymorphic VT/VF within the first 48 hours of acute MI is associated with greater in-hospital mortality, yet patients who survive to discharge are not at increased risk for later arrhythmic sudden death. Long-term risk after infarction is governed largely by residual LV function. In LQTS, higher risk is conferred by QTc >500 ms, female gender, and prior syncope or cardiac arrest. HCM is a prominent cause of sudden death before age 35; surgical myectomy carries a sudden death rate <1% per year, and transcoronary ethanol septal ablation has a reported annual rate of sustained VT or sudden death of roughly 1-5% (p.1969-1971).

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: Near-syncope, syncope, or cardiac arrest as the presenting event (p.1969)

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: Repeated episodes of polymorphic VT suggesting ongoing myocardial infarction/inadequate reperfusion (p.1969)

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: QTc exceeding 500 ms, female gender, and prior syncope or cardiac arrest as markers of increased risk in LQTS (p.1970)

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: Family history of sudden death (relevant in Brugada syndrome, early repolarization syndrome, and genetic cardiomyopathies) (p.1970-1971)

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: Febrile illness provoking cardiac arrest in Brugada syndrome (p.1970)

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: HCM features: young age, nonsustained VT, failure of blood pressure to rise with exercise, recent syncope (within 6 months), ventricular wall thickness >3 cm (p.1971)

chunks.diseaseName: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
chunks.text: No single formal severity grade; risk is stratified by substrate. In post-MI patients, an ICD is indicated for persistent severe LV dysfunction (LV ejection fraction <35%). In LQTS, high-risk features include QTc >500 ms, female gender, and prior syncope/cardiac arrest. In HCM, high-risk markers include young age, nonsustained VT, failure of blood pressure to rise with exercise, recent syncope, and ventricular wall thickness >3 cm (p.1969-1971).

chunks.text: Polytrauma involves injury to two or more body regions or systems, at least one of which is life-threatening. Simultaneous tissue damage triggers haemorrhage, hypovolaemic shock, and a systemic inflammatory response. Hypoperfusion causes tissue hypoxia and lactic acidosis, while ongoing bleeding and crystalloid dilution impair clotting. Hypothermia further inhibits enzymatic coagulation, and the resulting lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy establishes a self-reinforcing cycle. Later, immune activation predisposes to systemic inflammatory response syndrome, acute respiratory distress, and multi-organ dysfunction.

source.ref: ATLS / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine (critical care)

Hereditary tyrosinemia type 1 (succinylacetone inhibits ALA-dehydratase, mimicking acute porphyria) (p.3342)
Guillain-Barre syndrome (acute attack with ascending weakness mimics GBS) (p.3603)
Chronic liver disease (can cause nonspecific increases in urinary porphyrins leading to misdiagnosis) (p.3345)
Spot (single-void) urine for porphobilinogen (PBG) — first-line; always raised in acute attacks of AIP/HCP/VP and specific; 24-h collection unnecessary (p.3345-3346)
Quantitative urinary ALA, PBG, and creatinine on the same spot sample (also detects ADP) (p.3345)
Total urinary porphyrins (interpret cautiously — often nonspecific) (p.3345)
Urinary, fecal, and plasma porphyrins to distinguish AIP from HCP and VP (fecal porphyrins normal/minimal in AIP) (p.3346)
Total plasma porphyrins with fluorometric scanning of diluted plasma at neutral pH (distinguishes VP from PCT; VP emission peak ~626 nm) for cutaneous porphyrias (p.3346, 3348)
Erythrocyte protoporphyrin (more sensitive for EPP/XLP; confirm EPP by predominant free, not zinc, protoporphyrin) (p.3346)
Isocoproporphyrins in feces — diagnostic of hepatic URO-decarboxylase deficiency (PCT) (p.3348)
Erythrocyte URO-decarboxylase activity (~50% in type 2 PCT; markedly deficient, 3-10%, in HEP) (p.3348)
Molecular genetic mutation analysis of the relevant heme-pathway gene (definitive; diagnostic even when precursor levels have normalized, and for latent heterozygotes/relatives) (p.3342, 3346)
Acute surgical abdomen / intestinal obstruction (acute hepatic porphyria attack mimics this) (p.3344, ch.40)
Lead poisoning (lead colic and neuropathy mimic acute porphyria) (p.3342)
Guillain-Barre syndrome (ascending motor weakness in an acute attack) (p.3603)
Hereditary tyrosinemia type 1 (biochemical and clinical mimic of acute porphyria) (p.3342)

Each porphyria results from deficient (or, in XLP, increased) activity of one of the eight enzymes of the heme biosynthetic pathway converting glycine and succinyl-CoA to heme. In acute hepatic porphyrias, half-normal enzyme activity becomes limiting when hepatic heme synthesis is increased: induction of the rate-limiting hepatic gene ALAS1 (regulated in part by PGC-1alpha, which is induced by fasting) leads to accumulation and urinary excretion of the porphyrin precursors ALA and PBG, which underlie the acute neurovisceral attacks. Common precipitating factors include endogenous and exogenous steroids (estrogens/progestins), porphyrinogenic drugs (often P450-metabolized), alcohol, low-calorie/low-carbohydrate diets, infections, and surgery. AIP is almost always latent before puberty, suggesting adult steroid hormone levels drive expression; symptoms are commoner in women, with premenstrual (luteal-phase progesterone) attacks. Hyponatremia results from hypothalamic involvement with inappropriate vasopressin secretion or from electrolyte depletion (vomiting, diarrhea, poor intake, renal sodium loss). In PCT, substantial deficiency of hepatic URO-decarboxylase (to ~20% of normal or less, via an iron- and oxidative-stress-dependent uroporphomethene inhibitor) causes accumulation of porphyrins that, on excitation by long-wave UV light in the skin, produce blistering photosensitivity (p.3340, 3345-3347).

The porphyrias are metabolic disorders, each from deficient (or, for XLP, increased) activity of a specific enzyme in the heme biosynthetic pathway; inherited as autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked, except porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) which is usually sporadic (p.3340).
PCT is the most common porphyria overall; hepatic URO-decarboxylase is deficient in all types, and ~80% of patients have no UROD mutation (sporadic type 1) (p.3347).

PCT presents with blistering, photosensitive skin lesions most commonly on the backs of the hands that rupture, crust, and scar, with skin friability, milia, hypertrichosis, and hyperpigmentation; neurologic features are absent (p.3347).

An acute attack may begin with sharp abdominal pain, then agitation/hallucinations/seizures, with back and extremity pain followed by weakness several days later, mimicking Guillain-Barre syndrome; weakness may be asymmetric, proximal or distal, and involve facial/bulbar muscles (p.3602-3603).
Urine may appear brownish during an attack due to high porphyrin metabolite concentration (p.3602-3603).
Classified as hepatic or erythropoietic (by primary site of porphyrin/precursor overproduction) and as acute or cutaneous (by clinical manifestation) (p.3340, 3344).
Acute hepatic porphyrias (AIP, HCP, VP) usually present in adult life after puberty with acute attacks of neurovisceral symptoms and elevated urinary porphyrin precursors ALA and/or PBG (p.3344).

Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is autosomal dominant from half-normal HMB-synthase (porphobilinogen deaminase) activity; the most common acute hepatic porphyria (~1 in 20,000 Caucasians), especially frequent in Scandinavia and Great Britain (p.3340, 3346).
AIP abdominal pain is the most common symptom: poorly localized, often with cramping, ileus, distention, and decreased bowel sounds (though increased bowel sounds and diarrhea may occur) (p.3346).

AIP attacks also feature nausea, vomiting, constipation, tachycardia, hypertension, mental symptoms, limb/head/neck/chest pain, muscle weakness, sensory loss, dysuria, and urinary retention; tachycardia, hypertension, restlessness, tremor, and sweating reflect sympathetic overactivity (p.3346).

AIP peripheral neuropathy is due to axonal degeneration (not demyelination) and primarily affects motor neurons; proximal muscles (shoulders/arms) are involved first, and it may be focal or involve cranial nerves (p.3346).
Mental symptoms in acute attacks include anxiety, insomnia, depression, disorientation, hallucinations, and paranoia; seizures may be neurologic or due to hyponatremia (p.3346).

Diagnosis of an acute attack rests on substantial elevation of urinary PBG (and ALA); urinary PBG is always increased during acute attacks of AIP, HCP, and VP and is not substantially raised in any other condition, making a spot urine PBG both sensitive and specific (p.3345-3346).

A great mimic of the acute abdomen: porphyric (and lead colic) pain is hard to distinguish from intestinal obstruction because of prominent hyperperistalsis — risking unnecessary surgery (p.3344, ch.40).
Because symptoms are nonspecific and rarely occur before puberty, diagnosis is often delayed; a high index of suspicion is required (p.3340, 3346).
Measuring urinary porphyrins alone for screening should be avoided — minimal nonspecific increases (e.g., in chronic liver disease) cause misdiagnosis; use urinary PBG (p.3345).

Erythrocyte HMB-synthase assay is not a useful first-line test: activity is not decreased in all AIP patients, borderline-low values are not diagnostic, and it is not deficient in other acute porphyrias; some HMBS mutations give normal erythrocyte enzyme so genetic testing is needed (p.3345-3346).
ALA/PBG levels often remain high after symptoms resolve, so diagnosing an acute attack in a biochemically proven AIP patient relies primarily on clinical features (p.3346).
Most antiseizure drugs can exacerbate AIP, making seizure treatment difficult (clonazepam may be safer than phenytoin or barbiturates) (p.3346).
Abdominal tenderness, fever, and leukocytosis are usually absent or mild in AIP because the process is neurologic, not inflammatory — their prominence should prompt reconsideration (p.3346).
In PCT, neurologic features are absent — abdominal/neurovisceral attacks should not be attributed to it (p.3347).

AIP can be disabling but is rarely fatal; the prognosis of individuals with HMBS mutations is generally favorable, and most heterozygotes remain latent. When an attack resolves, abdominal pain may disappear within hours and paresis begins to improve within days, sometimes continuing to improve over years; recovery from severe motor neuropathy may take months to years and depends on the degree of neuronal damage and early treatment. Long-term complications of AIP include increased risk of hypertension and chronic kidney disease (up to 59% develop CKD), chronic liver function abnormalities with increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (warranting hepatic imaging at least every 6 months), and persistent neuropathy, fatigue, chronic pain, nausea, depression, and anxiety. Homozygous dominant AIP usually presents in infancy and most affected children die at an early age. PCT can almost always be brought into complete remission with treatment, but patients characteristically have chronic liver disease, sometimes cirrhosis, and are at risk for hepatocellular carcinoma (p.3346-3348).

Acute neurovisceral attack: severe poorly-localized abdominal pain with autonomic instability (tachycardia, hypertension, sweating), motor neuropathy/weakness, and psychiatric disturbance — the AIP acute hepatic porphyria red-flag constellation (p.3346)
Hyponatremia (from inappropriate vasopressin secretion or electrolyte depletion) and seizures during an attack (p.3346)
Markedly raised urinary PBG/ALA in a patient with abdominal pain after puberty (p.3345-3346)
Exposure to a porphyria-precipitating drug, low-calorie diet, alcohol, infection, or surgery preceding the attack (p.3346)
Progression to respiratory and bulbar paralysis; sudden death may result from sympathetic overactivity and cardiac arrhythmia, especially with delayed diagnosis/treatment (p.3346)

Porphyrias are classified by primary overproduction site (hepatic vs erythropoietic) and by clinical manifestation (acute neurovisceral vs cutaneous). Acute hepatic porphyrias: AIP, HCP, VP (and the rare autosomal recessive ADP) present with acute neurovisceral attacks and raised ALA/PBG; AIP causes neurovisceral disease without photosensitivity, whereas HCP and VP can have both neurovisceral attacks and PCT-like cutaneous photosensitivity. Cutaneous: PCT (and HEP) present with chronic blistering photosensitivity. Erythropoietic porphyrias (CEP, EPP, XLP) present with cutaneous photosensitivity (EPP/XLP non-blistering, immediate and painful). Acute-attack severity ranges from mild (abdominal pain without paresis or hyponatremia, manageable with carbohydrate loading) to severe (paresis, hyponatremia, bulbar/respiratory paralysis) (p.3340, 3344, 3346-3347).
Porphyria (non-infective) — Metabolic / Hematology Also: acute intermittent porphyria, porphyria cutanea tarda

chunks.text: Uterine atony
Genital tract trauma including cervical or vaginal lacerations and haematomas
Retained placenta or retained products of conception
Placenta accreta spectrum
Uterine inversion or rupture
Inherited or acquired coagulopathy including disseminated intravascular coagulation
Quantitative measurement of blood loss and continuous vital sign monitoring
Full blood count and serial haemoglobin
Coagulation screen with fibrinogen level
Group and cross-match with early activation of transfusion support
Examination under anaesthesia and ultrasound to identify retained tissue or genital tract trauma

Normal postpartum haemostasis depends on vigorous myometrial contraction that mechanically compresses the spiral arteries of the placental bed, supported by the clotting cascade. Postpartum haemorrhage results when one or more of these mechanisms fail: the uterus fails to contract (atony, often from overdistension, prolonged or augmented labour, infection, or retained tissue); vessels are torn by genital tract trauma; retained placental tissue or invasive placentation prevents effective contraction; or coagulation is impaired by dilution, consumption, or a pre-existing disorder. Ongoing loss can precipitate hypovolaemic shock and a self-perpetuating coagulopathy.
Postpartum haemorrhage is excessive bleeding after birth; primary PPH occurs within the first 24 hours and secondary PPH from 24 hours up to about 12 weeks postpartum
The causes are usefully remembered as the four Ts: tone (uterine atony), trauma (genital tract lacerations), tissue (retained placenta or products), and thrombin (coagulopathy)
Uterine atony is by far the commonest cause, so uterine massage and uterotonic agents are first-line alongside resuscitation
Active management of the third stage of labour with a prophylactic uterotonic reduces the incidence and severity of PPH
Blood loss is frequently underestimated visually, so vital signs, quantitative assessment, and a high index of suspicion are essential

A structured stepwise escalation moves from uterotonics to mechanical measures (bimanual compression, balloon tamponade) and then to surgical options such as compression sutures, vessel ligation, or hysterectomy
Tranexamic acid given early reduces death from bleeding and should be administered promptly
Early involvement of senior obstetric, anaesthetic, and haematology teams with activation of a massive transfusion protocol improves outcomes
Underestimating blood loss by visual assessment alone
Failing to recognise ongoing bleeding masked by the physiological cardiovascular reserve of pregnancy until late collapse
Not systematically excluding retained tissue and genital tract trauma when atony seems controlled but bleeding persists
Delaying tranexamic acid and blood product replacement
Escalating too slowly to mechanical and surgical measures when medical therapy fails

With prompt recognition, resuscitation, and stepwise treatment most women recover fully. Delay in diagnosis or treatment can lead to shock, organ failure, need for hysterectomy with loss of fertility, and death; postpartum haemorrhage remains one of the leading causes of maternal mortality worldwide, particularly in low-resource settings.
Tachycardia, hypotension, and other signs of hypovolaemic shock
Continued brisk bleeding despite uterotonics and uterine massage
Clinical or laboratory evidence of coagulopathy
A high uterine fundus with a boggy uterus indicating atony, or a suddenly inverted uterus
Suspected placenta accreta spectrum after a difficult placental delivery
Postpartum haemorrhage (non-infective) — Obstetrics / Gynaecology Also: postpartum hemorrhage, PPH, obstetric haemorrhage after delivery
IgA nephropathy
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
Lupus nephritis
Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) nephritis
Haemolytic uraemic syndrome
Alport syndrome or thin basement membrane disease
Serum complement C3 (and C4) with follow-up to document normalisation
Antistreptococcal serology (ASO, anti-DNase B) or streptozyme panel
Throat or skin swab and culture if active infection present
Urinalysis with microscopy for red cell casts and dysmorphic red cells
Serum urea, creatinine, and electrolytes to assess renal function
Renal biopsy only in atypical or progressive cases

Infection with nephritogenic strains of group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus triggers an immune-complex-mediated glomerular injury. Streptococcal antigens (such as nephritis-associated plasmin receptor and streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin B) deposit in the glomeruli and, together with circulating and in situ immune complexes, activate the complement system, predominantly via the alternative pathway. The resulting inflammation causes endocapillary proliferation and neutrophil infiltration, reducing glomerular filtration and producing sodium and water retention, which manifests as haematuria, oedema, and hypertension.
A classic cause of acute nephritic syndrome in children, most often between about 5 and 12 years of age.
Follows infection with specific nephritogenic strains of group A streptococcus, typically 1-2 weeks after pharyngitis or 3-6 weeks after skin infection.
Presents with the nephritic picture of haematuria (often cola- or tea-coloured urine), oedema, hypertension, and variable reduction in urine output.
Complement C3 is characteristically low and typically returns to normal within about 6-8 weeks; persistently low C3 beyond this window suggests another diagnosis.
Evidence of preceding streptococcal infection is supported by elevated or rising antistreptococcal antibodies such as ASO or anti-DNase B.
Management is largely supportive, centred on salt and fluid restriction and control of hypertension and fluid overload.
Antibiotics treat any active streptococcal infection but do not alter the course of the established nephritis.
Renal biopsy is usually unnecessary and reserved for atypical features such as persistent low complement, progressive kidney failure, or nephrotic-range proteinuria.
The prognosis in children is excellent, with the large majority recovering complete renal function.
Attributing every child with haematuria and low C3 to PSGN without follow-up complement testing
Overlooking hypertensive complications by not monitoring blood pressure closely
Failing to consider alternative glomerulonephritides when complement stays low beyond eight weeks
Aggressive fluid administration worsening volume overload in an oliguric child

Most children recover fully; acute complications resolve over days to weeks, complement normalises within about two months, and microscopic haematuria may persist for up to a year with an excellent long-term outlook.
Severe or refractory hypertension, including hypertensive encephalopathy
Rapidly rising creatinine suggesting rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis
Pulmonary oedema or heart failure from fluid overload
Marked oliguria or anuria
Persistently low complement or nephrotic-range proteinuria indicating an alternative diagnosis
Post-streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (infective) — Renal Also: PSGN, acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, APSGN, acute post-infectious glomerulonephritis
Premature thelarche (benign isolated breast development)
Premature adrenarche (early pubic/axillary hair without other puberty)
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Gonadal or adrenal tumour
McCune-Albright syndrome
CNS lesion (hamartoma, tumour, prior irradiation, or injury)
Exogenous sex steroid exposure
Bone age radiograph
Basal and GnRH-stimulated LH and FSH
Sex steroid levels (oestradiol or testosterone)
Adrenal androgens and 17-hydroxyprogesterone when a peripheral cause is suspected
Pelvic ultrasound in girls to assess ovarian and uterine development
MRI of the brain, particularly in boys or where a central lesion is suspected

In central precocious puberty the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis reactivates prematurely, with pulsatile GnRH secretion stimulating pituitary gonadotropins and subsequent gonadal sex steroid production, reproducing normal but early puberty. In peripheral precocious puberty sex steroids arise independently of GnRH from the gonads, adrenals, tumours, or exogenous sources, producing secondary sexual characteristics without central axis activation. Sex steroids accelerate growth and skeletal maturation, so advanced bone age can ultimately limit final height.
Precocious puberty is conventionally defined as the onset of secondary sexual characteristics before about 8 years in girls and 9 years in boys.

It is broadly classified as central (gonadotropin-dependent, from early activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis) or peripheral (gonadotropin-independent, from sex steroids produced outside the normal axis).
Central precocious puberty is far more common in girls and is usually idiopathic, whereas in boys an underlying CNS lesion is more likely and must be excluded.
Accelerated linear growth and advanced bone age are typical; paradoxically, premature epiphyseal fusion can compromise final adult height.
A GnRH (or GnRH-agonist) stimulation test helps distinguish central from peripheral causes by assessing the gonadotropin response.
Isolated premature thelarche or premature adrenarche are usually benign normal variants but should be monitored to ensure they are not the start of true precocity.
Peripheral causes include congenital adrenal hyperplasia, gonadal or adrenal tumours, McCune-Albright syndrome, and exogenous sex steroid exposure.
Beyond physical changes, early puberty can carry psychosocial consequences that warrant support for the child and family.
Assuming precocious puberty is idiopathic in a boy without imaging to exclude a CNS lesion
Confusing benign premature thelarche or adrenarche with true central precocity
Overlooking the impact of advanced bone age on final adult height
Neglecting the psychosocial needs of a child developing ahead of peers

Idiopathic central precocious puberty generally has a good outcome, and appropriate treatment can preserve growth potential and address psychosocial concerns; prognosis in secondary forms depends on the underlying cause, such as a CNS lesion or hormone-secreting tumour.
Neurological signs, headaches, or visual disturbance suggesting an intracranial lesion
Rapidly progressive virilisation or a palpable abdominal/gonadal mass suggesting a hormone-secreting tumour
Precocious puberty in a boy, which more often has a serious underlying cause
Very early or rapidly advancing puberty threatening severe height compromise
Cafe-au-lait macules with bony abnormalities suggesting McCune-Albright syndrome
Precocious Puberty (non-infective) — Endocrine Also: sexual precocity, central precocious puberty, peripheral precocious puberty, early puberty
Chronic (pre-existing) hypertension
Gestational hypertension without organ involvement
Chronic kidney disease with proteinuria
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura or haemolytic uraemic syndrome
Systemic lupus erythematosus flare
Serial blood pressure measurement and urine protein quantification (protein:creatinine ratio or 24-hour collection)
Full blood count for thrombocytopenia and evidence of haemolysis
Liver transaminases and lactate dehydrogenase
Renal function including serum creatinine and urate
Angiogenic markers (sFlt-1/PlGF ratio) where available to aid risk stratification
Fetal assessment with ultrasound growth, amniotic fluid volume, and umbilical artery Doppler

Pre-eclampsia originates in abnormal placentation: inadequate remodelling of the maternal spiral arteries by trophoblast leads to a poorly perfused, ischaemic placenta. The ischaemic placenta releases anti-angiogenic factors (such as soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 and soluble endoglin) that antagonise vascular endothelial and placental growth factors, producing widespread maternal endothelial dysfunction. This causes vasospasm, increased vascular permeability, activation of coagulation, and multi-organ hypoperfusion, manifesting as hypertension, proteinuria, hepatic and cerebral involvement, and fetal growth restriction.

Defined by new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks' gestation combined with proteinuria or evidence of maternal organ dysfunction (renal, hepatic, neurological, haematological) or uteroplacental compromise

Proteinuria is no longer mandatory for diagnosis when hypertension is accompanied by features such as thrombocytopenia, raised transaminases, renal impairment, pulmonary oedema, or cerebral/visual symptoms
Warning symptoms include persistent severe headache, visual disturbance (flashing lights, blurring), right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, and rapid oedema of the face and hands
HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) is a severe variant that can occur with only modest blood pressure elevation
Definitive treatment is delivery of the placenta; timing balances gestational age against maternal and fetal risk
Magnesium sulfate is used for seizure prophylaxis in severe disease and to treat eclamptic seizures, not as an antihypertensive
Antihypertensive therapy aims to lower dangerously high blood pressure to reduce maternal stroke risk while preserving placental perfusion
Low-dose aspirin from early pregnancy reduces incidence in women at high risk (prior pre-eclampsia, chronic hypertension, renal disease, diabetes, multiple pregnancy, antiphospholipid syndrome)
Excluding the diagnosis because proteinuria is absent despite organ dysfunction
Underestimating severity in HELLP syndrome where blood pressure may be only mildly raised
Over-aggressive blood pressure lowering compromising placental perfusion
Failing to continue monitoring postpartum, when eclampsia and severe hypertension can still occur
Treating magnesium sulfate as an antihypertensive rather than as seizure prophylaxis

With timely surveillance, blood pressure control, seizure prophylaxis, and appropriately timed delivery most women recover fully postpartum, though there is an increased lifetime risk of cardiovascular and renal disease. Severe or early-onset disease carries higher maternal and perinatal morbidity, and recurrence in future pregnancies is common.
Severe hypertension unresponsive to treatment threatening maternal stroke
Neurological signs (severe headache, visual loss, hyperreflexia with clonus) heralding impending eclampsia
Right upper quadrant pain with abnormal liver enzymes suggesting HELLP or hepatic haematoma/rupture
Pulmonary oedema or oliguria indicating organ failure
Fetal growth restriction with abnormal Dopplers or non-reassuring fetal status
Pre-eclampsia (non-infective) — Obstetrics / Gynaecology Also: preeclampsia, pre-eclampsia, PET, pregnancy-induced hypertension with proteinuria, gestational proteinuric hypertension

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: PVCs arise via enhanced (abnormal) automaticity, triggered activity, or localized reentry. They are frequently sympathetically sensitive and can reflect heightened sympathetic tone, myocardial ischemia, hypoxia, electrolyte disturbances (notably hypokalemia), or underlying structural heart disease. The site of earliest ventricular activation dictates the activation sequence and therefore the QRS morphology, allowing the surface ECG to suggest the anatomic origin and the likelihood of structural disease. In the setting of ischemia or structural disease, PVCs and NSVT can be harbingers of sustained VT or VF. AIVR is typically driven by automaticity, though rare reentrant circuits in diseased myocardium can produce it. PVC-induced ventricular dysfunction is thought to act through a mechanism akin to chronic tachycardia or through ventricular dyssynchrony.

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: Ventricular ectopy spanning PVCs, nonsustained VT (NSVT), and accelerated idioventricular rhythm (AIVR) is very common and is most often asymptomatic, detected incidentally on telemetry or prompted by palpitations.

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: Frequent ectopy can itself depress ventricular function (PVC-induced cardiomyopathy), but this rarely occurs unless PVCs account for at least 10-20% of total beats over 24 hours, and only a minority of such patients develop reversible cardiomyopathy.

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: Smooth, sharp QRS deflections of a PVC suggest a focus in relatively normal myocardium, whereas broad notching and slurring suggest a diseased substrate.

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: Recently inflammation has been recognized as contributing to PVC genesis in inflammatory and inherited cardiomyopathies.

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: A PVC is a single ventricular beat occurring earlier than the next expected supraventricular beat; PVCs from one focus share an identical QRS morphology (unifocal), while differing morphologies indicate multifocal origin and raise suspicion for structural or myopathic disease.

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: Two consecutive ventricular beats form a couplet; three or more consecutive beats above 100/min define VT, and VT terminating spontaneously within 30 seconds is termed nonsustained.

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: QRS morphology localizes the focus: a dominant S wave in V1 (left bundle branch block-like) points to the right ventricle or septum, whereas a dominant R wave in V1 (right bundle branch block-like) points to the left ventricle; the frontal-plane axis distinguishes superior (inferior-wall) versus cranial origin.

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: Most ventricular arrhythmias without structural disease have a left bundle branch block-like pattern, while a right bundle branch block configuration or multiple PVC morphologies more often signal structural heart disease.

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: Idiopathic ectopy commonly arises from the right or left ventricular outflow tracts near the valve annuli, and also from papillary muscles and fascicular tissue; benign idiopathic NSVT is usually monomorphic with rates under 200/min.

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: Bigeminy (every other beat a PVC) can cause pseudobradycardia because the premature beats may not generate a palpable pulse, so counted rate can read falsely low.

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: In the peri-infarct period, PVCs and NSVT are common early manifestations of ischemia and can herald ventricular fibrillation.

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: AIVR is defined as three or more ventricular beats at a rate slower than 100/min, usually due to enhanced automaticity; it is common during acute MI and may emerge during sinus bradycardia or sleep.

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: Bigeminal PVCs can produce pseudobradycardia, leading to an erroneously low measured heart rate.

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: Asymptomatic PVCs and NSVT discovered in a hospitalized or acutely ill patient generally do not require specific antiarrhythmic treatment beyond addressing the underlying illness and correcting aggravating factors.

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: Assuming all ventricular ectopy is benign; very rapid, polymorphic, short-coupled, or multifocal patterns and any ECG/structural abnormality demand evaluation for sudden-death risk.

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: Overlooking reversible PVC-induced cardiomyopathy in patients with very frequent ectopy and otherwise unexplained left ventricular dysfunction.

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: Attributing a wide-complex rhythm to VT without distinguishing it from supraventricular tachycardia with aberrancy.

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: PVCs, NSVT, and AIVR are most often benign when they occur in structurally normal hearts with normal ECGs, and idiopathic ectopy generally has excellent long-term arrhythmia-free outcomes (catheter ablation suppresses idiopathic PVCs in roughly 90% of patients). In contrast, the same arrhythmias carry prognostic weight in the presence of structural disease: after MI and in heart failure, frequent (typically >10 PVCs/h), repetitive PVCs, couplets, and NSVT are markers of depressed ventricular function and increased mortality, and they are likewise associated with worse outcomes in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and congenital heart disease with ventricular dysfunction. AIVR is usually well tolerated, though loss of AV synchrony may cause hemodynamic compromise in susceptible patients.

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: Syncope or near-syncope, especially without prodrome, during exertion, or with an abnormal ECG or structural heart disease

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: Very rapid or polymorphic NSVT, or a 'short-coupled' first beat occurring before the peak of the T wave

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: Family history of sudden death prompting evaluation for inherited cardiomyopathy or channelopathy

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: Any abnormality on the 12-lead ECG (Q waves of prior infarction, ventricular hypertrophy, repolarization abnormalities of long QT/Brugada/ARVC)

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: Right bundle branch block-like or multifocal PVC morphology suggesting structural disease

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: Depressed ventricular function with frequent/repetitive ectopy

chunks.diseaseName: Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm
chunks.text: Risk is stratified less by ectopy count alone than by context: (1) structurally normal heart with normal ECG and monomorphic NSVT under 200/min - benign/low risk; (2) structural heart disease (post-MI, heart failure, HCM, congenital disease) where greater frequency and complexity (couplets, NSVT) mark more severe disease and higher mortality; (3) high-risk features warranting concern - syncope, very rapid/polymorphic/short-coupled NSVT, multifocal or RBBB-like morphology, abnormal ECG, or family history of sudden death. PVC burden of at least 10-20% of total beats over 24 hours is the threshold associated with potential PVC-induced ventricular dysfunction.

chunks.text: Presbycusis results from cumulative degenerative changes in the auditory system with age. Several subtypes are described: sensory presbycusis from loss of hair cells in the basal (high-frequency) cochlea; neural presbycusis from loss of spiral ganglion neurons, which particularly impairs speech discrimination; strial or metabolic presbycusis from atrophy of the stria vascularis affecting the endocochlear potential across frequencies; and cochlear conductive (mechanical) presbycusis from stiffening of the basilar membrane. Central auditory pathway changes further degrade processing of speech, especially in noise. Genetic predisposition, lifelong noise exposure, vascular and metabolic disease and ototoxins accelerate these changes.

chunks.text: Presbycusis is the progressive, symmetrical sensorineural hearing loss that accompanies ageing and is the commonest cause of hearing loss in older adults
