Preterm labour is a syndrome with multiple pathways converging on premature activation of the mechanisms of labour: uterine contractility, cervical ripening, and decidual-membrane activation. Recognised triggers include intrauterine infection and inflammation, uteroplacental ischaemia or haemorrhage (decidual bleeding), excessive uterine distension (as in multiple pregnancy or polyhydramnios), cervical insufficiency, and maternal or fetal stress activating the corticotrophin-releasing hormone axis. These pathways generate prostaglandins and inflammatory mediators that stimulate contractions and cervical change ahead of term.
Preterm labour is regular uterine contractions with cervical change occurring before 37 completed weeks of gestation
It is the leading cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality, largely through complications of prematurity such as respiratory distress, intraventricular haemorrhage, and necrotising enterocolitis
The strongest predictors are a previous preterm birth and a short cervix on transvaginal ultrasound
Antenatal corticosteroids given to accelerate fetal lung maturation are among the most effective interventions to improve neonatal outcomes
Magnesium sulfate given before anticipated early preterm birth provides fetal neuroprotection, reducing the risk of cerebral palsy
Tocolytic drugs are used mainly to delay delivery briefly to allow steroids to act and to enable transfer to a unit with neonatal intensive care
Fetal fibronectin testing and cervical length measurement help identify women at genuinely high or low risk of imminent delivery
Group B streptococcus status guides intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis, and progesterone supplementation can reduce risk in selected high-risk women
Mistaking true preterm labour for Braxton Hicks contractions and delaying steroids
Overtreating with tocolytics when there is a contraindication such as chorioamnionitis or significant abruption
Failing to give antenatal corticosteroids and magnesium neuroprotection within the appropriate window
Not arranging timely transfer to a unit with adequate neonatal facilities
Overlooking an underlying infection driving the labour

Outcome depends heavily on gestational age at delivery; each additional week in utero at early gestations substantially improves survival and reduces disability. Antenatal steroids, magnesium neuroprotection, and delivery in a centre with neonatal intensive care improve results. Women with a prior spontaneous preterm birth remain at increased risk in subsequent pregnancies.
Signs of chorioamnionitis such as maternal fever, uterine tenderness, and fetal tachycardia
Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes with cord prolapse risk
Vaginal bleeding suggesting abruption or praevia
Non-reassuring fetal status
Advanced cervical dilatation with imminent delivery at a very early gestation

chunks.text: Priapism reflects a disturbance of the normal mechanisms that terminate erection. In ischaemic (low-flow) priapism, veno-occlusion persists so blood becomes trapped in the corpora cavernosa, producing stagnant, hypoxic, acidotic blood and a compartment-syndrome-like state; prolonged ischaemia leads to smooth muscle necrosis and corporal fibrosis. Causes include sickle cell disease and other haemoglobinopathies, leukaemic infiltration, and pharmacological agents. Non-ischaemic (high-flow) priapism results from unregulated arterial inflow, typically through a cavernosal artery fistula created by perineal or penile trauma, so oxygenation is maintained and tissue ischaemia does not occur.

source.ref: Smith & Tanagho's General Urology / Campbell-Walsh Urology

chunks.text: Priapism is a prolonged penile erection (typically beyond four hours) unrelated to sexual stimulation, and the critical first step is to distinguish ischaemic (low-flow) from non-ischaemic (high-flow) types

source.ref: Smith & Tanagho's General Urology / Campbell-Walsh Urology

chunks.text: Ischaemic priapism is a painful, rigid erection representing a compartment syndrome of the corpora cavernosa and is a urological emergency because prolonged ischaemia causes fibrosis and permanent erectile dysfunction

chunks.text: Non-ischaemic (high-flow) priapism is usually painless, semi-rigid, and follows perineal or penile trauma with an arteriolar-sinusoidal fistula; it is not an emergency and often resolves or is managed by embolisation

chunks.text: Cavernosal blood gas analysis distinguishes the two: ischaemic blood is dark and hypoxic/acidotic, whereas high-flow blood is bright red with near-arterial values

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: Most primary brain tumors have no identified cause; established risk factors are limited to ionizing radiation exposure (meningiomas, gliomas, schwannomas) and immunosuppression (primary CNS lymphoma), while electromagnetic field/cell-phone exposure, head injury, dietary N-nitroso compounds, and occupational factors are not proven. Tumors arise through a multistep accumulation of genetic alterations: loss of tumor-suppressor genes (p53, CDKN2A/B, PTEN) and amplification/overexpression of proto-oncogenes (EGFR, PDGFR), producing uncontrolled growth; many gliomas show marked molecular heterogeneity. The 2016 and 2021 WHO classifications integrate molecular parameters (e.g., IDH mutation, 1p/19q co-deletion, H3 K27/G34 alterations) with histology. Brain metastases spread hematogenously, lodging in terminal arterioles at the gray-white junction; leptomeningeal disease reaches the subarachnoid space via arterial circulation or retrograde venous flow and may also follow resection of a cerebellar metastasis. Epidural cord compression generally results from metastases to the axial skeleton (typically breast and prostate), though lymphoma can invade through an intervertebral foramen without bone destruction (Harrison 22e p.717, p.719, p.723, p.724-725).

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: Brain tumors of any histology tend to present with a mixture of generalized features (headache, nausea/vomiting, cognitive decline, personality change, gait disturbance from raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus) and focal features (hemiparesis, aphasia, visual-field defect) (Harrison 22e p.716).

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: Most brain metastases lodge at the gray-white junction in watershed territories; ~85% are supratentorial and ~15% in the posterior fossa, and distribution roughly mirrors regional blood flow (Harrison 22e p.723).

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: Melanoma has the greatest propensity to seed the brain (found in ~80% at autopsy), but lung and breast carcinomas are the most common sources overall; prostate and breast cancers also favor dural metastases that can mimic meningioma (Harrison 22e p.723).

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: In epidural spinal metastasis, back pain is the presenting symptom in virtually all patients and may precede neurologic signs by weeks to months; the pain characteristically worsens on lying down, in contrast to arthritic pain which eases with recumbency (Harrison 22e p.725).

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: Any cancer patient with severe back pain should undergo whole-spine MRI; plain films, bone scan, or CT may show bony disease but only MRI reliably delineates epidural tumor (Harrison 22e p.725).

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: The classic morning-predominant brain tumor headache that eases through the day is actually seen in only a minority of patients; tumor headaches may be holocephalic, ipsilateral to the lesion, or even migraine-like with throbbing pain and scotoma (Harrison 22e p.716).

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: Seizures occur in roughly 25% of patients with brain metastases or malignant gliomas but are the presenting symptom in up to 90% of low-grade gliomas; all tumor-related seizures have a focal onset whether or not that is clinically apparent (Harrison 22e p.716).

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: Contrast (gadolinium) MRI is the preferred diagnostic study; CT is reserved for patients who cannot undergo MRI. Neuroimaging is generally the only test needed to diagnose a brain tumor, and laboratory tests are rarely useful (Harrison 22e p.716).

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: Malignant tumors (primary or metastatic) typically enhance with gadolinium, show central necrosis, and are ringed by white-matter edema, whereas low-grade gliomas usually do NOT enhance and are best seen on FLAIR sequences (Harrison 22e p.716).

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: Meningiomas are dural-based enhancing extra-axial masses with a characteristic dural tail that compress but do not invade brain; their principal differential is a dural metastasis or dural lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.716, p.722).

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: Adult diffuse gliomas are now classified molecularly: IDH-mutant astrocytoma (1p/19q intact), IDH-mutant oligodendroglioma (1p/19q co-deleted), and IDH wild-type glioblastoma; these molecular markers carry major prognostic weight (Harrison 22e p.718-719).

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: An unmethylated MGMT promoter predicts relative temozolomide resistance and a worse glioblastoma prognosis; MGMT promoter hypermethylation (gene silencing) predicts better response (Harrison 22e p.720).

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: Meningiomas are the most common primary brain tumor (~35%), are more common in women and with prior cranial irradiation and NF2, and many are found incidentally; small asymptomatic ones can simply be monitored with serial MRI (Harrison 22e p.721-722).

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: Forgetting that the smallest brain metastases can produce extensive edema while large ones cause little, and that imaging appearance is nonspecific.

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: Overlooking that ~10% of systemic cancers can first present with a brain metastasis, sometimes requiring biopsy of the brain lesion when no accessible systemic site exists.

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: Treating low-grade glioma as benign — most ultimately transform to higher grade.

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: Outcome is highly histology- and molecular-subtype-dependent. Low-grade IDH-mutant astrocytomas have median survival around 10 years (most eventually transform to higher grade); oligodendrogliomas (1p/19q co-deleted) generally exceed 10 years. Glioblastoma carries a poor prognosis with median survival in the 15-18 month range with combined therapy and ~10% 5-year survival; adverse factors are older age, unmethylated MGMT promoter, poor Karnofsky status, and unresectable tumor. H3 K27-altered diffuse midline glioma has a median survival of roughly 1 year regardless of grade; H3 G34-mutant hemispheric glioma about 18-22 months. Medulloblastoma achieves long-term survival in ~70% but often with neurocognitive cost, varying by molecular subgroup (WNT best; group 3 worst). Completely resected meningiomas and schwannomas can be cured. Brain metastases treated with whole-brain radiotherapy alone yield median survival of only ~4-6 months, though stereotactic radiosurgery achieves local control in 80-90% and occasional cure. Leptomeningeal metastasis is treated palliatively with no curative therapy. In epidural metastasis, patients fare well if treated before a severe deficit develops, but overall survival is often short owing to widespread systemic disease (Harrison 22e p.718-725).

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: New focal neurologic deficit (hemiparesis, aphasia, visual-field loss) that is subacute and progressive

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: New-onset focal seizures, especially in an adult without prior epilepsy

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: Severe back pain in a cancer patient (suggests epidural metastasis) — warrants urgent whole-spine MRI

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: Leg weakness, sensory level, or sphincter dysfunction suggesting evolving spinal cord compression (a neuro-oncologic emergency)

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: New limb pain in a patient with breast, lung cancer, or melanoma (consider leptomeningeal spread)

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: Signs of raised intracranial pressure / hydrocephalus (worsening headache, vomiting, declining consciousness)

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: Multilevel neuraxis signs (combined cranial neuropathies plus radiculopathies) suggesting leptomeningeal carcinomatosis

chunks.diseaseName: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
chunks.text: Gliomas are graded by the WHO into grades 2-4 (low- vs high-grade) integrating histology with molecular markers (IDH mutation, 1p/19q co-deletion; CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion upgrades an IDH-mutant astrocytoma to grade 4). Meningiomas are WHO grade I (benign), II (atypical), or III (malignant). Brain tumor symptoms are categorized as generalized (raised-ICP related) versus focal/lateralizing. Nervous-system metastatic disease is grouped clinically into intraparenchymal brain metastases, leptomeningeal (carcinomatous meningitis) metastases, and epidural spinal cord compression (Harrison 22e p.716, p.719, p.722).

Primary hyperoxaluria results from autosomal recessive defects in enzymes of hepatic glyoxylate detoxification. In type 1, deficiency of the peroxisomal enzyme alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase allows glyoxylate to be oxidised to oxalate; types 2 and 3 involve other enzymes in the same pathway. The liver overproduces oxalate, which the kidneys excrete in high amounts, promoting calcium oxalate crystallisation, stone formation, and nephrocalcinosis. Because oxalate is poorly cleared once renal function fails, it accumulates systemically and is deposited in multiple tissues as oxalosis.
Primary hyperoxaluria is a group of inherited disorders of glyoxylate metabolism that cause marked overproduction of oxalate by the liver
It typically presents with recurrent calcium oxalate kidney stones and nephrocalcinosis, often from childhood, and can progress to renal failure
Type 1, from deficiency of the hepatic enzyme alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase, is the most common and generally the most severe form
As renal function declines, oxalate can no longer be cleared and deposits throughout the body (systemic oxalosis), affecting bone, heart, retina, and vessels
The diagnosis should be considered in any patient with recurrent oxalate stones, especially with early onset, a family history, or nephrocalcinosis
Elevated urinary oxalate, genetic testing, and sometimes liver biopsy establish the diagnosis, and high fluid intake with crystallisation inhibitors is a supportive measure

A subset of type 1 disease responds biochemically to pyridoxine, and definitive treatment historically involved combined or sequential liver and kidney transplantation, with newer RNA-targeted therapies now available
Treating recurrent stones symptomatically without recognising an underlying inherited metabolic cause
Confusing primary with enteric hyperoxaluria, which have different mechanisms and management
Overlooking systemic oxalosis as renal function falls
Performing isolated kidney transplantation in type 1 disease without addressing continued hepatic oxalate overproduction

The outlook varies with type and genotype; type 1 disease can progress to end-stage renal failure and life-threatening systemic oxalosis, whereas some pyridoxine-responsive and non-type-1 forms are milder, and early diagnosis with modern therapies has improved outcomes considerably.
Progressive decline in renal function toward end-stage disease
Systemic oxalosis with cardiac, skeletal, retinal, or vascular involvement
Recurrent obstructing stones with infection or acute kidney injury
Early-onset stone disease with nephrocalcinosis suggesting a severe genotype

PIDs are predominantly Mendelian genetic diseases that arise whenever the expression or function of a nonredundant effector or mediator of the immune system is genetically impaired. More than 550 conditions have been described, with deleterious mutations identified in roughly 500 genes; estimated prevalence is 5-10 per 100,000 (probably an underestimate). They are increasingly grouped within the broader category of inborn errors of immunity that also includes autoinflammatory syndromes. Defects can involve any aspect of innate or adaptive immunity, cell differentiation, effector function, or immune regulation. The clinical consequence is multiple levels of vulnerability to infection, ranging from extremely broad (as in SCID, where T-cell development is blocked) to narrowly restricted to a single class of organism (as in Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease, an IL-12-IFN-gamma axis defect). Antibody (B-cell) defects (agammaglobulinaemia from BTK and pre-B-cell-receptor gene defects, hyper-IgM from class-switch-recombination defects such as CD40L/CD40, IgA deficiency, and CVID) impair production or class switching of immunoglobulins, leaving patients unable to opsonise and neutralise pyogenic encapsulated bacteria. Cellular (T-cell) defects impair help for antibody production, macrophage activation, and cytotoxicity, causing susceptibility to viral, fungal (Candida), and opportunistic infections (e.g., Pneumocystis jirovecii, Cryptosporidium). Combined defects (SCID) abolish both arms. Innate defects affect phagocyte number (severe congenital neutropenia), adhesion (LAD), or microbial killing (chronic granulomatous disease, from defective NADPH-oxidase reactive-oxygen-species production), as well as complement components and innate receptor/signalling pathways (TLR adaptors IRAK4/MYD88). Beyond infection, PIDs can drive immunopathology including allergy, lymphoproliferation, autoimmunity, and an increased risk of malignancy (notably lymphoma) (Harrison 22e p.2793-2794, 2796-2802).

The most frequent symptom prompting the diagnosis of a PID is recurrent or unusually severe infection; recurrent allergic or autoimmune manifestations may also be the alerting feature (Harrison 22e p.2793).
Immunoglobulin replacement should be guided by the occurrence of infection, not by laboratory IgG/antibody levels alone, to avoid unjustified infusions; it is lifelong therapy (Harrison 22e p.2802).

A precise molecular/genetic diagnosis has become a milestone in the care of PID patients, guiding treatment selection, genetic counselling, and prenatal diagnosis; suspected cases should be referred to experienced centres (Harrison 22e p.2804).

PIDs are classified by (1) the arm of the immune system that is defective and (2) the mechanism of the defect; the major categories are antibody/B-cell defects (agammaglobulinaemia, CVID, hyper-IgM, IgA deficiency), T-cell/cellular defects, combined defects (SCID), and innate-immune defects of phagocytes, complement, or innate receptors/signalling (Harrison 22e p.2794).

The site of infection and the causal microorganism point to the affected compartment: respiratory-tract (sinus, bronchial) infection mostly suggests defective antibody responses; invasive bacterial infection can result from complement deficiency, innate-signalling defects, asplenia, or antibody defects; viral, recurrent Candida, and opportunistic infections suggest impaired T-cell immunity; skin infections and deep abscesses primarily reflect innate (phagocyte) defects such as chronic granulomatous disease (Harrison 22e p.2794).

B-lymphocyte (antibody) deficiencies are the most frequent PIDs, accounting for 60-70% of all cases; T-cell deficiencies account for ~20% and innate-immune defects for ~10% (Harrison 22e p.2794, 2796, 2797).

Encapsulated/pyogenic bacteria (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis) and recurrent sinopulmonary infection are the hallmark of defective antibody production; untreated recurrent bronchial infection leads to bronchiectasis, cor pulmonale, and death (Harrison 22e p.2801).

Invasive Neisseria infection points to deficiencies of the complement lytic phase (C5-C9) or the alternative pathway (factors D, properdin); classic-pathway and lytic-phase complement deficiencies may also predispose to autoimmune disease, notably SLE (Harrison 22e p.2797).

CVID is recognised predominantly in adults, although clinical manifestations can begin earlier in life; in most cases no molecular cause is identified and the diagnosis is made only after excluding hypomorphic agammaglobulinaemia mutations and more subtle T-cell defects, especially in children (Harrison 22e p.2802).

First-line laboratory work-up is guided by the clinical picture and includes blood cell counts/morphology, serum immunoglobulin levels (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE), specific antibody responses to vaccines (tetanus toxoid, unconjugated pneumococcal polysaccharide), and lymphocyte subset phenotyping; more specific (genetic) tests then confirm a definitive diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2794-2795).

Even with profound B-cell deficiency, infections rarely occur before 6 months of age because of transplacental maternal IgG; conversely, in SCID clinical consequences typically appear within 3-6 months of birth (Harrison 22e p.2801, 2799).
CVID can present in adulthood and is easily missed; it is recognised predominantly in adults although manifestations may begin earlier (Harrison 22e p.2802).

High variability of expression for a given PID (e.g., WAS, XLA, CTLA4 deficiency) can hamper diagnosis; modifier genes and environmental triggers such as EBV (in XLP) modulate the phenotype (Harrison 22e p.2804).
Leaky BTK mutations causing mild hypogammaglobulinaemia with low but detectable B cells should not be confused with CVID (Harrison 22e p.2802).
T-cell lymphopenia in SCID may be masked by maternally-engrafted T cells, so screening for maternal cells with genetic markers should be performed when needed (Harrison 22e p.2799).

Somatic mutations in an affected gene can attenuate the phenotype of T-cell PIDs (described for ADA, X-linked SCID, RAG, NEMO, and most often WAS), while somatic mutations can also create PID-like disease (as in ALPS) (Harrison 22e p.2804).
Cytokine-neutralising autoantibodies (to IFN-gamma, IL-6, IL-7, type I interferon) can mimic a PID (Harrison 22e p.2804).

Caution with immunoglobulin replacement in patients with complete IgA deficiency and residual antibody production: anti-IgA antibodies can trigger anaphylactic shock, so IgA-free IgG preparations should be used (Harrison 22e p.2803).

Ataxia-telangiectasia should be considered in young children with IgA deficiency and recurrent problematic infections, as ataxia and telangiectasia may not appear before age 3-4 years (Harrison 22e p.2799-2800).

Prognosis varies widely with the molecule and arm of immunity affected. T-cell and combined defects generally carry a poor prognosis and require early diagnosis and intervention; SCID is fatal in infancy without treatment, but allogeneic HSCT offers a high curative potential in patients in otherwise reasonable condition, and gene therapy has succeeded in X-linked (gamma-c) SCID, ADA-SCID, and Artemis deficiency. Functional T-cell defects carry a worse HSCT prognosis than SCID because many patients are already chronically infected at diagnosis. For antibody deficiencies, lifelong immunoglobulin replacement combined with management of chronic lung disease reduces respiratory infections and prevents progression to bronchiectasis and cor pulmonale; in CVID, lymphoproliferation, granulomatous disease, autoimmunity, and lymphoma define long-term prognosis. DNA-repair disorders such as ataxia-telangiectasia are progressive and carry a very high risk of lymphoma, leukaemia, and (in adulthood) carcinoma. Newborn TREC screening, by enabling treatment of uninfected SCID patients, maximises the chance of cure. Early diagnosis with referral to experienced centres is essential to optimal outcome (Harrison 22e p.2794, 2799-2800, 2802, 2804).
Recurrent, unusually severe, or persistent infections, or infection by unusual/opportunistic organisms
A family history of early childhood deaths (suggesting X-linked or recessive inheritance, e.g., SCID)
Lymphocytopenia in an infant (strongly suggestive of SCID in >90% of cases) or absent thymic shadow on chest x-ray
Failure to thrive with protracted diarrhoea, recurrent oral candidiasis, or Pneumocystis pneumonia in early infancy
Complications of live vaccines (e.g., BCG dissemination, rotavirus diarrhoea) signalling a severe T-cell defect
Invasive Neisseria infection (complement lytic-phase or alternative-pathway deficiency) or recurrent encapsulated-organism sepsis with asplenia
Recurrent infection accompanied by autoimmunity, lymphoproliferation, granulomatous disease, or lymphoma
Absence of pus at sites of infection (hallmark of severe congenital neutropenia)

PIDs are classified along two axes: (1) the arm of the immune system that is defective and (2) the mechanism of the defect (when known). The two main divisions are deficiencies of the innate immune system (phagocytic cells - impaired production [severe congenital neutropenia], asplenia, impaired adhesion [LAD], impaired killing [CGD]; innate-immunity receptors/signal transduction [TLR-signalling defects, MSMD]; complement deficiencies of the classical/alternative/lectin pathways and the lytic phase) and deficiencies of the adaptive immune system (T lymphocytes - SCID, DiGeorge, combined immunodeficiencies, hyper-IgE, DOCK8, CD40L, Wiskott-Aldrich, ataxia-telangiectasia and DNA-repair defects; B lymphocytes - X-linked/AR agammaglobulinaemia, hyper-IgM, CVID, IgA deficiency), together with regulatory defects (autoinflammatory syndromes, severe colitis, HLH, ALPS, autoimmunity such as IPEX and APECED). The classification is acknowledged to involve some arbitrary decisions because of overlap and incomplete data (Harrison 22e p.2794).

chunks.text: Primary open-angle glaucoma is a progressive optic neuropathy in which aqueous outflow through an anatomically open trabecular meshwork is impaired, raising resistance to drainage. The resulting intraocular pressure, sometimes within the normal range, contributes to mechanical and vascular stress at the optic nerve head, causing loss of retinal ganglion cell axons. This produces characteristic cupping of the optic disc and a corresponding pattern of arcuate and peripheral visual field loss that advances slowly over years.

Prion diseases are caused by prions, host-encoded proteins (the prion protein) that adopt an alternative, abnormal conformation (misfolded PrPSc) which undergoes self-propagation. PrPSc imposes its conformation on the normal precursor protein, which in turn becomes self-templating, producing faithful copies; the misfolded protein is enriched for beta-sheet and assembles into amyloid fibrils. The amyloid plaques in kuru and CJD are filled with PrPSc prions assembled into fibrils. CJD is one of the major degenerative dementias characterized by abnormal aggregation of a specific protein (misfolded prion protein, PrPSc). Familial CJD is genetically linked to mutations in the PrP gene (p.237, p.3400-3401).
CJD is a rapidly progressive disorder associated with dementia, focal cortical signs, rigidity, and myoclonus, causing death less than 1 year after first symptoms appear (p.3525-3526).

CJD is the classic cause of a rapidly progressive dementia (RPD: progression from symptom onset to dementia within a year or less), especially when associated with myoclonus, though more often RPD is due to AD, another neurodegenerative disorder, or autoimmune encephalitis (p.237).
On examination, CJD is suggested by diffuse rigidity, an akinetic-mute state, and prominent, often startle-sensitive myoclonus (p.239).

MRI diffusion-weighted imaging reveals restricted diffusion within the cortical ribbon and/or basal ganglia in most patients; basal ganglia or thalamus hyperintensity may also be seen on diffusion/FLAIR MRI (p.240, p.3526).
EEG is not routinely used but can suggest CJD by showing repetitive bursts of diffuse high-amplitude sharp waves (periodic complexes) (p.241).

Prion diseases such as CJD are rare (prevalence ~1 per million); the rapidity of progression distinguishes CJD from AD, though AD can occasionally present as a rapidly progressive dementia (p.3525-3526).
Prion disease is one cause of subacute progressive ataxia, especially when an infectious etiology such as transmission from contaminated human growth hormone is responsible (p.3590).

Must exclude treatable causes of rapidly progressive dementia (e.g., autoimmune/paraneoplastic encephalitis, Hashimoto's encephalopathy, CNS vasculitis, CNS infection, lymphoma) before attributing a rapidly progressive dementia to CJD.
More rapid degenerative dementias with prominent movement abnormalities (CBD, DLB) are more likely to be mistaken for CJD.
Rarely, prolonged focal or generalized seizures can produce an MRI appearance similar to CJD.
Uniformly fatal. CJD causes death less than 1 year after the first symptoms appear (p.3525-3526).

The prostate (pelvic, adjacent to rectum, bladder, neurovascular bundles and urinary sphincter) is composed of tubuloalveolar glands in fibromuscular stroma. PSA is produced by epithelial cells; both epithelial and stromal cells express androgen receptors (AR) and depend on androgens for growth. Testosterone is converted by prostatic 5alpha-reductase to the more potent dihydrotestosterone. BPH is non-malignant proliferation of the periurethral transition zone (begins at puberty, accelerates after age 55) producing bladder-outlet obstruction; symptoms also reflect age-related detrusor dysfunction. Malignancy usually arises in the peripheral zone; the cancer continuum runs from preneoplastic/localized lesion to metastatic, symptomatic, lethal disease over years to decades. Prostate cancer is AR-signaling dependent, so androgen deprivation is the mainstay of metastatic therapy; castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) progresses despite castrate testosterone (<=50 ng/mL) because most CRPCs continue to express and signal through the AR, and androgen-resistant cells are present from diagnosis (cure is not achieved by androgen depletion alone). (p.695-696, 702-703)

Both benign and malignant prostate changes rise sharply with age: autopsies of men in the eighth decade show hyperplastic changes in >90% and malignant changes in >70%, so management is risk-adapted and weighed against competing causes of morbidity and mortality (p.695).

BPH arises in the periurethral transition zone surrounding the urethra, whereas most cancers arise in the peripheral zone; peripheral-zone cancers may or may not be palpable on digital rectal exam (DRE) (p.696).

BPH causes lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) split into obstructive symptoms (hesitancy, straining, weak stream, terminal dribbling, prolonged voiding, incomplete emptying) and irritative symptoms (frequency, urgency, urge incontinence, small voided volumes); LUTS reflect both prostatic enlargement and age-related detrusor dysfunction, not mass effect alone (p.703).

PSA (kallikrein KLK3) is prostate specific, NOT prostate cancer specific: it can rise from prostatitis, BPH, or cancer; a lower free PSA fraction is more likely associated with cancer at biopsy (p.696-697).

After radical prostatectomy PSA should become undetectable within about 6 weeks (no prostate = no detectable PSA); persistence of measurable PSA after gland removal is typical of recurrent cancer (p.696-697).
Only 20-25% of patients with an abnormal DRE have prostate cancer; carcinoma is characteristically hard, nodular, irregular, asymmetric, but induration can also be BPH or calculi (p.696).
>95% of prostate cancers are adenocarcinomas; the remainder are squamous, transitional cell, rarely carcinosarcoma or small-cell histologies (p.697).

Most men diagnosed with prostate cancer will NOT die of it; the incidence/mortality ratio is extremely high relative to other malignancies, which drives the active-surveillance vs treatment balance (p.695).

Multiparametric prostate MRI (mpMRI) graded by PI-RADS is now obtained in most cases BEFORE biopsy: PI-RADS 1-2 lesions can safely avoid biopsy; PI-RADS 3-5 lesions get targeted biopsy, reducing detection of indolent Gleason 6 (grade group 1) cancers without missing clinically relevant ones (p.697).

PSA screening is controversial: it generates both false positives and false negatives and can lead to diagnosis and treatment of indolent cancers that pose little risk; the decision (USPSTF: individual shared decision for men 55-69, recommended AGAINST screening at age >=70; AUA: shared decision, earlier for Black ancestry/germline mutations/strong family history) must balance benefit against overtreatment harm.
PSA is prostate specific, not cancer specific - do not equate an elevated PSA with cancer; BPH and prostatitis also raise it.
There is NO PSA level below which prostate cancer risk is zero (Prostate Cancer Prevention Trial); a 'normal' PSA does not exclude cancer.
DRE alone is inaccurate for staging (capsular invasion, seminal-vesicle and nodal involvement) and is not a validated screening test by itself.
Patients misread Gleason 6 as 'mid-scale' and assume aggressive disease; the grade group system was created because Gleason 6 (grade group 1) is actually the lowest, favorable-risk category.
PSMA PET, despite high sensitivity, cannot detect low-volume microscopic nodal disease - a negative scan does not exclude micrometastasis.
A negative biopsy in a patient with elevated PSA does NOT rule out a future cancer diagnosis - continue follow-up.
No agent is currently approved for prostate cancer prevention (5-alpha-reductase inhibitors reduced mainly low-risk indolent cancers; vitamins/supplements showed no benefit).
No rationale to screen asymptomatic men with short life expectancy; antiandrogen monotherapy gives inferior cancer-specific outcomes versus castration.

Most men with prostate cancer do not die from it; >70-80% of newly diagnosed cancers are now organ-confined. Nonmetastatic disease is stratified low/intermediate/high (and very-high) risk; grade group system accurately predicts prognosis with grade group 1 (Gleason <=6) being favorable. A single PSA at age 60 correlates strongly (AUC 0.90) with lifetime risk of death from prostate cancer, and ~90% of prostate-cancer deaths occur in the top PSA quartile (>2 ng/mL), though only a minority of those men develop lethal disease. Androgen deprivation produces an initial response and dormant period but is not curative; PSA normalizes in 60-70% and measurable disease regresses in >50%, with survival inversely proportional to disease extent at treatment start and to the 6-8 month nadir PSA. Castration-resistant prostate cancer is lethal for most patients; multiple agents (abiraterone, enzalutamide, docetaxel, cabazitaxel, radium-223, Lu-177 PSMA-617, PARP inhibitors for BRCA/DNA-repair mutations, checkpoint inhibitors for MSI-high/dMMR) prolong survival. (p.695, 697, 701-703)

Osteoblastic bone metastases (prostate cancer characteristically produces bone-forming metastases) presenting as back/skeletal pain; bone is the dominant site of metastatic and castration-resistant progression
Spinal cord compression / cord compromise or base-of-skull symptoms from metastatic disease require EMERGENCY evaluation because loss of neurologic function may be permanent if not treated quickly

GnRH agonists are relatively contraindicated in patients with significant urinary obstruction, cancer-related pain, or spinal cord compromise because the initial testosterone surge can cause a disease flare (AR antagonists are added to blunt flare; GnRH antagonists and abiraterone do not cause a surge)

Rising nadir PSA >4 ng/mL at 6-8 months after starting androgen deprivation predicts markedly inferior survival

Gleason grade group system: grade group 1 (Gleason <=6), 2 (3+4=7), 3 (4+3=7), 4 (4+4=8), 5 (Gleason 9-10). TNM staging: T1c clinically inapparent PSA-detected; T2 palpable, confined within prostate; T3 extends through capsule/seminal vesicles (T3b); T4 fixed or invading adjacent structures. Nonmetastatic risk groups: low (organ-confined, PSA <10, grade group 1); intermediate (organ-confined, PSA 10-20, or grade group 2 favorable / 3 unfavorable, with >50% positive cores = unfavorable); high (extraprostatic, PSA >20, or grade group 4-5); very-high (seminal vesicle T3b or adjacent-organ T4 invasion or multiple high-grade biopsy samples). Metastatic states: noncastrate metastatic (testosterone >50 ng/dL) vs castration-resistant (CRPC, testosterone <=50 ng/mL). (p.697-698, 701-703)

Plasma proteins normally enter the gut lumen only in small amounts. In protein-losing enteropathy this loss is markedly increased by one of two general processes. In lymphatic disorders, obstructed or high-pressure intestinal lymphatics (from congenital lymphangiectasia or raised systemic venous pressure, as after Fontan surgery) leak protein-rich lymph into the lumen. In mucosal disorders, inflammation, ulceration, or increased epithelial permeability from infectious, allergic, inflammatory, or infiltrative disease allows serum proteins to escape across the damaged barrier. Because the loss is non-selective, albumin, immunoglobulins, and other proteins are depleted, producing hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, and sometimes immune compromise.
This is a syndrome, not a single disease, in which excessive loss of plasma proteins into the gastrointestinal tract leads to hypoproteinaemia and oedema.
It should be suspected in a child with hypoalbuminaemia and oedema once liver disease, kidney protein loss, and inadequate intake have been excluded.
Underlying mechanisms fall into two broad groups: lymphatic obstruction or elevated lymphatic pressure, and mucosal disease with increased permeability or erosion.

Lymphatic causes include intestinal lymphangiectasia and elevated central venous pressure after cardiac surgery (notably the Fontan circulation), while mucosal causes include inflammatory, allergic, infectious, and infiltrative enteropathies.
Because losses are non-selective, other serum proteins such as immunoglobulins and clotting factors may also fall, sometimes causing lymphopenia and predisposing to infection.
A stool alpha-1-antitrypsin measurement is a useful non-invasive marker of enteric protein loss because it is not degraded in the gut.
Management is directed at the underlying cause together with nutritional support, and in lymphatic causes a low-fat diet enriched with medium-chain triglycerides can reduce lymphatic protein loss.
Peripheral oedema, ascites, or effusions in a child with unexplained low albumin should prompt evaluation of the gut as a source.
Attributing hypoalbuminaemia and oedema to renal or hepatic causes without considering the gut
Overlooking accompanying immunoglobulin loss and infection risk
Failing to identify and treat the specific underlying disorder
Neglecting nutritional support and the role of a low-fat, medium-chain triglyceride diet in lymphatic loss

Outlook depends heavily on the underlying cause; some mucosal causes resolve when the primary disease is treated, whereas lymphangiectasia and Fontan-associated protein loss can be chronic and difficult to manage.

Most of these protozoa are acquired by fecal-oral ingestion of environmentally resistant cysts or oocysts (Trichomonas is the exception, being venereally transmitted). Giardia trophozoites excyst in the small intestine, adhere to but do not invade the proximal small-bowel epithelium, and may cause enterocyte apoptosis, epithelial barrier dysfunction, and malabsorption/secretion; the precise mechanism of diarrhea is unknown, and consequent loss of brush-border enzyme activity produces lactose intolerance and, in some chronic cases, malabsorption with villous flattening resembling tropical sprue or celiac disease. Cryptosporidium sporozoites infect intestinal epithelial cells within an intracellular vacuole, completing asexual and sexual cycles to generate immediately infectious oocysts; the means of secretory diarrhea are uncertain, infection can be patchy in the small bowel, and biliary tract involvement may cause papillary stenosis, sclerosing cholangitis, or cholecystitis, especially in AIDS. Cystoisospora and Cyclospora similarly invade small-bowel epithelial cells (Cyclospora oocysts must mature in the environment before becoming infectious). Microsporidia inject sporoplasm into host cells via an extruded polar tubule and replicate by merogony and sporogony, releasing spores in stool, urine, respiratory secretions, or other fluids. Hypogammaglobulinemia predisposes to prolonged, severe, treatment-refractory giardiasis, indicating humoral immunity is important for control.

Giardia (G. duodenalis, assemblages A and B in humans) is a non-invasive parasite confined to the proximal small bowel that does not spread hematogenously; an inoculum of as few as ~10 cysts can establish infection, and cysts resist routine chlorination but are killed by boiling or filtration.
Blastocystis hominis has uncertain pathogenicity; finding it in stool warrants a full search for other bacterial, viral, or protozoal causes of diarrhea before attributing symptoms to it.

Dientamoeba fragilis is unique among intestinal protozoa in having only a trophozoite stage and no cyst stage; immediate fixation of stool improves detection of the labile trophozoites and NAATs outperform microscopy.

Trichomonas vaginalis is one of the most prevalent protozoal parasites in the United States (an estimated 2-3 million infections per year); it is essentially always transmitted venereally, and most infected men are asymptomatic, serving as a reservoir for reinfection.

Giardiasis classically presents with upper-intestinal/small-bowel features (nausea, vomiting, bloating, belching, sulfurous flatus, abdominal pain) and non-bloody diarrhea; fever, blood, or mucus in stool point away from giardiasis toward colitis or a concomitant illness.

Cryptosporidium (C. hominis, C. parvum) is self-limited (about 1-2 weeks) in immunocompetent hosts but causes chronic, profuse watery diarrhea with stool volumes ranging from 1 to 25 L/day in AIDS patients with CD4 counts below 100/uL.

Cystoisospora belli is distinctive among enteric protozoa in that it can produce peripheral eosinophilia in immunocompetent hosts; in AIDS it mimics cryptosporidiosis with chronic profuse watery diarrhea.

Cyclospora cayetanensis is linked to foodborne outbreaks from imported produce (basil, sweet peas, raspberries) and waterborne spread, and characteristically causes prolonged diarrhea that may persist beyond one month; absence of fecal blood and leukocytes indicates the small-bowel mucosa is not destroyed.

Conventional ova-and-parasite (O+P) stool examination does NOT reliably detect Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, or microsporidia; specific tests (modified acid-fast stain, immunoassays, direct fluorescent antibody, or NAATs) must be requested explicitly.

Microsporidia are obligate intracellular spore-forming organisms that are small and gram-positive; they are most often opportunistic in AIDS, where Enterocytozoon bieneusi and Encephalitozoon intestinalis cause chronic diarrhea and wasting and have been found in 10-40% of patients with chronic diarrhea.

Encephalitozoon species can disseminate beyond the gut to cause keratoconjunctivitis, sinusitis, bronchiolitis/respiratory disease, cholangitis, nephritis, and cystitis, so microsporidiosis is not solely an intestinal disease.

Balantidium coli is a large ciliated protozoan producing a large-bowel disease resembling amebiasis (mucosal invasion, focal necrosis, ulceration); it is zoonotic from pigs and, unlike amebiasis, only rarely disseminates hematogenously to other organs.
Relying on routine stool O+P examination, which misses Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, and microsporidia - specific stains or NAATs must be ordered
Stopping at a single stool exam: cyst/oocyst excretion is variable and intermittent, so repeated sampling or duodenal aspiration/biopsy may be needed
Attributing symptoms to Blastocystis hominis without excluding other pathogens, given its uncertain pathogenicity
Missing Dientamoeba fragilis because of delayed fixation of stool, which degrades its labile trophozoites (it has no cyst stage)
Assuming routine water chlorination eliminates Giardia and Cryptosporidium - their cysts/oocysts resist standard chlorination; boiling or submicron filtration is needed
Diagnosing trichomonal vaginitis by wet mount alone, given its modest (~50-60%) sensitivity
Treating trichomoniasis without concurrently treating sexual partners, leading to apparent treatment failure that is actually reinfection (true high-level metronidazole resistance also occurs)

Outcomes depend heavily on immune status. Giardiasis ranges from asymptomatic carriage to fulminant diarrhea and malabsorption; most patients are cured, though some with chronic infection have delayed symptom resolution attributed to slow brush-border enzyme regeneration, and hypogammaglobulinemic or AIDS patients may have refractory disease. Cryptosporidiosis is self-limited (1-2 weeks) in immunocompetent hosts but can be chronic and severe in AIDS, where improved immune status from antiretroviral therapy can lead to resolution. Cystoisosporiasis and cyclosporiasis can be self-limited but tend to relapse and become chronic in HIV-infected patients. Microsporidiosis can be self-limited in the immunocompetent but contributes to chronic diarrhea and wasting in AIDS, and definitive therapy is not well established. Balantidiasis ranges from asymptomatic to fulminant dysentery; sarcocystosis and most Blastocystis or Dientamoeba infections are mild or self-limited.
CD4+ T-cell count below 100/uL with watery diarrhea (risk of severe, chronic, profuse cryptosporidiosis)
Very high stool output (up to 25 L/day) with marked fluid and electrolyte depletion in immunocompromised cryptosporidiosis

Fever, blood, or mucus in stool during presumed giardiasis - suggests an alternative diagnosis or coinfection
Eosinophilia with enteric symptoms (suggests cystoisosporiasis among the enteric protozoa, or sarcocystosis-associated myositis)
Disseminated microsporidiosis (fever, sinusitis, cholangitis, bronchiolitis, keratoconjunctivitis, encephalitis) in AIDS

No formal staging; severity is gauged clinically by host immune status (notably CD4 count below 100/uL marking risk of severe cryptosporidiosis), stool volume and degree of fluid/electrolyte loss (up to 25 L/day in severe cryptosporidiosis), presence of malabsorption/weight loss/wasting, dehydration, growth retardation in children, and biliary or disseminated extraintestinal involvement.

chunks.text: Psoriasis is a chronic immune-mediated disorder driven by dysregulated activation of the innate and adaptive immune systems, particularly the interleukin-23/T-helper-17 axis and tumour necrosis factor signalling. Activated T cells and dendritic cells release cytokines that drive keratinocyte hyperproliferation and abnormal differentiation, dramatically shortening epidermal turnover time and producing thickened, scaly plaques. Dilated dermal vessels and a neutrophilic and lymphocytic infiltrate account for the erythema and, in pustular variants, sterile collections of neutrophils. A strong polygenic predisposition (including PSORS1/HLA-C associations) interacts with triggers such as infection, trauma, drugs, and stress.

Drug- or medication-induced psychosis (parkinsonian agents, clonidine, quinacrine, procaine derivatives) mimicking schizophrenia

Psychiatric disorders are conceptualized as CNS disorders arising from interacting genetic, developmental, and environmental factors, with substantial heritability and considerable overlap of genetic risk variants across diagnoses (pleiotropy). Anxiety and panic involve noradrenergic discharge from the locus coeruleus and serotonergic dorsal-raphe pathways, with lactate, yohimbine, CCK-4, and CO2 capable of provoking attacks; generalized anxiety implicates the GABA-A receptor/chloride-channel complex and serotonergic modulation. PTSD is associated with excessive locus coeruleus norepinephrine release facilitating fear-memory encoding, insular threat-detection overactivity, and blunted pituitary-adrenal responses. OCD involves orbitofrontal cortex-caudate-globus pallidus circuitry. Major depression shows elevated cortisol and CRH, dexamethasone non-suppression, blunted TSH response to TRH, shortened REM latency with increased REM density and reduced slow-wave sleep, altered proinflammatory cytokines and neurotrophins, oxidative stress, telomere shortening, and possible gut-microbiome changes; delayed therapeutic action of antidepressants implicates adaptive second-messenger and neurotrophic changes. Bipolar disorder shows very high monozygotic concordance (approaching 80%) with risk genes (CACNA1C, ANK3, NCAN, ODZ4, TRANK1) shared with schizophrenia and autism, plus circadian and calcium dysregulation. Schizophrenia involves dopamine D2/D3 signaling in the ventral striatum, many small-effect GWAS loci and rare copy-number variants, and pathways of immunity, inflammation, and cell signaling.

Mental or substance use disorders affect roughly 30% of the U.S. population, yet only about one-third of those affected are currently in treatment; four of the ten leading causes of global disability are psychiatric in origin, and depression is the single largest contributor to disability worldwide.

Schizophrenia requires at least two characteristic symptoms (positive and/or negative) over a 1-month period with continuous signs for at least 6 months; about 10% of patients die by suicide, and negative symptoms predominate in roughly one-third and predict poor drug response.

Personality change can be the first manifestation of serious neurologic, endocrine, or other medical disease (e.g., a frontal-lobe tumor presenting with altered motivation while the neurologic exam stays normal), so a personality disorder is a diagnosis that requires exclusion of such causes.

In somatic symptom disorder the defining feature is the patient's disproportionate interpretation and preoccupation with symptoms, not the absence of a medical explanation; patients with genuine medical disease can still qualify, and repeated tests and exploratory surgery are counterproductive.

Brief validated office instruments (PRIME-MD / Patient Health Questionnaire, SDDS-PC, the four-item PC-PTSD screen) take only minutes and map patient responses onto formal DSM criteria, helping primary care clinicians make the initial diagnosis.

Panic attacks reach peak intensity within about 10 minutes and usually resolve within an hour; up to ~75% of panic disorder patients eventually meet criteria for major depression, and panic is a frequent occult cause of chest pain with normal coronary angiograms and of unexplained syncope.

Agoraphobia and housebound behavior are often concealed out of embarrassment, so the syndrome is missed unless the clinician asks directly; about one-third of patients presenting with anxiety have an underlying medical etiology.

Major depression requires depressed mood or anhedonia plus a total of at least 5 of 9 symptoms for a minimum of 2 weeks; key distinguishing features from grief are pervasive worthlessness/self-loathing and persistent (rather than wave-like) dysphoria.

Suicide risk must be probed by direct, empathic questioning: about 4-5% of depressed patients die by suicide, and most have seen a physician within the month before death; coexisting anxiety, panic, or agitation raises near-term risk.

Recognizing a bipolar diathesis in a patient presenting with depression is essential because antidepressant monotherapy can worsen symptoms and accelerate cycling; clues include childhood onset, antidepressant treatment failure, atypical features (hypersomnia, weight gain), and marked irritability/impulsivity.

Anorexia nervosa carries the highest mortality of any psychiatric disorder (~5.1 per 1000 untreated); characteristic lab and exam findings include leukopenia with relative lymphocytosis, raised BUN, metabolic alkalosis and hypokalemia with purging, amenorrhea, lanugo, hypotension, hypothermia, and sinus bradycardia.

Bulimia nervosa usually occurs at normal or slightly above-normal weight, and physical exam is often unremarkable except for dental enamel erosion and parotid gland enlargement; medical danger stems from purging-related fluid/electrolyte disturbance and cardiac conduction abnormalities.
Basing psychiatric referral on the mere absence of a physical explanation rather than on positive signs/symptoms of a mental disorder
Failing to ask directly about agoraphobia, OCD behaviors, or suicidal ideation, all of which patients commonly conceal
Subjecting somatic symptom disorder patients to repeated tests and exploratory surgery, or confronting them in a way that causes humiliation and treatment abandonment
Treating an unrecognized bipolar depression with antidepressant monotherapy, risking induction of mania or cycle acceleration
Prescribing benzodiazepines beyond 4-6 weeks (tolerance, abuse, dependence) and not anticipating withdrawal, which can include seizures
Giving benzodiazepines or SSRIs in the immediate aftermath of trauma, and using debriefing, which does not prevent PTSD and may worsen symptoms
Using TCAs in patients with serious cardiovascular risk or bundle branch block, and providing large supplies to suicidal patients (TCA overdose can be lethal, desipramine highest risk)
Overlooking lithium's narrow therapeutic index and its antithyroid/renal effects during maintenance monitoring

Outcomes vary widely by disorder. Panic disorder responds to treatment in 75-85% of patients, though complete remission is somewhat lower. Most depressed patients (60-70%) respond to an adequately dosed antidepressant over 6-8 weeks, and about three-quarters improve by ~2 months; the best predictor of recurrence is the number of prior episodes (50-60% of first-episode patients have at least one or two recurrences). Bipolar disorder is recurrent and requires maintenance therapy; lithium responses are 70-80% in acute mania and a sustained level >=0.8 meq/L reduces suicide risk. About 4-5% of depressed and ~10% of schizophrenic patients die by suicide. Anorexia nervosa has the highest mortality of any psychiatric condition (~5.1/1000 untreated), though most patients achieve remission within 5 years; binge-eating disorder has the most favorable prognosis among eating disorders. Schizophrenia often has a poor outcome with insidious onset, but positive symptoms tend to attenuate with age and permanent remission occasionally occurs.
Suicidal or homicidal ideation, a specific plan, or prior attempts - warrants immediate referral to a mental health specialist
Psychotic symptoms, mania, or severe depression/anxiety failing first-line treatment - indications for psychiatric consultation or transfer of care
Coexisting anxiety, panic, or agitation in a depressed patient, which raises near-term suicide risk
Critical weight loss, hypotension, hypothermia, bradycardia, or electrolyte/cardiac conduction abnormalities in eating disorders
Refeeding syndrome risk when restoring weight too rapidly in anorexia nervosa (target gain ~0.5-1 lb/week)
Serotonin syndrome (myoclonus, agitation, abdominal cramping, hyperpyrexia, hypertension) - a contraindication to combining MAOIs with SSRIs
Hypertensive crisis from tyramine-containing foods or sympathomimetics in patients taking MAOIs
New-onset psychosis requiring exclusion of a drug/medication cause before diagnosing schizophrenia

Diagnoses are framed by DSM-5-TR (with ICD-10-CM used more widely worldwide); alternative research frameworks include NIMH RDoC and the dimensional HiTOP taxonomy, none yet adequately validated. Severity and subtyping markers within disorders include: bipolar I (full manic episode >=1 week) vs bipolar II (hypomania >=4 days plus recurrent depression) vs cyclothymia (>=2 years of subthreshold fluctuations); rapid cycling defined as >=4 mood episodes per year; persistent depressive (dysthymic) disorder as chronic symptoms >=2 years; PTSD specifiers (with dissociative symptoms, with delayed expression >=6 months); anorexia nervosa restricting type vs binge-eating/purging type; and Munchausen's syndrome as the most severe form of factitious disorder.

chunks.text: Ptosis results from impaired elevation of the upper lid, which is normally raised by the levator palpebrae superioris (oculomotor nerve) and Muller muscle (sympathetic). Aponeurotic ptosis is caused by dehiscence or stretching of the levator aponeurosis with age. Neurogenic ptosis follows interruption of the nerve supply, as in third nerve palsy or sympathetic denervation (Horner syndrome). Myogenic ptosis reflects muscle disease such as myasthenia gravis, chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia, or myotonic dystrophy. Mechanical ptosis arises from lid mass or scarring, and congenital ptosis from maldevelopment of the levator muscle.

PAH arises from apoptosis resistance, cell proliferation, dysregulated metabolism and increased oxidant stress in pulmonary vascular cells, pericytes and adventitial fibroblasts, producing hypertrophic, fibrotic and plexogenic remodelling of distal (small) pulmonary arterioles with extracellular-matrix expansion, reduced vascular compliance and in-situ thrombosis. This raises pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) and mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP). To preserve cardiac output against the elevated right-ventricular afterload, RV work increases; sustained overload depletes myocardial energy and causes right ventricular-pulmonary arterial uncoupling, and in end-stage disease cardiac output and mPAP both fall. The most common germline driver of hereditary PAH is a BMPR2 variant (a TGF-beta superfamily receptor) with variable penetrance (as low as ~20%); other drivers include TBX4 and SOX17, and EIF2AK4 for pulmonary veno-occlusive disease. In group 2 PH the hallmark is elevated left atrial pressure causing pulmonary venous hypertension, venule sclerosis and secondary arteriolar remodelling. (p.2185-2192)

PH is diagnosed when mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) is >20 mmHg by right heart catheterisation; this threshold was lowered from the older >=25 mmHg cut-off to emphasise earlier disease detection (p.2185, 2191).

CTEPH is curable in many patients by surgical pulmonary endarterectomy but is widely underdiagnosed; ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scanning remains the primary screening test and should be considered in any PH of unclear cause (p.2190-2191).
The most common causes of PH are left heart disease or primary lung disease; pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is an uncommon but distinct subtype with an obliterative arteriopathy (p.2185).
Most patients present with dyspnoea and/or fatigue; oedema, chest pain, presyncope and syncope are less common and signal more advanced disease (p.2188).

The current WSPH classification (last revised 2018, Sixth World Symposium) defines five groups: 1 = PAH; 2 = PH due to left heart disease; 3 = PH due to chronic lung disease/hypoxia or sleep-disordered breathing; 4 = chronic thromboembolic PH (CTEPH); 5 = miscellaneous/multifactorial (p.2191).

Echocardiography with agitated-saline (bubble) study is the most important initial screening test; estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure >35 mmHg, a notched continuous-wave Doppler waveform, or a hypertrophied/dilated right ventricle supports the diagnosis (p.2188).

Hemodynamic subtypes by RHC: precapillary PH = PAWP/LVEDP <=15 mmHg with PVR >2.0 Wood units; isolated postcapillary PH = PAWP >15 mmHg with PVR <=2.0 WU; combined pre-/postcapillary PH = mPAP >20 mmHg with PAWP >15 mmHg and PVR >2.0 WU (p.2191).
In PAH, an isolated reduction in diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) on pulmonary function testing is a classic finding (p.2189).

BNP and NT-proBNP correlate with right ventricular dysfunction, hemodynamic severity and functional status in PAH, and NT-proBNP can serve as a biomarker of treatment response once a baseline is established (p.2191).

Vasoreactivity testing (with short-acting agents such as inhaled nitric oxide or inhaled epoprostenol) is reserved for idiopathic or hereditary PAH; a positive response is a fall in mPAP by >=10 mmHg to an absolute level <=40 mmHg without a fall in cardiac output, seen in <5% of patients but carrying a particularly favourable prognosis (p.2191).

Right heart catheterisation - not echocardiography - is the diagnostic gold standard; echocardiography only screens, and an echo in which tricuspid regurgitation is simply not detected does NOT exclude PH (PH is found in one-third of such patients).
PH symptoms are nonspecific, insidious and overlap with asthma, HFpEF and deconditioning, so the diagnosis is frequently missed without a reasonable index of suspicion.
Do not assume that PH in patients with comorbid cardiopulmonary disease (e.g. ILD, mitral valve disease) is merely an extension of the underlying condition rather than a specific entity.
Patients with left heart disease aggressively diuresed before RHC may falsely appear to have an isolated precapillary (PAH-like) profile - diuresis can mask the true hemodynamic classification.
A low peak VO2 occurs across the heart-lung disease spectrum and is NOT diagnostic of PH per se.

Chronic thromboembolic disease (thrombotic remodelling with reduced exercise capacity but without PH) requires consideration in patients with prior PE and dyspnoea even when echocardiography is reassuring.

If left untreated, PH carries a high mortality rate, largely owing to decompensated right heart failure. Idiopathic PAH is progressive and leads to right heart failure and early mortality; in left-sided heart failure or HFpEF even mildly elevated mPAP carries adverse outcome. Among IPAH, prevalence favours women ~3:1 but hemodynamics are more severe and prognosis less favourable in men. Hereditary BMPR2 PAH presents younger with more severe hemodynamics and greater clinical risk (conversion ~2.3%/year in carriers). Vasoreactive responders (<5%) have a particularly favourable prognosis. Scleroderma-associated PAH and HIV-PAH carry especially poor prognoses; portopulmonary hypertension is a marker of adverse post-liver-transplant outcome (up to 100% mortality reported with mPAP >=50 mmHg in one study). Peak VO2 <15 mL/kg/min is prognostic. (p.2185, 2191-2192)

Pulmonic stenosis is defined hemodynamically by a systolic pressure gradient between the right ventricle and the main pulmonary artery. Sustained obstruction to RV outflow drives RV hypertrophy and prolongs systolic ejection; because the RV adapts poorly to pressure overload, dysfunction from afterload mismatch develops earlier and at lower pressures than analogous left-sided changes in aortic stenosis. The right atrial a wave rises in proportion to the higher pressures needed to fill a stiff, hypertrophied RV, and a prominent RA v wave reflects functional tricuspid regurgitation from RV and annular dilation; cardiac output is preserved until late. Pulmonic stenosis rarely progresses when mild but can worsen with age in moderate disease owing to valve thickening and calcification. In pulmonic regurgitation, severe disease causes RV chamber enlargement and eccentric hypertrophy, creating a state of increased preload and afterload. The diastolic pressure gradient from pulmonary artery to RV that drives the regurgitant flow falls progressively through diastole, explaining the decrescendo murmur, and the murmur shortens as RV diastolic pressure rises. Forward output is preserved early but fails to augment normally with exercise and declines over time; advanced stages show marked RV and RA enlargement with elevated jugular venous pressure. PR arises from primary valve pathology, annular enlargement (e.g., long-standing severe pulmonary hypertension dilating the valve ring), or their combination, and may follow surgical relief of RV outflow obstruction or balloon valvotomy.
Pulmonic stenosis is overwhelmingly a congenital lesion; the valve is typically domed in isolated cases, and the pulmonic valve is only very rarely affected by the rheumatic process.
A reduction in RV ejection fraction may be an early sign of hemodynamic compromise in pulmonic regurgitation, before overt symptoms develop.
Trace or mild pulmonic regurgitation of no hemodynamic significance is frequently seen on transthoracic echocardiography even when the valve is structurally normal.
Carcinoid characteristically produces mixed pulmonic valve disease, combining both regurgitation and stenosis.
Dysplastic pulmonic valves occur as a feature of Noonan syndrome (mapped to chromosome 12), with PTPN1 gene mutations identified in roughly half of Noonan cases.
The pulmonic ejection sound (click) is the single right-sided acoustic event that DECREASES in intensity with inspiration, because elevated RV end-diastolic pressure pre-opens the valve.
As pulmonic stenosis worsens, the ejection sound migrates toward S1 and eventually becomes inaudible, the systolic murmur peaks later and may extend past A2, and P2 becomes reduced or absent.
The systolic murmur of pulmonic stenosis is mid-systolic and crescendo-decrescendo, best heard in the left second interspace, and it increases in intensity during inspiration.

The Graham Steell murmur of pulmonic regurgitation is a high-pitched, decrescendo diastolic murmur along the left sternal border that can be mistaken for aortic regurgitation; it tends to grow louder with inspiration.

In survivors of childhood tetralogy of Fallot or PS/pulmonary atresia repair, an RV-PA conduit lacking a valve can be freely regurgitant, producing a misleadingly low-pitched, short diastolic murmur despite significant PR and RV volume overload.

Right ventricular dysfunction from afterload mismatch appears earlier and at lower peak systolic pressures in pulmonic stenosis than left ventricular failure does in aortic stenosis, because the RV tolerates pressure overload poorly.
Cardiac output is maintained until late in pulmonic stenosis, so many patients with mild or even moderate disease are asymptomatic and are detected only by an incidental murmur or click.
The Graham Steell murmur of PR is easily confused with aortic regurgitation along the left sternal border.
A valveless RV-PA conduit after congenital repair can give a low-pitched, short diastolic murmur that understates the true severity of PR and RV volume overload.
Doppler peak instantaneous gradient correlates only weakly with the catheterization peak-to-peak gradient; the catheter peak-to-peak value tends to track better with the Doppler MEAN gradient.
Trace or mild PR seen on echocardiography is usually of no clinical or hemodynamic consequence and should not be over-interpreted.
Relying on the systolic ejection sound can mislead in severe PS, where the click moves toward S1 and may become inaudible.

Mild pulmonic stenosis rarely progresses, whereas moderate disease may worsen with age due to valve thickening and calcification. Because cardiac output is maintained until late, many patients remain asymptomatic for years; severe disease eventually brings RV dysfunction and, uncommonly and only very late, overt right heart failure. In pulmonic regurgitation, forward output is preserved early but does not rise normally with exertion and declines over time, with a falling RV ejection fraction serving as an early marker of compromise and advanced disease producing marked RV/RA enlargement and elevated jugular venous pressure.

Progressive hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the circular smooth muscle of the pylorus narrows and elongates the pyloric channel, obstructing gastric emptying. The exact cause is unknown but involves genetic and environmental factors. Persistent vomiting of gastric contents leads to loss of hydrogen and chloride ions, producing a hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis; ongoing losses and renal compensation drive potassium loss and, later, paradoxical aciduria. Fluid losses cause dehydration. The obstruction is proximal to the biliary drainage, so vomitus is non-bilious.
Hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle causing gastric outlet obstruction, typically presenting between 3 and 6 weeks of age and more common in firstborn males.
The hallmark is progressive, forceful non-bilious (projectile) vomiting shortly after feeds, with the infant remaining hungry and eager to feed again.
The classic metabolic picture is a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from loss of gastric acid and chloride.
A palpable olive-shaped mass in the epigastrium/right upper quadrant and visible gastric peristalsis are classic but not always present.
Ultrasound is the diagnostic investigation of choice, demonstrating a thickened and elongated pyloric muscle.
The vomiting is characteristically non-bilious, because the obstruction is proximal to the ampulla of Vater; bilious vomiting should prompt consideration of other diagnoses.
Initial management is medical resuscitation: correcting dehydration and the electrolyte and acid-base disturbance before any operation.
Definitive treatment is surgical pyloromyotomy, which is not an emergency and should follow adequate fluid and electrolyte correction.

Prognosis is excellent after appropriate resuscitation and pyloromyotomy, with prompt recovery and no long-term gastrointestinal sequelae.

Rabies virus, a single-strand negative-sense RNA lyssavirus (family Rhabdoviridae), is usually inoculated by an animal bite. During most of the incubation period the virus remains at or near the inoculation site; in muscle it binds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at neuromuscular junctions. It spreads centripetally along peripheral nerves toward the spinal cord or brainstem by retrograde fast axonal transport (up to ~250 mm/d, with ~12-h delays at each synapse). Once in the CNS it disseminates rapidly along neuroanatomic connections; neurons are prominently infected while astrocyte infection is unusual. After CNS infection is established there is centrifugal spread along sensory and autonomic nerves to salivary glands, heart, adrenal glands, and skin; viral replication in salivary gland acinar cells leads to secretion in saliva (the vehicle of animal transmission). There is no well-documented evidence for hematogenous spread. CNS inflammatory changes are mild (mononuclear infiltrate, perivascular cuffing, microglial Babes nodules) with little neuronal death; clinical disease is attributed to neuronal dysfunction rather than death, with oxidative stress from mitochondrial dysfunction implicated. (p.1650-1652)

Rabies is a rapidly progressive acute CNS infection by rabies virus (a lyssavirus, family Rhabdoviridae), normally transmitted via the bite of an infected animal; it has encephalitic and paralytic forms that progress to death (p.1650).

The Negri body (eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusion in brain neurons, e.g. cerebellar Purkinje cells and hippocampal pyramidal neurons) is the most characteristic pathologic finding, but is NOT seen in all cases (p.1651-1652).

Diagnosis should be considered in patients with acute atypical encephalitis or acute flaccid paralysis, including those in whom Guillain-Barre syndrome is suspected; absence of an animal-bite history is common in North America due to unrecognized bat exposures (p.1653).
Postexposure prophylaxis must be initiated after a recognized exposure and before any symptoms or signs develop; the emphasis for prevention is on PEP (p.1652).

Worldwide, ~99% of human rabies is transmitted from dogs in countries with endemic canine rabies; endemic canine rabies causes an estimated 59,000 human deaths annually, with most deaths in Asia and Africa and rural populations and children disproportionately affected (p.1650-1651).
Incubation period is usually 20-90 days but in rare cases may be as short as a few days or longer than 1 year (p.1651).

Earliest specific neurologic symptoms are paresthesias, pain, or pruritus near the exposure site, occurring in 50-80% of patients and strongly suggesting rabies; the wound has usually healed by this point (p.1652).
Two acute neurologic forms occur: encephalitic (furious) in ~80% and paralytic (dumb) in ~20% (p.1652).

Encephalitic rabies presents as atypical encephalitis with relative preservation of consciousness; episodes of hyperexcitability alternate with periods of complete lucidity that shorten as disease progresses (p.1652).

Early brainstem involvement produces the classic hydrophobia (involuntary painful contraction of diaphragm and accessory respiratory, laryngeal, and pharyngeal muscles on swallowing liquids) and aerophobia (same response to a draft of air) (p.1652).

Autonomic dysfunction is common and may cause hypersalivation, gooseflesh, cardiac arrhythmia, and priapism; hypersalivation plus pharyngeal dysfunction produces the classic 'foaming at the mouth' (p.1652).

Paralytic rabies features early prominent flaccid weakness often beginning in the bitten extremity, progressing to quadriparesis and facial weakness, with sphincter involvement common and sensory involvement usually mild (p.1652).
Rabies is often not considered until late in the clinical course in North America even with a typical presentation.
Relying on a history of animal bite to make the diagnosis - many cases (especially bat-associated) have no recalled exposure.
Assuming absence of hydrophobia excludes rabies - lack of hydrophobia is not unusual.
Misdiagnosing paralytic rabies as Guillain-Barre syndrome.
Treating negative antemortem rabies-specific tests as exclusionary.
Severe CSF pleocytosis (>1000 white cells/uL) is unusual for rabies and should prompt a search for an alternative diagnosis.
Delaying local wound care while awaiting the 10-day animal observation period - wound care should not be delayed.

Administering passive immunization (RIG) more than 7 days after the first vaccine dose, when endogenous antibody production has begun and passive immunization may be counterproductive; rabies vaccine and RIG must never be given at the same site.
Minor deviations from current PEP recommendations can lead to prophylaxis failure.

Rabies is an almost uniformly fatal disease but is nearly always preventable after recognized exposures with appropriate postexposure therapy during the early incubation period. Most patients die within several days of symptom onset despite aggressive critical-care support. There is no established treatment and no antiviral has demonstrated efficacy; aggressive supportive care has yielded at least 33 documented survivors (many recently reported from India), but recent treatment failures (>60) have far outnumbered successes. All but 2 of the 33 documented survivors had received one or more doses of rabies vaccine before disease onset, and the unvaccinated survivors had neutralizing antibodies in CSF at presentation. A palliative approach may be appropriate for patients who are not candidates for aggressive management. (p.1654)
Near-100% fatal once symptomatic, so post-exposure prophylaxis is everything - do NOT delay PEP after a recognized exposure.
Paresthesias, pain, or pruritus at a healed animal-bite site preceding neurologic illness strongly suggest rabies.
Hydrophobia or aerophobia with preserved consciousness (atypical encephalitis) is essentially diagnostic of encephalitic rabies.

Absence of a recalled animal bite does NOT exclude rabies - bat exposures are frequently unrecognized; consider PEP when a small child or sleeping adult shared a space with a bat and an unrecognized bite cannot be reliably excluded.
Negative antemortem rabies-specific laboratory tests never exclude the diagnosis; repeat testing may be needed.
Acute flaccid paralysis resembling Guillain-Barre syndrome may be paralytic rabies - fever, bladder dysfunction, normal sensory exam, and CSF pleocytosis favor rabies.

Clinical stages: incubation period (20-90 days, asymptomatic); prodrome (2-10 days: fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting; paresthesias/pain/pruritus at the wound site); acute neurologic disease - encephalitic form (~80%, 2-7 days: anxiety, agitation, hyperactivity, bizarre behavior, hallucinations, autonomic dysfunction, hydrophobia) or paralytic form (~20%, 2-10 days: flaccid limb paralysis progressing to quadriparesis with facial paralysis); then coma and death (0-14 days; recovery rare). (p.1653)
