Borrelia are slender, double-membrane spirochetes that are extracellular pathogens with a limited biosynthetic genome about one-quarter the size of E. coli; their flagella lie between the two membranes. Tick-borne spirochetes enter in tick saliva at the onset of feeding, and from a small inoculum STRF organisms proliferate in blood (doubling roughly every 6 h) to 10^6-10^7/mL or more, while HTRF organisms grow more slowly to lower densities. Although they lack potent exotoxins and lack lipopolysaccharide endotoxin, abundant Borrelia lipoproteins activate Toll-like receptors, driving an endotoxemia-like proinflammatory response with elevated TNF-alpha, IL-6, and IL-8. Spirochete binding to erythrocytes causes red cell aggregation, splenic/hepatic sequestration, hepatosplenomegaly, and anemia; bleeding reflects thrombocytopenia, impaired hepatic clotting-factor production, and small-vessel blockage by aggregates of spirochetes, erythrocytes, and platelets. Serotype-specific IgM appears after a few days and lyses circulating bacteria by bactericidal action or opsonization; release of bacterial products from dying organisms drives a spontaneous 'crisis,' the antibiotic-triggered counterpart of which is the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction. Antigenic variation of surface lipoproteins produces successive bacteremic relapses, each ended by variant-specific antibody. Some species are neurotropic and enter the relatively immune-sheltered brain, and spirochetes can cross the maternal-fetal barrier to cause placental damage, intrauterine growth retardation, and congenital infection (p.1444-1447).

Relapsing fever is caused by several Borrelia spirochete species and occurs in three epidemiologic forms: louse-borne (LBRF, B. recurrentis), soft tick-borne (STRF, multiple Ornithodoros-transmitted species), and hard tick-borne (HTRF, mainly B. miyamotoi and B. lonestari) (p.1444).

B. miyamotoi disease (HTRF) is less distinctive, often presenting as acute fever with chills, headache, and myalgia 1-2 weeks after a tick bite, and has been mistaken for undifferentiated sepsis; meningoencephalitis occurs particularly in patients with impaired humoral immunity (e.g., after rituximab) (p.1446).

Diagnosis of LBRF/STRF rests on direct microscopic detection of spirochetes in blood (Wright, Giemsa, or Giemsa-Wright stain), best collected at or just before the fever peak; spirochete density in B. miyamotoi/B. lonestari may be too low for smear alone (p.1447).

Outbreaks of LBRF (often alongside typhus) cluster in settings of famine, war, refugee migration, homelessness, and incarceration, and can appear in migrant camps far from the country of origin (p.1445).

The hallmark is two or more febrile episodes separated by afebrile intervals of well-being; the relapsing course reflects antigenic variation of the spirochete's surface lipoproteins, with each variant cleared as specific antibody develops (p.1444-1446).

In LBRF the first fever is typically unremitting for 3-6 days and is usually followed by a single milder relapse, whereas STRF produces multiple febrile periods of 1-3 days each; interfebrile intervals span roughly 4-14 days (p.1446).

A 'crisis' may terminate the first fever episode (rigors, a further rise in temperature, increased pulse and blood pressure for about 15-30 min), followed by drenching sweats, falling temperature, and hypotension lasting several hours (p.1446).
Soft ticks (Ornithodoros) feed briefly, often under 30 minutes and usually while the victim sleeps, then leave undetected, so the exposure may go unrecognized (p.1445).
Transovarial transmission in soft ticks means infection risk can persist in a dwelling for years, and a case may be diagnosed long after the last reported local case (p.1445-1447).

LBRF is acquired not from the louse bite itself but by rubbing crushed louse hemolymph into the bite site or auto-inoculating it into conjunctivae or a wound; humans are the sole reservoir of B. recurrentis (p.1445).
Jaundice, epistaxis, and subconjunctival hemorrhages are common in LBRF but typically absent in STRF and HTRF; splenomegaly or splenic tenderness is common in both LBRF and STRF (p.1446).

Localizing neurologic signs are more frequent in STRF than in LBRF/HTRF; B. turicatae is notably neurotropic, and unilateral or bilateral Bell's palsy (cranial neuritis) characteristically appears in the second or third febrile episode rather than the first (p.1446).
Whole-cell serologic assays (including ELISA and the C6 peptide ELISA for Lyme disease) can be falsely positive in relapsing fever due to antigenic cross-reactivity among spirochetes (p.1447).
Serology cannot distinguish among Borrelia species as the cause, and a positive IgG on a single specimen may reflect past infection rather than the current illness (p.1447).
Specific serologic assays (e.g., GlpQ-based) are commonly negative at the very time a blood smear or PCR would be positive (p.1447).
Spirochete density in B. miyamotoi or B. lonestari infection may be too low for diagnosis by blood smear alone, so PCR is preferred (p.1447).
Smears drawn during afebrile intervals may miss spirochetemia; sampling at/just before the fever peak (or using NAAT) improves yield (p.1447).
For B. miyamotoi HTRF, prompt removal of an embedded tick may not prevent infection because transmission occurs soon after feeding begins (p.1447).
STRF presenting with Bell's palsy can be misdiagnosed as Lyme disease in co-endemic regions (p.1447).
Co-infections (malaria, typhus, typhoid with relapsing fever; B. miyamotoi with Lyme disease) may obscure the diagnosis (p.1447).
A Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction can be provoked even by antibiotics with suboptimal antiborrelial activity (e.g., ciprofloxacin) given for an unsuspected case (p.1448).

Untreated mortality is approximately 10-70% for LBRF and 4-10% for STRF, depending heavily on coexisting conditions (e.g., malnutrition, other infection) and available medical support. With prompt antibiotic treatment, mortality falls to about 2-5% for LBRF and under 2% for STRF; no deaths from HTRF have been reported. Poor-prognosis features include concurrent malaria, typhus, or typhoid; pregnancy; stupor or coma at admission; diffuse bleeding; poor liver function; myocarditis; and bronchopneumonia. The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction in LBRF carries roughly a 5% mortality without adequate monitoring and resuscitation. LBRF or STRF in pregnancy frequently causes abortion, stillbirth, or perinatal death, though congenital malformations have not been reported. Documented posttreatment sequelae and prolonged disability have not been established for any form, and partial immunity to reinfection appears to develop in residents of perennially high-risk areas (p.1448).

No formal numeric severity score is given. Clinically, severity is stratified by relapsing-fever type and complications: LBRF carries higher untreated mortality (about 10-70%) than STRF (about 4-10%), while HTRF/B. miyamotoi disease is mildest with no reported deaths. CNS involvement (confirmed or suspected meningitis/meningoencephalitis, supported by CSF mononuclear pleocytosis and elevated protein) marks severe disease warranting parenteral therapy. Features defining a severe/poor-prognosis course include concurrent malaria, typhus, or typhoid; pregnancy; stupor or coma at admission; diffuse bleeding; poor liver function; myocarditis; and bronchopneumonia (p.1446-1448).

The exact mechanisms remain unclear despite study of genetic, environmental, and immunologic factors. Limited animal-model data suggest autoimmunity against cartilage components may contribute: immunizing certain animals against type II collagen, type IX collagen, or matrilin-1 can reproduce aspects of the human phenotype. However, autoantibodies (including anti-type II collagen) are neither sensitive nor specific enough for diagnosis, and observational data showing B-cell-depleting therapy is not particularly effective argue against a dominant antibody-mediated mechanism. Proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines linked to both innate and adaptive immunity have been associated with RP but are inconsistent. Histologically, acute cartilage shows a mixed myeloid and lymphoid inflammatory infiltrate at the cartilage interface; over time there is lacunar breakdown, loss of chondrocytes, and replacement by fibrosis (p.2918).

Rare systemic disease defined by recurrent inflammation of cartilaginous structures, with the ears, nose, respiratory tract, and joints as hallmark sites; the eyes, inner ear, nervous system, skin, and cardiovascular system may also be involved (p.2917).

MAGIC syndrome (mouth and genital ulcers with inflamed cartilage) overlaps with Behcet's syndrome features such as pathergy and GI involvement and may include large-vessel vasculitis of the aorta (p.2920).
Some patients carry concurrent rheumatologic diagnoses such as Sjogren's syndrome or systemic lupus erythematosus (p.2917).
Neurologic attribution to RP is a diagnosis of exclusion; infection and malignancy must be ruled out first, though encephalitis and meningitis can occur in RP (p.2920).

Ear involvement is the most common manifestation, affecting roughly 80-90% of patients, and typically spares the non-cartilaginous lobule; pain may occur with minimal visible swelling or erythema (p.2918).

Triggers for ear pain often include minor trauma (lying on the affected side, wearing glasses) or temperature change; 'cauliflower ear' from cartilage damage occurs only in a small subset after recurrent episodes (p.2918).

Nasal disease often presents as a pressure sensation at the bridge of the nose; a saddle-nose deformity may develop but is not universal, and unlike GPA the nasal perforations in RP are usually anterior rather than septal (p.2918-2919).

Airway involvement such as subglottic stenosis may be misdiagnosed as adult-onset asthma; severe narrowing can cause stridor and is a medical emergency, and chronic damage can lead to tracheomalacia, bronchomalacia, or tracheal calcification (p.2919).

Costochondral joint inflammation can produce severe bilateral chest pain that is reproducible on palpation and not movement-related, sometimes mimicking acute coronary syndrome and prompting emergency evaluation (p.2919-2920).

Recurrent chondritis of the ears and nose in older male patients with severe systemic inflammation and progressive bone marrow failure should prompt evaluation for VEXAS syndrome (somatic UBA1 mutation) (p.2917, 2920).
Episcleritis is the most frequent ocular manifestation; scleritis is rare but warrants urgent ophthalmologic evaluation given the risk of vision loss, scleromalacia, or globe rupture (p.2920).

Because disease activity is intermittent and patients may appear non-inflamed during a clinic visit, a longitudinal history and review of patient-provided photographs are essential to diagnosis (p.2918).
Airway involvement is commonly misdiagnosed as adult-onset asthma, delaying treatment and risking chronic large-airway damage (p.2919)
Normal ESR and CRP do not exclude active RP, as acute-phase reactants are not reliably elevated (p.2918)
There is no diagnostic blood or tissue biomarker; relying on a single test is a pitfall - diagnosis rests on clinical pattern recognition over time (p.2918, 2920)
Cartilage biopsy yields nonspecific findings and can cause morbidity; it should not be expected to confirm RP (p.2918, 2921)
Patients may appear non-inflamed at a single visit because disease activity is intermittent (p.2918)
Published diagnostic criteria were derived from small cohorts, are largely expert-opinion-based, and have not been formally validated (p.2920)
Assuming a saddle nose implies GPA - in RP the deformity usually lacks septal perforation (perforations are anterior) (p.2918-2919)

Outcomes depend heavily on organ involvement. Airway disease can progress to tracheomalacia, bronchomalacia, or tracheal calcification, and severe subglottic narrowing carries mortality risk. Scleritis can lead to vision loss or globe rupture. VEXAS-associated disease involves progressive bone marrow failure and is potentially life-threatening, so prompt recognition is essential. Acute-phase reactants (ESR, CRP) are not reliably elevated, so they cannot be used to gauge severity (p.2917-2920).
Stridor from severe airway/subglottic narrowing - a medical emergency requiring urgent attention to avoid mortality (p.2919)
Features of scleritis - urgent ophthalmology referral due to risk of vision loss, scleromalacia, or globe rupture (p.2920)
Cytopenia with macrocytosis and lymphopenia in older males - suggests VEXAS and possible progressive bone marrow failure (p.2917, 2920)
Severe costochondral chest pain that can mimic acute coronary syndrome (p.2919-2920)

No formally validated severity grading exists. Several diagnostic schemes have been proposed: McAdam's criteria require 3 of 6 features (bilateral auricular chondritis, nonerosive seronegative inflammatory polyarthritis, nasal chondritis, ocular inflammation, respiratory-tract chondritis, vestibular/cochlear dysfunction); the Damiani-Levine modification accepts 3 clinical features, or 1 feature plus histologic chondritis, or 2 features plus clinical response to treatment; Michet's criteria use 3 major criteria (ear, nose, or respiratory-tract inflammation) and 4 minor criteria (ocular inflammation, hearing loss, vestibular dysfunction, seronegative inflammatory arthritis), requiring 2 major or 1 major plus 2 minor. All are limited by lack of precise organ-involvement definitions (p.2920).

RCC is a heterogeneous group of tumors. Most cases are sporadic, but familial forms exist. Clear cell RCC (the predominant subtype) is characterized by loss of chromosome 3p as the earliest event, causing loss of heterozygosity for 3p genes including VHL, PBRM1, BAP1, and SETD2. VHL encodes a tumor-suppressor protein that regulates transcription of VEGF and other effectors via ubiquitination of hypoxia-inducible factors (HIF); VHL inactivation upregulates VEGF signaling, promoting tumor angiogenesis and growth and rendering clear cell RCC susceptible to antiangiogenic therapy. Clear cell RCC also arises in von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (autosomal dominant, VHL gene on chromosome 3p), which carries a ~70% lifetime risk of clear cell RCC. Papillary subtypes are linked to activating MET mutations or gain of chromosome 7; chromophobe tumors originate from the distal nephron and typically show aneuploidy. Early loss of chromosome 9p confers high risk of early metastatic dissemination and correlates with poor cancer-specific survival (p.687-688).

RCC accounts for 90-95% of malignant neoplasms arising from the kidney; the remaining 5-10% are transitional (urothelial) cell carcinomas of the renal pelvis (covered separately in Chap. 91) (p.687-688).

The classic triad of hematuria, flank pain, and a palpable abdominal mass is now uncommon; most tumors are detected incidentally on cross-sectional imaging (CT/MRI) performed for other reasons (p.688-689).
Other presenting features include fever, weight loss, anemia, and a varicocele (p.688).
Once called the "internist's tumor" because it was frequently first detected via a paraneoplastic syndrome before modern imaging was common (p.688-689).
Clear cell is the predominant histology (~70% of cases) and is found in >80% of patients who develop metastases; it arises from epithelial cells of the proximal tubules (p.688).
Any solid renal mass should be considered malignant until proven otherwise; a definitive diagnosis is required (p.689).
Most common sites of distant metastasis are the lungs, lymph nodes, liver, bone, and brain; the clinical course can be unpredictable and protracted (p.689).
RCC is associated with anecdotal reports of spontaneous regression (p.687).
Increasing detection of incidental low-stage tumors has improved 5-year survival and increased use of nephron-sparing surgery (partial nephrectomy) (p.689).
Relying on the classic triad (hematuria, flank pain, palpable mass) for diagnosis - it is now uncommon, and most tumors present incidentally (p.688-689).
Assuming chemotherapy will help - metastatic RCC is refractory to cytotoxic chemotherapy; treatment relies on molecularly targeted agents and checkpoint immunotherapy (p.689).
Treating a solid renal mass as benign without proof - any solid renal mass should be considered malignant until proven otherwise (p.689).
Despite many candidate biomarkers investigated for predictive value in metastatic RCC, none have been validated for clinical use to date (p.690).
Renal vein or inferior vena cava invasion does not preclude surgical resection if no metastases are present (p.689).

Staging uses the AJCC TNM system. Stage I tumors are <=7 cm and confined to the kidney; stage II are >7 cm and confined to the kidney; stage III extend through the renal capsule but remain within Gerota's fascia, grossly infiltrate the renal vein, or involve regional nodes (N1); stage IV invades adjacent organs or involves nonregional nodes or distant metastases. About 65% present at stage I-II, 15-20% at stage III, and 15-20% at stage IV. Overall 5-year survival is currently ~77% but varies greatly by stage. For metastatic disease, the IMDC risk model uses six factors associated with worse survival (poor performance status, low hemoglobin, high serum calcium, high neutrophils, high platelets, and <1-year interval from diagnosis to systemic treatment). Zero risk factors confer significantly longer median survival (>=5 years) than one to two factors (~4 years) or three to six factors (~3 years) with first-line checkpoint-inhibitor-containing regimens. Projected overall survival for newly diagnosed metastatic disease has tripled over the past 15-20 years (p.688-690).

Ruptured/impending-rupture abdominal aortic aneurysm — abdominal pain radiating to the flank, sacral region, or genitalia should always raise suspicion of a leaking AAA; pain may precede rupture by days (p.154).
Acute mesenteric ischemia (pain out of proportion to exam in a vascular patient) (p.154).

Other causes of acute lower abdominal pain such as appendicitis, salpingitis, ectopic pregnancy, inguinal hernia, inflammatory bowel disease, and bowel obstruction (p.18 abdominal pain differential table).
Ureteric obstruction due to extrinsic malignancy (pelvic/prostatic/gynecologic tumors, retroperitoneal nodes) or post-radiation ureteric fibrosis, which can mimic stone-related obstruction (p.631).
Acute pyelonephritis (flank pain, fever, pyuria) (p.1118).

Perinephric or renal abscess — flank/abdominal pain, fever in at least half; suspect when pyelonephritis remains febrile after 4-5 days, when urine culture is polymicrobial, when stones are known, or when fever and pyuria coexist with a sterile urine culture (p.1118).

Renal ultrasonography — useful to identify hydronephrosis/ureteric and pelvic dilation, though it may be falsely negative early or when ureteric dilation is prevented (e.g., retroperitoneal fibrosis or tumor encasement) (p.383, p.631).
Abdominal CT and renal ultrasound are the most useful modalities when perinephric/renal abscess is suspected (p.1118).

Urinalysis showing alkaline urine plus a urease-producing organism (e.g., Proteus) may prompt evaluation for urolithiasis, though Harrison notes clinical support for routine action on this finding is lacking (p.1334).
Serum calcium / PTH and metabolic workup when an underlying stone-promoting metabolic disorder (e.g., primary hyperparathyroidism) is suspected (p.406).
Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm with flank/genital radiation, especially in older patients (p.154).
Ureteric obstruction from malignancy or retroperitoneal fibrosis presenting with flank pain (p.631).

Colicky flank pain arises from acute distention of the renal collecting system and ureter when a stone obstructs urinary outflow, producing visceral cramping pain (p.551). Obstruction proximal to the bladder produces hydroureter and renal pelvic dilation (hydronephrosis); if unrelieved this impairs glomerular filtration and causes postrenal azotemia (p.383). In urease-producing infection (e.g., Proteus), hydrolysis of urea to ammonia raises urinary pH; the resulting alkaline environment precipitates struvite and carbonate-apatite, building staghorn calculi that perpetuate infection and obstruction (p.1118, p.1334). Stones also serve as a chronic nidus that promotes recurrent and recalcitrant urinary infection (p.1118).
Renal colic is classic visceral pain from distention of a hollow viscus (the obstructed collecting system/ureter): cramping and intermittent rather than constant (p.551).
Stones obstructing urinary flow are the single most important risk factor for perinephric/renal abscess; 20-60% of patients with perinephric abscess have renal stones (p.1118).

Urea-splitting organisms (notably Proteus, also other urease producers) alkalinize the urine, favoring precipitation of struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) and carbonate-apatite, which can form staghorn calculi in the renal pelvis (p.1118, p.1334).
Struvite stones act as a persistent nidus for recurrent UTI and typically cannot be eradicated by antibiotics alone without removal of the stone (p.1118, p.1334).

Stone-associated obstruction is a recognized cause of postrenal azotemia/AKI; because one functioning kidney clears adequately, obstructive renal failure from stones generally requires bilateral ureteric obstruction or unilateral obstruction in a solitary/single functioning kidney (p.383).
Nephrolithiasis can be the presenting feature of an underlying metabolic disorder such as primary hyperparathyroidism/hypercalcemia (p.406).
Imaging of the upper tracts is advised in any patient with hematuria, a history of calculi, or prior urinary tract problems (p.747).
Assuming flank pain radiating to the groin is always a stone — in older patients a ruptured/leaking AAA can present identically and is rapidly fatal if missed (p.154).
Relying on a negative ultrasound to exclude obstruction; dilation may be absent early or when the ureter cannot distend (p.383).
Failing to recognize an infected obstructed system / perinephric abscess in a patient with known stones who stays febrile or has polymicrobial or sterile-but-pyuric urine (p.1118).
Overlooking an underlying metabolic cause (e.g., hyperparathyroidism) in a stone former (p.406).

Stone-related obstruction is usually reversible if relieved promptly; urinary tract obstruction accounts for under 5% of acute renal failure and must be excluded early because it is correctable (p.383). When obstruction is complicated by infection (abscess), diagnosis is frequently delayed and mortality is appreciable, though lower than historically (p.1118). Struvite/staghorn stones tend to recur and perpetuate infection unless the stone is removed (p.1118, p.1334).
Pain radiating to flank, sacral region, or genitalia in an older patient — exclude a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm (p.154).
Rising serum creatinine, oliguria, or anuria — suggests obstruction of a solitary kidney or bilateral obstruction and warrants immediate evaluation (p.383, p.631).

Persistent fever after several days of treatment for presumed pyelonephritis, polymicrobial urine, or fever/pyuria with sterile culture — suspect perinephric/renal abscess complicating an obstructing stone (p.1118).

The renal cortex receives high arteriolar flow in excess of its metabolic needs for filtration, while the postglomerular medullary circulation has lower flow yet high oxygen consumption, leaving the deeper medulla near the margin of hypoxemia. Large-vessel occlusive disease (atherosclerosis, fibromuscular dysplasia, dissection, extrinsic compression, aortic stent graft) reduces perfusion pressure to the kidney. Once stenosis is hemodynamically significant (typically >70 to 80% lumen occlusion), the drop in perfusion pressure activates the renin-angiotensin system, reduces sodium excretion, and stimulates sympathetic adrenergic pathways, producing angiotensin-dependent systemic hypertension. Sustained pressure and ischemia drive endothelial injury (reflected by increased urinary albumin excretion), microvascular proliferation in early atherosclerosis and later microvascular rarefaction in chronic ischemia, with consequent tubulointerstitial fibrosis and loss of function. In atheroembolic disease, cholesterol crystals from fractured plaque occlude microvessels leaving a characteristic 'cleft' on biopsy (Harrison 22e p.2150-2152).
Renovascular disease is a specifically treatable 'secondary' cause of hypertension because restoring renal perfusion pressure can reverse the pressor pathways it activates (Harrison 22e p.2150).
The presence of ARAS independently predicts cardiovascular morbidity and mortality regardless of whether revascularization is performed (Harrison 22e p.2150).

Atheroembolic renal disease most often follows arterial procedures (e.g., coronary angiography), with cholesterol crystals lodging in downstream microvessels; manifestations typically appear 1 to 14 days after the inciting event (Harrison 22e p.2152).

Thromboembolic renal disease can cause flank pain, fever, leukocytosis, nausea and vomiting, and a transient extreme rise in LDH if infarction occurs; bilateral involvement causes precipitous functional decline and reduced urine output (Harrison 22e p.2153).

Roughly 90% of renovascular hypertension is due to atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis (ARAS), which is typically unilateral with a discrete lesion near the renal artery origin in older patients with a broader atherosclerotic risk profile (Harrison 22e p.2139, 2150).

Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) accounts for a minority of cases and characteristically affects younger patients aged ~15 to 50, predominantly women; lesions are more diffuse with an irregular 'sawtooth/string-of-beads' appearance located in the distal renal artery (Harrison 22e p.2139, 2150).

FMD should be suspected with abrupt-onset hypertension (especially in young women) or resistant/recently worsening hypertension; ARAS should be suspected in older patients with other ASCVD evidence or otherwise unexplained decline in kidney function (Harrison 22e p.2139).

Critical stenosis (usually >70 to 80% luminal obstruction) reduces perfusion pressure, activating the renin-angiotensin system, reducing sodium excretion, and engaging sympathetic pathways (Harrison 22e p.2150).

Early renovascular hypertension is angiotensin-dependent and marked by widely varying pressures, loss of circadian BP rhythm, and accelerated target organ injury including left ventricular hypertrophy and renal fibrosis (Harrison 22e p.2150).
An abdominal renal artery bruit, or carotid/femoral bruits, may be audible and supports the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2139, 2150).

When large-vessel disease primarily threatens kidney function the entity is termed ischemic nephropathy; gradually reduced flow can leave function reduced but stable for years, whereas advanced disease produces cortical hypoperfusion and overt tissue hypoxia (Harrison 22e p.2150).

ARAS commonly coexists with preexisting small-vessel disease from hypertension, aging, and diabetes; nearly 85% of patients considered for revascularization already have stage 3 to 5 CKD (eGFR <60) (Harrison 22e p.2150).
Plasma renin activity is transient and influenced by drugs/sodium/timing, so it does not reliably predict response to revascularization; over-reliance on it is misleading (Harrison 22e p.2151).

Multiple randomized trials show no compelling benefit of revascularization over optimal medical therapy for moderate ARAS regarding BP or renal function over 3 to 5 years; revascularization should not be assumed beneficial just because flow is restored (Harrison 22e p.2139, 2150).
Revascularization rarely normalizes BP alone because most patients have preexisting hypertension and need continued drug therapy (Harrison 22e p.2150).
Atheroembolic complications of revascularization can be catastrophic and accelerate the very hypertension and renal failure the procedure intended to prevent (Harrison 22e p.2151).

Atheroembolic renal disease is frequently underdiagnosed and is often a diagnosis of exclusion; systemic features (fever, abdominal pain, weight loss) are present in fewer than half of patients (Harrison 22e p.2152).

Hypertensive nephrosclerosis is often assigned without specific etiologic proof; nephrosclerosis changes also occur with aging, dyslipidemia, and glucose intolerance with only modest association with BP, and antihypertensive therapy does not alter its course (Harrison 22e p.2154).

FMD patients are usually younger with otherwise normal vessels and long life expectancy and often respond well to angioplasty; FMD seldom threatens kidney function. Untreated ARAS progresses in nearly 50% of cases over 5 years, sometimes to total occlusion, though intensive BP and statin therapy slow progression. After endovascular stenting renal function recovers in only ~25%, is unchanged in ~50%, and deteriorates in the remainder. ARAS independently predicts cardiovascular events and death. Atheroembolic renal disease carries an ominous prognosis with 1-year mortality exceeding 38%; untreated malignant hypertension historically had 1-year mortality over 90% (and >50% at 6 to 12 months with target organ injury), but current 5-year survival exceeds 50% with effective antihypertensive therapy (Harrison 22e p.2150-2154).

Progressive decline in GFR during BP treatment, or decline associated with ACE inhibitor/ARB therapy
Recurrent flash pulmonary edema / congestive heart failure not explained by LV dysfunction
Abrupt-onset hypertension in a young woman (suggests FMD) or worsening kidney function in an older patient with ASCVD (suggests ARAS)
New worsening hypertension and deteriorating renal function days after an arterial/angiographic procedure (atheroembolism), possibly reaching a malignant phase
Acute flank pain with fever and markedly elevated LDH suggesting renal infarction; anuria with bilateral acute occlusion

No formal staging is given; severity is gauged by degree of luminal stenosis (hemodynamically critical at >70 to 80% occlusion), CKD stage (most revascularization candidates are stage 3 to 5 with eGFR <60), and clinical syndrome (stable medically managed disease versus rapidly progressive/resistant disease). Table 289-2 outlines clinical factors favoring revascularization plus medical therapy (progressive GFR decline, medical failure of BP control, GFR decline with ACEi/ARB, recurrent unexplained heart failure) versus medical therapy with surveillance (controlled BP with stable function, stable non-progressing stenosis, advanced age/limited life expectancy, high atheroembolic risk, concomitant parenchymal disease with proteinuria) (Harrison 22e p.2152).

chunks.text: Restless legs syndrome is a sensorimotor disorder linked to dysfunction of central dopaminergic transmission and to abnormal brain iron handling, since iron is a cofactor for dopamine synthesis. Reduced iron availability within the central nervous system, even with normal peripheral stores, is thought to impair dopaminergic signalling in circuits including the spinal cord and diencephalon. There is a strong genetic contribution, and it may be primary or secondary to iron deficiency, uraemia, pregnancy, or neuropathy.

chunks.text: In rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, a full-thickness retinal break (usually from vitreous traction as the vitreous separates with age) allows liquefied vitreous to track through the tear into the potential space between the neurosensory retina and the retinal pigment epithelium, lifting the photoreceptor layer off its blood supply. Tractional detachment occurs when contracting fibrovascular membranes (as in proliferative diabetic retinopathy) pull the retina forward, and exudative detachment when fluid accumulates beneath an intact retina from inflammatory, vascular, or neoplastic processes. Separated photoreceptors become ischaemic and, if not reattached, degenerate.

chunks.text: Retinitis pigmentosa comprises inherited dystrophies caused by mutations in numerous genes essential to photoreceptor and retinal pigment epithelium function. Progressive apoptosis of rod photoreceptors, followed later by cones, leads to loss of peripheral and night vision that spreads centrally over time. Degenerating photoreceptors and migration of retinal pigment epithelial cells into the retina produce the characteristic bone-spicule pigmentation, while secondary changes cause arteriolar narrowing and optic disc pallor. The underlying genetic defect determines the pattern of inheritance and the rate of progression.

Retinoblastoma results from biallelic inactivation of the RB1 tumour suppressor gene in developing retinal cells. In heritable disease one mutated allele is inherited or arises in the germline, and a second somatic hit inactivates the remaining allele, producing early, often bilateral, multifocal tumours (consistent with the two-hit hypothesis). Loss of functional RB protein removes control of the cell cycle at the G1-S checkpoint, driving unregulated proliferation of retinal precursor cells and tumour formation.
The most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood, usually diagnosed before 5 years of age.
Leukocoria (a white pupillary reflex, sometimes first noticed in photographs) is the most common presenting sign and warrants urgent ophthalmology referral.
Strabismus is the second most common presentation and should never be dismissed without excluding an intraocular cause.
Disease may be unilateral or bilateral; bilateral and multifocal tumours are almost always heritable.
Heritable retinoblastoma arises from germline mutation of the RB1 tumour suppressor gene and carries a lifelong risk of second malignancies, especially osteosarcoma.
Diagnosis is made clinically by an experienced ophthalmologist under examination, supported by imaging; biopsy is avoided because of the risk of tumour seeding.
Treatment aims to save life first, then preserve the eye and vision, using approaches such as chemotherapy, focal therapies, and enucleation for advanced disease.
Children with heritable disease and affected families need genetic counselling and long-term surveillance for new tumours and secondary cancers.
Dismissing leukocoria or a subtle white reflex noticed in photographs as artefact
Attributing strabismus solely to a benign squint without a dilated fundus examination
Delaying urgent referral, which can be the difference between saving and losing an eye or life
Overlooking the need for genetic testing and family screening in apparently unilateral disease

With early diagnosis and modern therapy, survival in high-resource settings exceeds 95 percent for intraocular disease; extraocular or metastatic spread markedly worsens outcome. Children with heritable disease remain at elevated lifelong risk of second malignancies.

chunks.text: Retinopathy of prematurity results from disordered development of the retinal vasculature in the incompletely vascularised preterm retina. In an initial phase, the relatively hyperoxic extrauterine environment (worsened by supplemental oxygen) suppresses vascular growth factors and halts normal vessel growth, leaving peripheral avascular retina. As the metabolically active retina matures, the resulting hypoxia drives excessive vascular endothelial growth factor production and pathological neovascularisation at the junction of vascular and avascular retina. These new vessels can bleed and form fibrovascular tissue, exerting traction that leads to retinal detachment.

When Rh(D)-positive fetal red cells enter the circulation of a Rh(D)-negative mother, her immune system mounts an antibody response, initially IgM and then IgG anti-D. In a later pregnancy with a Rh(D)-positive fetus, maternal IgG crosses the placenta, binds fetal red cells, and leads to their destruction in the fetal reticuloendothelial system. The resulting fetal anaemia drives extramedullary haematopoiesis and, when severe, high-output cardiac failure with generalised oedema known as hydrops fetalis, alongside accumulation of bilirubin that threatens the neonate after birth.
Rhesus isoimmunisation occurs when a Rh(D)-negative mother is exposed to Rh(D)-positive fetal red cells and develops anti-D antibodies that can cross the placenta in subsequent pregnancies
Sensitising events include delivery, miscarriage, termination, ectopic pregnancy, antepartum bleeding, abdominal trauma, and invasive procedures such as amniocentesis
Because sensitisation usually produces no maternal symptoms, prevention and surveillance depend on routine antenatal blood grouping and antibody screening
Prophylactic anti-D immunoglobulin given after sensitising events and routinely in the third trimester has dramatically reduced the incidence of the disease
Once a woman is sensitised, anti-D immunoglobulin is no longer protective, and management focuses on monitoring the fetus for anaemia
Fetal anaemia is assessed non-invasively by Doppler measurement of the middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity, which rises as anaemia develops
Severe fetal anaemia can be treated by intrauterine transfusion, and timing of delivery is balanced against the severity of disease
Other red cell antibodies such as anti-Kell and anti-c can also cause severe haemolytic disease, so screening is not limited to the D antigen
Omitting anti-D prophylaxis after a sensitising event or assuming it helps an already sensitised woman
Focusing only on anti-D and overlooking other antibodies such as anti-Kell
Relying on antibody titres alone without fetal Doppler surveillance in established sensitisation
Underestimating small but sensitising fetomaternal haemorrhages
Failing to quantify large fetomaternal haemorrhage so that the anti-D dose is inadequate

With routine antenatal screening, effective anti-D prophylaxis, non-invasive monitoring, and intrauterine transfusion, most affected pregnancies now achieve good outcomes. Prognosis worsens with early-onset severe anaemia and hydrops, and sensitised pregnancies tend to be affected earlier and more severely in successive gestations, making specialist surveillance essential.

Ultrasound evidence of hydrops fetalis signalling severe disease
A significant sensitising event without timely anti-D prophylaxis

Previous pregnancy affected by severe haemolytic disease, predicting earlier and more severe recurrence

Clostridial myositis/myonecrosis — predictably precipitates acute rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.1096).
Streptococcal (group A) myositis — also predictably causes acute rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.1096).
Viral myositis — influenza, echovirus, coxsackievirus and Epstein-Barr virus infections may be associated with rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.1096).
Legionella infection — reported association with rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.1096).
Urine dipstick for blood with microscopy — dipstick blood-positive but RBC-negative supports myoglobinuria rather than true haematuria (Harrison 22e p.343).
Urine sediment / microscopy for muddy-brown (pigmented) granular casts and tubular epithelial cells, indicating accompanying acute tubular necrosis (Harrison 22e p.343).
Serum phosphate and calcium — hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia accompany acute muscle injury (Harrison 22e p.359, p.363).
Fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) — may be <1% in early rhabdomyolysis-associated ATN, limiting its discriminatory value (Harrison 22e p.343).

Massive skeletal muscle breakdown releases intracellular contents — including myoglobin, potassium, phosphate and creatine kinase — into the circulation. Filtered myoglobin (a heme protein) is nephrotoxic and contributes to pigment-induced acute tubular necrosis; the released heme pigment also causes a false-positive dipstick reaction for blood. Concurrent volume sequestration into injured muscle produces a prerenal/hypovolaemic insult that compounds the tubular injury (Harrison 22e p.343).

Myoglobinuria characteristically produces a positive urine dipstick for blood while urine microscopy shows no (or few) red cells — a key clue distinguishing pigment nephropathy from true haematuria (Harrison 22e p.343).

In rhabdomyolysis-associated acute tubular necrosis the fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) may be paradoxically low (<1%), unlike the classic >1% of established ATN, because the injury is often early/non-oliguric (Harrison 22e p.343).
Rhabdomyolysis is listed among the 'don't-miss' metabolic emergencies whose urgency can be underappreciated, alongside malignant hyperthermia and tumour lysis syndrome (Harrison 22e p.102).

Heat-related exertional rhabdomyolysis is a recognised, albeit rare, cause of sudden death in sickle cell trait carriers during strenuous exercise — a reason to counsel carriers before sports participation (Harrison 22e p.818).
Interpreting a dipstick-positive 'haematuria' as bleeding from the urinary tract when no RBCs are seen on microscopy — this pattern reflects myoglobinuria in rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.343).
Relying on a low FENa to exclude ATN: rhabdomyolysis-related ATN can present with FENa <1% (Harrison 22e p.343).

Acute rhabdomyolysis typically causes hypocalcaemia, but the recovery phase (with renal failure) can produce rebound hypercalcaemia — calcium should not be over-corrected early (Harrison 22e p.362, p.363).

Rhabdomyolysis-associated acute kidney injury is frequently of the milder, non-oliguric ATN type and is potentially reversible with adequate perfusion; the recovery phase may be complicated by rebound hypercalcaemia (Harrison 22e p.343, p.362).
Hyperkalaemia from release of intracellular potassium during muscle necrosis — predictable and potentially life-threatening (Harrison 22e p.359).
Rising creatinine with pigmented granular casts signalling evolving pigment-induced acute tubular necrosis (Harrison 22e p.343).

[guideline] management → Aggressive IV crystalloid (cornerstone) Early, aggressive isotonic fluids maintain renal perfusion and flush myoglobin, the single most effective measure to prevent pigment-induced AKI.

[guideline] adjunct → Cardiac membrane stabilisation (hyperkalaemia with ECG changes) / Potassium shift (with glucose) / Hypoglycaemia cover for insulin / Nebulised beta-agonist (potassium shift) / Urinary alkalinisation (selected cases — controversial) Stabilises the myocardium against hyperkalaemic arrhythmia; does not lower potassium.

Primary Sjogren's syndrome - polyarthralgia and mild synovitis can mimic RA, and ~50% are RF-positive; distinguished by predominant sicca symptoms, ANA positivity and anti-Ro/SSA in about two-thirds (Harrison 22e p.2847).

Spondyloarthropathies (psoriatic arthritis, enteropathy-associated arthritis) - distinguished by sacroiliitis, enthesopathy, and presence of psoriasis or inflammatory bowel disease (Harrison 22e p.2847).

Polymyalgia rheumatica in elderly patients - can resemble seronegative RA; PMR centres on neck/shoulder and hip girdle, whereas RA predominantly affects wrists/hands and ankles/feet, especially at onset (Harrison 22e p.2847).

Remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema (RS3PE) - features prominent distal-limb pitting edema (unusual in RA) and responds promptly to low-dose prednisone (Harrison 22e p.2847).
Paraneoplastic syndromes - may be confused with early RA (Harrison 22e p.2847).
Virus-related polyarthritis syndromes - can mimic RA and cause transient RF production, but usually resolve within 2-3 weeks (Harrison 22e p.2847).
Hepatitis C-related arthropathy - often involves small joints of the hands and is RF-positive in about half of cases, but generally anti-CCP negative (Harrison 22e p.2847).
Subacute bacterial endocarditis and chronic hepatitis B/C - chronic infections that can produce a positive RF and confound interpretation (Harrison 22e p.2847).
Anti-CCP (ACPA) antibodies - high specificity (~95%) for RA; useful diagnostically and prognostically (Harrison 22e p.2847).
Synovial fluid aspiration with cell count and crystal/microbiology analysis - confirms inflammatory arthritis and excludes infection or crystal disease (Harrison 22e p.2847).
MRI - greatest sensitivity for synovitis, effusions and early bone/bone-marrow changes; bone marrow edema predicts subsequent erosions (Harrison 22e p.2848).
Musculoskeletal ultrasound with power Doppler - detects synovitis, increased joint vascularity and erosions, often more than plain films; portable and radiation-free (Harrison 22e p.2848).
ANA and ANCA - may be positive in RA (~30% ANA, occasional p-ANCA), but anti-MPO/anti-PR3 should be negative (Harrison 22e p.2847).
High-resolution chest CT - to detect and characterise interstitial lung disease (UIP vs NSIP patterns) when respiratory symptoms arise (Harrison 22e p.2840).
Chronic tophaceous gout - can mimic severe RA, and tophi may be mistaken for rheumatoid nodules (Harrison 22e p.2847).
Pseudogout (CPPD crystal arthritis) - inflammatory arthritis excluded via synovial fluid crystal analysis (Harrison 22e p.2847).
Osteoarthritis - non-inflammatory; DIP involvement and synovial fluid under 2,000 WBC/uL favour OA over RA (Harrison 22e p.2839, p.2847).

RA is a chronic, systemic, symmetric erosive polyarthritis driven by an interaction of genetic predisposition (e.g., the HLA shared epitope) and environmental triggers such as cigarette smoking. Antigen-presenting cells activate synovial CD4+ T cells (via TCR-MHC class II and CD28-CD80/86 co-stimulation), which differentiate into TH1 and TH17 subsets. These activate B cells that mature into plasma cells producing autoantibodies (RF and anti-CCP/ACPA); immune complexes form within the joint and activate complement, amplifying inflammation. T effector cells stimulate synovial macrophages and fibroblasts to release pro-inflammatory cytokines, with TNF-alpha playing a central role by upregulating endothelial adhesion molecules and driving IL-1, IL-6 and GM-CSF production. TNF-alpha also disrupts the bone balance: it raises DKK-1 (inhibiting Wnt-driven osteoblastic bone formation) and promotes osteoclastogenesis through M-CSF and RANKL signalling, with osteoprotegerin acting as a decoy that limits bone loss. The net result is pannus formation, cartilage and bone erosion, and generalised inflammatory bone loss (Harrison 22e p.2845).

Early-morning joint stiffness lasting more than 1 hour that improves with activity is characteristic; the earliest joints involved are typically the small joints of the hands and feet (Harrison 22e p.2839).
Wrists, MCP and PIP joints are most often affected; isolated DIP involvement usually reflects coexistent osteoarthritis rather than RA itself (Harrison 22e p.2839).

Flexor tendon tenosynovitis is a frequent hallmark, producing reduced range of motion, weakened grip and trigger fingers, and can lead to tendon rupture (most commonly flexor pollicis longus) (Harrison 22e p.2839-2840).
Anti-CCP (ACPA) and RF are useful both diagnostically and as prognostic biomarkers; anti-CCP carries the most value for predicting worse outcomes (Harrison 22e p.2839, p.2847).

Anti-CCP has sensitivity similar to RF but much higher specificity (approaching 95%), so a positive anti-CCP in early inflammatory arthritis helps distinguish RA from other arthritides; testing both RF and anti-CCP adds incremental yield because some patients are positive for only one (Harrison 22e p.2847).
About three-quarters of RA patients are seropositive (RF and/or ACPA) and one-quarter are seronegative; seronegative RA is a clinical diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2847).
A fever above 38.3C (101F) at any point in the course should raise suspicion of systemic vasculitis or superimposed infection rather than being attributed to RA activity alone (Harrison 22e p.2840).

Approximately 30% of RA patients are ANA-positive and some have p-ANCA, but anti-MPO and anti-PR3 are not expected and their presence points to an ANCA-associated vasculitis instead (Harrison 22e p.2847).

Synovial fluid in RA is inflammatory (typically 5,000-50,000 WBC/uL, neutrophil-predominant) versus under 2,000 WBC/uL in osteoarthritis; aspiration is most useful to confirm inflammation and to exclude infection or crystal arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2847).

The 2010 ACR-EULAR criteria are classification (not diagnostic) criteria intended to identify early patients likely to progress; a positive RF or anti-CCP alone does not establish the diagnosis without supporting clinical features (Harrison 22e p.2847).

A negative RF does not exclude RA - IgM RF is found in only ~75% of patients, and RF also occurs in other connective tissue diseases, chronic infections and 1-5% of healthy people (Harrison 22e p.2847).
Accelerated growth of subcutaneous nodules can occur in up to 10% of patients on long-term methotrexate and should not automatically be read as worsening disease (Harrison 22e p.2840).
Rheumatoid nodules and chronic tophaceous gout tophi can be confused with one another (Harrison 22e p.2840, p.2847).
Periarticular osteopenia, the classic earliest x-ray finding, is difficult to appreciate on plain (especially digitised) films, so early radiographs may appear normal (Harrison 22e p.2848).

Most patients show persistent, waxing-and-waning progressive disease; about 10% (particularly seronegative) remit spontaneously within 6 months, while a minority follow either a relapsing explosive course or an aggressively erosive course (now less common with modern therapy). Early disability is driven mainly by joint inflammation (potentially reversible) and later by cumulative irreversible joint damage. Overall mortality is roughly twice that of the general population, with excess deaths from respiratory illness, cardiovascular disease and infection; median life expectancy is shortened by about 7 years in men and 3 years in women. Worse survival is associated with systemic extraarticular involvement, low functional capacity, low socioeconomic status, low education and chronic prednisone use. Cardiovascular disease is the most common cause of death (Harrison 22e p.2848). Seropositivity for RF and especially anti-CCP predicts worse outcomes (Harrison 22e p.2847).
Fever above 38.3C (101F) during the course should prompt evaluation for systemic vasculitis or infection rather than being ascribed to RA activity (Harrison 22e p.2840).

RA patients have the highest incidence of septic (most often S. aureus) arthritis due to chronically inflamed joints, glucocorticoid therapy and breakdown of nodules/vasculitic ulcers; TNF inhibitors add risk of mycobacterial and other infections (Harrison 22e Chap. 124, p.~).
Atlantoaxial (C1-C2) subluxation can cause compressive myelopathy; neurologic signs may evolve slowly with progressive instability (now seen in under 10% of patients) (Harrison 22e p.2840).
New-onset numbness, tingling or focal weakness (mononeuritis multiplex) suggests systemic rheumatoid vasculitis (Harrison 22e p.2841).
Two- to fourfold increased risk of lymphoma (most often diffuse large B-cell), greatest with high disease activity or Felty's syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2841).

Diagnosis is supported by the 2010 ACR-EULAR classification criteria (for patients with at least one joint of definite clinical synovitis not better explained by another disease), scored 0-10 across four domains - joint involvement (0-5), serology (RF/ACPA, 0-3), acute-phase reactants (CRP/ESR, 0-1), and symptom duration (0-1); a score of 6 or more fulfils requirements for definite RA. Disease activity (the main driver of treatment decisions) is tracked with composite indices: ACR 20/50/70 improvement criteria (mainly for trials) and continuous measures including DAS, SDAI, CDAI and RAPID3 used in practice. Functional disability is measured with the Health Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ) (Harrison 22e p.2847-2848).

The spotted fever and typhus group organisms (Rickettsia and Orientia) infect vascular endothelial cells and disseminate lymphohematogenously, producing widespread small-vessel infection. The fundamental injury is increased vascular permeability rather than occlusive thrombosis or ischemic necrosis; resulting edema, hypovolemia, and tissue ischemia drive the clinical picture. Platelet consumption causes thrombocytopenia in roughly a third to half of RMSF cases, but overt DIC with hypofibrinogenemia is rare; thrombin generation and fibrinolysis appear to be homeostatic responses to nonocclusive hemostatic plugs at sites of endothelial injury. Hyponatremia reflects appropriate ADH secretion in response to hypovolemia. Pathogenic rickettsiae have small, reductively evolved genomes lacking biosynthetic genes for intracellularly available molecules. Ehrlichia and Anaplasma instead parasitize vacuoles of hematopoietic cells; vasculitis and granulomas are not features of HME or HGA. Coxiella burnetii is genetically distinct from the Rickettsiaceae, survives harsh environments, escapes macrophage killing by inhibiting the final step of phagosome maturation, and adapts to the acidic phagolysosome.

Rickettsiae are small, obligately intracellular, gram-negative coccobacilli/short bacilli, most spread by a tick, mite, flea, or louse; except for louse-borne typhus, humans are incidental hosts. The agents span seven genera (Rickettsia, Orientia, Ehrlichia, Anaplasma, Neorickettsia, Candidatus Neoehrlichia, and Coxiella).

Of the rickettsial agents, only C. burnetii is documented to cause chronic illness, and only R. prowazekii causes a recrudescent illness (Brill-Zinsser disease) when latent infection reactivates years after the acute episode (p.1454, p.1459).

Q fever is an inhalational zoonosis from sheep, goats, and cattle (organism shed heavily in parturition material); the infectious dose is extremely low (probably 1-10 organisms) and ~60% of infections are asymptomatic seroconversions. Acute disease presents geographically as either pneumonia or hepatitis (p.1462).

Scrub typhus shows remarkable antigenic diversity with rapid loss of cross-protective immunity, so reinfection can occur within weeks to months; the classic eschar/rash/lymphadenopathy triad is often absent, with under half of travelers developing an eschar and under 40% a rash (p.1460).

During the first roughly 5 days the acute presentations are largely indistinguishable: fever, headache, and myalgia, with or without nausea, vomiting, and cough; later differentiating features such as rash, eschar, pneumonitis, or meningoencephalitis emerge. Heightened clinical suspicion based on exposure history should prompt empiric antibiotics rather than waiting for confirmation (p.1454).

A characteristic laboratory triad supports the diagnosis across many of these infections: thrombocytopenia, a normal or low white-cell count, mildly to moderately elevated hepatic aminotransferases, and hyponatremia (p.1454).

Coxiella burnetii, R. prowazekii, and R. typhi can survive long periods outside the host and are highly infectious by inhalation (a single Coxiella organism can cause pneumonia), making several agents bioterrorism concerns (p.1454).

In Rocky Mountain spotted fever the rash is progressive and unreliable: present in only about 14% on day 1 and roughly 49% by day 3, appearing on day 6 or later in ~20% and never appearing in about 10% of cases; classic palm/sole involvement tends to come late and may not occur at all (p.1456-1457).

Only about 3% of RMSF patients show the classic triad of fever, rash, and tick exposure in the first 3 days, and only ~60% recall a tick bite; serology is typically negative at presentation, so treatment must not await a positive result (p.1457).

An eschar (tache noire) at the bite site is a useful clue in several spotted fevers (notably African tick-bite fever ~90%, rickettsialpox, Mediterranean spotted fever ~50%) and in scrub typhus, but is absent in the typhus group (epidemic and murine typhus have no eschar) (p.1455).

Ehrlichioses/anaplasmoses (Anaplasmataceae) target hematopoietic cells: E. chaffeensis (HME) and E. muris infect mononuclear phagocytes, while E. ewingii and A. phagocytophilum (HGA) infect neutrophils; intracytoplasmic morulae may be seen on blood smear but only in a minority (about 20% or less in HME, 20-75% in HGA) (p.1460-1462).

Of the Rickettsiaceae, in descending case-fatality order the life-threatening species are R. rickettsii (RMSF), R. prowazekii (louse-borne typhus), Orientia tsutsugamushi (scrub typhus), R. conorii (MSF), and R. typhi (murine typhus); many spotted-fever species (e.g., R. parkeri, R. africae, R. akari, R. felis) have never been documented to cause a fatal illness (p.1456).
Waiting for serologic confirmation before treating - serology is usually negative at acute presentation; delay worsens outcome and empiric doxycycline should not be withheld
Excluding RMSF because there is no rash or no recalled tick bite (~10% never rash; only ~60% recall a bite) or because palms/soles are not involved

Interpreting a single acute-phase positive titer as diagnostic in endemic areas - cross-reactive preexisting antibody (e.g., from the highly prevalent R. amblyommatis or in HGA-endemic regions) can mislead; the recent apparent RMSF surge largely reflects cross-reactive single-titer enzyme immunoassays rather than true R. rickettsii disease
Relying on blood PCR for RMSF or typhus - insufficiently sensitive because organisms reside in endothelium, not blood; skin/eschar biopsy is preferable
Assuming negative HME serology because E. chaffeensis tests can cross-react when the true agent is another Ehrlichia; separate specific tests are needed for HME vs HGA

Overlooking chronic Q fever as a cause of culture-negative endocarditis or unexplained infected aneurysm/vascular prosthesis - median latency from primary infection is ~13 months and can exceed 9 years
Mislabeling epidemic typhus as typhoid fever in tropical/resource-limited settings
Attributing prolonged post-Q-fever fatigue to active infection and prescribing antibiotics - a randomized trial showed long-term doxycycline did not reduce fatigue versus placebo

Outcome depends heavily on early recognition and prompt empiric therapy. RMSF mortality was 20-25% before antibiotics and is roughly 3-5% now, principally driven by diagnostic/treatment delay; confirmed-case fatality is higher (~9-10% in regions where R. rickettsii is the sole spotted-fever species), is highest in children under 10 and adults over 70, and approaches 50% in parts of Mexico and Brazil for unknown reasons. Untreated fatal RMSF typically dies 8-15 days after onset. Survivors usually recover fully, but severe disease can leave permanent neurologic deficits or gangrene requiring amputation. Mediterranean spotted fever has a severe form (~50% mortality) in patients with diabetes, alcoholism, or heart failure. Epidemic (louse-borne) typhus is fatal in 7-40% of untreated cases. Untreated classic scrub typhus has ~6% case-fatality. Acute Q fever case-fatality is ~1-2%; chronic Q fever carries high mortality (~25% in proven Dutch-outbreak cases, highest at 33% when both endocarditis and vascular infection are present). Q fever fatigue syndrome follows up to 20% of acute cases. Many SFG species (e.g., R. parkeri, R. africae, R. akari, R. felis) have never caused documented fatal illness, and African tick-bite fever is typically mild.

No single unified rickettsial severity score; severity is judged by organ-system involvement and progression. Across the group, escalating clinical lines after nonspecific fever are: (1) macular/maculopapular rash; (2) eschar at the bite site; (3) vesicular rash; (4) pneumonitis with radiographic opacities/rales; (5) meningoencephalitis; and (6) progressive hypotension and multiorgan failure (sepsis/toxic-shock-like). For Q fever, the Dutch consensus group classifies chronic disease as proven, probable, or possible based on PCR positivity in blood/tissue or phase I IgG IFA >=1:800/1:1024 combined with endocarditis (modified Duke criteria), proven large-vessel/prosthetic infection on imaging, or compatible clinical and histologic findings.

chunks.text: Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory disorder of uncertain cause with several contributing mechanisms. Dysregulation of the innate immune system with abnormal cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide processing promotes inflammation and vascular changes. Neurovascular dysregulation drives flushing and persistent erythema, while an increased density of Demodex mites and altered cutaneous microbiome may stimulate the inflammatory response. Ultraviolet radiation, chronic inflammation, and vascular and lymphatic changes contribute to telangiectasia and, over time, the fibrous and sebaceous overgrowth of phymatous disease. Genetic predisposition and environmental triggers modulate expression.

chunks.text: The rotator cuff (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis) stabilises the humeral head in the glenoid and enables elevation and rotation. Tendon integrity is compromised by age-related degeneration, hypovascularity near the supraspinatus insertion, and mechanical impingement beneath the coracoacromial arch, making tears increasingly common with age. Repetitive overhead loading and acute trauma superimpose on this degeneration. Once a tear occurs, the tendon tends to retract and the corresponding muscle undergoes atrophy and fatty infiltration over time, reducing repairability and allowing superior migration of the humeral head, which can eventually produce cuff-tear arthropathy.

Rotavirus infects the mature enterocytes at the tips of the small intestinal villi, causing villous blunting and loss of absorptive surface. This produces malabsorption of nutrients and water with an osmotic diarrhoea, while the viral nonstructural protein NSP4 acts as an enterotoxin that triggers secretory diarrhoea and disrupts calcium homeostasis. The combination of impaired absorption, secretion, and reduced disaccharidase (including lactase) activity leads to voluminous watery stool and rapid fluid and electrolyte losses.
A leading cause of severe dehydrating diarrhoea in infants and young children, especially between about 3 and 24 months of age.
Typically presents with abrupt onset of vomiting followed by profuse watery, non-bloody stools, often with fever.
Spread is faecal-oral; the virus is highly contagious and stable in the environment, so outbreaks in daycare and hospital settings are common.
Assessment of hydration status guides management far more than laboratory testing, which is rarely needed for diagnosis.
Oral rehydration therapy is the cornerstone of treatment for mild to moderate dehydration; intravenous fluids are reserved for severe dehydration or failed oral therapy.
Early refeeding with an age-appropriate diet is encouraged once rehydration is achieved; prolonged fasting and dilute feeds are discouraged.
Antibiotics and antimotility agents have no role and may be harmful; routine antiemetics are generally avoided in young children.
Live oral rotavirus vaccines given in infancy substantially reduce severe disease and hospitalisation.
Antigen immunoassay or PCR on stool can confirm the pathogen when confirmation is required for epidemiologic or infection-control purposes.

Serology: rubella IgM in an acute-phase serum specimen, or a fourfold rise in IgG titer between acute- and convalescent-phase sera; IgM-capture ELISA is regarded as most accurate (Harrison 22e p.1644).

Timing of paired sera: acute specimen within 7-10 days of illness onset, convalescent specimen about 14-21 days later; repeat IgM testing if an early specimen (before day 5 after rash) is negative (Harrison 22e p.1644).

IgG avidity testing to distinguish primary infection (low-avidity antibodies, recent infection) from reinfection (mature high-avidity IgG indicating infection at least ~2 months earlier); especially useful in pregnant women to assess CRS risk (Harrison 22e p.1644).

RT-PCR for viral RNA detection (preferred from nasopharyngeal swab; throat swab or urine acceptable), collected as soon as possible after onset, ideally 1-3 days and no later than 7 days; virus isolation by culture also possible (Harrison 22e p.1644).

CRS confirmation: serum IgM (normally present up to ~6 months, sometimes up to 1 year; may be absent at birth and require retesting at 1 month), and persistence of rubella IgG beyond the expected decline of passively transferred maternal antibody (titer not declining at the expected twofold-per-month rate); RT-PCR/culture of nasopharyngeal, throat, or urine specimens, most likely positive within the first 6 months (Harrison 22e p.1644).
Routine prenatal screening for rubella IgG; a positive IgG indicates immunity (Harrison 22e p.1644-1645).
Scarlet fever (toxin-mediated streptococcal exanthem clinically similar to rubella)
Other drug or hypersensitivity maculopapular eruptions

Rubella virus spreads person to person via respiratory droplets. After primary implantation and replication in the nasopharynx it spreads to regional lymph nodes, followed by viremia. In pregnant women the viremia frequently infects the placenta; placental replication can then seed fetal organs. In the infected fetus nearly all organs may be involved, and the hallmark is a chronic infection that persists throughout intrauterine development and for up to 1 year after birth. Tissue effects of rubella virus range from no obvious impact to cell destruction. The pathology of postnatal (acquired) rubella is limited because the disease is mild, whereas the pathology of CRS is well defined even though its pathogenesis remains poorly delineated (Harrison 22e p.1643).

Caused by rubella virus, an enveloped single-stranded positive-sense RNA virus of the Matonaviridae family (genus Rubivirus); only a single antigenic type exists and humans are the only known reservoir (Harrison 22e p.1643).
Infants with CRS can shed large quantities of virus (notably from throat secretions and urine) for up to 1 year, so only rubella-immune individuals should care for them (Harrison 22e p.1643).
Reinfection with rubella virus, although uncommon, is possible and may produce detectable IgM antibodies (Harrison 22e p.1644).

Rubella is no longer endemic in the United States (endemic transmission interrupted by 2001), but importations and sporadic cases continue, so vigilance is warranted in adults migrating from or returning from areas without rubella control (Harrison 22e p.1643).

Acquired rubella typically presents as a mild generalized maculopapular rash lasting up to about 3 days, but as many as roughly half of infections are subclinical or occur without a rash (Harrison 22e p.1643).

Incubation period averages 14 days (range about 12-23 days); in older children and adults a 1- to 5-day prodrome of low-grade fever, malaise, and upper respiratory symptoms may precede the rash, whereas in young children rash is often the first sign (Harrison 22e p.1643).
Occipital and postauricular lymphadenopathy is characteristic and may appear during the second week after exposure (Harrison 22e p.1643).
Arthralgia and arthritis are common complications in infected adults, particularly women; thrombocytopenia and encephalitis are less common (Harrison 22e p.1643).

Persons with acquired rubella may shed virus from about 7 days before rash onset to roughly 5-7 days afterward, and both clinical and subclinical infections are considered contagious (Harrison 22e p.1643).

The most serious consequence is congenital rubella syndrome (CRS), which results from maternal infection during pregnancy, especially the first trimester; the classic triad is cataracts, hearing impairment, and heart defects (Harrison 22e p.1644).
Hearing impairment is the single most common defect of CRS, and the classic complete triad is seen in only about 10% of CRS infants (Harrison 22e p.1644).

Maternal infection within the first 10 weeks of gestation carries roughly a 90% risk of delivering an infant with CRS; risk declines later in pregnancy and fetal defects are rare after about 16 weeks, though sensorineural hearing deficit can still occur with infection up to about 20 weeks (Harrison 22e p.1644-1645).

Relying on clinical diagnosis is unreliable because rubella mimics many rash illnesses, has varied presentations, and is frequently subclinical or mild; laboratory confirmation is the only reliable way to confirm acute disease (Harrison 22e p.1644).
A negative rubella IgM drawn before day 5 after rash onset does not exclude infection and should be repeated (Harrison 22e p.1644).
Rubella IgM testing is not recommended in pregnant women without a history of illness or contact with a rubella-like illness because of the risk of false-positive results (Harrison 22e p.1645).
An infant with suspected CRS who tests IgM-negative shortly after birth should be retested at 1 month, since IgM may not yet be detectable (Harrison 22e p.1644).

Worldwide rubella case counts are likely underestimated because disease is often mild, care may not be sought, cases may go unrecognized or unreported, and some countries detect cases only through measles surveillance (Harrison 22e p.1643).

Live attenuated rubella-containing vaccine should not be given to women known to be pregnant, and pregnancy should be avoided for 28 days after vaccination; however, inadvertent vaccination during pregnancy is not ordinarily a reason to consider termination, as no CRS occurred among ~3000 such pregnancies followed (Harrison 22e p.1645).

Acquired rubella is generally a mild, self-limited illness; the rash usually resolves within about 3 days, and serious complications such as encephalitis and thrombocytopenia are uncommon. The major prognostic concern is congenital infection: maternal infection in early pregnancy may lead to miscarriage, fetal death, premature delivery, or live birth with severe and often permanent defects (eyes, ears, heart, and CNS). Permanent CRS manifestations include deafness, congenital heart defects, cataracts and other eye defects, microcephaly, and neurodevelopmental sequelae, whereas manifestations such as hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenic purpura, and adenopathy are transient. Immunity following infection or a single dose of rubella-containing vaccine (seroconversion in >=95%) is considered long-term and probably lifelong (Harrison 22e p.1644-1645).
Maternal rubella infection during the first trimester (highest risk of CRS, up to ~90% within the first 10 weeks of gestation) (Harrison 22e p.1644).
A susceptible pregnant woman with exposure to or symptoms of a rubella-like illness, requiring IgM testing and low-avidity IgG confirmation (Harrison 22e p.1645).
A neonate with cataracts, hearing impairment, congenital heart defects, or 'blueberry muffin' purpura suggestive of CRS (Harrison 22e p.1644).
Encephalitis or significant thrombocytopenia complicating acquired rubella (Harrison 22e p.1643).
An index case of CRS in a nosocomial or congregate setting, given prolonged viral shedding and outbreak potential (Harrison 22e p.1643).

No formal severity grading system is described. Clinically, infection is categorized by host and timing: subclinical/mild acquired rubella; symptomatic acquired rubella (rash with possible arthralgia/arthritis, rarely thrombocytopenia or encephalitis); congenital rubella virus infection without apparent signs; and congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) with transient versus permanent manifestations, where fetal risk is greatest with maternal infection in the first 10 weeks of gestation (~90%) and declines markedly after ~16 weeks (Harrison 22e p.1644-1645).

Excluding trauma, the commonest cause is rupture of a saccular ('berry') aneurysm, which forms at bifurcations of large- to medium-sized intracranial arteries (about 89% in the anterior circulation, mostly on the circle of Willis). Aneurysm walls show loss of the internal elastic lamina at the neck base with medial thinning and replacement of smooth muscle by connective tissue; rupture is usually at the thin-walled dome through a tear often <=0.5 mm. Rupture deposits blood in the subarachnoid space of the basal cisterns (and sometimes adjacent parenchyma), abruptly raising ICP. Other causes include vascular malformations (AVM, dural arteriovenous fistula) and subarachnoid extension of a primary intracerebral haemorrhage. Roughly 2% of adults harbour intracranial aneurysms and about 20% of affected patients have multiple aneurysms (frequently mirror-image bilateral). Delayed cerebral ischaemia is thought to arise from clot breakdown products acting on basal arteries to cause vasospasm and vessel-wall thickening, but also from vasospasm-independent mechanisms (microthrombosis, inflammation, microvascular dysregulation, cortical spreading depolarisation). Hyponatraemia results from natriuresis with volume depletion ('cerebral salt wasting'), mediated by atrial and brain natriuretic peptides (p.3457-3461).

The single most important feature of aneurysmal SAH headache is its sudden (abrupt) onset, even more than its severity; ruptures may occasionally present as only moderate headache or as a change in the patient's usual headache pattern (p.3458).

Transient loss of consciousness occurs in nearly half of patients at the moment of rupture, reflecting an abrupt rise in intracranial pressure; many patients only report the headache after regaining consciousness (p.3458).

A third nerve palsy with pupillary dilation and pain around/behind the eye suggests an expanding aneurysm at the posterior communicating artery-internal carotid junction; a sixth nerve palsy may indicate a cavernous-sinus aneurysm (p.3458).
Quivering, jerking, or extensor posturing accompanying loss of consciousness at SAH onset is usually caused by the sharp ICP rise rather than true seizure activity (p.3461).

ECG changes mimicking cardiac ischaemia (ST/T changes, long QT, peaked or deeply inverted T waves) and a reversible (catecholamine-mediated) cardiomyopathy with regional wall-motion abnormalities can occur after SAH; an asymptomatic troponin rise is common (p.3459-3460).
Nimodipine improves outcomes in aneurysmal SAH, apparently by limiting ischaemic injury rather than by reducing vasospasm itself (knowledge, no dose) (p.3461).
Perimesencephalic (idiopathic) SAH localised to the perimesencephalic cisterns is benign, probably venous/capillary in origin, and angiography is typically unrevealing (p.3458).

A normal CT does not exclude SAH, especially as time elapses or with small or infratentorial bleeds; if CT is non-diagnostic and there is no mass lesion/obstructive hydrocephalus, lumbar puncture for xanthochromia is required (p.3458-3459).
Xanthochromia (yellow CSF from haemoglobin-to-bilirubin conversion) takes 6-12 h to appear, peaks at ~48 h, and persists 1-4 weeks; an LP performed too early may miss it (p.3459).
Free-water restriction should NOT be used to treat SAH-associated hyponatraemia (cerebral salt wasting): the resulting hypovolaemia/hypotension can precipitate cerebral ischaemia (p.3459, p.3461).
Marked hyponatraemia of several days' duration must not be corrected too rapidly because of the risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome (p.3461).
Lumbar puncture before imaging is appropriate only when CT is unavailable at the time of suspected SAH (p.3459).

Overall mortality of aneurysmal SAH is about 35%, with roughly a third dying before reaching hospital; over half of survivors are left with significant neurologic deficits from the initial bleed, delayed cerebral ischaemia, or hydrocephalus. Outcome worsens with increasing presentation grade: grade 1 (Hunt-Hess) patients rarely die if treated, whereas mortality for grades 4-5 may reach about 60%. In an untreated aneurysm, rebleeding risk is about 20% in the first 2 weeks, 30% in the first month, then about 3% per year; rerupture (~30% in the first month, peaking in the first 7 days) carries about 50% mortality. Delayed cerebral ischaemia occurs in about 30% and is the leading cause of delayed morbidity and death among initial survivors. Unruptured aneurysms <7 mm had ~0% 5-year rupture risk in a large study (though many ruptured aneurysms are <6 mm); giant aneurysms (>25 mm) carry ~8-10% annual rupture risk (p.3458-3460).
Sudden unexplained headache of any location may represent a sentinel bleed (small aneurysmal leak) heralding imminent major haemorrhage and must be investigated (p.3459)
Declining mental status with worsening headache 4-14 days after SAH suggests delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm (p.3459-3460)
High ICP refractory to treatment is a poor prognostic sign (p.3461)

Two presentation-based clinical grading scales are used: the Hunt-Hess scale (1 = asymptomatic/minimal headache and slight nuchal rigidity through 5 = coma with reflex posturing or flaccidity) and the World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies (WFNS) scale based on Glasgow Coma Scale score and motor deficits (1 = GCS 15 no motor deficit through 5 = GCS 3-6). Higher grade predicts worse outcome. The modified Fisher CT grading system predicts symptomatic vasospasm by the amount and distribution of subarachnoid/intraventricular blood ('thin' <1 mm vs 'thick' >=1 mm), with risk rising from 0% (grade 0) to ~40% (grade 4, thick blood with intraventricular blood) (p.3459-3460).

Salicylate increases sensitivity of the CNS respiratory center and directly stimulates the medullary chemoreceptor, driving hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis. It also uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, inhibits Krebs cycle enzymes, and stimulates carbohydrate and lipid metabolism, generating unmeasured endogenous anions (and increased lactate) that produce a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (p.376, p.3714).

Classic course: early nausea/vomiting and hyperventilation with respiratory alkalosis and alkaline urine, evolving to a mixed respiratory alkalosis plus high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with paradoxical aciduria; late stages show acidemia with CNS and respiratory depression (p.3714).
Salicylates are the most common cause of drug-induced respiratory alkalosis, acting by direct stimulation of the medullary respiratory chemoreceptor (p.376).
Only part of the elevated anion gap is attributable to salicylate itself; concurrent lactic acid production and other endogenous unmeasured anions also contribute (p.370, p.3714).
Cerebral and pulmonary edema can develop in severe poisoning; non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema (ARDS) is a recognized complication (p.3705, p.3714).
Hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, hypokalemia, and seizures can occur in salicylate toxicity (p.3714).
Ketosis can accompany salicylate poisoning and may mimic other causes of ketoacidosis (p.3705).
Salicylate is detected on quantitative serum assay; serum levels guide management and are usually available within an hour (p.3706).

Enteric-coated and sustained-release salicylate preparations cause delayed/slow absorption and can form gastric concretions (bezoars), acting as a 'toxic time-bomb' with continued rising levels (p.3705, p.3752).
Vigorous gastric lavage, if used, should be with isotonic saline, NOT NaHCO3 (p.370).
Only a portion of the anion gap is due to salicylate itself; do not assume the whole gap reflects drug level (p.370).
Acid (acidic) diuresis is never indicated and is potentially harmful (p.3752).
Acetazolamide can cause systemic metabolic acidosis if excreted bicarbonate is not replaced, which markedly reduces salicylate clearance (p.370).
