All Salmonella infections begin with ingestion of organisms, usually in contaminated food or water; the infectious dose ranges from ~200 to 10^6 CFU, and the ingested dose helps determine incubation period and severity. Conditions reducing gastric acidity (age <1 year, acid-suppression therapy, achlorhydria) or compromising intestinal integrity (inflammatory bowel disease, cytotoxic chemotherapy, prior GI surgery, antibiotic-induced microbiome alteration) increase susceptibility. In contrast to enteric fever (mononuclear infiltration of small-bowel mucosa), NTS gastroenteritis is characterized by massive polymorphonuclear leukocyte infiltration into both large- and small-bowel mucosa. This response depends largely on induction of interleukin 8, a strong neutrophil chemoattractant secreted by intestinal cells in response to NTS colonization and translocation of bacterial proteins and LPS into host cytoplasm with subsequent inflammasome activation; neutrophil degranulation and release of toxic substances damages the mucosa, producing inflammatory diarrhea. NTS persistence is aided by its ability to use tetrathionate (generated from thiosulfate via inflammatory reactive oxygen species) for metabolism in a microaerophilic, inflamed gut, allowing it to outcompete endogenous flora. Unlike typhoidal serotypes, NTS effectively colonizes the intestinal tract rather than evolving as a primarily systemic pathogen.

NTS infection most often produces a gastroenteritis that is clinically indistinguishable from that caused by other enteric pathogens, with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea beginning 6-48 h after ingestion of contaminated food or water; stools are usually loose, nonbloody, and of moderate volume, though large-volume watery stools, bloody stools, or frank dysentery can occur (p.1320).
NTS gastroenteritis is usually self-limited: diarrhea resolves within 3-7 days and fever within 72 h; stool cultures may remain positive for 4-5 weeks after infection (p.1320).

Globally S. Typhimurium and S. Enteritidis are the most common serotypes causing human disease; in the United States NTS is the second most common cause of foodborne outbreaks after norovirus (p.1319).

Unlike S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi (human-only reservoir), NTS is acquired from multiple animal and plant reservoirs - especially eggs, poultry, undercooked ground meat, and dairy, plus produce contaminated with animal waste and contact with animals (reptiles, amphibians, chicks, etc.) (p.1319).

Up to 8% of patients with NTS gastroenteritis develop bacteremia, and of those 5-10% develop localized (metastatic) infections; bacteremia and metastatic infection are most common with S. Choleraesuis and S. Dublin and among infants, the elderly, and the immunocompromised, especially those with HIV (p.1320).

Invasive NTS disease (predominantly S. Typhimurium ST313 and S. Enteritidis ST11) is a leading cause of bacteremia in children and HIV-infected adults in sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia; it typically presents as a nonspecific febrile illness resembling enteric fever and uncommonly causes diarrhea (p.1319-1320).

Diagnosis rests on isolating the organism from freshly passed stool or from blood or another normally sterile fluid; culture-independent molecular tests are increasingly used but positive specimens should still undergo primary isolation, and all NTS isolates should be referred to public health for serotyping (p.1320-1321).
Reactive arthritis can follow NTS gastroenteritis, occurring most frequently in persons carrying the HLA-B27 antigen (p.1321).

Localized NTS infections include intraabdominal (hepatic/splenic abscess, cholecystitis), CNS (meningitis - chiefly in infants 1-4 months and HIV-infected adults), pulmonary (lobar pneumonia), urinary/genital, and bone/joint disease; Salmonella osteomyelitis classically affects the femur, tibia, humerus, or lumbar vertebrae and is strongly linked to sickle cell disease and hemoglobinopathies (p.1320-1321).

Antibiotics should NOT be used routinely to treat uncomplicated NTS gastroenteritis - the illness is usually self-limited and antibiotics do not significantly shorten fever or diarrhea, while they have been associated with increased relapse rates, prolonged fecal/gastrointestinal carriage, and adverse drug reactions.
Only ~1% of clinical isolates ferment lactose, so a high index of suspicion is needed to detect rare lactose-fermenting strains.

Decreased-ciprofloxacin-susceptibility NTS strains may not be reliably detected by nalidixic acid susceptibility testing or standard ciprofloxacin disk diffusion, risking missed resistance and treatment failure.

Neonates, the elderly, and immunosuppressed patients with NTS gastroenteritis are especially prone to dehydration and invasive infection and may need hospitalization and antibiotic therapy - they are exceptions to the no-routine-antibiotics rule.

NTS gastroenteritis is usually self-limited, with diarrhea resolving in 3-7 days and fever within 72 h; chronic carriage develops in <1% of cases. Outcomes worsen markedly with invasive disease: endocarditis and arteritis are rare (<1%) but carry serious, potentially fatal complications (valve perforation, endomyocardial abscess, infected mural thrombus, pericarditis, mycotic aneurysm, aneurysm rupture, aortoenteric fistula, vertebral osteomyelitis), and NTS meningitis is fatal in up to 60% of cases. In 2017 there were ~535,000 invasive NTS cases and ~77,500 deaths worldwide, ~80% in sub-Saharan Africa. Acute NTS gastroenteritis was associated with a threefold increased risk of dyspepsia and irritable bowel syndrome at 1 year in a Spanish study.
Invasive disease / bacteremia and endovascular seeding in the elderly, immunocompromised (including HIV), infants/neonates, and patients with sickle cell disease or other hemoglobinopathies

Harrison does not provide a formal graded severity score for NTS. Disease is described along a clinical spectrum: (1) uncomplicated self-limited gastroenteritis; (2) bacteremia (low-grade defined as <50% of blood cultures positive vs high-grade >50% of three or more sets positive, the latter raising concern for endovascular infection); and (3) localized/metastatic infection (intraabdominal, CNS, pulmonary, urinary/genital, bone/joint/soft tissue) and endovascular infection (endocarditis, arteritis). Host-risk stratification for invasive disease includes neonates (up to ~3 months), persons >50 years with atherosclerosis, and those with immunosuppression, cardiac valvular/endovascular abnormalities, or significant joint disease.

Sarcoidosis is thought to arise from a heightened, antigen-driven host immune response to an undetermined (likely inhaled bioaerosol or inorganic) environmental antigen in a genetically susceptible person; the inciting antigen may differ between individuals/populations. A poorly degradable material is presented to lymphocytes by dendritic cells/macrophages via MHC, triggering an innate cytokine/chemokine cascade and recruitment of adaptive immune cells. The immunopathologic hallmark is highly polarized CD4+ TH1 lymphocytes (less so CD8+) producing IFN-gamma, with upregulation of TH1-promoting cytokines/chemokines (IL-1, IL-2, IL-15, IL-18, CXCR3) that activate macrophages and drive formation of tightly organized nonnecrotizing (noncaseating) granulomas. Altered regulatory T-cell and TH17 responses are implicated in failure to resolve and in progression to fibrosis. Granulomas comprise macrophages, epithelioid cells, and multinucleated giant cells rimmed by lymphocytes/fibroblasts (CD4+ central, CD8+ and B cells peripheral). Mycobacterial proteins (mKatG, ESAT-6, superoxide dismutase A, antigen 85A, heat-shock proteins) and Cutibacterium acnes have been disproportionately implicated; the transmissibility seen with the Kveim-Siltzbach reagent and via organ transplantation supports an antigenic trigger (p.2922-2923).

Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease of unknown cause; the lung is involved in over 90% of cases, but roughly half of patients have extrapulmonary disease and almost any organ can be affected (p.2921, p.2924).

Baseline workup in every patient should include PFTs, chest imaging, an ophthalmologic exam (to detect clinically silent uveitis), an ECG, and serum creatinine/alkaline phosphatase/calcium/CBC (p.2924).

Hypercalcemia from dysregulated macrophage/granuloma production of calcitriol (1,25-(OH)2 vitamin D) occurs despite suppressed PTH; patients should limit vitamin D intake, avoid excess sunlight, and stay hydrated (p.2927-2928).
Optic neuropathy in ocular sarcoidosis is an emergency requiring immediate immunosuppression to prevent sudden permanent vision loss (p.2927).
Smoking is a consistent NEGATIVE predictor of incident sarcoidosis (reduced odds), an unusual feature among lung diseases (p.2921-2922).

Diagnosis rests on three criteria: a compatible clinical picture, nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation on tissue, AND exclusion of other causes of granulomas — it is never made with absolute certainty, so new signs during follow-up should be re-evaluated (p.2923-2924).

Löfgren syndrome (fever, erythema nodosum, ankle arthralgias, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy) occurs in up to ~10% of cases and, like Heerfordt syndrome, carries an excellent prognosis with frequent spontaneous resolution (p.2923).
Heerfordt syndrome = facial nerve palsy, fever, anterior uveitis, and bilateral parotid gland enlargement (p.2923, p.2928).

In very compelling presentations (classic Löfgren, Heerfordt, lupus pernio, or asymptomatic symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy), biopsy may be deferred, but close clinical follow-up is still required (p.2924).

A BAL CD4:CD8 lymphocyte ratio >3.5 supports the diagnosis when combined with consistent clinical/radiographic findings, but a normal ratio does NOT exclude sarcoidosis; BAL is also important to exclude infection (p.2924).
Endobronchial ultrasound-guided lymph node sampling has high diagnostic yield with low procedural risk when hilar/mediastinal nodes are the prominent feature (p.2924).

Sarcoidosis is upper-lobe predominant on imaging with a lymphangitic (perilymphatic/subpleural/peribronchovascular) nodular distribution; airflow obstruction can occur in up to one-third of patients despite the classically restrictive pattern (p.2924-2925).

Every sarcoidosis patient should be screened for cardiac involvement (baseline ECG) because severity of lung disease does not predict cardiac sarcoidosis and sudden death can be the initial presentation (p.2925-2926).
A normal BAL CD4:CD8 ratio, normal PFTs, or a normal lung exam does NOT exclude sarcoidosis despite active granulomatous inflammation (p.2924).
Serum ACE has low sensitivity and is not a reliable diagnostic or prognostic test; it only roughly tracks granuloma burden and is best used to monitor activity (p.2929).
Scadding (CXR) stages reveal overall resolution rates but do NOT predict disease activity, lung-function progression, or extrapulmonary involvement in an individual (p.2929).

Cardiac involvement is frequently subclinical and endomyocardial biopsy has poor sensitivity (patchy granulomas, basal predominance, sparing of the right ventricle), so a negative biopsy does not exclude cardiac sarcoidosis (p.2926).
Failing to screen for cardiac, ocular, and neurologic disease at baseline misses life- or sight-threatening involvement because pulmonary severity does not predict it (p.2924-2926).
Isolated extrapulmonary sarcoidosis (cardiac, hepatic, neurologic) can occur without lung disease and is easily overlooked (p.2926-2927).
Loosely formed granulomas suggest hypersensitivity pneumonitis and abundant necrosis suggests infection — misreading these as sarcoidosis is a classic error (p.2924).
Always re-evaluate alternative causes for isolated hepatic granulomas, which carry a broad differential (p.2927).

Disease resolves spontaneously in just over half of patients, but 30-40% develop chronic disease threatening vital organs or causing debilitating symptoms. Most patients show radiographic or spirometric improvement by 2 years (treated or untreated). Death attributable to sarcoidosis occurs in roughly 1-5%, most often from progressive respiratory insufficiency/pulmonary fibrosis (leading cause in the US/Northern Europe) or cardiac involvement (predominant cause of death in Japan). A robust acute initial immune response predicts a better outcome: Löfgren and Heerfordt syndromes remit spontaneously in up to ~80%, and immunosuppression is rarely needed. Adverse prognostic factors include lupus pernio, chronic uveitis, older age, chronic hypercalcemia, nephrocalcinosis, African ancestry, pulmonary hypertension, fibrotic pulmonary disease, sinus involvement, cystic bone lesions, neurosarcoidosis, and cardiac involvement. Relapses are common and associated with shorter treatment duration (p.2928-2929).

New reproductive-organ nodules/masses require exclusion of malignancy given the rarity of genital sarcoidosis

Scadding chest x-ray stages describe the pulmonary pattern and correlate with spontaneous resolution rates (NOT with activity or prognosis in the individual): Stage 1 = bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy without parenchymal involvement (resolution ~55-90%); Stage 2 = bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy WITH parenchymal involvement (resolution ~40-70%); Stage 3 = parenchymal involvement without lymphadenopathy (resolution ~10-20%); Stage 4 = pulmonary fibrosis with architectural distortion and volume loss (resolution ~0%) (p.2925).

chunks.text: Scabies is caused by infestation with the mite Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis. The fertilised female mite burrows into the stratum corneum, laying eggs and depositing faeces as she tunnels. The clinical eruption and intense pruritus are largely due to a delayed type IV hypersensitivity response to the mite, its eggs, and its excreta, which explains the delay in symptoms after primary infestation. In classic scabies the mite burden is low (typically a small number of adult mites), whereas in crusted scabies impaired immune control permits proliferation of thousands to millions of mites, producing thick hyperkeratotic crusts and extreme infectivity.

Free-swimming cercariae released from infected freshwater snails penetrate intact skin within minutes, transform into schistosomula, enter veins/lymphatics, traverse the lungs and heart, and mature in the portal vein into paired adult male and female worms that migrate to the mesenteric (S. mansoni, S. japonicum) or pelvic/vesical (S. haematobium) venous plexus. The prepatent period is 5-7 weeks (up to 12 for S. haematobium). About half of the eggs produced are excreted in feces or urine; the remainder become trapped in tissue. Most morbidity results from egg-induced, TH2-driven granulomatous immune responses (lymphocytes, eosinophils, alternatively activated macrophages; IL-4/5/13). Egg antigen excess early in infection forms soluble immune complexes causing a serum sickness-like illness (Katayama fever). Hepatic egg deposition leads to periportal (Symmers) fibrosis, portal-branch occlusion, and portal hypertension; S. haematobium egg deposition in the bladder/ureters causes inflammation, fibrosis, obstructive uropathy, and predisposes to squamous bladder carcinoma (p.1826-1829).
Infection is contracted through contact with freshwater bodies harboring infected intermediate-host snails; cercariae penetrate intact human skin within a few minutes (p.1826).
S. haematobium is an IARC group 1 carcinogen; chronic infection is associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the urinary bladder (p.1829).

Detection of schistosome eggs in stool or urine indicates active infection and is the standard diagnostic method; S. haematobium eggs (terminal spine) are excreted in urine, other species (S. mansoni lateral spine, S. japonicum small lateral knob) in feces (p.1826, p.1829).

Neuroschistosomiasis is one of the most severe forms: S. mansoni/S. haematobium can cause transverse myelitis (an acute complication in returning travelers), while S. japonicum causes cerebral granulomas with seizures and focal neurologic deficits (p.1829).
A travel/migration history of freshwater exposure (bathing, washing, fishing, rice-field work, swimming) in an endemic area is central to the diagnosis, especially in travelers (p.1827, p.1829).
Most disease manifestations are due to immunologic granulomatous reactions to eggs retained in host tissues, not to the adult worms; about half of eggs are trapped in tissue (p.1827).

Cercarial dermatitis ('swimmer's itch') is a maculopapular rash from cercarial skin penetration; a severe form follows exposure to avian schistosomes (e.g., lakes in Europe/US) that die in the skin (p.1828).

Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama fever) occurs 2 weeks to 3 months after exposure, usually in first-time-infected travelers, with fever, myalgia, malaise, headache, nonproductive cough, and abdominal symptoms (p.1828).
Eosinophilia is a common finding and is often associated with schistosomiasis; transient pulmonary infiltrates may accompany Katayama fever (p.1828, p.1829).

Intestinal schistosomiasis (S. mansoni, S. japonicum): worms in mesenteric veins; eggs trapped in intestinal tissue cause granulomatous inflammation, microulceration, intermittent abdominal pain, and sometimes bloody diarrhea (p.1829).

Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis (S. mansoni, S. japonicum): late disease produces periportal (Symmers clay-pipestem) fibrosis with portal vein occlusion, portal hypertension, splenomegaly, esophageal varices, and hematemesis; hepatic function usually remains normal (p.1827, p.1829).

Urogenital schistosomiasis (S. haematobium): hallmark of the active stage is painless terminal hematuria, with dysuria and suprapubic discomfort; eggs in bladder mucosa cause inflammation, fibrosis, 'sandy patches', and possible ureteric obstruction with hydronephrosis (p.1829).
Patients with periportal fibrosis (late hepatosplenic disease) may excrete very few or no eggs in feces, so a negative stool exam does not exclude advanced disease (p.1829).
In the chronic urogenital stage, urinary egg excretion may be sparse or absent despite ongoing urogenital tract pathology (p.1829).
Egg excretion may be very low in people from nonendemic areas (travelers), requiring larger samples and concentration methods (p.1829).
Katayama fever is rare in people chronically exposed in S. mansoni- or S. haematobium-endemic areas, so its absence does not exclude infection in residents (p.1829).
CAA/CCA antigen detection is not currently suitable for diagnosing travelers, who have low worm burdens (p.1830).
Serology is less useful in people from endemic areas with ongoing transmission (p.1829-1830).

Many patients recover spontaneously from acute schistosomiasis after 2-10 weeks, though some follow a more severe course, and the acute syndrome can rarely be fatal. In hepatosplenic disease, hepatic function usually remains normal even with marked periportal fibrosis and portal hypertension; however, severe periportal (Symmers) fibrosis is often irreversible, and hematemesis from variceal bleeding may be fatal. Early inflammatory hepatosplenomegaly in children generally decreases over time as immunity develops. Ureteral fibrosis can cause irreversible obstructive uropathy progressing to uremia. The adult worm lifespan averages 3-5 years but can reach 30 years (p.1826-1829).
Hematemesis or melena from esophageal varices in hepatosplenic disease - the most severe complication; death may result from massive blood loss (p.1829)
Acute transverse myelitis or other cerebral/spinal cord manifestations - neuroschistosomiasis, even from light infections (p.1829)
Severe Katayama fever with weight loss, dyspnea, diarrhea, and hepatomegaly; rarely fatal (p.1829)
Painless terminal hematuria in a traveler/migrant from an endemic area (urogenital S. haematobium) (p.1829)
Obstructive uropathy progressing to uremia from ureteral fibrosis (p.1829)

Disease is staged clinically by duration and intensity of infection into three phases - acute (cercarial dermatitis and Katayama fever), active/established, and chronic (e.g., late hepatosplenic periportal fibrosis with portal hypertension, or chronic urogenital fibrosis with sandy patches and obstructive uropathy). Severity of early hepatosplenomegaly is closely associated with infection intensity (p.1828-1829).

chunks.text: Scleritis is inflammation of the sclera, frequently immune-mediated and often a manifestation of systemic autoimmune or vasculitic disease. Immune-complex deposition and T-cell-mediated inflammation cause oedema and cellular infiltration of the sclera and episclera; in necrotising disease, occlusive vasculitis of the deep episcleral vessels leads to scleral ischaemia, necrosis, and thinning, with risk of perforation. chunks.text: Scoliosis is a structural lateral deviation of the spine accompanied by rotation of the vertebrae, which produces the characteristic rib or paravertebral prominence. In adolescent idiopathic scoliosis the cause is unknown but multifactorial, with genetic, growth-related, and neuromuscular balance factors implicated, and the deformity tends to worsen during periods of rapid skeletal growth. Congenital scoliosis results from failures of vertebral formation or segmentation present from birth, while neuromuscular scoliosis arises from asymmetrical muscle forces acting on the growing spine in conditions such as cerebral palsy. Progressive rotation and wedging of vertebrae make the curve increasingly rigid, and large thoracic curves can distort the chest and compromise lung capacity.

chunks.text: Scorpion venom contains peptide neurotoxins that delay inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels and block potassium channels at nerve terminals, causing repetitive depolarisation and unregulated release of neurotransmitters. This produces an initial cholinergic outpouring followed by an overwhelming sympathetic (catecholamine) surge. The resulting effects include hypertension, tachyarrhythmias, increased systemic vascular resistance, and direct catecholamine-mediated myocardial injury. Myocarditis, transient left ventricular dysfunction, and increased capillary permeability lead to acute pulmonary oedema, which is the principal cause of death, especially in children.

chunks.text: Seborrhoeic dermatitis is a chronic inflammatory disorder occurring in sebaceous-rich skin, driven by an abnormal host inflammatory response to Malassezia yeasts that are part of the normal skin flora. The yeasts metabolise sebum lipids, releasing free fatty acids and other products that irritate the skin and provoke inflammation in susceptible individuals. Sebaceous gland activity, an altered skin barrier, individual immune reactivity, and neurological or immunosuppressive comorbidities all influence expression. This explains its predilection for sebum-rich sites, its association with hormonal activity in infancy and adulthood, and its increased severity in HIV infection and Parkinson's disease.

chunks.text: Secondary peritonitis is inflammation of the peritoneum caused by spillage of gastrointestinal contents and micro-organisms into the peritoneal cavity following a breach of a hollow viscus or transmural necrosis. Gut flora, typically a mix of coliforms and anaerobes, provoke an intense inflammatory response with fibrinopurulent exudate, large third-space fluid losses, and paralytic ileus. Absorption of bacteria and endotoxin across the vast peritoneal surface drives systemic inflammatory response, sepsis, and septic shock. The peritoneum may localise infection into abscesses, but diffuse contamination overwhelms these defences and threatens life.

chunks.text: Syncope (vasovagal, cardiac arrhythmia, valvular heart disease, cardiac failure, orthostatic hypotension) - the most frequent diagnostic dilemma versus generalized seizure (p.3418-3419)
Transient ischemic attack, particularly basilar artery TIA (p.3419)
Migraine - confusional migraine, basilar migraine (p.3419)
Acute psychosis (p.3416)
Sleep disorders - narcolepsy/cataplexy, benign sleep myoclonus (p.3419)
Movement disorders - tics, nonepileptic myoclonus, paroxysmal choreoathetosis (p.3419)
In children: breath-holding spells, benign paroxysmal vertigo, night terrors, sleepwalking, apnea, abdominal migraine with cyclic vomiting (p.3419)

CNS infection (meningitis/encephalitis) presenting with seizures and altered mentation - lumbar puncture indicated if suspected and mandatory in all HIV-infected patients even when asymptomatic (p.3417)
Parasitic CNS infection such as neurocysticercosis as a cause of seizures in adolescents/young adults from endemic areas (p.3413)
Complete blood count, magnesium, liver and renal function tests, and urinalysis in addition to glucose/electrolytes/calcium to find metabolic causes (p.3416)
Toxicology screen of blood and urine, especially when no clear precipitant is identified (p.3417)
Lumbar puncture when meningitis/encephalitis is suspected; mandatory in all HIV-infected patients even without signs of infection (p.3417)
Serum and CSF autoantibody testing when epilepsy onset is fulminant or accompanied by psychiatric/cognitive disturbance (autoimmune/paraneoplastic encephalitis) (p.3417)
MRI preferred over CT for detecting structural lesions; CT performed emergently when MRI is not immediately available or when a mass/infection is suspected (p.3417-3418)

Interictal and ictal EEG, with activating procedures (hyperventilation, photic stimulation, sleep, sleep deprivation); a normal routine interictal EEG does NOT exclude epilepsy - it is normal in 50-80% of known epileptics initially (p.3416-3417)
Continuous video-EEG telemetry for poorly characterized events or seizures that are difficult to control, and to distinguish epileptic from psychogenic events (p.3417, p.3419)
Genetic testing in infants/children with suspected genetic epilepsy syndromes, and selected older patients with an undiagnosed early-life epilepsy syndrome (p.3418)

Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (PNES) - nonepileptic behaviors, often a conversion reaction; clues include side-to-side head turning, ictal eye closure, asynchronous large-amplitude limb shaking, four-limb twitching without loss of consciousness, pelvic thrusting, and prolonged waxing/waning episodes; surface EEG may be normal especially for frontal-lobe-like events, and PNES can coexist with true epilepsy (p.3419)

Convulsive syncope - a brief (1-10 s) burst of convulsive movements at the onset of a faint, especially if the patient stays upright; postictal confusion is much less prominent than after a true seizure (p.3419)
Alcoholic blackouts and delirium tremens (p.3419)
Hypoglycemia and hypoxia as metabolic mimics of seizure (p.3419)
Hyperventilation and panic attack (p.3419)
Effects of psychoactive drugs / hallucinogens (p.3419)

A seizure reflects a shift in the normal balance between excitation and inhibition in the CNS. At the cellular level the hallmark of focal seizure activity is the electrographic spike, generated by near-simultaneous bursting (the 'paroxysmal depolarization shift') of local excitatory neurons - a prolonged membrane depolarization driven by calcium influx that opens voltage-gated sodium channels, followed by a GABA- or potassium-mediated hyperpolarizing afterpotential. Surrounding inhibition normally limits spread; when recruitment overwhelms it (via rising extracellular potassium, presynaptic calcium accumulation with enhanced transmitter release, NMDA-receptor activation, and ephaptic effects), activity propagates through local cortical and long commissural pathways (e.g., corpus callosum). Generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges of absence seizures arise from thalamocortical oscillatory circuits involving GABA-B receptors, T-type calcium channels, and potassium channels. Many causes converge on three interacting factor classes: endogenous (genetic/developmental seizure-threshold) factors, epileptogenic factors (CNS injury such as severe penetrating head trauma, stroke, infection, or neurodegeneration that, over months to years, transforms a normal network into a chronically hyperexcitable one - 'epileptogenesis'), and precipitating factors (sleep deprivation, stress, hormonal change, toxins, certain drugs, photic stimulation). Many inherited epilepsies are channelopathies due to ion-channel mutations (p.3411-3415).

A seizure is a transient event from abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity; epilepsy is the distinct condition of recurrent unprovoked seizures from a chronic underlying process. A single seizure, or seizures due to a correctable/avoidable cause, is not by itself epilepsy (p.3408).

If the sole cause of a seizure is a correctable metabolic disturbance (e.g., electrolyte or glucose abnormality), or a precipitant drug/illicit substance, treatment targets the underlying problem and chronic antiseizure drugs are usually unnecessary (p.3419).

An apparently unprovoked first seizure carries a recurrence risk estimated at roughly 31-71% in the first 12 months; accepted risk factors favoring treatment are prior brain insult (stroke/trauma), epileptiform EEG, a significant imaging abnormality, or a nocturnal seizure (p.3420).

A serum prolactin rise in the 30 min after most generalized and some focal seizures can support an epileptic cause, but it is unreliable because baseline levels are rarely available and some drugs elevate prolactin (p.3419).
The clinical range of focal seizure behaviors is extremely broad, so caution is advised before dismissing paroxysmal stereotypic bizarre episodes as non-epileptic (p.3409).

The age of the patient strongly informs the likely etiology of new seizures - e.g., febrile seizures and genetic/developmental causes in young children versus cerebrovascular disease, tumor, metabolic disturbance and degenerative disease in older adults (p.3411-3414).
Operationally, epilepsy is defined as two or more unprovoked seizures, though a single seizure with clinical or EEG features portending high recurrence risk can establish the diagnosis (p.3408-3409).

Seizures are fundamentally classified as focal (network limited to one hemisphere; often structural) versus generalized (rapidly engaging both hemispheres) versus unknown onset; the older terms 'partial', 'simple/complex partial' are no longer used (p.3409).

Focal seizures are subclassified by awareness (intact vs impaired) and onset (motor vs nonmotor); a focal seizure can evolve to a bilateral tonic-clonic seizure (formerly 'secondary generalization') (p.3409).

Distinguishing a focal seizure that evolves to generalized from a primary generalized tonic-clonic seizure is critical but difficult, because bystanders emphasize the dramatic convulsive phase and overlook the subtle focal onset; a careful history for a preceding aura or focal features, and EEG, are needed because evaluation and treatment differ substantially (p.3410).

Status epilepticus is continuous seizures, or repetitive discrete seizures with impaired consciousness between them; for generalized convulsive status epilepticus the practical operational threshold is seizures lasting beyond 5 minutes (older definitions used 15-30 min) (p.3425).

Generalized convulsive status epilepticus (GCSE) is a medical emergency: prolonged seizures cause cardiorespiratory dysfunction, hyperthermia, and metabolic derangements that can produce irreversible CNS injury (p.3425-3426).

Treatment principle for status epilepticus is an escalating sequence beginning with a benzodiazepine, followed by an IV antiseizure drug, with anesthetic agents for refractory cases - alongside attention to airway, oxygenation, glucose, and reversible metabolic causes (no doses given here) (p.3426).

After 30-45 min of uninterrupted GCSE the motor signs can become very subtle (only fine finger twitching or rapid eye movements); if a patient stops overt convulsions yet remains comatose, an EEG is required to exclude ongoing (nonconvulsive) status epilepticus (p.3426).

Failing to exclude a treatable provoking cause (metabolic, toxic, structural, or infective) before labeling a patient as having epilepsy - many such seizures need only correction of the underlying problem, not chronic antiseizure drugs (p.3408, p.3419, p.3416-3417).
Assuming a normal interictal EEG rules out epilepsy - the initial routine EEG is normal in 50-80% of patients with known epilepsy, and EEG has limited sensitivity (p.3417).

Missing nonconvulsive status epilepticus: in altered consciousness or persistent coma without overt convulsions, NCSE can be present and is only revealed by EEG; intermittent seizures with prolonged postictal states are easily overlooked as causes of unexplained encephalopathy (p.3426).
Overlooking a focal onset by focusing on the dramatic generalized convulsive phase, thereby misclassifying the seizure and choosing the wrong evaluation/treatment pathway (p.3410).

Mistaking psychogenic nonepileptic seizures for epilepsy (or vice versa) on clinical grounds alone - even experienced epileptologists err; PNES and epilepsy can coexist, and video-EEG is the arbiter (p.3419).
Misinterpreting convulsive syncope (brief convulsive jerks at the start of a faint) as a primary seizure (p.3419).
Relying on headache or incontinence to distinguish seizure from syncope - these features are unreliable (p.3419).
Forgetting that the postictal Todd's paralysis (focal weakness for minutes to hours after a focal seizure) can mimic an acute structural deficit such as stroke (p.3409).
Misdiagnosing childhood absence epilepsy as attention deficit disorder or simple 'daydreaming' (p.3410).

About half of people respond to the first antiseizure drug; roughly 30% have ongoing seizures despite drug combinations (refractory epilepsy). People with epilepsy have a 2-3 times higher mortality than matched controls, mostly driven by the underlying etiology (e.g., tumor, stroke); excess deaths also arise from accidents, status epilepticus, and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP), which typically affects young patients with convulsive seizures and tends to occur at night, possibly via brainstem-mediated cardiorespiratory/arousal effects. Simple febrile seizures do not raise the risk of later epilepsy, whereas complex febrile seizures carry a 2-5% risk. Severe penetrating head trauma carries up to a ~45% (penetrating/depressed fracture/hemorrhage/prolonged coma: 30-50%) risk of subsequent epilepsy, closed head injury with contusion 5-25%, and mild concussion only slightly increased risk. Favorable factors for staying seizure-free after planned drug withdrawal include 1-5 years of control, a single seizure type, normal exam/intelligence, normal EEG, and no family history (p.3411, p.3414, p.3420, p.3424, p.3426-3427).
Generalized convulsive status epilepticus - immediate emergency due to risk of cardiorespiratory failure, hyperthermia, metabolic derangement, and irreversible CNS injury (p.3425-3426)
Persistent coma after overt convulsions stop - suspect ongoing nonconvulsive status epilepticus and obtain EEG (p.3426)
Focal features, focal neurologic deficit, or abnormal/changing neurologic exam - points to a structural cause (mass, stroke, infection, trauma, degenerative disease) requiring imaging (p.3416)
Fulminant new-onset seizures with psychiatric symptoms and cognitive change - suspect autoimmune/antibody-mediated encephalitis (p.3413-3414, p.3417)
First seizure in a patient with HIV - lumbar puncture is mandatory even without signs of infection (p.3417)
Atonic ('drop attack') seizures - substantial risk of direct head injury from the fall (p.3410)

Seizures are classified (ILAE 2017) by onset: (1) Focal onset (with intact or impaired awareness; motor or nonmotor onset; may evolve to bilateral tonic-clonic); (2) Generalized onset - motor (tonic-clonic, or other such as atonic/myoclonic) or nonmotor (absence); (3) Unknown onset. Status epilepticus is staged by duration/refractoriness in management terms: impending/early (5-30 min), established and early-refractory (30 min to 48 h), and late refractory (>48 h), with subtypes generalized convulsive (GCSE) versus nonconvulsive (NCSE) (p.3409, p.3425-3426).

Seizures arise from a shift in the normal balance between neuronal excitation and inhibition in the CNS. Focal seizure activity begins in a discrete cortical region and can invade surrounding cortex; the hallmark is the electrographic spike produced by near-simultaneous bursting of many excitatory neurons (hypersynchronization). At the cellular level, a prolonged paroxysmal depolarization shift driven by calcium influx opens voltage-dependent sodium channels and generates repetitive action potentials, followed by a GABA- or potassium-channel-mediated hyperpolarizing afterpotential. Spread is normally limited by intact hyperpolarization and feedforward surround inhibition; recruitment of neighboring neurons occurs through rising extracellular potassium, presynaptic calcium accumulation enhancing transmitter release, NMDA-receptor activation, and ephaptic effects, allowing propagation via local and commissural (corpus callosum) pathways. Epilepsy results from a dynamic interplay of endogenous (often genetic, maturational) factors, epileptogenic factors (e.g., severe head trauma, stroke, infection, neurodegeneration, developmental malformations), and precipitating factors (sleep deprivation, stress, hormonal change, toxins, photic stimulation). Many gene mutations affecting ion channels (e.g., SCN1A, KCNQ2), neurotransmitter receptors, and metabolic transporters (e.g., SLC2A1/GLUT-1) underlie specific syndromes.

A seizure is a transient event caused by abnormal excessive or hypersynchronous neuronal activity; epilepsy is the distinct condition of a chronic underlying tendency to recurrent unprovoked seizures, so a single or provoked seizure does not by itself constitute epilepsy (though a single seizure with high-risk clinical/EEG features may suffice).

Distinguishing seizure from syncope: aura, cyanosis, prolonged motor activity (30-60 s), and many minutes to hours of postictal confusion favor seizure, whereas brief loss of consciousness with rapid recovery, pallor, and provocation by pain/standing favor syncope; headache and incontinence are unreliable discriminators.

A transient serum prolactin rise in the first 30 minutes after most generalized and some focal seizures can support a true seizure over a psychogenic event, but is unreliable without a baseline and because some drugs elevate prolactin.
Penetrating head injury carries up to a 45% risk of subsequent epilepsy via epileptogenesis, illustrating how an acquired structural lesion can permanently lower seizure threshold.
Roughly 5-10% of people experience at least one seizure in life, with peaks in early childhood and late adulthood; epilepsy prevalence is approximately 5-30 per 1000.

The 2017 ILAE scheme classifies seizures by onset as focal, generalized, or unknown; focal seizures are described by awareness (intact vs impaired) and motor vs nonmotor onset, replacing the older 'simple/complex partial' and 'secondary generalization' terms.
Focal motor seizures may show a Jacksonian march (spread along the motor strip), and a postictal focal weakness (Todd's paralysis) lasting minutes to hours can mimic a stroke.
Auras are themselves focal seizures with intact awareness; temporal-lobe auras include rising epigastric sensations, foul smells/tastes, fear, deja vu, and micropsia/macropsia.

Typical absence seizures produce brief lapses of consciousness without postural loss or postictal confusion, with a 3-Hz generalized spike-and-wave EEG provoked by hyperventilation; they are frequently misdiagnosed as attention-deficit disorder or daydreaming.

Generalized tonic-clonic seizures begin with a tonic phase (ictal cry, apnea/cyanosis, tongue biting, sympathetic surge) evolving to a clonic phase, followed by postictal flaccidity, confusion, headache, and myalgia.

Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis is the most common cause of focal seizures with impaired awareness and is characteristically medically refractory but responds well to surgery.

Etiology is strongly age-dependent: neonates - perinatal hypoxia-ischemia, infection, and metabolic derangements; young children - febrile seizures; adolescents/young adults - trauma, genetic syndromes, drugs, autoantibodies; older adults - cerebrovascular disease (up to ~50% of new epilepsy over 65), tumor, and degenerative disease.

Failing to distinguish a focal seizure that secondarily generalizes from a primary generalized tonic-clonic seizure because bystanders emphasize the convulsive phase and overlook subtle focal onset/aura - a distinction that materially changes evaluation and treatment.
Misdiagnosing absence epilepsy as attention-deficit disorder or simple daydreaming.
Concluding bizarre paroxysmal stereotyped behavior is non-epileptic; focal (especially frontal-lobe) seizures can produce highly unusual behaviors.
Assuming a normal interictal EEG excludes epilepsy, or that epileptiform discharges by themselves prove epilepsy.
Over-relying on incontinence or headache to separate seizure from syncope, as these are unreliable.
Assuming psychogenic nonepileptic seizures exclude true epilepsy - the two frequently coexist.
Misreading subtle late-stage status epilepticus as resolution when damaging electrographic seizures persist.

Outcome varies widely by syndrome and etiology. Typical absence epilepsy and juvenile myoclonic epilepsy generally respond well to medication (though JME remission is uncommon), whereas mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, and epilepsies tied to structural lesions or developmental delay are often refractory. About half of patients do not respond to the first medication, and roughly 30% have ongoing seizures despite optimal drug therapy. Favorable predictors for successfully discontinuing therapy include 1-5 years of complete control, a single seizure type (generalized carrying a better prognosis than focal), normal neurologic examination and intelligence, no family history of epilepsy, and a normal EEG; a normal EEG generally implies a better prognosis. People with epilepsy have a death rate roughly 2-3 times that of matched controls, mostly attributable to the underlying cause but also to accidents, status epilepticus, and SUDEP.

Generalized convulsive status epilepticus - continuous or repetitive seizures (practically, GCSE lasting beyond ~5 min); a medical emergency that can cause cardiorespiratory failure, hyperthermia, metabolic derangement, and irreversible CNS injury
After 30-45 minutes of uninterrupted seizures the clinical signs may become subtle while damaging electrographic seizures continue, including in patients paralyzed by neuromuscular blockade
Fulminant new-onset seizures with psychiatric symptoms and cognitive change suggesting autoimmune (e.g., anti-potassium-channel or anti-glutamate-receptor) epilepsy
New seizure in an older adult suggesting cerebrovascular disease, tumor, or degenerative disease

Atonic 'drop attacks' with high risk of head injury

Seizures are classified by ILAE 2017 onset: focal (with intact or impaired awareness, motor or nonmotor), generalized (motor such as tonic-clonic, atonic, myoclonic; or nonmotor/absence), or unknown onset. Severity at the syndromic extreme is status epilepticus: continuous or repetitive seizures with impaired interictal consciousness, subdivided into generalized convulsive status epilepticus (GCSE) and nonconvulsive status epilepticus (NCSE). Although traditionally defined as 15-30 minutes of activity, GCSE is practically treated as an emergency when convulsions last beyond about 5 minutes. Febrile seizures are graded as simple (single, brief, symmetric) versus complex (repeated, lasting over 15 minutes, or with focal features).

chunks.text: Serotonin syndrome results from excess CNS and peripheral serotonergic activity — promotion of serotonin release, inhibition of its reuptake, or direct stimulation of serotonin receptors (chiefly 5-HT1A and 5-HT2), occurring alone or when serotonergic drugs are combined. NMS, in contrast, is linked to dopamine-antagonist (neuroleptic) exposure or abrupt loss of dopaminergic tone, producing central hyperthermia, rigidity and autonomic dysfunction; central dopamine depletion impairs hypothalamic (preoptic/anterior) thermoregulation. Both are classified among the hypothalamic disorders of autonomic/temperature regulation (Harrison 22e p.3541, p.3517, p.3715).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.3517 (Ch.446/447, drug-induced movement disorders), p.3667 (Ch.463, SSRIs), p.3715 (Ch.470, toxidromes), p.3541 (Ch.451, hypothalamic autonomic disorders), p.3773 (Ch.478, heat illness differential), p.1172 (Ch.149, antibacterial drug interactions)

chunks.text: Serotonin syndrome and NMS overlap closely (both cause fever, altered mental status, rigidity and autonomic instability), but prominent myoclonus is characteristically a feature of serotonin syndrome and helps separate it from NMS (p.3517).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.3517 (Ch.446/447, drug-induced movement disorders), p.3667 (Ch.463, SSRIs), p.3715 (Ch.470, toxidromes), p.3541 (Ch.451, hypothalamic autonomic disorders), p.3773 (Ch.478, heat illness differential), p.1172 (Ch.149, antibacterial drug interactions)

chunks.text: NMS typically evolves over days to weeks after a neuroleptic/dopamine-antagonist is started or up-titrated, i.e. a comparatively slow, subacute onset (p.3517).

chunks.text: NMS is not only triggered by antipsychotics: it can also be precipitated by abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic medication in Parkinson's disease patients (p.3517).

chunks.text: Serotonin syndrome arises from agents with serotonin-like activity or that block serotonin reuptake (e.g. tryptophan, MDMA/'ecstasy', meperidine, SSRIs), and is rare but potentially fatal (p.3517).

chunks.text: The serotonin-syndrome picture is attributed to hyperstimulation of brainstem 5-HT1A (and 5-HT2) receptors (p.3667).

chunks.text: The antibiotic linezolid (and to a lesser degree tedizolid) is a monoamine-oxidase inhibitor: combined with serotonergic agents such as SSRIs it can precipitate serotonin syndrome (p.1172).

chunks.text: Combining an MAOI with an SSRI is an absolute contraindication because of serotonin-syndrome risk; serotonergic agonists (tryptophan, fenfluramine, triptans) carry a similar hazard (p.3667).

chunks.text: Both syndromes are toxidromes in the CNS-syndrome / 'stimulated' physiologic category, alongside lithium toxicity, extrapyramidal reactions and strychnine (p.3715).

chunks.text: Mistaking one syndrome for the other: rapid-onset hyperreflexia/myoclonus/clonus after a serotonergic drug points to serotonin syndrome, whereas slow (days-to-weeks) lead-pipe rigidity with bradyreflexia after a dopamine-antagonist points to NMS — the offending drug class and onset tempo are the key discriminators (p.3517).

chunks.text: Overlooking non-psychiatric culprits: the antibiotic linezolid is an MAOI and can trigger serotonin syndrome with concurrent SSRIs (p.1172).

chunks.text: Some atypical antipsychotics (e.g. chlorpromazine used for agitation) can themselves cause or worsen NMS — adding a neuroleptic to an undifferentiated hyperthermic patient can be harmful (p.3776).

chunks.text: Both syndromes are potentially fatal; serotonin syndrome is described as rare but able to progress to death, and NMS can be lethal (e.g. typical neuroleptics in Lewy body disease can cause NMS and death). The duration of hyperthermia drives morbidity and mortality, and progression to rhabdomyolysis, renal failure, DIC and multisystem organ failure marks severe disease (Harrison 22e p.3517, p.3715, p.3773).

chunks.text: Harrison frames severity by the physiologic toxidrome state (stimulated vs depressed vs discordant) and by the degree of physiologic derangement on serial vital signs; escalating findings — hyperthermia, lactic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis and multisystem organ failure — mark severe serotonin syndrome, while marked CK elevation with renal failure and labile autonomic signs marks severe NMS. No formal numeric grading scale is given in the source (Harrison 22e p.3715, p.3517).

chunks.text: Medication review (serotonergics/antipsychotics)
CK, renal function
Temperature
Serotonin syndrome / NMS (non-infective) — Toxicology / Neuro
Fever with rigidity/clonus and altered mental state after serotonergic or antipsychotic drugs suggests a toxidrome, not infection.
Red flags: Hyperthermia + rigidity — stop agent, cooling, supportive ICU care

[guideline] management → Benzodiazepine (agitation/rigidity) / IV crystalloid First-line supportive measure for agitation, rigidity and autonomic instability in both serotonin syndrome and NMS; helps lower temperature.

[guideline] adjunct → Serotonin antagonist (serotonin syndrome) / Muscle relaxant (severe NMS/hyperthermia) / Dopamine agonist (NMS) 5-HT2A antagonist considered in moderate–severe serotonin syndrome not settling with supportive care.
Oedema from nephrotic syndrome or cardiac/hepatic failure
Chronic infection (including tuberculosis and HIV)
Malabsorption syndromes (e.g. coeliac disease, cystic fibrosis)
Chronic diarrhoeal disease
Underlying malignancy or chronic illness causing wasting
Weight, height/length, and mid-upper arm circumference with oedema assessment
Blood glucose (to detect hypoglycaemia)
Electrolytes including potassium, magnesium, and phosphate
Haemoglobin and assessment for anaemia
Screening for infection (including tuberculosis, HIV where relevant) and malaria in endemic areas
Assessment of hydration status, which is difficult to judge clinically in SAM

Prolonged inadequate intake of energy, protein, and micronutrients forces the body into a state of reductive adaptation: metabolic rate falls, organ function is downregulated, and body composition shifts with loss of fat and muscle. Sodium-potassium pump activity is impaired, causing intracellular sodium retention and total-body potassium and magnesium depletion despite oedema. Hepatic and cardiac function, immune competence, and thermoregulation are all compromised. In kwashiorkor, hypoalbuminaemia and increased capillary permeability contribute to oedema. These adaptations make the child dangerously intolerant of the metabolic demands of aggressive feeding and fluid loads.
Defined in young children by severe wasting (weight-for-height well below the reference median, or a very low mid-upper arm circumference) and/or bilateral pitting oedema of nutritional origin.
Marasmus is severe wasting from overall energy deficit; kwashiorkor is characterised by oedema, and mixed pictures occur.
Kwashiorkor features include oedema, sparse depigmented hair, skin changes (flaky-paint dermatosis), an enlarged fatty liver, and apathy.
Children with SAM are highly vulnerable to hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, and overwhelming infection, which is often present without classic signs.
Refeeding must be cautious and staged to avoid refeeding syndrome; overly rapid feeding and excess fluid or sodium can precipitate cardiac failure and death.
Initial stabilisation prioritises treating and preventing hypoglycaemia and hypothermia, correcting dehydration carefully, and giving broad micronutrient support.
Rehydration is preferably oral or nasogastric with a low-sodium, higher-potassium solution, because intravenous fluids readily cause fluid overload.
Management follows a stabilisation phase with cautious feeding, followed by a rehabilitation phase with catch-up growth once appetite and stability return.
Feeding too much too quickly and precipitating refeeding syndrome and heart failure
Using standard intravenous rehydration and causing fluid overload
Relying on usual signs of infection, which are often absent
Missing hypoglycaemia and hypothermia because signs are subtle
Treating oedema as fluid overload rather than recognising nutritional kwashiorkor

With careful phased management and treatment of complications, most children recover, but case fatality is high when complications such as hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, sepsis, or refeeding syndrome are missed or when rehydration is too aggressive.
Hypoglycaemia and hypothermia
Signs of shock or severe dehydration (difficult to assess and easy to overtreat)
Developing signs of heart failure during rehydration or refeeding (refeeding syndrome)
Severe anaemia requiring careful transfusion
Lethargy, hypothermia, or hypoglycaemia as subtle markers of serious infection

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Acute epididymitis must be distinguished from testicular torsion (a surgical emergency with sudden pain, testicular elevation, and absent Doppler flow), testicular tumor, and trauma (Harrison 22e p.1101)

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Dysuric women: STI-associated urethral syndrome (sterile pyuria, <10^2 conventional uropathogens/mL) versus bacterial cystitis (single uropathogen >=10^2/mL) versus acute pyelonephritis (costovertebral tenderness/fever) (Harrison 22e p.1100-1101)

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Persistent genital ulcer not resolving with syndrome-based therapy: consider donovanosis, carcinoma, and other nonvenereal dermatoses on biopsy (Harrison 22e p.1108)

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Pelvic inflammatory disease that is not due to specific STIs (secondary to appendicitis, regional ileitis, diverticulitis, hematogenous tuberculosis or staphylococcal bacteremia, or tropical disease such as schistosomiasis) (Harrison 22e p.1104)

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Chronic granulomatous epididymal disease such as tuberculosis mimicking sexually acquired epididymitis when symptoms persist after therapy (Harrison 22e p.1101)

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Risk assessment using a structured sexual-history questionnaire (e.g., the eleven-question STD/HIV risk assessment) to guide screening and presumptive treatment decisions (Harrison 22e p.1098)

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Urethral Gram's stain to confirm urethritis and detect gram-negative diplococci, recognizing that up to ~30% of gonococcal urethral infections can yield a negative Gram's stain (Harrison 22e p.1099)

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) for N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, M. genitalium, and T. vaginalis on appropriate genital/urine specimens (Harrison 22e p.1099-1100)

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Genital ulcer workup: dark-field examination, direct fluorescent antibody, or PCR for T. pallidum; RPR/VDRL/EIA serology for syphilis; culture, FA, ELISA, or PCR for HSV; HSV-2 type-specific serology; PCR or culture for H. ducreyi in chancroid-endemic settings (Harrison 22e p.1108-1109)

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Biopsy of a genital ulcer persisting beyond the expected natural history (herpes 2-3 weeks; chancroid or syphilis up to 6 weeks) to exclude donovanosis and malignancy (Harrison 22e p.1108)

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Aspiration of fluctuant inguinal nodes for culture/PCR (H. ducreyi) plus Gram's stain to exclude other pyogenic bacteria (Harrison 22e p.1108)

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Cervical ectopy (columnar epithelium on the ectocervix), often mislabeled 'cervical erosion,' confused with infectious endocervicitis but showing clear/cloudy mucus and intact epithelium on colposcopy (Harrison 22e p.1104)

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Testicular tumor or trauma presenting as scrotal pain/swelling mimicking epididymitis (Harrison 22e p.1101)

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Genital carcinoma or nonvenereal dermatoses presenting as a persistent genital ulcer (Harrison 22e p.1108)

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: STIs are acquired through sexual exposure to a susceptible person from an infectious one, with spread amplified within highly interconnected sexual networks marked by high partner-change rates or concurrent partners (e.g., transactional sex, some MSM, drug-using populations), while infections such as chlamydia, genital HPV, and genital herpes propagate efficiently even in relatively low-risk populations. Many of these organisms colonize or invade genital, anal, oral, or systemic epithelium; ascending spread from cervix or vagina to endometrium and fallopian tubes underlies PID, with potential extension to pelvic peritonitis, perihepatitis, perisplenitis, or abscess. Immunopathology contributes to tissue damage in chlamydial salpingitis, where repeated exposure produces the greatest inflammation. Hormonal and anatomic factors modulate susceptibility (e.g., cervical ectopy may increase susceptibility to gonococcus, chlamydia, and HIV; oral contraceptives favor ectopy persistence; menstruation appears to facilitate ascending gonococcal/chlamydial infection).

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: STIs are syndrome-driven in practice: most patients are managed initially by presenting symptoms, signs, and risk factors rather than by a confirmed microbial diagnosis, with common syndromes including male urethritis, epididymitis, mucopurulent cervicitis, vulvovaginitis, genital/perianal ulcers, PID, and proctitis (Harrison 22e p.1100).

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: STI control combines reducing exposure (education, behavior change, post-exposure prophylaxis), shortening infectivity (early diagnosis and curative or suppressive treatment), and reducing per-exposure transmission (condoms, vaccines, male medical circumcision) (Harrison 22e p.1096).

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Despite the strong epidemiologic HSV-HIV link, randomized trials of antiviral HSV suppression showed no protective effect against HIV acquisition or transmission (Harrison 22e p.1097).

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: More than 40 microorganisms are now recognized as predominantly sexually transmitted or frequently sexually transmissible, spanning bacteria, viruses, protozoa, fungi, and ectoparasites (Harrison 22e p.1096).

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: The initial rate of spread of any STI in a population is the product of three factors: the rate of sexual exposure of susceptible to infectious persons, the per-exposure transmission efficiency, and the duration of infectivity (Harrison 22e p.1096).

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Genital HPV is described as the most common sexually transmitted pathogen in the United States, and HPV and hepatitis B virus remain major causes of cervical and hepatocellular carcinoma respectively in the developing world (Harrison 22e p.1096-1097).

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Reported syphilis in the United States in 2022 (207,255 cases, all stages and congenital) was the highest since 1950, with congenital syphilis rate of 102.5 per 100,000 live births and 282 congenital syphilis-related stillbirths/infant deaths (Harrison 22e p.1097).

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: All four major curable STIs (gonorrhea, chlamydial infection, syphilis, trichomoniasis) plus bacterial vaginosis have been associated with increased risk of HIV transmission or acquisition (Harrison 22e p.1097).

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Acute epididymitis in sexually active men under 35 is most often due to C. trachomatis (less often N. gonorrhoeae) and usually accompanies overt or subclinical urethritis, whereas in older men or after urinary instrumentation it is usually caused by urinary pathogens (Harrison 22e p.1101).

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Unsolicited reporting of abnormal vaginal discharge (increased amount or abnormal odor) most often denotes bacterial vaginosis or trichomoniasis, not cervical gonorrhea or chlamydia, which usually do not increase discharge volume or odor (Harrison 22e p.1101).

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Sexually transmitted HSV causes most genital ulcer disease worldwide; HSV-2 produces more frequent genital recurrences and is more infectious to partners than HSV-1, so typing has prognostic value (Harrison 22e p.1097, 1108).

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Treating genital symptoms without performing the microbiologic tests needed to establish a cause; self-diagnosis of vulvovaginal candidiasis is often incorrect (Harrison 22e p.1101)

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Relying on urethral Gram's stain alone to exclude gonorrhea, since up to ~30% of gonococcal urethral infections are smear-negative (Harrison 22e p.1099)

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Misreading cervical ectopy as infectious endocervicitis and unnecessarily cauterizing it (Harrison 22e p.1104)

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Assuming a positive HSV-2 serology proves current lesions are herpetic, when nearly one-fifth of the U.S. population becomes HSV-2 seropositive in early adulthood and type-specific assays are not 100% specific (Harrison 22e p.1108)

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Failing to evaluate and treat sexual partners with contact in the relevant window (e.g., within the prior 60 days for urethritis), allowing reinfection (Harrison 22e p.1099)

chunks.diseaseName: Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach
chunks.text: Withholding presumptive syphilis treatment in a high-risk patient with a genital ulcer while awaiting seroconversion (Harrison 22e p.1108)

chunks.text: Attributing male urethritis recurrence to treatment failure without considering reexposure to an untreated partner or M. genitalium (often resistant to doxycycline and azithromycin) (Harrison 22e p.1100, 1099)

chunks.text: Many STIs are curable when diagnosed and treated early, and prompt treatment shortens infectivity and reduces onward transmission. Outcomes worsen with delayed care: untreated chlamydial and gonococcal infection can ascend to cause PID with risk of tubal damage and infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain, and immunopathology contributes to chlamydial tubal injury. HPV and HBV carry long-term oncogenic risk (cervical and other anogenital cancers; hepatocellular carcinoma). HSV-2 causes lifelong recurrent infection with asymptomatic shedding and ongoing transmission risk. In men, urethritis with neither chlamydiae nor gonococci detected carries a higher risk of recurrent nongonococcal urethritis, and most persistent urethritis is attributable to M. genitalium. Congenital syphilis can result in stillbirth or infant death.

chunks.text: No single staging system applies to STIs as a group; severity is assessed by syndrome and complications. Localized lower-tract syndromes (uncomplicated urethritis, cervicitis, vulvovaginitis, genital ulcer) are distinguished from complicated or upper-tract/disseminated disease (PID with peritonitis, perihepatitis, perisplenitis, or pelvic abscess; disseminated gonococcal infection; epididymo-orchitis), and from long-term oncologic or reproductive sequelae (cervical/anogenital neoplasia, infertility). Genital ulcer evaluation also uses lesion natural-history timelines (herpes 2-3 weeks; chancroid and syphilis up to ~6 weeks) to flag atypical persistence (Harrison 22e p.1104, 1108).

Stool culture is the gold standard; sample the bloody/mucopurulent portion directly, or use rectal swabs (highest yield in the acute phase).
Because Shigella is fragile and dies during transport, use a holding medium (buffered glycerol saline or Cary-Blair) with prompt inoculation onto isolation media.

Use multiple media to raise yield: nonselective (bromocresol-purple lactose), low-selectivity (MacConkey, eosin-methylene blue), and high-selectivity (Hektoen, Salmonella-Shigella, or xylose-lysine-deoxycholate agar).
Microscopy of stool smears: bacterial enteroinvasive infection (including shigellosis) shows high PMN counts per field, whereas E. histolytica shows erythrophagocytic trophozoites with very few PMNs.
Identify shigellae as non-lactose-fermenting colonies that are glucose-positive (usually no gas), lactose-negative, H2S-negative, and nonmotile; confirm serogroup by slide agglutination.
Blood cultures are positive in fewer than 5% of cases but should be obtained when there is a clinical picture of severe sepsis.
Abdominal x-ray when toxic megacolon is suspected (transverse colon dilation, thumbprinting, loss of haustra, pseudopolyps; pneumoperitoneum if perforated).
In HUS: full blood count and smear (schizocytes), platelets, LDH, free hemoglobin, reticulocytes, creatinine; Coombs test (HUS is Coombs-negative).
PCR for Shigella virulence genes or mass spectrometry are available but not yet standardized for global use.
Inflammatory bowel disease - Crohn's disease
Inflammatory bowel disease - ulcerative colitis

Pathogenicity is governed by a ~214-kb virulence plasmid encoding a type III secretion system that injects effectors into host cells. After acid-resistant passage through the stomach, bacteria invade colonic epithelium either directly at crypt openings or after crossing M cells over mucosal lymphoid follicles; they induce apoptosis of resident macrophages, drive cytoskeletal uptake, lyse the containing vacuole to reach the cytosol, then spread cell-to-cell using actin-based motility. A massive cytokine-driven influx of polymorphonuclear leukocytes destabilizes the epithelial barrier and produces the acute colitis of shigellosis. Early watery diarrhea is attributed to combined enterotoxin (ShET-1) action and mucosal inflammation. In S. dysenteriae type 1, Shiga toxin (an A1-B5 toxin binding globotriaosylceramide and inhibiting protein synthesis via 28S rRNA N-glycosidase activity) is translocated into the circulation and, by acting on renal target cells, can cause hemolytic-uremic syndrome (p.1322-1323).
Classic dysentery is a syndrome of fever, intestinal cramps, and frequent passage of small, bloody, mucopurulent stools; tenesmus is characteristic (p.1322).

Shigella has a very low infectious dose; experimental infection of volunteers occurs with as few as ~100 CFU, accounting for high attack rates in day-care centers (33-73%) and high secondary attack rates among family members (26-33%) (p.1322).
Spread is primarily fecal-oral via hand carriage; the organism survives gastric passage owing to acid resistance, and can also be transmitted sexually (p.1322-1323).
Shigellosis typically evolves through four phases: incubation (usually 1-4 days, up to 8), watery diarrhea, dysentery, and a postinfectious phase (p.1323).

Dysentery reflects invasion of the colonic mucosa, producing acute colitis mainly involving the distal colon and rectum, with uninterrupted small-volume bloody mucopurulent stools, tenesmus, and cramps (p.1323).

Of the four species, S. flexneri predominates in least-developed areas while S. sonnei is more common in industrialized/emerging economies; S. dysenteriae type 1 (Shiga-toxin producer) drives the most severe epidemic disease (p.1322).

With effective antibiotics, clinical improvement occurs within ~48 h, with fewer complications, shorter symptoms, and clearance of Shigella from stool; in the US every culture-confirmed case is recommended for treatment because of transmissibility (p.1324).

Reactive arthritis (arthritis, ocular inflammation, urethritis) can develop weeks to months after infection, almost exclusively after S. flexneri and in HLA-B27-positive patients (about 3% of S. flexneri infections) (p.1323-1324).

Avoid antimotility agents in bloody diarrhea: they have been implicated in prolonged fever in shigellosis, are suspected of increasing the risk of toxic megacolon, and were implicated in HUS in children with EHEC infection.
Because shigellosis often manifests only as watery diarrhea, systematic attempts to isolate Shigella are necessary - a watery presentation does not exclude the diagnosis.
Shigella is fragile and commonly disappears during transport with changes in temperature and pH; failure to use a holding medium and prompt inoculation leads to false-negative cultures.
Negative initial blood cultures do not exclude shigellosis (positive in fewer than 5% of cases).
Predisposing factors for toxic megacolon - hypokalemia and use of opioids, anticholinergics, loperamide, psyllium seeds, and antidepressants - should be sought and addressed.
In HUS, oral rehydration solutions and potassium-rich nutrition must be discontinued (water restriction is required), in contrast to routine rehydration management.
Bacteriologic proof in mild adult cases often arrives only after symptoms have resolved, so empiric decisions cannot await culture in fragile patients.

Most episodes are self-limited and resolve without treatment within about 1 week; with appropriate therapy recovery occurs within a few days to a week, usually without sequelae. Acute life-threatening complications occur most often in children under 5 (especially the malnourished) and the elderly. In HUS, acute renal failure occurs in 55-70% of cases but renal function recovers in most (up to ~70%). S. dysenteriae type 1 epidemics historically caused high mortality. Shigellosis is a major contributor to stunted growth among children in endemic regions because of the exudative enteropathy and anorexia it causes.
Nonbloody diarrhea, moderate-to-severe dehydration, bacteremia, absence of fever, abdominal tenderness, and rectal prolapse are risk factors for death in clinically severe cases.
Altered consciousness (seizures, delirium, coma), especially in children under 5, carries a poor prognosis.
Abdominal distention and tenderness suggesting toxic megacolon, with or without peritonitis.
Pallor, asthenia, irritability, oliguria, increasing edema, or mucosal bleeding heralding hemolytic-uremic syndrome (most often after several days of diarrhea).
Fever persisting beyond 48-72 h in toxic megacolon raises the possibility of local perforation or abscess.
Severe, unusual manifestations such as meningitis in the absence of serious malnutrition may indicate an inborn innate-immune defect (e.g., IRAK-4 deficiency) and warrant genetic investigation.

Harrison does not provide a formal grading scale. Severity is described as depending on infecting serotype and, more importantly, on host age, immunologic and nutritional status. The clinical course is staged in four phases (incubation, watery diarrhea, dysentery, postinfectious). Severe/complicated disease is recognized by markers of poor outcome (nonbloody diarrhea, moderate-to-severe dehydration, bacteremia, absence of fever, abdominal tenderness, rectal prolapse, altered consciousness) and by major complications: intestinal (toxic megacolon, perforation, rectal prolapse), metabolic (hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, dehydration), and HUS (in S. dysenteriae type 1).

Linear growth depends on an intact growth plate responding to growth hormone, insulin-like growth factor 1, thyroid hormone, and sex steroids, supported by adequate nutrition and freedom from chronic illness. Short stature arises when any of these are disturbed: genetic determination of a lower height potential, temporary delay in the tempo of maturation, endocrine deficiency, chronic systemic disease, undernutrition, or intrinsic bone/cartilage disorders. The pattern of growth velocity, body proportions, and bone age reflects which mechanism predominates.
Short stature is generally defined as height more than about 2 standard deviations below the mean for age and sex, but the growth velocity and trajectory matter more than a single measurement.
The two most common causes are normal variants: familial (genetic) short stature and constitutional delay of growth and puberty.
Serial, accurately measured heights plotted on a growth chart are the single most valuable assessment, since a falling growth velocity is a key warning sign.
Bone age radiography helps distinguish constitutional delay (delayed bone age, preserved height potential) from familial short stature (bone age near chronological age).
A low or crossing-down growth velocity with poor weight gain suggests systemic disease or malnutrition, whereas short but proportionate growth with normal velocity favours a normal variant.
Endocrine causes such as growth hormone deficiency and hypothyroidism typically produce a child who is relatively overweight for height, in contrast to malnutrition or chronic illness.
Disproportionate short stature points towards a skeletal dysplasia and warrants assessment of body segment ratios.
Estimating mid-parental target height helps interpret whether a child's growth is appropriate for their genetic background.
Relying on a single height measurement rather than growth velocity over time
Labelling a child as a normal variant without excluding treatable disease when velocity is poor
Missing an intracranial cause of growth hormone deficiency

Normal variants such as familial short stature and constitutional delay have an excellent prognosis with normal health, and constitutional delay usually reaches a normal adult height; outcomes for pathological causes depend on early identification and treatment of the underlying condition.

chunks.text: Salivary glands are normally protected from ascending infection by continuous salivary flow, which flushes the ducts, and by antibacterial constituents of saliva. When flow is reduced, by dehydration, poor oral intake, debility, medications that dry the mouth, or mechanical obstruction from a duct stone or stricture, oral bacteria ascend the duct and infect the gland, producing acute suppurative sialadenitis with parenchymal inflammation and pus. Stasis of saliva also predisposes to stone formation, and calculi in turn obstruct outflow, causing painful mealtime swelling and recurrent infection. Repeated episodes lead to chronic inflammation, ductal changes and glandular fibrosis. Viral sialadenitis such as mumps causes a non-suppurative inflammatory swelling.
