chunks.text: Acute chest syndrome (pneumonia-like illness with chest pain, cough, fever, hypoxia and a pulmonary infiltrate) closely resembles and may coexist with bacterial pneumonia; antibiotics are almost always used even though a causative bacterium is often not cultured (p.775).
Multiorgan failure accompanying severe acute chest syndrome is often confused with, and can coexist with, sepsis (p.774, Table 103-3).

High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) and hemoglobin electrophoresis to quantify hemoglobin fractions (HbS, HbF, HbA, HbA2, HbC) and distinguish trait, sickle cell anaemia and HbSC disease (Table 103-2, Fig. 103-4, p.772).

Peripheral blood film: irreversibly sickled cells, target cells and nucleated red cells in HbSS/HbS-beta0 thalassaemia; HbC crystals, taco-folded cells and contracted microspherocytes in HbSC disease (Fig. 103-4, p.772-774).
DNA-based diagnosis for genetic counselling and family planning; antenatal diagnosis by chorionic villus sampling or cell-free DNA (p.772, 776).
Transcranial Doppler screening in children (ages 2-16) to identify stroke risk (Table 103-3, p.776).
Echocardiographic measurement of tricuspid regurgitant jet velocity (TRV) annually to screen for pulmonary hypertension.
Screening for microalbuminuria from age 10 for nephropathy, and annual fluorescein angiography from age 10 for retinopathy.

HbS behaves like HbA except that it polymerises when deoxygenated: contacts between beta6 valine residues of deoxy-HbS and beta/alpha-globin residues form hemoglobin fascicles that injure the sickle erythrocyte, after a delay between initiation of polymerisation and accumulation of damaging polymer. Polymerisation depends on roughly the 30th power of hemoglobin concentration, so small changes in concentration or cell dehydration have large effects. Membrane vesiculation/microparticle release, activation of dehydrating channels (Gardos, K/Cl cotransport, Psickle) which raise mean corpuscular HbS concentration and reduce deformability, translocation of phosphatidylserine to the outer membrane leaflet, and oxidation produce irreversibly sickled cells (ISCs) that remain deformed regardless of oxygenation. Sickle erythrocytes adhere to endothelium and other blood cells, occluding small and large vessels (vaso-occlusion), and survive <20 days (normal ~120), haemolysing intra- and extravascularly. Intravascular haemolysis depletes haptoglobin and hemopexin and liberates heme, arginase and other DAMPs which scavenge nitric oxide, activate platelets and endothelium, reduce antioxidant activity, cause vasoconstriction and drive inflammation (p.772-774).

Sickle cell disease is a clinical/haematologic phenotype caused by an assortment of genotypes; sickle cell anaemia (HbSS, homozygosity for the HbS Glu6Val mutation) is the most common, followed by HbSC disease (compound heterozygosity for HbS and HbC) and the HbS-beta thalassaemias (p.772).
The chief presenting symptom is pain: a hand-foot syndrome (dactylitis) in young children, and typical acute painful episodes in older children and adults (p.772).

Acute painful episodes are the most common acute events; pain is typically unprovoked, severe, in extremities or torso, often symmetrical and stereotypical for each patient, and lasts days to weeks (p.773).

In HbSC disease and HbS-beta+ thalassaemia, acute vaso-occlusive episodes occur at about half the rate of sickle cell anaemia and complications develop later; rarely such patients are asymptomatic (p.772).

Complications fall into two related groups: those driven by sickle vaso-occlusion (pain, acute chest syndrome, osteonecrosis, splenic infarction) and those driven by intravascular haemolysis (stroke, pulmonary/systemic vasculopathy, nephropathy, leg ulcers, gallstones, priapism); vaso-occlusive complications respond best to HbF induction (p.772-773).

Carriers of sickle cell trait (HbAS) outnumber patients with disease ~25 to 1; trait is usually benign with normal life expectancy, but carries a small risk of sudden death from heat-related exertional rhabdomyolysis and complications such as haematuria, papillary necrosis, hyposthenuria, splenic infarction at altitude and increased VTE risk (p.772, 775).

Autosplenectomy from repeated childhood splenic infarction is usual in sickle cell anaemia; a palpable spleen after age 5 suggests a coexisting genotype (e.g. thalassaemia or HbC) (p.769-770 reference and Table 103-2).

Hydroxyurea (acting mainly by inducing HbF) is standard of care for all patients with sickle cell anaemia and HbS-beta0 thalassaemia regardless of symptoms; in adults it roughly halves pain and acute chest syndrome and reduced mortality by 49% over 17.5 years (p.775).

Cure is possible with HLA-identical related-donor allogeneic stem cell transplant (event-free survival >95%, though only ~15% of patients have a fully matched donor) and with two approved ex vivo autologous gene therapies (lentiviral betaT87Q HbA gene; CRISPR/Cas9 disruption of the BCL11A enhancer) (p.775-776).
No diagnostic test can confirm or refute an acute pain episode; physical examination is often unhelpful and the presence of ISCs and the reticulocyte count are of no diagnostic value (p.773).

Supplemental oxygen is unnecessary unless hypoxia is present, and NSAIDs add little once intravenous opioids are given; overhydration and excessive opioids can compound dyspnoea and hypoxia in acute chest syndrome (p.773, 775).

Opioids should not be dosed on an 'as-needed' schedule - patient-controlled or fixed scheduled dosing with rescue doses is preferred, with monitoring to avoid excessive sedation; many patients are opioid-tolerant and need higher doses (p.773).
Transfusions are both overutilised and underutilised; they should usually be avoided in acute pain episodes and for stable chronic anaemia (p.776).
A palpable spleen after age 5 in sickle cell disease suggests a coexisting genotype rather than simple HbSS (p.769-770).

In the United States childhood death is now rare and the median age of death in sickle cell anaemia is in the fifth or sixth decade; by contrast in high-burden regions such as Nigeria most affected newborns die before age 5. Hydroxyurea reduced mortality by 49% over 17.5 years of follow-up. Genotype modifies severity: HbSC disease and HbS-beta+ thalassaemia have about half the complication rate of HbSS, and coexistent alpha thalassaemia (present in ~30% of HbSS) is associated with fewer strokes and leg ulcers and less pulmonary vascular and renal disease. Allogeneic transplantation and gene therapy offer potential cure (p.772, 775-776).

Acute chest syndrome - chest pain, cough, fever, hypoxia and a pulmonary infiltrate; can be devastating with multilobar involvement, severe hypoxia, ARDS, multiorgan failure and rapid death (often from embolised necrotic marrow) (p.775).
Splenic sequestration (acute anemic episode) - rapid drop in hemoglobin; recurrent episodes are an indication for splenectomy (Table 103-3, p.774).
Aplastic crisis from parvovirus B19 infection causing acute worsening of anaemia with reticulocytopenia (Table 103-3, p.774; reticulocytopenia in acute worsening noted elsewhere).

Stroke and silent infarction - occur in 10-15% of cases, from early childhood into adulthood, with neurocognitive abnormalities even without apparent stroke; haemorrhagic stroke in adults (Table 103-3, p.773).

Functional/anatomic asplenia (autosplenectomy) places patients at high risk of overwhelming infection with encapsulated organisms, notably overwhelming pneumococcal disease (p.776, 769/Table; pneumococcal chapter p.999).

Sudden unexpected death shortly after admission for acute pain (possible arrhythmia or pulmonary embolism); thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis >20,000 and rapidly developing acute anaemia portend severe acute chest syndrome and multiorgan failure (p.773, 775).
Multiorgan failure - can accompany severe acute chest syndrome, affecting CNS, liver, muscle, lung and kidney (Table 103-3, p.774).

Severity is largely defined by genotype: sickle cell trait (HbAS, usually benign); sickle cell anaemia (HbSS, vaso-occlusion- and haemolysis-related complications, Hb ~7-10 g/dL); HbS-beta0 thalassaemia (complication rate similar to HbSS); HbS-beta+ thalassaemia (~half the rate of HbSS depending on percent HbA); HbSC disease (near-asymptomatic to as severe as HbSS, ~half the complication rate, increased retinopathy risk); HbSE (resembles HbS-beta+ thalassaemia, often Asian/Indian ancestry); and HbSS-alpha thalassaemia (phenocopies HbS-beta0 thalassaemia with fewer strokes/leg ulcers and less pulmonary/renal disease). HbF level (influenced by HbS haplotype) modifies severity (p.772).

chunks.text: Sigmoid volvulus occurs when a redundant, elongated sigmoid loop twists around its narrow mesenteric pedicle, producing a closed-loop large bowel obstruction. Chronic constipation and a lengthy, mobile sigmoid on a narrow mesenteric base predispose to torsion. The twist obstructs the lumen at both ends, and progressive distension raises intraluminal and intramural pressure. If the mesenteric vessels are compromised by the torsion, the loop becomes ischaemic, progressing to gangrene and perforation with faeculent peritonitis and sepsis. Massive gaseous distension of the closed loop is characteristic.

Activated T lymphocytes are the major infiltrating cells in affected exocrine (chiefly salivary and lacrimal) glands, with B-cell populations prevailing in heavily infiltrated labial minor salivary gland tissue; follicular, myeloid, and plasmacytoid dendritic cells and macrophages are also present, the latter (with inflammasome activation) being linked to lymphoma risk. Ductal and acinar epithelial cells play an active pathogenic role: they aberrantly express costimulatory molecules and surface Ro/La autoantigens, secrete proinflammatory cytokines and lymphocyte-attracting chemokines that support ectopic germinal center formation, express innate-immunity Toll-like receptors (TLR3, 7, 9), and display immunoregulatory molecules (ICAM, CD40). Epithelial cells produce B cell–activating factor (BAFF), induced by type I and II interferons, and circulating BAFF is elevated (especially with hypergammaglobulinemia and autoantibodies), exerting an antiapoptotic effect on B lymphocytes; epithelial cells themselves show increased apoptosis. Disease initiation and perpetuation reflect interplay of endogenous triggers (intracellular stress, inappropriate expression of endogenous nucleic acids) and exogenous triggers (viruses, hormonal factors, stressful life events) on a genetically hyperactive immune background. Established genetic loci include HLA-DQA1*0501, interferon/BAFF axis variants (IRF5, STAT4, BAFF), B-cell function genes (EBF1, BLK), and combined deficiencies of the classical complement pathway.
Prototype autoimmune disease defined by lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands causing xerostomia and dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca), together with marked B-cell hyperactivity.
Most patients (about two-thirds) have an elevated ESR, hypergammaglobulinemia, antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, and anti-Ro52/Ro60 and anti-La autoantibodies.
The disease course is usually slow and benign in the majority of patients; antecedent major stressful life events have been reported prior to onset.
Recently described as triggerable by PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitor therapy.
Strongly female-predominant (female-to-male ratio roughly 10–20:1) and chiefly affects middle-aged women, but can present at any age including childhood; prevalence is approximately 0.5–1%.
Earlier age at onset tends to mark a more aggressive phenotype with more systemic manifestations and more serum autoantibodies.

Can occur alone or in association with other systemic rheumatic diseases, most commonly rheumatoid arthritis, limited scleroderma, and systemic lupus erythematosus; 5–20% of patients with other autoimmune diseases can have sicca features.

Principal oral symptom is dryness (xerostomia) with difficulty swallowing dry food, burning mouth, increased dental caries; examination may show dry erythematous sticky mucosa, atrophic tongue papillae, and a deeply fissured tongue.
Intermittent or persistent enlargement of the parotid or other major salivary glands occurs in about two-thirds of patients.

Ocular involvement classically produces a sandy or gritty sensation under the lids, with burning, stranded secretions at the inner canthi, reduced tearing, redness, and photosensitivity from corneal and conjunctival epithelial destruction (keratoconjunctivitis sicca).
Extraglandular (systemic) manifestations occur in about one-third of patients and are categorized as nonspecific, periepithelial, immune complex–mediated, and lymphoma.

Carries the highest risk of lymphoma among all autoimmune diseases; most are extranodal, low-grade, marginal zone (MALT) B-cell lymphomas, often found incidentally on labial minor salivary gland biopsy.
Failing to take a careful medication history — diuretics, antihypertensives, anticholinergics, and antidepressants can themselves cause dryness and mimic or worsen sicca.
Overlooking HIV- or HCV-associated sicca syndrome, which can closely resemble Sjögren’s but lacks anti-Ro/La and has distinct demographics and glandular infiltrate phenotype.
Missing renal tubular dysfunction: interstitial nephritis may be asymptomatic, presenting only as hyposthenuria or renal tubular acidosis, and untreated acidosis can progress to nephrocalcinosis.
Attributing all salivary gland enlargement to benign disease and missing an incidental MALT lymphoma on labial biopsy.
Not excluding sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, IgG4-related disease, graft-versus-host disease, and prior head/neck radiation before diagnosing Sjögren’s disease.
Assuming arthritis is erosive — arthritis in primary Sjögren’s disease is characteristically nonerosive (may lead to Jaccoud’s arthropathy).

The disease usually evolves slowly and follows a benign course in most patients. The dominant adverse outcome is malignant transformation: Sjögren’s disease carries the highest lymphoma risk of any autoimmune disease, with clinical (parotid enlargement, severe tongue atrophy, palpable purpura), hematologic/serologic (leukopenia, autoantibodies, low C4, monoclonal gammopathy, cryoglobulins), and histopathologic (germinal center formation, heavy focal lymphocytic infiltrates) risk factors. Survival is reduced in patients with B symptoms, lymph node mass >7 cm, and high or intermediate histologic grade. Patients also have an increased risk of cardiovascular disease, paralleling rheumatoid arthritis and SLE.
Parotid or major salivary gland enlargement, especially persistent or with a lymph node mass >7 cm — concern for lymphoma
Palpable purpura, urticarial lesions, skin ulcerations, or mononeuritis multiplex (immune complex–mediated vasculitis)

Diagnosis/classification per the 2016 ACR-EULAR criteria: suspect in patients with dry eyes and/or dry mouth (or systemic features such as major salivary gland enlargement, fatigue, Raynaud’s, small-joint arthralgia/arthritis, palpable purpura/urticaria, renal tubular acidosis/membranoproliferative GN, ILD/small airway disease, autoimmune cholangitis, peripheral neuropathy, or MS-like lesions), supported by objective findings: unstimulated whole saliva flow ≤0.1 mL/min, Schirmer’s test ≤5 mm/5 min, ocular staining score ≥5 (or van Bijsterveld ≥4), serum anti-Ro antibodies, and minor salivary gland biopsy focus score ≥1. Exclusions include prior head/neck radiation, active HCV, AIDS, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, graft-versus-host disease, and IgG4-related disease. Extraglandular disease severity is gauged by the categories of involvement (nonspecific, periepithelial, immune complex–mediated, and lymphoma).

chunks.text: A delayed, T-cell-mediated (type IVa, cytotoxic) severe cutaneous adverse reaction. A drug or metabolite-altered antigen is presented in association with a risk HLA class I allele by keratinocytes or other antigen-presenting cells; a restricted T-cell receptor on skin-enriched CD8+ T cells recognizes this drug-HLA complex, triggering activation and release of cytolytic mediators (notably granulysin) that cause full-thickness epidermal keratinocyte death and detachment. Proposed antigen-presentation models include hapten/prohapten covalent binding, the pharmacologic-interaction (p-i) noncovalent model, and the altered-peptide-repertoire model (as proven for abacavir-HLA-B*57:01). Carbamazepine SJS/TEN shows a highly restricted V-alpha/V-beta TCR repertoire shared among HLA-B*15:02 patients. A risk HLA allele alone is insufficient; non-MHC factors such as drug metabolism (e.g., CYP2C9*3 slow metabolism with phenytoin) contribute. (Harrison 22e p.417-420)

Melanoma is a malignancy of melanocytes, neural-crest-derived pigment-producing cells; most melanomas arise in skin but can occur in mucosa, eye, meninges, and upper esophagus. UV radiation is the dominant environmental driver, and cutaneous melanomas carry one of the highest somatic mutation rates of any cancer (>10 mutations/Mb), the majority bearing a UV signature. Key driver mutations affect the MAP-kinase and PI3K/AKT proliferative pathways: BRAF (commonly V600E) in 40-50% of cutaneous melanomas, NRAS in ~20%, and loss-of-function NF1 in 10-15%; germline CDKN2A (p16/ARF, RB and p53 pathways), CDK4, MITF, BAP1, POT1, TERT, and moderate-risk MC1R variants underlie inherited susceptibility. Nonmelanoma skin cancers are also UV-driven: SCC is associated with p53 and N-RAS damage, whereas BCC is driven by hedgehog (Hh) pathway activation, usually loss of function of the tumor-suppressor PTCH1 (which normally inhibits SMO). Merkel cell carcinoma is linked to the oncogenic Merkel cell polyomavirus, present in ~80% of tumors (p.598-607).

Apply the ABCDE rule to pigmented lesions to detect melanoma early: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variegation, Diameter >6 mm (pencil-eraser size), and Evolving (any change in size, shape, color, elevation, or new symptoms such as bleeding, itching, or crusting) (p.601).
The 'ugly duckling' sign: any nevus that looks atypical and different from the rest of an individual's nevi should be considered suspicious (p.601).
Melanoma is an aggressive malignancy of melanocytes and accounts for over half of all deaths from skin cancer, even though it is far less common than nonmelanoma skin cancer (p.598).

Basal cell carcinoma is among the most common cancers; its natural history is a slowly enlarging, locally invasive neoplasm with low metastatic potential (~0.1% in immunocompetent patients), though the risk of recurrence or a new primary NMSC is about 40% over 5 years (p.607).

Nodular BCC classically presents as a pearly nodule with tortuous telangiectatic vessels, rolled borders, and a central crust; pigmented BCC may contain melanin and be confused with melanoma (p.606-607).

Squamous cell carcinoma arises from keratinizing epidermal cells on sun-exposed skin and can metastasize (0.3-5.2%), most often to regional lymph nodes; lower-lip and ear tumors metastasize in 13% and 11% respectively (p.606-607).

Actinic keratoses and actinic cheilitis are premalignant forms of SCC; SCC in situ (Bowen's disease) presents as a scaling erythematous plaque, and treating premalignant/in-situ lesions reduces subsequent invasive disease (p.607).
NMSCs (SCC ~80%, BCC ~18% of cases) are the most common cancers in the US, with an estimated >5.3 million cases annually (p.606).

Breslow thickness (greatest tumor thickness measured from the top of the granular layer or ulcer base to the bottom of the tumor) is the best predictor of melanoma recurrence and, with ulceration, defines the T stage (p.601-602).
Morpheaform, infiltrative, and micronodular BCCs have indistinct borders and subtle presentation, so treatment is often delayed and tumors are more extensive than they appear clinically
SCC can be mistaken for a benign wart or callus when the inflammatory response is minimal

Melanoma frequently develops on non-sun-exposed skin (acral, mucosal); in dark-skinned, Hispanic, and East Asian populations melanoma is often non-UV-related, diagnosed at higher stage, and has worse outcomes
The 31-gene GEP can estimate distant-relapse probability but has not supplanted prognostic estimates from surgical staging, and genomic pathway data are not yet incorporated into AJCC staging
Standard labs and imaging rarely detect occult metastatic disease in early melanoma and should be directed by symptoms/exam findings

Melanoma prognosis is dominated by Breslow thickness and ulceration (T stage); favorable primary sites are the forearm and leg, unfavorable sites the scalp, hands, feet, and mucous membranes. 10-year melanoma-specific survival ranges from >99% for stage 0 (in situ) and ~98% for stage IA down to ~24-30% for stage IIID. Women with stage I/II disease and younger patients do better; older men have worse outcomes (delayed diagnosis, thicker tumors, more head/neck, acral and BRAF wild-type tumors). High mitotic rate and lymphatic/vascular invasion are additional adverse factors. Overall melanoma mortality has been falling, attributed to immunotherapy and targeted therapy. BCC rarely metastasizes (~0.1% in immunocompetent patients) but recurs frequently. Cutaneous SCC metastasizes in 0.3-5.2% of cases overall, higher for lip/ear/recurrent/immunosuppressed disease. Merkel cell carcinoma is aggressive: ~90% cure with local disease but ~52% survival with nodal and ~10% with distant disease (p.602-609).

Merkel cell carcinoma has its own TNM staging incorporating tumor size (<2 cm vs >2 cm), nodal status, and distant metastases (p.602-609).

SLE arises from overactive innate and adaptive immunity with autoantibodies directed at nuclear components (nucleic acids, nucleosomes, RNA-binding proteins). Impaired clearance of cellular debris — driven by high neutrophil turnover/NETosis and defective complement-mediated phagocytosis — overwhelms macrophages and dendritic cells. Accumulated nucleic acids engage toll-like receptors and nucleic-acid sensors in plasmacytoid dendritic cells, driving type 1 interferon production that primes the immune response. Autoreactive B cells (including expanded age-associated B cells) lose tolerance and, with help from T follicular/T peripheral helper cells, mature into autoantibody-secreting plasma cells, while regulatory T-cell function is defective. Resulting immune complexes deposit in tissues and cause inflammation, repair, and eventual fibrosis after recurrent flares. Strong genetic component (monozygotic twin concordance 24% vs 2% dizygotic; >150 GWAS loci, with the MHC the strongest and nearly half of loci linked to type 1 interferon; monogenic complement-pathway deficiencies — C1q, C1r/s, C2, C4 — cause severe SLE). Environmental triggers include UV light, smoking, crystalline silica, mercury/toxins, sex hormones, EBV, and gut microbiome/permeability changes (p.2827-2829).

Roughly 90% of SLE patients are women, most of childbearing age; prevalence is highest among Black women, then Hispanic, White, and Asian/Pacific Islander women; disease tends to be more severe in non-White patients (p.2827).

Antiphospholipid antibodies/APS coexist in about a third of SLE patients and markedly raise risk of arterial/venous thrombosis, stroke (reported in up to 19%), Libman-Sacks endocarditis, and pregnancy loss (p.2829, 2830, 2831).
Autoantibodies can be detectable years before clinical diagnosis, so a positive serology in a symptomatic patient supports attributing nonspecific complaints to SLE (p.2827, 2829).
Most patients have active disease despite therapy or recurrent flares; treatment goals are low disease activity (SLEDAI 0-4) or remission on ≤5 mg/day prednisone equivalent (p.2829, 2832).

A proposed clinical split distinguishes type 1 lupus (classic inflammatory/organ manifestations such as nephritis, arthritis, vasculitis that respond to immunosuppression) from type 2 lupus (fatigue, diffuse pain, brain fog, depression, sleep disturbance that respond poorly to immunosuppression) (p.2827).

Anti-dsDNA titers and C3/C4 levels track disease activity: anti-dsDNA is produced by short-lived plasmablasts that turn over quickly, and complement falls during high activity as it is consumed by immune complexes (p.2832).
Rising anti-dsDNA and falling C3/C4 can serve as warning signs of impending active nephritis even in an asymptomatic patient (p.2830).
Lupus arthritis is typically non-erosive (Jaccoud-like reversible deformity from ligamentous laxity); overlap with rheumatoid arthritis is termed 'rhupus' (p.2829).
Pain out of proportion in a single hip, shoulder, or knee — especially with prior corticosteroid use — should raise concern for avascular necrosis of bone (p.2829).

Accelerated atherosclerosis is a major cause of premature death, notably myocardial infarction and stroke in young patients without traditional risk factors, and is the leading cause of death after ~5 years of disease (p.2829, 2836).

Distinguishing flare from infection is a central challenge: cytopenias and constitutional symptoms can stem from disease activity, medication, OR infection, and acute lupus pneumonitis can look identical to pneumonia on imaging — infection must be excluded before escalating immunosuppression (p.2829-2830).

Classification criteria (2019 EULAR/ACR; 2012 SLICC) were built for trial enrollment, not diagnosis — diagnosis remains an individualized clinical judgment; relying on criteria alone can mislead, and ANA-negative or incomplete-lupus patients are excluded by EULAR/ACR (p.2827).

A positive ANA or even antihistone antibody alone does not confirm SLE — many drugs induce a positive ANA in patients who never develop symptoms, and antihistone antibodies occur in most SLE cases too (p.2835).

Drug-induced lupus can be hard to separate from SLE because skin biopsy and many labs overlap; presence of additional SLE-specific autoantibodies (rarely seen in DIL) and symptom resolution after stopping the drug help distinguish (p.2835).
Acute psychosis/confusion may be glucocorticoid-induced rather than neuropsychiatric lupus — and infectious encephalitis must also be ruled out (p.2829).
Single-joint pain out of proportion may be avascular necrosis (steroid-related), not arthritis flare (p.2829).
Estrogen-containing contraceptives/HRT should be avoided in patients with antiphospholipid antibodies or moderate-severe/active lupus due to thromboembolism risk (p.2836).

Prognosis and survival vary widely by geography, race/ethnicity, and access to care/medications. Renal disease, especially class IV nephritis, carries substantial risk of ESRD and death (~20% within 10 years), and is more severe in non-White patients. Accelerated atherosclerosis is a major cause of premature death and the leading cause after ~5 years of disease, driven by both traditional risk factors and lupus-specific factors (antiphospholipid antibodies, high disease activity, low C3, high glucocorticoid dose, high homocysteine/leptin). Glucocorticoid exposure independently accrues irreversible organ damage (cataracts, osteoporotic fractures, avascular necrosis, diabetes) even at doses as low as 5 mg prednisone equivalent. Class V (membranous) nephritis has a better prognosis than class III/IV. Sustained low disease activity (LLDAS) for 2+ years is associated with significantly less damage. Recent meta-analyses suggest an increased overall cancer risk and cancer-related mortality (p.2830, 2835-2836).
Rapidly declining eGFR, rising proteinuria, or active urinary sediment — class III/IV proliferative lupus nephritis; ~20% of class IV patients die or reach ESRD within 10 years (p.2830)

Disease activity is graded for treatment using SLEDAI/SLEDAI-2K (low disease activity = SLEDAI 0-4; remission/DORIS = SLEDAI 0). EULAR severity tiers: mild (constitutional symptoms, mild arthritis, rash <=9% BSA, platelets 50-100, SLEDAI <=6); moderate (RA-like arthritis, rash 9-18% BSA, platelets 20-50, serositis, SLEDAI 7-12); severe (major organ-threatening disease e.g. cerebritis, myelitis, pneumonitis, mesenteric vasculitis; platelets <20; TTP-like or acute hemophagocytic syndrome; rash >18% BSA; SLEDAI >12). Lupus nephritis is graded by ISN/RPS renal biopsy classes I-V (class I mesangial deposits; II mesangial proliferative; III focal proliferative; IV diffuse proliferative; V membranous; III/IV +/- V combinations), with class III/IV (and III/IV+V) being proliferative forms warranting aggressive therapy (p.2827, 2830-2831, 2833-2834).

In OSA the pharyngeal airway lacks fixed bony/cartilaginous support, so patency depends on pharyngeal dilator muscles. Inspiration generates increasingly negative intraluminal pressure (a suctioning force); at sleep onset neuromuscular output to these muscles declines, and in a collapsible airway this causes transient pharyngeal collapse (apnoea) or near-collapse (hypopnoea), typically terminated by an arousal that restores muscle activity. Collapse sites include the soft palate (most common), tongue base, lateral pharyngeal walls, and epiglottis. OSA is often worst in REM sleep (lowest skeletal-muscle output) and supine (gravity). A small pharyngeal lumen (soft-tissue enlargement from fat, lymphoid tissue, or genetic variation; craniofacial factors such as mandibular retroposition/micrognathia), low lung volume (reduced caudal pharyngeal traction, pronounced in obesity), and high nasal resistance all predispose to collapse. Pharyngeal muscle activation is linked to ventilatory drive: an over-sensitive ventilatory control system, a low arousal threshold (preempting CO2-mediated muscle compensation), or a high arousal threshold (prolonging apnoeas) all contribute. In OSA-related disease, sleep fragmentation, cortical arousals, and intermittent hypoxaemia/hypercapnia drive sympathetic overactivity, blood-pressure surges, a prothrombotic/proinflammatory state, insulin resistance, and large negative intrathoracic pressure swings that alter cardiac preload/afterload and promote cardiac/electrical remodelling. CSA is usually caused by increased PCO2 sensitivity producing hyperventilation alternating with apnoea, plus prolonged circulatory delay (heart failure) giving Cheyne-Stokes breathing.

OSA diagnosis requires either symptoms of nocturnal breathing disturbance (snoring, snorting, gasping, breathing pauses) impairing quality of life or unexplained daytime sleepiness/fatigue, PLUS at least 5 obstructive apnoeas/hypopnoeas per hour of sleep (apnoea-hypopnoea index, AHI) on a sleep study; OSA may also be diagnosed without symptoms if AHI is at least 15 episodes/h (p.2277-2278).

Large randomized trials have FAILED to show that CPAP reduces cardiovascular/stroke events or prolongs survival, possibly because sleepy patients (who may have the greatest risk) were excluded and because of limited treatment adherence (p.2281).

Central sleep apnoea (CSA) is less common than OSA and may occur alone or, more often, combined with obstructive events as mixed apnoeas; it is often driven by increased sensitivity to PCO2 causing unstable breathing, and a prolonged circulation delay (as in congestive heart failure) produces the crescendo-decrescendo Cheyne-Stokes pattern (p.2282).

Treatment of CSA has NOT been shown to improve long-term health outcomes, so specific treatment is generally indicated only for symptomatic CSA; unlike OSA, treatment is difficult and depends on the underlying cause (p.2282).
Each apnoea/hypopnoea is a reduction in breathing for at least 10 s, commonly causing a fall in oxygen saturation of at least 3% or a cortical arousal (p.2278).
The major risk factors for OSA are obesity, male sex, and older age; roughly 40-60% of cases are attributable to excess weight, but the absence of obesity does NOT exclude the diagnosis (p.2278).

Snoring is the most common symptom, but its absence does NOT exclude OSA because pharyngeal collapse can occur without tissue vibration; the most common daytime symptom is excessive sleepiness, though women preferentially report fatigue rather than sleepiness (p.2279).
Dyspnoea is unusual in OSA, and its absence generally distinguishes OSA from paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, nocturnal asthma, and acid reflux with laryngospasm (p.2279).

Overnight in-laboratory polysomnography (PSG) is the gold standard for diagnosis; a negative in-lab PSG usually rules out OSA, but false-negatives can occur with night-to-night variation, insufficient REM sleep, or less supine sleep than typical (p.2279).
Home sleep tests recording only respiratory and cardiac channels are a cost-effective option; when prior probability of OSA is high, a negative home study should be followed by PSG (p.2279).

CPAP is the standard medical therapy with the highest level of evidence; it acts as a mechanical splint to hold the airway open during sleep, and auto-titrating (APAP) home devices have eliminated the need for titration studies in many patients (p.2281).

Although CPAP reduces 24-h ambulatory blood pressure, the overall effect is modest (averaging 2-4 mmHg), with larger improvements in patients with high AHI, daytime sleepiness, or resistant hypertension (p.2280-2281).
Assuming absence of snoring excludes OSA - pharyngeal collapse can occur without tissue vibration.
Assuming a normal weight excludes OSA - absence of obesity does NOT exclude the diagnosis.
Underrecognising OSA in women, who have a lower arousal threshold, shorter and more REM-predominant apnoeas, and tend to report fatigue/insomnia rather than classic sleepiness.
Relying on symptoms/signs to gauge severity - they do not accurately predict the severity of sleep-related breathing disturbance; objective measurement is required.
Treating a single negative home sleep study as definitive when prior probability is high - follow with PSG.
Attributing right-heart failure/cor pulmonale to OSA alone, which is not thought to cause it - look for a comorbid cardiopulmonary condition.
Using adaptive servoventilation in patients with CSA and LVEF below 45% (FDA warning following increased mortality).
Sedative-hypnotics have inconsistent effects and should be avoided in most patients with moderate-to-severe OSA; opioids worsen CSA in a dose-dependent way.

OSA is the most common medical cause of daytime sleepiness and reduces quality of life. It is strongly associated with cardiac, cerebrovascular and metabolic disease (coronary artery disease, heart failure with and without reduced EF, atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, atherosclerosis, stroke, diabetes), premature death, and increased risk of certain cancers. Untreated OSA carries a roughly twofold risk of occupational accidents and a two- to threefold increase in motor-vehicle crashes. CPAP improves alertness, mood, quality of life, blood pressure and insulin sensitivity, but randomized trials have NOT shown that CPAP reduces cardiovascular/stroke events or prolongs survival. CSA carries increased risk for heart failure and atrial fibrillation, and its treatment has not been shown to improve long-term outcomes; adaptive servoventilation showed no cardiovascular or mortality benefit and increased mortality in patients with LVEF below 45%.

Evidence of cor pulmonale, suggesting a comorbid cardiopulmonary condition (OSA alone is NOT thought to cause right-heart failure)
Resistant or uncontrolled hypertension
Excessive daytime sleepiness with occupational accident or motor-vehicle-crash risk (drowsy driving)

OSA severity by apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI = apnoeas plus hypopnoeas per hour of sleep): mild OSAHS = AHI 5-14 events/h; moderate OSAHS = AHI 15-29 events/h; severe OSAHS = AHI at least 30 events/h. The respiratory disturbance index (RDI) additionally counts respiratory effort-related arousals (RERAs). Each AHI level can be further qualified by the degree of sleepiness and associated hypoxaemia (Table 308-2, p.2280).

chunks.text: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis occurs when shear forces exceed the strength of the proximal femoral physis, allowing the epiphysis to displace, typically posteriorly and inferiorly, relative to the femoral neck (so the neck effectively rotates anteriorly and externally on the head). The physis is mechanically weakest during the adolescent growth spurt, and obesity increases the mechanical load, while hormonal factors influence physeal strength, explaining associations with endocrine disorders. In unstable slips the epiphyseal blood supply, which runs along the femoral neck, is at high risk of disruption, predisposing to avascular necrosis. Residual deformity from a healed slip alters femoral head-neck morphology and can cause femoroacetabular impingement and early osteoarthritis.

chunks.text: Social anxiety disorder reflects an interaction between heritable temperamental traits, notably behavioural inhibition in early childhood, and altered function of fear and threat-appraisal circuits involving the amygdala and prefrontal cortex. Dysregulation of serotonergic and dopaminergic systems, heightened sensitivity to social evaluation, and learned avoidance that prevents disconfirmation of feared outcomes together maintain the condition.

chunks.text: Benign soft tissue tumor / well-differentiated liposarcoma (atypical lipomatous tumor) - lacks metastatic potential
Benign bone lesions with malignant potential: enchondroma and osteochondroma (to chondrosarcoma); fibrous dysplasia, bone infarcts, Paget's disease (to UPS or osteosarcoma)
Lymphoma, embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, and small-cell carcinoma (can be confused with the small round blue cells of Ewing's sarcoma)
Osteoporosis vs metastatic spine disease in older patients (cortical bone preserved in osteoporosis; cortical destruction with metastases)
Plasma cell tumors (the most common malignant tumor of bone)
Core-needle (cutting needle) or small-incision biopsy of all new, persistent, or growing masses, placed so it can be encompassed in the definitive resection
Plain radiographs and MRI for primary tumors of extremities or head/neck (MRI best for intramedullary and soft-tissue extension)
CT for tumors of the chest, abdomen, or retroperitoneum (CT best for bone destruction and calcification pattern in osteosarcoma)
Chest radiograph and chest CT to detect lung metastases
Bone scan or FDG-PET to detect skeletal metastases (almost all osteosarcomas are hypervascular and PET-avid)
Radionuclide bone scanning (sensitive to new bone formation) for osteoblastic lesions; plain radiography for osteolytic lesions (may not be apparent until >1 cm)
Serum alkaline phosphatase (elevated with prominent osteoblastic activity) and monitoring for hypercalcemia (osteolytic) or hypocalcemia (extensive osteoblastic)
Osteoporotic vertebral disease mimicking spinal bone metastasis in older patients
Benign enchondroma / osteochondroma mimicking low-grade chondrosarcoma (difficult to distinguish by x-ray or histology; new pain, inflammation, or progressive size increase suggests malignancy)
Well-encapsulated benign-appearing lesion produced by the compressed pseudocapsule of a soft tissue sarcoma

Sarcomas are mesenchymal neoplasms (mostly mesodermal, occasionally neuroectodermal) classified into ~20 groups by their pattern of differentiation toward normal tissue (e.g., rhabdomyosarcoma shows skeletal-muscle cross-striations, leiomyosarcoma shows smooth-muscle spindle fascicles, liposarcoma contains adipocytes). Malignant transformation of benign soft tissue tumors is extremely rare, except that malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (neurofibrosarcoma, malignant schwannoma) can arise from neurofibromas in neurofibromatosis. Etiologic contributors include radiation (tumor arises in the irradiated field, risk rising with time), scar tissue (prior surgery, burn, fracture, foreign body), chemical carcinogens (polycyclic hydrocarbons, asbestos, dioxin), HHV-8 (Kaposi's sarcoma - the only sarcoma virus-associated), and immunodeficiency/immunosuppression. Genetic syndromes include Li-Fraumeni (germline p53), neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1 on chr 17, encoding neurofibromin which inhibits ras), and germline RB1 mutation (chr 13q14, predisposing to osteosarcoma and radiation-unrelated soft tissue sarcomas). About one-third of soft tissue sarcomas carry characteristic translocations; most malignant GISTs have activating c-kit (KIT receptor tyrosine kinase) mutations, fewer have PDGFRA mutations. Bone metastases occur via hematogenous spread (or local invasion); tumors produce osteolytic lesions (via PTH-related peptide, vitamin D-like steroids, prostaglandins, IL-1, TNF inducing osteoclasts) and/or osteoblastic lesions (cytokines activating osteoblasts), with most lesions showing a mix.

Sarcomas are rare (<1% of all malignancies) mesenchymal neoplasms arising in bone and soft tissues, usually of mesodermal origin and biologically distinct from the more common epithelial cancers (p.727).
The most important predictive factor for long-term survival in osteosarcoma is response to chemotherapy; long-term survival in extremity osteosarcoma ranges from 60-80% (p.730).

Ewing's sarcoma (~10-15% of bone sarcomas) peaks in the second decade, shows an 'onion peel' periosteal reaction with a soft-tissue mass, expresses p30/32 (MIC-2 product), and carries the t(11;22) translocation fusing fli-1 (chr 11) and ews (chr 22) (p.730).

Chondrosarcoma (~20-25% of bone sarcomas) is a tumor of adulthood/old age (peak 4th-6th decades) with predilection for flat bones (shoulder, pelvic girdles); it has an indolent natural history and is mostly chemoresistant, with surgical resection the mainstay (p.730).
Prostate, breast, and lung primaries account for 80% of all bone metastases; metastatic bone tumors are more common than primary bone tumors (p.730).

Bone is a common metastatic site for prostate, breast, lung, kidney, bladder, and thyroid carcinomas and for lymphomas and sarcomas; in descending frequency the sites are vertebrae, proximal femur, pelvis, ribs, sternum, proximal humerus, and skull (p.730).
When a patient with back pain develops neurologic signs or symptoms, emergency evaluation for spinal cord compression is indicated (p.730).
The most common presentation of a soft tissue sarcoma is an asymptomatic mass; mechanical symptoms from pressure, traction, or entrapment of nerves or muscles may also occur (p.728).

Approximately 60% of soft tissue sarcomas arise in the extremities (lower limbs involved three times as often as upper), 30% in the trunk (retroperitoneum = 40% of trunk lesions), and 10% in the head and neck (p.727).
The pulmonary parenchyma is the most common site of metastasis for soft tissue sarcomas; lung radiograph plus chest CT is important for detecting lung metastases (p.728).
Histologic grade and primary tumor size are the most important prognostic factors; prognosis is related to AJCC stage and cure is common in the absence of metastatic disease (p.728).
About one-third of soft tissue sarcomas carry a characteristic translocation with diagnostic/prognostic relevance (e.g., t(X;18)(p11;q11) involving SYT in ~90% of synovial sarcomas) (p.728).

Most malignant GISTs carry activating c-kit mutations causing ligand-independent KIT receptor tyrosine kinase activation; ~5-10% have PDGFRA mutations, and KIT/PDGFRA wild-type GISTs may show SDH B/C/D mutations (p.728).

Osteosarcoma accounts for almost 45% of bone sarcomas, is a spindle-cell neoplasm producing osteoid/bone, with predilection for metaphyses of long bones (distal femur, proximal tibia, proximal humerus); ~60% occur in the second decade (p.729-730).

Classic osteosarcoma radiographic findings: a destructive moth-eaten lesion, spiculated periosteal reaction (sunburst appearance), and a cuff of periosteal new bone at the soft-tissue mass margin (Codman's triangle) (p.730).

Soft tissue sarcomas grow along fascial planes and compress surrounding tissue into a pseudocapsule, giving a deceptive well-encapsulated appearance; 'shelling out' (marginal excision / enucleation) results in a 50-90% probability of local recurrence - wide excision with a negative margin incorporating the biopsy site is standard.

A biopsy of an enlarging/deep/large mass must be planned so the tract can be encompassed in the definitive resection and does not compromise a limb-sparing operation; an inappropriately placed incision compromises future limb salvage.
Low-grade chondrosarcoma is difficult to distinguish from benign lesions on x-ray or histology, so diagnosis is influenced by clinical history and examination.
Osteosarcoma is radioresistant - radiation therapy has no role in routine management.

Forgetting non-pulmonary metastatic patterns: GISTs metastasize to liver, myxoid liposarcomas seek fatty tissue (retroperitoneum, mediastinum, subcutaneous), clear cell sarcomas may go to bone, and alveolar soft part sarcoma to CNS.
In older patients (especially women), metastatic spine disease must be distinguished from osteoporosis - cortical bone is preserved in osteoporosis but destroyed by metastatic cancer.

For soft tissue sarcoma, histologic grade and size are the most important prognostic factors and prognosis tracks AJCC stage; cure is common without metastatic disease, and a small number with metastases can still be cured. Metastatic soft tissue sarcomas are largely incurable, but up to 20% achieving complete response become long-term survivors. Historically most stage IV patients died within 12 months, but with multiple treatment lines, median survival in second-line and beyond is now 13-18 months and some live with stable/slowly progressive disease for years. Extremity osteosarcoma long-term survival is 60-80%, with response to chemotherapy the key predictor. Ewing's sarcoma overall cure rates approach 60-70% for localized tumors. For bone metastases, overall survival is related to the prognosis of the underlying tumor; some (lymphoma, Hodgkin's lymphoma) are curable while most are treated palliatively.
An enlarging, deep, or large soft tissue mass requires biopsy - all new, persistent, or growing masses should be biopsied rather than ignored
Back pain with new neurologic signs or symptoms mandates emergency evaluation for spinal cord compression
New onset of pain, signs of inflammation, and progressive size increase in a cartilaginous lesion suggest malignant (chondrosarcoma) transformation
Bone pain that develops gradually over weeks, is localized, and is more severe at night suggests bone metastasis
Pathologic fracture, nerve root or cord compression, or myelophthisis from a destructive bony lesion
Hypercalcemia symptoms in the setting of bony destruction

Soft tissue sarcomas use the AJCC (8th edition) TNM/grade system: T1 (<=5 cm), T2 (>5-10 cm), T3 (>10-15 cm), T4 (>15 cm); N0/N1; M0/M1; with grade G1-G3 driving stage grouping (e.g., Stage IA = T1 N0 M0 G1; Stage IV = any T N1 M0, or any T any N M1). Bone sarcomas use the Musculoskeletal Tumor Society system (stage I low grade, II high grade, III nodal/distant metastases; A = intracompartmental, B = extracompartmental) and a TNM system: T1 (<=8 cm), T2 (>8 cm), T3 (discontinuous tumors in the primary bone); M1a (lung) vs M1b (other sites); grade G1-G4 (Ewing's always G4).

Loss of functional SMN protein, resulting from homozygous deletion or mutation of SMN1, leads to degeneration and loss of the motor neurons of the anterior horn of the spinal cord and brainstem motor nuclei. The nearly identical SMN2 gene produces only a small amount of full-length functional protein, so a higher SMN2 copy number partially compensates and mitigates severity. Denervation of skeletal muscle causes progressive weakness and atrophy, with the respiratory and bulbar musculature critically affected in severe forms, resulting in hypoventilation, impaired airway clearance, aspiration, and respiratory failure.
An autosomal recessive disorder of anterior horn (lower motor neuron) degeneration, most commonly caused by homozygous loss of function of the SMN1 gene.
It produces progressive, symmetrical muscle weakness and wasting that is typically more marked proximally and in the legs more than the arms.
Disease severity is graded into types (from severe infantile-onset to milder later-onset forms) and correlates broadly with the number of copies of the modifying SMN2 gene.
Severe infantile SMA (type 1) presents with profound hypotonia, poor head control, a weak cry, feeding and swallowing difficulty, and paradoxical (belly) breathing with a bell-shaped chest.
Tongue fasciculations and absent deep tendon reflexes are characteristic, while cognition and sensation are preserved.
Respiratory muscle and bulbar weakness drive the major morbidity and mortality, particularly recurrent aspiration and respiratory failure in the most severe forms.
Diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing showing biallelic SMN1 loss, with SMN2 copy number providing prognostic information.
Disease-modifying therapies that increase SMN protein have substantially changed the outlook, and newborn screening enables early, presymptomatic treatment.
Multidisciplinary supportive care addresses respiratory support, nutrition, orthopaedic complications such as scoliosis and contractures, and physiotherapy.
Attributing infantile hypotonia to a central cause and missing the lower motor neuron pattern
Overlooking tongue fasciculations and preserved cognition as clues to anterior horn disease
Underestimating respiratory and bulbar risk, especially during intercurrent illness
Delaying genetic confirmation and thereby missing the window for early therapy
Failing to organise multidisciplinary respiratory, nutritional, and orthopaedic support

Historically severe infantile-onset disease carried a very poor prognosis with early respiratory failure, while later-onset forms had longer survival with variable disability. Early diagnosis through newborn screening and initiation of SMN-directed disease-modifying therapy have markedly improved motor outcomes and survival, especially when started presymptomatically.

Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD) and gout (may coexist with/mimic PsA) (Harrison 22e p.2889)
SAPHO and hidradenitis suppurativa (may mimic palmoplantar psoriasis/PsA) (Harrison 22e p.2889)

SpA is a prototypic chronic immune-mediated inflammatory disease that couples inflammation to structural damage, with the unique feature that inflammation-induced bone loss coexists with pathologic new bone formation at specific skeletal sites (sacroiliac joints, anterior spinal ligaments, peripheral entheses). HLA-B27, an MHC class I allele, is the strongest genetic risk factor; proposed mechanisms include the arthritogenic peptide theory (HLA-B27 presenting microbial peptides to CD8+ T cells with molecular mimicry), HLA-B27 homodimerization engaging innate receptors (KIR3DL2) to drive IL-17, and unfolded protein response/autophagy promoting IL-23-driven type 17 immunity. Disease requires additional factors beyond HLA-B27 (only ~5% of HLA-B27-positive people, and 20% of HLA-B27-positive first-degree relatives, develop axSpA); key instigators are loss of intestinal barrier integrity with microbial dysbiosis (germ-free HLA-B27 transgenic rats fail to develop disease) and aberrant response to mechanical stress. The IL-23/IL-17 axis and TNF-alpha are central, with overlapping yet domain-distinct cytokine signatures across gut, joint, entheses, and skin (Harrison 22e p.2880-2882).

Spondyloarthritis (SpA) is a family of immune-mediated inflammatory arthritides sharing clinical, genetic, and pathologic features; classified by ASAS (2009) into axial (axSpA) and peripheral (pSpA). Axial skeletal involvement is hinted at in the name but is NOT mandatory (Harrison 22e p.2879).

Persistent axial inflammation leads to bony fusion of sacroiliac and apophyseal joints and syndesmophyte formation; complete ankylosis of the spine is termed 'bamboo spine,' seen in only a very small percentage of late-stage AS patients (Harrison 22e p.2880, 2884).

Typical SpA syndesmophytes are vertically oriented, distinguishing them from the horizontal osteophytes of spinal osteoarthritis; PsA syndesmophytes are often chunky and nonmarginal (Harrison 22e p.2884, 2889).

Reactive arthritis follows infectious gastroenteritis (Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter) or genitourinary Chlamydia; classic features include urethritis, conjunctivitis, mucosal ulcers, and keratoderma blennorrhagica (Harrison 22e p.2880).

IBD-associated arthritis: r-axSpA develops in up to 10% of IBD patients and pSpA in 10-30%; conversely axSpA patients have a 5-10% risk of developing IBD. HLA-B27 is NOT a risk factor for IBD itself (Harrison 22e p.2891-2892).

axSpA is subdivided into radiographic (r-axSpA, = ankylosing spondylitis [AS]) and nonradiographic (nr-axSpA), the difference based on presence/absence of definitive sacroiliitis on plain radiographs; the two share the same clinical features and disease burden (Harrison 22e p.2880, 2883).

pSpA encompasses psoriatic arthritis (PsA), reactive arthritis (ReA), IBD-associated arthritis, and undifferentiated pSpA; SAPHO, acne-associated, and hidradenitis suppurativa-associated arthritis are sometimes included (Harrison 22e p.2880).
HLA-B27 is the strongest genetic risk factor: present in 85-90% of r-axSpA and 50-90% of nr-axSpA, versus ~5% of the healthy Caucasian population (Harrison 22e p.2881).

Inflammatory back pain (IBP): insidious onset, age <45, chronic (>3 months), improves with exercise/activity but NOT with rest, worse in second half of night with improvement after getting up, and prolonged (>30 min) morning stiffness; this distinguishes it from mechanical back pain (Harrison 22e p.2883).

Characteristic SpA pattern is asymmetric mono-/oligoarticular (<=4 joints) inflammatory arthritis of large lower-limb joints (usually knee) with enthesitis, tendonitis, and dactylitis (sausage digits), contrasting with the symmetric polyarticular MCP/PIP involvement of rheumatoid arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2879).
Hips are the most common nonspinal ('root') joints affected in axSpA; peripheral arthritis occurs in ~30-40% of axSpA patients (Harrison 22e p.2883).

Uveitis is the most common extramusculoskeletal manifestation (~40% of axSpA), typically acute, anterior, unilateral, and episodic; other extra-articular features include psoriasis (~10%) and IBD (frank IBD ~10%, subclinical gut inflammation up to 50%) (Harrison 22e p.2883-2884).

Enthesitis (inflammation at tendon/ligament insertions) is common in axSpA, presenting as heel pain (plantar fasciitis, Achilles insertion), chest wall pain, epicondylitis, or pelvic rim pain; dactylitis is relatively rare in axSpA but common in PsA (Harrison 22e p.2883).

PITFALL: confusing inflammatory back pain with common mechanical back pain - mechanical causes must be considered first since axSpA is the etiology in only 4-5% of chronic back pain; conversely IBP improves with exercise and worsens with rest, the reverse of mechanical pain (Harrison 22e p.2883, 2885).
The term 'inflammatory back pain' is itself a partial misnomer - only ~15% of patients with IBP have demonstrable axial inflammation (Harrison 22e p.2883).
Diagnostic delay of 5-14 years is common, worse in women (back pain/enthesitis mistaken for fibromyalgia) and in nonwhite populations with lower HLA-B27 prevalence (Harrison 22e p.2884).
Interreader reliability for distinguishing r-axSpA from nr-axSpA on radiographs is poor (kappa 0.35-0.45), even between trained musculoskeletal radiologists (Harrison 22e p.2883).
MRI overdiagnosis: osteitis-type and fat-metaplasia changes occur from mechanical stress in athletes, postpartum women, degenerative arthritis, and normal individuals >40 (Harrison 22e p.2885).
Normal/negative inflammatory markers do NOT exclude axSpA - ESR/CRP elevated in only 30-40% of active disease (Harrison 22e p.2884).
Plain spine radiographs should generally be avoided in chronic back pain; multiple oblique sacroiliac views add little but increase gonadal radiation (Harrison 22e p.2884).

Avoid glucocorticoid injection around lower-extremity weight-bearing entheses due to risk of tendon rupture; in IBD-associated arthritis anti-IL17 therapy is contraindicated and NSAIDs may trigger IBD flares (Harrison 22e p.2890-2892).

Course is variable: ~50% of patients progress from nonradiographic to radiographic stage over 20 years, but <10% progress to significant spinal involvement with bamboo spine. Risk factors for osteoproliferation (worse structural outcome) include male sex, persistent inflammation (MRI sacroiliac/spine activity, high CRP), existing syndesmophytes, HLA-B27 positivity, and smoking. With increased awareness and earlier treatment, structural damage has steadily decreased over recent decades, with a shift toward higher prevalence of nr-axSpA over r-axSpA. axSpA significantly impairs well-being, function, productivity, and quality of life. Reactive arthritis is often self-limiting but may become chronic, with HLA-B27 linked to chronicity (Harrison 22e p.2880, 2884, 2891).
Fever, weight loss, advanced age, or past malignancy in a back-pain patient - prompt evaluation for osteomyelitis, osteoporotic fracture, or metastatic disease (Harrison 22e p.2886)
Cauda equina syndrome (urinary hesitancy and/or saddle anesthesia) - late axSpA complication (Harrison 22e p.2884)
Cardiac conduction abnormalities (heart block) at any stage; aortic valve insufficiency as a late complication (Harrison 22e p.2884)
AA (renal) amyloidosis causing nephrotic syndrome after prolonged uncontrolled inflammation; IgA nephropathy with microscopic hematuria (Harrison 22e p.2884)
Spinal fractures in ankylosed (bamboo) spine - consider if back pain persists/relapses despite therapy (Harrison 22e p.2888)
Atlantoaxial subluxation (rare, in PsA) with potentially serious neurologic consequences (Harrison 22e p.2889)
Acute anterior uveitis (eye pain, redness, photophobia, miosis) requiring urgent ophthalmologic care (Harrison 22e p.2884)

axSpA is classified as radiographic (r-axSpA / ankylosing spondylitis) vs nonradiographic (nr-axSpA) using definitive sacroiliitis on plain radiographs per the modified New York criteria: definitive = grade 2 bilateral OR grade 3-4 unilateral or bilateral (r-axSpA); lower-grade sacroiliitis = nr-axSpA. ASAS criteria further split SpA into axial (axSpA) and peripheral (pSpA). Diagnosis of axSpA in chronic back pain follows the schema of Figure 374-2 (definite sacroiliitis on x-ray -> AS; otherwise count SpA features >=4 or compelling clinical picture plus MRI sacroiliitis/HLA-B27 -> nr-axSpA). Disease activity graded with BASDAI/ASDAS; PsA classified with CASPAR criteria, activity by DAPSA/MDA (Harrison 22e p.2883-2884, 2889).

chunks.text: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma is a malignant proliferation of epidermal keratinocytes that have acquired full-thickness atypia and then breached the basement membrane to invade the dermis. Cumulative ultraviolet radiation is the dominant driver, producing signature mutations including in TP53 and other tumour-suppressor and oncogene pathways, with additional contributions from immunosuppression, human papillomavirus in some tumours, chronic inflammation or scarring, and carcinogen exposure. Progression typically follows a continuum from dysplastic keratinocytes (actinic keratosis) through in-situ disease (Bowen's) to invasive carcinoma. Invasive nests of atypical keratinocytes with variable keratinisation can track along nerves and invade lymphatics, giving the potential for metastasis that distinguishes it from basal cell carcinoma.

STEMI usually results from abrupt thrombotic occlusion of a coronary artery already affected by atherosclerosis. Vascular injury promoted by smoking, hypertension, lipid accumulation, and inflammation leads to disruption of an atherosclerotic plaque by erosion or rupture, exposing its contents to blood under conditions favoring thrombogenesis. A platelet monolayer forms first; agonists such as collagen, ADP, epinephrine, and serotonin activate platelets, releasing thromboxane A2 (a local vasoconstrictor) and converting the glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor to a high-affinity state that binds fibrinogen and cross-links platelets. Exposure of tissue factor activates the coagulation cascade (factors VII and X), generating thrombin, which converts fibrinogen to fibrin; an autoamplifying thrombin reaction culminates in an occlusive thrombus of platelet aggregates and fibrin. The extent of necrosis depends on the territory supplied, completeness and duration of occlusion, collateral supply, myocardial oxygen demand, endogenous thrombolysis, and adequacy of reperfusion. Microvascular dysfunction can produce no-reflow. Healing proceeds through acute (first hours-7 days), healing (7-28 days), and healed (29+ days) stages, with polymorphonuclear leukocytes then proinflammatory and reparative monocytes driving clearance, angiogenesis, extracellular matrix production, scar formation, and ventricular remodeling (Harrison 22e pp.2113-2116).

STEMI typically arises when coronary flow drops abruptly after a thrombus forms over an atherosclerotic plaque that has eroded or ruptured; slowly progressive high-grade stenoses less often cause STEMI because collaterals develop over time (Harrison 22e p.2113).

Wall-motion abnormalities on two-dimensional echocardiography are almost universal in STEMI and aid triage, but acute infarction cannot be distinguished from old scar or severe acute ischemia by echo alone (Harrison 22e p.2116).

The two major classes of complications determining prognosis in the primary-PCI era are electrical (arrhythmias) and mechanical (pump failure); most out-of-hospital STEMI deaths result from sudden ventricular fibrillation (Harrison 22e p.2117).

Temperature can rise up to 38 degrees C during the first week, and a nonspecific leukocytosis (often 12,000-15,000/microL) appears within hours and persists 3-7 days, with the ESR rising more slowly and peaking in the first week (Harrison 22e pp.2114, 2116).

Plaques prone to disruption tend to have a large lipid core and a thin fibrous cap, yet fewer than 5% of such thin-capped fibroatheromas actually become the nidus for an acute MI during long-term follow-up (Harrison 22e p.2113).

Deep, visceral chest pain described as heavy, squeezing, or crushing, usually central and/or epigastric and lasting longer than angina, is the most common presentation; it may radiate to the arms, back, lower jaw, or neck but not below the umbilicus (Harrison 22e p.2114).

Pain is not universal: painless STEMI is more frequent in patients with diabetes mellitus and increases with age, and the event may instead present as sudden breathlessness, syncope, confusion, profound weakness, arrhythmia, peripheral embolism, or an unexplained fall in blood pressure (Harrison 22e p.2114).

Anterior infarction may produce sympathetic overactivity (tachycardia/hypertension), whereas inferior infarction may produce parasympathetic overactivity (bradycardia/hypotension) (Harrison 22e p.2114).
Substernal chest pain lasting more than 30 minutes combined with diaphoresis strongly suggests STEMI (Harrison 22e p.2114).

The 12-lead ECG is the pivotal triage tool: total epicardial coronary occlusion produces ST-segment elevation, and most patients presenting with ST elevation ultimately evolve Q waves (Harrison 22e p.2115).

Cardiac troponin T and I are the preferred biomarkers when measured with high-sensitivity assays and may rise to roughly 20-50 times the upper reference limit in classic MI, remaining elevated for at least 7-10 days after STEMI (Harrison 22e pp.2115-2116).

Because urgent reperfusion decisions rest on clinical and ECG findings, high-sensitivity troponin is of less immediate value in confirmed STEMI than in the broader chest-pain workup (Harrison 22e p.2116).
Equating absence of pain with absence of STEMI: painless infarction is common in diabetics and older patients and may present only as dyspnea, syncope, or hypotension (Harrison 22e p.2114).
Misattributing xiphoid/epigastric pain to indigestion, compounded by the patient's own denial of a heart attack (Harrison 22e p.2114).

Older terms Q-wave/non-Q-wave and transmural/nontransmural MI correlate poorly with pathology and have been replaced by STEMI and NSTEMI; Q-wave development depends more on infarct volume than on transmurality (Harrison 22e p.2115).

Peak biomarker concentration correlates only weakly with infarct size, and early reperfusion causes earlier biomarker peaking from rapid washout, so peak levels should not be used to gauge infarct size (Harrison 22e p.2116).
Echocardiographic wall-motion abnormalities cannot distinguish acute STEMI from old scar or severe acute ischemia (Harrison 22e p.2116).
Radionuclide perfusion 'cold spots' cannot distinguish acute infarct from chronic scar, so they are not specific for acute MI (Harrison 22e p.2117).

About half of AMI-related deaths occur before the patient reaches the hospital. In-hospital mortality after admission for AMI has fallen from roughly 10% to about 5%, and the 1-year mortality after AMI is approximately 15%. Mortality is roughly fourfold higher in patients older than 75 years than in younger patients. Up to one-third of STEMI patients achieve spontaneous reperfusion of the infarct-related artery within 24 hours with improved healing. Outcome hinges largely on electrical (arrhythmic) and mechanical (pump failure) complications (Harrison 22e pp.2113, 2117).
Sudden development of ventricular fibrillation, the leading cause of out-of-hospital STEMI death, with most such deaths occurring within the first 24 hours and over half within the first hour
Hypotension or unexplained drop in arterial pressure
Sudden loss of consciousness, confusional state, or profound weakness as an atypical STEMI presentation
New apical systolic murmur suggesting mitral valve apparatus dysfunction, a serious mechanical complication
Inferior infarction with elevated jugular venous pressure, clear lungs, and hypotension suggesting right ventricular infarction
Pericardial friction rub in transmural STEMI
Signs of pump failure / cardiogenic shock and mechanical complications such as ventricular septal defect

Patients with prolonged ischemic discomfort are first classified as an acute coronary syndrome and triaged by the 12-lead ECG into ST-segment elevation versus no ST-segment elevation; biomarkers then separate unstable angina from NSTEMI. The Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction classifies MI into five types: type 1 (atherothrombotic), type 2 (oxygen supply-demand imbalance unrelated to acute atherothrombosis), type 3 (cardiac death with presumed new ischemic ECG changes before troponin became available), type 4 (PCI-related, including 4a, 4b stent thrombosis, 4c restenosis), and type 5 (CABG-related). Procedure-related MI within 48 h is defined by troponin elevation greater than 5-fold (type 4a) or greater than 10-fold (type 5) the 99th percentile URL with additional ischemic criteria (Harrison 22e pp.2114, 2117-2118).

S. aureus expresses cell wall-anchored adhesins called MSCRAMMs (microbial surface components recognizing adhesive matrix molecules, e.g., SdrC) that mediate binding to host extracellular-matrix proteins and underpin adherence and colonization (p.967). Like other extracellular pathogens it can form biofilms, which contribute to device- and prosthesis-associated infection (p.967). Disease is driven partly by potent secreted toxins. Superantigens — including toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1) and the staphylococcal enterotoxins — bind invariant regions of MHC class II molecules and the T-cell receptor, nonspecifically activating vast numbers of T cells and triggering a cytokine storm responsible for fever, rash, and the shock of TSS (p.974, p.402). S. aureus also produces an erythrotoxin causing scarlatiniform rash and exfoliative toxin ("exfoliatin") that cleaves the superficial epidermis to produce bullous impetigo and SSSS (p.402, p.389). It elaborates several pore-forming toxins — leukocidins, alpha- and gamma-hemolysins, and phenol-soluble modulins — that lyse host cells, protect the organism from phagocytosis, and impair development of protective adaptive immunity (p.975). Methicillin resistance results from acquisition of the mobile mecA gene carried on the SCCmec cassette, which has spread widely through the S. aureus population (p.1195).

Staphylococcus aureus causes a wide spectrum of disease, ranging from localized skin and soft-tissue infection to invasive bloodstream, endocardial, and bone infection and to toxin-mediated syndromes; methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) is now common in both community and health-care settings (p.1195, p.389).

Furunculosis (boils) is caused by S. aureus and has risen in prominence with community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA); patients frequently mistake furuncles for spider or insect bites, and family members or close contacts may also be affected (p.389).

Whenever possible, send lesional material from staphylococcal skin infection for culture; incision and drainage may be adequate therapy for a small solitary furuncle without surrounding cellulitis or systemic symptoms (p.389).

Impetigo is caused most often by S. aureus (and sometimes group A streptococci) and forms a characteristic honey-colored crust; bullous impetigo, with tense clear bullae, is produced by S. aureus exfoliative toxin (phage type II) (p.389).

In staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome (SSSS) the site of staphylococcal infection is usually extracutaneous (e.g., conjunctivitis, rhinorrhea, otitis media, pharyngitis) and the skin lesions themselves are sterile, whereas in bullous impetigo the skin lesions are the actual site of infection (p.402).

Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is defined by clinical criteria — fever, diffuse macular (sunburn-type) erythroderma, hypotension, and multiorgan involvement — with three criteria involving mucocutaneous sites (diffuse skin erythema, desquamation of palms and soles 1-2 weeks after onset, and mucous-membrane hyperemia of the vagina, oropharynx, or conjunctivae) (p.402, p.993).

In staphylococcal TSS, the vagina or a postoperative wound is typically colonized rather than overtly infected, and mucosal areas appear hyperemic but not infected; this contrasts with streptococcal TSS, which is more often linked to overt skin/soft-tissue infection and bacteremia (p.993).

Acute bacterial endocarditis from S. aureus follows a far more aggressive course than subacute endocarditis, can attack previously normal native valves, and native-valve S. aureus (including MRSA) endocarditis is increasing in frequency (p.994).

Coagulase-negative staphylococci are skin commensals; a single positive blood-culture bottle for skin flora (especially one taking >24 h to turn positive) should raise suspicion of contamination or catheter colonization rather than true bloodstream infection, and cultures should be repeated from both central and peripheral sites (p.581).

Attributing a single positive blood culture for coagulase-negative staphylococci to true bacteremia when it may represent skin-flora contamination or catheter colonization — repeat paired cultures and assess time-to-positivity (p.581).
Assuming a primary skin focus is present in staphylococcal TSS; colonization (vaginal or wound) without overt infection is typical, so the portal may be subtle (p.993).
Missing the diagnosis of S. aureus endocarditis in older patients, whose nonspecific presentation delays recognition (p.994).

Confusing SSSS with toxic epidermal necrolysis or severe drug eruption; SSSS occurs mainly in infants/toddlers, is more superficial, spares the oral mucosa, and is toxin- rather than drug-mediated (p.402).
Inducible clindamycin resistance can cause treatment failure in apparently clindamycin-susceptible isolates unless the double-disk (D-zone) test is performed (p.383).

Outcome varies sharply by syndrome. For TSS, reported mortality is about 5% for menstruation-associated and 10-15% for nonmenstrual disease (compared with 30-70% for streptococcal TSS) (p.993). Acute bacterial endocarditis, including native-valve S. aureus/MRSA disease, carries mortality of roughly 10-40%, and older patients with S. aureus endocarditis often present with nonspecific symptoms that delay diagnosis and worsen prognosis (p.994). Rapid recognition and intervention are crucial across invasive staphylococcal syndromes.
S. aureus bacteremia warrants an active search for infective endocarditis and metastatic/seeded foci, because any primary focus can give rise to bloodstream infection with secondary seeding (p.994).

In TSS, rapid hypotension developing within hours of symptom onset, and early renal failure preceding hypotension, are warning features (early renal failure helps distinguish TSS from other septic shock syndromes) (p.993).

Acute S. aureus endocarditis: a changing murmur, congestive heart failure, rapid valvular destruction (especially aortic) with pulmonary edema and hypotension, myocardial abscess with conduction block/arrhythmia, and large friable vegetations causing arterial emboli, metastatic infection, or stroke (p.994).
Widespread skin blistering or radial perioral crusting with diffuse tenderness suggests SSSS and demands prompt evaluation (p.402).
S. aureus among organisms that can present as intractable hypotension/septic shock with a primary soft-tissue focus (p.993).

No single graded severity scale is presented; staphylococcal disease is categorized by clinical syndrome and invasiveness — superficial skin/soft-tissue infection (impetigo, furunculosis), toxin-mediated syndromes (TSS, SSSS, scarlatiniform eruption), and invasive disease (bacteremia, infective endocarditis, osteomyelitis, septic intracranial/epidural infection). TSS is defined by formal clinical criteria (fever, diffuse erythroderma, hypotension, multiorgan involvement with mucocutaneous features) (p.402, p.993).

chunks.text: Strabismus arises from a failure of the normal binocular alignment maintained by coordinated extraocular muscle action and central fusional control. Causes include refractive error (notably hypermetropia driving accommodative esotropia), sensory deprivation from poor vision in one eye, abnormalities of the neuromuscular pathways (cranial nerve palsies), mechanical restriction of muscles, and disorders of central fusion. In children, misalignment during the critical period of visual development leads to suppression of the deviating eye's image and can result in amblyopia and loss of binocular single vision.
