Pharyngitis differential includes group C/G streptococci, mixed anaerobes (Vincent's angina), Arcanobacterium haemolyticum, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Corynebacterium diphtheriae, EBV/CMV/HIV, and other viruses (Table 153-2, p.1208)
Impetigo differential: bullous impetigo due to S. aureus, and herpetic lesions (orolabial HSV, chickenpox, or zoster), distinguished by grouped discrete vesicles and positive Tzanck/PCR (p.1210)
Staphylococcus aureus cellulitis/soft tissue infection mimicking streptococcal cellulitis (suspect S. aureus when cellulitis develops around a wound or ulcer) (p.1210-1211)
Bullous impetigo (S. aureus) mimicking streptococcal impetigo (p.1210)
Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome (shares features with streptococcal TSS, but staph TSS patients are usually not bacteremic) (p.1211-1212)
Herpes simplex virus or varicella-zoster lesions mimicking impetigo (p.1210)

Throat culture (gold standard; vigorous rubbing of both tonsillar pillars) and rapid antigen test (latex agglutination/EIA, specificity >95%, relative sensitivity 70-90%); confirm negative rapid test with culture in higher-risk individuals (p.1208)
Antibody tests to streptolysin O (ASO) and DNase B for serodiagnosis of preceding streptococcal infection in suspected ARF or PSGN (p.1207)
emm-typing by PCR/sequencing of the variable region of the emm gene (CDC database) for strain typing (p.1207)
In streptococcal TSS, laboratory findings: marked left shift with immature granulocytes, hypocalcemia, hypoalbuminemia, and thrombocytopenia (worsening on day 2-3) (p.1211)
Blood cultures (most streptococcal TSS patients are bacteremic) (p.1211-1212)
Early surgical exploration of suspected necrotizing fasciitis for diagnosis (reveals fascial-plane necrosis and inflammatory fluid without muscle involvement) (p.1211)
Cultures of vesicular fluid in difficult impetigo cases; culture to rule out MRSA if empirical treatment fails (p.1210)
Kawasaki disease (mimics scarlet fever) (p.1209)
Systemic allergic reactions / drug eruptions (mimic scarlet fever) (p.1209)

GAS (S. pyogenes) is the single species of Lancefield group A, a beta-hemolytic, chain-forming, gram-positive facultative anaerobe. M protein (encoded by the emm gene, >200 emm types) is the major surface protein and chief virulence factor: it resists phagocytic killing partly by binding plasma fibrinogen and interfering with complement deposition, and type-specific anti-M antibody confers protection only against the same M type. A hyaluronic acid capsule (a weak immunogen owing to structural identity with mammalian connective tissue) protects against phagocytosis and aids pharyngeal colonization via CD44 binding; capsule is not essential for virulence. GAS elaborates streptolysins S and O, streptokinase, DNases, SpyCEP (cleaves IL-8 to impair neutrophil recruitment), and pyrogenic exotoxins (formerly erythrogenic toxins) that cause the scarlet fever rash and act as superantigens triggering T-cell cytokine release, implicated in severe invasive disease including necrotizing fasciitis and streptococcal TSS. The post-infectious sequelae ARF (uniquely associated with S. pyogenes) and PSGN are thought to result from immune responses to streptococcal infection. GBS is encapsulated by 1 of 10 polysaccharides; the capsule is a key virulence factor and type-specific anticapsular antibody is protective.

Group A Streptococcus (GAS; S. pyogenes) is the only common cause of sore throat that should be treated with antibiotics; GAS accounts for 20-40% of exudative pharyngitis in children and is rare under age 3 (p.1208).

Streptococcal cellulitis favors sites of disrupted lymphatic drainage (prior cellulitis, post-mastectomy/axillary dissection arm, prior DVT or lymphedema leg, saphenous vein harvest site); treating tinea pedis can stop recurrent leg cellulitis after vein harvest (p.1210-1211).
GAS is among the few pathogens producing wound infection and surrounding cellulitis within the first 24 h after surgery, with thin exudate and rapid spread (p.1211).

Necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical emergency: GAS is implicated in ~60% of cases; early surgical exploration and extensive debridement are diagnostic, therapeutic, and life-saving, with antibiotics as a critical adjunct (p.1211).

Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (TSS) features fever, hypotension, renal impairment, and respiratory distress; in contrast to staphylococcal TSS, most patients with streptococcal TSS are bacteremic, rash usually does NOT develop, and the most common associated infection is a soft tissue infection (necrotizing fasciitis, myositis, or cellulitis) (p.1211-1212).
Streptococcal TSS carries a mortality rate of >=30%, mostly from shock and respiratory failure; because of its rapidly progressive lethal course, early recognition is essential (p.1212).

Group B Streptococcus (GBS; S. agalactiae) is a leading cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis and of peripartum fever; early-onset disease (first week, median 20 h) is acquired from the colonized maternal genital tract, while late-onset disease (1 week-3 months) most often presents as meningitis, frequently capsular type III (p.1212-1213).

GBS infection in adults increasingly affects the elderly and those with chronic illness (e.g., diabetes, malignancy), presenting as cellulitis/soft-tissue infection including diabetic ulcers, UTI, pneumonia, endocarditis, and septic arthritis (p.1213-1214).

Streptococcal pharyngitis cannot be reliably diagnosed on clinical grounds alone given overlap with many viral and bacterial causes; throat culture remains the diagnostic gold standard, with rapid antigen tests (specificity >95%) a useful adjunct (p.1208).
Antibiotic treatment of GAS pharyngitis is given primarily to prevent suppurative complications and acute rheumatic fever; symptoms resolve in 3-5 days and are shortened little by treatment (p.1208).
Prevention of ARF depends on eradicating the organism from the pharynx (not just symptom resolution) and requires a 10-day penicillin course; a single dose or short course is inadequate (p.1208).
Penicillin treatment of streptococcal pharyngitis reduces the likelihood of ARF but NOT of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (p.1209).

Worldwide, GAS infections and their post-infectious sequelae (chiefly ARF and rheumatic heart disease) cause an estimated 500,000 deaths/year; incidence of GAS disease and RHD is roughly tenfold higher in resource-limited countries (p.1206-1207).

Scarlet fever is streptococcal infection (usually pharyngitis) plus a rash from pyrogenic exotoxins: blanching sandpaper-textured papular rash on trunk and extremities sparing palms and soles, with circumoral pallor, strawberry tongue, and Pastia's lines in skin folds, followed by desquamation of palms and soles (p.1209).

Impetigo is most often a superficial GAS infection (occasionally other streptococci or S. aureus) of young children; honey/amber crusted lesions on face and legs; lesions are generally NOT painful and fever is NOT a feature — if fever is present, suspect deeper infection or another diagnosis (p.1209-1210).

Erysipelas is a streptococcal cellulitis of the superficial dermis: bright red, warm, shiny, edematous plaque with a sharply demarcated raised border and peau d'orange texture, typically on the face (malar) or lower extremities, with abrupt onset, fever and chills; classic cases are almost always due to beta-hemolytic streptococci (usually GAS) (p.1210).
Diagnosing streptococcal pharyngitis on clinical grounds alone is unreliable; clinicians over-prescribe antibiotics for sore throat (p.1208)
Rapid antigen tests are less sensitive than culture (relative sensitivity 70-90%), so a negative rapid test should be confirmed by throat culture in higher-risk patients (p.1208)
Improper swab technique lowers rapid-test sensitivity; both tonsillar pillars (and any exudate/ulceration) must be vigorously sampled (p.1208)
In necrotizing fasciitis, early physical findings may be unimpressive despite severe pain; relying on skin appearance delays diagnosis (p.1211)
Macrolide resistance is common in many countries and rising in invasive US GAS isolates (>30% since 2021); avoid macrolides where resistance exceeds 5-10% unless susceptibility is known (p.1208-1209)
Clindamycin resistance occurs in >=30% of invasive GAS isolates; susceptibility should not be assumed without in vitro testing before relying on clindamycin (p.1212)

Aggressive eradication of asymptomatic GAS pharyngeal carriage is usually not justified (carriers have lower risk of ARF and of transmission than symptomatic patients); exceptions arise when a carrier is a source of transmission to others (p.1209)

Endocarditis due to nonenterococcal group D streptococci (S. gallolyticus/S. bovis group) is associated with occult GI neoplasm (often colon carcinoma/polyp; abnormalities in >60%) and should prompt GI evaluation (p.1214)

Uncomplicated GAS pharyngitis is self-limited, with symptoms resolving in 3-5 days. Suppurative complications (peritonsillar/retropharyngeal abscess, cervical lymphadenitis, sinusitis, otitis, meningitis, bacteremia, endocarditis, pneumonia) are now uncommon with antibiotics; nonsuppurative sequelae are ARF and PSGN. Necrotizing fasciitis and streptococcal TSS are rapidly progressive and life-threatening; streptococcal TSS has a mortality rate of >=30%. Globally GAS sequelae account for ~500,000 deaths/year. Neonatal GBS incidence has fallen from ~2-3 to ~0.6 per 1000 live births with prenatal screening. Recurrent invasive GBS in adults occurs in ~4% of cases.

Necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical emergency: severe pain out of proportion to physical findings, with only minimal early skin erythema; progression over hours to dusky/mottled erythema and edema; tenderness evolving into anesthesia from infarction of cutaneous nerves — demands early surgical exploration and debridement (p.1211)
Streptococcal TSS: rapidly progressive, lethal (mortality >=30%) with hypotension and multiorgan failure; early recognition essential (p.1211-1212)
Fever in a patient with impetigo suggests extension to deeper tissues or an alternative diagnosis (p.1210)
GAS bacteremia without an identified source raises the possibility of endocarditis, occult abscess, or osteomyelitis (p.1212)
Unusually severe or prolonged pharyngitis, or localized pain with high fever and toxic appearance, suggests a peritonsillar or parapharyngeal abscess (p.1209)

Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome case definition (CDC, 1993; updated 2010; Table 153-4): I. Isolation of GAS from (A) a normally sterile site or (B) a nonsterile site; II. Clinical signs of severity = (A) hypotension AND (B) >=2 of: renal impairment, coagulopathy, liver function impairment, ARDS, generalized erythematous macular rash that may desquamate, or soft tissue necrosis (including necrotizing fasciitis or myositis) or gangrene. A DEFINITE case meets IA + IIA + IIB; a PROBABLE case meets IB + IIA + IIB if no other etiology is identified. Pharyngitis pretest risk is stratified clinically by the Centor criteria (fever history, absence of cough, tender anterior cervical adenopathy, tonsillar exudate/swelling).

chunks.text: Filariform larvae penetrate the skin, migrate through the circulation to the lungs, ascend the airways and are swallowed, maturing into adult worms in the small intestine. Females produce eggs that hatch into rhabditiform larvae; some transform into infective filariform larvae within the gut or perianal skin and reinvade the host, sustaining autoinfection. When host cellular immunity is impaired, this autoinfective cycle accelerates uncontrollably, causing massive larval migration through multiple organs (hyperinfection and dissemination) and carrying enteric bacteria that seed the bloodstream, meninges and other sites.

Subacute thyroiditis is thought to result from a viral infection or post-viral inflammatory response affecting the thyroid, producing granulomatous inflammation with giant cells and destruction of thyroid follicles. Disruption of follicles releases stored thyroid hormone into the circulation, causing an initial destructive thyrotoxicosis with suppressed TSH and low radioiodine uptake. As follicular stores are depleted and the gland heals, patients pass through a hypothyroid phase before glandular recovery restores normal hormone production in most cases.
Typically follows a viral upper respiratory illness by a few weeks and presents with a painful, tender thyroid and referred pain to the jaw or ears
Classically evolves through phases: an early thyrotoxic phase from follicular disruption, followed by transient hypothyroidism, and usually a return to euthyroidism
In the thyrotoxic phase radioiodine uptake is characteristically low, which distinguishes it from Graves' disease where uptake is high
The erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are markedly elevated, reflecting the inflammatory process
Thyrotoxic symptoms arise from release of preformed hormone rather than increased synthesis, so antithyroid drugs are ineffective
Management is largely symptomatic, with anti-inflammatory agents for milder disease and corticosteroids reserved for severe pain, alongside beta-blockade for adrenergic symptoms
A minority of patients are left with permanent hypothyroidism, so thyroid function should be monitored during recovery
Mistaking destructive thyrotoxicosis for Graves' disease and prescribing ineffective antithyroid drugs
Failing to check radioiodine uptake or ultrasound vascularity to separate the two
Overlooking the later hypothyroid phase and not monitoring thyroid function through recovery
Attributing a painful gland to malignancy without recognising the inflammatory picture

The illness is usually self-limiting over weeks to months with full recovery of thyroid function in most patients, though pain can be prolonged, recurrences occur occasionally, and a small proportion develop permanent hypothyroidism.

Persistent hypothyroid symptoms indicating the need for hormone replacement

chunks.text: A subconjunctival haemorrhage is bleeding from small conjunctival or episcleral vessels into the potential space between the conjunctiva and the underlying sclera. Because blood is confined to this superficial layer, it appears as a well-demarcated red sheet without affecting the cornea or intraocular structures. Rises in venous pressure (Valsalva), fragile vessels, trauma, or impaired haemostasis predispose to rupture. The blood is gradually cleared by resorption, passing through the usual colour changes of a resolving bruise.

Bleeding occurs beneath the dura (subdural space). The bleeding producing larger subdural haematomas is primarily venous in origin, classically from torn bridging veins, although arterial bleeding sites are occasionally found at operation and a few large haematomas are purely arterial. Chronic subdural haematomas develop days to weeks after (often trivial) injury, favoured by age-related cerebral atrophy that stretches bridging veins; they organise into a vascular fibrous capsule, and weeks-old collections often contain a mixture of blood and serous fluid. Anticoagulant-related intracranial haemorrhages are often subdural and may continue to evolve over 24-48 h if coagulopathy is insufficiently reversed (pp.3572-3573, 3498).

Direct cranial trauma may be minor and is not always required for an acute subdural bleed, particularly in the elderly and those on anticoagulants; acceleration forces alone (e.g. whiplash) can suffice (p.3572).
Up to one-third of patients with acute subdural haematoma have a lucid interval of minutes to hours before coma supervenes, but most are drowsy or comatose from the moment of injury (p.3572).
A unilateral headache with a slightly enlarged pupil on the side of the haematoma is frequently, though not invariably, present (p.3572).
Small subdural haematomas may be asymptomatic and usually do not require evacuation unless they enlarge (p.3572).
In chronic subdural haematoma, drowsiness, inattentiveness and incoherent thinking are generally more prominent than focal signs such as hemiparesis (p.3573).
Chronic subdural haematoma headache typically fluctuates in severity, sometimes with changes in head position (p.3573).
A history of trauma may be absent in chronic subdural haematoma; the injury may have been trivial and forgotten, especially in the elderly and those with clotting disorders (p.3572).
Recurrent falls in older adults place them at risk for subdural haematoma; brain imaging is warranted when neurologic signs are present (pp.222-223, 3927, 3929).
Trauma should be considered in any patient with an unexplained acute neurologic deficit (hemiparesis, stupor, confusion), particularly after a fall (p.3498).
Subacute pitfall: between roughly 2 and 6 weeks after the initial bleed the clot becomes isodense relative to adjacent brain on non-contrast CT and may be inapparent/missed (p.3573).

Acute subdural produces more horizontal displacement (mass effect) than expected from its thickness because of its large rostral-caudal extent, so mass effect can be underestimated from clot thickness alone (p.3572).
Absence of a trauma history does not exclude chronic subdural haematoma in the elderly or anticoagulated (p.3572).
Skull fractures are markers of injury site/severity, not the haematoma itself, and may be absent (p.3572).

In contrast to epidural haematomas, acute subdural haematomas requiring surgery carry significant morbidity and mortality, partly reflecting frequently associated underlying cortical brain damage. Chronic subdural collections evacuated through burr holes are usually treated successfully when a postoperative cranial drain is used; encapsulating fibrous membranes may require craniotomy to prevent recurrent fluid accumulation (pp.3572-3573).
Stupor or coma, hemiparesis, and unilateral pupillary enlargement indicate a larger acute haematoma (p.3572)
Acutely deteriorating patient requiring emergency craniotomy (p.3572)
Repetitive vomiting, nystagmus, drowsiness and unsteadiness may signal a posterior fossa subdural haematoma (p.3619)
Large bleed after only minor trauma should raise concern for coagulopathy or anticoagulant therapy (p.3573)

chunks.text: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss reflects acute dysfunction of the cochlea or auditory nerve. Although often idiopathic, proposed mechanisms include viral infection or inflammation of the labyrinth, microvascular compromise of the cochlear blood supply, rupture of intracochlear membranes, and autoimmune injury. These processes damage the delicate hair cells and neural elements or disturb the cochlear ionic and metabolic environment, producing abrupt hearing loss. A minority result from identifiable structural causes such as a vestibular schwannoma compressing the cochlear nerve, which is why imaging is required.

Superficial fungi inhabit only the keratinized superficial layers (stratum corneum, hair follicles, nail plate) and do not invade beneath the stratum corneum. Dermatophytes live within keratin and produce disease through host inflammatory responses to fungal antigens rather than by direct tissue invasion; nail involvement begins via the lateral or superficial nail plate then spreads, and hair-shaft invasion may be intra- or peri-shaft. Host defense is mediated by IL-17 responses, which restrict dermatophyte growth and control cutaneous Malassezia; infections are more frequent in males, and progesterone can inhibit dermatophyte growth. Malassezia organisms are lipophilic commensals of sebaceous areas that elicit little inflammation but, when IL-17 responses are excessive, can exacerbate atopic inflammation. Candida species are mucosal/cutaneous commensals; control depends on IL-17-producing lymphoid cells (TH17, gamma-delta T cells, innate lymphoid cells) at barrier sites, and defects in IL-17 signaling predispose to oral and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis.

Superficial fungal infections are caused by molds and yeasts that colonize the outer skin layers, hair follicles, and nails without invading deeper tissue; they are the most common human fungal infections but rarely cause serious disease.

Mucocutaneous candidiasis is most often caused by Candida albicans; oral thrush yields white mucosal plaques that scrape off, and antibiotic use, diabetes, and pregnancy are major risk factors for vulvovaginal candidiasis.

Candida auris is an emerging multidrug-resistant species that persistently colonizes human skin, hair follicles, healthcare environments, and devices, grows avidly in human sweat, and drives nosocomial outbreaks.

Seborrheic dermatitis (a Malassezia-associated condition) can be especially severe in patients with AIDS, and Malassezia fungemia, though rare, occurs almost exclusively in premature neonates receiving parenteral lipid nutrition.

Dermatophytes (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton) are not part of normal skin flora and confine themselves to keratinized structures; symptoms arise from inflammatory reaction to fungal antigens rather than tissue invasion, and an estimated billion people are affected worldwide.

The annular, ring-shaped cutaneous lesion ('ringworm') results from centrifugal outward growth of the organism in the stratum corneum; the term tinea (Latin for worm) is preferred and is paired with the affected body site.
Tinea capitis predominantly affects children aged 3 to 7 years, producing well-demarcated scaly patches with hair shafts broken off near the skin surface and possible alopecia.

Tinea pedis typically begins in the toe web spaces with peeling, maceration, and pruritus, and is a recognized portal of entry for streptococci and staphylococci, predisposing to lower-extremity cellulitis through interdigital fissures.

Onychomycosis affects toenails more often than fingernails, is most common in those with tinea pedis, and shows thickened, discolored, crumbling nails with onycholysis; older age, vascular disease, diabetes, and nail trauma are risk factors.

Malassezia yeasts (notably M. furfur, M. pachydermatis) are lipophilic commensals of sebum-rich areas (back, chest, scalp, face) and cause tinea/pityriasis versicolor, folliculitis, and seborrheic dermatitis; cutaneous IL-17 signaling normally controls them.
Tinea versicolor appears as flat round scaly hypo- or hyperpigmented patches on the neck, chest, or upper arms, usually asymptomatic, and can be confused with vitiligo (which is non-scaly).

KOH (potassium hydroxide) preparation of lesion-edge scrapings demonstrating hyphae is the key bedside diagnostic test; Malassezia shows a characteristic mix of budding bottle-shaped yeasts and short septate hyphae.

The outcome of rare systemic Malassezia infection depends on the host's underlying condition, though most affected neonates do well.

Sustained monomorphic VT most commonly results from reentry around a fixed substrate. In structural heart disease this substrate is an area of patchy replacement fibrosis (from infarction, inflammation, fibrosis, or surgical scar) creating anatomic or functional reentrant circuits; the uniform QRS reflects a single focal origin or repetitive exit from a stable circuit. In coronary artery disease the typical setting is a remote large myocardial infarction with a remodeled ventricle and depressed LV function, where the infarct scar provides a durable reentry substrate that is not generally dependent on ongoing acute ischemia. In nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy, scar-related reentry from progressive replacement fibrosis underlies VT, with scars often intramural or subepicardial and frequently adjacent to a valve annulus; sarcoidosis, Chagas' disease, and Lamin A/C mutation cardiomyopathy are particularly associated. Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy involves fibrofatty replacement chiefly of right ventricular myocardium producing a left bundle branch block-like VT. Bundle branch reentry VT (about 5% of monomorphic VT with structural disease) uses a macroreentrant circuit through the Purkinje system, usually retrograde up the left bundle and anterograde down the right bundle, generating a left bundle branch block configuration. Idiopathic VT in structurally normal hearts arises either from focal triggered automaticity (outflow tract foci near the pulmonic or aortic annuli) or from small reentry circuits in the Purkinje system (fascicular VT). Rapid or scar-associated monomorphic VT may degenerate into ventricular fibrillation.

Sustained monomorphic VT is a wide-QRS ventricular arrhythmia lasting at least 30 seconds, or one requiring intervention (antitachycardia pacing or cardioversion) for termination; each QRS resembles the others, pointing to a single focal origin or repetitive exit from a fixed reentry circuit.

Outflow tract VT most often arises in the right ventricular outflow tract, producing a left bundle branch block pattern in V1 with an inferiorly directed axis (tall R waves in II, III, aVF); a prominent R wave in V1 or V2 suggests a left ventricular outflow tract or aortic-root origin.

LV fascicular VT (Belhassen's / verapamil-sensitive VT) is the second most common idiopathic form: it shows a right bundle branch block-like configuration negative in the inferior leads and is due to a small reentry circuit near the septal ramifications of the left Purkinje system; despite being reentrant its course is typically benign.

Repeated incessant bursts of nonsustained monomorphic VT (repetitive monomorphic VT) can produce a tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy with depressed ventricular function that recovers once the arrhythmia is suppressed.

In structural heart disease the usual substrate is patchy replacement fibrosis from prior infarction, fibrosis, inflammation, or previous cardiac surgery, which sets up anatomic or functional reentry; less often VT arises from reentry or automaticity in diseased Purkinje conduction tissue.

Clinical tolerance depends on rate, baseline ventricular function, and autonomic response: rapid VT may cause hypotension and syncope (especially with poor LV function), while patients with normal function may have only palpitations despite fast rates.
Hemodynamic stability during a wide-complex tachycardia does NOT distinguish VT from supraventricular tachycardia with aberrancy; tolerance of the rhythm should never be used to exclude VT.

Ventriculoatrial (AV) dissociation is a reliable marker of VT, provided the atrial rate is slower than the ventricular rate; however a P wave following every QRS does not exclude VT because 1:1 ventriculo-atrial conduction can occur.
A monophasic R or Rs complex in lead aVR, or concordance (all monophasic R or all S waves) across V1 to V6, is relatively specific for VT.

In a patient with known structural heart disease, a wide-QRS tachycardia is most likely VT regardless of QRS morphology; depressed LV function or evidence of structural disease makes scar-related reentry the most likely mechanism of sustained monomorphic VT.
Scar is suggested by pathologic Q waves on ECG, segmental wall-motion abnormalities on echo or nuclear imaging, and areas of delayed gadolinium enhancement on cardiac MRI.

Idiopathic VT occurs in structurally normal hearts (normal sinus ECG, normal function and no scar on imaging), is provoked by sympathetic stimulation or acute sympathetic withdrawal (e.g. immediately post-exercise), and is generally benign with low risk of sudden death.
Using hemodynamic stability to rule out VT - tolerance of the rhythm does not exclude VT.
Assuming a P wave after every QRS excludes VT, when 1:1 ventriculo-atrial conduction can mimic this.
Relying on a single QRS-morphology criterion; all such criteria have limitations and are unreliable in severe heart disease, and bundle branch reentry VT can closely resemble the native sinus QRS.

Interpreting troponin/CK-MB elevations during VT as proof of an acute coronary event - these usually reflect demand ischemia from hypotension and fixed coronary disease; acute MI is rarely the cause of sustained monomorphic VT.
Mistaking telemetry noise or movement artifact for VT, leading to unnecessary tests and interventions.
Attributing a typical outflow-tract QRS morphology automatically to benign idiopathic VT, since cardiomyopathies (notably ARVC) can produce PVCs/VT from the same region and must be excluded.
Failing to recognize repetitive monomorphic (incessant nonsustained) VT as a reversible cause of tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy.

Prognosis hinges on the presence and type of underlying heart disease. Scar-related monomorphic VT in structural heart disease carries a high recurrence risk; with ischemic cardiomyopathy and a prior large MI, up to 70% of patients have arrhythmia recurrence within 2 years, and even after device-based secondary prevention the depressed-ejection-fraction population remains at risk for heart failure, recurrent ischemic events, and recurrent VT, with a 5-year mortality exceeding 30%. Device shocks and antitachycardia pacing are themselves adverse events linked to higher rates of heart failure, mortality, and psychological stress. By contrast, idiopathic VT in a structurally normal heart is generally benign, sudden death is rare, and a defibrillator is not recommended; LV fascicular (Belhassen's) VT likewise follows a benign course despite being reentrant. In ARVC, clinical heart failure is rare until late stages and survival to advanced age can be expected provided the VT is controlled. In repaired tetralogy of Fallot the risk of sudden cardiac death may reach roughly 1% per year in adulthood by the fourth or fifth decade.

Harrison classifies sustained ventricular arrhythmias by substrate/etiology rather than a graded severity scale: (1) idiopathic VT without structural heart disease - outflow tract (RV outflow: LBBB pattern in V1 with inferior axis and late precordial transition; LV outflow: inferior axis with early precordial transition and prominent R in V2-V3), LV fascicular VT (RBBB pattern in V1 with left axis deviation), and papillary muscle VT; (2) ischemic cardiomyopathy (monomorphic VT common after large prior MI); (3) nonischemic cardiomyopathy (fibrotic scar VT, e.g. sarcoidosis, Chagas', Lamin A/C); (4) arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy (RV-origin LBBB-pattern VT); (5) repaired tetralogy of Fallot (RV-origin VT); (6) hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; and (7) genetic arrhythmia syndromes (long QT, Brugada, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT, short QT/early repolarization). Practically, the most important severity distinction is between benign idiopathic VT in a structurally normal heart and scar-related VT in structural heart disease, the latter conferring substantial sudden-death risk.

chunks.text: SVC syndrome results from obstruction of the superior vena cava causing a severe reduction in venous return from the head, neck, and upper extremities. Obstruction may be due to external compression, direct tumour invasion, intraluminal thrombosis (often device-related), or fibrosis. Venous congestion produces facial/upper-body swelling, distended neck veins, and development of collateral venous channels over the chest wall. The 'hot quadrate' focal hepatic hotspot on CT reflects portosystemic shunting between the SVC and portal vein. Chronic SVCS can produce 'downhill' oesophageal varices (cephalad-to-caudad flow, opposite to portal-hypertension 'uphill' varices), which may bleed late.

Treponema pallidum subsp. pallidum is a thin spiral organism with a lipid-rich outer membrane and periplasmic endoflagella that drive motility; it has severely limited metabolic capacity and depends on host amino acids, carbohydrates, and lipids. Humans are the only known natural host. After penetrating intact mucous membranes or skin abrasions, treponemes reach the lymphatics and blood within hours, producing systemic dissemination and metastatic foci well before the primary lesion appears (median incubation ~21 days, rarely >6 weeks). Tissue damage reflects the host immune response rather than a direct treponemal toxin: lesions show perivascular infiltration by CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, plasma cells, and macrophages with endarteritis obliterans (obliteration of small vessels). Antigenic variation of the TprK outer-membrane protein allows immune evasion and persistence, explaining the paradoxical appearance of secondary lesions after primary lesions clear. Tertiary lesions (gumma, aortitis of the vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta, parenchymal neurosyphilis) arise from a slowly progressive inflammatory process that begins early in infection (Harrison 22e p.1428-1430, p.1432).

Chronic systemic infection by Treponema pallidum subsp. pallidum, usually sexually transmitted, characterized by episodes of active disease separated by asymptomatic latent periods (Harrison 22e p.1428).
Penicillin is the drug of choice for all stages as a principle; its efficacy against T. pallidum remains undiminished after decades of use (Harrison 22e p.1434).

Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction (fever, chills, myalgia, headache, tachycardia) may follow the start of therapy, thought to be a response to lipoproteins released by dying treponemes; it occurs in ~50% of primary and ~90% of secondary cases, defervesces within 12-24 h, is self-limited, and does not require steroids (Harrison 22e p.1435).

Earliest manifestations of early congenital syphilis include rhinitis ('snuffles'), mucocutaneous lesions, periostitis/bone changes, and hepatosplenomegaly; classic late stigmata include Hutchinson's teeth, mulberry molars, saddle nose, and saber shins (Harrison 22e p.1432-1433).

Staging is the organizing framework: a primary chancre at the site of inoculation, then generalized secondary mucocutaneous disease, followed by latency, and in a minority of untreated patients tertiary disease (gumma, cardiovascular, late neurosyphilis) (Harrison 22e p.1428, p.1430).

Primary chancre is typically a single painless papule that erodes into an indurated ulcer with a firm cartilaginous edge; it is accompanied by regional (usually inguinal) lymphadenopathy that is firm, nonsuppurative, and painless, and heals spontaneously in about 4-6 weeks (Harrison 22e p.1430).

Secondary syphilis classically produces a widespread macular-to-papular, nonpruritic rash that frequently involves the palms and soles, plus generalized nontender lymphadenopathy (noted in ~85% of patients) (Harrison 22e p.1430-1431).

Condylomata lata (broad, moist, highly infectious lesions in intertriginous areas, ~10% of secondary cases) and mucous patches (painless silver-gray erosions of oral/genital mucosa) are characteristic secondary lesions (Harrison 22e p.1431).

Latent syphilis is defined by reactive serology with a normal CSF and no clinical manifestations; early latent is within the first year, late latent is >=1 year or of unknown duration (Harrison 22e p.1431).

Two classes of serologic tests: lipoidal (nontreponemal) RPR/VDRL, which are quantitative and reflect disease activity, and treponemal tests (FTA-ABS, TPPA, EIA/CIA); a reactive lipoidal screen must be confirmed by a treponemal test (Harrison 22e p.1433).
RPR is preferred for rapid serologic diagnosis; the VDRL remains the standard for CSF examination and is superior to RPR for that purpose (Harrison 22e p.1433-1434).

After treatment of early syphilis a fourfold (two-dilution) fall in VDRL/RPR titer (e.g., 1:32 to 1:8) signals adequate response; treponemal tests typically remain reactive and are not useful for monitoring therapy (Harrison 22e p.1433, p.1435).

Prozone phenomenon: a high-titer specimen may give a nonreactive or only weakly reactive lipoidal test with undiluted serum that becomes reactive only on dilution—a falsely negative screen if dilution is not performed (Harrison 22e p.1433).

Primary syphilis is often missed in women and in MSM because chancres on the cervix, vaginal wall, anal canal, rectum, or mouth go unseen; atypical or trivial dark-field-negative genital lesions should still prompt consideration of syphilis (Harrison 22e p.1430).

Both lipoidal and treponemal tests may be nonreactive in early primary syphilis; an early primary ulcer can present with nonreactive serology, so negative serology does not exclude it (Harrison 22e p.1431-1433).

Biological false-positive lipoidal tests occur (usually titer <=1:8, e.g., in autoimmune disease or injection drug use); a nonreactive treponemal test excludes syphilis in this setting (Harrison 22e p.1433-1434).
Treponemal tests usually remain reactive for life after treatment and cannot distinguish active from past infection or gauge response to therapy (Harrison 22e p.1433, p.1435).
CSF VDRL is highly specific but insensitive—it may be nonreactive even in symptomatic neurosyphilis—and RPR must not be substituted for VDRL on CSF (Harrison 22e p.1434).

Benzathine penicillin does not achieve treponemicidal levels in CSF even at high doses, so it is inadequate for neurosyphilis and viable T. pallidum has been recovered from CSF after such treatment (Harrison 22e p.1434).
Syphilis is a 'great imitator': its protean mucocutaneous and systemic features overlap with many other diseases, so it must be considered broadly (Harrison 22e p.1430-1431).

Untreated primary and secondary lesions resolve spontaneously, but infection persists. In the preantibiotic era about one-third of untreated patients with latent infection progressed to tertiary disease; the Tuskegee Study showed untreated syphilis raised the death rate ~17%, largely from cardiovascular disease. With early treatment, prognosis is excellent and tertiary syphilis is now nearly eliminated in Western countries; the clinical response to therapy for benign tertiary (gumma) disease is usually impressive. Congenital syphilis prognosis is poor when fulminant disease is clinically apparent at birth, but adequate maternal treatment before the 16th week of pregnancy should prevent fetal damage. Response to therapy is monitored by a fourfold decline in VDRL/RPR titer (Harrison 22e p.1430, p.1432, p.1435).

Neurosyphilis at any stage: meningeal syphilis (headache, neck stiffness, cranial nerve involvement, seizures, mental status change), meningovascular syphilis (stroke syndrome in a relatively young adult), or late parenchymatous disease (general paresis, tabes dorsalis) (Harrison 22e p.1432)
Ocular syphilis (uveitis, iritis, optic neuritis, pupillary abnormalities)—permanent blindness may result without prompt diagnosis and treatment (Harrison 22e p.1431)
Otic syphilis (sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo, tinnitus)—deafness may result if untreated (Harrison 22e p.1431)
Cardiovascular syphilis: aortitis with aortic regurgitation, saccular aneurysm of the ascending aorta, or coronary ostial stenosis (Harrison 22e p.1432)
Maternal syphilis in pregnancy: high risk of fetal loss, stillbirth, prematurity, neonatal death, and congenital syphilis (Harrison 22e p.1432)
Serum RPR titer >=1:32 marks higher risk of neurosyphilis (Harrison 22e p.1432, p.1434)

Disease is described by clinical stage rather than a graded severity score: primary syphilis (chancre with regional lymphadenopathy); secondary syphilis (generalized mucocutaneous rash including palms and soles, condylomata lata, mucous patches, constitutional symptoms); latent syphilis (reactive serology, normal CSF, no clinical signs; early latent <1 year vs late latent >=1 year or unknown duration); tertiary/late syphilis (gumma, cardiovascular syphilis, late neurosyphilis). Neurosyphilis spans a continuum: early (asymptomatic meningitis, meningeal and meningovascular syphilis) and late parenchymatous disease (general paresis, tabes dorsalis). Congenital syphilis is divided into early (within first 2 years) and late (after 2 years) (Harrison 22e p.1428, p.1431-1433).

chunks.text: Syringomyelia is characterised by a longitudinal cavity within the spinal cord that disrupts neural tissue from the centre outward. Altered cerebrospinal fluid dynamics, often related to obstruction at the craniocervical junction as in Chiari I malformation, are thought to drive fluid accumulation and cavity expansion. The central location preferentially damages the decussating spinothalamic fibres, producing dissociated sensory loss, and progressive enlargement affects anterior horn cells, long tracts, and autonomic pathways.

SLE arises from multiple immunoregulatory defects in genetically predisposed individuals interacting with environmental triggers. There is a strong genetic component (24% vs 2% concordance in monozygotic vs dizygotic twins; >150 GWAS susceptibility loci), with the MHC the most common association and nearly half of loci tied to type 1 interferon production or signaling (e.g., TLR7, IRF5/7/8, STAT4); complement-cascade defects (C1q, C1r, C1s, C2, C4) impair clearance of apoptotic debris and immune complexes and underlie severe monogenic disease. Environmental contributors include UV light, crystalline silica, smoking, sex hormones, Epstein-Barr virus, and gut-microbiome-related increased intestinal permeability. Innate defects cause excess cellular debris (high neutrophil turnover and NETosis) that overwhelms macrophage/dendritic clearance, triggering nucleic-acid sensors and TLRs in plasmacytoid dendritic cells to produce type 1 interferon, which sensitizes the adaptive immune system. Loss of B- and T-cell tolerance (including expansion of age-associated B cells, T follicular/peripheral helper cell help, and defective regulatory T cells) drives production of pathogenic autoantibodies; autoantibody-nucleic acid immune complexes deposit in tissue, activate monocytes, and produce inflammation, repair, and eventually fibrosis after recurrent flares.

SLE is an autoimmune disease driven by overactive innate and adaptive immunity, with tissue injury mediated by autoantibodies and immune complexes; cutaneous, musculoskeletal, and renal systems are most often affected, followed by pulmonary, hematologic, cardiovascular, serosal, and CNS involvement (p.2827).

Anti-Ro/SSA antibodies can cross the placenta and cause neonatal lupus (transient rash/lab abnormalities or, less commonly, congenital heart block); high-titer Ro warrants fetal echocardiography screening (p.2836).
Avascular (osteo)necrosis should be suspected when pain is out of proportion in a single hip, shoulder, or knee, particularly with prior corticosteroid use (p.2829).

Some patients are categorized as 'type 1 lupus' (classic immune-driven features such as nephritis, arthritis, vasculitis, generally steroid-responsive) versus 'type 2 lupus' (fatigue, diffuse pain, cognitive dysfunction/'brain fog', less responsive to immunosuppression) (p.2827-2828).

Roughly 90% of patients are women, most of childbearing age; in the US the highest prevalence is in Black women, then Hispanic, White, and Asian/Pacific Islander women, and non-White patients tend to have more severe disease (p.2827).
Autoantibodies can be detectable years before clinical diagnosis, so seropositivity helps attribute nonspecific constitutional symptoms to SLE (p.2827, p.2830).

ANA at a titer of at least 1:80 is the best screening test and is present in nearly all patients; repeatedly negative immunofluorescence ANA makes the diagnosis unlikely, though about 5% of patients are ANA-negative (p.2832).

Anti-dsDNA (present in ~40-60%, specificity ~75-99%) and anti-Sm (present in ~30%, highly specific) are the only ANA subtypes in the EULAR/ACR criteria; rising anti-dsDNA with falling C3/C4 signals active disease, especially impending nephritis (p.2832, p.2830).

Lupus arthritis is a nonerosive polyarthritis of wrists, MCP/PIP joints, and knees; periarticular ligament damage can cause reversible Jaccoud-like deformities, and overlap with rheumatoid arthritis is termed 'rhupus' (p.2829).

The classic malar 'butterfly' rash spares the nasolabial folds (distinguishing it from rosacea); subacute cutaneous lupus is photosensitive and linked to anti-Ro/SSA, while discoid lesions are the most common chronic cutaneous form (p.2829).

Nephritis occurs in about 35% of patients, may be asymptomatic, and warrants screening every 3 months with a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio; biopsy is generally prompted by UPCr >0.5 or declining renal function (p.2830, p.2833).

Antiphospholipid antibodies are present in ~50% of patients and markedly raise risk of arterial/venous thrombosis, thrombocytopenia, recurrent fetal loss, Libman-Sacks endocarditis, and stroke (p.2830, p.2832).

Treating ANA positivity as diagnostic: ANA occurs at low titer in healthy people and in many other autoimmune diseases; diagnosis ultimately rests on clinical judgment, and classification criteria were designed for trial enrollment, not diagnosis.
Excluding SLE because ANA is negative: about 5% of patients are ANA-negative, where anti-Ro/SSA can support the diagnosis.
Missing asymptomatic lupus nephritis or cytopenias by not screening quarterly, since renal and hematologic disease can be present without symptoms.
Attributing acute pulmonary infiltrates to lupus pneumonitis when infection looks identical on imaging.
Ascribing psychosis or confusion to neuropsychiatric lupus without ruling out glucocorticoid-induced psychosis and infectious encephalitis.
Overlooking avascular necrosis as a cause of disproportionate single-joint pain in patients on corticosteroids.
Confusing drug-induced lupus (antihistone-positive, usually sparing kidney/brain, resolving after withdrawal) with idiopathic SLE.
Using estrogen-containing contraceptives or HRT in patients with antiphospholipid antibodies or active disease, increasing thromboembolism risk.
Using direct oral anticoagulants instead of warfarin for concomitant APS, or continuing teratogenic agents (mycophenolate, methotrexate, warfarin) in pregnancy.

Prognosis and survival vary widely by geographic region, race/ethnicity, and access to care and medications. Most patients have active disease despite therapy or recurrent flares; about 15% have relatively mild disease. Renal disease is a major determinant of outcome: roughly 20% of US patients with class IV lupus nephritis die or develop ESRD within 10 years, and non-White patients more often progress to ESRD. Accelerated atherosclerosis becomes a leading cause of death after about 5 years of disease, with elevated myocardial infarction and stroke rates driven by both traditional risk factors and lupus-specific factors (antiphospholipid antibodies, high disease activity, low C3, high glucocorticoid dose, elevated homocysteine/leptin). Glucocorticoids contribute to irreversible, dose-dependent organ damage (cataracts, osteoporotic fractures, avascular necrosis, diabetes) even at low doses; class V nephritis carries a better renal prognosis than class III/IV. Sustained low disease activity (LLDAS) for 2 or more years is associated with significantly less damage, and meta-analyses suggest an increased overall risk of cancer and cancer-related death.
Rapidly declining renal function or rising proteinuria suggesting class III/IV proliferative lupus nephritis (~20% of class IV cases die or reach ESRD within 10 years)
Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage or acute pneumonitis (life-threatening pulmonary involvement)
Severe neuropsychiatric disease: psychosis, seizures, transverse myelitis, stroke
Severe thrombocytopenia (<20,000-50,000/uL) with bleeding risk, or life-threatening hemolytic anemia
Atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome / thrombotic microangiopathy (hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, schistocytes, low ADAMTS13, high LDH)
Mesenteric vasculitis (risk of intestinal perforation, bleeding, ischemia)
Antiphospholipid syndrome with arterial/venous thrombosis or catastrophic APS
Pulmonary arterial hypertension or prior arterial thrombosis in pregnancy (highest maternal mortality risk)
New chest pain in a young patient given accelerated atherosclerosis and premature coronary disease

Lupus nephritis is graded by the International Society of Nephrology/Renal Pathology Society (ISN/RPS) classes: I (mesangial deposits without hypercellularity), II (mesangial proliferative), III (focal proliferative glomerulonephritis), IV (diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis), and V (membranous), with III/IV +/- V combinations carrying the highest risk; class V (~20% of nephritis) more often presents with nephrotic syndrome but has a better prognosis than III/IV. Disease activity is quantified with the SLEDAI (and SLEDAI-2K), where low disease activity is a score of 0-4 and remission a score of 0 (with stable hydroxychloroquine/immunosuppressive use and prednisone equivalent 5 mg/day or less). Overall disease severity is also stratified clinically as mild (constitutional symptoms, mild arthritis, rash <=9% BSA, platelets 50-100, SLEDAI <=6), moderate (rheumatoid-like arthritis, rash 9-18% BSA, platelets 20-50, serositis, SLEDAI 7-12), and severe (major organ-threatening disease such as cerebritis, myelitis, pneumonitis, mesenteric vasculitis; platelets <20; TTP-like or hemophagocytic syndrome; rash >18% BSA; SLEDAI >12). Treat-to-target endpoints include LLDAS and DORIS remission, and trials use SRI, BICLA, and CLASI instruments.

Nailfold capillaroscopy (low-power stereomicroscope or videocapillaroscopy under immersion oil) (p.2867)
High-resolution chest CT (HRCT) for ILD detection and prognostic assessment of fibrosis extent (p.2868)
Pulmonary function testing including FVC and DLCO for ILD monitoring (a DLCO reduction out of proportion to lung volumes suggests pulmonary vascular disease) (p.2868)
Doppler echocardiography for PAH screening; right heart (cardiac) catheterization to confirm PAH and exclude venoocclusive/postcapillary causes (p.2868)

Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (associated with gadolinium exposure) (p.2860)

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura / thrombotic microangiopathy - scleroderma renal crisis is sometimes initially misdiagnosed as TTP (p.2871)

SSc is a chronic, often progressive disease of unknown etiology defined pathologically by widespread microangiopathy (fibroproliferative vasculopathy with capillary loss and obliteration) combined with multiorgan fibrosis, on a background of autoimmunity. An initial vascular insult in a genetically predisposed individual (modest HLA class II and immune-regulatory gene associations) triggers inflammation, generation of SSc-specific autoantibodies, and sustained activation of fibroblasts/myofibroblasts driven by mediators such as TGF-beta, IL-6, CTGF, PDGF and endothelin. Maladaptive repair leads to replacement of normal tissue with rigid, avascular, acellular connective tissue affecting skin, lungs, heart, GI tract, kidneys and other organs (p.2859-2866).

Two major subsets: limited cutaneous SSc (lcSSc) with skin confined to fingers, distal limbs and face (trunk spared) and an indolent course; and diffuse cutaneous SSc (dcSSc) with rapidly progressive skin involvement of fingers, extremities, face and trunk (p.2859, 2866).
SSc patients should be screened for PAH at initial evaluation and annually thereafter, and screened for ILD with regular pulmonary monitoring for several years after diagnosis (p.2868, 2872).
SSc sine scleroderma: characteristic Raynaud's plus typical clinical/serologic features of SSc in the absence of detectable skin thickening (~10% of patients) (p.2859, 2866, 2872).

In lcSSc, Raynaud's phenomenon typically precedes sclerodactyly and other manifestations, sometimes by years; the CREST constellation (calcinosis cutis, Raynaud's, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia) is a distinct lcSSc subset (p.2859).
Bilateral symmetrical skin thickening starting in the fingers and advancing distal-to-proximal is the hallmark distinguishing SSc from other connective tissue diseases (p.2867).

SSc-specific autoantibodies are mutually exclusive and aid risk stratification: anti-centromere is associated with lcSSc and isolated PAH (renal crisis rare); anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70) with dcSSc, extensive skin, early ILD and cardiac involvement; anti-RNA polymerase III with rapidly progressive skin, renal crisis and contemporaneous cancer (p.2864, 2871).
Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) are detectable in virtually all SSc patients, even in early/preclinical stages (p.2864, 2871).

Nailfold capillaroscopy distinguishes primary Raynaud's disease (regular, evenly spaced parallel hairpin loops) from secondary Raynaud's/SSc (giant capillaries, dilated and distorted loops, microhemorrhages, capillary dropout) and helps establish early SSc diagnosis (p.2867, 2871).
ILD and pulmonary vascular disease together account for the majority of SSc-related deaths; survival is particularly poor when both coexist (p.2868).

Scleroderma renal crisis presents with accelerated hypertension plus acute kidney injury, occurs in <15% of patients almost always within 4 years of onset, and is associated with diffuse/progressive skin involvement and anti-RNA polymerase III (up to 50%); anti-centromere appears protective (p.2870-2871).
Palpable tendon friction rubs are associated with increased risk of renal and cardiac complications and reduced survival, and may be a harbinger of impending renal crisis (p.2871).

Early dcSSc may present with only upper-extremity edema and puffy fingers and Raynaud's may be absent, leading to misdiagnosis as arthritis, SLE, myositis or undifferentiated connective tissue disease (p.2872)
Scleroderma renal crisis can be misdiagnosed as TTP or other thrombotic microangiopathy; renal biopsy and von Willebrand factor-cleaving protease activity may help (p.2871)
Glucocorticoids (especially prednisone >=10 mg/d) are associated with precipitating scleroderma renal crisis and should be used only when essential and at low dose in high-risk patients (p.2870)
PFTs and conventional echocardiography are relatively insensitive for early ILD and early cardiac involvement, respectively (p.2868, 2871)
Echocardiography can over- or underestimate pulmonary artery pressures, so PAH must be confirmed by cardiac catheterization (p.2868)
SSc sine scleroderma can be missed because diagnostic skin induration is absent despite organ involvement (p.2872)

Highly variable; dcSSc carries a more rapidly progressive course and worse prognosis than lcSSc. SSc confers a fivefold to eightfold higher age/sex-adjusted mortality, with median survival ~11 years; 5- and 10-year survival are ~70%/55% in dcSSc and ~90%/75% in lcSSc. Major causes of death are PAH, pulmonary fibrosis, GI involvement and cardiac disease. Scleroderma renal crisis carries ~30% 3-year mortality (markedly improved by ACE inhibitors). Poor-prognosis markers include male sex, African ancestry, older age at onset, extensive truncal skin involvement, palpable tendon friction rubs, significant/progressive visceral involvement, and laboratory findings of elevated ESR, anemia, proteinuria and anti-topoisomerase I antibodies (p.2873).

Scleroderma renal crisis: accelerated/new hypertension (generally >150/90 mmHg) with progressive oliguric renal failure - a medical emergency (note ~10% present normotensive, with poorer outcome) (p.2870-2871)
Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with fragmented red cells and thrombocytopenia (hallmark of renal crisis) (p.2871)
New unexplained anemia, thrombocytopenia, pericardial effusion or new tendon friction rubs as harbingers of impending renal crisis (p.2871)
Pulmonary arterial hypertension: exertional dyspnea, near-syncope, loud P2, right heart failure - 3-year survival of untreated PAH <50% (p.2868)
Rapidly progressive ILD with declining FVC (can fall ~30%/year), most rapid in the first 3-5 years (p.2868)
Critical digital ischemia with fingertip ulceration/necrosis and acro-osteolysis (p.2867)

ACR/EULAR classification criteria are >90% specific and sensitive but are intended for research rather than clinical practice; weighted items include skin thickening proximal to MCP joints (score 9), sclerodactyly/puffy fingers, fingertip lesions, telangiectasia, abnormal nailfold capillaries, ILD/PAH, Raynaud's phenomenon, and SSc-specific autoantibodies (anti-centromere, Scl-70, RNA polymerase III). Clinically, patients are stratified into limited cutaneous and diffuse cutaneous subsets by extent of skin involvement (p.2860).

Massive pulmonary embolism (shares hypotension/tachycardia and pulsus paradoxus) (p.147, p.1906)

Hemorrhagic shock (cause of pulsus paradoxus) (p.1906)
Severe obstructive lung disease / asthma (cause of pulsus paradoxus) (p.1906)
Acute MI with cardiogenic shock (hypotension + tachycardia in chest-pain patient) (p.147)
Acute aortic dissection (may extend into the pericardium and itself cause tamponade) (p.147, p.1938)

Pericardial fluid accumulates between the visceral (epicardial) and parietal pericardial layers. Tamponade develops when intrapericardial pressure rises enough to exceed the filling pressures of the cardiac chambers, generally the right ventricle, impairing diastolic filling. Because the relatively non-distensible pericardial sac determines tolerance, the rate of fluid accumulation is more important than absolute volume: slow accumulation allows large effusions without compromise, while rapid accumulation (trauma, cardiac rupture, procedural perforation, aortic dissection into the pericardium) causes tamponade at small volumes. Inspiratory augmentation of right-heart filling at the expense of the left, mediated by exaggerated interventricular dependence within the fixed pericardial space, produces pulsus paradoxus (p.1906, p.1938).

Tamponade is fundamentally a clinical diagnosis in an unstable patient; the textbook triad is hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure with neck-vein distention, and quiet/muffled heart sounds (p.630).
It is the balance between intrapericardial pressure and ventricular (especially right ventricular) filling pressure that drives compression, not the absolute volume of fluid (p.1938).

Rate of accumulation matters more than total volume: slowly forming effusions (e.g. malignant) can become large without classic tamponade physiology, whereas rapid accumulation (e.g. cardiac rupture, perforation, aortic dissection into the pericardium) can cause tamponade with only a small effusion (p.1938).
Pulsus paradoxus is an inspiratory fall in systolic pressure of more than 10 mmHg and represents an exaggerated form of normal interventricular dependence (p.1906).

Measure pulsus paradoxus by deflating the cuff slowly and noting the gap between the pressure where Korotkoff sounds are first heard (only in expiration) and the pressure where they are heard with every beat regardless of respiration; a difference >15 mmHg may even be palpable at the brachial or femoral pulse (p.1906).
A pulsus paradoxus exceeding 12 mmHg in a patient with a large pericardial effusion is highly predictive of tamponade (reported sensitivity ~98%, specificity ~83%) (p.1910).

The ECG triad of sinus tachycardia, low QRS voltage, and total electrical alternans (beat-to-beat P-QRS-T alternation) strongly suggests pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology, though it is insensitive (p.1917).

Total electrical alternans (whole-complex) is relatively specific for effusion/tamponade; in contrast, pure repolarization (ST-T/U-wave) alternans signals electrical instability and risk of ventricular arrhythmia, not tamponade (p.1917).
Echocardiography is the initial test of choice for suspected effusion/tamponade and can usually be done rapidly at the bedside (p.1938).

Do not delay decompression in a hemodynamically unstable patient waiting for confirmatory tests; tamponade is a clinical/emergency diagnosis and instability requires immediate drainage (p.147, p.630).
Failing to appreciate the urgency of the situation is a recognized diagnostic error for tamponade (listed among can't-miss time-critical diagnoses) (p.102).
Pulsus paradoxus can be hard to measure or unreliable in tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, or tachypnea (p.1906).

A large slowly-accumulating effusion may lack classic tamponade signs, while a small rapidly-accumulating effusion may already be causing tamponade; judging severity by volume alone is misleading (p.1938).

In malignant tamponade, relatively specific signs (paradoxical pulse, diminished heart sounds, pulsus alternans, friction rub) are LESS common than in nonmalignant disease, so their absence does not exclude tamponade (p.630).
ECG and chest radiograph are abnormal in ~90% of malignant pericardial cases but about half of those abnormalities are nonspecific (p.630).

Outcome depends heavily on cause and timeliness of drainage. Untreated tuberculous pericarditis is usually fatal and even treated TB pericarditis carries case-fatality rates up to ~40% in some series, with risk of progression to constrictive pericarditis. Cancer patients whose pericardial fluid contains malignant cells on cytology have very poor survival. After percutaneous catheter drainage of malignant effusions the recurrence rate is ~20%, and a subset develop paradoxical hemodynamic worsening after drainage (post-drainage low cardiac output syndrome) (p.630, p.1432).
Hypotension with tachycardia in a chest-pain patient mandates rapid evaluation for tamponade as one of the immediately life-threatening causes (p.147)
Life-threatening hemodynamic instability with acute tamponade requires immediate fluid drainage (p.630)
Hemorrhagic tamponade from cardiac rupture, procedural perforation, or aortic dissection into the pericardium can be catastrophic at small effusion volumes (p.1938)

chunks.text: A panarteritis of medium- and large-sized arteries, classically branches of the carotid (especially the temporal artery) but systemically involving the aorta and its branches. Histology shows mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate within the vessel wall with frequent giant cell formation, intimal proliferation, and fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina; organ damage results from ischemia of involved vessels. It is considered an antigen-driven process: CD4+ T cells enter via the adventitial vasa vasorum, become activated, and drive macrophage differentiation, with restricted clonal T-cell expansion suggesting an arterial-wall antigen. Lesional T cells produce mainly IL-2 and IFN-gamma; both IFN-gamma-producing TH1 and IL-17-producing TH17 lineages contribute and may differ in glucocorticoid responsiveness. Associated with HLA-DR4 and HLA-DRB1*04 variants. (Harrison 22e p.2902)

chunks.text: A one-way valve mechanism allows air to enter the pleural space during inspiration but prevents its escape, so intrapleural pressure rises progressively. The affected lung collapses, and mounting pressure pushes the mediastinum towards the opposite side, compressing the other lung and, critically, kinking the great veins to impair venous return to the heart. The combination of impaired gas exchange and obstructed venous return produces profound hypoxia and obstructive shock. Positive-pressure ventilation can accelerate air accumulation and the development of tension physiology.

GCTs originate from the primordial germ cell, and most malignant GCTs arise from germ cell neoplasia in situ; the precise molecular steps driving progression from in situ neoplasia to invasive tumor are not fully defined. Genetic analysis shows excess copy number of isochromosome 12p in most cases, and genome-wide studies implicate several loci, most strongly KITLG on chromosome 12. Tumors are classified as seminoma (must be 100% seminoma; any mixed tumor is treated as nonseminomatous) or nonseminoma. Seminomas may contain syncytiotrophoblastic cells that secrete hCG but never secrete AFP. Nonseminomatous subtypes include embryonal carcinoma (the most undifferentiated, able to differentiate into the others, and may secrete AFP and/or hCG), yolk sac tumor (often AFP-secreting), choriocarcinoma (aggressive, often very high hCG), and teratoma (mature, immature, or malignant somatic tissue derived from two or more germ layers).

Germ cell tumors (GCTs) account for about 95% of all testicular neoplasms; non-GCTs of the testis are much less common, and roughly 5% of GCTs arise in extragonadal sites such as the mediastinum, retroperitoneum, and pineal gland.
Genetically, most GCTs show excess copies of isochromosome 12p (i[12p]); the strongest heritable-risk locus identified is KITLG (KIT ligand) on chromosome 12, and overall heritability is nearly 50%.
Teratoma is chemotherapy-resistant and must be managed surgically; the other nonseminomatous subtypes (embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma) and seminomas are chemosensitive.

Sperm banking should be offered before chemotherapy: about 30% of newly diagnosed patients already have severe oligospermia or azoospermia, and treatment-related sterility is common (though ~80% recover spermatogenesis over years).
Testicular cancer is regarded as a model curable neoplasm: about 95% of newly diagnosed patients are cured, and treatment is dictated by pathology (seminoma vs nonseminoma) and stage.
It is the most common malignancy in adolescent and young adult males (age 15-39), most often diagnosed in Caucasians and much less common in African Americans; incidence in those over 50 is rising.

Strongest risk factors are a prior history of GCT, cryptorchidism, and germ cell neoplasia in situ; a prior GCT carries a 1-2% risk of a contralateral tumor (usually metachronous), and cryptorchidism raises risk roughly four- to sixfold.
Orchidopexy before puberty reduces but does not eliminate the cryptorchidism-associated risk, and the contralateral normally descended testis also remains at risk.

A solid mass on scrotal ultrasound (typically hypoechoic, sometimes multifocal) must be considered malignant until proven otherwise; transscrotal aspiration or biopsy must never be performed because it risks seeding the scrotum or inguinal nodes.

Tumor marker biology is key: seminomas never secrete AFP, so a histologic seminoma with elevated AFP is managed as a nonseminomatous GCT; hCG can be elevated in both seminoma and nonseminoma, and choriocarcinoma may produce markedly high hCG.

Serum tumor markers (AFP, hCG, LDH) should be measured before and after orchiectomy; AFP is elevated in roughly 60-70% of nonseminomatous GCTs, while most seminomas and up to a third of nonseminomas have no marker elevation.

Lymphatic spread follows a predictable pattern: left-sided tumors drain first to left paraaortic nodes below the left renal vessels, right-sided tumors to aortocaval nodes below the right renal vessels, then to retrocrural, mediastinal, and supraclavicular nodes; the lung is the most common hematogenous site.
Performing transscrotal biopsy or aspiration of a testicular mass, which can seed the scrotum or inguinal nodes and should never be done.
Misclassifying a histologic seminoma with elevated AFP as a true seminoma, when it must be approached as a nonseminomatous GCT.
Over-relying on tumor markers for diagnosis, since most seminomas and up to a third of nonseminomas have no marker elevation.
Diagnostic delay (not uncommon) leading to more advanced stage at presentation, including mislabeling a GCT as epididymitis/orchitis.

Assuming residual postchemotherapy masses are benign: imaging cannot distinguish necrosis/fibrosis from teratoma or viable tumor, and enlarging cystic retroperitoneal masses with normalized markers may represent growing teratoma syndrome.
Forgetting that LDH is a nonspecific marker whose main role is risk classification in metastatic disease, not diagnosis.

Outcomes are excellent overall, with about 95% of newly diagnosed patients cured. Nearly all stage I patients (seminoma and nonseminoma) achieve cure. In metastatic (stage III) disease classified by the International Germ Cell Consensus Classification, most patients have good-risk disease with >90% cure; intermediate- and poor-risk groups have approximately 80% and 50% five-year survival, respectively. About 20-30% of patients with metastatic GCT treated with cisplatin-based chemotherapy do not achieve durable control, with most relapses occurring within 2 years of completing treatment.

Three main AJCC TNM-based stages: Stage I limited to the testis; Stage II involving retroperitoneal lymph nodes (subgrouped IIA/IIB/IIC by node size: <=2 cm, >2-5 cm, >5 cm); Stage III with lymph node involvement beyond the retroperitoneum and/or distant metastases. Stage III is further stratified into good-, intermediate-, and poor-risk groups by the International Germ Cell Consensus Classification using histology, primary site, presence of nonpulmonary visceral metastases, and postorchiectomy marker levels (e.g., for NSGCT good-risk: AFP <1000 ng/mL, hCG <5000 mIU/mL, LDH <1.5x ULN; poor-risk: AFP >10,000 ng/mL, hCG >50,000 mIU/mL, LDH >10x ULN, mediastinal primary, or nonpulmonary visceral metastases). Marker half-lives: AFP 5-7 days, hCG 24-36 hours.

chunks.text: Testicular torsion is twisting of the spermatic cord that obstructs venous drainage first and then arterial inflow, producing ischaemia and, if unrelieved, haemorrhagic infarction of the testis. The intravaginal form, most common in adolescents, is facilitated by the bell-clapper deformity where the tunica vaginalis surrounds the testis and epididymis completely, allowing the testis to rotate freely within it. Extravaginal torsion occurs in neonates when the entire tunica and its contents twist above the level of attachment. The degree of twisting and the duration of ischaemia determine the likelihood of viability.

Tetanus is caused by tetanus toxin (tetanospasmin) produced by Clostridium tetani, an anaerobic, gram-positive, spore-forming rod whose resilient environmental spores enter through wounds, abrasions, or the umbilical stump and germinate in anaerobic tissue. Only toxin-producing organisms cause disease. The toxin is a 150-kDa protein cleaved into a heavy (100-kDa) and light (50-kDa) chain joined by a disulfide bond; the heavy-chain carboxy terminal binds presynaptic motor nerve terminals, leading to internalization and retrograde intra-axonal transport to motor nuclei of cranial nerves and spinal cord ventral horns. The toxin then crosses the synapse into GABA-ergic presynaptic inhibitory interneurons, where the light chain (a zinc-dependent endopeptidase) cleaves VAMP2 (synaptobrevin), blocking inhibitory neurotransmitter release. Loss of inhibition produces unregulated motor activity (muscle rigidity and spasms), and similar disinhibition in the autonomic system produces autonomic instability; elevated circulating catecholamines in severe disease drive cardiovascular complications.

Trismus (lockjaw) is typically the earliest symptom, progressing to neck and trunk rigidity, dysphagia, and pharyngeal/laryngeal spasm; risus sardonicus and opisthotonos reflect the characteristic sustained muscle rigidity.
Natural infection does not confer protective immunity because tetanus toxin is poorly immunogenic, so survivors still require a full primary immunization course.
Generalized tetanus is the most common form, characterized by muscle rigidity with generalized spasms; localized tetanus affects only isolated muscle groups but can progress to the generalized form.
Cephalic tetanus is a localized form involving the cranial nerves, which can cause pharyngeal or laryngeal spasm leading to aspiration, airway obstruction, or respiratory failure.

Neonatal tetanus classically presents with loss of the ability to suck and cry (a newborn normal in the first 2 days who deteriorates between days 3 and 28), poor feeding, rigidity, and generalized spasms.
Laryngeal spasm causing apnea or respiratory failure is a life-threatening event and, without immediate respiratory support, is the most common cause of death.

Autonomic nervous system disturbance characteristically emerges in the second week of severe disease, with fluctuating heart rate and blood pressure, sweating, gastrointestinal stasis, and increased tracheal secretions; cardiovascular events then become the major threat.
Disease severity is graded with the Ablett classification (Grades I-IV), where Grade IV is Grade III plus autonomic dysfunction.
Abdominal rigidity in tetanus is characteristically continuous, distinguishing it from the rigidity of peritonitis or an acute abdomen.

Roughly 20-30% of cases have no identifiable entry wound; superficial limb abrasions are the most common portal of entry in adults, while deeper injuries (open fractures, drug injection) are linked to more severe disease.
Diagnosis is clinical - waiting for laboratory confirmation is misguided; a positive wound culture does not confirm and a protective antitetanus IgG (>0.1 IU/mL) argues against the diagnosis.
Treatment should not be delayed once tetanus is clinically diagnosed.
Assuming natural infection confers immunity: tetanus toxin is poorly immunogenic, so survivors still require a full primary immunization course.
Overlooking absence of a wound: about 20-30% of cases have no identifiable entry site, so a negative wound history does not exclude tetanus.
Failure to identify and debride the entry wound (to remove anaerobic foci) can lead to recurrent or prolonged disease.

Long-term ICU care with deep sedation predisposes to hospital-acquired infections (ventilator-associated pneumonia, bloodstream and urinary tract infection, sepsis), venous thromboembolism, and other complications - prognosis depends on controlling these.

Tetanus has a high survival rate when complications are controlled and interventions are prompt, though recovery is prolonged, typically taking about 4-6 weeks. Rapid onset predicts more severe disease: the shorter the incubation period (wound to first symptom) and the period of onset (first symptom to first generalized or pharyngeal/laryngeal spasm), the worse the prognosis. The Tetanus Severity Score (TSS) outperforms the Dakar and Philips scores for predicting severity and outcome (sensitivity ~66%, specificity ~91%; a cutoff score of >=8 predicts death). Surviving adults, especially the elderly, may have reduced long-term functional outcomes, while affected children and neonates have a higher incidence of neurologic sequelae (neonates may face increased risk of learning disabilities, behavioral problems, cerebral palsy, and deafness).
Laryngeal spasm with apnea or respiratory failure - life-threatening and the most common cause of death.

Autonomic nervous system disturbance (labile heart rate and blood pressure, sweating, GI stasis, increased tracheal secretions), typically in the second week, marking high cardiovascular mortality risk.
Short incubation period (wound to first symptom) and short period of onset (first symptom to first generalized/pharyngeal/laryngeal spasm) - rapid progression predicts worse outcome.
Dysphagia with laryngeal hyperactivity, which makes airway management difficult and raises aspiration risk.

Ablett classification of tetanus severity: Grade I (mild) - mild trismus, general spasticity, no respiratory compromise, no spasms, no dysphagia; Grade II (moderate) - moderate trismus and rigidity, short spasms, mild dysphagia, moderate respiratory involvement, respiratory rate >30/min; Grade III (severe) - severe trismus, generalized rigidity, prolonged spasms, severe dysphagia, apneic spells, pulse >120/min, respiratory rate >40/min; Grade IV (very severe) - Grade III features plus autonomic dysfunction. Prognostic scoring is provided by the Tetanus Severity Score (TSS), which is superior to the Dakar and Philips scores.

Anterior and cephalad deviation of the infundibular septum during development produces right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, a malaligned ventricular septal defect, and an aorta that overrides the defect. Obstruction to pulmonary outflow, combined with the large communication between the ventricles, allows deoxygenated right ventricular blood to shunt right-to-left into the aorta, producing systemic desaturation. The volume of pulmonary blood flow and the resulting cyanosis depend dynamically on the balance between the fixed and dynamic outflow obstruction and systemic vascular resistance; a fall in systemic resistance or a spasm of the infundibulum increases right-to-left shunting and precipitates a hypercyanotic spell.

The most common cyanotic congenital heart lesion beyond infancy, comprising four features: a large ventricular septal defect, an overriding aorta, right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, and right ventricular hypertrophy.
The degree of cyanosis reflects the severity of right ventricular outflow obstruction; some infants are minimally cyanotic (so-called pink Fallot) while others present with marked desaturation.

A harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border arises from the outflow obstruction, not from the septal defect itself; the murmur softens during a hypercyanotic spell as flow across the outflow tract falls.
Hypercyanotic (tet) spells are episodes of sudden, worsening cyanosis with agitation and deep breathing, often on waking or after feeding or crying, and can be life-threatening.

Calming manoeuvres for a spell aim to increase systemic vascular resistance and outflow through the lungs: comforting the child, bringing the knees to the chest, and giving oxygen, with pharmacological support as needed.
The chest radiograph classically shows a boot-shaped heart with a concave main pulmonary artery segment and normal or reduced pulmonary vascularity.
Echocardiography confirms the anatomy and defines the outflow tract, pulmonary arteries, and coronary artery course before surgery.
Older, unrepaired children may adopt squatting to relieve exertional cyanosis by transiently raising systemic resistance and pulmonary blood flow.
Complete surgical repair, involving closure of the septal defect and relief of outflow obstruction, is the definitive treatment and is usually performed in infancy.
Interpreting a softening or absent murmur reassuringly when it actually signals a severe hypercyanotic spell
Aggressively sedating or agitating an infant in a spell rather than using calming, resistance-raising manoeuvres
Overlooking a duct-dependent lesion in a neonate whose cyanosis worsens as the ductus arteriosus closes
Attributing exertional symptoms or squatting in an older child to behaviour rather than underlying cyanotic heart disease
Failing to screen for associated 22q11.2 deletion and other anomalies

With timely complete surgical repair the long-term outlook is generally good, though survivors need lifelong cardiology follow-up for pulmonary regurgitation, residual outflow obstruction, arrhythmia, and possible need for pulmonary valve replacement. Untreated disease carries high morbidity and mortality from progressive cyanosis, spells, and complications.
Hypercyanotic (tet) spell with deepening cyanosis, agitation, and a disappearing murmur
Loss of consciousness, seizures, or limpness during a spell
Duct-dependent presentation with severe outflow obstruction and cardiovascular collapse as the ductus closes
Profound or worsening hypoxaemia unresponsive to calming measures
Metabolic acidosis indicating inadequate pulmonary blood flow
