chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: AV nodal myocytes sit at a relatively high resting membrane potential (~-60 mV), exhibit slow phase-0 upstrokes mediated by L-type calcium current (with a relative lack of fast sodium current), and show spontaneous phase-4 depolarization, conferring backup automaticity. Weak electrical coupling from sparse gap junctions (predominantly connexin-40) plus increased extracellular volume slows conduction and protects the ventricle. The AV junction comprises a transitional (atrionodal) cell zone showing decremental conduction, the compact node, and the penetrating His bundle; conduction continues through the His, right and left bundle branches, and the fast-conducting Purkinje network (1-3 m/s). Bradycardia and block arise when conduction across this axis is compromised by fibrosis/sclerosis, calcification (Lev, Lenegre disease), ischemia/infarction, infiltrative or inflammatory disease, drugs, heightened vagal tone, or congenital/genetic abnormalities; consequences range from fatigue and syncope to asystolic death if no reliable escape emerges. Functional (autonomic/metabolic/drug) causes are often reversible while structural fibrosis is typically permanent.

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: The AV node is specialized for slow conduction, creating a delay between atrial and ventricular activation and acting as the electrical gatekeeper to the ventricle; its intrinsic backup pacemaker (escape) rate is roughly 20-60 beats/min, normally overridden by the faster sinus node (60-100 beats/min).

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: Congenital complete heart block with a narrow QRS typically increases heart rate with exercise, whereas acquired complete heart block (especially wide QRS) does not respond to exercise.

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: Acquired persistent AV conduction failure is rare in healthy adults (estimated incidence about 1 per 5000 per year in the U.S.), but becomes much more common with ischemia, aging/fibrosis, or infiltrative disease.

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: Idiopathic progressive fibrosis/sclerosis of the conduction system is the most common acquired cause, accounting for roughly 50% of AV block; it often begins in the fourth decade and is accelerated by atherosclerosis, hypertension, and diabetes.

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: First-degree AV block means every atrial impulse still conducts but with an abnormally prolonged PR interval (>200 ms); the term block is a misnomer since conduction is delayed, not interrupted.

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: Mobitz I (Wenckebach) second-degree block shows progressive PR lengthening before a dropped beat with grouped beating and progressive RR shortening; it is typically within the AV node, hemodynamically stable, and usually does not warrant pacing when asymptomatic.

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: Mobitz II second-degree block shows a fixed PR interval before a dropped beat, is usually infranodal with a wider QRS, carries a risk of sudden death from an unreliable escape rhythm, and warrants permanent pacing even without symptoms.

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: In 2:1 AV block the ECG cannot reliably distinguish type I from type II; a PR <160 ms with a wide QRS before the conducted beat favors infranodal (type II) block.

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: QRS width of the escape rhythm localizes the block: a narrow QRS escape implies block in the AV node or proximal His with a faster, more stable junctional rhythm, whereas a wide QRS escape (without preexisting bundle branch block) implies distal His or bundle branch block and a slower, less reliable rhythm.

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: Vagal maneuvers and carotid sinus massage slow AV nodal conduction but may paradoxically improve infranodal conduction, while atropine, isoproterenol, and exercise improve AV nodal conduction but may worsen infranodal conduction - useful for localizing the level of block.

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: On the His bundle electrogram, the AH interval (AV nodal conduction) is normally <130 ms and the HV interval (His-Purkinje conduction) is normally <=55 ms; a markedly prolonged HV interval predicts progression to higher-grade block.

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: Functional causes of AV block (autonomic, metabolic/endocrine, drug-related) tend to be reversible, whereas most structural causes producing fibrosis are permanent.

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: Mislabeling 2:1 AV block as type I when it may be infranodal type II - the surface ECG cannot reliably distinguish them

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: Assuming all AV block is benign vagal phenomenon and missing serious infranodal disease that warrants pacing despite absent symptoms

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: Overlooking reversible/treatable causes (offending drugs, electrolyte derangement, ischemia, hypothyroidism, sleep apnea, Lyme carditis) before committing to permanent therapy

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: Failing to pursue advanced imaging for infiltrative disease (e.g., sarcoidosis) when AV block presents at a younger age (<=60 years)

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: Misinterpreting Mobitz I at very short paced cycle lengths as pathologic - it can be a normal physiologic response; it is abnormal at cycle lengths >500 ms (<120 beats/min) without high vagal tone

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: Not recognizing that a new perivalvular abscess in endocarditis can present as AV block requiring urgent surgery

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: Prognosis depends heavily on the level of block. AV-nodal (proximal) block - including Mobitz I and most inferior-MI-related block - tends to have a faster, stable narrow-complex escape and is often reversible with a favorable outcome. Infranodal (distal His-Purkinje) block, Mobitz II, and high-grade block in anterior MI carry unstable wide-complex escape rhythms, higher mortality, and a risk of sudden asystolic death, so pacing is indicated even when asymptomatic. Functional/reversible causes generally resolve; structural fibrotic disease is usually permanent and progressive.

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: Wide-complex escape rhythm at a slow rate (e.g., ~30 beats/min) implying infranodal block and an unreliable escape

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: Mobitz II second-degree or complete (third-degree) heart block

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: Syncope or presyncope attributable to bradycardia

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: Markedly prolonged HV interval (>100 ms carries an annual incidence of complete AV block approaching 10%)

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: High-grade AV block complicating anterior MI (distal block, wide unstable escape, high mortality)

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: New AV block with infective endocarditis suggesting perivalvular abscess

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: Alternating bundle branch block or bifascicular/trifascicular block with intermittent third-degree block

chunks.diseaseName: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
chunks.text: Electrocardiographic grading: First-degree AV block - all atrial impulses conduct but PR is prolonged (>200 ms), delay usually within the AV node. Second-degree AV block - intermittent failure of AV conduction; Type I/Mobitz I/Wenckebach (progressive PR prolongation until a dropped beat, usually AV-nodal) and Type II/Mobitz II (fixed PR before a dropped beat, usually infranodal, often with wide QRS). Third-degree (complete) AV block - complete AV dissociation with a ventricular (escape) rate slower than the atrial rate.

Fractionation of serum bilirubin into conjugated (direct) and unconjugated (indirect) components

Bilirubin, the end product of heme degradation (chiefly from senescent erythrocyte hemoglobin), circulates tightly bound to albumin and is processed by hepatocytes in four steps: carrier-mediated uptake, intracellular binding to glutathione-S-transferases, conjugation with glucuronic acid by UGT1A1 (the physiologically critical isoform encoded by exon A1 plus shared exons 2-5 of the UGT1 gene complex on chromosome 2), and ATP-dependent canalicular excretion of mono- and diglucuronides via MRP2. A portion of glucuronides is also exported into the portal circulation by MRP3 and recaptured by sinusoidal OATP1B1/OATP1B3. Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia arises from overproduction (hemolysis, ineffective erythropoiesis, resorption of large hematomas/infarcts), decreased hepatic uptake (drugs such as rifampin, novobiocin; contributory in Gilbert syndrome), or impaired conjugation (neonatal immaturity, breast-milk jaundice, drug inhibition of UGT1A1, and hereditary UGT1A1 defects of Crigler-Najjar I/II and Gilbert syndrome). Gilbert syndrome most often reflects a homozygous extra TA insertion (A[TA]7TAA rather than A[TA]6TAA) in the UGT1A1 promoter reducing enzyme expression; Crigler-Najjar reflects coding/structural UGT1 mutations causing absent (type I) or markedly reduced (type II) activity. Predominantly conjugated familial hyperbilirubinemias result from defective canalicular excretion: Dubin-Johnson from MRP2 (ABCC2) mutation and Rotor from combined OATP1B1/OATP1B3 deficiency impairing reuptake of refluxed conjugated bilirubin.

Bilirubin is the terminal product of heme catabolism, with roughly 70-90% derived from breakdown of hemoglobin in senescent red cells; hepatic handling involves four linked steps: carrier-mediated uptake, intracellular binding to glutathione-S-transferases (ligandins), conjugation by UGT1A1, and canalicular excretion (Harrison 22e p.2637-2638).

A rapidly rising neonatal unconjugated bilirubin, or absolute levels above ~340 micromol/L (20 mg/dL), risks bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus) as pigment crosses an immature blood-brain barrier and deposits in the basal ganglia (Harrison 22e p.2639).

Acquired liver disease (acute hepatitis, common bile duct stone) generally produces a mixed conjugated and unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and serum levels or fractions cannot reliably distinguish intrahepatic from extrahepatic obstruction (Harrison 22e p.2640).

Gilbert syndrome impairs glucuronidation of the irinotecan (CPT-11) active metabolite SN-38, predisposing to severe diarrhea and myelosuppression; the HIV protease inhibitors indinavir and atazanavir inhibit UGT1A1 and worsen hyperbilirubinemia, most markedly in preexisting Gilbert syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2640).

Conjugation by UGT1A1 adds one or two glucuronic acid moieties, disrupting internal hydrogen bonding so the resulting glucuronides become water-soluble; conjugation is obligatory for biliary excretion (Harrison 22e p.2638).

Unconjugated bilirubin is too tightly albumin-bound to be filtered and does not appear in urine, whereas conjugated (water-soluble) bilirubin is readily filtered, so bilirubinuria indicates a conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia; the kidney acts as an overflow valve so renal failure can amplify jaundice in conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (Harrison 22e p.2638).

Isolated hemolysis in an otherwise healthy person produces a purely unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with direct fraction <=15% of total; because marrow erythropoiesis can rise only about eightfold, hemolysis alone rarely sustains a bilirubin above ~68 micromol/L (4 mg/dL), so higher values imply concomitant hepatic dysfunction (Harrison 22e p.2638-2639).

Gilbert syndrome is a common, benign cause of mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (usually <51 micromol/L, <3 mg/dL) with normal liver tests and histology; levels rise with fasting, stress, fatigue, alcohol, and intercurrent illness and fall with caloric intake or enzyme inducers (Harrison 22e p.2640).

Crigler-Najjar type I shows extreme lifelong unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (~340-765 micromol/L, 20-45 mg/dL) with essentially absent UGT1A1 activity, no response to phenobarbital, and high kernicterus risk; type II has lower levels, detectable enzyme, pigmented bile, and a >25% bilirubin fall with phenobarbital (Harrison 22e p.2639-2640).

Dubin-Johnson syndrome is a benign, autosomal recessive predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (typically 34-85 micromol/L) caused by mutation of the canalicular transporter MRP2 (ABCC2); the liver is grossly black from lysosomal pigment and urinary coproporphyrin is >=80% isomer I despite a normal total (Harrison 22e p.2640-2641).

Rotor syndrome resembles Dubin-Johnson clinically (conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, bilirubinuria) but the liver is normal in color, the gallbladder is visualized on oral cholecystography, and total urinary coproporphyrin is markedly increased with isomer I usually <70%; it results from combined deficiency of OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 (Harrison 22e p.2641-2642).

Most neonates develop mild physiologic unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia between days 2 and 5 (peak typically <85-170 micromol/L, 5-10 mg/dL) due to low UGT1A1 and enterohepatic recycling, resolving within about 2 weeks (Harrison 22e p.2639).

Mistaking the first episodes of benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis for acute viral hepatitis
Prescribing drugs cleared by glucuronidation (notably irinotecan) without caution in Gilbert syndrome given risk of severe toxicity

Gilbert, Dubin-Johnson, and Rotor syndromes are benign with normal life expectancy and no progression to chronic liver disease. Crigler-Najjar type I carries a grave prognosis: before phototherapy most patients died of kernicterus in infancy or early childhood, and even survivors developed bilirubin-induced neurologic dysfunction, with early liver transplantation the best means to prevent brain injury and death. Crigler-Najjar type II is far less often complicated by kernicterus and is generally compatible with normal life, though intercurrent illness, fasting, or low albumin can precipitate dangerous bilirubin elevations. BRIC is benign and does not cause cirrhosis, whereas PFIC progresses to end-stage liver disease in childhood.

Inherited unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia forms a severity continuum by residual UGT1A1 activity: Crigler-Najjar type I (activity absent; bilirubin ~340-765 micromol/L, 20-45 mg/dL; no phenobarbital response; usual kernicterus), Crigler-Najjar type II (reduced activity, typically <=10% of normal; bilirubin ~100-430 micromol/L, 6-25 mg/dL; >25% phenobarbital response; rare kernicterus), and Gilbert syndrome (activity ~10-35% of normal; bilirubin usually <=70 micromol/L, 4 mg/dL absent fasting/hemolysis; normal histology). Familial conjugated hyperbilirubinemias of canalicular function (Dubin-Johnson, Rotor) are benign, distinguished from the progressive cholestatic disorders BRIC (episodic, non-progressive) and PFIC (progressive to end-stage liver disease).

Insulin resistance is the most widely accepted unifying mechanism. Early insulin resistance manifests as postprandial then fasting hyperinsulinemia, eventually progressing to hyperglycemia as compensatory beta-cell secretion fails. An overabundance of circulating free fatty acids (FFAs), released from expanded adipose tissue and from lipoprotein-lipase-mediated lipolysis, drives the process: FFAs impair insulin-mediated glucose uptake in muscle, promote intramuscular and cardiac triglyceride accumulation, and increase hepatic glucose and triglyceride production with VLDL secretion. Insulin normally suppresses lipolysis (its most sensitive action), so resistance amplifies FFA release in a self-perpetuating loop. Increased VLDL/apoB and elevated apoC-III inhibit lipoprotein lipase, raising triglyceride-rich remnants; HDL becomes small, dense, and cleared faster, lowering HDL cholesterol. Loss of insulin-mediated vasodilation (nitric oxide) with preserved renal sodium reabsorption and sympathetic activation, plus adipose angiotensinogen expression, contributes to hypertension. Contributing/associated mechanisms include leptin resistance, reduced anti-inflammatory adiponectin, increased proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, IL-18, TNF-alpha, resistin) from adipose-derived macrophages, a prothrombotic state (fibrinogen, PAI-1), oxidative stress with mitochondrial dysfunction, and alterations in the gut microbiome (increased Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio).

Metabolic syndrome is a clustering of metabolic abnormalities (central obesity, hypertriglyceridemia, low HDL cholesterol, hyperglycemia, and hypertension) that together raise the risk of cardiovascular disease and diabetes.

Conditions strongly associated with insulin resistance and the syndrome include metabolic-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD/MASH), polycystic ovary syndrome, and obstructive sleep apnea, which should be screened for during evaluation.
Obstructive sleep apnea can predict metabolic syndrome even without excess adiposity, and insulin resistance tends to be more severe in apnea patients than in weight-matched controls.

Hyperuricemia reflects insulin-resistance-related defects in renal tubular handling of uric acid and may itself contribute to hypertension via effects on endothelial nitric oxide synthase and activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

Diagnosis under NCEP:ATPIII (2001) requires three or more of: waist circumference >102 cm in men or >88 cm in women; triglycerides >=150 mg/dL; HDL <40 mg/dL (men) or <50 mg/dL (women); BP >=130/85 mmHg; fasting glucose >=100 mg/dL (or specific medication for, or prior diagnosis of, the relevant condition).

The Harmonizing definition uses ethnicity-specific waist circumference cutoffs (e.g., for South Asian and Chinese men >=90 cm, Europid men >=94 cm, Japanese men >=85 cm), reflecting that risk at a given waist circumference differs between populations.

Visceral (intra-abdominal) adipose tissue is more strongly linked to insulin resistance, diabetes, and CVD than subcutaneous fat, but waist circumference alone cannot reliably distinguish the two depots; DEXA, CT, or MRI is needed for that distinction.

Normal-weight individuals can still be insulin-resistant and meet criteria for metabolic syndrome, a phenotype that is particularly evident in populations from India, Southeast Asia, and Central America.
The syndrome is typically asymptomatic; physical examination often shows only elevated waist circumference and blood pressure, which should trigger a search for the other biochemical components.
Lipoatrophy and acanthosis nigricans, when present, signal severe insulin resistance, though they are far less common than the standard components.

Hypertriglyceridemia is an excellent marker of the insulin-resistant state; fasting triglycerides above roughly 180 mg/dL (~2.0 mM) are typically accompanied by a predominance of small, dense, more atherogenic LDL particles.
Most patients (~75%) with type 2 diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance have metabolic syndrome, and its presence in these groups marks a higher CVD burden than in those without the syndrome.
Waist circumference does not reliably separate subcutaneous from visceral fat, so it can misestimate true metabolic risk without imaging.
A single ethnicity-blind waist cutoff under- or over-estimates risk across populations; ethnicity-specific thresholds are needed.
Normal body weight does not exclude the syndrome, so insulin resistance can be missed in lean individuals.
Whether metabolic syndrome adds CVD or diabetes risk beyond the simple sum of its individual components remains debated, so it should not be over-interpreted as an independent diagnosis.
Fasting insulin levels or HOMA capture only part of insulin resistance, so they inadequately quantify the contribution of resistance to hypertension.
Obstructive sleep apnea and PCOS are commonly overlooked associated conditions if not actively screened for.

Metabolic syndrome roughly doubles the risk of cardiovascular death and confers about a threefold higher risk of acute myocardial infarction or stroke; the risk for type 2 diabetes is increased three- to fivefold (fasting glucose explaining most of this). In the REGARDS cohort, metabolic syndrome carried a relative risk of about 1.34 for all-cause mortality, with the relationship to hsCRP and mortality stronger in white than in black participants. Prevalence among patients with coronary heart disease may reach up to 60% in those over 75. Risk and prevalence are modifiable: cardiac rehabilitation and lifestyle change (improved nutrition, physical activity, weight reduction) can reduce the prevalence of the syndrome.

There is no graded severity scale; the syndrome is defined categorically by meeting three or more of the five diagnostic components (NCEP:ATPIII 2001 or the ethnicity-adjusted Harmonizing definition, Table 420-1). Risk rises with the number of components present and with associated markers such as elevated hsCRP.

Most vasculitic syndromes are thought to be at least partly immune-mediated responses to antigenic stimuli, with the precise mechanism varying by disease. Three principal hypothesized mechanisms are recognized. (1) Pathogenic immune-complex formation/deposition (e.g., IgA vasculitis, lupus vasculitis, serum-sickness/cutaneous syndromes, HCV-associated cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, HBV-associated vasculitis): antigen-antibody complexes formed in antigen excess deposit in vessel walls whose permeability has been raised by vasoactive amines, activate complement (notably chemotactic C5a), recruit neutrophils that phagocytose complexes and release intracytoplasmic enzymes damaging the wall, with later mononuclear infiltration and luminal compromise. (2) ANCA production (GPA, microscopic polyangiitis, EGPA): when neutrophils/monocytes are primed by TNF-alpha or IL-1 or alternative-complement activation, PR3 and MPO translocate to the cell membrane where ANCA can engage them, triggering degranulation, reactive oxygen species, endothelial injury, and release of IL-1/IL-8; however, some patients have active GPA without ANCA and titers correlate poorly with activity, so a primary pathogenic role remains debated. (3) Pathogenic T-lymphocyte responses and granuloma formation (giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis, GPA, EGPA): cytokine-activated endothelium expresses HLA class II and secretes IL-1, enabling CD4+ T-cell interactions; IL-1 and TNF-alpha upregulate ELAM-1 and VCAM-1 to enhance leukocyte adhesion. In GCA the disease is antigen-driven, with clonally restricted T cells suggesting an arterial-wall antigen, and both TH1 (IFN-gamma) and TH17 (IL-17) CD4 lineages contribute. The size, type, and location of affected vessels, host genetic predisposition, environmental exposures, reticuloendothelial clearance of complexes, hemodynamic factors, and endothelial integrity all influence the ultimate phenotype.

Vasculitis is inflammation of and damage to blood vessel walls that typically narrows the lumen and produces downstream tissue ischemia; it may be the sole disease, may be secondary to another disease, and may be single-organ or multisystem.

Polymyalgia rheumatica (aching/stiffness of neck, shoulder and hip girdles with raised ESR/CRP) coexists with GCA in 40-50% of GCA patients; creatine kinase is normal and RF/anti-CCP should be negative. ~10-20% with isolated PMR later develop GCA.

Takayasu arteritis is a large-vessel panarteritis with strong predilection for the aortic arch and its branches, classically in adolescent girls and young women; suspect it in a young woman with diminished or absent pulses, an interarm blood-pressure discrepancy, or arterial bruits.

IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein) is a small-vessel, immune-complex (IgA) vasculitis most common in children 4-7 years, with palpable purpura over buttocks/lower limbs, arthralgias, colicky GI symptoms (intussusception risk), and usually mild self-limited glomerulonephritis; serum complement is normal and IgA is elevated in about half.

Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis is most often associated with hepatitis C (estimated in ~5% of chronic HCV); rheumatoid factor is almost always present, hypocomplementemia occurs in ~90%, and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis accounts for ~80% of renal lesions.

Temporal artery biopsy yield improves with a 3-5 cm segment and serial sectioning because involvement is segmental; biopsy may still show arteritis after about 14 days of glucocorticoid therapy, so starting treatment promptly does not preclude later diagnosis.

Suspect vasculitis in any unexplained systemic illness; clinical clues include palpable purpura, pulmonary infiltrates with microscopic hematuria, chronic sinusitis, mononeuritis multiplex, unexplained ischemic events, and glomerulonephritis with multisystem disease.

Definitive diagnosis usually rests on biopsy of clinically involved tissue; 'blind' biopsy of organs without subjective or objective involvement has very low yield and should be avoided. Catheter-directed arteriography is used when PAN, Takayasu, or primary CNS vasculitis is suspected.

ANCA subtypes: cANCA targets proteinase-3 (>90% positive in active granulomatosis with polyangiitis); pANCA most relevantly targets myeloperoxidase (variably positive in microscopic polyangiitis, EGPA, and isolated necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis). Only anti-MPO and anti-PR3 are convincingly vasculitis-associated.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis classically combines granulomatous vasculitis of the upper and lower respiratory tracts with glomerulonephritis; upper airway involvement occurs in ~95% and renal disease (~77% over course) dominates prognosis. Renal lesion is pauci-immune (no immune-complex deposition).

Microscopic polyangiitis resembles GPA but lacks granulomatous inflammation; it favors small vessels (capillaries, venules, arterioles), with glomerulonephritis in at least 79% and alveolar hemorrhage in ~12%. Upper airway disease and lung nodules are atypical and, if present, point instead to GPA. ANCA (usually anti-MPO) in ~75%.

EGPA (Churg-Strauss) is defined by asthma, blood and tissue eosinophilia, and vasculitis; eosinophilia exceeds 1000 cells/uL in >80% and ANCA (usually anti-MPO) is present in ~48%. Cardiac involvement is the leading cause of death, so echocardiography is advised at diagnosis.

Polyarteritis nodosa is a necrotizing vasculitis of small- and medium-sized muscular arteries that spares pulmonary arteries and does NOT cause glomerulonephritis, granuloma, or significant eosinophilia; renal involvement is arteritis (microaneurysms, hypertension), not glomerular. ANCA are rarely found; screen all patients for hepatitis B and C.

Giant cell arteritis occurs almost exclusively after age 50, presents with fever, anemia, high ESR/CRP, and headache; ischemic optic neuropathy with sudden blindness is the dreaded complication, and patients carry an ~18-fold increased risk of thoracic aortic aneurysm. Treatment should not be delayed for biopsy.
Do NOT treat a rise in ANCA titer alone as evidence of relapse; only ~43% of patients relapsed within a year of an ANCA rise, and many remain ANCA-positive for years in remission.

ANCA predictive value falls sharply when renal disease is absent (~30-60% with sinus/lung-only disease vs ~90% with active glomerulonephritis), so biopsy is needed to exclude infection or malignancy that can cause false-positive ANCA.

Upper airway lesions in GPA should NEVER be irradiated; midline destructive disease mimics include NK/T-cell lymphoma and cocaine/levamisole injury (anti-neutrophil-elastase ANCA, granulocytopenia point to levamisole).
Eosinophilia is rare in PAN; when markedly elevated it should redirect toward EGPA.
In PAN, MR and CT arteriography lack the resolution to visualize the small/medium aneurysms, so catheter-directed dye arteriography is required.
When tocilizumab or other IL-6 blockade is used in GCA, ESR and CRP normalize and can no longer be used to gauge disease activity or detect infection.
TMP-SMX should never be used alone to treat active GPA involving organs beyond the sinonasal tissue.
Failure to exclude infection (especially endocarditis) before starting empirical immunosuppression in a rapidly deteriorating patient can be catastrophic.
Glucocorticoids do not reliably benefit the skin or renal disease of IgA vasculitis and do not shorten its course or reduce recurrence.

Outcome varies markedly by syndrome and by treatment. Untreated granulomatosis with polyangiitis was once uniformly fatal within months; modern cyclophosphamide- or rituximab-based regimens with glucocorticoids achieve improvement in >90% and remission in ~75%, with 5-year survival >80%, though 50-70% of remissions are followed by relapse and many patients accrue irreversible damage (renal insufficiency, hearing loss, subglottic stenosis, saddle-nose deformity). Treated microscopic polyangiitis has ~74% 5-year survival with relapse in at least 34%, mortality from alveolar hemorrhage or GI/cardiac/renal disease. Untreated EGPA has a ~25% 5-year survival; with treatment about 72% survive at 78 months, and myocardial involvement causes ~39% of deaths. Untreated PAN carries a 10-20% 5-year survival (death from bowel infarction/perforation and cardiovascular causes); combination immunosuppression markedly improves survival, with relapse in ~10-20%. GCA seldom causes acute death but carries late risk of aortic aneurysm rupture/dissection; PMR generally responds well. Takayasu is usually chronic and relapsing with widely variable reported survival. IgA vasculitis prognosis is excellent (mortality exceedingly rare; 1-5% of children reach end-stage renal disease, possibly higher in adults; recurrences in 10-40%). In cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, glomerulonephritis is a poor prognostic sign (~15% progress to end-stage renal disease, 40% of whom later die of cardiovascular disease, infection, or liver failure).

For ANCA-associated vasculitis (GPA/microscopic polyangiitis), Harrison frames management by severe vs nonsevere disease. Severe disease involves life- or organ-threatening manifestations and is judged by both extent and the specific organ affected: pulmonary disease may be nonsevere (nodules without respiratory compromise) or severe (alveolar hemorrhage), whereas active glomerulonephritis is ALWAYS considered severe even when renal function is normal. Treatment is conceptually divided into a remission-induction phase followed by a maintenance phase, with regimen choice stratified by this severity assessment along with relapse history and comorbidities.

Thrombotic renovascular disorders share endothelial injury of the renal microvasculature (terminal arterioles and capillaries) leading to platelet/hyaline thrombi and microangiopathic hemolysis. In TTP, deficient ADAMTS13 activity (below ~5-10%, from congenital mutation in cTTP/Upshaw-Schulman syndrome or acquired autoantibody in iTTP) allows ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers to accumulate, forming platelet-rich thrombi that shear red cells; an inflammatory trigger is often required to manifest disease. In atypical HUS, dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway (commonly factor H deficiency, or defects in factor I, factor B, CD46/membrane cofactor protein, C3, CFHR1/3/5, thrombomodulin, or autoantibody to factor H in DEAP HUS) causes complement-mediated endothelial damage. STEC HUS results from Shiga toxins (Stx1/Stx2, verotoxins) binding the glycolipid receptor Gb3 on renal microvascular cells, inducing inflammatory cytokines (IL-8, MCP-1, SDF-1) and chemokine receptors (CXCR4/CXCR7) with platelet aggregation; Streptococcus pneumoniae neuraminidase can expose the cryptic Thomsen-Friedenreich antigen so preformed IgM triggers MAHA. Scleroderma renal crisis features arcuate artery intimal/medial proliferation with onion-skinning, fibrinoid necrosis, and thrombosis. Antiphospholipid syndrome causes intralobular fibrous intimal hyperplasia and arterial/arteriolar occlusion. Renal vein thrombosis results from endothelial damage, venous stasis, or hypercoagulability (notably nephrotic syndrome, especially membranous nephropathy).

Thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) is a pathologic lesion of endothelial injury in terminal arterioles and capillaries, with platelet and hyaline thrombi causing partial or complete occlusion; it is usually but not always accompanied by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) featuring thrombocytopenia and schistocytes.

Renal vein thrombosis can present with flank pain, tenderness, hematuria, rapid renal decline, and proteinuria, or be silent and discovered during a pulmonary embolism workup; the left renal vein is more commonly involved and two-thirds of cases are bilateral.

Sickle cell nephropathy arises from occlusion of the vasa recta in the renal medulla, where low oxygen tension and high osmolarity favor hemoglobin S polymerization and sickling; sequelae include hyposthenuria, hematuria, and papillary necrosis (which can also occur in sickle trait).

Drug-induced TMA occurs via two mechanisms: dose-dependent toxic/endothelial damage (chemotherapeutics such as proteasome inhibitors, mitomycin C, gemcitabine; immunosuppressives such as calcineurin inhibitors, interferon, sirolimus) or non-dose-dependent drug-induced autoantibodies (e.g., quinine, which can react even after a single re-exposure).

Renal histology of TMA shows swollen endocapillary cells (endotheliosis), fibrin thrombi, platelet plugs, arterial intimal fibrosis, and a membranoproliferative glomerular pattern; fibrin thrombi may extend into the arteriolar pole producing glomerular collapse and at times cortical necrosis, and recovered kidneys may develop secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.

The classic TTP pentad (MAHA, thrombocytopenia, neurologic symptoms, fever, renal failure) is rare: fewer than 5% of immune-mediated TTP cases show the full pentad, so do not wait for all five to act.

TTP is defined as MAHA associated with ADAMTS13 activity below 5-10%; ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers accumulate, form clots, and shear erythrocytes, but loss of ADAMTS13 alone may need an additional trigger (infection, surgery, pancreatitis, pregnancy) to provoke clinical disease.

Atypical (complement-mediated) HUS reflects alternative complement pathway dysregulation; affected patients often have low C3 with normal C4, and factor H deficiency is the most common defect, with more than 70 factor H gene mutations described.

Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) HUS, classically D+ (diarrhea-associated) HUS, mostly affects children under 5 but can affect adults; bloody diarrhea precedes MAHA within one week in over 80% of cases, fever is typically absent, and neurologic involvement is common, especially in adults.

Scleroderma renal crisis presents with acute kidney injury, abrupt-onset hypertension, and a normal urine sediment (though none is strictly required); it occurs in about 12% of diffuse but only ~2% of limited systemic sclerosis, and its renal histology of 'onion-skinning' arcuate artery intimal/medial proliferation is indistinguishable from malignant hypertension.

Antiphospholipid syndrome produces a predisposition to arterial and venous thrombosis and recurrent fetal loss; 'triple positivity' (lupus anticoagulant, anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I, and anticardiolipin antibodies) carries the highest thrombosis risk, and APLS is the leading cause of stroke in patients under 45.

HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) is a microvascular pregnancy complication; the defining organ is the liver (subcapsular hematoma with potential rupture), renal failure occurs in about half of patients, and proteinuria is present in 86-100%.
Waiting for the full TTP pentad before acting is a mistake, since fewer than 5% of immune-mediated TTP cases display all five features.

Assuming TMA always shows MAHA can mislead: TMA is usually but not always accompanied by microangiopathic hemolysis, and in antiphospholipid syndrome renal TMA is common while signs of MAHA and platelet consumption are usually absent.

Scleroderma renal crisis is histologically indistinguishable from malignant hypertension and the two can coexist, so renal biopsy is recommended for atypical renal involvement, especially when hypertension is absent.
ADAMTS13 reduction in HELLP (30-60%) is milder than in TTP (below ~10%), so interpreting modest reductions as diagnostic of TTP can mislead during pregnancy when aHUS and TTP can also be triggered.

Thrombocytopenia in HIV-related TMA may prohibit renal biopsy, yet biopsy is required for diagnosis because other HIV-associated renal diseases mimic it; ADAMTS13 activity is not reduced in HIV-related TMA.
In drug-induced autoantibody TMA (e.g., quinine), disease can recur after even a single re-exposure in a previously sensitized patient, so it is not strictly dose-dependent.
Distinguishing HSCT-associated TMA is difficult because thrombocytopenia, anemia, and renal insufficiency are common after transplantation for other reasons.

Prognosis varies by subtype. Untreated immune-mediated TTP has a mortality exceeding 90%, and even with modern therapy about 20% die within the first month from microvascular thrombosis. HSCT-associated TMA is highly lethal, with roughly 75% mortality within 3 months. Scleroderma renal crisis historically had over 90% mortality at 1 month, reduced to about 30% at 3 years with renin-angiotensin system blockade; nearly two-thirds of patients may require dialysis, with renal recovery in about half (median ~1 year). HELLP syndrome carries a mortality of about 7.4-34% and usually resolves spontaneously after delivery. POEMS syndrome rarely progresses to end-stage renal disease. Renal injury in aHUS can be severe and progress to end-stage renal disease, with recurrence risk after transplant depending on the complement-regulatory protein involved. Chronic kidney disease develops in roughly 25-33% of sickle cell nephropathy patients, and nephrotic-range proteinuria predicts progression to renal failure.

No single unified severity scale; classification is by etiologic subtype and laboratory criteria. TTP is defined as MAHA with ADAMTS13 activity below 5-10% and subdivided into congenital (cTTP/Upshaw-Schulman) and immune (iTTP) forms. HUS variants include STEC/D+ HUS, pneumococcal neuraminidase-associated HUS, atypical complement-mediated HUS (aHUS), and DEAP HUS. HSCT-associated TMA has formal diagnostic criteria (Harrison Table 329-1): the International Working Group requires schistocytes (over 4% in one set, or RBC fragmentation with at least 2 schistocytes per high-power field), de novo/progressive thrombocytopenia, rising LDH, falling hemoglobin or increased transfusion need, negative Coombs, falling haptoglobin, and concurrent renal/neurologic dysfunction without other explanation. Antiphospholipid syndrome severity is stratified by antibody profile, with 'triple positivity' conferring the highest thrombosis risk and a catastrophic variant defined by rapid multiorgan failure.

Thyroid nodular disease reflects disordered growth of thyroid cells that may be hyperplastic or neoplastic. Thyroid neoplasms can arise from follicular cells (papillary, follicular, oncocytic, poorly differentiated, anaplastic carcinomas), calcitonin-producing C cells (medullary carcinoma), lymphocytes (lymphoma), or stromal/vascular elements. Cancers are monoclonal, arising from mutations conferring a growth advantage or resistance to cell death. Activation of the RET-RAS-BRAF (MAPK) signaling pathway is seen in up to 70% of PTCs; BRAF V600E mutations occur in up to 60% of PTC, RET rearrangements in ~15% (more frequent after Chernobyl fallout), and RAS mutations in ~15%. FTCs harbor BRAF/RAS mutations plus PAX8-PPARgamma rearrangements (~70% have a mutation/rearrangement). Anaplastic cancers accumulate additional TERT promoter, BRAF, CTNNB1 (beta-catenin), and TP53 mutations driving dedifferentiation and genetic instability. MEN 2-associated MTC carries inherited activating RET point mutations and is preceded by C-cell hyperplasia. External and fallout radiation predispose to chromosomal breaks and increase risk of benign and malignant nodules, especially in children. Most differentiated cancers retain TSH receptor expression and respond to TSH, the basis for both LT4 suppression and radioiodine uptake.

Thyroid nodules are common: ~3-7% of adults by palpation, but up to 50% have nodules on ultrasound, with the majority <1 cm. The vast majority of nodules are benign (Harrison 22e p.3040, p.3044, p.3048).

Serum thyroglobulin (Tg) is a sensitive marker of residual/recurrent disease for PTC, FTC, and oncocytic carcinoma after total thyroidectomy and radioablation, while calcitonin serves this role for MTC (Harrison 22e p.3045, p.3047).

Molecular diagnostic panels (next-generation sequencing, microRNA, gene expression) are increasingly used on FNA samples with indeterminate cytology (AUS, follicular neoplasm) to distinguish benign from malignant lesions and reduce unnecessary diagnostic surgery; current validated tests have negative predictive values >95% (Harrison 22e p.3046, p.3050).

Initial workup of a nodule begins with a TSH level. If TSH is suppressed, a radionuclide scan is done; a hyperfunctioning ('hot') nodule is almost never malignant, so FNA is unnecessary. Otherwise proceed to thyroid ultrasound (Harrison 22e p.3048).

Thyroid ultrasound with a validated risk-stratification system (e.g., ACR TI-RADS, TR1-TR5) is used to decide which nodules need fine-needle aspiration (FNA), combining sonographic pattern with nodule size; more suspicious patterns warrant FNA at lower size cutoffs (Harrison 22e p.3042, p.3048).

FNA, ideally ultrasound-guided, is the diagnostic procedure of choice for nodules. Cytology is reported with the six-tier Bethesda System (version 3): benign ~4% malignancy risk, AUS ~22%, follicular neoplasm ~30%, suspicious for malignancy ~74%, malignant ~97% (Harrison 22e p.3044, p.3049).

Papillary thyroid cancer (PTC) is the most common type (80-85% of well-differentiated cancers); classic and follicular variants are usually indolent, spread mainly via lymphatics, and have an excellent prognosis (>95% present at stage I or II) (Harrison 22e p.3046).

Follicular thyroid cancer (FTC) accounts for ~5% of US thyroid cancers and cannot be distinguished from benign follicular lesions by FNA cytology alone; diagnosis requires histologic evidence of capsular and/or vascular invasion (Harrison 22e p.3046-3047, p.3048).

Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) arises from calcitonin-producing C cells, accounts for ~5% of thyroid cancers, and can be sporadic or familial (MEN 2A, MEN 2B, familial MTC); elevated serum calcitonin is a marker of residual/recurrent disease (Harrison 22e p.3048).

All patients with MTC should be tested for RET mutations so that genetic counseling and family testing can be offered; pheochromocytoma must be excluded before surgery in any patient with a RET mutation (Harrison 22e p.3048).
Anaplastic thyroid cancer (ATC) is poorly differentiated and aggressive with a bleak prognosis; most patients die within 6 months of diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.3040, p.3048).

Thyroid cancer is being overdiagnosed: rising incidence is driven by small T1 papillary tumors while disease-specific mortality has not changed in 40 years; routine FNA is not recommended for nodules <1 cm unless metastatic cervical nodes are present.
For thyroid lymphoma, initial surgical resection should be avoided because it may spread otherwise localized disease.
A hyperfunctioning ('hot') nodule on radionuclide scan is almost never malignant; FNA is unnecessary and should not be performed for these.

FNA cytology cannot reliably distinguish benign follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma because nuclear features do not differ; the distinction requires histologic evidence of capsular/vascular invasion.

LT4 (TSH-suppression) therapy does NOT shrink nodules in iodine-replete (iodine-sufficient) populations and should not be used for that purpose; if it has not reduced nodule size after 6-12 months it should be stopped.
Spongiform nodules (TR1) have <3% cancer risk and warrant observation rather than FNA.
Iodine-containing contrast agents should be avoided in nodular goiter due to the risk of the Jod-Basedow effect (iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis from autonomous nodules).
NIFTP can only be diagnosed on surgical pathology, so it is still included within Bethesda malignancy risk estimates.
Hoarseness more commonly reflects benign causes (e.g., reflux) than malignancy, but new vocal cord paralysis is a genuine red flag.
In MTC, surgery should not proceed until pheochromocytoma has been excluded in any patient with a RET mutation.

Prognosis spans a wide range by histologic type. Differentiated cancers (PTC and FTC) are often curable with good prognosis in early-stage disease; the 20-year disease-specific mortality for low-risk thyroid cancer is ~1%, and most PTC present at stage I/II with survival similar to expected. Mortality rises markedly in stage IV disease, especially with distant metastases (stage IVB, ~1% of patients). FTC, particularly angioinvasive, carries less favorable outcomes than PTC partly due to more stage IV presentation; poor features include distant metastases, age >55, tumor >4 cm, and marked vascular invasion. MTC is more aggressive in MEN 2B than MEN 2A, and familial MTC more aggressive than sporadic. Anaplastic thyroid cancer is aggressive with a bleak prognosis, most patients dying within 6 months. Older age (>65) and male gender are associated with worse outcomes overall.

Histologic classification (WHO/Table 397-1): follicular cell-derived (benign follicular/oncocytic adenoma; low-risk neoplasms including NIFTP; malignant - papillary, follicular, oncocytic, differentiated/poorly differentiated high-grade, anaplastic), C-cell-derived medullary carcinoma, mixed medullary-follicular, lymphoma, and others. Staging uses the AJCC/UICC 8th-edition TNM system (tumor size and extrathyroidal invasion, regional nodal metastases, distant metastases) for differentiated and anaplastic cancers. Sonographic risk stratification uses ACR TI-RADS levels TR1 (benign) to TR5 (highly suspicious). FNA cytology uses the six-tier Bethesda System v3 (I nondiagnostic ~13%, II benign ~4%, III AUS ~22%, IV follicular neoplasm ~30%, V suspicious for malignancy ~74%, VI malignant ~97% malignancy risk). MTC risk in MEN 2 is further stratified by specific RET mutation.

chunks.text: Thyroid eye disease is an autoimmune inflammatory disorder of the orbit linked to Graves disease. Autoantibodies against the thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor, expressed on orbital fibroblasts, drive activation and differentiation of these cells. The resulting inflammation causes accumulation of glycosaminoglycans, oedema, and enlargement of the extraocular muscles and orbital fat. The expanded orbital contents within a fixed bony cavity produce proptosis, restrictive myopathy, and, when the crowded orbital apex compresses the optic nerve, dysthyroid optic neuropathy. Over time inflammation gives way to fibrosis, leaving fixed muscle restriction and lid changes.

The hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis is a classic endocrine feedback loop. Hypothalamic TRH stimulates pituitary thyrotrope production of TSH, which binds the TSH-R (a Gs-coupled seven-transmembrane GPCR) on the basolateral surface of thyroid follicular cells, activating adenylyl cyclase/cAMP and phospholipase C to drive gland growth and hormone synthesis. Iodide is actively trapped by the sodium-iodide symporter (NIS), transported apically via pendrin, and oxidized/organified onto tyrosyl residues of thyroglobulin by thyroid peroxidase using DUOX-generated hydrogen peroxide; iodotyrosines are coupled to form T4 and T3, which are released after lysosomal proteolysis of reabsorbed thyroglobulin. Circulating hormone is largely protein-bound (TBG, transthyretin, albumin) with only the small unbound fraction biologically available; deiodinases (types I, II, III) regulate peripheral conversion of T4 to active T3 or inactivating reverse T3. T3 acts mainly through nuclear receptors TRalpha and TRbeta, which heterodimerize with RXR on thyroid response elements, exchanging co-repressors for co-activators upon ligand binding. Thyroid hormones feed back, predominantly via TRbeta2 in hypothalamus and pituitary, to suppress TRH and TSH, establishing the axis set point.
TSH is the single most useful physiologic marker of thyroid hormone action; because of its long plasma half-life (~50 min) a single measurement reliably reflects circulating levels (p.3021).

After total thyroidectomy and radioablation for thyroid cancer, thyroglobulin should be <0.2 ng/mL in the absence of anti-Tg antibodies; a measurable level suggests incomplete ablation or recurrence (p.3026).
A normal TSH essentially excludes a primary thyroid abnormality, so the logical first step in evaluation is to determine whether TSH is suppressed, normal, or elevated (p.3026).

Primary hyperthyroidism produces a low/suppressed TSH and primary hypothyroidism produces an elevated TSH because thyroid hormone exerts dominant negative feedback on TSH gene expression (p.3021, p.3026).

TSH is a glycoprotein with an alpha subunit shared with LH, FSH, and hCG and a unique beta subunit; the structurally similar hCG weakly stimulates the TSH-R, lowering TSH in the first trimester of pregnancy (p.3021, p.3024).
T4 is secreted in roughly 15-fold excess over T3 and acts largely as a prohormone, being converted peripherally to the more potent T3 by deiodinases (p.3023-3024).

Nuclear thyroid hormone receptors silence target genes when unliganded by binding co-repressors, so hormone deficiency causes both loss of stimulation and active gene repression, giving deficiency a more profound effect than receptor gene deletion (p.3025).

About 5-15% of euthyroid women and up to 2% of euthyroid men carry thyroid (anti-TPO) antibodies and are at increased risk of future thyroid dysfunction; nearly all autoimmune hypothyroid patients and up to 80% of Graves' patients have TPO antibodies (p.3026).
Functioning (hot) thyroid nodules are almost never malignant and do not require fine-needle aspiration, whereas non-functioning (cold) nodules carry a ~5-10% malignancy risk (p.3026-3027).

Serum thyroglobulin is elevated in all forms of thyrotoxicosis except factitious thyrotoxicosis (exogenous hormone), and its principal clinical use is surveillance after thyroidectomy/radioablation for thyroid cancer (p.3026).
Treating low total T4 in TBG deficiency: attempts to normalize total T4 cause thyrotoxicosis and are futile due to rapid clearance.
Relying on TSH alone in suspected hypothalamic-pituitary (secondary) hypothyroidism, where TSH is inappropriately low-to-normal for a low T4; free T4 must also be measured.
Failing to stop biotin supplements >=2 days before testing, leading to falsely low TSH and falsely high T4/T3.
Missing T3 toxicosis (2-5% of cases) if only free T4 is checked when TSH is suppressed.
Misinterpreting transiently low TSH (0.01-0.1 mIU/L) of early pregnancy, recent hyperthyroidism treatment, or glucocorticoid/dopamine therapy as true thyrotoxicosis.
Performing fine-needle aspiration on a hot/functioning nodule, which is almost never malignant; scintigraphy should precede biopsy when TSH is subnormal.
Confusing thyroid hormone resistance or a TSH-secreting adenoma with simple primary hyperthyroidism because of elevated hormones with non-suppressed TSH.

Most physiologic and binding-protein variants (TBG abnormalities, familial dysalbuminemic hyperthyroxinemia, classic TRbeta resistance) are benign and require no treatment once recognized, the main goal being avoidance of inappropriate therapy. Early thyroid hormone replacement in congenital hypothyroidism prevents severe developmental abnormality, whereas untreated iodine deficiency in early life causes irreversible cretinism and even mild deficiency can subtly reduce IQ.

Thyroid nodules arise from focal proliferation of follicular cells and may be colloid nodules, adenomas, cysts, areas of thyroiditis, or carcinomas. Autonomously functioning nodules develop constitutive activation of thyroid hormone production, often through activating mutations of the TSH-receptor or G-protein signalling pathway, suppressing TSH and appearing 'hot' on scanning. Malignant nodules result from oncogenic alterations (for example in the MAPK pathway) driving unregulated growth, and their behaviour ranges from indolent differentiated cancers to aggressive anaplastic disease.
Thyroid nodules are common and usually benign, but the central task is to identify the minority that are malignant
Initial evaluation begins with a serum TSH; a suppressed value points towards an autonomously functioning (usually benign) nodule and warrants a radionuclide scan
Ultrasound characterises nodules and stratifies malignancy risk, with features such as marked hypoechogenicity, microcalcifications, irregular margins, and a taller-than-wide shape raising concern
Fine-needle aspiration is the key diagnostic test, with results reported using standardised cytology categories that guide management
Hot (functioning) nodules on scanning rarely harbour malignancy, so aspiration is generally directed at non-functioning nodules
History of childhood neck irradiation, family history of thyroid cancer, rapid growth, hoarseness, or fixed hard nodules increase suspicion of cancer

Most nodules are benign and can be followed conservatively, and even most malignant nodules are differentiated cancers with an excellent prognosis after treatment, though anaplastic and some medullary cancers carry a poor outlook.

Other causes of thyrotoxicosis besides Graves' disease must be considered (e.g. toxic adenoma, toxic multinodular goitre, destructive thyroiditis, ectopic thyroid tissue, factitious thyrotoxicosis); radionuclide scan/uptake or color-flow Doppler ultrasonography helps distinguish hyperthyroidism from destructive thyroiditis (Harrison 22e p.3078).

Watch for confounding biochemistry: elevated bilirubin, liver enzymes and ferritin, plus microcytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia, may accompany thyrotoxicosis (Harrison 22e p.3078).

Thyroid storm represents a severe, decompensated form of thyroid hormone excess (thyrotoxicosis), typically arising when an acute stressor is superimposed on partially treated or untreated hyperthyroidism. Excess circulating thyroid hormone drives a hypermetabolic, hyperadrenergic state; high cardiac output produces a bounding pulse, widened pulse pressure and may precipitate or worsen heart failure or angina, particularly in the elderly or those with pre-existing heart disease (Harrison 22e p.3077, p.3080).
Thyrotoxic crisis (thyroid storm) is a rare, life-threatening exacerbation of hyperthyroidism (Harrison 22e p.3080).
Characteristic features include fever, delirium, seizures, coma, vomiting, diarrhoea and jaundice (Harrison 22e p.3080).

Often precipitated by an acute intercurrent illness (e.g. stroke, infection, trauma, diabetic ketoacidosis), by surgery (especially thyroid surgery), or by radioiodine treatment given to a patient whose hyperthyroidism is only partially treated or untreated (Harrison 22e p.3080).
Apathetic thyrotoxicosis: in the elderly, features may be subtle or masked, presenting mainly with fatigue and weight loss, and can be mistaken for depression (Harrison 22e p.3076).
Thyrotoxicosis may be complicated by a form of hypokalaemic periodic paralysis, particularly common in Asian males (Harrison 22e p.3076).
Treatment of the thyrotoxic state alone restores sinus rhythm in up to 75% of patients with thyrotoxicosis-associated atrial fibrillation who have no underlying cardiac disease (Harrison 22e p.3077).
Radioiodine therapy in a patient with partially treated or untreated hyperthyroidism can itself precipitate thyrotoxic crisis (Harrison 22e p.3080).
In the elderly, thyrotoxicosis may be masked (apathetic thyrotoxicosis), delaying recognition (Harrison 22e p.3076).
Mortality remains high (4-17%) even with treatment, usually from cardiac failure, arrhythmia or hyperthermia (Harrison 22e p.3080).
Fever, delirium, seizures or coma in a thyrotoxic patient indicate thyroid storm (Harrison 22e p.3080).
Death is most often due to cardiac failure, arrhythmia or hyperthermia (Harrison 22e p.3080).

A TIA results from transient focal cerebral ischaemia when blood flow falls for longer than several seconds; neurons lack glycogen so deficits appear within seconds, but because the occluded vessel reopens and flow is restored before infarction occurs, symptoms resolve completely. Mechanisms mirror ischaemic stroke: emboli to the brain (cardiac or proximal arterial source) or in-situ thrombosis of an intracranial vessel. Small-vessel (lacunar) TIAs may recur several times a day and last only minutes (Harrison 22e p.3428, 3448, 3447).
TIA classically produces 'negative' symptoms (transient loss of function); positive sensory symptoms or involuntary movements point instead to seizure (p.3378).
Most TIAs last under 1 hour, well within the historical 24-hour window (p.3448).

About 25% of symptomatic internal carotid disease is heralded by recurrent transient monocular blindness (amaurosis fugax), typically described as a horizontal shade sweeping down or up across one eye, lasting a few minutes (p.3430).
A high-pitched carotid bruit fading into diastole suggests a tight stenosis; paradoxically the bruit may fade or vanish as occlusion becomes imminent and flow drops (p.3430).
Causes of TIA and ischaemic stroke are identical, so the diagnostic evaluation of a TIA should parallel that of a completed stroke (p.3448).
A TIA is a clinical diagnosis: a normal brain imaging study does NOT rule it out (p.3448).

If a relevant infarction is seen on imaging, the event is reclassified as a stroke regardless of how briefly symptoms lasted — the modern definition is tissue-based, not purely time-based (p.3428, p.3448).
Patients with carotid/vertebrobasilar TIA may report symptoms 'in one eye' when the deficit is actually a homonymous hemifield loss affecting both eyes (p.3430-equivalent / cortical visual TIA).
Acephalgic migraine can mimic TIA even with no prior migraine history and even after age 65 (p.3428).

Stroke risk after a TIA is approximately 10-15% within the first 3 months, with most events occurring in the first 2 days; this early risk is well predicted by the ABCD2 score, so urgent evaluation and treatment are justified (Harrison 22e p.3448).
Most strokes after a TIA occur within the first 2 days — the early window is the highest-risk period and warrants urgent (not deferred) workup (p.3448)
Stuttering or crescendo course of small-vessel TIAs heralding lacunar infarct can progress to severe permanent disability (p.3447)
Amaurosis fugax indicates a symptomatic internal carotid source needing prompt carotid evaluation (p.3430)

ABCD2 score (Harrison 22e p.3448) stratifies early stroke risk after TIA: 1 point each for Age >=60, BP (SBP >140 or DBP >90 mmHg), and Diabetes; for Clinical features 2 points for unilateral weakness or 1 for speech disturbance without weakness; for Duration 2 points for >=60 min or 1 for 10-59 min. The 3-month stroke rate rises with the total: ~0% at score 0-1, ~3% at 2-3, ~8% at 4, ~12% at 5, ~17% at 6, and ~22% at 7.

chunks.text: Tinea versicolor results from overgrowth of lipophilic Malassezia yeasts that are normal residents of sebum-rich skin. Under predisposing conditions such as heat, humidity, occlusion, and increased sebum, the yeast converts to its hyphal, pathogenic form and proliferates within the stratum corneum. The organism produces dicarboxylic acids, notably azelaic acid, that inhibit melanocyte tyrosinase and cause the hypopigmented patches, while an associated low-grade inflammatory and hyperkeratotic response produces the scale and, in some, hyperpigmentation. Because the yeast is part of the normal flora, the condition is more a disturbance of host-commensal balance than a transmissible infection, and it readily recurs.

chunks.text: Subjective tinnitus is thought to arise from aberrant neural activity generated when the cochlea or auditory nerve is damaged; loss of input leads to maladaptive changes and increased spontaneous firing and reorganisation in the central auditory pathways, so the brain perceives sound that is not present. Emotional and attentional networks amplify and sustain the perception, which explains why distress and the loudness of tinnitus are only loosely related. Objective tinnitus, in contrast, has a genuine internal acoustic source: turbulent or pulsatile blood flow in vascular lesions, or repetitive contraction of palatal, tensor tympani or stapedius muscles, generates a real sound transmitted to the ear.

Hepatotoxicity arises from direct hepatocyte injury (free radicals or reactive metabolites causing membrane lipid peroxidation) or from drug/metabolite activation of innate or adaptive immune pathways, apoptotic signaling, and disruption of bile excretory transport. Interference with canalicular pumps allows injurious endogenous bile acids to accumulate, producing cholestasis; other mechanisms inhibit protein synthesis or impair mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation, leading to lactic acidosis and microvesicular steatosis. Most drugs are metabolized via phase I cytochrome P450 (oxidation) followed by phase II conjugation (glucuronidation, sulfation) or glutathione inactivation; most toxicity reflects formation of a reactive phase I metabolite, with glutathione depletion removing a protective pathway. For acetaminophen, phase II conjugation yields harmless metabolites, but a fraction is converted by CYP2E1 to the toxic intermediate NAPQI, normally detoxified by glutathione; when glutathione is overwhelmed or depleted, NAPQI binds covalently to hepatocyte macromolecules forming protein adducts that drive necrosis. Susceptibility to idiosyncratic injury is influenced by HLA haplotypes (e.g., amoxicillin-clavulanate, flucloxacillin), polymorphisms in metabolizing pathways and protective cytokines, and activation of nuclear receptors such as CAR and PXR. Factors potentiating acetaminophen injury include enzyme induction (alcohol via CYP2E1, phenobarbital, isoniazid), fasting/starvation and other states that lower hepatic glutathione (Harrison 22e p.2665-2666, 2668-2670).

Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) is the single most common cause of acute liver failure, and hepatotoxicity signals are the leading reason candidate compounds fail to gain approval during drug development; a meticulous history covering prescription, over-the-counter, herbal, dietary, occupational and household chemical exposures is essential (Harrison 22e p.2665).

Certain drugs produce an autoimmune-hepatitis-like phenotype with positive antinuclear antibodies, classically nitrofurantoin, minocycline, hydralazine and alpha-methyldopa (Harrison 22e p.2667, 2670-2671).

Immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-CTLA-4 ipilimumab; anti-PD-1 pembrolizumab and nivolumab) cause an immune-mediated hepatitis within weeks, often ANA-positive, mediated predominantly by CD8+ lymphocytes and responsive to glucocorticoids; concurrent immune injury to thyroid, muscle and colon may occur (Harrison 22e p.2671-2672).

Withdrawal of the suspected agent at the first sign of an adverse reaction, or when aminotransferases reach five times the upper limit of normal, is critical, because continued use despite symptoms and signs is associated with lethal outcomes (Harrison 22e p.2668).

Two broad categories are recognized: direct (intrinsic) toxic injury, which is predictable, dose-dependent and has a short latency (often hours), and idiosyncratic injury, which is infrequent (roughly 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 100,000 exposures), less clearly dose-related and typically appears 5-90 days after starting the drug (Harrison 22e p.2665-2666).

The R value, the ratio of ALT to alkaline phosphatase (each as a multiple of the upper limit of normal), classifies the injury pattern: R greater than 5 indicates hepatocellular injury, R less than 2 indicates cholestatic injury, and R of 2-5 indicates a mixed pattern (Harrison 22e p.2667).

Hy's Law, named for Hyman Zimmerman, holds that drug-induced jaundice during a trial predicts serious liver injury, with roughly a 10-to-1 ratio of jaundiced cases to cases of acute liver failure; such cases often portend failure of drug approval (Harrison 22e p.2667).

Acetaminophen is the prototypic direct hepatotoxin and the most prevalent cause of acute liver failure in the Western world; it produces dose-related centrilobular necrosis, and aminotransferases can exceed 10,000 IU/L, far above levels seen in viral hepatitis, often with a relatively low bilirubin in this hyperacute injury (Harrison 22e p.2668).

A characteristic biochemical clue to acetaminophen toxicity is the combination of extremely high aminotransferases with low bilirubin; clinical suspicion should prompt empiric N-acetylcysteine even before history is confirmed, since denial or altered mentation can obscure the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2668).

Isoniazid causes transient mild aminotransferase elevation in about 10% of recipients early in therapy (an 'adaptive' response that usually resolves despite continued use); clinically significant hepatocellular injury can appear over a latency of up to 6 months and rises sharply with age, being highest in those over 50 and lowest in those under 20 (Harrison 22e p.2670).

Amoxicillin-clavulanate is the most commonly implicated single agent in DILI in the United States and Europe, producing a fairly specific mixed or predominantly cholestatic injury that may begin after the drug has already been stopped owing to a long latency (Harrison 22e p.2667, 2670-2671).

Complementary and alternative medicines, including herbal and dietary weight-loss and body-building products, now account for more than 20% of DILI cases in the United States; implicated agents include green tea extract (Camellia sinensis), kava, germander, chaparral, comfrey (pyrrolizidine alkaloids), Hydroxycut and OxyElite Pro (Harrison 22e p.2671).
DILI is nearly always a diagnosis of exclusion; causality is hard to prove and many disorders produce an identical clinicopathologic picture
Mild transient aminotransferase elevations that resolve during continued therapy ('adaptation,' seen with isoniazid, valproate, phenytoin and statins) can be mistaken for significant toxicity
Long latency drugs (notably amoxicillin-clavulanate and nitrofurantoin) may cause injury that manifests only after the drug has been stopped
Idiosyncratic reactions occurring in under 1 in 10,000 recipients are missed by clinical trials and only detected through postmarketing surveillance (e.g., troglitazone)
In chronic alcohol users, glutathione depletion and CYP2E1 induction can make the toxic acetaminophen dose as low as 2 g
Activated charcoal or cholestyramine are ineffective if given more than 30 minutes after acetaminophen ingestion
Routine liver test monitoring during statin therapy is not recommended, and asymptomatic isolated aminotransferase elevations need not prompt discontinuation
Herbal/dietary supplements may contain undeclared pharmaceuticals (e.g., diclofenac in antirheumatic 'herbs'), so the history must specifically probe alternative-medicine use

Most DILI is self-limited and resolves after withdrawal of the offending agent. Acute liver failure develops in about 10% of DILI cases; once that threshold (coagulopathy plus encephalopathy) is reached, spontaneous recovery occurs in fewer than 30%, and over 40% of those patients undergo liver transplantation. Survivors of acetaminophen overdose rarely have lasting liver injury, though the associated acute kidney injury (seen in nearly 75% of severe cases) is almost always self-limited. Anabolic steroid cholestasis typically resolves over weeks to months with prolonged jaundice. Some agents cause chronic injury: methotrexate, tamoxifen and amiodarone can lead to cirrhosis, and several drugs cause chronic autoimmune-like hepatitis (Harrison 22e p.2668-2670).
Jaundice arising during drug exposure (Hy's Law) predicts serious injury and possible liver failure
Coagulopathy and hepatic encephalopathy - markers of acute liver failure, which develops in about 10% of DILI cases
Aminotransferases above 10,000 IU/L with a low bilirubin - hyperacute acetaminophen pattern
Continued ingestion despite nausea, fatigue or jaundice (common scenario in fatal isoniazid and acetaminophen toxicity)
Acetaminophen ingestion of 25 g or more, or high timed plasma levels on the nomogram
Arterial lactate above 3.5 mmol/L in acetaminophen acute liver failure
Concurrent renal failure or myocardial injury in acetaminophen overdose

Injury pattern is graded by the R value (ALT/ALP as multiples of ULN): hepatocellular (R > 5), cholestatic (R < 2), or mixed (R 2-5). Severity is judged clinically by progression to acute liver failure (coagulopathy plus encephalopathy). Causality likelihood is assessed by structured tools including the DILIN expert-opinion scale (definite, highly likely, probable, possible, unlikely), RUCAM, and the newer RECAM. Hy's Law identifies high-risk hepatocellular injury when jaundice accompanies hepatocellular enzyme elevation (Harrison 22e p.2667-2668).

chunks.text: Liver injury can follow ingestion of essentially any xenobiotic (industrial toxins, drugs, herbal/dietary supplements). Most drugs are lipophilic and undergo phase I oxidation/methylation by cytochrome P450 enzymes followed by phase II conjugation (glucuronidation, sulfation) or glutathione inactivation to a water-soluble form for renal/biliary excretion; most hepatotoxicity arises from a reactive phase I metabolite, and glutathione depletion compounds the injury. Damage occurs through several overlapping routes: direct hepatocyte injury via free radicals/reactive intermediates causing membrane lipid peroxidation; activation of innate or adaptive immune responses (HLA-haplotype-dependent hapten binding, cytotoxic lymphocytes, antibody-mediated cytotoxicity); triggering of apoptosis via TNF-alpha/Fas pathways; disruption of bile canalicular transport pumps (e.g., MRP3) leading to toxic bile-acid accumulation and cholestasis; and inhibition of mitochondrial beta-oxidation/respiration producing lactic acidosis and microvesicular steatosis. Nuclear receptors such as CAR and PXR can also induce hepatotoxicity. For acetaminophen specifically, a minor fraction is converted by CYP2E1 to the reactive metabolite NAPQI, normally detoxified by conjugation with hepatoprotective glutathione; when NAPQI overwhelms or glutathione is depleted, NAPQI binds covalently to hepatocyte macromolecules forming protein adducts that drive centrilobular necrosis.

chunks.text: Most DILI is self-limited and resolves after the offending agent is withdrawn. However, acute liver failure develops in about 10% of DILI cases; once that threshold (coagulopathy plus hepatic encephalopathy) is reached, spontaneous recovery occurs in fewer than 30%, and liver transplantation is undertaken in more than 40% of these patients (p.2668). For acetaminophen, up to 72% of poisoned patients in some Scandinavian series progress to encephalopathy and coagulopathy (lower in the UK/US); a single dose of 10-15 g can cause clinical injury and fulminant fatal disease is usually associated with >=25 g; the N-acetylcysteine antidote markedly reduces severity and is most effective given early (within ~8-12 h), though it retains some benefit up to 24-36 h. Survivors of acetaminophen overdose rarely have ongoing liver injury (p.2668, p.2670). Several agents cause chronic injury or progression to cirrhosis (methotrexate, tamoxifen, amiodarone), and the autoimmune-pattern agents (nitrofurantoin, minocycline, hydralazine, methyldopa) can lead to cirrhosis if not recognised early (p.2668-2670).

chunks.text: Injury pattern is classified by the R value (ALT/ALP as multiples of ULN): R >5.0 hepatocellular, R <2.0 cholestatic, R 2.0-5.0 mixed (p.2667). Hy's Law serves as a severity/prognostic marker: jaundice (significant bilirubin rise) accompanying hepatocellular DILI predicts a markedly higher risk of acute liver failure (about a 10:1 jaundice-to-failure ratio) (p.2667). The aminotransferase threshold of >5x ULN (or >3x ULN with symptoms) marks the point at which the offending agent should be withdrawn (p.2668). Causality (not severity) is graded on a five-point likelihood scale by DILIN (definite, highly likely, probable, possible, unlikely) (p.2668). The clinical endpoint of severity is acute liver failure, defined by coagulopathy plus hepatic encephalopathy (p.2668).
