T. gondii is an intracellular coccidian. Ingested tissue cysts (bradyzoites) or oocysts (sporozoites) release organisms that invade gut epithelium and transform into rapidly dividing tachyzoites, which can infect and replicate in all nucleated mammalian cells via a parasitophorous vacuole, causing cell death and focal necrosis with an acute mononuclear inflammatory response. Parasites disseminate as free tachyzoites or within phagocytic 'Trojan horse' cells through blood and lymphatics to lymphatic tissue, skeletal muscle, myocardium, retina, placenta, and CNS. In the immunocompetent host, humoral and cell-mediated immunity (parasiticidal antibody, macrophage activation, IFN-gamma, IL-12-driven TH1 response, CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes) controls infection; tissue cysts containing bradyzoites then form 7-10 days after systemic infection and persist principally in the CNS and muscle, completing the asexual cycle and establishing lifelong chronic infection. Subclinical cycles of cyst rupture and reformation are the probable source of recrudescent infection. Immunocompromised or fetal hosts lack the immune factors (notably CD8+ T cells; reactivating T cells fail to secrete IFN-gamma and IL-2) needed to contain tachyzoite spread, allowing progressive focal destruction (necrotizing encephalitis, pneumonia, myocarditis). The sexual stage occurs only in the cat (definitive host), producing oocysts shed in feces (Harrison 22e p.1797-1800).
Caused by the obligate intracellular parasite Toxoplasma gondii; up to a third of the world's population is latently infected (Harrison 22e p.1797).

Antibody titers are NOT useful for establishing reactivation or following infection activity in immunocompromised patients; however, an absence of positive serology suggests an alternative diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1800).
Diagnosis rests on serology (combined IgG and IgM, with circulating IgA favoring acute infection) and PCR; PCR of body fluids is specific but its sensitivity may be low (Harrison 22e p.1801).

A therapeutic trial of anti-Toxoplasma medications is frequently used in AIDS patients with CNS mass lesions: >50% improve by day 3 and >90% by day 7, whereas worsening by day 7 (or lymphoma) prompts brain biopsy (Harrison 22e p.1802).

Two transmissible stages reach humans: tissue cysts containing bradyzoites in undercooked meat (e.g., lamb, pork, venison, ground beef), and sporulated oocysts shed in cat feces that contaminate soil, food, or water; sporulated oocysts are environmentally hardy and highly infectious (Harrison 22e p.1797).
In the immunocompetent host, acute infection is usually asymptomatic and self-limited, going unrecognized in 80-90% of acquired infections (Harrison 22e p.1799).

The most common manifestation of symptomatic acute toxoplasmosis in immunocompetent patients is cervical lymphadenopathy; nodes are usually nontender and discrete, with associated headache, malaise, fatigue, and low-grade fever (temperature usually <40 degrees C) (Harrison 22e p.1799).

The classic severe presentation is reactivation encephalitis in immunocompromised hosts (especially HIV-positive individuals or transplant recipients) in whom latent infection has reactivated (Harrison 22e p.1797).

In AIDS, >95% of Toxoplasma encephalitis cases are due to recrudescent infection, typically developing when the CD4+ T-cell count falls below 100/microL; encephalitis is the predominant manifestation while meningeal involvement is uncommon (Harrison 22e p.1800).

On MRI/CT, Toxoplasma encephalitis classically produces multiple ring-enhancing lesions, most often in the basal ganglia and corticomedullary junction; a single lesion increases the likelihood of primary CNS lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.1801-1802).

T. gondii is the most common cause of posterior uveitis in immunocompetent individuals and is estimated to cause about 35% of all chorioretinitis cases in the US and Europe (Harrison 22e p.1799, p.1801).

Congenital toxoplasmosis results from transplacental passage during primary maternal infection; infants may be asymptomatic at birth but later manifest chorioretinitis, strabismus, epilepsy, hydrocephalus, microcephaly, intellectual disability, and psychomotor retardation (Harrison 22e p.1797, p.1799).

Acute toxoplasmosis is asymptomatic and self-limited in 80-90% of immunocompetent adults and children, so the diagnosis is easily missed (in one epidemic, toxoplasmosis was correctly diagnosed in only 3 of 25 patients who sought care) (Harrison 22e p.1799).
If a patient is seronegative for T. gondii, the likelihood that a CNS mass lesion is due to toxoplasmosis is <10%, favoring earlier biopsy (Harrison 22e p.1802).
Antibody titers do not establish reactivation or track infection activity in immunocompromised patients; do not rely on serial titers to gauge active disease (Harrison 22e p.1800).
A negative PCR does not rule out toxoplasmosis - PCR is specific but may be of low sensitivity depending on the body fluid (Harrison 22e p.1801).

Isolation/demonstration of tissue cysts (bradyzoites) from biopsied tissue indicates only the presence of cysts and should NOT be misinterpreted as evidence of acute toxoplasmosis; only demonstration of tachyzoites (e.g., in lymph nodes) establishes acute infection (Harrison 22e p.1801).

IgM can persist for >1 year, so a positive IgM with positive IgG should not necessarily be interpreted as acute disease; a negative IgM with positive IgG indicates distant infection (Harrison 22e p.1801).
MRI/CT findings are not pathognomonic - 40% of CNS lymphomas are multifocal and 50% are ring-enhancing, and the false-negative rate for both MRI and CT is ~10% (Harrison 22e p.1802).

In AIDS patients with TE, IgM is usually undetectable and titers may be borderline/low (or transplant patients on B-cell-targeted immunosuppression may become seronegative); fewer than 3% have no demonstrable antibody at diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1800, p.1801).
Up to 25% of congenitally infected newborns may be seronegative with normal routine physical examinations, so eye, brain, CSF, and radiologic assessment are needed (Harrison 22e p.1802).
Toxoplasma pneumonia can be confused with Pneumocystis pneumonia, and organisms may also be found in healthy tissue, complicating interpretation (Harrison 22e p.1800).

In immunocompetent individuals, acute infection is usually asymptomatic and self-limited, resolving within several weeks though lymphadenopathy may persist for months; chronic infection persists lifelong with little consequence. Ocular disease can be self-limited but episodic chorioretinitis flares progressively destroy retinal tissue and may lead to glaucoma. In immunocompromised hosts, disease may be rapidly fatal if untreated, mandating prompt diagnosis and therapy; with treatment of Toxoplasma encephalitis, >50% improve by day 3 and >90% by day 7, but relapses are common and maintenance/secondary prophylaxis is needed while CD4+ counts remain low. For congenital toxoplasmosis, factors associated with severe disability include delayed diagnosis/treatment, neonatal hypoxia and hypoglycemia, profound visual impairment, uncorrected hydrocephalus, and raised intracranial pressure; with appropriate treatment upward of 70% of children have normal developmental, neurologic, and ophthalmologic findings at follow-up. Infected infants normal at birth may still have higher rates of learning disabilities and chronic neurologic sequelae (Harrison 22e p.1797-1801).

Focal neurologic deficits, seizures, altered mental status, or ring-enhancing CNS mass lesion(s) in an HIV/AIDS patient (especially CD4+ <100/microL) - reactivation Toxoplasma encephalitis, which is rapidly fatal if untreated (Harrison 22e p.1800).
A solitary ring-enhancing CNS lesion - increases the likelihood of primary CNS lymphoma over toxoplasmosis (Harrison 22e p.1802).
Failure to improve clinically by day 7 of empiric anti-Toxoplasma therapy - prompts brain biopsy and consideration of lymphoma or alternative diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1802).
Fulminant sepsis, fever of unknown origin, or pneumonia in an immunocompetent person with travel to or residence in South/Central America - virulent atypical genotypes (Harrison 22e p.1797-1799).

Toxoplasma pneumonia / disseminated disease in immunocompromised hosts may progress to acute respiratory failure with hemoptysis, metabolic acidosis, hypotension, and disseminated intravascular coagulation (Harrison 22e p.1800).
Acute maternal infection in pregnancy (risk of transplacental transmission; severity highest with first-trimester infection) (Harrison 22e p.1798).

Harrison does not provide a formal severity grading system for toxoplasmosis. Clinical stratification is by host immune status and syndrome: (1) immunocompetent acute infection - usually asymptomatic/self-limited (most commonly cervical lymphadenopathy); (2) ocular toxoplasmosis (chorioretinitis); (3) reactivation disease in the immunocompromised host - most importantly Toxoplasma encephalitis in AIDS (typically CD4+ <100/microL), which is rapidly fatal if untreated, plus pneumonitis, myocarditis, and disseminated disease; and (4) congenital toxoplasmosis, with severity inversely related to gestational age at maternal infection (earliest infection = lowest transmission but most severe fetal disease) (Harrison 22e p.1797-1800).

Abnormal separation of the primitive foregut into trachea and oesophagus during embryogenesis leaves an abnormal connection between the two and, commonly, a discontinuous oesophagus (atresia). In the common configuration, the upper oesophagus ends in a blind pouch while the lower oesophagus connects to the trachea. Swallowed secretions collect in and overflow from the upper pouch into the airway, and the distal fistula allows gastric contents to reflux into the trachea and air to distend the stomach. These mechanisms produce aspiration, chemical pneumonitis, and, with a large distal fistula, gaseous abdominal distension that further impairs ventilation.

An abnormal congenital communication between the trachea and oesophagus, most often occurring together with oesophageal atresia; the commonest anatomical type is proximal oesophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula.
Typical newborn features include excessive drooling and frothy secretions, choking, coughing, and cyanosis with feeds, and inability to pass a nasogastric tube into the stomach.

A characteristic radiographic clue is a feeding tube coiling in the upper oesophageal pouch; gas in the stomach and bowel indicates a distal fistula, while a gasless abdomen suggests atresia without a distal fistula.
Aspiration of saliva and, via the fistula, gastric contents into the airway causes respiratory compromise and pneumonitis.
An isolated H-type fistula without atresia may present later with recurrent coughing during feeds, cyanotic spells, and recurrent respiratory infections.
Initial management protects the airway and lungs: keep the infant nil by mouth, apply continuous suction to the upper pouch, and position to reduce aspiration and reflux through the fistula.
It is frequently part of the VACTERL association, so evaluation for vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, renal, and limb anomalies is important.
Definitive treatment is surgical division of the fistula and repair of the oesophageal atresia, timed according to the infant's stability and anatomy.
Long-term issues can include anastomotic stricture, gastro-oesophageal reflux, tracheomalacia, and dysphagia requiring ongoing follow-up.

With early diagnosis and surgical repair the outlook is generally favourable, and prognosis is influenced strongly by prematurity, birth weight, and associated anomalies, particularly cardiac lesions. Many children require management of later complications such as strictures, reflux, and tracheomalacia but achieve good long-term function.

Adverse reactions to blood components arise via immune or nonimmune mechanisms. Immune-mediated acute haemolysis occurs when recipient preformed antibodies (anti-A/anti-B IgM/IgG, or alloantibodies to Rh, Kell, Duffy) lyse transfused donor RBCs, with complement activation; ABO incompatibility classically results from clerical/identification error. Delayed haemolysis reflects an anamnestic alloantibody response (neoformed allogeneic IgG, C3b-mediated opsonisation and ADCC-mediated phagocytosis) detectable 1-2 weeks later. FNHTR is driven by proinflammatory cytokines accumulated in the component or recipient antibodies against donor leukocyte antigens. Allergic/anaphylactic reactions relate to plasma proteins and soluble mediators triggering histamine/serotonin release (IgA-deficient recipients may react to IgA). TRALI results from donor anti-HLA (class II, also class I) or anti-HNA antibodies binding recipient antigen, or cytokine/chemokine priming, causing neutrophil aggregation in pulmonary vasculature and release of inflammatory mediators producing noncardiogenic pulmonary oedema. TACO is hydrostatic circulatory overload from excessive volume/rate relative to cardiac/renal reserve. Transfusion-associated GVHD is mediated by engrafted donor T lymphocytes attacking host HLA antigens. (Harrison 22e p.906-912)

Acute immune-mediated haemolytic reactions occur when recipient preformed antibodies lyse transfused donor RBCs, during or up to 24 h after transfusion; anti-A/anti-B antibodies cause most of the most severe (potentially fatal) reactions, though alloantibodies against Rh, Kell, and Duffy antigens can also cause severe haemolysis (Harrison 22e p.906).

Most allergic transfusion reactions are mild (rash, pruritus, urticaria, localised oedema) and relate to plasma proteins; rarely they are severe/anaphylactic with bronchospasm, respiratory distress, hypotension, nausea, vomiting and shock - anaphylaxis can occur after only a few millilitres of component (Harrison 22e p.911).

TRALI is characterised by occurrence or worsening of hypoxia and NONcardiogenic pulmonary oedema with bilateral interstitial infiltrates on chest x-ray during or within 6 h of transfusion (delayed cases up to 72 h); it is among the most common causes of transfusion-related fatalities and treatment is supportive only (Harrison 22e p.911).

TRALI usually results from donor plasma containing high-titre anti-HLA class II antibodies binding recipient cognate antigen (anti-HLA class I and anti-HNA antibodies may also be involved); a cytokine/chemokine-mediated mechanism without HLA interaction can also occur (Harrison 22e p.911).

TACO (transfusion-associated circulatory overload) is common and underrecognised and is now the main cause of transfusion-related death since TRALI risk was mitigated; it presents with dyspnoea, hypoxia, bilateral and predominantly ALVEOLAR infiltrates on chest x-ray, frequent systolic hypertension, and elevated BNP (fever may also occur) (Harrison 22e p.912).

TRALI vs TACO distinction: TRALI gives noncardiogenic oedema with predominantly interstitial infiltrates within 6 h, whereas TACO is volume overload with predominantly alveolar infiltrates (within 12 h), systolic hypertension and elevated BNP; TACO risk factors include older age, renal failure, preexisting fluid overload, cardiac dysfunction, large transfusion volume and excessive transfusion rate (Harrison 22e p.911-912).

Transfusion-related GVHD is extremely rare but fatal in over 90% of cases; mediated by engrafted donor T lymphocytes in a recipient unable to reject them, it presents 5-10 days post-transfusion with cytopenia, fever, characteristic skin rash, diarrhoea and liver function abnormalities, and is prevented by irradiation (minimum 25 Gy) of cellular components in at-risk patients (Harrison 22e p.911).

Transfusion-transmitted bacterial infection remains a significant concern, notably with platelet concentrates stored at room temperature; some gram-negatives such as Yersinia grow at 4 degrees C and can contaminate RBC units - recipients may develop abrupt fever and chills deteriorating to septic shock, DIC and death, and after culture sampling broad-spectrum antibiotics should be started promptly (Harrison 22e p.913).

Iron overload: each RBC concentrate contains 200-250 mg of iron; in frequently transfused recipients untreated accumulation impairs endocrine, hepatic and cardiac function (death may occur from cardiac failure or arrhythmia), assessed by serum ferritin, MRI and liver biopsy, and prevented/treated by monitoring and iron chelation (Harrison 22e p.912).

Acute hypotensive transfusion reactions are an abrupt drop in systolic blood pressure of more than 30 mmHg early after starting transfusion that resolves once transfusion is stopped; they are more likely in patients taking ACE inhibitors (impaired bradykinin metabolism) and the same product should NOT be restarted (Harrison 22e p.912).

The most dramatic acute haemolytic reactions are usually caused by a failure in product or patient identification, erroneous blood grouping, or unidentified recipient anti-RBC alloimmunisation - i.e. a clerical/identification error (Harrison 22e p.906).

Acute haemolytic reactions may present with hypotension, tachypnoea, tachycardia, fever (rise of 1-2 degrees C), chills, chest and back/flank pain, haemoglobinuria, and haemoglobinemia; in the most severe cases DIC, acute renal failure, shock, and death may occur (Harrison 22e p.906).

RED FLAG: when an adverse reaction is suspected the transfusion must be STOPPED, the recipient's clinical status assessed, and supportive care initiated; a thorough clerical check is crucial to prevent a possible second misidentified transfusion (Harrison 22e p.908).

Management of acute immune haemolytic reaction is mainly supportive: prompt interruption of transfusion, biological workup, vigorous isotonic saline hydration with diuretics to maintain urine output; may require forced alkaline diuresis, electrolyte correction, and pressor support, and in DIC with bleeding, platelet/plasma/cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen (Harrison 22e p.908).

Diagnosis of transfusion-associated haemolysis relies on persistent/worsening anaemia, depleted haptoglobin, haemoglobinemia and haemoglobinuria, and elevated LDH and unconjugated bilirubin; the direct antiglobulin test (DAT/direct Coombs) is most often positive, as is the indirect antiglobulin test (IAT) (Harrison 22e p.908).

Delayed haemolytic reactions present with icterus and persisting or worsening anaemia and result from an anamnestic response in previously sensitised patients who had a negative alloantibody screen at transfusion (low antibody levels); the alloantibody becomes detectable 1-2 weeks after transfusion (Harrison 22e p.906).

FNHTR (febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction) is the most frequent reaction to cellular components (up to 300 per 100,000), characterised by chills, rigors and a rise of at least 1 degree C, caused by proinflammatory cytokines in the component or recipient antibodies against donor antigens; it is a diagnosis of exclusion once infection and haemolysis are ruled out (Harrison 22e p.911).
Leukocyte reduction (especially prestorage) can prevent FNHTR; premedication with antipyretics has generally proven ineffective and may mask relevant clinical symptoms (Harrison 22e p.911).

Most adverse reactions are non-life-threatening, though serious reactions can present with mild symptoms. An average of ~37 transfusion-associated fatalities (possible-to-definite imputability) were reported yearly to the FDA between 2017-2021 among ~15 million transfused components, with leading causes of death being TACO (32%), TRALI (21%), haemolysis (21%) and microbial contamination (13%). Acute haemolysis is often self-limiting but can be fatal (DIC, acute renal failure, shock). Transfusion-associated GVHD is fatal in over 90% of cases and highly resistant to treatment. (Harrison 22e p.906-911)

Temperature rise over 2 degrees C - favours transfusion-transmitted bacterial infection or haemolysis
Rash over two-thirds of body within 5 minutes with dyspnoea and shock - anaphylaxis
Development of DIC, acute renal failure or shock during/after transfusion

Warning-sign based recognition of transfusion adverse reactions (Harrison Table 118-5): fever of at least 38 degrees C (rise of 1-2 degrees C within 4 h favours FNHTR or TRALI; rise over 2 degrees C favours bacterial infection/haemolysis); hypotension (systolic drop of at least 30 mmHg) suggesting haemolytic, anaphylactic or septic shock; dyspnoea (TRALI within 6 h, TACO within 12 h, severe allergy within 4 h); haemoglobinuria (intravascular haemolysis); rash (minor allergy if under two-thirds body, severe if over two-thirds, anaphylaxis if with dyspnoea/shock within 5 min); icterus (delayed haemolysis); rash/diarrhoea/fever 2 days-6 weeks (GVHD); gum bleeding/purpura 5-12 days (posttransfusion purpura). Reactions are also categorised as immune-mediated vs nonimmunologic, and by timing (acute vs delayed). (Harrison 22e p.908)
Transfusion Reactions (non-infective) — Hematology / Transfusion Also: hemolytic transfusion reaction, TRALI, TACO

During fetal life the lungs are filled with fluid that is normally cleared around birth by labour-associated catecholamine and hormonal surges that switch alveolar epithelial cells from fluid secretion to sodium-driven absorption, aided by mechanical squeeze during vaginal delivery. When this clearance is delayed or incomplete, residual fluid remains in the interstitium and air spaces, reducing lung compliance and causing tachypnoea and mild hypoxaemia until the fluid is reabsorbed.
A common, benign, self-limited cause of respiratory distress in term and late-preterm newborns caused by delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid.
It typically presents soon after birth with tachypnoea, mild grunting, nasal flaring, and mild recession, usually without severe distress.
Delivery by caesarean section (especially without labour), maternal diabetes, and rapid or precipitous delivery are recognised risk factors.
The chest radiograph classically shows prominent perihilar vascular markings, fluid in the interlobar fissures, hyperinflation, and sometimes small pleural effusions.
It is largely a diagnosis of exclusion, and sepsis and pneumonia should be considered, particularly if distress is marked or prolonged.
Management is supportive with oxygen as required and attention to feeding; the condition usually resolves within the first day or two of life.
Oxygen requirement is generally modest, and the need for high oxygen or escalating support should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis.
Distress persisting well beyond 2-3 days argues against transient tachypnoea and warrants further evaluation.
Anchoring on transient tachypnoea and missing early sepsis or pneumonia
Overlooking congenital heart disease presenting with tachypnoea
Failing to reconsider the diagnosis when oxygen needs are high or distress is prolonged
Unnecessarily delaying feeding or investigation in a stable infant
Attributing every caesarean-born tachypnoeic infant to TTN without appropriate observation
The condition is benign and self-limited, resolving within hours to a few days with supportive care and no long-term respiratory sequelae in the great majority of infants.
High or rising oxygen requirement
Distress persisting beyond the first few days of life
Marked recession, grunting, or signs of respiratory failure
Features suggesting sepsis or pneumonia
Differential pre- and post-ductal saturations suggesting pulmonary hypertension or cardiac disease

Echocardiography to confirm ventriculoarterial discordance, mixing sites, and coronary anatomy

Chest radiograph looking for an egg-on-a-string silhouette
Blood gas to assess hypoxaemia and acidosis
Pulse oximetry, including pre- and post-ductal comparison

Abnormal division of the truncus arteriosus results in the aorta connecting to the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery to the left ventricle. As a consequence, deoxygenated systemic venous blood is pumped back to the body and oxygenated pulmonary venous blood is returned to the lungs, forming two separate parallel circuits. Life is only possible if oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix through a communication at the atrial, ventricular, or ductal level. Inadequate mixing produces severe systemic hypoxaemia and progressive metabolic acidosis, which worsens as the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale close after birth.
In d-transposition the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle, so the systemic and pulmonary circulations run in parallel rather than in series.
It is a leading cause of cyanosis presenting in the newborn period, often in an otherwise well-grown, term infant.
Survival depends on mixing between the two parallel circuits through a patent foramen ovale, atrial or ventricular septal defect, or the ductus arteriosus.
Cyanosis is typically profound and, unlike many respiratory causes, does not improve substantially with supplemental oxygen.
A prostaglandin infusion is started to maintain ductal patency and improve intercirculatory mixing while the infant is stabilised.
Balloon atrial septostomy may be performed to enlarge the atrial communication and improve mixing when cyanosis is severe.
Chest radiograph may show an egg-on-a-string cardiac silhouette with a narrow mediastinum, though this is not always present.
Echocardiography confirms the discordant great-artery connections, defines associated defects, and maps the coronary arteries before surgery.
The arterial switch operation, restoring normal ventriculoarterial connections, is the definitive repair and is performed in the neonatal period.
Attributing severe neonatal cyanosis to lung disease and delaying cardiac evaluation because oxygen does not help
Failing to start prostaglandin promptly, allowing the ductus to close and mixing to fail
Overlooking the need to enhance mixing (septostomy) in a critically hypoxaemic infant
Assuming a normal chest radiograph excludes the diagnosis
Not mapping coronary anatomy before surgical planning

With prompt stabilisation and an arterial switch operation in the neonatal period, most children do well with good long-term function, though follow-up is required for coronary, valve, and great-artery complications. Without intervention the condition is rapidly fatal.
Severe cyanosis in a newborn that fails to improve with supplemental oxygen
Rapid deterioration and acidosis as the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale close, restricting mixing
Duct-dependent collapse before prostaglandin is established
Worsening metabolic acidosis indicating inadequate systemic oxygen delivery
Inadequate intercirculatory mixing requiring urgent septostomy
Transposition of the Great Arteries (non-infective) — Paediatric cardiology Also: TGA, d-TGA, transposition of great vessels
Compressive myelopathy from disc, tumour, abscess, or haematoma

chunks.text: Transverse myelitis is focal inflammation of the spinal cord causing demyelination and axonal injury across one or more segments, disrupting ascending sensory and descending motor tracts as well as autonomic pathways. It may follow infection or vaccination as a para- or post-infectious immune response, arise from autoimmune demyelinating disease such as multiple sclerosis, NMOSD, or MOG antibody disease, or occur with systemic autoimmune conditions. Breakdown of the blood-cord barrier and inflammatory cell infiltration produce cord swelling and dysfunction.

chunks.text: The primary injury is the mechanical damage sustained at impact, which cannot be reversed. Secondary injury develops over hours to days from hypoxia, hypotension, oedema, haematoma expansion, seizures, and disturbed autoregulation. Because the skull is a fixed compartment, expanding blood or oedema raises intracranial pressure; once compensatory mechanisms are exhausted, small volume increases cause steep pressure rises. Rising intracranial pressure reduces cerebral perfusion pressure and drives ischaemia, and pressure gradients can force brain tissue across dural folds or the foramen magnum, producing herniation and brainstem compression.

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: These are zoonotic tissue-dwelling nematode infections arising from incidental human exposure; symptoms derive largely from invasive larval stages that (except for Trichinella) do not mature in humans. In trichinellosis, ingested encysted larvae are freed by gastric acid and proteases, invade small-bowel mucosa, mature to adults, and after about one week females release newborn larvae that migrate via the circulation to striated muscle, where most species encyst by radically transforming muscle-cell architecture into a 'nurse cell'; host immune responses help expel adult intestinal worms but have little effect on muscle larvae. Migrating larvae provoke a marked local and systemic hypersensitivity reaction with eosinophilia. In visceral larva migrans, ingested Toxocara eggs hatch, penetrate the gut, and disseminate to liver, lungs, CNS, and other tissues, eliciting intense eosinophilic granulomatous inflammation. In cutaneous larva migrans, animal hookworm larvae penetrate skin and burrow along the dermal-epidermal junction. In angiostrongyliasis, ingested infective larvae migrate to the brain and die there, inciting eosinophilic inflammation, hemorrhage, necrosis, and granuloma formation. In gnathostomiasis, aberrant migration of a single larva into cutaneous, visceral, neural, or ocular tissue causes local inflammation, including ascending migration along nerve tracts producing myeloencephalitis (Harrison 22e p.1810-1813).

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Trichinellosis follows ingestion of meat (classically pork, but increasingly wild game such as bear and walrus) containing encysted Trichinella larvae; most infections are mild or asymptomatic, but heavy burdens can be life-threatening (Harrison 22e p.1810).

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Angiostrongylus cantonensis (rat lungworm) is the most common cause of human eosinophilic meningitis; CSF shows elevated opening pressure, pleocytosis (150-2000 cells/uL) with eosinophilic pleocytosis >20%, elevated protein, and normal glucose (Harrison 22e p.1813).

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Gnathostomiasis is acquired from raw fish/poultry (e.g., som fak, sashimi) and causes migratory, recurrent pruritic cutaneous swellings; CNS invasion produces eosinophilic myeloencephalitis with agonizing radicular pain followed by paraplegia, and cerebral involvement is often fatal (Harrison 22e p.1813).

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Stool examination is worthless in toxocariasis because the larvae never develop into egg-producing adults in the human host (Harrison 22e p.1812).

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Disease severity tracks larval burden: light infections (<10 larvae/g muscle) tend to be asymptomatic, whereas heavy infections (>50 larvae/g muscle) can be life-threatening (Harrison 22e p.1811).

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Clinical course is biphasic: an early enteric phase (diarrhea, abdominal pain, constipation, nausea) in the first weeks, followed in the second week by larval-migration symptoms (fever, periorbital/facial edema, eosinophilia) and then a myositis phase as larvae encyst (Harrison 22e p.1811).

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Periorbital and facial edema with subconjunctival, retinal, and nail-bed (splinter) hemorrhages are characteristic of the migratory phase of trichinellosis (Harrison 22e p.1811).

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Most deaths in trichinellosis result from myocarditis (with tachyarrhythmias or heart failure) and, less commonly, encephalitis or pneumonitis (Harrison 22e p.1811).

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Muscle involvement preferentially affects the extraocular muscles, biceps, and the jaw, neck, lower back, and diaphragm muscles, with symptoms peaking around 3 weeks (Harrison 22e p.1811).

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Visceral larva migrans (most often Toxocara canis) chiefly affects preschool children who ingest soil contaminated with embryonated eggs, producing fever, hepatosplenomegaly, wheezing, and extraordinary eosinophilia that can approach 90% (Harrison 22e p.1812).

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Ocular larva migrans typically occurs in older children/young adults without pica and usually lacks eosinophilia or visceral signs; the retinal granuloma can mimic retinoblastoma and lead to unnecessary enucleation if misdiagnosed (Harrison 22e p.1812).

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Cutaneous larva migrans ('creeping eruption'), usually from the dog/cat hookworm Ancylostoma braziliense, produces an intensely pruritic serpiginous track that advances several centimeters per day; the larvae cannot mature in humans and self-resolve over weeks to a couple of months (Harrison 22e p.1812).

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Most mild trichinellosis cases remain undiagnosed; a high index of suspicion and a careful dietary/exposure history are needed.

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Trichinella serology is typically negative until after the third week, so a presumptive clinical diagnosis (fever, eosinophilia, periorbital edema, myalgia after a suspect meal) may be required early.

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Stool examination is useless in toxocariasis because larvae do not mature into egg-producing adults in humans.

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Ocular toxocariasis can be mistaken for retinoblastoma, risking unnecessary enucleation; it often lacks eosinophilia and visceral signs.

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: In angiostrongyliasis, A. cantonensis larvae are only rarely seen in CSF and serologic tests are unstandardized and may be negative at symptom onset.

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Arctic T. nativa larvae in walrus or bear meat are relatively freeze-resistant and may remain viable despite freezing, so usual freezing prevention may fail.

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Gnathostomiasis may present with ocular or CNS involvement without antecedent cutaneous swellings.

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Most lightly infected trichinellosis patients recover uneventfully, with symptoms peaking near 3 weeks and subsiding gradually over a prolonged convalescence; heavy infections can be life-threatening, with death usually due to myocarditis. Most visceral larva migrans infections are self-limited (rare deaths from severe organ involvement). Cutaneous larva migrans self-resolves over weeks to a couple of months as the larvae die. Cerebral angiostrongyliasis is usually self-limited with complete recovery, though heavy infections can leave permanent neurologic sequelae or cause death. Gnathostomiasis cutaneous swellings can recur intermittently over years; CNS gnathostomiasis is a serious complication and cerebral involvement is often fatal (Harrison 22e p.1811-1813).

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Myocarditis with tachyarrhythmias or heart failure (leading cause of death in trichinellosis)

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Encephalitis or pneumonitis in trichinellosis

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Dysphagia, dyspnea, or diaphragmatic muscle involvement

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Severe neurologic, pneumonic, or myocardial involvement in visceral larva migrans (rare deaths)

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Ascending radicular pain and paresthesias followed by paraplegia in gnathostomiasis (myeloencephalitis)

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Cerebral involvement with focal hemorrhages in gnathostomiasis (often fatal)

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Permanent neurologic sequelae from heavy CNS angiostrongyliasis

chunks.diseaseName: Trichinellosis and Other Tissue Nematode Infections
chunks.text: Trichinellosis severity correlates with muscle larval burden: light/asymptomatic infection <10 larvae per gram of muscle; heavy, potentially life-threatening infection >50 larvae per gram of muscle. Clinically graded as mild, moderate, and severe (severe = significant myositis/myocarditis) per Harrison's tissue nematode framework (Harrison 22e p.1811-1812).

Tricuspid stenosis is defined by a diastolic pressure gradient between the right atrium and right ventricle that increases with inspiration (greater transvalvular flow) and falls with expiration. A mean diastolic gradient of about 4 mmHg is usually enough to raise mean right atrial pressure to levels causing systemic venous congestion - hepatomegaly, ascites, and edema. Resting cardiac output is typically depressed and fails to rise with exercise. In tricuspid regurgitation, the incompetent valve allows backward flow from RV to RA, with the regurgitant volume governed by RV systolic driving pressure and the size of the regurgitant orifice; severity is modulated by pulmonary artery systolic pressure, annular dimensions, respiratory changes in RV preload, and RA compliance. Significant TR enlarges the right atrium, raises RA and jugular venous pressures with prominent c-v waves, can 'ventricularize' the RA waveform, and leads to RV volume overload, dilation, and eventual systolic dysfunction - accelerated by any added pressure load from pulmonary hypertension or prior myocardial fibrosis (Harrison 22e p.2059-2061).

Tricuspid stenosis is far less common than mitral stenosis in North America and Western Europe, is usually rheumatic in origin, occurs more often in women, and essentially never appears as an isolated lesion (it is typically combined with mitral stenosis) (Harrison 22e p.2059).

On ECG, absence of right ventricular hypertrophy in a patient with right-sided heart failure who is presumed to have mitral stenosis should raise suspicion for coexisting tricuspid valve disease; right atrial enlargement gives tall peaked P waves in lead II and prominent upright P waves in V1 (Harrison 22e p.2060).

A distinct category of tricuspid regurgitation is caused by cardiac implantable electronic device (CIED) leads crossing the valve, producing leaflet entrapment or perforation; right ventricular apical pacing can additionally cause dyssynchronous contraction and functional TR (Harrison 22e p.2060-2061).

Coexisting tricuspid stenosis can mask the hemodynamic and clinical features of associated mitral stenosis by lowering cardiac output and keeping left atrial, pulmonary artery, and RV systolic pressures only normal or mildly elevated (Harrison 22e p.2059).

Hemodynamically significant tricuspid stenosis is seen in roughly 5-10% of patients with severe mitral stenosis, and rheumatic tricuspid stenosis is commonly accompanied by some tricuspid regurgitation; nonrheumatic causes of stenosis are rare (Harrison 22e p.2059).

More than 85% of tricuspid regurgitation encountered clinically is secondary (functional), arising from tricuspid annular dilation and leaflet tethering in the setting of RV remodeling from pressure/volume overload, MI, or trauma rather than from intrinsic valve disease (Harrison 22e p.2060).
New-onset atrial fibrillation, especially in older patients, can produce 'atrial functional' tricuspid regurgitation through atrial and annular remodeling (Harrison 22e p.2060-2061).

Patients with severe tricuspid stenosis characteristically complain of relatively little dyspnea given the marked hepatomegaly, ascites, and edema present, because the right-sided obstruction limits pulmonary congestion (Harrison 22e p.2059).
Tricuspid regurgitation is more often detected by inspecting the neck veins (prominent c-v waves with rapid y descent) than by cardiac auscultation (Harrison 22e p.2061).

Carvallo's sign - inspiratory accentuation of the holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border - helps distinguish the murmur of tricuspid regurgitation from that of mitral regurgitation; it diminishes on expiration or during the Valsalva strain phase (Harrison 22e p.2061).

The murmur of tricuspid stenosis resembles that of mitral stenosis but is best heard at the lower left sternal border/xiphoid, is most prominent in presystole during sinus rhythm, and increases with inspiration while decreasing during expiration and Valsalva strain (Harrison 22e p.2060).

In tricuspid stenosis with sinus rhythm, the right atrial a wave can be enormous (approaching RV systolic pressure) and the y descent is prolonged; presystolic pulsations of an enlarged liver may also be palpable (Harrison 22e p.2059).

Tricuspid stenosis is easily overlooked because it almost always occurs alongside obvious mitral disease and its diastolic murmur resembles that of mitral stenosis - the diagnosis must be deliberately considered (Harrison 22e p.2059-2060).
The TR murmur may be mistaken for mitral regurgitation unless its inspiratory accentuation and the degree of RV enlargement are appreciated (Harrison 22e p.2061).
Accurate echocardiographic quantification of TR severity, PA pressure, and RV size/function is genuinely difficult in many patients (Harrison 22e p.2062).
Continuous-wave Doppler estimation of PA systolic pressure can be falsely low when TR is very severe because the jet velocity is blunted by rapidly rising RA pressure (Harrison 22e p.2062).

Mild-to-moderate tricuspid regurgitation is generally well tolerated when there is no other hemodynamic disturbance. Because TR commonly coexists with left-sided valve lesions, LV dysfunction, or pulmonary hypertension, those conditions often dominate the clinical course. As isolated severe TR progresses, reduced forward cardiac output causes fatigue and exertional dyspnea, and declining RV function leads to cervical pulsations, abdominal fullness, anorexia, muscle wasting, weight gain, and painful lower-extremity swelling. Severe TR is associated with markedly reduced cardiac output and elevated mean RA and RV end-diastolic pressures (Harrison 22e p.2061-2062).
Severe hepatic congestion progressing to cirrhosis, jaundice, serious malnutrition, anasarca, and ascites in severe tricuspid valve disease
Persistent right-sided failure after an adequate mitral commissurotomy, suggesting unrecognized tricuspid stenosis
Progressive RV dilation and declining systolic function in severe TR
Marked reduction in cardiac output with prominent c-v wave and rapid y descent and loss of the x descent in severe TR

Severe tricuspid stenosis is defined echocardiographically by a tricuspid valve area of 1 cm2 or less, or a pressure half-time of 190 ms or more; a mean diastolic gradient around 4 mmHg is hemodynamically significant. For tricuspid regurgitation, severity is staged (progressive Stage B, asymptomatic severe Stage C, symptomatic severe Stage D); annular dilation is defined as >40 mm (>21 mm/m2) on transthoracic echocardiography or >70 mm on direct intraoperative measurement, and severe TR is accompanied by hepatic vein systolic flow reversal (Harrison 22e p.2060-2062).

chunks.text: Tricyclic antidepressants exert several toxic actions. Blockade of fast cardiac sodium channels slows myocardial depolarisation, widening the QRS and predisposing to ventricular arrhythmia and myocardial depression; this effect is worsened by acidosis. Anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) activity produces the classic peripheral and central anticholinergic features. Antagonism of peripheral alpha-adrenergic receptors causes vasodilatation and hypotension, and central effects plus GABA and other receptor actions lower the seizure threshold. Seizures worsen acidosis, which in turn intensifies sodium-channel blockade in a dangerous positive-feedback loop.

chunks.diseaseName: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders
chunks.text: The cranial nerves are 12 paired nerves with mixed motor, sensory, and autonomic functions linked by their close brainstem relationships; nine connect directly to brainstem nuclei, while CN I and II are effectively brain fiber tracts and CN XI arises largely from upper cervical cord. In trigeminal neuralgia, symptoms arise from ectopic action-potential generation in pain-sensitive afferents of the fifth-nerve root just proximal to its entry at the lateral pons; demyelination of large myelinated (non-nociceptive) fibers renders them hyperexcitable and electrically coupled to adjacent small unmyelinated/poorly myelinated pain fibers, so tactile input can ignite paroxysms of pain. Compression of the root by a blood vessel—most often the superior cerebellar artery (or a tortuous vein)—is implicated in most cases; age-related brain sagging and increased vascular tortuosity may explain its predilection for later life. The trigeminal nerve carries oligodendrocyte-derived (central-type) myelin for up to ~7 mm beyond the brainstem, which may underlie trigeminal neuralgia in MS. In Bell’s palsy there is inflammation of the facial nerve with mononuclear cell infiltration suggesting an infectious/immune mechanism; reactivation of herpes simplex virus type 1 in the geniculate ganglion is thought to cause most cases, with varicella-zoster reactivation implicated in up to one-third (Ramsay Hunt syndrome). The vagus and other lower cranial nerves can be injured along their medullary, meningeal, foraminal, or extracranial courses; the recurrent laryngeal nerve (especially the left) is most often damaged by intrathoracic disease.

chunks.diseaseName: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders
chunks.text: Trigeminal neuralgia produces brief (seconds to a minute or two) paroxysms of excruciating, superficial, stabbing pain usually in the lips, gums, cheek, or chin (V2/V3); ophthalmic-division (V1) involvement is rare. Attacks may be triggered by light tactile stimuli at facial, lip, or tongue trigger zones (washing, brushing teeth, a draft of air) and by speaking, chewing, or smiling.

chunks.diseaseName: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders
chunks.text: Cavernous sinus syndrome is frequently life-threatening: orbital/facial pain, orbital swelling, chemosis, fever, ophthalmoplegia (III, IV, VI), and V1 (±V2) trigeminal involvement—cavernous sinus thrombosis from facial/orbital/sinus infection (including mucormycosis in diabetics) is the most common cause and demands early diagnosis.

chunks.diseaseName: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders
chunks.text: Tolosa-Hunt syndrome (idiopathic granulomatous cavernous-sinus/orbital inflammation) causes painful ophthalmoparesis with V1/V2 numbness and shows a dramatic response to glucocorticoids, but its picture can be mimicked by sarcoid, vasculitis, IgG4-related disease, lymphoma, and fungal infection—so confirm before attributing to it.

chunks.diseaseName: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders
chunks.text: An eleventh-nerve (spinal accessory) palsy causes little overt neck weakness because other muscles assist head turning; detection relies on palpating absent sternocleidomastoid contraction during head turning and on noting a lower shoulder, scapular winging, and inability to abduct the arm beyond 90 degrees.

chunks.diseaseName: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders
chunks.text: An essential diagnostic feature of classic trigeminal neuralgia is the ABSENCE of demonstrable objective sensory loss on examination; demonstrable trigeminal sensory or motor deficit instead points to a structural trigeminal neuropathy or secondary cause.

chunks.diseaseName: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders
chunks.text: Trigeminal neuralgia is relatively common (incidence ~4–8 per 100,000/year), affects mainly middle-aged and elderly persons, and roughly 60% of cases occur in women; bouts persist for weeks to months and tend to remit then recur.

chunks.diseaseName: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders
chunks.text: When trigeminal neuralgia occurs in a young adult or is bilateral, suspect multiple sclerosis (demyelinating plaque near the trigeminal root entry zone in the pons), especially if subtle facial sensory loss is present.

chunks.diseaseName: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders
chunks.text: Bell’s palsy is the most common form of facial paralysis (annual incidence ~25 per 100,000; lifetime risk ~1 in 60); onset is abrupt with maximal weakness by 48 h, often preceded by retroauricular pain for a day or two, and may include loss of taste and hyperacusis.

chunks.diseaseName: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders
chunks.text: A peripheral (lower motor neuron) facial palsy weakens the whole hemiface including the forehead and eyelid closure, whereas a supranuclear (central) lesion relatively spares the forehead and orbicularis oculi because upper-face muscles receive bilateral corticobulbar innervation.

chunks.diseaseName: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders
chunks.text: Localizing the seventh-nerve lesion: loss of taste over the anterior two-thirds of the tongue points to a middle-ear-segment lesion; hyperacusis indicates involvement of the nerve to stapedius; accompanying deafness, tinnitus, or vertigo suggests an internal auditory meatus lesion affecting the eighth nerve.

chunks.diseaseName: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders
chunks.text: Glossopharyngeal neuralgia resembles trigeminal neuralgia but is much less common; pain is paroxysmal and intense, arises in the tonsillar fossa/throat, may radiate to the ear, and is provoked by swallowing or coughing; rarely it triggers bradycardia/asystole, hypotension, and syncope.

chunks.diseaseName: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders
chunks.text: Anatomic clustering of cranial nerves yields recognizable syndromes: jugular foramen (IX, X, XI), cavernous sinus (III, IV, V1, VI), pontocerebellar angle (V, VI, VII, VIII), and retroparotid space (IX, X, XI, XII plus Horner’s).

chunks.diseaseName: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders
chunks.text: Diagnosing classic trigeminal neuralgia despite objective trigeminal sensory loss—such findings indicate trigeminal neuropathy from a structural/secondary cause (aneurysm, neurofibroma, acoustic schwannoma, meningioma).

chunks.diseaseName: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders
chunks.text: Overlooking multiple sclerosis as the cause of trigeminal neuralgia in a young adult or when symptoms are bilateral.

chunks.diseaseName: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders
chunks.text: Mistaking a central (supranuclear) forehead-sparing facial weakness for peripheral Bell’s palsy and missing a stroke or hemispheric lesion.

chunks.diseaseName: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders
chunks.text: Failing to examine the eighth and other cranial nerves in a patient with facial palsy—the eighth nerve runs close to the facial nerve at the pontomedullary junction and in the temporal bone.

chunks.diseaseName: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders
chunks.text: Attributing an insidious, progressive facial weakness to Bell’s palsy when it actually reflects a temporal bone or pontine tumor.

chunks.diseaseName: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders
chunks.text: Missing Ramsay Hunt syndrome by not inspecting the external auditory canal and palate for zoster vesicles.

chunks.diseaseName: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders
chunks.text: Misdiagnosing vagal/laryngeal or pharyngeal muscle disease (polymyositis, dermatomyositis, myotonic dystrophy) as a primary vagus nerve lesion in dysphagia/dysphonia.

chunks.diseaseName: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders
chunks.text: Searching intracranially for an isolated vocal cord palsy when intrathoracic disease (aortic aneurysm, enlarged left atrium, mediastinal/bronchial tumor) is the far more common cause.

chunks.diseaseName: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders
chunks.text: Delaying recognition and treatment of cavernous sinus thrombosis, an early-diagnosis emergency.

chunks.diseaseName: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders
chunks.text: Trigeminal neuralgia characteristically remits spontaneously after bouts lasting weeks to months, and remissions can be long-lasting, though the disorder ultimately recurs in most patients. In Bell’s palsy, about 80% of patients recover within a few weeks to months; incomplete paralysis during the first week is the most favorable prognostic sign, whereas EMG evidence of denervation after 10 days predicts axonal degeneration with delayed (typically ~3 months) and possibly incomplete recovery, and recurrences occur in roughly 7% of cases. Idiopathic trigeminal neuropathy usually recovers gradually. Most patients with isolated spinal accessory neuropathy recover. Post-intubation Tapia syndrome (vagal plus hypoglossal palsy) usually resolves within a few months.

chunks.diseaseName: Trigeminal Neuralgia, Bell’s Palsy, and Other Cranial Nerve Disorders
chunks.text: No formal grading scale is presented in this chapter. In Bell’s palsy, clinical severity is gauged by completeness of paralysis, with incomplete paralysis in the first week being the most favorable prognostic indicator and electromyographic denervation after 10 days indicating axonal degeneration and a worse, more prolonged recovery. The diagnosis of Bell’s palsy is supported clinically by a typical presentation, absence of other risk factors/symptoms, no zoster lesions in the ear canal, and a normal neurologic examination apart from the facial nerve.

chunks.text: TTP arises from deficient or antibody-inhibited ADAMTS13, the metalloprotease that cleaves von Willebrand factor (VWF). VWF is secreted by endothelium as ultra-large multimers; when these are not cleaved they persist and drive pathological platelet adhesion and aggregation, producing microvascular thrombi. ADAMTS13 deficiency alone is not sufficient — congenitally ADAMTS13-deficient individuals develop TTP only episodically, implying a second trigger. In HUS the dominant lesion is endothelial injury with deposition of fibrin in capillary/arteriolar walls, predominantly in the kidney; typical (diarrhoea-associated) HUS is driven by Shiga toxin from E. coli O157:H7, while atypical HUS results from dysregulated activation of the complement alternative pathway with consequent endothelial damage. The shared downstream picture is microvascular platelet/fibrin thrombi causing red-cell fragmentation (MAHA), consumption thrombocytopenia and end-organ ischaemia (Harrison 22e pp.967-968, 800-801).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chap. 120 pp.967-968 (TTP/HUS); Chap. 105 pp.800-801 (familial/atypical HUS); Chap. on cutaneous purpura p.450; oncologic-emergencies HUS p.638; blood-smear schistocytes p.~640

chunks.text: The thrombotic microangiopathies are unified by microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA): thrombocytopenia plus fragmented red cells (schistocytes) on the smear, biochemical haemolysis (high LDH, high unconjugated bilirubin, low haptoglobin) and microvascular thrombosis (Harrison 22e p.967).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chap. 120 pp.967-968 (TTP/HUS); Chap. 105 pp.800-801 (familial/atypical HUS); Chap. on cutaneous purpura p.450; oncologic-emergencies HUS p.638; blood-smear schistocytes p.~640

chunks.text: TTP was classically described as a pentad of MAHA, thrombocytopenia, renal failure, neurologic changes and fever; the full pentad is now seen less often because earlier diagnosis and treatment intervene before it evolves (Harrison 22e pp.967-968).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chap. 120 pp.967-968 (TTP/HUS); Chap. 105 pp.800-801 (familial/atypical HUS); Chap. on cutaneous purpura p.450; oncologic-emergencies HUS p.638; blood-smear schistocytes p.~640

chunks.text: ADAMTS13 activity below 10% is diagnostic of TTP; the assay (activity level plus anti-ADAMTS13 antibody) is central to working up any MAHA (Harrison 22e p.968).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chap. 120 pp.967-968 (TTP/HUS); Chap. 105 pp.800-801 (familial/atypical HUS); Chap. on cutaneous purpura p.450; oncologic-emergencies HUS p.638; blood-smear schistocytes p.~640

chunks.text: ADAMTS13 levels are generally normal in HUS, although they have occasionally been reported as decreased — so a normal ADAMTS13 does not exclude a thrombotic microangiopathy other than TTP (Harrison 22e p.968).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chap. 120 pp.967-968 (TTP/HUS); Chap. 105 pp.800-801 (familial/atypical HUS); Chap. on cutaneous purpura p.450; oncologic-emergencies HUS p.638; blood-smear schistocytes p.~640

chunks.text: Schistocytes are red-cell fragments produced by physical disruption against intravascular platelet/fibrin strands or external forces, and are the morphologic hallmark of MAHA (Harrison 22e p.~640).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chap. 120 pp.967-968 (TTP/HUS); Chap. 105 pp.800-801 (familial/atypical HUS); Chap. on cutaneous purpura p.450; oncologic-emergencies HUS p.638; blood-smear schistocytes p.~640

chunks.text: The Coombs (direct antiglobulin) test is negative in microangiopathic haemolysis, helping separate it from autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (Harrison 22e p.638).

chunks.text: TTP is more common in women than men, and is over-represented in HIV infection and in pregnancy; congenital ADAMTS13 deficiency (Upshaw-Schulman) may first declare itself during a first pregnancy (Harrison 22e p.968).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chap. 120 pp.967-968 (TTP/HUS); Chap. 105 pp.800-801 (familial/atypical HUS); Chap. on cutaneous purpura p.450; oncologic-emergencies HUS p.638; blood-smear schistocytes p.~640

chunks.text: In a classic HUS presentation, a preceding episode of diarrhoea (often bloody) in a child points to Shiga-toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7 as the commonest, though not the only, cause (Harrison 22e p.968).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chap. 120 pp.967-968 (TTP/HUS); Chap. 105 pp.800-801 (familial/atypical HUS); Chap. on cutaneous purpura p.450; oncologic-emergencies HUS p.638; blood-smear schistocytes p.~640

chunks.text: Atypical HUS is essentially a complement-alternative-pathway disease — driven by mutations in complement components/regulators (C3, CFB, CFH, CD46/MCP, CFI, THBD) or anti-factor-H antibodies — and clinical disease usually requires a trigger such as infection, so penetrance is incomplete (Harrison 22e pp.800-801).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chap. 120 pp.967-968 (TTP/HUS); Chap. 105 pp.800-801 (familial/atypical HUS); Chap. on cutaneous purpura p.450; oncologic-emergencies HUS p.638; blood-smear schistocytes p.~640

chunks.text: Do not reflexively transfuse platelets in TTP — platelet transfusion may fuel further microvascular thrombosis and is reserved for life-threatening bleeding (principle, Harrison 22e Chap. 120).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chap. 120 pp.967-968 (TTP/HUS); Chap. 105 pp.800-801 (familial/atypical HUS); Chap. on cutaneous purpura p.450; oncologic-emergencies HUS p.638; blood-smear schistocytes p.~640

chunks.text: Do not assume normal coagulation excludes a thrombotic microangiopathy: PT and aPTT are characteristically normal in TTP/HUS, whereas they are abnormal in DIC — use them to discriminate, not to exclude (Harrison 22e p.967).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chap. 120 pp.967-968 (TTP/HUS); Chap. 105 pp.800-801 (familial/atypical HUS); Chap. on cutaneous purpura p.450; oncologic-emergencies HUS p.638; blood-smear schistocytes p.~640

chunks.text: A normal ADAMTS13 does not point to TTP; ADAMTS13 is usually normal in HUS, so the diagnosis there rests on the clinical picture and complement work-up (Harrison 22e p.968).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chap. 120 pp.967-968 (TTP/HUS); Chap. 105 pp.800-801 (familial/atypical HUS); Chap. on cutaneous purpura p.450; oncologic-emergencies HUS p.638; blood-smear schistocytes p.~640

chunks.text: Atypical HUS is a diagnosis of exclusion; patients may be started on plasma exchange until ADAMTS13 returns and the diagnosis clarifies, even though plasma exchange has not been shown to change clinical outcomes in aHUS (Harrison 22e p.968).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chap. 120 pp.967-968 (TTP/HUS); Chap. 105 pp.800-801 (familial/atypical HUS); Chap. on cutaneous purpura p.450; oncologic-emergencies HUS p.638; blood-smear schistocytes p.~640

chunks.text: Plasma infusion/exchange does not alter the course of typical HUS or aHUS except in the subgroup with anti-factor-H antibodies (Harrison 22e p.968).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chap. 120 pp.967-968 (TTP/HUS); Chap. 105 pp.800-801 (familial/atypical HUS); Chap. on cutaneous purpura p.450; oncologic-emergencies HUS p.638; blood-smear schistocytes p.~640

chunks.text: Drug-induced microangiopathy may improve simply on withdrawing or reducing the offending endothelial-toxic agent, so reflexive long-term plasma exchange may be unnecessary (Harrison 22e p.968).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chap. 120 pp.967-968 (TTP/HUS); Chap. 105 pp.800-801 (familial/atypical HUS); Chap. on cutaneous purpura p.450; oncologic-emergencies HUS p.638; blood-smear schistocytes p.~640

chunks.text: Cancer-associated HUS can present without an evident malignancy — in one series 35% had no apparent cancer when the syndrome appeared, and it may surface weeks to months after the last chemotherapy dose (Harrison 22e p.638).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chap. 120 pp.967-968 (TTP/HUS); Chap. 105 pp.800-801 (familial/atypical HUS); Chap. on cutaneous purpura p.450; oncologic-emergencies HUS p.638; blood-smear schistocytes p.~640

chunks.text: Plasma exchange transformed TTP outcomes, reducing mortality from roughly 85-100% to about 10-30%. Relapse is common: 25-45% of plasma-exchange-treated patients relapse within 30 days of apparent remission and 12-40% relapse late, with relapse more frequent in those with severe ADAMTS13 deficiency at presentation. In diarrhoea-associated HUS roughly 40% of children need some dialysis but overall mortality is <5%; non-diarrhoeal HUS carries higher mortality (~26%). Untreated atypical HUS had acute-phase mortality up to ~15% with up to 50% progressing to end-stage renal disease, though spontaneous remission occurs and relapse is likely with re-exposure to a trigger. Cancer-/chemotherapy-associated HUS has a high case-fatality rate, with most patients dying within months (Harrison 22e pp.968, 800-801, 638).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chap. 120 pp.967-968 (TTP/HUS); Chap. 105 pp.800-801 (familial/atypical HUS); Chap. on cutaneous purpura p.450; oncologic-emergencies HUS p.638; blood-smear schistocytes p.~640

chunks.text: New unexplained thrombocytopenia with MAHA is a haematologic emergency — TTP is devastating if not recognised and treated promptly (Harrison 22e p.968)

source.page: Harrison 22e Chap. 120 pp.967-968 (TTP/HUS); Chap. 105 pp.800-801 (familial/atypical HUS); Chap. on cutaneous purpura p.450; oncologic-emergencies HUS p.638; blood-smear schistocytes p.~640

chunks.text: Plasma exchange should be initiated urgently on clinical suspicion without waiting for confirmatory ADAMTS13 results, and likewise re-initiated promptly on suspected relapse (Harrison 22e p.968)

chunks.text: In cancer-/transfusion-associated HUS, severe hypertension, pulmonary oedema and rapid worsening of haemolysis and renal function can follow a blood or blood-product transfusion (Harrison 22e p.638)

chunks.text: Harrison does not give a formal TTP/HUS severity score in this material. Functional stratification used: ADAMTS13 activity <10% is diagnostic of TTP and severe deficiency at presentation predicts relapse and worse sequelae. HUS is grouped clinically into diarrhoea-associated (typical, Shiga-toxin) HUS versus non-diarrhoea-associated/atypical (complement-mediated) HUS, which carries higher mortality. (No PLASMIC score is described in the source and none is asserted here.) (Harrison 22e pp.968, 800-801).
