Anti-Ro (SS-A) and anti-La (SS-B) antibodies when Sjogren's syndrome suspected (Harrison 22e p.2438)
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis and immunofixation, plus serum/urine free light chains, when light chain cast nephropathy suspected (Harrison 22e p.2440)

Renal ultrasonography - 'medical renal disease' changes (increased echogenicity, loss of corticomedullary differentiation); asymmetric scarred kidneys in reflux nephropathy (Harrison 22e p.2437, p.2441)

Kidney biopsy - not usually required for AIN diagnosis but shows interstitial/tubular leukocyte infiltration including eosinophils; required (with other criteria) for aristolochic acid nephropathy (Harrison 22e p.2438, p.2442)
Acute tubular necrosis and other causes of unexplained AKI (biopsy-proven AIN accounts for no more than ~15% of unexplained AKI, likely an underestimate) (Harrison 22e p.2437)
Primary glomerulonephritis causing secondary tubulointerstitial damage; in advanced disease the initial cause is often difficult to discern on biopsy (Harrison 22e p.2442)
Behcet's disease and sarcoidosis as alternative causes of uveitis when considering TINU (Harrison 22e p.2439)

A group of disorders that primarily affect the renal tubules and interstitium with relative sparing of the glomeruli and vessels, divided into acute and chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis (TIN) (Harrison 22e p.2437). Acute TIN causes AKI either via aggressive inflammatory infiltrates producing tissue edema, tubular cell injury, and compromised tubular flow, or via frank tubular obstruction by casts, cellular debris, or crystals; flank pain may arise from renal capsule distention (Harrison 22e p.2437). Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) is most commonly an allergic, immune-mediated drug reaction (antibiotics such as beta-lactams/sulfonamides/quinolones/vancomycin/rifampin, NSAIDs/COX-2 inhibitors, proton pump inhibitors, diuretics, anticonvulsants, allopurinol, immune checkpoint inhibitors), but may also be immune-mediated within autoimmune syndromes (Sjogren's, SLE, TINU, granulomatous/sarcoid, IgG4-related disease) or infection-associated (Harrison 22e p.2437-2438). Chronic TIN produces interstitial fibrosis with patchy mononuclear cell infiltration, widespread tubular atrophy, luminal dilation, and thickened tubular basement membranes, manifesting as tubular dysfunction (nephrogenic DI, Fanconi's syndrome, RTA) and progressive azotemia (Harrison 22e p.2437). Because the chronic histopathology is nonspecific, biopsy rarely yields a specific diagnosis, so diagnosis relies on history, drug/toxin exposure, associated symptoms, and imaging (Harrison 22e p.2437).

Tubulointerstitial diseases primarily affect the tubules and interstitium with relative sparing of the glomeruli and renal vessels, and are divided into acute and chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis (TIN) (Harrison 22e p.2437).
Papillary necrosis is a key feature of analgesic nephropathy; a sloughed necrotic papilla can cause gross hematuria and ureteric colic from ureteral obstruction (Harrison 22e p.2442).
Renal ultrasound in reflux nephropathy characteristically shows asymmetric small kidneys with irregular outlines, thinned cortices, and regions of compensatory hypertrophy (Harrison 22e p.2441).

Classic allergic acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) presents with fever, rash, peripheral eosinophilia, and oliguric acute kidney injury occurring after 7-10 days of a beta-lactam (e.g., methicillin) - but this classic tetrad is the exception rather than the rule; patients are more often found incidentally to have a rising creatinine (Harrison 22e p.2438).
Acute TIN most often presents as acute kidney injury; today AIN is far more often an allergic reaction to a drug than a postinfectious phenomenon (Harrison 22e p.2437).

Urinalysis in allergic AIN shows pyuria with white blood cell casts and hematuria; white blood cell (leukocyte) casts are a characteristic finding of interstitial nephritis (Harrison 22e p.2438, p.2456).

The mainstay of treatment for drug-induced AIN is discontinuation of the offending agent, which often leads to reversal of kidney injury; glucocorticoids may accelerate recovery but are NOT required in most cases and are reserved for severe injury (Harrison 22e p.2438).

Chronic TIN is more indolent and manifests with disorders of tubular function: polyuria from impaired concentrating ability (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), Fanconi's syndrome from defective proximal reabsorption (glycosuria, phosphaturia, aminoaciduria, hypokalemia, and type II/proximal RTA from bicarbonaturia), or non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with hyperkalemia (type IV RTA) from impaired ammoniagenesis (Harrison 22e p.2437).

Proteinuria in chronic TIN is usually modest (rarely >2 g/d) from decreased tubular reabsorption of filtered proteins, but nephrotic-range albuminuria may occur when secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) develops (Harrison 22e p.2437).

Tubulointerstitial nephritis with uveitis (TINU) accounts for <5% of AIN, affects females 3x more than males, with median onset age 15 years; hallmark is painful anterior uveitis plus lymphocyte-predominant interstitial nephritis, with sterile pyuria, mild proteinuria, features of Fanconi's syndrome, and elevated ESR (Harrison 22e p.2439).

Sterile pyuria with elevated creatinine and features of Fanconi's syndrome should raise suspicion for TINU; ocular symptoms precede or accompany kidney disease in only one-third of cases (Harrison 22e p.2439).
The classic AIN tetrad (fever, rash, eosinophilia, oliguric AKI) is the exception rather than the rule; relying on it misses most cases (Harrison 22e p.2438).
NSAID-induced AIN often lacks fever, rash, and eosinophilia but presents with AKI and heavy proteinuria (Harrison 22e p.2438).
Urinary eosinophil testing is neither sensitive nor specific for AIN and is not recommended (Harrison 22e p.2438).
Absence of peripheral eosinophilia does not exclude AIN, as it is present in only a minority of patients (Harrison 22e p.2438).

A negative urine dipstick for protein with elevated total spot urine protein is highly suggestive of Bence-Jones protein (light chains), which dipsticks do not detect - missing myeloma kidney (Harrison 22e p.2440).
Reflux nephropathy may go unnoticed until adulthood and can be mistaken for 'chronic pyelonephritis'; a single affected kidney may be silent except for hypertension (Harrison 22e p.2441).
Because chronic TIN histopathology is nonspecific, biopsy rarely gives a specific diagnosis; over-reliance on biopsy without history/exposure analysis is a pitfall (Harrison 22e p.2437).

In allergic/drug-induced AIN, discontinuation of the offending agent often reverses the kidney injury, though recovery may be incomplete depending on duration of exposure and degree of tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis (Harrison 22e p.2438). Granulomatous, idiopathic, TINU, and Sjogren's-related interstitial nephritis generally respond to glucocorticoids, especially when treated early before significant fibrosis, but may relapse and require maintenance immunosuppression (Harrison 22e p.2438-2439). Chronic TIN damage that has already occurred is impossible to reverse, but further deterioration may be slowed by treating glomerular hypertension (Harrison 22e p.2440). Reflux nephropathy affecting both kidneys often progresses inexorably to ESRD over years even without ongoing infection or reflux (Harrison 22e p.2441). Lithium-associated CKD is often irreversible and slowly progresses to ESRD even after lithium is stopped (Harrison 22e p.2443). AKI from acute hypercalcemia may be fully reversible, whereas chronic hypercalcemic kidney dysfunction may not improve even after correcting the calcium disorder (Harrison 22e p.2443).
Classic allergic AIN tetrad: fever, rash, peripheral eosinophilia, and oliguric AKI after a drug (Harrison 22e p.2438)
Particularly severe and rapid-onset AIN upon reintroduction of rifampin after a drug-free period (Harrison 22e p.2438)
Painful anterior uveitis (often bilateral, with blurred vision and photophobia) with sterile pyuria and AKI - suggests TINU (Harrison 22e p.2439)
Gross hematuria with ureteric colic from a sloughed necrotic papilla in analgesic or sickle cell nephropathy (Harrison 22e p.2442)
Triad of saturnine gout, hypertension, and impaired kidney function suggesting lead nephropathy (Harrison 22e p.2443)
Anemia disproportionately severe relative to kidney dysfunction in aristolochic acid nephropathy (with very high risk of upper urinary tract urothelial cancer) (Harrison 22e p.2442)

Harrison classifies tubulointerstitial diseases into Acute Tubulointerstitial Disorders - acute interstitial nephritis (therapeutic agents/drugs, infection, autoimmune including TINU, Sjogren's, SLE, granulomatous, IgG4-related) and acute obstructive disorders (light chain cast nephropathy, acute phosphate nephropathy, acute urate nephropathy) - versus Chronic Tubulointerstitial Disorders (reflux nephropathy, sickle cell disease, chronic toxin/drug exposure such as analgesics, lithium, heavy metals, aristolochic acid, calcineurin inhibitors), metabolic disturbances (hypercalcemia/nephrocalcinosis, hyperuricemia, hypokalemia, hyperoxaluria, cystinosis), cystic/hereditary disorders, and miscellaneous causes (aging, chronic glomerulonephritis, obstruction, ischemia, radiation) (Harrison 22e p.2437).
Tubulointerstitial Kidney Disease (non-infective) — Nephrology Also: interstitial nephritis, acute interstitial nephritis, renal tubular acidosis
Lung cancer (pulmonary nodules or dense consolidation can mimic malignancy, prompting CT/PET and biopsy before tularemia is suspected) (Harrison 22e p.1337, 1339)
Head and neck cancer (Harrison 22e p.1337)
Lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.1337)
Tuberculosis (Harrison 22e p.1337)
Unspecified viral infection / 'a severe virus' (Harrison 22e p.1337)
Common skin and soft tissue infection (Harrison 22e p.1337)
Community-acquired pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.1337)
Undifferentiated fever or sepsis (Harrison 22e p.1337)
Tuberculosis (Harrison 22e p.1337)
Community-acquired pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.1337)
Common skin and soft tissue infection (Harrison 22e p.1337)
Unspecified viral infection (Harrison 22e p.1337)

Laboratory confirmation by recovery of an F. tularensis isolate, detection of F. tularensis-specific antigens or nucleic acids, or detection of specific antibodies by serology (Harrison 22e p.1338-1339)
Direct detection by PCR/nucleic acid testing of clinical specimens is rapid and reliable; for ulcer specimens it is comparable to culture in sensitivity and specificity (Harrison 22e p.1339)

Appropriate specimens for direct detection or culture: ulcer specimens (sampled from the wound edge), lower respiratory tract specimens (sputum, tracheal washing, bronchoalveolar lavage), lymph node biopsies or aspirates, and blood cultures (Harrison 22e p.1339)

Blood culture: F. tularensis is slow-growing and a 10-day incubation is recommended for optimal sensitivity; MALDI-TOF identification from blood cultures is an increasingly common, sometimes unexpected, finding (Harrison 22e p.1339)

Serology (ELISA or microagglutination) is the mainstay in many laboratories and is especially useful when tularemia is suspected at a later stage; antibodies are generally detectable 10-20 days post-infection (Harrison 22e p.1339)

Chest imaging in respiratory tularemia: single or multifocal consolidation, pleural effusion, and hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy; CT may show rounded subpleural consolidations and necrotic lymph nodes; pathology resolution on imaging can be slow and take months (Harrison 22e p.1339)
Lung cancer (Harrison 22e p.1337, 1339)
Head and neck cancer (Harrison 22e p.1337)
Lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.1337)
Suspected tumor with lymphoid tissue engagement (Harrison 22e p.1337)

Natural transmission is usually through the skin or by inhalation of aerosols, but ingestion of contaminated food/water can also infect. An extremely low dose of about 10-50 organisms inoculated through skin microtrauma or inhaled suffices to cause disease, whereas roughly 10^6-10^8 organisms are required by the oral route. Tissue-resident macrophages (alveolar macrophages in lung, Langerhans cells in skin) transport the organism via blood and lymphatics to lymph nodes, spleen, and bone marrow; in skin, neutrophils phagocytose F. tularensis early. After uptake, the bacterium escapes the phagosome into the cytosol, replicates, exits the cell, and disseminates. F. tularensis is a 'stealth pathogen' that manipulates host-cell signaling, delaying the immune response and permitting rapid systemic spread. Characteristic tissue reactions are granuloma formation and necrotic foci surrounded by macrophages, lymphocytes, and giant cells in lymph nodes, lung, spleen, kidney, and liver; pulmonary autopsy findings show necrotizing pneumonia with fibrin, cellular debris, and neutrophils. Effective protective immunity requires both B and T cells, and antigen-specific recall T-cell responses can persist 25-30 years after infection or vaccination (Harrison 22e p.1337, 1339).

Zoonosis caused by Francisella tularensis, a small facultatively intracellular aerobic gram-negative coccobacillus; humans are infected via arthropod bites (ticks, tabanid/deer flies, mosquitoes), inhalation of infectious aerosols, handling infected animals, or ingestion of contaminated water/food (Harrison 22e p.1335-1336).

Typhoidal form (~14% of US cases): an older term for a typhoid-like syndrome with prolonged high fever, fatigue, headache, and nausea; Harrison recommends avoiding the term because most historic typhoidal cases were in fact respiratory/pneumonic tularemia acquired by inhalation (Harrison 22e p.1338).

Routine blood biochemistry is generally unhelpful; findings are nonspecific and may or may not show elevated liver enzymes or hematuria. In a Swedish type B outpatient series, white-cell counts stayed within normal limits in 70% of patients and CRP was only moderately elevated (Harrison 22e p.1338).

When tularemia is clinically suspected, communicate the suspicion to the microbiology laboratory in advance so that cultures are handled safely, because F. tularensis causes laboratory-acquired infection and culture requires BSL-3 containment; it is also a US HHS Tier 1 Select Agent (Harrison 22e p.1335, 1339).
For ulcer sampling, swab the edge of the wound (remove any scab first) and rub firmly so the specimen is slightly blood-tinged to maximize yield (Harrison 22e p.1339).

Take a deliberate exposure history: wild animal contact (rodents, rabbits, hares), inhalation of dust contaminated with their urine or feces, recent tick/fly/mosquito bites, brush-cutting or grass-trimming, handling wood or hay, and walking or hunting in wildlife habitats; cluster cases sharing the same exposure are a clue (Harrison 22e p.1337).

The most common initial manifestation is an influenza-like illness with high fever (acute onset, myalgia, headache, constitutional symptoms); fever may be persistent or intermittent. Incubation is usually 3-5 days but may range from 1 to 21 days (Harrison 22e p.1337).

Inflamed, swollen, tender regional lymph nodes are typical; the initial infection route determines which lymphoid tissue is engaged (skin or pharyngeal entry gives regional nodes; inhalation gives mediastinal/hilar nodes) (Harrison 22e p.1337).

Ulceroglandular form (most common, ~47% of US cases): skin inoculation by a blood-feeding arthropod or direct contact with an infected animal/contaminated material produces a primary ulcer plus tender regional lymphadenopathy; the primary ulcer is often a small skin break with limited inflammation that requires careful examination to detect (Harrison 22e p.1337-1338).
Glandular form (~18% of US cases): regional lymphadenopathy without a detectable primary skin ulcer (Harrison 22e p.1338).

Oculoglandular form (~2% of US cases): conjunctivitis with pronounced local inflammation plus regional (e.g., preauricular) lymphadenopathy, acquired by touching the eye with contaminated fingers or by contaminated aerosol (Harrison 22e p.1338).

Oropharyngeal form (~2% of US cases): acute pharyngitis with pronounced local inflammation following ingestion of contaminated water or food, with cervical/tonsillar lymphadenopathy (Harrison 22e p.1338).

Respiratory/pneumonic form (~17% of US cases): acquired by inhaling contaminated aerosol; more often bacteremic and more likely to progress to severe disease requiring inpatient care, particularly in patients aged 65 and over and those with comorbidities. Onset of a dry cough may occur more than 7 days after the influenza-like illness; engaged lymphoid tissue is in the mediastinum or lung hila (Harrison 22e p.1338).

Clinical recognition is challenging, especially if the patient does not spontaneously report fever; tularemia may not be suspected until after extensive and costly investigations, and even in high-endemic areas patients are often initially mistreated for other conditions. A high index of suspicion is critical (Harrison 22e p.1337).
If care is sought several weeks after symptom onset, the acute fever onset may not be reported spontaneously and must be actively elicited (Harrison 22e p.1337).

The primary ulcer can be a small, minimally inflamed skin break that is easily missed or may be undetectable, in which case the disease is classified as glandular rather than ulceroglandular (Harrison 22e p.1338).

Failure to alert the microbiology laboratory to suspected tularemia risks laboratory-acquired infection, as F. tularensis is highly virulent and requires BSL-3 culture conditions (Harrison 22e p.1335, 1339).

Acute-phase serology can be misleading because F. tularensis antibodies persist (single titers can remain above the diagnostic cutoff for at least 1 year), so reliable acute diagnosis should rely on a significant rise between paired sera taken 2-4 weeks apart (Harrison 22e p.1339).
Culture specimens taken from an established lymph node abscess are typically F. tularensis negative (Harrison 22e p.1340).
Tularemia patients do not require isolation because there is no human-to-human transmission (Harrison 22e p.1340).

Before antibiotics, US case-fatality rates were typically 5-15% and could reach as high as 60% in respiratory/pneumonic tularemia. Recent US surveillance (2006-2021) showed 27 of 903 patients (3.0%) with available outcome data died; treatment with at least one high-efficacy antimicrobial class was independently associated with greatly increased odds of survival. Type A is generally more lethal than type B, though there is heterogeneity among type A genetic varieties. Overall type B fatality is estimated at less than 1% in Sweden, where severe respiratory type B tularemia carried about 1.5% fatality. Recovery (and resolution of imaging abnormalities) may be slow, and some patients report postinfectious persisting fatigue and disability of uncertain cause (Harrison 22e p.1339-1340).

Respiratory/pneumonic form, which is more often bacteremic and may progress to severe disease requiring inpatient care, particularly in patients aged 65 and over and those with comorbidities (Harrison 22e p.1338)
Multiorgan involvement or hemodynamic instability, indicating need for inpatient care (Harrison 22e p.1337)
Host factors increasing risk of severe infection: geriatric frailty, immunosuppression, severe lung and/or heart impairment, and other significant comorbidities (Harrison 22e p.1337)
Lymph node abscess formation, which occurs in about one-third of patients and is associated with antibiotic treatment delay of more than 2-3 weeks after disease onset (Harrison 22e p.1340)
Severe complications reported: adult respiratory distress syndrome, myocarditis, pericarditis, endocarditis, meningitis, osteomyelitis, hepatitis, and renal failure (Harrison 22e p.1340)

Harrison does not provide a formal severity score. Clinically, management level is decided by physical examination of the anatomic site and extent of inflammation (pneumonitis, lymph node inflammation, skin ulcers/pustules, pharyngitis), the rate of progression, and host risk factors: localized symptoms are generally suitable for outpatient care, whereas multiorgan involvement or hemodynamic instability suggests inpatient care. The recognized clinical forms (ulceroglandular, glandular, oropharyngeal, oculoglandular, respiratory/pneumonic, typhoidal) are classified by F. tularensis infection route rather than by severity (Harrison 22e p.1337-1338).
Tularemia (infective) — Infectious Diseases Also: Francisella tularensis infection

chunks.diseaseName: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree

chunks.diseaseName: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree

chunks.diseaseName: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree
chunks.text: HCC develops through a multistep process beginning with precancerous low-grade dysplastic nodules that progress to high-grade dysplastic nodules and then early HCC; adult hepatocytes are the principal cell of origin, either transforming directly or de-differentiating into precursor cells, with progenitor cells contributing in a subset. It is a prototypical inflammation-associated cancer in which oxidative stress and the immune microenvironment of chronically damaged liver drive mutation. Tumors accumulate roughly 40-60 somatic alterations, of which 4-8 are driver genes; the leading drivers are TERT promoter mutations (~56%), TP53 (~27%), and CTNNB1 (~26%), all currently non-actionable. Aflatoxin B1 produces a characteristic TP53 R249S hotspot mutation. Only about 20-25% of HCCs carry an actionable mutation. Two molecular subclasses exist: a proliferative class (poor outcome, HBV-related, AFP overexpression, Ras/mTOR/IGF activation) and a nonproliferative class (often CTNNB1-mutated, better outcome). Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma arises from adult cholangiocytes, transdifferentiated hepatocytes, or progenitor-cholangiocyte precursors, whereas extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma arises from biliary epithelium and peribiliary glands. Hepatic adenomas are clonal proliferations from single-gene driver mutations (e.g., CTNNB1, HNF1A inactivation, inflammatory or Hedgehog pathway activation), and focal nodular hyperplasia is a polyclonal hepatocellular proliferation secondary to an arterial malformation (Harrison 22e p.660-670).

chunks.diseaseName: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree
chunks.text: Liver cancer is the sixth most common cancer worldwide and the third leading cause of cancer-related death; hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) makes up about 85% of primary liver cancers, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma about 10%, with rarer entities including fibrolamellar HCC, mixed HCC-iCCA, epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, and pediatric hepatoblastoma (Harrison 22e p.659).

chunks.diseaseName: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree
chunks.text: Gallbladder cancer is the most common biliary tract malignancy worldwide, has a female-to-male ratio of about 3:1, and cholelithiasis is the major risk factor though fewer than 1% of patients with gallstones develop it; gallbladder polyps 10 mm or larger carry transformation risk (Harrison 22e p.669-670).

chunks.diseaseName: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree
chunks.text: Fibrolamellar HCC typically affects children and young adults (10-30 years) without underlying liver disease, carries the PRKACA-DNAJB1 fusion oncogene in 80-100% of cases, and has a better prognosis than conventional HCC (Harrison 22e p.670).

chunks.diseaseName: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree
chunks.text: Hepatic (hepatocellular) adenomas occur predominantly in women aged 35-40 (female-to-male ratio ~10:1), are linked to oral contraceptive use in women and anabolic androgenic steroid use in male bodybuilders, and carry risk of hemorrhage and malignant transformation, particularly when larger than 5 cm (Harrison 22e p.670).

chunks.diseaseName: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree
chunks.text: Cirrhosis of any cause is the dominant risk factor for HCC; about one-third of cirrhotic patients develop HCC over their lifetime, with an annual risk of roughly 3-8% in HBV- or HCV-related cirrhosis and a lower 1-2% per year in cirrhosis from alcohol, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, autoimmune hepatitis, Wilson's disease, and cholestatic disorders (Harrison 22e p.659-660).

chunks.diseaseName: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree
chunks.text: HBV accounts for roughly 50% of HCC cases globally (about 60% in Asia and Africa, about 20% in the West) and can cause tumors via insertional mutagenesis; importantly, 25-30% of MASH-associated HCCs arise in the absence of cirrhosis (Harrison 22e p.660).

chunks.diseaseName: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree
chunks.text: HCC has a strong male preponderance (male-to-female ratio about 2.5:1) and incidence peaks at 65-70 years, though it presents earlier (40-50 years) in populations with vertical HBV transmission (Harrison 22e p.659).

chunks.diseaseName: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree
chunks.text: The radiologic hallmark of HCC on four-phase CT or dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI is arterial-phase contrast uptake with washout in the portal venous or delayed phase, a pattern with about 95-100% specificity that can make biopsy unnecessary in cirrhotic patients (Harrison 22e p.661).

chunks.diseaseName: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree
chunks.text: The Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) system is the most accepted staging scheme; the TNM staging system is NOT used in HCC because it does not capture liver function and performance status, the key prognostic variables (Harrison 22e p.662-664).

chunks.diseaseName: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree
chunks.text: Cholangiocarcinoma is the second most common primary liver cancer and is classified by location into intrahepatic (iCCA, ~20-30%), perihilar (pCCA, ~50-60%), and distal (dCCA, ~20-30%); perihilar and distal forms together are termed extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (Harrison 22e p.667).

chunks.diseaseName: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree
chunks.text: FGFR2 fusions and IDH1/2 mutations occur mostly in iCCA, whereas ERBB2/3 amplifications and SMAD4 aberrations characterize extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma; up to about 40% of iCCAs carry a targetable mutation (Harrison 22e p.667).

chunks.diseaseName: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree
chunks.text: Acute painless jaundice occurs in about 90% of perihilar cholangiocarcinoma patients, while roughly 10% present with cholangitis; distal cholangiocarcinoma can be hard to distinguish from early pancreatic cancer (Harrison 22e p.668-669).

chunks.diseaseName: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree
chunks.text: A negative liver biopsy does NOT exclude HCC; sensitivity falls below 50% for tumors 1-2 cm, and a second biopsy is advised if findings are inconclusive or the lesion grows/changes enhancement

chunks.diseaseName: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree
chunks.text: Nodules under 1 cm are unlikely to be HCC and are difficult to diagnose; short-interval ultrasound follow-up (every 3-4 months) is recommended rather than immediate biopsy

chunks.diseaseName: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree
chunks.text: PET and contrast-enhanced ultrasound perform poorly for early HCC diagnosis and are not recommended as primary diagnostic tools

chunks.diseaseName: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree
chunks.text: An AFP of >=400 ng/dL is highly suspicious but NOT diagnostic of HCC by guidelines

chunks.diseaseName: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree
chunks.text: TNM staging should NOT be applied to HCC because it omits liver function and performance status

chunks.diseaseName: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree
chunks.text: About 25-30% of MASH-related HCCs occur without cirrhosis, so absence of cirrhosis does not exclude HCC in this group

chunks.diseaseName: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree
chunks.text: Surveillance is generally NOT recommended in advanced (Child-Pugh C) cirrhosis since curative therapy is precluded, except for liver transplant waiting-list patients

chunks.diseaseName: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree
chunks.text: Liver biopsy carries a ~2-3% risk of complications including tumor seeding and bleeding

chunks.diseaseName: Tumors of the Liver and Biliary Tree
chunks.text: Prognosis depends on stage, tumor burden, liver function, and performance status. About 40% of HCC patients are diagnosed at BCLC stage 0 or A and are eligible for potentially curative resection, transplantation, or ablation, with median overall survival beyond 5 years (up to ~10 years after transplantation). Optimal surgical resection candidates have 5-year survival of 60-70% (35-55% in suboptimal candidates); RFA achieves ~60% 5-year survival; liver transplantation within Milan criteria yields 70-80% 5-year survival with ~10-15% recurrence at 5 years. Intermediate-stage (BCLC B) untreated natural history is about 16 months, improved to ~25-30 months with TACE. Symptomatic/advanced disease has median survival under 1 year; end-stage (BCLC D) survival is about 3-6 months. Cholangiocarcinoma overall carries a 5-year survival of about 10%; resectable iCCA single tumors have median survival ~40-50 months. Gallbladder cancer 5-year survival ranges 60-90% in resected localized disease but only ~10-12 months median in advanced disease. Fibrolamellar HCC has better prognosis (median ~70 months after resection). Hepatoblastoma overall 5-year survival is ~70% (50-90% by PRETEXT stage); notably, low AFP (<100 ng/mL) indicates poor prognosis in hepatoblastoma, opposite to HCC.

chunks.text: Hepatocellular carcinoma is staged by the Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) system into five stages: very early (BCLC 0, single nodule <=2 cm, Child-Pugh A, ECOG 0), early (BCLC A, single or up to three nodules <=3 cm, Child-Pugh A-B, ECOG 0), intermediate (BCLC B, multinodular, Child-Pugh A-B, ECOG 0), advanced (BCLC C, portal/macrovascular invasion, N1 or M1, or ECOG 1-2), and terminal (BCLC D, Child-Pugh C or ECOG >2). Liver function is graded by the Child-Pugh score (classes A-C) and performance by ECOG. Milan criteria (single tumor <=5 cm, or up to three nodules each <=3 cm, no macrovascular invasion or extrahepatic spread) define transplant eligibility. Cholangiocarcinoma is classified anatomically into intrahepatic, perihilar, and distal subtypes; hepatoblastoma uses the PRETEXT (Pretreatment Extent of Tumor) classification (Harrison 22e p.661-669).

Loss of all or part of the second sex chromosome causes haploinsufficiency of genes that normally escape X-inactivation and are needed in two copies. Deficiency of the SHOX gene contributes to short stature and skeletal features, while accelerated loss of ovarian follicles leads to gonadal dysgenesis and oestrogen deficiency. Abnormal fetal lymphatic development produces the lymphoedema, nuchal changes, and associated features such as the webbed neck, and disrupted development contributes to the cardiovascular and renal malformations.
A chromosomal disorder affecting females caused by complete or partial absence of one X chromosome, most commonly a 45,X karyotype, with mosaic forms also occurring.
The two most consistent features are short stature and gonadal dysgenesis leading to ovarian failure.
Newborns may show puffiness of the hands and feet (lymphoedema) and redundant nuchal skin; a fetal cystic hygroma may be detected antenatally.
Characteristic features can include a webbed neck, low posterior hairline, widely spaced nipples on a broad chest, and a wide carrying angle at the elbows.
Congenital cardiovascular anomalies, particularly bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation of the aorta, carry a risk of aortic dilatation and dissection and require ongoing surveillance.
Renal anomalies such as a horseshoe kidney are common, as are recurrent otitis media and hearing loss.
Most girls have normal intelligence but may have specific difficulties with visuospatial and mathematical tasks.
Growth hormone therapy is used to improve final height, and oestrogen replacement is used to induce puberty and maintain bone and uterine health.
Diagnosis is confirmed by karyotype, and lifelong multidisciplinary follow-up addresses cardiac, endocrine, and reproductive needs.

With appropriate hormone therapy and surveillance most girls achieve improved height, undergo induced puberty, and have a good quality of life; long-term outlook is influenced chiefly by cardiovascular complications, and fertility is usually impaired though assisted reproduction may be possible.

chunks.text: The tympanic membrane can be breached when middle ear pressure rises from suppurative infection until necrosis of the drum produces a perforation, or when external forces (direct trauma, sudden pressure change, or a foreign body) tear it mechanically. Loss of an intact vibrating surface and of the round window sound-shielding effect reduces the efficiency of sound transfer to the cochlea, producing conductive hearing loss proportional to the area lost and its position. Small tears usually re-epithelialise and heal, but persistent perforation, ongoing infection, or ingrowth of squamous epithelium through a marginal or attic defect can prevent closure and predispose to cholesteatoma and chronic disease.

Type 1 diabetes results from T-cell mediated autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing pancreatic beta cells in genetically predisposed children, often triggered by environmental factors. Progressive beta-cell loss produces absolute insulin deficiency, so glucose cannot enter cells and hyperglycaemia develops. Without insulin the body shifts to lipolysis and ketogenesis; unrestrained ketone production causes metabolic acidosis, while osmotic diuresis from glycosuria leads to dehydration and electrolyte loss, culminating in diabetic ketoacidosis if untreated.
The most common form of diabetes in children, caused by autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells leading to absolute insulin deficiency.
Classic presenting features are polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, and fatigue, often over a few weeks; new secondary enuresis in a previously dry child is a useful clue.
A substantial proportion of children present in diabetic ketoacidosis, which can be the first manifestation of the disease.
Lifelong insulin replacement is essential; unlike type 2 diabetes, it cannot be managed by lifestyle measures or oral agents alone.
A 'honeymoon' period of partial remission with reduced insulin needs may follow initial stabilisation but is temporary.
Management is multidisciplinary, combining insulin, carbohydrate awareness, glucose monitoring, and structured education for the child and family.
Careful attention to preventing and recognising hypoglycaemia is central to safe day-to-day care.
Long-term care includes screening for associated autoimmune conditions (such as thyroid disease and coeliac disease) and for microvascular complications over time.

With modern insulin regimens, glucose monitoring, and multidisciplinary support most children live full lives; long-term outcome depends heavily on sustained glycaemic control, which reduces the risk of microvascular and macrovascular complications. Acute risks include ketoacidosis and severe hypoglycaemia.

chunks.text: Umbilical and paraumbilical hernias arise from a defect at or adjacent to the umbilical cicatrix. In infants the umbilical ring fails to close fully after cord separation. In adults, weakening and separation of the linea alba fibres around the umbilicus, combined with sustained raised intra-abdominal pressure from obesity, pregnancy, or ascites, allows protrusion of preperitoneal fat, omentum, or bowel through a paraumbilical defect. The characteristically narrow, fibrous neck restricts reduction and readily compromises the vascular supply of trapped contents, predisposing to incarceration and strangulation.

Most of these fungi enter through inhalation of environmental conidia, with a smaller number introduced by traumatic skin or corneal inoculation or by injection of contaminated material. Dimorphic fungi (Paracoccidioides, Talaromyces, Emergomyces, Emmonsia crescens) convert from mold to invasive yeast/adiaspore form under thermal pressure in the lungs and then disseminate hematogenously to the reticuloendothelial system and other organs; granulomatous inflammation is typical. Disease frequently reflects host immune deficits: inborn errors affecting the IL-12/IFN-gamma axis predispose to severe paracoccidioidomycosis and talaromycosis, and IFN-gamma-primed monocytes/macrophages and neutrophils control Talaromyces. Molds such as Fusarium, Scedosporium, and Lomentospora are angioinvasive, and protection against Fusarium and Trichosporon depends heavily on neutrophils and their oxidative burst, explaining the strong link with profound prolonged neutropenia and with chronic granulomatous disease (defective NADPH oxidase). Dematiaceous molds use melanin as a virulence factor; defense against disseminated phaeohyphomycosis involves Dectin-1 (CLEC7A) and the adaptor CARD9, and deficiencies in this pathway predispose to disseminated and brain infection even in otherwise immunocompetent hosts. In adiaspiromycosis, inhaled E. crescens conidia enlarge into nonreplicating thick-walled adiaspores (up to ~500 micrometers) that drive a granulomatous inflammatory response.

This group spans endemic dimorphic fungi (paracoccidioidomycosis, talaromycosis, emergomycosis, adiaspiromycosis), hyaline and dematiaceous molds (fusariosis, scedosporiosis/lomentosporiosis, phaeohyphomycoses), and the yeast-like Trichosporon; the more common invasive mycoses (histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, blastomycosis, sporotrichosis, candidiasis, cryptococcosis, aspergillosis, mucormycosis) are covered separately (Harrison 22e p.1725).

Phaeohyphomycoses are caused by melanin-producing (dematiaceous/brown-black) molds; melanin is a virulence factor, certain species (Cladophialophora bantiana, Rhinocladiella mackenziei) are neurotropic, and golden-brown hyphae are highlighted by the Fontana-Masson melanin stain (Harrison 22e p.1728).

Trichosporonosis (most often Trichosporon asahii) resembles invasive candidiasis with fungemia, but the presence of arthroconidia helps distinguish it from candidemia, and the serum cryptococcal antigen latex agglutination test can be falsely positive because T. asahii shares polysaccharide antigens with Cryptococcus neoformans (Harrison 22e p.1729).

Scedosporiosis (Scedosporium apiospermum complex) and lomentosporiosis (Lomentospora prolificans) mimic aspergillosis radiographically and histologically; L. prolificans can grow in blood cultures whereas S. apiospermum usually does not (Harrison 22e p.1729).

Dimorphic fungi exist as conidia-producing molds in the environment (the infectious form) and convert to yeast (or spherules/adiaspores) at temperatures above about 35 degrees C in tissue; infection generally begins with inhalation of conidia (Harrison 22e p.1725).

Paracoccidioidomycosis (Paracoccidioides brasiliensis complex, P. lutzii) is acquired by inhalation in humid Central/South American forests, with highest incidence in Brazil; chronic disease shows a striking male predominance (reported male-to-female ratios from 14:1 up to ~70:1) (Harrison 22e p.1726).

The acute/juvenile form of paracoccidioidomycosis is uncommon, occurs typically in those under 30, primarily disseminates through the reticuloendothelial system, and often shows peripheral eosinophilia; the chronic/adult form accounts for ~90% of cases (Harrison 22e p.1726).

On tissue, Paracoccidioides yeast classically appears as a central yeast ringed by narrow-necked daughter buds (the 'mariner's wheel'); some commercial serologic tests may fail to detect P. lutzii (Harrison 22e p.1726).

Talaromycosis (Talaromyces marneffei, formerly Penicillium marneffei) is endemic in Vietnam, Thailand, and other Southeast Asian countries, is epidemiologically linked to bamboo rats, and occurs mostly in advanced AIDS; its presentation mimics disseminated histoplasmosis with umbilicated molluscum-like skin papules (Harrison 22e p.1727).

In culture T. marneffei produces a distinctive diffusible red pigment, and tissue/blood smears show yeast-like organisms reproducing by bipolar fission (two ellipses with a central septum) (Harrison 22e p.1727).

Emergomycosis (Emergomyces, several formerly Emmonsia) is an emerging dimorphic-fungus infection of patients with impaired cellular immunity; cutaneous involvement (disseminated ulcers, papules, nodules) accompanies pulmonary disease in most patients, while CNS spread is rare (Harrison 22e p.1727).

Fusariosis is angioinvasive and mimics aspergillosis, but is distinguished by very common, often painful, nodular or necrotic skin lesions appearing around the onset of fever and by frequently positive blood cultures (~50%); banana-shaped macroconidia are characteristic on culture (Harrison 22e p.1728).

Misidentifying tissue forms: Emergomyces can be mistaken for Histoplasma, and Fusarium/Scedosporium/Lomentospora are difficult to distinguish from Aspergillus on histology, so culture identification is essential
Cross-reacting antigen tests can mislead: Histoplasma antigen cross-reacts with Emergomyces, and cryptococcal antigen may be positive in Trichosporon asahii infection
Assuming AmB activity is universal: many of these molds (Scedosporium, Lomentospora) are intrinsically resistant to amphotericin B, and Fusarium MICs are relatively high
Treating a respiratory mold isolate as disease without evidence of tissue invasion, since Scedosporium/Lomentospora may merely colonize the airway (e.g., in bronchiectasis)
In vitro susceptibility of dematiaceous molds may not reflect response because muriform/tissue forms can behave differently from hyphal forms
Overlooking Fusarium onychomycosis as a portal for later disseminated disease in patients heading into neutropenia or transplantation
Missing the diagnosis in 'immunocompetent' patients with disseminated/brain phaeohyphomycosis who may carry CLEC7A/CARD9 pathway defects

Outcomes vary widely by organism and host immune status. Paracoccidioidomycosis generally responds well, though pulmonary fibrosis can progress in chronic disease. Untreated disseminated talaromycosis is usually fatal, but treated mortality is about 10%. Disseminated fusariosis carries high mortality (historically up to ~85%, now around 50% with better therapy) and approaches 100% if neutropenia persists; survival hinges on neutrophil recovery. Invasive S. apiospermum infection has roughly 50% mortality, whereas L. prolificans remains about 85-100% lethal. Disseminated trichosporonosis mortality has been as high as 70% and remains very high with persistent neutropenia. Disseminated and visceral phaeohyphomycoses, particularly with CNS involvement, have high mortality.
Persistent fever in a profoundly neutropenic patient despite broad-spectrum antibiotics (suggests angioinvasive mold such as Fusarium or Scedosporium/Lomentospora)
New painful nodular or necrotic skin lesions in a neutropenic or leukemic patient, especially appearing with the onset of fever (fusariosis)
Positive fungal blood culture in an immunocompromised host (disseminated fusariosis or Lomentospora)
Disseminated cutaneous ulcers/papules/nodules with pulmonary disease in an HIV/AIDS or transplant patient (emergomycosis, talaromycosis)
Indolent brain abscess with golden-brown pigmented hyphae, or intraventricular CNS spread (neurotropic dematiaceous molds such as Cladophialophora bantiana)
CNS involvement in any of these disseminated infections, which carries notably high mortality

No single formal staging applies across this heterogeneous group. Practically, infections are stratified by extent and host status: localized cutaneous/keratitis/onychomycosis or pulmonary-limited disease versus disseminated/angioinvasive infection; presence of CNS involvement marks the most severe end (associated with the highest mortality). For dimorphic fungi (e.g., paracoccidioidomycosis, talaromycosis, emergomycosis), disease is broadly described as mild/moderate versus severe, and as acute (juvenile) versus chronic (adult) forms for paracoccidioidomycosis.

Staging laparoscopy with peritoneal washing cytology for GEJ/gastric tumors with advanced T stage to detect peritoneal involvement
Bronchoscopy for mid/upper esophageal tumors to exclude tracheobronchial invasion (its presence precludes curative surgery)
Molecular/NGS profiling, PD-L1 IHC, HER2/ERBB2 (IHC/FISH/NGS), and MSI/mismatch-repair-protein testing on metastatic tumors to guide systemic therapy
Plasma circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) when biopsy tissue is insufficient, and as an investigational measure of minimal residual disease
H. pylori status assessment in all gastric lymphoma patients (histology, and if negative, stool antigen or urea breath test); HBV testing before lymphoma therapy
Benign gastric or duodenal ulcer
Reflux esophagitis / Barrett's esophagus
Achalasia or benign esophageal stricture
Submucosal benign tumors (lipoma, leiomyoma, neurofibroma, lymphoid nodular hyperplasia)

Esophageal SCC is linked to mucosal injury from alcohol and tobacco (synergistic), ingestion of very hot beverages, areca/betel-nut chewing, chronic achalasia, prior radiation, lye-induced strictures, and Plummer-Vinson (Patterson-Kelly) syndrome; genomically it resembles SCCs of other sites (e.g., head and neck) more than esophageal adenocarcinoma, and HPV is not implicated. Esophageal/GEJ adenocarcinoma arises in the setting of chronic gastroesophageal reflux producing inflammation and Barrett's metaplasia (glandular gastric-type mucosa extending into the esophagus); progression through dysplasia accumulates TP53 mutations and aneuploidy, with annual risk of progression of Barrett's to cancer about 0.4-0.5%. Gastric adenocarcinoma is predominantly an inflammation-driven malignancy: H. pylori (and the broader gastric microbiome) and ingestion of nitrate-rich smoked/salted/dried foods generate carcinogenic nitrites; the intestinal Lauren subtype associates with H. pylori and atrophic gastritis, while the diffuse subtype (~20%) associates with germline or somatic CDH1 loss. TCGA defines four molecular subtypes (EBV-positive, microsatellite-unstable/hypermutated, genomically stable [diffuse], and chromosomally unstable). The proximal esophagus-GEJ-gastric cardia adenocarcinomas share a similar genomic profile suggesting common driving factors. Gastric MALT lymphoma is driven by chronic antigenic stimulation from H. pylori, with the t(11;18) API1-MALT1 fusion activating NF-kB signaling. GISTs originate from Cajal cells via gain-of-function KIT or PDGFRA mutations.

Two biologically distinct esophageal cancers arise in the same organ: squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), favoring the upper and mid esophagus, and adenocarcinoma, almost always in the lower esophagus and at the gastroesophageal junction (GEJ); globally SCC predominates while adenocarcinoma now accounts for over 75% of incident U.S./Western European cases.

GISTs arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal and are driven by activating cKIT (~majority) or PDGFRA mutations; the stomach is the most frequent primary site (~60%), followed by small bowel (~25%); spindle-cell histology predominates (~70%) and KIT expression is found in ~95%.

Small-bowel neoplasms account for only about 3% of GI tumors; in the U.S., neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors (40-45%) slightly outnumber adenocarcinomas (30-40%), and the duodenum is the most common site (~50%).

EBV is associated with a distinct gastric cancer subtype (identified in roughly 8-10% of gastric cancer patients) and is described as a driver in some esophageal/GEJ adenocarcinomas; current EBV positivity does not by itself change therapeutic options.

Because dysphagia and odynophagia are typically not noticed until the lumen is substantially obstructed, most esophageal cancers are locally advanced or metastatic at diagnosis; any patient with these symptoms warrants upper endoscopy with biopsy.

Helicobacter pylori is a major chronic-inflammation driver of gastric cancer, but cancer develops in only a small subset of the roughly half of humans infected; eradication has been shown in prospective trials to lower subsequent gastric cancer risk, supporting treatment of asymptomatic H. pylori in those with a first-degree relative with gastric cancer or a prior early-stage gastric cancer.

Physical findings suggesting advanced/metastatic gastric cancer include left supraclavicular adenopathy (Virchow's node), a periumbilical nodule (Sister Mary Joseph nodule), a palpable rectal-shelf mass (Blumer's shelf), ascites, and an ovarian mass (Krukenberg tumor); more commonly the exam is unrevealing.

Diffuse (signet-cell) gastric cancer may not form a discrete mass or ulcer, instead producing thickened gastric rugae and tracking beneath an intact mucosal surface, so initial superficial biopsies can be falsely negative and EUS-guided deeper biopsy may be required.

Germline CDH1 (e-cadherin) mutation markedly increases risk of the diffuse/signet-cell gastric cancer subtype and also raises lobular breast cancer risk; prophylactic gastrectomy is an option in CDH1 carriers.

Molecular profiling is therapeutically decisive: roughly 20-25% of esophageal/GEJ and about 20% of gastric adenocarcinomas overexpress or amplify HER2/ERBB2, and MSI-high/mismatch-repair-deficient and PD-L1-high (high combined positive score) tumors identify candidates for immune-modulating therapy; NGS plus PD-L1 IHC should be routine in metastatic disease.

Gastric lymphomas (about 3% of gastric malignancies) are extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphomas; the GI tract is the most common extranodal NHL site and the stomach is the most common GI site, with MALT (~40%) and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (~55%) being the dominant subtypes.

MALT lymphoma of the stomach is strongly H. pylori-associated, and the stomach accounts for about 35% of all MALT lymphomas; the t(11;18) translocation marks tumors less likely to respond to H. pylori eradication.
Falsely reassuring superficial endoscopic biopsies in diffuse-type gastric cancer or gastric lymphoma, which track below the mucosa; adequate deep tissue or EUS-guided sampling is required.
Relying on FDG-PET to exclude disease in diffuse-type gastric cancer, which is often not FDG-avid (PET may be non-informative).
Using tumor markers (CEA, CA19-9) for diagnosis; they are nonspecific and elevated in many cancers, and are better for monitoring response/progression.
Attributing alarm symptoms in patients under 50 to benign illness and delaying diagnostic workup, given rising early-onset upper GI cancer incidence.
Missing tracheobronchial invasion in mid/upper esophageal tumors, which precludes curative surgery, by omitting bronchoscopy.
Treating gastric lymphoma like adenocarcinoma; surgical resection has no role in primary gastric lymphoma and MALT may respond to H. pylori eradication alone, so accurate subtyping is critical.
Assuming a t(11;18)-positive MALT lymphoma will respond to H. pylori eradication; this subgroup is less likely to respond.
Forgetting HBV testing before initiating lymphoma therapy (risk of reactivation).

Esophageal cancer prognosis remains poor overall but is slowly improving; by clinical (pretreatment) AJCC staging, 5-year survival ranges from about 75-82% for stage 0-I down to roughly 5-18% for metastatic (stage IVB) disease, and most U.S. patients present with locally advanced or metastatic disease. For gastric cancer, surgery alone yields about 25% overall 5-year survival, with stage-dependent rates falling from about 90% (stage 0) to roughly 3% for stage IV; multimodality therapy (perioperative chemotherapy plus surgery) improves 5-year survival by about 10-15% over surgery alone (e.g., MAGIC trial 36% vs 23%). Even with modern systemic and immune-modulating therapy, overall survival for stage IV gastric cancer is still only about 12-15 months. Gastric MSI-high tumors had the best outcomes and genomically stable (diffuse)/mesenchymal subtypes the worst in genomic series. Lynch-syndrome-associated small-bowel cancers probably have a better prognosis. For nonmetastatic gastric GIST, resected tumors 2 cm or smaller with a mitotic index of 5% or less carry near-zero progression risk, whereas tumors 10 cm or larger with mitotic index above 5% are moderate-to-high risk.
New or progressive dysphagia or odynophagia, especially with weight loss
Hematemesis or melena, or unexplained iron-deficiency anemia from occult GI bleeding
Anorexia, early satiety, and unexplained weight loss
Left supraclavicular (Virchow's) node, Sister Mary Joseph periumbilical nodule, Blumer's shelf, ascites, or Krukenberg ovarian mass indicating advanced disease
Dysphagia, odynophagia, or upper abdominal discomfort in a patient under 50, given the rising incidence of early-onset upper GI cancers (symptoms must not be dismissed as benign)
Small-bowel obstruction, perforation, or intussusception as a presentation of small-bowel neoplasm

Esophageal and gastric cancers are staged with the AJCC TNM system (eighth edition; ninth edition expected 2024), with separate clinical (cTNM, pretreatment), pathologic (pTNM, for patients undergoing initial surgery), and post-neoadjuvant (ypTNM) classifications. The esophageal T stage reflects depth of penetration through the wall (which over most of its course lacks serosa); regional nodal disease is still potentially curable while metastatic disease is generally treated palliatively. Gastric staging similarly progresses from Tis (mucosa-confined, stage 0) through wall penetration and increasing nodal involvement to distant metastasis (stage IV). Gastric lymphomas are NOT staged by TNM; the Lugano system (an Ann Arbor modification) is used: stage I confined to the gastric wall, stage II regional nodal or local-structure involvement, stage III nodes on both sides of the diaphragm, stage IV more extensive nodal or distant/extranodal (including marrow) disease. GIST recurrence risk is stratified by primary tumor size, mitotic index, and GI location. Neuroendocrine tumors are graded 1-3 by Ki-67 positivity, distinct from fully malignant small-/large-cell neuroendocrine carcinomas.

chunks.text: A urethral stricture is the result of scarring within the corpus spongiosum (spongiofibrosis) and urethral epithelium following injury or inflammation. Trauma, infection, instrumentation, or inflammatory disease such as lichen sclerosus provokes healing by fibrosis, which contracts and narrows the lumen. The narrowed segment increases outflow resistance, causing high-pressure voiding, turbulent flow, and incomplete emptying. Persistent obstruction leads to proximal urethral dilatation, bladder wall changes, stasis with infection and stone formation, and in severe cases upper tract dilatation and retention.

source.ref: Smith & Tanagho's General Urology / Campbell-Walsh Urology

chunks.text: A urethral stricture is a fibrotic narrowing of the urethral lumen, largely a condition of the male anterior urethra, presenting with obstructive voiding symptoms such as a weak, splayed, or spraying stream, straining, and incomplete emptying

source.ref: Smith & Tanagho's General Urology / Campbell-Walsh Urology

chunks.text: Common causes include prior instrumentation or catheterisation, straddle and pelvic trauma, infection (historically gonococcal urethritis), and lichen sclerosus affecting the meatus and distal urethra

chunks.text: Urethritis is inflammation of the urethral mucosa, usually caused by sexually transmitted organisms ascending the urethra. Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis are the principal pathogens, with Mycoplasma genitalium, Trichomonas vaginalis, and other organisms also implicated. Infection provokes a neutrophilic inflammatory response in the urethral epithelium, producing discharge and dysuria. Non-infective urethritis can follow trauma or instrumentation. Untreated infection may ascend or spread, causing epididymo-orchitis, prostatitis, disseminated gonococcal infection, or, historically, inflammatory urethral stricture, and in women pelvic inflammatory disease.

chunks.text: Urethritis is inflammation of the urethra presenting with urethral discharge, dysuria, and urethral itch or discomfort, most often sexually transmitted

chunks.text: It is broadly divided into gonococcal urethritis (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) and non-gonococcal urethritis, of which Chlamydia trachomatis is the leading cause, along with Mycoplasma genitalium and others

chunks.text: Gonococcal urethritis classically produces a profuse purulent discharge, whereas non-gonococcal urethritis tends to cause a scantier, more mucoid discharge, though overlap is common and co-infection frequent

chunks.text: Continence requires coordinated bladder storage at low pressure with a competent, closed outlet, governed by autonomic and somatic innervation. Stress incontinence arises from a weakened pelvic floor and urethral sphincter (from childbirth, ageing, or prostatic surgery) so that raised abdominal pressure overcomes closure. Urgency incontinence results from involuntary detrusor contractions (detrusor overactivity), which may be idiopathic or neurogenic. Overflow incontinence occurs when a chronically overdistended bladder leaks around an obstruction or fails to contract effectively, as in outlet obstruction or an underactive/neurogenic detrusor. Mixed incontinence combines these mechanisms.

chunks.text: Urinary incontinence is any involuntary leakage of urine, and classifying the type guides management: stress, urgency, mixed, overflow, and functional (continuous) incontinence

chunks.text: Urgency incontinence is leakage accompanied by a sudden compelling desire to void, usually from detrusor overactivity, and is part of the overactive bladder syndrome

chunks.text: Overflow incontinence is dribbling from a chronically distended, poorly emptying bladder, often due to outlet obstruction or an underactive detrusor, and must not be missed

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
chunks.text: The urinary tract behaves as a continuous column of urine from kidney to urethra. Most UTIs arise by ascending infection: periurethral and vaginal-introital colonization by intestinal flora (usually E. coli) is the critical first step, followed by ascent up the urethra to the bladder and, in renal infection, up the ureter to the kidney. Hematogenous seeding accounts for less than 2% of UTIs and usually involves virulent organisms (e.g., S. aureus, Salmonella). Outcome depends on the interplay of host, pathogen, and environmental factors. The flushing action of normal voiding clears bacteria; urinary stasis, obstruction, foreign bodies (stones, catheters), and biofilm formation favor infection. Uropathogenic E. coli express virulence factors: type 1 pili bind mannose on bladder uroepithelium to initiate cystitis, while P fimbriae bind the P blood-group antigen on renal epithelium and are important in pyelonephritis and bloodstream invasion; toxins, iron-acquisition systems, biofilms, and capsules also contribute. Host susceptibility has a hereditary component (familial/maternal history; non-secretor blood-group phenotypes increasing E. coli adherence; Toll-like receptor and IL-8 receptor gene variants). Disruption of vaginal lactobacilli (spermicide/nonoxynol-9, menopausal atrophy) promotes E. coli colonization (Harrison 22e pp.1087-1088).

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
chunks.text: UTI denotes symptomatic infection somewhere along the urinary tract; bacteria in urine WITHOUT related symptoms is asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB), not UTI, and generally should NOT be treated (Harrison 22e p.1086).

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
chunks.text: In catheterized patients bacteriuria and pyuria are essentially inevitable, so an abnormal urinalysis alone cannot diagnose CAUTI; localizing or systemic symptoms must be present and other causes excluded (Harrison 22e p.1090).

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
chunks.text: Recurrent UTI is not automatically 'complicated' - individual episodes can be uncomplicated; early recurrence (within 2 weeks) is usually relapse rather than reinfection and should prompt a search for a sequestered focus (Harrison 22e pp.1086-1087).

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
chunks.text: Treatment of ASB is discouraged except in two settings: pregnancy (untreated ASB is linked to pyelonephritis, preterm delivery, and low birth weight) and before urologic procedures causing mucosal injury such as lithotripsy or transurethral prostate resection (Harrison 22e p.1086).

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
chunks.text: Cystitis presents with dysuria, frequency, and urgency, often with suprapubic discomfort, new nocturia, hesitancy, or gross hematuria; fever, rigors, and unilateral flank/back pain are INCONSISTENT with uncomplicated cystitis and point to infection beyond the bladder (Harrison 22e p.1088).

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
chunks.text: Fever is a key feature distinguishing cystitis from pyelonephritis; mild pyelonephritis may show only low-grade fever with or without costovertebral angle pain, while severe disease brings high fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting, and flank pain (Harrison 22e p.1089).

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
chunks.text: E. coli is the predominant uropathogen across UTI syndromes, accounting for roughly 75-90% of acute cystitis isolates; Staphylococcus saprophyticus causes about 5-15% (more in younger women) (Harrison 22e p.1087).

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
chunks.text: Isolation of S. aureus or Salmonella from urine should raise suspicion of concomitant bacteremia, since hematogenous seeding (<2% of UTIs) typically involves these more virulent organisms (Harrison 22e p.1088).

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
chunks.text: Acute bacterial prostatitis (ABP) is a typically severe illness with dysuria, frequency, and prostatic/pelvic/perineal pain, sometimes with fever, rigors, or bladder outlet obstruction; chronic bacterial prostatitis (CBP) presents insidiously as recurrent cystitis episodes, often without systemic signs (Harrison 22e p.1088).

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
chunks.text: Chronic pelvic pain syndrome (formerly chronic prostatitis) is far more common than bacterial prostatitis, is NOT associated with bacteriuria, and does NOT improve with antibiotics; obtaining urine cultures in male UTI helps distinguish these entities (Harrison 22e p.1088).

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
chunks.text: Diagnostic stewardship - not culturing urine in patients lacking UTI signs/symptoms (except pregnancy or pre-urologic-procedure screening) - is the key intervention to reduce misdiagnosis and overtreatment of ASB (Harrison 22e p.1088).

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
chunks.text: Diagnosing UTI from pyuria/bacteriuria alone without requiring symptoms - this conflates ASB with true UTI; degree of pyuria in an asymptomatic patient should not drive the diagnosis (very high pyuria is common with urinary stasis, ESRD, or obstructed catheters).

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
chunks.text: Treating ASB outside pregnancy or pre-urologic-procedure settings - it does not reduce future UTIs and may even increase infection risk (e.g., in renal transplant recipients).

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
chunks.text: Premature diagnostic closure: attributing an older patient's isolated altered mentation to 'UTI' without excluding sepsis and other time-sensitive causes of delirium; a reported history of recurrent UTIs may actually reflect persistent ASB.

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
chunks.text: Relying on a negative dipstick to rule out UTI - false negatives occur with non-Enterobacterales organisms, dilute frequently-voided urine, and it is insufficiently sensitive to exclude bacteriuria in pregnancy.

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
chunks.text: Mistaking an STI (especially C. trachomatis) for UTI, or treating dysuria due to vaginitis/cervicitis as UTI; vaginal discharge should prompt STI evaluation.

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
chunks.text: Assuming all male UTI is 'complicated' or that complicated-UTI guidelines apply to prostatitis; not all men with UTI have urinary tract abnormalities, especially those 45 years or younger.

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
chunks.text: Misinterpreting a mixed-flora culture as infection - usually contamination except in long-term catheterization, chronic retention, or urinary-enteric/genital fistula.

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
chunks.text: UTI is common and patients typically respond favorably and rapidly to appropriately chosen modern antimicrobials. Uncomplicated cystitis in low-risk women carries a low risk of serious complications and can often be managed remotely. About 20-30% of women with one UTI develop recurrences (average ~2.6 reinfections/year; rate 0.3-7.6 per patient-year), with likelihood of recurrence decreasing as time since the last infection lengthens. Up to 80% of women have at least one UTI in their lifetime; lifetime prevalence in U.S. men is about 14%. Untreated ASB in pregnancy carries risk of pyelonephritis, preterm delivery, and low birth weight. Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis causes suppurative destruction of renal tissue and its mass effect can mimic renal malignancy (Harrison 22e pp.1086-1089).

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
chunks.text: Fever, rigors, or unilateral flank/back pain in a patient with urinary symptoms (suggests pyelonephritis, prostatitis, or bloodstream involvement)

chunks.text: Severe pyelonephritis with high fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting, and flank pain

chunks.text: Emphysematous pyelonephritis (gas in renal/perinephric tissue), occurring almost exclusively in poorly controlled diabetes

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
chunks.text: Signs of sepsis in an older patient with altered mentation

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
