chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
chunks.text: Clinical syndrome-based: asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) vs symptomatic UTI. Uncomplicated UTI = infection confined to the bladder (cystitis) in a woman or man without a urinary catheter. Complicated UTI = infection extending beyond the bladder (prostatitis, pyelonephritis, bacteremia) or in the setting of catheterization (CAUTI). Pyelonephritis is graded clinically from mild (low-grade fever +/- back/CVA pain) to severe (high fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting, flank pain). Severe/special forms: emphysematous pyelonephritis and xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis. Lab/diagnostic thresholds: pyuria conventionally >10 WBCs/HPF (poor specificity ~36%; a cutoff nearer 250 WBCs/HPF correlates better with symptoms in older women); for women with cystitis symptoms a colony count >10^2 bacteria/mL is more sensitive (95%) than the classic 10^5/mL; CAUTI bacteriuria threshold is >=10^3 CFU/mL (Harrison 22e pp.1086-1092).

chunks.diseaseName: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis
chunks.text: Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis (infective) — Genitourinary Also: UTI, Acute cystitis, Acute bacterial prostatitis (ABP), Chronic bacterial prostatitis (CBP), Pyelonephritis, Catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI)
Benign prostatic hyperplasia (bladder outlet obstruction)
Neurogenic bladder / functional obstruction (diabetic neuropathy, spinal cord disease, cauda equina syndrome)
Pregnant uterus / uterine leiomyomata
Accidental surgical ligation or injury of the ureter during pelvic or colonic surgery
Aortic aneurysm (extrinsic ureteric compression)
Drug-related urinary retention (anticholinergics, alpha-adrenergic agonists, opiates)
Carcinoma of prostate, bladder, cervix, colon, or rectum
Retroperitoneal fibrosis
Lymphoma (particularly follicular) with retroperitoneal involvement
Calculi (ureteric, bladder, urethral)
Urethral stricture
Ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) narrowing/obstruction
Vesicoureteral reflux
Posterior urethral valves (boys)
Pyelonephritis (urinary stasis from obstruction encourages organism growth; UTO must always be considered with UTIs)
Generalized sepsis from an infected obstructed system
Bladder catheter insertion and postvoid residual measurement
Abdominal scout film/KUB (insensitive; may show nephrocalcinosis or radiopaque stone)
Furosemide-augmented imaging to distinguish functional from anatomic obstruction
Bedside bladder ultrasound to assess bladder volume
Abdominal ultrasonography (~90% sensitive and specific for hydronephrosis)
Noncontrast multidetector CT (test of choice for acute flank pain; visualizes retroperitoneum and intrinsic/extrinsic sites of obstruction; characterizes stones by Hounsfield units)
Duplex Doppler ultrasonography (increased resistive index)
Retrograde or antegrade urography (no contrast-induced AKI risk in renal insufficiency)
Voiding cystourethrography (vesicoureteral reflux, bladder neck and urethral obstruction; postvoid residual urine)
Cystourethroscopy and urodynamic studies (cystometry, pressure-flow analysis)
Radionuclide (renal) scan for differential renal function and to predict reversibility after prolonged decompression
Prerenal azotemia (acute partial bilateral obstruction may mimic it with high BUN-to-creatinine ratio, concentrated urine, and sodium retention)
Renal cystic disease (congenital UPJ obstruction may be mistaken for it; extrarenal pelvis is a normal variant causing false-positive hydronephrosis)
Other causes of polyuria/nocturia and concentrating defects
ADPKD and other ciliopathies (cystic compression of normal nephrons leading to fibrosis)

Obstruction to urine flow produces stasis and a rise in hydrostatic pressure proximal to the blockade; this pressure is transmitted to the glomerular urinary space, decreasing or stopping filtration. Acutely, bilateral obstruction increases renal blood flow with rising ureteral/tubule pressures (mediated by vasodilator prostaglandins and nitric oxide), then renal blood flow and GFR fall with chronicity as vasoconstrictor prostaglandins and renin-angiotensin production increase. Tubular dysfunction develops: loss of medullary hypertonicity and concentrating ability (AVP-insensitive polyuria, a form of acquired nephrogenic diabetes insipidus from dysregulation of aquaporin-2 water channels), natriuresis from downregulation of proximal salt reabsorption and transporters (Na+/K+-ATPase, NKCC2, ENaC), and partial bilateral UTO causing acquired distal RTA with hyperkalemia and renal salt wasting (disrupted H+-ATPase trafficking in alpha-intercalated cells, reduced ENaC-driven Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion, impaired ammonium excretion). The renal interstitium becomes edematous with mononuclear infiltrate early; later interstitial fibrosis and atrophy of papillae and medulla precede cortical involvement. Increased angiotensin II drives inflammation and fibroblast accumulation via profibrotic cytokines, progressing to chronic kidney damage and permanent loss of renal mass (renal atrophy). Obstruction can be mechanical (intrinsic or extrinsic) at any level from the renal tubules to the urethral meatus, or functional from abnormal pontine/sacral micturition control (e.g., neurogenic bladder). Genetic/fetal causes (CAKUT, LUTO) reflect reduced nephron number, as there is no nephrogenesis after birth (p.2453-2456).

Urinary tract obstruction (UTO) is a common and potentially reversible cause of both acute and chronic kidney disease (obstructive nephropathy); early recognition and prompt relief can prevent or reverse devastating effects on kidney structure and function (p.2453).

Posterior urethral valves are the most common cause of bilateral hydronephrosis in boys; in adults UTO is usually due to acquired defects, with pelvic tumors, calculi, and urethral stricture predominating (p.2454).
As many as 50% of men aged >40 years may have lower urinary tract symptoms associated with benign prostatic hypertrophy, but these symptoms may occur without bladder outlet obstruction (p.2454).

Noncontrast CT is the imaging test of choice for acute flank pain and improves visualization of the urinary tract in renal impairment; retrograde/antegrade urography carry no risk of contrast-induced AKI in patients with renal insufficiency (p.2455-2456).

Any patient with otherwise unexplained renal failure, or with a history of nephrolithiasis, hematuria, diabetes mellitus, prostatic enlargement, pelvic surgery, trauma, or tumor should be evaluated for UTO (p.2455-2456).

When suspected, a bladder catheter should be inserted and abdominal ultrasonography performed to assess renal/bladder size and pyelocalyceal contour; bladder volume can be readily assessed at the bedside by ultrasound (p.2454-2455).

Flank pain is the most common presenting symptom and is due to distention of the collecting system or renal capsule; its severity is influenced more by the rate at which distention develops than by the degree of distention (p.2454).
Complete bilateral obstruction should be suspected when acute renal failure is accompanied by anuria (p.2455).
Wide fluctuations in urine output in an azotemic patient should always raise the possibility of intermittent or partial UTO (p.2455).
Azotemia with hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis (acquired distal renal tubular acidosis pattern) should prompt consideration of UTO (p.2455).
Flank pain that occurs only with micturition is pathognomonic of vesicoureteral reflux (p.2455).
Lower obstruction above the bladder causes unilateral hydroureter and hydronephrosis, whereas lesions at or below the bladder cause bilateral involvement (p.2454).

UTO is a reversible cause of AKI that must be actively excluded in any unexplained AKI (insert bladder catheter and perform bladder scan/ultrasound) - the urine sediment is often normal even with marked azotemia and extensive structural damage.

Hydronephrosis may be ABSENT on ultrasound when obstruction is <48 h in duration, or associated with volume contraction, staghorn calculi, retroperitoneal fibrosis, or infiltrative renal disease - a negative ultrasound does not exclude obstruction when suspicion remains high.
False-positive hydronephrosis can occur with diuresis, renal cysts, or a normal extrarenal pelvis.

Insidious obstruction (e.g., chronic UPJ narrowing) may cause little or no pain yet result in total destruction of the affected kidney; unilateral ureteric injury during surgery may remain undetected.

After relief, anticipate postobstructive diuresis (see below) - iatrogenic over-replacement of fluids can sustain the diuresis, while under-recognition can lead to profound dehydration and vascular collapse.
NSAIDs for renal colic must account for potential renal harm, and opiates in patients with decreased renal function may be dangerous and used with caution.
Alpha-adrenergic blockers for BPH carry a risk of intraoperative floppy iris syndrome during cataract surgery.

With relief of obstruction, return of renal function depends largely on whether irreversible renal damage has occurred. If obstruction is not relieved, course depends on whether it is complete or incomplete, bilateral or unilateral, and whether infection coexists. Complete obstruction with infection can destroy the kidney within days. Partial return of GFR may follow relief of complete obstruction of 1-2 weeks' duration, but after 8 weeks of obstruction recovery is unlikely. In the absence of definitive evidence of irreversibility, every effort should be made to decompress; a renal radionuclide scan after a prolonged period of decompression may predict reversibility. Chronic fibrotic progression to a failing kidney has no demonstrated reversal of scarring to date (p.2453, 2456-2457).

UTO complicated by infection (infected obstructed system) requires immediate relief of obstruction to prevent generalized sepsis and progressive renal damage; sepsis necessitates prompt urologic intervention with drainage (nephrostomy, ureterostomy, or catheterization)
Acute renal failure with anuria suggesting complete bilateral obstruction
Overflow incontinence with sudden-onset fecal incontinence, severe lower back pain, and saddle anesthesia requires emergency evaluation for cauda equina syndrome
Complete obstruction with infection can lead to total destruction of the kidney within days
Fetal LUTO with maternal oligohydramnios or anhydramnios (risk of pulmonary hypoplasia and infant death if untreated)

No formal severity grade; characterized along clinically meaningful axes per Tables 331-1 and 331-2: by level (upper tract/ureter vs bladder outlet vs urethra), laterality (unilateral hydroureter/hydronephrosis vs bilateral involvement at/below the bladder), completeness (complete vs partial/incomplete), acuity (acute vs chronic vs release/postobstructive phase), and presence of superimposed infection. Postobstructive diuresis follows relief of bilateral, but not unilateral, complete obstruction.
Urinary Tract Obstruction (non-infective) — Nephrology / Urology Also: obstructive uropathy, hydronephrosis
Acute vs chronic urticaria/angioedema (cutoff 6 weeks duration)
Serum sickness and hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis

Allergic rhinitis: nonallergic rhinitis with eosinophilia (NARES), vasomotor/perennial nonallergic rhinitis, rhinitis medicamentosa, gustatory rhinitis, hormonal (pregnancy) rhinitis, drug-induced rhinitis, hypothyroidism, anatomic/structural nasal defects, nasal foreign body
Inducible (physical) urticarias: dermatographism, cholinergic, cold, solar, pressure, vibratory, heat, aquagenic, contact
Urticarial vasculitis (immune-complex disease; small-vessel leukocytoclastic vasculitis)
Mastocytosis (cutaneous or systemic; urticaria pigmentosa)
Hereditary angioedema (C1INH type 1/2; type 3 with normal C1INH e.g. factor XII mutation)
Acquired C1INH deficiency (lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disease)
ACE inhibitor-induced (bradykinin-mediated) angioedema
CIAS1/NLRP3-associated periodic fever syndromes (familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome, Muckle-Wells syndrome)
Schnitzler's syndrome, Gleich's syndrome, hypereosinophilic syndrome
Viral infection-associated acute urticaria (a common trigger of new-onset acute urticaria)
Bacterial or parasitic infection-associated urticaria (travel history should prompt parasite evaluation)
Hepatitis B or C and SARS-CoV-2 infection associated with urticaria/urticarial vasculitis
Upper respiratory tract infection mimicking rhinitis; secondary bacterial sinusitis/otitis from mucosal swelling
History-directed skin testing (puncture/prick) or serum allergen-specific IgE for suspected allergen triggers
Provocation/threshold testing for inducible urticaria (e.g. ice-cube test for cold urticaria; stroking for dermatographism)
Limited labs in unrevealing chronic urticaria: CBC with eosinophil assessment, ESR or CRP (most chronic urticaria has no lab abnormality)
Skin biopsy for lesions lasting >36 h, scarring, or painful/non-pruritic - to assess for urticarial vasculitis (cellular infiltrate, nuclear debris, fibrinoid venular necrosis)
For isolated angioedema: basic chemistries with liver function tests and complement levels
C1INH antigen level and functional (catalytic inhibition) assay, with C4 and C2 levels, for suspected HAE; C1q and C1 function additionally reduced in acquired C1INH deficiency
Evaluation for paraproteinemia/lymphoproliferative disease where presentation suggests acquired C1INH deficiency
Autologous serum skin test and basophil activation markers (CD63/CD203) for autoimmune chronic urticaria; antithyroid antibodies
Nasal secretion eosinophils and serum/skin specific IgE for allergic rhinitis (skin test more sensitive; serum specific IgE less sensitive but highly specific)
Urticarial vasculitis (lesions >24 h, painful/burning rather than pruritic, residual petechiae/bruising)
Mastocytosis presenting with flushing and hyperpigmented papules that urticate on stroking (Darier's sign)
Thyroid disease (hypo-/hyperthyroidism) and autoimmune thyroiditis
Serum sickness / serum sickness-like reactions
Vasomotor (nonallergic) rhinitis and NARES mimicking allergic rhinitis

Atopy is a tendency to manifest asthma, rhinitis, urticaria, food allergy, and atopic dermatitis in association with allergen-specific IgE, though urticaria and anaphylaxis can also occur in non-atopic individuals. Mast cells are the key effector cells: IgE binds the high-affinity receptor FcepsilonRI (sensitization), and antigen-driven receptor aggregation triggers Lyn/Syk/Fyn tyrosine-kinase signaling, calcium influx, and degranulation. This releases preformed granule mediators (histamine, tryptase, chymase, carboxypeptidase A, proteoglycans), newly generated lipid mediators (PGD2 via cyclooxygenase; LTB4 and cysteinyl leukotrienes LTC4/D4/E4 via 5-lipoxygenase/FLAP; PAF), and cytokines/chemokines (TNF-alpha, IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, GM-CSF). Mast cells can also be activated IgE-independently via C5a/C3a anaphylatoxin receptors, TLRs, alarmin (TSLP, IL-33) receptors, and MRGPRX2 (a target of small-molecule drugs such as ciprofloxacin and rocuronium and of neuropeptides). Histamine and lipid mediators increase venular permeability producing dermal edema (urticaria) or deeper subcutaneous/dermal edema (angioedema). Cold urticaria provides the best evidence for IgE/mast-cell involvement, with documented mast cell degranulation and elevated lesional histamine. In contrast, bradykinin-mediated angioedema (HAE from C1INH deficiency, or ACE inhibitor-induced) results from excess bradykinin: C1INH normally inhibits activated factor XII, kallikrein, and C1r/C1s, and its deficiency leads to bradykinin accumulation with falling C4/C2. Allergic rhinitis arises from sensitized intraepithelial and perivenular nasal mast cells that, on allergen exposure, release histamine, PGD2, and leukotrienes, producing submucosal edema and eosinophilic infiltration.

Urticaria (hives) are well-circumscribed wheals (dilation of superficial dermal vessels) that are intensely pruritic, often migrate, individually last <24 h, and resolve without bruising or scarring; angioedema arises from deeper dermis/subcutaneous tissue with more pain than pruritus and minimal erythema, taking hours to days to resolve (p.2807).

Allergic rhinitis usually occurs in atopic individuals and overlaps strongly with other atopic disease: up to 50% of allergic rhinitis patients have asthma, while 70-80% of asthmatics and 80% of those with chronic bilateral sinusitis have allergic rhinitis (p.2809).

Seasonal allergic rhinitis is elicited by wind-pollinated tree, grass, and weed pollens (in temperate North America: trees Mar-May, grasses Jun-early Jul, weeds mid-Aug-early Oct); perennial rhinitis is driven by year-round allergens such as dust mites (Dermatophagoides), animal dander, cockroach proteins, and mold spores (p.2809).
Pollen-associated (oral allergy) food syndrome causes oropharyngeal pruritus and/or mild swelling after ingesting plant foods cross-reactive with the offending tree, grass, or weed pollen (p.2809).

Urticaria and angioedema reflect similar pathophysiology at different skin levels and often co-occur, with roughly 40% of patients reporting both; together they affect >20% of the population at some point in life (p.2807).

Acute urticaria/angioedema are episodes lasting <6 weeks (usually food, environmental, or drug allergen, or viral infection); attacks persisting >6 weeks are termed chronic and are often spontaneous/idiopathic with no identifiable cause. More than two-thirds of new-onset cases are ultimately diagnosed as acute (p.2807).

Inducible (physical) urticarias are identified by the precipitating stimulus: dermatographism (linear wheal after brisk stroke, affects 2-5%), cholinergic urticaria (small 1-2 mm pruritic wheals with large surrounding erythema triggered by a rise in core body temperature such as fever, hot bath, or exercise), cold, solar, pressure, vibratory, heat, aquagenic, and contact urticaria; most inducible-urticaria lesions individually last <2 h (p.2807-2808).

Hereditary angioedema (HAE) is a fully penetrant autosomal dominant disorder from SERPING1 mutation causing C1 inhibitor (C1INH) deficiency (type 1, ~85%) or dysfunctional protein (type 2); presentation in childhood/adolescence and a family history of angioedema are distinguishing features (p.2808).

HAE diagnosis is suggested by family history, early age of onset, lack of pruritus and urticarial lesions, recurrent gastrointestinal colic, episodes of laryngeal edema, and failure to respond to H1 antihistamines; laboratory confirmation shows low C1INH antigen (type 1) or nonfunctional protein (type 2), with chronically depleted C4 and C2 that fall further during attacks (p.2808-2809).

Cold urticaria can be confirmed by ice-cube placement on the volar forearm provoking a wheal within minutes; cryoglobulins or cold agglutinins are present in up to 5% of these patients, and immersion in cold water (swimming) can progress to vascular collapse (p.2807-2808).

Up to 45% of chronic urticaria has an autoimmune basis, including autoantibodies to IgE or to the alpha chain of FcepsilonRI, and may be associated with antithyroid antibodies (antimicrosomal peroxidase/thyroglobulin) in both Hashimoto's thyroiditis and a euthyroid state (p.2808).

Allergic rhinitis is characterized by sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal obstruction, lacrimation, and itching of the conjunctiva/nasal mucosa/oropharynx; the nasal mucosa is classically pale and boggy. It requires a temporal relationship to allergen exposure plus documented IgE sensitization (p.2808-2809).

Failing to distinguish histaminergic from bradykinin-mediated angioedema: bradykinin-mediated angioedema (hereditary angioedema from C1INH deficiency, and ACE inhibitor-induced) is conspicuously WITHOUT concomitant urticaria or pruritus, frequently involves the GI tract, lasts >24 h, and characteristically does NOT respond to H1 antihistamines (nor to adrenaline) - treat with C1INH replacement, bradykinin B2-receptor antagonist (icatibant), or kallikrein inhibitor rather than antihistamines.

Mistaking urticarial vasculitis for simple urticaria: individual lesions persist >24 h, may leave bruising/petechiae and scarring, and cause burning rather than pruritus - biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis and may signal underlying SLE, Sjogren's, or complement deficiency.
Overlooking laryngeal angioedema as an airway emergency, or mistaking GI angioedema for a surgical abdomen.
Topical glucocorticoids are of no value in urticaria, and systemic glucocorticoids are generally avoided in idiopathic, allergen-induced, or inducible urticaria due to long-term toxicity.
Prolonged use of topical alpha-adrenergic nasal decongestants (7-14 days) causes rebound rhinitis medicamentosa.

Concomitant beta-adrenergic blocker therapy increases the risk of severe/refractory anaphylaxis during allergen immunotherapy; immunotherapy is contraindicated in significant cardiovascular disease or unstable asthma.

More than two-thirds of new-onset urticaria cases are ultimately acute and self-limited. Chronic spontaneous urticaria is most common in the third to fifth decades and the vast majority shows no laboratory abnormality. Dermatographism generally has a duration of <5 years. Allergic rhinitis prevalence in North America is 10-30% (peak >30% in the fifth decade). Allergen immunotherapy (SCIT/SLIT) for allergic rhinitis provides durable symptom benefit and can reduce asthma symptoms; guidelines recommend 3-5 years of SCIT with discontinuation after minimal symptoms over two consecutive allergen seasons.
Angioedema of the upper respiratory tract / larynx may be life-threatening due to transient laryngeal obstruction - airway emergency
Gastrointestinal angioedema with abdominal colic can mimic an acute abdomen and lead to unnecessary surgical intervention
Cold urticaria with cold-water immersion may progress to vascular collapse
Progression of urticaria/angioedema to anaphylaxis with vascular collapse (e.g. exercise-induced anaphylaxis, food/drug triggers)
Urticarial lesions lasting >24-36 h with bruising/petechiae, scarring, or burning/pain rather than pruritus suggest urticarial vasculitis and warrant biopsy

Urticaria/angioedema classified by duration: acute = episodes lasting <6 weeks; chronic = attacks persisting >6 weeks (Table 363-1 further classifies by precipitating factor into acute vs chronic categories, including drug, food, infection, physical/inducible, autoimmune, vasculitic, mastocytosis, and hereditary forms). Hereditary angioedema typed as: type 1 (low C1INH antigen, ~85%), type 2 (dysfunctional C1INH protein), and type 3 (normal C1INH/complement, often identifiable gene mutation e.g. factor XII). Allergic rhinitis classified as seasonal vs perennial, and managed by severity (mild vs moderate-to-severe).
Urticaria, Angioedema & Allergic Rhinitis (non-infective) — Immunology / Allergy Also: hives, urticaria, hereditary angioedema, allergic rhinitis

Endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma as a cause of abnormal bleeding
Transvaginal and transabdominal ultrasound to characterise number, size, and location
Saline infusion sonohysterography or hysteroscopy to define submucosal fibroids and the cavity
MRI for detailed mapping before myomectomy or embolisation and to help distinguish adenomyosis
Full blood count to detect iron-deficiency anaemia from heavy bleeding
Endometrial sampling when there is abnormal bleeding with risk factors for endometrial pathology

Fibroids arise from a single transformed myometrial smooth muscle cell that proliferates under the influence of ovarian sex steroids to form a well-circumscribed, pseudo-encapsulated mass of smooth muscle and extracellular matrix. Oestrogen and progesterone, along with local growth factors, drive their growth, which is why they enlarge in the reproductive years and shrink after menopause. Heavy bleeding results from an increased and distorted endometrial surface, altered local vasculature and prostaglandins, and impaired uterine contraction. As fibroids outgrow their blood supply they can undergo hyaline, cystic, calcific, or red degeneration.
Fibroids are benign monoclonal tumours of uterine smooth muscle and are the most common pelvic tumour in women
Many are asymptomatic; when symptomatic, they commonly cause heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding, pelvic pressure, bulk-related urinary or bowel symptoms, and sometimes subfertility
Location matters more than size: submucosal fibroids are most associated with abnormal bleeding and reproductive problems, while subserosal fibroids tend to cause pressure symptoms
They are oestrogen and progesterone dependent, so they typically grow during the reproductive years and regress after the menopause

Treatment is guided by symptoms, fibroid characteristics, and the woman's fertility wishes, ranging from expectant management to medical therapy, uterine artery embolisation, myomectomy, or hysterectomy
Medical options aim to reduce bleeding and shrink fibroids, including hormonal treatments and agents that suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis
Rapid growth, particularly after the menopause, should raise suspicion of the rare leiomyosarcoma
In pregnancy fibroids may undergo red (carneous) degeneration causing acute pain, and can be associated with malpresentation and obstructed labour
Assuming all abnormal bleeding in a woman with fibroids is due to the fibroids and missing coexisting endometrial pathology
Overlooking submucosal fibroids as a cause of infertility or recurrent bleeding when only transabdominal imaging is used
Attributing a rapidly growing mass to a benign fibroid without considering sarcoma
Neglecting to treat iron-deficiency anaemia
Failing to consider fibroid degeneration as a cause of acute pain in pregnancy

Fibroids are benign and most women have a good outcome; malignant transformation is very rare. Symptoms often stabilise or regress after the menopause. Recurrence after uterine-conserving treatments such as myomectomy is possible, whereas hysterectomy is definitive but ends fertility.
Rapidly enlarging uterine mass or postmenopausal growth suggesting leiomyosarcoma
Severe anaemia from heavy menstrual bleeding
Acute severe pain from fibroid degeneration or torsion of a pedunculated fibroid
Hydronephrosis from ureteric compression by a large mass
Acute urinary retention from a large or cervical fibroid
Uterine fibroids (non-infective) — Obstetrics / Gynaecology Also: leiomyoma, myoma, fibromyoma, uterine leiomyomata
Cystocele or rectocele without significant uterine descent
Vaginal vault prolapse after hysterectomy
Enterocele
Large vaginal or cervical cyst or fibroid
Chronic uterine inversion
Urethral diverticulum or other vaginal mass
Pelvic examination in different positions and with straining to define the compartments and stage
Assessment of pelvic floor muscle strength
Urinary assessment including post-void residual and urodynamics where incontinence complicates management
Consideration of imaging for large or atypical masses
Evaluation and treatment of contributing factors such as constipation, chronic cough, and atrophy

The uterus and vagina are held in position by the levator ani muscles and the endopelvic fascia and ligaments, including the uterosacral and cardinal ligaments. Damage to these supports, most often from stretching and denervation during vaginal delivery, together with age-related and oestrogen-deficiency-related weakening of connective tissue and muscle, allows the pelvic organs to descend. Sustained increases in intra-abdominal pressure accelerate this process. As support fails, the uterus and cervix prolapse downward, frequently dragging the vaginal walls and adjacent bladder and rectum with them.

Uterine prolapse is descent of the uterus and cervix into or beyond the vagina due to weakening of the pelvic floor supports, and it often coexists with prolapse of the vaginal walls, bladder, and rectum
Typical symptoms include a sensation of vaginal bulge or something coming down, pelvic heaviness or dragging, and symptoms that worsen through the day and with standing or straining
Associated urinary, bowel, and sexual dysfunction are common and should be assessed directly, as women may not volunteer them
Major risk factors include vaginal childbirth, increasing age and menopause, chronically raised intra-abdominal pressure from obesity, chronic cough or constipation, and connective tissue laxity
Severity is graded by how far the leading part of the prolapse descends relative to the hymen, using a standardised staging system
Conservative management with pelvic floor muscle training and vaginal pessaries is appropriate for many women, particularly if surgery is undesirable or unsafe
Surgical options range from uterine-preserving procedures to hysterectomy with vault support, and the choice depends on symptoms, fertility wishes, and fitness
Vaginal oestrogen can improve atrophic tissue and support pessary use in postmenopausal women
Failing to ask about associated urinary, bowel, and sexual symptoms
Overlooking coexisting prolapse in other vaginal compartments
Missing occult stress incontinence unmasked after prolapse correction
Neglecting to exclude malignancy in a woman with abnormal bleeding
Not treating vaginal atrophy or constipation that undermines pessary use and surgical outcomes

Uterine prolapse is a benign but often progressive quality-of-life condition; conservative measures relieve symptoms in many women, and surgery provides good results though prolapse can recur in other compartments over time. Prognosis is favourable overall, and attention to modifiable risk factors such as weight, constipation, and chronic cough helps limit progression and recurrence.
Ulceration, bleeding, or infection of exposed prolapsed tissue
Urinary retention or obstructed voiding from advanced prolapse
Hydronephrosis or renal impairment from ureteric kinking in severe procidentia
New abnormal bleeding requiring exclusion of malignancy
Complete procidentia that cannot be reduced, needing prompt specialist assessment
Uterine Prolapse (non-infective) — Obstetrics / Gynaecology Also: pelvic organ prolapse, uterovaginal prolapse, descent of the uterus, genital prolapse
Peptic ulcer disease — the most common cause of upper GI bleeding (~50% of UGIB hospitalisations) (p.360)
Mallory-Weiss tear — ~2-10% of UGIB, classically preceded by vomiting/retching/coughing, usually on the gastric side of the gastro-oesophageal junction; stops spontaneously in ~80-90% (p.360)
Bleeding gastric varices, intestinal varices, and portal hypertensive gastropathy/enterocolopathy — other portal-hypertension-related sources distinct from oesophageal varices (p.361, p.2714)
Erosive disease — erosive oesophagitis, gastritis, duodenitis (up to ~30% of UGIB), commonly NSAID-related (p.361)
Stress-related gastric mucosal injury in the critically ill (p.361)

Less common: neoplasm, vascular ectasias (including hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, gastric antral vascular ectasia), Dieulafoy's lesion, aortoenteric fistula, haemobilia/haemosuccus pancreaticus (p.361)

Upper endoscopy within 24 h is first-line both to diagnose the bleeding source and to treat acutely; more urgent endoscopy (6-12 h) does not improve outcomes and may worsen them in high-risk patients (p.362, p.2714)

Endoscopic surveillance for varices: recommended at diagnosis of compensated cirrhosis, then every 2 years (active liver disease) or every 3 years (inactive); also at the time of hepatic decompensation (p.2714)
Liver stiffness by transient elastography — if <20 kPa and no thrombocytopenia, high-risk varices are rare and screening endoscopy may be deferred (p.2714)
HVPG measurement by interventional radiology (hepatic vein cannulation) in selected cases to confirm/quantify portal hypertension (p.371, p.2714)

Complete blood count (thrombocytopenia from hypersplenism is often the first marker of portal hypertension), liver biochemistry, albumin, and prothrombin time/INR to assess hepatic function and severity (p.371, p.2714)

Endoscopic stigmata predicting bleeding risk: red wale signs, hematocystic spots, diffuse erythema, bluish colour, cherry-red spots, white-nipple spots; larger varices and worse Child-Pugh/MELD also predict bleeding (p.2713)

Portal hypertensive gastropathy — snakeskin-like mosaic mucosal pattern on endoscopy; can cause acute or chronic (iron-deficiency) GI bleeding and mimics variceal bleeding as a cause of haematemesis/melaena in the same cirrhotic patient (p.2714)
Gastric varices — also driven by portal hypertension but managed differently from oesophageal varices (p.361, p.2714)

Oesophageal varices are a consequence of portal hypertension, defined as an HVPG >5 mmHg. Portal hypertension arises from two simultaneous haemodynamic processes: (1) increased intrahepatic resistance to portal blood flow (from cirrhosis, regenerative nodules and microthrombi) and (2) increased splanchnic blood flow secondary to splanchnic vasodilation. Cirrhosis is associated with decreased intrahepatic endothelial nitric oxide synthase and nitric oxide, causing intrahepatic vasoconstriction, while systemically nitric oxide, VEGF and TNF rise, driving splanchnic vasodilation. In advanced stages, neurohumoral and vasoconstrictor activation causes sodium/water retention, increased blood volume and a hyperdynamic circulation that further raises portal pressure. Intrahepatic causes (mainly cirrhosis) account for >95% of portal hypertension; pre-hepatic (portal/splenic vein thrombosis) and post-hepatic (Budd-Chiari, right-heart congestion) causes also occur. Elevated portal pressure decompresses into portosystemic collaterals, producing gastro-oesophageal varices that can rupture and bleed. (p.2713-2714)

Portal hypertension is defined as a hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) >5 mmHg; compensated cirrhosis typically has an HVPG of 5-10 mmHg, while clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH), defined as HVPG ≥10 mmHg, carries substantial risk of decompensation (variceal bleeding, ascites, encephalopathy). Patients with a gradient >12 mmHg are at risk for variceal haemorrhage (p.2713-2714).
Each episode of variceal haemorrhage carries a 20-30% mortality rate, making it an immediate life-threatening complication of portal hypertension (p.2713).

In cirrhotic patients presenting with upper GI bleeding, prophylactic antibiotics (typically ceftriaxone) started before endoscopy reduce bacterial infections, recurrent bleeding AND mortality — this is a mortality-altering intervention, not merely supportive (p.362, p.2714).

A vasoactive/vasoconstricting agent (somatostatin, octreotide, terlipressin, vapreotide) improves initial bleeding control, reduces transfusion needs and reduces all-cause mortality; combined endoscopic plus pharmacologic therapy is superior to either alone (p.360, p.2714).

A restrictive transfusion strategy (transfuse when haemoglobin <7 g/dL, target 7-9 g/dL) reduced early rebleeding and mortality compared with a liberal threshold in randomised trial; haemoglobin may be normal at initial presentation because plasma and red-cell volumes fall proportionately ("people bleed whole blood") and may take up to 72 h to fall (p.362, p.2714).

Roughly one-third of patients with histologically confirmed cirrhosis have varices; about 5-15% of cirrhotics develop varices per year, and roughly one-third of patients with varices will bleed (p.2713).
IV erythromycin given shortly before endoscopy is suggested as a promotility agent to improve endoscopic visualisation in UGI bleeding, reducing the need for repeat endoscopy (p.362, p.2713).

Routine correction of an elevated prothrombin time with fresh frozen plasma is NOT recommended in acute variceal bleeding unless there is evidence of coagulopathy such as bleeding at other sites (e.g. IV-line sites) (p.2714).

Bleeding gastric varices, especially when entirely within the stomach or extending into the proximal stomach, are often not amenable to band ligation; tissue-adhesive injection (e.g. cyanoacrylate), TIPS, or balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration (BRTO) are alternative principles (p.361, p.2714).

Assuming a normal initial haemoglobin excludes severe bleeding — haemoglobin may be normal or only minimally reduced at presentation and can take up to 72 h to fall as extravascular fluid re-equilibrates (p.362)

Reflexively correcting a prolonged prothrombin time with FFP — not recommended in variceal bleeding without evidence of true coagulopathy, and FFP can raise portal pressure and cause volume overload (p.2714)
Over-liberal transfusion — a liberal threshold (Hb 9 g/dL) increased early rebleeding and mortality versus a restrictive (<7 g/dL) threshold (p.362, p.2714)
Omitting antibiotics in a cirrhotic UGI bleed — prophylactic antibiotics reduce infection, rebleeding and mortality and are a core, not optional, intervention (p.362, p.2714)
Attempting band ligation on gastric or proximal-stomach varices, where it is often unsuccessful — consider tissue adhesive, TIPS or BRTO (p.2714)
Forgetting that TIPS causes new or worsened hepatic encephalopathy in as many as 20% of patients, especially the elderly and those with pre-existing encephalopathy (p.2714)

Variceal haemorrhage carries a 20-30% mortality rate with each bleeding episode and patients with variceal haemorrhage have poorer outcomes than those with other UGIB sources. Control of acute bleeding is achievable in the vast majority of cases, but bleeding recurs in the majority of patients unless definitive endoscopic therapy is instituted; oesophageal varices reflect clinically significant portal hypertension (HVPG ≥10 mmHg), and once cirrhosis decompensates the median survival is <2 years. Prophylactic antibiotics, vasoactive drugs and a restrictive transfusion strategy each independently reduce mortality. (p.360, p.2713-2714)
Variceal haemorrhage is immediately life-threatening with 20-30% mortality per bleeding episode — treat as a major haemorrhage with airway/haemodynamic priority (p.2713)
Hemodynamic compromise (tachycardia, hypotension), increasing age and comorbidities predict rebleeding and death (p.362)
Increased frequency of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) in patients with variceal haemorrhage — SBP prophylaxis is recommended at presentation with upper GI bleeding (p.2715)

Persistent or recurrent bleeding despite endoscopic and medical therapy, and advanced liver disease (Child-Pugh B score 8-9 with active bleeding, or Child-Pugh C score 10-13), mark patients who benefit from early/salvage TIPS (p.360-361)

Bleeding/decompensation risk is stratified by Child-Pugh class and MELD score, by HVPG/wedged-hepatic-vein pressure (CSPH ≥10 mmHg; variceal bleeding risk at >12 mmHg), by varix size and location, and by endoscopic high-risk stigmata (red wale signs, cherry-red spots, etc.). For triage of UGIB generally, the Glasgow-Blatchford score (0-23) identifies very-low-risk patients (score 0-1) suitable for outpatient management. Advanced-disease thresholds favouring early TIPS: Child-Pugh B 8-9 with active bleeding at endoscopy, or Child-Pugh C 10-13. (p.362, p.2713-2714)

Haematemesis/melaena in a patient with chronic liver disease suggests variceal bleeding.
Red flags: Major haemorrhage — resuscitate; antibiotics reduce mortality in cirrhotic GI bleed

[guideline] empiric → Ceftriaxone — antibiotic prophylaxis in cirrhotic upper-GI bleeding Short-course antibiotic prophylaxis at presentation reduces bacterial infection, rebleeding and mortality in cirrhotic UGIB and is a standard adjunct to vasoactive therapy + endoscopy (Baveno VII / AASLD).

For chickenpox: disseminated HSV infection in patients with atopic dermatitis; disseminated vesiculopapular lesions of coxsackievirus or echovirus infection; atypical measles (these rashes are more often morbilliform/hemorrhagic than vesicular) (p.1506)
Rickettsialpox - distinguished by the 'herald spot' (eschar) at the mite-bite site and a more pronounced headache; serology helps differentiate it from varicella (p.1506)
Mpox - consider in travelers from endemic areas and in HIV-infected individuals (p.1506)
Smallpox - bioterrorism concern; smallpox lesions are larger than chickenpox lesions and all at the same stage of evolution at any given time (p.1506)
For herpes zoster: both HSV and coxsackievirus infections can cause dermatomal vesicular lesions (p.1506)
Disseminated HSV infection (notably in atopic dermatitis) (p.1506)
Coxsackievirus infection (p.1506)
Echovirus infection (p.1506)
Atypical measles (p.1506)
Rickettsialpox (p.1506)
Mpox (p.1506)
Smallpox (p.1506)
HSV and coxsackievirus causing dermatomal vesicular lesions (mimicking zoster) (p.1506)
PCR for VZV DNA in vesicular fluid - diagnostic method of choice; also performed on lesions, blood, and saliva (p.1507)
Tzanck smear (scraping of lesion base for multinucleated giant cells) - rapid but low sensitivity (~60%) (p.1507)
Viral isolation in susceptible tissue-culture cell lines (unequivocal confirmation) (p.1507)
Direct immunofluorescent staining of cells from the lesion base or immunoperoxidase detection of viral antigens (p.1507)

Serology: seroconversion or fourfold rise in antibody titer between acute- and convalescent-phase sera; FAMA (fluorescent antibody to membrane antigen) test and ELISA are the most sensitive serologic tools (p.1507)

VZV is a member of the Herpesviridae with double-stranded DNA (~125,000 bp), a lipid envelope, and an icosahedral nucleocapsid (~180-200 nm). Primary transmission is by the respiratory route, with localized replication (presumably nasopharynx) seeding the lymphatic/reticuloendothelial system and producing viremia, which manifests as diffuse, scattered skin lesions. Vesicles involve the corium/dermis with ballooning degeneration, multinucleated giant cells, and eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions; localized skin blood-vessel involvement can cause necrosis and epidermal hemorrhage. During chickenpox the virus infects dorsal root ganglia and remains latent (in sensory dorsal, cranial, and enteric ganglia) until an unknown trigger causes reactivation, producing herpes zoster; active zoster ganglia show hemorrhage, edema, and lymphocytic infiltration. Pulmonary involvement shows interstitial pneumonitis with giant cells, intranuclear inclusions, and hemorrhage; CNS infection produces perivascular cuffing similar to other viral encephalitides, while focal hemorrhagic necrosis (characteristic of HSV encephalitis) develops infrequently in VZV infection (p.1504).

VZV causes two distinct clinical syndromes: primary infection (varicella/chickenpox), usually a benign childhood exanthematous vesicular illness, and reactivation of latent virus (herpes zoster/shingles), a dermatomal vesicular rash usually associated with severe pain (p.1504).

In chickenpox, skin lesions appear in successive crops over a 2-4 day period and are present in various stages of evolution simultaneously (maculopapules, vesicles, and scabs) on a given body region - the classic small vesicle on an erythematous base ('dewdrop on a rose petal') (p.1505).

Chickenpox is highly contagious (attack rate >=90% in seronegatives); patients are infectious ~48 h before the rash appears, throughout vesicle formation, and until all vesicles are crusted. Incubation is usually 14-17 days (range 10-21) (p.1505).

Herpes zoster results from reactivation of latent VZV in dorsal root ganglia; most patients have no recent exposure to others with VZV. Incidence is highest in the sixth decade of life and beyond; recurrent zoster is exceedingly rare except in immunocompromised hosts, especially those with AIDS (p.1505).
Zoster pain (dermatomal) may precede visible lesions by 48-72 h; in the prodromal stage before the rash appears, the diagnosis can be exceedingly difficult (p.1505-1506).
Dermatomes T3 to L3 are most frequently involved in herpes zoster (p.1505).

PCR detection of VZV DNA in vesicular fluid is the diagnostic method of choice; specimens for PCR include lesions, blood, and saliva. The Tzanck smear gives a rapid impression but has low sensitivity (~60%) (p.1507).
Patients with herpes zoster can transmit infection to seronegative individuals, resulting in chickenpox (not zoster) in the contact (p.1506).
Aspirin should never be given to children with chickenpox because of its association with Reye syndrome; aspirin is no longer used for this reason (p.1505, 1507)
Zoster sine herpetica: dermatomal pain with serologic evidence of zoster can occur in the absence of any skin lesions - shingles without a rash has been reported, making diagnosis difficult (p.1506)
In the prodromal stage of herpes zoster (before lesions appear), diagnosis may be possible only after lesions emerge or by retrospective serology (p.1506)

Glucocorticoids for zoster should not be used without concomitant antiviral therapy, and steroid use is appropriate only for relatively healthy elderly patients with moderate/severe pain; patients with osteoporosis, diabetes mellitus, glycosuria, or hypertension may not be appropriate candidates (p.1507)
VZIG is NOT indicated for a newborn if the mother has zoster (as opposed to varicella); it is indicated when maternal varicella onsets within 5 days before to 48 h after delivery (p.1507-1508)

In the immunocompetent host chickenpox is usually benign and self-limited (total duration ~7-10 days; skin may take 2-4 weeks to fully normalize). Childhood acute cerebellar ataxia is generally benign and does not require hospitalization. Postherpetic neuralgia is the most debilitating complication of zoster: uncommon in the young but affects at least 50% of patients over age 50, who report dermatomal pain for months after cutaneous healing. Even in immunocompromised patients, disseminated zoster is rarely fatal. Hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients are at particularly high risk, with a mortality rate of ~10% for posttransplantation VZV infection. The Shingrix subunit vaccine showed 97.2% efficacy in adults >=50 years, although vaccine immunity wanes over time (p.1505-1507).

Zoster ophthalmicus - involvement of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve; a debilitating condition that can result in blindness in the absence of antiviral therapy. Lesions on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson sign) signal likely ocular involvement; refer immediately to an ophthalmologist (p.1505-1507)

Ramsay Hunt syndrome - geniculate ganglion (sensory branch of facial nerve) involvement causing pain and vesicles in the external auditory canal, loss of taste in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, and ipsilateral facial palsy (p.1506)

Disseminated/progressive herpes zoster in immunocompromised hosts - patients with Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma are at greatest risk; cutaneous dissemination occurs in ~40% untreated, raising the risk of pneumonitis, meningoencephalitis, and hepatitis by 5-10% (p.1506)

Varicella pneumonia - the most serious complication of chickenpox; more common in adults (up to 20%) than children and particularly severe in pregnant women; typically requires ventilatory support (p.1505, 1507)
Visceral dissemination in immunocompromised patients - occurs in 30-50% of cases and is fatal 15% of the time without antiviral therapy (p.1505)
Perinatal varicella - mortality as high as 30% when maternal disease begins within 5 days before to 48 h after delivery (p.1505)

CNS involvement: encephalitis (0.1-0.2% of children with chickenpox), aseptic meningitis, transverse myelitis, Guillain-Barre syndrome; in zoster, symptomatic meningoencephalitis and rare granulomatous angiitis with contralateral hemiplegia (p.1505-1506)

chunks.text: A varicocele results from incompetent or absent valves in the internal spermatic (testicular) veins, leading to retrograde flow and dilatation of the pampiniform plexus. The predominance on the left relates to the anatomy of left testicular venous drainage into the left renal vein at a right angle with a longer, higher-pressure course. The resulting venous stasis is thought to impair testicular function through elevated scrotal temperature, venous hypertension, hypoxia, and reflux of adrenal or renal metabolites, contributing to defective spermatogenesis and, in some cases, testicular atrophy.

chunks.text: Varicose veins develop when incompetent valves in the superficial venous system, or at the saphenofemoral or saphenopopliteal junctions, permit reflux of blood back down the leg. The resulting venous hypertension dilates and elongates the superficial veins, making them tortuous. Sustained ambulatory venous hypertension is transmitted to the skin microcirculation, causing capillary leakage, fibrin deposition, inflammation, and progressive skin changes that culminate in venous ulceration. Contributing factors include heredity, prolonged standing, pregnancy, obesity, and previous deep vein thrombosis, the last causing secondary varicosities through deep venous obstruction or valvular damage.

Brain MRI is the mainstay for detection and subtyping of cerebrovascular disease; should include FLAIR, diffusion-weighted, and T2*-weighted sequences to detect large and small chronic infarcts, acute microinfarcts, microbleeds, and white matter hyperintensities (p.3491)
Diffusion tensor MRI (e.g., peak width of skeletonized mean diffusivity, PSMD) detects white matter disconnection (largely research use) (p.3490)
Vessel imaging (CT or MR angiography) is not required for initial cognitive evaluation but may help determine the cause of identified macroscopic infarcts (p.3491)
Screening for atrial fibrillation in individuals with asymptomatic infarcts; prolonged cardiac monitoring for embolic-appearing infarcts (p.3491)
Genetic testing for hereditary VCID (CADASIL, hereditary cerebral amyloid angiopathy) when young onset, positive family history, or suggestive imaging—otherwise unnecessary (p.3491)
Alzheimer's disease (frequently coexists as mixed dementia—a key pitfall)
Normal pressure hydrocephalus (shares gait disturbance)
Delirium (prominent attention/executive deficits)

Vascular dementia results from the cumulative impact of cerebrovascular disease on age-related cognitive decline. Symptomatic strokes (ischemic or hemorrhagic) produce irreversible injury whose cognitive effect depends on size and location. Cerebral small-vessel disease—principally arteriolosclerosis (thickening of arterioles from plasma-protein infiltration; risk factors age, hypertension, diabetes; centered on deep penetrating territories such as thalamus, basal ganglia, brainstem) and cerebral amyloid angiopathy (beta-amyloid deposition in walls of small cortical arteries/arterioles/capillaries; main risk factor advancing age; favoring lobar cortex and subcortical white matter)—is often clinically asymptomatic and produces lacunar infarcts, microinfarcts, cerebral microbleeds, and white matter hyperintensities. These small distributed injuries disconnect nodes within distributed brain networks. Mixed pathology is the rule: cerebrovascular lesions frequently co-occur with neurodegenerative disease (most commonly Alzheimer's), producing greater impairment than either mechanism alone, possibly via loss of blood-brain barrier integrity and impaired perivascular clearance of beta-amyloid (p.3489-3491).

Traditionally defined as dementia due primarily to one or more symptomatic strokes; ranked the second most frequent cause of dementia after Alzheimer's disease, and especially common where vascular risk factors are undertreated (p.3489).

The concept has been broadened to vascular contributions to cognitive impairment and dementia (VCID), reflecting that cerebrovascular pathology is highly prevalent in the elderly and contributes to cognitive impairment, whether in isolation or—more commonly—combined with neurodegenerative processes (p.3489).

Clinical evaluation focuses on identifying vascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, tobacco use, atrial fibrillation, coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease), prior stroke/TIA, and family history of early stroke or vascular disease (p.3491).

Although stepwise progression and deficits such as loss of executive function are particularly suggestive, most individuals with VCID follow the more typical pattern of gradual progression of impaired episodic memory (p.3491).

Patients often show a mixture of executive and visuospatial deficits with prominent psychomotor slowing, and may present with psychiatric symptoms such as depression, anxiety, delusions, disinhibition, or apathy (p.196).
Gait disturbance is common in vascular dementia (as well as PD/DLB and NPH) (p.195).

Strategic single infarcts in locations such as thalamus, medial temporal cortex, anterior corpus callosum, or dominant-side angular gyrus can sufficiently impair episodic memory and function to meet memory-based dementia criteria (p.3489).

At least some cognitive impairment is present in approximately half of stroke survivors and increases with longer follow-up; even patients with good cognitive recovery show accelerated poststroke cognitive decline (p.3489).

One late-onset community autopsy cohort attributed 25% of dementia risk to cerebrovascular disease (vs 39% Alzheimer's, 17% LATE, 12% Lewy body), and most late-onset dementia involves multiple coexisting pathologies (p.195).

Mixed dementia is the rule rather than the exception—cerebrovascular disease commonly co-occurs with Alzheimer's and other neurodegenerative pathologies, so attributing cognitive impairment to a single etiology is often incorrect (p.3489).
Most individuals with VCID do not show classic stepwise decline but instead a gradual progression of impaired episodic memory resembling Alzheimer's (p.3491).
White matter hyperintensities are an almost ubiquitous, nonspecific feature of aging (gliosis, demyelination, or increased water content) and should not be over-interpreted (p.3490).
Many chronic lacunar infarcts and microinfarcts cannot be readily identified on routine imaging, so absence of visible lesions does not exclude small-vessel disease (p.3490).

Stroke survivors show accelerated poststroke cognitive decline even after good initial recovery; in one longitudinal study trajectory shifted from a prestroke cognitive gain to poststroke loss. Multiple strokes and larger infarcted volumes raise the likelihood of poststroke cognitive dysfunction. Epidemiologic data show declining age-adjusted dementia incidence paralleling improved hypertension control and stroke prevention, and the SPRINT-MIND trial showed intensive systolic blood pressure lowering reduced rates of mild cognitive impairment and combined MCI/probable dementia, underscoring VCID as a target for prevention (p.3489).
Young onset, positive family history, or suggestive neuroimaging—consider hereditary forms such as CADASIL or hereditary cerebral amyloid angiopathy (p.3491)
Lobar intracerebral hemorrhage or convexity subarachnoid blood, suggesting cerebral amyloid angiopathy (p.3490)
Rapid progression with motor rigidity and myoclonus suggests CJD rather than vascular dementia (p.195)

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) - upper + lower respiratory tract granulomatous vasculitis plus pauci-immune glomerulonephritis; PR3/cANCA in >90% of active disease (Harrison 22e p.2939-2940)
Lymphomatoid granulomatosis - EBV-positive angiocentric B-cell proliferation with lung/skin/CNS/kidney involvement that mimics GPA but is not a true vasculitis (Harrison 22e p.2941)

Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) - pauci-immune small-vessel necrotizing vasculitis with frequent glomerulonephritis and pulmonary capillaritis but no granulomas; MPO/pANCA in ~75% (Harrison 22e p.2942)
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis / Churg-Strauss (EGPA) - asthma, eosinophilia, extravascular granuloma, vasculitis; ANCA (anti-MPO) in ~48% (Harrison 22e p.2943-2944)

Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) - necrotizing vasculitis of small/medium muscular arteries with microaneurysms, sparing lungs and glomeruli; associated with hepatitis B (and C); consider DADA2 in early-onset disease (Harrison 22e p.2944-2945)
Giant cell (temporal) arteritis with polymyalgia rheumatica - medium/large-vessel arteritis in patients over 50 (Harrison 22e p.2945-2946)
Takayasu arteritis - large-vessel arteritis of the aorta and its branches in young women (Harrison 22e p.2946-2947)
IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein) - small-vessel immune-complex vasculitis with palpable purpura, arthralgia, GI symptoms, glomerulonephritis; IgA/C3 on biopsy (Harrison 22e p.2947-2948)
Cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis - strongly associated with hepatitis C virus infection (Harrison 22e p.2936)
Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease (Goodpasture's syndrome) - other cause of pulmonary-renal syndrome to distinguish from ANCA-associated vasculitis (Harrison 22e p.2941)
Bacterial (infective) endocarditis - can produce a false-positive pANCA and a vasculitis-like multisystem picture (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and rhinoscleroma - midline destructive infections that mimic GPA upper-airway disease (Harrison 22e p.2941)
Disseminated gonococcal infection (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Pulmonary histoplasmosis (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Coccidioidomycosis (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Syphilis (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Lyme disease (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Rocky Mountain spotted fever (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Whipple's disease (Harrison 22e p.2937)
Bacterial airway infection in cystic fibrosis - associated with a non-anti-MPO pANCA pattern (Harrison 22e p.2937)
ANCA with antigen specificity - anti-proteinase-3 (cANCA) and anti-myeloperoxidase (pANCA) testing, interpreting in light of pretest probability (Harrison 22e p.2937, p.2941)
Hepatitis B and C serology in all suspected PAN (and in cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis) (Harrison 22e p.2945)
Echocardiography in all newly diagnosed EGPA because cardiac involvement drives mortality (Harrison 22e p.2944)
Serum complement and IgA levels in IgA vasculitis (complement normal; IgA elevated in about half) (Harrison 22e p.2948)

Tissue biopsy of a clinically involved organ for definitive diagnosis; in GPA, lung biopsy has the highest yield (necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis), upper-airway biopsy often shows only inflammation, renal biopsy shows pauci-immune GN (Harrison 22e p.2941)
Skin biopsy with immunofluorescence in IgA vasculitis (leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA and C3 deposition) (Harrison 22e p.2948)
Catheter-directed dye arteriography for PAN (microaneurysms of renal/hepatic/visceral arteries) - MR/CT angiography lack adequate resolution (Harrison 22e p.2945)
Temporal artery biopsy (3-5 cm segment, serial sections, because involvement is patchy/segmental); may remain positive up to ~14 days after starting glucocorticoids (Harrison 22e p.2946)
Temporal +/- axillary artery ultrasonography for the noncompressible 'halo' sign in GCA (Harrison 22e p.2946)
MR/CT angiography (and investigational PET) to assess large-vessel disease in GCA and to image the whole aorta and branches in Takayasu arteritis (Harrison 22e p.2946, p.2947)
Acute-phase reactants - ESR and/or CRP (note IL-6 inhibitors suppress CRP/ESR, removing them as activity markers in treated GCA) (Harrison 22e p.2946)
Complete blood count - anaemia, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis as inflammatory markers; striking eosinophilia in EGPA (Harrison 22e p.2940, p.2943)

Drug toxicity - cocaine (cocaine-induced midline destructive lesions can show anti-human-neutrophil-elastase ANCA), levamisole (cocaine adulterant; causes cutaneous infarction, granulocytopenia, vasculitis-mimicking serology), amphetamines, ergot alkaloids, methysergide, arsenic (Harrison 22e p.2937, p.2941)

Vasculitis is inflammation of and damage to blood vessel walls, usually compromising the lumen and causing ischaemia of supplied tissues; any size, type, or location of vessel may be affected, and disease may be primary/single-organ or secondary to another illness. Most syndromes are at least partly immune-mediated through three broad mechanisms (Harrison 22e p.2936): (1) Immune-complex formation/deposition (e.g., IgA vasculitis, lupus vasculitis, serum sickness, hepatitis-B-associated vasculitis, hepatitis-C cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis) - resembling serum sickness, complexes deposit in vessel walls, activate complement (notably C5a, chemotactic for neutrophils), and neutrophils infiltrate and release enzymes that damage the wall. (2) ANCA production (GPA, MPA, EGPA) - when neutrophils/monocytes are primed by TNF-alpha, IL-1, or alternative-complement activation, PR3 and MPO translocate to the cell membrane where ANCA can engage them, triggering degranulation, reactive oxygen species, endothelial injury, and release of IL-1/IL-8. (3) Pathogenic T-lymphocyte responses and granuloma formation (GCA, Takayasu, GPA, EGPA) - cytokine (IFN-gamma) activated endothelium expresses HLA class II and interacts with CD4+ T cells, with IL-1/TNF-alpha inducing adhesion molecules (ELAM-1, VCAM-1). The 1992/2012 Chapel Hill Consensus nomenclature underpins the classification of these syndromes by predominant vessel size (Harrison 22e p.2936, p.2942).

Suspect vasculitis in any patient with an unexplained multisystem illness; specific clues include palpable purpura, pulmonary infiltrates with microscopic hematuria, chronic sinusitis, mononeuritis multiplex, unexplained ischemic events, and glomerulonephritis with multisystem disease (Harrison 22e p.2937).
Saddle-nose deformity (from nasal septal perforation) and subglottic stenosis (~16% of GPA, may cause severe airway obstruction) are characteristic upper-airway sequelae of GPA (Harrison 22e p.2940).
Mononeuritis multiplex is a recurring vasculitic clue - common in EGPA (up to ~72%) and PAN (~51%), and also seen in GPA and MPA (Harrison 22e p.2940, p.2943, p.2944).

EGPA (Churg-Strauss) requires asthma, peripheral blood eosinophilia (>1000 cells/uL in >80%), and clinical features of vasculitis; eosinophilic tissue infiltration and extravascular granulomas are characteristic (Harrison 22e p.2943-2944).

Cardiac involvement (myocarditis, pericarditis, coronary vasculitis) is the leading cause of death in EGPA, accounting for ~39% of mortality; echocardiography is advised in all newly diagnosed patients (Harrison 22e p.2943-2944).

PAN does NOT involve pulmonary arteries and does NOT cause glomerulonephritis, granuloma, or significant eosinophilia; venule involvement points away from PAN and toward microscopic polyangiitis (Harrison 22e p.2944).

PAN classically causes microaneurysms of small- and medium-sized renal, hepatic, and visceral arteries; catheter-directed dye arteriography (MR/CT lack resolution) can be diagnostic when accessible tissue is unavailable (Harrison 22e p.2944-2945).

Giant cell arteritis occurs almost exclusively in those over 50; jaw/tongue claudication, scalp tenderness, and headache precede the dreaded complication of ischemic optic neuropathy with sudden blindness - therapy should not be delayed for diagnostic testing (Harrison 22e p.2945).
GCA and polymyalgia rheumatica are considered spectrums of one disease - PMR occurs in 40-50% of GCA, and 10-20% of isolated PMR later develop GCA (Harrison 22e p.2945).
Takayasu arteritis should be strongly suspected in a young woman with diminished/absent peripheral pulses, an inter-arm blood pressure discrepancy, or arterial bruits (Harrison 22e p.2946-2947).
Hemoptysis may be the first sign of alveolar haemorrhage in MPA (~12%); upper-airway disease and pulmonary nodules are atypical for MPA and instead suggest GPA (Harrison 22e p.2942).

The first step in suspected vasculitis is to exclude conditions that mimic it - especially infections - particularly before starting empirical immunosuppression in a deteriorating patient (Harrison 22e p.2937).
GPA carries an increased risk of venous thrombotic events (DVT/PE); maintain a heightened awareness even though routine anticoagulation is not recommended (Harrison 22e p.2940).

Definitive diagnosis usually rests on biopsy of clinically involved tissue; 'blind' biopsy of organs with no clinical evidence of involvement has very low yield and should be avoided. Arteriography is used when PAN, Takayasu, or primary CNS vasculitis is suspected (Harrison 22e p.2937-2938).

ANCA-associated vasculitides (GPA, MPA, EGPA) share small-vessel involvement and ANCA positivity but have distinct clinical phenotypes and should be regarded as separate entities (Harrison 22e p.2937).

cANCA targets proteinase-3 (PR3) - present in >90% of active GPA; pANCA targets myeloperoxidase (MPO) - only anti-MPO antibodies are convincingly linked to vasculitis (MPA, EGPA, GPA, isolated necrotizing crescentic GN) (Harrison 22e p.2937).

A pANCA pattern NOT due to anti-MPO can occur in nonvasculitic conditions: rheumatic/nonrheumatic autoimmune disease, inflammatory bowel disease, certain drugs, and infections including endocarditis and bacterial airway infection in cystic fibrosis (Harrison 22e p.2937).

ANCA titres do not reliably track disease activity - GPA can be active despite negative ANCA, titres correlate poorly with activity, and patients in remission may keep high ANCA for years (Harrison 22e p.2937, p.2941).

Predictive value of a positive ANCA in GPA is ~90% with active glomerulonephritis but falls to 30-60% in sinus/lung disease without renal involvement; tissue biopsy is then needed to exclude infection or malignancy that may give a false-positive ANCA (Harrison 22e p.2941).

In GPA the renal lesion is a pauci-immune (no immune-complex deposition) focal segmental glomerulitis that can evolve into rapidly progressive crescentic glomerulonephritis (Harrison 22e p.2939-2940).

Treating a rise in ANCA titre as a relapse - only ~43% relapse within 1 year of an ANCA increase, so a rising ANCA alone should not prompt reinstitution or escalation of immunosuppression (Harrison 22e p.2941).
Missing DADA2 (adenosine deaminase 2 deficiency) in early-onset PAN-like vasculitis, which responds to TNF inhibitors rather than standard PAN therapy (Harrison 22e p.2944).

Relying on ANCA to diagnose vasculitis in sinus/lung disease without renal involvement, where positive predictive value is only 30-60% and biopsy is needed to exclude infection/malignancy with false-positive ANCA (Harrison 22e p.2941).
Performing 'blind' biopsies of clinically uninvolved organs - yield is very low (Harrison 22e p.2937).
Starting immunosuppression before excluding infectious mimics, especially in a rapidly deteriorating patient (Harrison 22e p.2937).
Irradiating upper-airway lesions assuming GPA when the diagnosis is actually NK/T-cell lymphoma - GPA airway lesions should never be irradiated (Harrison 22e p.2941).
Overlooking cocaine/levamisole-induced midline destruction, which can produce vasculitis-mimicking serology (anti-elastase ANCA) and granulocytopenia (Harrison 22e p.2941).
Using CRP/ESR to monitor disease activity or assess infection in GCA patients on IL-6 inhibitors, which suppress these acute-phase reactants (Harrison 22e p.2946).
Attributing every minor ESR/CRP rise during a GCA prednisone taper to a flare - small increases may not reflect arteritis, and can also be caused by infection (Harrison 22e p.2946).
Mislabelling a necrotizing vasculitis with venule involvement as PAN - venule involvement indicates microscopic polyangiitis, not PAN (Harrison 22e p.2944).

Untreated GPA was historically fatal within months; with cyclophosphamide-based therapy >90% improve, ~75% achieve complete remission, and 5-year survival exceeds 80%, but 50-70% of remissions later relapse and many accrue irreversible damage (renal insufficiency, hearing loss, subglottic stenosis, saddle-nose deformity, chronic sinus dysfunction) (Harrison 22e p.2941). Treated MPA has a ~74% 5-year survival, with deaths from alveolar haemorrhage or GI/cardiac/renal disease, and relapse in at least ~34% (Harrison 22e p.2942). Untreated EGPA has a ~25% 5-year survival; treated, prognosis is favourable (~72% at 78 months), but myocardial involvement causes ~39% of deaths (Harrison 22e p.2944). Untreated PAN has a poor 5-year survival of 10-20% (deaths from GI and cardiovascular causes); prednisone plus cyclophosphamide markedly improves survival, with relapse in ~10-20% (Harrison 22e p.2944-2945). In GCA acute death is uncommon, but patients face late mortality from aortic aneurysm rupture/dissection (18x more likely to develop thoracic aortic aneurysm than the general population) (Harrison 22e p.2946). Takayasu outcomes vary widely (overall survival >=94% in some North American series; 5-year mortality 0-35% elsewhere), and the disease is usually chronic and relapsing (Harrison 22e p.2947). IgA vasculitis has an excellent prognosis with rare mortality and only 1-5% of children progressing to end-stage renal disease (Harrison 22e p.2948).
Active glomerulonephritis is always classed as severe disease even with normal renal function (Harrison 22e p.2941)
Alveolar/pulmonary haemorrhage - severe manifestation of GPA/MPA; hemoptysis may be the first symptom of alveolar haemorrhage in MPA (Harrison 22e p.2941, p.2942)

Visual symptoms in a patient over 50 with headache - ischemic optic neuropathy in GCA can cause sudden, irreversible blindness; do not delay treatment for diagnostic workup (Harrison 22e p.2945, p.2946)
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with rising creatinine in ANCA-associated vasculitis (Harrison 22e p.2939-2940, p.2942)
Jaw/tongue claudication, scalp tenderness, or a tender/nodular temporal artery - cranial ischaemic features of GCA (Harrison 22e p.2945)
Inter-arm blood pressure discrepancy, absent pulses, or bruits in a young woman - suggests Takayasu large-vessel involvement (Harrison 22e p.2947)
Bowel infarction/perforation and GI bleeding in PAN - leading causes of death (Harrison 22e p.2944-2945)
Cardiac involvement in EGPA - the chief cause of death (Harrison 22e p.2944)
Signs of deep-vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism in GPA given the increased venous thrombotic risk (Harrison 22e p.2940)

Vasculitides are classified by predominant vessel size per the Chapel Hill Consensus nomenclature (Harrison 22e p.2936, p.2942): LARGE-VESSEL (giant cell/temporal arteritis, Takayasu arteritis); MEDIUM-VESSEL (polyarteritis nodosa, Kawasaki disease); SMALL-VESSEL, which splits into ANCA-associated (GPA, MPA, EGPA) and immune-complex (IgA vasculitis/Henoch-Schonlein, cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis). The chapter also separates PRIMARY syndromes from SECONDARY vasculitis (associated with probable etiology e.g. drug-induced, hepatitis-B/C-related, cancer-associated; or with systemic disease e.g. lupus, rheumatoid, sarcoid vasculitis), and single-organ vasculitis (cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis, cutaneous arteritis, primary CNS vasculitis, isolated aortitis) (Harrison 22e p.2936). For management stratification, ANCA-associated vasculitis is divided into SEVERE (life- or organ-threatening; e.g., alveolar haemorrhage, and active glomerulonephritis is severe even with normal renal function) versus NONSEVERE/limited disease - severity depends on both extent and the specific organ involved (e.g., nodular pulmonary disease without respiratory compromise is nonsevere, whereas alveolar haemorrhage is severe) (Harrison 22e p.2941).

12-lead ECG when arrhythmia or underlying cardiac disease is suspected; look for brady-/tachyarrhythmias, AV block, acute or old myocardial ischemia/infarction, long QT, and bundle branch block.

Supine and standing (3 min) blood pressure and heart rate to detect orthostatic hypotension.

Tilt-table testing (autonomic testing) to distinguish autonomic-failure orthostatic hypotension from the hypotensive-bradycardic response of neurally mediated syncope, and to identify immediate or delayed orthostatic hypotension; may also reproduce psychogenic syncope when symptoms occur without hemodynamic change.

Autonomic function testing in specialized centers: heart rate variability to deep breathing and Valsalva (parasympathetic), thermoregulatory sweat test and quantitative sudomotor axon reflex test (sympathetic cholinergic), and BP response to Valsalva/tilt (sympathetic adrenergic).

Carotid sinus massage (under continuous ECG and BP monitoring) for suspected carotid sinus syncope and in patients >40 years with recurrent unexplained syncope; avoid with carotid bruits, plaque, or stenosis.

Inpatient ECG monitoring for high arrhythmia risk; ambulatory Holter monitoring for frequent (near-daily) episodes; external or implantable loop recorders for less frequent episodes (monitor for at least twice the interspell interval).

Echocardiography for patients with cardiac history or abnormal exam/ECG (may reveal aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, cardiac tumors, aortic dissection, pericardial tamponade; also stratifies sudden-death risk by ejection fraction).
Treadmill exercise testing with ECG and BP monitoring for syncope during or shortly after exercise.
Invasive electrophysiologic studies (low sensitivity/specificity, rarely used) only when pretest probability is high in structural heart disease with ECG abnormalities.

Standing pools 500-1000 mL of blood in the lower extremities, buttocks, and splanchnic circulation, reducing venous return, ventricular filling, cardiac output, and blood pressure. Normally baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch trigger a compensatory reflex that raises sympathetic outflow and lowers vagal activity, increasing peripheral resistance, venous return, and cardiac output. In neurally mediated (reflex/vasovagal) syncope this reflex transiently fails: there is a paroxysmal shift in autonomic efferent activity with increased parasympathetic outflow plus sympathoinhibition, producing bradycardia, vasodilation/loss of vasoconstrictor tone (vasodepressor response), and reduced cardiac output. The resulting fall in systemic blood pressure drops cerebral blood flow below the limits of autoregulation, causing transient global cerebral hypoperfusion and loss of consciousness. Multiple afferent triggers (orthostatic stress, carotid sinus, gastrointestinal tract, bladder) converge on the central autonomic network in the medulla. Hyperventilation-induced hypocarbia (cerebral vasoconstriction) and raised intrathoracic pressure (impaired venous return) contribute to many situational reflex syncopes. By contrast, orthostatic hypotension reflects chronic impairment of these homeostatic reflexes (autonomic failure), and cardiac syncope results from arrhythmias or structural disease reducing cardiac output.

Syncope is a transient, self-limited loss of consciousness from acute global cerebral hypoperfusion, with rapid onset, brief duration, and spontaneous complete recovery; reorientation is almost immediate after a syncopal event.
A clinically meaningful syncope usually corresponds to a fall in systolic BP to roughly 50 mmHg or lower; cessation of cerebral blood flow for 6-8 s produces loss of consciousness.
Causes fall into three categories: neurally mediated (reflex/vasovagal) syncope, orthostatic hypotension, and cardiac syncope; clinical features, mechanisms, and prognosis differ markedly among them.

Neurally mediated syncope is the most common cause overall in population-based studies and accounts for the vast majority of syncope in the young (peak incidence ~age 15); incidence is higher in women, and a first-degree family history is common in young patients.

Vasovagal syncope (the common faint) is provoked by intense emotion, pain, the sight of blood, venipuncture, and/or orthostatic stress; situational reflex syncopes have specific localized triggers (cough, micturition, swallow, defecation, carotid sinus pressure).
Premonitory (prodromal) features of autonomic activation in neurally mediated syncope include diaphoresis, pallor, palpitations, nausea, lightheadedness, hyperventilation, and yawning.
A functioning autonomic nervous system is required to develop neurally mediated syncope, in contrast to syncope from autonomic failure (orthostatic hypotension).
Neurally mediated syncope can be subdivided by efferent pathway: vasodepressor (sympathetic vasoconstrictor failure), cardioinhibitory (bradycardia/asystole from vagal outflow), or mixed.

Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a fall in systolic BP of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic BP of at least 10 mmHg within 3 min of standing or head-up tilt; supine and standing BP/HR at 3 min should be measured in every initial evaluation.
Initial clinical assessment plus ECG identifies a cause in about 50% of patients and stratifies cardiac mortality risk.

Convulsive syncope mimics seizure: myoclonic and other movements occur in up to ~90% of syncopal episodes, but syncope-related jerks are typically arrhythmic, multifocal/generalized, and brief (<30 s), with mild flexor/extensor posturing; EEG seizure discharges are absent during syncope.

Distinguishing features from seizure: seizure loss of consciousness usually lasts >5 min with prolonged postictal drowsiness/disorientation, whereas reorientation after syncope is almost immediate; muscle aches are longer and more severe after seizures; seizures are rarely provoked by emotion or pain.
Urinary incontinence can occur in both syncope and seizure and does not distinguish them; fecal incontinence is very rare in syncope and postictal confusion is rare after syncope.
During neurally mediated syncope the eyes typically remain open and deviate upward with dilated pupils, and grunting/moaning/stertorous breathing may occur, which can be mistaken for a seizure.
Orthostatic hypotension syncope is usually preceded by warning symptoms but may occur suddenly, mimicking a seizure or cardiac cause.
Supine hypertension is common (>50%) in autonomic-failure orthostatic hypotension; treating one condition can unmask or worsen the other.

Initial orthostatic hypotension (BP fall within 15 s, resolving by 45 s) and delayed orthostatic hypotension (beyond 3 min) can be missed by a single 3-min standing measurement; initial orthostatic hypotension does not represent autonomic failure.

Syncope of noncardiac and unexplained origin in younger individuals carries an excellent prognosis with unaffected life expectancy. In contrast, cardiac syncope (structural heart disease or primary arrhythmia) is associated with an increased risk of sudden cardiac death and overall mortality, and mortality is also increased with orthostatic hypotension related to age and comorbidities. Hospitalization and mortality risk are higher in older adults.
Syncope during exertion, or while seated or supine.

ECG features: ischemia, history of ventricular arrhythmias, prolonged QT (>500 ms), repetitive SA block or sinus pauses, persistent sinus bradycardia, bi-/trifascicular block or QRS >=120 ms, atrial fibrillation, nonsustained VT, preexcitation, or a Brugada pattern.
