New chest discomfort, abdominal pain, shortness of breath, or headache associated with the episode.
Exam: unexplained systolic BP <90 mmHg, signs of GI hemorrhage, persistent bradycardia <40 beats/min, or an undiagnosed systolic murmur.

Harrison categorizes syncope by mechanism rather than a graded severity score: (1) neurally mediated (reflex/vasovagal) syncope, (2) orthostatic hypotension, and (3) cardiac syncope. For risk stratification, Table 23-1 lists high-risk features indicating hospitalization or intensive evaluation (e.g., ischemic chest pain, heart failure, significant valvular/structural disease, ECG ischemia, ventricular arrhythmia history, QT >500 ms, SA block/sinus pauses, persistent sinus bradycardia, bi-/trifascicular block or QRS >=120 ms, atrial fibrillation, nonsustained VT, family history of sudden death, preexcitation, Brugada pattern, palpitations at syncope, syncope at rest or during exercise). Neurally mediated efferent subtypes are vasodepressor, cardioinhibitory, and mixed.

A communication in the ventricular septum allows blood to shunt according to the pressure and resistance gradient between the ventricles. After birth, as pulmonary vascular resistance declines, left-to-right shunting increases, raising pulmonary blood flow and volume-loading the left atrium and left ventricle. A large, sustained shunt increases pulmonary artery pressure and flow, and over time medial hypertrophy and intimal changes in the pulmonary vasculature raise resistance irreversibly; when pulmonary resistance exceeds systemic, the shunt reverses and produces cyanosis (Eisenmenger syndrome).
The most common congenital heart malformation, an opening in the interventricular septum that permits shunting between the ventricles; most are membranous or muscular in location.

The direction and size of the shunt depend on the defect size and the relative resistances of the pulmonary and systemic circulations, so many defects become clinically apparent only as pulmonary resistance falls in the first weeks of life.
Small defects produce a loud, often harsh holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border but little haemodynamic burden, and many close spontaneously.
Large defects cause a significant left-to-right shunt with excessive pulmonary blood flow, leading to heart failure signs such as tachypnoea, poor feeding, sweating, and failure to thrive in infancy.
A large shunt may generate a mid-diastolic rumble at the apex from increased flow across the mitral valve.
Untreated large defects risk progressive pulmonary vascular disease that can eventually reverse the shunt (Eisenmenger physiology), a late and largely irreversible complication.
Echocardiography defines the defect location and size, estimates shunt magnitude, and assesses chamber enlargement and pulmonary pressures.

Management of a haemodynamically significant defect focuses on treating heart failure and supporting growth, with surgical or catheter closure for defects that do not shrink or that cause failure or pulmonary hypertension.
Many small muscular and membranous defects close on their own during early childhood.
Assuming a loud murmur means a large, dangerous defect when small defects are often the loudest
Missing a large defect in the newborn period before pulmonary resistance falls and the murmur becomes apparent
Overlooking progression to pulmonary vascular disease by delaying closure of a significant shunt
Attributing poor growth to feeding problems rather than an underlying significant shunt
Failing to recognise shunt reversal when cyanosis appears in a previously acyanotic child

Small defects have an excellent outlook and often close spontaneously. Large defects, if repaired before irreversible pulmonary vascular disease develops, generally have a good outcome; delayed closure risks fixed pulmonary hypertension and a markedly worse prognosis.

chunks.text: Vesicoureteric reflux occurs when the valve-like mechanism of the vesicoureteric junction fails, allowing urine to reflux from the bladder into the ureter and renal pelvis. Normally an adequate length of submucosal ureter within the bladder wall is compressed during bladder filling and voiding, preventing reflux; in primary VUR this tunnel is congenitally short or laterally placed. Secondary VUR develops when high intravesical pressures from bladder outlet obstruction or neurogenic/dysfunctional voiding overcome the junction. Reflux of infected urine and elevated pressures transmitted to the kidney cause pyelonephritis and scarring (reflux nephropathy), which underlies later hypertension and renal impairment.

In many viral exanthems the rash reflects the systemic phase of infection when virus disseminates through the bloodstream and, together with the host immune response, involves the skin. Some eruptions result from direct viral infection of skin cells (as in varicella, where the virus produces vesicular lesions), while others are largely immune-mediated, appearing as the immune response develops and sometimes coinciding with defervescence, as in roseola. The specific morphology, distribution, and timing are determined by the particular virus, its tropism, and the character of the immune reaction, which is why individual exanthems have recognisable patterns.
Viral exanthems are widespread skin eruptions accompanying systemic viral infections and are among the most common causes of rash with fever in children.
The classic childhood exanthems include measles, rubella, erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19), roseola (human herpesvirus 6/7), and varicella, each with fairly characteristic patterns.
Diagnosis is often clinical, based on the morphology and distribution of the rash, its timing relative to fever, and associated features such as enanthems and prodromal symptoms.
Measles is distinguished by high fever with cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis, Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa, and a rash spreading from the head downward.
Roseola typically causes several days of high fever in a well-appearing infant, followed by a rash that appears as the fever resolves.
Erythema infectiosum produces the characteristic slapped-cheek facial appearance followed by a lacy, reticular rash on the limbs.
Most viral exanthems are self-limiting and managed supportively, but measles carries a notable risk of complications and remains vaccine-preventable.
Recognising non-viral mimics, especially meningococcaemia, scarlet fever, Kawasaki disease, and drug reactions, is essential because some require urgent specific treatment.

Failing to consider Kawasaki disease in a child with prolonged fever and rash
Overlooking measles and its public health and complication implications
Attributing a drug hypersensitivity eruption to a viral cause

The great majority of viral exanthems are benign and self-limiting with full recovery, though certain infections, notably measles and varicella in vulnerable hosts, and parvovirus in specific settings, can cause significant complications.

Enteric viruses injure the small-intestinal mucosa to produce predominantly watery diarrhea. With human caliciviruses (Norwalk/norovirus), carbohydrates resembling human histo-blood group antigens on the gastroduodenal epithelium of secretor-phenotype individuals appear to serve as attachment ligands; infection causes reversible lesions of the upper jejunum with broadening and blunting of villi, microvillar shortening, epithelial vacuolization, crypt hyperplasia, and lamina propria infiltration by neutrophils and lymphocytes. These changes persist for at least 4 days after symptom resolution and produce malabsorption of carbohydrates and fats with reduced brush-border enzymes; adenylate cyclase activity is unchanged. No histopathologic change occurs in stomach or colon, but delayed gastric motor function is thought to drive the characteristic nausea and vomiting. Rotavirus infects and destroys mature enterocytes of the proximal small-intestinal villous epithelium; loss of absorptive cells plus proliferation of secretory crypt cells yields secretory diarrhea, while reduced brush-border enzymes leave unmetabolized disaccharides that cause osmotic diarrhea. The nonstructural rotavirus protein NSP4 acts as an enterotoxin altering epithelial permeability and function, and rotavirus may also stimulate fluid secretion via activation of the enteric nervous system.

Most viral gastroenteritis is caused by RNA viruses, but DNA enteric adenoviruses (types 40 and 41) are also recognized causes; the principal pathogens are rotavirus, norovirus, sapovirus, astrovirus, and enteric adenovirus.

In temperate climates viral gastroenteritis shows winter seasonality, whereas in tropical/year-round settings seasonal peaks are less pronounced; before vaccination, US rotavirus season began in the Southwest in autumn/early winter and migrated to peak in the Northeast in late winter/spring.
Fever is common with both rotavirus and norovirus but uncommon with the other viral agents; up to one-third of rotavirus patients may have a temperature above 39 degrees C.

Death is a rare outcome and usually results from severe dehydration in vulnerable hosts such as debilitated elderly patients and young children; acute gastroenteritis is a leading cause of childhood death in developing countries (roughly 0.5 million deaths annually) and a major cause of pediatric hospitalization (6-8%) in industrialized nations.

Illness presents with acute onset of vomiting and/or diarrhea, often with fever, nausea, abdominal cramps, anorexia, and malaise; the diarrhea is characteristically watery and nonbloody, without mucus or fecal leukocytes.

Norovirus has become the leading cause of medically attended gastroenteritis in young children in the United States and other developed countries following the decline in severe rotavirus disease after routine rotavirus vaccination, and it affects all age groups.

Norovirus is responsible for roughly half of all reported gastroenteritis outbreaks in the United States and is the major cause of gastroenteritis epidemics worldwide; it also causes traveler's diarrhea and outbreaks among deployed military personnel.

The infectious dose for most viral agents is very low (about 10-100 viral particles), in contrast to the higher inoculum typically required for many bacterial pathogens; norovirus can spread by fecal-oral route, aerosolization of vomitus, contaminated fomites, and person-to-person contact.

Nearly all children worldwide are infected with rotavirus by 3-5 years of age; first symptomatic infection usually occurs after 3 months of age, disease incidence peaks at 4-23 months, and severity decreases with each repeat infection.

Protection against rotavirus correlates with virus-specific secretory IgA in the intestine (and to some degree serum); because intestinal IgA is short-lived, full protection is temporary, but successive reinfections build progressively greater immunity.

Susceptibility to norovirus is influenced by host genetics: histo-blood group antigen (HBGA) phenotype and secretor status affect attachment, and functional antibodies that block norovirus binding to HBGAs correlate with protective immunity.

Rotavirus antigenemia and viremia are common in acutely infected children, although serum antigen and RNA levels are far lower than stool levels; rotavirus is shed in very large quantities in stool (10^7-10^12 per gram).

Distinguishing viral from bacterial gastroenteritis on clinical and epidemiologic grounds alone is often unreliable; laboratory testing may be needed, and viral gastroenteritis is frequently a diagnosis of exclusion in practice.
Antibiotics and antimotility agents are inappropriate for viral gastroenteritis and are contraindicated.
Commercial stool EIA kits for norovirus have limited sensitivity and are most useful in outbreak investigation (many specimens tested) rather than for diagnosing individual patients.

Higher preexisting antibody to Norwalk virus does not guarantee protection - early studies paradoxically found higher antibody levels associated with greater susceptibility, later explained by host HBGA genetics rather than simple antibody titer.

Rotavirus has been associated with diverse conditions (SIDS, necrotizing enterocolitis, intussusception, Kawasaki disease, type 1 diabetes) and with respiratory/neurologic features, but no causal relationship has been confirmed for any of these.

Asymptomatically infected and pre-symptomatic persons can shed norovirus, and shedding can persist for weeks after recovery (prolonged in immunocompromised hosts), so a single negative or positive result must be interpreted with care.

Viral gastroenteritis is generally self-limited. Human calicivirus illness has a sudden onset after a mean incubation of about 24 hours (range 12-72 h) and typically lasts 12-60 h; norovirus and sapovirus illness usually resolves in 1-3 days. Rotavirus illness begins abruptly after a 1-3 day incubation, with vomiting often preceding diarrhea, and gastrointestinal symptoms generally resolve in 3-7 days. Among healthy young adults the illness is rarely fatal but causes substantial morbidity and lost work time. The main serious complication is dehydration; death is uncommon and concentrated in the very young, the elderly, and those with debilitating conditions. Severely immunodeficient children may develop protracted rotavirus diarrhea with prolonged shedding and, rarely, systemic dissemination.
Signs of severe dehydration (especially in young children and debilitated elderly)
Inability to tolerate oral intake due to frequent vomiting
Bloody diarrhea or fecal leukocytes - should prompt evaluation for a bacterial/inflammatory cause rather than viral gastroenteritis
Protracted diarrhea with prolonged viral excretion or systemic dissemination in severely immunocompromised hosts (e.g., post-bone-marrow transplant rotavirus disease)

Harrison does not provide a formal grading scale; clinical severity is described per agent and ranges from subclinical/mild infection to severe gastroenteritis with life-threatening dehydration. Relative clinical severity by virus: group A rotavirus is the most severe (predominantly children under 5), norovirus is moderate (all ages), and sapovirus, astrovirus, and enteric adenovirus are generally milder (mainly children under 5).

RT-PCR targeting one or more filovirid genes is the diagnostic assay of choice; in-field PCR platforms (e.g., Cepheid GeneXpert) are deployed during outbreaks
Acute-phase blood/serum is the preferred specimen as it usually contains high virion titers
Antigen-capture ELISA / immunochromatographic rapid diagnostic tests (currently limited; EBOV antigen RDT sensitivity restricts use largely to postmortem samples)
IgM- and IgG-capture ELISAs (including multiplex) for antibodies in later disease and in survivors
Virus isolation/plaque assays and electron microscopy require maximum-containment laboratories; in-field genome sequencing supports outbreak epidemiology

Supportive labs typically show leukopenia (then leukocytosis), thrombocytopenia, raised aminotransferases (AST > ALT) and GGT, raised creatinine/urea with proteinuria, electrolyte derangement, hypoglycemia, hypoalbuminemia, prolonged PT/PTT, elevated CPK, and markedly elevated CRP in severe illness
Hemoconcentration from vascular leakage is usually evident (most marked in HFRS and severe dengue)
Venomous snakebite
Warfarin (anticoagulant) intoxication
Acquired or inherited coagulopathies in the bleeding patient

Across VHFs, direct or indirect microvascular damage increases vascular permeability and (when platelet function is reduced) causes disruption and local hemorrhage, most evident in skin and mucous membranes; hypotension and shock reflect generalized circulatory dysfunction rather than life-threatening blood loss. Pathogenesis is incompletely understood and varies by virus, with direct vascular/parenchymal damage in some and soluble mediators dominating in others. For filovirids specifically, virions enter via skin lesions, mucosal surfaces, or parenteral inoculation; GP1,2 spikes engage cell-surface molecules and the intracellular receptor NPC1. First targets are macrophages, monocytes, and dendritic cells, and viral proteins (VP35, VP40, VP24) suppress innate immunity (e.g., type I interferon pathways), enabling high viral titers and widespread tissue dissemination. Hallmarks include profound immune dysregulation, massive lymphoid depletion with severe lymphopenia, coagulopathy (thrombocytopenia, elevated tissue factor, consumption of clotting factors, raised D-dimers, falling protein C; possible DIC, though controversial), hepatocyte necrosis with synthetic dysfunction contributing to coagulopathy, and endothelial dysfunction with increased vascular permeability leading to fluid redistribution, interstitial edema, and hypovolemic or septic shock (pp.1674-1675, 1683-1685).

VHF is an acute viral syndrome of severe disease and multisystem organ dysfunction sharing a common disruption of vascular function, stability, and integrity; overt hemorrhage is often NOT the most prominent or severe feature, so absence of bleeding does not exclude VHF (p.1674).

Travel to an endemic or active-outbreak area within the incubation period is a major diagnostic clue; rural exposures more often suggest VHF except for urban-host/vector agents (Seoul virus, dengue, yellow fever) (p.1675).

For filovirid (Ebola/Marburg) disease, the incubation period is 2-25 days (most commonly 7-10 days), beginning with a nonspecific influenza-like illness (sudden fever/chills, headache, myalgia, pharyngitis, arthralgia, maculopapular rash) before a second phase (~5-7 days on) with GI, respiratory, cardiovascular, and CNS involvement (p.1685).

Common filovirid hemorrhagic signs are subconjunctival injection, petechial rash, gingival bleeding, and bleeding at injection sites; frank epistaxis, hematemesis, hematuria, and melena occur but are LESS common, and severe blood loss is rare (except during/after childbirth) (pp.1684-1685).
Ebola/Marburg present with very similar clinical phenotypes that cannot be distinguished at the bedside and, for practical purposes, may be managed as the same disease (p.1685).
Early recognition is crucial: prompt isolation and hospitalization are indicated even in the absence of clinical signs, with rapid triage and ongoing vital-sign monitoring (p.1675).

Filovirids are highly infectious but not exceptionally contagious; human-to-human spread occurs by direct contact with an infected person or their body fluids/tissues, with NO evidence of aerosol or respiratory droplet transmission in natural outbreak settings (p.1679).

Persistence of filovirids in immune-privileged sites (most commonly semen of male survivors; rarely CNS, eye, placenta) can cause recrudescent disease and rare reignition of outbreaks; sexual abstinence or condom use is advised for male survivors until semen is shown to be filovirid-RNA free (pp.1686-1687).

Filovirid/VHF disease cannot be diagnosed on clinical presentation alone; numerous more common febrile illnesses (especially malaria and typhoid) closely mimic it and are far more likely in non-outbreak settings, so do not anchor on VHF without epidemiologic context and laboratory confirmation.
Absence of overt hemorrhage does not exclude VHF, since hemorrhagic manifestations are often neither the most prominent nor the most severe feature.
Treat DIC only with clear laboratory evidence and feasible monitoring; there is no proven benefit otherwise.

Fluid management is a balancing act: VHF patients are commonly hypovolemic from insensible and GI losses, yet may also have decreased cardiac output, capillary leak, and oliguria requiring judicious fluids and inotropic/vasopressor support.
Do not assume respiratory/aerosol spread for filovirids in natural settings and do not reuse medical equipment (gloves, syringes) used for an infected patient.

FVD is among the most severe acute human viral diseases and generally carries a poor prognosis, though with far more heterogeneity than historically assumed (the long-cited 70-90% case-fatality rate for EVD has required revision). Outcome likely depends on the specific filovirid, host factors (age, immune status, coinfections, host genetics), exposure route and dose, viral load, presence and severity of organ dysfunction, and critically the availability of filovirid-specific countermeasures and supportive/critical care. Even with effective EBOV-specific therapeutics, outcomes in severe EVD with high viral loads and complex organ dysfunction remain suboptimal. For other VHFs prognosis varies widely by agent (e.g., Argentinian/Bolivian hemorrhagic fevers can have case-fatality rates exceeding 50% in individual outbreaks) (pp.1675, 1685-1687).

Strict barrier nursing and infection-control isolation with appropriate PPE are mandatory for suspected VHF (except dengue, orthohantavirus, RVFV, or yellow fever); isolate and hospitalize even before clinical signs appear
Immediately notify infectious disease specialists and public health authorities if filovirid disease is suspected on epidemiologic or clinical grounds
Progressive multiorgan dysfunction: shock, acute kidney injury, CNS injury (encephalopathy, coma, seizures), respiratory failure, and severe hemorrhage signal critical illness

Exposure history raising suspicion: caves/mines, direct contact with bats, nonhuman primates, or bushmeat, contact with severely ill local residents, or patient-to-patient/healthcare-worker clusters in rural hospitals
Hemodynamic instability/hypotension and capillary leak with effusions and edema
Pregnancy and labor are associated with severe complications and poor outcomes (clotting-factor consumption, fetal loss, severe peripartum hemorrhage)

No formal numeric severity score is provided; clinically, the illness progresses from an incubation period through a nonspecific febrile prodrome (early phase) to a peak phase, with severity marked by progressive multiorgan dysfunction (shock, acute kidney injury, respiratory failure, CNS injury, severe hemorrhage). Filovirid disease course is depicted across incubation, early, peak, and recovery phases. Severity and case-fatality vary by causative virus and the availability of specific countermeasures and supportive care (pp.1675, 1683-1686).

chunks.text: Viral warts result from infection of keratinocytes by human papillomavirus, which enters through microabrasions and drives epidermal proliferation and hyperkeratosis. Different HPV genotypes show tropism for particular sites and clinical morphologies. The virus establishes infection in the basal layer and completes its life cycle as keratinocytes differentiate towards the surface, producing the koilocytic changes seen histologically. Clearance depends on an effective cell-mediated immune response, which explains both spontaneous resolution over time and the persistence or proliferation of warts in immunocompromised patients. Certain high-risk genital genotypes carry oncogenic potential.

chunks.text: Other causes of night blindness (retinitis pigmentosa)
Fat malabsorption syndromes (cystic fibrosis, cholestatic liver disease, coeliac disease)
Protein-energy malnutrition with multiple deficiencies
Infective keratoconjunctivitis
Zinc deficiency
Dry eye from other causes
Serum retinol level
Clinical ocular examination for Bitot spots, xerosis, and corneal changes
Assessment of nutritional status and dietary intake
Investigation for fat malabsorption where suspected
Screening for coexisting micronutrient deficiencies

Vitamin A (retinol) is essential for the visual cycle, where its aldehyde form retinal combines with opsin to form rhodopsin in rod cells; deficiency reduces rhodopsin regeneration and causes night blindness. Retinoic acid also regulates differentiation and maintenance of epithelial tissues and mucosal barriers, so deficiency leads to squamous metaplasia and keratinisation of conjunctival and corneal epithelium (xerophthalmia) and of other epithelia. Impaired epithelial barriers and immune regulation increase susceptibility to and severity of infection.
A major cause of preventable childhood blindness and increased infection-related mortality in low- and middle-income countries.
The earliest and most sensitive symptom is night blindness, reflecting impaired rod photoreceptor function.
Progressive ocular signs (xerophthalmia) include conjunctival dryness, Bitot spots, corneal xerosis, and ultimately corneal ulceration and keratomalacia that can rapidly destroy the eye.
Deficiency also impairs epithelial integrity and immune function, increasing severity of infections such as measles and diarrhoeal disease.
It commonly coexists with protein-energy malnutrition and other micronutrient deficiencies.
Measles can precipitate acute deficiency and corneal damage, so supplementation is recommended during measles infection in at-risk children.
Diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by a low serum retinol level and dietary history.
High-dose vitamin A supplementation reverses early ocular signs and reduces mortality, and periodic supplementation programmes are a key public health measure.
Excessive vitamin A intake is toxic, so dosing schedules must be followed carefully.
Overlooking night blindness as an early, treatable warning sign
Failing to supplement vitamin A during measles in at-risk children
Missing underlying fat malabsorption in a child with deficiency and adequate intake
Causing toxicity by exceeding recommended supplementation doses

Early ocular changes are fully reversible with prompt supplementation, but corneal ulceration and keratomalacia can cause permanent blindness; adequate vitamin A status also lowers infection-related mortality.
Corneal ulceration or keratomalacia threatening irreversible blindness
Rapidly progressing ocular signs, particularly during measles
Severe concurrent infection in a malnourished child

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Vitamins are organic micronutrients that the body cannot synthesize in adequate amounts and that act largely as coenzymes or prosthetic groups (e.g., thiamine pyrophosphate in alpha-ketoacid decarboxylation; FAD/FMN flavoenzymes; NAD/NADP in redox reactions; pyridoxal phosphate in amino-acid metabolism). Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) require intact fat absorption and act in vision, gene transcription, calcium homeostasis, antioxidant defense, and gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors. Trace minerals function within metalloenzymes (zinc in numerous metalloenzymes and transcription factors; copper in ceruloplasmin/ferroxidase, cytochrome c oxidase, superoxide dismutase; selenium in glutathione peroxidase and deiodinases). Deficiency arises from inadequate intake, malabsorption, increased losses (hemodialysis, diuretics, increased urinary excretion), drug interference (isoniazid-B6, warfarin-vitamin K, metformin-B12/thiamine, penicillamine-zinc), or genetic transport/enzyme defects. Conversely, supplements, fortification, and occupational exposures can cause clinically important toxicities; in the inflammatory/acute-phase state, micronutrients redistribute and standard laboratory levels become unreliable.

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Overt single-nutrient deficiencies are uncommon in Western settings, but subclinical 'hidden hunger' is frequent in the elderly and the socioeconomically deprived; multiple deficiencies cluster in the chronically ill, those with alcohol use disorder, the impoverished, and post-bariatric-surgery patients.

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Copper deficiency causes an anemia refractory to iron plus neutropenia and can be precipitated by chronic high-dose zinc; inherited disorders include Menkes kinky-hair syndrome (ATP7A) and aceruloplasminemia.

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Selenium deficiency causes Keshan cardiomyopathy in low-soil regions; combined iodine and selenium deficiency can aggravate cretinism, while selenium excess causes selenosis (hair/nail loss, garlic breath, neuropathy).

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Biotin and choline deficiencies occur mainly with inborn errors or parenteral nutrition; high-dose biotin supplements can spuriously skew streptavidin-biotin immunoassays (e.g., falsely high free T4, falsely low TSH or troponin).

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Body stores differ enormously: vitamin B12 and vitamin A reserves are large (deficiency may take a year or more to appear), whereas folate and thiamine can be depleted within weeks of an inadequate diet.

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Thiamine should be replenished before or during refeeding of malnourished or alcoholic patients, because giving carbohydrate (especially IV glucose) without thiamine can precipitate acute deficiency with lactic acidosis and Wernicke encephalopathy.

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Wernicke encephalopathy is the classic triad of ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus, cerebellar ataxia, and confusion; addition of memory loss and confabulation defines Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, which is underdiagnosed despite a typical history.

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Pellagra (niacin deficiency) is remembered as the 'four Ds' - dermatitis (notably the photosensitive Casal's necklace), diarrhea, dementia, and death; it arises with corn-based diets, alcoholism, Hartnup disease, carcinoid syndrome, and isoniazid use.

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Pyridoxine (B6) should be co-administered with isoniazid to prevent neuropathy; paradoxically, chronic high-dose B6 (above ~100 mg/d) itself causes a reversible severe sensory neuropathy, so long-term supplementation should be discouraged.

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Vitamin A deficiency is the leading cause of preventable childhood blindness worldwide (xerophthalmia, Bitot's spots, keratomalacia) and impairs immune defenses, increasing mortality from diarrhea, measles, malaria, and respiratory infection.

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies (A, D, E, K) characteristically accompany fat-malabsorptive states such as celiac disease, cholestatic liver disease, cystic fibrosis, short-bowel syndrome, and bariatric surgery.

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Zinc deficiency presents with growth retardation/dwarfism, hypogonadism, hypogeusia, alopecia, immune dysfunction, and a periorificial/acral rash; the inherited form is acrodermatitis enteropathica, and penicillamine or chronic zinc itself (via copper depletion) can be culprits.

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Interpreting micronutrient blood levels during inflammation/acute illness without accounting for acute-phase redistribution (e.g., copper rises with ceruloplasmin, zinc and retinol fall), leading to over- or under-diagnosis

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Refeeding a malnourished or alcoholic patient with carbohydrate before giving thiamine, precipitating acute deficiency and lactic acidosis

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Attributing a prolonged prothrombin time solely to vitamin K deficiency in liver disease - if it fails to correct with vitamin K, the cause is hepatocellular

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Overlooking drug-induced deficiencies (isoniazid-B6, warfarin/orlistat-vitamin K, metformin-B12, chronic zinc-copper, penicillamine-zinc) and chronic high-dose B6 causing neuropathy

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Missing biotin supplement interference with streptavidin-biotin immunoassays (spurious thyroid, troponin, or hCG results)

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Assuming carotenemia (yellow palms/soles, spared sclerae) indicates jaundice; and giving high-dose beta-carotene to smokers, which raises lung cancer risk

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Most deficiency syndromes respond well and reversibly to timely repletion: thiamine produces cardiovascular and ophthalmoplegic improvement within ~24 hours and scurvy improves within days, although Wernicke-Korsakoff psychosis may be permanent and vitamin E or B12 neurologic deficits may only partially recover if advanced. Vitamin A deficiency carries substantial mortality - keratomalacia blinds an estimated quarter-million children yearly with case-fatality of 4-25%, and supplementation in deficient populations reduces childhood mortality by roughly 23-34%. Untreated severe thiamine, niacin (death is the fourth 'D'), or selenium (Keshan) deficiency can be fatal, as can acute vitamin A or D intoxication.

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Confusion, ophthalmoplegia, or ataxia in an alcoholic or malnourished patient before/during refeeding - possible Wernicke encephalopathy requiring immediate thiamine

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: High-output cardiac failure with edema (wet beriberi) or Keshan-type cardiomyopathy (selenium)

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Night blindness, corneal xerosis, or keratomalacia signaling sight-threatening vitamin A deficiency

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Bleeding/hemorrhage with prolonged prothrombin time, especially neonatal intracranial or GI bleeding (vitamin K deficiency)

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Increased intracranial pressure, bulging fontanels, hypercalcemia, or papilledema suggesting vitamin A or D intoxication

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Iron-refractory anemia with neutropenia (copper deficiency, often from chronic high-dose zinc)

chunks.diseaseName: Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess
chunks.text: Deficiency severity is graded from subclinical/biochemical (laboratory abnormality without symptoms - 'hidden hunger') through overt clinical deficiency syndromes (beriberi, pellagra, scurvy, xerophthalmia, rickets) to life-threatening complications (Wernicke-Korsakoff, keratomalacia/blindness, hemorrhage, cardiomyopathy). Thiamine deficiency is classically dichotomized into wet (cardiovascular) and dry (neuropathic) beriberi with considerable overlap, and vitamin A xerophthalmia is staged from night blindness and conjunctival xerosis/Bitot's spots to corneal ulceration and keratomalacia.

chunks.text: Vitiligo is an acquired disorder characterised by immune-mediated destruction of epidermal melanocytes, leading to loss of pigment. Current understanding emphasises an interplay of genetic susceptibility, intrinsic melanocyte vulnerability with oxidative stress, and an autoimmune response in which CD8 cytotoxic T cells and interferon-gamma signalling target and destroy melanocytes. The absence of functioning melanocytes leaves affected skin devoid of melanin, producing the characteristic depigmented macules. Non-segmental vitiligo tends to be symmetrical and progressive with autoimmune associations, whereas segmental vitiligo is localised to a dermatomal-like distribution and often stabilises after an early active phase.

chunks.text: Vitreous haemorrhage is extravasation of blood into or around the vitreous cavity. It occurs when abnormal new vessels (as in proliferative diabetic retinopathy or ischaemic vein occlusion) bleed, when normal retinal vessels are torn during posterior vitreous detachment or a retinal tear, or when trauma ruptures vessels. Blood disperses through the vitreous gel, scattering light and obscuring vision. Clearance is slow because the avascular vitreous reabsorbs blood inefficiently, and long-standing blood can lead to fibrosis and tractional complications.

chunks.text: Vocal cord nodules form in response to repeated mechanical trauma from vocal abuse. Forceful or excessive vocal fold collision, especially at the midpoint of the membranous cord where impact stress is greatest, causes localised oedema and microhaemorrhage in the superficial lamina propria. With continued strain this reactive change organises into fibrosis and thickening of the overlying epithelium, producing symmetrical nodules on the medial edges of both folds. These masses prevent complete glottic closure and add mass to the vibrating edge, disrupting the mucosal wave and generating hoarseness and a breathy voice. Because both folds strike each other, lesions are characteristically bilateral and roughly symmetrical.

chunks.text: Vocal cord palsy arises from interruption anywhere along the motor pathway to the larynx, from the brainstem nucleus through the vagus and recurrent laryngeal nerves to the intrinsic laryngeal muscles. Loss of innervation impairs abduction and adduction of the affected fold, so it rests in a position determined by the residual muscle tone and any compensatory changes. The recurrent laryngeal nerve's long course, especially on the left where it loops under the aortic arch, exposes it to compression or invasion by neck and chest disease and to iatrogenic injury during surgery. The functional consequence depends on the resting position of the cords and whether one or both are affected.

Candida species colonise the vagina asymptomatically in many women, kept in check by the resident lactobacillus-dominant flora and local immunity. Disturbance of this balance, for example by antibiotics, or increased glycogen availability from high oestrogen states and hyperglycaemia, allows the yeast to proliferate and transform into an invasive hyphal form. Adherence to and penetration of the vaginal epithelium triggers a brisk inflammatory response, producing the pruritus, erythema, and discharge characteristic of symptomatic infection.
Most infections are caused by Candida albicans, a commensal yeast that becomes symptomatic when the vaginal environment or host defences change
Typical features are intense vulval itching, soreness, and a thick, white, non-malodorous discharge often likened to cottage cheese, with vulval erythema and sometimes fissuring
The vaginal pH usually remains normal and acidic, which helps distinguish it from bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis
Predisposing factors include recent antibiotic use, pregnancy, diabetes, immunosuppression, and high oestrogen states
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by microscopy showing budding yeasts and pseudohyphae, and culture is useful in recurrent or treatment-resistant cases to identify non-albicans species
Uncomplicated disease responds well to topical or oral antifungal therapy, whereas recurrent disease often needs a longer induction and maintenance approach
Recurrent or resistant infection should prompt evaluation for diabetes, immunosuppression, and non-albicans species such as Candida glabrata, which are less responsive to standard azoles
It is not classed as a sexually transmitted infection, and routine treatment of asymptomatic male partners is not indicated
Diagnosing thrush on symptoms alone and missing bacterial vaginosis or dermatoses
Repeatedly treating recurrent infection without investigating for diabetes or immunosuppression
Assuming all cases are Candida albicans and overlooking azole-resistant species
Unnecessarily treating asymptomatic partners
Attributing chronic vulval symptoms to candidiasis when a dermatological condition is responsible

Uncomplicated vulvovaginal candidiasis responds rapidly to antifungal treatment with an excellent outlook. A minority of women develop recurrent disease that is troublesome and requires prolonged maintenance therapy, and outcomes in these cases improve when underlying predisposing factors and non-albicans species are identified and addressed.

chunks.text: Wernicke disease results from thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency. Thiamine is a cofactor for several enzymes including transketolase, pyruvate dehydrogenase, and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. Deficiency causes a diffuse fall in cerebral glucose utilization and mitochondrial damage; impaired alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase leads to glutamate accumulation, which together with the energy deficit may produce excitotoxic neuronal injury. Lesions are periventricular, surrounding the third ventricle, aqueduct, and fourth ventricle, with predilection for midline structures (dorsomedial thalamus, mammillary bodies, midline cerebellum, periaqueductal gray, and trochlear/abducens nuclei). Acute cases may show petechial hemorrhages; chronic cases show mammillary body atrophy.

chunks.text: Outcome depends on early thiamine administration. Ocular palsies improve within hours of thiamine; horizontal nystagmus may persist. Ataxia improves more slowly than ocular signs, and roughly half of patients recover incompletely, left with a slow, wide-based, shuffling gait and inability to tandem walk. Apathy, drowsiness, and confusion resolve gradually. Korsakoff psychosis is frequently persistent, with permanent gaps in memory, confabulation, and disordered temporal sequencing; prolonged untreated deficiency can cause an irreversible profound amnestic syndrome or death. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is underdiagnosed despite a typical history and picture.

Confusion, ataxia and eye signs in an alcohol-dependent or malnourished patient is Wernicke until proven otherwise.
Red flags: Reversible — treat empirically with thiamine, do not delay

[guideline] management → High-dose IV thiamine (Pabrinex) / Magnesium replacement (cofactor) Treats established Wernicke's encephalopathy; must be given before any glucose load, which can otherwise precipitate or worsen it. Delivered as Pabrinex (thiamine with other B vitamins).
[guideline] adjunct → Oral thiamine maintenance Continues repletion after the parenteral course, particularly in ongoing alcohol misuse or malnutrition.

Lymphoma (mesenteric/retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy on CT commonly raises this concern) (p.1368)

Postbulbar (more distal) duodenal biopsies with PAS staining for diastase-resistant inclusions in lamina propria macrophages plus PCR for T. whipplei (tissue yield exceeds body-fluid yield) (p.1369)
Video-capsule endoscopy to identify more distal small-bowel lesions when initial duodenal biopsy is nondiagnostic (p.1368)

Urine PCR as a potential noninvasive test and therapeutic-monitoring tool (positive in ~75% of cases pretreatment in one small study); plasma cell-free DNA next-generation sequencing for endocarditis (p.1369, p.1370)
PCR of duodenal biopsy: a cycle threshold of <=30 can help confirm the diagnosis even when PAS staining is negative (p.1369)
Immunohistochemistry (greater specificity and sensitivity than PAS, usable on archived fixed tissue) and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) as complementary tools (p.1369)

Echocardiography for suspected endocarditis (vegetations seen in 50-75%) (p.1368)
FDG-PET may show uptake at affected sites and can guide tissue sampling (p.1368, p.1369)
Biopsy of normal-appearing skin may detect T. whipplei as a minimally invasive diagnostic route in classic WD (p.1369)

Other rheumatologic disorders during the early arthralgic stage (p.1368)

T. whipplei is a weakly staining gram-positive, non-acid-fast bacillus with a small (<1-megabase) genome and incomplete biosynthetic pathways, consistent with an intracellular/nutritionally dependent pathogen; it is one of the slowest-growing human pathogens (doubling time ~18 days). Exposure is far more common than disease, and chronic infection (WD) is a rare outcome (<0.01% of those exposed). Establishing chronic infection involves both an impaired host inflammatory response and pathogen-driven immune modulation: HLA alleles DRB1*13 and DQB1*06 (favoring humoral over cell-mediated responses) raise risk, an impaired TH1 response with increased anti-inflammatory cytokines and regulatory T-cell activity, M2 macrophage polarization with impaired phagosome-lysosome fusion, and blunted T. whipplei-specific T-cell development occur. The organism has tropism for myeloid cells, which it invades and within which it avoids killing; affected tissue is infiltrated by foamy macrophages containing PAS-staining inclusions (ingested bacteria). In the small intestine, villus atrophy, lymphangiectasia, crypt hyperplasia, and surface epithelial apoptosis lead to malabsorptive diarrhea. (p.1367, p.1368)

Whipple disease is a rare chronic infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei; because it is uncommon, mimics many other conditions, and needs nonroutine tests, years typically pass between symptom onset and diagnosis (p.1367).

"Classic" Whipple disease presents as some combination of migratory arthralgias/seronegative arthritis, weight loss, chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fever, with the duodenum and/or jejunum involved over years (p.1367, p.1368).

Migratory oligo- or polyarthralgia (knees, wrists, ankles, MCP joints) typically precedes gastrointestinal symptoms by an average of 6-8 years; joint disease is present in >80% of patients (p.1368, p.2546).

CNS disease (detected by CSF PCR for T. whipplei) develops in roughly 50% of patients and many are asymptomatic; manifestations include cognitive decline progressing to dementia, personality/mood change, and hypothalamic involvement, and portend a poor prognosis (p.1368).
Oculomasticatory and oculofacial myorhythmia are highly suggestive of Whipple disease; supranuclear gaze palsy (usually vertical) is another neuro-ophthalmologic clue (p.1368).

Diagnosis rests on small-bowel (postbulbar duodenal) biopsy showing lamina propria infiltration by foamy macrophages with diastase-resistant PAS-positive inclusions, combined with PCR for T. whipplei; PCR has substantially improved sensitivity and specificity (p.1368, p.1369).
It is prudent to collect CSF even without CNS symptoms, because asymptomatic CNS disease is common and the CNS is the most common site of relapse, informing treatment duration (p.1369).

Treatment requires prolonged therapy; clinical response is often rapid, but eradication and durable cure are challenged by relapse and host predisposition to reinfection, which can occur years to decades later (p.1369, p.1370).

WD should be considered in any chronic multisystemic process, especially the combination of rheumatologic and intestinal disease with weight loss, with or without neurologic and cardiac involvement (p.1368, p.1369).
Serology is of little value: patients with active infection mount a poor IgM/IgG response, and a positive result most likely reflects prior exposure and clearance (p.1369)
A normal macroscopic duodenal appearance is common, and a negative test does not exclude WD; pretest probability must be considered (p.1369)
Histology/PAS alone is not optimally sensitive and is nonspecific (also positive with mycobacteria and other organisms); anti-TNF-alpha therapy may decrease PAS sensitivity (p.1369)

Saliva and fecal PCR are inappropriate as sole diagnostic tools because of low positive predictive value (more often reflecting colonization than disease); a positive result needs confirmation from end-organ tissue or body fluid (p.1370)

Treating presumed inflammatory arthritis or uveitis with glucocorticoids or anti-TNF-alpha agents can accelerate disease progression and unmask/precipitate disease; consider screening for WD before immunosuppression (p.1368)

Oral tetracycline or TMP-SMX monotherapy has unacceptable relapse rates, particularly for CNS disease; sequence data indicate TMP is not active against T. whipplei (no dihydrofolate reductase) (p.1369, p.1370)
Detection of T. whipplei sequence in BALF of asymptomatic individuals does not establish disease; caution is needed before diagnosing isolated pneumonia on sequence alone (p.1368)
Culture is not practical for diagnosis as it takes months to turn positive (p.1370)

Untreated Whipple disease is often fatal, and delayed diagnosis can lead to irreparable organ damage, particularly in the CNS. With appropriate treatment, clinical response is often rapid and at times remarkable, and timely recognition may yield cure with medical management alone; however, eradication requires prolonged therapy and a durable response is challenged by relapse (especially CNS relapse) and host predisposition to reinfection occurring years to decades later. CNS disease carries a significant mortality risk and may leave neurologic sequelae. (p.1367, p.1368, p.1369, p.1370)

CNS involvement (cognitive decline/dementia, personality change, hypothalamic dysfunction such as polyuria/polydipsia or sleep-cycle disorder, supranuclear gaze palsy, oculomasticatory myorhythmia) portends a poor prognosis with significant mortality risk and neurologic sequelae (p.1368)
Endocarditis (often afebrile, Duke criteria rarely met) may be complicated by congestive heart failure (~40%), embolic events, arrhythmias, or mycotic aneurysm (p.1368)
Progressive weight loss with chronic diarrhea and malabsorption (p.1367, p.1368)

Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) after treatment, with recurrent fever, arthritis, skin lesions, pleuritis, uveitis, and periorbital inflammation; some cases have been fatal (p.1369)

Harrison frames the disease by clinical syndrome rather than a graded severity score: asymptomatic colonization/carriage (PCR-detectable T. whipplei in stool, saliva, or duodenal tissue without symptoms); acute infection (e.g., gastroenteritis in children, febrile bacteremia, acute pneumonia); chronic infection comprising "classic" Whipple disease (intestinal involvement with multisystem disease) and "isolated" infection (organ disease such as endocarditis, neurologic, ocular, or pulmonary disease without intestinal symptoms); and reinfection/relapsing disease, including treatment-associated IRIS. (p.1367, p.1368, p.1369)

Wilms tumour arises from embryonal nephrogenic (metanephric) blastema, often showing a classic triphasic pattern of blastemal, epithelial, and stromal elements. It is linked to abnormalities of genes involved in kidney development, including WT1, and to epigenetic changes at chromosome 11p; persistent nephrogenic rests are precursor lesions. Anaplastic histology confers a worse prognosis and greater treatment resistance.
The most common primary renal malignancy of childhood, typically presenting in preschool children around 2-5 years of age.
The usual presentation is an asymptomatic, smooth abdominal mass discovered by a parent or on routine examination, sometimes with abdominal pain, haematuria, or hypertension.
The mass characteristically does not cross the midline, in contrast to neuroblastoma.
Associated with syndromes and anomalies such as WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann, and Denys-Drash, and with hemihypertrophy and aniridia; these children warrant surveillance.
Examination should be gentle, avoiding vigorous palpation of the mass because of the risk of tumour rupture.
Staging and histology (favourable versus anaplastic) guide a multimodal approach combining surgery, chemotherapy, and sometimes radiotherapy.
Bilateral disease occurs in a minority and requires nephron-sparing strategies to preserve renal function.
The lungs are the most common site of metastatic spread, so chest imaging is part of staging.
Overall survival is high, making Wilms tumour one of the success stories of paediatric oncology.
Aggressive palpation of the abdominal mass, risking rupture
Confusing it with neuroblastoma, which typically crosses the midline and has different markers
Missing hypertension as an associated finding
Failing to screen children with predisposing syndromes
Overlooking the contralateral kidney for bilateral disease
With risk-adapted multimodal therapy, most children with favourable-histology disease are cured; prognosis is worse with anaplastic histology, advanced stage, or unfavourable biological features.
Rapidly enlarging abdominal mass
Gross haematuria or significant hypertension
Features of tumour rupture (acute abdominal pain, distension, haemodynamic instability)
Respiratory symptoms suggesting pulmonary metastases
Signs of vascular (caval) extension

Cirrhosis of other cause (p.3338)

Autosomal recessive disease caused by loss-of-function variants in ATP7B, a highly conserved P-type copper-transporting ATPase expressed primarily in liver and kidney. ATP7B normally mediates copper removal from the liver via biliary excretion and prevents brain copper accumulation; its loss leads to pathologic copper accumulation, primarily impacting the liver and brain. Neurologic disease reflects copper toxicity in the basal ganglia (caudate, putamen, striatum) with neurodegeneration and astrogliosis. Copper also deposits in the cornea (Kayser-Fleischer ring) and lens (sunflower cataract), and renal copper toxicity produces tubular (Fanconi) dysfunction. Massive sudden release of hepatic copper into the circulation directly damages red cell membranes, causing hemolytic anemia (p.3338-3339).

Autosomal recessive disorder of copper transport caused by loss-of-function variants in ATP7B (a P-type copper-transporting ATPase), which normally mediates copper removal from the liver via biliary excretion and prevents brain copper accumulation (p.3338).

Typically affects adolescents and young adults; presenting features include nonspecific liver disease, neurologic abnormalities, psychiatric illness, hemolytic anemia, renal tubular Fanconi syndrome, and skeletal abnormalities (p.3338).

Age influences presentation: nearly all individuals presenting with liver disease are <30 years, whereas neurologic or psychiatric presentations may range from the first to the fifth decade; regardless of presentation, some degree of liver disease is invariably present (p.3338).

Neurologic presentation reflects basal ganglia (caudate, putamen) involvement: dysarthria, dystonia (including facial grimacing/risus sardonicus), rigidity, tremor (classically 'wing-beating'), choreiform movements, abnormal gait, and uncoordinated handwriting; WD can properly be classified as a movement disorder (p.3338, p.3518).

Kayser-Fleischer ring (golden to greenish-brown band in the peripheral cornea, from copper deposition in Descemet's membrane) is pathognomonic; present in ~95% of patients with neurologic signs but only about two-thirds of those with hepatic presentations (p.3339).
Supportive biochemistry: low serum copper, low serum ceruloplasmin, increased 24-h urinary copper excretion (>100 ug/24 h), elevated transaminases, aminoaciduria, and hemolytic anemia (p.3339).
Hepatic copper >200 ug per gram dry weight (normal 20-50) on percutaneous needle liver biopsy is a gold-standard biochemical diagnostic finding (p.3339).

Diagnosis relies on a combination of clinical, biochemical, and molecular features; the Leipzig scoring system (2001), endorsed by EASL, weights and collates these features as a valuable diagnostic guide (p.3339).

One of the best-characterized and most effectively managed inborn errors of metabolism; prompt diagnosis in the presymptomatic or early symptomatic phase plus lifelong treatment are needed to prevent premature mortality (p.3338).

WD is treatable and progression is preventable, so it is critical to test for it in any young patient with liver disease and/or a movement disorder or new psychiatric illness; missed diagnoses are tragic (p.3338, p.3518).
Normal blood copper, ceruloplasmin, or urinary copper levels do NOT exclude the diagnosis (p.3518).
WD in adolescence may present with chronic-hepatitis features long before neurologic manifestations or Kayser-Fleischer rings appear (p.427/355).
Kayser-Fleischer rings are absent in about one-third of patients with hepatic presentations, so their absence does not rule out WD (p.3339).
In patients with neurologic presentations, penicillamine treatment can induce paradoxical worsening of neurologic status (p.3340).

In the absence of treatment, the course is progressive, leading to severe neurologic dysfunction and early/premature death in most patients, although a small proportion experience a relatively benign course. WD is one of the most effectively managed inborn errors of metabolism: prompt diagnosis in the presymptomatic or early symptomatic phase and lifelong treatment prevent premature mortality. Liver transplantation, generally needed only when delayed diagnosis or poor compliance has caused irreversible hepatic damage, can correct both hepatic failure and crippling neurologic impairment (p.3338, p.3340, p.3518).
Hemolytic anemia from sudden, massive release of hepatic copper into the circulation directly toxic to red cell membranes can be sudden and catastrophic (p.3339).
Any teenager or young adult with new-onset psychiatric signs should have WD formally excluded (p.3339).
WD should always be considered in the differential of a movement disorder, particularly when arising in the first decades of life (p.3518).

No single graded severity scale is given in the source; diagnosis is formalized using a combination of clinical, biochemical, and molecular features, collated by the Leipzig scoring system (2001, endorsed by EASL). Disease is broadly staged as presymptomatic/early symptomatic versus advanced; advanced or medically unresponsive hepatic disease is the indication for liver transplantation (p.3339-3340).

chunks.text: Yellow fever virus, an RNA flavivirus, is inoculated by an infected mosquito and spreads via lymphatics and blood to target organs, with marked hepatotropism. Infection and death of hepatocytes (with characteristic midzonal necrosis and Councilman bodies) impair synthesis of clotting factors and cause jaundice, while direct renal injury produces acute kidney injury. The combination of coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia and vascular injury drives the haemorrhagic manifestations, and a dysregulated inflammatory response contributes to shock and multi-organ failure in the toxic phase.

chunks.text: Zika virus is an RNA flavivirus that, after inoculation by an Aedes mosquito, replicates in dendritic cells and spreads via lymphatics and blood. It has particular tropism for neural progenitor cells, which underlies its ability to disrupt fetal brain development when it crosses the placenta, producing microcephaly and other structural anomalies. Immune-mediated mechanisms, including molecular mimicry, are implicated in the associated Guillain-Barre syndrome. The virus can persist in immune-privileged sites such as semen, enabling sexual transmission.
